advanced cardiac life support.definition: An evidence-based protocol used by healthcare providers for the urgent management of cardiac arrest and other life-threatening cardiopulmonary emergencies, incorporating high-quality CPR, airway management, defibrillation as indicated, vascular access, administration of medications (eg, epinephrine and antiarrhythmics), rhythm analysis, and post-arrest care, in accordance with ACLS guidelines.

attention deficit disorder.definition: A neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interferes with functioning or development; the current diagnosis is attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), with presentations that are predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, or combined.

activities of daily living.definition: An assessment of a person's ability to perform basic self-care tasks required for daily living, such as bathing, dressing, transferring, toileting, continence, and feeding, to determine level of independence and need for assistance.

acquired immunodeficiency syndrome.definition: The most advanced stage of infection with HIV, in which the immune system is severely weakened, leading to increased susceptibility to opportunistic infections and certain cancers.

aids.definition: Abbreviation for acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, the most advanced stage of infection with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).

amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.definition: A disease that attacks the nerve cells in your brain and spinal cord that carry messages to your muscles. Also called ALS, Lou Gehrig's Disease, or motor neuron disease.

acute myocardial infarction.definition: A sudden, irreversible death of heart muscle due to acute loss of blood supply from a blocked coronary artery, usually from rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque with thrombus; presents with chest pain and elevated cardiac biomarkers and requires urgent reperfusion therapy (e.g., PCI or thrombolysis).

atrial septal defect.definition: A congenital heart defect characterized by a hole in the interatrial septum (the wall between the atria) that allows blood to shunt from the left to the right atrium, potentially causing increased pulmonary blood flow and right-sided heart strain; many defects are small and asymptomatic, but larger defects may require closure.

aspartate aminotransferase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the transfer of an amino group from aspartate to α‑ketoglutarate, forming oxaloacetate and glutamate; a clinical biomarker used to detect hepatocellular injury and is also present in heart and skeletal muscle.

arteriovenous.definition: Relating to or involving arteries and veins; a direct connection between an artery and a vein, bypassing the capillary network.

atrioventricular.definition: Relating to the atrium and the ventricle of the heart; used to describe structures bridging the two chambers, such as the atrioventricular valves (mitral and tricuspid) and the atrioventricular node.

barium enema.definition: Radiographic examination of the colon in which barium sulfate contrast is instilled via enema to outline the large intestine on X-ray, often with air for double-contrast imaging to detect mucosal abnormalities.

breast self-examination.definition: A technique by which a person visually inspects and palpates their own breasts to detect abnormalities such as lumps, thickening, changes in size or contour, skin changes, or nipple discharge.

blood pressure.definition: The force of your blood pressing against the walls of your arteries. The high number (systolic pressure) measures when your heart beats and the low number (diastolic pressure) measures between beats.

benign prostatic hypertrophy.definition: A noncancerous enlargement of the prostate gland that occurs with aging in men; it is not cancer. Also called enlarged prostate gland.

bowel movement.definition: The last step of food moving through your body. Also called poop, stool, or feces.

basal metabolic rate.definition: The amount of energy the body requires at rest in a fasting, awake state to maintain basic physiological functions such as breathing, circulation, and cellular metabolism; it represents the minimum energy expenditure necessary to sustain life, and is influenced by factors like age, sex, body composition, and hormones.

blood urea nitrogen.definition: A laboratory value representing the amount of nitrogen in the blood as urea, a waste product of protein metabolism; used to assess kidney function and hydration status.

biopsy.definition: When a piece of tissue from a part of your body is taken for testing.

coronary artery bypass graft.definition: A surgical procedure in which a healthy blood vessel from another part of the body or a synthetic graft is used to bypass a blocked coronary artery, restoring blood flow to the heart muscle.

coronary artery disease.definition: When the blood vessels that bring blood and oxygen to the heart become narrow. Also called coronary heart disease or CAD.

computed tomography.definition: A special type of imaging that creates three-dimensional X-rays. Also called CT scans or CAT scans (computed axial tomography).

axial tomography.definition: A tomographic imaging technique that reconstructs cross-sectional (axial) images of the body from multiple X-ray projections around the patient; the method laid the foundation for modern computed tomography (CT).

complete blood count.definition: A broad panel of screening tests that examine different parts of the blood and can be used to diagnose anemia, infection, and many other diseases.

coronary care unit.definition: A ward in a hospital that provides specialized care and monitoring for patients with heart problems.

cystic fibrosis.definition: A hereditary disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene that disrupts chloride channel function, leading to thick, sticky mucus in the lungs, pancreas, and other organs with resulting chronic respiratory infections and pancreatic exocrine insufficiency.

congenital heart disease.definition: A group of structural or functional heart defects present at birth, arising from abnormal development of the heart or great vessels, that disrupt normal blood flow and can range from mild to life-threatening.

coronary heart disease.definition: When the arteries that supply the heart with blood and oxygen become narrowed or blocked, reducing blood flow to the heart muscle; also called coronary artery disease (CAD).

congestive heart failure.definition: When your heart can't pump enough blood. Also called heart failure or CHF.

creatinine kinase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the reversible transfer of a phosphate group from phosphocreatine to ADP to form ATP and creatine; found mainly in skeletal muscle, heart, and brain; serum levels rise with muscle injury or myocardial infarction; has isoenzymes CK-MM, CK-MB, and CK-BB.

cytomegalovirus.definition: A ubiquitous human herpesvirus (HHV‑5) that establishes lifelong latent infection after primary exposure; most infections are asymptomatic, but it can cause a mononucleosis‑like illness in healthy people and severe disease (e.g., retinitis, pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis) in immunocompromised patients, and congenital infection can lead to fetal/neonatal complications such as sensorineural deafness.

central nervous system.definition: The brain and spinal cord; the main integrating and control center of the nervous system.

cardiac output.definition: The amount of blood the heart is able to pump into circulation; specifically measured as the amount of blood the left side of the heart can pump in one minute.

carbon dioxide.definition: A colorless, odorless gas produced by cellular metabolism and respiration; transported in the blood mainly as bicarbonate and exhaled by the lungs, it regulates acid-base balance and respiratory drive; elevated levels cause respiratory acidosis, low levels cause respiratory alkalosis.

chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.definition: Lung diseases, such as chronic bronchitis or emphysema.

cyclooxygenase.definition: An enzyme that helps blood cells known as platelets stick to each other, a key step in the formation of a blood clot.

cerebral palsy.definition: A group of permanent disorders of movement and posture resulting from non-progressive disturbances in the developing fetal or infant brain; often associated with motor impairment and may include sensory, cognitive, communication, and behavioral difficulties, as well as epilepsy.

continuous positive airway pressure.definition: A therapy for obstructive sleep apnea in which a machine delivers a continuous stream of air which prevents the collapse of the airway during sleep.

creatine phosphokinase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the transfer of a phosphate group from ATP to creatine to form phosphocreatine; measured in blood as a marker of muscle damage or myocardial injury, with isoenzymes CK-MM (skeletal muscle), CK-MB (heart), and CK-BB (brain).

cardiopulmonary resuscitation.definition: A combination of chest compressions and mouth-to-mouth breathing that keeps oxygenated blood circulating to the brain and tissues.

cerebrospinal fluid.definition: A clear, colorless body fluid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord; produced mainly by the choroid plexuses in the ventricles; circulates within the ventricular system and subarachnoid space, providing buoyant support to the brain, cushioning against impact, and helping to maintain chemical stability and remove waste.

cerebrovascular accident.definition: The medical term for a stroke.

costovertebral angle.definition: An angle on the back formed by the 12th rib and the vertebral column overlying the kidney; tenderness to percussion at this site (costovertebral angle tenderness) suggests renal inflammation such as pyelonephritis.

dilation and curettage.definition: A gynecologic procedure in which the cervix is dilated and the uterine lining (endometrium) is scraped or suctioned to remove tissue for biopsy or to treat conditions such as miscarriage, heavy uterine bleeding, or retained products of conception.

disseminated intravascular coagulation.definition: A systemic process characterized by widespread activation of the coagulation cascade, leading to microvascular thrombosis and consumption of platelets and clotting factors, which can cause organ dysfunction and paradoxical bleeding; often triggered by sepsis, trauma, malignancy, or obstetric complications.

differential blood count.definition: A laboratory test that measures the percentages (and often absolute counts) of the five major white blood cell types in peripheral blood—neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils—to aid in diagnosing and monitoring infection, inflammation, hematologic disorders, and other disease processes.

diabetic ketoacidosis.definition: A serious complication of diabetes characterized by hyperglycemia, anion-gap metabolic acidosis, and ketonemia/ketonuria due to insulin deficiency, leading to dehydration and metabolic instability; precipitated by infection or missed insulin and treated with IV fluids, insulin, and electrolyte correction.

diabetes mellitus.definition: A group of metabolic disorders characterized by chronic hyperglycemia due to impaired insulin secretion, insulin action, or both, with disturbances in carbohydrate, fat, and protein metabolism.

deoxyribonucleic acid.definition: Double-stranded nucleic acid that carries the genetic information of most living organisms; built from deoxyribose‑phosphate backbones with four bases (adenine, thymine, cytosine, guanine) paired A–T and C–G, organized as a double helix, and used as a template for replication and transcription.

do not resuscitate.definition: A Do Not Resuscitate (DNR) order is a medical directive indicating that if a patient experiences cardiopulmonary arrest, CPR and other resuscitative efforts should not be performed. It reflects the patient’s or surrogate’s wishes and does not necessarily preclude other medical treatments or palliative care unless otherwise stated.

dead on arrival.definition: A person who is dead on arrival (DOA) is someone found to be dead with no signs of life (no pulse, no respirations, no brain activity) upon arrival at a healthcare facility or during transport, with resuscitation not attempted or considered futile.

diphtheria-pertussis-tetanus.definition: A combined vaccine that protects against three bacterial diseases—diphtheria, pertussis (whooping cough), and tetanus; administered in childhood as a series of injections (historically DTP, now commonly DTaP for primary series and Tdap for boosters) to induce immunity.

diagnosis-related group.definition: A hospital payment classification system that groups inpatient stays into categories designed to reflect similar resource use, based on diagnoses, procedures, and patient characteristics, and used to determine reimbursement by Medicare and other payers.

diagnostic and statistical manual of men.word: diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders
diagnostic and statistical manual of men.definition: A manual published by the American Psychiatric Association that provides standardized, criteria-based definitions and diagnostic codes for mental disorders to guide clinical diagnosis, research, and billing; it outlines specific symptom requirements, duration, and impairment for each disorder and is currently in its fifth edition (DSM-5-TR).

delirium tremens.definition: A severe, potentially life-threatening form of alcohol withdrawal characterized by delirium, autonomic hyperactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, fever), marked tremors, agitation, and perceptual disturbances (often visual or auditory hallucinations), typically developing 48–72 hours after last drink in heavy drinkers; requires inpatient care with benzodiazepines, supportive care, IV fluids, electrolyte correction, and thiamine.

dextrose 5% in water.definition: A sterile intravenous solution of 5% dextrose in water that provides free water and calories; it is isotonic initially but becomes hypotonic as glucose is metabolized, and is commonly used for hydration or as a diluent for IV medications.

diagnosis.definition: The identification of a disease or condition by evaluating a patient’s symptoms, medical history, physical examination, and diagnostic test results.

epstein-barr virus.definition: A ubiquitous human herpesvirus (HHV-4) that infects B lymphocytes and epithelial cells; transmitted mainly via saliva; establishes lifelong latent infection and is associated with infectious mononucleosis as well as several malignancies, including Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

electrocardiogram.definition: A recording of the heart's electrical activity obtained by placing electrodes on the skin; used to assess heart rhythm, rate, and conditions affecting the heart such as ischemia, infarction, and conduction abnormalities.

echocardiography.definition: A noninvasive imaging test in which ultrasound is used to visualize the heart in real time, assessing cardiac structure and function, including chamber size, wall motion, valve anatomy and function, and blood flow with Doppler.

electroconvulsive therapy.definition: A procedure in which brief electrical stimulation is applied to the brain under anesthesia to induce a controlled generalized seizure, used to treat severe depression and other psychiatric conditions when other treatments have failed; typically given as a series of sessions with anesthesia and muscle relaxation, and may cause temporary memory impairment.

emergency department.definition: A hospital-based department that provides rapid assessment and treatment for patients with urgent or life-threatening conditions, offering triage, stabilization, diagnostic evaluation, and initial management with disposition by discharge, admission, or transfer.

estimated date of delivery.definition: Predicted date when the baby is likely to be born, typically calculated as 40 weeks from the first day of the last menstrual period or adjusted by ultrasound dating.

electroencephalogram.definition: Test that records the brain's electrical activity via scalp electrodes, producing a tracing of brain waves over time; used to diagnose and monitor epilepsy and other seizure disorders, sleep disorders, and various neurological conditions.

eent.definition: Abbreviation for Eyes, Ears, Nose, and Throat

enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay.definition: A plate-based immunoassay in which an antigen or antibody is immobilized on a solid surface and detected with an enzyme-conjugated partner; upon adding a substrate, the enzyme produces a colorimetric, fluorometric, or luminescent signal proportional to the amount of target analyte in the sample.

electromyogram.definition: The graphic recording of the electrical activity of skeletal muscle produced by electromyography, obtained with surface or intramuscular electrodes and used to evaluate neuromuscular disorders.

emergency medical service.definition: A coordinated system that provides prehospital emergency medical care and transportation for people with acute illness or injury, including dispatch, on-scene assessment and treatment, and rapid transport to an appropriate healthcare facility.

emergency medical technician.definition: A trained prehospital care professional who provides basic emergency medical care and transports patients to medical facilities; responsibilities include scene assessment, airway management, CPR, bleeding control, wound care, splinting, oxygen administration, and monitoring vital signs, with levels ranging from basic to advanced life support.

ear, nose, and throat.definition: A medical specialty focusing on diseases and conditions of the ear, nose, throat, and related head and neck structures; practitioners diagnose and treat hearing and balance disorders, sinus and airway problems, swallowing and voice disorders, sleep apnea, and head and neck cancers, often using both medical and surgical approaches.

emergency room.definition: A hospital department that delivers rapid evaluation and treatment for patients with acute, urgent, or life-threatening conditions, using triage to prioritize care and providing stabilization, diagnostic testing, and initial management before admission or discharge.

expiratory reserve volume.definition: The volume of air that can be forcibly exhaled from the lungs after a normal, resting exhalation.

erythrocyte sedimentation rate.definition: A blood test that measures the rate at which red blood cells settle in a sample over one hour, used as a nonspecific marker of inflammation.

end-stage renal disease.definition: An irreversible, final stage of chronic kidney disease in which kidney function is insufficient to sustain life without renal replacement therapy (dialysis or kidney transplantation), usually defined by an estimated glomerular filtration rate below 15 mL/min/1.73 m2.

fasting blood sugar.definition: A blood glucose measurement taken after an overnight fast (usually 8–12 hours) used to screen for and diagnose diabetes and prediabetes. Normal is <100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L); 100–125 mg/dL (5.6–6.9 mmol/L) indicates impaired fasting glucose (prediabetes); ≥126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) on two occasions indicates diabetes.

forced expiratory volume.definition: The volume of air that can be forcibly exhaled from the lungs after a maximal inhalation, typically measured during spirometry in liters; used to assess pulmonary function and airway obstruction. If you meant forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1), I can define that specifically.

family history.definition: Health information about your close relatives.

fetal heart rate.definition: The fetal heart rate is the heart rate of a fetus, measured in beats per minute (bpm) using Doppler ultrasound, a fetoscope, or electronic fetal monitoring; normal rates are roughly 110–160 bpm in the third trimester, and the pattern of the rate (variability, accelerations, decelerations) helps assess fetal well-being.

failure to thrive.definition: A condition in which a child does not gain weight or grow as expected for age and sex, usually shown by weight-for-age below the 5th percentile or crossing growth-chart percentiles, often due to inadequate intake, malabsorption, chronic illness, or psychosocial factors (organic or nonorganic).

fracture.definition: A break or crack in a bone, disrupting its continuity; may be closed (skin intact) or open (bone exposed) and may be displaced or nondisplaced.

gallbladder.definition: An organ located near your liver that stores a fluid (bile) that helps to digest fat.

gonococcus.definition: A Gram-negative diplococcus bacterium (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) that causes gonorrhea, a sexually transmitted infection.

gonorrheal.definition: Relating to gonorrhea, a sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

gastrointestinal.definition: Relating to the stomach and intestines; the gastrointestinal (GI) tract is the continuous digestive tube from the esophagus to the anus.

gravida.definition: An obstetric term meaning the number of times a woman has been pregnant, including the current pregnancy if applicable; counted regardless of pregnancy outcome.

gunshot wound.definition: A penetrating traumatic injury caused by a discharged firearm, where a projectile enters the body (entrance wound) and may exit, causing tissue disruption, bleeding, and potential injury to internal organs, vessels, or bones.

genitourinary.definition: Relating to the genital organs and the urinary tract; pertaining to both the urinary and reproductive (genitourinary) systems.

gynecology.definition: The study of the functions and diseases that are specific to women and girls.

history and physical.definition: A comprehensive medical assessment in which the clinician collects the patient’s medical history (symptoms, past illnesses, medications, allergies, family and social history) and performs a physical examination to evaluate current health, identify problems, and guide diagnostic testing and management.

hepatitis a virus.definition: A nonenveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus of the family Picornaviridae (genus Hepatovirus) that causes acute hepatitis A; transmitted primarily by the fecal-oral route, infection is usually self-limited and does not progress to chronic hepatitis; vaccination is available for prevention.

hemoglobin.definition: A protein within red blood cells that binds oxygen via heme iron and transports it from the lungs to tissues, while also carrying a portion of carbon dioxide from tissues back to the lungs for exhalation.

hepatitis b virus.definition: A small enveloped DNA virus of the Hepadnaviridae family that infects hepatocytes and can cause acute or chronic hepatitis; transmitted via blood and bodily fluids; has a circular, partially double-stranded genome that replicates via reverse transcription; chronic infection increases risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma; prevented by vaccination and treated with antivirals (e.g., tenofovir, entecavir) and sometimes pegylated interferon.

human chorionic gonadotropin.definition: A glycoprotein hormone produced by placental trophoblast after implantation; it acts like LH to maintain the corpus luteum and progesterone production in early pregnancy and is the basis for pregnancy tests.

hematocrit.definition: A blood test that measures the amount of red blood cells in your blood

high-density lipoprotein.definition: A lipoprotein particle that transports cholesterol from peripheral tissues to the liver for excretion, considered the “good” cholesterol because higher levels are associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular disease.

hiv.definition: A retrovirus that primarily infects CD4+ T lymphocytes, compromising the immune system and, if untreated, leading to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome; it is transmitted through blood, sexual contact, shared needles, and from mother to child; treated with combination antiretroviral therapy to suppress viral replication.

hydrogen peroxide.definition: A colorless, unstable inorganic compound that acts as a strong oxidizing agent; in dilute solutions it is used as a topical antiseptic and wound-cleaning agent, while higher concentrations are caustic and can cause tissue damage; it decomposes into water and oxygen.

herpes simplex virus.definition: A DNA virus of the Herpesviridae family that causes oral and genital herpes (HSV-1 and HSV-2); it establishes lifelong latent infection in sensory neurons with periodic reactivation and transmission by direct contact; no cure, but antiviral therapy can manage symptoms.

hypertension.definition: When your low pressure (diastolic) is 90 or higher or the high pressure (systolic) is 140 or higher. Also called high blood pressure.

intrauterine device.definition: A type of birth control that is placed inside the womb (uterus). Also called an IUD.

intravenous.definition: To put a substance in a vein.

intravenous pyelogram.definition: Radiographic imaging of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder after intravenous injection of iodinated contrast, to visualize anatomy and assess urinary tract function. Also known as intravenous urography.

potassium chloride.definition: A potassium salt used medically as an electrolyte replenisher to treat or prevent potassium deficiency (hypokalemia); given orally or by IV and sometimes used as a salt substitute; excessive dosing can cause hyperkalemia and potentially dangerous cardiac arrhythmias.

kub.definition: Abbreviation for Kidney, Ureter, and Bladder

lumbar puncture.definition: A procedure in which a hollow needle is inserted into the lower part of the spinal canal to withdraw fluid for testing. Also called a spinal tap.

lactated ringer’s.definition: A sterile isotonic crystalloid solution used for fluid resuscitation and electrolyte replenishment; it contains sodium chloride, sodium lactate, potassium chloride, and calcium chloride. The lactate component is metabolized to bicarbonate by the liver, providing a buffering effect.

left ventricular hypertrophy.definition: A thickening of the wall of the lower left chamber of the heart, which is responsible for pumping blood to organs throughout the body.

mean arterial pressure.definition: The average arterial pressure during a single cardiac cycle, representing organ perfusion. It is often estimated as MAP ≈ DBP + 1/3(SBP − DBP) or MAP ≈ (SBP + 2×DBP)/3, expressed in mmHg.

muscular dystrophy.definition: A group of inherited disorders characterized by progressive weakness and degeneration of skeletal muscles caused by defects in muscle fiber proteins (most notably dystrophin) or their supporting complexes, with muscle tissue progressively replaced by fat and connective tissue.

metered dose inhaler.definition: A handheld inhaler that delivers a specific, premeasured dose of medication as an aerosol with each puff, using a propellant; used for inhaled therapies in asthma and COPD, and often requires coordination with inhalation (sometimes aided by a spacer).

milliequivalent.definition: A unit of chemical quantity equal to one-thousandth of an equivalent; it expresses the amount of a substance that can donate or accept one mole of electrical charge in reactions. In solution concentrations, mEq/L = (valence of ion) × (mmol/L); for monovalent ions this equals mmol/L, while for divalent ions it equals 2 × mmol/L.

myocardial infarction.definition: Occurs when the flow of blood to the heart is stopped by a blood clot or a spasm of an artery. Also called a heart attack or MI.

measles-mumps-rubella.definition: A combined live attenuated vaccine that provides immunity against the viral diseases measles, mumps, and rubella; typically given to children in two doses.

magnetic resonance imaging.definition: A scan that creates detailed pictures of internal organs; commonly referred to as MRI. Magnetic resonance imaging uses radio waves, a strong magnetic field, and a computer to produce images of organs and internal tissues.

sodium chloride.definition: An inorganic ionic compound consisting of sodium cations (Na+) and chloride anions (Cl−) in a 1:1 ratio; the major extracellular electrolyte and dietary salt; used medically as intravenous saline solutions for fluid therapy.

north american nursing diagnosis associa.definition: An organization that developed and maintains a standardized taxonomy of nursing diagnoses used to identify patient problems that nurses can address with independent interventions; the group originated with a North American focus and is now known as NANDA International.

nasogastric.definition: Relating to the nose and stomach; describes a device or procedure that passes from the nose into the stomach (e.g., a nasogastric tube used for feeding or drainage).

neonatal intensive care unit.definition: A specialized hospital unit that provides intensive monitoring, life-support, and advanced medical care for ill or premature newborns.

no known allergies.definition: A statement in a medical history that there are no documented allergies or known hypersensitivities to medications, foods, or environmental agents.

nothing by mouth.definition: A medical instruction to withhold all oral intake—food, fluids, and medications given by mouth—for a defined period, often prior to anesthesia or certain procedures, to reduce the risk of aspiration or to ensure an empty stomach.

nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drug.definition: A drug that reduces swelling and pain.

normal sinus rhythm.definition: A normal heart rhythm originating from the sinoatrial node with a regular rate and rhythm, typically 60–100 beats per minute in adults, with upright P waves preceding each QRS complex and a normal PR interval.

oxygen.definition: A colorless, odorless diatomic gas (O2) essential for aerobic cellular respiration; makes up about 21% of Earth's atmosphere and is carried in the bloodstream bound to hemoglobin; can be administered medically as supplemental gas.

obstetrics.definition: The branch of medicine that focuses on pregnancy, labor, delivery, and the postpartum period, including prenatal care and the medical and surgical management of both uncomplicated and high-risk pregnancies to ensure the health of the mother and fetus.

organic brain syndrome.definition: An umbrella term for cognitive and behavioral changes caused by an identifiable brain disease or dysfunction, such as delirium, dementia, brain injury, infection, or metabolic/vascular brain disorders, rather than a primary psychiatric illness.

operating room.definition: A sterile, specialized hospital suite equipped for performing surgical procedures under anesthesia, with sterile instrumentation, lighting, monitoring and anesthesia equipment, and immediate access to resuscitation resources.

over-the-counter.definition: A medication or other health product that can be bought by consumers without a prescription from a licensed healthcare professional, typically labeled with usage directions and safety information.

pediatric advanced life support.definition: Pediatric Advanced Life Support is the American Heart Association–recognized program of guidelines and training for the resuscitation and emergency cardiovascular care of infants and children (birth through adolescence), including high‑quality CPR, airway and ventilation management, vascular access and medications, and algorithmic treatment of pediatric shock, respiratory failure/arrest, and cardiac arrest.

postanesthesia care unit.definition: A specialized hospital area where patients recover from anesthesia and are closely monitored after surgery, with ongoing assessment of airway, breathing, circulation, vital signs, pain, and nausea, until stable and ready for discharge home or transfer to a regular inpatient unit.

patient-controlled analgesia.definition: A method that allows a person to control, within limits, the amount and timing of pain medication they receive, typically by pressing a button to release medication from a computerized pump into an IV.

positive end-expiratory pressure.definition: A ventilatory setting that maintains airway pressure above atmospheric pressure at the end of expiration to prevent alveolar collapse, improve oxygenation, and increase functional residual capacity; commonly used during mechanical ventilation with typical levels around 5 cm H2O, adjustable to balance oxygenation and hemodynamics.

positron emission tomography.definition: A medical imaging test that uses a radioactive substance to assess organ and tissue function in the body and to look for disease. Commonly called a PET scan.

percutaneously inserted central catheter.definition: A central venous catheter inserted through the skin into a central vein with the tip terminating in the superior vena cava or right atrium, used for long-term venous access to administer medications, parenteral nutrition, or for frequent blood sampling.

pelvic inflammatory disease.definition: When a woman's reproductive organs, like the womb, are infected and swollen. Also called PID

phenylketonuria.definition: A disease in which the body can't process a substance found in most foods. Because this condition can lead to serious health problems, all babies are tested at birth.

past medical history.definition: A patient's record of previously diagnosed medical conditions and significant health events—such as prior illnesses, surgeries, hospitalizations, and chronic diseases—that may influence current care.

point of maximal impulse.definition: The point of maximal impulse (PMI) is the location on the chest wall where the heartbeat is most strongly felt, representing the apex of the left ventricle; normally felt at the left midclavicular line around the 5th intercostal space, and may be displaced in cardiomegaly or other cardiac conditions.

polymorphonuclear neutrophil leukocytes.definition: White blood cells that seek out and engulf foreign cells.

premenstrual syndrome.definition: A recurring set of physical, emotional, and behavioral symptoms that arise in the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle and resolve with the start of menstruation; common features include mood changes (irritability, depression), anxiety, bloating, breast tenderness, headaches, fatigue, and sleep disturbance.

orally.definition: By mouth; administered through the oral route, i.e., taken by mouth rather than by injection.

prothrombin time.definition: A blood test that measures how long plasma takes to clot after the addition of tissue factor (thromboplastin) and calcium, assessing the extrinsic coagulation pathway; used to monitor warfarin therapy and to evaluate suspected coagulation disorders.

partial thromboplastin time.definition: Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) is a blood test that measures the time for plasma to clot after activation, evaluating the intrinsic and common coagulation pathways; it is used to investigate bleeding disorders and to monitor unfractionated heparin therapy.

premature ventricular contraction.definition: An early beat in a ventricle that feels like the heart skipped a beat.

rickettsia.definition: An obligate intracellular, Gram-negative bacterial genus transmitted by arthropod vectors (ticks, fleas, lice, and mites) that causes rickettsial diseases such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever and typhus; they reproduce within the cytoplasm of host cells and depend on host cell machinery for survival.

roentgen.definition: A legacy unit of exposure to ionizing radiation, defined as the amount of X-ray or gamma-ray radiation that produces 2.58 × 10^-4 coulombs of charge per kilogram of dry air at standard conditions; it has been superseded by SI units such as coulomb per kilogram (C/kg) for exposure and gray (Gy) for absorbed dose.

red blood cell.definition: A biconcave, anucleate cell in the blood that contains hemoglobin and carries oxygen from the lungs to tissues throughout the body, while also helping transport carbon dioxide from tissues back to the lungs.

recommended daily/dietary allowance.definition: The average daily amount of a nutrient that will meet the nutritional needs of almost all (97%–98%) healthy people at specific stages of their lives.

respiratory distress syndrome.definition: A condition in premature infants caused by insufficient pulmonary surfactant, leading to alveolar collapse, poor gas exchange, and respiratory failure.

rh factor.definition: A surface antigen (D antigen) on red blood cells that defines the Rh blood group; presence of the antigen makes an individual Rh-positive, while its absence makes them Rh-negative. Immune sensitization to this antigen can cause hemolytic transfusion reactions and, in pregnancy, hemolytic disease of the newborn if an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive fetus.

ribonucleic acid.definition: A nucleic acid composed of ribonucleotides linked by phosphodiester bonds that carries genetic information and participates in protein synthesis; in cells it is typically single-stranded and includes types such as mRNA, tRNA, and rRNA, functioning in transcription and translation.

range of motion.definition: The extent of movement—and thus flexibility—in a joint, measured in the degrees of a circle.

review of systems.definition: A systematic part of the medical history in which the clinician asks the patient about symptoms affecting each major organ system to identify current or past problems not volunteered.

recovery room.definition: A post-anesthesia care area (PACU) where patients are monitored as they awaken from anesthesia after surgery, with ongoing monitoring of vital signs, airway and breathing, circulation, and pain and nausea management until stable for transfer or discharge.

respiratory rate.definition: The number of breaths taken per minute; a basic vital sign used to assess ventilation and respiratory effort.

serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase.definition: An enzyme also known as aspartate aminotransferase (AST) that catalyzes the transfer of an amino group from aspartate to alpha-ketoglutarate to form oxaloacetate and glutamate; present mainly in liver, heart, and skeletal muscle; elevated serum levels indicate hepatocellular injury and are used in liver function testing.

serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase.definition: An enzyme (alanine aminotransferase, ALT) in the liver that catalyzes transfer of an amino group from alanine to α-ketoglutarate, forming pyruvate and glutamate; measured in blood as a marker of hepatocellular injury, with elevations suggesting liver damage.

sudden infant death syndrome.definition: The sudden, unexplained death of a baby less than one year old. Also called SIDS or crib death.

systemic lupus erythematosus.definition: A disease where the immune system of your body attacks healthy tissue by mistake (autoimmune). It can be mild or severe and can affect many parts of the body.

shortness of breath.definition: When you have a hard time breathing.

staphylococcus.definition: A genus of Gram-positive cocci that occur in grape-like clusters; facultatively anaerobic; catalase-positive; includes several human pathogens, notably species that cause skin and soft tissue infections, pneumonia, sepsis, and toxin-mediated diseases; some are coagulase-positive and others coagulase-negative.

sexually transmitted disease.definition: An infection transmitted primarily through sexual contact (vaginal, anal, or oral) with an infected person; caused by bacteria, viruses, or parasites; may be asymptomatic or symptomatic and is often preventable and treatable.

streptococcus.definition: A specific germ (a bacteria). Also called strep.

signs and symptoms.definition: Signs are objective, observable evidence of disease detected by examination or tests (e.g., fever, rash, abnormal lab results). Symptoms are subjective experiences reported by the patient (e.g., pain, nausea, fatigue).

tonsillectomy adenoidectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove both the palatine tonsils and the adenoids (pharyngeal tonsils) to reduce recurrent throat infections and relieve nasal obstruction or sleep-disordered breathing, most commonly performed in children.

tuberculosis.definition: An infection caused by a bacteria, often located in the lungs. Also called TB.

transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulat.definition: The use of low-voltage electrical current (through electrodes placed on the skin) to provide pain-suppressing stimulation.

transient ischemic attack.definition: Happens when the blood supply to the brain is blocked briefly. Also called a TIA.

temporomandibular joint.definition: A bilateral synovial articulation between the mandibular condyle and the articular fossa of the temporal bone, separated by an articular disc into upper and lower compartments; permits hinge (opening/closing) and gliding (protrusion, retrusion, lateral movement) movements essential for chewing and speech.

total parenteral nutrition.definition: An intravenous method of providing all daily caloric and nutrient needs (carbohydrates, protein, fats, fluids, electrolytes, vitamins, and trace elements) directly into the bloodstream, bypassing the gastrointestinal tract, usually via a central venous catheter; used when the GI tract cannot absorb nutrients or is unusable.

tpr.definition: Abbreviation for temperature pulse and respiration

testicular self-examination.definition: An examination performed by an individual to palpate each testicle for lumps, swelling, or changes in size, shape, or consistency; typically done monthly, usually after a warm shower or bath to relax the scrotum, with prompt medical evaluation if an abnormal lump, swelling, or persistent pain is detected.

thyroid-stimulating hormone.definition: A hormone produced by the pituitary gland that stimulates the thyroid gland; measuring TSH levels helps determine if thyroid hormone levels are normal.

urinalysis.definition: A test of your urine to check for diseases, such as diabetes, urinary tract infections, or kidney problems.

upper respiratory infection.definition: An infection of the upper airway structures (nose, paranasal sinuses, pharynx, and larynx) most commonly caused by viruses; presents with nasal congestion or discharge, sore throat, cough, sneezing, and sometimes fever, and is usually self-limited.

urinary tract infection.definition: A bacterial infection of the urinary tract that most often involves the bladder or urethra; presents with dysuria, urinary frequency and urgency, and sometimes suprapubic pain or hematuria; diagnosed by urinalysis and urine culture; treated with antibiotics.

vital capacity.definition: The maximum amount of air a person can exhale after a maximum inhalation; the sum of inspiratory reserve volume, tidal volume, and expiratory reserve volume. It is a standard measure of lung function obtained with spirometry.

volume.definition: The amount of space that a substance or object occupies; in physiology, the volume of fluid or gas within a body compartment (e.g., blood volume, extracellular fluid volume, tidal volume).

vital signs.definition: Measurements that indicate how well the body is functioning, including pulse rate, respiration (breathing rate), temperature, and blood pressure.

ventricular septal defect.definition: One or more holes in the septum, the muscular wall separating the right and left sides of the heart.

white blood cell.definition: A leukocyte; a blood cell that defends the body against infection by recognizing and destroying pathogens and coordinating immune responses. Leukocytes originate in the bone marrow and include neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils.

endometriosis.definition: Occurs when tissue like the lining of the uterus grows in other places in your body.

anesthesia.definition: A drug that reduces pain (a local anesthetic) or that puts you to sleep (a general anesthetic), as during surgery.

anesthetist.definition: An anesthetist is a clinician who administers anesthesia and oversees perioperative care, including airway management, monitoring vital signs, adjusting anesthetic agents, and providing analgesia; the title's meaning varies by country, sometimes referring to physician anesthesiologists and other times to nurse anesthetists (CRNAs).

hemostasis.definition: The physiological process that stops bleeding by constricting damaged vessels, forming a platelet plug (primary hemostasis), and activating the coagulation cascade to produce a fibrin clot (secondary hemostasis), which is eventually dissolved during fibrinolysis as healing occurs.

infection.definition: When germs get in your body and you get sick.

anatomy.definition: The branch of biology that studies the structure of living organisms and the relationships among their parts; in humans, the organization of tissues, organs, and body systems, typically investigated by dissection and imaging.

imaging.definition: Imaging refers to techniques that create visual representations of the body's internal structures for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes, using modalities such as X-ray radiography, CT, MRI, ultrasound, and nuclear medicine.

radiography.definition: A diagnostic imaging technique that uses X-ray radiation to visualize internal body structures by recording the differential absorption of the beams, producing radiographs (X-ray images) on film or a digital detector.

pharmacotherapy.definition: Using drugs to treat a disease or condition.

pharmacology.definition: The science that studies how drugs interact with living organisms, including their origin, chemical properties, absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (pharmacokinetics); their mechanisms of action and effects on the body (pharmacodynamics); therapeutic uses; and their adverse effects and toxicology.

supplements.definition: A product intended to supplement the diet that contains one or more dietary ingredients (e.g., vitamins, minerals, herbs, amino acids, or botanicals) and is taken by mouth in pill, capsule, tablet, powder, or liquid form; not a substitute for a healthy diet and not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent disease.

analgesic.definition: A pain reliever, available over the counter (such as aspirin or acetaminophen) or by prescription.

artificial lung.definition: A device or circuit that oxygenates blood and removes carbon dioxide outside the body, functioning as a temporary lung substitute for patients with severe respiratory failure (most commonly via an extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, ECMO, oxygenator).

anal membrane.definition: An embryologic, transient structure formed by the union of endoderm and ectoderm at the end of the hindgut (the cloacal/anal membrane) that covers the future anal opening and ruptures to form the anal canal opening.

artificial menopause.definition: Induced cessation of ovarian function from medical interventions (such as surgical removal of the ovaries, chemotherapy, or pelvic radiotherapy), leading to menopause-like hormone deficiency, cessation of menses, and estrogen-deprivation symptoms.

menopause.definition: The time in a woman's life when her periods stop. Also known as "the change."

acquired immunity.definition: An adaptive immune response that develops after exposure to specific antigens, mediated by B and T lymphocytes, producing targeted antibodies and cellular responses, and characterized by immunological memory that enables faster and stronger responses upon re-exposure.

nilstat.definition: A brand-name antifungal medication (nystatin) used to treat Candida infections of the mouth, throat, esophagus, and skin; it binds ergosterol in fungal cell membranes, creating pores and causing cell leakage and death; it is poorly absorbed from the GI tract when given orally.

11-hydroxycorticosteroid.definition: A corticosteroid with a hydroxyl group at the 11β position; a class including cortisol (hydrocortisone) and corticosterone, and their urinary metabolites used as markers of adrenal cortical activity.

11-hydroxyetiocholanolone.definition: A steroid metabolite; the 11-hydroxylated derivative of etiocholanolone produced by hepatic metabolism of androgens and excreted in urine.

5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid.definition: A major urinary metabolite of serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) produced by MAO-initiated oxidation followed by aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction; excreted in urine and used as a biomarker for carcinoid syndrome and other conditions with increased serotonin turnover.

hydroxychloroquine sulfate.definition: An oral antimalarial and disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD); the sulfate salt of a 4-aminoquinoline used to prevent and treat malaria and to manage autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis. Its immunomodulatory effects are thought to arise from increasing lysosomal pH and interfering with antigen processing and presentation.

hydroxychloroquine.definition: A 4-aminoquinoline antimalarial drug also used as a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug for autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis; it modulates immune function by increasing lysosomal pH and inhibiting toll-like receptor signaling.

eastern equine encephalitis.definition: An arboviral, mosquito‑borne encephalitis caused by an alphavirus; it begins with fever and flu-like symptoms and may progress to severe brain inflammation with confusion, seizures, coma, and death. There is no specific antiviral treatment; management is supportive. Birds are the natural reservoir and mosquitoes the vector; humans and horses are dead‑end hosts. A vaccine exists for horses but not for humans.

western equine encephalitis.definition: A mosquito-borne viral encephalitis caused by an alphavirus; ranges from febrile illness to severe encephalitis with confusion and neurologic deficits; occurs in North America; no specific antiviral therapy; management is supportive.

venezuelan equine encephalitis.definition: A mosquito-borne RNA alphavirus infection causing febrile illness and sometimes encephalitis in humans; horses are primary amplifying hosts, with outbreaks occurring in the Americas. Diagnosis is via serology or PCR; there is no specific antiviral therapy, and management is supportive. Prevention relies on mosquito control and vaccination of horses.

equine encephalitis.definition: A group of mosquito-borne viral infections causing encephalitis in horses, typically due to Eastern, Western, or Venezuelan equine encephalitis viruses; signs include fever, ataxia, depression, seizures, and recumbency, and the disease can be fatal. Vaccination is available for horses (and humans can be affected rarely).

encephalitis.definition: Inflammation of the brain caused by an infectious germ (typically a virus or bacteria), leading to swelling of brain tissue.

rectal suppositories.definition: A solid dosage form inserted into the rectum that melts or dissolves at body temperature to release a drug for local action (e.g., laxatives, hemorrhoidal therapies) or systemic absorption, often using a waxy base such as cocoa butter.

dermatological agents.definition: Substances used in the diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of skin diseases; includes topical and systemic medications and preparations such as corticosteroids, antifungals, antibiotics, retinoids, keratolytics, immunomodulators, moisturizers, and sunscreens.

abdominal.definition: Relating to the abdomen, the region of the body between the thorax and pelvis; used to describe anatomy, diseases, or procedures involving the abdominal cavity and its organs.

abdominal surgery.definition: Any surgical procedure performed within the abdomen (the peritoneal cavity) or on abdominal organs to diagnose, repair, remove, or treat disease or injury; commonly done via open or minimally invasive (laparoscopic) approaches.

surgery.definition: To change the organs or tissues in your body through cutting. Also called an operation.

achondroplastic.definition: Relating to achondroplasia, a congenital form of dwarfism characterized by disproportionately short limbs with a normal-sized trunk, due to FGFR3 gene mutation.

dwarf.definition: An individual of unusually short stature, typically defined as an adult height of about 147 cm (4 feet 10 inches) or less, caused by a medical or genetic condition that impairs growth; can be disproportionate (limbs and trunk not in proportion) or proportionate.

achondroplastic dwarf.definition: Disproportionate dwarfism caused by an FGFR3 gain‑of‑function mutation that disrupts endochondral ossification; features include rhizomelic (proximal) limb shortening, a relatively normal trunk, macrocephaly with frontal bossing, midface hypoplasia, and often lumbar lordosis or spinal stenosis.

adie's syndrome.definition: A benign autonomic neuropathy characterized by a tonically dilated pupil that poorly reacts to light but slowly accommodates, due to postganglionic parasympathetic denervation of the iris, often with diminished or absent deep tendon reflexes (areflexia).

symmers' disease.definition: A hepatic periportal fibrosis (“pipe-stem fibrosis”) due to chronic Schistosoma mansoni infection, leading to presinusoidal portal hypertension.

bernard-soulier syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal recessive bleeding disorder due to deficiency or dysfunction of the platelet GPIb-IX-V complex (von Willebrand factor receptor), causing defective platelet adhesion, macrothrombocytopenia, and mucocutaneous bleeding; ristocetin-induced aggregation is reduced and does not correct with normal plasma.

hematoma.definition: A bruise or when your skin is black and blue after an injury.

hematomata.definition: Multiple localized collections of blood outside vessels, typically within tissues, arising from rupture of blood vessels after injury or surgery; they present as swellings that may be tender and discolored and usually resolve over time, though large or expanding hematomata may require drainage.

haematology.definition: The branch of medicine that studies and treats diseases of the blood and blood-forming tissues, including disorders of red cells, white cells, platelets, plasma, and the coagulation system.

foramen.definition: An opening or hole in a bone or other structure through which nerves, blood vessels, or ligaments pass.

foramina.definition: Openings or holes in bones through which nerves and blood vessels pass.

calculus.definition: A hard crusty coating on teeth or a "stone" in an organ (kidney or bladder stones, for example).

calculi.definition: A stone formed by precipitation or crystallization of minerals within a hollow organ or duct; common sites include the kidneys, ureters, bladder, and gallbladder.

cocci.definition: Round-shaped bacteria; a common bacterial morphology that can occur singly or in characteristic arrangements such as pairs (diplococci), chains (streptococci), or clusters (staphylococci). Includes medically important genera such as Streptococcus and Staphylococcus.

coccus.definition: A spherical bacterium; the basic bacterial cell shape, with cocci occurring alone or in arrangements such as pairs (diplococci), chains (streptococci), or clusters (staphylococci).

epulis.definition: A benign gingival (gum) mass arising from the gingival mucosa; it can be fibrous or vascular (e.g., pyogenic granuloma) and is often related to local irritation, trauma, plaque, or hormonal factors.

epulides.definition: Plural form of a gingival (gum) growth; benign, tumor-like overgrowths of the gingival tissue, often fibrous or inflammatory in nature.

corpus.definition: The main body or central portion of an organ or structure; the substantive mass of an organ, as distinct from its extremities or specialized parts.

corpora.definition: Plural of corpus; in anatomy, a body or rounded structure within an organ; used in the names of several structures (e.g., corpora cavernosa, corpora lutea, corpora quadrigemina).

femur.definition: Your thigh bone that connects your hip and knee.

femora.definition: Plural form of the thigh bone; the thigh bone is the longest bone in the human skeleton, extending from the hip to the knee. Proximally it articulates with the acetabulum of the pelvis, and distally with the tibia and patella.

analyses.definition: A detailed examination of the components or elements of a subject or specimen, typically to interpret data, determine composition, or derive meaning; in medicine, the testing and interpretation of laboratory results and patient samples.

incus.definition: One of the three small bones of the middle ear (the anvil). It transmits sound vibrations from the malleus (hammer) to the stapes (stirrup) as part of the ossicular chain that conducts and amplifies vibrations to the inner ear.

ductus.definition: A tubular passage in the body that transports fluids or secretions from one location to another, often connecting an organ to another structure or to the exterior.

coxa adducta.definition: A fixed deformity of the hip in which the thigh is adducted toward the midline; the limb cannot be abducted and lies closer to the body's midline, often due to contracture of the hip adductor muscles or other hip pathology.

coxa flexa.definition: Flexion of the hip joint; movement that decreases the angle between the femur and the pelvis, bringing the thigh toward the abdomen.

coxa vara.definition: A deformity of the hip in which the femoral neck–shaft angle is decreased (varus) relative to the normal hip angle (about 120–135 degrees), causing limb shortening and a limp; it can be congenital, developmental, or due to fracture or disease.

acoustic neurilemmoma.definition: A benign tumor arising from Schwann cells of the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII), typically located in the internal auditory canal or cerebellopontine angle; it commonly presents with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and disequilibrium, and may cause facial weakness if large.

acoustic neurinoma.definition: A benign tumor of the vestibulocochlear nerve (cranial nerve VIII), typically arising from Schwann cells in the internal auditory canal or cerebellopontine angle; causes unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and balance disturbance; management ranges from observation to microsurgical resection or stereotactic radiotherapy.

acoustic neurofibroma.definition: A benign tumor of the vestibulocochlear nerve (cranial nerve VIII) arising from Schwann cells; typically located in the internal auditory canal or cerebellopontine angle and commonly called vestibular schwannoma or acoustic neuroma.

acoustic nerve.definition: A cranial nerve (CN VIII) that transmits auditory information from the cochlea and balance information from the vestibular apparatus to the brain; consists of cochlear and vestibular divisions and traverses the internal auditory meatus.

abducens nerve.definition: A motor cranial nerve (cranial nerve VI) that innervates the lateral rectus muscle to abduct the eye; dysfunction causes horizontal diplopia and medial deviation (esotropia).

bacteriophage.definition: A virus that specifically infects bacteria; it carries its own nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) enclosed in a protein capsid (often with a tail) and uses the bacterial machinery to replicate, typically causing lysis of the bacterial cell, though some phages can establish lysogeny by integrating into the host genome.

bacteriophagy.definition: The engulfment and intracellular digestion of bacteria by phagocytic immune cells (such as macrophages and neutrophils).

aura.definition: Sensations such as chills, flashes of light, or a blind spot that come just before the occurrence of medical problems such as migraines or seizures.

defibrillate.definition: To restore a normal heart rhythm by delivering a controlled electric shock to the heart, typically to treat life-threatening arrhythmias such as ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia.

coccyx.definition: The last bone at the bottom of the spine. Also called tailbone.

sternum.definition: A bone in the middle of the chest that connects the first couple ribs. Also called breastbone.

ribs.definition: One of the 12 paired, curved bones forming the rib cage that protect the thoracic organs; the first seven pairs connect directly to the sternum via costal cartilage, the next three attach indirectly through the cartilage of the rib above, and the last two do not attach to the sternum anteriorly.

vertebral column.definition: A segmented bony axis of the axial skeleton that houses the spinal cord and provides upright support and motion; it comprises the vertebrae (cervical, thoracic, lumbar) and the fused sacral and coccygeal vertebrae, separated by intervertebral discs.

ilium.definition: The broad, wing-shaped bone forming the upper portion of each hip bone; it articulates with the sacrum at the sacroiliac joint and provides attachment for many hip and thigh muscles.

sacrum.definition: A triangle-shaped bone at the bottom of the spine and connected to the hips.

frontal bone.definition: A single, unpaired cranial bone forming the forehead and the roof of the orbits; it consists of the squamous part (forehead) and the orbital part (roof of the orbit) and contains the frontal sinuses.

zygomatic bone.definition: A paired facial bone that forms the cheek prominence and part of the orbit, articulating with the maxilla, frontal bone, sphenoid, and temporal bone; it has four processes (frontal, orbital, maxillary, and temporal) that connect to neighboring bones.

scapula.definition: A wide, flat bone at the back of the shoulder.

xiphoid process.definition: A small, pointed projection at the inferior end of the sternum; initially cartilaginous and ossifying with age, it is the lowest part of the sternum and serves as an attachment for the rectus abdominis and other abdominal muscles, and is a commonly used CPR landmark.

costal cartilage.definition: Hyaline cartilage that connects the anterior ends of the ribs to the sternum (directly for true ribs and indirectly via the cartilage above for false ribs), contributing to the elasticity and expansion of the thoracic cage.

humerus.definition: The bone in the upper arm that connects the shoulder to the elbow.

ulna.definition: A bone in the lower part of the arm, closer to the body.

radius.definition: A bone in the lower part of the arm, towards the outside edge.

carpal bones.definition: Eight small irregular bones forming the wrist, arranged in two rows (proximal and distal) between the forearm and the metacarpals, enabling wrist movements and providing stability.

metacarpal bones.definition: Five long bones of the hand extending from the carpal (wrist) bones to the proximal phalanges; they form the palm and are numbered I–V from the thumb to the little finger. Each bone has a base that articulates with the carpal bones, a shaft, and a head that forms the knuckles with the proximal phalanges.

phalanges.definition: The bones that make up the fingers and the toes.

patella.definition: A large sesamoid bone in front of the knee, embedded in the quadriceps tendon; it protects the knee joint and increases the mechanical advantage of the quadriceps during leg extension.

tibia.definition: A bigger bone in the bottom half of the leg that connects the ankle to the knee.

fibula.definition: A thin bone in the bottom half of the leg.

tarsal bones.definition: Seven irregular bones of the foot that form the ankle and proximal foot: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and the three cuneiforms (medial, intermediate, lateral); they articulate with the tibia and fibula to form the ankle joint and contribute to the foot arches and weight transfer.

metatarsal bones.definition: Five long bones in the forefoot that extend from the tarsal bones to the proximal phalanges of the toes; they bear weight and aid in movement, and form the transverse and longitudinal arches of the foot. They are numbered I to V from the medial (big toe) side; each has a base, shaft, and head.

occipital bone.definition: The bottom of the back of the skull.

parietal bone.definition: A paired skull bone forming the superior lateral wall and roof of the cranial cavity; it articulates with the frontal, occipital, temporal, and sphenoid bones at the coronal, lambdoid, squamous, and sphenoparietal sutures; it consists of outer and inner compact bone with a middle diploë (spongy) layer.

temporal bone.definition: A paired bone forming part of the side and base of the skull; it contains the middle and inner ear structures (in the petrous part) and provides attachment for muscles and the temporomandibular joint. It is subdivided into the squamous, tympanic, mastoid, and petrous parts and features the external auditory meatus, mandibular fossa, carotid canal, and jugular foramen.

sphenoid.definition: A central, butterfly-shaped bone at the base of the skull that forms part of the cranial floor and the orbits; contains the sella turcica for the pituitary gland and the sphenoid sinuses.

nasal bone.definition: A pair of small, rectangular facial bones that form the superior part of the nasal bridge; they articulate with the frontal bone superiorly and with the maxillae laterally, and with each other at the midline, forming the bony nasal skeleton that supports the nasal cartilage.

lacrimal bone.definition: A small, delicate bone forming part of the medial wall of the orbit; it contains the lacrimal groove for the lacrimal sac and contributes to the nasolacrimal canal, articulating with the ethmoid, maxilla, frontal bone, and sphenoid.

atlas.definition: The topmost vertebra of the neck, lying just beneath the skull; the first cervical vertebra (C-1).

axis.definition: The second vertebra of the neck (from the skull); also called the C-2 vertebra.

greater trochanter.definition: A large bony prominence on the lateral aspect of the proximal femur, just distal to the femoral neck; it serves as the insertion site for the hip abductor muscles (gluteus medius and minimus) and as an attachment for the piriformis and other structures.

pubis.definition: The anterior portion of the pelvic bone; one of the paired pubic bones that join at the pubic symphysis to form the anterior part of the pelvis.

ischium.definition: One of the three fused bones of the pelvis (os coxae); it forms the posteroinferior portion of the acetabulum and includes the body and ramus, with the ischial tuberosity that bears weight when sitting.

intervertebral foramen.definition: An opening between adjacent vertebrae on the lateral aspect of the spine through which the spinal nerve roots exit the vertebral canal; it is bounded anteriorly by the intervertebral disc and vertebral bodies and posteriorly by the facet joints and ligamentum flavum.

vertebral canal.definition: The bony-tunnel within the vertebral column formed by the aligned vertebral foramina, extending from the foramen magnum to the sacral canal, that houses the spinal cord (or cauda equina in adults) along with the meninges and cerebrospinal fluid.

vertebral body.definition: The large, anterior portion of a vertebra that bears the body's weight; a block of cancellous bone surrounded by a thin cortical shell, with superior and inferior endplates that articulate with the adjacent intervertebral discs and vertebrae.

lamina.definition: One of the two thin, plate-like parts of each vertebra.

pedicle.definition: A narrow stalk attaching a structure to the body, containing its blood vessels (and often nerves) that supply it.

spinous process.definition: The lever-like backward projection extending off each vertebra, to which muscles and ligaments are attached.

transverse process.definition: A lateral bony projection of a vertebra, extending from the junction of the pedicle and lamina; it serves as an attachment site for muscles and ligaments and, in the thoracic spine, articulates with a rib at the costotransverse joint.

dens.definition: A peg-like projection from the body of the axis (C2 vertebra), called the odontoid process, that acts as a pivot for the atlas (C1) and enables rotation of the head.

optic foramen.definition: An opening in the posterior orbit formed by the sphenoid bone (lesser wing) through which the optic nerve (cranial nerve II) and the ophthalmic artery pass.

infraorbital foramen.definition: An opening in the maxilla below the orbit that transmits the infraorbital nerve (a branch of CN V2) and accompanying vessels from the infraorbital canal to the midface.

supraorbital foramen.definition: An opening in the frontal bone at the superior orbital margin (often a foramen or notch) that transmits the supraorbital nerve and its accompanying vessels from the orbit.

mental foramen.definition: An opening on the anterior surface of the mandible, typically near the premolars, that transmits the mental nerve and vessels to supply sensation to the chin and lower lip; a key landmark for inferior alveolar/mental nerve blocks.

coronal suture.definition: A fibrous joint between the frontal bone and the parietal bones of the skull; it runs across the top of the head and allows skull growth during infancy.

sagittal suture.definition: A dense fibrous joint between the two parietal bones along the midline of the skull; it is an immovable cranial suture (synarthrosis) that ossifies with age.

lambdoidal suture.definition: A dense fibrous joint between the occipital bone and the parietal bones at the posterior aspect of the skull; it allows growth of the skull during infancy and typically ossifies with age.

squamosal suture.definition: A cranial suture between the squamous part of the temporal bone and the parietal bone; a fibrous joint that allows skull growth in infancy and typically fuses with age.

frontal suture.definition: A cranial suture along the midline of the forehead that unites the two halves of the frontal bone; it typically fuses in early childhood, and persistence is referred to as the metopic suture.

nasal conchae.definition: Three bony shelves on the lateral wall of the nasal cavity (superior, middle, and inferior conchae/turbinates) lined with respiratory mucosa. They increase nasal surface area to warm and humidify inspired air, filter particles, and direct airflow to help condition air and support olfaction.

nasal cavity.definition: An air-filled space inside the nose, extending from the nares to the choanae, lined by respiratory mucosa; it filters, warms, and humidifies inhaled air and houses the olfactory epithelium in its superior portion.

external auditory meatus.definition: The external auditory meatus is the outer ear canal that extends from the auricle to the tympanic membrane; it conducts sound to the middle ear and protects it, comprising a lateral cartilaginous portion and a medial bony portion, lined with skin bearing hairs and ceruminous glands.

mastoid fontanel.definition: A soft membranous gap on the posterolateral aspect of an infant's skull near the mastoid region, between growing bones, allowing skull growth; it normally closes by about 1–2 years of age.

styloid process.definition: A slender, pointed projection of the temporal bone that extends downward from the skull and serves as the attachment site for the muscles stylopharyngeus, styloglossus, and stylohyoid, as well as for the ligaments stylohyoid and stylomandibular.

orbit.definition: The bony socket that holds the eyeball.

zygomatic process.definition: A projection on certain skull bones that articulates with the zygomatic bone; examples include the zygomatic process of the temporal bone (forming part of the zygomatic arch) and the zygomatic process of the maxilla (contributing to the orbital rim).

parotid gland.definition: A major salivary gland located anterior to the ear in the cheek region; the largest of the salivary glands, producing serous saliva that drains into the mouth via Stensen’s duct.

masseter.definition: A thick muscle of mastication on the lateral jaw that elevates the mandible to close the mouth; it originates from the zygomatic arch and inserts on the mandible (ramus/angle) and is innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3).

temporalis.definition: A broad, fan-shaped muscle of mastication located in the temporal fossa on the side of the skull; it elevates the mandible to close the jaw (with posterior fibers also retracting the mandible) and is innervated by the deep temporal nerves (mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve) and supplied by the deep temporal arteries.

buccinator.definition: A thick, quadrilateral muscle forming the muscular wall of the cheek that compresses the cheek against the teeth during chewing and helps blow air; it originates from the alveolar processes of the maxilla and mandible and the pterygomandibular raphe and inserts into the orbicularis oris; innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII).

orbicularis oculi.definition: A circular muscle surrounding the eye that closes the eyelids; composed of orbital and palpebral portions and innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII).

orbicularis oris.definition: A circular muscle that encircles the mouth and acts as a sphincter to close and purse the lips; essential for speech, kissing, and facial expressions; innervated by the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII).

zygomaticus major.definition: A facial expression muscle arising from the zygomatic bone and inserting at the angle of the mouth; it elevates and draws the corner of the mouth upward and laterally (smiling). Innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII).

zygomaticus minor.definition: A small facial muscle that originates from the zygomatic bone and inserts into the skin of the upper lip; it elevates the upper lip, aiding in smiling.

nasalis.definition: A paired facial muscle of the nose, consisting of two parts: the transversus nasalis, which compresses the nostrils, and the alaris (alar) portion, which dilates the nostrils; innervated by the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII).

levator labii superioris.definition: A facial expression muscle that elevates the upper lip; innervated by the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII).

levator labii superioris alaeque nasi.definition: A facial muscle that elevates the upper lip and widens the nostril (naris); it originates from the frontal process of the maxilla and inserts into the upper lip and the ala of the nose.

risorius.definition: A thin superficial muscle of facial expression that pulls the corners of the mouth laterally (outward), aiding in smiling; innervated by the buccal branch of the facial nerve.

mentalis.definition: A small paired muscle of the chin that elevates and protrudes the lower lip and wrinkles the skin of the chin; innervated by the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII).

platysma.definition: A broad, thin superficial neck muscle that tenses the skin of the neck and helps depress the lower jaw and corners of the mouth; it extends from the fascia of the chest and shoulder to the lower face.

sternocleidomastoid.definition: Paired superficial neck muscle that originates from the sternum and medial clavicle and inserts on the mastoid process; it flexes the neck when both sides contract and rotates the head to the opposite side when contracting unilaterally; it can assist in elevating the sternum during deep inspiration. Innervated by the spinal accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI).

trapezius.definition: A large superficial back muscle that extends from the occipital bone and cervical and upper thoracic spinous processes to the clavicle, acromion, and spine of the scapula; it elevates, retracts, and upwardly rotates the scapula and helps stabilize the shoulder girdle. Innervated primarily by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) with proprioceptive fibers from C3–C4.

pectoralis major.definition: A large, fan-shaped muscle of the anterior chest wall. It originates from the medial clavicle, sternum, and upper costal cartilages and inserts onto the lateral lip of the intertubercular (bicipital) groove of the humerus. It adducts and medially rotates the humerus; the clavicular portion flexes the arm and the sternocostal portion can extend a flexed arm. It is innervated by the medial and lateral pectoral nerves and vascularized by branches of the thoracoacromial trunk.

serratus anterior.definition: A large, fan-shaped muscle on the lateral thorax that protracts and stabilizes the scapula against the chest wall and assists in upward rotation of the scapula; innervated by the long thoracic nerve (C5–C7).

rectus abdominis.definition: A paired muscle of the anterior abdominal wall that runs vertically and flexes the trunk; it originates from the pubic crest and symphysis and inserts on the xiphoid process and costal cartilages of ribs 5–7, and is enclosed within the rectus sheath.

external abdominal oblique.definition: One of the flat muscles of the anterolateral abdominal wall; it originates from the external surfaces of ribs 5–12 and inserts into the iliac crest and the linea alba via its aponeurosis. Its fibers run inferomedially and it functions to flex and rotate the trunk and to increase intra-abdominal pressure; innervation is by the thoracoabdominal nerves (T7–T11) and the subcostal nerve (T12).

tensor fasciae latae.definition: A muscle of the hip that originates from the anterior part of the iliac crest and anterior superior iliac spine and inserts into the iliotibial tract; it flexes, abducts, and medially rotates the thigh and helps stabilize the pelvis by tensing the iliotibial band. Innervated by the superior gluteal nerve (L4–S1).

vastus lateralis.definition: A large muscle of the quadriceps femoris group on the anterior-lateral thigh that extends the knee and helps stabilize the patella; it is the largest of the quadriceps muscles.

vastus medialis.definition: A muscle of the quadriceps femoris group on the inner thigh that extends the knee and helps stabilize the patella (kneecap) during movement.

rectus femoris.definition: An anterior-thigh muscle of the quadriceps femoris group that crosses both the hip and knee joints; it originates from the anterior inferior iliac spine and inserts into the patella (via the quadriceps tendon) and the tibial tuberosity (via the patellar ligament). It extends the knee and flexes the hip.

patellar tendon.definition: A strong band of dense connective tissue that extends from the inferior pole of the patella to the tibial tuberosity, transmitting the force of the quadriceps to the tibia to extend the knee; part of the knee's extensor mechanism.

gastrocnemius.definition: A large two-headed muscle of the posterior leg (calf) that plantarflexes the foot at the ankle and flexes the knee; it originates from the femoral condyles and inserts into the calcaneus via the Achilles tendon.

soleus.definition: A muscle of the posterior leg, part of the triceps surae, that plantarflexes the foot at the ankle; originates from the posterior surfaces of the tibia and fibula and inserts into the calcaneus via the Achilles tendon; innervated by the tibial nerve.

iliotibial tract.definition: A thick band of fascia on the lateral thigh (fascia lata) that runs from the iliac crest to the lateral tibia (Gerdy’s tubercle); it stabilizes the knee laterally and serves as an aponeurosis for the tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus.

adductor magnus.definition: Large triangular muscle of the medial thigh that adducts the femur. It has two parts: an anterior adductor part and a posterior hamstring part. The adductor part originates from the inferior pubic ramus and ischial ramus and inserts along the linea aspera; the hamstring part originates from the ischial tuberosity and inserts on the adductor tubercle of the femur.
