Innervation: obturator nerve (adductor part) and tibial part of the sciatic nerve (hamstring part). Function: adducts the thigh; the anterior part flexes the hip, while the posterior part extends it.

gracilis.definition: An elongated, slender muscle of the medial thigh that adducts the thigh and flexes the knee; originates from the inferior pubic ramus and inserts on the medial tibial surface as part of the pes anserinus.

gluteus maximus.definition: A large, powerful muscle of the buttock that extends the thigh at the hip and assists with external rotation; it originates from the ilium, sacrum, and coccyx and inserts into the iliotibial tract and the gluteal tuberosity of the femur; innervated by the inferior gluteal nerve.

sartorius.definition: A long, strap‑like superficial muscle of the anterior thigh that originates from the anterior superior iliac spine and inserts on the medial proximal tibia (via the pes anserinus); it flexes, abducts, and laterally rotates the hip, and flexes the knee. Innervated by the femoral nerve.

biceps femoris.definition: Two-headed muscle of the posterior thigh (one of the hamstrings) that extends the hip and flexes the knee; the long head originates from the ischial tuberosity and is innervated by the tibial nerve, the short head from the femur and is innervated by the common fibular nerve; it inserts on the head of the fibula.

semitendinosus.definition: One of the hamstring muscles of the posterior thigh; it extends the hip, flexes the knee, and medially rotates the leg when the knee is flexed. It originates from the ischial tuberosity and inserts at the pes anserinus on the medial tibia; innervated by the tibial portion of the sciatic nerve.

semimembranosus.definition: One of the hamstring muscles in the posterior thigh; it originates from the ischial tuberosity and inserts on the posteromedial surface of the proximal tibia, extending the hip, flexing the knee, and medially rotating the leg when flexed; innervated by the tibial portion of the sciatic nerve.

tibialis anterior.definition: A muscle of the anterior compartment of the leg that dorsiflexes the ankle and inverts the foot; it originates from the upper tibia and interosseous membrane and inserts on the medial cuneiform and base of the first metatarsal.

peroneus longus.definition: A long muscle of the lateral leg (fibularis longus) that everts the foot and plantarflexes the ankle; it originates from the head and shaft of the fibula and inserts on the plantar base of the first metatarsal and the medial cuneiform, helping support the transverse arch of the foot. Innervated by the superficial peroneal nerve.

peroneus brevis.definition: A muscle of the lateral compartment of the leg that originates from the distal fibula, inserts on the base of the fifth metatarsal, and everts the foot while assisting in plantarflexion of the ankle, helping stabilize the lateral aspect of the ankle.

calcaneal tendon.definition: A thick fibrous tendon that attaches the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles (the triceps surae) to the posterior calcaneus (heel bone), enabling plantarflexion of the foot; commonly known as the Achilles tendon.

calcaneus.definition: The largest bone of the foot’s tarsal bones, forming the heel; a weight-bearing bone that articulates with the talus superiorly and the cuboid anteriorly, with the Achilles tendon attaching to its tuber.

achilles tendon.definition: A dense collagenous tendon that anchors the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles to the calcaneus (heel bone); it transmits plantarflexion force from the calf muscles to the foot during standing, walking, and running.

splenius capitis.definition: A broad, superficial muscle of the posterior neck that extends and rotates the head. It originates from the lower part of the nuchal ligament and the spinous processes of C7–T4 and inserts on the mastoid process and the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone.

splenius cervicis.definition: An intrinsic neck muscle of the splenius group; it originates from the spinous processes of the upper thoracic vertebrae (T3–T6) and inserts on the transverse processes of the upper cervical vertebrae (C1–C3). It extends, laterally flexes, and rotates the neck to the same side; it works with the splenius capitis to extend the head and neck.

latissimus dorsi.definition: A large, broad back muscle that extends, adducts, and medially rotates the humerus. It originates from the lower thoracic and lumbar spine, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, and lower ribs, and inserts into the intertubercular groove of the humerus; it is innervated by the thoracodorsal nerve (C6–C8).

teres major.definition: A thick muscle of the posterior shoulder girdle that extends, adducts, and medially rotates the arm; it originates from the inferior angle of the scapula and inserts on the medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus. Innervated by the lower subscapular nerve (C5–C7).

teres minor.definition: A narrow rotator cuff muscle originating from the upper two-thirds of the lateral border of the scapula and inserting on the inferior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus; it laterally rotates the arm and stabilizes the glenohumeral joint, innervated by the axillary nerve (C5–C6).

supraspinatus.definition: A rotator cuff muscle that originates from the supraspinous fossa of the scapula and inserts on the greater tubercle of the humerus; initiates the first ~15 degrees of arm abduction and helps stabilize the glenohumeral joint (innervated by the suprascapular nerve).

infraspinatus.definition: A rotator cuff muscle located in the infraspinous fossa of the scapula; it externally rotates the humerus and helps stabilize the glenohumeral joint. Innervated by the suprascapular nerve (C5–C6).

erector spinae.definition: A group of deep back muscles (iliocostalis, longissimus, and spinalis) that extends and maintains the vertebral column; they run along the spine from the sacrum and iliac crest to the ribs, vertebrae, and skull and are innervated by the dorsal rami of the spinal nerves.

sternocleidomastoideus.definition: A paired neck muscle that originates from the manubrium of the sternum and the medial clavicle and inserts on the mastoid process of the temporal bone; it flexes the neck and rotates the head to the opposite side when contracting unilaterally, and serves as an accessory muscle of respiration.

galea aponeurotica.definition: A broad, fibrous connective-tissue layer (epicranial aponeurosis) forming the middle layer of the scalp; it extends between the frontal and occipital muscles and serves as their shared tendon.

thymus.definition: A specialized organ of the immune system located in the upper-middle chest where T cells mature.

thyroid.definition: A gland in your neck that is shaped like a butterfly. It makes hormones that help your body work normally.

parathyroid.definition: One of usually four small endocrine glands located on the posterior surface of the thyroid; it secretes a hormone that regulates blood calcium and phosphate levels.

pineal.definition: Relating to the pineal gland, a small endocrine gland in the brain that secretes melatonin and helps regulate circadian rhythms.

pancreas.definition: A gland behind the stomach that helps with digestion.

islets.definition: Small clusters of endocrine cells scattered among the pancreatic exocrine tissue that secrete insulin, glucagon, somatostatin, and pancreatic polypeptide into the bloodstream to regulate blood glucose; they are richly vascularized.

testes.definition: The male gonads that produce sperm and the hormone testosterone.

ovaries.definition: Paired female reproductive organs that produce oocytes (egg cells) and secrete the hormones estrogen and progesterone.

hypothalamus.definition: Controls some basic functions of your body, such as how hot or cold you feel, if you are hungry, and how happy or sad you feel.

pituitary.definition: A pea-sized endocrine gland at the base of the brain (hypophysis) with anterior and posterior lobes that regulates growth, metabolism, reproduction, and water balance by releasing hormones such as ACTH, TSH, GH, prolactin, FSH, and LH (anterior) and vasopressin (ADH) and oxytocin (posterior) under hypothalamic control.

pineal body.definition: A small endocrine gland in the brain, located near the center in the epithalamus between the two hemispheres. It secretes melatonin, regulating circadian rhythms and sleep-wake cycles; melatonin production is influenced by light exposure.

adrenals.definition: A pair of small endocrine glands located on top of the kidneys; they secrete steroid hormones (cortisol and aldosterone) and catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine) involved in stress response, metabolism, electrolyte balance, and blood pressure regulation.

hepatopancreatic ampulla.definition: A dilation at the junction of the common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct that drains bile and pancreatic juice into the duodenum via the major duodenal papilla, regulated by the sphincter of Oddi.

head of pancreas.definition: The expanded, right end of the pancreas that lies within the C-shaped loop of the duodenum; it is the broadest portion of the gland.

tail of pancreas.definition: A slender leftward end of the pancreas that extends toward the spleen and ends at the splenic hilum; it lies within the splenorenal ligament and is supplied by branches of the splenic artery.

bile duct.definition: A duct that carries bile from the liver and gallbladder to the duodenum; the common bile duct is formed by the union of the hepatic and cystic ducts and opens into the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla, regulated by the sphincter of Oddi.

main pancreatic duct.definition: The main pancreatic duct (duct of Wirsung) is the principal excretory duct of the pancreas, collecting secretions from pancreatic acinar cells and draining them into the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla, typically joining the common bile duct near the ampulla of Vater.

minor duodenal papilla.definition: An opening in the mucosa of the second part of the duodenum that drains the accessory pancreatic duct (duct of Santorini); it serves as an alternative outlet for pancreatic secretions besides the main papilla (ampulla of Vater) and is typically located proximal to the major papilla.

major duodenal papilla.definition: An opening in the descending part of the duodenum through which the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct empty their secretions; guarded by the sphincter of Oddi and associated with the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater).

tonsils.definition: Tonsils are the paired lymphoid tissues located at the back of the throat (part of Waldeyer's ring) that sample inhaled and ingested pathogens and mount immune responses; they can become inflamed in tonsillitis.

lymph node.definition: A small, encapsulated, bean-shaped structure along lymphatic vessels that filters lymph and initiates immune responses by housing lymphocytes and other immune cells.

spleen.definition: An organ in your belly that helps fight diseases and balance fluids in your body.

red pulp.definition: A region of the spleen composed of splenic cords (Cords of Billroth) and venous sinusoids where aging or damaged red blood cells are removed by macrophages; it also serves as a reservoir for platelets.

white pulp.definition: An area of the spleen consisting of lymphoid tissue around central arteries, including periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths (T cells) and lymphoid follicles (B cells); it mediates immune responses to blood-borne antigens and is separated from the red pulp by a marginal zone.

hilum.definition: An anatomical depression or indentation on an organ where vessels, nerves, and ducts enter and exit; for example, the lung hilum contains the main bronchus and pulmonary vessels, and the kidney hilum is the medial entry/exit point for the renal artery, vein, and ureter.

trabecula.definition: A small beam or rod of tissue that forms a supporting lattice within an organ; in bone, the thin, lattice-like plates of cancellous (spongy) bone; in the heart, the muscular ridges on the inner surfaces of the ventricles.

capsule.definition: A fibrous or membranous envelope that surrounds and protects an organ or anatomical structure (for example, a joint capsule); in pharmacology, a capsule is a dosage form consisting of a gelatin shell enclosing a drug substance.

germinal center.definition: A specialized structure within secondary lymphoid organs (e.g., lymph nodes and spleen) formed after antigen exposure, where activated B cells proliferate in the dark zone, undergo somatic hypermutation and class-switch recombination, and are selected for high-affinity antibodies in the light zone.

medullary sinus.definition: A large, irregular lymphatic channel in the medulla of a lymph node that receives lymph from the cortical and medullary sinuses and efferent vessels; lined by discontinuous endothelium with resident macrophages.

medullary cords.definition: In a lymph node, medullary cords are strands of lymphoid tissue in the medulla formed mainly by B lymphocytes and plasma cells; they extend from the cortex into the medulla and are separated by medullary sinuses.

efferent lymph vessel.definition: A lymphatic vessel that carries lymph away from a lymph node, draining it into larger lymphatic vessels toward the venous system.

thoracic duct.definition: The thoracic duct is the largest lymphatic vessel; it collects lymph (including chyle) from the lower body, left thorax, head, and neck, and drains into the left venous angle at the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins. It begins as the cisterna chyli in the abdomen and ascends through the posterior mediastinum.

right lymphatic duct.definition: A short lymphatic vessel that drains lymph from the right side of the head and neck, right upper limb, and right thorax, emptying into the right venous angle (junction of the right internal jugular and right subclavian veins).

axillary lymph node.definition: A lymph node in the armpit (axilla) that filters lymph from the upper limb, chest wall, and breast; part of the axillary lymphatic basin, draining toward central and apical nodes and contributing to immune defense.

great saphenous vein.definition: The largest superficial vein of the leg, running from the medial foot up the medial leg to the saphenofemoral junction where it drains into the femoral vein; commonly used as a graft in bypass procedures.

small saphenous vein.definition: A superficial vein of the lower limb that runs along the posterior aspect of the leg from the lateral malleolus to the popliteal fossa, draining the superficial posterior and lateral leg and typically joining the popliteal vein; commonly used as a conduit for bypass grafts.

femoral vein.definition: A deep vein of the thigh that drains blood from the lower limb; it accompanies the femoral artery through the femoral triangle, receives the profunda femoris (deep femoral) vein and superficial tributaries such as the great saphenous via the saphenofemoral junction, and becomes the external iliac vein as it passes under the inguinal ligament.

popliteal vein.definition: A deep vein located in the popliteal fossa behind the knee; it drains the calf and knee regions, runs with the popliteal artery, and continues as the femoral vein after passing through the adductor hiatus.

fibular vein.definition: A deep vein of the leg that accompanies the fibular (peroneal) artery in the posterior compartment; it drains the lateral aspect of the leg and typically empties into the posterior tibial vein or contributes to the formation of the popliteal vein.

dorsal venous arch.definition: A superficial venous network on the dorsum of the foot formed by the dorsal digital and dorsal metatarsal veins; it crosses the top of the foot and drains medially into the great saphenous vein and laterally into the small saphenous vein via perforating branches.

cephalic vein.definition: A superficial vein of the upper limb that runs along the lateral aspect of the arm from the dorsal venous network of the hand, ascends through the forearm and arm, passes in the deltopectoral groove, and drains into the axillary vein; commonly used for venous access.

basilic vein.definition: A large superficial vein of the upper limb that runs along the medial aspect of the forearm and arm, drains into the brachial veins to form the axillary vein, and is commonly used for venipuncture and for creation of arteriovenous fistulas in dialysis.

median cubital vein.definition: A superficial forearm vein that crosses the elbow (cubital fossa) and connects the cephalic and basilic veins; commonly used for venipuncture.

hepatic portal vein.definition: A large vein that drains nutrient-rich blood from the gastrointestinal tract and spleen and transports it to the liver as part of the portal venous system; formed by the union of the splenic and superior mesenteric veins behind the neck of the pancreas.

inferior vena cava.definition: A large vein that returns deoxygenated blood from the lower half of the body to the right atrium of the heart; formed by the union of the common iliac veins, it ascends on the right side of the vertebral column and passes through the diaphragm at the caval opening.

superior vena cava.definition: The major vein that carries deoxygenated blood from the upper body to the heart.

internal jugular vein.definition: A large vein in the neck that drains venous blood from the brain, face, and neck; it begins at the jugular foramen as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus, travels in the carotid sheath lateral to the internal carotid artery, and drains into the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.

external jugular vein.definition: A superficial vein of the neck that drains blood from the scalp and exterior face; formed behind the angle of the mandible by the union of the posterior auricular vein and the posterior division of the retromandibular vein, it runs obliquely downward across the sternocleidomastoid and empties into the subclavian vein.

common iliac vein.definition: A vein formed by the union of the internal and external iliac veins on each side; it drains the pelvis and lower limb and unites with the contralateral common iliac vein to form the inferior vena cava around the level of L5.

internal iliac vein.definition: A major pelvic vein that drains blood from pelvic organs and surrounding structures; accompanies the internal iliac artery and typically empties into the common iliac vein, returning blood to the inferior vena cava.

external iliac vein.definition: A deep vein of the lower limb and pelvis that accompanies the external iliac artery; it begins as the femoral vein as it passes beneath the inguinal ligament, ascends to become the external iliac vein, and drains into the common iliac vein at the pelvic brim, receiving tributaries such as the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac veins.

coronary sinus.definition: A large venous channel in the posterior coronary sulcus that drains most of the heart’s venous blood into the right atrium (via the coronary sinus ostium).

great cardiac vein.definition: A large vein that accompanies the anterior interventricular artery in the anterior interventricular sulcus, drains blood from the areas supplied by the left coronary artery, and empties into the coronary sinus.

circumflex artery.definition: A branch of the left coronary artery that travels in the left atrioventricular groove to supply the left atrium and the lateral and often posterior walls of the left ventricle; gives obtuse marginal branches and, in left-dominant circulation, may give rise to the posterior descending artery.

left coronary artery.definition: An artery arising from the left aortic sinus that supplies oxygenated blood to the left atrium, most of the left ventricle, and the interventricular septum; it typically divides into the left anterior descending and left circumflex arteries.

right coronary artery.definition: One of the principal coronary arteries that supplies blood to the heart; this vessel supplies the right and lower part of the heart.

anterior interventricular artery.definition: An artery running in the anterior interventricular sulcus, usually the left anterior descending artery, that supplies the anterior wall of the left ventricle and most of the interventricular septum; a major branch of the left coronary artery.

pulmonary trunk.definition: The large artery that originates from the right ventricle and divides into the left and right pulmonary arteries, carrying deoxygenated blood to the lungs for oxygenation as part of the pulmonary circulation.

arch of aorta.definition: The curved portion of the thoracic aorta between the ascending and descending aorta, giving rise to the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery, and left subclavian artery.

left subclavian artery.definition: A major artery arising from the aortic arch that supplies the left upper limb and portions of the thorax; it travels laterally across the thorax, gives off branches such as the vertebral, internal thoracic, thyrocervical trunk, and costocervical trunk, and becomes the axillary artery at the lateral border of the first rib.

right subclavian artery.definition: A major artery of the upper limb that arises from the brachiocephalic trunk on the right; it travels laterally, coursing past the scalenes, and becomes the axillary artery at the lateral border of the first rib.

common carotid artery.definition: A major neck artery that supplies the head and brain; the left arises from the aortic arch and the right from the brachiocephalic trunk, ascends within the carotid sheath, and bifurcates at about the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C4) into the internal and external carotid arteries, with no branches in the neck.

internal carotid artery.definition: A major artery that supplies blood to the brain; arising from the common carotid in the neck, it ascends into the skull, gives off the ophthalmic artery, and ends by dividing into the anterior and middle cerebral arteries, forming part of the brain's anterior circulation.

external carotid artery.definition: Artery arising from the bifurcation of the common carotid artery at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage; supplies extracranial head and neck structures and gives branches such as facial, lingual, maxillary, superficial temporal, occipital, posterior auricular, ascending pharyngeal, and superior thyroid arteries before dividing into the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries.

brachiocephalic artery.definition: A short branch of the aortic arch (the first branch) that divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries, supplying the head, neck, and right upper limb.

radial artery.definition: A major forearm artery that originates from the brachial artery and runs along the lateral aspect of the forearm to the wrist, supplying oxygenated blood to the forearm and hand; commonly palpated at the wrist to assess the pulse and used for arterial cannulation or arterial blood gas sampling.

ulnar artery.definition: A major artery of the forearm; the continuation of the brachial artery at the elbow, running on the medial (ulnar) side of the forearm with the ulnar nerve, supplying the forearm and hand and contributing to the superficial palmar arch.

femoral artery.definition: A large artery in the thigh, continuation of the external iliac artery after crossing the inguinal ligament; it supplies oxygenated blood to the lower limb, giving off the deep femoral (profunda femoris) branch and, after passing through the adductor hiatus, continuing as the popliteal artery.

deep femoral artery.definition: A large branch of the femoral artery that arises just below the inguinal ligament and runs deep to the thigh, supplying the deep thigh muscles and hip region by giving off perforating branches to the posterior compartment and the lateral and medial circumflex femoral arteries.

medial circumflex femoral artery.definition: A branch of the profunda femoris (deep femoral) artery that courses medially around the femoral neck, giving ascending retinacular branches to the femoral head and neck; it supplies the hip joint and, with anastomoses from the lateral circumflex femoral and inferior gluteal arteries, is the principal arterial supply to the femoral head in adults.

lateral circumflex femoral artery.definition: A branch of the femoral artery (often arising from the profunda femoris) that runs laterally around the thigh and divides into ascending, transverse, and descending branches; it supplies the hip joint and thigh muscles such as tensor fasciae latae, gluteus medius/minimus, and vastus lateralis.

perforating arteries.definition: Small arteries that pass through a muscle or fascia to reach and supply tissues beyond that layer, often providing cutaneous or deep arterial branches.

obturator artery.definition: A branch of the internal iliac artery that accompanies the obturator nerve through the obturator canal to supply the medial thigh muscles (adductors and obturator externus) and the hip joint.

descending branch of lateral circumflex.word: descending branch of lateral circumflex femoral artery
descending branch of lateral circumflex.definition: An inferiorly directed branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery that supplies the quadriceps femoris muscle group and the knee region, and forms anastomoses with the descending genicular and other genicular arteries.

popliteal artery.definition: Continuation of the femoral artery after it passes through the adductor hiatus; travels in the popliteal fossa behind the knee, supplying the knee joint and posterior leg muscles, and it divides into the anterior tibial artery and the tibioperoneal trunk (which further divides into the posterior tibial and peroneal arteries).

anterior tibial artery.definition: A branch of the popliteal artery that passes into the anterior compartment of the leg, through the interosseous membrane, supplying the muscles of the anterior leg (tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, and fibularis tertius) and continuing distally as the dorsalis pedis artery on the dorsum of the foot.

posterior tibial artery.definition: A major artery of the lower leg that arises from the popliteal artery in the posterior compartment, travels down the leg behind the tibia and behind the medial malleolus, supplying the posterior compartments and the plantar surface of the foot; at the ankle it typically bifurcates into the medial and lateral plantar arteries.

fibular artery.definition: A branch of the posterior tibial artery that descends in the posterior leg along the fibula, supplying the deep posterior and lateral compartments (via perforating branches) and the tibia via a nutrient artery, with communications to the anterior tibial artery near the ankle.

dorsalis pedis artery.definition: Continuation of the anterior tibial artery as it crosses the ankle, running on the dorsum of the foot to supply the dorsal structures of the foot and toes; it gives branches such as the lateral and medial tarsal arteries, the arcuate artery, the first dorsal metatarsal artery, and a deep plantar branch that anastomoses with the plantar arterial arch.

genicular arteries.definition: Arteries around the knee derived mainly from the popliteal artery that supply the knee joint and periarticular structures; they include the superior medial genicular, superior lateral genicular, inferior medial genicular, inferior lateral genicular, and middle genicular arteries, which form an anastomotic network around the joint.

internal iliac artery.definition: An artery arising from the common iliac artery that enters the pelvis and divides into anterior and posterior divisions to supply pelvic organs, pelvic walls, and the perineum, with branches including those to the gluteal region, internal pudendal, obturator, and pelvic viscera (e.g., vesical, uterine/vaginal, and middle rectal).

hepatic artery.definition: An artery that supplies oxygenated blood to the liver; the hepatic artery proper typically originates from the common hepatic artery (a branch of the celiac trunk) and divides into right and left hepatic arteries within the liver.

splenic artery.definition: An artery originating from the celiac trunk that supplies the spleen; it runs along the superior border of the pancreas, gives off short gastric arteries and the left gastroepiploic artery, and ends at the splenic hilum.

renal artery.definition: One of the two arteries that branch from the abdominal aorta to supply the kidneys with oxygenated blood.

inferior mesenteric artery.definition: A major abdominal artery arising from the aorta around the level of L3 that supplies the distal part of the large intestine—the descending colon, sigmoid colon, and upper rectum—via its branches (left colic, sigmoid arteries, and superior rectal artery), and forms anastomoses with the middle and superior rectal arteries via the marginal artery.

superior mesenteric artery.definition: An abdominal artery arising from the anterior aspect of the aorta just below the celiac trunk, supplying the midgut; its branches (jejunal, ileal, ileocolic, right colic, and middle colic) distribute blood to the small intestine (distal duodenum to proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon) and the proximal portion of the large intestine (cecum and ascending colon).

celiac artery.definition: The celiac artery is the first major visceral branch of the abdominal aorta, arising near the T12–L1 level and dividing into the left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries to supply the foregut (esophagus to proximal duodenum) including the stomach, liver, spleen, pancreas, and proximal duodenum.

internal thoracic artery.definition: A branch of the subclavian artery that descends along the inner surface of the anterior chest wall, about 1–2 cm lateral to the sternum; it supplies the chest wall and breasts via perforating branches and terminates as the superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries. It is commonly used as a conduit in coronary artery bypass grafting.

lateral thoracic artery.definition: A branch of the axillary artery (usually from the second part) that runs along the lateral chest wall to supply the serratus anterior, pectoral muscles, lateral breast tissue, and overlying skin.

axillary artery.definition: A continuation of the subclavian artery that passes through the axilla and becomes the brachial artery at the inferior border of the teres major; it supplies the upper limb and gives branches such as the superior thoracic, thoracoacromial, lateral thoracic, subscapular, and anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries.

subscapular artery.definition: A large branch of the axillary artery (usually arising from the third part) that supplies the subscapular region and gives rise to the circumflex scapular artery and the thoracodorsal artery.

deep palmar arch.definition: Formed mainly by the radial artery’s deep branch and the deep branch of the ulnar artery; located deep in the palm on the bases of the metacarpals, it gives rise to the palmar metacarpal arteries and perforating branches that anastomose with the superficial palmar arch.

superficial palmar arch.definition: A shallow arterial arch in the palm formed primarily by the superficial palmar branch of the ulnar artery and reinforced by a branch from the radial artery; it lies superficial to the flexor tendons and deep to the palmar aponeurosis, giving rise to the common palmar digital arteries that divide into the proper palmar digital arteries, and it communicates with the deep palmar arch.

digital arteries.definition: Arteries that supply blood to the digits (fingers and toes); they run along the sides of each digit and originate from the palmar arches in the hand (and plantar arches in the foot), branching into the proper digital arteries that perfuse the digits.

facial artery.definition: A branch of the external carotid artery that supplies blood to the face; it courses upward and forward along the lower border of the mandible, gives off the inferior and superior labial arteries, and ends near the medial canthus as the angular artery, with anastomoses to branches of the ophthalmic artery.

superior thyroid artery.definition: A branch of the external carotid artery that supplies the thyroid gland, especially its upper pole, and gives the superior laryngeal artery to the larynx; it is typically the first anterior branch of the external carotid artery.

ascending pharyngeal artery.definition: An artery arising from the external carotid artery that ascends along the wall of the pharynx to supply the pharyngeal mucosa and surrounding structures, with pharyngeal branches and occasional meningeal branches.

superficial temporal artery.definition: A terminal branch of the external carotid artery that ascends in the temple to supply the scalp, running superficial to the temporalis muscle and ending as the frontal and parietal branches.

maxillary artery.definition: A large terminal branch of the external carotid artery that runs through the infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae, supplying the deep face—including the maxilla, teeth, muscles of mastication, nasal cavity, and palate—with branches such as the middle meningeal artery to the dura.

lingual artery.definition: A branch of the external carotid artery that supplies the tongue and floor of the mouth; it gives rise to the deep lingual and sublingual arteries as it runs anterior to the hyoglossus.

vertebral artery.definition: One of two blood vessels that run up the back of the neck and join at the base of the skull to form the basilar artery. The vertebral arteries carry blood from the heart to the brain.

azygos vein.definition: A vein in the posterior mediastinum that drains the thoracic wall and mediastinal structures on the right; it ascends on the right side of the vertebral column and arches over the root of the right lung to join the superior vena cava, serving as a collateral pathway between the superior and inferior vena cavae.

internal jugular.definition: A large neck vein that drains blood from the brain, face, and neck; it runs within the carotid sheath with the artery and vagus nerve and empties into the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.

external jugular.definition: A superficial neck vein that drains blood from the scalp and exterior face; it runs obliquely across the sternocleidomastoid muscle and empties into the subclavian vein, typically formed by the union of the posterior auricular vein and the posterior division of the retromandibular vein.

left brachiocephalic vein.definition: Formed by the union of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins, it courses obliquely across the superior mediastinum from left to right, anterior to the aortic arch vessels, receiving tributaries such as the left superior intercostal and left inferior thyroid veins, and joins the right brachiocephalic vein to form the superior vena cava.

nervous system.definition: A person’s brain, spinal cord, and nerves. Your nervous system controls your thinking, feeling, smelling, touching, seeing, hearing, and moving.

intermediate mass.definition: A midline patch of gray matter that connects the two thalami across the third ventricle; also known as the interthalamic adhesion; its presence is variable, and its exact function is not well understood.

thalamus.definition: A brain structure that relays sensory information to other parts of the brain; also plays a role in memory consolidation.

optic chiasm.definition: An X-shaped structure at the base of the brain where the optic nerves partially cross (nasal retinal fibers decussate to the opposite optic tract while temporal fibers stay on the same side), forming part of the visual pathway and enabling binocular vision.

pyramid.definition: Two longitudinal ridges on the ventral surface of the medulla oblongata formed by corticospinal and corticobulbar motor fibers; these fibers decussate (cross to the opposite side) at the caudal medulla.

diencephalon.definition: A part of the forebrain located between the brainstem and the cerebral hemispheres, comprising the thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus, and subthalamus; it acts as a major relay for sensory information (thalamus), regulates autonomic and endocrine functions (hypothalamus), and interfaces with limbic systems.

midbrain.definition: The mesencephalon, the upper portion of the brainstem between the pons and the diencephalon; it contains the cerebral peduncles, the tectum with the superior and inferior colliculi, and the tegmentum (including the red nucleus and substantia nigra). It houses the nuclei of cranial nerves III and IV and coordinates eye movements, as well as visual and auditory reflexes and other motor pathways.

superior colliculus.definition: A paired midbrain structure in the tectum that receives retinal and other sensory input and coordinates reflexive visual orienting and saccadic eye movements.

inferior colliculus.definition: Principal midbrain auditory relay nucleus that receives input from brainstem auditory pathways (via the lateral lemniscus) and sends output to the thalamic medial geniculate body; involved in sound localization and auditory reflexes.

cerebral peduncle.definition: Two large bundles of descending projection fibers on the ventral midbrain (crus cerebri) that connect the cerebral cortex to the brainstem and spinal cord, containing corticospinal, corticobulbar, and corticopontine tracts.

superior cerebellar peduncle.definition: A major cerebellar efferent pathway that carries fibers from the deep cerebellar nuclei (primarily the dentate nucleus) to the contralateral midbrain (via the red nucleus) and to the ventral lateral nucleus of the thalamus, aiding coordination and timing of voluntary movement.

fourth ventricle.definition: Diamond-shaped cavity in the brainstem's ventricular system, located between the pons/medulla anteriorly and the cerebellum posteriorly; communicates with the third ventricle via the cerebral aqueduct and with the subarachnoid space through the foramina of Magendie (median) and Luschka (lateral).

inferior cerebellar peduncle.definition: A major cerebellar peduncle (restiform body) connecting the medulla oblongata to the cerebellum; it contains predominantly afferent fibers from the spinal cord and brainstem to the cerebellum (including the dorsal spinocerebellar, cuneocerebellar, and olivocerebellar tracts) conveying proprioceptive and vestibular information, and also carries some cerebellar efferents to vestibular and reticular nuclei.

brainstem.definition: A structure at the base of the brain that connects the cerebrum and cerebellum to the spinal cord, comprising the midbrain, pons, and medulla; it houses cranial nerve nuclei and centers regulating vital autonomic functions such as breathing, heart rate, and blood pressure, and it serves as a conduit for motor and sensory information between the brain and spinal cord.

middle cerebellar peduncle.definition: A tract of transverse fibers (brachium pontis) connecting the pons to the cerebellum; the largest cerebellar peduncle, it carries pontocerebellar afferent fibers from the contralateral pontine nuclei to the cerebellar hemispheres (mainly via mossy fibers) to provide input for movement coordination. Efferent cerebellar output uses the superior and inferior peduncles.

pons.definition: A structure in the brainstem between the midbrain and medulla oblongata that contains cranial nerve nuclei for V–VIII, relays signals between the cerebrum and cerebellum (via pontine nuclei and middle cerebellar peduncles), and participates in respiration and arousal/sleep regulation.

olive.definition: An oval-shaped bulge on the ventrolateral medulla formed by the inferior olivary nucleus; part of the olivary bodies that relays information to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle and is involved in motor coordination and motor learning.

medulla oblongata.definition: Lower portion of the brainstem, continuous with the spinal cord, containing vital autonomic centers for cardiovascular and respiratory regulation, as well as nuclei for cranial nerves IX–XII and reflex centers such as coughing, swallowing, and vomiting.

cerebellum.definition: The part of the brain that controls coordinated movement.

accessory nerve.definition: A motor cranial nerve (cranial nerve XI) with spinal and cranial roots; the spinal portion innervates the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, enabling head rotation and shoulder elevation; injury causes weakness in turning the head and shrugging the shoulder.

hypoglossal nerve.definition: A pure motor cranial nerve (CN XII) that innervates the intrinsic tongue muscles and most extrinsic tongue muscles (genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus) to control tongue movement; exits the skull through the hypoglossal canal; lesion causes ipsilateral tongue weakness with deviation toward the affected side.

vagus nerve.definition: A mixed cranial nerve (the tenth cranial nerve) that provides parasympathetic innervation to the heart, lungs, and most of the digestive tract, supplies motor fibers to the pharynx and larynx, and carries visceral sensory information; it originates in the medulla, exits the skull, and travels in the neck to distribute branches to thoracic and abdominal organs.

glossopharyngeal nerve.definition: A mixed cranial nerve (CN IX) that supplies taste and general sensation to the posterior one-third of the tongue and oropharynx; carries visceral sensory information from the carotid body and sinus; provides motor innervation to the stylopharyngeus; and carries parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland; exits the skull via the jugular foramen.

vestibulocochlear nerve.definition: A sensory cranial nerve (CN VIII) that transmits auditory information from the cochlea and balance information from the vestibular apparatus to the brain; it has cochlear and vestibular divisions, passes through the internal acoustic meatus, and synapses in the cochlear and vestibular nuclei of the brainstem.

facial nerve.definition: A cranial nerve (CN VII) that provides motor innervation to the muscles of facial expression; carries parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the lacrimal, submandibular, and sublingual glands; conveys taste from the anterior two‑thirds of the tongue; traverses the facial canal and exits the skull at the stylomastoid foramen.

trigeminal nerve.definition: A mixed cranial nerve (the fifth CN) that provides sensory innervation to the face and motor innervation to the muscles of mastication; it has three divisions: V1 ophthalmic, V2 maxillary, and V3 mandibular.

trochlear nerve.definition: Motor cranial nerve IV that innervates the superior oblique muscle, enabling eye intorsion and depression; palsy causes vertical diplopia that worsens on downward gaze and can be improved with head tilt toward the opposite shoulder. It arises from the dorsal brainstem and travels to the orbit via the superior orbital fissure.

oculomotor nerve.definition: A cranial nerve (CN III) that provides motor innervation to most of the extraocular muscles (superior, medial, and inferior rectus; inferior oblique) and the levator palpebrae superioris, and carries parasympathetic fibers to the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle for pupil constriction and accommodation; it originates from the oculomotor nucleus in the midbrain.

optic nerve.definition: A cable of specialized nerve fibers that transmit visual impulses from the eye to the brain.

olfactory nerve.definition: Purely sensory cranial nerve for the sense of smell; carries olfactory information from receptors in the nasal epithelium through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb, then to the primary olfactory cortex and related limbic areas.

anterior cerebral artery.definition: A terminal branch of the internal carotid artery that courses in the interhemispheric fissure to supply the medial aspects of the frontal and parietal lobes, including the leg areas of the primary motor and sensory cortices and parts of the corpus callosum; its branches include the pericallosal and callosomarginal arteries.

circle of willis.definition: A circle of arteries at the base of the brain, connecting major brain arteries and supplying blood to all parts of the brain.

pituitary gland.definition: Controls other glands (like the thyroid) and also how you grow.

middle cerebral artery.definition: A major branch of the internal carotid artery that supplies the lateral aspects of the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes, including the primary motor and sensory cortices and parts of the language cortex; occlusion can cause contralateral weakness and sensory loss, aphasia (in the dominant hemisphere), and hemispatial neglect (in the non-dominant hemisphere).

posterior communicating artery.definition: An artery within the Circle of Willis that links the internal carotid artery to the posterior cerebral artery, enabling collateral blood flow between the anterior and posterior cerebral circulations; aneurysms at its junction can cause subarachnoid hemorrhage.

posterior cerebral artery.definition: A major artery of the brain's posterior circulation arising from the basilar artery, typically as a terminal branch, that supplies the occipital lobe, calcarine cortex, inferior and medial temporal lobes, and parts of the thalamus; occlusion can cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia and memory/visual processing deficits.

superior cerebellar artery.definition: An artery arising from the basilar artery that supplies the superior aspect of the cerebellum (including the superior surface of the cerebellar hemispheres and the superior vermis) and gives perforating branches to the midbrain and upper brainstem; it courses laterally around the brainstem.

basilar artery.definition: The artery that supplies blood to the cerebellum, the brainstem, and the back of the brain.

internal auditory artery.definition: A small artery that supplies the inner ear (cochlea and vestibular apparatus); typically arising from the basilar artery or the anterior inferior cerebellar artery and traveling through the internal auditory canal with cranial nerves VII and VIII, giving rise to cochlear and vestibular arteries that perfuse the labyrinth.

anterior inferior cerebellar artery.definition: A branch of the basilar artery that supplies the anterior inferior surface of the cerebellum and portions of the lateral pons; it commonly gives rise to the labyrinthine (internal auditory) artery to the inner ear.

anterior spinal artery.definition: A vessel running along the anterior midline of the spinal cord, supplying the anterior two-thirds of the cord via sulcal branches; formed primarily by branches of the vertebral arteries and reinforced by segmental medullary arteries (including the artery of Adamkiewicz).

posterior inferior cerebellar artery.definition: A major branch of the vertebral artery that supplies the posterior-inferior aspect of the cerebellum and the dorsolateral medulla, with contributions to the fourth ventricle via the posterior inferior choroidal arteries; occlusion can cause lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome.

temporal lobe.definition: One of the four major subdivisions of the two hemispheres of the brain’s cerebral cortex. The temporal lobe plays a role in hearing, long-term memory, and behavior.

right lobe of cerebellum.definition: The right cerebellar hemisphere, the right lateral portion of the cerebellum, coordinates smooth, precise voluntary movements on the right side of the body, helps maintain posture and balance, and participates in motor learning and timing of movements. It receives input via the cerebellar peduncles and projects to motor pathways through the deep cerebellar nuclei.

dendrite.definition: A branched projection of a neuron that receives synaptic input from other neurons and conducts impulses toward the cell body.

mitochondrion.definition: An organelle within most eukaryotic cells that generates most of the cell’s ATP through oxidative phosphorylation; enclosed by a double membrane with folds (cristae), contains its own circular DNA and ribosomes, and participates in various metabolic pathways and apoptosis.

cell body.definition: Central region of a neuron containing the nucleus and most of the cytoplasm; the metabolic and synthetic center of the neuron, housing organelles and supporting protein synthesis and energy production, and it integrates incoming synaptic inputs before they are transmitted along the axon.

axon.definition: The long, slender extension of a nerve cell that conducts electrical impulses away from the nerve's cell body and on to nearby nerves.

axon hillock.definition: A cone-shaped region of a neuron at the junction of the soma and axon where action potentials are typically initiated; it contains a high density of voltage-gated sodium channels and serves as the neuron's trigger zone, converting summed postsynaptic potentials into an action potential.

schwann cell.definition: A glial cell of the peripheral nervous system that insulates axons by wrapping around them to form the myelin sheath; each Schwann cell myelinates a single segment of an axon and supports regeneration, while non-myelinating Schwann cells ensheath multiple small-diameter fibers without forming myelin.

myelin sheath.definition: A fatty insulating layer around axons in the central and peripheral nervous systems, formed by oligodendrocytes (CNS) and Schwann cells (PNS), that increases the speed of electrical impulse conduction via saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier.

node of ranvier.definition: A gap in the myelin sheath of a myelinated axon where voltage-gated sodium (and other ion) channels are concentrated, enabling saltatory conduction and faster propagation of action potentials.

telodendria.definition: The fine terminal branches at the distal end of a neuron’s axon that contact target cells via synaptic boutons, enabling transmission of nerve impulses to multiple postsynaptic sites.

synaptic knob.definition: The distal, enlarged end of a neuron's axon at a synapse (terminal bouton) that contains synaptic vesicles and releases neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft to transmit signals to the postsynaptic cell.

golgi apparatus.definition: A stack of flattened membrane-bound sacs that modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and lipids for secretion or delivery to other organelles; it receives from the rough endoplasmic reticulum at the cis face and ships via vesicles from the trans face, performing post-translational modifications such as glycosylation.

neurofilament.definition: A neuronal intermediate filament protein that forms part of the cytoskeleton in neurons, especially within axons; provides structural support, helps determine axonal diameter, and supports axonal transport; composed of light, medium, and heavy chain subunits (NFL, NFM, NFH). Elevated levels of its breakdown products in CSF or blood reflect axonal injury and can serve as biomarkers in neurodegenerative diseases.

microfilament.definition: A thin cytoskeletal filament made of polymerized actin (F-actin), about 7–9 nanometers in diameter, that supports cell shape and enables movement and muscle contraction through actomyosin interactions; dynamic and continually assembled/disassembled.

microtubule.definition: A hollow cytoskeletal filament composed of tubulin heterodimers (α- and β-tubulin); provides structural support, helps organize the cytoplasm, and serves as tracks for motor proteins during transport; exhibits dynamic instability and forms the mitotic spindle and the axoneme of cilia and flagella.

neurilemma.definition: Outer cytoplasmic sheath of a Schwann cell surrounding a peripheral nerve axon; contains the Schwann cell nucleus and forms the outermost layer of the nerve fiber, supporting peripheral nerve regeneration.

alveoli.definition: The tiny air sacs in the lungs.

alveolar duct.definition: A small airway in the lung that conducts air from the respiratory bronchioles to the alveolar sacs; its walls are lined by alveolar epithelium and supported by elastic tissue, and it ends in clusters of alveoli (alveolar sacs).

alveolar sac.definition: A cluster of alveoli at the end of a respiratory bronchiole (the terminal part of the respiratory acinus) where gas exchange occurs; multiple alveoli share a common duct/ostium, forming the primary surface for diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide across the alveolar–capillary membrane.

capillary.definition: Tiny blood vessels that connect the small arteries and veins.

alveolar epithelium.definition: Thin epithelial lining of the alveoli in the lungs, consisting mainly of type I pneumocytes (gas-exchange barrier) and type II pneumocytes (surfactant production and progenitors for type I cells); together with the underlying capillary endothelium, it forms the alveolar–capillary barrier for gas transfer.

capillary endothelium.definition: Thin, single-layer of squamous endothelial cells lining the interior of capillaries, forming the inner surface of microvessels and regulating vascular permeability and exchange of fluids, solutes, and gases between blood and surrounding tissues (varying by capillary type: continuous, fenestrated, or sinusoidal).

basement membrane.definition: Thin extracellular matrix layer between epithelial or endothelial cells and the underlying connective tissue that anchors the cells to the stroma and regulates diffusion and signaling. It comprises two components: the basal lamina (secreted by epithelial cells; rich in type IV collagen, laminin, entactin/nidogen, and proteoglycans) and the reticular lamina (produced by connective tissue; rich in type III collagen).

respiratory membrane.definition: A thin barrier between the alveolar air and pulmonary capillary blood through which oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse during gas exchange; formed by the alveolar epithelium (primarily type I pneumocytes), the capillary endothelium, and their fused basement membranes (the alveolar–capillary barrier).

interstitial space.definition: An extracellular compartment between cells in tissues, outside of blood vessels, filled with interstitial fluid; the space through which nutrients, gases, and waste diffuse between capillaries and cells.

tongue.definition: The organ inside your mouth that helps you to taste, swallow, chew, and speak.

cricoid cartilage.definition: A complete ring of hyaline cartilage forming the lower part of the larynx, immediately inferior to the thyroid cartilage. It encircles the airway, providing structural support to keep the airway open and serving as an attachment site for laryngeal muscles and ligaments; it articulates with the thyroid cartilage above and with the arytenoid cartilages posteriorly.

arytenoid muscle.definition: An intrinsic laryngeal muscle attaching to the arytenoid cartilage; it participates in moving the arytenoids to regulate the glottal opening and vocal fold tension for breathing and phonation.

vestibular fold.definition: One of the two mucous-membrane folds in the larynx located above the true vocal cords (false vocal cords); they protect the airway by sealing the laryngeal inlet during swallowing and do not vibrate during normal voice production.

false vocal fold.definition: One of the paired mucosal folds of the larynx located above the true vocal cords; it does not normally vibrate during phonation and primarily functions to protect the airway and help close the larynx during swallowing or coughing.

vocal fold.definition: One of the paired mucosal folds of the larynx (the true vocal cords) that vibrate as air passes through the glottis to produce phonation; composed of epithelium overlying connective tissue and controlled by intrinsic laryngeal muscles, they adduct to phonate and abduct to breathe.

ventricle.definition: One of the two lower chambers of the heart. The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs; the left ventricle pumps blood to the rest of the body.

hyoid bone.definition: A U-shaped bone in the neck that does not articulate with any other bone; it lies around the level of C3 and serves as an anchor for the tongue and as an attachment point for muscles of the floor of the mouth, tongue, pharynx, and larynx. It is suspended by ligaments from the temporal bone and thyroid cartilage.

epiglottis.definition: A leaf-shaped cartilage flap at the entrance of the larynx that folds down to cover the glottis during swallowing, preventing aspiration.

thyroid cartilage.definition: A large hyaline cartilage of the larynx that forms the anterior wall and laryngeal prominence; it consists of two laminae that fuse anteriorly and sits above the cricoid cartilage, providing protection for the vocal cords and serving as an attachment for laryngeal muscles and membranes.

adam’s apple.definition: A protrusion on the front of the neck formed by the thyroid cartilage (laryngeal prominence); part of the larynx that houses the vocal cords, typically more noticeable in males after puberty due to laryngeal growth.

corniculate cartilage.definition: Paired small, cone-shaped cartilages on the apex of each arytenoid cartilage in the larynx, within the aryepiglottic folds; they contribute to the structure of the laryngeal inlet and support the overlying mucosa.

cuneiform cartilage.definition: Two small elastic cartilages in the larynx, embedded in the aryepiglottic folds, that reinforce the laryngeal inlet by stiffening the aryepiglottic folds; they are normally present but may be absent in some individuals.

vestibule.definition: An anatomical space at the entrance of a body cavity or canal; in anatomy it refers to spaces at the nasal opening, the oral cavity between lips/cheeks and teeth, and the central cavity of the inner ear involved in balance.

sublingual gland.definition: One of the major salivary glands; a mucus-secreting gland located in the floor of the mouth beneath the tongue, the smallest of the major salivary glands, with multiple short ducts that open along the sublingual fold.

hepatic duct.definition: Bile duct that drains bile from the liver; the right and left hepatic ducts merge to form the common hepatic duct, which joins with the cystic duct to form the common bile duct.

cystic duct.definition: A duct that connects the gallbladder to the common bile duct, allowing bile to flow between these structures; it contains spiral valves (valves of Heister) that regulate bile flow.

common bile duct.definition: A conduit that carries bile from the liver and gallbladder to the duodenum; formed by the union of the common hepatic duct and the cystic duct, it joins with the main pancreatic duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla and opens at the major duodenal papilla in the descending part of the duodenum.

villi.definition: Finger-like projections of the mucosal lining of the small intestine that increase surface area for nutrient absorption; each projection has a core of lamina propria with a capillary network and a central lacteal, and is covered by a single layer of absorptive epithelial cells with microvilli (plus goblet cells).

brunner’s glands.definition: Mucus-secreting glands in the submucosa of the proximal duodenum that secrete an alkaline mucus containing bicarbonate to neutralize gastric acid and protect the duodenal mucosa.

ampulla.definition: A dilated, saclike enlargement at the end of a duct or canal, often at a junction with another structure.

duodenum.definition: The first portion of the small intestine; a short, C-shaped segment about 25–30 cm long that begins at the pylorus and ends at the duodenojejunal flexure, receiving chyme and pancreatic/biliary secretions, neutralizing gastric acid, and initiating digestion.

pancreatic duct.definition: Main duct of the pancreas that carries pancreatic juice rich in digestive enzymes and bicarbonate from the pancreatic acini to the duodenum; it typically joins the common bile duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla and opens at the major duodenal papilla.

stomach.definition: The place in your upper belly where food is first broken down (digested). It is between the tube that takes food from your mouth to your stomach (esophagus) and your small intestine.

liver.definition: The largest organ inside your body. It helps to digest food, store energy, and remove poisons from your body.

ascending colon.definition: A portion of the large intestine that extends upward on the right side from the ileocecal junction to the hepatic flexure; it absorbs water and electrolytes from indigestible chyme.

ileum.definition: The final portion of the small intestine, extending from the jejunoileal junction to the ileocecal valve; about 3–4 meters long in adults; absorbs bile acids, vitamin B12, and other nutrients, and contains Peyer’s patches, ending at the ileocecal valve.

cecum.definition: The cecum is the blind-ended pouch that forms the first part of the large intestine; it receives contents from the ileum via the ileocecal valve and begins absorption, while hosting gut bacteria.

vermiform appendix.definition: A narrow, blind-ended tubular extension of the cecum in the large intestine, typically about 6–9 cm long in adults, containing lymphoid tissue; its precise function is not essential, though it can become inflamed in appendicitis.

rectum.definition: The last 12 centimeters of the colon, through which waste is eliminated from the body.

transverse colon.definition: A portion of the large intestine that runs horizontally across the upper abdomen from the hepatic (right colic) flexure to the splenic (left colic) flexure; intraperitoneal and suspended by the transverse mesocolon; functions in absorbing water and electrolytes and forming feces.

haustrum.definition: A pouch-like sacculation of the colon wall formed by the taenia coli, giving the colon its segmented appearance and aiding in slow mixing and absorption of contents.

sigmoid colon.definition: Section of the colon leading to the rectum that makes an S-shaped curve.

anal canal.definition: The last inch of the large intestine, leading to the anal opening.

submandibular gland.definition: A pair of major salivary glands located beneath the floor of the mouth; they are mixed seromucous glands that secrete most of the unstimulated saliva and drain into the oral cavity via the submandibular (Wharton’s) duct.

lymph nodule.definition: A small, localized cluster of lymphoid tissue (a lymphoid follicle) within lymphoid organs or mucosa, typically containing a germinal center of proliferating B cells surrounded by a mantle zone of resting B cells.

duct from gland.definition: A tubular channel that conveys secretions from a gland to an epithelial surface or to another organ; exocrine glands discharge their products into ducts.

gland in submucosa.definition: A gland located in the submucosa—the connective tissue layer beneath the mucosa—that secretes mucus or serous fluid to lubricate and protect the mucosal surface; examples include Brunner’s glands in the duodenum and the esophageal submucosal glands.

mesentery.definition: A fold of the peritoneum that attaches the intestines to the posterior abdominal wall, containing blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatics; it supports the intestines and provides a conduit for their vessels and nerves.

myenteric plexus.definition: An intrinsic neural network of the enteric nervous system located between the circular and longitudinal layers of the GI tract’s muscularis externa (Auerbach’s plexus); it coordinates gut motility by regulating smooth muscle tone and peristaltic contractions.

submucosal plexus.definition: A network of neurons in the submucosa of the gastrointestinal tract (Meissner's plexus) that regulates local secretions, absorption, and mucosal blood flow by modulating glandular activity and epithelial transport; part of the enteric nervous system.

intramural plexus.definition: A network of neurons and supporting glial cells located within the wall of an organ, especially the gastrointestinal tract, that autonomously regulates local functions such as smooth muscle contraction and secretions; in the gut it includes the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus between the muscular layers and the submucosal (Meissner) plexus in the submucosa.

submucosa.definition: A connective tissue layer beneath the mucosa of the gastrointestinal tract (between the mucosa and muscularis externa) that contains blood and lymphatic vessels, nerves (Meissner’s plexus), and glands in some regions; it supports the mucosa, provides vascular supply, and houses immune cells.

serosa.definition: A smooth serous membrane that lines body cavities (peritoneal, pleural, and pericardial) and covers visceral surfaces; composed of mesothelium with underlying connective tissue and secretes serous fluid to reduce friction.

mucous epithelium.definition: A moist epithelium lining mucous membranes that secretes mucus (via goblet cells) to lubricate and protect surfaces and trap particulates; its cell type varies by location (often pseudostratified ciliated columnar in the respiratory tract, simple columnar in parts of the GI tract).

circular muscle layer.definition: A layer of smooth muscle arranged circumferentially around a hollow organ’s lumen, forming the inner layer of the muscularis externa; its contraction constricts the lumen and, with the outer longitudinal layer, drives peristalsis and segmentation.

longitudinal muscle layer.definition: A layer of smooth muscle in the gastrointestinal tract’s muscularis externa with fibers oriented longitudinally; its contraction shortens the gut segment and works with the inner circular layer to facilitate peristalsis and propulsion of contents.

mucosa.definition: Tissue that lines the tube-like structures of the body such as the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts.

muscularis.definition: The thin layer of smooth muscle lining of the colon or rectum.

lamina propria.definition: A thin layer of loose connective tissue beneath the epithelium of mucosal membranes, containing capillaries, nerves, lymphatics, and resident immune cells; it supports the epithelium and binds it to the underlying tissues (often the muscularis mucosae).

muscularis mucosae.definition: Thin layer of smooth muscle in the mucosa of the gastrointestinal tract, located just beneath the lamina propria and superficial to the submucosa, typically arranged as inner circular and outer longitudinal fibers; its contractions produce localized mucosal movements to facilitate contact with luminal contents, aiding secretion and absorption.

blood vessels.definition: Hollow tubes that transport blood throughout the body; includes arteries, veins, and capillaries.

connective tissue layer.definition: A layer of connective tissue consisting mainly of extracellular matrix with collagen and other fibers, embedded with cells such as fibroblasts, that provides structural support, binding, and protection between tissues or organs; it can be loose (areolar) or dense in its arrangement.

peritoneum.definition: The thin lining of your belly area.

bile.definition: A thick, yellow-green fluid produced by the liver that aids in digestion.

pancreatic juice.definition: An alkaline digestive secretion produced by the pancreas, containing bicarbonate-rich fluid and digestive enzymes (amylase, lipase, and proteases such as trypsinogen) that are released into the duodenum to digest carbohydrates, fats, and proteins; secretion is stimulated by secretin and cholecystokinin.

frenulum of tongue.definition: A small fold of mucous membrane that connects the underside of the tongue to the floor of the mouth, anchoring the tongue and limiting its movement.

minor sublingual ducts.definition: Numerous small excretory ducts of the sublingual gland that open on the sublingual fold or floor of the mouth; collectively known as the ducts of Rivinus, they drain saliva from the sublingual gland and may join the main sublingual duct (duct of Bartholin) or open directly into the oral cavity.

major sublingual ducts.definition: The major sublingual ducts (ducts of Bartholin) are the principal excretory ducts of the sublingual salivary gland, transporting saliva into the floor of the mouth. They typically open at the sublingual caruncle, and are associated with numerous smaller ducts (ducts of Rivinus) that open along the sublingual fold.

mylohyoid muscle.definition: A paired muscle forming the floor of the mouth; it originates from the mylohyoid line on the inner surface of the mandible and inserts into the body of the hyoid via a midline raphe, elevating the floor of the mouth and the hyoid during swallowing and speech (and aiding in depressing the mandible when the hyoid is fixed). Innervation: nerve to mylohyoid (branch of V3). Blood supply: submental artery and mylohyoid branch of the inferior alveolar artery.

digastric muscle.definition: Two-bellied suprahyoid neck muscle that elevates the hyoid bone during swallowing and speaking; when the hyoid is fixed it assists in depressing the mandible. Anterior belly innervated by the nerve to the mylohyoid (branch of V3) and posterior belly by the facial nerve (CN VII).

submandibular duct.definition: A duct of the submandibular gland that transports saliva from the gland to the floor of the mouth, opening at the sublingual caruncle (Wharton’s duct).

wharton’s duct.definition: A major duct of the submandibular salivary gland that carries saliva from the gland to the floor of the mouth, opening at the sublingual caruncle near the base of the tongue.

sternocleidomastoid muscle.definition: A paired superficial neck muscle originating from the manubrium of the sternum and the medial clavicle, inserting on the mastoid process and superior nuchal line; it rotates the head to the opposite side and flexes the neck, and is innervated by the spinal accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI).

parotid duct.definition: Excretory duct of the parotid gland (Stensen's duct) that carries saliva from the gland into the oral cavity; it crosses the masseter, pierces the buccinator, and opens opposite the second maxillary molar.

common hepatic duct.definition: Formed by the union of the left and right hepatic ducts, it carries bile from the liver to the common bile duct. It courses in the hepatoduodenal ligament and joins with the cystic duct to form the common bile duct.

gallbladder neck.definition: The narrow, tapered portion of the gallbladder between the body and the cystic duct.

hepatic flexure.definition: A bend in the colon where the ascending colon turns into the transverse colon, located in the right upper quadrant near the liver; also known as the right colic flexure.

right colic flexure.definition: The bend in the large intestine where the ascending colon transitions to the transverse colon, located in the right upper quadrant near the liver.

portal vein.definition: A large vein formed by the union of the splenic and superior mesenteric veins behind the neck of the pancreas; it transports nutrient-rich blood from the gastrointestinal tract to the liver via the hepatic portal system and contains no valves.

inferior mesenteric vein.definition: A vein that drains the hindgut, including the descending colon, sigmoid colon, and upper rectum, ascends on the left side of the mesentery and typically empties into the splenic vein (via the splenomesenteric confluence).

taeniae coli.definition: Three longitudinal bands of smooth muscle on the colon that contract to shorten the colon and create sacculations (haustra); they converge at the base of the appendix.

renal vein.definition: A blood vessel that drains deoxygenated blood from the kidney and returns it to the inferior vena cava; there are left and right renal veins, with the left vein crossing anterior to the aorta and receiving tributaries such as the left gonadal and left suprarenal veins.

kidney.definition: A pair of bean-shaped organs that filter blood, removing wastes and excess fluids to form urine.

adrenal gland.definition: An endocrine gland located on top of each kidney; it consists of a cortex and a medulla and secretes hormones such as cortisol, aldosterone, epinephrine, and norepinephrine that regulate metabolism, electrolyte balance, and the body’s stress response.

urinary bladder.definition: A muscular, hollow organ in the pelvis that stores urine produced by the kidneys until it is excreted through the urethra.

urethra.definition: A tube that carries urine out of your body.

epididymis.definition: A highly coiled duct attached to the posterior surface of the testis that stores and matures sperm as they pass from the testes to the vas deferens.

testis.definition: A paired male gonad that produces sperm and testosterone; located in the scrotum and encased by the tunica albuginea; contains seminiferous tubules where spermatogenesis occurs.

scrotum.definition: A pouch of skin and underlying tissue that contains the testes and, via the cremaster and dartos muscles, helps regulate testicular temperature for spermatogenesis; it forms part of the external male genitalia.

foreskin.definition: A fold of skin and mucous membrane that covers the glans penis (prepuce) in uncircumcised males and can retract to expose the glans.

prepuce.definition: The foreskin of the penis. It is removed when a person is circumcised.

vas deferens.definition: A muscular duct of the male reproductive tract that carries sperm from the tail of the epididymis to the ejaculatory ducts; it traverses the spermatic cord and inguinal canal and is the target of a vasectomy.

seminal vesicle.definition: A paired gland in the male reproductive system located near the posterior aspect of the bladder; it secretes a viscous, alkaline fluid rich in fructose and prostaglandins that constitutes a major component of semen.

prostate gland.definition: A walnut-shaped gland at the base of the male bladder. It produces a fluid that forms part of semen.

bulbourethral gland.definition: A pair of small mucous-secreting glands in the deep perineal pouch of males that release clear pre-ejaculatory fluid into the bulbar urethra during sexual arousal to lubricate the urethra and help neutralize residual urine.

tunica vaginalis.definition: A double-layered serous membrane surrounding the testis and epididymis in the scrotum, consisting of visceral and parietal layers with a potential space containing a small amount of lubricating fluid; derived from peritoneum via the processus vaginalis.

cremaster muscle.definition: A thin layer of striated muscle fibers derived from the internal oblique that surrounds the spermatic cord and testis; its contraction elevates the testis (cremasteric reflex) to help regulate temperature and protect the testes. Innervated by the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1–L2).

internal spermatic fascia.definition: The innermost fascial covering of the spermatic cord, derived from the transversalis fascia, surrounding the testicular vessels, vas deferens, and pampiniform plexus as they pass through the inguinal canal.

spermatic cord.definition: A cord-like structure in the male groin extending from the inguinal canal to the testis, containing the vas deferens, testicular vessels (artery and pampiniform venous plexus), nerves, lymphatics, and the cremaster muscle, enclosed by fascial coverings; it serves as the conduit for sperm transport and supplies the testis with blood.

dartos fascia.definition: Layer of loose connective tissue beneath the scrotal and penile skin that contains the dartos muscle; part of the superficial fascia of the scrotum and penis; its contraction wrinkles the scrotal skin to help regulate testicular temperature.

dartos muscle.definition: A layer of smooth muscle in the scrotal wall (tunica dartos) that contracts to wrinkle the scrotal skin, reducing surface area and heat loss to help regulate testicular temperature; innervated by sympathetic nerves.

internal urethral meatus.definition: Opening at the bladder neck where the urethra begins; the proximal (internal) opening of the urethra into the urinary bladder (also called the internal urethral orifice).

left kidney.definition: A retroperitoneal, bean-shaped organ of the urinary system in the left upper abdomen that filters blood to form urine; receives arterial blood from the left renal artery and drains to the left renal vein, with the hilum oriented medially.

abdominal aorta.definition: A segment of the aorta that runs through the abdomen from the aortic hiatus (around T12) to its bifurcation into the common iliac arteries at about L4; it supplies abdominal organs and the abdominal wall via visceral branches (e.g., celiac trunk, superior and inferior mesenteric arteries, renal and gonadal arteries) and parietal branches.

common iliac artery.definition: A paired artery that arises from the bifurcation of the abdominal aorta around the level of L4, divides into the internal iliac artery and external iliac artery, and supplies the pelvis and lower limb (the external iliac continuing as the femoral artery).

renal pyramid.definition: A cone-shaped portion of the renal medulla containing collecting ducts (and associated loop of Henle thinnings); bounded by renal columns, its apex (renal papilla) drains urine into a minor calyx.

arcuate arteries.definition: Renal arteries that course along the corticomedullary junction, arching over the bases of the renal pyramids, and giving rise to the interlobular (cortical radiate) arteries.

interlobular arteries.definition: Small renal arteries arising from the arcuate arteries that project into the renal cortex as cortical radiate arteries and give rise to the afferent arterioles supplying the glomeruli.

segmental arteries.definition: An artery that supplies a discrete anatomical segment of an organ, typically arising from a larger parent vessel and giving rise to branches that nourish that specific segment (e.g., segmental pulmonary arteries feeding bronchopulmonary segments in the lung; hepatic segmental arteries supplying liver segments).

interlobar arteries.definition: A branch of the renal artery that runs through the renal columns between the pyramids, arising from the segmental arteries and giving rise to the arcuate arteries at the corticomedullary junction.

lobar arteries.definition: Arteries arising from the pulmonary arteries that supply the lobes of the lungs; the right lung has arteries to three lobes (superior, middle, inferior) and the left to two (superior, inferior). They give rise to the segmental (bronchopulmonary) arteries that perfuse the bronchopulmonary segments.

renal tubule.definition: The portion of the nephron after Bowman's capsule where filtrate is reabsorbed and secreted to form urine; it includes the proximal tubule, loop of Henle, and distal tubule (with the collecting duct often described as the final segment).

renal corpuscle.definition: An anatomical unit in the kidney cortex consisting of the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule; it filters plasma to form the initial filtrate, with blood supplied by the afferent arteriole and drained by the efferent arteriole.
