acorn-tipped.definition: Describes a structure with a rounded, bulbous tip resembling an acorn; a descriptive term used to characterize the morphology of a structure or lesion apex.

acoustic.definition: Relating to sound or hearing; used to describe the auditory system or procedures, measurements, or phenomena involving sound.

vestibulocochlear.definition: Relating to the vestibule and cochlea of the inner ear; most often used to describe the vestibulocochlear nerve (cranial nerve VIII), which transmits auditory (hearing) and vestibular (balance) information from the inner ear to the brain.

acoustic neuroma.definition: A benign tumor arising from Schwann cells of the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII), typically located at the internal auditory canal or cerebellopontine angle; presents with progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and balance disturbance.

neuroma.definition: A benign growth of nerve tissue or nerve sheath origin forming a localized mass; it can cause pain, numbness, or functional impairment depending on its location.

meatus.definition: An opening or canal in the body that leads to an internal cavity or passage; examples include the ear canal and the nasal passages.

tympanometry.definition: A test of the eardrum's motion and pressure in the middle ear. Also known as impedance testing.

audiometry.definition: A complete hearing test that involves listening to sounds of different frequencies and volume.

impedance.definition: Opposition to the flow of an alternating electrical current in a circuit, determined by resistance and reactance; measured in ohms. In biological tissues, it describes the impedance to current flow and is used in bioimpedance analysis to assess body composition and tissue properties.

prostate-specific.definition: Relating to the prostate gland; produced by or specific to prostate tissue.

antigen.definition: An abnormal substance in your body that must be fought off by antibodies.

semen.definition: A viscous, whitish fluid containing spermatozoa (gametes) and secretions from the seminal vesicles, prostate, and other glands; ejaculated during ejaculation and capable of fertilizing an ovum.

salivary.definition: Relating to saliva; produced by, or associated with, the salivary glands.

gland.definition: An organ or group of cells that produces and releases substances. Exocrine glands secrete into ducts onto surfaces (such as skin or mucous membranes), while endocrine glands secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream.

sebaceous.definition: Relating to the glands that secrete sebum; oily, waxy substance that lubricates the skin and hair.

follicle.definition: A small sac or cavity in an organ or tissue, often containing secretions or a developing reproductive cell; for example, a hair follicle is the epidermal invagination surrounding the hair shaft, and an ovarian follicle is a fluid-filled sac containing an immature oocyte and secreting hormones during its development.

folliculitis.definition: Inflammation of one or more hair follicles, usually caused by infection (most commonly Staphylococcus aureus) or irritation; presents as small red papules or pustules centered on follicles, often itchy or tender, typically superficial but can be deeper, and managed with hygiene and topical antiseptics or antibiotics (more extensive disease may require oral antibiotics).

comedones.definition: A plug of keratin and sebum within a hair follicle, seen in acne; open comedones appear as darkened surface plugs (blackheads) and closed comedones are skin-colored or white bumps (whiteheads).

pus.definition: A thick, yellow or green liquid that is composed of dead cells and bacteria, most often found at the site of a bacterial infection.

scarring.definition: Scar formation is the process by which damaged tissue is repaired by laying down fibrous connective tissue, replacing normal tissue with scar tissue that may differ in appearance and function; scars can be flat, raised (hypertrophic or keloid), or atrophic.

dermabrasion.definition: A procedure in which the superficial layers of the skin are abraded or removed with a rotating instrument to resurface the skin and improve scars, wrinkles, and other superficial irregularities.

isotretinoin.definition: An oral retinoid (vitamin A derivative) used to treat severe acne that is refractory to other therapies; it reduces sebaceous gland activity and keratinization in hair follicles. It is highly teratogenic and requires strict pregnancy prevention; adverse effects include mucocutaneous dryness and cheilitis, with potential serious risks including hepatic toxicity, hyperlipidemia, and mood changes.

estrogen-progesterone.definition: A combined hormonal therapy containing estrogen and progesterone (or a progestin) used in contraception and hormone replacement; estrogen promotes menstrual-cycle regulation and endometrial proliferation, while progesterone counteracts estrogen’s effects on the endometrium, helps stabilize it, and contributes to ovulation suppression and cervical mucus changes.

antibiotics.definition: Substances that kill bacteria or inhibit their growth to treat bacterial infections; they may be bactericidal (kill) or bacteriostatic (inhibit growth) and can be natural, semi-synthetic, or synthetic. They are generally ineffective against viruses and misuse can promote antibiotic resistance.

intralesional.definition: Relating to or occurring within a lesion; administered by injection directly into a lesion.

steroids.definition: Another term for corticosteroids—steroid medications made to mimic hormones produced naturally by the adrenal glands. They are used to treat a wide range of health problems.

antimicrobial.definition: Describes something that kills or slows things like bacteria, viruses, and fungi.

antiinfective.definition: An agent that prevents or treats infection by inhibiting the growth or destruction of pathogenic microorganisms; includes antibiotics, antivirals, antifungals, antiparasitics, and antiseptics.

topical.definition: Pertaining to an external surface of the body, such as the skin, mouth, vagina, or anus; often used to describe the administration of medicine that is applied directly to such a surface.

bicarbonate.definition: A negatively charged polyatomic ion (HCO3−) that acts as a base and buffer in body fluids, especially blood, forming the carbonic acid–bicarbonate buffering system that maintains acid–base balance; commonly present as sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3) in solution.

prostatic.definition: Relating to the prostate gland, a male reproductive organ located below the bladder that contributes fluid to semen.

pneumonia.definition: An infection in one or both lungs.

bacteremia.definition: Presence of viable bacteria in the bloodstream, which can be transient and asymptomatic or indicate a systemic infection; typically detected by positive blood cultures.

meningitis.definition: Occurs when the thin tissue around the brain and spinal cord (called the meninges) becomes swollen. It can be caused by different germs (a virus or bacteria).

wound.definition: An injury to body tissues, typically the skin, caused by physical trauma that disrupts tissue continuity; may involve bleeding, inflammation, and potential infection, and can be acute or chronic.

wounds.definition: A wound is an injury to body tissues, typically involving a breach of the skin or mucous membranes caused by physical trauma; wounds may be open (with a skin break) or closed, and healing proceeds through inflammation, tissue repair, and remodeling, often requiring cleansing, debridement, and dressings to prevent infection.

immunocompromised.definition: Having a weakened or impaired immune system, which increases susceptibility to infections and reduces the ability to fight pathogens; caused by diseases (e.g., HIV/AIDS), immunosuppressive therapy (e.g., steroids, chemotherapy), organ transplantation, malnutrition, or congenital immune deficiencies.

enteric.definition: Relating to the intestines, especially the small intestine; pertaining to the gastrointestinal tract.

gram-negative.definition: Bacteria that do not retain the crystal violet stain in Gram staining due to a thin peptidoglycan layer and the presence of an outer membrane with lipopolysaccharide; they appear pink to red after counterstaining with safranin.

neisseriaceae.definition: A family of Gram-negative, typically nonmotile cocci or coccobacilli in the order Neisseriales; includes clinically important genera such as Neisseria, Kingella, and Eikenella; many species inhabit human mucous membranes and range from normal flora to opportunistic pathogens, notably Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

oxidase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes oxidation–reduction reactions by transferring electrons from a substrate to molecular oxygen, typically producing hydrogen peroxide or water.

catalase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide into water and molecular oxygen, protecting cells from oxidative damage; it typically functions as a tetramer in peroxisomes (2 H2O2 → 2 H2O + O2).

baumannii.definition: A Gram-negative, aerobic, nonmotile coccobacillus of the genus Acinetobacter, commonly an opportunistic nosocomial pathogen associated with pneumonia, bacteremia, wound and soft-tissue infections, and notable for frequent multidrug resistance and environmental persistence.

tracheostomy.definition: A hole created through the front of the neck and into the windpipe (trachea). It provides an air passage when the usual route for breathing is obstructed, such as after a traumatic injury to the face or neck, or when long-term use of a breathing machine (ventilator) is needed.

sputum.definition: A mixture of saliva and mucus coughed up from the respiratory tract; it may be examined in a laboratory for signs of disease.

insulin.definition: A hormone produced by the beta cells of the pancreas that promotes the uptake of glucose from the blood into body cells, lowering blood glucose levels and supporting energy metabolism.

calcium carbonate.definition: An inorganic compound used as a calcium supplement to prevent or treat calcium deficiency and as an antacid to neutralize stomach acid.

sodium bicarbonate.definition: A white, crystalline, water-soluble salt with the formula NaHCO3; a weak base and bicarbonate source used clinically as an antacid to neutralize gastric acid and as a systemic buffering agent to treat metabolic acidosis and to alkalinize urine.

calcium.definition: A mineral that makes your bones and teeth strong.

carbonate.definition: A salt or ester of carbonic acid (H2CO3). The CO3^2− ion is a negatively charged polyatomic ion that forms salts with metals and is used medically as an antacid and as a dietary calcium supplement.

tubular.definition: Relating to or resembling a tube; cylindrical in form with a hollow lumen, as seen in tubular anatomical structures such as ducts, vessels, and portions of the gastrointestinal tract.

acoustic reflex.definition: An involuntary contraction of the stapedius muscle in the middle ear in response to loud sounds, which stiffens the ossicular chain to reduce tympanic membrane movement and protect the inner ear; mediated by a brainstem reflex arc in the auditory pathway.

neurilemmoma.definition: A benign tumor arising from Schwann cells of the nerve sheath (peripheral nerves), typically encapsulated and slow-growing; also known as a schwannoma.

neurinoma.definition: A benign neoplasm arising from Schwann cells of a nerve sheath, most commonly on the vestibulocochlear nerve (vestibular schwannoma/acoustic neuroma); it often presents with progressive hearing loss, tinnitus, and balance disturbance.

neurofibroma.definition: A benign tumor of the peripheral nerve sheath arising from Schwann cells (and associated neural elements); typically presents as soft, painless cutaneous or subcutaneous nodules and may occur solitary or as multiple lesions in neurofibromatosis type 1 (plexiform neurofibromas involve a network of nerves and can be more extensive).

schwannoma.definition: A benign neoplasm derived from Schwann cells of the nerve sheath; typically encapsulated and slow-growing, occurring along peripheral or cranial nerves (most often the vestibulocochlear nerve), and may cause neurologic symptoms by compression.

stapedius muscle.definition: A small middle-ear muscle that originates from the pyramidal eminence and inserts on the neck of the stapes; its contraction reduces the amplitude of the stapes’ vibrations in response to loud sounds (the stapedius reflex), protecting the inner ear. It is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII).

tensor tympani muscle.definition: A small skeletal muscle of the middle ear that, when contracted, tenses the tympanic membrane by pulling on the handle of the malleus to dampen sound transmission and protect the inner ear; innervated by the nerve to the tensor tympani (a branch of CN V3, the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve).

middle ear.definition: The air-filled cavity behind the eardrum that contains the three small bones that transmit sound vibrations to the inner ear.

inner ear.definition: That part of the inner ear containing the cochlea for hearing and the vestibular apparatus (semicircular canals, utricle, and saccule) for balance; it houses the bony and membranous labyrinth and transduces mechanical vibrations into neural signals carried by the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII).

acoustic reflex threshold.definition: The lowest sound level that elicits a measurable stapedius reflex (acoustic reflex) in the middle ear, used to assess the integrity of the auditory pathway up to the brainstem; typically around 70–95 dB SPL in normal ears, depending on frequency.

conductive hearing loss.definition: Hearing loss caused by a blockage in the middle ear that prevents sound waves from reaching the inner ear.

sensorineural hearing loss.definition: Permanent hearing loss caused by damage to the cochlea, hair cells, or auditory nerve.

cochlear hearing loss.definition: A type of sensorineural hearing loss due to damage within the cochlea (inner ear), especially the hair cells or organ of Corti, causing reduced hearing sensitivity and usually poorer speech understanding.

acoustics.definition: The branch of physics that studies sound—its generation, propagation, and interaction with matter; in medicine, it encompasses ultrasound imaging and therapeutic uses of high-frequency sound waves.

acoustic shadow.definition: An area on ultrasound images where echoes are absent or markedly reduced posterior to a highly attenuating structure (e.g., a calcified stone or dense bone), due to absorption and scattering of the ultrasound waves by the structure.

ultrasound.definition: A type of imaging that uses high sound waves to see things inside your body.

biliary calculi.definition: Formation of stones within the biliary tract, most often in the gallbladder; these stones (cholesterol, pigment, or mixed) may be asymptomatic or cause biliary colic, cholecystitis, or obstruction of the bile ducts.

acoustic trauma.definition: An injury to the inner ear caused by exposure to a high-intensity sound (often an impulse noise such as an explosion or gunfire), resulting in sudden sensorineural hearing loss and commonly tinnitus; may be temporary or permanent.

noise-induced hearing loss.definition: Noise-induced hearing loss is a sensorineural hearing loss resulting from exposure to damaging levels of noise, either acutely from a single event or chronically from prolonged exposure, causing damage to cochlear hair cells (especially outer hair cells) and/or auditory nerve synapses; it typically produces a high-frequency notch around 3–6 kHz and may be temporary or permanent, and is preventable with hearing protection and exposure management.

acoustooptics.definition: An interaction between acoustic (sound) waves and light within a medium in which the sound modulates, diffracts, or steers light, enabling control or sensing of light with ultrasound in optical devices and related imaging techniques.

acoustooptic devices.definition: An optical device that uses the acousto‑optic effect—interaction of an acoustic wave with light in a crystal—to diffract, modulate, or filter a light beam; enabling rapid electronic control of beam direction, intensity, or wavelength for imaging and laser systems.

acquired cystic kidney disease.definition: A form of cystic kidney disease that develops in people with chronic kidney disease, especially after long-term dialysis, characterized by multiple bilateral renal cysts arising in the absence of inherited polycystic kidney disease; it is associated with an increased risk of renal cell carcinoma and infection.

acquired epileptic aphasia.definition: An acquired pediatric language disorder in which previously normal children experience loss or severe impairment of language abilities (aphasia) due to epileptiform activity in the language-dominant cortex (often temporoparietal/perisylvian regions), with preserved nonverbal intelligence and commonly associated with focal seizures; often referred to as Landau-Kleffner syndrome.

landau-kleffner syndrome.definition: A rare childhood epilepsy syndrome characterized by acquired loss of language skills (often with preserved nonverbal intelligence) due to epileptiform brain activity, typically accompanied by seizures and an abnormal EEG; language impairment may improve with treatment.

acquired hypogammaglobulinemia.definition: A non-genetic decrease in serum immunoglobulin levels (IgG, IgA, and/or IgM) due to external factors such as immunosuppressive therapy, hematologic malignancies, protein-losing states (nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy), malnutrition, or chronic infections, resulting in increased susceptibility to infections.

aids-dementia complex.definition: A late-stage HIV-related neurocognitive disorder characterized by progressive impairment of memory, attention, and executive function, with behavioral changes and motor abnormalities due to HIV infection of the central nervous system; historically termed AIDS-dementia complex and now referred to as HIV-associated dementia (a form of HAND).

aids-wasting syndrome.definition: Unintentional, progressive loss of body weight in a person with HIV/AIDS, typically >10% of baseline, often with chronic diarrhea, fever, and/or weakness, lasting more than 30 days and not explained by other causes.

acquired pellicle.definition: A thin, acellular film of salivary glycoproteins and other macromolecules that rapidly adsorbs to exposed tooth surfaces (and dental materials) within minutes after cleaning; provides lubrication and protection and serves as a substrate for bacterial adhesion, initiating plaque formation.

pellicle.definition: A thin film or layer on a surface; in dentistry, the acquired pellicle is a proteinaceous film of salivary glycoproteins that forms on tooth enamel within minutes after cleaning; in microbiology, it can refer to a loosely adherent film of microorganisms on a liquid surface.

salivary glycoproteins.definition: Proteins secreted into saliva that are glycosylated (carbohydrate-modified) and produced by the salivary glands; they contribute to lubrication and viscosity, form the acquired enamel pellicle, protect oral tissues, and participate in innate antimicrobial defense.

plaque.definition:
- A layer of bacteria that forms on the surface of a tooth and can cause dental disease.
- A fatty deposit in or on the walls of an artery, as part of atherosclerosis.

brown pellicle.definition: An acquired pellicle on tooth enamel that has become brown-stained from chromogenic substances (e.g., coffee, tea, tobacco); a thin film of salivary glycoproteins that forms within minutes and can be removed by cleaning.

bacterial plaque.definition: A sticky biofilm of bacteria that forms on teeth and other surfaces, embedded in a self-produced extracellular matrix; it adheres to the tooth surface via the acquired pellicle and, if not removed, can lead to dental caries and periodontal disease.

acquired sterility.definition: Acquired sterility is the inability to reproduce that develops after birth due to acquired damage or dysfunction of the reproductive organs or their regulatory systems (for example, gonadal failure from infections, chemotherapy/radiation, autoimmune disease, or surgical removal), as opposed to a congenital cause.

one-child sterility.definition: Secondary infertility is the inability to conceive or carry a pregnancy to a live birth after a prior pregnancy or birth, despite regular unprotected intercourse for at least 12 months.

acquired trait.definition: An attribute or characteristic developed during an individual's life due to environmental influences or experience that is not encoded in the germline DNA and is not inherited by offspring.

acrocentric.definition: Describing a chromosome in which the centromere is near one end, producing a short p arm and a much longer q arm; in humans, acrocentric chromosomes include 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22 and typically have satellites on the short arm.

acrocyanosis.definition: A chronic, symmetric bluish discoloration of the hands and feet caused by vasospasm of small cutaneous vessels, often precipitated by cold; arterial oxygen saturation is typically normal, distinguishing it from systemic hypoxemia.

acrodermatitis.definition: Inflammation of the skin of the distal extremities (hands and feet), usually with redness, scaling, and crusting; historically associated with zinc deficiency (acrodermatitis enteropathica).

acrodermatitis enteropathica.definition: A rare autosomal recessive disorder of zinc absorption caused by mutations in the intestinal zinc transporter ZIP4 (SLC39A4), leading to zinc deficiency with a characteristic dermatitis around body orifices and on the extremities, alopecia, diarrhea, and growth retardation; treated with lifelong zinc supplementation.

acrodermatitis papulosa infantum.definition: A zinc-deficiency dermatitis of infancy characterized by erythematous papules and pustules around body orifices (perioral, perianal) and on acral surfaces, often with alopecia and diarrhea; improves with zinc supplementation.

acrodynia.definition: A rare pediatric mercury poisoning syndrome caused by exposure to inorganic mercury, characterized by irritability, tachycardia, sweating, photophobia, insomnia, and desquamation with pink discoloration of the hands and feet (pink disease).

acroesthesia.definition: Abnormal sensation localized to the extremities (hands and feet), such as tingling, numbness, burning, or heightened sensitivity.

acrokeratosis verruciformis.definition: Rare autosomal dominant keratoderma characterized by flat-topped, warty papules on the dorsum of the hands and feet (acral surfaces), often beginning in childhood and sometimes involving elbows and knees; mucosal involvement is usually absent and it can resemble Darier disease.

acroosteolysis.definition: Resorption of the distal phalanges (terminal tufts) of the fingers and toes, a radiographic finding associated with ischemia, frostbite, systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), hyperparathyroidism, and other inflammatory or metabolic conditions; may result in shortened or deformed digits.

acroparesthesia.definition: Abnormal sensory perception (paresthesias) localized to the distal extremities, most often the hands and feet, such as tingling, prickling, burning, or numbness.

acrophobia.definition: A persistent, irrational fear of heights that leads to anxiety and avoidance of situations involving elevations, often classified as a specific phobia.

acrosomal cap.definition: A cap-like region of the acrosome covering the anterior portion of the sperm head; formed during spermiogenesis from the Golgi-derived acrosomal vesicle and containing hydrolytic enzymes (e.g., hyaluronidase and acrosin) that enable penetration of the zona pellucida during fertilization.

acrosomal head cap.definition: A cap-like organelle covering the anterior portion of the sperm head (the acrosome) containing hydrolytic enzymes such as acrosin and hyaluronidase that enable penetration of the egg’s zona pellucida during fertilization; formed from the Golgi apparatus during spermiogenesis.

acrosome.definition: A cap-like organelle over the anterior portion of the sperm head that contains hydrolytic enzymes (notably acrosin and hyaluronidase) used to digest the zona pellucida during fertilization.

gianotti-crosti syndrome.definition: A self-limited papular eruption of childhood characterized by symmetric, flat-topped papules on the cheeks/facial area and extensor surfaces of the limbs (often involving the buttocks), frequently associated with a viral infection such as hepatitis B or others.

pneumocystis pneumonia.definition: A fungal pneumonia caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii that mainly affects immunocompromised individuals; it presents with progressive dyspnea, nonproductive cough, and fever, with diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates on imaging. Diagnosis is by detecting Pneumocystis in respiratory specimens (stain or PCR); treatment is high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, with adjunctive corticosteroids if hypoxemic, and prophylaxis is recommended for high-risk patients.

aspergillosis.definition: A fungal infection caused by Aspergillus species (most often A. fumigatus) that can manifest as allergic disease (e.g., allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis), colonization with an aspergilloma, chronic pulmonary aspergillosis, or invasive disseminated disease in immunocompromised individuals.

candidiasis.definition: A fungal infection caused by Candida species, most commonly Candida albicans, affecting skin and mucous membranes (e.g., oral thrush, vulvovaginal candidiasis) and, in immunocompromised individuals, potentially causing disseminated disease.

cryptococcosis.definition: A fungal infection caused by the encapsulated yeasts Cryptococcus neoformans and Cryptococcus gattii, typically affecting the lungs and central nervous system; it can disseminate, particularly in immunocompromised individuals.

cytomegalovirus infection.definition: A viral infection caused by cytomegalovirus (CMV, a member of the herpesvirus family). It is often asymptomatic or mild in healthy individuals, but can cause congenital CMV disease with hearing loss and neurodevelopmental impairment, and severe organ disease (retinitis, pneumonitis, colitis, encephalitis) in immunocompromised patients or with primary infection/reactivation.

toxoplasmosis.definition: A disease caused by a small bug (parasite). You can get it from cat litter, infected meat, and other sources. If you are pregnant or your immune system does not work well, this disease can be very serious.

herpes simplex.definition: The germ (a virus) that causes cold sores.

kaposi's sarcoma.definition: A vascular neoplasm caused by infection with human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), characterized by endothelial spindle-cell proliferation with slit-like vascular spaces, presenting as violaceous patches, plaques, or nodules on the skin and mucous membranes and often involving viscera, especially in immunocompromised individuals (notably those with HIV/AIDS).

burkitt's lymphoma.definition: An aggressive B‑cell non‑Hodgkin lymphoma driven by MYC oncogene translocations (most often t(8;14) involving the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus), leading to rapid tumor growth; endemic form is EBV-associated and often presents with jaw involvement, while sporadic form frequently presents as an abdominal mass; highly chemosensitive to intensive chemotherapy.

non-hodgkin's lymphoma.definition: A heterogeneous group of lymphoid cancers arising from B cells, T cells, or natural killer cells, excluding Hodgkin lymphoma; they typically present with painless lymphadenopathy and may involve extranodal sites, with clinical behavior ranging from indolent to aggressive.

t cells.definition: A type of lymphocyte that matures in the thymus and mediates cell‑mediated immunity; they recognize peptide antigens presented by MHC molecules and differentiate into subtypes (e.g., helper CD4+, cytotoxic CD8+, regulatory, and memory T cells) to coordinate and execute immune responses.

b cells.definition: A type of lymphocyte derived from the bone marrow that mediates humoral immunity by recognizing antigens and differentiating into antibody-producing plasma cells and memory B cells; they express surface immunoglobulin as receptors and can function as antigen-presenting cells to helper T cells.

reverse transcriptase inhibitors.definition: A class of antiretroviral drugs that inhibit reverse transcriptase, the viral enzyme that copies RNA into DNA in retroviruses (notably HIV), thereby preventing viral replication. They are subdivided into nucleoside/nucleotide RT inhibitors (NRTIs) and non-nucleoside RT inhibitors (NNRTIs).

zidovudine.definition: A nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) used to treat HIV infection; a thymidine analog that, after phosphorylation to zidovudine triphosphate, inhibits HIV DNA synthesis by chain termination and reduces perinatal transmission of HIV.

dideoxyinosine.definition: A purine nucleoside analog reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) used in HIV therapy; it terminates viral DNA synthesis by being incorporated by reverse transcriptase, thereby inhibiting HIV replication.

ritonavir.definition: A protease inhibitor antiretroviral used to treat HIV infection; it inhibits the HIV-1 protease, preventing maturation of viral particles. It is often given at low doses to boost the levels of other protease inhibitors by inhibiting hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes (notably CYP3A4).

indinavir.definition: A protease inhibitor antiretroviral used to treat HIV infection by inhibiting the HIV-1 protease, preventing maturation of viral particles; typically used as part of combination antiretroviral therapy. Common adverse effects include nephrolithiasis (kidney stones), hyperbilirubinemia, and gastrointestinal symptoms; adequate hydration is advised to reduce stone risk.

hiv protease inhibitors.definition: HIV protease inhibitors are a class of antiretroviral drugs that block the HIV protease enzyme, preventing processing of viral Gag-Pol polyproteins into mature, functional proteins; this inhibits viral maturation and replication and is used in combination with other antiretrovirals as part of HAART.

hiv-1.definition: A retrovirus that infects and destroys CD4+ T lymphocytes, causing progressive immune deficiency and, if untreated, Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS); transmitted through blood and certain body fluids (e.g., sexual contact, sharing needles, from mother to child) and treated with antiretroviral therapy.

hiv-2.definition: A retrovirus in the genus Lentivirus that causes HIV infection; HIV-2 is genetically distinct from HIV-1, generally less transmissible and less pathogenic, with slower progression to AIDS and is predominantly found in West Africa and among people of West African origin.

cd4+ helper t lymphocytes.definition: A subset of T lymphocytes that express the CD4 surface receptor and coordinate the adaptive immune response by recognizing antigens presented by MHC class II, secreting cytokines to activate B cells, macrophages, and other T cells; they differentiate into helper subsets (e.g., Th1, Th2, Th17, Tfh, Treg).

cd4+.definition: A subset of T lymphocytes that express the CD4 surface glycoprotein; these helper T cells coordinate the adaptive immune response by activating B cells, cytotoxic T cells, and macrophages. They are targeted by HIV, and their numbers reflect immune function.

pneumococcal influenza vaccines.definition: Two separate vaccines: pneumococcal vaccines protect against diseases caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae (e.g., PCV13 and PPSV23); influenza vaccines protect against seasonal influenza viruses (e.g., inactivated, recombinant, or live-attenuated formulations).

pneumococcal.definition: Relating to Streptococcus pneumoniae, a gram-positive diplococcus bacterium that can cause illnesses such as pneumonia, meningitis, otitis media, and sinusitis.

influenza.definition: An infection by a virus that affects your mouth, nose, and throat.

hepatitis b.definition: A disease that affects your liver. You get it from contact with someone else's blood or body fluids.

vaccines.definition: A biological preparation that activates the immune system to recognize and defend against a specific pathogen by presenting harmless antigens or genetic instructions, thereby inducing immunity without causing the disease.

vaccination.definition: A method of protecting the body against disease by injecting parts or all of a microorganism that will cause the body to develop antibodies against the microorganism and later fight off disease.

colostrum.definition: An antibody-rich form of breast milk, produced at the end of pregnancy and for a short time after birth, which strengthens a newborn’s immune system.

antibodies.definition: Immunoglobulin proteins produced mainly by B cells that bind specifically to antigens on pathogens or foreign substances, neutralizing them and marking them for attack by other immune cells; a central component of the adaptive immune response.

gamma globulin.definition: A fraction of serum proteins consisting mainly of antibodies (immunoglobulins), especially IgG, that mediates humoral immunity by binding to specific antigens.

macrophages.definition: A large phagocytic white blood cell derived from monocytes that resides in tissues; it engulfs and digests microbes and debris, presents antigens to T cells via MHC class II, and secretes cytokines to coordinate immune responses.

feer's disease.definition: A rare, inherited neurologic disorder characterized by bilateral, symmetric calcifications of the basal ganglia and other brain structures (visible on neuroimaging), typically presenting with movement disorders (parkinsonism, dystonia, chorea), neuropsychiatric symptoms, cognitive impairment, and sometimes seizures; most cases are familial with autosomal dominant inheritance and involve mutations in genes regulating brain mineralization.

pink disease.definition: An obsolete, nonspecific descriptor used in historical medical literature for conditions presenting with a pinkish skin eruption or pallor; it is not a current, precise medical term and does not correspond to a single modern diagnosis. If you provide context (dermatology, pediatrics, era), I can map it to the closest contemporary term.

erythroderma polyneuropathy.definition: Simultaneous widespread redness and scaling of the skin (erythroderma) with symmetric peripheral nerve dysfunction causing sensory disturbance and motor weakness; not a single established diagnosis, but a description of two coexisting findings.

mercury poisoning.definition: Toxicity from exposure to mercury or its compounds (elemental, inorganic, or organic), causing multisystem illness—most notably neurotoxicity and nephrotoxicity—with symptoms such as tremor, cognitive/behavioral changes, sensory disturbances, gingivitis, and renal impairment; exposure routes include inhalation of mercury vapor and ingestion of contaminated seafood. Management includes removing exposure and chelation therapy as indicated.

acromegalic eunuchoidism.definition: An uncommon phenotypic description in which acromegaly features (enlarged hands and feet, prognathism, coarse facial features) occur in a eunuchoid body habitus (tall stature with long limbs and hypogonadal characteristics due to reduced gonadal function).

acromial.definition: Relating to the acromion, the lateral bony projection of the scapula that forms the highest point of the shoulder.

acromioclavicular articulation.definition: A synovial plane joint between the acromion of the scapula and the distal end of the clavicle that allows slight gliding movements; stabilized by the acromioclavicular ligaments and the coracoclavicular ligaments (conoid and trapezoid).

acromiocoracoid.definition: Relating to the region between the acromion and coracoid processes of the scapula; it typically denotes the ligament spanning these two processes (the coracoacromial ligament), forming part of the shoulder’s protective arch and contributing to stability.

acromiohumeral.definition: Relating to the acromion and the humerus; used to describe structures between or connecting the acromion and the humeral head (e.g., the acromiohumeral ligament).

acromion.definition: A bony projection of the scapula; the lateral continuation of the scapular spine that overhangs the shoulder joint and articulates with the clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint.

acromion process.definition: A bony projection on the scapula that extends laterally over the shoulder joint; it forms the apex of the shoulder and articulates with the clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint, providing attachment for the deltoid and trapezius muscles.

acromioscapular.definition: Relating to the acromion (the lateral bony projection of the scapula) and the scapula itself; typically used to describe the shoulder region near the acromion, noting there is no distinct acromioscapular joint.

acrocephalosyndactyly.definition: A congenital craniosynostosis syndrome characterized by premature fusion of skull sutures (craniosynostosis) with syndactyly of the fingers and toes; part of a spectrum of related disorders such as Apert and Pfeiffer syndromes.

acrocephaly.definition: A cranial deformity in which the head is abnormally tall and tower‑shaped, often due to premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures (craniosynostosis) or other growth disturbances.

oxycephaly.definition: A form of craniosynostosis in which premature fusion of the coronal sutures (often with involvement of other sutures) produces a tall, narrow, and often pointed skull (turricephaly/acrocephaly).

acrochordon.definition: Benign, soft, small, pedunculated skin lesion caused by fibroepithelial proliferation; commonly arises in skin folds such as the neck, axillae, groin, and eyelids and is often related to friction. It is usually asymptomatic but may be irritated or bleed, and removal by snip excision, cryotherapy, or electrocautery can be performed for cosmetic or symptomatic reasons.

acremonium.definition: A genus of hyaline, septate filamentous fungi (molds); some species are opportunistic human pathogens causing keratitis, endophthalmitis, and disseminated infections in immunocompromised individuals; historically classified as Cephalosporium and known for producing the antibiotic cephalosporin.

cephalosporin.definition: A class of beta-lactam antibiotics derived from the fungus Cephalosporium that kill bacteria by inhibiting cell wall synthesis through binding to penicillin-binding proteins; they are grouped into generations with progressively broader activity against Gram-negative bacteria and greater beta-lactamase stability.

cephalosporium.definition: A historic genus of filamentous fungi that was identified as the source of cephalosporin antibiotics; the producing organism is now classified as Acremonium chrysogenum.

acrosomal reaction.definition: A calcium-dependent exocytosis of the acrosome on the sperm head triggered by contact with the zona pellucida, releasing hydrolytic enzymes that digest the zona pellucida and enable fertilization.

actinomyces.definition: A genus of Gram-positive, non-spore-forming, anaerobic (often microaerophilic) filamentous bacteria that are part of the normal oral, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary flora and can cause actinomycosis, a chronic granulomatous infection with draining sinus tracts and sulfur granules.

actinomyces israelii.definition: A Gram-positive, anaerobic, filamentous bacterium that is part of the normal oral flora and is the principal cause of actinomycosis—a chronic granulomatous infection presenting with draining sinus tracts and sulfur granules, commonly affecting the jaw and face.

actinomycosis.definition: A chronic, granulomatous bacterial infection caused by Actinomyces species (most commonly Actinomyces israelii), characterized by abscesses and draining sinus tracts with sulfur granules, most often in the cervicofacial region but can affect the thorax, abdomen, or pelvis; commonly follows mucosal disruption and requires prolonged antibiotic therapy.

orocervicofacial actinomycosis.definition: A chronic cervicofacial infection caused by Actinomyces species (most often Actinomyces israelii), typically following dental disease or trauma, characterized by indurated facial swelling, abscesses with draining sinus tracts, and sulfur granules; treated with prolonged high‑dose penicillin or other antibiotics, sometimes with surgical drainage.

cervicofacial actinomycosis.definition: A chronic cervicofacial bacterial infection caused primarily by Actinces israelii, presenting with indurated facial/jaw masses that form abscesses and draining sinus tracts with sulfur granules; typically follows dental trauma or poor oral hygiene and is treated with prolonged high‑dose penicillin and surgical drainage if needed.

thoracic actinomycosis.definition: A chronic granulomatous and suppurative infection of the thorax caused by Actinomyces species (most often Actinomyces israelii), characterized by pulmonary consolidation or masses with abscess formation and draining sinus tracts, often following dental disease or aspiration; diagnosed by histology or culture showing sulfur granules; treated with prolonged high‑dose penicillin therapy, with surgical drainage as needed.

abdominal actinomycosis.definition: A chronic, suppurative granulomatous infection of the abdomen caused by Actinomyces species (most often A. israelii), presenting as indolent masses with abscesses and draining sinus tracts (often containing sulfur granules); it can involve the peritoneum, ileocecal region, or intra-abdominal organs and may mimic cancer or Crohn disease. Management typically requires prolonged high-dose penicillin therapy, with surgical drainage or debridement as needed.

pelvic actinomycosis.definition: A chronic pelvic infection caused by Actinomyces species (most often Actinomyces israelii), typically associated with long-term intrauterine device use; it presents with pelvic pain, adnexal masses or abscesses and sometimes sinus tracts, and can mimic malignancy. Treatment requires prolonged high‑dose antibiotics (often penicillin) and may include surgical drainage or excision.

central nervous system actinomycosis.definition: An uncommon, chronic granulomatous infection of the central nervous system caused by Actinomyces species (most often A. israelii or A. meyeri), typically arising from contiguous spread or hematogenous seeding; presents as brain abscess or granulomatous mass with sulfur granules; diagnosed by histopathology and culture; treated with prolonged high-dose penicillin and often surgical drainage.

brain abscess.definition: A focal intracerebral infection that results in a pus-filled cavity within brain parenchyma, typically arising from contiguous spread or hematogenous seeding; presents with fever, headache, focal neurologic deficits, and sometimes seizures; treated with IV antibiotics and often surgical drainage.

actinobacillus.definition: Genus of Gram-negative, nonmotile, rod-shaped bacteria in the Pasteurellaceae family; several species are animal pathogens (e.g., porcine pleuropneumonia) and taxonomy has led some species to be reclassified into Aggregatibacter or Haemophilus.

actinobacillus actinomycetemcomitans.definition: Gram-negative, nonmotile, facultatively anaerobic bacterium of the Pasteurellaceae family; a primary periodontal pathogen linked to aggressive periodontitis and capable of causing endocarditis and other focal infections.

actinomycin.definition: A chromopeptide antibiotic produced by Streptomyces species; it intercalates into DNA and inhibits RNA synthesis, and is used as a chemotherapeutic agent for certain cancers.

actinomycin a.definition: A polypeptide antibiotic produced by Streptomyces species that intercalates into DNA and inhibits RNA synthesis, yielding antitumor activity; the clinically used derivative is dactinomycin (actinomycin D).

actinomycin b.definition: An antibiotic in the actinomycin family; a chromopeptide that intercalates into DNA and inhibits transcription, produced by Streptomyces species; closely related to actinomycin D (dactinomycin) and used mainly for research due to toxicity.

actinomycin d.definition: A cytotoxic antibiotic (dactinomycin) produced by Streptomyces that intercalates into DNA and inhibits RNA synthesis, acting as an antineoplastic (chemotherapy) agent. It is used to treat certain cancers, such as Wilms tumor, rhabdomyosarcoma, and Ewing sarcoma.

dactinomycin.definition: A chemotherapy drug (antineoplastic antibiotic) that intercalates into DNA and inhibits RNA synthesis, used to treat certain cancers.

actinomyosin.definition: An actin–myosin protein complex in muscle fibers that enables contraction by the cycling of myosin cross-bridges along actin filaments (sliding filament mechanism) powered by ATP hydrolysis.

actinotherapy.definition: A medical treatment that uses ultraviolet light (actinic radiation) to treat certain conditions, particularly skin disorders; delivered with UV lamps or sunlight and includes modalities such as UVB or UVA phototherapy, sometimes with photosensitizing agents (PUVA).

actinic.definition: Relating to or produced by light, especially sunlight or ultraviolet radiation.

actinic conjunctivitis.definition: Inflammation of the conjunctiva due to exposure to actinic (ultraviolet) radiation from sunlight; presents with red eye, irritation, tearing, and photophobia, often after outdoor exposure. Management centers on UV protection, lubricants, and symptomatic relief.

actinic ophthalmia.definition: A phototoxic inflammatory eye condition caused by actinic (ultraviolet) radiation from sunlight, typically affecting the conjunctiva and cornea and presenting with irritation, redness, tearing, and photophobia.

actinic dermatitis.definition: A photosensitive inflammatory skin reaction caused by ultraviolet radiation from sunlight, typically presenting as red, itchy patches on sun-exposed skin, sometimes with vesicles or eczema-like plaques.

actinic keratosis.definition: Scaly pink or red-brown raised spots or patches on the skin caused by overexposure to the sun. Actinic keratosis may be a precursor to skin cancer.

senile keratosis.definition: An outdated term for actinic (solar) keratosis—a rough, scaly patch on sun-exposed skin that is premalignant and may progress to squamous cell carcinoma.

solar keratosis.definition: Premalignant skin lesion caused by chronic UV damage to keratinocytes, presenting as a rough, scaly patch on sun-exposed areas with potential progression to squamous cell carcinoma.

actinium.definition: Radioactive chemical element in the actinide series (atomic number 89). It emits alpha particles and is used primarily in scientific research; some isotopes have been investigated for targeted alpha therapy in cancer.

actinomycetes.definition: Gram-positive, filamentous, branching bacteria (phylum Actinobacteria) that resemble fungi; most are saprophytic soil organisms, but some species, notably Actinomyces israelii and Nocardia spp., cause chronic granulomatous infections in humans.

penicillin.definition: A group of beta-lactam antibiotics produced by Penicillium species that kill or inhibit bacteria by blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking in the cell wall via inhibition of transpeptidase (PBPs); used to treat a range of bacterial infections.

bacterial endocarditis.definition: An infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, most often involving the valves, caused by bacteria after bacteremia; characterized by fever, a new or changing murmur, positive blood cultures, and the formation of vegetations that can embolize and cause valvular or systemic complications.

endocarditis.definition: An inflammation of the inner lining of the heart, most often caused by bacterial infections.

appendicitis.definition: Inflammation of the vermiform appendix, usually due to luminal obstruction, presenting with migratory abdominal pain (often starting near the umbilicus and localizing to the right lower quadrant), fever, anorexia, and nausea; commonly treated with surgical removal of the appendix (appendectomy) and often antibiotics, with possible complications including perforation, abscess, and peritonitis.

diverticulum.definition: A pouch or outpouching of the wall of a hollow organ formed by herniation of mucosa and submucosa through the muscular layer; in the colon these are common, with true outpouchings involving all layers of the wall and false outpouchings involving only mucosa and submucosa.

diverticulum of the large bowel.definition: A sac-like pouch formed by mucosa and submucosa protruding through the muscular wall of the colon, most often in the sigmoid region; usually asymptomatic but may cause inflammation (diverticulitis) or bleeding.

perforation.definition: A hole that develops into an organ.

intestines.definition: A pair of tubular organs in the digestive tract between the stomach and anus, comprising the small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum) where most digestion and nutrient absorption occurs, and the large intestine (cecum, colon, rectum) where water absorption and feces formation occur.

large bowel.definition: Part of the digestive tract consisting of the cecum, colon, and rectum; it absorbs water and electrolytes from indigestible material and forms and stores feces.

esophagus.definition: The tube that carries food and liquids from your mouth to your stomach.

bronchi.definition: Either of the two main air passages that carry air from the trachea into the lungs and branch within the lungs to form the bronchial tree.

mouth.definition: An entry to the digestive tract consisting of the lips, teeth, gums, hard and soft palate, and tongue; a mucosa-lined cavity that enables ingestion, mastication, taste, salivation, and the initiation of swallowing and speech.

throat.definition: The throat is the region of the neck that includes the pharynx and larynx; a muscular passage that connects the back of the nose and mouth to the esophagus and trachea, and is involved in swallowing, breathing, and voice production.

neck.definition: A region of the body that connects the head to the trunk; the cervical area containing the cervical spine, airway (larynx and trachea), esophagus, major vessels and nerves, and the muscles that move and support the head.

jaw.definition: The jaw comprises the upper jaw (maxilla) and the lower jaw (mandible); the maxilla forms the fixed upper portion of the mouth, while the mandible is the movable lower bone that articulates with the temporal bones at the temporomandibular joints.

cervix.definition: The lower part of the womb, where the baby grows during pregnancy.

intrauterine devices.definition: A type of birth control that is placed inside the womb (uterus). Also called an IUD.

birth canal.definition: The passage through which a fetus is delivered during vaginal birth, formed by the cervix and vagina and the surrounding pelvic soft tissues (including the perineum).

uterine contractions.definition: Rhythmic shortening of the uterine smooth muscle (the myometrium) that raises intrauterine pressure; during labor, these contractions dilate and efface the cervix and move the fetus through the birth canal.

alveolar process.definition: The portion of the jawbone that forms the tooth sockets and supports the teeth in the maxilla and mandible.

muscle.definition: Contractile tissue composed of elongated cells that shorten in response to neural stimulation to produce movement or generate force; it exists in three principal forms: skeletal, smooth, and cardiac.

subcutaneous tissue.definition: Deepest layer of skin, which consists of connective tissue and fat.

brain.definition: The organ that controls your thoughts, memory, speech, and movements. It also controls the functions of many organs.

urogenital system.definition: A body system consisting of the urinary tract (kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra) and the genital/reproductive organs; it functions to form, store, and eliminate urine and to produce gametes and support reproduction.

tumor-associated antigen.definition: An antigen expressed by tumor cells that is either an overexpressed normal self-protein or a differentiation/ lineage-specific antigen, typically with limited expression in normal tissues, and that can be recognized by the immune system as a target for anti-tumor responses.

tumor-associated antigens.definition: Antigens expressed on tumor cells that originate from normal self-proteins but are overexpressed, aberrantly expressed, or re-expressed in cancer (e.g., differentiation or embryonic/cancer-testis antigens); they can be recognized by the immune system and targeted in immunotherapy, but are not exclusively cancer-specific.

antiserum.definition: A serum containing specific antibodies against a particular antigen, obtained from an immunized donor (animal or human) and used to provide passive immunity or to neutralize toxins or pathogens.

acute confusional state.definition: An acute, fluctuating disturbance of consciousness and cognition, typically caused by an underlying medical, metabolic, or drug-related condition, characterized by inattention, disorganized thinking, altered awareness, and rapid changes in mental status.

immunotherapy.definition: Treatment to make the immune system work better.

specific immunotherapy.definition: A treatment that uses progressively larger doses of a specific antigen (typically an allergen) to alter the immune response and promote tolerance, thereby reducing allergic symptoms in conditions such as allergic rhinitis, asthma, and venom allergy.

active immunity.definition: Being able to fight off a disease once you have had that disease. Also called adaptive immunity.

passive immunity.definition: When a baby is protected from disease by its mother. This lasts 6 to 12 months.

actifed.definition: A brand-name combination oral medication containing a decongestant (pseudoephedrine) and an H1 antihistamine (triprolidine) used to relieve nasal congestion, runny nose, sneezing, and other cold- or allergy-related symptoms.

actigraph.definition: A wearable accelerometer-based device, typically worn on the wrist, that records movement in defined time intervals to estimate physical activity and sleep–wake patterns; used in sleep research and activity monitoring.

electrocardiograph.definition: A device that detects and records the heart’s electrical activity via surface electrodes, producing a tracing known as an electrocardiogram.

activase.definition: Recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) thrombolytic agent used to dissolve pathologic clots in acute ischemic stroke, acute myocardial infarction, and pulmonary embolism; administered intravenously; activates plasmin to degrade fibrin; risk of serious bleeding.

alteplase.definition: A recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rt-PA) thrombolytic that dissolves clots by converting plasminogen to plasmin; administered intravenously, indicated for acute ischemic stroke within a specified time window, and for certain cases of pulmonary embolism or ST-elevation myocardial infarction when reperfusion therapy is appropriate; bleeding risk is the main safety concern.

tissue plasminogen activator.definition: A clot-dissolving enzyme produced naturally in the blood vessels and used medically as a drug to break down clots in conditions such as heart attack, ischemic stroke, and pulmonary embolism. It must be administered within a few hours of symptom onset.

activated charcoal.definition: A highly porous form of carbon processed to have a large surface area that adsorbs a wide range of toxins in the gastrointestinal tract; used as an antidote for certain ingested poisons and overdoses and is not absorbed systemically.

activated clotting time.definition: A whole-blood assay that measures the time (in seconds) for a clot to form after an activating agent is added, used to monitor the level of anticoagulation (especially unfractionated heparin) during procedures such as cardiopulmonary bypass.

activated partial thromboplastin time.definition: A laboratory assay that measures the time for plasma to clot after activation of the intrinsic coagulation pathway, typically used to evaluate intrinsic pathway factor deficiencies (e.g., factors VIII, IX, XI, XII) and to monitor unfractionated heparin therapy.

aptt.definition: A laboratory test that measures the time it takes for plasma to clot after activation of the intrinsic and common coagulation pathways; used to monitor unfractionated heparin therapy and to evaluate suspected coagulation disorders and factor deficiencies.

activated prothrombin complex concentrat.definition: A plasma-derived hemostatic product containing factors II, IX, and X with activated factor VII (FVIIa) that bypasses inhibitors to factor VIII or IX to promote clotting; used to control severe bleeding in patients with factor VIII inhibitors and as a bypassing agent for anticoagulant-related bleeding.

Could you specify the medical field or provide the full form of the acronym you’re using (e.g., oncology, pathology, coding, etc.)? If you’d like, I can also list common expansions once you share the field.

activated resin.definition: A resin that has been induced to polymerize and harden by an activation process (e.g., light-activated or chemically activated initiators), yielding a solid polymer used in dental restorations and other biomedical applications.

self-curing resin.definition: A resin that hardens by a chemical reaction initiated within the material itself (auto-polymerization) without external light or heat activation; it uses an internal initiator–activator system and is commonly used for self-cured dental resins such as provisional restorations and denture bases.

activation.definition: The process by which a cell, receptor, or tissue becomes biologically active in response to a stimulus, initiating signaling pathways that produce a functional response (for example, immune cells becoming active after antigen exposure or platelets initiating aggregation in hemostasis).

activation energy.definition: The minimum amount of energy required to start a chemical reaction, sufficient to overcome the activation barrier between reactants and products; this energy influences the reaction rate and can be lowered by catalysts, including enzymes.

activator.definition: A molecule or substance that increases the activity of an enzyme or biochemical pathway, typically by binding to the enzyme (often at an allosteric site) or by enhancing receptor-mediated signaling.

adenosine triphosphate.definition: An energy-storing molecule that is found in all human cells. Usually abbreviated as ATP.

atp.definition: An energy-carrying molecule in cells consisting of adenosine, ribose, and three phosphate groups; energy is released by hydrolysis of its phosphate bonds to power numerous cellular processes.

acusis.definition: The sense of hearing; auditory perception.

adl.definition: Basic self-care tasks essential for independent living, including bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, continence, and feeding.

barthel index.definition: A scale that quantifies a person’s ability to perform activities of daily living (ADLs). It assesses 10 items (feeding, bathing, grooming, dressing, bowel and bladder control, toilet use, transfers, mobility on level surfaces, and stairs) and yields a total score from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating greater independence; it is widely used to evaluate functional status in stroke rehabilitation and geriatrics.

actomyosin.definition: An actin-myosin complex consisting of actin filaments bound by myosin motor proteins that converts ATP energy into mechanical work, enabling muscle contraction and cellular contractility.

cautery.definition: The destruction or coagulation of tissue by heat, electrical current, or caustic chemicals, used in surgery to achieve hemostasis or to remove or ablate tissue.

focal spot.definition: The small area on the anode of an X-ray tube from which X-rays are emitted; the size of this area affects geometric image sharpness (unsharpness) and the tube’s heat loading.

acute abdomen.definition: A clinical syndrome of sudden, severe abdominal pain often with tenderness or peritoneal signs, typically requiring urgent diagnostic evaluation to identify potentially life-threatening intra-abdominal pathology such as perforation, obstruction, ischemia, or acute inflammatory processes.

acute abscess.definition: A localized collection of pus within tissue or a confined space, usually due to bacterial infection, that presents with acute inflammation (pain, swelling, warmth, redness) and often requires incision and drainage plus antibiotic therapy.

acute air trapping.definition: A pattern of rapid onset retention of air in the lungs from acute obstruction of the small airways, causing incomplete expiration and hyperinflation; often due to acute bronchospasm, mucus plugging, edema, or inflammatory processes.

acute alcoholism.definition: An episode of acute alcohol intoxication from recent heavy ethanol ingestion, causing central nervous system depression with confusion or stupor, ataxia, slurred speech, slowed reflexes, and impaired judgment; typically self-limited as blood alcohol level falls, but severe intoxication can require emergency medical care.

acute angle.definition: An angle that measures less than 90 degrees; in medical or anatomical contexts, it describes a sharp or narrow angle between two structures (for example, the angle between the iris and cornea in the eye) but the term alone does not imply disease.

acute anicteric hepatitis.definition: An acute hepatitis in which jaundice is absent (anicteric); characterized by hepatocellular inflammation with elevated liver enzymes, possible malaise and fatigue, and variable bilirubin levels that do not produce visible jaundice (often due to viral hepatitis or drug-induced liver injury).

acute anterior poliomyelitis.definition: An acute viral infection caused by poliovirus that damages motor neurons in the anterior horn of the spinal cord, producing sudden-onset, asymmetric flaccid paralysis; may involve bulbar or respiratory muscles; transmitted via the fecal-oral route and preventable by vaccination.

acute articular rheumatism.definition: An acute inflammatory arthritis historically used to describe the arthritis component of acute rheumatic fever, presenting with sudden, often migratory joint pain and swelling after a preceding streptococcal infection.

acute ascending myelitis.definition: An acute inflammatory disorder of the spinal cord with rapid, upward progression of neurological deficits (motor, sensory with a defined level, and autonomic dysfunction) over hours to days, often associated with longitudinal spinal cord lesions on MRI.

acute ascending spinal paralysis.definition: An acute, rapidly progressive weakness syndrome in which paralysis begins in the legs and ascends to involve the trunk, arms, and potentially the respiratory muscles; most commonly due to an acute inflammatory polyneuropathy (e.g., Guillain-Barré syndrome) and requiring urgent evaluation.

acute atrophic paralysis.definition: An abrupt onset of paralysis accompanied by rapid muscle wasting, reflecting an acute neurogenic or myopathic process affecting motor neurons, peripheral nerves, or muscle fibers.

acute bacterial arthritis.definition: An acute infection of a joint caused by bacterial invasion of the synovial space (septic arthritis). It presents with sudden onset joint pain, swelling, warmth, and restricted movement, often with fever; usually affects a single joint and requires urgent antibiotics and prompt joint drainage to prevent cartilage destruction.

acute bronchitis.definition: A short-term inflammation of the bronchi, typically triggered by a viral infection, presenting with a persistent cough (with or without sputum) that lasts up to several weeks; may include wheeze, chest discomfort, and mild fever, but without evidence of pneumonia. Management is supportive; antibiotics are not routinely indicated unless bacterial infection is suspected.

acute care.definition: Care for a sudden or urgent medical condition that requires rapid evaluation, stabilization, and short-term treatment, typically in hospital, emergency, or other acute-care settings.

acute catarrhal sinusitis.definition: Acute inflammation of the mucous membrane lining one or more paranasal sinuses, characterized by mucous (catarrhal) nasal discharge, nasal obstruction, facial pain or pressure, and mucosal edema, usually following a viral upper respiratory infection and lasting up to about four weeks.

acute cervicitis.definition: Acute cervicitis is abrupt inflammation of the cervix, typically presenting with cervix erythema and friability and mucopurulent vaginal discharge, and sometimes postcoital bleeding; most commonly caused by sexually transmitted infections such as Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

acute childhood leukemia.definition: An aggressive pediatric hematologic malignancy characterized by clonal proliferation of immature leukocytes (lymphoblasts or myeloblasts) in the bone marrow and peripheral blood, leading to bone marrow failure; the most common form in children is acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

acute lymphoblastic leukemia.definition: An aggressive hematologic malignancy in which lymphoid precursor (lymphoblast) cells clonally proliferate in the bone marrow and spill into the blood, causing marrow failure (anemia, thrombocytopenia) and systemic symptoms; characterized by rapid onset and requiring intensive multi-agent chemotherapy with CNS prophylaxis.

acute myeloid leukemia.definition: A fast-growing disease that occurs when there are too many of a type of white blood cell (myeloblast) that crowds out other types of blood cells. It is the most common type of leukemia in adults. Also called AML.

bone marrow aspiration.definition: A procedure in which a small sample of bone marrow is removed from a bone and sent to a laboratory for examination.

bone marrow biopsy.definition: When a small sample of bone is removed and sent to a laboratory to be studied.

chemotherapy.definition: A drug that kills cancer cells.

down syndrome.definition: A chromosomal condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21) that results in intellectual disability, characteristic facial features, and an increased risk of health problems such as congenital heart defects, thyroid issues, hearing and vision problems, and leukemia.

perforating ulcer.definition: An ulcer that has eroded through the full thickness of the wall of a hollow organ (most commonly the stomach or duodenum), creating a perforation with leakage of luminal contents into the peritoneal cavity, often causing acute peritonitis.

abdominal pain.definition: Pain or discomfort localized to the abdomen, arising from irritation or disease of abdominal organs (stomach, intestines, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, kidneys, or peritoneum) or the abdominal wall; it can be acute or chronic and varies in location, quality, duration, and intensity, often with associated symptoms that help determine the cause.

bowel habits.definition: The typical pattern of an individual's bowel movements, including frequency, stool form/consistency, and ease or difficulty of passage, used to assess normal gut function and disorders such as constipation or diarrhea.

weight loss.definition: A decrease in total body weight resulting from a sustained energy deficit, often involving loss of fat mass and sometimes lean body mass and body water; it can be intentional (as in dieting) or unintentional (which may indicate an underlying illness).

bloody stool.definition: A condition in which stool contains visible blood, indicating a gastrointestinal bleed; the blood may be bright red (hematochezia) from lower GI or anorectal sources, or dark, tarry, and black (melena) when the bleed is higher in the GI tract and has been digested; evaluation is recommended to determine the cause and severity.

menses.definition: The monthly shedding of the uterine endometrium (lining) through the vagina that occurs as part of the menstrual cycle, typically lasting 3 to 7 days and driven by hormonal changes (estrogen and progesterone).

clay-colored stool.definition: Clay-colored stool is pale, light-gray stool resulting from a lack of bile pigments in the intestine, usually due to reduced bile flow (cholestasis) from biliary obstruction or liver disease; it may be associated with dark urine and itching.

surgical abdomen.definition: An acute abdominal condition that necessitates operative treatment rather than nonoperative management; symptoms suggest a surgical cause (e.g., perforation, obstruction, strangulation, or ischemia) and require urgent or emergent surgery.

sore throat.definition: Pain, scratchiness, or irritation in the throat due to inflammation of the pharynx (pharyngitis), most often from viral infection but can be bacterial or irritant-related; may be accompanied by fever and painful swallowing.

gastroesophageal reflux.definition: When your stomach contents come back up into your esophagus, causing heartburn, also called acid reflux. Also called GERD.

hyperacidity.definition: A condition defined by excess production of gastric acid in the stomach, typically presenting with heartburn, sour stomach, and indigestion; associated with gastritis, peptic ulcers, or GERD, and treated with acid-suppressing therapy and lifestyle changes.

peptic ulcer disease.definition: A condition characterized by ulcers in the stomach or duodenum resulting from an imbalance between mucosal defenses and gastric acid, most commonly due to Helicobacter pylori infection or NSAID use.

spastic colon.definition: A historical term for irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), a functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by recurrent abdominal pain or discomfort associated with altered bowel habits (diarrhea, constipation, or both) in the absence of an identifiable organic disease.

urinary incontinence.definition: When you lose control of your bladder and the fluids it holds.

infertility.definition: Inability to conceive after 12 months of regular, unprotected intercourse (or after 6 months for individuals aged 35 years or older).

dysmenorrhea.definition: Painful menstruation with cramps during your period.

memory problems.definition: Difficulty encoding, storing, or retrieving information, affecting short- or long-term memory; may arise from aging, sleep deprivation, stress, medications, head injury, mood disorders, substance use, or neurological conditions such as dementia or Alzheimer's disease.

sensory disturbances.definition: An alteration in sensation, including numbness, tingling (paresthesias), burning or electric pain, or reduced/increased sensitivity, due to dysfunction of peripheral nerves or central sensory pathways in the nervous system.

leukemia.definition: A cancer of the blood caused by rapid growth of white blood cells that crowd out other blood cells. There are different types, including acute lymphocytic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, and chronic myeloid leukemia.

erythrocytes.definition: A mature red blood cell that carries oxygen from the lungs to tissues and carbon dioxide from tissues back to the lungs, via hemoglobin. In humans, erythrocytes are anucleate and lack mitochondria, produced in the bone marrow and circulating for about 120 days.

neutropenia.definition: A condition characterized by an abnormally low number of neutrophils, a type of white blood cell, resulting in increased susceptibility to bacterial and fungal infections; typically defined as an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) below about 1.5 x 10^9/L (1500/µL) in adults, with lower cutoffs used to indicate severity.

lymph nodes.definition: Glands that contain white blood cells that help protect you against germs.

reticuloendothelial system.definition: An older term for the mononuclear phagocyte system: a network of phagocytic macrophages and related cells distributed throughout reticuloendothelial tissues (eg, Kupffer cells in the liver, splenic and lymph node macrophages, alveolar macrophages) that clear debris and aged cells, remove pathogens, and present antigens to initiate immune responses.

fever.definition: A body temperature that is higher than normal. Also called pyrexia.

pyrexia.definition: A body temperature that is higher than normal. Also called fever.

pallor.definition: When your skin is more pale than usual.

dehydration.definition: When you lose too much fluid or water from your body.

bone marrow.definition: The tissue inside some of your larger bones where blood cells are made.

lymphoblasts.definition: Immature precursor cells of the lymphoid lineage that develop into mature B or T lymphocytes; large cells with a high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio and a prominent nucleolus, produced during lymphopoiesis in bone marrow and thymus.

lymphoid.definition: Relating to lymph or the lymphatic system; consisting of lymphoid tissue or cells, such as lymphocytes.

lymphocytic.definition: Relating to lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell involved in the adaptive immune response; describes samples or tissues in which lymphocytes predominate or conditions affecting lymphocytes.

lymphoblastic.definition: Relating to lymphoblasts, immature precursor cells of the lymphoid lineage that develop into lymphocytes (B and T cells).

lymphoblastoid.definition: Relating to lymphoblasts or to cells that resemble them; commonly used for immortalized B-lymphocyte cell lines produced by Epstein-Barr virus transformation.

granulocytic.definition: Relating to granulocytes, a class of white blood cells with cytoplasmic granules (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils); used to describe cells of granulocytic lineage.

myelocytic.definition: Pertaining to myelocytes, immature bone marrow cells that give rise to granulocytes and other cells of the myeloid lineage.

monocytic.definition: Relating to monocytes, a type of white blood cell; monocytes are large phagocytes that migrate into tissues to ingest pathogens and debris and to present antigens to T cells.

myelogenous.definition: Relating to the bone marrow; arising from or produced in the bone marrow (myeloid lineage).

monoblastic.definition: Relating to monoblasts, the immature precursor cells of the monocytic lineage that differentiate into promonocytes and then monocytes; an excess of monoblasts is seen in acute monocytic leukemia.

monomyeloblastic.definition: Relating to monoblasts, the immature precursors of monocytes; describes leukemic cells of the monocytic lineage in which blasts predominate.

leukocytes.definition: White blood cells; immune system cells produced in the bone marrow that defend the body against infection and foreign substances, circulating in blood and lymph, and differentiating into main subtypes including neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils.

megakaryocytes.definition: Large cells in the bone marrow that give rise to platelets; they are polyploid cells of the myeloid lineage that extend proplatelets into sinusoidal blood vessels to release platelets into the circulation.

leukemic meningitis.definition: Meningeal involvement by leukemic cells causing meningitis-like symptoms (headache, fever, neck stiffness) in patients with leukemia; CSF often contains leukemic blasts.

tumor lysis syndrome.definition: A potentially life-threatening metabolic complication occurring after initiation of cytotoxic cancer therapy (or spontaneously in cancers with high tumor burden). It results from rapid breakdown of malignant cells, releasing intracellular potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids into the bloodstream, causing hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia (secondary), and hyperuricemia, which can lead to acute kidney injury, arrhythmias, seizures, and other organ dysfunction. Prevention and management include aggressive IV hydration, monitoring and correction of electrolytes, and urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol or rasburicase); renal replacement therapy may be needed in severe cases.

rasburicase.definition: A recombinant urate oxidase enzyme used to rapidly lower serum uric acid levels in patients at risk for tumor lysis syndrome; it catalyzes the oxidation of uric acid to allantoin, a more soluble metabolite, and is given by intravenous infusion.

allopurinol.definition: A xanthine oxidase inhibitor that decreases uric acid production by blocking the conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid; used for chronic gout and hyperuricemia, prevention of uric acid stones, and reduction of uric acid elevations after chemotherapy (tumor lysis syndrome). Dose is adjusted for renal impairment; adverse effects include rash and hypersensitivity; may precipitate gout flares when started.

l-asparaginase.definition: An enzyme used in chemotherapy that hydrolyzes circulating L-asparagine to aspartate and ammonia, depleting extracellular asparagine and inhibiting protein synthesis in asparagine-dependent leukemic cells; derived from bacterial sources (e.g., Escherichia coli or Erwinia) and used primarily to treat acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

vincristine sulfate.definition: A vinca alkaloid chemotherapy agent that binds tubulin to prevent microtubule assembly, halting cell division (mitosis); used to treat various cancers and is a vesicant with potential neurotoxic adverse effects.

corticosteroids.definition: A type of drug used to treat a variety of diseases and conditions; they reduce swelling and suppress or modulate the immune response.

irradiation.definition: Exposure of tissue to ionizing radiation, typically for therapeutic purposes (radiation therapy) or other medical uses, delivering a prescribed dose to the target tissue.

tinnitus.definition: Noise in your ears that does not come from outside of your body. Also called ringing in the ears.

acute coronary syndrome.definition: An umbrella term for clinically recognized acute myocardial ischemia due to a sudden reduction in coronary blood flow, usually from rupture or erosion of an atherosclerotic plaque with superimposed thrombosis; it includes unstable angina, non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), and ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).

methotrexate.definition: A folic acid analog antimetabolite that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, impairing DNA synthesis; used as chemotherapy for various cancers and as a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug for autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis; administered orally or by injection.

mercaptopurine.definition: A purine analog antimetabolite used in chemotherapy and immunosuppression. It is converted in the body to active thioinosinic acid, which inhibits de novo purine synthesis and disrupts DNA replication, reducing proliferation of leukemic and immune cells. Clinically used to treat acute lymphoblastic leukemia and inflammatory bowel diseases (e.g., Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis).
