adnexal.definition: Relating to the adnexa; in anatomy, the adnexa are the accessory structures of an organ—most commonly the ovaries, fallopian tubes, and surrounding supporting tissues in the pelvis.

scheuermann’s disease.definition: A juvenile-onset structural thoracic kyphosis caused by anterior wedging of three or more consecutive thoracic vertebral bodies (typically ≥5° per vertebra), producing a rigid hyperkyphotic curvature often accompanied by back pain and stiffness; radiographs commonly show wedged vertebrae with irregular endplates and Schmorl’s nodes.

adolescent vertebral epiphysitis.definition: Inflammation of the vertebral growth plates (epiphyses) occurring during adolescence.

autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney dis.definition: A hereditary kidney disorder characterized by the development of numerous bilateral renal cysts due to mutations in PKD1 or PKD2, leading to enlarged kidneys, hypertension, and progressive renal failure; inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with a 50% transmission risk.

polycystic kidney disease.definition: A genetic disorder characterized by numerous fluid-filled cysts in the kidneys that enlarge the kidneys and progressively impair renal function; most often autosomal dominant (PKD1/PKD2 mutations) with autosomal recessive forms occurring less commonly. It is frequently associated with hypertension and can involve liver cysts. Management is supportive, including blood pressure control, pain management, and eventually kidney replacement therapy (dialysis or transplantation).

adpkd.definition: A hereditary kidney disease characterized by the development of numerous bilateral renal cysts, leading to enlarged kidneys and progressive decline in renal function. It is most commonly caused by autosomal dominant mutations in PKD1 or PKD2, and may be associated with hypertension and extrarenal cysts (e.g., in the liver) and, rarely, berry aneurysms.

adrenal cortex.definition: The outer part of the adrenal gland, located above the kidney, that produces corticosteroid hormones—mineralocorticoids (e.g., aldosterone), glucocorticoids (e.g., cortisol), and androgens—organized into three zones (glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis).

adrenal cortical carcinoma.definition: A rare malignant neoplasm arising from the adrenal cortex; often hormonally active, producing cortisol and/or androgens (causing Cushing syndrome or virilization) but can be nonfunctional. Primary treatment is surgical resection; adjuvant therapy (e.g., mitotane-based chemotherapy) and/or radiation may be used for advanced disease. Prognosis depends on stage and completeness of resection.

addison’s disease.definition: A disorder of the adrenal cortex causing primary adrenal insufficiency due to deficient cortisol (and often aldosterone) production, most commonly from autoimmune destruction; presents with fatigue, weight loss, abdominal pain, hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hyperpigmentation; requires lifelong glucocorticoid replacement and often mineralocorticoid therapy.

adrenocortical.definition: Relating to the adrenal cortex, the outer portion of the adrenal gland that produces corticosteroid hormones (e.g., cortisol, aldosterone) and androgens.

aldosterone.definition: A hormone secreted by the adrenal glands that helps regulate blood pressure by controlling sodium and potassium levels in the body.

androgens.definition: A group of steroid hormones that promote the development and maintenance of male characteristics and reproductive function; the principal androgen is testosterone, produced mainly in the testes (also by the adrenal glands and, to a lesser extent, the ovaries), and they act by binding androgen receptors to influence sexual differentiation, muscle and bone mass, and libido.

intracranial pressure.definition: The pressure within the skull caused by brain tissue, blood, and cerebrospinal fluid; normally about 7–15 mmHg in adults, with elevations indicating intracranial hypertension.

diabetes insipidus.definition: A disease where your kidneys don't work well and you need to pee a lot.

hyposecretion of antidiuretic hormone.definition: Deficiency of antidiuretic hormone resulting in impaired water reabsorption in the kidney collecting ducts, causing polyuria, polydipsia, and dilute urine; central diabetes insipidus due to hypothalamic or pituitary dysfunction.

hyperkalemia.definition: An elevated level of potassium in the blood, defined as a serum potassium concentration above the upper limit of normal (approximately >5.0 mEq/L), which can cause cardiac conduction abnormalities and neuromuscular symptoms.

cushing’s syndrome.definition: A disorder caused by high levels of the stress-hormone cortisol resulting in damage to the body, including abdominal obesity, rounded red face, and other symptoms.

adrenal virilism.definition: Excess androgen production by the adrenal glands leading to virilization (masculinization) in females or prepubertal children; commonly due to congenital adrenal hyperplasia, adrenal tumors, or ACTH excess.

meibomian gland.definition: A type of sebaceous gland in the eyelid margin (tarsal plates) that secretes meibum, an oily substance that coats the tear film and reduces evaporation, helping to lubricate the eye.

tarsal plate.definition: A dense fibrous plate in the eyelid that forms the tarsus; provides lid rigidity and shape, contains the meibomian (tarsal) glands, and serves as the attachment site for the levator palpebrae superioris via its aponeurosis; its posterior surface is lined by palpebral conjunctiva.

palpebral conjunctiva.definition: The mucous membrane that lines the inner surface of the eyelids, extending from the eyelid margin to the conjunctival fornix and continuous with the bulbar conjunctiva on the eyeball.

conjunctiva.definition: The clear, thin membrane that covers the inside of the eyelid and the white part of the eyeball.

premedications.definition: Medications given before a medical procedure or anesthesia to improve comfort and safety by reducing anxiety, providing sedation or analgesia, and preventing perioperative complications such as nausea and vomiting; common examples include benzodiazepines for anxiolysis, opioids for analgesia, antiemetics, and anticholinergics.

opioid analgesics.definition: Medications that relieve pain by binding to and activating opioid receptors in the brain and spinal cord; they include natural, semi-synthetic, and synthetic compounds (e.g., morphine, codeine, fentanyl, oxycodone) and can cause analgesia, euphoria, sedation, constipation, dependence, tolerance, and potentially respiratory depression.

benzodiazepines.definition: Anti-anxiety medications that work by helping to maintain levels of the neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) in the brain.

sedatives.definition: A drug that depresses central nervous system activity to produce calmness, relaxation, or sleep; used to relieve anxiety and agitation and to treat insomnia; may cause drowsiness, slowed reaction, impaired coordination, and potential dependence with prolonged use.

hypnotics.definition: A class of medications that induce sleep or sedation, used to treat insomnia; they are CNS depressants (often GABAergic) and can cause daytime drowsiness, cognitive impairment, tolerance, and dependence.

phenothiazines.definition: Powerful tranquilizing drugs used to treat schizophrenia and, sometimes, severe nausea.

anticholinergics.definition: A class of medications that block acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, reducing parasympathetic nervous system activity.

antihistamines.definition: Drugs that block histamine receptors (primarily H1) to reduce the effects of histamine in allergic reactions, thereby alleviating symptoms such as sneezing, itching, runny nose, and urticaria; they can be sedating (first-generation) or non-sedating (second-generation).

antianxiety agents.definition: A class of medications that reduce anxiety and excessive worry; they are called anxiolytics or anti-anxiety agents and include benzodiazepines (e.g., diazepam, lorazepam), nonbenzodiazepine agents such as buspirone, certain antidepressants (SSRIs/SNRIs), and other drugs like hydroxyzine or propranolol used for specific anxiety symptoms.

adjuvant.definition: Something that is added to a vaccine to make it work better.

adjuvant therapy.definition: Extra therapy given after a primary treatment, to increase the effectiveness of the primary treatment. For example, using chemotherapy after surgery or radiation treatment for cancer.

adjuvant chemotherapy.definition: Chemotherapy given after primary treatment (usually surgery) to eradicate microscopic residual cancer cells and reduce the risk of recurrence, with the goal of improving cure rates.

radiotherapy.definition: The medical use of ionizing radiation to treat disease, most commonly cancer, by damaging the DNA of cells to prevent replication and promote cell death; delivered externally (external beam radiotherapy) or internally (brachytherapy), typically in fractionated doses to spare normal tissue.

nasogastric intubation.definition: The insertion of a flexible tube through the nose into the stomach for purposes such as gastric decompression, drainage, administration of medications or enteral nutrition, and sampling of gastric contents.

suction.definition: The creation of negative pressure to draw out liquids or gases from a body cavity or wound, typically using a suction device or catheter.

lysis.definition: Breakdown or destruction of cells, tissues, or other biological structures, typically by rupture of the cell membrane or wall or by enzymatic digestion; in microbiology it denotes the bursting of a cell, and in hematology it may refer to hemolysis or fibrinolysis (clot dissolution).

excision.definition: The surgical removal of tissue or a lesion by cutting it out, typically with a scalpel, sometimes with margins to ensure complete removal.

obesity.definition: A condition defined by excessive body fat that increases health risks, commonly defined as a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or higher.

adrenalectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove one or both adrenal glands, typically to treat adrenal tumors or excessive hormone production.

adrenergic receptor.definition: Receptors that bind catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine) and mediate sympathetic nervous system effects; they are G protein–coupled receptors with α (α1, α2) and β (β1, β2, β3) subtypes that activate different second-messenger pathways to produce tissue-specific responses.

coma.definition: When a person is deeply unconcious because of illness or injury. A person in a coma cannot move or talk.

vasomotor tone.definition: The baseline level of continuous constriction of vascular smooth muscle in systemic arterioles, maintained largely by sympathetic autonomic activity and modulated by local and humoral factors, which regulates systemic vascular resistance and arterial pressure.

exogenous steroids.definition: Steroid hormones or steroid-like drugs that originate outside the body and are administered externally (exogenous), such as corticosteroids or anabolic steroids, which can suppress the body's own steroid production.

steroid.definition: A kind of drug that reduces swelling and helps your body’s natural defense against sickness (your immune system). Also called corticosteroids or glucocorticoids.

isotonic solution.definition: A solution that has the same osmotic pressure as body fluids, causing no net movement of water into or out of cells when infused; commonly 0.9% saline (normal saline) and lactated Ringer's solution.

vasopressor.definition: A medication that increases blood pressure by causing vasoconstriction and increasing systemic vascular resistance, used to treat hypotension and shock.

aspiration.definition: The inhalation of a foreign object into the airway; also, the process of removing fluids, tissue, or other substances from the body by suction.

hyperemesis.definition: Excessive, persistent vomiting that leads to dehydration, electrolyte disturbances, and often weight loss; most commonly used to describe severe vomiting in pregnancy (hyperemesis gravidarum).

bed rest.definition: An ordered period of minimal physical activity, typically spent in bed, prescribed by a clinician to reduce bodily stress and promote healing after injury, surgery, or certain medical conditions.

corticosteroid.definition: A class of steroid hormones produced by the adrenal cortex and their synthetic analogues, with anti-inflammatory, immunosuppressive, and metabolic effects; used to treat inflammatory and autoimmune diseases (e.g., prednisone, dexamethasone).

crisis.definition: An acute, time-limited episode of severe illness or distress that rapidly changes a patient’s condition and usually requires urgent assessment and intervention; in psychiatry, it refers to an emotional or behavioral emergency needing immediate help.

cushing's syndrome.definition: A disorder caused by high levels of the stress-hormone cortisol resulting in damage to the body, including abdominal obesity, rounded red face, and other symptoms.

pheochromocytoma.definition: A rare adrenal gland tumor that secretes hormones that narrow blood vessels and increase blood pressure.

osteoporosis.definition: A systemic skeletal disorder characterized by decreased bone mass and deterioration of bone microarchitecture, leading to bones that are fragile and prone to fractures.

adrenal medulla.definition: The inner portion of the adrenal gland consisting of chromaffin cells derived from neural crest; a neuroendocrine tissue that secretes catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine) into the bloodstream in response to sympathetic stimulation, mediating the fight-or-flight response.

suprarenal gland.definition: An endocrine gland located on the superior aspect of each kidney; it has a cortex and a medulla and secretes corticosteroids (including cortisol and aldosterone) and catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine), regulating metabolism, electrolyte balance, stress response, and cardiovascular function.

central vein.definition: The venule at the center of a hepatic lobule that collects blood from hepatic sinusoids and drains into sublobular veins, ultimately joining the hepatic veins and the inferior vena cava.

cortex.definition: The middle layer and main structure of the hair shaft, consisting mainly of compact bundles of the protein keratin.

medulla.definition: Anatomical inner region or core of an organ; used to describe the inner part of structures such as the kidney or brainstem.

adrenalin.definition: A catecholamine hormone and neurotransmitter produced by the adrenal medulla (epinephrine) that mediates the fight-or-flight response by increasing heart rate, blood pressure, and airway dilation; used clinically as a life-saving drug for anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest, and severe bronchospasm.

adrenaline.definition: Stress hormone that puts the body on high alert. Changes include faster heartbeat, more rapid breathing, greater energy, and higher blood pressure. Also called epinephrine.

epinephrine.definition: A catecholamine hormone and neurotransmitter produced by the adrenal medulla that activates adrenergic receptors, increasing heart rate and contractility, bronchodilation, and glucose mobilization; used clinically as a vasopressor and emergency treatment for anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest, and profound hypotension.

norepinephrine.definition: A hormone produced by adrenal glands that puts the body on heightened alert when a threat is perceived (the fight-or-flight response). Also known as noradrenaline.

adrenal insufficiency.definition: A condition in which the adrenal cortex fails to produce adequate cortisol (and often aldosterone), leading to fatigue, weakness, nausea or vomiting, abdominal pain, hypotension, hyponatremia, and possible hypoglycemia; it can be primary (adrenal destruction) or secondary/tertiary (pituitary/hypothalamic dysfunction), with a life-threatening crisis requiring prompt glucocorticoid replacement and fluid resuscitation.

adrenocortical cytomegaly.definition: Enlargement of cells in the adrenal cortex (cytomegaly) with expanded, often foamy cytoplasm due to lipid accumulation; a histopathologic finding rather than a distinct disease.

adrenocortical hormone.definition: A hormone produced by the adrenal cortex; the major classes are mineralocorticoids (e.g., aldosterone), glucocorticoids (e.g., cortisol), and adrenal androgens, which regulate electrolyte balance, metabolism and the stress response, and contribute to sexual development.

acth.definition: A peptide hormone produced by the anterior pituitary that stimulates the adrenal cortex to synthesize and secrete glucocorticoids (predominantly cortisol); derived from proopiomelanocortin (POMC) and regulated by corticotropin-releasing hormone with negative feedback by cortisol.

corticotropin.definition: A peptide hormone from the anterior pituitary (adrenocorticotropic hormone, ACTH) that stimulates the adrenal cortex to release glucocorticoids (primarily cortisol) and androgens; used in diagnostic ACTH stimulation tests to evaluate adrenal function and, historically, as a treatment for adrenal insufficiency.

cosyntropin.definition: A synthetic peptide analogue of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) consisting of the first 24 amino acids of ACTH; it stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete cortisol and is used in the ACTH stimulation test to evaluate adrenal insufficiency.

metyrapone.definition: A selective inhibitor of adrenal 11β-hydroxylase (CYP11B1) that blocks cortisol synthesis, leading to accumulation of 11-deoxycortisol; used clinically to test the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis and, in some cases, to treat Cushing's syndrome by lowering cortisol production.

adrenal hyperplasia.definition: Enlargement of the adrenal glands due to increased proliferation of adrenal cortical cells (bilateral hyperplasia), typically resulting from chronic adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimulation or as part of congenital adrenal hyperplasia; a non-neoplastic process.

adrenal adenoma.definition: A benign neoplasm of the adrenal cortex that may be nonfunctioning or secrete hormones (most often cortisol or aldosterone), potentially causing Cushing syndrome or primary hyperaldosteronism; many are incidental findings on imaging.

adrenal carcinoma.definition: A rare, malignant tumor of the adrenal cortex (adrenocortical carcinoma), often aggressive and sometimes hormonally active (secreting cortisol or androgens), presenting as an enlarging adrenal mass and primarily treated with surgical resection, with mitotane-based or systemic therapy for advanced disease.

gonadotropin.definition: A hormone that stimulates the gonads (ovaries or testes). In humans, the principal examples are luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone, produced by the anterior pituitary, which regulate gamete production and sex steroid synthesis.

corticotropin-releasing hormone.definition: A hypothalamic neuropeptide that stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) by acting on receptors on corticotroph cells, thereby activating the adrenal cortex to produce cortisol; a central regulator of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis in response to stress.

acth stimulation test.definition: A diagnostic test to evaluate adrenal gland function by giving synthetic ACTH (cosyntropin) and measuring serum cortisol before and after; a normal cortisol rise argues against adrenal insufficiency, while a blunted/absent rise suggests adrenal insufficiency (primary or secondary).

acth stimulation.definition: A diagnostic test that evaluates adrenal gland function by measuring the cortisol response after administration of synthetic adrenocorticotropic hormone (cosyntropin); used to diagnose adrenal insufficiency and assess adrenal reserve.

stimulation test.definition: A diagnostic test in which a stimulus is applied to an organ or gland to provoke a measurable response, used to assess its function or reserve.

adrenogenital syndrome.definition: A disorder of adrenal androgen excess, most often due to congenital adrenal hyperplasia (classically 21-hydroxylase deficiency), that leads to virilization of female genitalia and signs of precocious puberty in males.

adrenarche.definition: Adrenarche is the maturation of the adrenal cortex (zona reticularis) with increased production of adrenal androgens (primarily DHEA and DHEA-S), occurring around ages 6–8 in girls and 7–9 in boys and preceding gonadal puberty.

adrenergic.definition: Relating to adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrinephrine (norepinephrine) receptors or to nerves that release these catecholamines; mediates sympathetic nervous system responses.

adrenergic blocking agent.definition: A drug that blocks adrenergic receptors, preventing norepinephrine and epinephrine from activating sympathetic nervous system responses; includes alpha-adrenergic blockers and beta-adrenergic blockers.

adrenergic bronchodilator.definition: A medication that relaxes bronchial smooth muscle by stimulating adrenergic receptors (primarily beta-2 receptors), causing bronchodilation and relief of bronchospasm; commonly used to treat asthma and COPD.

adrenergic fiber.definition: A nerve fiber that releases norepinephrine (noradrenaline) as its neurotransmitter at synapses; the typical postganglionic sympathetic fiber involved in adrenergic signaling.

alpha-adrenergic.definition: Relating to the adrenergic receptor subclasses alpha-1 and alpha-2, which respond to catecholamines such as norepinephrine and epinephrine; activation increases vascular tone and blood pressure (alpha-1) and inhibits norepinephrine release (alpha-2).

beta-adrenergic.definition: Relating to a class of catecholamine receptors (β1, β2, β3) of the sympathetic nervous system. These G protein–coupled receptors respond to epinephrine and norepinephrine, increasing intracellular cAMP via adenylate cyclase and producing tissue-specific effects such as increased heart rate and contractility (β1), bronchodilation (β2), and lipolysis (β3).

sympathomimetic.definition: A drug or endogenous substance that mimics or enhances sympathetic nervous system activity by stimulating adrenergic receptors (mainly alpha and beta), either directly as receptor agonists or indirectly by increasing synaptic catecholamines.

antiadrenergic.definition: A drug or substance that inhibits the effects of adrenergic neurotransmitters (epinephrine and norepinephrine) by blocking α- or β-adrenergic receptors or by reducing norepinephrine release, thereby decreasing sympathetic nervous system activity.

adrenodoxin.definition: An iron–sulfur mitochondrial protein that acts as an electron carrier in steroid biosynthesis, receiving electrons from adrenodoxin reductase and delivering them to mitochondrial cytochrome P450 enzymes such as CYP11A1 (P450scc) to drive pregnenolone formation.

adrenoleukodystrophy.definition: A peroxisomal, X-linked inherited disorder caused by ABCD1 gene mutations, leading to accumulation of very long-chain fatty acids in the brain and adrenal glands with progressive demyelination and adrenal insufficiency.

ald.definition: Not a standard medical term; when used as ALD, it refers to a genetic disorder causing progressive demyelination of the central nervous system and adrenal insufficiency due to accumulation of very long‑chain fatty acids, typically from ABCD1 gene mutations.

adrenomegaly.definition: Enlargement of one or both adrenal glands (the glands perched on the kidneys), which can result from hyperplasia, benign or malignant tumors, or other adrenal disorders.

adrenomimetic.definition: An adrenomimetic is a substance that mimics the actions of adrenaline (epinephrine) by stimulating adrenergic receptors (alpha and/or beta), producing sympathetic (fight-or-flight) effects.

adrenotropic.definition: Relating to or affecting the adrenal glands; capable of stimulating adrenal activity (e.g., catecholamine release from the adrenal medulla).

adriamycin.definition: A chemotherapy drug (the anthracycline antibiotic doxorubicin) used to treat various cancers; it intercalates DNA and inhibits topoisomerase II, leading to DNA damage and cell death.

adrucil.definition: A chemotherapy agent containing 5-fluorouracil, a pyrimidine analogue antimetabolite used to treat various solid tumors; it inhibits thymidylate synthase and disrupts DNA synthesis (and can be incorporated into RNA).

fluorouracil.definition: An antimetabolite chemotherapy agent that inhibits thymidylate synthase, leading to impaired DNA synthesis and cell death; used systemically for various solid tumors (often in combination regimens) and topically for actinic keratoses and certain skin cancers.

rotavirus.definition: A germ (a virus) that causes you to feel sick to your stomach, throw up, or have diarrhea.

adult rotavirus.definition: An infection by rotavirus occurring in adults, presenting as acute gastroenteritis with watery diarrhea, vomiting, and sometimes fever; primarily transmitted via the fecal-oral route and typically milder in adults than in children, managed with supportive care such as hydration and electrolyte repletion.

adrv.definition: Not a recognized medical term; no standard definition available. Please provide context or the full form of the acronym to define it accurately.

ards.definition: A life-threatening acute inflammatory lung injury causing noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and severe hypoxemia, typically resulting from direct or indirect insults (e.g., sepsis, trauma, pneumonia) and often requiring mechanical ventilation.

paraquat.definition: A highly toxic nonselective herbicide (paraquat dichloride) whose ingestion or exposure causes rapid systemic oxidative injury, especially to the lungs, leading to pulmonary edema and progressive fibrosis; there is no specific antidote and management is supportive.

chlorine.definition: A chemical element whose biologically important form is the chloride ion (Cl−), an extracellular anion essential for maintaining fluid and electrolyte balance and acid-base homeostasis, and for stomach acid production; it is ingested mainly as sodium chloride in salt, while inhalation of chlorine gas is a highly toxic respiratory irritant.

ammonia.definition: A colorless, highly soluble inorganic gas (NH3) produced by the breakdown of nitrogenous compounds and amino acid deamination; in the body it is detoxified in the liver by the urea cycle, and elevated levels (hyperammonemia) are toxic and can cause encephalopathy.

phosgene.definition: A highly toxic, colorless gas (carbonyl chloride, COCl2) that causes severe pulmonary edema and chemical pneumitis after inhalation, with a potential delayed onset; historically used as a choking warfare agent.

barbiturates.definition: A class of sedative-hypnotic drugs derived from barbituric acid that act as CNS depressants by enhancing GABA-A receptor activity; historically used for anesthesia, sleep induction, and seizure control, but associated with tolerance, dependence, and risk of respiratory depression.

chlordiazepoxide.definition: A long-acting benzodiazepine with anxiolytic, sedative, anticonvulsant, and skeletal muscle relaxant properties; used for anxiety disorders, alcohol withdrawal, and preoperative sedation; it enhances GABA-A receptor–mediated neurotransmission.

heroin.definition: An illegal semi-synthetic opioid analgesic (diacetylmorphine) derived from morphine; it is rapidly converted to morphine in the brain and activates mu-opioid receptors, producing profound euphoria and analgesia with a high risk of tolerance, dependence, and fatal respiratory depression.

methadone hydrochloride.definition: A long-acting synthetic opioid analgesic in the hydrochloride salt form, used for moderate to severe pain and for maintenance therapy in opioid dependence; acts as a mu-opioid receptor agonist with a risk of respiratory depression and dependence.

propoxyphene hydrochloride.definition: A synthetic opioid analgesic (mu-opioid receptor agonist) in the hydrochloride salt form, formerly used for mild to moderate pain but withdrawn in many markets due to risk of serious cardiotoxicity and arrhythmias.

uremia.definition: A clinical syndrome from advanced renal failure in which accumulation of nitrogenous wastes and other toxins in the blood causes nausea, vomiting, fatigue, confusion or altered mental status, anorexia, pruritus, and sometimes pericarditis; typically treated with dialysis or renal transplantation.

diabetes mellitus type 2.definition: A chronic metabolic disorder characterized by hyperglycemia due to insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency, typically associated with obesity and progressive β-cell dysfunction.

adult-onset diabetes.definition: A chronic metabolic disorder characterized by insulin resistance and progressive relative insulin deficiency, resulting in hyperglycemia; typically diagnosed in adulthood and associated with overweight/obesity and sedentary lifestyle; managed with diet and exercise, glucose-lowering medications, and sometimes insulin.

rheumatoid arthritis.definition: A kind of joint disease that causes pain and swelling.

myasthenia.definition: An abnormal weakness in a muscle or group of muscles.

demyelination.definition: The loss or damage of the myelin sheath surrounding nerve fibers, causing slowed or disrupted conduction of electrical impulses along nerves.

schilder's disease.definition: A rare pediatric inflammatory demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system characterized by large, bilateral, symmetric demyelinating lesions in cerebral white matter (often periventricular, sometimes involving the corpus callosum), presenting with acute/subacute neurologic deficits; considered by many as a variant of ADEM/diffuse leukoencephalitis with variable prognosis and usually responsive to corticosteroids.

oily skin.definition: An overactive sebaceous gland–driven skin type producing excess sebum, leading to a shiny appearance, enlarged pores, and a propensity for acne.

ovarian changes.definition: Alterations in the ovaries' size, structure, or function, often related to hormonal changes, aging, pregnancy, or menopause, and may reflect pathology such as cysts, neoplasms, or inflammatory conditions.

muscular hypertrophy.definition: An increase in the size of skeletal muscle fibers, resulting in greater muscle mass, typically in response to mechanical overload such as resistance training; can be physiological or, less commonly, pathological.

atrophy.definition: Wasting away of an organ or tissue due to undernourishment, disease, or aging.

breasts.definition: A pair of mammary glands on the anterior chest that produce milk; composed of glandular tissue organized into lobes and ducts, embedded in connective tissue and fat; their primary function is lactation after puberty; in males they are typically small or vestigial.

pubic hair.definition: Hair in the genital region that appears during puberty as part of secondary sexual characteristics; it is typically coarser and darker than other body hair, and growth is influenced by androgens.

axillary hair.definition: Hair located in the armpit (axilla); typically develops during puberty under androgen influence and is usually coarser and darker than other body hair, representing a secondary sexual characteristic.

precocious development.definition: Development occurring earlier than the typical age or stage for an individual; in pediatrics, most often refers to precocious puberty—the early onset of secondary sexual characteristics and rapid maturation.

clitoral enlargement.definition: An abnormal enlargement of the clitoris (clitoromegaly), typically due to excess androgens causing virilization; can be congenital or acquired and may indicate underlying endocrine disorders such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia or exposure to androgens.

labial fusion.definition: Partial or complete fusion of the labia minora at the midline of the vulva, typically near the posterior aspect, most common in prepubertal girls or in states of low estrogen; may be asymptomatic or cause urinary symptoms.

epiphyses.definition: The ends of a long bone, formed from secondary ossification centers; their surfaces are covered by articular cartilage, and they are separated from the shaft by the metaphysis (growth plate) in children and later fuse with the diaphysis in adulthood.

premature closure.definition: Early fusion or closure of a structure that normally remains open, most commonly cranial sutures or epiphyseal growth plates, which can restrict normal growth and cause deformities.

androgenic hormones.definition: Hormones that promote the development and maintenance of male secondary sexual characteristics; they are androgens that bind to androgen receptors, chiefly testosterone and its potent metabolite dihydrotestosterone, produced mainly by the testes and adrenal glands.

aec syndrome.definition: A rare genetic disorder defined by the triad of eyelid fusion at birth (ankyloblepharon), ectodermal dysplasia (abnormal development of hair, teeth, nails, and sweat glands), and facial clefting (such as cleft lip/palate); most cases are due to TP63 gene mutations with autosomal dominant inheritance, with variable expressivity and may include skin erosions or limb anomalies.

acls.definition: An evidence-based course and set of guidelines for the advanced management of life-threatening cardiac emergencies—covering high-quality CPR, airway management, defibrillation, rhythm analysis, drug therapy, and post-resuscitation care; typically provided as an American Heart Association certification.

advanced life support.definition: Advanced life support is the level of emergency medical care for life-threatening emergencies that extends basic life support by providing advanced airway management, ventilation support, circulatory support and monitoring, defibrillation or cardioversion, and administration of resuscitation medications according to standardized guidelines (e.g., ACLS).

als.definition: A progressive neurodegenerative disease affecting upper and lower motor neurons in the brain and spinal cord, leading to progressive muscle weakness and atrophy, spasticity, fasciculations, and eventually paralysis with respiratory failure; no cure and supportive multidisciplinary management.

airway.definition: A passage for air between the outside environment and the lungs, comprising the upper airway (nostrils/mouth, pharynx, larynx) and lower airway (trachea, bronchi, bronchioles); it conducts air to the lungs and conditions it by warming, humidifying, and filtering, while protecting the lower respiratory tract.

ventilatory.definition: Relating to ventilation; the process of moving air into and out of the lungs, or to methods/devices that support breathing.

fluid resuscitation.definition: Rapid intravenous administration of fluids to restore intravascular volume and tissue perfusion in states of hypovolemia or shock. It commonly uses isotonic crystalloids (e.g., normal saline or lactated Ringer's) and may include colloids or blood products depending on the clinical scenario.

defibrillation.definition: A medical procedure that delivers a controlled electric shock to the heart to depolarize cardiac cells and restore a normal rhythm, used to treat life-threatening arrhythmias such as ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia; can be delivered externally (via an AED/defibrillator) or internally (via an implanted device).

endotracheal intubation.definition: Placement of a tube through the mouth or nose into the trachea to secure an airway and enable ventilation, typically during anesthesia or critical illness, with protection against aspiration.

intravenous therapy.definition: A method of delivering fluids, medications, or nutrients directly into the venous system via an IV line (catheter or needle) for hydration, treatment, or nutrition.

cardiac arrhythmias.definition: Group of conditions characterized by abnormal heart rhythm due to dysfunction of the heart's electrical system—impaired impulse formation and/or conduction—producing rates or rhythms that are too fast, too slow, or irregular; ranges from benign to life-threatening and may cause palpitations, dizziness, syncope, or heart failure depending on type and severity.

heart failure.definition: When your heart can't pump enough blood. Also called congestive heart failure or CHF.

emphysema.definition: A lung disease that makes it hard to breathe. It gets worse over time. It is a type of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or COPD.

copd.definition: A lung disease that makes breathing hard. Also known as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, emphysema, or chronic bronchitis.

bronchospasm.definition: A sudden constriction of the smooth muscle in the walls of the bronchi and bronchioles, causing narrowing of the airways and wheezing; typically reversible with bronchodilator therapy and commonly seen in asthma, allergies, and other obstructive lung conditions.

wheezes.definition: A high-pitched, musical breath sound caused by turbulent airflow through narrowed or obstructed airways, most often heard during expiration in conditions such as asthma, bronchitis, or COPD.

rhonchi.definition: Coarse, low-pitched breath sounds heard on auscultation, produced by secretions or obstruction in the larger airways; often described as snoring or gurgling and may be relieved by coughing.

crackles.definition: An abnormal lung sound heard on auscultation characterized by brief, discontinuous noises produced by the sudden opening of collapsed small airways or by movement of fluid/secretions in the airways; it is categorized as fine (soft, high-pitched) or coarse (louder, lower-pitched).

pleural friction rub.definition: A dry, scratchy, grating auscultatory sound heard when inflamed pleural surfaces rub together during respiration, usually due to pleuritis (pleurisy).

pulmonary infarction.definition: Localized necrosis of lung tissue caused by ischemia from occlusion of a pulmonary artery or its branches, most often due to pulmonary embolism; the infarct is typically wedge-shaped and subpleural, and may be hemorrhagic due to the lung's dual blood supply.

atrial flutter.definition: A supraventricular tachycardia due to a reentrant circuit in the atria (often the right atrium) that produces a rapid, regular atrial rate of about 250–350 beats per minute with characteristic sawtooth flutter waves on ECG; ventricular rate is commonly slower due to AV nodal conduction, often around 150 bpm with 2:1 conduction.

acid-fast bacillus.definition: A bacterium that retains the carbol fuchsin dye after decolorization with acid-alcohol in acid-fast staining, due to a waxy, mycolic-acid–rich cell wall; classically refers to Mycobacterium species (e.g., M. tuberculosis).

automated external defibrillator.definition: A portable, battery-powered device that analyzes the heart rhythm and, if a shockable rhythm is detected (eg, ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia), delivers an electric shock to restore a normal rhythm; designed for use by laypersons with guided audio-visual prompts.

aedes.definition: A genus of mosquitoes (Culicidae), including Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, that are vectors for dengue, Zika, chikungunya, and yellow fever.

st. louis encephalitis.definition: A mosquito-borne viral infection of the central nervous system caused by a flavivirus transmitted primarily by Culex mosquitoes. It ranges from asymptomatic or mild febrile illness to severe encephalitis with fever, headache, confusion, and sometimes seizures or coma. Diagnosis is by serology (IgM antibodies in serum or CSF) or PCR. Treatment is supportive; prevention emphasizes mosquito control and avoiding bites.

yellow fever.definition: Caused by a germ (a virus) that lives in mosquitoes. It affects many parts of your body. The yellow fever virus is found in certain parts of Africa and South America.

tularemia.definition: A zoonotic bacterial infection caused by Francisella tularensis; transmitted to humans by bites from infected arthropods (ticks, deerflies), contact with infected animals, or inhalation of contaminated aerosols; it commonly presents as ulceroglandular disease (skin ulcer with tender regional lymphadenopathy) and can also appear in glandular, oculoglandular, pneumonic, or systemic forms; treated with antibiotics such as streptomycin, gentamicin, doxycycline, or ciprofloxacin.

barosinusitis.definition: Barosinusitis is inflammation of the paranasal sinuses caused by rapid ambient-pressure changes that impair sinus drainage (ostial patency), most often during diving or air travel, leading to facial pain/pressure and nasal congestion.

aerosinusitis.definition: Inflammation of the paranasal sinuses caused by exposure to aerosolized irritants or particles, leading to mucosal swelling, impaired sinus drainage, and symptoms of sinusitis such as nasal congestion, facial pressure, and discharge.

barotitis.definition: Inflammation or injury of the ear caused by changes in ambient barometric pressure (barotrauma), typically during rapid ascent or descent (e.g., flying or diving), causing ear pain, fullness, hearing loss, and possible tympanic membrane rupture or middle-ear effusion due to Eustachian tube dysfunction.

barotitis media.definition: Inflammation and/or injury of the middle ear caused by rapid changes in barometric pressure between the environment and the middle ear (barotrauma), typically during ascent or descent in flying or diving; symptoms include ear pain, fullness, muffled hearing, and sometimes tympanic membrane rupture or middle-ear effusion.

aerosol therapy.definition: Delivery of medications to the respiratory tract as an inhaled aerosol, using devices such as nebulizers, metered‑dose inhalers, or dry powder inhalers. It is used to treat respiratory diseases by delivering bronchodilators, corticosteroids, mucolytics, or antibiotics directly to the airways.

aerosol bronchodilator therapy.definition: Delivery of bronchodilator medications to the airways as an inhaled aerosol (via nebulizers or inhalers) to relax airway smooth muscle, dilate the bronchi, and improve airflow and symptoms in obstructive lung diseases such as asthma and COPD.

bronchodilator.definition: A drug that helps you breathe easier.

flunisolide.definition: A synthetic corticosteroid (glucocorticoid) used as an anti-inflammatory medication in the management of asthma and allergic rhinitis; administered by inhalation (metered-dose inhaler) for asthma or as a nasal spray for rhinitis, and works by suppressing airway inflammation with minimal systemic effects at usual doses.

aeromonas.definition: A genus of Gram-negative, oxidase-positive, facultatively anaerobic, rod-shaped bacteria commonly found in fresh water; some species are opportunistic human pathogens causing gastroenteritis, wound infections, and septicemia.

aerobe.definition: An organism that requires oxygen for growth and metabolism; it uses molecular oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor in aerobic respiration.

aerobic.definition: Relating to or requiring oxygen; a metabolic process that uses oxygen to produce energy.

aerobic capacity.definition: The maximal rate at which the body can consume and utilize oxygen during incremental aerobic exercise, reflecting cardiorespiratory endurance and usually measured as VO2 max.

aerobics.definition: A form of sustained, rhythmic physical activity using large muscle groups to improve cardiovascular endurance and oxygen uptake (aerobic capacity), typically performed at moderate to vigorous intensity and often done to music.

aeration.definition: The introduction or presence of air or gas in a substance or space; in medical contexts, it refers to delivering air or oxygen to tissues or body cavities.

air embolism.definition: Blockage of a blood vessel by air bubbles in the circulation, causing impaired blood flow and tissue oxygenation; it can occur during medical procedures, trauma, or rapid decompression and is treated with 100% oxygen and measures to remove the air and prevent further entry.

aerodermectasia.definition: A historical term referring to the presence of air in the dermal or subcutaneous tissues, causing gaseous swelling and crepitus; essentially subcutaneous emphysema of the skin.

aerodontalgia.definition: A dental pain provoked by changes in ambient air pressure (barometric pressure), commonly occurring during aviation or scuba diving, often due to trapped air in a tooth or restoration.

aerophagy.definition: The act of swallowing air into the stomach, leading to belching and abdominal distension; it can be a normal habit or a pathological condition when persistent, often associated with anxiety or developmental/psychiatric disorders.

pseudocyst.definition: A fluid-filled cavity surrounded by a nonepithelial fibrous wall (a false cyst), typically arising after pancreatitis or pancreatic injury.

adventitia.definition: Outer connective tissue coat that surrounds and anchors a hollow organ or vessel to surrounding tissues; in blood vessels it is the tunica externa and may contain small vessels (vasa vasorum) and nerves (nervi vasorum).

adventitious bursa.definition: A bursar sac that forms de novo in soft tissue in response to chronic friction or pressure, typically over a bony prominence where no normal bursa exists; it functions to reduce friction but can become inflamed (adventitious bursitis).

adventitious cyst.definition: An adventitious cyst is a cyst that develops in an abnormal, non-native location (an adventitial location), often acquired rather than congenital, and arising from trauma, inflammation, or displacement of tissue rather than from a primary developmental process.

adventitious sound.definition: An abnormal breath sound heard on auscultation of the chest that is not normally present in healthy lungs, such as crackles (rales), wheezes, rhonchi, or pleural friction rub, indicating airway or parenchymal pathology.

affective disorder.definition: Mood disorder characterized by a primary disturbance of mood, including depressive and/or manic/hypomanic episodes; examples include major depressive disorder, bipolar I/II disorder, and cyclothymic disorder.

mood disorder.definition: A group of mental health disorders in which a disturbance of mood is the central feature, with episodes of depressed mood and/or elevated or irritable mood that significantly impair thinking, energy, sleep, appetite, and functioning; includes depressive disorders and bipolar and related disorders.

afterdepolarization.definition: An abnormal depolarizing change in a cell’s membrane potential that occurs after the preceding action potential has repolarized, commonly seen in cardiac tissue as early afterdepolarizations (during repolarization) and delayed afterdepolarizations (after repolarization), both of which can trigger arrhythmias.

melancholia.definition: Historically, a severe depressive illness marked by profound sadness or despondency, anhedonia, psychomotor retardation or agitation, unreactive mood, early morning awakening, significant weight loss or loss of appetite, and excessive guilt; in contemporary psychiatry this corresponds to major depressive disorder with melancholic features.

bipolar disorder.definition: A chronic mental health disorder marked by alternating or episodic mood states of mania or hypomania and depression, with periods of normal mood in between; mania/hypomania include elevated or irritable mood, increased energy, diminished need for sleep, grandiosity, rapid speech, and risk-taking; depressive episodes feature persistent low mood, anhedonia, fatigue, sleep/appetite changes, poor concentration, and possible suicidal thoughts.

psychosis.definition: A mental state characterized by a loss of contact with reality, with symptoms such as delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thinking, and impaired insight or behavior; it can occur in primary psychiatric disorders, mood disorders, substance effects, or medical illnesses.

glomerular arteriole.definition: A small-diameter renal arteriole that supplies blood to the glomerulus of the nephron; the afferent arteriole brings blood into the glomerulus and the efferent arteriole drains it, helping regulate glomerular filtration rate through constriction and dilation.

afferent.definition: Carrying toward a center, especially toward the brain or spinal cord; in physiology, describing sensory pathways that transmit information from peripheral receptors to the central nervous system.

afferent nerve.definition: A nerve that transmits sensory information from peripheral receptors toward the central nervous system; essentially a sensory nerve.

afferent pathway.definition: Afferent pathway: the neural route by which sensory information is transmitted from peripheral receptors toward the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord); it includes primary sensory neurons and their synapses, conveying modalities such as touch, pain, temperature, and proprioception.

afferent tract.definition: Afferent tract: a neural pathway in the central nervous system that carries sensory information from peripheral receptors toward the brain or spinal cord; these are ascending tracts, in contrast to efferent (descending) tracts that carry motor commands away from the CNS.

left ventricle.definition: The left lower chamber of the heart. It pumps blood out of the heart to other organs in the body.

atrial tachycardia.definition: Atrial tachycardia is a type of supraventricular tachycardia caused by an ectopic focus in the atria (outside the sinoatrial node) that fires impulses rapidly and regularly, typically at 100–250 beats per minute, with abnormal P-wave morphology and usually a narrow QRS complex.

ventricular tachycardia.definition: A very fast heartbeat that starts in the ventricles. It can be deadly if it renders the heart unable to pump enough blood to the body.

lymphadenopathy.definition: Enlargement of one or more lymph nodes, usually resulting from infection, inflammation, or malignant disease; can be localized or generalized and may be tender or painless.

chills.definition: A sensation of cold with involuntary shivering caused by a rise in the body's core temperature set-point during fever or infection.

lethargy.definition: A feeling of low energy, low motivation, or sleepiness.

sleepiness.definition: Subjective feeling of drowsiness and an increased propensity to fall asleep; often due to fatigue, inadequate sleep, circadian disruption, medications, or underlying sleep disorders.

maculopapular rash.definition: A diffuse skin eruption consisting of flat red patches (macules) and small raised lesions (papules) that may coalesce; typically erythematous, blanching, and pruritic, seen in many viral exanthems and drug eruptions.

parasympathetic ganglion cells.definition: Postganglionic neurons of the parasympathetic nervous system, located in or near visceral target organs (intramural/terminal ganglia); they receive input from preganglionic parasympathetic neurons and release acetylcholine to innervate smooth muscle and glands, mediating rest-and-digest effects.

ganglion.definition: A knot-like collection of nerve cell bodies in the peripheral nervous system; it is also commonly used to describe a benign, fluid-filled cyst that arises near a joint or tendon sheath (ganglion cyst).

nerve.definition: A bundle of peripheral nerve fibers (axons) enclosed by connective tissue that conducts electrical impulses between the central nervous system and the body; these nerves can be sensory, motor, or mixed and are organized into endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium.

nerve fiber.definition: A single neuron axon (myelinated or unmyelinated) that conducts an action potential, forming the basic unit of a nerve.

veins.definition: The vessels that carry blood back to the heart.

lymphatic vessels.definition: Thin-walled, valved vessels of the lymphatic system that carry lymph—interstitial fluid rich in proteins, lipids, and immune cells—from tissues toward the venous circulation, beginning as blind-ended lymphatic capillaries and converging into larger collecting vessels, trunks, and ducts; they aid in fluid balance, fat absorption, and immune defense.

amni on.definition: An innermost fetal membrane that lines the amniotic cavity, surrounding the developing embryo and containing the amniotic fluid; it forms the amniotic sac that cushions and protects the fetus.

chorion.definition: The outer fetal membrane surrounding the developing embryo; formed from trophoblast and extraembryonic mesoderm, and contributing to the placenta through chorionic villi that invade the maternal endometrium.

amniotic fluid.definition: The fluid surrounding unborn baby in a mother's womb.

blood clots.definition: A coagulated mass that occurs when blood cells stick together and form a solid.

afterbirth.definition: The placenta and fetal membranes that are expelled from the uterus after the birth of the infant.

african hemorrhagic fever.definition: A broad term for severe viral hemorrhagic fevers occurring in Africa, caused by pathogens such as Ebola virus, Marburg virus, and Lassa virus; characterized by abrupt fever, malaise, myalgias, and bleeding, which can progress to shock and organ failure; transmission via contact with infected bodily fluids, contaminated materials, or animal reservoirs; diagnosed by molecular or serologic testing; management is supportive with strict infection control.

ebola virus disease.definition: A severe, often fatal viral hemorrhagic fever caused by infection with Ebola virus (a filovirus). Transmission occurs via direct contact with the blood, body fluids, or tissues of an infected person or animal, or with contaminated objects; incubation is typically 2–21 days. Early symptoms include abrupt fever, fatigue, muscle pains, headache, and sore throat, followed by vomiting, diarrhea, rash, impaired kidney and liver function, and sometimes bleeding. Case fatality varies by outbreak and viral species; supportive care improves outcomes, and targeted therapies and vaccines exist for outbreak control.

african sleeping sickness.definition: A parasitic infection caused by the protozoan Trypanosoma brucei (subspecies gambiense or rhodesiense) transmitted by tsetse flies; it begins with fever and lymphadenopathy and progresses to a fatal central nervous system stage with sleep disturbances, behavioral changes, and coma if untreated.

african trypanosomiasis.definition: A parasitic disease caused by Trypanosoma brucei transmitted by tsetse fly bites, presenting as African sleeping sickness with an early febrile/lymphadenopathic phase and a late meningoencephalitic phase affecting the central nervous system.

sleeping sickness.definition: A parasitic infection caused by Trypanosoma brucei (African trypanosomiasis), transmitted by tsetse flies; it starts with fever, lymphadenopathy, and malaise and progresses to neurological involvement with sleep disturbances, behavioral changes, and, if untreated, coma and death.

trypanosomiasis.definition: An infection caused by protozoan parasites of the genus Trypanosoma, transmitted by insect vectors; includes African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) caused by T. brucei and American trypanosomiasis (Chagas disease) caused by T. cruzi, and can lead to fever, neurological or cardiac complications, and potentially death if untreated.

gambian trypanosomiasis.definition: A form of West African human African trypanosomiasis caused by Trypanosoma brucei gambiense, transmitted by tsetse flies; it is a chronic parasitic infection that begins with nonspecific symptoms (fever, fatigue, lymphadenopathy) and can progress to central nervous system involvement if untreated.

rhodesian trypanosomiasis.definition: An acute form of African sleeping sickness caused by Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense, transmitted by tsetse flies; presents with fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy, and edema, and progresses rapidly to central nervous system involvement if untreated (more fulminant than the gambiense form).

trypanosoma brucei gambiense.definition: A subspecies of the flagellated protozoan parasite that causes human African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness), typically presenting as a chronic form in West and Central Africa and transmitted to humans by infected tsetse flies (Glossina spp.).

trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense.definition: An acute zoonotic subspecies of the flagellated protozoan parasite Trypanosoma brucei, transmitted by tsetse flies, that causes human African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) with rapid onset and progression to central nervous system involvement if untreated, primarily in East Africa.

relapsing fever.definition: A tick- or louse-borne infection caused by Borrelia spirochetes, characterized by recurrent fever episodes separated by afebrile intervals due to antigenic variation in Borrelia.

dutton's relapsing fever.definition: Tick-borne relapsing fever caused by Borrelia duttonii, transmitted by Ornithodoros soft ticks in East Africa; presents with recurrent febrile episodes due to transient spirochetemia, often with headache and myalgias, and is treated with tetracyclines or penicillin.

tick-borne fever.definition: A febrile illness transmitted by tick bites, caused by a variety of pathogens (bacteria such as Borrelia, Rickettsia, and Anaplasma; protozoa such as Babesia); symptoms are usually nonspecific and include fever, headache, malaise, and myalgias, with possible rash or organ-specific findings depending on the pathogen. Diagnosis relies on exposure history and laboratory testing; treatment depends on the causative organism (commonly doxycycline for many bacterial tick-borne diseases).

african tick fever.definition: Tick-borne rickettsial infection caused by Rickettsia africae, transmitted by Amblyomma ticks; presents with fever, headache, malaise, myalgias, regional lymphadenopathy, and often inoculation eschars at bite sites; typically mild and self-limiting; treated with doxycycline.

african tick typhus.definition: Tick-borne rickettsial infection caused by Rickettsia africae, transmitted by Amblyomma ticks (e.g., Amblyomma hebraeum/variegatum) in sub-Saharan Africa; presents with fever, headache, malaise, regional lymphadenopathy, and inoculation eschars at bite sites; usually mild and self-limited and responsive to doxycycline, with diagnosis by serology or PCR.

rocky mountain spotted fever.definition: A tick-borne infection caused by the bacterium Rickettsia rickettsii, characterized by abrupt fever, severe headache, myalgias, and often a maculopapular or petechial rash that may begin on the wrists/ankles and spread to the trunk; transmitted by Dermacentor ticks and can cause vasculitis with potentially life-threatening complications; treated with doxycycline.

burkitt lymphoma.definition: An aggressive B‑cell non‑Hodgkin lymphoma driven by translocations involving the MYC gene (most commonly t(8;14)(q24;q32)) that lead to rapid tumor growth; variants include endemic (often involving the jaw and EBV-associated), sporadic (abdomen/pelvis), and immunodeficiency-associated forms; highly chemosensitive and often curable with intensive short‑course chemotherapy.

african lymphoma.definition: An historical term for endemic Burkitt lymphoma, a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma seen most often in children in equatorial Africa. It is strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection and malaria; typically presents with jaw/facial bone tumors or abdominal masses and is treated with short, intensive combination chemotherapy, with a high cure rate in children when treated early.

liver cancer.definition: A malignant neoplasm arising in the liver, most commonly hepatocellular carcinoma, typically developing in the setting of chronic liver disease (e.g., cirrhosis from hepatitis B or C, alcohol, or nonalcoholic fatty liver disease). It may invade blood vessels and metastasize; diagnosis relies on imaging and biomarkers, and treatment depends on tumor stage and liver function.

hirschsprung disease.definition: Congenital absence of enteric ganglion cells in the distal colon (aganglionosis) due to failed neural crest cell migration, causing a nonrelaxing, obstructed bowel segment; most commonly involves the rectosigmoid colon; presents in neonates with delayed passage of meconium and abdominal distension; treated by surgical resection of the aganglionic segment with a pull-through procedure.

aganglionic megacolon.definition: Congenital absence of enteric ganglion cells in a distal segment of the colon, leading to a functional obstruction with proximal bowel dilation. This is the pathophysiologic basis of Hirschsprung disease; diagnosis is by rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells, and treatment is surgical resection of the aganglionic segment.

aganglionosis.definition: A congenital absence of autonomic ganglion cells in a segment of the intestine, leading to impaired peristalsis and functional obstruction (classically associated with Hirschsprung disease).

agastria.definition: A congenital absence or failure of development of the stomach.

agastric.definition: Lacking a stomach; absence of the stomach, either congenitally or following gastrectomy.

afibrinogenemia.definition: An extremely rare congenital bleeding disorder characterized by absent (undetectable) fibrinogen (factor I) in the blood due to biallelic mutations in fibrinogen genes (FGA, FGB, or FGG), leading to defective fibrin formation and severe bleeding from infancy; inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.

afibrinogenaemia.definition: A rare inherited bleeding disorder characterized by undetectable or severely reduced plasma fibrinogen (factor I) levels due to mutations in fibrinogen genes, resulting in defective fibrin formation and a severe bleeding tendency; usually autosomal recessive.

aflatoxins.definition: A family of highly toxic mycotoxins produced by Aspergillus species (notably A. flavus and A. parasiticus) that contaminate food; they are potent hepatocarcinogens associated with liver cancer and can cause acute aflatoxicosis at high exposures.

aspergillus flavus.definition: A species of mold (filamentous fungus) in the genus Aspergillus; a common contaminant of stored grains and nuts that produces aflatoxins, potent hepatocarcinogens, and can cause invasive disease in immunocompromised individuals.

fabry disease.definition: A rare X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of the enzyme alpha-galactosidase A, leading to accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) in vascular endothelium and other tissues, which can cause angiokeratomas, acroparesthesias (neuropathic pain), hypohidrosis, corneal verticillata, and progressive kidney, heart, and central nervous system involvement.

agalsidase beta.definition: Recombinant human alpha-galactosidase A used as enzyme replacement therapy for Fabry disease; it substitutes the deficient lysosomal enzyme to decrease accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (GL-3) and is given by intravenous infusion every two weeks.

alpha-fetoprotein.definition: A fetal glycoprotein produced mainly by the fetal liver, yolk sac, and gastrointestinal tract; in pregnancy, maternal serum AFP is screened to assess risk of neural tube defects and ventral wall defects, while in adults elevated AFP can indicate hepatocellular carcinoma and certain germ cell tumors.

absolute granulocyte count.definition: The total number of granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils) in a given volume of blood, typically reported as cells per microliter (µL) or per liter (L); derived by multiplying the total white blood cell count by the percentage of granulocytes on a differential.

absolute neutrophil count.definition: An absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is the number of neutrophils in peripheral blood, calculated from the white blood cell count and the neutrophil percentage (segmented plus band neutrophils); expressed as cells per microliter (or x10^9/L).

immunoglobulin.definition: A large glycoprotein antibody produced by plasma cells that binds specific antigens to neutralize pathogens or mark them for attack by immune cells; these antibodies are classified into IgA, IgD, IgE, IgG, and IgM, with distinct roles in humoral immunity.

antigen-antibody reaction.definition: A specific immune interaction in which an antibody binds its antigen, forming an antigen–antibody complex; this binding can neutralize pathogens, cause agglutination or precipitation of antigens, activate complement, and promote phagocytosis (opsonization) or inflammatory responses.

agammaglobulinemia.definition: A primary immunodeficiency characterized by profoundly low or absent serum immunoglobulins due to defective B-cell development, resulting in recurrent bacterial infections (often beginning in infancy or early childhood).

agammaglobulinaemia.definition: A primary humoral immunodeficiency characterized by markedly reduced or absent immunoglobulins and B cells due to defective B cell development, leading to recurrent bacterial infections; most commonly X-linked (Bruton) type, treated with immunoglobulin replacement.

bruton's agammaglobulinemia.definition: A genetic X-linked primary immunodeficiency caused by BTK mutations that prevents maturation of B cells, resulting in absent or markedly reduced immunoglobulins (hypogammaglobulinemia) and recurrent bacterial infections, especially of the respiratory tract; managed with lifelong immunoglobulin replacement therapy.

suramin sodium.definition: A large polysulfonated antiparasitic agent supplied as its disodium salt, used to treat early-stage human African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) caused by Trypanosoma brucei gambiense or rhodesiense; administered intravenously; mechanism includes inhibition of parasite enzymes and energy metabolism, with potential adverse effects such as hypersensitivity reactions, nephrotoxicity, and hepatotoxicity.

pentamidine isothionate.definition: A diamidine antiparasitic drug used to treat Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and African trypanosomiasis; administered parenterally (and inhaled for PCP prophylaxis); it binds to parasite DNA and inhibits replication.

organic arsenicals.definition: Compounds in which arsenic is bonded to carbon (organoarsenicals). A class of organoarsenical drugs and pesticides historically used as antimicrobial or antiparasitic agents; many are highly toxic and tightly regulated today.

difluoromethylorthinine.definition: An irreversible inhibitor of ornithine decarboxylase, the enzyme in polyamine biosynthesis; it is a difluoromethyl analog of ornithine that depletes cellular polyamines (putrescine, spermidine, spermine) and inhibits cell growth. Clinically used as an antiparasitic agent against African trypanosomiasis and studied for cancer prevention.

eflornithine.definition: An irreversible inhibitor of ornithine decarboxylase (difluoromethylornithine) that decreases polyamine synthesis; used systemically for African sleeping sickness and topically to reduce facial hair growth.

oxymetazoline hydrochloride.definition: A topical alpha-adrenergic agonist; the hydrochloride salt of oxymetazoline used as a nasal decongestant (and in some ophthalmic preparations to relieve conjunctival redness) by vasoconstricting nasal/ocular mucosa. Onset is within minutes and effects last several hours; prolonged use risks rebound congestion and should be limited to short-term therapy.

culture media.definition: Substrates prepared to support the growth, isolation, and maintenance of microorganisms in a laboratory; typically liquids or gels (broth or agar) containing nutrients (carbon and energy sources, minerals, vitamins, and growth factors) and may be selective or differential to favor or identify particular organisms.

electrophoresis.definition: An analytical technique in which charged molecules (such as DNA, RNA, or proteins) are driven through a gel or other medium by an applied electric field, separating them based on size, charge, and shape.

serum.definition: The clear fluid that remains after blood has clotted; the liquid portion of blood lacking fibrinogen and other clotting factors.

hemoglobin variants.definition: Structural variants of hemoglobin arising from mutations in globin genes that produce abnormal hemoglobin molecules (e.g., HbS, HbC, HbD). They can alter stability, oxygen affinity, or polymerization, potentially causing hemolytic anemia or sickling in some cases; detection is usually by hemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC, with DNA analysis for confirmation.

lipoprotein fractions.definition: Lipoprotein fractions are the discrete density- and size-defined classes of circulating lipoprotein particles that transport lipids in the bloodstream; the major fractions are chylomicrons, VLDL, IDL, LDL, and HDL, each differing in lipid-to-protein content and density, and they are separated and quantified in the lab by ultracentrifugation or other fractionation methods to assess lipid risk profiles.

rickettsia africae.definition: A species of pathogenic, obligate intracellular, Gram-negative bacteria of the spotted fever group (genus Rickettsia); transmitted by Amblyomma ticks and causes African tick bite fever in humans.

tsetse fly.definition: A blood-sucking fly native to sub-Saharan Africa of the genus Glossina that transmits the protozoan parasites Trypanosoma brucei gambiense and Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense to humans and animals, causing African sleeping sickness (African trypanosomiasis).

plasma.definition: The liquid part of your blood.

agenesis.definition: Agenesis is the congenital absence of an organ or body part due to failure of development during embryogenesis.

agenesis of the corpus callosum.definition: A congenital absence (agenesis) or severe underdevelopment (hypoplasia) of the corpus callosum, the major fiber tract that connects the brain's two hemispheres; it can be isolated or associated with other brain abnormalities or syndromes, and it yields a wide range of neurodevelopmental outcomes, from normal to intellectual disability and seizures. Diagnosis is typically by MRI.

corpus callosum.definition: The large bundle of nerve fibers linking the left and right sides of the brain.

ageniocephaly.definition: A severe congenital neural tube defect in which a major portion of the brain and skull are absent at birth, typically incompatible with life. If you meant a different term, please provide more context.

ageniocephalia.definition: Not a widely recognized medical term; etymology would suggest congenital absence of the chin within the head. Closest established concepts are agnathia (absence of the mandible) or micrognathia (a small mandible). If you have a spelling variant (e.g., agnathia, agenesis), I can look that up.

agnathia.definition: A rare congenital absence of the jaw (mandible), leading to an absent lower facial skeleton and typically associated with severe craniofacial anomalies.

agnathocephaly.definition: A rare congenital condition characterized by absence of the jaw (agnathia) with abnormal development of the head and facial structures, resulting in severe craniofacial deformities.

agnathocephalic.definition: Relating to the head in which the jaw is absent or underdeveloped; a jawless cephalic condition.

agnathocephalous.definition: Having a head that lacks jaws; jawless.

agnathous.definition: Lacking a jaw or jaws; jawless.

agnathus.definition: Relating to jawless vertebrates; lacking true jaws, as in jawless fishes such as lampreys and hagfishes.

agnosia.definition: A rare disease in which a person can’t recognize objects, shapes, or people. Often due to a brain or neurological condition.

autotopagnosia.definition: A neurological disorder in which a person cannot identify or point to parts of their own body on command, despite intact sensation and movement; typically due to parietal lobe damage and disruption of body schema (somatognosia).

paragnosia.definition: A nonstandard or rarely used term for a partial agnosia in which recognition of sensory stimuli is impaired despite preserved basic sensory perception, often modality-specific (e.g., visual object or facial recognition) after brain injury.

ageusia.definition: Complete loss of the sense of taste (gustation) due to dysfunction of taste receptors or gustatory pathways; can result from neural injury (eg, chorda tympani or glossopharyngeal nerve), zinc deficiency, medications, or viral infections.

gustatory anesthesia.definition: Temporary loss or impairment of taste sensation in the tongue due to anesthesia or injury of the gustatory pathways (most often from block or damage to chorda tympani fibers with the lingual nerve, or involvement of the glossopharyngeal nerve).

aggressive infantile fibromatosis.definition: A rare, benign but locally infiltrative fibrous tumor of infancy composed of proliferating myofibroblasts that forms rapidly enlarging soft-tissue masses, may invade adjacent tissues including bone, and tends to recur after treatment but does not metastasize.

aggressive periodontitis.definition: An early-onset, rapidly progressive form of periodontitis occurring in otherwise healthy individuals, characterized by rapid attachment loss and alveolar bone destruction disproportionate to plaque, often localized (first molars and incisors) or generalized and with a familial tendency; frequently associated with infection by Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans.

porphyria cutanea tarda.definition: A form of porphyria caused by deficient activity of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase, leading to hepatic overproduction and accumulation of porphyrins (especially uroporphyrin) and resulting in photosensitive blistering and fragility of sun-exposed skin, commonly on the dorsal hands; often associated with liver disease, iron overload, and certain drugs or alcohol use.

birth defects.definition: A problem that happens while a baby is developing in the mother's body, often very early in pregnancy. Birth defects affect how the body looks and works. They include heart disease, cleft lip, and Fragile X Syndrome.

otocephaly.definition: A rare, severe congenital craniofacial malformation arising from abnormal development of the first pharyngeal (branchial) arches, typically characterized by extreme mandibular deficiency or agenesis (agnathia) with malformations of the external ears; often described as the agnathia-otocephaly complex and usually lethal.

presbyopia.definition: When you can't see close up as you get older.

mental retardation.definition: An outdated label for a neurodevelopmental condition marked by significantly subaverage intellectual functioning and impairments in adaptive behavior, with onset during the developmental period (before age 18).

agitated depression.definition: A depressive episode with prominent psychomotor agitation—restlessness, inability to sit still, and pacing—occurring with typical depressive symptoms such as low mood and anhedonia; often seen in major depressive disorder with agitation or bipolar depression and can be associated with higher suicidality risk.

agitation.definition: An abnormal state of marked restlessness and increased motor activity with heightened emotional arousal, often with irritability or verbal/physical outbursts; commonly seen with delirium, anxiety, pain, withdrawal, intoxication, or other medical or psychiatric conditions.

snakebite.definition: Envenomation after a venomous snake bite, with venom injected by fangs; presentation ranges from local pain and swelling to systemic toxicity, depending on species; management includes assessment for envenomation and antivenom when indicated, with supportive care.

cortical cells.definition: Cells comprising the cerebral cortex, chiefly neurons and glial cells, involved in higher brain functions such as perception, cognition, and voluntary movement.

pyramidal cells.definition: A neuron with a pyramid-shaped soma, a long apical dendrite extending toward the pial surface, multiple basal dendrites, and a single axon; the principal excitatory projection neuron of the cerebral cortex and hippocampus, typically glutamatergic and involved in synaptic integration and long-range signaling.

lower jaw.definition: A U-shaped bone forming the lower jaw; the largest movable bone of the skull, consisting of a curved body with two rami, housing the lower teeth and articulating with the temporal bones at the temporomandibular joints to enable chewing and speech.

cranial vault.definition: A domed portion of the skull forming the skullcap that encloses the brain; the calvaria is formed by the frontal bone, the parietal bones, the squamous parts of the temporal bones, and the squamous part of the occipital bone.

zygomas.definition: Paired facial bones forming the cheekbones and part of the orbital rim; they articulate with the maxilla, temporal bone, frontal bone, and sphenoid.

agglutination.definition: The clumping together of particles (such as red blood cells or bacteria) caused by antibodies cross-linking their surface antigens; a basis for serologic agglutination tests.

agglutinin.definition: A substance, typically an antibody, that binds to antigens on the surface of particles (often red blood cells) causing them to clump together (agglutinate). Agglutinins are usually IgM or IgG antibodies involved in immune reactions and phenomena such as blood typing.

agglutinin absorption.definition: A laboratory technique in which specific agglutinins (antibodies that cause red cell agglutination) are removed from serum by adsorption onto antigen-bearing cells or other adsorbents, so that the remaining serum can be tested for other antibodies or to determine antibody specificity.

agglutination-inhibition test.definition: A serologic assay in which antibodies in a sample inhibit the agglutination of indicator particles by a specific antigen; the extent of inhibition correlates with the amount of antibody present, enabling detection or quantification of the antibody.

blood typing.definition: A laboratory test that determines a person's blood group by identifying red blood cell antigens (ABO and Rh); used to ensure safe transfusions and to assess pregnancy-related risks.

dioxin.definition: A member of the chlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxin family of persistent environmental pollutants; highly toxic compounds that bioaccumulate in fat and act by activating the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, causing chloracne, liver toxicity, immune and developmental effects, and increased cancer risk.

cholangiopathy.definition: A disease or disorder of the bile ducts (the biliary tree), which may involve injury, inflammation, obstruction, or cholestasis, and can be congenital or acquired.

agoraphobia.definition: Fear and avoidance of public places and open spaces.

agonal respiration.definition: An abnormal, irregular, gasping or labored breathing pattern seen in severe illness or during cardiac arrest, representing an ineffective or inadequate attempt at ventilation.

cheyne-stokes respiration.definition: An abnormal breathing pattern in which breathing cycles alternate between deep, rapid breaths and shallow breaths, often followed by a period of no breathing (apnea).

agranulocytosis.definition: A severe decrease in circulating neutrophils (neutropenia), typically with an absolute neutrophil count below about 500 cells per microliter, leading to a high risk of life-threatening infections; commonly drug-induced.
