allochesthesia.definition: A mislocalization of a sensory stimulus; the sensation is perceived as arising from a different part of the body than the area actually stimulated.

allantois.definition: An extraembryonic membrane derived from the caudal yolk sac that extends into the connecting stalk; it contributes to the formation of the umbilical vessels and the urachus, and is vestigial in humans after birth.

allantoidoangiopagus.definition: A form of conjoined twinning in which the twins are joined through the allantoic membranes and share a substantial vascular connection.

omphaloangiopagus.definition: An extremely rare form of conjoined twinning in which the two fetuses are joined at the umbilical region with shared vascular connections between their circulations, often with some shared abdominal organs such as the liver.

allen's test.definition: A quick bedside test to assess collateral circulation and patency of the hand’s arterial supply by temporarily occluding the radial and ulnar arteries at the wrist, having the patient make a fist to blanch the hand, then releasing one artery to observe the return of color; prompt flushing indicates adequate collateral flow through the palmar arches.

allen-doisy test.definition: Definition not found in standard medical dictionaries. It may be a misnomer or a historical/field-specific term. If you can share the context (medical specialty) or confirm the spelling/capitalization, I can help more. Alternatively, you might mean "Allen's test" (hand vascular patency) or a separate "Doisy test."

patch test.definition: A test used to diagnose whether a rash was caused by a reaction to certain allergens, such as poison ivy or a cosmetic ingredient, or an irritant such as soap.

scratch test.definition: A diagnostic skin test in which small amounts of suspected allergens are scratched or pricked into the epidermis to elicit a local IgE-mediated reaction; a positive result is indicated by a raised, itchy wheal with surrounding redness within about 15–20 minutes.

radioallergosorbent test.definition: A blood test used for identifying allergens.

prausnitz-küstner test.definition: A historical skin test for immediate-type hypersensitivity in which serum from a patient is injected intradermally into a healthy volunteer; the suspected allergen is then injected at the same site. A wheal-and-flare reaction indicates the presence of allergen-specific IgE antibodies in the patient's serum.

allergen.definition: Something, like pollen, dust, mold, or animal dander, that causes a reaction in your body, such as a rash or sneezing.

allergen extract.definition: A prepared solution containing allergenic proteins from a defined source (e.g., pollen, dust mites, foods, venom) used for allergy diagnosis (such as skin testing) and for allergen immunotherapy (desensitization); potency is standardized to defined units.

allergenic.definition: Capable of triggering an allergic reaction in susceptible individuals, typically by inducing an IgE-mediated immune response.

allergic rhinitis.definition: Caused by your body's reaction in your nose to mold, pollen, or dust. Also called hay fever.

allergic conjunctivitis.definition: Inflammation of the conjunctiva caused by an IgE-mediated allergic reaction to environmental allergens (e.g., pollen, dust mites, pet dander), presenting with itching, redness, tearing, and eyelid swelling; commonly seasonal or perennial and often associated with other atopic diseases.

allergic dermatitis.definition: An inflammatory skin condition caused by a sensitized individual’s immune reaction to a contact allergen (delayed-type hypersensitivity), presenting with pruritic, erythematous, vesicular or oozing lesions at the contact site.

allergic granulomatosis.definition: A systemic vasculitis of small- to medium-sized vessels characterized by eosinophilia, asthma or allergic rhinitis, and necrotizing granulomatous inflammation; commonly affects the lungs, skin, nerves, and heart; historically known as Churg–Strauss syndrome and now referred to as eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA).

churg-strauss syndrome.definition: A systemic necrotizing vasculitis of small- to medium-sized vessels characterized by adult-onset asthma, marked eosinophilia, and granulomatous inflammation with eosinophilic tissue infiltration, leading to multi-organ involvement (commonly lungs, skin, nerves, and heart). It is now termed eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) and is part of the ANCA-associated vasculitides.

allergic interstitial nephritis.definition: An acute inflammatory condition of the renal interstitium, most often a drug-induced hypersensitivity reaction, characterized by interstitial edema and infiltration of inflammatory cells (classically eosinophils) leading to impaired kidney function; management centers on stopping the offending drug and providing supportive care (corticosteroids may be used in selected cases).

allergic interstitial pneumonitis.definition: A hypersensitivity-type interstitial lung disease caused by an allergic immune reaction to inhaled environmental antigens (eg, birds, moldy hay, certain chemicals). It features inflammation of the interstitium and alveolar spaces (alveolitis) and may include noncaseating granulomas; clinically presents with cough and dyspnea (acute, subacute, or chronic) and may show restrictive lung physiology and diffuse infiltrates on imaging. Management centers on avoidance of the offending antigen, with corticosteroids used for symptomatic or progressive disease.

allergic proctitis.definition: Inflammation of the rectal mucosa caused by a hypersensitivity (allergic) reaction to an external agent, such as rectal medications or irritants, presenting with anal itching, pain or burning, mucus discharge, and sometimes bleeding; management centers on avoiding the offending agent and providing symptom relief.

allergic gastroenteropathy.definition: A gastrointestinal disorder caused by an immune-mediated hypersensitivity to dietary antigens (most commonly cow's milk or other food proteins) that leads to symptoms such as chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, vomiting, and malabsorption with possible growth or weight faltering; managed by dietary avoidance and confirmation with elimination and food challenges.

allergic purpura.definition: A small-vessel vasculitis due to IgA immune complex deposition (IgA vasculitis) presenting with palpable purpura, typically on the lower extremities, often accompanied by arthralgia, abdominal pain, and potential renal involvement, and usually following an infection or drug exposure.

allergic vasculitis.definition: A hypersensitivity-driven small-vessel vasculitis (immune complex–mediated) that occurs after exposure to an allergen, drug, or infection, commonly presenting with palpable purpura and histology showing leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.definition: A hypersensitivity reaction to colonization of the airways by Aspergillus species (most commonly A. fumigatus) in individuals with asthma or cystic fibrosis, leading to eosinophilia, elevated IgE (and Aspergillus-specific IgE/IgG), recurrent pulmonary infiltrates and mucus plugging, bronchial inflammation, and often central bronchiectasis.

aspergillus fumigatus.definition: An airborne filamentous fungus and the most common cause of aspergillosis in humans; a saprophytic mold found in soil and decaying vegetation; inhalation of its conidia can trigger allergic reactions, colonization of the respiratory tract, and, in immunocompromised individuals, invasive pulmonary or disseminated infection.

charcot-leyden crystals.definition: Hexagonal bipyramidal crystals formed from the eosinophil-derived protein galectin-10 (Charcot-Leyden crystal protein); they arise with eosinophil degranulation/lysis and are seen in secretions or tissues during eosinophilic inflammation, such as in asthma, allergic diseases, and parasitic infections.

hay fever.definition: An IgE-mediated allergic condition (allergic rhinitis) characterized by sneezing, itching, nasal congestion, and runny nose, often with itchy, watery eyes, triggered by environmental allergens such as pollen.

pollen.definition: A fine powder produced by the male reproductive organs of seed plants (stamens in flowering plants; cones in conifers) that contains the male gametophyte; dispersed by wind or animals to enable fertilization and commonly acts as an environmental allergen.

house dust.definition: A mixture of fine particles that accumulates indoors, primarily skin scales, fibers, and other organic debris, plus dust mites and their feces, insect fragments, pet dander, mold spores, pollen, and other organic and inorganic matter; a major source of indoor allergens associated with allergic rhinitis, asthma, and dermatitis.

animal dander.definition: Small airborne particles made up of shed animal skin (commonly from cats and dogs) that can act as allergens, triggering IgE-mediated reactions and symptoms such as sneezing, nasal congestion, itchy or watery eyes, and asthma in sensitive individuals.

mold.definition: Very small growths on food and damp surfaces. They can be harmful to your health.

hyposensitization.definition: A treatment to reduce an individual’s sensitivity to an allergen by gradually increasing exposure to it, thereby desensitizing the immune system and decreasing allergic symptoms (commonly referred to as allergen immunotherapy, delivered by injections or sublingual methods).

mast cells.definition: Mast cells are tissue-resident immune cells derived from hematopoietic stem cells that contain cytoplasmic granules rich in histamine, heparin, and proteases and express high-affinity IgE receptors; upon activation they degranulate, releasing mediators that mediate allergic reactions, inflammation, and defense against parasites.

histamine.definition: A biogenic amine derived from histidine that is released by mast cells and basophils during allergic and inflammatory responses; it increases vascular permeability, causes vasodilation, and stimulates gastric acid secretion, acting on histamine receptors (H1–H4).

bronchial tree.definition: The bronchial tree is the branching system of airways within the lungs that conducts air from the trachea to the bronchioles. It begins with the right and left main (primary) bronchi, which give rise to lobar (secondary) and segmental (tertiary) bronchi and continue as progressively smaller bronchi and bronchioles, forming the conducting airways and conditioning air for gas exchange.

bronchial mucosa.definition: The mucous membrane lining the bronchi, composed of pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells over a lamina propria (often with submucosal glands in larger bronchi). It functions in mucociliary clearance by producing mucus and moving it toward the pharynx to trap and remove inhaled particles and pathogens.

allergic alveolitis.definition: An immune-mediated inflammatory reaction of the alveoli (hypersensitivity pneumonitis) caused by inhaled environmental organic antigens (e.g., moldy hay, bird proteins), leading to alveolar inflammation and symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and fever with diffuse interstitial changes.

diffuse hypersensitivity pneumonia.definition: An immune-mediated interstitial lung disease caused by inhalation of environmental antigens (e.g., mold spores, bird or animal proteins) that leads to diffuse alveolitis and interstitial inflammation. It can present acutely after exposure with fever, cough, and dyspnea, or chronically with progressive dyspnea and possible fibrosis. Management focuses on avoiding the offending antigen; corticosteroids may be used for symptomatic or severe cases.

hypersensitivity pneumonitis.definition: An immune‑mediated interstitial lung disease caused by inhalation of environmental organic antigens (e.g., moldy hay, bird proteins) that induces alveolitis with granulomatous inflammation; exposure leads to acute/subacute flu‑like symptoms (fever, cough, dyspnea) and may progress to chronic fibrotic lung disease with ongoing exposure.

body stalk.definition: A narrow embryonic connection between the developing embryo and the chorion that contains primitive umbilical vessels and extraembryonic mesoderm; it later forms the umbilical cord.

umbilical cord.definition: A flexible, tube-like structure that connects the developing fetus to the placenta, containing two arteries and one vein encased in Wharton’s jelly; it transports oxygenated blood and nutrients from the placenta to the fetus and returns deoxygenated blood and waste from the fetus to the placenta.

umbilical vessels.definition: The two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein in the umbilical cord that connect the fetus to the placenta; they transport blood between the fetus and placenta—arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta, and the vein carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus.

yolk sac.definition: A membranous extraembryonic structure derived from the hypoblast that surrounds the early yolk; in humans it is the site of primitive hematopoiesis (early blood cell formation), contributes to germ cell development, and helps form the primitive gut; its function diminishes as placental nourishment becomes established.

chorionic villi.definition: Fingerlike projections of the chorion that extend into the maternal endometrium, forming the placental villous tree and containing fetal blood vessels to enable nutrient, gas, and waste exchange between mother and fetus.

vascular hypertension.definition: Chronic elevation of pressure within the arterial vasculature (often systemic arterial hypertension or, in the pulmonary circuit, pulmonary hypertension), typically due to increased vascular resistance and/or increased blood volume, and associated with risk of target-organ damage if untreated.

acute interstitial nephritis.definition: An acute kidney injury caused by inflammation and edema of the renal interstitium, usually a hypersensitivity reaction to medications (e.g., penicillins, cephalosporins, NSAIDs, rifampin) or infections. It presents with fever, rash, eosinophilia, and sterile pyuria or hematuria, with a rise in serum creatinine; management centers on stopping the offending agent and providing supportive care, with corticosteroids reserved for persistent or severe cases.

kidney stones.definition: A solid piece of material that forms in the kidney from material in the urine. They can be tiny or large. While most kidney stones pass without help sometimes a stone will get stuck, blocking urine and causing great pain.

dexamethasone.definition: A potent synthetic glucocorticoid corticosteroid with anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressant effects; used to treat inflammatory and autoimmune conditions, severe allergic reactions, certain cancers, cerebral edema, and to prevent chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.

glottis.definition: The opening between the true vocal folds (vocal cords) in the larynx; its size is adjusted by the laryngeal muscles to regulate airflow for breathing and sound production, and it closes to protect the airway.

alloplasty.definition: A surgical reconstruction or repair of a body part using tissue grafts from a donor (allograft) or implantation of a prosthetic material, as opposed to using the patient’s own tissue.

gout.definition: A form of inflammatory arthritis caused by deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints and soft tissues due to hyperuricemia, characterized by sudden, severe joint pain, swelling, and redness, often starting in the big toe (podagra).

malignancy.definition: A malignant neoplasm; a cancerous tumor that invades surrounding tissue and can metastasize to distant sites.

islet.definition: A small cluster of endocrine cells in the pancreas that secretes hormones such as insulin and glucagon to regulate blood glucose.

migraine.definition: A primary headache disorder characterized by recurrent, typically unilateral, pulsating headaches lasting 4–72 hours, accompanied by nausea and/or vomiting and photophobia or phonophobia, and worsened by routine activity; may occur with or without an aura (reversible neurological symptoms preceding the headache).

almotriptan.definition: An oral triptan medication that acts as a selective 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonist for the acute treatment of migraine, causing cranial vasoconstriction and inhibition of neuropeptide release.

prausnitz-küstner.definition: A historical skin test (passive cutaneous anaphylaxis) in which serum from an allergic person containing IgE is injected into the skin of a nonallergic recipient, who is then challenged with the allergen to produce a local wheal-and-flare reaction, demonstrating IgE-mediated hypersensitivity.

radioallergosorbent.definition: An allergen-coated solid phase (sorbent) used in the radioallergosorbent test to capture allergen-specific IgE antibodies from a patient's serum, enabling measurement by radiolabeled detection.

conjunctival.definition: Of or relating to the conjunctiva, the thin mucous membrane that covers the sclera (front of the eyeball) and lines the inner surfaces of the eyelids.

intradermal.definition: Located in or administered into the dermis, the layer of skin beneath the epidermis and above the subcutaneous tissue.

patch.definition: A small adhesive device or skin-applied material used to deliver a drug through the skin over time, or to test for allergic reactions; in dermatology it can also refer to a flat, nonpalpable area of skin larger than 1 cm in diameter.

allogeneic.definition: Relating to or derived from a donor who is genetically different from the recipient but of the same species, as in allogeneic organ, tissue, or cell transplantation.

homograft.definition: A graft of tissue or an organ obtained from a donor of the same species and transplanted into a recipient; also known as an allograft.

isograft.definition: A graft transplanted between genetically identical individuals of the same species (e.g., between monozygotic twins); typically free from immunologic rejection due to identical genetic makeup.

autograft.definition: A graft of tissue harvested from one part of a patient's body and transplanted to another part of the same patient; it reduces rejection risk because the tissue is autologous.

isoantigen.definition: An antigen that is present in some individuals of a species but absent in others; when encountered by a genetically different individual, it can trigger an immune response (alloimmunity), as in transfusion, transplantation, or pregnancy incompatibility.

dyscrasia.definition: An abnormality or disorder of the blood or its cellular components (red cells, white cells, or platelets), often referring to a disturbance in hematopoiesis or blood cell function.

dermographia.definition: A benign form of physical urticaria in which stroking or scratching the skin induces linear wheals and redness (often called "skin writing"), caused by histamine release from cutaneous mast cells; lesions typically appear within minutes and resolve within about 1–2 hours.

inflammation.definition: Redness or swelling of the body while it tries to heal or fight off bacteria and viruses.

antibiotic.definition: A drug used to treat bacterial infections.

dust.definition: A fine, dry collection of particles suspended in air; inhalation can irritate the respiratory tract and provoke coughing or allergic reactions, and ongoing exposure to certain dusts can contribute to occupational or environmental lung diseases.

alopecia areata.definition: An autoimmune condition that appears as patchy hair loss on the scalp that may result in permanent hair loss.

alopecia totalis.definition: Hair loss that involves the entire scalp.

alopecia universalis.definition: Hair loss that involves the entire body.

alopecia toxica.definition: A form of diffuse hair loss due to exposure to toxic substances (such as certain medications, chemicals, or poisons) that damages hair follicles; it is typically non-scarring and often reversible after removal of the toxin, with mechanisms including toxic injury to rapidly dividing hair matrix cells (anagen effluvium) or disruption of the hair growth cycle.

aloxi.definition: Brand-name antiemetic containing palonosetron; a selective serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonist used to prevent chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting and postoperative nausea and vomiting.

palonosetron.definition: A selective 5-HT3 receptor antagonist antiemetic used to prevent both acute and delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting and postoperative nausea and vomiting; it has a long half-life, enabling single-dose regimens.

alpha-adrenergic receptor.definition: A class of G protein–coupled receptors activated by catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine); they include alpha-1 receptors (Gq/11) that promote vasoconstriction and smooth muscle contraction by increasing intracellular calcium, and alpha-2 receptors (Gi/o) that inhibit adenylyl cyclase, decrease cAMP, and reduce neurotransmitter release.

alpha1-antitrypsin.definition: A liver-produced serine protease inhibitor that protects lung tissue by inhibiting neutrophil elastase; inherited deficiency due to SERPINA1 gene mutations increases the risk of early-onset emphysema and liver disease.

alpha1-antitrypsin test.definition: A blood test that measures the level of alpha-1 antitrypsin in the blood, used to diagnose alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and to identify genetic variants (phenotype/genotype) that affect risk of lung and liver disease.

alpha1-proteinase inhibitor.definition: An inherited liver-produced serine protease inhibitor (serpin) that inhibits neutrophil elastase (and other proteases) in the lungs, protecting pulmonary tissue from proteolytic damage; deficiency leads to early-onset emphysema and may be associated with liver disease; replacement therapy is used for deficiency.

alpha2-interferon.definition: A subtype of type I interferon produced mainly by leukocytes; a cytokine with antiviral, antiproliferative, and immunomodulatory effects, used clinically as interferon alfa-2a or alfa-2b for certain viral infections and malignancies.

alphavirus.definition: A genus of enveloped, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses in the Togaviridae family, transmitted by arthropods (primarily mosquitoes); causes arboviral diseases in humans such as fever, rash, and joint pain, and includes notable pathogens like chikungunya virus, Sindbis virus, and Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus.

afp.definition: A fetal plasma protein produced by the yolk sac and fetal liver; in adults it serves as a tumor marker for hepatocellular carcinoma and germ cell tumors, and elevated maternal levels during pregnancy can signal neural tube defects or other fetal anomalies.

alt.definition: A liver enzyme that catalyzes the transamination of L-alanine to pyruvate and α-ketoglutarate to glutamate; elevated blood levels suggest hepatocellular injury.

ataxia-telangiectasia syndrome.definition: An autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder caused by biallelic mutations in the ATM gene, presenting with progressive cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasias, immunodeficiency with recurrent infections, a markedly increased risk of malignancies, and hypersensitivity to ionizing radiation.

alport's syndrome.definition: A hereditary nephropathy caused by defects in type IV collagen (COL4A5, COL4A3, COL4A4) leading to progressive kidney disease with persistent hematuria; often associated with sensorineural hearing loss and ocular abnormalities (e.g., anterior lenticonus).

alström's syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal recessive ciliopathy due to ALMS1 mutations, characterized by early-onset cone-rod dystrophy with vision loss, obesity and insulin resistance/diabetes, sensorineural hearing loss, dilated cardiomyopathy, hepatic and renal dysfunction, and short stature.

alpha-methyldopa.definition: An antihypertensive drug that is a prodrug converted to alpha-methyl norepinephrine, a central alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that decreases central sympathetic outflow to reduce vascular resistance and lower blood pressure; commonly used to treat hypertension in pregnancy.

alpha-thalassemia.definition: An inherited blood disorder caused by deletions or mutations of the alpha-globin genes (HBA1 and HBA2) on chromosome 16, leading to reduced synthesis of alpha-globin chains and imbalanced globin production; clinical severity depends on the number of gene deletions, ranging from silent carrier (one deleted) or alpha-thalassemia trait (two deletions) to HbH disease (three deletions) with chronic hemolytic anemia, to hydrops fetalis when all four genes are deleted (usually fatal in infancy).

alpha-tocopherol.definition: Most biologically active form of vitamin E; a fat-soluble antioxidant that protects cell membranes from lipid peroxidation by neutralizing lipid radicals.

alpha wave.definition: An EEG rhythm of about 8–12 Hz seen during relaxed wakefulness, especially with eyes closed; most prominent in the occipital cortex and reduced with eye opening or mental activity.

alpha particle.definition: A positively charged helium-4 nucleus (two protons and two neutrons) emitted in radioactive decay; it has a +2e charge, high ionizing power, and a short range in matter (stopped by a sheet of paper or skin).

alpha-l-fucosidase.definition: A lysosomal hydrolase that hydrolyzes terminal α-L-fucose residues from fucosylated glycoproteins and glycolipids; deficiency causes fucosidosis, a rare autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder.

alpha-aminoisovaleric acid.definition: A branched-chain essential amino acid; chemical name 2-amino-3-methylbutanoic acid; required in the human diet for protein synthesis and nitrogen balance; catabolized to enter the citric acid cycle (e.g., as succinyl-CoA). Formula: C5H11NO2.

pancreatic islets.definition: A cluster of endocrine cells in the pancreas (islets of Langerhans) that secrete hormones—primarily insulin and glucagon, but also somatostatin and pancreatic polypeptide—into the bloodstream to regulate blood glucose.

glucagon.definition: A hormone produced by pancreatic alpha cells that raises blood glucose by promoting hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; counterregulatory to insulin; used clinically to treat severe hypoglycemia and to facilitate certain radiologic imaging procedures.

hepatocellular carcinoma.definition: A primary malignant tumor of the liver arising from hepatocytes, typically in a chronically diseased or cirrhotic liver; risk factors include hepatitis B or C infection, alcohol-related liver disease, and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. It often invades hepatic vessels and can metastasize.

hepatoma.definition: A malignant tumor of liver cells (hepatocytes); the most common primary liver cancer, usually arising in a cirrhotic or chronically damaged liver.

neural tube defects.definition: A group of congenital malformations resulting from failure of the neural tube to close properly during early embryonic development, leading to defective brain and/or spinal cord formation; examples include anencephaly and spina bifida. Many can be prevented with adequate maternal folic acid intake before conception and in early pregnancy.

spina bifida.definition: A congenital defect in which part of the spinal column fails to develop completely, leaving part of the spinal cord exposed.

anencephaly.definition: A birth defect in which an infant is born without most of the brain or without the skull bones covering the brain.

ischemic.definition: Relating to reduced blood flow to a tissue or organ, causing insufficient oxygen and nutrient delivery and potentially leading to cellular injury or death.

intracranial bleeding.definition: Bleeding within the cranial cavity from ruptured blood vessels, which may involve brain tissue (intracerebral hemorrhage) or spaces around the brain (epidural, subdural, or subarachnoid hemorrhages) or the ventricular system.

intracranial trauma.definition: Injury to the brain and other intracranial structures caused by mechanical energy transmitted to the skull from an external force, resulting in focal injuries (contusions, hematomas, lacerations) and/or diffuse brain injury with potential neurological deficits.

brain tumor.definition: A brain tumor is an abnormal growth of cells within the brain that can be benign (noncancerous) or malignant (cancerous); it may arise from brain tissue or represent metastatic cancer from another site and can cause symptoms by pressing on or invading brain structures, disrupting normal function.

retroperitoneal bleeding.definition: Bleeding into the retroperitoneal space, the area behind the peritoneum; commonly due to trauma, rupture of retroperitoneal vessels or organs (e.g., aneurysm, renal injury), or iatrogenic causes, and may present with back or flank pain, abdominal pain, hypotension, anemia, and a delayed or difficult-to-detect hematoma.

gi bleeding.definition: Bleeding occurring anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract, manifesting as hematemesis (vomiting blood), melena (black, tarry stools), hematochezia (passage of fresh blood per rectum), or occult blood in stool; classified as upper GI bleeding (proximal to the ligament of Treitz) or lower GI bleeding (distal to it).

gastrointestinal bleeding.definition: Gastrointestinal bleeding is the loss of blood from any part of the gastrointestinal tract (from the esophagus to the anus), which may present as hematemesis (vomiting blood), melena (black, tarry stools), or hematochezia (bright red or maroon stools); it can be overt or occult and ranges from mild to life-threatening.

tetralogy of fallot.definition: A cyanotic congenital heart defect defined by four anatomical abnormalities: a ventricular septal defect, pulmonary (outflow) tract obstruction (pulmonary stenosis), an overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy.

tricuspid atresia.definition: A congenital heart defect in which the tricuspid valve is absent or imperforate, resulting in a hypoplastic right ventricle and reliance on an atrial (and usually a ventricular) septal defect to allow blood to reach the pulmonary circulation, causing mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood and often cyanosis; typically treated with staged surgical palliation.

idioventricular rhythm.definition: A ventricular escape rhythm originating from the Purkinje system or ventricular myocardium, with a slow rate (about 20–40 beats per minute), wide QRS complexes, and typically absent or dissociated P waves; it occurs when higher‑order pacemakers fail (e.g., due to complete heart block or severe bradycardia) and can be seen in acute myocardial infarction or other causes of reduced conduction. It may require urgent intervention if symptomatic.

neoplasms.definition: An abnormal, uncontrolled growth of tissue arising from neoplastic transformation of cells, forming a discrete mass that can be benign (noninvasive and often well-differentiated) or malignant (invasive and capable of metastasis).

teratomas.definition: A germ cell tumor composed of tissues derived from two or more embryonic germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm); often contains differentiated tissues such as skin, hair, or teeth, and can be mature (benign) or immature (potentially malignant, with malignant potential). Most commonly arises in the ovaries or testes, but can occur in midline locations such as the sacrococcygeal region.

hodgkins disease.definition: A malignant lymphoma characterized by the presence of Reed-Sternberg cells; typically presents with painless lymphadenopathy (often in the neck or chest) and B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss); generally has a favorable prognosis with modern treatment.

lymphoma.definition: Cancer of lymphatic system, an important part of your immune system.

alveolar.definition: Relating to an alveolus, a small cavity or socket in bone or tissue; in dentistry, to the dental alveolar bone surrounding a tooth socket, and in the lungs, to the tiny air sacs (alveoli) where gas exchange occurs.

alveolus.definition: A small air-filled sac in the lung where gas exchange occurs between inhaled air and the blood; lined by a thin epithelium, coated with surfactant, and surrounded by a dense capillary network.

alveolar bone.definition: The part of the jawbone that supports the teeth.

alveolar ridge.definition: A bony ridge of the jaw that contains the tooth sockets (alveoli) and forms the supporting alveolar process for the teeth.

alveolar socket.definition: A bony cavity in the jawbone's alveolar process that houses and supports the root of a tooth.

alveolar canal.definition: A bony passage in the jawbone that contains the neurovascular bundle supplying the teeth; most commonly, the mandibular canal carries the inferior alveolar nerve and vessels.

dental canal.definition: An internal hollow space within a tooth that houses the dental pulp (nerve and vessels), extending from the pulp chamber in the crown to the root apex; it is responsible for tooth sensation and nourishment and can become inflamed or infected (pulpitis), often requiring root canal therapy.

cementoenamel junction.definition: The anatomical boundary where enamel of the crown meets cementum of the root at the cervical region of a tooth; it marks the interface between crown and root and serves as a landmark for assessing periodontal attachment and recession.

cementum.definition: A hard covering of the outside of the root of your tooth below the gum line.

periodontal ligament.definition: A dense, vascularized connective tissue located in the periodontal space between cementum and the alveolar bone; anchors the tooth to the bone via collagen fibers (Sharpey's fibers), cushions occlusal forces, and houses vessels, nerves, and cells involved in remodeling of the periodontium.

alveolar periosteum.definition: The periosteum covering the alveolar bone of the jaws—the dense fibrous membrane lining the tooth sockets; it has an outer fibrous layer and an inner cellular layer with osteogenic cells, supplies blood and nerves, and participates in remodeling of the alveolar process and anchoring the periodontal ligament.

periosteum.definition: An outer, vascular membrane that covers the surface of a bone (except where cartilage is present at joints); it comprises an outer fibrous layer and an inner cellular (osteogenic) layer containing osteoblasts and progenitor cells. It provides blood supply and nutrients to bone, participates in growth in thickness (appositional growth) and fracture repair, and serves as the attachment site for tendons and ligaments.

alveolar crest.definition: The most coronal edge of the alveolar bone that forms the tooth-supporting ridge around the tooth roots; the crest of the alveolar process (typically about 1–2 mm apical to the cementoenamel junction in a healthy dentition).

alveolar crestal fiber.definition: A principal group of periodontal ligament fibers that extends from cementum near the cemento-enamel junction to the alveolar crest, helping stabilize the tooth in its socket and maintain the height of the alveolar crest.

alveolar capillary membrane.definition: A very thin barrier between the air-filled alveolus and the surrounding pulmonary capillary blood, formed by the alveolar epithelium (primarily type I pneumocytes), the capillary endothelium, and their fused basement membranes; it facilitates gas exchange by diffusion of oxygen into blood and carbon dioxide into the alveolus.

alveolar-capillary membrane.definition: A thin barrier formed by alveolar epithelium (primarily type I pneumocytes), the capillary endothelium, and their fused basement membranes (the respiratory membrane); it separates air in the alveolus from the blood and facilitates gas exchange (O2 and CO2).

alveolar septum.definition: The thin wall separating adjacent alveoli, composed of alveolar epithelium (primarily type I pneumocytes), a fused basement membrane, and surrounding interstitium containing capillaries; forms part of the alveolar–capillary barrier essential for gas exchange.

interalveolar septum.definition: The thin wall separating adjacent alveoli in the lung, formed by the alveolar epithelium (primarily type I pneumocytes) with its fused basement membranes and underlying interstitial connective tissue, containing a dense network of pulmonary capillaries that facilitates gas exchange.

alveolar macrophage.definition: A resident phagocytic macrophage located in the alveolar airspaces of the lung, derived from monocytes, that engulfs inhaled particles, microbes, and excess surfactant to maintain alveolar sterility and homeostasis.

alveolar microlithiasis.definition: A rare autosomal recessive lung disorder in which calcium phosphate microliths accumulate within the alveolar spaces, often due to mutations in a phosphate transporter gene (e.g., SLC34A2), producing a diffuse “sandstorm” chest radiograph pattern and progressive dyspnea.

alveolar proteinosis.definition: A rare lung disease in which surfactant-derived lipoprotein accumulates within the alveoli because alveolar macrophages fail to clear it, leading to impaired gas exchange and progressive dyspnea; it can be autoimmune (GM-CSF autoantibodies) or secondary to exposures or other underlying conditions.

alveolar edema.definition: Fluid accumulation within the alveolar air spaces of the lungs, causing impaired gas exchange and hypoxemia; commonly due to cardiogenic heart failure (increased hydrostatic pressure) or noncardiogenic injury that increases alveolar-capillary permeability.

alveolar ventilation.definition: The volume of air per unit time that reaches the alveoli and participates in gas exchange, calculated as (tidal volume − dead space) × respiratory rate.

alveolar gas.definition: The gas mixture occupying the alveolar spaces; the air in the lungs after gas exchange with pulmonary capillary blood, with lower oxygen and higher carbon dioxide than inspired air, reflecting the balance of alveolar ventilation and perfusion.

alveolar gas volume.definition: The volume of gas contained in the alveoli that participates in gas exchange—the portion of inspired air that reaches the alveolar sacs after dead space is accounted for.

alveolar-arterial gas pressure differenc.definition: Difference between the alveolar oxygen tension (PAO2) and arterial oxygen tension (PaO2); a measure of the efficiency of pulmonary gas exchange (PAO2 − PaO2). Normal values are small (roughly 5–15 mm Hg on room air) and increase with age; an elevated gradient suggests V/Q mismatch, diffusion impairment, or shunt.

alveolar-arterial end-capillary gas pres.definition: The difference between the alveolar oxygen partial pressure (PAO2) and the arterial oxygen partial pressure (PaO2); a measure of the efficiency of oxygen transfer from the alveoli to the blood, with higher values indicating impaired gas exchange.

alveolar carcinoma.definition: An historical term for a lung adenocarcinoma characterized by malignant cells spreading along the alveolar walls (lepidic growth) with little or no invasion; in modern WHO classification these lesions are categorized as adenocarcinoma in situ or invasive adenocarcinomas with lepidic features (including mucinous and non-mucinous subtypes).

alveolar cell carcinoma.definition: An older term for a malignant tumor of the lung arising from alveolar cells; historically used for bronchioloalveolar carcinoma, now reclassified as a form of pulmonary adenocarcinoma (often mucinous or non-mucinous) depending on histology and invasion.

alveolar adenocarcinoma.definition: A malignant neoplasm of the lung arising from gland-forming epithelial cells, typically peripheral and often mucin-producing; historically termed bronchioloalveolar carcinoma, with current classification including adenocarcinoma in situ and lepidic-predominant invasive adenocarcinoma.

alveolar air.definition: The gas mixture inside the alveoli of the lungs, the site of external respiration; it is humidified and has a composition different from inspired air, with roughly 13–14% O2 and about 5% CO2 (the remainder being mostly nitrogen), corresponding to alveolar partial pressures of O2 around 100 mmHg and CO2 around 40 mmHg.

alveolar air equation.definition: A formula that estimates alveolar oxygen tension (PAO2) from inspired oxygen fraction (FiO2) and other constants: PAO2 ≈ FiO2 (PB − PH2O) − PaCO2/R, where PB is barometric pressure, PH2O is water vapor pressure, PaCO2 is arterial CO2, and R is the respiratory quotient; used to assess gas exchange and the alveolar–arterial gradient.

alveolar period.definition: A developmental phase in dentistry during which the alveolar process of the jaws forms and remodels to accommodate erupting teeth and provide their support.

alveolar cyst.definition: A cystic lesion within the alveolar bone of the jaw (the tooth sockets), typically benign and lined by epithelium; may arise from odontogenic tissues or inflammatory processes.

alveolar dead space.definition: That portion of the tidal volume consisting of alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused, so gas exchange does not occur; a component of physiologic dead space.

alveolar fistula.definition: A chronic draining sinus tract that communicates between a periapical dental infection (often from pulpal necrosis) and the oral mucosa over the alveolar ridge, allowing pus to drain onto the gingiva or alveolar mucosa.

altitude sickness.definition: An acute altitude-related illness that occurs after rapid ascent to high altitude (typically above about 2,500 meters/8,000 feet) due to hypobaric hypoxia and inadequate acclimatization. It usually presents within hours to a day with headache and at least one of nausea/vomiting, fatigue, dizziness, insomnia, or loss of appetite; mild cases improve with rest and acclimatization or descent, while severe forms—high-altitude cerebral edema and high-altitude pulmonary edema—are life-threatening and require urgent descent and medical care.

acute mountain sickness.definition: A syndrome of altitude illness caused by inadequate acclimatization after rapid ascent to high altitude, usually within hours to a day, presenting with headache plus fatigue, dizziness, nausea or vomiting, and sleep disturbance; commonly occurring above about 2,500–3,000 meters (8,200–9,800 feet).

altitude anoxia.definition: A condition of near-complete oxygen deprivation to body tissues caused by exposure to very high altitude, due to extremely low inspired oxygen partial pressure.

alupent.definition: A bronchodilator medication (metaproterenol sulfate), a short-acting nonselective beta-adrenergic agonist used to treat or prevent acute bronchospasm in asthma and other obstructive airway diseases; it relaxes airway smooth muscle by stimulating beta-adrenergic receptors.

metaproterenol sulfate.definition: A beta-adrenergic agonist bronchodilator (sulfate salt) used to relieve bronchospasm in asthma and other obstructive airway diseases; it stimulates beta-2 receptors in bronchial smooth muscle to cause relaxation and bronchodilation.

aluminum hydroxide.definition: An inorganic compound (Al(OH)3) used medically as an oral antacid to neutralize stomach acid and as a phosphate binder in chronic kidney disease; it is poorly absorbed from the GI tract and may cause aluminum toxicity with prolonged high-dose use; also used as a vaccine adjuvant in some formulations.

aluminum oxide.definition: An inorganic compound of aluminum and oxygen (Al2O3); a hard, thermally stable, chemically inert oxide used as an industrial abrasive and as a ceramic/bioceramic material in some medical implants and dental applications.

aluminum acetate solution.definition: A topical astringent solution containing aluminum acetate used as soaks or compresses to relieve itching and inflammation in minor skin irritations (such as dermatitis and poison ivy/oak reactions); commonly sold as Burow's solution.

aluminum hydroxychloride.definition: An inorganic aluminum salt containing hydroxide and chloride ligands; used topically as an astringent and antiperspirant ingredient in dermatologic and cosmetic products.

aluminum salts.definition: A group of aluminum-containing inorganic compounds (for example aluminum hydroxide and aluminum phosphate) used medicinally as antacids to neutralize gastric acid, as topical astringents, and as vaccine adjuvants.

burow’s solution.definition: An astringent topical solution of aluminum acetate in water, used as wet dressings or soaks to relieve itching, inflammation, and discharge in inflammatory skin conditions such as dermatitis and contact dermatitis (e.g., poison ivy).

antineoplastic agent.definition: A drug used in oncology to treat cancer by inhibiting or killing malignant cells; includes cytotoxic chemotherapy agents, targeted therapies that block specific molecular pathways, hormonal therapies, and immunotherapies.

induction therapy.definition: An initial treatment phase aimed at rapidly reducing disease burden and inducing remission or significant disease control, usually given before definitive local therapy or consolidation; in oncology, it typically uses chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy.

ovarian cancer.definition: A malignant neoplasm arising in the ovary, most often from epithelial cells, with several histologic subtypes; it commonly presents with nonspecific symptoms such as abdominal bloating or pelvic/abdominal pain and may form a pelvic mass, often diagnosed at an advanced stage. Management typically includes cytoreductive surgery followed by platinum-based chemotherapy.

hepatic toxicity.definition: Liver injury caused by exposure to toxic substances (such as drugs, chemicals, or herbal supplements), which can present as hepatocellular damage, cholestasis, or liver failure.

bone marrow depression.definition: Decreased activity of the bone marrow resulting in reduced production of blood cells (red cells, white cells, and platelets), leading to anemia, infection risk, and bleeding; may be caused by chemotherapy, radiation, drugs, or toxins.

difficulty sleeping.definition: A sleep disorder characterized by problems with initiating or maintaining sleep or experiencing nonrestorative sleep, resulting in daytime distress or impairment in functioning.

alzheimer’s sclerosis.definition: Not a standard medical term; when used, it usually refers to the brain changes seen in Alzheimer's disease, which include amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles with progressive neuronal loss and brain atrophy.

senile dementia.definition: Diagnosis once given to people over 65 with dementia.

amyloid plaques.definition: Extracellular aggregates of misfolded amyloid proteins, most often beta-amyloid, deposited in brain tissue and forming plaques; a histopathologic hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease associated with neurodegeneration.

bagassosis.definition: An occupational hypersensitivity pneumonitis caused by inhalation of dust from bagasse (the fibrous residue after extracting juice from sugarcane), typically contaminated with thermophilic actinomycetes or molds; presents with acute fever, cough, dyspnea, and diffuse interstitial infiltrates after exposure, and improves with avoidance of exposure.

farmer’s lung.definition: A hypersensitivity pneumonitis caused by inhalation of organic dusts from moldy hay, straw, or grain containing thermophilic actinomycetes; an immune-mediated inflammatory reaction in the lungs that can present acutely after exposure with flu-like symptoms and dyspnea, or chronically with progressive shortness of breath and potential fibrosis with continued exposure.

pigeon breeder’s lung.definition: A hypersensitivity pneumonitis caused by inhalation of avian antigens from pigeons, leading to an immune-mediated inflammatory reaction in the lungs (often with flu-like symptoms after exposure; can be acute, subacute, or chronic).

bronchopulmonary lavage.definition: A procedure performed via bronchoscopy in which sterile saline is instilled into the bronchial and/or alveolar spaces and then aspirated to wash the airways for diagnostic sampling (e.g., cytology, microbiology) or therapeutic clearance of secretions.

ambiguous genitalia.definition: A congenital condition in which the external genitalia do not have a clearly male or female appearance, often reflecting disorders of sex development due to genetic, gonadal, or hormonal factors; evaluation is needed to determine diagnosis and management.

antimitochondrial antibody.definition: An autoantibody directed against mitochondrial antigens, most often the E2 subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex; strongly associated with primary biliary cholangitis and used as a diagnostic marker.

antimyocardial antibody.definition: Autoantibodies directed against cardiac muscle antigens (most commonly cardiac myosin) that can be found in immune‑mediated myocarditis and other inflammatory cardiac diseases; their presence reflects an immune attack on the myocardium.

amalgam.definition: An alloy of mercury with other metals (usually silver, tin, and copper) used as a dental filling material.

amalgam tattoo.definition: Benign pigmented lesion of the oral mucosa caused by implantation of dental amalgam particles during dental procedures, presenting as a flat blue-gray to black macule commonly on the gingiva or buccal mucosa.

amantadine.definition: A synthetic antiviral and antiparkinsonian medication that inhibits the influenza A M2 ion channel and enhances dopamine release; used for influenza A prophylaxis and treatment and for the symptomatic treatment of Parkinson's disease and drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms.

amantadine hydrochloride.definition: A salt form of an antiviral and antiparkinsonian agent used to prevent and treat influenza A infections and to manage Parkinson disease and certain drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms, primarily by increasing dopaminergic activity and antagonizing NMDA receptors.

amastia.definition: A congenital absence of breast tissue (mammary gland) resulting in no breast development; can be unilateral or bilateral and may be accompanied by absence of the nipple-areolar complex.

amaurosis.definition: Partial or complete loss of vision (blindness); may be temporary or permanent and can result from retinal or optic nerve disease, vascular ischemia, or other ocular/neurologic causes.

amaurosis fugax.definition: A transient, painless monocular loss of vision due to temporary retinal ischemia, usually from emboli or hypoperfusion related to carotid artery disease; episodes typically last seconds to minutes and resolve completely, and it is a warning sign for potential ischemic stroke.

amaurosis partialis fugax.definition: A transient, partial loss of vision in one eye caused by temporary retinal ischemia, often lasting seconds to minutes; considered a form of amaurosis fugax and a warning sign for carotid artery disease or cerebrovascular risk.

amaurotic.definition: Relating to amaurosis; blind or nearly blind.

amaurotic familial idiocy.definition: A historical, obsolete term for a familial, inherited syndrome in which affected individuals are congenitally or early-blind (amaurosis) and have severe intellectual disability (idiocy); not a precise modern diagnostic label.

tay-sachs disease.definition: An uncommon disease that you get from your parents that causes mental and physical problems.

ambrisentan.definition: A selective endothelin receptor antagonist (ET_A–preferring) used to treat pulmonary arterial hypertension by blocking endothelin-1–mediated vasoconstriction, thereby dilating pulmonary arteries and reducing pulmonary vascular resistance.

ambulatory anesthesia.definition: Anesthesia administered for outpatient, same-day procedures, allowing discharge home after full recovery, typically using general, regional, or monitored anesthesia care.

ambulatory blood pressure monitoring.definition: A method in which a portable blood pressure monitor is worn for 24 hours to automatically measure BP at regular intervals during daily activities and sleep, providing average values, daytime versus nighttime readings, and BP variability to aid in diagnosing hypertension and assessing control.

ambulatory electrocardiograph.definition: A portable device that records the heart’s electrical activity (ECG) over an extended period, typically 24–48 hours, while the patient engages in normal daily activities, to detect intermittent arrhythmias or ischemia.

holter monitor.definition: A portable, ambulatory electrocardiography device that records the heart's electrical activity continuously for 24–48 hours (often during daily activities) to detect intermittent arrhythmias or other cardiac abnormalities.

ambulatory schizophrenia.definition: Outpatient management of schizophrenia; treatment of schizophrenia in an ambulatory (outpatient) setting rather than as an inpatient, typically with antipsychotic medication and psychosocial interventions.

ambulatory splint.definition: A removable or semi-rigid orthopedic device applied to an injured limb in the outpatient setting to immobilize it for healing while allowing the patient to ambulate, typically used for fractures or sprains of the extremities.

ambulatory surgery center.definition: A facility where elective surgical procedures are performed on an outpatient basis, with patients admitted and discharged on the same day after anesthesia or sedation.

amcinonide.definition: A potent synthetic topical corticosteroid used to treat inflammatory skin conditions such as eczema, dermatitis, and psoriasis by reducing inflammation, itching, and redness; applied to the skin as a cream, ointment, or lotion.

amdinocillin pivoxil.definition: An oral prodrug form of amdinocillin in which a pivoxil ester is attached to improve oral absorption; after administration, it is hydrolyzed to active amdinocillin, a beta-lactam antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins.

amdinocillin.definition: A penicillin-class beta-lactam antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins, used to treat susceptible bacterial infections.

ameba.definition: A single-celled, motile protozoan that moves by extending cytoplasmic processes called pseudopodia and feeds by phagocytosis; commonly free-living or parasitic in humans and animals.

amebae.definition: Unicellular eukaryotic organisms that move by pseudopodia and ingest food by phagocytosis; found in soil and aquatic environments, with some species parasitic in humans and capable of causing diseases such as amebic dysentery and liver abscess (e.g., Entamoeba histolytica).

amebiasis.definition: A parasitic intestinal infection caused by Entamoeba histolytica, presenting as amebic dysentery or colitis and, in some cases, extraintestinal disease such as liver abscess; transmitted by ingestion of cysts in contaminated water or food.

amebic abscess.definition: A localized collection of pus in the liver caused by Entamoeba histolytica infection, typically following intestinal amebiasis.

amebic dysentery.definition: An intestinal infection caused by Entamoeba histolytica that produces dysentery with bloody, mucus-containing stools, abdominal pain, and tenesmus; it can invade the colonic mucosa and may spread to the liver (amoebic liver abscess).

hepatic amebiasis.definition: Amebic liver abscess due to Entamoeba histolytica infection spreading from intestinal amebiasis; an extraintestinal manifestation presenting with fever, right upper quadrant pain and hepatomegaly, treated with systemic anti-amoebic therapy (e.g., metronidazole) followed by a luminal agent.

amebicide.definition: Amebicide: a drug or chemical that kills or inhibits Entamoeba species (amoebae), used to treat amebic infections; can be luminal (acting in the intestinal lumen) or systemic/tissue-acting.

amebic liver abscess.definition: A focal hepatic abscess caused by Entamoeba histolytica infection, usually arising from intestinal amebiasis; presents with fever and right upper-quadrant pain and is diagnosed by imaging and serology. Treatment is metronidazole or another nitroimidazole followed by a luminal agent, with percutaneous drainage reserved for large or nonresolving abscesses.

amoeboid movement.definition: An actin-mediated mode of locomotion in which a cell extends cytoplasmic projections called pseudopodia (false feet); the cytoplasm streams into these extensions, pulling the cell forward to move along a surface.

amelanotic melanoma.definition: A malignant melanoma that lacks pigment because the tumor cells produce little or no melanin, presenting as a nonpigmented, pink, red, or flesh-colored lesion that can be mistaken for benign conditions and may be diagnosed at a later, more advanced stage.

amelanotic malignant melanoma.definition: A malignant melanoma that produces little or no melanin, presenting as a nonpigmented pink or skin-colored lesion and often diagnosed late; histology shows malignant melanocytes with scant or absent pigment and immunohistochemical positivity for melanocytic markers.

amelia.definition: Congenital absence of one or more limbs (arms or legs) at birth; a severe limb deficiency that may be unilateral or bilateral and can occur as an isolated anomaly or with other anomalies.

amelogenesis.definition: The biological process by which dental enamel is formed during tooth development, in which ameloblasts secrete an organic enamel matrix that is subsequently mineralized to become hard, acellular enamel.

amelogenesis imperfecta.definition: An inherited disorder of enamel formation in which enamel is defective, resulting in thin, soft, or poorly mineralized enamel that is discolored and prone to rapid wear and breakage; enamel defects may be hypoplastic, hypomature, or hypocalcified.

ameloblast.definition: Enamel-forming cells of the developing tooth; tall, columnar cells derived from the inner enamel epithelium that secrete enamel matrix proteins which mineralize to enamel; these cells degenerate after enamel formation, leaving the enamel.

ameloblastoma.definition: An odontogenic tumor of epithelial origin that is typically benign but locally aggressive, arising from enamel-forming cells (ameloblasts); most often located in the mandible and presenting as a slow-growing jaw swelling with a multilocular radiolucent appearance; management usually requires wide surgical excision due to risk of recurrence.

ameloblastic fibroma.definition: Benign odontogenic tumor composed of ameloblast-like epithelial nests and a primitive ectomesenchymal stroma resembling dental papilla; typically occurs in children and young adults, presenting as a slow-growing intraosseous jaw swelling (most often in the posterior mandible); radiographically often a radiolucent lesion; treated with surgical enucleation/curettage with relatively low recurrence.

ameloblastic fibro-odontoma.definition: A benign mixed odontogenic tumor characterized by ameloblast-like epithelial tissue within odontogenic ectomesenchyme that forms enamel- and dentin-like hard tissues; considered a developing odontoma variant, typically occurring in children and adolescents and usually treated with conservative surgical enucleation.

ameloblastic hemangioma.definition: A rare benign odontogenic lesion characterized by concurrent ameloblastoma-type epithelial proliferation and a prominent vascular (hemangiomatous) component; most often arising in the mandible of children and young adults.

ameloblastic sarcoma.definition: A rare malignant odontogenic tumor with an ameloblastoma-like epithelial component and a malignant mesenchymal (sarcomatous) stroma; it can arise de novo or from a preexisting ameloblastoma and may invade surrounding tissues and metastasize, with treatment typically involving wide surgical excision and consideration of adjuvant radiotherapy or chemotherapy.

adamantinoma.definition: A rare, slow-growing malignant bone tumor most often arising in the tibial diaphysis, characterized by epithelial (odontogenic-type) nests within a fibrous stroma; locally aggressive with a high recurrence rate after intralesional procedures, treated primarily by wide surgical excision.

adamantoblastoma.definition: An historical term for ameloblastoma, a benign but locally aggressive odontogenic tumor of the jaw arising from enamel organ–type epithelium; management typically requires wide surgical excision to reduce recurrence.

epithelioma adamantinum.definition: A benign, locally aggressive odontogenic tumor of the jaw derived from enamel organ epithelium (ameloblastoma); it grows slowly, often causes jaw swelling and tooth displacement, and tends to infiltrate surrounding bone with a high risk of recurrence after conservative excision, requiring wide surgical resection.

amelodentinal.definition: Relating to both enamel and dentin, the two hard tissues of a tooth; used to describe structures or processes that involve both tissues (e.g., the enamel–dentin interface).

odontogenic neoplasm.definition: A neoplasm arising from odontogenic (tooth-forming) tissue of the jaws, derived from the odontogenic epithelium and/or ectomesenchyme (enamel organ, dental papilla, or dental sac); it can be benign or malignant (e.g., ameloblastoma, odontogenic carcinomas, odontogenic sarcomas).

enamel.definition: The hard covering on the outside of each tooth.

dentin.definition: The main bone-like part of a tooth.

enamel cell.definition: An enamel-forming cell of the developing tooth; a tall secretory cell derived from the inner enamel epithelium that synthesizes and secretes the enamel matrix and initiates mineralization to form dental enamel; these cells degenerate and are lost after enamel maturation.

teeth.definition: Hard calcified structures in the jaws used for biting and chewing; composed of enamel, dentin, pulp, and cementum; function to mechanically break down food and assist in speech.

gingiva.definition: The part of the gums surrounding the teeth.

buccal membrane.definition: The mucous membrane lining the inside of the cheek (buccal mucosa) in the oral cavity; it consists of stratified squamous epithelium overlying connective tissue.

endodontically treated tooth.definition: Tooth that has undergone endodontic therapy (root canal treatment), in which infected or necrotic pulp is removed, the root canals are cleaned, disinfected, and filled with an inert obturant (usually gutta-percha) to seal the canal system, typically followed by a restoration or crown to restore function and prevent fracture.

carotid artery disease.definition: When the arteries in your neck become narrow or blocked.

autosomal recessive.definition: A pattern of inheritance in which two copies of a pathogenic variant on an autosome are required for disease expression; carriers with one copy are typically asymptomatic. Each pregnancy of two carriers has a 25% chance of an affected child, a 50% chance of a carrier, and a 25% chance of an unaffected non-carrier; affects males and females equally.

paromomycin.definition: A poorly absorbed aminoglycoside antibiotic used as a luminal agent to treat intestinal protozoal infections (e.g., Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia lamblia); it inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding the 30S ribosomal subunit and is not suitable for systemic infections due to limited absorption. Potential nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

iodoquinol.definition: A luminal amebicide derived from hydroxyquinoline that remains in the intestinal lumen to eradicate Entamoeba histolytica infections; poorly absorbed from the gut and often used with metronidazole for invasive disease.

metronidazole.definition: A nitroimidazole antibiotic and antiproprotozoal agent that disrupts DNA synthesis in anaerobic bacteria and protozoa; used to treat infections such as amebiasis, giardiasis, trichomoniasis, and anaerobic bacterial infections, with alcohol avoidance advised during treatment due to a potential disulfiram-like reaction.

chloroquine hydrochloride.definition: A water-soluble salt form of chloroquine, a synthetic 4-aminoquinoline antimalarial drug. It is used for the treatment and prevention of malaria caused by susceptible Plasmodium species; its mechanism involves inhibiting heme detoxification in the parasite.

dysentery.definition: A condition characterized by inflammation of the intestines, especially the colon, with abdominal pain and frequent stools that contain blood and mucus.

nervousness.definition: A feeling of worry, anxiety, or unease, typically in anticipation of a perceived threat or stressor; often accompanied by autonomic arousal such as increased heart rate, sweating, tremor, or restlessness.

blurred vision.definition: Blurred vision is a lack of sharp vision in which objects appear out of focus or hazy; it can be temporary or persistent and may result from refractive errors (e.g., myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism), dry eye, cataracts, retinal or optic nerve disease, or systemic conditions such as diabetes or hypertension.

slurred speech.definition: Slurred speech is imprecise or slurred articulation of words caused by weakness or poor coordination of the muscles used for speaking (dysarthria), often due to neurological injury, stroke, or intoxication.

renal disease.definition: A disease of the kidneys that impairs their ability to filter waste, regulate fluids and electrolytes, and maintain acid-base balance.

mucous membrane.definition: A thin layer that lines many cavities and structures in the body that are exposed to air in the environment, such as the nose, mouth, and lungs.

livedo reticularis.definition: Netlike, violaceous-blue discoloration of the skin, typically on the legs, caused by dilation of cutaneous venules with sluggish or interrupted blood flow; often cold-induced and benign, but can be associated with vascular occlusive or autoimmune diseases (e.g., antiphospholipid syndrome).

orthostatic hypotension.definition: A sudden drop in blood pressure upon standing or getting out of bed, causing dizziness.

peripheral edema.definition: Swelling of the extremities from excess fluid in the interstitial spaces, most often in the feet and ankles, due to imbalances in forces governing fluid filtration and reabsorption (eg, increased capillary hydrostatic pressure, decreased oncotic pressure, lymphatic obstruction, or inflammation).

enamel hypoplasia.definition: A quantitative developmental defect of tooth enamel in which enamel is thinner than normal due to disrupted enamel matrix formation during tooth development, producing pits, grooves, or diffuse thinning in affected teeth; it may be localized or generalized and is associated with systemic disturbances (e.g., illness, fever, malnutrition) or local trauma during amelogenesis, often increasing caries risk.

hypoplasia.definition: Underdevelopment or incomplete development of a tissue or organ, typically due to a reduced number of cells during embryogenesis, resulting in a smaller-than-normal organ that is otherwise structurally normal.

hypocalcification.definition: Deficient or incomplete mineralization (calcification) of tissue, most notably tooth enamel during development, resulting in under-mineralized, chalky patches or discolored areas.

ameloblasts.definition: Tall, polarized cells of the enamel organ that synthesize and secrete the enamel matrix during tooth development; derived from the inner enamel epithelium, they differentiate to form enamel and are lost after enamel maturation and eruption.

dentinogenesis imperfecta.definition: An autosomal-dominant hereditary disorder of dentin formation characterized by opalescent, rapidly worn teeth due to defective dentin, with enamel usually normal and pulp chambers often obliterated on radiographs.

amentia.definition: An archaic medical term denoting mental deficiency or loss of cognitive function; a state of impaired intellect historically used to refer to dementia or intellectual disability.

ovary.definition: A paired female reproductive organ that produces ova (eggs) and secretes the hormones estrogen and progesterone; involved in follicle development, ovulation, and regulation of the menstrual cycle.

primary amenorrhea.definition: Failure to start menstruating by age 15 with normal growth and secondary sexual characteristics, or by age 13 in a girl without secondary sexual characteristics.

secondary amenorrhea.definition: The absence of menses for at least 3 consecutive cycles or for 6 months in a woman who has previously menstruated.

hypothalamic amenorrhea.definition: A form of functional hypothalamic hypogonadism in which reduced pulsatile GnRH secretion from the hypothalamus suppresses LH and FSH release, causing hypoestrogenic amenorrhea—often triggered by energy deficit/weight loss, excessive exercise, or significant stress.

postpill amenorrhea.definition: A temporary absence of menses after stopping hormonal contraception (such as combined oral contraceptive pills), caused by suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis; menses typically resume within a few months, but persistent amenorrhea warrants evaluation for other causes.

amenorrheic.definition: Relating to the absence of menstrual periods; the state of not menstruating.

leishmaniasis.definition: A vector-borne parasitic disease caused by Leishmania spp., transmitted by female sandflies, presenting as cutaneous ulcers, mucocutaneous lesions, or visceral organ involvement depending on species and host immunity.

chiclero ulcer.definition: A chronic ulcerating lesion of the ear (pinna) caused by infection with Leishmania mexicana, a form of cutaneous leishmaniasis transmitted by sandflies; classically seen in workers who harvested chicle.

espundia.definition: A form of mucocutaneous leishmaniasis caused by infection with Leishmania parasites (classically the Leishmania braziliensis complex), characterized by destructive ulcerative lesions of the nasal and oropharyngeal mucosa that can lead to deformity.

forest yaws.definition: A form of yaws occurring in forested tropical regions; a chronic infection caused by Treponema pertenue, transmitted by direct skin-to-skin contact, presenting with contagious skin lesions that may ulcerate and progress to bone or joint involvement; endemic in humid rainforest areas; treatable with penicillin or azithromycin.

mucocutaneous leishmaniasis.definition: Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis is a form of leishmaniasis in which Leishmania parasites invade mucosal tissues—most often the nasal, pharyngeal, and laryngeal mucosa—after an earlier cutaneous infection, causing progressive, destructive mucosal ulcers and deformities; it typically develops months to years after the initial skin lesion and is commonly caused by certain New World Leishmania species (e.g., the L. braziliensis complex).

new world leishmaniasis.definition: A form of leishmaniasis occurring in the Americas, caused by Leishmania parasites transmitted by phlebotomine sandflies; it most often presents as cutaneous ulcers at the bite site, with possible mucosal involvement (mucocutaneous leishmaniasis) in certain species.

leishmania.definition: A genus of parasitic, flagellated protozoa that cause leishmaniasis; transmitted by female phlebotomine sandflies; exists as promastigotes in the sandfly vector and as amastigotes inside mammalian macrophages.

cutaneous lesions.definition: Any localized abnormality of the skin or its appendages, presenting as changes in color, texture, or contour; includes primary lesions (e.g., macule, papule, vesicle, pustule, plaque, nodule, wheal) and secondary lesions (e.g., crust, scale, scar, erosion, ulcer).

colorado tick fever.definition: A viral illness caused by a coltivirus transmitted by Rocky Mountain wood ticks (Dermacentor andersoni) in western North America; incubation is about 2–6 days, with abrupt fever, severe headache, myalgias, and photophobia, often biphasic with a second fever during recovery. It is typically self-limited within 1–2 weeks and managed with supportive care; there is no specific antiviral treatment or vaccine.

american mountain fever.definition: A viral tick-borne illness occurring in mountainous regions of western North America, caused by Colorado tick fever virus. It presents with abrupt fever, chills, headache, myalgia, and photophobia; may be biphasic with a relapse of fever after temporary improvement; typically self-limited, resolving within 1–2 weeks; no specific antiviral treatment exists; management is supportive and focuses on tick-bite prevention.

intermenstrual phase.definition: The interval in the menstrual cycle from the end of one menstrual period to ovulation, corresponding to the follicular (proliferative) phase and characterized by follicle growth and rising estrogen leading to endometrial thickening.

temporomandibular joint disorders.definition: A group of conditions involving the temporomandibular joint and surrounding muscles and tissues, causing jaw pain, limited movement, and/or joint noises (clicking, crepitus); commonly associated with bruxism, arthritis, trauma, or bite misalignment, and usually managed with conservative therapies such as analgesics, physical therapy, occlusal splints, and lifestyle modification, with surgery reserved for refractory cases.

maxillofacial disorders.definition: Conditions affecting the maxillofacial region—jaws, face, and surrounding structures—encompassing dental and skeletal abnormalities, temporomandibular joint disorders, congenital anomalies (e.g., cleft lip/palate), trauma, infections, tumors, and other deformities.

dental prostheses.definition: Artificial devices used to replace missing teeth or surrounding tissues in the dental arch, including dentures (complete or partial), dental bridges, crowns, and implant-supported restorations.

surgical removal.definition: The surgical removal of tissue or an organ from the body; the excision or removal of diseased or unwanted tissue or structures.

radiology.definition: The study of diseases using X-rays.

mammography.definition: A radiographic imaging technique that uses low-dose X-rays to visualize the breast for the detection of breast cancer and other abnormalities; used in routine screening and diagnostic evaluation, with modern methods including digital mammography and 3D tomosynthesis.

sonography.definition: An imaging modality that uses high-frequency sound waves to produce real-time images of internal soft tissues and organs; noninvasive and does not involve ionizing radiation.

breast sonography.definition: An imaging modality that uses high-frequency ultrasound to produce real-time images of breast tissue; it is noninvasive and free of ionizing radiation, primarily used to differentiate cystic from solid masses, characterize lesions, guide needle biopsies, and evaluate abnormalities detected on clinical exam or mammography.

bone densitometry.definition: A noninvasive imaging test that measures bone mineral density (BMD), most commonly using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), to assess fracture risk, diagnose osteoporosis, and monitor treatment; results are reported as T-scores and Z-scores.

vascular interventional radiography.definition: A subspecialty of radiology that uses percutaneous catheter-based, fluoroscopy-guided techniques to diagnose and treat diseases of the blood vessels; common procedures include angiography, angioplasty and stenting, embolization, and thrombolysis.

cardiovascular-interventional radiograph.definition: A subspecialty of radiology that uses real-time imaging to guide catheter-based, minimally invasive procedures for diseases of the heart and blood vessels. It includes diagnostic angiography and therapeutic interventions such as angioplasty with or without stent placement, embolization, thrombectomy, and other vascular procedures performed under fluoroscopic guidance.

american trypanosomiasis.definition: A parasitic infection caused by the protozoan Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted by triatomine (kissing) bugs; it has acute and chronic phases, and chronic infection can cause dilated cardiomyopathy, megacolon, and megaesophagus.

chagas’ disease.definition: An infection caused by the protozoan Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted mainly by triatomine (kissing) bugs; it has acute and chronic phases, with chronic disease potentially causing cardiomyopathy and megasyndromes such as megacolon and megaesophagus. Transmission can also occur congenitally, by blood transfusion, or organ transplantation; treatment options include antiparasitic agents such as benznidazole or nifurtimox.

ames test.definition: An in vitro bacterial mutagenicity assay that uses histidine-auxotrophic strains (commonly Salmonella typhimurium) to detect mutagens by measuring the number of revertant colonies that grow on histidine-free medium, often with a metabolic activation system (S9 mix).

ametropia.definition: Ametropia is a refractive error in which the eye cannot focus light on the retina when the eye is relaxed, resulting in blurred vision; it includes myopia (nearsightedness), hyperopia (farsightedness), and astigmatism.

amevive.definition: A biologic fusion-protein therapy that binds CD2 on T cells (LFA-3–IgG1 fusion) to inhibit T-cell activation and deplete memory-effector T cells, used to treat plaque psoriasis.

aminocaproic acid.definition: A synthetic amino acid that acts as an antifibrinolytic agent by inhibiting plasminogen activation and plasmin activity, thereby reducing fibrinolysis and helping prevent or treat excessive bleeding.

amicar.definition: A brand name for aminocaproic acid, an antifibrinolytic agent that inhibits plasmin activity and plasminogen activation, thereby preventing fibrin clot breakdown and reducing bleeding.

amidase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of amide bonds, converting amides into a carboxylic acid and an amine; a member of the hydrolase family that acts on amide substrates.

local anesthetic.definition: A medication that reversibly blocks nerve conduction in a localized area to produce loss of sensation (local anesthesia), usually by inhibiting voltage-gated sodium channels in peripheral nerves.

lidocaine.definition: An amide-type local anesthetic that blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in nerve membranes, preventing initiation and propagation of action potentials. It is used for local anesthesia (infiltration, nerve blocks) and, intravenously, as a class IB antiarrhythmic for certain ventricular arrhythmias.

bupivacaine.definition: A long-acting amide local anesthetic that blocks voltage-gated sodium channels to produce regional anesthesia and analgesia; used for epidural, intrathecal, and peripheral nerve blocks, with higher potency and longer duration than lidocaine and a risk of cardiotoxicity and CNS toxicity.

prilocaine.definition: An amide-type local anesthetic used for infiltration and nerve blocks; commonly used in topical preparations (e.g., EMLA cream with lidocaine); can cause methemoglobinemia at high systemic doses or in susceptible individuals.

amifostine.definition: An intravenous cytoprotective prodrug (WR-1065) that is converted to an active thiol metabolite to scavenge free radicals and protect normal tissues from the toxic effects of radiation therapy and platinum‑based chemotherapy.

cisplatin.definition: A platinum-based chemotherapy agent that forms covalent DNA crosslinks, primarily intrastrand crosslinks, leading to inhibition of DNA replication and transcription and cancer cell death.
