It is used to treat various solid tumors (e.g., testicular, ovarian, bladder, head and neck) and is given intravenously with hydration to reduce nephrotoxicity; common adverse effects include nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neurotoxicity, nausea, and myelosuppression.

ovarian carcinoma.definition: Malignant tumor of the ovary, typically arising from the ovarian surface epithelium (epithelial ovarian cancers) with subtypes such as serous, mucinous, endometrioid, and clear cell; commonly presents at an advanced stage; treated with surgical cytoreduction and platinum-based chemotherapy; prognosis depends on stage and histology.

xerostomia.definition: A condition in which the mouth feels dry for a prolonged period due to reduced saliva production.

mannitol.definition: An intravenous osmotic diuretic (a hexitol sugar alcohol) that increases plasma osmolality to pull water from tissues and promote diuresis; used to reduce intracranial and intraocular pressure and to treat edema. Contraindicated in anuria, severe dehydration, and significant renal impairment.

aminothiol.definition: A molecule containing both an amino group (-NH2) and a thiol group (-SH) in its structure; i.e., an amino-thiol (mercaptoamine).

hypocalcemia.definition: A lower-than-normal level of calcium in the blood, often due to hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, kidney disease, or pancreatitis, and it can cause neuromuscular irritability (paresthesias, tetany) and may lead to seizures or cardiac rhythm abnormalities.

amikacin sulfate.definition: An aminoglycoside antibiotic in sulfate salt form used to treat serious infections caused by aerobic gram-negative bacteria (notably Pseudomonas and Enterobacteriaceae); administered parenterally (IV or IM), it inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of mRNA, with notable risks including nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

amikacin.definition: An aminoglycoside antibiotic active against many Gram-negative bacteria (notably Pseudomonas); bactericidal by irreversibly binding the 30S ribosomal subunit to inhibit bacterial protein synthesis, typically given IV or IM, with potential nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

ototoxicity.definition: An adverse effect in which toxic injury to the inner ear (cochlea and vestibular system) from certain medications or chemicals causes sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and/or balance problems.

neuromuscular blockade.definition: Pharmacologic paralysis of skeletal muscles produced by agents that interfere with transmission at the neuromuscular junction (primarily nicotinic acetylcholine receptors), used during anesthesia to facilitate intubation and surgery; consciousness and analgesia are not abolished by these agents and concomitant anesthesia with ventilation support is required.

amikin.definition: A brand-name aminoglycoside antibiotic used to treat serious infections caused by gram-negative bacteria; it is bactericidal and inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit; typically given IV or IM; adverse effects include nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

potassium-sparing diuretic.definition: A diuretic that increases urine output while conserving potassium, usually by blocking aldosterone receptors or inhibiting sodium reabsorption in the distal nephron; can cause hyperkalemia.

encephalopathy.definition: A broad term for diffuse brain dysfunction caused by various insults (metabolic, infectious, toxic, hypoxic, or structural), leading to altered mental status ranging from confusion and lethargy to coma.

impotence.definition: Inability to achieve or maintain an erection sufficient for satisfactory sexual intercourse; commonly referred to as erectile dysfunction.

muscle cramps.definition: A sudden, involuntary contraction of a muscle or part of a muscle, usually painful and lasting seconds to minutes; commonly affects the calves, thighs, or feet and often resolves with stretching and rest, though dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, or muscle overuse can contribute.

photosensitivity.definition: An abnormal sensitivity of the skin (and sometimes the eyes) to light, especially ultraviolet radiation, resulting in exaggerated sunburn, rashes, or ocular symptoms after light exposure; can be drug‑induced, hereditary, or associated with systemic diseases.

irregular heart rhythm.definition: A problem with the rate of your heart or when your heart doesn’t have a steady beat.

arrhythmia.definition: A problem with the rate of your heart or when your heart doesn’t have a steady beat.

amiodarone.definition: A class III antiarrhythmic medication that prolongs the cardiac action potential and refractory period by blocking potassium channels; used to treat and prevent various atrial and ventricular tachyarrhythmias, with a very long half-life and potential adverse effects including pulmonary toxicity, thyroid dysfunction, hepatotoxicity, photosensitivity, and multiple drug interactions.

amiodarone hydrochloride.definition: An iodinated, class III antiarrhythmic agent that blocks potassium channels to prolong the cardiac action potential and refractory period; used to treat and prevent a wide range of ventricular and supraventricular tachyarrhythmias, administered orally or intravenously, with potential thyroid, hepatic, pulmonary toxicities and numerous drug interactions.

monoamine oxidase inhibitor.definition: A class of medications that irreversibly or reversibly inhibit monoamine oxidase enzymes (MAO-A and/or MAO-B) in the brain, increasing synaptic levels of monoamines (serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine) to treat depression or Parkinson disease; nonselective or irreversible inhibitors require dietary tyramine restrictions and have significant drug interactions.

para-aminobenzoic acid.definition: A benzoic acid derivative that serves as a precursor for folate synthesis in bacteria; not an essential nutrient for humans; has been used in some sunscreens as a UV filter and historically as a dietary supplement, though its use is limited due to potential allergic reactions.

p-aminobenzoic acid.definition: An aromatic carboxylic acid bearing an amino group in the para position relative to the carboxyl group; a precursor in bacterial folate biosynthesis and historically used as a UV-filter in sunscreens; not an essential nutrient for humans and may cause photosensitivity or allergic reactions.

paba.definition: An aromatic carboxylic acid historically considered a B vitamin (vitamin Bx); in bacteria it serves as a precursor in folic acid synthesis and is not essential for human nutrition. It has been used in sunscreen formulations and can cause photosensitivity or allergic reactions in some individuals.

aminobenzoic acid.definition: A class of aromatic carboxylic acids in which an amino group is attached to the benzene ring; there are three isomers—ortho-, meta-, and para-aminobenzoic acid—differing by the position of the amino group relative to the carboxyl group.

aminotransferase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes transamination—the transfer of an amino group from an amino acid to a keto acid, using pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as a cofactor; clinically, examples include ALT and AST used to assess liver injury.

transaminase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the transfer of an amino group from an amino acid to an α-keto acid, producing a different amino acid and a different keto acid; a central step in amino acid metabolism and often measured clinically as a marker of liver injury.

amino acid.definition: An organic molecule that is the basic building block of proteins; it contains an amino group (–NH2), a carboxyl group (–COOH), a central α-carbon, and a variable side chain (R). Amino acids join through peptide bonds to form polypeptides; there are 20 standard amino acids, some of which are essential in humans.

glycine.definition: The smallest amino acid with a single hydrogen as its side chain; nonessential; used in protein synthesis and acts as an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord and brainstem; also a precursor in the synthesis of glutathione, creatine, porphyrins, and collagen-containing proteins.

isoleucine.definition: An essential amino acid and one of the branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs); it is required for protein synthesis and energy production. Humans cannot synthesize it, so it must be obtained from the diet (e.g., meat, dairy, eggs, soy, legumes).

leucine.definition: An essential amino acid that is one of the branched-chain amino acids; required for protein synthesis and muscle maintenance; strictly ketogenic and cannot be synthesized by humans; obtained from dietary proteins.

lysine.definition: An essential amino acid required for protein synthesis and growth; humans cannot synthesize it and must obtain it from the diet; it is a basic (positively charged) amino acid with a side chain that carries a positive charge at physiological pH.

methionine.definition: An essential sulfur-containing amino acid required for protein synthesis; it serves as the precursor to S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), the principal methyl donor in cells, and in humans often acts as the initiator amino acid for protein synthesis.

phenylalanine.definition: An essential aromatic amino acid with a benzyl side chain; required in the diet because humans cannot synthesize it, and it serves as a building block for proteins and as a precursor to tyrosine and downstream catecholamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine) and melanin.

threonine.definition: An essential amino acid required in the human diet for protein synthesis; a polar, uncharged amino acid with a β-hydroxyl side chain.

tryptophan.definition: An essential amino acid that must be obtained from the diet; it serves as a precursor to the neurotransmitter serotonin and the hormone melatonin and is also a precursor to niacin, and it is incorporated into body proteins during protein synthesis.

valine.definition: An essential, branched-chain amino acid that must be obtained from the diet; has an aliphatic isopropyl side chain and is primarily glucogenic, being catabolized to succinyl-CoA for energy production and glucose synthesis in muscle and other tissues.

arginine.definition: A semiessential (conditionally essential) amino acid with a positively charged guanidino side chain; it serves as a substrate for protein synthesis and is a precursor to nitric oxide via nitric oxide synthase, and it participates in the urea cycle to detoxify ammonia.

histidine.definition: An essential amino acid with an imidazole-containing side chain; basic and positively charged at physiological pH; required in the diet for protein synthesis and as a precursor to histamine.

alanine.definition: A nonessential amino acid that is one of the 20 standard amino acids used to build proteins; it has a nonpolar, aliphatic side chain and is synthesized from pyruvate, participating in glucose metabolism, notably the glucose–alanine cycle between muscle and liver.

asparagine.definition: A polar, uncharged amino acid with a carboxamide side chain (–CONH2); one of the 20 standard amino acids used in protein synthesis; encoded by the codons AAC and AAU; synthesized from aspartate via an amide-transfer enzyme; also serves as a site for N-linked glycosylation in proteins.

aspartic acid.definition: A standard amino acid with a side-chain carboxyl group that is negatively charged at physiological pH; one of the 20 protein-building amino acids; nonessential; encoded by the codons GAU and GAC.

glutamine.definition: An abundant, conditionally essential amino acid (the amide of glutamic acid) that serves as a major nitrogen donor and energy source for rapidly dividing cells (such as enterocytes and immune cells); important for protein and nucleotide synthesis and nitrogen transport, and becomes essential during critical illness or stress.

glutamic acid.definition: An acidic, nonessential amino acid with a carboxyl group on its side chain; one of the 20 standard amino acids; acts as an excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS and serves as a precursor for glutamine and GABA.

proline.definition: A nonessential, nonpolar amino acid with a cyclic pyrrolidine side chain; its amino group is bound to its side chain, forming a secondary amine (an imino acid); important for protein synthesis and collagen stability.

serine.definition: A nonessential amino acid with a polar, uncharged side chain containing a hydroxymethyl group (-CH2OH); synthesized from 3-phosphoglycerate and serving as a precursor for glycine, cysteine, sphingolipids, and phospholipids, and participating in one‑carbon metabolism via serine hydroxymethyltransferase.

cystinuria.definition: A rare autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by defective renal tubular reabsorption of dibasic amino acids, especially cystine, leading to high urinary excretion of cystine and a predisposition to recurrent cystine kidney stones.

aminoaciduria.definition: Excretion of amino acids in the urine, typically due to defective proximal tubular reabsorption of amino acids or underlying metabolic disorders.

amipaque.definition: A nonionic iodinated contrast agent used in radiology to enhance visualization of tissues and vessels during X-ray and CT imaging; administered intravenously or intra-arterially.

metrizamide.definition: A water-soluble iodinated contrast agent used for intrathecal administration in myelography and cisternography to visualize cerebrospinal fluid spaces; ionic, high-osmolar, with potential neurotoxic reactions and arachnoiditis, largely replaced by nonionic agents.

intrathecal.definition: Relating to or occurring within the thecal sac (the subarachnoid space of the brain or spinal cord); typically used to describe delivery of substances directly into cerebrospinal fluid.

intravascular.definition: Relating to or occurring within a blood vessel; within the vascular system.

nonhyperkeratotic actinic keratosis.definition: A sun-exposed skin premalignant lesion (actinic keratosis) in which epidermal keratinocyte atypia is present but there is little to no overlying keratin production, i.e., no pronounced hyperkeratosis; it typically appears as a red, flat or slightly scaly patch on sun-damaged skin and may progress to squamous cell carcinoma.

porphobilinogen.definition: An intermediate in the heme biosynthesis pathway; a pyrrole-containing compound produced from two molecules of delta-aminolevulinic acid by the enzyme ALA dehydratase; four of these units are condensed to form hydroxymethylbilane and eventually heme.

aminolevulinic acid hydrochloride.definition: A water-soluble salt form of 5-aminolevulinic acid that is metabolized in cells to protoporphyrin IX, a photosensitizer used in photodynamic therapy and fluorescence-guided procedures; its application varies by formulation and can include topical treatment of actinic keratoses and other cancers.

protoporphyrin ix.definition: An iron-free tetrapyrrole porphyrin that serves as the immediate precursor to heme in the heme biosynthesis pathway; insertion of ferrous iron by ferrochelatase yields heme (heme B).

photosensitizer.definition: A chemical compound that, after absorbing light, becomes excited and transfers energy to molecular oxygen to form reactive oxygen species, enabling photodynamic therapy.

head and neck cancer.definition: A group of malignant tumors arising in the head and neck region, most commonly squamous cell carcinomas of the mucosa of the upper aerodigestive tract (oral cavity, pharynx, and larynx); less often in the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, or salivary glands. Risk factors include tobacco and alcohol use, and HPV-associated cancers occur in the oropharynx.

antifibrotic.definition: Describing a substance or intervention that inhibits or reduces fibrosis, the excessive formation of scar tissue from abnormal deposition of extracellular matrix.

hemostatic agent.definition: A substance that promotes hemostasis by promoting coagulation and/or vasoconstriction to stop bleeding; applied topically or used systemically.

amitiza.definition: A brand-name medication (lubiprostone) that activates chloride channels in the intestinal lining to increase fluid secretion and promote bowel movements; approved to treat chronic idiopathic constipation, irritable bowel syndrome with constipation in adults, and opioid-induced constipation.

lubiprostone.definition: A medication that acts as a chloride channel activator in the intestinal epithelium, increasing chloride-rich fluid secretion and accelerating intestinal transit; used to treat chronic idiopathic constipation and irritable bowel syndrome with constipation.

amitriptyline.definition: A tricyclic antidepressant used to treat major depressive disorder and certain types of chronic or neuropathic pain; it works by inhibiting the reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin, increasing their synaptic concentrations, and it often has sedative and anticholinergic effects.

amlexanox.definition: A topical anti-inflammatory and anti-allergic medication used to treat aphthous ulcers (canker sores) and other mucosal ulcers; it reduces inflammation and relieves pain.

amlodipine.definition: A calcium channel blocker of the dihydropyridine class used to treat hypertension and angina by relaxing vascular smooth muscle and causing vasodilation.

amoxicillin.definition: An oral beta-lactam antibiotic in the penicillin class (an aminopenicillin) that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin‑binding proteins; used to treat a range of infections caused by susceptible bacteria, including respiratory tract infections, otitis media, sinusitis, pneumonia, and skin infections.

amoxil.definition: Amoxicillin, a penicillin-type antibiotic, inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis and is used to treat a variety of bacterial infections.

amoxapine.definition: A tricyclic antidepressant of the dibenzoxepin class used to treat major depressive disorder; it inhibits reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin and has dopamine D2 receptor antagonism, which can cause extrapyramidal and anticholinergic side effects.

amobarbital.definition: A short- to intermediate-acting barbiturate CNS depressant used as a sedative and hypnotic; it enhances GABA-A receptor activity, increasing chloride influx to produce sedation and sleep, with a high risk of dependence and respiratory depression.

amylobarbitone.definition: A barbiturate CNS depressant used as a sedative-hypnotic; enhances GABA-A receptor activity to produce sedation and sleep, historically used for insomnia and anxiety but largely replaced by safer agents due to risk of dependence and overdose.

amphotericin b.definition: A polyene antifungal antibiotic used to treat severe systemic fungal infections; it binds ergosterol in fungal cell membranes, forming pores that lead to fungal cell death. Typically given intravenously; associated with nephrotoxicity and infusion-related reactions, with liposomal formulations reducing toxicity.

amphotericin b cholesteryl complex.definition: A lipid complex formulation in which amphotericin B is bound to cholesterol to form a stable drug complex, used as an alternative to conventional amphotericin B for systemic fungal infections and typically associated with reduced nephrotoxicity and altered pharmacokinetics.

amphotericin.definition: An antifungal antibiotic of the polyene class used for serious systemic fungal infections; it binds ergosterol in fungal cell membranes, forming pores that disrupt membrane integrity and cause cell death; typically given IV, with potential nephrotoxicity and infusion-related reactions; available in conventional and lipid formulations.

amphojel.definition: A brand-name aluminum hydroxide product used as an antacid to neutralize stomach acid and as a phosphate binder to reduce hyperphatemia in chronic kidney disease.

amphetamines.definition: A class of potent central nervous system stimulants that increase synaptic dopamine and norepinephrine by promoting their release and inhibiting reuptake, producing heightened alertness, energy, and euphoria; used medically for ADHD and narcolepsy, but with a high risk of abuse, dependence, and cardiovascular or psychiatric adverse effects.

amphetamine.definition: A potent central nervous system stimulant that increases synaptic concentrations of dopamine and norepinephrine by promoting their release and inhibiting reuptake; used medically to treat ADHD and narcolepsy, but widely abused as a recreational drug and associated with dependence and cardiovascular and psychiatric adverse effects.

amphetamine sulfate.definition: A salt form of the stimulant drug amphetamine formed by combining the amphetamine base with sulfate; a central nervous system stimulant used medically for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and narcolepsy, with high abuse potential.

dextroamphetamine.definition: A potent central nervous system stimulant; the dextrorotatory enantiomer of amphetamine that increases the release of dopamine and norepinephrine in the brain and is used to treat ADHD and narcolepsy, with a high potential for abuse and dependence.

methamphetamine.definition: Potent central nervous system stimulant that increases release and blocks reuptake of dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin, producing heightened alertness, euphoria, and appetite suppression; illicit use (crystal meth) carries a high risk of addiction and serious health harms, with only very limited approved medical uses under strict control (e.g., for ADHD and obesity).

amniocentesis.definition: A way to check on a baby's health before it is born, using a small amount of fluid from around the baby.

amniography.definition: A radiographic examination in which contrast material is injected into the amniotic cavity to outline the fetus and membranes on x-ray, to assess fetal anatomy and placental location; largely obsolete due to ultrasound and MRI.

amnion.definition: An innermost fetal membrane that surrounds the developing embryo, forming the amniotic sac and containing amniotic fluid; it cushions and protects the fetus and is derived from the epiblast lining the amniotic cavity.

amnionitis.definition: Inflammation of the amnion, the innermost fetal membrane, typically due to intra-amniotic infection; it is a component of chorioamnionitis when the chorion is also involved, and is histologically marked by neutrophilic infiltration of the amnion.

amnioscopy.definition: A procedure in which the amniotic cavity is visually inspected by inserting an amnioscope (a small endoscope) through the cervix to examine the amniotic membranes, fetus, and placenta.

amnioinfusion.definition: An obstetric procedure performed during labor in which sterile saline (or lactated Ringer's solution) is infused into the amniotic cavity through a transcervical catheter to increase amniotic fluid volume, primarily to relieve umbilical cord compression and improve fetal heart tracing in cases of oligohydramnios.

amniotic band disruption sequence syndro.definition: A sporadic fetal disruption syndrome caused by rupture of the amnion with formation of fibrous amniotic bands that constrict or entangle developing fetal parts, leading to limb constriction rings, amputations, limb deformities, and sometimes craniofacial or body wall defects.

amniotic cavity.definition: The fluid-filled space inside the amniotic sac that surrounds and protects the developing fetus during pregnancy; it is lined by the amnion and contains amniotic fluid.

amniotic fluid embolism.definition: A rare, life-threatening obstetric emergency in which amniotic fluid, fetal cells, or other debris enter the maternal circulation, triggering a systemic inflammatory response and activation of the coagulation cascade, leading to cardiopulmonary collapse and disseminated intravascular coagulation.

amniotic sac.definition: A fluid-filled membranous sac that surrounds and protects the developing fetus in the uterus; formed by the amnion (inner membrane) and chorion (outer layer), and containing amniotic fluid; provides cushioning, temperature regulation, and space for fetal movement; usually ruptures during labor (rupture of membranes).

chorionic villus sampling.definition: A prenatal diagnostic procedure in which a small sample of placental tissue (chorionic villi) is obtained, usually via transabdominal or transcervical approach, to test fetal chromosomal abnormalities and genetic disorders; typically performed in the first trimester. It yields early results but carries a small risk of miscarriage.

decidua.definition: The decidua is the specialized, hormonally driven endometrium of the uterus during pregnancy, produced by decidualization of endometrial stromal cells to support implantation and placentation; it comprises decidua basalis, decidua capsularis, and decidua parietalis and is shed at delivery.

meconium.definition: The first stool passed by a newborn; a thick, tar-like, dark green to black stool formed in the fetal intestine and passed after birth, composed of desquamated intestinal cells, mucus, bile pigments, and swallowed amniotic fluid.

rh negative.definition: A blood type in which red blood cells lack the Rh(D) antigen; individuals are at risk for anti-D antibody formation if exposed to Rh-positive blood, which can cause hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn in pregnancy; management includes Rh immunoglobulin prophylaxis for at-risk pregnancies.

rho(d) immunoglobulin.definition: A preparation of anti-D immunoglobulin given to Rh-negative individuals during pregnancy and after delivery or fetomaternal hemorrhage to prevent sensitization to the Rh(D) antigen and reduce the risk of hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn in future pregnancies.

isoimmunization.definition: The development of maternal antibodies against fetal red blood cell antigens following exposure to those antigens, typically due to Rh incompatibility, which can lead to hemolytic disease of the fetus/newborn.

hemolytic disease of the fetus.definition: A condition in which maternal IgG antibodies directed against fetal red blood cell antigens cross the placenta and destroy fetal erythrocytes (alloimmune hemolysis), causing fetal anemia and, in severe cases, hydrops fetalis and neonatal hyperbilirubinemia; most commonly due to Rh(D) incompatibility, preventable with Rh immune globulin prophylaxis.

premature rupture of membranes.definition: Rupture of the fetal membranes (amnion and chorion) before the onset of labor, resulting in leakage of amniotic fluid; if before 37 weeks it is called preterm PROM (PPROM), and if at or after 37 weeks it is term PROM.

preterm labor.definition: Labor that begins before 37 completed weeks of gestation, characterized by regular uterine contractions and progressive cervical dilation or effacement, which may culminate in preterm birth.

fetal death.definition: Fetal death is the death of a fetus in utero, typically defined as death after about 20 weeks of gestation (stillbirth), though exact criteria such as gestational age or birth weight can vary by region.

genetic disorders.definition: A disease or condition caused by abnormalities of the genome—such as single-gene mutations, chromosomal abnormalities, or complex interactions of multiple genes and environmental factors—that can be inherited or arise de novo and affect the structure or function of the body.

inherited disorders.definition: Disorders caused by genetic alterations that are passed from parent to offspring through the germ line; they can be Mendelian (single-gene) conditions, chromosomal abnormalities, mitochondrial inheritance, or multifactorial/polygenic disorders, and may be evident at birth or manifest later in life.

sex-linked disorders.definition: Disorders caused by mutations in genes located on the sex chromosomes (X or Y). Most commonly X-linked, these conditions often affect males more than females (who may be carriers), while Y-linked disorders affect only males and are rare.

chromosomal aberrations.definition: Structural or numerical changes to chromosomes that deviate from the normal karyotype, including aneuploidies (e.g., monosomy, trisomy) and structural rearrangements (deletions, duplications, inversions, translocations, ring chromosomes, isochromosomes); these alterations can disrupt gene dosage and lead to developmental abnormalities, infertility, or cancer.

congenital anomalies.definition: Structural or functional abnormalities that are present at birth, arising during fetal development, due to genetic or chromosomal abnormalities, environmental exposures (teratogens), or other factors affecting embryogenesis; they range from minor variants to life-threatening malformations.

cardiovascular disease.definition: A broad category of diseases affecting the heart and blood vessels, typically caused by atherosclerosis and other vascular risk factors, and encompassing conditions such as coronary artery disease, stroke, heart failure, and peripheral vascular disease.

fulminant hepatitis.definition: An acute liver failure characterized by rapid deterioration of hepatic function with the development of hepatic encephalopathy within 8 weeks of onset, accompanied by marked coagulopathy (INR typically >1.5) and jaundice due to massive hepatocellular necrosis.

hepatic encephalopathy.definition: A neuropsychiatric syndrome from liver failure or portosystemic shunting due to accumulation of gut-derived toxins (notably ammonia) that the liver would normally detoxify; it ranges from subtle cognitive/mood changes to confusion and coma.

blood dyscrasia.definition: An abnormal or diseased condition of the blood, typically referring to disorders of its cellular elements (red cells, white cells, or platelets) or of plasma components.

thrombophlebitis.definition: An inflammatory process of a vein with thrombus formation inside the lumen, causing localized pain, warmth, and redness along the affected vein; it commonly involves superficial veins but may involve deeper venous systems.

neuropathic pain.definition: Pain caused by a lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system; often described as burning, shooting, or electric shock-like, and may be accompanied by allodynia or hyperalgesia.

pneumothorax.definition: Presence of air in the pleural space that disrupts the negative intrapleural pressure, causing partial or complete collapse of the affected lung; can be spontaneous or traumatic and may progress to a life-threatening tension pneumothorax requiring urgent intervention.

endoscope.definition: A flexible or rigid optical instrument with a light source and camera used to visualize the interior surfaces of hollow organs or body cavities during endoscopy.

a-mode.definition: An ultrasound display mode in which echoes are represented as spikes whose height corresponds to echo amplitude, plotted against depth (derived from time of flight); it yields a one-dimensional measurement useful for estimating distances (e.g., ocular axial length) and provides timing information but no cross-sectional image.

b-mode.definition: A two-dimensional grayscale ultrasound imaging modality in which the brightness of each display point corresponds to the strength of the reflected ultrasound echo, yielding a cross-sectional image of tissues.

m-mode.definition: Motion mode (M-mode) is a one-dimensional ultrasound imaging mode that records motion along a single scan line, plotting depth versus time to visualize and quantify the motion and dimensions of cardiac structures (e.g., chamber sizes and wall motion).

a-mode ultrasound.definition: One-dimensional ultrasound display in which echoes are plotted as spikes along a depth axis; depth reflects time‑of‑flight and spike height reflects echo amplitude, allowing precise measurements of distances to tissue interfaces (e.g., ocular axial length) but not forming a two‑dimensional image.

amputation.definition: The surgical removal of a limb or other body part.

ampicillin.definition: A broad-spectrum beta-lactam antibiotic of the penicillin class (an aminopenicillin) that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins; used to treat infections caused by susceptible organisms and can be given orally or by injection.

sodium.definition: An essential extracellular cation (Na+) and major electrolyte that maintains extracellular fluid volume and osmolality; vital for nerve impulse transmission and muscle contraction; normal serum level roughly 135–145 mEq/L.

amprenavir.definition: A protease inhibitor antiretroviral medication used to treat HIV-1 infection; it inhibits the HIV-1 protease enzyme, preventing processing of viral polyproteins and maturation of infectious virions. It is typically given with ritonavir boosting and in combination with other antiretrovirals.

kalaazar.definition: A severe systemic parasitic infection caused by Leishmania donovani complex, transmitted by sandflies, presenting with prolonged fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, and pancytopenia; if untreated, it can be fatal and is treated with antileishmanial medications (e.g., liposomal amphotericin B, miltefosine).

liposome.definition: A spherical vesicle formed from a lipid (phospholipid) bilayer that encloses an aqueous interior; used to carry and deliver drugs, vaccines, or genetic material, with hydrophilic cargo in the core and hydrophobic cargo in the bilayer.

liposomal.definition: Relating to liposomes; describing substances encapsulated within lipid bilayer vesicles (liposomes) used to improve delivery, stability, and bioavailability of drugs or nutrients.

lipid.definition: A diverse group of hydrophobic biological molecules that are insoluble in water; major types include triglycerides, phospholipids, sterols, and fatty acids, and they function in energy storage, membrane structure, and signaling.

fungal.definition: Relating to fungus; produced by or caused by a fungus.

invasive.definition: In medicine, invasive means entering or penetrating the body or surrounding tissues, or a disease that spreads beyond its original site (e.g., invasive cancer).

tubal.definition: Relating to a tube; specifically, pertaining to the fallopian (uterine) tube in the female reproductive system or to other tubular structures.

flap.definition: A piece of tissue (such as skin, muscle, fat, or composite) moved from its original site to cover a defect while preserving its own blood supply; can be pedicled (local/regional) or free via microvascular anastomosis.

stump.definition: The residual limb remaining after amputation; the end portion of a limb that may be fitted with a prosthesis.

amputee.definition: A person who has had one or more limbs surgically removed or lost due to injury or disease.

cast.definition: A rigid external immobilization device, usually made of plaster or fiberglass, applied to a limb or body part to immobilize a fracture or severe injury and support healing.

gangrene.definition: Tissues in the body die due to loss of blood supply.

phantom.definition: A perceptual phenomenon in which a person experiences sensations (such as pain, warmth, tingling, or movement) in a limb or body part that has been amputated or is otherwise absent.

aplastic.definition: Relating to aplasia; characterized by absence or failure of development or function of an organ or tissue; in hematology, describing bone marrow failure to produce adequate blood cells.

hemolytic.definition: Relating to the destruction of red blood cells (hemolysis), which can occur due to immune, mechanical, infectious, or toxic processes.

protease.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of peptide bonds in proteins, breaking them down into smaller peptides and amino acids.

inhibitor.definition: A drug that slows down or stops a process.

amylase.definition: An enzyme secreted by the pancreas that breaks starch into sugar.

amyloidosis.definition: A group of diseases in which misfolded amyloid proteins accumulate extracellularly as insoluble fibrils in tissues and organs, causing progressive dysfunction; most forms are systemic (eg, AL/light-chain and AA/serum amyloid A) but localized forms exist.

amylopectinosis.definition: A rare glycogen storage disorder in which an amylopectin-like polysaccharide accumulates in tissues due to deficiency of the glycogen branching enzyme (GBE1), most often corresponding to glycogen storage disease type IV (Andersen disease).

amylophagia.definition: A form of pica characterized by persistent ingestion of starch.

crohn.definition: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease causing relapsing inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract, often affecting the terminal ileum and/or colon, with symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and fatigue; complications can include fistulas and strictures.

osteomyelitis.definition: A bone infection caused by bacteria or fungi.

alzheimer.definition: A progressive brain disease that causes memory loss, impaired thinking, and personality changes.

hemodialysis.definition: A treatment that does the work of your kidneys when they can't. Also called dialysis.

amygdala.definition: Part of the brain involved in memory and emotion.

amygdaloid.definition: Almond-shaped; in neuroanatomy, relating to the amygdala, a limbic system structure in the temporal lobe involved in emotional processing, fear responses, and memory formation.

fossa.definition: A shallow depression or hollow on a bone or organ, often serving as an articular surface or a space to accommodate another structure.

nucleus.definition: A membrane-bound organelle in eukaryotic cells that contains the cell's DNA, organized into chromosomes, and regulates gene expression and DNA replication; it is enclosed by the nuclear envelope with nuclear pores and houses the nucleolus.

ampullary.definition: Relating to an ampulla; a dilated, sac-like enlargement of a duct or canal, such as the ampulla of Vater at the junction of the bile and pancreatic ducts with the duodenum.

duodenal.definition: Relating to the duodenum, the first portion of the small intestine.

obstruction.definition: An obstruction is a blockage that prevents the normal passage of a substance (air, fluid, or contents) through a hollow organ or duct, and can be partial or complete, mechanical or functional.

cyanide.definition: A group of chemical substances containing the cyanide (CN−) group, including hydrogen cyanide and cyanide salts; they inhibit mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV), blocking oxidative phosphorylation and causing histotoxic hypoxia; acute exposure can cause headache, confusion, seizures, coma, and metabolic acidosis; treatment includes antidotes such as hydroxocobalamin and nitrite/thiosulfate therapies plus supportive care.

angina.definition: Chest pain or discomfort that occurs when there is not enough blood flowing to the heart. Stable angina is also called angina pectoris.

amylopsin.definition: A pancreatic enzyme (α-amylase) that digests starch by hydrolyzing α-1,4-glycosidic bonds to maltose and dextrins, facilitating carbohydrate digestion.

glycoprotein.definition: A protein with covalently attached carbohydrate (glycan) chains, typically via N- or O-glycosylation; glycosylation modulates folding, stability, and function and glycoproteins mediate cell recognition, signaling, adhesion, and immune responses.

protein.definition: One of the three major nutrients (along with carbohydrates and fats). It is used by the body for building and repairing tissues. Protein is derived primarily from animal sources but can be obtained from nuts and seed, some grains, and other plant sources.

endocytosis.definition: A cellular process by which cells internalize extracellular material by invagination of the plasma membrane to form vesicles, including phagocytosis, pinocytosis, and receptor-mediated endocytosis.

angiospasm.definition: A transient, involuntary constriction of a blood vessel (usually an artery or arteriolar) causing sudden narrowing and reduced blood flow to the supplied tissue, often occurring in vasospastic disorders (e.g., coronary vasospasm).

anoxia.definition: A total lack of oxygen supply to the body's tissues; a severe form of hypoxia that can result from impaired oxygen delivery or uptake (e.g., respiratory failure, airway obstruction, or circulatory failure).

dna.definition: The part of your genes that influences the way you look and grow.

pcr.definition: A laboratory method that rapidly amplifies a specific DNA sequence by cycling denaturation, primer annealing, and extension with a DNA polymerase, enabling detection and analysis from small starting amounts. Variants include real-time (quantitative) PCR for quantification and reverse-transcription PCR for RNA templates.

anacusis.definition: Complete loss of hearing in both ears; total deafness.

anaemia.definition: An abnormal condition in which the blood has a lower-than-normal level of red blood cells or hemoglobin, reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.

anaesthesia.definition: A reversible state of insensitivity to pain created intentionally for medical procedures, typically by drugs or techniques that block sensation and may include loss of consciousness; includes general, regional, and local approaches.

anaesthetic.definition: A drug that induces anesthesia, causing loss of sensation (and possibly consciousness) for a medical procedure; includes local, regional, and general anesthetics.

anadicrotic.definition: Describing a pulse waveform lacking the dicrotic notch on an arterial pressure tracing; the small secondary deflection following the main systolic peak is absent.

pulse.definition: A rhythmic palpable expansion of an artery produced by the systolic contraction of the heart, used to estimate heart rate and assess circulation.

anadidymus.definition: No recognized medical term by that spelling. If you meant the epididymis: a coiled tube at the posterior aspect of each testis where sperm mature and are stored. Please confirm spelling or provide context.

anadipsia.definition: A lack of thirst; absence or diminished drive to drink fluids, typically due to dysfunction of the hypothalamic thirst center or related central nervous system or metabolic disorders, which can lead to dehydration and electrolyte disturbances.

anadrol-50.definition: A potent synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid (oxymetholone) used to treat certain anemias and to stimulate weight gain in malnourished or debilitated patients; it can cause liver toxicity and other androgenic side effects.

oxymetholone.definition: A potent orally active synthetic anabolic steroid (androgen) used to treat severe anemia and promote weight gain in wasting syndromes; commonly known by the brand name Anadrol-50.

anaerobe.definition: An organism that does not require oxygen for growth and is often inhibited or killed by exposure to atmospheric oxygen (obligate anaerobe).

anaerobic.definition: Relating to or occurring in the absence of oxygen; an organism that does not require oxygen to live or grow.

clostridium.definition: A genus of Gram-positive, spore-forming, obligate anaerobic bacilli found in soil and in the intestinal tracts; several species produce potent toxins and cause diseases such as botulism, tetanus, gas gangrene, and antibiotic-associated diarrhea.

botulinum.definition: A potent neurotoxin produced by Clostridium botulinum that blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, causing flaccid paralysis; used therapeutically in small doses to reduce wrinkles and treat certain muscle spasticity disorders.

tetanus.definition: A serious infectious disease caused by the bacterium Clostridium tetani, found in soil, that produces toxins causing painful muscle stiffness and spasms, often starting with lockjaw.

myositis.definition: Inflammation of skeletal muscle tissue, often with proximal muscle weakness and sometimes muscle pain; may be idiopathic or autoimmune (as in polymyositis and dermatomyositis) and can be associated with elevated muscle enzymes.

anagen.definition: The active growth phase of the hair-growth cycle.

anagrelide.definition: A selective phosphodiesterase-III inhibitor that reduces platelet production by inhibiting megakaryocyte maturation; used to treat essential thrombocythemia to lower platelet counts; common adverse effects include headache, tachycardia, palpitations, edema, and dizziness.

anakinra.definition: A recombinant human interleukin-1 receptor antagonist that blocks IL-1 by competitively inhibiting its binding to IL-1 receptors; used as an anti-inflammatory biologic for rheumatoid arthritis and various autoinflammatory disorders (e.g., cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes, systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis).

fissure.definition: An elongated crack or split in tissue, especially skin or mucous membranes; can be a natural groove or a pathologic tear caused by trauma, infection, or disease.

fistula.definition: A connection that is not normal between 2 organs or blood vessels. You can be born with a fistula or it can develop after surgery or a disease.

hemorrhoids.definition: Engorged or inflamed venous cushions in the anal canal. When located above the dentate line, these cushions typically cause painless rectal bleeding or prolapse; when located below the line, they are often painful. Risk factors include constipation, straining, diarrhea, and pregnancy. Management ranges from a high-fiber diet and fluids to topical therapies, and, for persistent or prolapsed disease, procedures such as rubber-band ligation or surgical removal.

anal.definition: Relating to the anus; pertaining to the distal end of the digestive tract.

canal.definition: A natural tubular passage within the body; a long, narrow channel through which substances (air, fluids, nerves, or other materials) pass.

sphincter.definition: A ring of muscle that surrounds an opening and can be contracted to close the opening. For example, the muscles found at the anus and the opening of the bladder are sphincters.

perianal.definition: Relating to or located around the anus; the region surrounding the anal opening.

perineal.definition: Relating to the perineum—the area between the anus and the genitals; in humans, the region between the pubic symphysis and coccyx, bounded laterally by the ischial tuberosities.

cloacal.definition: Relating to a posterior body cavity into which the intestinal, urinary, and genital tracts open in birds, reptiles, amphibians, and monotremes; in human embryology, pertaining to the embryonic structure that divides to form the anorectal canal and the urogenital sinus.

membrane.definition: A thin layer of tissue that surrounds or lines organs or cavities.

cryptitis.definition: Inflammation of the intestinal crypts (crypts of Lieberkühn), typically with neutrophilic infiltration of the crypt epithelium and sometimes crypt abscess formation; a histologic sign of active colitis.

crypt.definition: A tubular invagination or gland in a mucous membrane, lined by epithelium; in the gastrointestinal tract, the crypts of Lieberkühn are glands at the base of intestinal villi that contain stem cells responsible for renewing the epithelium.

analogue.definition: A chemical compound that resembles another in chemical structure and often in pharmacological activity, usually produced by modifying the original molecule while keeping similar biological effects.

crohns.definition: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease of unknown cause characterized by transmural, segmental inflammation that can involve any part of the gastrointestinal tract (most often the terminal ileum and colon), with skip lesions and potential fistulas or strictures; symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and malabsorption, and it may have extraintestinal manifestations.

anus.definition: The external opening at the end of the digestive tract where feces are expelled.

chlorpheniramine.definition: A first-generation antihistamine (H1 receptor antagonist) used to relieve symptoms of allergic rhinitis, conjunctivitis, and urticaria, and sometimes as a sedative for insomnia; it blocks histamine receptors in the body and brain, often causing drowsiness and anticholinergic side effects.

orthostatic.definition: Relating to standing upright; in medicine, describing physiological changes that occur when shifting from lying or seated to standing, commonly involving a drop in blood pressure.

palpitations.definition: A subjective sensation of the heartbeat that feels unusually fast, irregular, or strong (e.g., racing, fluttering, pounding, or skipped beats); not a diagnosis in itself but may reflect benign conditions or underlying arrhythmias or other medical issues.

seizures.definition: Episodes of transient, abnormal electrical activity in the brain that disrupt normal function, causing convulsions, altered awareness or sensation, or other sudden changes in behavior.

ecchymosis.definition: A large bruise; a subcutaneous extravasation of blood from ruptured vessels, producing a bluish-purple discoloration under the skin that often changes hue as it heals.

lymphadenoma.definition: A benign, tumor-like proliferation of lymphoid tissue within a lymph node.

myocardiopathy.definition: A disease of the heart muscle (myocardium) that impairs the heart’s ability to pump blood; it encompasses a family of conditions called cardiomyopathies, including dilated, hypertrophic, and restrictive types.

cardiomegaly.definition: Enlargement of the heart seen on imaging due to dilation or hypertrophy of the cardiac chambers; commonly caused by hypertension, cardiomyopathy, valvular disease, or heart failure, and not a disease itself.

epidural.definition: A shot of medicine in the lower back that causes pain to be dulled in some parts of the body.

intraspinal.definition: Located within the spinal canal (inside the vertebral column).

analeptic.definition: A drug that stimulates the central nervous system, particularly the respiratory centers, used to counteract central nervous system depression or anesthesia.

erotism.definition: State of sexual arousal or erotic excitement in response to stimuli; used in psychology and psychiatry to denote sexual desire or arousal.

perspiration.definition: The secretion of sweat from the sweat glands in the skin, consisting mainly of water and electrolytes with small amounts of waste products; its primary function is thermoregulation through evaporative cooling, regulated by the sympathetic nervous system.

electrolyte.definition: A substance that dissociates into positively and negatively charged ions in solution and conducts electricity; in biology, key ions such as sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, calcium, and phosphate regulate fluid balance, nerve and muscle function, and acid-base balance.

imbalance.definition: A state in which the body's normal balance of substances or regulatory processes is disrupted, resulting in abnormal levels or distribution (for example, electrolyte imbalances, hormonal imbalances, or acid–base imbalances).

bipolar.definition: Relating to two poles; in psychiatry, a mood disorder characterized by episodes of elevated or irritable mood (mania or hypomania) and depressive episodes, with periods of normal mood in between.

manic.definition: Pertaining to mania; a mood state of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable affect with increased energy and activity, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts, grandiosity, distractibility, and often impulsive or risky behavior. It is a feature of bipolar disorder; when sustained for at least one week (or with hospitalization) and causing marked impairment, it constitutes a manic episode.

anamnesis.definition: The patient's account of their medical history and current symptoms, gathered through clinician interview, including past illnesses, medications, allergies, family history, and relevant lifestyle and psychosocial factors.

anamnestic.definition: Relating to memory; in medicine, pertaining to anamnesis (the recall of a patient’s medical history) or to a memory-driven immune response that is enhanced upon re-exposure to an antigen.

anaphylactic.definition: Relating to anaphylaxis, a severe, potentially life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction that occurs rapidly after exposure to an allergen, causing symptoms such as widespread hives or swelling, bronchospasm, airway obstruction, hypotension, and shock.

anaphylactoid purpura.definition: IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis presenting with palpable purpura (usually on the legs/buttocks), abdominal pain, arthritis/arthralgia, and possible renal involvement; most common in children; pathogenesis involves IgA immune-complex deposition in vessel walls; historically described as Henoch–Schönlein purpura.

henoch-schönlein purpura.definition: A small-vessel leukocytoclastic vasculitis caused by IgA immune complex deposition; classically presents with palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs, often with arthralgia, abdominal pain, and possible renal involvement (hematuria/proteinuria); most common in children and usually self-limited.

anaphylatoxin.definition: Small peptide fragments (C3a, C4a, C5a) produced during complement activation that act as inflammatory mediators by causing degranulation of mast cells and basophils, increasing vascular permeability, and recruiting leukocytes.

anastrozole.definition: A non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor that reduces estrogen production by inhibiting the aromatase enzyme; used to treat estrogen receptor–positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women (adjuvant and metastatic settings).

anastomosis.definition: A surgical or natural connection between two hollow tubular structures (such as blood vessels or intestinal segments) to restore continuity and enable flow between them.

end-to-end anastomosis.definition: A surgical technique that connects the two ends of a tubular organ (most commonly the intestine) after removal of a diseased segment, to restore a continuous lumen. The join is typically created with sutures or surgical staples to reestablish continuity and function.

end-to-side anastomosis.definition: A surgical connection in which the end of one hollow organ or vessel is joined to the side of another, creating a channel that preserves the recipient lumen while attaching the donor end to its side. Commonly used in vascular grafting and bowel surgery to restore continuity or divert flow.

side-to-side anastomosis.definition: A surgical connection between the sidewalls of two hollow structures (often segments of intestine or ducts) to create a single channel between their lumens; the anastomosis joins the lateral aspects rather than the ends, often to bypass a stricture or widen the passage.

anastomotic.definition: Relating to an anastomosis, a surgical or natural connection between two hollow structures (such as blood vessels or segments of intestine) that enables continuity of flow between them.

anastomos is.definition: A connection between two hollow tubular structures (e.g., blood vessels or segments of the intestine) that permits flow or passage between them; can be natural (physiologic) or surgically created.

anatomical.definition: Relating to anatomy; pertaining to the structure of the body or its parts.

anatomical snuffbox.definition: A triangular depression on the dorsoradial aspect of the wrist at the base of the thumb, bounded medially by the tendon of extensor pollicis longus and laterally by the tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis; its floor overlies the scaphoid and trapezium, with the radial artery coursing beneath. Clinically important for palpating the radial pulse and assessing suspected scaphoid fractures.

anatomical neck of humerus.definition: The narrow region immediately below the humeral head that forms the boundary between the articular head and the greater/lesser tubercles; the joint capsule attaches there.

anatomical position.definition: An upright standing posture used as the reference position in anatomy: the person stands erect, facing forward, with feet together or slightly apart and arms at the sides with palms facing forward and thumbs directed away from the body.

anaplasia.definition: Loss of cellular differentiation and tissue organization, characterized by pleomorphic, hyperchromatic cells and increased mitotic activity, commonly seen in malignant tumors.

anaplastic.definition: Describing cells that have lost differentiation and resemble primitive, immature forms; in pathology, cells are undifferentiated and pleomorphic with hyperchromatic nuclei and increased mitotic activity, typically indicating a highly malignant, poorly differentiated tumor.

anaplastic astrocytoma.definition: A malignant glioma of astrocytic origin (WHO grade III) characterized by marked cellular atypia, increased mitotic activity, and infiltrative growth; more aggressive than a low-grade astrocytoma but less aggressive than glioblastoma (grade IV).

anaprox.definition: A brand-name nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) containing naproxen; used to relieve pain, inflammation, and fever.

anconeus.definition: A small triangular muscle on the posterior aspect of the elbow that extends the forearm and stabilizes the elbow joint; originates from the lateral epicondyle of the humerus and inserts onto the olecranon and proximal ulna; innervation: radial nerve (posterior interosseous branch).

ancrod.definition: A defibrinogenating enzyme derived from the venom of the Malayan pit viper that cleaves fibrinogen, reducing plasma fibrinogen levels and inhibiting clot formation; previously used as an anticoagulant/antithrombotic agent but associated with bleeding risk and limited current use.

ancylostoma.definition: A genus of parasitic nematodes (hookworms) that infect the small intestine of mammals; in humans, infection can cause iron-deficiency anemia and gastrointestinal symptoms, typically transmitted by skin penetration of infective larvae in contaminated soil.

ancylostomiasis.definition: An intestinal nematode infection caused by hookworms (Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus) acquired through skin penetration by larvae in contaminated soil, leading to chronic intestinal blood loss and iron-deficiency anemia; treated with antihelminthic agents such as albendazole or mebendazole.

ancylostoma duodenale.definition: A parasitic nematode (hookworm) of humans that inhabits the proximal small intestine, causing hookworm disease with iron-deficiency anemia and protein malnutrition; transmission occurs when filariform larvae in contaminated soil penetrate the skin and migrate to the small intestine.

ancylostoma braziliense.definition: A zoonotic parasitic nematode (hookworm) primarily infecting dogs and cats; human infection occurs when larvae penetrate the skin, causing cutaneous larva migrans (creeping eruption) with serpiginous, pruritic skin tracks.

ancylostoma caninum.definition: A parasitic nematode (hookworm) that infects dogs and other canids; resides in the small intestine and feeds on host blood, causing anemia, with larvae that can penetrate human skin to cause cutaneous larva migrans.

necator americanus.definition: A species of intestinal nematode (hookworm) that infects humans; larvae penetrate the skin from contaminated soil and mature in the small intestine, where adults attach to the mucosa and feed on blood, causing iron-deficiency anemia and protein loss, especially in tropical and subtropical regions.

andersen's disease.definition: An autosomal recessive glycogen storage disease (type IV) due to deficiency of the glycogen branching enzyme (GBE1), causing accumulation of abnormal, poorly branched glycogen (polyglucosan) in liver, heart, and muscle with progressive hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis, hypotonia, cardiomyopathy, and early death in infancy.

glycogen storage disease.definition: A group of inherited metabolic disorders caused by deficiencies of enzymes involved in glycogen synthesis or breakdown, leading to abnormal glycogen accumulation and impaired glucose release from the liver; clinical features vary by subtype but often include fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, and growth or muscle problems (weakness, myopathy, or cardiomyopathy).

glycogen storage disease type iv.definition: An autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of the branching enzyme (amylo-1,4→1,6-transferase, encoded by GBE1), leading to accumulation of insoluble, poorly branched glycogen (polyglucosan) in liver, heart, and muscle. It typically presents with hepatosplenomegaly and liver dysfunction, progressing to cirrhosis, failure to thrive, hypotonia, cardiomyopathy, and often early death in infancy.

brancher glycogen storage disease.definition: An autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of the glycogen branching enzyme, leading to accumulation of abnormal, poorly branched glycogen in liver, heart, and muscle; presents with progressive hepatosplenomegaly, liver fibrosis or cirrhosis, possible cardiomyopathy, and failure to thrive, usually in infancy; diagnosed by enzyme assay or genetic testing; management is supportive with variable prognosis.

andersen's syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal dominant channelopathy caused by mutations in the KCNJ2 gene (Kir2.1) that presents with a combination of congenital long QT syndrome and episodic muscle weakness (periodic paralysis); may include additional dysmorphic features.

andersen's triad.definition: I can’t find a standard medical definition for “Andersen’s triad.” It may be a misspelling or a very rare/obsolete term. pyeloplasty.definition: A surgical procedure to repair a blockage at the ureteropelvic junction by reconstructing the renal pelvis and ureter (often resecting the obstructed segment and reattaching the healthy ends) to restore normal urine drainage; performed open, laparoscopically, or robotically.

anderson-hynes pyeloplasty.definition: A dismembered surgical repair of ureteropelvic junction obstruction in which the obstructed UPJ segment is excised and the healthy ureter is reimplanted into the renal pelvis to restore drainage, commonly performed openly or via minimally invasive approaches and typically with a ureteral stent.

androgen.definition: Any of a group of male sex hormones, including testosterone, that controls male characteristics such as beard growth.

androgamone.definition: A male gamete; the reproductive cell that fuses with the female gamete during fertilization, typically produced by male gametangia (such as antheridia) in plants and algae.

androblastoma.definition: A rare androgen-secreting sex cord–stromal tumor of the gonad (most often the ovary); composed of Sertoli and Leydig cells and historically called arrhenoblastoma, often presenting with virilization.

arrhenoblastoma.definition: An androgen-secreting ovarian tumor of sex cord-stromal origin (Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor); often produces virilization in women and may be benign or malignant.

androsterone.definition: A naturally occurring weak androgen steroid; a metabolite of testosterone and dihydrotestosterone, chemically 3α-hydroxy-5α-androstan-17-one.

hookworm disease.definition: An intestinal infection caused by hookworms (Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus) that occurs when larvae penetrate the skin, migrate to the small intestine, and attach to the mucosa to feed on blood, often causing iron‑deficiency anemia and nutritional loss; symptoms may include abdominal pain and fatigue, and diagnosis is by stool egg examination; treatment involves antiparasitic drugs and iron supplementation, with prevention by improved sanitation and wearing shoes.

hookworm.definition: Parasitic infection of the small intestine caused by blood-sucking nematodes (primarily Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus) acquired when larval forms in contaminated soil penetrate the skin; produces iron-deficiency anemia and gastrointestinal symptoms; diagnosed by stool eggs and treated with antiparasitic drugs such as albendazole or mebendazole.

graft.definition: A piece of tissue or an organ transplanted surgically from one site to another to replace damaged tissue; may be autograft, allograft, or xenograft.

greater saphenous vein.definition: A large superficial vein of the leg, the longest in the body; it begins at the medial dorsal venous arch of the foot, ascends along the medial aspect of the leg and thigh, and drains into the femoral vein at the saphenous opening in the fascia lata.

saphenous vein.definition: A superficial blood vessel that extends from the thigh to the calf; it can be removed and used as a coronary bypass graft.

elbow.definition: A hinge-type synovial joint formed by the articulation of the distal humerus with the proximal radius and ulna; it primarily permits flexion and extension of the forearm, with the proximal radioulnar joint allowing forearm rotation (pronation and supination).

olecranon.definition: A large projection of the ulna at the elbow (the proximal posterior part of the ulna) that forms the point of the elbow; the triceps brachii tendon inserts here and it participates in the elbow joint by articulating with the trochlea of the humerus.

brachial artery.definition: The major blood vessel of the upper arm; a continuation of the axillary artery that travels down the arm and bifurcates into the radial and ulnar arteries at the elbow, supplying oxygenated blood to the arm and forearm.

deep brachial arteries.definition: Branch of the brachial artery in the arm that travels posteriorly with the radial nerve in the spiral/Radial groove, supplying the posterior arm muscles (notably the triceps) and giving off posterior radial collateral arteries that contribute to elbow collateral circulation; also provides a nutrient artery to the humerus.

pharynx.definition: A muscular, mucosa‑lined tube behind the nasal and oral cavities that funnels air to the larynx and food to the esophagus; it is divided into the nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx.

crown.definition: A covering on a tooth. Can be made from different materials, including porcelain or gold.

snuffbox.definition: Anatomical region on the dorsoradial wrist at the base of the thumb; a triangular depression bounded medially by the tendon of extensor pollicis longus and laterally by the tendons of extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus, overlying the scaphoid bone with the radial artery coursing in its floor.

cefazolin.definition: A first-generation cephalosporin antibiotic used for perioperative prophylaxis and for treating susceptible Gram-positive bacterial infections; it inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin‑binding proteins and is given by IV or IM administration, with limited activity against Gram-negative bacteria and no reliable activity against MRSA.

ancef.definition: A brand-name injectable cephalosporin antibiotic (cefazolin) used for perioperative surgical prophylaxis and for treatment of infections caused by susceptible bacteria.

cefazolin sodium.definition: A sodium salt form of cefazolin, a first-generation cephalosporin antibiotic given by IV or IM injection for prophylaxis of surgical infections and treatment of susceptible bacterial infections; it is bactericidal by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis.

naproxen.definition: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that relieves pain and inflammation and reduces fever by reversibly inhibiting cyclooxygenase (COX‑1 and COX‑2), thereby decreasing prostaglandin synthesis; commonly used for arthritis, musculoskeletal pain, and cramps.

naproxen sodium.definition: A salt form of naproxen, a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that relieves pain, inflammation, and fever by nonselectively inhibiting cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2) and decreasing prostaglandin synthesis; used for mild-to-moderate pain such as arthritis, musculoskeletal injuries, and cramps.

tamoxifen.definition: A drug used by women to prevent breast cancer or its recurrence.

allergens.definition: A substance that triggers an allergic reaction in susceptible individuals, such as pollen, dust, mold, or animal dander.

antigen-antibody.definition: A specific binding interaction in which an antibody attaches to its corresponding antigen (epitope), forming an immune complex that can neutralize the antigen and promote its clearance by other immune mechanisms.

ige.definition: A class of antibody (immunoglobulin E) produced by plasma cells; mediates type I hypersensitivity reactions and helps defend against parasites; binds to Fc receptors on mast cells and basophils, and cross-linking by an allergen triggers release of histamine and other mediators.

igg.definition: An abundant class of antibodies in human serum that provides the majority of antibody-mediated immunity; it neutralizes pathogens and toxins, promotes opsonization, activates the classical complement pathway, and crosses the placenta to confer passive fetal immunity; it comprises four subclasses (IgG1–IgG4).

complement.definition: A group of serum proteins that augment immunity by promoting inflammation, opsonization, chemotaxis, and lysis of pathogens; activated through classical, lectin, or alternative pathways in a proteolytic cascade, culminating in membrane attack complex formation.

mast cell.definition: A cell involved in allergic reactions. When stimulated, it releases chemicals like histamine that signal infection and cause inflammation.

mast cell activation.definition: Process by which mast cells become activated and release mediators (histamine, tryptase, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, cytokines) in response to various triggers (e.g., allergen–IgE cross-linking, physical stimuli, drugs), producing inflammatory and allergic symptoms.

fibroblasts.definition: Fibroblasts are spindle-shaped cells of connective tissue that synthesize and remodel the extracellular matrix, especially collagen types I and III, and glycosaminoglycans; they play a central role in wound healing and tissue repair.

antibiotic therapy.definition: Treatment of a bacterial infection with medications that kill or inhibit the growth of bacteria; selection depends on the suspected or confirmed organism and site of infection, and administration can be oral, intravenous, or topical.

insect venom.definition: A toxic secretion produced by venomous insects and delivered through a sting or bite to defend the insect or subdue prey; it contains diverse components (peptides, enzymes, amines) that commonly cause immediate pain and swelling, and may provoke systemic symptoms or severe allergic reactions in susceptible individuals.

bee venom.definition: A venom produced by the venom glands of honeybees (Apis mellifera) that is injected via stings; it contains peptides such as melittin and enzymes (e.g., phospholipase A2) and can cause local pain and swelling, with potential for systemic allergic reactions including anaphylaxis in susceptible individuals.

bee sting.definition: A sting from a bee in which venom is injected into the skin by the insect’s barbed stinger; commonly causes immediate sharp pain, swelling, redness, and itching at the site and may trigger systemic allergic reactions (including anaphylaxis) in sensitive individuals. Management includes removing the stinger, cold application, analgesics, and antihistamines; severe reactions require epinephrine and emergency care.

iodide.definition: The negatively charged iodide ion (I−); the conjugate base of hydroiodic acid, forming iodine salts, and biologically required for thyroid hormone synthesis.

contrast media.definition: A substance used to enhance visualization of internal structures in imaging by altering tissue contrast; examples include iodinated agents for CT/X-ray and gadolinium-based agents for MRI, administered intravenously, orally, or rectally.

contrast media containing iodide.definition: A radiopaque iodine-containing contrast agent used to enhance visualization on X-ray–based imaging by increasing X-ray attenuation; typically water-soluble and given intravenously or intra-arterially, available in ionic (high-osmolar) and nonionic (low-osmolar) formulations.

hyperemia.definition: An increased volume of blood in the microvasculature of a tissue, often causing redness and warmth; caused by arteriolar dilation (active hyperemia) or venous congestion (passive hyperemia) during inflammation.

abdominal cramps.definition: A sensation of pain or cramping in the abdomen caused by rhythmic contractions or spasms of the smooth muscles of the intestines or uterus; commonly due to gas, indigestion, constipation, diarrhea, infection, or menstrual cramps.

dysphagia.definition: When you have trouble or pain when you swallow.

stridor.definition: A high-pitched, wheezing sound produced by turbulent airflow through a narrowed or obstructed upper airway, typically heard on inspiration and indicating partial airway obstruction at the larynx or trachea.

endotracheal tube.definition: An artificial airway device inserted through the mouth or nose into the trachea to secure a patent airway and allow ventilation and oxygen delivery, typically with an inflatable cuff to seal the trachea and prevent aspiration, and connected to a ventilator or anesthesia machine.

cricothyrotomy.definition: A rapid emergency surgical airway created by incising the skin and cricothyroid membrane to enter the trachea and insert a tube to bypass an upper airway obstruction when conventional methods fail.

oxygen therapy.definition: Oxygen therapy is the medical administration of supplemental oxygen to treat or prevent hypoxemia by increasing the amount of oxygen in inspired air. It is delivered via devices such as a nasal cannula, face mask, or ventilatory support and is titrated to a target arterial oxygen saturation (SpO2) or PaO2 based on the patient's condition (commonly SpO2 94–98%, or 88–92% for some COPD patients).

intramuscular.definition: To put into a muscle. Some shots are given intramuscularly.

subcutaneous.definition: Situated beneath the skin; pertaining to the subcutaneous tissue (hypodermis), the fatty layer located beneath the dermis.

iv solutions.definition: Sterile intravenous fluids given through a vein to restore or maintain circulating volume, supply electrolytes and calories, and facilitate medication administration. They include crystalloids (e.g., normal saline 0.9% NaCl, lactated Ringer's, dextrose-containing solutions) and, less commonly, colloids, and are chosen based on tonicity (isotonic, hypotonic, or hypertonic) and clinical need.

vasoconstrictors.definition: Substances that induce contraction of vascular smooth muscle, narrowing blood vessels and increasing vascular resistance and blood pressure; includes endogenous mediators (e.g., norepinephrine, angiotensin II, vasopressin) and pharmacologic agents (e.g., phenylephrine, norepinephrine) used to treat hypotension or reduce bleeding.

ventilation.definition: The process of moving air into and out of the lungs to facilitate gas exchange; it can occur through normal breathing or via artificial/mechanical ventilation in clinical settings.

tissue perfusion.definition: The flow of blood through the capillary networks of a tissue, delivering oxygen and nutrients while removing carbon dioxide and waste products; it reflects the adequacy of tissue blood supply.

prophylaxis.definition: Something that prevents disease or infection, such as drugs taken before travel to prevent malaria, or shots given after an animal bite to prevent rabies.

medic alert.definition: A medical identification bracelet or similar ID that communicates critical health information to emergency responders, including medical conditions, allergies, medications, and contact details, often linked to a secure patient record.

androgenetic alopecia.definition: Female- and male-pattern baldness. The condition appears to involve a heightened response by the hair follicle to androgen levels in the body.

scalp.definition: The skin and subcutaneous tissue that cover the skull, including the hair-bearing outer layer.

hair.definition: A filamentous keratinized outgrowth produced by hair follicles in the skin; the visible portion is the hair shaft, while the root remains in the follicle. Hair grows in cycles (anagen, catagen, telogen) and varies in color due to melanin; it provides insulation, protection, and tactile sensation.

telogen.definition: The resting phase of the hair growth cycle, during which hair follicles are inactive, club hairs form, and shedding occurs; it lasts about 2–4 months before follicles re-enter the growth phase.

android obesity.definition: A pattern of fat distribution in which most adiposity is centralized in the abdomen (visceral/central obesity), giving an "apple-shaped" body; associated with a higher risk of metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease.

android pelvis.definition: An android pelvis is a male-type maternal pelvis characterized by a heart-shaped pelvic inlet and a narrow, funnel-shaped true pelvis with an acute subpubic angle; it often results in a relatively narrow birth canal and is associated with obstructed labor.

gynecoid pelvis.definition: A female-typical pelvic morphology with a rounded or oval pelvic inlet and a spacious true pelvis, featuring a broad subpubic angle and wide pelvic outlet, making it the most favorable type for vaginal delivery.

pelvis.definition: A bowl-shaped set of bones that connects the upper part of your body with your legs.

vaginal delivery.definition: Vaginal delivery is the birth of a baby through the birth canal (vagina) after the onset of labor, which can be spontaneous or assisted with instruments (e.g., vacuum extraction or forceps).

placental abnormalities.definition: Structural or functional disorders of the placenta—the organ that nourishes the fetus during pregnancy—that disrupt placental development, implantation, blood flow, or nutrient transfer, potentially leading to fetal growth restriction, preterm birth, or maternal hemorrhage.

uterine atony.definition: Failure of the uterus to contract effectively after delivery, leading to postpartum hemorrhage from inadequate compression of placental vessels.

postpartum.definition: Pertaining to the period after giving birth.

anephric.definition: Relating to or denoting absence of a kidney.

anephrogenesis.definition: A congenital absence of kidney tissue due to failure of nephrogenesis; complete lack of kidney development, typically bilateral, resulting in absent kidneys at birth and usually incompatible with life or causing severe oligohydramnios.

anergia.definition: A persistent lack of energy and initiative (psychomotor energy deficiency) with diminished motivation and activity, often seen in depression or chronic illness.

aneroid.definition: A device for measuring pressure that contains no liquid; it uses a sealed flexible metal chamber that expands or contracts with pressure and drives a mechanical gauge, as in aneroid sphygmomanometers or barometers.

anesthetic.definition: A substance used to reduce sensitivity to pain. See also anesthesia.

anesthesia machine.definition: A device that delivers a precisely controlled mixture of oxygen and volatile anesthetic agents to a patient during anesthesia, while providing ventilation support and monitoring; comprises gas sources, delivery lines, vaporizers, a breathing circuit, a ventilator, a CO2 absorber, and a scavenging system.
