anesthesiologist.definition: A physician who specializes in anesthesia, responsible for administering anesthesia, monitoring patients during surgery, and managing perioperative pain and recovery.

anesthesiologist assistant.definition: A non-physician anesthesia professional who, under an anesthesiologist's supervision, helps plan and administer anesthesia—including preoperative assessment, induction, maintenance, airway management, intraoperative monitoring, and emergence—with a master’s degree from an accredited anesthesiologist assistant program and board certification.

anesthesiologist's assistant.definition: A certified nonphysician anesthesia provider who assists anesthesiologists in the perioperative management of patients, including preoperative assessment, induction and maintenance of anesthesia, airway management, intraoperative monitoring, and postoperative care, typically with graduate-level training and licensure, working under an anesthesiologist's supervision.

local anesthesia.definition: A drug that causes numbness in a localized area of the body where it is administered, such as at the site of a dental procedure.

regional anesthesia.definition: A regional anesthesia is a technique that blocks sensation in a defined body region by injecting local anesthetic near targeted nerves or neuraxial structures (spinal/epidural or peripheral nerve/plexus), providing surgical anesthesia or analgesia while the patient remains awake or lightly sedated.

spinal anesthesia.definition: A regional anesthesia technique in which a local anesthetic is injected into the subarachnoid (intrathecal) space to block sensory and motor function below the injection level, providing rapid-onset anesthesia for procedures of the lower abdomen, pelvis, and lower extremities.

epidural analgesia.definition: Regional anesthesia produced by injecting a local anesthetic (often with an opioid) into the epidural space around the spinal cord to block pain signals, providing targeted analgesia for labor, surgery, or other procedures.

nerve block.definition: Injection of a medication into one or more nerves to relieve pain.

bier block.definition: A regional anesthesia technique in which the limb is exsanguinated and confined with a tourniquet, then local anesthetic is injected into a peripheral vein to anesthetize the entire limb for surgery (intravenous regional anesthesia, IVRA).

general anesthesia.definition: To put to sleep before surgery or another medical procedure.

inhalation anesthesia.definition: A method of general anesthesia in which volatile or gaseous anesthetic agents are inhaled and absorbed through the lungs (usually in a mixture of oxygen) to produce unconsciousness, analgesia, and muscle relaxation, with delivery via an anesthesia machine.

intravenous sedation.definition: A technique of pharmacologic sedation in which sedative medications are administered intravenously to achieve a controlled level of consciousness—typically from anxiolysis to conscious/moderate sedation—for a procedure, while monitoring vital signs and preserving airway and spontaneous breathing.

minimal sedation.definition: A drug-induced state in which the patient responds normally to verbal commands; cognitive function and coordination may be impaired, but ventilatory and cardiovascular functions are unaffected.

sedation.definition: Sedation is a medically controlled state of diminished consciousness and responsiveness induced by sedative medications, used to relieve anxiety and discomfort and to facilitate procedures; it ranges from minimal (anxiolysis) to deep sedation, with higher levels increasing risk and potentially requiring airway support.

anxiolysis.definition: Anxiolysis is the pharmacologic or nonpharmacologic reduction of anxiety or tension, especially prior to a medical procedure, typically producing calmness with little or no sedation or impairment of consciousness.

amnesia.definition: When you are not able to remember new information.

ultrasonography.definition: A diagnostic imaging technique that uses high-frequency sound waves emitted by a transducer and the returned echoes to produce real-time images of internal structures; it is noninvasive and does not involve ionizing radiation; commonly used for obstetric, abdominal, cardiac (echocardiography), and vascular assessments.

folic acid.definition: A water-soluble B vitamin (B9) essential for one-carbon metabolism, DNA synthesis, and cell division; it supports fetal neural tube development, and deficiency can cause megaloblastic anemia and neural tube defects. It is found in leafy greens and fortified foods, and synthetic folic acid is commonly taken as a supplement during pregnancy to prevent neural tube defects.

neural tube defect.definition: A congenital malformation due to failure of the neural tube to close during early embryogenesis (about days 21–28), resulting in brain and/or spinal cord defects (e.g., anencephaly or spina bifida); folic acid supplementation before conception reduces risk.

sickle cell disease.definition: A hereditary autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the beta-globin (HBB) gene producing abnormal hemoglobin S; deoxygenated hemoglobin S polymerizes, causing red blood cells to sickle, leading to chronic hemolytic anemia and recurrent vaso-occlusive crises with ischemia in various organs; lifelong management includes pain control, hydroxyurea, transfusion, and potential curative hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

sickle cell.definition: An inherited hemoglobinopathy caused by a mutation in the beta-globin gene producing abnormal hemoglobin S; under low oxygen, red blood cells deform into a sickle shape, leading to chronic hemolytic anemia, painful vaso-occlusive crises, and risk of organ damage.

anemia of chronic disease.definition: Anemia of chronic disease is a normocytic to mildly microcytic anemia that occurs with chronic inflammation, infection, or malignancy. It results from cytokine-mediated iron sequestration and an impaired erythropoietin response, typically showing low serum iron and low transferrin saturation with normal to elevated ferritin; it often improves when the underlying condition is treated.

anemia of pregnancy.definition: A physiologic, dilutional anemia of pregnancy in which plasma volume expands more than red cell mass, causing a fall in hemoglobin and hematocrit during pregnancy (commonly Hb <11 g/dL in the first and third trimesters, or <10.5 g/dL in the second trimester), often with iron deficiency contributing.

iron.definition: An essential trace mineral required for oxygen transport and energy metabolism; a key component of hemoglobin and myoglobin, enabling red blood cells and muscle tissue to use oxygen; stored in ferritin and hemosiderin and absorbed mainly in the duodenum, with levels regulated by hepcidin.

vitamin b12.definition: A water-soluble vitamin (cobalamin) essential for DNA synthesis, red blood cell formation, and maintenance of myelin and nervous system function. It is absorbed in the terminal ileum with intrinsic factor and stored in the liver; deficiency can cause megaloblastic anemia and progressive neurologic damage. Dietary sources are mainly animal products; the average adult requirement is about 2.4 mcg per day.

folate.definition: A water-soluble B vitamin (B9) essential for one-carbon metabolism, DNA synthesis, and cell division. It occurs naturally in foods in multiple forms; the synthetic form used in supplements and fortification is the one commonly added to foods and prenatal vitamins. Deficiency can cause megaloblastic anemia and, in early pregnancy, neural tube defects.

mild diabetes.definition: A nonstandard, informal phrase referring to diabetes with relatively mild hyperglycemia and few symptoms, often representing early type 2 diabetes or good glycemic control; formal diagnosis and severity are defined by established criteria (HbA1c, fasting glucose, oral glucose tolerance test, and clinical symptoms).

chronic bronchitis.definition: Chronic bronchitis is a form of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease characterized by chronic productive cough due to inflammation and mucus hypersecretion of the bronchial mucosa, typically defined clinically as coughing up sputum for at least 3 months in each of two consecutive years without another identifiable cause.

autoimmune diseases.definition: An umbrella term for disorders in which the immune system mistakenly targets the body's own tissues, causing chronic inflammation and tissue damage; these diseases can be organ-specific or systemic and often involve autoantibodies or autoreactive T cells.

microangiopathy.definition: Microangiopathy is a disease of the small blood vessels (capillaries, arterioles, and venules) characterized by structural changes—such as basement-membrane thickening and hyalinization—that impair microcirculation; it commonly accompanies diabetes mellitus and other conditions causing microvascular injury (e.g., diabetic retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy).

hematologic disease.definition: A disease of the blood or blood-forming organs, including disorders of blood cells (red cells, white cells, platelets) or of the coagulation system.

erythrocyte.definition: A mature red blood cell that carries oxygen from the lungs to body tissues and carbon dioxide from tissues back to the lungs, via hemoglobin.

packed red blood cells.definition: A blood product in which red blood cells are concentrated with most plasma removed, produced by removing plasma from whole blood; transfused to raise hemoglobin/hematocrit and improve oxygen-carrying capacity in patients with anemia or acute blood loss.

transfusion.definition: The process of taking blood from a healthy person and infusing it into a person whose own blood has been depleted during surgery or an accident, or is for some reason not functioning correctly. Transfusions of whole blood or of specific blood cells (such as red cells, white cells, or platelets) are possible.

erythropoietin.definition: A glycoprotein hormone produced mainly by the kidneys that stimulates red blood cell production by acting on erythroid progenitor cells in the bone marrow; its release increases in response to hypoxia.

splenectomy.definition: Removal of the spleen by surgical means; commonly performed for splenic injury, certain hematologic disorders, or splenic tumors; can be done via open or laparoscopic approach; results in loss of splenic immune function and increased risk of severe infection with encapsulated bacteria.

adrenal corticosteroids.definition: Corticosteroid hormones produced by the adrenal cortex, mainly glucocorticoids (e.g., cortisol) and mineralocorticoids (e.g., aldosterone); they regulate metabolism, immune and inflammatory responses, stress response, and electrolyte–water balance, and synthetic forms are used as anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive drugs.

adrenal.definition: Relating to the adrenal glands (suprarenal glands), the paired endocrine glands atop the kidneys that secrete hormones such as cortisol, aldosterone, and catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine).

testosterone esters.definition: Esters of testosterone are derivatives in which the 17β-hydroxyl group is esterified with fatty acids, creating long-acting injectable prodrugs that slowly release active testosterone after administration (e.g., testosterone enanthate, testosterone cypionate).

iron metabolism.definition: An integrated set of processes that regulate the acquisition, transport, storage, recycling, and utilization of iron to meet physiological needs while preventing iron toxicity. It includes intestinal iron absorption (primarily in the duodenum), plasma transport by transferrin, cellular uptake via transferrin receptors, storage as ferritin (and hemosiderin), and recycling from senescent erythrocytes, with systemic control largely governed by hepcidin and ferroportin.

hypochromic.definition: Red blood cells with reduced hemoglobin content, causing paler staining and a low mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC); commonly seen in iron deficiency anemia.

normochromic.definition: Describes red blood cells with normal hemoglobin content, yielding normal staining on a peripheral smear and indicating no hypochromia.

macrocytic.definition: Having larger than normal red blood cells; macrocytosis is defined by an increased mean corpuscular volume (MCV > 100 fL) on a CBC, commonly due to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, liver disease, alcoholism, hypothyroidism, or certain medications.

normocytic.definition: Describes red blood cells that are normal in size, with a mean corpuscular volume in the reference range (about 80–100 fL).

microcytic.definition: Microcytic refers to red blood cells that are smaller than normal in size, typically with a low mean corpuscular volume (MCV); commonly seen in iron deficiency anemia and thalassemia.

hemolytic anemia.definition: A form of anemia caused by the accelerated destruction of red blood cells, either within blood vessels or by splenic clearance, leading to a reduced lifespan of erythrocytes; it can be inherited or acquired and often presents with reticulocytosis and elevated bilirubin.

neural tube.definition: An embryonic precursor to the central nervous system formed when the neural plate folds and closes into a hollow tube; its closure occurs early in development, and failure to close can cause neural tube defects such as spina bifida and anencephaly.

dyspepsia.definition: When you are uncomfortable or feel burning around your stomach.

confusion.definition: A state of reduced awareness and impaired attention, with disorganized thinking and memory problems, often acute and reversible, commonly due to delirium or other medical illness, medications, or substance withdrawal.

disorientation.definition: A state of confused awareness in which a person is not oriented to time, place, or person, with impaired recognition of surroundings; may result from delirium, dementia, stroke or brain injury, intoxication, or metabolic disturbances.

pulmonary embolus.definition: A blockage of the pulmonary arteries by an embolus, usually a clot that has traveled from the deep veins of the legs, causing impaired blood flow through the lungs and potentially life-threatening respiratory or cardiovascular compromise.

ruptured abdominal aneurysm.definition: A life-threatening rupture of a previously dilated abdominal aortic aneurysm, causing massive intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal hemorrhage; presents with sudden severe abdominal or back pain, hypotension and shock; requires emergent surgical repair (open or endovascular).

anesthesiology.definition: A medical specialty focused on the administration of anesthesia and perioperative care for patients undergoing procedures, including anesthesia planning, airway management, analgesia, monitoring, and postoperative recovery.

aneurysmal.definition: Relating to an aneurysm; describing a localized, abnormal dilation of a blood vessel due to weakness in the vessel wall, which can be fusiform or saccular and may predispose to rupture or thrombosis.

varix.definition: A dilated, tortuous vein; a single instance of a venous dilation, commonly referring to dilated esophageal or rectal veins seen in portal hypertension.

preanesthesia.definition: The preoperative phase in which the anesthesia team evaluates and optimizes a patient before anesthesia, including history and physical examination, risk assessment, medication review and adjustments, perioperative instructions, and planning for anesthesia and airway management.

induction.definition: Initiation or start of a physiological state or medical procedure, such as the induction of anesthesia or the induction of labor, typically achieved by pharmacologic or other therapeutic means.

maintenance.definition: In medicine, a long-term treatment strategy begun after initial therapy to maintain disease control or remission, prevent relapse, and minimize toxicity; often involves a reduced dose or less intensive regimen compared with induction therapy.

vasodilators.definition: A class of drugs that dilate (widen) blood vessels by relaxing vascular smooth muscle, thereby reducing vascular resistance and the heart’s workload. They are used to prevent or relieve angina and other forms of coronary artery disease; examples include nitroglycerin and isosorbide derivatives.

postanesthesia.definition: Relating to the period after anesthesia; the recovery phase during which a patient regains consciousness and vital signs stabilize under close monitoring.

monitoring.definition: A systematic, ongoing observation and measurement of a patient's physiological status, clinical findings, or laboratory data to detect changes, guide treatment decisions, and evaluate response to therapy.

nurse anesthetist.definition: An advanced practice registered nurse who specializes in the administration of anesthesia and perioperative care. They assess patients preoperatively, develop and implement anesthesia plans, administer anesthetic agents, monitor patients during surgery, manage airway and vital signs, and provide postoperative pain management and recovery support; many are certified as CRNAs (Certified Registered Nurse Anesthetists) and may practice independently or under physician supervision depending on jurisdiction.

anetoderma.definition: A rare dermatologic disorder characterized by focal loss of elastic tissue in the dermis, producing soft, atrophic, pouch-like patches that are often asymptomatic; lesions may be primary (idiopathic) or secondary to inflammatory or autoimmune conditions.

aneuploid.definition: An abnormal number of chromosomes in a cell, not an exact multiple of the haploid chromosome number, typically arising from nondisjunction; examples include monosomy (loss of a chromosome) and trisomy (gain of a chromosome).

aneuploidy.definition: A deviation from the normal chromosome number in a cell, due to gain or loss of one or more chromosomes, usually arising from nondisjunction during cell division; often results in congenital abnormalities or pregnancy loss (examples include trisomy 21 and monosomy X).

aneurysmectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove an aneurysm, typically by excising the aneurysm sac and repairing the parent vessel.

aneurysm needle.definition: Not a standard medical term; if used, it would denote a needle intended to puncture or access an aneurysm sac during vascular procedures, such as aspirating the sac or delivering therapy, though most aneurysm interventions use catheters rather than a specific "aneurysm needle."

phencyclidine.definition: A dissociative anesthetic drug that acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist, producing dissociative anesthesia, analgesia, and amnesia; at recreational doses it can cause delirium, hallucinations, agitation, and autonomic instability (tachycardia, hypertension).

phencyclidine hydrochloride.definition: An illicit dissociative hallucinogenic drug; the hydrochloride salt of a synthetic arylcyclohexylamine that acts as a noncompetitive NMDA receptor antagonist, causing dissociation from the environment, analgesia, delirium, and often agitation or psychosis.

angelica.definition: A genus of herbaceous plants in the Apiaceae family; used in traditional herbal medicine with preparations from roots, seeds, or aerial parts for digestive aid; contains essential oils and furanocoumarins, which can cause photosensitivity and may interact with certain medications.

angelmans syndrome.definition: A genetic neurodevelopmental disorder caused by loss of maternal UBE3A gene expression on chromosome 15 (most commonly from a maternal 15q11-q13 deletion, paternal uniparental disomy, imprinting defect, or UBE3A mutation). It presents with severe developmental delay, minimal or absent speech, ataxia and movement disorders, seizures, a happy, excitable demeanor with frequent laughter, and distinctive EEG findings.

angina pectoris.definition: Temporary chest pain that occurs when the heart isn’t getting enough oxygen and blood, usually occurring in response to physical activity or stress.

nitroglycerin.definition: A drug that relaxes blood vessels and increases the supply of blood and oxygen to the heart while reducing its workload. It is commonly used to treat angina.

prinzmetal angina.definition: A form of chest pain caused by transient coronary artery vasospasm that leads to brief episodes of myocardial ischemia, typically occurring at rest and often accompanied by transient ST-segment elevation on ECG; usually occurs without fixed, significant coronary obstruction (though atherosclerosis may coexist); managed with calcium channel blockers and nitrates, and by avoiding triggers such as smoking or cocaine.

stable angina.definition: Angina pectoris (chest pain with exertion or stress) that is well-controlled with medicines and lifestyle changes.

unstable angina.definition: Chest pain that occurs or worsens in frequency, severity, or duration when a person is at rest or engaging in mild activity.

stress test.definition: A diagnostic test in which cardiovascular measurements such as heart rate, blood pressure, and electrical activity are recorded while the heart is being stressed (usually by having the person exercise on a treadmill or bicycle).

electrocardiographic.definition: Relating to electrocardiography; describing or produced by an electrocardiogram, which records the heart's electrical activity.

ecg.definition: A recording of the heart’s electrical activity over time, obtained with surface skin electrodes, producing a tracing that shows P waves, QRS complexes, and T waves; used to evaluate heart rhythm and conduction, detect ischemia or infarction, and monitor cardiac conditions.

cardiac enzyme.definition: Enzymes released into the bloodstream from damaged heart muscle after myocardial injury; used as biomarkers to diagnose myocardial infarction. Historically CK-MB is the classic cardiac enzyme, with elevations also seen in CK and LDH; today troponin I or T are the preferred biomarkers, though troponin is a regulatory protein, not an enzyme.

nuclear scanning.definition: A diagnostic imaging technique in which small amounts of radioactive tracers are administered and detected by a gamma camera or PET scanner to visualize the function and metabolism of organs, producing functional rather than purely anatomical images.

angiography.definition: A test that shows how blood moves through the blood vessels and heart. It uses x-rays and the injection of a fluid called a contrast agent that can be seen on the x-rays.

angiocardiography.definition: A radiographic imaging technique in which radiopaque contrast is injected into the heart and great vessels (usually via cardiac catheterization) to visualize the heart’s chambers, valves, and coronary arteries for assessment of anatomy and blood flow.

angiocarditis.definition: Inflammation of the heart and its blood vessels.

angio catheter.definition: A flexible catheter placed into a blood vessel for vascular imaging or intervention, typically used to inject contrast dye during angiography or to deliver medications and withdraw samples.

angiochondroma.definition: A rare benign tumor composed of mature cartilage with an abundant vascular component.

angioneurotic edema.definition: A localized, non-pitting swelling of the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissues (and often mucosa) due to transient increased vascular permeability, usually in response to an allergic reaction or hereditary C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency; commonly affects the face, lips, tongue, or airway and can be life-threatening if the airway is involved.

angioendothelioma.definition: A vascular neoplasm arising from endothelial cells of blood vessels; it forms abnormal vascular channels and ranges from benign to low- to intermediate-grade malignant tumors (e.g., epithelioid angioendothelioma, retiform angioendothelioma).

angiofibroma.definition: A benign lesion composed of fibrous tissue with a rich network of blood vessels; classically used to describe juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma, a highly vascular tumor of the nasopharynx in adolescent males.

telangiectatic fibroma.definition: A benign fibrous tumor in which the stroma is markedly vascular, containing numerous dilated capillaries (telangiectasia); typically presents as a small, red-to-purple papule or nodule that grows slowly.

angiogenesis.definition: The formation of new blood vessels.

angiogenesis inhibitor.definition: A substance that inhibits the growth of new blood vessels (angiogenesis), thereby reducing blood supply to tissues; used in cancer therapy and in certain ocular diseases, often by blocking VEGF signaling or other angiogenic pathways.

angiogenic cell cluster.definition: A group of cells that promotes the growth of new blood vessels; typically includes endothelial and supporting stromal or inflammatory cells that secrete proangiogenic factors (such as VEGF) and coordinate endothelial sprouting and tube formation during angiogenesis.

angiogenin.definition: A secreted ribonuclease of the RNase A superfamily that promotes angiogenesis by stimulating endothelial cell proliferation and migration; encoded by the RNASE5 gene.

angioglioma.definition: A rare glial brain tumor characterized by prominent vascular proliferation within the tumor (angiomatous stroma), essentially a glioma variant with extensive blood vessels.

angiogram.definition: A radiographic imaging test in which a contrast agent is injected into the bloodstream to visualize blood vessels on X-ray or fluoroscopy, used to evaluate arteries and veins for blockages, aneurysms, and other vascular abnormalities.

angiograph.definition: A radiographic image of blood vessels produced during angiography, usually obtained after injection of a contrast agent to visualize the vascular system.

angioimmunoblastic lymphadenopathy.definition: A pattern of generalized lymph node enlargement associated with immune dysregulation and hypergammaglobulinemia, histologically showing prominent vascular proliferation (high endothelial venules) and expansion of the follicular dendritic cell network; historically described as angioimmunoblastic lymphadenopathy and now largely associated with angioimmunoblastic T‑cell lymphoma (AITL).

dysproteinemia.definition: An abnormal pattern or concentration of serum proteins in the blood, indicating disturbances in protein production, breakdown, or loss—often seen with monoclonal gammopathies, liver disease, nephrotic syndrome, or chronic inflammation.

aild.definition: Not a recognized medical term; there is no standard definition without additional context or correct spelling.

night sweats.definition: Episodes of excessive sweating during sleep, often soaking clothing or bedding; commonly related to fever, hormonal changes (e.g., menopause), infections, malignancies, medications, or other systemic conditions.

angiohemophilia.definition: An historical term describing a bleeding tendency due to vascular fragility or vessel-wall defects, in which bleeding is disproportionate to routine coagulation tests; not a currently recognized, specific inherited coagulopathy.

von willebrand disease.definition: A common inherited bleeding disorder caused by deficiency or dysfunction of von Willebrand factor, a protein that enables platelets to adhere to damaged vessels and to each other.

endocardial tubes.definition: Two paired endocardial (endothelial) tubes in the embryonic cardiogenic region that fuse to form the primitive heart tube; they contribute to the endocardial lining and set the stage for the development of the heart chambers.

aneurysmal bone cyst.definition: A benign, expansile bone lesion characterized by multiple blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa; often occurs in the metaphyses of long bones in adolescents and young adults and can be primary or secondary to other bone lesions. Treatment typically involves curettage with bone grafting or resection, with a risk of recurrence.

mycotic aneurysm.definition: An infectious aneurysm of a blood vessel caused by infection of the arterial wall (often bacterial, from septic emboli or bacteremia), weakening the wall and producing focal dilation with risk of rupture; commonly associated with infective endocarditis.

berry aneurysm.definition: A small, sac-like outpouching of a cerebral artery, most often at branch points in the circle of Willis, caused by weakness in the arterial wall; prone to rupture, leading to subarachnoid hemorrhage.

saccular aneurysm.definition: A focal, berry-shaped outpouching of an artery that involves only a portion of the vessel wall and is connected by a narrow neck; a true aneurysm typically occurring at arterial bifurcations, with risk of rupture and hemorrhage (often intracranial).

fusiform aneurysm.definition: A true aneurysm characterized by circumferential, spindle-shaped dilation of a segment of an artery, involving all layers of the vessel wall.

dissecting aneurysm.definition: A dissecting aneurysm is a condition in which a tear in the inner lining of a blood vessel allows blood to enter and split the wall layers, creating a false lumen alongside the true lumen; most commonly it involves the aorta and can progress, rupture, or cause organ ischemia.

pseudoaneurysm.definition: A pulsatile hematoma resulting from a breach in an artery, in which blood escapes into surrounding tissue but remains in communication with the arterial lumen; it is contained by perivascular tissue rather than by the arterial wall (also known as a false aneurysm).

rasmussens aneurysm.definition: A pulmonary artery pseudoaneurysm arising within a tuberculous cavity, caused by erosion of a pulmonary artery branch by tuberculosis; rupture can lead to massive hemoptysis.

aortic.definition: Relating to the aorta, the largest artery of the body that carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the systemic circulation.

popliteal.definition: Relating to the popliteal region—the hollow behind the knee; used for structures such as the popliteal artery and popliteal vein.

artery.definition: Vessels that carry blood from the heart to the body's organs.

vein.definition: A vessel that carries blood back to the heart.

heart.definition: An organ made of muscles that pumps blood through your body. It is on the left side of your body.

intracoronary.definition: Within or inside a coronary artery; used to describe administration or delivery of substances directly into a coronary artery.

atherosclerosis.definition: A disease in which arteries become stiff and clogged by substances in the blood, such as fat and calcium, forming plaques.

atherosclerotic plaque.definition: A mixture of fats, cholesterol, and other tissue that builds up on artery walls.

myocardial.definition: Relating to the myocardium, the muscular middle layer of the heart wall; pertaining to heart muscle.

perfusion.definition: Passage of a fluid through a specific organ or an area of the body.

bypass.definition: A procedure to divert the flow of blood or other fluids around a blocked vessel or organ; in cardiology, surgery that reroutes blood around a blocked coronary artery to restore blood flow.

coronary artery bypass.definition: A surgical procedure to restore blood flow to the heart by bypassing blocked coronary arteries with grafts (commonly internal mammary artery or saphenous vein), creating new routes for blood to reach the myocardium; typically performed for multivessel coronary artery disease and may be done with or without cardiopulmonary bypass.

coronary intervention.definition: A catheter-based procedure to treat coronary artery disease by opening narrowed or blocked coronary arteries, typically using balloon angioplasty with stent placement (percutaneous coronary intervention); may include atherectomy or other adjunct devices.

stent.definition: A wire mesh device inserted into an artery to prop it open once a blockage has been cleared by angioplasty.

heparin.definition: An anticoagulant that enhances antithrombin III activity, inhibiting thrombin (IIa) and factor Xa to prevent and treat thrombosis; available as unfractionated and low-molecular-weight forms.

statins.definition: A type of drug that lowers the amount of cholesterol in your blood. There are many names for these drugs, including atorvastatin, simvastatin, and rosuvastatin.

nitrates.definition: Medications that widen blood vessels; usually used to treat chest pain from angina and other heart problems.

beta-blockers.definition: A class of medications that antagonize beta-adrenergic receptors (primarily in the heart), reducing heart rate, contractility, and conduction, thereby lowering blood pressure and myocardial oxygen demand; used to treat hypertension, angina, certain arrhythmias, and heart failure.

channel.definition: A tubular passage in the body that allows the movement or transmission of substances, such as fluids or ions, or of electrical signals (for example, ion channels in cell membranes or biological ducts/vessels).

blockers.definition: A substance, usually a medication, that prevents or reduces a physiological response by blocking a receptor, ion channel, or enzyme, thereby inhibiting signaling pathways (e.g., beta-blockers block β-adrenergic receptors; calcium channel blockers block calcium influx).

iodinated.definition: Containing iodine; a compound in which iodine atoms have been incorporated, often referring to iodine-containing contrast media used in radiographic imaging.

contrast.definition: In medical imaging, contrast is the difference in radiodensity or signal intensity between two tissues or structures that allows them to be distinguished; contrast media (agents) are substances given to enhance this difference and improve visualization.

nephrotoxic.definition: Adjective: Toxic to the kidneys; capable of causing kidney injury or impairing renal function.

renal neoplasms.definition: Tumors arising from kidney tissue; they can be benign (e.g., oncocytoma, angiomyolipoma) or malignant (most commonly renal cell carcinoma).

neoplasm.definition: An abnormal growth of tissue, either cancerous or benign.

serum sickness.definition: A type III (immune complex–mediated) hypersensitivity reaction to exogenous proteins (often animal serum or antitoxins) that typically occurs about 1–2 weeks after exposure, caused by immune complex deposition with complement activation, presenting with fever, urticarial rash, arthralgias/arthritis, malaise, and sometimes lymphadenopathy or nephritis.

angiokeratoma.definition: A benign vascular skin lesion in which dilated capillaries in the dermal papillae produce superficial dark red to blue‑black papules with overlying epidermal hyperkeratosis.

angiokeratoma circumscriptum.definition: A congenital vascular malformation of the skin characterized by dilated superficial capillaries with overlying epidermal hyperkeratosis, presenting as clustered violaceous to dark red papules or plaques commonly on the legs; lesions may blanch with pressure and can bleed or enlarge with trauma.

angiokeratoma corporis diffusum.definition: A diffuse eruption of numerous small, dark red to blue-black keratotic papules on the trunk and proximal limbs, representing a cutaneous manifestation of Fabry disease (X-linked α-galactosidase A deficiency).

fabry's disease.definition: A rare X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of the enzyme alpha-galactosidase A, leading to accumulation of globotriaosylceramide in vascular endothelium and various tissues; it presents with episodic neuropathic pain (acroparesthesias), angiokeratomas, hypohidrosis, corneal verticillata, and progressive renal, cardiac, and cerebrovascular disease.

fabry's syndrome.definition: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient activity of the enzyme alpha-galactosidase A, leading to systemic accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) in vascular endothelium and other tissues; presents with acroparesthesias, angiokeratomas, hypohidrosis, corneal verticillata, and progressive renal, cardiac, and cerebrovascular disease.

angiokeratoma serpiginosum.definition: A rare cutaneous vascular lesion consisting of dilated superficial dermal capillaries with overlying epidermal hyperkeratosis, presenting as bright-red to violaceous punctate papules arranged in a serpiginous (snake-like) pattern, typically on the lower extremities or trunk of adolescents, usually without systemic involvement.

angiolipoma.definition: A benign subcutaneous tumor composed of mature adipose tissue with a prominent vascular component (capillary-sized blood vessels); typically painful and most often located on the forearm.

telangiectatic lipoma.definition: A benign adipose-tissue tumor (lipoma) variant in which numerous dilated small blood vessels (telangiectasias) are present within or adjacent to the lipomatous tissue, giving a vascular-appearing lesion. Histology shows mature adipocytes with capillary-sized vessels and no malignant features.

angioma.definition: A benign proliferation of blood vessels forming a vascular lesion in the skin or mucosa; usually noncancerous and asymptomatic, often presenting as a small red to purple spot or nodule.

hemangioma.definition: A benign vascular tumor consisting of an abnormal proliferation of blood vessels; most often seen in infancy, typically presenting as a red or purple raised lesion (strawberry mark) that enlarges during early life and gradually involutes over several years; can involve the skin or internal organs.

cavernous hemangioma.definition: A benign vascular lesion made up of large, dilated, blood-filled channels (sinusoids) in the dermis or subcutaneous tissue, lined by endothelium with scant intervening tissue; a low-flow vascular tumor typically present at birth or in early infancy and can occur in skin, mucosa, or visceral organs (e.g., liver).

cavernous hemangiomas.definition: A benign vascular lesion consisting of large, dilated, blood-filled vascular spaces (caverns) lined by endothelium and separated by fibrous stroma; commonly occurs in skin or liver and may be asymptomatic or cause symptoms depending on location.

lymphangioma.definition: A benign congenital malformation of the lymphatic vessels resulting in dilated lymphatic channels or cystic masses, usually present at birth or in early infancy, most commonly in the head and neck (cystic hygroma).

angioma cutis.definition: A benign lesion of the skin consisting of an abnormal proliferation of blood vessels (mainly capillaries) in the dermis.

nevus.definition: A benign pigmented skin lesion caused by localized proliferation of melanocytes (nevus cells), commonly called a mole; can be flat or raised and vary in color.

angioma arteriale racemosum.definition: A congenital vascular malformation consisting of a dense, branching network of arteries with abnormal arteriovenous connections, producing high-flow shunting; essentially another description of an arteriovenous malformation (AVM).

angiomatosis.definition: A diffuse proliferation of blood vessels resulting in numerous angiomas (benign vascular lesions) that can involve the skin, mucosa, and sometimes internal organs; can be congenital or acquired and may be part of a vascular malformation syndrome.

angiomyoma.definition: Benign neoplasm composed of smooth muscle cells associated with blood vessels; a vascular leiomyoma (angioleiomyoma).

angiomyomata.definition: Benign neoplasm composed of smooth muscle cells with vascular channels (a vascular leiomyoma/angioleiomyoma). It typically presents as a small, often painful subcutaneous nodule, most commonly in the extremities.

angiomyoneuroma.definition: A benign neoplasm composed of a mixed proliferation of vascular channels, smooth muscle, and neural elements.

angiomyosarcoma.definition: A malignant tumor derived from smooth muscle cells that shows prominent vascular (blood vessel–forming) features; a soft tissue sarcoma with mixed myogenic differentiation and angioarchitectural patterns.

angiomyosarcomata.definition: A malignant neoplasm arising from the walls of blood vessels, composed of malignant smooth muscle (myogenic) cells; often regarded as a variant of angiosarcoma.

angioneuroma.definition: A rare benign neoplasm composed of mature neural elements (neurons and Schwann cells) with a prominent vascular (angiomatous) stroma.

glomangioma.definition: A benign vascular malformation consisting of dilated venous channels surrounded by glomus cells (a glomus tumor variant), typically congenital or present in childhood, presenting as blue-to-purple skin nodules or plaques on the extremities and sometimes painful.

angiosarcoma.definition: A malignant neoplasm arising from endothelial cells lining blood vessels (and sometimes lymphatic vessels), characterized by aggressive growth and a high propensity for local invasion and metastasis; commonly affects skin and soft tissues but can involve the liver, spleen, breast, and other organs, and may be associated with prior radiation exposure or chronic lymphedema.

hemangiosarcoma.definition: A malignant neoplasm of vascular endothelial cells, forming irregular, blood-filled vascular channels; an aggressive sarcoma with a high potential for invasion and metastasis.

malignant hemangioendothelioma.definition: Historically a malignant vascular tumor arising from endothelial cells; the term has been used to describe high-grade angiosarcoma and is now largely considered synonymous with angiosarcoma, characterized by aggressive growth, early metastasis, and a poor prognosis.

angiosclerosis.definition: Hardening or thickening of a blood vessel wall, usually arteries or arterioles, resulting in reduced elasticity and compliance and potentially impaired blood flow; a non-specific degenerative vascular change that can be age-related or associated with other vascular diseases (distinct from plaque-related atherosclerosis).

angioscope.definition: An angioscope is an endoscope used to visualize the inside of blood vessels, typically introduced via catheter to inspect vascular lumens for lesions and to guide endovascular procedures.

vasospasm.definition: Uncontrollable contraction or spasm of a blood vessel.

balloon angioplasty.definition: A procedure to open clogged heart arteries. A surgeon inserts and inflates a tiny balloon. It widens the blocked artery then expands a small wire mesh tube to keep the artery open.

angiostrongyliasis.definition: A zoonotic parasitic infection caused by Angiostrongylus species (most commonly Angiostrongylus cantonensis) acquired by ingestion of larvae in mollusks (snails/slugs) or contaminated produce; larvae migrate to the central nervous system, causing eosinophilic meningitis or meningoencephalitis (neuroangiostrongyliasis), and may also affect the eye or abdomen.

angiostrongylus.definition: A genus of parasitic nematodes that primarily infect the pulmonary arteries of rodents; humans are accidental hosts, and infection can cause eosinophilic meningitis or abdominal angiostrongyliasis after ingestion of molluscan intermediate hosts or contaminated food.

angiostrongylus cantonensis.definition: An infectious nematode (rat lungworm) whose humans are accidental hosts; it causes eosinophilic meningitis (neuroangiostrongyliasis) after ingestion of third-stage larvae in contaminated mollusks (commonly raw or undercooked snails or slugs) or paratenic hosts; the life cycle normally involves rats as the definitive hosts.

angiotensin.definition: A protein that raises blood pressure by narrowing blood vessels and causing the kidneys to store more sodium and water.

ace inhibitor.definition: A class of medications that inhibits the angiotensin-converting enzyme, reducing angiotensin II formation and aldosterone secretion, leading to vasodilation and lower blood pressure; used to treat hypertension and heart failure and to protect renal function in diabetes.

angiotensinogen.definition: A liver-derived glycoprotein that serves as the substrate for renin in the renin–angiotensin system; it is cleaved by renin to form angiotensin I, the precursor to angiotensin II, and helps regulate blood pressure and fluid balance.

angiotensin i.definition: An inactive form of the protein angiotensin. It is the precursor to the active form, angiotensin II.

angiotensin ii.definition: The active form of the protein angiotensin, which raises blood pressure by narrowing blood vessels and causing the kidneys to store more sodium and water.

bradykinin.definition: A nonapeptide mediator of the kinin–kallikrein system that promotes vasodilation and increases vascular permeability, contributing to inflammation and pain. It is formed from kininogen by kallikrein and is rapidly degraded by kinases, including angiotensin‑converting enzyme (ACE).

angiotensin-converting enzyme test.definition: Serum ACE activity test; a laboratory assay measuring angiotensin-converting enzyme activity in the blood, used as a supportive aid in diagnosing sarcoidosis and other granulomatous diseases. Elevated levels suggest granulomatous activity but are not specific or sensitive, and results can be affected by ACE inhibitors and other factors; a normal result does not exclude disease.

ace test.definition: A blood test that measures serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) level; elevations can occur with sarcoidosis and other granulomatous diseases, but the test is not specific and is used as an adjunct to diagnosis rather than a definitive test.

angiotensin sensitivity test.definition: A diagnostic procedure that assesses the body's responsiveness to angiotensin II by administering the peptide and measuring the resulting changes in blood pressure and hormonal or renal parameters (e.g., plasma renin activity, aldosterone).

angle-closure glaucoma.definition: An ocular condition in which the iridocorneal angle closes or narrows, blocking aqueous humor outflow and causing a rapid or gradual rise in intraocular pressure with potential optic nerve damage and vision loss; it may present acutely with severe eye pain, halos around lights, headache, nausea, and a red eye.

anhedonia.definition: A reduced ability to experience pleasure from normally enjoyable activities (loss of interest or reduced positive affect), commonly seen in major depressive disorder and other psychiatric or neurological conditions; may include anticipatory anhedonia (decreased anticipation of pleasure) and consummatory anhedonia (reduced pleasure in the moment).

anhidrosis.definition: A condition characterized by the absence or severe reduction of sweating, impeding the body's ability to regulate its temperature; it may be localized or generalized and can result from dysfunction of the sweat glands or autonomic innervation.

anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia.definition: A hereditary disorder of ectodermal structures characterized by hypohidrosis/anhidrosis (reduced or absent sweating), hypotrichosis (sparse hair), and hypodontia or anodontia (missing teeth), often with heat intolerance; most commonly caused by mutations in EDA/EDAR/EDARADD and transmitted in X-linked or autosomal patterns.

ectodermal dysplasia.definition: An inherited disorder spectrum characterized by abnormal development of ectodermal structures—primarily hair, teeth, nails, and sweat glands—leading to sparse hair (hypotrichosis), missing or peg-shaped teeth (hypodontia/oligodontia), dry skin, and reduced sweating with possible heat intolerance; with multiple genetic forms and inheritance patterns.

christ-siemens-touraine syndrome.definition: A hereditary angioedema caused by deficiency or dysfunction of C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH), resulting in recurrent, nonpitting swelling of subcutaneous tissue and mucosa (often face, GI tract, airway) due to excessive bradykinin; usually autosomal dominant.

hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia.definition: A genetic disorder of ectodermal development characterized by hypohidrosis (reduced or absent sweating), hypotrichosis (sparse hair), and hypodontia (missing teeth), typically due to mutations in the EDA/EDAR/EDARADD signaling pathways.

anhydrase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the reversible hydration or dehydration of a substrate to form or break an anhydride linkage; the best-known example is carbonic anhydrase, which interconverts carbon dioxide and water with carbonic acid.

carbonic anhydrase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the reversible hydration of carbon dioxide to bicarbonate and a proton, facilitating CO2 transport in blood and maintenance of acid–base balance.

anicteric.definition: Not jaundiced; without yellowing of the skin or sclera due to elevated bilirubin levels.

anicteric hepatitis.definition: A form of hepatitis characterized by liver inflammation without clinically detectable jaundice (no icterus); may present with malaise, elevated liver enzymes, and hepatomegaly.

anodontia.definition: A congenital absence of all teeth in the jaws (complete agenesis of both primary and permanent dentitions); teeth fail to develop.

conical teeth.definition: Teeth with crowns that are cone-shaped, tapering to a point and typically narrower than normal; a crown morphology often described as peg-shaped (as in peg lateral incisors) and may occur as an isolated developmental anomaly.

saddle nose.definition: A nasal deformity in which the nasal dorsum is sunken or depressed, giving a saddle-shaped contour due to loss of support from the nasal septal cartilage and adjacent structures; it can result from trauma, chronic inflammatory or granulomatous diseases, infections, or septal necrosis.

front bossing.definition: A prominent, protruding forehead resulting from frontal bone overgrowth or thickening; a clinical sign seen in various craniofacial and systemic conditions (e.g., hydrocephalus, rickets, achondroplasia, acromegaly, craniosynostosis).

midfacial hypoplasia.definition: Underdevelopment of the midfacial skeleton, particularly the maxilla, resulting in a retruded midface relative to the cranial base and often associated with dental malocclusion and airway or esthetic concerns.

sudoriferous glands.definition: Exocrine sweat glands in the skin that secrete sweat onto the surface via ducts; they aid thermoregulation and waste excretion, and consist of eccrine (merocrine) glands distributed widely and apocrine glands concentrated in the axillae and groin.

casts.definition: A rigid external immobilization device, usually made of plaster or fiberglass, that encases a limb to immobilize fractures or soft-tissue injuries and allow healing.

urine.definition: A pale yellow, sterile liquid waste produced by the kidneys, consisting mainly of water and dissolved solutes (urea, electrolytes, creatinine, uric acid); formed by filtration and tubular processing and excreted through the urinary tract.

muscle bundles.definition: A bundle of skeletal muscle fibers bound together by connective tissue and surrounded by perimysium; this unit is called a fascicle. Several fascicles make up a whole muscle, which is enclosed by epimysium.

glycolipids.definition: Glycolipids are lipid molecules with covalently attached carbohydrate (sugar) residues, typically containing a ceramide backbone, that reside in cell membranes and participate in cell recognition, signaling, and membrane stability.

juxtaglomerular cells.definition: Specialized smooth muscle cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus in the kidney's afferent arterioles that synthesize, store, and secrete renin in response to decreased renal perfusion, decreased NaCl delivery to the macula densa, or sympathetic stimulation; renin initiates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system to regulate blood pressure and electrolyte balance.

polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia.definition: An increase in gamma globulins due to activation of multiple B-cell clones, producing a broad range of immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM), typically seen in chronic inflammation, persistent infection, autoimmune disease, or liver disease; contrasts with a monoclonal gammopathy, where a single clone predominates.

hypergammaglobulinemia.definition: An abnormal increase in gamma globulins (immunoglobulins) in the blood, reflecting increased antibody production; commonly polyclonal and seen in chronic infections, autoimmune or inflammatory diseases, or liver disease.

immunoblasts.definition: A large activated lymphocyte arising in response to antigen exposure, typically from a B or T cell. It has abundant basophilic cytoplasm, a vesicular nucleus with a prominent nucleolus, and it proliferates as part of the immune response; in the B-cell lineage, such cells may differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells.

hepatosplenomegaly.definition: Simultaneous enlargement of the liver and spleen, often due to infections, liver disease with portal hypertension, hematologic disorders, storage diseases, or malignancy.

coombs' positive hemolytic anemia.definition: An immune‑mediated hemolytic anemia in which red blood cells are coated with antibodies or complement, so the direct Coombs (direct antiglobulin) test is positive, indicating antibody- or complement‑mediated RBC destruction.

anileridine.definition: A potent synthetic opioid analgesic in the 4-phenylpiperidine class that acts as a mu-opioid receptor agonist to produce analgesia; used for moderate to severe pain in some settings and carries typical opioid risks such as respiratory depression, sedation, constipation, dependence, and tolerance; regulated as a controlled substance.

anisokaryosis.definition: Variation in the size of cell nuclei within a tissue, reflecting nuclear pleomorphism; commonly observed in malignant neoplasms.

anilism.definition: A form of occupational poisoning caused by exposure to aniline dyes, characterized by methemoglobinemia with cyanosis and hypoxia, often presenting with headache, dizziness, and fatigue. Management includes removing exposure and treating methemoglobinemia (e.g., methylene blue); severe cases may require supplemental oxygen or exchange transfusion.

aniridia.definition: Congenital absence or extreme underdevelopment of the iris, typically present at birth, causing photophobia and reduced visual acuity; often bilateral and may occur as an isolated condition or as part of syndromes such as WAGR, usually due to PAX6 gene mutations.

anisakiasis.definition: A parasitic infection caused by ingestion of Anisakis larvae from raw or undercooked seafood, in which the larvae invade the gastric or intestinal mucosa, causing acute abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting, and occasionally allergic reactions.

anisakis marina.definition: A marine parasitic nematode of the genus Anisakis; it infects marine fish and marine mammals, and humans can become accidental hosts through ingestion of raw or undercooked seafood, causing anisakiasis and possible allergic reactions.

aniseikonia.definition: A binocular vision condition in which the images seen by the two eyes appear different in size or shape, leading to difficulty with fusion and reduced depth perception; commonly caused by anisometropia or differences in retinal image magnification, and corrected with specially prescribed lenses (magnifying or minifying lenses) or contact lenses.

anisometropia.definition: A condition in which the two eyes have markedly different refractive errors, causing images to be focused at different distances on the two retinas; can lead to impaired binocular vision and amblyopia in children if uncorrected.

anisopia.definition: Unequal visual fields between the two eyes; an abnormal condition in which the extent of the visual field differs from one eye to the other, often due to a unilateral field defect.

anistreplase.definition: A thrombolytic agent formed as a complex of streptokinase and plasminogen (APSAC) that acts as a prodrug releasing plasmin to promote fibrinolysis; used to dissolve clots in acute myocardial infarction and other thrombotic conditions.

streptokinase.definition: A thrombolytic (clot-dissolving) agent designed to dissolve the blood clots that block an artery during a heart attack or stroke.

anoplasty.definition: Plastic or reconstructive surgery of the anus and anal canal to correct defects or restore function, commonly performed to treat anal stenosis and often using local tissue flaps or grafts.

anorectal abscess.definition: An accumulation of pus in the tissues around the anus or rectum from infection of anal glands (cryptoglandular infection); presents with acute anal/rectal pain and swelling, may have fever, and is typically treated with incision and drainage; may be associated with fistula-in-ano.

anodyne.definition: A substance that relieves pain; also, something that is soothing or innocuous and unlikely to provoke strong emotion or controversy.

anomia.definition: A language impairment characterized by difficulty retrieving or naming words or objects, despite intact comprehension and fluent speech; commonly associated with aphasia due to left-hemisphere brain damage.

aphasia.definition: Difficulty speaking or comprehending language; a common occurrence after a stroke affecting the left hemisphere of the brain, where language is processed.

anopsia.definition: A loss or defect of vision in part or all of the visual field; a visual field defect that may result from disease or damage to the eye, optic nerve, or visual pathways in the brain.

anopia.definition: Complete loss of vision in one eye; monocular blindness.

ankyloglossia.definition: A congenital condition in which the lingual frenulum is abnormally short, thick, or tight, restricting tongue movement and potentially causing feeding difficulties in infancy and speech issues; also known as tongue-tie.

ankyloblepharon.definition: Fusion of the upper and lower eyelids, resulting in partial or complete adhesion that restricts eyelid opening; can be congenital or acquired (e.g., due to inflammation, burns, or scarring).

ankyloblepharon–ectodermal dysplasia–cle.definition: A rare autosomal dominant ectodermal dysplasia syndrome characterized by congenital ankyloblepharon (fused eyelids), sparse or abnormal hair and teeth with nail and skin changes, and orofacial clefting; most cases are due to TP63 gene mutations (Hay-Wells syndrome is a classic TP63-related form).

hay-wells syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal dominant ectodermal dysplasia syndrome caused by TP63 mutations, presenting at birth with fusion of the eyelids (ankyloblepharon), sparse or abnormal hair, nail and tooth abnormalities, skin defects, and orofacial clefts; also called ankyloblepharon-ectodermal dysplasia-clefting syndrome.

ankylosing spondylitis.definition: A disease that leads to swelling between the disks of the spine and in the joints where the pelvis and spine meet. Causes back pain and stiffness and can limit movement.

ankylosis.definition: The loss of mobility of a joint due to abnormal fusion of the bones (bony ankylosis) or bridging fibrous tissue (fibrous ankylosis), often resulting from inflammation, injury, infection, or degenerative disease.

arthrodesis.definition: Joining together two bones to reduce pain and provide stability to a damaged, arthritic, or painful joint.

ankle.definition: The ankle is the joint that connects the leg to the foot, formed by the articulation of the tibia and fibula with the talus (the talocrural joint); it allows dorsiflexion and plantarflexion and is stabilized by ligaments and surrounding soft tissues.

ankle-arm index.definition: A noninvasive test that compares systolic blood pressure at the ankle with systolic blood pressure at the arm to detect peripheral artery disease. A lower ankle-to-arm ratio suggests PAD.

ankle joint.definition: A hinge-type synovial joint between the distal tibia and fibula and the talus (the talocrural joint) forming the ankle mortise; it primarily allows dorsiflexion and plantarflexion and is stabilized by the deltoid ligament medially and the lateral ligament complex.

ankle reflex.definition: A deep tendon reflex produced by tapping the Achilles (calcaneal) tendon behind the ankle, causing plantar flexion of the foot; it assesses the integrity of the S1–S2 spinal nerve roots and related peripheral nerves.

ankle clonus.definition: A sign of upper motor neuron dysfunction in which, after a rapid stretch of the ankle muscles (often by sudden dorsiflexion), the muscles undergo a series of rhythmic, involuntary contractions (beats), reflecting spasticity and central nervous system pathology such as stroke or multiple sclerosis.

ankle bandage.definition: A bandage wrapped around the ankle to apply compression and provide support for soft-tissue injuries (e.g., sprains) and to help reduce swelling; typically an elastic or gauze wrap applied firmly but not so tight as to cut off circulation.

calcaneonavicular ligament.definition: A strong plantar ligament connecting the calcaneus to the navicular bone; part of the plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament, it supports the head of the talus and helps maintain the medial longitudinal arch of the foot.

long plantar ligament.definition: A strong band on the sole of the foot that extends from the plantar surface of the calcaneus to the cuboid and the bases of the second through fifth metatarsals; it helps maintain the lateral longitudinal arch and stabilizes the calcaneocuboid joint, lying deep to the plantar aponeurosis.

short plantar ligament.definition: A plantar ligament extending from the calcaneus to the cuboid bone; it stabilizes the lateral longitudinal arch of the foot and helps maintain the arch during weight-bearing.

plantar.definition: Relating to the sole of the foot; the plantar surface is the bottom of the foot.

annulus conjunctivae.definition: A circular band of bulbar conjunctiva surrounding the corneal limbus (the border between the cornea and sclera).

annulus.definition: Term used to describe ring or circle shaped objects or body parts.

conjunctivae.definition: Thin, transparent mucous membranes that cover the front of the eyeball and line the inside of the eyelids, forming the ocular surface and producing mucus to keep the eye moist and protected.

conjunctival ring.definition: Not a standard ophthalmologic term. If used descriptively, it may refer to an annular band of conjunctival tissue encircling the corneal limbus, but its exact meaning should be clarified from the clinical context.

anal sphincter.definition: A muscular ring surrounding the anal canal that maintains continence; it comprises the internal anal sphincter (involuntary smooth muscle) and the external anal sphincter (voluntary skeletal muscle), which relax to permit defecation.

cyanosis.definition: A condition in which skin turns blue due to a lack of oxygen in the blood, often because of heart failure or lung disease.

methemoglobinemia.definition: A condition in which an excess of methemoglobin (ferric [Fe3+] iron) forms in the blood, impairing oxygen delivery to tissues and causing hypoxia; can be congenital or acquired (eg, exposure to oxidizing agents or nitrates).

lactic acidosis.definition: A rare but potentially lethal condition in which blood lactic acid levels increase.

cerebral embolism.definition: An embolus that travels through the bloodstream and lodges in a brain artery, causing cerebral ischemia and typically presenting as an ischemic stroke.

intracranial hemorrhage.definition: Bleeding within the cranial cavity from a ruptured cerebral vessel, which may occur in brain tissue or the surrounding meningeal spaces (subarachnoid, subdural, or epidural), often causing raised intracranial pressure and neurologic deficits.

genitourinary bleeding.definition: Bleeding from any part of the genitourinary tract (kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra, and genital organs), which may present as hematuria or visible bleeding from the urinary or genital tract.

dysrhythmias.definition: Disorders of the heart's rhythm caused by abnormal electrical activity, leading to heartbeats that are too fast (tachyarrhythmias), too slow (bradyarrhythmias), or irregular; they may cause palpitations, dizziness, syncope, or chest discomfort and can range from benign to life-threatening depending on the type and effect on cardiac output.

sweating.definition: The secretion of sweat from the sweat glands (primarily eccrine glands) in the skin, mainly for thermoregulation via evaporative cooling; it also assists in electrolyte excretion and, in apocrine-rich areas, can contribute to body odor; regulated by the sympathetic nervous system.

tremor.definition: When part of your body is shaking or trembling and you can't control it.

vertigo.definition: The sensation that you or your surroundings are spinning.

phlebitis.definition: Inflammation of a vein, usually due to irritation, injury, or infection, presenting with pain, redness, warmth, and swelling along the affected vessel; may involve superficial veins or extend to deep venous systems and may be associated with clot formation.

itching.definition: An unpleasant skin sensation that elicits the urge to scratch; medically termed pruritus, it can arise from skin disorders (e.g., eczema, psoriasis), dry skin, allergies, insect bites, infections, medications, or systemic diseases.

flushing.definition: Transient redness of the skin caused by dilation of superficial cutaneous blood vessels, most often affecting the face and neck, commonly triggered by heat, emotional states, alcohol, spicy foods, or certain medications.

low back pain.definition: Pain or discomfort localized to the lumbar region of the spine, often due to musculoskeletal strain or degenerative changes; a symptom rather than a diagnosis, typically self‑limited and described as acute or chronic based on duration.

thrombi.definition: A blood clot that forms within a blood vessel or heart chamber during life, adherent to the vessel wall, composed of platelets, fibrin, and blood cells, and capable of obstructing blood flow or embolizing to distant sites.

coronary artery thrombi.definition: A thrombus that forms inside a coronary artery, typically at sites of a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque, leading to partial or complete vascular occlusion and potentially causing myocardial ischemia or infarction.

embolism.definition: Sudden blockage of a blood vessel by an embolus (a piece of material traveling in the bloodstream from a distant site), most often a thrombus but also air, fat, or tumor fragments, leading to ischemia or infarction of the affected tissue.

acute myelocytic leukemia.definition: A malignant neoplasm of the myeloid lineage characterized by rapid proliferation of clonal myeloid blasts in the bone marrow and blood, leading to bone marrow failure (anemia, infections, and bleeding); treated with intensive chemotherapy and often stem cell transplantation.

malaria.definition: A disease that you get when you are bitten by a mosquito in certain parts of the world.

plasmodium.definition: A genus of parasitic protozoa that causes malaria in humans; transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes and includes species such as P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, and P. knowlesi.

anorectal stricture.definition: A narrowing of the anorectal lumen (distal rectum and anal canal) due to fibrosis or scar tissue, causing obstructive defecation symptoms; common causes include radiation, prior surgery (anastomotic stricture), inflammatory diseases (e.g., Crohn’s), infection, and trauma.

submucosal abscess.definition: A localized collection of pus beneath a mucous membrane, within the submucosa, caused by bacterial infection; presents with tenderness and swelling and may require drainage plus antibiotics.

ischiorectal abscess.definition: A deep bacterial infection of the ischiorectal fossa resulting in a pus-filled collection adjacent to the rectum; it typically presents with severe perianal or perineal pain, swelling, and fever and is usually treated with incision and drainage plus antibiotics.

perianal abscess.definition: A localized collection of pus in the perianal tissues resulting from infection of the anal glands, causing anal pain, swelling, and often fever; usually treated with surgical incision and drainage.

pelvirectal abscess.definition: A deep-seated pus collection in the pelvic space surrounding the rectum, typically arising from anorectal infection; presents with rectal or pelvic pain, fever, and malaise and often requires antibiotics with surgical drainage.

anorectal fistula.definition: An abnormal channel that connects the anorectal canal to the perianal skin, usually arising from infection of anal glands with prior abscess formation; it causes chronic drainage and recurrent infections and is typically treated surgically.

anal fissure.definition: A small tear in the lining of the anal canal (anoderm), usually at the posterior midline, causing intense pain with defecation and often bright red bleeding; commonly associated with constipation or hard stools and typically healing with conservative measures (fiber, stool softeners, sitz baths, topical vasodilators); persistent fissures may require surgical intervention.

anal crypt.definition: A small mucosal recess between the anal columns at the base of the anal canal (crypts of Morgagni); the openings for the anal glands reside in these crypts and can become infected, leading to an abscess or fistula.

anorexia nervosa.definition: A serious eating disorder defined by severe restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight, an intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, and a distorted perception of body weight or shape; often accompanied by physiological and psychological complications.

anorexiant.definition: A drug that suppresses appetite, used to aid weight loss by reducing hunger and caloric intake; many act on the central nervous system to promote satiety and some have cardiovascular or psychiatric side effects.

anorectic.definition: A substance that suppresses appetite; an appetite-suppressing drug or agent.

anorgasmy.definition: A persistent or recurrent inability to achieve orgasm despite adequate sexual arousal and stimulation, which can be lifelong or acquired and may involve psychological, neurologic, hormonal, or pharmacologic factors.

anorthopia.definition: A rare term for misalignment of the visual axes that produces diplopia (double vision).

anosmia.definition: Loss of the ability to detect odors, which may be complete or partial and can result from nasal obstruction or disease, infections, trauma, or neurological conditions.

anosmia gustatoria.definition: Loss or impairment of the sense of taste (gustation), including complete loss (ageusia) or distorted taste (dysgeusia); caused by damage to taste buds, the gustatory nerves (facial VII via chorda tympani, glossopharyngeal IX, vagus X), or central gustatory pathways, and can be influenced by concurrent olfactory dysfunction.

anosognosia.definition: A deficit in awareness of one's own neurological deficits, most often after a brain injury or stroke; patients may be unaware of or deny paralysis or other impairments.

anotia.definition: Congenital absence of the external ear (auricle). It is often unilateral but can be bilateral and is frequently associated with absence or malformation of the external auditory canal and other craniofacial anomalies.

anoxemia.definition: A deficiency of oxygen content in arterial blood (reduced PaO2 and/or SaO2), leading to inadequate tissue oxygenation; it differs from anoxia, which is a complete lack of oxygen.

ansa cervicalis.definition: A loop of nerves in the neck formed by C1–C3 fibers of the cervical plexus that supplies motor innervation to the infrahyoid muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid).

ansa hypoglossi.definition: A loop of nerves in the neck formed by C1 fibers hitchhiking with the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) to join fibers from C2–C3, forming part of the ansa cervicalis and innervating the infrahyoid muscles.

anovulation.definition: The failure of the ovaries to release a mature egg during a menstrual cycle, leading to irregular or absent menses and possible infertility; often due to hormonal disruption of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis.

anovarianism.definition: A condition in which the ovaries are absent or nonfunctional, resulting in impaired ovarian hormonal activity and reproductive capability.

anovular menstruation.definition: A menstrual cycle in which ovulation does not occur; the endometrium proliferates under estrogen and sheds without luteal-phase progesterone, often resulting in irregular or unpredictable bleeding and potential infertility.

anovulatory.definition: Not ovulating; relating to anovulation, a menstrual cycle in which ovulation does not occur.

hypoxemia.definition: A lower-than-normal level of oxygen in the arterial blood, indicated by decreased PaO2 and/or decreased SaO2, typically caused by respiratory or circulatory dysfunction.

antabuse.definition: A medication used to treat alcohol dependence by inhibiting aldehyde dehydrogenase, causing acetaldehyde buildup when alcohol is consumed and producing unpleasant symptoms (such as flushing, nausea, and palpitations) to discourage drinking.

antacid.definition: A substance that neutralizes gastric acid in the stomach to relieve heartburn and indigestion. Common antacids include calcium carbonate, magnesium hydroxide, aluminum hydroxide, and sodium bicarbonate; they provide rapid symptomatic relief but do not address underlying causes.

antagonism.definition: A relationship in which one substance or action opposes, counteracts, or reduces the effect of another; in pharmacology, a substance that blocks or diminishes the action of another drug or endogenous mediator, often by occupying a receptor without activating it.

antagonist.definition: The muscle opposing the major muscle required to do a task. It works to help balance movement and ward off injury.

antimetabolite.definition: A substance that interferes with normal cellular metabolism by acting as an analog or antagonist of a key metabolite, inhibiting nucleotide synthesis and DNA/RNA replication; widely used as chemotherapy.

antebrachial.definition: Relating to the forearm, the region of the upper limb between the elbow and the wrist.

antebrachial region.definition: The region of the upper limb between the elbow and the wrist; the forearm.

antebrachium.definition: The forearm; the region of the upper limb between the elbow and the wrist that contains the radius and ulna bones and their associated muscles, nerves, and vessels, enabling forearm rotation (pronation/supination) and wrist/hand movements.

antecubital.definition: Relating to the front of the elbow; the anterior aspect of the elbow.

antecubital fossa.definition: Triangular depression on the anterior aspect of the elbow, bounded medially by pronator teres, laterally by brachioradialis, and superiorly by a line between the epicondyles; it contains the biceps brachii tendon, brachial artery with its bifurcation into radial and ulnar arteries, median nerve, and accompanying veins. It is a common site for venipuncture and arterial access.

antecurvature.definition: A forward (anterior) bend or curvature of a body part or anatomical structure; the curvature oriented toward the front.

antefebrile.definition: Relating to or occurring before the onset of fever; preceding fever.

anteflexion.definition: Forward bending or flexion of a part on its axis; in gynecology, the uterus is anteflexed when the body bends forward on the cervix, with the fundus directed toward the bladder.

antegonial notch.definition: A notch or concavity on the inferior border of the mandible just anterior to the gonial angle (the antegonial region), typically identified on radiographs.

antegrade.definition: Moving forward in the direction of normal physiological flow; opposite of retrograde.

antegrade colonic enema.definition: A bowel-management procedure in which enema solution is delivered antegradely into the colon through a surgically created access (commonly an appendicostomy) to promote controlled stool evacuation; used for neurogenic bowel or refractory constipation; also known as antegrade continence enema (ACE).

antegrade colonic irrigation.definition: A bowel-management technique in which irrigation solution is infused into the colon in an antegrade direction (typically via a surgically created catheter/appendicostomy) to cleanse the colon and facilitate scheduled, controlled emptying, used to treat constipation and fecal incontinence, especially in neurogenic bowel.

antepartum hemorrhage.definition: Bleeding from the genital tract after 20 weeks of gestation and before delivery, usually due to placental disorders such as placenta previa or placental abruption, and requiring prompt evaluation and management.

antenatal.definition: Relating to the period before birth; occurring during pregnancy; prenatal.

antenatal care.definition: Care given to a pregnant person before birth, including scheduled prenatal visits, screening and prevention for mother and fetus, health education, nutrition advice, and planning for a safe delivery.

antenatal diagnosis.definition: The identification of fetal diseases or abnormalities before birth, using prenatal screening and diagnostic tests such as ultrasound, fetal echocardiography, and invasive genetic testing (e.g., amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling).

antepartal.definition: Relating to the period before birth; occurring during pregnancy prior to delivery.

antepartal care.definition: Care given to a pregnant person from conception to delivery, involving regular medical checkups, screening and management of maternal and fetal health, and counseling on nutrition, lifestyle, and labor planning.

antepartum.definition: Pertaining to the period of pregnancy before childbirth; occurring before labor begins.

anterior atlantoaxial ligament.definition: A fibrous band forming part of the anterior atlantoaxial membrane that extends between the anterior arch of the atlas (C1) and the body/odontoid region of the axis (C2), stabilizing the C1–C2 joint.

anterior atlantooccipital membrane.definition: A broad fibrous band spanning the craniocervical junction from the anterior arch of the atlas (C1) to the anterior border of the foramen magnum, continuous with the anterior longitudinal ligament, reinforcing the anterior aspect of the atlantooccipital joint and helping to limit excessive extension between the skull and atlas.

anterior axillary line.definition: A vertical surface landmark that runs along the anterior edge of the axilla (the front armpit) down the chest; used to describe the location of structures on the thorax and abdomen.

anterior cardiac vein.definition: Small veins on the anterior surface of the heart that drain directly into the right atrium, bypassing the coronary sinus; they collect venous blood from the anterior portion of the right ventricle and empty it into the right atrium.

anterior central gyrus.definition: Region of the frontal lobe immediately anterior to the central sulcus that contains the primary motor cortex; it mediates voluntary movement of the contralateral skeletal muscles and is organized somatotopically as the motor homunculus.

anterior cerebral commissure.definition: A small cross-hemispheric bundle of axons that connects the left and right temporal lobes, including olfactory areas and the amygdalae; it serves interhemispheric communication for olfactory and limbic pathways.
