anterior cervical decompression and fusi.definition: An anterior approach surgical procedure in the neck to relieve compression of the spinal cord or nerve roots by removing the offending intervertebral disc or bone spurs (decompression), followed by fusion of the adjacent cervical vertebrae with bone graft and often instrumentation to stabilize the spine.

acdf.definition: A surgical procedure to remove a damaged cervical intervertebral disc through an anterior approach and fuse the adjacent vertebrae to relieve nerve root or spinal cord compression and stabilize the cervical spine.

anal fistula.definition: A persistent, abnormal channel that forms between the anal canal or rectum and the skin near the anus, usually arising from an infected anal gland after an anorectal abscess, causing ongoing perianal drainage; typically treated surgically to eradicate the tract while preserving continence.

anorectoperineal muscle.definition: A muscle located in the anorectal region that functions to constrict the anal canal and maintain continence; this term typically corresponds to the external anal sphincter, a part of the pelvic-floor musculature.

anorectal canal.definition: A region of the digestive tract that includes the distal rectum and the anal canal, extending from the anorectal junction to the anal opening; about 2–4 cm long. The mucosa transitions from rectal columnar epithelium to anal squamous epithelium at the dentate (pectinate) line, and it is bounded by the internal and external anal sphincters, facilitating continence and defecation.

perineal region.definition: The perineal region is the area between the pubic symphysis and the coccyx, bounded laterally by the ischial tuberosities, containing the openings of the urogenital and digestive tracts and divided into the urogenital (anterior) and anal (posterior) triangles.

papanicolaou smear.definition: A cervical cytology test in which cells from the cervix are collected and examined microscopically to detect precancerous or cancerous changes, used for cervical cancer screening.

pap smear.definition: A cervical cancer screening test in which epithelial cells are collected from the cervix and examined under a microscope to detect cervical dysplasia and cervical cancer.

neisseria gonorrhoeae.definition: A fastidious, Gram-negative diplococcus that colonizes mucous membranes of the genitourinary tract, rectum, and oropharynx; the etiologic agent of gonorrhea, a sexually transmitted infection that can cause urethritis, cervicitis, pharyngitis, and proctitis, and may disseminate to cause septic arthritis with dermatitis.

chlamydia species.definition: Caused by a germ (a bacteria) that is passed during oral or genital sex from one person to another.

trichomonas vaginalis.definition: A flagellated, anaerobic protozoan parasite that infects the human urogenital tract and causes trichomoniasis, a common sexually transmitted infection; transmission is sexual, with women often presenting with vaginal discharge, itching, and dysuria, while men are frequently asymptomatic; diagnosed by NAAT or microscopy; treated with nitroimidazole antibiotics such as metronidazole or tinidazole, and sexual partners should be treated.

herpes genitalis.definition: A sexually transmitted infection caused primarily by herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2; HSV-1 can also cause genital infection) characterized by painful genital vesicular lesions, itching or dysuria, and episodic recurrences; transmitted by sexual contact and managed with antiviral therapy.

rubella titers.definition: A laboratory measurement of rubella-specific antibodies in the blood, used to determine immune status or to detect acute infection; IgG indicates past exposure or vaccination, while IgM indicates recent infection.

fetal heart.definition: The developing heart of a fetus, formed from the primitive cardiac tube; it begins beating around 4–5 weeks of gestation and pumps blood through the fetal circulatory system, which includes shunts such as the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus that bypass the nonfunctional fetal lungs.

ovarian dysgenesis.definition: A developmental disorder in which the ovaries fail to develop properly (gonadal dysgenesis), resulting in streak ovaries with little or no estrogen production, leading to hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, primary amenorrhea, and infertility.

ovarian pregnancy.definition: A very rare form of ectopic pregnancy in which the fertilized ovum implants within ovarian tissue (usually the ovarian cortex) rather than in the uterus or fallopian tube.

ovarian dysfunction.definition: Impaired ovarian function resulting in abnormal ovulation and altered ovarian hormone production (estrogen and progesterone), often presenting as irregular or absent menses, infertility, and/or hypoestrogenic symptoms.

ovulation.definition: The release of a mature egg from the ovary, at which time it is available to be fertilized by sperm.

oral contraceptives.definition: Pills taken by mouth to prevent pregnancy, usually containing estrogen and progestin and primarily working by suppressing ovulation; they also thicken cervical mucus and thin the endometrium. Progestin-only formulations (mini-pills) are an alternative option.

diskectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove all or part of a herniated or damaged intervertebral disc to relieve nerve root or spinal cord compression and alleviate associated back or leg pain.

albert's disease.definition: There is no widely recognized medical condition named "Albert's disease." If you meant Alzheimer's disease, it is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by memory loss, impaired thinking and judgment, and changes in behavior and function. If you had a different term in mind (e.g., Albert's syndrome), please clarify.

achilles bursitis.definition: Inflammation of the bursa located near the Achilles tendon (most often the retrocalcaneal bursa), causing posterior heel pain and swelling; usually due to overuse, repetitive friction, or trauma and may be associated with Achilles tendinopathy.

asynclitism.definition: An obstetric malposition in which the fetal head descends through the birth canal with the sagittal suture obliquely oriented to the maternal pelvis, so the head engages at an angle and deflects to one side.

triangle of the neck.definition: Posterior triangle of the neck: a region bounded anteriorly by the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, posteriorly by the anterior border of the trapezius, and inferiorly by the clavicle; contains the spinal accessory nerve, portions of the brachial plexus, the external jugular vein, and cervical lymph nodes.

bone graft.definition: A surgical procedure in which bone tissue is transplanted to replace missing bone or enhance healing; grafts may be autograft, allograft, or synthetic substitutes and provide structural support plus osteoconductive scaffolding, osteoinductive growth factors, and sometimes osteogenic cells to promote new bone formation.

disk space.definition: The space between adjacent vertebral bodies occupied by the intervertebral disc; its height reflects disc health and is reduced with degenerative disc disease.

spinal stability.definition: The ability of the spine to maintain vertebral alignment and spacing under normal physiological loads, resisting excessive motion to protect neural elements and enable functional movement; achieved by the coordinated action of passive structures (vertebrae, discs, ligaments, facet joints) and active stabilizers (paraspinal muscles) with neuromuscular control.

spinal plate.definition: A rigid implant used to stabilize the spine, typically attached to vertebral bodies with screws to immobilize segments for fracture fixation or spinal fusion.

screws.definition: A threaded metal implant used in surgery to fasten bone fragments or anchor implants to bone, providing stabilization for fracture fixation or fusion.

postoperative.definition: After surgery. Also called recovery from surgery.

recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy.definition: Paralysis or weakness of the intrinsic laryngeal muscles innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, resulting in impaired vocal fold movement and hoarseness; commonly due to surgical injury, tumor, or neuritis and may be unilateral or bilateral.

anterior horn.definition: Ventral (anterior) gray-matter region of the spinal cord containing motor neuron cell bodies; their axons form the ventral roots and innervate skeletal muscles.

ventral horn.definition: The anterior (ventral) portion of the spinal cord’s gray matter containing the cell bodies of lower motor neurons whose axons exit via the ventral roots to innervate skeletal muscle.

anterior column.definition: The anterior column of the spine refers to the anterior portion of the vertebral column, including the anterior longitudinal ligament and the anterior two‑thirds of the vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs; in Denis' three‑column stability model, it bears most of the axial load.

anterior longitudinal ligament.definition: A broad, strong band of dense connective tissue that runs along the anterior aspect of the vertebral column from the base of the skull to the sacrum, attaching to the anterior margins of the vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs and limiting spinal extension to provide anterior stability.

anterior cruciate ligament.definition: A strong ligament inside the knee that connects the femur to the tibia, preventing the tibia from sliding forward relative to the femur and providing rotational stability.

femoral nerve.definition: A major mixed motor-sensory nerve from the lumbar plexus (L2–L4) that supplies the anterior thigh muscles (iliopsoas, sartorius, quadriceps, pectineus) and provides cutaneous sensation to the anterior thigh and medial leg via the saphenous branch; it travels under the inguinal ligament within the femoral triangle.

anterior crural nerve.definition: Historically, this term designates the femoral nerve, a major lower-limb nerve arising from the L2–L4 ventral rami. It travels through the femoral triangle under the inguinal ligament, supplying motor innervation to the anterior thigh muscles (iliopsoas, quadriceps, sartorius, pectineus) and providing sensory innervation to the anterior thigh and, via the saphenous branch, to the medial leg.

anterior cutaneous nerve.definition: A cutaneous sensory nerve that supplies the skin on the front (anterior) aspect of a body region, usually the anterior branch of a spinal nerve (for example, the anterior cutaneous branches of intercostal nerves supplying the chest wall and abdomen).

cervical plexus.definition: A network of nerves in the neck formed by the anterior rami of C1–C4 (often with contributions from C5) spinal nerves. It supplies motor innervation to certain neck muscles (via the ansa cervicalis) and provides cutaneous sensation to the neck and parts of the head and shoulder, giving rise to branches such as the lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical, and supraclavicular nerves.

intercondylar eminence.definition: A raised area on the proximal tibia, between the medial and lateral condyles of the tibial plateau; it serves as the attachment site for the cruciate ligaments (anterior and posterior) and for the horns of the menisci.

incisal guide.definition: A dental concept describing the anterior guidance provided by the incisal edges of the maxillary and mandibular incisors during forward (protrusive) jaw movement; it is defined by the inclination of the incisal edges and influences posterior tooth disclusion and occlusal contacts.

anterior guide.definition: An anterior guide is the pattern of contact and alignment of the anterior teeth that directs mandibular movements—especially during protrusive and lateral excursions—resulting in disclusion of the posterior teeth and influencing overall occlusion.

incisal guide pin.definition: An adjustable pin on a dental articulator used to set and reproduce the incisal (anterior) guidance by contacting the incisal edges, guiding posterior tooth movement during occlusal analysis and fabrication.

condylar guide.definition: The path traced by the mandibular condyle within the temporomandibular joint during functional movements (especially protrusion), determined by the shape of the articular eminence and disc; used to set and simulate patient-specific mandibular motion on dental articulators and influence occlusion.

anterolateral thoracotomy.definition: A surgical approach to the chest achieved by an incision in the anterolateral chest wall (usually left), typically through the 4th or 5th intercostal space, to access the heart, lungs, and great vessels—commonly used in emergent trauma or thoracic surgery.

posterolateral thoracotomy.definition: A surgical approach to the thoracic cavity via a posterolateral chest-wall incision (typically through the 4th–8th intercostal spaces) with retraction or division of chest wall muscles (often latissimus dorsi and serratus anterior) to expose the lungs, pleura, esophagus, or mediastinum for procedures such as lobectomy, pneumonectomy, or esophagectomy.

anterior mediastinal node.definition: A lymph node located in the anterior mediastinum; part of the mediastinal (prevascular) lymph node group that drains anterior mediastinal structures such as the thymus and pericardium, and can be involved in diseases or metastasis affecting the anterior mediastinum.

anterior mediastinum.definition: An anatomical subdivision of the inferior mediastinum, located between the sternum and the pericardium; its contents include thymic tissue (thymus in children, residual thymic tissue in adults), fat and connective tissue, and anterior mediastinal lymph nodes and small vessels.

middle mediastinum.definition: That portion of the inferior mediastinum surrounding the pericardial sac that contains the heart, the roots/proximal portions of the great vessels (e.g., ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk), the main bronchi, and related pericardial structures and nerves.

posterior mediastinum.definition: Portion of the thoracic mediastinum located behind the pericardium and in front of the thoracic vertebral column, extending from the superior thoracic aperture to the diaphragm; contains the esophagus, descending thoracic aorta and its branches, thoracic duct, azygos and hemiazygos venous systems, thoracic sympathetic trunks, and the esophageal plexus formed by the vagus nerves.

superior mediastinum.definition: The portion of the mediastinum located above the plane through the sternal angle (T4–T5), extending from the superior thoracic aperture to that plane. It contains the thymus (often small in adults), the origins of the great vessels (aortic arch and branches), the superior vena cava and azygos system, the trachea and esophagus, the thoracic duct, and the vagus and phrenic nerves (including the left recurrent laryngeal nerve).

brachiocephalic vein.definition: A large vein formed by the union of the internal jugular and subclavian veins on each side; it drains blood from the head, neck, and upper limbs and joins to form the superior vena cava.

aortic arch.definition: A curved portion of the thoracic aorta between the ascending and descending aorta that gives rise to the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery, and left subclavian artery; located in the superior mediastinum and supplies oxygenated blood to the head, neck, and upper limbs.

thoracic visceral node.definition: A lymph node located in the thoracic cavity that drains lymph from thoracic viscera (such as the lungs, heart, pericardium, and mediastinal structures) and participates in immune surveillance; typically part of the mediastinal/tracheobronchial lymph node groups.

lateral anterior malleolar artery.definition: An artery arising from the anterior tibial artery that supplies the lateral aspect of the ankle joint and the lateral malleolus; it accompanies the anterior talofibular ligament and participates in the ankle's arterial anastomosis.

medial anterior malleolar artery.definition: A branch of the anterior tibial artery that supplies the medial aspect of the ankle and the medial malleolus, forming part of the ankle’s arterial anastomotic network with branches from the posterior tibial and perforating peroneal arteries.

lateral malleolar rete.definition: A vascular network around the lateral malleolus formed by anastomosing arteries (primarily perforating branches of the peroneal/fibular artery with contributions from the anterior and posterior tibial arteries) that supplies the lateral ankle region.

medial malleolar rete.definition: A vascular network around the inner ankle formed by arterial connections between branches of the anterior tibial and posterior tibial arteries (and perforators), supplying the medial ankle and the ankle joint with collateral circulation.

interosseous membrane.definition: A dense fibrous sheet that binds two long bones along their interosseous borders (such as the radius and ulna or the tibia and fibula), forming a syndesmosis, providing muscle attachments, and distributing loads between the bones.

anterior tibial node.definition: A deep lymph node located along the anterior tibial vessels in the lower leg; part of the deep lymphatic drainage of the limb.

inguinal node.definition: A lymph node in the groin (inguinal region) that filters lymph from the lower limb, lower abdomen, perineum, and external genitalia; part of the superficial and deep inguinal lymph node groups.

popliteal node.definition: An lymph node located in the popliteal fossa behind the knee; part of the lower limb lymphatic drainage, receiving lymph from deep tissues of the leg and foot and draining into the deep inguinal lymph nodes.

anterior nares.definition: The external openings of the nasal cavity (the nostrils) at the front of the nose; they allow air to pass into the nasal passages.

posterior nares.definition: The two internal openings between the nasal cavity and the nasopharynx; the posterior nasal apertures, also called the choanae.

anterior nasal spine.definition: A sharp bony projection on the anterior border of the maxilla at the inferior margin of the nasal aperture; the most anterior point of the maxilla, used as a cephalometric radiographic landmark.

nasal fossae.definition: Two hollow cavities within the nose, separated by the nasal septum, extending from the nares to the choanae; lined by respiratory mucosa and bounded by surrounding facial bones, they condition inhaled air (warming, humidifying, filtering) and serve as resonating chambers for the voice.

anterior ethmoidal artery.definition: A branch of the ophthalmic artery that supplies the anterior nasal cavity and the anterior ethmoidal air cells; it travels medially in the orbit, enters the nasal cavity through the anterior ethmoidal foramen, and gives off the internal and external nasal branches, with anastomoses to the sphenopalatine and posterior ethmoidal arteries.

anterior ethmoidal nerve.definition: A sensory branch of the nasociliary nerve (V1) that traverses the anterior ethmoidal foramen into the nasal cavity, supplying sensation to the anterior part of the nasal septum and adjacent nasal mucosa; its terminal divisions include the internal nasal nerve within the nasal cavity and the external nasal branch to the skin of the nose, and it also gives a small meningeal branch to the dura.

cranial fossa.definition: A depression on the inner surface of the skull forming the floor of the cranial cavity; there are three fossae—anterior, middle, and posterior—that house brain structures and define neurovascular pathways.

fontanel.definition: A soft, membranous gap between the bones of an infant's skull where the sutures have not yet fused, allowing for skull growth; these gaps (anterior and posterior) gradually ossify and close by about 18–24 months.

fontanelle.definition: A soft membranous interval between cranial bones in an infant where sutures have not yet fused; allows skull growth and birth passage; the anterior fontanelle is the largest, typically closing by 18–24 months, while the posterior fontanelle usually closes by 2–3 months.

anterior tubercle of the atlas.definition: A small midline projection on the anterior arch of the atlas (C1); serves as the attachment site for the anterior longitudinal ligament and for the longus colli muscle.

septum pellucidum.definition: A thin, vertical, double-layered membrane that separates the anterior horns of the left and right lateral ventricles of the brain; located at the midline and typically containing a cavum septi pellucidi when present.

lentiform nucleus.definition: A subcortical gray-matter structure of the basal ganglia consisting of the putamen and the globus pallidus (external and internal segments); located lateral to the internal capsule; modulates and coordinates voluntary motor movements as part of the extrapyramidal motor system.

caudate nucleus.definition: A C-shaped mass of gray matter in each hemisphere, part of the basal ganglia; forms the dorsal striatum with the putamen and receives widespread cortical input to influence movement and certain learning and memory processes; degeneration is characteristic of Huntington disease.

artery of adamkiewicz.definition: A large radiculomedullary artery, typically arising from a left intercostal or lumbar artery around the T9–L2 level, that enters the spinal canal and joins the anterior spinal artery to supply the lower two-thirds of the spinal cord (including the lumbosacral enlargement); interruption can cause ischemia of the distal spinal cord (anterior spinal artery syndrome).

anterior temporal artery.definition: A branch of the middle cerebral artery that supplies the anterior portion of the temporal lobe, including the temporal pole.

anterior temporal lobe.definition: The front portion of the temporal lobe of the brain, including the temporal pole and adjacent anterior temporal cortex; involved in semantic memory, language, and social–emotional processing.

bacillus anthracis.definition: A Gram-positive, rod-shaped, spore-forming bacillus that causes anthrax in humans and animals; encapsulated with poly-D-glutamic acid and producing virulence factors (protective antigen with edema factor and lethal factor); infection occurs via spores entering through skin, inhalation, or ingestion; treated with antibiotics and, in severe cases, antitoxins; vaccine available for at-risk individuals.

anthrax.definition: A zoonotic bacterial infection caused by Bacillus anthracis, presenting in cutaneous, inhalational, or gastrointestinal forms after exposure to infected animals or contaminated animal products; virulence arises from a poly-D-glutamic acid capsule and tripartite toxins; treated with specific antibiotics; vaccination is available for some at-risk groups.

inhalational anthrax.definition: An acute, potentially fatal infection caused by inhaling Bacillus anthracis spores, characterized by initial nonspecific flu‑like symptoms that rapidly progress to severe respiratory distress, mediastinal involvement, and sepsis.

woolsorter’s disease.definition: Inhalational anthrax, a form of anthrax caused by inhaling Bacillus anthracis spores; historically linked to wool workers and processing of animal hair, hides, and wool. It begins with nonspecific flu-like symptoms and can rapidly progress to severe respiratory distress, mediastinal widening, and septicemia if untreated.

malignant edema.definition: A rapidly progressive, life-threatening infection of soft tissue caused by clostridial bacteria (often Clostridium septicum or Clostridium perfringens) characterized by marked edema with extensive necrosis, gas production, and systemic toxicity (sepsis), often following trauma or surgery.

malignant pustule.definition: A cutaneous lesion caused by Bacillus anthracis infection (cutaneous anthrax); it starts as a painless papule that progresses to a vesicle or pustule and then to a necrotic, painless black eschar with surrounding edema.

ragpicker disease.definition: A historical term for dermatitis among rag-pickers, typically chronic irritant or allergic contact dermatitis of the hands and forearms due to prolonged exposure to dirty rags, waste, and irritants; today this is classified as occupational dermatitis.

anthracosis.definition: Deposition of carbon pigment (coal dust) in the lungs and regional lymph nodes from inhalation; typically asymptomatic and nonfibrotic, often an incidental finding and not a progressive pneumoconiosis.

anthraconecrosis.definition: Necrosis of tissue associated with anthracosis (coal dust deposition), in which dark carbon pigment is present within the necrotic area; occurs with chronic inhalation exposure and may be seen in the lungs and regional lymph nodes.

black lung disease.definition: A chronic occupational lung disease caused by inhaling coal dust, leading to inflammation and fibrotic nodules in the lungs and, in advanced cases, progressive massive fibrosis with impaired respiratory function.

coal worker’s pneumoconiosis.definition: A lung disease caused by chronic inhalation of coal dust, primarily in coal miners, characterized by coal macules and nodular interstitial fibrosis that may progress to progressive massive fibrosis and impaired gas exchange; also known as black lung disease.

miner’s pneumoconiosis.definition: A lung disease caused by chronic inhalation of coal dust, resulting in coal dust–induced nodular fibrosis in the lungs that can progress to extensive scarring (progressive massive fibrosis), typically affecting coal miners.

pneumoconiosis.definition: A group of interstitial lung diseases caused by chronic inhalation of mineral dusts (e.g., coal dust, silica, asbestos), leading to inflammation, fibrotic scarring, and impaired respiratory function.

anthelmintic.definition: A drug used to treat infections caused by parasitic worms (helminths). It kills or disables helminths by targeting their metabolism or neuromuscular systems and is effective against nematodes, cestodes, and trematodes.

piperazine.definition: A saturated six-membered heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms (a diamine), commonly used as a chemical building block in medicinal chemistry and as the core scaffold for many pharmaceutical piperazine derivatives.

pyrantel pamoate.definition: An anthelmintic used to treat common intestinal nematode infections, including pinworm, roundworm, and hookworm infestations. It acts by causing depolarizing neuromuscular paralysis in the parasite, via stimulation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, leading to immobilization and expulsion in the stool. It is poorly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract and is given orally, typically in single-dose regimens with possible repeat dosing; adverse effects are usually mild and include GI upset, nausea, or vomiting.

pyrvinium pamoate.definition: An orally administered anthelmintic used to treat intestinal pinworm infections; it is poorly absorbed from the GI tract and acts locally in the intestine, likely by disrupting parasite energy metabolism (uncoupling oxidative phosphorylation).

mebendazole.definition: A benzimidazole broad-spectrum anthelmintic that binds nematode beta-tubulin, inhibiting microtubule formation and glucose uptake, causing energy depletion and parasite death; used to treat intestinal helminth infections such as pinworm, roundworm, whipworm, and hookworm; poorly absorbed from the GI tract (acts luminally).

niclosamide.definition: An anthelmintic drug used to treat intestinal cestode infections (such as Taenia species). It acts locally in the gastrointestinal tract by uncoupling oxidative phosphorylation in the parasite's mitochondria, depleting ATP and killing the tapeworm; it is poorly absorbed, with mainly GI side effects.

hexylresorcinol.definition: A resorcinol derivative (4-hexylresorcinol), a phenolic compound with antimicrobial activity and tyrosinase inhibition, used as an antiseptic in oral care and as a skin-lightening agent in cosmetics.

diethylcarbamazine.definition: A synthetic antifilarial medication used to treat filarial infections (most notably lymphatic filariasis); it primarily kills microfilariae and can provoke inflammatory reactions (Mazzotti reaction) due to rapid parasite death.

thiabendazole.definition: A benzimidazole-class antiparasitic used as an anthelmintic to treat intestinal nematode infections (e.g., ascariasis, hookworm, whipworm). It inhibits parasite tubulin polymerization by binding to beta-tubulin, disrupting microtubule formation and glucose uptake, leading to energy depletion and death of the worms.

ciprofloxacin.definition: A fluoroquinolone antibiotic that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, blocking DNA replication and causing bacterial death; used to treat a wide range of infections such as urinary tract infections, intra-abdominal infections, skin and respiratory tract infections, and certain sexually transmitted infections.

levofloxacin.definition: A fluoroquinolone antibiotic that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, used to treat a variety of infections including respiratory, urinary tract, skin, and certain gastrointestinal infections.

doxycycline.definition: A broad-spectrum tetracycline antibiotic that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by reversibly binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit; used to treat a wide range of infections and for malaria prophylaxis. It is contraindicated in pregnancy and in children under 8 due to effects on teeth and bone; common adverse effects include photosensitivity and gastrointestinal upset; absorption is reduced by calcium, iron, and dairy products.

vaccine.definition: A shot that protects you from certain diseases. Also called immunization.

chronic dermatitis.definition: A long-standing inflammatory skin condition characterized by pruritic, eczematous lesions that persist or recur for months to years, often with thickened (lichenified), scaly, or crusted skin, and commonly associated with atopy or ongoing exposure to irritants or allergens.

anthralin.definition: A topical antipsoriatic agent used to treat plaque psoriasis; it irritates the skin to produce a localized dermatitis that reduces epidermal cell proliferation, typically applied for short periods and washed off; can stain skin, hair, nails, and clothing and cause irritation or contact dermatitis.

anthranilic acid.definition: An aromatic carboxylic acid (2-aminobenzoic acid) with an amino group in the ortho position to the carboxyl group; used as a chemical building block in the synthesis of dyes, pharmaceuticals, and polymers, and as an intermediate in the biosynthesis of tryptophan and NAD in bacteria and plants.

anteversion.definition: Forward rotation or tilting of a body part toward the anterior (front) surface; used to describe, for example, the anterior rotation of the femoral neck relative to the shaft or the forward tilt of the uterus.

anterior vaginal repair.definition: A surgical repair of the anterior vaginal wall to correct pelvic organ prolapse (most commonly a cystocele) by tightening and reinforcing the pubocervical fascia to restore bladder support.

anterograde amnesia.definition: An inability to form new long-term memories after a brain injury or illness, with preserved recall of previously learned information; encoding and consolidation of new declarative memories are impaired, though short-term memory and some non-declarative (procedural) memory may be preserved.

retrograde amnesia.definition: An impairment in which memories formed before a specific event or injury cannot be recalled, while the ability to form new memories remains relatively preserved.

anteroposterior diameter of the pelvic o.word: anteroposterior diameter of the pelvic outlet
anteroposterior diameter of the pelvic o.definition: The sagittal distance from the inferior border of the pubic symphysis to the tip of the coccyx, representing the front-to-back extent of the pelvic outlet.

cutaneous anthrax.definition: Localized cutaneous infection caused by Bacillus anthracis spores entering through a break in the skin, typically starting as a painless papule that enlarges to a vesicle or bulla and then forms a necrotic black eschar; often acquired from contaminated animal products and may be accompanied by regional edema; generally curable with prompt antibiotic therapy.

inhalation anthrax.definition: Life-threatening form of anthrax caused by inhaling Bacillus anthracis spores; spores germinate in the lungs, causing rapid fever, malaise, cough, and dyspnea, often with mediastinal involvement, progressing to severe pneumonia, sepsis, and death if not treated promptly with antibiotics and supportive care.

gastrointestinal anthrax.definition: A rare form of anthrax caused by ingesting Bacillus anthracis spores, leading to infection of the gastrointestinal tract with symptoms such as severe abdominal pain, vomiting (often bloody), nausea, fever, and possible progression to sepsis if untreated.

eschar.definition: A dry, dark, leathery crust of necrotic tissue and dried exudate that forms over a burn or other wound; nonviable tissue that can impede healing and may require debridement.

vesicle.definition: A small, fluid-filled blister on the skin or mucous membrane, typically less than 1 centimeter in diameter and containing clear serous fluid.

necrotic center.definition: An area within a lesion where cells have died (necrosis), typically due to ischemia or infection; in tumors, central necrosis occurs when the blood supply cannot sustain rapid growth.

mediastinal widening.definition: An abnormal increase in the width of the mediastinal silhouette on chest radiography, suggesting enlargement or mass effect from mediastinal structures (e.g., aortic aneurysm/dissection, mediastinal tumor or lymphadenopathy, edema, or hemorrhage) and typically requiring further imaging to determine cause and urgency.

infiltrates.definition: An accumulation of fluid, inflammatory cells, pus, blood, or tumor cells in tissue or an organ; in radiology, patchy or confluent areas of increased opacity in the lungs representing such material (e.g., pneumonia, edema, or hemorrhage).

cipro.definition: A broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone antibiotic that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, used to treat a variety of infections including urinary tract, respiratory, skin, and gastrointestinal infections.

floxacin.definition: Suffix used in the names of a class of broad-spectrum antibacterial drugs called fluoroquinolones; these agents inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV and are used to treat a variety of infections.

penicillin g.definition: Penicillin G (benzylpenicillin) is a beta-lactam antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins. It is active mainly against Gram-positive organisms (including streptococci) and certain spirochetes; typically administered parenterally (IM/IV) as salt forms and used for infections such as syphilis and streptococcal infections, though it is inactivated by many beta-lactamase–producing bacteria.

gentamicin sulfate.definition: An aminoglycoside antibiotic in sulfate salt form used to treat serious Gram-negative infections; it inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit, leading to bacterial death, and is typically given by injection with potential nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

kanamycin sulfate.definition: An aminoglycoside antibiotic; the sulfate salt form of kanamycin used to treat serious infections caused by susceptible bacteria; administered by injection since it is poorly absorbed orally; it inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit; associated with nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity; use has declined with safer alternatives.

neomycin sulfate.definition: A broad-spectrum aminoglycoside antibiotic in the sulfate salt form that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding the 30S ribosomal subunit; used topically for skin, eye, and mucous membrane infections and orally to decontaminate the gastrointestinal tract before surgery; may cause nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

streptomycin sulfate.definition: An aminoglycoside antibiotic in the sulfate salt form that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of mRNA; used to treat certain serious infections (notably tuberculosis, plague, and tularemia) and usually administered by intramuscular injection, with adverse effects including ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity.

tobramycin sulfate.definition: A salt form of the aminoglycoside antibiotic tobramycin used to treat serious gram-negative bacterial infections. It binds to the 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of mRNA and inhibition of protein synthesis (bactericidal). Administered systemically or as topical formulations (ophthalmic/otic or inhalation) depending on the preparation; adverse effects include nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

lidocaine hydrochloride.definition: A hydrochloride salt of lidocaine used as a local anesthetic and antiarrhythmic agent; it blocks voltage-gated sodium channels to inhibit nerve conduction and stabilize cardiac membranes.

disopyramide phosphate.definition: A class IA antiarrhythmic agent (sodium-channel blocker) in phosphate salt form; used to treat certain ventricular and supraventricular tachyarrhythmias by slowing conduction and prolonging the ventricular action potential (QT interval), with risks of anticholinergic effects and proarrhythmia (torsades de pointes) and cautions in heart failure or conduction disturbances.

procainamide hydrochloride.definition: A class IA antiarrhythmic agent that blocks fast sodium channels to slow conduction and prolong repolarization; used to treat certain atrial and ventricular arrhythmias and is administered intravenously or orally as the hydrochloride salt.

quinidine.definition: A class IA antiarrhythmic drug that blocks cardiac sodium channels and prolongs the cardiac action potential, used to treat certain atrial and ventricular tachyarrhythmias; may cause QT prolongation and torsades de pointes.

propranolol hydrochloride.definition: A nonselective beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist (beta-blocker) used to treat hypertension, angina pectoris, certain cardiac arrhythmias, and to prevent migraine headaches; also used for tremors and some anxiety disorders.

isoproterenol hydrochloride.definition: A synthetic nonselective beta-adrenergic agonist (isoproterenol) in the hydrochloride salt form; stimulates beta-1 and beta-2 receptors, increasing heart rate, myocardial contractility, and bronchodilation; used in the management of bradycardia or heart block and, less commonly, bronchospasm.

atropine.definition: A tropane alkaloid antimuscarinic drug that competitively blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors; used to increase heart rate in bradycardia, reduce secretions, dilate pupils, and treat organophosphate poisoning.

digoxin.definition: A cardiac glycoside that increases myocardial contractility by inhibiting Na+/K+-ATPase, leading to increased intracellular calcium; used to treat heart failure and certain arrhythmias (notably atrial fibrillation) but has a narrow therapeutic index and potential toxicity.

calcium channel blockers.definition: This kind of drug lowers your blood pressure. It can also be used to treat chest pain and a heart beat that is not regular. There are many different names for these drugs, including amlodipine, diltiazem, and nifedipine.

antiarrhythmic.definition: A medication that treats or prevents abnormal heart rhythms by altering the electrical activity of the heart (e.g., modifying ion channel currents or conduction).

defibrillator.definition: A device that gives the heart an electrical shock to make it start beating normally again.

pacemaker.definition: A small battery-powered device implanted under the skin near the heart that delivers electrical impulses to stimulate heart contractions and maintain an appropriate heart rate and rhythm in people with slow or irregular heartbeats.

atrioventricular node.definition: A cluster of specialized cardiac cells at the base of the right atrium that delays the electrical impulse from the sinoatrial node before transmitting it to the ventricles, allowing atrial contraction to precede ventricular contraction.

complete heart block.definition: A severe atrioventricular block in which no conduction occurs from the atria to the ventricles; the atria and ventricles beat independently (AV dissociation) with the ventricles paced by a slower escape rhythm. It commonly causes marked bradycardia and symptoms such as dizziness or syncope; treatment typically involves pacemaker implantation.

ventricular arrhythmias.definition: Ventricular arrhythmias are abnormal heart rhythms that originate from the ventricles (the heart’s lower chambers). They include premature ventricular contractions, ventricular tachycardia, and ventricular fibrillation; these can be benign or life-threatening and may cause palpitations, dizziness, syncope, or sudden cardiac death.

antianemic.definition: A substance, treatment, or agent that counteracts anemia, usually by increasing red blood cell production or hemoglobin levels.

aplastic anemia.definition: A rare bone marrow failure in which hematopoietic stem cells are destroyed or suppressed, producing hypocellular marrow and pancytopenia (reduced red cells, white cells, and platelets); can be acquired (idiopathic or due to drugs, toxins, radiation, or infections) or inherited.

laennec's cirrhosis.definition: Forma de cirrosis hepática asociada al consumo crónico de alcohol, caracterizada por nodulación microscópica (micronodular) de la estructura hepática con fibrosis difusa, que provoca deterioro progresivo de la función hepática y hipertensión portal.

antianginal.definition: A drug or agent used to prevent or relieve angina pectoris by reducing myocardial oxygen demand or increasing myocardial oxygen supply.

beta-adrenergic blocking agents.definition: A class of medications that antagonize beta-adrenergic receptors (primarily β1 and β2), decreasing heart rate, contractility, and conduction velocity, thereby lowering blood pressure and myocardial oxygen demand; used to treat hypertension, angina, certain arrhythmias, and heart failure, with some agents more selective for β1 and others nonselective.

antiantibody.definition: An antibody that binds to another antibody; this includes anti-idiotype antibodies that recognize the target antibody’s antigen-binding (variable) region, as well as anti-immunoglobulin antibodies that bind other regions of immunoglobulins.

antiantitoxin.definition: A substance, typically an antibody, that neutralizes an antitoxin by binding to it, thereby diminishing the antitoxin's ability to neutralize a toxin.

antianxiety agent.definition: An anxiolytic is a medication that reduces anxiety symptoms; these agents act by dampening excessive brain activity through different mechanisms, most commonly by enhancing GABAergic inhibition (as with benzodiazepines) or by altering serotonin and/or norepinephrine signaling (as with SSRIs, SNRIs, and buspirone).

anxiolytic.definition: A drug or agent that reduces anxiety; used to treat anxiety disorders, often acting on GABA receptors (e.g., benzodiazepines) or other mechanisms (e.g., buspirone).

antiarthritic.definition: A substance (drug or treatment) used to treat arthritis by reducing inflammation and pain, and often slowing or preventing joint damage (as with disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs and related therapies).

antibacterial.definition: Relating to substances that kill bacteria or inhibit their growth; used to describe agents such as antibiotics, antiseptics, and disinfectants that act against bacteria.

chloramphenicol.definition: A broad-spectrum antibiotic that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by reversibly binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit and blocking peptidyl transferase; primarily bacteriostatic, but can be bactericidal for some organisms, and is limited by serious toxicity such as bone marrow suppression (including aplastic anemia) and gray baby syndrome in neonates.

cephalosporin antibiotics.definition: A class of beta-lactam antibiotics derived from the fungus Acremonium; they inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins, causing cell lysis. They are organized into generations with increasing activity against gram-negative bacteria and are used to treat a broad range of infections. They are generally bactericidal and may cause hypersensitivity reactions in penicillin-allergic patients; common adverse effects include diarrhea, rash, and, with some agents, disulfiram-like reactions with alcohol.

cephalosporins.definition: A class of beta-lactam antibiotics derived from the fungus Acremonium, which inhibit bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins and are used for a wide range of infections; they are grouped into generations with increasing activity against gram-negative bacteria and varying beta-lactamase resistance.

cefadroxil monohydrate.definition: A first-generation cephalosporin antibiotic; the monohydrate is the salt form of cefadroxil used to treat various susceptible bacterial infections (e.g., skin and soft-tissue, urinary tract, and certain respiratory infections). It inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins, resulting in bacterial lysis (bactericidal).

cefamandole nafate.definition: A parenteral cephalosporin antibiotic (the nafate salt of cefamandole), a second-generation beta-lactam that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis and is used to treat infections caused by susceptible gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria.

cephalexin.definition: An oral first-generation cephalosporin antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis and is used to treat mild to moderate infections such as skin and soft tissue infections, otitis media, respiratory tract infections, and urinary tract infections.

cephaloglycin.definition: A cephalosporin-type antibiotic (beta-lactam) used to treat various bacterial infections; it inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis.

cephaloridine.definition: A cephalosporin antibiotic (beta-lactam) historically used to treat bacterial infections; it is notably nephrotoxic, which has led to restricted or discontinued use in favor of safer cephalosporins.

cephalothin sodium.definition: A sodium salt of a first‑generation cephalosporin antibiotic used for parenteral therapy; it inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin‑binding proteins, producing bactericidal activity against susceptible organisms. Indicated for certain infections (eg, skin and soft tissue, urinary, respiratory); contraindicated in cephalosporin or penicillin allergy.

cephapirin.definition: A cephalosporin antibiotic (beta-lactam) used chiefly in veterinary medicine, typically as an intramammary infusion to treat bovine mastitis; it inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin‑binding proteins, with activity mainly against Gram-positive cocci and some Gram-negative bacteria.

cephradine.definition: An older first-generation cephalosporin antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins; active mainly against gram-positive cocci and some gram-negative rods, used for mild to moderate infections caused by susceptible organisms.

penicillinase.definition: An enzyme produced by certain bacteria that hydrolyzes the beta-lactam ring of penicillin, inactivating the antibiotic and enabling resistance.

haemophilus influenzae.definition: A small, Gram-negative coccobacillus that colonizes the human upper respiratory tract; it requires X (hemin) and V (NAD) factors for growth and can cause infections ranging from otitis media and conjunctivitis to meningitis and epiglottitis, with encapsulated type b associated with invasive disease and preventable by Hib vaccination.

haemophilus influenzae meningitis.definition: A bacterial meningitis caused by Haemophilus influenzae, most commonly type b (Hib); incidence has fallen with Hib vaccination.

rickettsial diseases.definition: A group of infections caused by obligate intracellular, Gram‑negative bacteria (primarily Rickettsia, Orientia, Ehrlichia, and Anaplasma) transmitted to humans by arthropod vectors (ticks, mites, fleas, lice). They typically cause febrile illness with headache and often a rash due to vasculitis of small vessels, and are treated with doxycycline.

enteropathogenic escherichia coli.definition: A diarrheagenic pathotype of Escherichia coli that causes watery diarrhea, especially in infants, by attaching to and effacing intestinal epithelial cells via a type III secretion system; typically does not produce Shiga toxin, with typical EPEC harboring the EAF plasmid (bundle-forming pili) and atypical EPEC lacking it.

typhoid fever.definition: A systemic febrile illness caused by Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi, acquired through ingestion of contaminated food or water; typically presents with prolonged fever, malaise, and abdominal pain, and can progress to serious intestinal complications if untreated.

staphylococcal infections.definition: An infection caused by Staphylococcus bacteria, most often Staphylococcus aureus, that can affect the skin and soft tissues (e.g., folliculitis, impetigo, abscesses, cellulitis) and may involve deeper structures or the bloodstream (e.g., pneumonia, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, bacteremia); many strains are methicillin-resistant (MRSA).

streptomyces.definition: A genus of Gram-positive, aerobic, filamentous bacteria (Actinobacteria) found in soil; notable for producing a large number of clinically important antibiotics and having a high GC content in its DNA.

erythromycin.definition: A macrolide antibiotic derived from Saccharopolyspora erythraea that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit; used to treat a range of infections, especially in penicillin-allergic patients.

oleandomycin.definition: A macrolide antibiotic that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit, blocking translocation.

bacitracin.definition: A polypeptide antibiotic produced by Bacillus species that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by interfering with the dephosphorylation of bactoprenol (bactoprenol pyrophosphate), blocking transport of peptidoglycan precursors. It is mainly active against gram-positive bacteria and has limited activity against gram-negatives due to the outer membrane. Used topically (including ophthalmic ointments) for local infections; systemic use is limited by nephrotoxicity. Often formulated in combination products (e.g., with polymyxin B and neomycin).

vancomycin.definition: A glycopeptide antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis by binding to the D-alanyl-D-alanine terminus of peptidoglycan precursors; active mainly against Gram-positive bacteria and used for serious infections such as MRSA; administered IV for systemic infections (oral for C. difficile colitis).

capreomycin.definition: An injectable cyclic peptide antibiotic used as a second-line treatment for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis; it inhibits protein synthesis in Mycobacterium tuberculosis and may cause nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

gramicidin.definition: A polypeptide antibiotic produced by Bacillus brevis that inserts into bacterial membranes to form channel-like pores, dissipating the proton motive force and causing leakage of ions and cell death; primarily active against Gram-positive bacteria and historically used topically, but unsuitable for systemic use due to toxicity.

colistin sulfate.definition: A polypeptide antibiotic (polymyxin E) in the sulfate salt form that disrupts the outer membrane of susceptible Gram-negative bacteria by binding lipopolysaccharides; used against certain multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infections, with significant nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity risk; administration can be systemic, topical, inhaled, or oral for GI decontamination.

serological testing.definition: A laboratory method that detects antibodies to a pathogen or antigens from a pathogen in a patient’s blood serum to determine current or past infection or immune status; used for diagnosis, confirmation, and surveillance with assays such as ELISA, immunofluorescence, agglutination, Western blot, and rapid tests.

antitoxin.definition: An antitoxin is a preparation of antibodies that neutralizes a specific toxin, used to provide passive immunity or treat exposure to the toxin.

post-exposure anthrax vaccine.definition: A vaccination given after suspected exposure to Bacillus anthracis to stimulate an immune response and reduce the risk of developing anthrax, typically used in conjunction with antibiotic prophylaxis and requiring a multi-dose schedule for longer-term protection.

immunization.definition: The process by which an individual becomes protected against a disease, typically through vaccination that stimulates an immune response and establishes immunological memory.

immunity.definition: The ability to fight off an illness.

anticancer.definition: Having the ability to prevent, inhibit, or treat cancer; describing agents or strategies that kill or slow the growth of cancer cells.

mitomycin.definition: An antitumor antibiotic produced by Streptomyces species that acts as a bifunctional alkylating agent, cross-linking DNA and inhibiting DNA synthesis; used in cancer chemotherapy and, in ophthalmology, to prevent scar formation after surgery.

b-lymphocytes.definition: A lymphocyte of the adaptive immune system that matures in the bone marrow; upon activation, it differentiates into antibody-secreting plasma cells and memory B cells, providing humoral immunity.

autoantibodies.definition: Proteins created by the immune system that mistakenly target healthy cells, tissues, or organs.

anticardiolipin.definition: Autoantibodies directed against cardiolipin, a phospholipid; they are serologic markers for antiphospholipid syndrome and can contribute to arterial or venous thrombosis and pregnancy morbidity, detected by anticardiolipin ELISA (IgG or IgM), and may cause prolonged phospholipid-dependent coagulation tests such as the aPTT.

anticentromere.definition: An autoantibody directed against centromere-associated proteins (e.g., CENP-A/B), most often seen in the limited form of systemic sclerosis (CREST) and associated with a relatively favorable prognosis but possible esophageal dysmotility.

anticholinergic.definition: A substance that inhibits the action of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, reducing parasympathetic nervous system activity.

belladonna.definition: A poisonous plant containing anticholinergic alkaloids—atropine, scopolamine, and hyoscyamine; produces delirium, tachycardia, dry mouth, and other anticholinergic effects, and can be fatal in overdose. Used in very small, controlled doses for pupil dilation and relief of cramps.

glycopyrrolate.definition: A quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) medication that blocks muscarinic receptors, thereby reducing secretions (salivary, bronchial, and GI) and providing antisialogogue and antisposmodic effects; used to decrease secretions preoperatively and to manage drooling, with minimal central nervous system effects due to limited blood-brain barrier penetration.

hyoscamine.definition: An antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) tropane alkaloid used as a gastrointestinal antispasmodic; it blocks muscarinic receptors, reducing smooth muscle contractions and secretions to relieve cramping.

methixene.definition: Not a recognized medical term; no established pharmacology, mechanism of action, or clinical use documented in standard references. If you have a different spelling or context (drug class, condition), please share it for a more precise definition.

trihexyphenidyl.definition: An anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) medication used to treat Parkinson disease and drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms; it reduces central acetylcholine activity to help decrease tremor, rigidity, and dystonia.

scopolamine.definition: An antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) medication that blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. It is used to prevent motion sickness and postoperative nausea and vomiting, commonly administered as a transdermal patch or oral formulation. Side effects include drowsiness, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, and confusion, especially in older adults.

anticholinesterase.definition: A substance that inhibits acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that hydrolyzes acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft, thereby increasing acetylcholine levels and enhancing cholinergic transmission; used therapeutically in conditions like myasthenia gravis and Alzheimer's disease and to reverse neuromuscular blockade; can be reversible or irreversible.

edrophonium.definition: An ultra-short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used diagnostically in myasthenia gravis (the Tensilon test) to transiently increase muscle strength; onset within seconds to a minute with effects lasting about 5–10 minutes.

neostigmine.definition: A reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that increases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction by carbamoylating acetylcholinesterase; used to treat myasthenia gravis, reverse nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade after surgery, and treat acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome).

pyridostigmine.definition: Long-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used to treat myasthenia gravis by increasing acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction; administered orally or by injection; limited CNS penetration due to its quaternary ammonium structure.

physostigmine.definition: A reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that increases acetylcholine at cholinergic synapses; used to treat anticholinergic toxicity and open-angle glaucoma (often as a topical ocular agent).

organophosphates.definition: A class of organophosphorus esters that irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase, leading to accumulation of acetylcholine and cholinergic toxicity; widely used as pesticides and includes nerve agents.

phenytoin.definition: A hydantoin anticonvulsant that stabilizes neuronal membranes by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels, reducing neuronal excitability; used to treat and prevent focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures; has nonlinear pharmacokinetics and potential for drug interactions and adverse effects.

vasopressin.definition: A peptide hormone produced in the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary; the antidiuretic hormone that promotes renal water reabsorption by increasing collecting duct water permeability via V2 receptors, and at higher concentrations can cause vasoconstriction via V1 receptors.

antidiuretic.definition: A substance that reduces urine production by promoting water reabsorption in the kidneys.

adh.definition:
- A fibrous band that binds two tissues or surfaces that are normally separate, often forming after inflammation, infection, or surgery.
- A hormone produced by the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary that promotes water reabsorption in the kidneys, thereby concentrating the urine (vasopressin).

neurohypophysis.definition: The posterior pituitary gland; a neural extension of the hypothalamus that stores and releases the hormones vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone) and oxytocin, produced in hypothalamic neurons.

crest.definition: A prominent linear ridge or border on a bone or other anatomical structure, typically serving as an attachment point for muscles or ligaments (e.g., the iliac crest).

streptococcal.definition: Relating to or caused by bacteria of the genus Streptococcus; infections by these bacteria are common and may affect the throat, skin, or other tissues.

addison.definition: A primary adrenal insufficiency caused by destruction or dysfunction of the adrenal cortex, leading to deficient cortisol (and often aldosterone) and presenting with fatigue, weight loss, hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and typically hyperpigmentation; lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement is required.

antistreptolysin.definition: An antibody against streptolysin O, a toxin of group A Streptococcus; used as a serologic marker of recent streptococcal infection (often measured as an ASO titer).

antideoxyribonuclease-b.definition: An antibody to DNase B (deoxyribonuclease B), an enzyme produced by group A Streptococcus; used as a serologic marker of prior Streptococcus pyogenes infection, with anti-DNase B titers rising after infection and aiding diagnosis of rheumatic fever and other post-streptococcal sequelae, especially when ASO results are negative or inconclusive.

anti-dna.definition: Antibodies directed against DNA, especially double-stranded DNA; commonly associated with autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus, where they can form immune complexes that contribute to tissue injury (notably lupus nephritis) and serve as a diagnostic marker and indicator of disease activity (anti-dsDNA).

antidote.definition: A substance that counteracts the effects of a poison or toxin, often by binding, neutralizing, or reversing its action.

anticoagulant.definition: A substance that helps prevent blood from clotting.

citrate.definition: A tricarboxylate anion derived from citric acid; a key metabolic intermediate in the citric acid (Krebs) cycle; citrate salts (e.g., sodium citrate) are used medically as anticoagulants and buffering/alkalinizing agents.

phosphate.definition: An inorganic phosphate (PO4^3−) or its salts/esters; an essential mineral involved in energy metabolism (ATP/ADP), bone and teeth mineralization, nucleic acid and phospholipid synthesis, and acid-base buffering; regulated by renal excretion.

dextrose.definition: The dextrorotatory enantiomer of glucose (a simple monosaccharide) that serves as a rapid energy source and is provided clinically as intravenous or oral sugar solutions (for example, 5% or 10% glucose in water).

adenine.definition: A purine nucleobase present in DNA and RNA; pairs with thymine in DNA and with uracil in RNA; a component of adenosine-containing nucleotides such as ATP, ADP, and AMP.

phenindione.definition: An oral anticoagulant of the indandione class that acts as a vitamin K antagonist, inhibiting synthesis of vitamin K–dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X to prevent thrombosis (historically used; now rarely used).

splint.definition: A rigid or flexible device applied to an injured or unstable body part to immobilize, support, and protect it to promote healing; commonly used temporarily for fractures or sprains.

insipidus.definition: A disorder of water balance caused by deficiency of or resistance to antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin), resulting in excessive urine production and increased thirst with very dilute urine.

nephrogenic.definition: Relating to the kidney; arising in or produced by the kidney.

rheumatic.definition: Relating to rheumatism; affecting the joints or connective tissues, typically with inflammation and pain.

myxedema.definition: A nonpitting edema due to accumulation of glycosaminoglycans (mucin) in the dermis and other tissues, seen in severe hypothyroidism; may progress to myxedema coma.

mononucleosis.definition: An infectious illness caused primarily by Epstein-Barr virus and transmitted via saliva, presenting with fever, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes, fatigue, and often splenomegaly. It is typically self-limited; diagnosis is supported by heterophile antibody tests; treatment is supportive (rest, fluids, analgesics).

biliary.definition: Relating to bile or the biliary tract, including the bile ducts and gallbladder.

viruses.definition: A virus is a small infectious agent that replicates only inside living cells of a host; it contains nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) enclosed in a protein coat, and sometimes a lipid envelope; viruses lack independent metabolism and are obligate intracellular parasites that hijack host cell machinery to reproduce.

titer.definition: A blood test that finds how much of a substance, like an immunization, remains in your body.

codon.definition: A sequence of three nucleotides in messenger RNA that specifies a particular amino acid or a stop signal during translation of proteins.

anticodon.definition: A sequence of three nucleotides on a transfer RNA (tRNA) molecule that is complementary to a specific codon on messenger RNA (mRNA), enabling the proper amino acid to be incorporated into a polypeptide during translation.

antigenic.definition: Relating to an antigen; capable of triggering an immune response or being recognized by antibodies or T cells due to specific antigenic determinants (epitopes).

tumor.definition: A growth or lump in your body. It may be cancer, but it also may not be cancer.

antiemetic.definition: A drug that prevents nausea and vomiting.

chlorpromazine.definition: A phenothiazine-class typical antipsychotic used to treat schizophrenia and other psychoses; it acts as a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist in the CNS and has antiemetic and sedative properties. Common adverse effects include extrapyramidal symptoms, sedation, orthostatic hypotension, and anticholinergic effects.

phenothiazine.definition: A class of heterocyclic, tricyclic compounds used as antipsychotic and antiemetic drugs; classic agents (e.g., chlorpromazine, promethazine) act mainly as dopamine D2 receptor antagonists in the CNS.

antihistamine.definition: Medications that treat allergies and reduce symptoms such as sneezing and itching by blocking histamine, the substance in the body which causes these symptoms.

dolasetron.definition: A selective serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonist antiemetic used to prevent nausea and vomiting, especially associated with chemotherapy or surgery; administered orally or intravenously; can cause QT interval prolongation and torsades de pointes, so use is cautioned in patients with prolonged QT or on QT-prolonging drugs.

dronabinol.definition: A synthetic form of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC); a cannabinoid receptor agonist used as an antiemetic for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting and as an appetite stimulant in AIDS-related wasting; administered orally and classified as a Schedule III controlled substance in the U.S.

antineoplastic.definition: A drug or agent that inhibits the growth of malignant cells or destroys neoplastic tissue; used in cancer chemotherapy to treat tumors.

antiestrogen.definition: A substance that inhibits the actions of estrogen by blocking estrogen receptors or reducing estrogen production.

mixed connective tissue disease.definition: A systemic autoimmune disease with overlapping features of systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis, often associated with anti-U1 RNP antibodies; common findings include Raynaud phenomenon, swollen hands, arthritis, myositis, and esophageal dysmotility.

goodpasture's disease.definition: An autoimmune disorder in which antibodies target the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes (anti-GBM antibodies), causing rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage; immunofluorescence shows linear IgG along basement membranes, and treatment includes plasmapheresis with immunosuppression (steroids and cyclophosphamide).

antigen-presenting cell.definition: Specialized white blood cells that detect harmful substances in the body and then signal other immune system defenders (known as T-cells) to mount a defense.

dendritic cell.definition: A professional antigen-presenting cell of the immune system that captures antigens in tissues, migrates to lymphoid organs, and presents peptide antigens to T cells (via MHC class II), providing co-stimulatory signals to activate naive T lymphocytes and initiate adaptive immunity.

major histocompatibility complex.definition: A cluster of highly polymorphic genes encoding cell-surface proteins that present peptide antigens to T cells, thereby directing the adaptive immune response and influencing tissue compatibility in transplantation. Class I molecules present endogenous peptides to CD8+ T cells; Class II molecules present exogenous peptides to CD4+ T cells.

hla class ii.definition: MHC class II proteins expressed on professional antigen-presenting cells that present extracellularly derived peptide antigens to CD4+ T helper cells; they are heterodimers of alpha and beta chains (e.g., HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) encoded in the HLA region on chromosome 6 and are essential for initiating CD4+ T-cell–mediated immune responses.

t cell.definition: Abbreviation for T lymphocyte, a type of white blood cell that is produced in the bone marrow and is part of the body’s immune system.

t cell receptor.definition: Membrane-bound receptor on T lymphocytes that recognizes peptide antigens presented by MHC molecules on antigen-presenting cells; typically a heterodimer of α and β chains (TCRαβ), often associated with CD3 and zeta chains to transduce activation signals upon antigen recognition (there is also a γδ TCR in a minority of T cells).

coombs' test.definition: An antiglobulin assay to detect antibodies or complement on red blood cells (direct antiglobulin test) or antibodies in serum against red cell antigens (indirect antiglobulin test); used to diagnose autoimmune hemolytic anemia, transfusion reactions, and hemolytic disease of the newborn, and to screen for blood compatibility in pregnancy or before transfusion.

antiglobulin test.definition: A laboratory test used to detect antibodies or complement bound to red blood cells; the direct antiglobulin test detects in vivo coating of RBCs by antibodies or complement, while the indirect antiglobulin test detects antibodies in patient serum by their ability to bind to red blood cell antigens in vitro.

antiglobulin serum.definition: A serum containing anti-human globulin antibodies (e.g., anti-IgG and/or anti-C3) used in the Coombs antiglobulin test to detect antibodies or complement bound to red blood cells.

anti-hu antibody.definition: An autoimmune antibody directed against neuronal Hu (ELAVL) RNA-binding proteins, associated with paraneoplastic neurologic syndromes (ANNA-1), most often presenting with sensory neuronopathy or encephalomyelitis and commonly linked to small cell lung carcinoma.

antihemophilic factor.definition: A coagulation factor (factor VIII) that acts as a cofactor for factor IXa to activate factor X in the intrinsic pathway of coagulation; deficiency causes hemophilia A; circulates in plasma bound to von Willebrand factor.

factor viii.definition: A plasma coagulation protein that serves as a cofactor for activated factor IX in the intrinsic pathway to activate factor X; it circulates bound to von Willebrand factor; deficiency causes hemophilia A; replacement therapy is available (recombinant or plasma-derived).

hemophilia a.definition: An X-linked inherited bleeding disorder caused by deficiency of coagulation factor VIII, leading to prolonged bleeding and spontaneous hemorrhages; treated with factor VIII replacement and, in some mild cases, desmopressin (DDAVP).

antihypercholesterolemic.definition: Describes a substance or intervention that lowers elevated cholesterol levels in the blood, especially reducing LDL cholesterol (e.g., statins, bile acid sequestrants, PCSK9 inhibitors).

antihyperglycemic.definition: A drug or agent that lowers elevated blood glucose levels, used in the treatment or management of hyperglycemia and diabetes.

antihyperkalemic.definition: A medication or intervention that lowers serum potassium or prevents its rise, used to treat or prevent hyperkalemia.

antihyperlipidemic.definition: A drug or agent that lowers lipid levels (cholesterol and triglycerides) in the blood to treat hyperlipidemia and reduce cardiovascular risk.

antihypertensive.definition: A medication or agent that lowers blood pressure, used to treat hypertension. Classes include diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers, alpha-blockers, and other vasodilators.

angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors.definition: A class of medications that inhibit the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), decreasing angiotensin II and aldosterone levels, leading to vasodilation and lower blood pressure; used to treat hypertension and heart failure and to protect renal function in diabetes.

angiotensin receptor blockers.definition: A class of antihypertensive medications that selectively block the angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptor, inhibiting angiotensin II–mediated vasoconstriction and aldosterone release, which lowers blood pressure and reduces fluid retention. Used to treat hypertension, heart failure, and diabetic nephropathy; examples include losartan, valsartan, and olmesartan.

carotid sinus.definition: A dilation at the bifurcation of the common carotid artery in the neck that contains baroreceptors (stretch receptors) detecting blood pressure and helping regulate heart rate and vascular tone via the carotid sinus reflex.

antiglaucoma.definition: A drug or agent used to treat glaucoma, typically by lowering intraocular pressure to prevent optic nerve damage; includes prostaglandin analogs, beta-blockers, alpha-adrenergic agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, and cholinergic agents.

antiglomerular basement membrane antibod.definition: Autoantibodies directed against the glomerular basement membrane, most commonly IgG antibodies against the NC1 domain of type IV collagen (α3 chain), causing rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and often with pulmonary hemorrhage (Goodpasture syndrome).

antifungal.definition: A substance or drug that inhibits the growth of fungi or kills them, used to treat fungal infections.

ketoconazole.definition: An azole antifungal that inhibits fungal ergosterol synthesis by blocking lanosterol 14α-demethylase; used topically for dermatophytoses, candidiasis, and seborrheic dermatitis, with oral use limited due to risk of hepatotoxicity and drug interactions.

griseofulvin.definition: A systemic antifungal medication (fungistatic) derived from Penicillium griseofulvum that inhibits fungal mitosis by binding to microtubules; used primarily to treat dermatophyte infections of the skin, hair, and nails (e.g., tinea capitis, tinea corporis, onychomycosis).

miconazole nitrate.definition: A topical azole antifungal agent used to treat fungal infections of the skin and mucous membranes (e.g., dermatophyte infections and candidiasis); it inhibits fungal cytochrome P450–dependent 14-α-demethylase, blocking ergosterol synthesis and disrupting fungal cell membranes.

nystatin.definition: A polyene antifungal antibiotic used to treat Candida infections; it binds to ergosterol in fungal cell membranes, forming pores and increasing membrane permeability, leading to fungal cell death.

dermatophytes.definition: A group of keratinophilic fungi that cause superficial infections of keratinized tissues such as skin, hair, and nails; they feed on keratin and include the genera Trichophyton, Microsporum, and Epidermophyton.

yeast.definition: A unicellular fungus that reproduces by budding or fission; yeasts include Saccharomyces species used in baking and brewing and Candida species that can cause opportunistic infections in humans.

antimycotic.definition: An antifungal drug; a substance that inhibits the growth of fungi or destroys them, used to treat fungal infections.

oat cell carcinoma.definition: A highly malignant neuroendocrine tumor of the lung, also known as small cell lung carcinoma; characterized by small cells with scant cytoplasm, high mitotic rate, rapid growth, and early metastasis, often smoking-related and treated primarily with chemotherapy and radiotherapy; prognosis is poor.

sarcoma.definition: A cancer that arises in the soft tissues of the body that connect, support, and separate other tissues or organs. These tumors can occur almost anywhere in the body.

neuroblastoma.definition: A malignant tumor of immature nerve cells (neuroblasts) arising from neural crest–derived cells of the sympathetic nervous system, most often in the adrenal medulla or along the sympathetic chain, and is the most common extracranial solid tumor in children.

breast cancer.definition: A malignant tumor that originates in breast tissue, most often from ductal or lobular cells, characterized by uncontrolled proliferation of abnormal cells that can invade surrounding tissue and metastasize to distant sites.

hemolytic disease of the newborn.definition: A condition in which maternal antibodies directed against fetal red blood cell antigens cross the placenta and destroy fetal red cells, causing fetal or neonatal anemia and hyperbilirubinemia; most commonly due to Rh incompatibility (Rh-negative mother with an Rh-positive fetus), with ABO and other antigen incompatibilities also contributing.

antigenuria.definition: Presence of a specific antigen in urine, detected by immunoassay, used as a diagnostic marker for certain infections or conditions.

antigenic drift.definition: A gradual accumulation of point mutations in a pathogen's surface antigens (e.g., influenza hemagglutinin/neuraminidase) that alters epitopes, reducing recognition by preexisting antibodies and enabling immune escape, contributing to seasonal epidemics.

antigenic shift.definition: A major genetic reassortment of the segmented influenza A genome that creates a new combination of surface antigens (typically hemagglutinin and/or neuraminidase), often resulting in an immune-escape virus and potential pandemic outbreaks.

epitope.definition: The specific part of an antigen that is recognized by an immune receptor (such as an antibody or a T-cell receptor), triggering an immune response. Epitopes may be linear (continuous sequence) or conformational (formed by protein folding).

antigenic determinant.definition: A site or region on an antigen that is specifically recognized and bound by an antibody or a T‑cell receptor; also called an epitope. An antigen may have multiple determinants, which can be linear or conformational.

immunoglobulin g.definition: An antibody isotype that makes up the majority of serum immunoglobulins; produced by plasma cells after B‑cell activation; exists as a monomer; mediates pathogen neutralization and opsonization, activates the classical complement pathway, and can cross the placenta to provide passive fetal immunity; has four subclasses (IgG1–IgG4).

antihypoglycemic.definition: An agent that prevents or treats hypoglycemia by raising blood glucose levels, such as glucagon or epinephrine.

antimyasthenic.definition: A drug that improves muscle weakness in myasthenia gravis by increasing acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, usually by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase (e.g., pyridostigmine or neostigmine).

antihypotensive.definition: An agent or treatment that raises and maintains blood pressure, used to prevent or correct hypotension (low blood pressure).

antiimmune.definition: Relating to suppression or inhibition of the immune response; describing agents or conditions that reduce immune activity or impair host defenses. Not a standard medical term; immunosuppressants or immune evasion are generally used instead.

antiinfection.definition: An intervention or agent that prevents or reduces infection by inhibiting, neutralizing, or eliminating pathogens (for example, vaccines, antiseptics, aseptic techniques, and prophylactic antimicrobials).
