lichen planus.definition: A chronic inflammatory disease of the skin and mucous membranes of unknown etiology, characterized by pruritic, violaceous, flat-topped polygonal papules and plaques, often with Wickham striae on mucous membranes; commonly involves the wrists, forearms, ankles, and oral mucosa; treatment typically starts with topical corticosteroids.

atabrine.definition: Brand name for quinacrine, an older acridine-based antimalarial drug used historically to treat malaria; it intercalates parasite DNA and inhibits replication; notable adverse effects include yellowing of the skin and sclera, along with gastrointestinal and neuropsychiatric symptoms, and it is now rarely used due to safety concerns and resistance.

hydrochloride.definition: A chemical salt formed when a basic compound (usually an amine) is protonated by hydrochloric acid; the resulting salt contains a positively charged cation and a chloride counterion, commonly used to improve water solubility and bioavailability of pharmaceutical agents.

bismuth stomatitis.definition: A mucosal inflammatory reaction of the oral cavity caused by exposure to bismuth salts (most often from long-term use of bismuth‑containing medications), characterized by irritation and erythema of the oral mucosa, sometimes ulceration, and typically resolving after discontinuation of the offending agent.

ataractic.definition: A drug or agent that relieves anxiety and emotional tension, producing calmness without significant psychomotor impairment; an anxiolytic tranquilizer used in older pharmacology contexts.

atarax.definition: Hydroxyzine; a first-generation antihistamine with sedative and anxiolytic properties used to treat anxiety and tension, pruritus (itching), and as an antiemetic or premedication for sedation.

hydroxyzine.definition: A first-generation antihistamine (H1 receptor antagonist) used to relieve itching due to allergic reactions, to treat anxiety and provide sedation, and as an antiemetic in certain settings.

ataraxia.definition: A state of serene calmness and freedom from anxiety or emotional disturbance; imperturbability.

atavism.definition: Reappearance in an organism of ancestral traits that were present in distant evolutionary ancestors but not in recent generations; typically due to reactivation of ancient developmental pathways.

atavistic.definition: Relating to atavism; the reappearance of ancestral traits in an individual, often due to reexpression of dormant genes from distant ancestors or a reversion to a more primitive developmental pattern.

ataxia.definition: Being unable to control movement; symptoms include shaking and an unsteady walk.

ataxiaphasia.definition: A language disturbance associated with cerebellar ataxia, characterized by dysprosodic, poorly coordinated speech with possible word-finding and grammatical difficulties, reflecting cerebellar involvement in language production rather than a primary cortical aphasia. The term is uncommon and may be considered part of cerebellar cognitive involvement rather than a distinct aphasia.

telangiectasia.definition: Dilation of small blood vessels (primarily capillaries and venules) in the skin or mucous membranes, producing visible fine red to purple lines or patches that may blanch with pressure.

louis-bar syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder caused by ATM gene mutations, characterized by progressive cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasias, immunodeficiency with recurrent infections, hypersensitivity to ionizing radiation, and elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein.

ataxic.definition: Relating to ataxia; lacking voluntary coordination of muscle movements, resulting in an unsteady, clumsy gait and impaired limb coordination.

ataxic aphasia.definition: Historically used to describe a language disturbance caused by cerebellar dysfunction, featuring ataxic, poorly coordinated speech with irregular prosody and articulatory inaccuracy; language content and comprehension are relatively preserved, and it is not considered a distinct modern aphasia syndrome—more accurately viewed as cerebellar dysarthria or apraxia of speech.

biot's respiration.definition: An irregular respiratory pattern consisting of groups of quick, shallow breaths followed by periods of apnea, with an unpredictable rhythm typically due to brainstem (medullary) injury or increased intracranial pressure.

ataxic breathing.definition: An irregular, unpredictable pattern of breathing with varying depth and rate and irregular pauses or periods of apnea, caused by dysfunction of the brainstem respiratory centers (medullary), typically indicating severe neurological injury and poor prognosis.

ataxic dysarthria.definition: A motor speech disorder caused by cerebellar dysfunction, characterized by imprecise consonants and vowels, irregular articulatory breakdowns, abnormal prosody with excessive and uneven stress, and a slowed or variable speech rate (often with scanning speech).

dysarthria.definition: When you have difficulty speaking because your muscles don't work well. Also called slurred speech.

ataxic gait.definition: An unsteady, wide-based gait due to cerebellar dysfunction or impaired proprioception, characterized by irregular steps, staggering, veering, and incoordination of the limbs (often with dysmetria and intended tremor).

ataxic speech.definition: A type of dysarthria due to cerebellar dysfunction, marked by irregular speech timing and rate, scanning speech, imprecise consonants, and abnormal prosody.

atazanavir.definition: An oral protease inhibitor used in combination antiretroviral therapy for HIV-1 infection; it inhibits HIV-1 protease, preventing maturation of viral particles and is commonly boosted with ritonavir.

stevens-johnson syndrome.definition: A rare, life-threatening mucocutaneous hypersensitivity reaction, usually triggered by medications or infections, characterized by fever, rapid onset of widespread painful skin lesions with epidermal detachment and mucous membrane involvement; requires prompt withdrawal of the offending agent and intensive medical care.

antithymocyte globulin.definition: An animal-derived polyclonal antibody preparation (often horse- or rabbit-derived) that targets human T lymphocytes to deplete them and suppress the immune response, primarily used as induction therapy or treatment for organ transplant rejection and, in some regimens, for aplastic anemia.

athereogenesis.definition: The development of atherosclerotic plaques in arteries, driven by endothelial dysfunction, lipid accumulation, inflammatory cell recruitment, and smooth muscle proliferation.

atherogenic.definition: Capable of promoting the formation of atherosclerotic plaques in arteries; refers to factors, lipoproteins, or processes that increase arterial lipid deposition and inflammation leading to atherosclerosis.

atheroma.definition: An abnormal build-up of fatty plaque inside an artery.

atheromatosis.definition: A degenerative process of medium- and large arteries characterized by the development of lipid-rich plaques within the intima, causing arterial narrowing (stenosis) and increasing the risk of thrombosis, embolism, and ischemia.

atheromatous.definition: Relating to or characterized by atheroma formation; consisting of or containing an atheromatous plaque associated with atherosclerosis.

atheromatous plaque.definition: A lipid-rich lesion of the arterial intima formed in atherosclerosis, composed of cholesterol-laden foam cells, extracellular lipid, a necrotic core, and a fibrous cap; it narrows the vessel lumen and may rupture, provoking thrombosis.

atherosclerotic.definition: Relating to atherosclerosis, a disease in which lipid-rich plaques accumulate in the inner lining of arteries, causing thickening, stiffening, and potential narrowing that can impair blood flow and lead to cardiovascular complications.

atherosclerotic aneurysm.definition: An aneurysm caused by atherosclerotic disease weakening the arterial wall, leading to progressive dilation—most commonly in the abdominal aorta—with potential mural thrombus and risk of rupture.

endarterectomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which the inner lining of a diseased artery is opened and the accumulated atherosclerotic plaque is removed to restore normal blood flow; commonly performed for carotid artery stenosis.

stents.definition: A stent is a small, expandable mesh tube implanted into a narrowed or blocked vessel or duct to maintain patency and restore normal flow; commonly used in coronary arteries after angioplasty and in other ducts, with variants such as bare-metal and drug-eluting stents.

bypass surgery.definition: A surgical procedure that reroutes blood flow around a blocked or damaged vessel or area to restore circulation or function; the best-known form is coronary artery bypass grafting, where grafts from another vessel are used to bypass narrowed coronary arteries.

thrombus.definition: A blood clot that stays where it has formed in your body.

endothelium.definition: The thin layer of specialized simple squamous epithelial cells lining the interior surface of blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, and the heart, forming a barrier between the blood/lymph and underlying tissues and regulating permeability, vascular tone, hemostasis, and inflammation.

cholesterol.definition: A kind of fat in your blood. Some cholesterol is useful in your body. Too much can lead to diseases such as hardening of your arteries (atherosclerosis) or coronary artery disease.

lipoprotein.definition: A combination of fat (lipid) and protein molecules bound together as packages. The combination allows fats and cholesterol to move easily through the blood.

smoking.definition: A habit of inhaling and exhaling the smoke produced by burning tobacco; contains nicotine and many toxic chemicals and is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, respiratory disease, and cancer.

head injury.definition: Trauma to the scalp, skull, or brain resulting from external mechanical force; ranges from mild concussion to severe traumatic brain injury, potentially causing neurologic impairment, loss of consciousness, or death.

cerebellar degeneration.definition: Progressive loss of neurons in the cerebellum (often Purkinje cells) leading to impaired coordination and balance, with features such as ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, and a wide-based gait.

cerebellar.definition: Relating to the cerebellum, the brain structure at the back of the brain involved in coordinating movement, balance, and motor learning.

bulbar conjunctiva.definition: The bulbar conjunctiva is the portion of the conjunctiva that covers the visible anterior sclera (the white of the eye) from the limbus to the edge of the cornea; it is a mucous membrane that is loosely attached and highly vascular, continuous with the palpebral conjunctiva.

autosomal-recessive.definition: An inheritance pattern in which a trait or disorder is caused by mutations in an autosomal gene and is expressed only when two pathogenic variants (one from each parent) are present; carriers with a single mutated copy are typically asymptomatic, affected individuals often have unaffected carrier parents, and males and females are equally affected, with about a 25% recurrence risk for each pregnancy when both parents are carriers.

thiamine.definition: An essential water-soluble B vitamin (B1) that serves as a cofactor for enzymes in carbohydrate metabolism. Deficiency causes beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome; dietary sources include fortified cereals, whole grains, pork, legumes, and yeast.

athiaminosis.definition: A deficiency of thiamine (vitamin B1) in the body, which can lead to beriberi and, in severe cases or with chronic alcoholism, Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome.

beriberi.definition: A nervous system or heart disorder caused by lack of the vitamin thiamine (B1).

athlete's heart.definition: Physiologic cardiac adaptation to sustained intensive training, characterized by benign enlargement of the heart (often increased left ventricular end-diastolic dimension and sometimes mild LV wall thickening) with preserved or enhanced systolic and diastolic function and resting bradycardia; asymptomatic and nonpathologic, distinguishing it from cardiomyopathy by lack of adverse remodeling.

athletic heart syndrome.definition: A physiologic cardiac remodeling seen in endurance-trained athletes, characterized by enlargement of the cardiac chambers (especially the left ventricle) and mild increases in wall thickness with preserved systolic function and often resting bradycardia; a benign adaptation that can resemble cardiomyopathy on ECG or imaging.

athletic habitus.definition: A descriptive body type characterized by well-developed skeletal muscles and low to moderate body fat, producing a lean, muscular physique typical of athletes; not a pathological condition.

athlete's foot.definition: A common fungal infection of the skin of the feet (tinea pedis), usually due to dermatophyte fungi such as Trichophyton rubrum, characterized by itching, burning, and scaling, especially between the toes; treated with topical antifungal agents and good foot hygiene.

tinea pedis.definition: A fungal infection of the skin of the feet (often between the toes) caused by dermatophyte fungi, presenting with itching, scaling, and sometimes fissures; may involve the soles and nails; also known as athlete’s foot.

atlantal.definition: Relating to the atlas, the first cervical vertebra (C1) of the spine.

atlantoaxial.definition: Relating to the atlas (C1) and axis (C2) vertebrae, especially the joint between them that enables head rotation.

atlantooccipital joint.definition: A pair of synovial condyloid joints between the atlas (C1) and the occipital condyles, permitting mainly flexion–extension (nodding) of the head with limited lateral flexion and minimal rotation; stabilized by ligaments such as the anterior and posterior atlantooccipital membranes.

occipital.definition: Relating to the back of the head or the posterior part of the skull; also used to describe structures in the posterior brain region involved in vision.

joint.definition: Where 2 or more bones come together, like your shoulder or ankle.

atls.definition: A structured, evidence-based course and protocol for the initial assessment and management of trauma patients, emphasizing a rapid primary survey (airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure), prompt resuscitation, a systematic secondary survey, and planned definitive care; developed to standardize trauma care and improve outcomes.

advanced trauma life support.definition: An evidence-based protocol for the initial assessment and resuscitation of trauma patients, organized around a rapid primary survey (airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure) with prompt hemorrhage control and timely transfer to definitive care.

pleural space.definition: A potential space between the visceral pleura covering the lungs and the parietal pleura lining the chest wall; normally contains a small amount of lubricating pleural fluid and maintains negative pressure to keep the lungs expanded; can accumulate air or fluid in disease (pneumothorax or pleural effusion).

mediastinal shift.definition: Mediastinal shift is the displacement of the mediastinal structures (heart, trachea, and great vessels) away from the midline on imaging, usually due to unilateral volume loss or increased intrathoracic pressure such as tension pneumothorax, large pleural effusion, or lobar collapse.

mediastinal.definition: Relating to the mediastinum, the central compartment of the thoracic cavity between the lungs that contains the heart, great vessels, trachea, esophagus, thymus, and other structures.

fluoroscopy.definition: An imaging modality that uses a continuous or pulsed X-ray beam and an image receptor to produce real-time, moving images of internal structures, allowing visualization of motion and the flow of contrast through body regions.

atopic.definition: Having an inherited predisposition to allergies.

atresia.definition: An absence or complete closure of a normally open hollow organ or passage (often congenital), leading to obstruction.

dermatitis.definition: When your skin swells and is itchy. Also called eczema.

eczema.definition: When your skin swells and is itchy. Also called dermatitis.

herpes.definition: A viral infection caused by herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 (HSV-1 and HSV-2), characterized by recurrent vesicular lesions on the skin or mucous membranes; HSV-1 most often affects the mouth and lips (oral herpes), while HSV-2 most often affects the genital area (genital herpes).

simplex.definition: A herpesvirus; specifically, a double-stranded DNA enveloped virus of the genus Simplexvirus (e.g., HSV-1 and HSV-2) that causes herpes simplex infections such as oral and genital herpes and can establish lifelong latency with episodic reactivation.

ichthyosis.definition: A group of inherited skin disorders characterized by defective keratinization, leading to dry, thick, scaly skin with a fish-scale appearance.

cheilitis.definition: Inflammation of the lips, causing redness, swelling, cracking, and crusting; can be acute or chronic and results from irritation, infection (e.g., herpes simplex, candidiasis), nutritional deficiencies, contact dermatitis, or sun exposure (actinic cheilitis).

papule.definition: A firm raised spot on your skin.

antipruritic.definition: Relieving or preventing itching; a medication or agent used to relieve pruritus.

pimecrolimus.definition: A topical calcineurin inhibitor used to treat mild-to-moderate atopic dermatitis; a macrolide immunosuppressant that binds FKBP12 to inhibit calcineurin, reducing T-cell activation and cytokine production.

tacrolimus.definition: A macrolide immunosuppressant calcineurin inhibitor used to prevent organ transplant rejection; inhibits T-lymphocyte activation by binding FKBP12 and blocking calcineurin signaling, leading to reduced IL-2 production. Available systemically and as a topical formulation.

atorvastatin.definition: A statin medication that inhibits hepatic HMG-CoA reductase, lowering LDL cholesterol and triglycerides (and modestly raising HDL), used to reduce cardiovascular risk in adults.

atovaquone.definition: An antiparasitic agent (a hydroxy-naphthoquinone) that inhibits mitochondrial electron transport in susceptible organisms, used to prevent or treat Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, babesiosis, and malaria.

clofibrate.definition: An older fibric acid derivative used as a hypolipidemic agent; it is a prodrug hydrolyzed to clofibric acid, which activates PPAR-α to reduce hepatic VLDL production and increase fatty acid oxidation, lowering triglycerides and modestly increasing HDL. Its use is limited by safety concerns such as hepatotoxicity and gallstone formation.

atromid.definition: An older lipid-lowering drug (clofibrate), a fibric acid derivative used to treat hyperlipidemia by lowering triglycerides and modestly raising HDL; it activates PPAR-α and is largely replaced by statins due to safety concerns.

pneumocystis.definition: A genus of fungi (obligate intracellular yeasts) that includes Pneumocystis jirovecii, the human pathogen causing Pneumocystis pneumonia in immunocompromised individuals; previously classified as a protozoan.

hemosiderosis.definition: Hemosiderosis is the deposition of hemosiderin, an iron-containing pigment, in body tissues due to excess iron from repeated bleeding, increased iron absorption, or transfusion; it is often asymptomatic but can lead to organ dysfunction with prolonged iron accumulation.

pernicious.definition: Having a harmful effect, especially in a gradual or subtle way.

glossitis.definition: Inflammation of the tongue, causing swelling, redness, pain, and often altered taste; it can result from infections, nutritional deficiencies (iron, vitamin B12, folate), irritation or trauma, allergies, or systemic diseases.

atrophic.definition: Relating to or characterized by atrophy; describing tissue that has wasted away, resulting in decreased size and function of an organ or structure.

flutter.definition: Rapid, regular atrial contractions caused by a reentrant circuit in the atria, typically at 250–350 beats per minute, producing a sawtooth pattern on ECG and often resulting in a rapid ventricular rate via AV conduction.

myxoma.definition: A benign tumor composed of spindle- or stellate-shaped mesenchymal cells embedded in an abundant myxoid (mucinous) extracellular matrix; most commonly arises in the heart but can occur in other tissues.

anp.definition: A peptide hormone produced by atrial cardiomyocytes that promotes natriuresis and diuresis, reduces plasma volume and blood pressure, and is released in response to atrial stretch; it operates via cGMP signaling to oppose the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system.

natriuretic.definition: Promoting the excretion of sodium in the urine (natriuresis); agents or hormones that increase sodium and water loss, such as atrial or brain natriuretic peptides that help regulate fluid and electrolyte balance.

peptide.definition: A molecule consisting of two or more amino acids connected by covalent peptide bonds; typically shorter than a protein and usually defined as 2–50 amino acids in length.

septum.definition: A wall or other structure that divides one cavity from another. For example, in the heart the muscular septum separates the right side of the heart from the left side.

atrium.definition: One of the heart's two upper chambers (the plural form is atria). The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body; the left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs.

node.definition: A small swelling or lump in tissue; most often refers to a lymph node, a bean-shaped organ of the lymphatic system that filters lymph and helps mount an immune response.

block.definition: An obstruction that prevents normal flow through a body channel (such as a blood vessel, airway, or duct) or a disturbance in electrical conduction in the heart (as in heart block).

echocardiogram.definition: A noninvasive ultrasound imaging test of the heart that produces real-time images to evaluate cardiac structure and function, including chamber size, wall motion, valve function, and blood flow (often with Doppler); can be transthoracic or transesophageal.

endocardial.definition: Relating to the endocardium, the innermost lining of the heart chambers and the heart valves.

cushion.definition: A soft pad or padding used to distribute pressure and reduce friction, protecting tissues and providing comfort in seating, footwear, or medical devices.

mitral.definition: Relating to the mitral valve of the heart, the valve between the left atrium and left ventricle.

bicuspid.definition: Having two cusps or leaflets; used to describe a valve with two flaps (such as the mitral/bicuspid valve of the heart) or a tooth with two cusps (premolar).

tricuspid.definition: Having three cusps; relating to the tricuspid valve, the three-cusped heart valve between the right atrium and right ventricle.

his.definition: An essential amino acid with an imidazole-containing side chain; positively charged at physiological pH and capable of acting as a proton donor/acceptor in enzyme active sites. It is a dietary essential for infants and is considered conditionally essential in adults; serves as a precursor for histamine and must be obtained from protein-containing foods.

purkinje.definition:
- Large neurons in the cerebellar cortex with extensive dendritic arbors, essential for coordinating movement.
- Specialized conducting fibers in the ventricles that rapidly propagate electrical impulses from the AV node to the ventricular myocardium, coordinating ventricular contraction.

sinoatrial.definition: Relating to the sinoatrial node, the heart’s natural pacemaker that initiates electrical impulses to set the heart rate.

abiotrophy.definition: A degenerative condition in which a tissue or organ loses cells prematurely due to a primary defect within the tissue’s own cells (often hereditary), so the tissue develops normally but then undergoes degeneration and dysfunction without an external injurious cause.

hyoscyamine.definition: An antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) alkaloid used as a GI smooth‑muscle antispasmodic and to reduce secretions. It blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, decreasing GI motility and cramps; derived from plants such as Datura and Belladonna. Common uses include relief of GI cramps and irritable bowel syndrome; adverse effects include dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, and tachycardia.

detrusor.definition: Smooth muscle layer of the urinary bladder wall that contracts to expel urine during micturition; relaxation allows urine storage.

uvea.definition: The pigmented, highly vascular middle coat of the eye, comprising the iris, ciliary body, and choroid; it lies between the sclera and retina and supplies blood to the eye’s internal structures.

eye pain.definition: Subjective sensation of discomfort, pain, or aching in the eye or adnexa, caused by ocular surface disease, intraocular pathology, trauma, or referred pain; may be accompanied by redness, tearing, photophobia, or vision changes.

dry mouth.definition: When your mouth feels dry for a long time. Also called xerostomia.

liver dysfunction.definition: An impairment of liver function in which the liver cannot adequately perform its normal metabolic, synthetic, detoxifying, and excretory roles, often indicated by abnormal liver tests (e.g., elevated transaminases, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase), coagulopathy, hypoalbuminemia, jaundice, or hepatic encephalopathy, arising from liver disease, toxin/drug injury, ischemia, or systemic illness.

attenuvax.definition: A vaccine containing a live, attenuated (weakened) form of a pathogen that stimulates an immune response without causing illness, often providing long-lasting immunity.

mycobacteria.definition: A genus of aerobic, acid-fast, rod-shaped bacteria with a waxy, lipid-rich cell wall containing mycolic acids; typically slow-growing and often intracellular; includes pathogens causing tuberculosis and leprosy, as well as numerous non-tuberculous species that cause a range of pulmonary and extrapulmonary infections.

nontuberculosis.definition: Not tuberculosis; relating to diseases or infections not caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, including infections caused by nontuberculous mycobacteria.

mycoplasma.definition: A genus of very small, cell-wall–deficient bacteria (Mollicutes) that require cholesterol for their membranes and cause various human infections, including respiratory disease (Mycoplasma pneumoniae) and urethritis (Mycoplasma genitalium).

pneumoniae.definition: A Latin genitive form meaning “of pneumonia”; used in biological nomenclature as the species epithet (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae).

somatoform.definition: Relating to disorders in which one or more physical symptoms cannot be fully explained by a medical condition after evaluation and are thought to be influenced by psychological factors; historically called somatoform disorders and now largely classified as somatic symptom and related disorders.

attenuation.definition: Reduction in the strength or intensity of a signal or beam as it passes through a medium; in radiology, the loss of X-ray beam intensity due to absorption and scattering by tissues, and in vaccinology, a weakened form of a pathogen used in vaccines.

epithelium.definition: A membranous tissue that lines body surfaces, cavities, and ducts and forms glands; composed of tightly joined cells with minimal extracellular matrix, often avascular, and primarily functions in protection, absorption, filtration, secretion, and sensation.

epitympanic.definition: Relating to the epitympanum (epitympanic recess): the attic or upper portion of the middle ear cavity above the tympanic membrane, containing the heads of the malleus and incus and communicating with the mastoid antrum.

attachment.definition: The anatomical site where a structure connects to another, such as where a muscle originates from or inserts on bone.

antithrombin.definition: A serine protease inhibitor (serpin) produced by the liver that inactivates thrombin (IIa) and factor Xa, thereby regulating the coagulation cascade; its anticoagulant action is markedly enhanced by heparin; deficiency or dysfunction predisposes to thrombosis.

cycloplegic.definition: Relating to cycloplegia; a drug that paralyzes the ciliary muscle, causing loss of accommodation and pupil dilation, used in ophthalmology for refraction and retinal examination.

refraction.definition: The deflection of light as it passes through one medium to another of different density; also refers an eye test to evaluate the eye’s ability to focus.

dilation.definition: The enlargement or widening of a hollow organ, duct, or body opening; can occur physiologically (such as the pupil widening) or be produced for medical purposes.

virus.definition: Germs or "bugs" that grow in your body and can make you sick.

auditory amnesia.definition: An informal term for impairment of auditory memory—the inability to encode, store, or retrieve memories of sounds, spoken language, or music—often due to brain injury or disease affecting memory networks (e.g., temporal lobe/hippocampus).

audiology.definition: A branch of science and medicine focused on hearing and balance, including the assessment, diagnosis, and management of hearing and balance disorders.

audiogram.definition: A chart that shows a person’s ability to hear at different pitches or frequencies.

audiometer.definition: A device used in audiology to present calibrated sounds and speech at controlled frequencies and intensities in order to determine a person’s hearing thresholds and overall auditory sensitivity.

audiometrist.definition: A professional who performs audiometric testing (hearing tests) using an audiometer to measure hearing thresholds and assist in diagnosing hearing loss and fitting hearing aids, typically working under supervision of an audiologist.

audiovisual.definition: Relating to both hearing and sight; involving or using both sound and image, commonly used to describe media, aids, or devices that combine audio and visual components.

auditory.definition: Relating to the sense of hearing or to the ear; pertaining to the auditory system.

auditory cortex.definition: Region of the cerebral cortex in the temporal lobe that processes auditory information; it includes the primary auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus) and surrounding auditory areas, receiving input from the thalamus (medial geniculate nucleus) and analyzing basic sound features (frequency, timing) as well as higher‑order aspects such as speech and music.

auditory nerve.definition: A nerve in the inner ear that transmits information about sound to the brain.

audiologist.definition: A health professional who assesses hearing and fits hearing aids.

organ of corti.definition: An organ within the cochlea of the inner ear containing inner and outer hair cells on the basilar membrane that transduce mechanical vibrations from sound into neural impulses, enabling hearing; located beneath the tectorial membrane.

spiral organ of corti.definition: A sensory organ of hearing located in the cochlea; contains inner and outer hair cells on the basilar membrane that transduce mechanical sound vibrations into neural impulses, which are conveyed to the brain via the cochlear (spiral) nerve.

hair cell.definition: A mechanosensory receptor cell of the inner ear that converts mechanical stimuli (sound vibrations in the cochlea and head movements in the vestibular system) into neural signals. Hair cells have apical stereocilia that bend in response to fluid motion, opening ion channels to generate receptor potentials and release neurotransmitter to afferent neurons; there are inner hair cells (primarily for auditory transduction) and outer hair cells (involved in amplification and tuning).

cilia.definition: Small, hairlike structures on the surface of some cells.

internal auditory meatus.definition: A narrow bony canal in the petrous part of the temporal bone that extends from the posterior cranial fossa to the inner ear, transmitting the facial nerve (CN VII), vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII), and the labyrinthine artery.

mastoid.definition: A bony prominence of the temporal bone behind the ear (the mastoid process) containing air-filled mastoid air cells; used to describe structures in this region or conditions such as mastoiditis.

tympanum.definition: The eardrum; a thin, concave, semi-transparent membrane that forms the boundary between the external auditory canal and the middle ear and vibrates in response to sound to transmit mechanical energy to the auditory ossicles.

ear canal.definition: The external auditory canal is the tube that conducts sound from the outer ear to the tympanic membrane; about 2.5 cm long in adults; lined with skin containing hair and ceruminous glands; the outer one-third is cartilaginous and the inner two-thirds is bony.

eustachian tube.definition: An air-filled canal that connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx; it equalizes middle-ear pressure by periodically opening during swallowing or yawning and drains secretions from the middle ear into the nasopharynx. It is normally closed and opens transiently; it is shorter and more horizontal in children.

rinne test.definition: A simple hearing test that uses a tuning fork to determine what type of hearing loss a person has.

weber test.definition: A hearing test that uses a tuning fork to diagnose one-sided hearing loss.

ototoxic medications.definition: Ototoxic medications are drugs that can cause damage to the inner ear (cochlea and/or vestibular system), potentially resulting in hearing loss, tinnitus, and/or balance disturbances.

aminoglycerides.definition: A class of bactericidal antibiotics that irreversibly bind to the 30S ribosomal subunit, inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis and causing misreading of mRNA; primarily active against aerobic Gram-negative bacteria; commonly used for serious infections; examples include gentamicin, tobramycin, and amikacin.

diuretics.definition: A group of drugs that help the body get rid of excess fluid by increasing urine production; also known as water pills.

prematurity.definition: The birth of a baby before 37 completed weeks of gestation (premature birth).

high-noise environment.definition: An environment where noise exposure is high enough to risk hearing damage or communication impairment, typically defined by occupational exposure limits (e.g., ≥85 dB SPL averaged over 8 hours). Prolonged exposure can cause noise-induced hearing loss and tinnitus; hearing protection is recommended.

auricular forceps.definition: A small, delicate pair of forceps used in ear surgery (otology/otolaryngology) to grasp and remove tissue or foreign bodies from the external auditory canal.

auricularis anterior.definition: A small muscle of the external ear (pinna) that pulls the ear forward; one of the auricular muscles innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII).

auricularis posterior.definition: A small muscle of the external ear that retracts the pinna (auricle); one of the trio of auricular muscles, largely vestigial in humans with only slight ear movement.

auricularis superior.definition: A small, variably present intrinsic muscle of the external ear that elevates the auricle; one of the three auricular muscles (anterior, superior, posterior) that move the ear, typically innervated by the facial nerve.

auricular tachycardia.definition: A tachyarrhythmia originating from an ectopic focus or reentrant circuit in the atria (a type of supraventricular tachycardia) that produces a rapid, usually regular heart rate with abnormal P-wave morphology and typically narrow QRS complexes.

auer rods.definition: Needle- or rod-shaped, azurophilic cytoplasmic inclusions in myeloid blasts, composed of fused primary granule material; commonly seen in acute myeloid leukemia (especially acute promyelocytic leukemia) and are peroxidase-positive on cytochemical staining.

auer body.definition: Needle-shaped, eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions in myeloid blasts (myeloblasts and promyelocytes) formed from azurophilic granules; typically MPO-positive and seen in acute myeloid leukemia, especially acute promyelocytic leukemia.

acute myelogenous leukemia.definition: Malignant hematologic neoplasm of myeloid origin marked by clonal expansion of immature myeloid blasts in the bone marrow with impaired differentiation, causing bone marrow failure; defined by ≥20% blasts in marrow or blood (or certain cytogenetic abnormalities); presents with fatigue, anemia, infection, and bleeding; treated with cytotoxic chemotherapy and often stem cell transplantation.

myelomonocytic leukemia.definition: An acute myeloid leukemia subtype in which malignant cells show both myeloid and monocytic differentiation (myeloblasts and monoblasts predominate), typically designated AML-M4; patients often present with anemia, thrombocytopenia, infections, gingival hyperplasia, and possible extramedullary involvement, and treatment follows AML-type induction chemotherapy.

acid phosphatase.definition: An enzyme that hydrolyzes phosphate esters at acidic pH; a member of the phosphatase enzyme family, with notable forms such as prostate-specific acid phosphatase that has historically been used as a tumor marker for prostate cancer.

peroxidase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the oxidation of diverse substrates by transferring electrons to hydrogen peroxide, reducing H2O2 to water; most are heme-containing proteins found throughout plants, animals, and microorganisms.

esterase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of ester bonds, converting esters into an alcohol and a carboxylic acid (carboxylate); esterase activity is found in enzymes such as cholinesterases, carboxylesterases, and lipases.

chrysiasis.definition: Bluish-gray hyperpigmentation of the skin caused by deposition of gold salts in the dermis, typically a complication of long-term systemic gold therapy (e.g., aurothiomalate, auranofin) for rheumatoid arthritis; discoloration may be accentuated by sun exposure and can be permanent.

aurantiasis cutis.definition: An orange-yellow discoloration of the skin due to elevated carotenoid levels (carotenemia), usually from excessive intake of carotene-rich foods or supplements; scleral coloration is typically spared and the changes resolve with reduced carotene intake.

auranofin.definition: An oral gold(I) compound used as a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) for rheumatoid arthritis; it suppresses inflammatory immune cell activity to reduce joint inflammation.

australian antigen.definition: A hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg); a viral envelope protein of the hepatitis B virus that is detectable in the blood during acute or chronic infection and is used in screening tests for hepatitis B (e.g., blood donor screening).

hepatitis b surface antigen.definition: A surface protein of the hepatitis B virus; its presence in blood indicates active HBV infection (acute or chronic) and infectiousness, and it is used as a diagnostic and screening marker.

hbsag.definition: Hepatitis B surface antigen; a viral protein on the surface of the hepatitis B virus detectable in blood during acute or chronic HBV infection and used as a marker of active infection; persistence beyond about 6 months defines chronic hepatitis B. The HBV vaccine contains recombinant HBsAg to induce immunity.

q fever.definition: An acute zoonotic infection caused by Coxiella burnetii, transmitted primarily by inhalation of contaminated birth products from livestock; presents with sudden fever, malaise, severe headache, and may involve pneumonia or hepatitis; treated with doxycycline, with chronic endocarditis possible in rare cases.

tubercle bacillus.definition: A slender, acid-fast, obligate-aerobe bacillus of the genus Mycobacterium (primarily M. tuberculosis) that causes tuberculosis in humans; it has a lipid-rich cell wall with mycolic acids and grows slowly, often within macrophages.

frankfort horizontal plane.definition: A reference plane in cephalometrics defined by the porion (the upper border of the external auditory meatus) and orbitale (the lowest point on the orbital margin) on both sides; it is used as a horizontal standard to orient cephalometric radiographs in the natural head position.

jugular vein.definition: A large vein in the neck that drains deoxygenated blood from the head and neck and returns it to the heart via the superior vena cava; the two main branches are the internal jugular vein and the external jugular vein.

burr hole.definition: A small hole drilled through the skull using a neurosurgical burr to access the brain for procedures such as hematoma drainage, biopsy, placement of monitoring devices, or CSF drainage; it may be part of a craniotomy.

hydrocephalus.definition: A condition in which cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) accumulates abnormally within the brain’s ventricles or subarachnoid space, causing ventricular dilation and increased intracranial pressure; results from impaired CSF flow, absorption, or overproduction.

ventriculoatrial shunt.definition: A cerebrospinal fluid diversion system that drains CSF from the cerebral ventricle into the right atrium via a catheter, used to treat hydrocephalus.

auriculoventriculostomy.definition: A nonstandard or historical term referring to creating a surgical connection between the atrial auricle (left atrial appendage) and a ventricle, effectively forming an intracardiac shunt; it is not an established or routinely performed procedure.

snellen’s reflex.definition: No widely recognized medical term by this name; Snellen relates to the visual acuity chart rather than a reflex. If referring to the pupillary light reflex: pupil constricts in response to bright light; afferent input from the retina via the optic nerve, efferent output via the oculomotor nerve, with constriction in both pupils.

gyrus.definition: A raised ridge on the surface of the brain, especially on the cerebral cortex, formed by the folds (convolutions) between sulci.

lateral fissure.definition: A deep groove on the lateral surface of the cerebrum that separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes; also known as the Sylvian fissure.

superior temporal gyrus.definition: A gyrus on the lateral surface of the temporal lobe, lying above the superior temporal sulcus, containing auditory cortex and, in the dominant hemisphere, language comprehension (Wernicke’s area) located in its posterior portion.

petrous part of temporal bone.definition: The dense, pyramidal portion of the temporal bone at the skull base (pars petrosa) that encases the inner ear and forms part of the cranial base, housing the inner ear structures and openings such as the internal acoustic (auditory) meatus and carotid canal.

autism.definition: A neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across contexts, and by restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities. Symptoms typically appear in early childhood and cause impairment in functioning; it presents along a spectrum with varying degrees of severity.

infantile autism.definition: An older term for autism spectrum disorder, describing a neurodevelopmental condition with onset in early childhood, characterized by deficits in social communication and interaction, and by restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities; the label is now largely replaced by autism spectrum disorder in modern diagnostic systems.

autoantibody.definition: An antibody produced by the immune system that mistakenly targets the body's own tissues or components, often associated with autoimmune diseases.

autoantigen.definition: A self-derived molecule or structure that can be recognized as an antigen by the immune system, potentially triggering an autoimmune response when immune tolerance to it fails.

autoimmune disease.definition: A disease in which the immune system mistakenly identifies healthy tissues and organs as threats and responds by attacking and destroying them.

autoimmune thyroiditis.definition: A chronic autoimmune inflammatory disorder in which the immune system attacks the thyroid gland, causing progressive destruction of thyroid tissue and usually resulting in hypothyroidism; commonly associated with thyroid autoantibodies (e.g., anti-thyroid peroxidase) and lymphocytic infiltration.

autoimmune thrombocytopenia.definition: A disorder in which the body's immune system produces autoantibodies against platelets, causing their destruction and reduced production, leading to low platelet counts and an increased risk of bleeding.

autoimmune hemolytic anemia.definition: An autoimmune disorder in which antibodies directed against red blood cell antigens cause immune-mediated hemolysis, resulting in anemia. It can be warm-type (usually IgG) or cold-type (IgM), and may be idiopathic or associated with other autoimmune diseases, infections, drugs, or lymphoproliferative disorders.

gastric parietal cells.definition: These gastric mucosal cells, located in the fundus and body of the stomach, secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor. They possess an extensive apical canalicular system and abundant mitochondria and use a H+/K+-ATPase proton pump to acidify the lumen. Activity is stimulated by gastrin, histamine, and acetylcholine.

parietal cells.definition: Specialized gastric gland cells in the fundus and body of the stomach that secrete hydrochloric acid (HCl) via the H+/K+-ATPase proton pump and intrinsic factor, the latter essential for vitamin B12 absorption; activity is stimulated by histamine, gastrin, and acetylcholine.

antigens.definition: An abnormal substance in your body that must be fought off by antibodies.

streptococcal antigens.definition: Antigens associated with Streptococcus species that elicit an immune response; include surface components such as the M protein, capsule polysaccharides (e.g., hyaluronic acid in S. pyogenes), and Lancefield group carbohydrates, which are targets of serologic testing (e.g., anti-streptolysin O, anti-DNase B) and contribute to immune recognition and pathogenicity.

myocardial tissue.definition: Heart muscle tissue that forms the myocardium, composed of cardiomyocytes arranged to produce rhythmic, involuntary contractions that pump blood; it is a striated muscle with high mitochondrial content and intercalated discs.

lupus erythematosus.definition: A chronic autoimmune disorder in which the immune system attacks multiple body tissues, causing inflammation in the skin, joints, kidneys, and other organs; often presents as systemic disease with fatigue, fever, arthritis, malar or other rashes, and photosensitivity, and can also present in cutaneous forms such as discoid lupus.

gardner-diamond syndrome.definition: A rare disorder characterized by spontaneous, recurrent, painful ecchymoses with normal coagulation tests, typically in women and often precipitated by emotional stress; thought to involve an autoimmune sensitivity to the patient’s own erythrocytes (autoerythrocyte sensitization syndrome, psychogenic purpura).

autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes.definition: A group of rare autoimmune disorders characterized by immune-mediated destruction or dysfunction of two or more endocrine glands (commonly the adrenal, parathyroid, thyroid, and pancreas), often with additional autoimmune features outside the endocrine system; subtypes include early-onset, AIRE-related forms and later-onset variants such as those with Addison disease plus other autoimmune endocrinopathies.

autodiploid.definition: A diploid cell or organism produced by duplication of its own genome (endoreduplication/autopolyploidization) rather than by fertilization or mating with another cell.

autodiploidy.definition: The formation of a diploid genome from an originally haploid genome within the same organism, usually by duplication of the genome (endoreduplication or failed cell division), resulting in two homologous chromosome sets derived from the same species.

autoimmunization.definition: The process by which the immune system becomes reactive against the body's own tissues (autoantigens), leading to autoantibody production and autoimmune disease.

autoantitoxin.definition: Not a standard medical term. Conceptually, it would refer to an autoantibody that neutralizes a toxin—that is, an antibody directed against a toxin within the same individual.

autoactivation.definition: Self-activation of a molecule (such as an enzyme or signaling protein) without an external activator, typically by autocatalytic processing or a conformational change that yields a constitutively active form.

autoamputation.definition: Self-removal or detachment of a body part by the person, usually a limb or digit, resulting from irreversible tissue damage (e.g., gangrene, frostbite, severe infection) or in certain psychiatric conditions; it occurs without planned medical surgical intervention.

autoagglutination.definition: Spontaneous clumping of a person’s own red blood cells caused by circulating autoantibodies against erythrocyte antigens; commonly seen in autoimmune hemolytic anemia and certain infections (e.g., cold agglutinin syndrome), and may yield a positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test.

autohemagglutination.definition: Clumping of the person’s own red blood cells caused by autoantibodies against RBC antigens (typically cold agglutinins, often IgM), usually occurring at low temperatures and seen in autoimmune hemolytic anemia or certain infections.

autohemolysis.definition: Destruction of one’s own red blood cells by immune-mediated processes (commonly autoantibodies), resulting in intravascular or extravascular hemolysis.

autoerythrocyte sensitization.definition: A hypersensitivity reaction to autologous red blood cell antigens that produces recurrent, painful ecchymoses (bruising), often following minor trauma or stress; sometimes demonstrated by a positive reaction to intradermal autologous erythrocyte testing, and also known as Gardner-Diamond syndrome.

autoerythrocyte sensitization syndrome.definition: A rare psychodermatologic disorder in which recurrent, spontaneous, painful bruises (ecchymoses) appear without clear trauma, often related to emotional or psychiatric stress; the presumed mechanism is hypersensitivity to one's own erythrocytes (autoerythrocyte sensitization).

autocatheterization.definition: A procedure in which a person inserts a urinary catheter through the urethra into the bladder to drain urine, performed by the patient themselves (self-catheterization), typically used for chronic urinary retention or neurogenic bladder to achieve bladder emptying.

self-catheterization.definition: A technique in which a person inserts a catheter into their own bladder (via the urethra or a surgically created opening) to drain urine, typically performed intermittently to maintain bladder emptying and prevent urinary retention.

catheterization.definition: The insertion of a catheter (a flexible tube) into a body passage or cavity to drain fluids, obtain samples, or administer medications; urinary catheterization specifically refers to placing a catheter through the urethra into the bladder to drain urine.

urinary catheterization.definition: Insertion of a sterile catheter through the urethra (or via a suprapubic route) into the bladder to drain urine or to instill fluids; can be performed intermittently or as an indwelling catheter with a retention balloon.

autogenous graft.definition: Transplantation of tissue from one site to another site in the same person (the patient's own tissue), used to repair or replace damaged tissue; immune-compatible and does not require donor matching or immunosuppression.

autogenous vaccine.definition: A vaccine prepared from a patient’s own pathogenic organism isolated from that patient’s infection, then inactivated or attenuated and re-administered to induce an immune response specific to that organism.

autogenesis.definition: The process by which a structure, tissue, or organism originates or develops from within the organism itself, arising endogenously rather than from an external source.

autogenic therapy.definition: A relaxation technique in which a person uses self-suggestion and focused attention to induce sensations of heaviness and warmth in the limbs, promoting a regulated autonomic state and reducing stress-related symptoms (closely related to autogenic training).

autoinfection.definition: Infection that results from parasites or pathogens originating within the same host, i.e., endogenous reinfection; infectious forms develop inside the host and re-enter the host without external exposure.

autoinfusion.definition: Infusion administered by the patient themselves using a programmable infusion device, i.e., self‑administered intravenous or subcutaneous drug delivery.

autodigestion.definition: Self-digestion of tissue by its own digestive enzymes, leading to destruction of its cells; commonly described in pancreatitis when pancreatic proteases become active within the pancreas and digest pancreatic tissue.

autoinoculation.definition: The self-transfer of an infectious agent from one site on the body to another, causing infection or new lesions—often via touching, scratching, or rubbing existing lesions.

autointoxication.definition: A historical, largely discredited theory that toxins produced by gut bacteria in the intestines (often associated with constipation or bowel stagnation) are absorbed into the circulation and cause systemic symptoms.

autokeratoplasty.definition: A corneal procedure in which tissue from the patient’s own cornea is used as a graft (autograft) to replace damaged tissue, typically by relocating a portion of cornea within the same eye to improve vision and avoid donor tissue.

autokinesia.definition: Self-generated movement; movement initiated by the individual rather than by external stimuli.

autolesion.definition: Self-inflicted physical injury to one's own body, typically performed as a coping mechanism to relieve emotional distress, usually without suicidal intent.

autolet.definition: The spelling you provided does not correspond to a recognized medical term. It may be a misspelling of a related concept. For example, a self-digestion of cells and tissues by their own enzymes, often occurring after death or during tissue processing.
