bertin's column hypertrophy.definition: Thickening of the normal renal columns that separate the renal pyramids; a benign anatomic variant that can appear as prominent linear bands on imaging and may mimic a renal mass.

berylliosis.definition: A chronic occupational lung disease caused by inhalation of beryllium dust or fumes, producing granulomatous pneumonitis that often resembles sarcoidosis; diagnosis includes history of exposure and a positive beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test (BeLPT).

beta-adrenergic antagonist.definition: A class of medications that block beta-adrenergic receptors, diminishing sympathetic stimulation of the heart and other tissues; reduces heart rate, contractility, and renin release, thereby lowering blood pressure and treating conditions such as hypertension, angina, certain arrhythmias, and heart failure; nonselective agents block both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors, while cardioselective agents preferentially block beta-1 receptors.

beta-adrenergic blocking agent.definition: A drug that blocks beta-adrenergic receptors (beta-1 and/or beta-2), reducing sympathetic stimulation of the heart and other tissues; used to treat hypertension, angina, certain arrhythmias, and heart failure; can be nonselective or cardioselective.

beta-adrenergic receptor.definition: A G protein–coupled receptor for catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine) that activates adenylate cyclase via Gs to increase intracellular cAMP; subtypes β1, β2, and β3 mediate diverse sympathetic effects such as increased heart rate (β1), bronchodilation (β2), and lipolysis (β3).

beta-adrenergic stimulating agent.definition: A drug that binds to and activates beta-adrenergic receptors (β1, β2, and/or β3), producing sympathetic effects such as increased heart rate and contractility, bronchodilation, and metabolic changes; commonly referred to as a beta-adrenergic agonist.

beta-alaninemia.definition: A biochemical state with abnormally high levels of beta-alanine in the blood, usually resulting from increased dietary exposure or impaired metabolism of beta-alanine; it is not widely recognized as a distinct clinical syndrome.

beta-blocker.definition: A medication that blocks beta-adrenergic receptors (beta-1 and/or beta-2), thereby reducing heart rate, contractility, and blood pressure; used to treat hypertension, angina, certain arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, and some types of heart failure and migraine prophylaxis; nonselective agents can cause bronchospasm in asthma/COPD and may mask hypoglycemia.

beta-carotene.definition: An orange-yellow fat-soluble carotenoid pigment that acts as a provitamin A; converted in the intestine to retinol (vitamin A), supporting vision and immune function, with antioxidant properties.

beta cells.definition: Cells that make and secrete insulin; located in the islets of Langerhans of the pancreas.

betadine.definition: A topical antiseptic solution containing povidone-iodine that slowly releases iodine to kill bacteria, fungi, and some viruses on the skin; commonly used for skin cleansing and preoperative preparation of the surgical site.

betagan.definition: A brand-name ophthalmic beta-blocker (levobunolol) used as eye drops to lower intraocular pressure by decreasing aqueous humor production in open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension.

levobunolol hydrochloride.definition: A nonselective beta-adrenergic receptor blocker given as an ophthalmic solution to reduce aqueous humor production and lower intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension.

beta-fetoprotein.definition: A fetal glycoprotein produced mainly by the fetal liver and yolk sac; in adults it serves as a tumor marker for hepatocellular carcinoma and certain germ cell tumors, and in pregnancy its levels in maternal serum or amniotic fluid are used to screen for neural tube defects and chromosomal abnormalities.

maple syrup urine disease.definition: An autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by deficiency of the branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, leading to accumulation of the branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine, and valine (and their corresponding keto acids) and a characteristic maple-syrup odor in urine; presents in newborns with poor feeding, vomiting, and lethargy and can cause severe brain injury or death if untreated; managed by strict dietary restriction of branched-chain amino acids with ongoing metabolic monitoring.

berlock dermatitis.definition: A phototoxic dermatitis caused by photosensitizing compounds (notably bergapten/bergamottin) in citrus oils and perfumes; it produces erythema and subsequent hyperpigmented streaks on sun-exposed skin (commonly the neck and face) after sun exposure, resolving with avoidance of the offending product and sun protection.

iga nephropathy.definition: An immune-complex–mediated kidney disease in which IgA-containing immune complexes deposit in the glomerular mesangium, causing mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis with episodic hematuria (often after an upper respiratory infection) and variable proteinuria; diagnosis is by kidney biopsy showing mesangial IgA deposition on immunofluorescence.

berger's paresthesia.definition: An abnormal skin sensation described as tingling, pricking, burning, or numbness, typically due to nerve irritation or damage; this eponym is not widely recognized in standard medical references. If you have a specific context or source, I can refine the definition.

renal column hypertrophy.definition: Thickening of the renal columns—the cortical tissue that separates the renal medullary pyramids in the kidney.

benzthiazide.definition: A diuretic medication of the thiazide class that inhibits the Na+/Cl− cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, increasing excretion of sodium and water; used to treat hypertension and edema; adverse effects may include hypokalemia, hyponatremia, and dehydration.

benzathine penicillin g.definition: Long-acting intramuscular antibiotic form of penicillin G in which benzathine creates a slow-release depot, providing prolonged penicillin levels; used to treat syphilis and to prevent rheumatic fever after streptococcal infection.

benzoyl peroxide.definition: A topical antimicrobial and keratolytic agent used to treat acne; it releases free radicals that oxidize and kill bacteria implicated in acne (Cutibacterium acnes) and helps shed follicular keratin. Common concentrations range from 2.5% to 10%; can cause skin dryness, irritation, and bleaching of fabrics.

benzyl alcohol.definition: A colorless, aromatic primary alcohol (C6H5CH2OH) used as a solvent and preservative in pharmaceutical and cosmetic preparations; caution in neonates due to risk of gasping syndrome, and it is flammable.

17β-hydroxycorticosterone.definition: A corticosteroid produced in the adrenal cortex; the 17β-hydroxylated derivative of corticosterone that functions as an intermediate in the biosynthesis of corticosterone and aldosterone, with relatively weak glucocorticoid or mineralocorticoid activity.

beta-lactam antibiotic.definition: A class of antibiotics that contain a beta-lactam ring and kill bacteria by inhibiting cell wall synthesis, specifically by binding penicillin-binding proteins; includes penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, and monobactams, and they are often inactivated by beta-lactamases.

beta-hemolytic streptococci.definition: A group of Streptococcus bacteria that produce beta-hemolysis on blood agar, yielding clear zones around colonies due to complete lysis of red blood cells; they are Gram-positive cocci in chains and are classified by Lancefield serogroups (A, B, C, G, etc.), with notable species including S. pyogenes (group A) and S. agalactiae (group B).

glomerular.definition: Relating to the glomerulus, the tuft of capillaries in the kidney nephron where blood plasma is filtered to form the filtrate that becomes urine.

iga.definition: A major antibody class found mainly in mucosal secretions and on mucosal surfaces; it provides immune protection by neutralizing pathogens and preventing their adherence at mucosal sites; produced by plasma cells in mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue; exists in two subclasses.

mesangial.definition: Relating to the mesangium, the central part of the renal glomerulus composed of mesangial cells and extracellular matrix that provides structural support to the glomerular capillaries and participates in regulation of filtration and immune-related functions.

beta-lactamase.definition: An enzyme produced by certain bacteria that hydrolyzes the beta-lactam ring of beta-lactam antibiotics (e.g., penicillins, cephalosporins), inactivating the drug and promoting antibiotic resistance.

cephalosporinase.definition: An enzyme produced by certain bacteria that hydrolyzes the beta-lactam ring of cephalosporin antibiotics, inactivating the drug and contributing to antibiotic resistance.

beta-lactamase-resistant.definition: Describes an antibiotic that remains active in the presence of beta-lactamase enzymes, i.e., resistant to beta-lactamase–mediated hydrolysis of the beta-lactam ring.

betamethasone.definition: A potent synthetic glucocorticoid corticosteroid with anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects; used in various formulations (topical, injectable, oral, inhaled) to treat inflammatory and allergic disorders, and in obstetrics to promote fetal lung maturation in preterm birth.

dermatoses.definition: A broad term for any disease or abnormal condition of the skin; a category of skin disorders or eruptions.

bursitis.definition: Joint pain caused by swelling in a tiny sac between your bones and muscles, tendons, or skin.

infections.definition: An invasion and growth of microorganisms (bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites) in body tissues, causing tissue injury and an immune or inflammatory response; infections may be localized or systemic and vary in severity.

endocrine.definition: The glands that produce hormones that flow through the blood to other parts of the body.

neurological.definition: Relating to the nervous system, including the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves; pertaining to its structure, function, or diseases.

beta2-microglobulin.definition: A small (about 11–12 kDa) protein that forms the light chain of MHC class I molecules and is present on nearly all nucleated cells. It is released into the bloodstream, filtered by the kidneys, and degraded in the proximal tubules; serum levels rise with reduced glomerular filtration rate or increased cell turnover, making it a marker of renal function and a prognostic indicator in certain hematologic cancers (e.g., multiple myeloma).

tubule.definition: A small tube-like structure in the body; a slender, hollow passage through which fluids or other substances flow within an organ or tissue.

beta-naphthylamine.definition: An aromatic amine (the beta isomer of naphthylamine; 2-naphthylamine) that is carcinogenic to the bladder and has been used as an intermediate in dye production; exposure is associated with urothelial cancer.

beta-oxidation.definition: A catabolic process in which fatty acids are oxidized in mitochondria (and in peroxisomes for very long chains) by successive removal of two-carbon units as acetyl-CoA, with concomitant production of NADH and FADH2 that feed the electron transport chain for ATP generation.

tca.definition: A class of antidepressant medications that increase synaptic norepinephrine and serotonin by inhibiting their reuptake; they often have anticholinergic and sedating side effects and are used to treat major depressive disorder and some chronic pain conditions.

receptor.definition: A protein or cellular structure that binds a signaling molecule (ligand) or detects a stimulus and triggers a biochemical or electrical response in the cell; can be located on the cell surface or intracellularly.

propranolol.definition: A non-selective beta-adrenergic blocker (beta-blocker) used to treat hypertension, angina, certain arrhythmias, and to prevent migraines; it also helps manage essential tremor and performance anxiety by reducing heart rate, myocardial contractility, and sympathetic outflow.

beta-thalassemia.definition: A hereditary autosomal recessive hemoglobinopathy caused by mutations in the beta-globin (HBB) gene that reduce or abolish beta-globin synthesis, leading to imbalanced globin chain production and a spectrum of anemia from mild (trait/minor) to severe (beta-thalassemia major/Cooley anemia).

thalassemia.definition: A group of inherited hemoglobin disorders characterized by reduced or absent synthesis of one or more globin chains (alpha or beta), resulting in microcytic, hypochromic anemia with variable clinical severity; caused by mutations in globin genes (HBA1/HBA2 for alpha, HBB for beta).

betatron.definition: A device that uses a changing magnetic field to accelerate electrons in a circular path, functioning as a type of particle accelerator; not typically used in medical settings.

beta-wave.definition: A type of brain electrical activity seen on electroencephalography (EEG) with a frequency of roughly 13–30 Hz and relatively low amplitude, typically present during wakeful, alert, and actively thinking states; increased beta activity can be associated with anxiety or stimulant use.

beta-rhythm.definition: Fast, low-amplitude electrical brain activity in the 13–30 Hz frequency range, typically seen during wakeful, alert, and cognitively engaged states; greatest over frontal regions and reduced during relaxation, drowsiness, or sleep.

betaxolol.definition: Cardioselective beta-adrenergic receptor blocker (beta-1 selective) used primarily as an ophthalmic preparation to lower intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension by reducing aqueous humor formation; systemic absorption can produce antihypertensive effects.

betoptic.definition: A brand-name ophthalmic solution of timolol maleate; a nonselective beta-adrenergic blocker used topically to lower intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension.

bethanechol.definition: A direct-acting muscarinic agonist (parasympathomimetic) that increases smooth muscle contractility in the bladder and GI tract; used to treat nonobstructive urinary retention and postoperative ileus.

cholinergic.definition: Relating to acetylcholine, the neurotransmitter; describes neurons that release acetylcholine, receptors that bind it (nicotinic and muscarinic), or drugs and actions that mimic or enhance acetylcholine's effects.

neurogenic.definition: Of or caused by the nervous system or nerves; arising from nerve tissue or nerve injury.

atony.definition: Atony is a state of reduced or absent tone in a muscle or hollow organ, resulting in flaccidity; for example, uterine atony is the uterus failing to contract after delivery, which can cause postpartum hemorrhage.

ocular hypertension.definition: A condition defined by elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), typically above about 21 mmHg, without detectable glaucomatous optic neuropathy or visual field loss; it is a risk factor for developing glaucoma.

open-angle glaucoma.definition: A chronic, progressive optic neuropathy characterized by retinal ganglion cell death with cupping of the optic disc and gradual loss of peripheral vision; typically due to impaired drainage of aqueous humor with an open anterior chamber angle, and is the most common form of glaucoma.

parkinson’s disease.definition: A movement disorder that occurs when the brain does not produce enough of a chemical.

nephritic.definition: Relating to nephritis (inflammation of the kidney) or to nephritic syndrome; a kidney disorder typically involving inflammation with hematuria and modest proteinuria.

colitis.definition: Inflammation of the lining of the colon (large intestine), causing abdominal pain and diarrhea, sometimes with blood or mucus; causes include infection, inflammatory bowel disease, ischemia, and antibiotic-associated colitis.

nephritic syndrome.definition: An inflammatory glomerulonephritis presenting with hematuria (often with red blood cell casts), variable proteinuria (typically sub-nephrotic), edema, hypertension, and often azotemia due to impaired glomerular filtration.

bicornate uterus.definition: A congenital uterine anomaly due to incomplete fusion of the Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts, resulting in a uterus with two horns (bicornuate) that share a single cervix; the fundal cleft depth varies from shallow to deep.

bicornuate.definition: Having two horns; in anatomy, a uterus with two uterine horns due to incomplete fusion of the Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts during embryogenesis.

bicameral.definition: Having two chambers or compartments; divided into two cavities by a septum.

bicipital.definition: Relating to the biceps brachii muscle.

bicipital aponeurosis.definition: A broad, flat tendon of the biceps brachii that fans out to blend with the forearm's antebrachial fascia; it forms the roof of the cubital fossa and helps transmit and distribute the biceps' contraction while protecting the neurovascular bundle (median nerve and brachial artery) as they pass anterior to the elbow.

bicipital groove.definition: A groove on the anterior proximal humerus between the greater and lesser tubercles that houses the tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii as it passes from the shoulder to the elbow; bridged by the transverse humeral ligament and lined by a synovial sheath for the tendon.

pronator teres.definition: A superficial muscle of the anterior forearm that pronates the forearm by rotating the radius medially and assists elbow flexion; originates from the medial epicondyle of the humerus and the coronoid process of the ulna, and inserts on the lateral surface of the mid-radius; innervated by the median nerve.

deep tendon reflex.definition: A monosynaptic stretch reflex elicited by tapping a tendon with a reflex hammer, causing a brief contraction of the attached muscle; it assesses the integrity of the spinal cord and peripheral nerves, mediated by muscle spindle Ia afferents forming a direct synapse with alpha motor neurons in the anterior horn.

bichat’s membrane.definition: Historically, Bichat’s membrane referred to the buccal mucosa—the mucous membrane lining the inside of the cheek.

bicillin-c-r.definition: A combination intramuscular penicillin antibiotic containing benzathine penicillin G and procaine penicillin G; provides immediate and prolonged penicillin activity to treat various bacterial infections such as streptococcal infections and certain stages of syphilis.

cannabis.definition: A plant genus whose dried inflorescences contain cannabinoids (chiefly delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, THC, and cannabidiol, CBD). It is used recreationally for its psychoactive effects and medically for pain, nausea, spasticity, and appetite stimulation. Adverse effects include cognitive impairment, anxiety, tachycardia, dependence with chronic use, and, in some individuals, psychosis.

bhang.definition: A traditional cannabis preparation made from the leaves and flowering tops of Cannabis sativa or Cannabis indica, usually ingested orally as an edible or beverage; contains THC and other cannabinoids and produces psychoactive effects.

cannabis sativa.definition: A tall annual plant of the genus Cannabis with narrow, palmate leaves; it produces cannabinoids such as tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabidiol (CBD) and is cultivated for industrial hemp fiber and seeds as well as for psychoactive or medicinal drug-type products depending on the cultivar.

benzene.definition: A colorless, highly flammable aromatic hydrocarbon with a six-carbon ring (C6H6) used as an industrial solvent and chemical precursor; prolonged exposure is hematotoxic and carcinogenic, with an increased risk of leukemia.

hexachloride.definition: A chemical compound containing six chlorine atoms bound to an organic framework; a hexachlorinated compound, typically belonging to the organochlorine class and often persistent and potentially toxic.

benzene hexachloride.definition: An organochlorine insecticide (gamma-hexachlorocyclohexane), historically used topically as a scabicide and pediculicide; it acts by antagonizing GABA receptors in insects, but can cause neurotoxic effects in humans (including seizures), leading to safety concerns and restricted medical use in many countries.

meprednisone.definition: A synthetic glucocorticoid corticosteroid related to prednisone, used for its anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects. It works by activating glucocorticoid receptors and modulating gene expression to suppress inflammatory mediators; it has potent anti-inflammatory activity with relatively low mineralocorticoid action.

betapar.definition: A brand-name beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist (beta-blocker) used to lower blood pressure or intraocular pressure, depending on the formulation.

strabismus.definition: When both of your eyes do not look in the same direction. Also called walleye.

bidactyly.definition: A congenital anomaly in which only two digits (fingers or toes) remain on a limb, with the other digits absent.

teratoid_neoplasm.definition: A germ cell–origin tumor containing tissues derived from more than one embryonic germ layer, resembling a teratoma.

ectoderm.definition: The outermost of the three primary germ layers in early embryonic development; it forms the epidermis and the nervous system, and neural crest–derived structures.

endoderm.definition: The innermost of the three primary germ layers formed during embryogenesis; it gives rise to the epithelial lining of the gastrointestinal and respiratory tracts and to the associated glands and organs such as the liver, pancreas, and thyroid.

mesoderm.definition: The middle of the three primary germ layers formed in the early embryo (gastrulation); it differentiates into most connective tissues and structures, including muscle, bone and cartilage, the cardiovascular and lymphatic systems, parts of the urogenital system, and the serous membranes (mesothelium).

blastoderm.definition: Thin, single-layered sheet of embryonic cells formed on the surface of the yolk during early embryogenesis; from this layer, the germ layers develop.

bilaminar.definition: Relating to or consisting of two layers; in embryology, describing the early embryonic disc composed of two cell layers, the epiblast and hypoblast.

bifid_tongue.definition: A rare congenital abnormality in which the tongue is divided or forked along the midline, resulting in two distinct tips or lobes; it may be isolated or occur with other midline craniofacial anomalies and can affect speech and swallowing depending on severity.

bifid_uvula.definition: An uvula that is split into two lobes (forked); a congenital variation of the soft palate that may be isolated or associated with submucous cleft palate and velopharyngeal insufficiency.

bifid_ureter.definition: A congenital anomaly in which the ureter bifurcates (splits into two branches) along its course, often near the renal pelvis; the two limbs may drain separately into the bladder or rejoin, and it can be associated with a duplicated collecting system or obstruction.

cleft_palate.definition: A congenital malformation in which there is a fissure or opening in the palate due to failure of fusion of the palatal shelves during embryonic development, resulting in communication between the oral and nasal cavities (often associated with cleft lip).

bifocal.definition: Relating to two focal points; in ophthalmology, a lens (usually glasses) with two areas of different optical power for distance and near vision to correct presbyopia.

contact_lens.definition: A thin, curved lens placed directly on the surface of the eye (over the cornea) to correct refractive errors or for therapeutic reasons; made of hydrogel or silicone hydrogel materials and worn on the tear film, with various wear schedules and hygiene requirements to prevent infection.

bifocal_glasses.definition: A type of eyeglasses whose lenses have two distinct focal powers in the same lens: an upper portion for distance vision and a lower segment for near vision, usually separated by a visible line; used to correct presbyopia and other refractive errors.

bifrontal_suture.definition: A cranial suture between the left and right frontal bones; in infancy it corresponds to the metopic (frontal) suture and typically fuses as the frontal bones unite during early childhood.

bifurcation.definition: The division of a structure into two branches; in anatomy, the point where a vessel, nerve, or airway splits into two distinct branches (e.g., the tracheal bifurcation into the left and right main bronchi, or the common carotid bifurcation into internal and external carotid arteries).

bifurcate_ligament.definition: A ligament that splits into two branches (bifurcates) to connect two anatomical structures, often forming a forked or Y-shaped cord and contributing to joint stability.

bifurcate.definition: To divide into two branches or forks.

lithotomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove stones (calculi) from the urinary tract by incision into the stone-bearing organ, most commonly the bladder.

lithotrite.definition: A surgical instrument used to mechanically crush or scoop urinary bladder stones during cystoscopic procedures; it has a hollow, scoop-shaped tip used to fragment and retrieve stone fragments.

bigeminal.definition: Occurring in pairs; in cardiology, describing a rhythm in which a normal heartbeat is regularly followed by a premature (ectopic) beat, yielding a two-beat pattern.

bigeminal_pregnancy.definition: A pregnancy in which two embryos develop in the uterus; most commonly due to two separate fertilizations (dizygotic twins), but can involve twins with shared placentation depending on chorionicity.

bigeminal_pulse.definition: A cardiac rhythm pattern in which a normal heartbeat is regularly followed by a premature beat (typically a premature ventricular contraction), producing a pulse that alternates in amplitude.

bigeminy.definition: A rhythm in which every normal heartbeat is followed by a premature ventricular contraction, producing a regular normal– PVC pattern (every other beat is abnormal). It is a ventricular arrhythmia that can be benign or related to underlying heart disease, with management based on symptoms and overall risk.

bilabial.definition: Relating to or produced with both lips; in phonetics, consonants articulated with both lips, such as p, b, and m.

spica_cast.definition: A hip spica cast is a rigid body cast that immobilizes the trunk and one or both legs, typically extending from the chest to the feet, used to stabilize the hip or femur after fracture, dislocation, or postoperative reduction.

long_leg_spica_cast.definition: A rigid orthopedic cast that extends from the trunk to the foot, immobilizing the hip and knee (and sometimes the ankle) to stabilize the pelvis and lower extremity after femur or hip injuries or surgery, commonly used in pediatric care.

cuboid.definition: A cube-shaped tarsal bone on the lateral side of the foot that forms part of the midfoot and articulates with the calcaneus, navicular, and the bases of the fourth and fifth metatarsals.

navicular.definition: Boat-shaped bone of the foot in the midfoot, located between the talus posteriorly and the three cuneiforms anteriorly, contributing to the medial longitudinal arch. In older anatomy texts, the same term is used for the scaphoid bone of the wrist.

cervical_vertebrae.definition: Seven vertebrae in the neck region (C1–C7) forming the upper part of the spine; they support the head, encase and protect the cervical spinal cord, and allow a wide range of head and neck motions. Notable features include the atlas (C1) and axis (C2) with the dens, and transverse foramina that transmit the vertebral arteries.

spinous_processes.definition: A slender bony projection that extends posteriorly from the vertebral arch (lamina) of each vertebra; serves as an attachment site for muscles and ligaments and forms the palpable midline bumps along the spine.

bile_duct.definition: A duct system that carries bile from the liver and gallbladder to the duodenum. It includes intrahepatic ducts, the common hepatic duct, the cystic duct, and the common bile duct; obstruction or injury can lead to jaundice and cholestasis.

common_bile_duct.definition: A duct that carries bile from the liver and gallbladder into the duodenum; it is formed by the union of the common hepatic duct and the cystic duct and drains at the major duodenal papilla via the hepatopancreatic ampulla, under control of the sphincter of Oddi.

hepatic_duct.definition: A bile duct draining bile from the liver; the left and right hepatic ducts merge to form the common hepatic duct, which becomes the common bile duct after joining with the cystic duct.

cystic_duct.definition: A duct that drains bile from the gallbladder into the common bile duct; it connects the gallbladder to the common hepatic duct and contains spiral valves (Heister's valves) that help maintain patency and regulate bile flow.

small_intestine.definition: A section of the digestive system that includes the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum and plays the major role in absorbing nutrients for the body.

greater_duodenal_papilla.definition: A major duodenal papilla (papilla of Vater) in the descending part of the duodenum; the opening for the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct into the duodenum, regulated by the sphincter of Oddi.

sphincter_of_oddi.definition: A smooth muscle ring at the junction of the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct near the ampulla of Vater that regulates the flow of bile and pancreatic juice into the duodenum; contraction closes the lumen, relaxation permits drainage, with tone modulated by hormonal and autonomic signals (e.g., cholecystokinin).

bilirubin.definition: A yellow pigment produced by the breakdown of heme from hemoglobin; exists in an unconjugated (indirect) form in the bloodstream and, after hepatic conjugation, as a conjugated (direct) form excreted in bile. Elevated levels cause jaundice and can indicate liver, biliary tract, or red blood cell turnover disorders.

bilirubin_cast.definition: A urinary cast containing bilirubin pigment, formed in the renal tubules during hepatic dysfunction or biliary obstruction, typically indicating cholestasis or severe liver disease.

ursodeoxycholic_acid.definition: A hydrophilic bile acid used therapeutically to treat certain cholestatic liver diseases (most notably primary biliary cholangitis) and, in some cases, to dissolve cholesterol-containing gallstones; it works by reducing hepatic cholesterol saturation and improving bile flow, and it has cytoprotective effects on hepatocytes and cholangiocytes.

choledocholithiasis.definition: The presence of gallstones within the common bile duct, which can obstruct bile flow and lead to jaundice, biliary colic, cholangitis, or pancreatitis.

cholangiography.definition: A radiologic examination of the biliary tract in which a radiopaque contrast medium is introduced into the bile ducts to visualize their structure and assess for obstruction, stones, strictures, or leaks.

biliary_calculus.definition: A stone formed in the biliary tract, usually in the gallbladder; gallstones consist mainly of cholesterol or bilirubin calcium salts and can be asymptomatic or cause biliary colic, cholecystitis, cholangitis, or pancreatitis.

biliary_obstruction.definition: A blockage of bile flow through the biliary tree, from the liver to the duodenum, causing cholestasis and usually jaundice; common causes include gallstones in the bile duct, biliary strictures, tumors, or inflammatory processes.

biliary_tract.definition: A system of ducts and the gallbladder that stores and transports bile from the liver to the duodenum, including the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts (right and left hepatic ducts, common hepatic duct, common bile duct) and the cystic duct.

biliary_pseudolithiasis.definition: A temporary appearance of stone-like material in the biliary system that mimics gallstones on imaging but consists of reversible precipitates (most commonly ceftriaxone-calcium in bile or biliary sludge) and typically resolves after stopping the offending agent.

biliary_system.definition: A system of organs and ducts that produce, transport, store, and excrete bile; comprising the liver (bile production), the gallbladder (bile storage and concentration), and the biliary ducts (intrahepatic and extrahepatic) that convey bile to the duodenum for fat digestion.

biliary_tract_cancer.definition: A malignant tumor arising from the biliary system, including cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct cancers) and gallbladder cancer. It often presents with jaundice, abdominal pain, and weight loss; risk factors include primary sclerosing cholangitis, biliary stones, cirrhosis, and congenital biliary anomalies. Diagnosis relies on imaging and histology; treatment depends on site and stage and may include surgical resection, liver transplantation for select perihilar cases, and chemotherapy (gemcitabine with cisplatin).

biliary_cirrhosis.definition: A chronic liver disease in which autoimmune destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts causes cholestasis, inflammation, and progressive fibrosis leading to cirrhosis; commonly referred to as primary biliary cholangitis (formerly primary biliary cirrhosis).

primary_biliary_cirrhosis.definition: A chronic autoimmune liver disease in which immune-mediated destruction of the small intrahepatic bile ducts causes cholestasis, leading to progressive fibrosis and ultimately cirrhosis; commonly presents with fatigue, pruritus, and positive anti-mitochondrial antibodies.

secondary_biliary_cirrhosis.definition: A chronic liver disease caused by prolonged obstruction of bile flow outside the liver (such as from gallstones, biliary strictures, or pancreatic head tumors) leading to persistent cholestasis, bile duct injury, and progressive fibrosis that culminates in cirrhosis.

gallstone.definition: A stone that forms in the gallbladder or biliary tract from bile constituents (most commonly cholesterol or bilirubin calcium salts) and can obstruct bile flow, causing biliary colic, cholecystitis, or pancreatitis.

crohn's_disease.definition: A disease that lasts for a long time and causes severe irritation in your digestive tract (bowels).

schistosomiasis.definition: An infection caused by parasitic trematodes (schistosomes) of the genus Schistosoma, acquired when skin contacts water contaminated with larval forms released by infected freshwater snails. Chronic disease can affect the intestines, liver, and urinary tract, causing abdominal pain, diarrhea or GI bleeding, hepatosplenic disease, hematuria, and bladder/urinary tract pathology; diagnosis is by eggs in stool or urine (with serology or PCR in some cases); treatment is with praziquantel.

bilharziasis.definition: A parasitic infection caused by Schistosoma species acquired through skin contact with freshwater containing infective cercariae; chronic disease affects the urinary tract or intestines, causing symptoms such as hematuria, abdominal pain, diarrhea, hepatosplenomegaly, and can lead to fibrosis or bladder cancer; treated with praziquantel.

bilharzia.definition: Infection caused by Schistosoma species acquired from contaminated freshwater; chronic disease with abdominal pain, diarrhea, and blood in stool or urine, and possible liver, spleen, or urinary tract involvement; diagnosed by detecting eggs in stool or urine; treated with praziquantel.

schistosoma.definition: A genus of parasitic flatworms (blood flukes) that infect humans; they reside in the venous circulation and cause schistosomiasis.

sclerosing_cholangitis.definition: A chronic liver disease characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, leading to multifocal strictures (beading) and cholestasis that can progress to biliary cirrhosis; commonly associated with inflammatory bowel disease, especially ulcerative colitis.

neonatal_hepatitis.definition: An inflammation of the liver occurring in newborns (neonates), presenting with jaundice and hepatocellular dysfunction; often due to infections, metabolic disorders, or biliary tract disease, and is a common cause of neonatal cholestasis.

portal_hypertension.definition: An elevation of pressure within the portal venous system, typically due to increased resistance to portal blood flow (most commonly from liver cirrhosis or portal vein thrombosis), which predisposes to complications such as esophageal varices, ascites, and splenomegaly.

choledystogram.definition: A radiographic study of the biliary ducts in which contrast material is introduced to visualize the biliary tree.

nasogastric_suctioning.definition: Insertion of a flexible nasogastric tube through the nose into the stomach, connected to suction, to evacuate gastric contents and gas for decompression or drainage, relieve distention, prevent aspiration, and obtain gastric secretions or samples.

parenteral_fluids.definition: Fluids administered by routes other than the gastrointestinal tract (most commonly intravenously or subcutaneously) to provide hydration and correct electrolyte imbalances, and sometimes to deliver nutrients; includes isotonic crystalloids such as normal saline and lactated Ringer’s.

electrolytes.definition: A group of minerals (mainly salt) in your blood.

fat_soluble_vitamins.definition: Vitamins soluble in fats; absorbed with dietary fat and bile, stored in liver and adipose tissue, and can accumulate to toxic levels with excess intake. They include vitamins A, D, E, and K.

vitamin_k.definition: A fat-soluble vitamin essential for the γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues in clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X and proteins C and S, enabling blood coagulation; it also supports bone metabolism. It exists as phylloquinone (K1) from plants and menaquinones (K2) produced by gut bacteria.

prothrombin.definition: A vitamin K–dependent plasma glycoprotein produced by the liver; the inactive precursor (zymogen) of thrombin that is activated to thrombin by the prothrombin activator complex in the coagulation cascade.

choledochal_cysts.definition: Congenital dilation of the biliary tree, most commonly the extrahepatic bile ducts, causing biliary obstruction; associated with an abnormal pancreaticobiliary junction and presenting with jaundice, abdominal pain, or a palpable mass; complications include cholangitis, pancreatitis, biliary stones, and increased risk of biliary malignancy; treated by surgical cyst excision with biliary reconstruction (eg, hepaticojejunostomy).

ureter.definition: The tube that connects each kidney to the bladder.

ileocecal_valve.definition: A sphincter at the ileocecal junction that regulates passage of chyme from the ileum into the cecum and prevents backflow from the colon.

bilirubinemia.definition: The presence of bilirubin in the bloodstream; when bilirubin levels are elevated, this is called hyperbilirubinemia and can result from increased production, impaired hepatic uptake or conjugation, or impaired excretion, often causing jaundice.

bilirubinuria.definition: The presence of bilirubin in the urine, typically due to elevated conjugated (direct) bilirubin in the blood from liver dysfunction or biliary obstruction, since conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and excreted in urine. Unconjugated bilirubin is not usually found in urine.

biliuria.definition: The presence of bile pigments, especially conjugated bilirubin, in the urine; typically indicates bilirubin in the bloodstream being excreted by the kidneys, usually due to hepatobiliary disease such as cholestasis, biliary obstruction, or hepatic dysfunction. Unconjugated bilirubin is not usually detectable in urine.

mesocolon.definition: A peritoneal fold that attaches the colon to the posterior abdominal wall, forming part of the mesentery and containing the vessels, nerves, and lymphatics that supply the colon.

gastrojejunostomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which a connection (anastomosis) is created between the stomach and the jejunum to bypass the duodenum, typically to relieve gastric outlet obstruction or after gastric surgery.

vagotomy.definition: An operation in which the vagus nerve supply to the stomach is severed to reduce gastric acid secretions, historically used to treat peptic ulcers; variants include truncal vagotomy, selective vagotomy, and highly selective (parietal) vagotomy.

vagus.definition: A mixed cranial nerve (CN X) that provides parasympathetic innervation to the heart, lungs, and most of the gastrointestinal tract; carries visceral sensory information from thoracic and abdominal organs; and supplies motor fibers to the pharynx and larynx, contributing to swallowing, voice, and reflexes such as coughing and the gag reflex.

bilobate placenta.definition: Two distinct placental lobes connected by a narrow band of placental tissue (an isthmus); a two-lobed placental morphology.

bilobed placenta.definition: A placental anomaly in which the placenta is divided into two lobes connected by a band of placental tissue (bridging tissue).

placenta bipartitia.definition: A two-lobed placenta consisting of two placental masses connected by bridging placental tissue within a single placental disc.

binswanger's disease.definition: A form of vascular dementia characterized by chronic hypertension–related small-vessel disease causing widespread demyelination and gliosis of the deep/subcortical white matter, leading to cognitive decline (often executive dysfunction) and slowed gait; MRI typically shows diffuse white-matter hyperintensities in periventricular and deep regions.

gastric cancer.definition: A malignant tumor arising from the stomach lining, most often gastric adenocarcinoma; it typically presents late with symptoms such as weight loss, epigastric pain, or early satiety, and treatment depends on stage, usually involving surgical resection with chemotherapy and/or radiation.

praziquantel.definition: A broad-spectrum antiparasitic medication used to treat cestode and trematode infections, including schistosomiasis, clonorchiasis, opisthorchiasis, taeniasis, and paragonimiasis; it increases calcium permeability of parasite membranes, causing paralysis and death.

bimatoprost.definition: A prostaglandin F2α analog used as an ophthalmic medication to lower intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension; it is also used topically to promote eyelash growth (cosmetic use).

bimanual examination.definition: A manual examination technique in which both hands are used to palpate internal or external structures; typically one hand applies pressure while the other palpates from the opposite side to assess size, shape, position, mobility, and tenderness of organs (for example, in gynecology, abdominal palpation with one hand and vaginal palpation with the other to evaluate the uterus, ovaries, and adnexa).

bimanual palpation.definition: A two-handed physical examination technique in which the examiner uses both hands to palpate a structure from opposing directions, allowing assessment of size, shape, consistency, mobility, tenderness, and the presence of masses; commonly used for abdominal, pelvic (gynecologic), or breast examinations.

bimanual percussion.definition: A form of indirect percussion in which the examiner places the non-dominant hand (pleximeter) on the body and strikes its middle finger with the dominant hand (plexor) to elicit a percussion tone that helps assess underlying tissue density.

billroth's operation i.definition: A surgical procedure in which the distal portion of the stomach is removed (antrectomy) and the remaining stomach is anastomosed to the duodenum (gastroduodenostomy).

billroth's operation ii.definition: Partial gastrectomy with antrectomy in which the remaining stomach is anastomosed to the jejunum (gastrojejunostomy), and the duodenal stump is closed; bypasses the duodenum.

cervical mucus.definition: Secretions produced by the cervical glands whose amount and consistency vary with the menstrual cycle; they become thin and stretchy around ovulation to facilitate sperm transport, and are thicker at other times to protect the uterus from infection.

transverse mesocolon.definition: A peritoneal fold that suspends the transverse colon from the posterior abdominal wall, carrying the middle colic vessels, and dividing the peritoneal cavity into supracolic and infracolic compartments.

bioimpedance analysis.definition: Noninvasive method that estimates body composition and hydration by passing a small alternating electrical current through the body and measuring impedance; because lean tissue conducts electricity well due to higher water content, while fat tissue conducts poorly, impedance data are used to estimate total body water, fat-free mass, and fat mass.

brain activity.definition: Electrical and metabolic activity of cerebral neurons as they process information, sense, move, and regulate bodily functions; manifested by neuronal firing and synaptic activity, with regional blood flow and metabolism changes detectable by EEG/MEG and imaging methods like fMRI or PET.

endomyocardial biopsy.definition: A procedure in which small samples of the endomyocardium (inner heart muscle) are obtained with a bioptome via a transvenous approach (usually from the right ventricle) under fluoroscopic guidance for histopathologic examination to diagnose myocarditis, cardiomyopathy, infiltrative diseases, or transplant rejection.

heart transplantation.definition: A surgical procedure in which a failing heart is removed and replaced with a healthy donor heart, typically for end-stage heart failure or certain cardiomyopathies; the recipient requires lifelong immunosuppression to prevent rejection.

electrocardiography.definition: A noninvasive test that records the heart's electrical activity over time using surface skin electrodes to assess rhythm and diagnose cardiac conditions such as arrhythmias and ischemia.

electromyography.definition: A diagnostic procedure that evaluates and records the electrical activity produced by skeletal muscles, typically using needle or surface electrodes, to assess muscle function and diagnose neuromuscular disorders.

electroencephalography.definition: A test that records the brain's electrical activity through electrodes placed on the scalp, yielding brain wave recordings used to diagnose epilepsy, sleep disorders, encephalopathies, and to assess brain function.

right ventricle.definition: The right lower chamber of the heart; it receives blood from the right atrium for distribution to the lungs.

septal wall.definition: A wall or partition that separates two cavities or chambers; for example, the heart’s interventricular septum divides the left and right ventricles, and the nasal septum divides the two nasal cavities.

aspiration biopsy.definition: A diagnostic procedure in which a needle is inserted into a lesion and suction is applied to aspirate cells or tissue for microscopic examination.

needle biopsy.definition: Use of a hollow needle to remove a small sample of tissue for examination.

punch biopsy.definition: A diagnostic procedure in which a circular blade is used to remove a cylindrical plug of skin tissue, including epidermis and dermis (and sometimes superficial subcutaneous fat), for histopathologic examination.

surface biopsy.definition: A biopsy technique that removes only the surface layer of tissue—typically the epidermis and possibly the superficial dermis—for histopathologic examination; usually performed by shaving or curettage and is less invasive than punch or full-thickness biopsies.

biological half-life.definition: The time required for the amount of a substance in the body to decrease by 50% due to metabolic and excretory (biological) processes.

biological monitoring.definition: Biological monitoring is the measurement of chemicals or their metabolites in a person’s biological specimens (such as blood or urine) to estimate internal exposure or dose from a chemical substance and to evaluate potential health risks.

biological rhythm.definition: A natural, endogenous, recurring pattern of physiological or behavioral changes in living organisms, governed by internal biological clocks and synchronized by external cues; examples include circadian (~24-hour) rhythms, ultradian rhythms, and infradian rhythms.

biotin.definition: A water-soluble B vitamin (vitamin B7) that acts as a coenzyme for carboxylase enzymes involved in fatty acid synthesis, gluconeogenesis, and amino acid metabolism; deficiency can cause dermatitis, alopecia, and enteritis.

biotin deficiency syndrome.definition: An condition due to insufficient biotin (vitamin B7) availability, causing dermatitis, alopecia, and often neurologic or metabolic disturbances; can result from poor intake, malabsorption, excess avidin from raw egg whites, or inherited biotinidase deficiency, and is typically corrected with biotin supplementation.

precordial distress.definition: Discomfort, pain, or a sense of tightness in the chest over the heart (the precordial region), often described as chest pressure; commonly due to cardiac causes such as angina or myocardial infarction but may have noncardiac etiologies.

hyperesthesia.definition: Heightened or abnormal sensitivity to sensory stimuli (such as touch or pain) beyond what is normally felt, often due to peripheral nerve damage, neuropathy, or central nervous system disorders.

interleukins.definition: A group of cytokines produced by leukocytes that regulate communication between immune cells, guiding the development, activation, and function of immune cells and modulating inflammation; they signal through specific receptors on target cells and can be pro-inflammatory or anti-inflammatory.

interferons.definition: A group of cytokines produced by host cells in response to viral infection and other immune triggers that induce antiviral states in neighboring cells, activate immune cells, and upregulate antigen presentation to coordinate the immune response.

hematopoietic growth factors.definition: A group of cytokines that regulate hematopoiesis by promoting the proliferation, differentiation, and survival of hematopoietic progenitor cells in the bone marrow (e.g., erythropoietin, G-CSF, GM‑CSF, thrombopoietin), used clinically to treat deficits in specific blood cell lines.

antitoxins.definition: Antibodies that neutralize specific toxins by binding to them, preventing their harmful effects; they can be produced by the host after exposure or vaccination, or administered as immune serum to provide passive protection against toxin-mediated disease.

sera.definition: Plural of serum; the clear, pale-yellow fluid that remains after blood has clotted and the clot is removed, containing antibodies and other soluble proteins but lacking fibrinogen and other clotting factors; used in serologic testing, diagnostics, and research.

bioassay.definition: A test that uses living organisms, cells, or biological systems to measure the potency, activity, or concentration of a substance by observing a quantifiable biological response.

endomyocardial.definition: Relating to the endocardium and myocardium; the inner lining and muscular middle layer of the heart.

heart rhythm.definition: The pattern of the heartbeats—their timing, regularity, and force—generated by the heart's electrical conduction system; normal rhythm is sinus rhythm with a regular rate appropriate for age/activity.

dizygotic twins.definition: Fraternal twins that arise when two separate eggs are fertilized by two separate sperm during the same pregnancy. They are genetically as related as ordinary siblings (about 50% shared DNA) and can be the same or different sexes.

bipalatinoid.definition: Relating to two palatine bones or two palatal structures; having a double palatal region.

gelatin capsule.definition: An oral dosage form in which the drug is enclosed in a gelatin shell (hard capsules are two-piece shells containing powders or pellets; soft capsules are one-piece, flexible shells containing liquids); the shell dissolves in the gastrointestinal tract to release the medication.

bipara.definition: A woman who has had two deliveries at or beyond 20 weeks' gestation (parity II).

biparental inheritance.definition: Transmission of genetic material from two parents to offspring; for nuclear genes, offspring are diploid and inherit one allele from each parent, yielding genetic contributions from both maternal and paternal lineages.

amphigenous inheritance.definition: Not a standard term in medical genetics; there is no established definition. If you have a source or context, please share it—this may be a misspelling or a nonstandard label. In the meantime, I can help explain established inheritance patterns (autosomal, X-linked, mitochondrial, Y-linked, polygenic) if that would help.

biparietal diameter.definition: A prenatal ultrasound measurement of the fetal head width in the axial view, taken at the level of the thalami, representing the distance between the two parietal bones; used to estimate gestational age and assess fetal growth.

biparietal suture.definition: A cranial suture between the left and right parietal bones of the skull; it runs along the midline and is the sagittal suture.

biparous.definition: Having given birth to two offspring; having had two births.

bipartite.definition: Divided into two parts; describing a structure that consists of two separate components or fragments.

biped.definition: An organism that walks on two legs; a two-footed creature (often used to describe humans).

bipedal.definition: Relating to or using two feet for walking; walking on two legs.

bipenniform.definition: Describing a muscle in which fascicles attach to a central tendon from both sides, creating a two-sided pennate (bipennate) arrangement.

biperiden lactate.definition: A muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist (anticholinergic) used as an antiparkinsonian medication and to treat extrapyramidal symptoms; the lactate salt form is used for injectable administration.

parkinson's disease.definition: A movement disorder that occurs when the brain does not produce enough of a chemical.

extrapyramidal disorders.definition: A group of movement disorders caused by dysfunction of the extrapyramidal system (basal ganglia and related circuits), presenting with features such as Parkinsonism (bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor), dystonia, akathisia, and tardive dyskinesia; can result from neurodegenerative disease, drug effects (notably antipsychotics), or lesions of the basal ganglia.

narrow-angle glaucoma.definition: A form of glaucoma in which the iridocorneal angle is narrowed or closed, restricting outflow of aqueous humor and causing elevated intraocular pressure with potential optic nerve damage; may present acutely with eye pain, red eye, halos around lights, headache, nausea, and vomiting.

genitourinary tract obstruction.definition: An obstruction that blocks the flow of urine at any point along the urinary tract (kidneys, ureters, bladder, or urethra), which can be partial or complete and may lead to hydronephrosis and impaired renal function.

gi tract obstruction.definition: A condition in which the lumen of the gastrointestinal tract is blocked, preventing the passage of contents; it can be mechanical (adhesions, hernias, tumors, volvulus) or functional (ileus), and typically causes abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and inability to pass gas or stools.

urinary retention.definition: An inability to empty the bladder completely, resulting in retention of urine; it can be acute (sudden, painful inability to urinate with a distended bladder) or chronic (incomplete emptying with a high postvoid residual).

postural hypotension.definition: A clinically significant drop in blood pressure within minutes of standing (typically a ≥20 mmHg systolic or ≥10 mmHg diastolic decrease) accompanied by dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting, due to inadequate autonomic vasoconstriction or reduced circulating volume.

decreased sweating.definition: Decreased sweating is a reduced ability to sweat, which can impair the body's ability to regulate temperature; it may be localized to a region or generalized and can result from sweat gland or autonomic nerve dysfunction, medications, or underlying medical conditions.

hypersensitivity reactions.definition: An immune-mediated adverse reaction to typically harmless antigens in which the immune response is exaggerated or misdirected, causing tissue injury or symptoms. Traditionally categorized into four mechanisms: Type I (IgE-mediated immediate reactions), Type II (antibody-mediated cytotoxic), Type III (immune complex–mediated), and Type IV (T-cell–mediated delayed hypersensitivity).

biphasic.definition: Having two distinct phases or components, each with different characteristics or effects; often describing a process or response that occurs in two sequential stages.

bipolar electrocautery.definition: A surgical diathermy technique in which electrical current flows between the two tips of a bipolar forceps to coagulate or cut tissue, achieving hemostasis with localized heating and without requiring a grounding pad (with less collateral thermal spread than monopolar electrocautery).

bipolar lead.definition: A pacing/monitoring lead configuration in which electrical activity is sensed and/or delivered between two closely spaced electrodes on the same lead (commonly a tip and ring), as opposed to a unipolar lead that uses a single electrode with a distant return.

bipotentiality.definition: An embryonic tissue or progenitor cell's ability to differentiate into two alternative cell lineages; for example, the bipotential gonad can develop into either a testis or an ovary depending on genetic and hormonal cues.

bird breeder's lung.definition: A hypersensitivity pneumonitis caused by inhalation of avian antigens from birds kept by breeders; an immune-mediated inflammatory lung disease that can present acutely after exposure or chronically with progressive dyspnea and cough.

pigeon breeder's lung.definition: A form of hypersensitivity pneumonitis (immune-mediated interstitial lung disease) caused by inhalation of avian proteins from pigeons (feathers, droppings, and dander). It presents acutely with fever, cough, dyspnea, and malaise after exposure, and can progress to chronic interstitial fibrosis with ongoing exposure.

retrognathism.definition: A condition in which the jaw is positioned posteriorly (receded) relative to the upper jaw and cranial base, most often referring to a retruded mandible, producing a convex facial profile and commonly associated with Class II malocclusion.

bird flu.definition: An infection caused by avian influenza viruses (influenza A) that primarily infect birds. Human infections are rare and usually occur through close contact with infected birds or contaminated environments; illness can range from mild respiratory symptoms to severe pneumonia and death, with certain subtypes (e.g., H5N1, H7N9) associated with higher severity and sustained human transmission being uncommon.

avian influenza.definition: An infection with influenza A viruses that primarily infect birds but can occasionally infect humans and other mammals; these viruses are categorized in birds by pathogenicity as low or highly pathogenic, with highly pathogenic strains causing severe disease and poultry outbreaks, while human infections are uncommon and usually occur after close contact with infected birds.

birth center.definition: A birth center is a licensed health care facility that provides comprehensive childbirth services for low-risk pregnancies in a home-like setting, typically staffed by midwives and nurses, offering prenatal care, labor and birth, and postpartum care with an established transfer plan to a hospital if complications arise.

birth certificate.definition: A government-issued document that records an individual's birth, including date, place, sex, and parentage; used as legal proof of identity, age, and citizenship and to obtain other civil documents.

birth control.definition: A method or device used to prevent pregnancy; also called contraception. Methods include hormonal pills, implanted devices, intrauterine devices, barrier methods, and sterilization (surgery) for women or men.

birth defect.definition: A birth defect is a structural or functional abnormality present at birth, resulting from abnormal development before birth and can be caused by genetic or environmental factors.

congenital anomaly.definition: A structural or functional abnormality of the body that is present at birth, arising from abnormal development during fetal life; it may be due to genetic factors, teratogenic environmental exposures, or multifactorial causes.

birthing.definition: The process of giving birth: the delivery of a fetus and placenta from the uterus, usually through the birth canal, following the stages of labor.

birthing chair.definition: A delivery chair designed to support a laboring person in a seated or semi‑upright position during labor and vaginal birth, with hips flexed and thighs apart to facilitate fetal descent; typically features a sturdy frame, padded seat, backrest, and armrests.

birth injury.definition: An injury sustained by a fetus or newborn during labor and delivery as a result of mechanical forces or instrumentation, distinct from congenital anomalies. Examples include clavicle fracture, brachial plexus injury, facial nerve palsy, skull injuries, and intracranial hemorrhages.

erb's palsy.definition: A brachial plexus traction injury most often involving the C5–C6 nerve roots, causing weakness of the shoulder and arm muscles and a characteristic waiter's-tip posture; typically results from obstetric birth trauma (e.g., shoulder dystocia) and often improves with conservative management, with surgery considered for persistent deficits.

birthmark.definition: A benign skin lesion present at birth or appearing shortly after birth; it may be pigmented or vascular and is usually harmless.

birth weight.definition: The weight of a baby at birth, typically measured in grams or pounds, used to assess neonatal health and growth; low birth weight is defined as less than 2,500 grams.

small for gestational age.definition: A fetus or newborn whose birth weight (or estimated fetal weight) is below the 10th percentile for its gestational age, indicating possible fetal growth restriction.

true birth rate.definition: An informal, nonstandard term; not found in standard medical dictionaries. If used, it would typically refer to the rate at which pregnancies result in live births—i.e., the number of live births per unit population (often per 1,000 people per year) adjusted to exclude fetal losses such as miscarriages or stillbirths. In formal terminology, the closest concepts are the crude birth rate and the live-birth rate per pregnancy.

crude birth rate.definition: The crude birth rate is the number of live births in a year per 1,000 people in the population, using the mid-year population as the denominator; it is unadjusted for the population’s age or sex structure.

refined birth rate.definition: Not a standard term in epidemiology; when used, it usually denotes an adjusted birth-rate estimate derived from the crude birth rate after refinement (e.g., age-standardization to account for different population age structures or corrections for data quality) to enable more accurate cross-population comparisons.

birth trauma.definition: Physical injuries sustained by the newborn or mother during labor and delivery, caused by passage through the birth canal or obstetric maneuvers, ranging from minor contusions to more serious injuries such as fractures, nerve injuries, intracranial hemorrhage, or uterine/perineal trauma.

breech birth.definition: A baby that is born feet or rear-end first.

live birth.definition: Live birth is the birth of a product of conception that shows signs of life (e.g., breathing, heartbeat, pulsation of the umbilical cord, or voluntary movement) after complete separation from the mother.

stillbirth.definition: The death of a fetus after 20 weeks of gestation; the baby is delivered with no signs of life.

malocclusion.definition: When your teeth do not fit together properly, such as when your teeth are crowded together or you have an overbite or an underbite.

rectal fissures.definition: A tear in the mucosa of the anal canal (often the anoderm), usually located in the posterior midline, causing sharp pain with defecation and bright red blood on stool. Commonly associated with constipation and hard stools; most acute fissures heal with conservative measures such as increased fiber and fluids, stool softeners, and sitz baths. Chronic or refractory fissures may require topical vasodilators (e.g., nitroglycerin, calcium-channel blockers) or surgical intervention (lateral internal sphincterotomy).

sore tongue.definition: A painful or uncomfortable tongue due to inflammation or irritation of the tongue surface (glossitis); commonly caused by trauma or irritation, infections such as candidiasis, nutritional deficiencies (iron, vitamin B12, folate), irritants (hot/spicy foods, tobacco, alcohol), medications, or systemic conditions.

metallic taste.definition: An unpleasant, metallic-tasting sensation (dysgeusia) in the mouth not related to food, which can be temporary or persistent. Causes include certain medications (e.g., some antibiotics, chemotherapy), dental issues, pregnancy, infections, kidney or liver disease, metabolic disorders, or exposure to metals.

burning sensation.definition: Subjective dysesthetic sensation described as hot, burning, or scalding warmth, usually due to irritation or injury of nerves or mucosa/skin (e.g., neuropathic pain, inflammatory conditions, infections, or chemical irritation).

bismuth subsalicylate.definition: A nonprescription bismuth salt used to relieve upset stomach, nausea, indigestion, heartburn, and diarrhea; it has mild antisecretory and antimicrobial effects in the GI tract and can discolor stools or tongue.

bismuth.definition: A chemical element (Bi, atomic number 83); a brittle, silvery-white heavy metal used in medicine in compounds such as bismuth subsalicylate as an antiseptic and antidiarrheal agent.

bisacodyl.definition: A stimulant laxative that increases bowel movements by irritating the intestinal mucosa and stimulating peristalsis; used to treat constipation and for bowel preparation before procedures. Available orally or as a rectal suppository; onset is typically about 6–12 hours (oral) or 15–60 minutes (rectal).

bisacromial.definition: Relating to or situated between the two acromions of the scapula (the outer bony projections at the top of each shoulder).

bisalbuminemia.definition: A rare lab finding characterized by two distinct albumin fractions in serum, usually seen as a double peak on serum protein electrophoresis, typically caused by an inherited albumin variant and generally of no clinical consequence.

bitartrate.definition: A salt of tartaric acid in which one or more acidic hydrogens are replaced by a metal or amine cation; the most common example is a potassium salt used as a food additive and in dietary supplements.

carboxylate.definition: A negatively charged ion that is the conjugate base of a carboxylic acid, formed by deprotonation of the carboxyl group (R-COO−); it forms carboxylate salts with cations.

biteplane.definition: A removable acrylic dental appliance that covers the biting surfaces of selected teeth to alter the occlusion, typically used to deprogram the bite, reduce bruxism, or manage temporomandibular joint disorders by temporarily separating posterior teeth and adjusting vertical dimension during treatment.

biteplate.definition: A dental occlusal appliance—a small acrylic plate placed on the biting surfaces of the teeth (removable or fixed) to alter or prevent occlusal contact, commonly used to protect teeth from grinding or wear and to relieve temporomandibular joint symptoms by allowing the jaw to rest.

bitegauge.definition: A dental instrument that measures the force and pattern of a person’s bite (occlusal force), typically using a pressure sensor or load device to quantify bite strength for occlusal analysis and temporomandibular joint assessment.

biteguard.definition: A dental appliance worn over the teeth to protect them from injury or wear; used to prevent dental trauma during sports and to mitigate tooth grinding (bruxism) and related jaw discomfort.

biteguard splint.definition: A dental appliance, usually made of acrylic, that fits over the teeth to protect them from wear due to grinding or clenching (bruxism), distribute occlusal forces, and reduce temporomandibular joint pain and headaches; commonly worn at night.

bitelock.definition: A device placed between the teeth to keep the mouth open during dental procedures or anesthesia, preventing biting and protecting the airway.

biteblock.definition: A biteblock is a device placed between the teeth to prevent biting and to help maintain mouth opening and airway protection during procedures such as anesthesia, intubation, or dental work, often protecting the endotracheal tube and instruments.

occlusal plane.definition: An imaginary reference plane formed by the incisal edges of the maxillary anterior teeth and the buccal cusps of the posterior teeth, used in dentistry to evaluate and plan occlusion and prosthetic restorations.

occlusion rim.definition: A wax or acrylic resin guide placed on an edentulous arch to establish and record the vertical dimension of occlusion and centric relation during complete denture fabrication; also known as a bite rim.

orthodontics.definition: A branch of dentistry that diagnoses, prevents, and treats irregularities of the teeth and jaws, especially misalignment of teeth and bite (malocclusion), using appliances such as braces, aligners, and retainers to straighten teeth and improve function and aesthetics.

prosthodontics.definition: Prosthodontics is the dental specialty concerned with the diagnosis, treatment planning, rehabilitation, and maintenance of missing or damaged teeth and oral tissues through the use of artificial devices such as dentures, crowns, bridges, implants, and other prostheses to restore function, aesthetics, and comfort.

labial wires.definition: A method in oral and maxillofacial surgery in which wires are attached to the labial (lip-facing) surfaces of teeth to immobilize the dental arches or stabilize fracture segments, typically as part of intermaxillary fixation.

wrought wire.definition: A metal wire formed by mechanical deformation (work hardening) of the metal, rather than by casting, yielding increased strength and hardness.

clasps.definition: A device or component that grips or holds something in place; in dentistry, a metal arm or hook of a removable partial denture that engages a tooth to provide retention.

biventricular pacing.definition: A form of cardiac resynchronization therapy that delivers coordinated pacing to the right and left ventricles (via a coronary sinus lead) from a tri-lead pacemaker to restore synchronized ventricular contraction in heart failure with dyssynchrony, improving symptoms and outcomes.

bite wing film.definition: A dental radiograph of the posterior teeth produced with the patient biting on a stabilizing bite-wing tab; it images the crowns of adjacent teeth and the interproximal bone to detect interproximal caries and assess crestal bone Levels.

bite wing radiograph.definition: A dental radiograph that images the crowns of posterior teeth and the height of the alveolar bone, obtained with the patient biting on a small tab to stabilize the film or sensor; used to detect interproximal caries and assess bone levels for periodontal health.

interproximal film.definition: A dental radiographic film (or sensor) placed between adjacent teeth to image the interproximal surfaces; it is typically used as a bitewing radiograph to detect proximal caries and to assess bone height/periodontal status.

interproximal film image.definition: A dental radiographic image focused on the interproximal surfaces between adjacent teeth (typically a bitewing), showing the crowns of posterior teeth and the crestal bone; used to detect interproximal caries and evaluate periodontal bone levels.

bithynia.definition: A genus of small freshwater snails in the family Bithyniidae; they serve as the first intermediate hosts in the life cycles of several trematode parasites, including the fish-borne liver fluke Opisthorchis felineus.

opisthorchis.definition: A genus of parasitic liver flukes (trematodes) in the family Opisthorchiidae; humans become infected by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish containing metacercariae, leading to opisthorchiasis with biliary disease and an increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma.

teething.definition: The process by which a tooth erupts through the gingiva (gum tissue) into the mouth, usually beginning around 6 months of age with the eruption of primary (deciduous) teeth and continuing as more teeth emerge.

teething process.definition: The teething process is the eruption of primary (deciduous) teeth through the gums in infants and young children, typically starting around 6 months of age and continuing for several years; it may be associated with gum soreness, drooling, irritability, and mild changes in sleep or appetite.

psychosexual development.definition: Freud's theory that personality develops through a sequence of childhood stages—oral, anal, phallic, latency, and genital—during which libidinal energy is focused on different erogenous zones; conflicts unresolved at any stage can lead to fixation, influencing later behavior and personality.

psychosocial development.definition: The development of social and emotional functioning across the lifespan, shaped by the interaction of individual factors and environmental influences, affecting relationships, self-identity, coping, and adaptation to social roles.

bitolterol.definition: A short-acting inhaled beta-2 adrenergic agonist bronchodilator that relaxes bronchial smooth muscle to relieve bronchospasm in asthma and other airway diseases.

bitolterol mesylate.definition: An inhaled beta-2 adrenergic agonist bronchodilator (the mesylate salt of bitolterol) used to relieve bronchospasm in asthma and other obstructive airway diseases by relaxing airway smooth muscle; typically provides rapid, short-acting relief and is administered by inhalation.

chronic obstructive airway disease.definition: A chronic, progressive inflammatory disease of the airways with persistent, not fully reversible airflow limitation, typically caused by smoking or environmental exposures; it encompasses chronic bronchitis and emphysema and presents with chronic cough, dyspnea, and sputum production. Management focuses on symptom control and slowing progression with bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids as needed, smoking cessation, vaccinations, pulmonary rehabilitation, and supplemental oxygen in advanced cases.

bronchitis.definition: Inflammation of the mucous membranes of the bronchi (airways) with cough and increased mucus production; acute bronchitis is a short-term illness usually viral, while chronic bronchitis is a long-term condition defined by a productive cough lasting at least three months in two consecutive years, typically linked to smoking or environmental irritants.

pulmonary emphysema.definition: Permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles with destruction of alveolar walls, causing loss of elastic recoil and air trapping; a major form of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) typically due to tobacco smoking.

bitot's spots.definition: A foamy, gray-white patch of keratinized conjunctival epithelium on the bulbar conjunctiva (typically the temporal side), an early ocular sign of vitamin A deficiency seen in xerophthalmia; may regress with vitamin A supplementation.

bitrochanteric lipodystrophy.definition: Loss or marked thinning of subcutaneous fat in the bilateral hip (trochanteric) regions, a manifestation of lipodystrophy characterized by reduced adipose tissue in those areas and possible compensatory fat redistribution elsewhere.

lipodystrophy.definition: An abnormal or degenerative disorder of adipose tissue distribution characterized by loss or redistribution of subcutaneous fat, often with fat accumulation in other areas and metabolic complications such as insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and fatty liver.

biuret.definition: A white, crystalline organic compound formed by the condensation of two urea molecules with the release of ammonia; in biochemistry, used in the Biuret test to detect proteins via formation of a copper–peptide complex that produces a violet color.

biuret reaction.definition: A chemical test for the presence of peptide bonds in proteins, in which copper(II) ions in alkaline solution react with peptide bonds to form a violet-colored complex; used to detect and estimate protein concentration.

bivalent.definition: Having two valences or binding sites. In immunology, describing an antibody with two antigen-binding sites or a vaccine formulated to present two different antigens or serotypes.

bivalent antibody.definition: An antibody molecule possessing two antigen-binding sites (two Fab regions) that can bind two epitopes simultaneously, increasing avidity and enabling cross-linking of antigens; typical IgG antibodies are bivalent.

bivalent chromosome.definition: During meiosis, a bivalent is the paired homologous chromosomes (each consisting of two sister chromatids) that align and are held together by synapsis and chiasmata to form a tetrad, enabling genetic recombination.

bivalirudin.definition: A synthetic direct thrombin inhibitor used as an anticoagulant, administered IV, that inhibits circulating and clot-bound thrombin to prevent fibrin formation and thrombin-mediated platelet activation; mainly used during percutaneous coronary intervention and as an alternative to heparin in patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; has a short half-life and is renally excreted.

unstable angina pectoris.definition: An acute coronary syndrome defined by new or worsening chest pain at rest or with minimal exertion due to partial thrombosis on a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque, without evidence of myocardial necrosis (troponin negative or not elevated initially).

percutaneous transluminal coronary angio.definition: A procedure to open blocked coronary arteries by threading a catheter with a small balloon to the narrowed segment, then inflating the balloon to widen the artery; a stent may be placed to keep it open. Also known as balloon angioplasty.

bladder augmentation.definition: A surgical procedure to increase bladder capacity and reduce bladder pressure by enlarging the bladder with a segment of intestine (commonly ileum), usually for neurogenic or poorly compliant bladder to protect kidney function.

augmentation cystoplasty.definition: A surgical procedure in which a segment of intestine, typically ileum or colon, is used to enlarge the bladder capacity and reduce intravesical pressure, creating a larger, more compliant urinary reservoir (enterocystoplasty).
