circumduction.definition: A conical, circular movement of a limb at a joint in which the distal end traces a circle while the proximal segment remains relatively fixed; produced by a combination of flexion, abduction, extension, and adduction (as at the shoulder or hip).

risser cast.definition: A long-body plaster cast used to immobilize the spine for scoliosis treatment, typically extending from the neck to the pelvis; largely historical and now largely replaced by bracing and surgical options.

thoracolumbosacral orthosis.definition: A rigid or semi-rigid back brace that immobilizes and stabilizes the thoracic, lumbar, and sacral spine to limit movement, used for fractures, post‑operative stabilization, scoliosis, and other spinal conditions.

orthosis.definition: A custom shoe insert that helps cushion or realign the foot.

spinal injury.definition: Damage to the spinal cord or surrounding spinal column (often from trauma) that results in impaired or lost motor, sensory, and autonomic function below the level of injury; can be complete or incomplete.

spinal surgery.definition: Procedures performed on the spine (vertebrae, intervertebral discs, spinal cord, and nerve roots) to treat disorders such as herniated discs, spinal stenosis, fractures, deformities, or tumors. The goal is to relieve pain, decompress neural structures, restore stability and alignment, and improve neurological function; common techniques include decompression (discectomy, laminectomy), fusion with instrumentation, disc replacement, and corrective osteotomies.

bone tissue.definition: A hard connective tissue that forms bones, consisting of osteocytes in lacunae within a mineralized extracellular matrix made primarily of collagen and hydroxyapatite; it provides structural support and protection, enables movement, stores minerals, and houses bone marrow.

osteocyte.definition: A mature bone cell derived from an osteoblast that is embedded in a lacuna within the mineralized bone matrix; it maintains bone tissue, senses mechanical strain, and coordinates remodeling by signaling to osteoblasts and osteoclasts via gap junctions.

osteoblast.definition: A bone-forming cell that secretes osteoid (the organic bone matrix) and enables mineralization to form new bone; derived from mesenchymal stem cells.

osteoclast.definition: A large multinucleated bone cell that resorbs bone tissue during remodeling by secreting acid and proteolytic enzymes; derived from the monocyte/macrophage lineage and forms resorption lacunae on the bone surface.

bone matrix.definition: Extracellular component of bone tissue composed of organic osteoid (primarily type I collagen and noncollagenous proteins) and inorganic hydroxyapatite mineral, produced by osteoblasts and later mineralized to give bone its strength and rigidity.

lamella.definition: A thin plate or layer; in biology, lamellae are the concentric sheets of mineralized bone matrix in compact bone (lamellar bone) and, more generally, any thin plate-like layer of tissue.

cancellous bone.definition: One of two types of tissue that form bone; this type is commonly found at the center of long bones and makes up a large part of the hip and spine. Also known as trabecular bone.

trabeculae.definition: Small, rod- or plate-like structural elements that form a supportive lattice within a tissue; in bone they comprise the cancellous (spongy) bone network, and in the heart they refer to the muscular trabeculae carneae lining the ventricles.

haversian canals.definition: A central channel within an osteon of compact bone that contains blood vessels and nerves, surrounded by concentric lamellae of calcified bone matrix.

volkmann canals.definition: Perforating (Volkmann's) canals are channels in bone that run perpendicular to the long axis and connect the Haversian (central) canals with each other and with the periosteum, allowing blood vessels and nerves to supply the osteons.

osteons.definition: The building blocks of compact bone, the hard, tightly-packed tissue that forms the outer shell of bones.

bony labyrinth.definition: A rigid bony cavity within the petrous portion of the temporal bone that encloses the membranous labyrinth of the inner ear, containing perilymph and housing the cochlea, vestibule, and semicircular canals; it protects and supports the sensory organs for hearing and balance.

membranous labyrinth.definition: An interconnected system of membranous sacs and ducts inside the inner ear's bony labyrinth that contains endolymph and houses the sensory organs for hearing and balance (cochlear duct/scala media, utricle, saccule, and semicircular ducts).

hard palate.definition: The bony anterior part of the palate that forms the roof of the mouth and the floor of the nasal cavity; composed of the palatine processes of the maxilla and the horizontal plates of the palatine bones, and covered by mucosa. It separates the oral and nasal cavities.

bony palate.definition: Rigid anterior portion of the palate (hard palate) formed by the palatine processes of the maxilla and the horizontal plates of the palatine bones; it forms the roof of the mouth, separates the oral and nasal cavities, and bears the upper teeth.

posterior superior iliac crest.definition: Prominent bony ridge on the back surface of the ilium, forming the upper (posterior) border of the iliac crest; a palpable pelvic landmark used to orient the sacral-hip region and guide certain regional procedures.

mandibular condyle.definition: The rounded articular end of the mandible (condylar head) that articulates with the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone to form the temporomandibular joint; it enables hinge and translational movements of the jaw and is separated from the temporal bone by an articular disc.

proximal epiphyses.definition: The ends of long bones nearest the trunk that articulate with adjacent bones at joints; in growing individuals they contain the epiphyseal (growth) plate, and in adulthood they are fused to the diaphysis and consist mainly of cancellous bone covered by articular cartilage.

vertebral bodies.definition: A large, cylindrical anterior part of a vertebra that bears weight and transmits load along the spine; composed of cancellous bone encased in a cortical shell, it forms the superior and inferior endplates and interfaces with the intervertebral disc and adjacent vertebrae.

thoracic vertebrae.definition: A vertebra in the mid-thoracic part of the spine (T1–T12), typically with a heart-shaped body bearing costal facets for rib articulation, facets on the transverse processes for rib tubercles, and a long downward-sloping spinous process; it forms the thoracic portion of the vertebral column and articulates with ribs.

bone marrow infusion.definition: Infusion of hematopoietic stem cells obtained from donor bone marrow into a recipient, typically after conditioning therapy, to re-establish bone marrow function and blood cell production; can be autologous or allogeneic.

bone marrow reserve.definition: The functional capacity of the bone marrow’s hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell compartment to produce adequate blood cells in response to physiologic demand or after injury, including recovery after cytopenias such as chemotherapy-induced myelosuppression.

hematopoietic system.definition: The organ system and process that produces and matures blood cells—red cells, white cells, and platelets—primarily through hematopoiesis in the bone marrow, with supportive roles from the liver and spleen (especially during fetal development) and other lymphoid organs.

hematopoietic.definition: Relating to the formation of blood cells; capable of producing blood cells, as in hematopoietic tissue (bone marrow) where hematopoiesis occurs.

megaloblastic anemia.definition: Fewer than normal healthy red blood cells in circulation due to deficiency of folate or vitamin B12, with red cells that are enlarged and deformed and have impaired oxygen-carrying capacity.

fibrosis.definition: Formation and deposition of excess fibrous connective tissue in an organ or tissue as part of a reparative or reactive response to injury or chronic inflammation, leading to scarring, architectural distortion, and potential impairment of function.

tumors.definition: A neoplastic mass formed by uncontrolled cell growth; may be benign (noncancerous) or malignant (cancerous). Benign tumors grow slowly and do not invade surrounding tissues or metastasize, while malignant tumors invade locally and can spread (metastasize) to distant sites.

immunological deficiencies.definition: Immunodeficiencies are disorders in which the immune system's ability to fight infections is reduced or absent, resulting in increased susceptibility to infections; they can be primary (congenital) or secondary (acquired) due to genetic defects, infections, illness, malnutrition, or immunosuppressive therapy.

inborn errors of metabolism.definition: A group of congenital genetic disorders caused by defects in enzymes or transport proteins of metabolism, leading to abnormal accumulation of substrates or deficiency of essential products and often presenting in infancy or early childhood with metabolic crises or multisystem disease.

total body irradiation.definition: A radiotherapy technique that delivers a uniform dose of ionizing radiation to the entire body, typically used as a myeloablative preparative regimen before hematopoietic stem cell (bone marrow) transplantation.

bone plate.definition: A rigid internal fixation plate used in orthopedic surgery, attached to a bone with screws to hold fracture fragments in alignment during healing.

bone recession.definition: Loss or apical migration of alveolar bone surrounding a tooth, leading to reduced supporting bone and potential tooth mobility; commonly associated with periodontal disease, trauma, or excessive occlusal forces.

bone resorption.definition: The process by which osteoclasts break down mineralized bone tissue, releasing calcium and other minerals into the bloodstream as part of normal bone remodeling; excessive resorption can contribute to bone loss and diseases such as osteoporosis.

bone scan.definition: A test in which radioactive material is injected into a person's bloodstream to help produce images of bones; often used to detect cancer or bone diseases.

single-photon absorptiometry.definition: A test using gamma rays to measure bone density, usually in the forearm.

dual-photon absorptiometry.definition: An older radiologic technique that estimates bone mineral content by transmitting photons at two different energies through bone and comparing their differential attenuation, typically used to measure bone mineral density at peripheral sites and largely superseded by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA).

dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry.definition: A radiologic technique that uses two-energy X-ray beams to differentiate bone from soft tissue and quantify bone mineral density, typically in the hip and lumbar spine; it is the standard method for diagnosing osteoporosis and assessing fracture risk, with results usually reported as T-scores and Z-scores.

quantitative computed tomography.definition: A modification of computed tomography that provides measurements of bone mass as well as an image.

radiographic absorptiometry.definition: An imaging method that estimates bone mineral density/content by measuring X‑ray attenuation through a bone (often the hand or distal radius) and comparing it to calibration standards; historically used but largely replaced by dual‑energy X‑ray absorptiometry (DXA).

quantitative ultrasound.definition: A set of ultrasound techniques that convert raw ultrasound signals into numerical tissue parameters (such as speed of sound, attenuation, backscatter, and scatterer-related metrics) to characterize tissue properties and detect pathology. Often used in bone densitometry and general tissue characterization.

bone turnover.definition: An ongoing process of bone remodeling in which existing bone is resorbed by osteoclasts and new bone is formed by osteoblasts, maintaining bone mass, microarchitecture, and mineral homeostasis.

bone turnover biochemical markers.definition: Biochemical markers of bone turnover are substances released during bone formation or bone resorption that can be measured in blood or urine to reflect the rate of bone remodeling. Examples include formation markers such as osteocalcin, bone-specific alkaline phosphatase, and P1NP, and resorption markers such as CTX and NTX.

bone turnover markers.definition: Biochemical indicators measured in blood or urine that reflect the rate of bone formation and bone resorption, used to assess bone remodeling and monitor treatment of osteoporosis and other metabolic bone diseases.

paget’s disease.definition: A chronic bone remodeling disorder characterized by excessive osteoclastic bone resorption followed by disorganized osteoblastic bone formation, resulting in enlarged, deformed, and structurally weaker bones; commonly affects the pelvis, femur, spine, and skull.

osteitis fibrosa.definition: A bone disorder caused by chronic hyperparathyroidism in which excessive parathyroid hormone–driven osteoclastic resorption is followed by fibrous replacement of bone, leading to weakened bones and characteristic subperiosteal bone loss and brown tumor–type lesions.

osteitis fibrosa cystica.definition: A bone disorder caused by chronic excess parathyroid hormone (hyperparathyroidism) in which bone is excessively resorbed and replaced by fibrous tissue and cystic brown tumors, leading to bone pain, deformities, and fragility. Also historically known as von Recklinghausen disease of bone.

parathyroid disorder.definition: A group of conditions caused by abnormal function of the parathyroid glands, which regulate calcium and phosphorus levels through parathyroid hormone (PTH). Common examples include hyperparathyroidism (excess PTH with elevated calcium) and hypoparathyroidism (insufficient PTH with low calcium).

bone tumors.definition: A growth arising from bone tissue that can be benign (noncancerous) or malignant (cancerous); examples include benign osteochondroma and enchondroma, and malignant osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, and chondrosarcoma.

bornholm disease.definition: An acute viral illness caused by Coxsackie B enteroviruses, characterized by sudden, severe pleuritic chest or upper abdominal pain, often with fever and malaise; commonly affects children and is also known as epidemic pleurodynia, epidemic myalgia, or devil's grip.

epidemic pleurodynia.definition: A viral illness caused by Coxsackie B viruses, also known as Bornholm disease, presenting with sudden focal chest or upper abdominal pain with pleuritic quality and fever; common in children and outbreaks; typically self-limited with supportive care.

turner syndrome.definition: A condition where a person's X chromosome is missing or partly missing. Only occurs in females.

bonwill triangle.definition: A theoretical dental occlusion model in which the centers of the two mandibular condyles and the incisal point of the lower central incisors form an equilateral triangle, with each side about 4 inches (102 mm) long.

retinoscopy.definition: An objective eye exam procedure in which a retinoscope's light reflex is observed as it is swept across the pupil to estimate refractive error and guide lens prescription.

book retinoscopy.definition: A retinoscopy technique in which the patient views a near target (e.g., a book) during the examination to stimulate accommodation while the examiner observes the reflex to estimate near refractive error and the accommodative response.

meclizine.definition: An antihistamine (H1 receptor antagonist) used to prevent and treat nausea, vomiting, and dizziness caused by motion sickness or vertigo; it has anticholinergic effects and may cause drowsiness.

boric acid.definition: A weak, boron-containing inorganic acid (chemical formula H3BO3) used topically as an antiseptic and in ophthalmic preparations; also functions as a buffering agent in borate buffers and is toxic if ingested in significant amounts.

borate.definition: A salt or ester of boric acid; a boron–oxygen compound formed from boric acid (H3BO3), such as borax (sodium borate) or borate esters.

borax.definition: A white, crystalline sodium borate compound (Na2B4O7·10H2O). Not a medication; historically used as a laxative and antiseptic in some preparations, but toxicity limits medical use.

boric acid poisoning.definition: Boric acid poisoning is the toxic condition produced by exposure to boric acid (H3BO3), most often from ingestion, presenting with gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea), dehydration and electrolyte disturbances, and potentially neurologic symptoms (headache, confusion, tremors, seizures), renal impairment, and metabolic disturbances; management is supportive with decontamination and close monitoring, as there is no specific antidote.

bordetella bronchiseptica.definition: Small Gram-negative coccobacillus; an animal respiratory pathogen (notably kennel cough in dogs) that can act as an opportunistic human pathogen, causing bronchitis or pneumonia in immunocompromised individuals and colonizing the upper respiratory tract.

bordetella parapertussis.definition: An aerobic Gram-negative coccobacillus of the Bordetella genus that causes parapertussis, a milder, pertussis-like respiratory illness in humans; transmitted via respiratory droplets; diagnosed by culture on selective media or PCR and treated with macrolide antibiotics.

bordetella pertussis.definition: A Gram-negative, encapsulated coccobacillus that causes pertussis (whooping cough) in humans; transmitted via respiratory droplets and colonizes the respiratory tract, leading to severe paroxysmal coughing, especially in infants and unvaccinated individuals.

irritability.definition: A tendency to become easily irritated or annoyed; in physiology, the inherent responsiveness of tissue or nerves to a stimulus.

high-pitched cry.definition: A shrill, piercing cry in an infant or child, reflecting severe distress or neurologic irritation; not specific and may indicate central nervous system pathology (e.g., meningitis, encephalopathy) or other serious illness, warranting urgent evaluation.

hyperthermia.definition: An abnormally high body temperature resulting from external heat or impaired heat dissipation, not caused by fever; often due to environmental heat exposure or conditions such as heat stroke, malignant hyperthermia, or drug-induced hyperthermia, and requiring rapid cooling and supportive care.

vitamin k.definition: A fat-soluble vitamin essential for the gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues on clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X and on proteins C and S, enabling normal blood coagulation; it also supports bone metabolism by activating osteocalcin and matrix Gla protein. Deficiency causes bleeding diathesis and can lead to hemorrhagic disease in newborns, with risk increased in fat malabsorption and prolonged antibiotic use; warfarin antagonizes its action.

silver nitrate.definition: An inorganic silver salt (AgNO3) used topically as a caustic agent and antiseptic, applied to tissue for chemical cautery and historically for neonatal conjunctival prophylaxis.

newborn.definition: A newborn (neonate) is a human infant in the first 28 days after birth.

congenital defect.definition: A structural or functional abnormality present at birth, arising from abnormal prenatal development.

cord stump.definition: The dried residual portion of the umbilical cord attached to a newborn after birth, which typically dries and falls off within 1–3 weeks; keep the area clean and dry to prevent infection.

epiphyseal.definition: Relating to the epiphysis, the end portion of a long bone; specifically to the epiphyseal (growth) plate between the epiphysis and diaphysis that enables longitudinal bone growth in children.

infant botulism.definition: Infant botulism is a form of botulism in which Clostridium botulinum spores colonize the infant’s immature gut and produce toxin in vivo, causing a symmetric descending flaccid weakness with features such as hypotonia, poor suck and cry, constipation, and potentially respiratory failure; it typically affects infants up to about 12 months, and treatment consists of supportive care with botulism immune globulin (BIG-IV).

food-borne botulism.definition: A rare, life-threatening illness caused by ingesting botulinum neurotoxin produced by Clostridium botulinum in improperly processed or stored foods; it causes symmetric descending flaccid paralysis beginning with cranial nerve palsies (e.g., diplopia, ptosis, dysarthria) and can progress to respiratory failure. Treatment includes prompt administration of botulinum antitoxin and supportive care.

wound botulism.definition: Wound botulism is a form of botulism caused by infection of a wound with Clostridium botulinum that produces botulinum toxin in situ, leading to symmetric cranial nerve dysfunction and descending flaccid paralysis, potentially causing respiratory failure.

botulinum toxin.definition: A potent neurotoxin produced by Clostridium botulinum that blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction by cleaving SNARE proteins, causing flaccid paralysis; used in small doses for cosmetic and therapeutic indications.

trivalent botulinal antitoxin.definition: A horse-derived antitoxin preparation containing antibodies to botulinum neurotoxins types A, B, and E, used to neutralize circulating toxin in botulism.

bourneville's disease.definition: A genetic neurocutaneous disorder (tuberous sclerosis complex) with multiple hamartomas in the brain, skin, kidneys, heart, and other organs; commonly presents with seizures, developmental delay/intellectual disability, ash-leaf hypomelanotic patches, facial angiofibromas, and renal angiomyolipomas.

tuberous sclerosis.definition: Genetic neurocutaneous disorder causing benign hamartomas in multiple organs (especially brain, skin, kidneys, heart, and lungs) due to TSC1 or TSC2 mutations; commonly presents with seizures, developmental delay or autism, and characteristic skin findings plus organ hamartomas.

bouchard's node.definition: A bony enlargement of the proximal interphalangeal joints of the fingers, commonly due to osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease) with osteophyte formation.

heberden's node.definition: A hard bony enlargement at the distal interphalangeal joint (DIP) due to osteophyte formation in osteoarthritis of the hand.

boston exanthema.definition: A historical term for a self-limited viral exanthem described in children in Boston; the exact causative agent is uncertain and the term is now largely obsolete.

exanthema.definition: A widespread erythematous skin eruption that accompanies a systemic illness, most commonly a viral infection.

borrelia burgdorferi.definition: A spirochete bacterium transmitted by Ixodes ticks and the primary etiologic agent of Lyme disease in humans.

borrelia.definition: A genus of Gram-negative, corkscrew-shaped (spirochete) bacteria transmitted by arthropods (primarily ticks; some species by lice); includes species such as Borrelia burgdorferi, the primary cause of Lyme disease, and others that cause relapsing fever.

back pain.definition: Pain localized to the back (cervical, thoracic, or lumbar region) that may result from musculoskeletal strain, degenerative spine conditions, nerve compression, fracture, infection, or other pathology. It can be acute or chronic; most episodes improve with conservative care, though persistent or red-flag symptoms require medical evaluation.

peripheral neuropathy.definition: Damage to the long nerves radiating from the spine to the arms and legs.

rigors.definition: An episode of intense shivering with a rising fever, typically due to acute infection; caused by pyrogen-induced resetting of the body's hypothalamic temperature set point.

cardiac sphincter.definition: A circular band of smooth muscle at the gastroesophageal junction (lower esophageal sphincter) that maintains tonic contraction to prevent reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus; it relaxes transiently to allow swallowing.

soft palate.definition: The velum is the flexible, muscular posterior part of the palate that separates the oral cavity from the nasopharynx; it elevates to close the nasopharynx during swallowing and speech, preventing nasal regurgitation and aiding resonance.

maculopapules.definition: Lesions on the skin that include both flat, discolored patches (macules) and small, raised bumps (papules). Often used to describe a maculopapular rash.

erythematous.definition: Relating to or characterized by redness of the skin due to dilation of superficial blood vessels, often from inflammation, irritation, or infection.

diplopia.definition: Happens when your eyes do not work together, so you see 2 images of the same thing. Also called double vision.

pupillary light reflex.definition: A reflex that causes the pupil to constrict in response to bright light; mediated by the afferent optic pathway (CN II) and the efferent oculomotor pathway (CN III) to the sphincter pupillae, producing both direct and consensual constriction.

cardiac disease.definition: A broad category of diseases that affect the heart's structure or function, including coronary artery disease, heart failure, arrhythmias, valvular disease, and cardiomyopathies.

boutonneuse fever.definition: A tick-borne rickettsial infection caused by Rickettsia conorii, transmitted by the dog tick (Rhipicephalus sanguineus); characterized by fever, severe headache and myalgias, a maculopapular rash (often trunk-to-extremities), and commonly an inoculation eschar at the bite site.

rickett s ia conorii.definition: An obligate intracellular, Gram-negative bacterium of the spotted fever group that causes Mediterranean spotted fever (boutonneuse fever); transmitted by ticks and typically presenting with fever, headache, malaise, rash, and a necrotic inoculation eschar at the bite site.

rickettsia conorii.definition: A Gram-negative, obligate intracellular bacterium transmitted by ticks that causes Mediterranean spotted fever, presenting with fever, headache, rash, and an inoculation eschar; treated with doxycycline.

tache noire.definition: A black necrotic skin lesion (an eschar): a dark, devitalized crust or spot resulting from tissue death, commonly seen at the site of certain infections such as cutaneous anthrax.

black spot.definition: A dark, pigmented skin lesion resulting from melanin; most are benign (e.g., nevus or lentigo), but some may be malignant (melanoma) and should be evaluated if there are changes in size, shape, color, or if it bleeds or itches.

papular erythematous rash.definition: A skin eruption consisting of small, raised, red (erythematous) papules due to superficial skin inflammation; the rash is a descriptive finding seen in many conditions (e.g., dermatitis, viral exanthems, drug eruptions) rather than a single diagnosis.

rickettsial disease.definition: An illness caused by obligate intracellular, gram-negative bacteria of the order Rickettsiales (e.g., Rickettsia, Orientia), transmitted to humans by arthropod vectors such as ticks, fleas, lice, or mites; typically presents with fever, headache, and rash and is treated with doxycycline.

boutonniere deformity.definition: A finger deformity in which the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint is flexed and the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint is hyperextended, caused by injury to the extensor mechanism (central slip) at the PIP joint; commonly treated with immobilization of the PIP in extension (often with a PIP extension splint) for several weeks, with surgical repair considered for chronic cases.

erythroplasia ofqueyrat.definition: A form of penile intraepithelial neoplasia (carcinoma in situ) presenting as a red, velvety patch or plaque on the glans penis (often involving the foreskin), associated with high-risk human papillomavirus infection and with potential to progress to invasive squamous cell carcinoma if untreated.

erythroplasia of queyrat.definition: A penile carcinoma in situ (high-grade intraepithelial neoplasia) involving the glans and/or foreskin, presenting as a red, velvet-like patch; commonly HPV-associated, with potential progression to invasive squamous cell carcinoma if untreated.

bowens disease.definition: An intraepidermal squamous cell carcinoma of the skin (SCC in situ), presenting as a persistent, slowly enlarging, scaly or crusted erythematous patch or plaque on sun-exposed areas; it can progress to invasive squamous cell carcinoma if untreated.

bowenoid papulosis.definition: An HPV-associated, sexually transmitted condition presenting as multiple pigmented genital papules, histologically resembling Bowen disease (squamous cell carcinoma in situ); considered a premalignant lesion with a potential, though low, risk of progression to invasive cancer.

bowen technique.definition: A gentle manual therapy in which the practitioner uses light, precise fingertip moves over muscles and fascia with brief pauses, aiming to stimulate the body's healing response and relieve musculoskeletal pain; typically performed with the client clothed and in a relaxed position, though high-quality evidence supporting its effectiveness is limited.

bovine spongiform encephalopathy.definition: A fatal prion disease of cattle causing progressive neurodegeneration with sponge-like vacuolation in brain tissue; caused by misfolded prion proteins and linked to human variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease after exposure to contaminated beef.

bovine tuberculosis.definition: A chronic infectious disease of cattle caused by Mycobacterium bovis, a member of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, characterized by granulomatous lesions in the lungs and regional lymph nodes; transmission occurs mainly by inhalation of aerosols from infected animals or ingestion of contaminated milk or dairy products; it is a zoonosis that can infect humans.

scrapie.definition: A fatal prion disease of sheep and goats; a transmissible spongiform encephalopathy caused by misfolded prion proteins (PrPSc) that leads to progressive neurodegeneration, with clinical signs such as pruritus (scratching), ataxia, and behavioral changes; transmitted via exposure to infected tissues or placental material; no cure or vaccine is available, and it is not known to infect humans.

creutzfeldt-jakob disease.definition: A rare, untreatable, rapid form of dementia that is fatal.

cjd.definition: A rare, untreatable, rapid form of dementia that is fatal.

mad cow disease.definition: A fatal prion disease of cattle causing neurodegeneration and sponge-like changes in the brain; transmission to humans through contaminated beef can cause variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

inflammatory bowel disease.definition: A group of chronic illnesses where your intestines are very painful and swollen. The two most common kinds are ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease.

bowel bypass syndrome.definition: An informal or nonstandard term referring to complications that may occur after surgically bypassing a portion of the bowel (as in certain bariatric procedures), typically involving malabsorption, chronic diarrhea or steatorrhea, nutritional deficiencies, electrolyte disturbances, dehydration, and weight loss.

bowel continence.definition: The ability to retain stool and gas and to control the timing of defecation, requiring intact anal sphincter function, pelvic floor muscles, and rectal sensation to prevent involuntary leakage.

bowel elimination.definition: The physiological process of expelling feces from the gastrointestinal tract through the rectum and anus (defecation), involving stool formation in the colon, rectal sensation and peristalsis, and coordinated relaxation of the anal sphincters to evacuate waste.

bowel incontinence.definition: An involuntary loss of stool or leakage arising from impaired anal sphincter or pelvic floor function, nerve damage, diarrhea, constipation with overflow, or other rectal diseases; severity ranges from minor leakage to complete loss of bowel control.

encopresis.definition: Repeated passage of feces in inappropriate places by a child who is at least 4 years old, not due to a medical illness; often linked to chronic constipation/overflow (fecal impaction) and may be primary (never attained daytime fecal continence) or secondary (loss of continence after a period of control).

bowel irrigation.definition: A procedure in which the intestines are flushed with large volumes of liquid (often isotonic saline or a polyethylene glycol solution) via the rectum to cleanse the colon of feces, typically used for colonoscopy preparation, relief of fecal impaction, or temporary bowel cleansing before or after certain medical procedures.

bowel management.definition: A structured, individualized program to regulate bowel function and prevent constipation, impaction, and incontinence. It typically includes scheduled bowel routines, hydration and fiber management, and the use of laxatives or stool softeners, stimulant agents, digital stimulation, and rectal evacuations.

bowel resection.definition: A surgical procedure in which a diseased or damaged segment of the bowel (small or large intestine) is removed and the remaining ends are reconnected (anastomosis).

reanastomosed.definition: To surgically form a new connection (anastomosis) between two tubular structures after a prior connection has been disrupted or revised.

autonomic hyperreflexia.definition: A life-threatening syndrome in people with spinal cord injury above the T6 level, caused by an unregulated sympathetic response to noxious stimuli below the level of injury (e.g., bladder distension, bowel impaction). It presents with abrupt, severe hypertension, headache, flushing above the lesion, sweating below the lesion, nasal congestion, and often bradycardia; immediate management includes removing the trigger, sitting the patient up to lower blood pressure, and treating hypertension as needed.

paroxysmal hypertension.definition: A syndrome of sudden, recurrent episodes of markedly elevated blood pressure with abrupt onset and spontaneous resolution, typically lasting minutes to hours, often accompanied by autonomic symptoms such as headache, sweating, tachycardia, flushing or pallor, and anxiety. Diagnosis is by exclusion after pheochromocytoma and other secondary causes have been ruled out; treatment focuses on mitigating episodes and addressing potential triggers such as stress or anxiety, with antihypertensive or anxiolytic therapy as needed.

laxative suppository.definition: A rectally inserted laxative medication that stimulates bowel movements or softens stool to relieve constipation; examples include glycerin and bisacodyl suppositories, which act locally in the rectum and typically produce an effect within minutes to an hour.

glycerin suppository.definition: A rectal laxative suppository containing glycerin that draws water into the stool, softening it and stimulating bowel movement; typically produces evacuation within about 15–60 minutes.

retention enema.definition: An enema in which a small volume of solution is instilled into the rectum and retained for several minutes to soften or lubricate stool and facilitate defecation, or to allow local absorption of administered medications.

oil retention enema.definition: A retention enema in which oil (typically mineral oil) is inserted into the rectum and retained to soften stool and lubricate the anal canal, thereby facilitating defecation in constipation.

tap water enema.definition: An irrigation enema using clean tap water as the cleansing solution, introduced into the rectum to soften stool and induce bowel movement; used to treat constipation or for bowel preparation; excessive use or high volumes can lead to electrolyte imbalance or water intoxication.

enema.definition: A medical procedure in which liquid or gas is introduced into the rectum via the anus to stimulate bowel movement, cleanse the colon, or administer medications.

bowel training.definition: A program to establish regular, predictable bowel movements by training the patient to defecate at scheduled times (often after meals) using behavioral strategies, dietary fiber and fluids, and, if needed, laxatives or stool-regulating techniques; aimed at reducing constipation and/or fecal incontinence.

bowel urgency.definition: A sudden, compelling urge to defecate that is difficult to defer, sometimes with leakage of stool; a symptom commonly associated with diarrhea, irritable bowel syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease, and other colorectal conditions.

bowman capsule.definition: A cup-shaped portion of the nephron that surrounds the glomerulus, forming the renal corpuscle; it collects the filtrate produced by the glomerular capillaries into a central space and channels it into the proximal tubule, and comprises an inner visceral layer with podocytes and an outer parietal layer.

bowman lamina.definition: An acellular, collagenous layer of the cornea located between the epithelial basement membrane and the stroma; it provides structural support and a barrier, but damaged this layer does not regenerate readily (thickness ~8–14 micrometers).

bowman glands.definition: Exocrine serous glands in the lamina propria of the olfactory mucosa that secrete a watery mucus to dissolve odorants, moisturize, and protect the olfactory epithelium (often containing antimicrobial enzymes).

bowman membrane.definition: An acellular, collagen-rich layer of the cornea lying between the epithelial basement membrane and the stroma; it forms the anterior limiting layer of the cornea and does not regenerate after injury.

glomerular capsule.definition: A cup-shaped membranous structure surrounding the glomerulus in the nephron that collects the filtrate produced by the glomerular capillaries (Bowman's capsule).

proximal tubule.definition: A segment of the nephron in the kidney (the part after Bowman's capsule, comprising the proximal convoluted and proximal straight tubules) in the renal cortex; lined by brush-border cuboidal cells, it reabsorbs the majority of filtered solutes and water (approximately 65–70% of Na+, Cl−, and water, and nearly all glucose and amino acids), reabsorbs bicarbonate, and secretes certain organic acids and bases, playing a key role in acid–base and fluid–electrolyte balance.

distal tubule.definition: A segment of the nephron in the renal cortex between the loop of Henle and the collecting duct; it reabsorbs sodium and chloride (via the Na-Cl cotransporter) and calcium (influenced by parathyroid hormone), secretes potassium and hydrogen ions, and is relatively impermeable to water, contributing to urine dilution.

efferent arteriole.definition: A small renal arteriole that carries blood away from the glomerulus after filtration; typically narrower than the afferent arteriole, it maintains high glomerular capillary pressure and helps regulate glomerular filtration rate, draining into the peritubular capillaries or vasa recta depending on nephron type.

afferent arteriole.definition: A small renal artery that delivers blood to the glomerulus; it arises from a renal artery, forms the glomerular capillary tuft, and drains into the efferent arteriole. Its caliber helps regulate glomerular filtration rate through autoregulation.

interlobar artery.definition: A renal artery branch that runs through the renal columns between the renal pyramids, supplying the kidney and giving rise to the arcuate arteries at the corticomedullary junction.

interlobar vein.definition: A vein draining a renal lobe, running in the renal columns between the renal pyramids and joining the renal vein.

arcuate artery.definition: An artery that travels along the corticomedullary (cortical-medullary) junction of the kidney, parallel to the bases of the renal pyramids; it arises from an interlobar artery and gives off the cortical radiate (interlobular) arteries to supply the renal cortex.

arcuate vein.definition: A vein that runs along the corticomedullary junction of the kidney, accompanying the arcuate artery, and drains blood from the renal cortex into the interlobar veins.

descending limb.definition: The portion of the loop of Henle that descends into the renal medulla; highly permeable to water but relatively impermeable to solutes, so water is reabsorbed and tubular fluid becomes more concentrated as it descends, helping establish the medullary osmotic gradient.

ascending limb.definition: Part of the loop of Henle in the nephron; the thick ascending limb reabsorbs sodium, potassium, and chloride ions via the NKCC symporter and is impermeable to water, thereby diluting the tubular fluid and helping establish the medullary osmotic gradient.

nephron loop.definition: A U-shaped segment of a nephron in the kidney with descending and ascending limbs; it concentrates urine by countercurrent multiplication, reabsorbing water in the descending limb and solutes (notably Na+, K+, and Cl−) in the thick ascending limb to create and maintain a hyperosmotic medullary gradient.

innominate artery.definition: First branch of the aortic arch that bifurcates to form the right common carotid artery and the right subclavian artery.

innominate vein.definition: A large central vein formed by the union of the internal jugular and subclavian veins on each side; the right and left brachiocephalic veins unite to form the superior vena cava and drain blood from the head, neck, upper limbs, and upper thorax.

brachiocephalic trunk.definition: A short artery arising from the right side of the aortic arch that immediately bifurcates into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries, supplying the right head, neck, and upper limb. Also known as the innominate artery.

brachiocubital.definition: Relating to the upper arm (brachium) and the elbow region (cubital); describing structures or areas located in the arm–elbow region.

brachial plexus.definition: A network of nerves that are rooted at the cervical spine and provide sensation and movement to the shoulder and arm.

brachial plexus anesthesia.definition: A regional anesthesia technique in which a local anesthetic is injected around the brachial plexus nerves (e.g., interscalene, supraclavicular, infraclavicular, or axillary blocks) to produce anesthesia and sometimes motor blockade of the upper limb for surgical procedures and postoperative analgesia, often avoiding general anesthesia.

brachial plexus block.definition: A regional anesthesia technique in which local anesthetic is injected near the brachial plexus to produce sensory and motor block of the upper limb for shoulder, arm, forearm, or hand procedures; commonly performed via interscalene, supraclavicular, infraclavicular, or axillary approaches, often with ultrasound guidance, and with potential complications including pneumothorax, hematoma, nerve injury, and systemic local anesthetic toxicity.

horner syndrome.definition: A disorder caused by interruption of the oculosympathetic (sympathetic) pathway to the eye, resulting in ipsilateral ptosis (drooping eyelid), miosis (constricted pupil), and often facial anhidrosis; can be congenital or acquired from lesions such as carotid artery dissection or apical lung (Pancoast) tumor along the sympathetic chain.

phrenic nerve block.definition: A regional anesthesia technique in which local anesthetic is injected near the phrenic nerve to temporarily block its motor and sensory function, causing ipsilateral diaphragmatic paralysis and providing analgesia for thoracic procedures; respiratory function may be affected.

recurrent laryngeal paralysis.definition: Paralysis of the intrinsic laryngeal muscles innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, leading to immobility of one or both vocal cords; unilateral involvement typically causes hoarseness and dysphonia, while bilateral involvement can cause airway obstruction and dyspnea. Causes include nerve injury from surgery, tumor, trauma, infection/inflammation, or neuropathy.

persistent sensory deficits.definition: A lasting impairment or loss of sensation in a region due to damage to peripheral nerves or central pathways, with modalities such as touch, pain, temperature, vibration, or proprioception remaining reduced or absent beyond the expected recovery period.

venous puncture.definition: A procedure in which a needle is inserted into a vein to obtain a blood sample or to administer medications or fluids.

arterial puncture.definition: A puncture of an artery with a needle to obtain arterial blood samples (often for arterial blood gas analysis) or to place an arterial line for monitoring; it carries risks such as bleeding, hematoma, infection, thrombosis, or arterial injury.

subarachnoid injection.definition: Administration of a substance directly into the cerebrospinal fluid by injecting into the subarachnoid space (between the arachnoid and pia mater), typically via lumbar puncture; used for spinal anesthesia or intrathecal analgesia, and for certain diagnostic or therapeutic injections.

erbs palsy.definition: An injury to the upper part of the brachial plexus (typically C5–C6), causing weakness or paralysis of the shoulder and elbow muscles; classically presents with an adducted, internally rotated arm and extended elbow (waiter’s tip), most often due to birth trauma or traction injury, with recovery varying from spontaneous improvement to requiring therapy or surgery.

erb palsy.definition: A brachial plexus injury of the upper trunk (C5–C6) causing weakness or paralysis of the shoulder and elbow flexors (notably deltoid and biceps), resulting in the arm held adducted and internally rotated with the elbow extended and forearm pronated—the classic "waiter's tip" posture; most often from traction on the neck during childbirth (neonatal) or acute trauma.

brachial pulse.definition: The palpable arterial pulse of the brachial artery, usually felt in the antecubital fossa; used to assess heart rate and rhythm, peripheral perfusion, and as the site for cuff-based blood pressure measurement.

brachial vein.definition: Paired deep veins of the upper arm that accompany the brachial artery (veinæ comitantes); they drain the arm’s deep tissues and typically join with the basilic vein to form the axillary vein.

suprascapular nerve.definition: A branch of the brachial plexus (mainly C5–C6) that innervates the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles and provides sensory innervation to the shoulder joint.

subclavian nerve.definition: A motor branch of the brachial plexus (nerve to subclavius) that arises from the upper trunk (C5–C6) and innervates the subclavius muscle, helping depress and stabilize the clavicle during shoulder movements.

axillary nerve.definition: Branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus (C5–C6) that winds around the surgical neck of the humerus; motor to the deltoid and teres minor; sensory to the skin over the lateral/superolateral shoulder (regimental badge area); provides articular branches to the shoulder joint.

radial nerve.definition: A major peripheral nerve of the upper limb arising from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus (C5–T1). It travels in the radial groove with the profunda brachii vessels, supplying the posterior compartments of the arm and forearm (including the triceps brachii and forearm extensors) and providing cutaneous sensation to the posterior arm, forearm, and dorsum of the hand; near the elbow it divides into a superficial (sensory to the dorsum of the hand) and a deep/posterior interosseous branch (motor to most forearm extensors).

median nerve.definition: A major nerve of the upper limb derived from C5–T1 ventral rami of the brachial plexus, formed from contributions of the lateral and medial cords. It travels through the arm and forearm, innervating most of the forearm flexors and several intrinsic hand muscles, and provides sensory innervation to the palmar surface of the lateral three-and-a-half digits (and dorsal fingertips). It passes through the carpal tunnel at the wrist and may be compressed in carpal tunnel syndrome.

ulnar nerve.definition: A major peripheral nerve of the upper limb arising from the medial cord of the brachial plexus (C8–T1) that supplies motor innervation to most intrinsic hand muscles and to the flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of the flexor digitorum profundus, and sensory innervation to the medial one-and-a-half digits; it runs along the medial aspect of the arm and enters the hand through the wrist via Guyon’s canal.

musculocutaneous nerve.definition: Motor and sensory nerve of the upper limb arising from the brachial plexus (C5–C7) that innervates the anterior arm muscles (coracobrachialis, biceps brachii, brachialis) and continues as the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve to provide sensation on the lateral forearm; it facilitates elbow flexion and forearm supination.

long thoracic nerve.definition: A motor nerve arising from the C5–C7 roots of the brachial plexus that innervates the serratus anterior muscle; injury can cause scapular winging.

medial brachial cutaneous nerve.definition: A cutaneous nerve arising from the medial cord of the brachial plexus (C8–T1) that provides sensory innervation to the medial aspect of the upper arm (from the axilla to the elbow).

medial and lateral pectoral nerves.definition:
- Medial pectoral nerve: A branch of the medial cord (C8–T1) of the brachial plexus that provides motor innervation to the pectoralis minor and, typically, to the sternocostal part of the pectoralis major (often piercing pectoralis minor to reach pectoralis major).

- Lateral pectoral nerve: A branch of the lateral cord (C5–C7) of the brachial plexus that supplies motor innervation to the pectoralis major (clavicular and sternocostal heads) and does not innervate the pectoralis minor.

brachioradialis.definition: A muscle of the forearm that flexes the elbow; it originates from the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus and inserts on the distal radius at the radial styloid process. It is most active when the forearm is in a neutral (midpronated) position and is innervated by the radial nerve (C5–C7).

transverse processes.definition: The ringlike projection on each side of a vertebra to which muscles and ligaments are attached and, in the chest area, to which the ribs are connected.

boxers fracture.definition: Fracture of the neck of the fifth metacarpal bone of the hand, typically caused by punching a hard object with a clenched fist; presents with swelling and angular deformity of the little finger due to palmar (volar) displacement of the distal fragment.

pachyotia.definition: A nonstandard or rare term suggesting thickening of ear structures (thickened ear tissue or ear canal); derived from pachy- meaning thick and ot- meaning ear, but not a widely recognized medical diagnosis in standard references. If you meant pachyostosis (bone thickening) or pachyderma (thick skin), those are established terms.

brachioradialis reflex.definition: A deep tendon reflex elicited by tapping the brachioradialis tendon at the distal forearm with the forearm in a neutral position; the normal response is elbow flexion (often with slight forearm rotation), mediated primarily by the C5–C6 nerve roots.

cervical vertebra.definition: A vertebra in the cervical region of the spine (the neck); one of seven cervical vertebrae (C1–C7) that support the skull and enable head movement, with C1 (atlas) and C2 (axis) having specialized anatomy for nodding and rotation.

parkinson\u001fs disease.definition: A movement disorder that occurs when the brain does not produce enough of a chemical.

cerebral hemorrhage.definition: A hemorrhagic stroke caused by rupture of a blood vessel in the brain, resulting in bleeding into brain tissue.

brain concussion.definition: A head injury caused by a big impact or shaking.

brain death.definition: Irreversible loss of all brain function, including brainstem, diagnosed by clinical criteria (unresponsiveness, absence of brainstem reflexes, and apnea) and often supported by ancillary testing; it constitutes legal death in many jurisdictions.

brain edema.definition: Swelling of brain tissue caused by abnormal fluid accumulation, leading to increased intracranial pressure and risk of brain herniation; commonly due to trauma, stroke, infection, tumor, or metabolic disturbances and classified as cytotoxic or vasogenic.

intracranial abscess.definition: A localized, pus-filled collection within the intracranial contents (usually the brain parenchyma) caused by bacterial infection, often from contiguous spread or hematogenous seeding, typically with a surrounding capsule and presenting with focal neurological deficits and increased intracranial pressure.

glioma.definition: A neoplasm arising from glial cells of the brain or spinal cord; includes astrocytomas, oligodendrogliomas, and ependymomas; typically infiltrative and graded by malignancy (low-grade to high-grade), with treatment guided by histology and grade.

medulloblastoma.definition: A malignant cerebellar primitive neuroectodermal tumor; the most common malignant brain tumor in children, often presenting with gait ataxia and truncal imbalance, with a tendency to disseminate via cerebrospinal fluid, treated with surgical resection followed by craniospinal irradiation and chemotherapy.

gliomas.definition: A group of primary brain tumors arising from glial cells (astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, or ependymal cells). They are typically infiltrative and range from low-grade lesions (WHO grades I–II) to highly malignant tumors (e.g., glioblastoma, WHO grade IV).

astrocytomas.definition: A type of glial tumor arising from astrocytes in the central nervous system, typically in the brain; it ranges from low-grade, slow-growing lesions to high-grade, aggressive tumors such as glioblastoma, and commonly presents with headaches, seizures, or focal neurologic deficits.

medulloblastomas.definition: A highly malignant cerebellar tumor of childhood, classified as a primitive neuroectodermal tumor of the posterior fossa; histologically consists of densely packed small round blue cells often with Homer-Wright rosettes and has a tendency to disseminate via cerebrospinal fluid.

brain scan.definition: An imaging study of the brain (most commonly a CT or MRI) used to visualize brain structure and identify injury, stroke, tumors, or other abnormalities.

beta wave.definition: A fast EEG brain wave with a frequency of approximately 12–30 Hz, associated with wakeful, alert, and cognitively active states; typically of low amplitude and desynchronized activity, often most prominent in frontal regions.

gamma wave.definition: A high-frequency brain oscillation in EEG/MEG signals, typically 30–100 Hz, associated with attention, perception, and working memory, reflecting synchronized activity of cortical neuronal assemblies.

kappa wave.definition: Not a standard term in medical references; there is no widely accepted definition. If you meant something else, please provide context (e.g., EEG/sleep, immunology, radiology) and I can give the closest defined concept (for example, a K-complex in EEG during stage 2 sleep).

theta wave.definition: An EEG brain rhythm in the 4–7 Hz range (theta range), typically seen during drowsiness and light sleep, and associated with memory encoding and spatial navigation (notably in the hippocampus).

brain attack.definition: A medical emergency in which blood flow to a part of the brain is interrupted or reduced, causing brain tissue injury or death; most often due to an ischemic event (arterial blockage) or a hemorrhagic event (bleeding).

craniostenosis.definition: Premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures, causing restricted skull growth and an abnormal skull shape; may lead to increased intracranial pressure and potential neurodevelopmental issues, and can occur as an isolated condition or as part of craniosynostosis syndromes.

brachycephaly.definition: A skull shape characterized by a shortened front-to-back (anterior-posterior) dimension with a broad, short appearance; may result from premature fusion of the cranial sutures (craniosynostosis) or from positional molding in infancy.

brachycephalia.definition: A skull shape in which the head is shorter from front to back and broader from side to side, resulting in a short, wide head; may be due to premature closure of cranial sutures (craniosynostosis) or positional molding.

brachycephalism.definition: A condition of the skull characterized by a shortened front-to-back length and increased breadth, producing a short, broad head (brachycephaly); can result from premature fusion of cranial sutures or deformational factors.

brachycephalic.definition: A skull shape that is broad and short from front to back (high cephalic index); in humans, generally defined as a cephalic index around 80 or higher, opposite of dolichocephalic.

brachycephalous.definition: Having a short, broad skull; a cranial shape with a high cephalic index (usually CI > 80%).

micrognathia.definition: An abnormally small mandible (lower jaw) that can be present at birth, often producing retrognathia, dental crowding, and possible airway or feeding difficulties; it can be an isolated finding or part of syndromes such as Pierre Robin sequence or Treacher Collins.

brachygnathia.definition: A condition in which the jaws are abnormally short relative to the skull, causing dental malocclusion; commonly denotes a shortened mandible that can produce a functional underbite.

brachytherapy.definition: Treatment in which a surgeon implants seeds or pellets of radioactive material in the body to destroy cancer cells.

teletherapy.definition: The remote delivery of psychotherapy or counseling services using telecommunications technology (most commonly real-time video conferencing) to allow clinicians and patients to connect remotely for therapy sessions.

pet.definition: A nuclear medicine imaging modality that uses radiolabeled tracers to visualize metabolic activity and function in tissues; it detects gamma rays produced by positron annihilation to create functional images, usually fused with CT or MRI for anatomical localization. Widely used in oncology, neurology, and cardiology to assess tumors, brain function, and myocardial viability.

electroencephalograms.definition: A recording of the brain's electrical activity obtained via scalp electrodes during electroencephalography (EEG); used to evaluate brain function and diagnose conditions such as epilepsy, sleep disorders, and encephalopathies.

spinal fluid.definition: A clear, colorless fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord; produced mainly by the choroid plexuses, it circulates within the ventricular system and subarachnoid space to cushion the CNS, provide buoyancy, and maintain chemical balance while removing metabolic waste.

papilledema.definition: A swelling of the optic disc (optic nerve head) due to increased intracranial pressure, typically affecting both eyes and indicating intracranial pathology that requires urgent evaluation.

visual field.definition: The full scope of what the eye sees; includes central and peripheral vision.

funduscopic examination.definition: An examination of the interior surface of the eye (fundus) using an ophthalmoscope to assess the retina, optic disc, macula, and retinal vessels for signs of disease.

cranial nerves.definition: Twelve paired nerves that arise directly from the brain and brainstem, supplying sensory and motor innervation to the head and neck and mediating the special senses, somatic motor functions, and autonomic activities.

occipital neoplasm.definition: A tumor located in the occipital region, arising from the occipital bone or occipital cortex, which may be benign or malignant.

sick sinus syndrome.definition: A group of sinoatrial node disorders causing abnormal heart rates due to SA node dysfunction, resulting in bradycardia, sinus pauses/arrests, and/or tachyarrhythmias (tachycardia-bradycardia syndrome); symptoms often include dizziness, syncope, or fatigue, especially in older adults, with pacemaker therapy commonly used for persistent bradycardia or symptomatic tachy-brady conditions.

bradyarrhythmia.definition: An abnormally slow heart rate caused by reduced electrical activity in the heart, often defined as a resting heart rate <60 bpm in adults; may result from sinus bradycardia, AV block, or other conduction disturbances and can cause dizziness, fatigue, or syncope.

bradykinesia.definition: A slowing of voluntary movement with reduced amplitude and difficulty initiating movements; a core feature of Parkinson disease and other movement disorders.

bradyphasia.definition: Slowness of speech production, including delayed initiation and reduced rate of verbal expression, often seen with Parkinsonian or other neurodegenerative/extrapyramidal disorders.

bradypnea.definition: A slower-than-normal respiratory rate, typically defined as fewer than 12 breaths per minute in adults.

bradyuria.definition: A slower-than-normal rate of urination (reduced urinary flow or delayed voiding), often resulting from urinary tract obstruction, detrusor underactivity, or neurogenic bladder dysfunction.

tachycardia-bradycardia syndrome.definition: A form of sick sinus syndrome characterized by alternating episodes of tachyarrhythmia (often atrial tachycardia or atrial fibrillation with rapid conduction) and bradycardia due to sinus node dysfunction or AV nodal conduction disease, commonly causing dizziness or syncope; management includes rhythm/rate control for tachyarrhythmias and often pacemaker implantation for persistent bradycardia.

atrioventricular block.definition: Disorder of cardiac conduction in which the electrical signal from the atria to the ventricles is delayed or blocked at the AV node or His-Purkinje system, producing bradycardia that ranges from asymptomatic to symptomatic (dizziness, syncope). It is classified by degree: first-degree (prolonged PR interval with 1:1 atrial-to-ventricular conduction), second-degree (intermittent non-conducted beats—Mobitz I/Wenckebach or Mobitz II with dropped beats and usually constant PR), and third-degree (complete AV dissociation with no atrial-to-ventricular conduction). Causes include ischemia/infarction, medications (e.g., beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers), degenerative conduction disease, myocarditis, and electrolyte disturbances. Management depends on degree and symptoms, from observation for benign first-degree blocks to pacemaker therapy for high-grade or symptomatic blocks.

digitalis toxicity.definition: Toxic effect from digitalis glycosides (most often digoxin) due to excess drug levels, presenting with GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, anorexia), CNS changes (confusion, weakness, visual disturbances such as blurred or yellow vision), and potentially dangerous cardiac arrhythmias or conduction abnormalities; management includes stopping the drug, correcting electrolytes, and, in severe cases, administering digoxin-specific antibody fragments.

breakthrough pain.definition: A transient flare of moderate to severe pain that occurs despite otherwise well-controlled baseline analgesia, typically with rapid onset and short duration, often in cancer patients, treated with a rescue dose of a fast-acting analgesic.

breakthrough analgesia.definition: An episodic flare of pain that occurs despite ongoing, baseline analgesia (e.g., regular opioid therapy); it is typically rapid-onset and short-lived and is treated with rescue analgesics.

breakthrough bleeding.definition: Vaginal bleeding that occurs outside the expected menstrual period, typically light and brief; it is commonly seen with hormonal fluctuations or estrogen-containing contraception and may also occur with pregnancy, perimenopause, or other conditions.

breakthrough dose.definition: An extra dose of a drug given to rapidly relieve symptoms that occur despite ongoing, regular dosing (commonly a rescue dose for breakthrough pain in patients on chronic opioid therapy).

branched-chain ketoaciduria.definition: An autosomal recessive metabolic disorder due to deficiency of the branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, causing accumulation of branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine) and their α-ketoacids in blood and urine, with infantile feeding difficulties, vomiting, lethargy, and a characteristic maple-syrup odor of the urine.

branched-chain amino acids.definition: An essential trio of amino acids—leucine, isoleucine, and valine—with branched aliphatic side chains; they cannot be synthesized by humans and are primarily metabolized in skeletal muscle, where they stimulate protein synthesis and provide energy, with leucine particularly activating mTOR signaling.

branchial arches.definition: A series of paired embryologic structures in the developing head and neck; each arch contains a mesenchymal core with an artery, a cranial nerve, a cartilage element, and muscle precursors, and they give rise to many facial, neck, and pharyngeal structures (typically six arches form in humans, with the fifth being rudimentary).

branchial cleft.definition: An embryologic ectodermal groove between the pharyngeal (branchial) arches that normally involutes during development; persistent remnants may form branchial cysts or fistulas.

branchial cyst.definition: A congenital epithelial or lymphoepithelial cyst in the lateral neck arising from residual branchial apparatus (most commonly the second branchial cleft); presents as a painless, slow-growing lateral neck mass in children or young adults and may become infected or form a sinus; management is complete surgical excision.

branchial fistula.definition: A congenital, persistent fistulous tract that connects the skin on the lateral neck to the oropharynx (often the tonsillar fossa), arising from incomplete involution of branchial apparatus remnants (most commonly the second branchial cleft).

cervical fistula.definition: An abnormal passage or tract between the cervix and another organ or surface (most commonly the vagina), through which fluids can pass; often due to obstetric injury, infection, surgery, or radiation.

branchial pouch.definition: An embryologic endoderm-lined outpocketing of the developing pharynx (the branchial apparatus) located between the pharyngeal arches; each pouch differentiates into specific head and neck structures (e.g., parts of the middle ear, tonsils, thymus, and parathyroid glands).

branchial remnant.definition: An embryologic residual tissue of the branchial (pharyngeal) apparatus in the neck, which may present as a congenital cyst, sinus, or fistula—most commonly a branchial cleft cyst.

branchio-oto-renal syndrome.definition: An autosomal dominant genetic disorder characterized by branchial cleft anomalies (cervical fistulas or cysts), outer/middle ear malformations with hearing loss, and renal anomalies (hypoplasia or dysplasia); most cases are due to mutations in EYA1, with additional cases linked to SIX1 or SIX5.

brandt-andrews maneuver.definition: Definition not found in standard medical dictionaries. If you mean the maneuver used to treat benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, it is a vestibular rehabilitation exercise in which the patient repeatedly moves from a seated position to lying on each side, holding briefly, to habituate vertigo and facilitate repositioning of canaliths. Would you like me to confirm spelling or provide a definition for Brandt–Daroff specifically?

braschi valve.definition: Not a recognized medical term; no standard definition available. It may be a misspelling or a term from a specific device or source. If you can share context (anatomical system, condition, or source) or confirm the spelling, I can provide a precise definition.

metal fume fever.definition: A self-limited febrile illness caused by inhalation of metal oxide fumes (most commonly zinc oxide) during welding or other metalworking; onset occurs within hours of exposure and is characterized by fever, chills, malaise, myalgias, cough, dyspnea, and headache, resolving within 24–48 hours after removal from exposure.

brassy cough.definition: A harsh, metallic-sounding cough caused by irritation or obstruction of the central airways (larynx/trachea); often described as "brassy" and may occur with laryngotracheal infections, croup, or airway lesions.

chalkitis.definition: Not a recognized medical term; there is no established condition by this name in standard medical references. If encountered, it is likely a misspelling, misnomer, or obsolete term.

braun's canal.definition: No widely recognized anatomical structure by this name appears in standard medical references; the term may be a misspelling or an obscure/nonstandard eponym. If you can provide the context (organ system, source, or spelling), I can help identify the correct term and definition.

brawny arm.definition: A thick, muscular arm with well-developed muscles (hypertrophy), often due to strength training; describes physical appearance rather than a pathology.

lymphedema.definition: A type of swelling that occurs when a type of fluid (lymph) builds up.

braxton hicks contractions.definition: Irregular, usually painless uterine contractions during pregnancy that do not cause progressive cervical dilation; often called "practice contractions" and typically subside with rest, hydration, or change in activity.

braxton hicks version.definition:
Not a standard term. Likely meant one of the following:

- Irregular, often painless uterine contractions that occur during pregnancy (usually in the second or third trimester) and help prepare the uterus for labor but do not signify true labor; contractions typically decrease with rest or hydration.

- A late-pregnancy procedure to turn a fetus from breech or transverse lie to head-down position using manual manipulation of the abdomen (often with ultrasound guidance), sometimes aided by medications to relax the uterus.

brazelton assessment.definition: A neonatal behavioral assessment tool that evaluates a newborn's neurological status and neurobehavioral organization—reflexes, motor behavior, state regulation, autonomic function, and social-interactive abilities—to describe neonatal functioning and screen for potential developmental concerns.

neonatal behavioral assessment scale.definition: A standardized, comprehensive assessment of a newborn's neurobehavioral status and neurologic integrity, evaluating how the infant regulates arousal and states, responds to stimuli, and displays motor, autonomic, and social behaviors. Used to identify early neurological issues and to understand neonatal behavioral organization.

chagas' disease.definition: A tropical parasitic infection caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted primarily by triatomine kissing bugs (and can also be spread congenitally, by blood transfusion or organ transplantation, or by ingesting contaminated food). It has an acute phase that is often mild or asymptomatic, and a chronic phase that can cause cardiomyopathy and megasy (megaesophagus and megacolon); antiparasitic treatment with benznidazole or nifurtimox is most effective in the acute phase.

brca1.definition: A tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 17 that encodes a protein essential for repair of double-strand DNA breaks by homologous recombination; pathogenic variants markedly increase risk of breast and ovarian cancers and are associated with hereditary breast-ovarian cancer syndrome.

brca2.definition: A tumor suppressor gene encoding a protein essential for repair of double-strand DNA breaks via homologous recombination; pathogenic variants markedly increase lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer (with elevated risk for pancreatic and prostate cancers and other cancers).

brca3.definition: Not a formally recognized human gene; there is no officially designated BRCA3 in standard gene nomenclature. BRCA1 and BRCA2 are the established breast cancer susceptibility genes, and references to BRCA3 are informal, historical, or nonstandard and not used in clinical genetic testing.

ductule.definition: A small duct; a minute channel that conveys secretions from a glandular secretory unit to a larger duct or to an epithelial surface.

duct.definition: A tubular structure that conducts secretions or fluids from a gland or organ to a target site or to the exterior.

lactiferous sinus.definition: A dilated segment of the breast's lactiferous duct that acts as a milk reservoir just beneath the nipple, storing milk before it is released through the nipple.

lactiferous duct.definition: A duct in the breast that carries milk produced by the mammary glands to the nipple during lactation; part of the ductal system that drains the lobules and opens at the nipple.

areolar.definition: Relating to the areola; in anatomy, areolar tissue is a loose connective tissue beneath epithelium, consisting of a mesh of collagen and elastic fibers with cells such as fibroblasts, macrophages, and mast cells.

suspensory ligaments of cooper.definition: Fibrous connective tissue septa extending from the pectoral fascia to the dermis of the breast, forming a supportive lattice that suspends the breast tissue and helps maintain its contour; traction or thickening of these ligaments by tumors can cause skin dimpling.

pectoralis major muscle.definition: A large chest muscle with clavicular and sternocostal parts that originates from the medial clavicle, sternum, and upper costal cartilages and inserts on the lateral lip of the intertubercular groove of the humerus; it adducts and medially rotates the arm, with the clavicular portion flexing the arm and the sternocostal portion extending a flexed arm. Innervated by the medial and lateral pectoral nerves.

intercostal muscle.definition: Muscles between the ribs that aid breathing; the external intercostals elevate the ribs during inspiration and the internal intercostals depress the ribs during forced expiration (innermost intercostals lie deeper).

axillary lymph nodes.definition: A group of lymph nodes located in the armpit (axilla) that drain lymph from the upper limb, chest wall, and breast; they filter lymph and initiate immune responses.

breast abscess.definition: A localized collection of pus within breast tissue caused by bacterial infection, typically arising from mastitis or lactational mastitis; presents with pain, swelling, warmth, erythema, fever, and sometimes purulent drainage; often treated with antibiotics and drainage (needle aspiration or surgical incision and drainage).

breast augmentation.definition: Cosmetic surgery to increase the size of the breasts.

augmentation mammoplasty.definition: A surgical procedure to increase breast size and alter contour, usually achieved by placing breast implants (silicone or saline) or by fat grafting (lipofilling), for cosmetic enhancement or reconstructive purposes.

infiltrating ductal carcinoma.definition: A malignant breast cancer that begins in the lining of a milk duct and invades surrounding breast tissue; the most common type of invasive breast cancer.

infiltrating lobular carcinoma.definition: A type of invasive breast cancer that arises from the lobular cells of the breast and then invades surrounding tissue. It features small, discohesive cancer cells that infiltrate in single-file patterns due to loss of E-cadherin adhesion. It often presents as a subtle abnormality on imaging and is more likely to be multifocal or bilateral; most tumors are estrogen receptor–positive and HER2-negative.

infiltrating medullary carcinoma.definition: An invasive malignant neoplasm of the medullary type, most commonly medullary thyroid carcinoma arising from parafollicular (C) cells; it shows invasion into surrounding thyroid tissue and beyond, may secrete calcitonin, and histology typically shows nests or sheets of polygonal to spindle-shaped cells with an amyloid-rich stroma; can be associated with MEN2 syndromes.

colloid carcinoma.definition: A histologic variant of adenocarcinoma in which malignant glandular cells are embedded in, or float within, large pools of extracellular mucin; a mucin-producing tumor seen in several organs (most commonly colon, stomach, and breast).

comedo carcinoma.definition: A high-grade ductal carcinoma in situ of the breast characterized by malignant ductal cells with central necrosis (comedonecrosis) and dystrophic calcifications; an aggressive DCIS pattern with a higher risk of progression to invasive ductal carcinoma if untreated.

papillary carcinoma.definition: A malignant neoplasm characterized by papillary (finger-like) fronds with fibrovascular cores lined by neoplastic epithelial cells; most commonly refers to papillary thyroid carcinoma, the common form of thyroid cancer with an often favorable prognosis after treatment.

scirrhous carcinoma.definition: A carcinoma in which malignant cells elicit extensive fibrous tissue (desmoplasia), producing a firm, scar-like (hard) tumor; commonly used to describe certain breast cancers such as invasive ductal carcinoma with dense desmoplastic stroma.

inflammatory carcinoma.definition: An aggressive presentation of breast cancer characterized by rapid onset diffuse erythema, warmth, and edema of the skin (peau d’orange) due to tumor emboli obstructing dermal lymphatics; commonly associated with inflammatory breast cancer and a poor prognosis.

sentinel lymph node biopsy.definition: A surgical procedure to identify and remove the sentinel lymph node—the first lymph node to receive drainage from a primary tumor—for histopathologic examination to assess whether cancer has spread.

incisional biopsy.definition: A biopsy in which only a portion of a lesion or mass is removed for histopathologic examination, with the remainder left in place (as opposed to an excisional biopsy that removes the entire lesion).

excisional biopsy.definition: A diagnostic surgical procedure in which an entire lesion or suspected area is excised and submitted for histopathology; it differs from an incisional biopsy, which samples only part of the lesion.

fine-needle biopsy.definition: A minimally invasive procedure in which a thin needle is inserted into a lesion to withdraw cells or small amounts of fluid for cytologic examination, typically performed under imaging guidance (such as ultrasound or CT).

stereotactic core biopsy.definition: An image-guided percutaneous biopsy of a breast lesion performed using stereotactic imaging (commonly mammography) to precisely target and sample a non-palpable lesion with a core needle, often vacuum-assisted, to obtain tissue for histologic analysis.

ductal lavage.definition: A procedure in which a catheter is inserted into a major breast duct via the nipple to flush saline and collect ductal fluid containing epithelial cells for cytologic analysis, primarily studied for detecting atypia or early cancer but not routinely used in clinical practice.

breast ductal lavage.definition: A procedure in which a small catheter is inserted into a breast duct, saline is flushed through the duct to collect exfoliated ductal cells, and the fluid is analyzed cytologically to detect atypical or malignant cells (often used to evaluate nipple discharge or assess cancer risk).
