self-breast examination.definition: An at-home procedure in which a person inspects and palpates their own breasts to detect lumps, thickening, changes in size or contour, skin, or nipple discharge; typically performed monthly as part of breast health awareness and may involve visual inspection and systematic palpation of the breasts and underarm areas; not a substitute for professional screening such as clinical breast examination or mammography.

clinical breast examination.definition: A physical examination performed by a clinician that involves inspecting and palpating the breasts and surrounding areas (including the axillae) to detect lumps, skin or nipple changes, tenderness, or enlarged lymph nodes.

mammogram.definition: An X-ray picture of the breast, that is helpful in finding diseases.

genetic screening test.definition: A genetic screening test is a test performed on individuals or populations to identify those who are at increased risk of having or transmitting a genetic condition, typically before symptoms arise, so that confirmatory diagnostic testing or counseling can be pursued. It is not diagnostic by itself.

brca genetic testing.definition: A laboratory test analyzing BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes to detect inherited pathogenic variants that increase breast, ovarian, and certain other cancer risks; used for personal risk assessment and to guide screening, preventive, and treatment decisions; results can be positive, negative, or show a variant of uncertain significance.

breast cancer genetic testing.definition: Testing to identify inherited genetic variants that increase breast cancer risk (most commonly BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations) using germline DNA analysis to inform risk assessment, surveillance, and preventive management for the patient and at-risk relatives.

breast cancer tumor analysis.definition: A set of laboratory analyses on a breast tumor specimen (biopsy or surgical) to characterize histology and molecular features, including tumor type (e.g., ductal, lobular), grade, receptor status (estrogen and progesterone receptors), HER2 status, proliferation index (e.g., Ki-67), and genomic risk assays, to guide prognosis and treatment planning.

tumor analysis.definition: A systematic evaluation of a tumor, typically via tissue analysis, to determine histologic type and grade, assess extent, and identify molecular/biomarker features that inform diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment.

tumor cells.definition: Neoplastic cells that comprise a tumor; they typically show autonomous, uncontrolled proliferation and may be benign or malignant, with malignant tumor cells capable of invading nearby tissues and spreading to distant sites (metastasis).

axillary glands.definition: Small, bean-shaped lymph nodes in the armpit (axilla) that drain lymph from the upper limb, breast, and chest wall; they filter lymph and participate in immune defense. Enlargement may indicate infection, inflammation, or malignancy.

lymphatic system.definition: A system of channels that drains excess clear fluid, called lymph, from tissues and returns it into the bloodstream.

renal dysplasia.definition: An congenital disorder in which renal tissue differentiates abnormally during fetal development, resulting in disorganized, dysplastic renal parenchyma often with cyst formation and fibrous stroma, leading to structurally abnormal kidneys that may have reduced function.

klinefelter's syndrome.definition: A chromosomal disorder in males caused by an extra X chromosome (most often 47,XXY), leading to testicular dysgenesis and hypogonadism with low testosterone, reduced fertility, gynecomastia, tall stature, and sometimes language or learning difficulties.

progesterone.definition: A female steroid hormone produced by the ovaries that prepares the uterine lining for pregnancy.

antiestrogen therapy.definition: Treatment that blocks or lowers estrogen activity or production, thereby inhibiting estrogen-driven growth of certain tissues; commonly used for estrogen receptor–positive breast cancer. It may involve selective estrogen receptor modulators (e.g., tamoxifen), aromatase inhibitors (e.g., letrozole, anastrozole), or estrogen receptor downregulators.

herceptin.definition: A monoclonal antibody that targets the HER2/neu receptor, used to treat HER2-positive breast cancer and some HER2-overexpressing gastric cancers by inhibiting HER2 signaling and promoting immune-mediated tumor cell death.

trastuzumab.definition: A humanized monoclonal antibody that targets the HER2/neu (ERBB2) receptor. It binds the extracellular domain to inhibit HER2 signaling and mediate antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity; used in HER2-positive breast cancer and some HER2-positive gastric cancers.

stem cell transplantation.definition: A medical procedure in which hematopoietic stem cells are infused into a patient to reestablish bone marrow function after intensive chemotherapy or radiation; the cells may be autologous (from the patient), allogeneic (from a donor), or from umbilical cord blood.

phenylalanine mustard.definition: A nitrogen mustard alkylating agent linked to the amino acid phenylalanine to form a prodrug that targets tumor cells via amino acid transporters; after activation it releases the active mustard that alkylates DNA, causing cross-links and cytotoxicity.

l-pam.definition: Not found as a standard medical term in major dictionaries. If you meant “PAM” as an acronym, it stands for a positive allosteric modulator—a substance that binds to an allosteric site on a receptor and enhances the receptor’s response to its endogenous ligand; benzodiazepines are classic examples at GABA-A receptors. If you have context or an alternate spelling, please share it for a precise definition.

estrogen receptor.definition: An intracellular, ligand-activated nuclear receptor that binds estrogen and functions as a transcription factor to regulate estrogen-responsive genes; main subtypes are ER-α and ER-β, expressed in various tissues; clinically, estrogen receptor status guides prognosis and endocrine therapy in breast cancer.

estrogen receptors.definition: Proteins that bind estrogen and mediate its effects; they function as intracellular receptors that regulate gene expression when activated by estrogen (genomic actions) and also mediate rapid non-genomic signaling via membrane-associated receptors; mainly two subtypes, ERα and ERβ, encoded by ESR1 and ESR2 and widely expressed in many tissues.

reconstructive surgery.definition: A surgical discipline dedicated to restoring form and function after injury, illness, or congenital defects, using tissue transfer (grafts and flaps), implants, and other reconstructive techniques to repair and rebuild affected structures.

preauricular pits.definition: A congenital indentation or small sinus opening located just anterior to the external ear, resulting from incomplete obliteration of the first pharyngeal groove during embryologic development; usually asymptomatic but can become infected or drain mucoid material and may be associated with other ear anomalies or BOR (branchio-oto-renal) syndrome.

branchial pits.definition: An embryologic remnant along the lateral neck stemming from persistent branchial clefts, presenting as a small skin opening (pit) or sinus that may drain mucus and become infected; may be associated with branchial cleft cysts or fistulas.

intrinsic positive end-expiratory pressu.definition: Intrinsic positive end-expiratory pressure (iPEEP) is the positive pressure that remains in the lungs at the end of expiration due to incomplete lung emptying (air trapping), commonly from high airway resistance or shortened expiratory time during ventilation; it can cause dynamic hyperinflation and increased work of breathing.

recurrent pharyngeal nerve.definition: A branch of the vagus nerve that supplies motor innervation to most intrinsic laryngeal muscles and provides sensory input below the vocal cords; it courses inferiorly, then recurs to ascend in the tracheoesophageal groove, with the left side looping around the aortic arch and the right around the subclavian artery.

ionizing radiation.definition: Radiation with enough energy to ionize atoms or molecules by ejecting electrons; typically photons above about 10 eV, and includes X-rays, gamma rays, alpha and beta particles, and neutrons. It can cause chemical changes and biological damage.

self-examination.definition: An individual's examination of their own body to detect signs or symptoms of disease or abnormality, often performed for early detection (e.g., breast self-exam, testicular self-exam).

breast examination.definition: A clinical procedure in which a health care professional visually inspects the breasts for skin changes, contour, symmetry, and nipple changes, and then palpates the breast tissue and regional lymph nodes to identify masses, tenderness, or other abnormalities.

breech.definition: An obstetric presentation in which the fetus is positioned to be born buttocks or feet first rather than head first; a non-cephalic presentation.

examination.definition: A systematic clinical evaluation of a patient that includes taking the medical history and performing a physical assessment (inspection, palpation, percussion, and auscultation) to identify signs, assess function, and guide diagnosis and management.

extraction.definition: An act of removing something from the body or a sample, typically by pulling it out; most commonly the removal of a tooth.

bregma.definition: A skull landmark at the intersection of the sagittal and coronal sutures; roughly corresponds to the anterior fontanelle in infants.

sutures.definition: Stitches used to close a cut or wound, such as after an injury or during surgery.

coronal.definition: Relating to the crown of a tooth; in anatomy, describing a vertical plane that divides the body into anterior (front) and posterior (back) portions.

sagittal.definition: An anatomical plane that divides the body or an organ into left and right parts; it runs longitudinally from front to back. The central division is the midline (median) plane, with planes offset from it lying off-center; the term is also used for a skull suture along this line.

granulosa.definition: A layer of cells surrounding the oocyte in the ovarian follicle; granulosa cells support follicle development and, under FSH, convert androgens to estrogens.

theca.definition: A sheath or envelope surrounding a structure; in the ovary, the two layers surrounding the follicle (an inner endocrine layer and an outer fibrous layer) involved in steroid hormone production.

brenner.definition: A rare ovarian neoplasm composed of nests of transitional (urothelial-like) epithelial cells within fibrous stroma; most tumors are benign, with malignant Brenner tumors being rare.

breslow.definition: A histopathologic measurement of melanoma thickness in millimeters, from the top of the epidermal granular layer to the deepest point of tumor invasion; used to stage melanoma and estimate prognosis.

kernicterus.definition: Permanent brain damage caused by deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in brain tissue (most often the basal ganglia) in newborns with severe hyperbilirubinemia, leading to movement disorders, sensorineural hearing loss, gaze abnormalities, and intellectual disability.

ondine.definition: A historical term referring to central congenital hypoventilation syndrome (Ondine's curse), a rare disorder in which automatic control of breathing is diminished during sleep, resulting in hypoventilation, hypercapnia, and potentially hypoxemia.

phototherapy.definition: A treatment that uses light of specific wavelengths to produce a therapeutic effect, such as blue light for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia and ultraviolet light for certain skin conditions, or light-activated therapy in photodynamic therapy for cancer.

helicobacter.definition: A genus of Gram-negative, curved bacteria that are microaerophilic and motile; the best-known species, Helicobacter pylori, colonizes the stomach and is associated with gastritis, peptic ulcers, and gastric cancer.

pylori.definition: A spiral-shaped, microaerophilic Gram-negative bacterium that colonizes the stomach; a common cause of chronic gastritis and peptic ulcers and is associated with gastric cancer and MALT lymphoma.

scintigraphy.definition: A diagnostic technique based on the detection of energy emitted by radioactive substances injected into the body; also called radionuclide scanning.

sonogram.definition: An image produced by ultrasonography, created by transmitting high-frequency sound waves into the body and recording the echoes to visualize soft tissues and organs.

transillumination.definition: A diagnostic technique in which a bright light is placed against or behind a body part to see whether light passes through; it helps distinguish fluid-filled or hollow structures from solid tissues, since fluid-filled or hollow areas typically transmit light, while solid masses do not.

diaphanography.definition: A historical imaging technique that uses transillumination—passing light through tissues—to visualize internal structures or fluid-filled areas and detect abnormalities; largely obsolete today.

nasotracheal.definition: Relating to the nose and trachea; commonly used to describe a route or device (such as a tube) inserted through the nasal passage into the trachea to secure the airway.

presentation.definition: The clinical manifestation of a disease; the signs and symptoms with which a patient first presents or is observed upon examination.

version.definition: A procedure in obstetrics in which the fetus is manually turned within the uterus to change its presenting part, usually from breech or transverse lie to cephalic presentation to facilitate vaginal delivery.

cocktail.definition: An intentional combination of two or more drugs given together to treat a condition; used to enhance efficacy, reduce resistance, or target multiple pathways (e.g., in antiretroviral therapy or chemotherapy).

bronchiectasis.definition: Chronic, irreversible dilation and destruction of the bronchi, leading to impaired mucociliary clearance and recurrent respiratory infections, typically presenting with a daily productive cough and sputum production; often diagnosed by CT showing dilated airways.

drowsiness.definition: A state of sleepiness or reduced alertness, with a tendency to fall asleep, often due to fatigue, sleep deprivation, medications, or illness.

morphine.definition: A potent opioid analgesic that acts as a mu-opioid receptor agonist to relieve moderate to severe pain; it can cause respiratory depression, sedation, nausea, constipation, miosis, and has potential for tolerance and dependence. Routes include oral and various parenteral forms, with active metabolites that can accumulate in renal impairment.

bronchial.definition: Relating to the bronchi, the major air passages that branch from the trachea into the lungs and conduct air to the smaller airways.

postural.definition: Relating to posture; pertaining to the position and alignment of the body.

fremitus.definition: A palpable vibration transmitted to the chest wall when the patient speaks; assessed by placing the hands on the chest, it is increased with lung consolidation (e.g., pneumonia) and decreased with air or fluid in the pleural space or a thick chest wall.

hyperreactivity.definition: An exaggerated physiological response of an organ or tissue to a stimulus, indicating increased sensitivity or reactivity beyond normal levels (for example, airway hyperreactivity in asthma).

secretion.definition: The release of chemical substances produced by the body; or the substance that is produced.

spasm.definition: The sudden, strong tightening or jerk of a muscle.

toilet.definition: An area or fixture designated for urination and defecation; in medical and caregiving contexts, it also refers to assisting a patient with using these facilities and maintaining personal hygiene.

tree.definition: A branching system of airways within the lungs that conducts air from the trachea to the alveoli, comprising the trachea, main bronchi, and progressively smaller bronchioles.

washing.definition: A cleansing process using water or a sterile solution to remove dirt, debris, or contaminants from a body surface, wound, or cavity.

rsv.definition: A common respiratory virus that often causes mild cold‑like illness but can provoke bronchiolitis and pneumonia, especially in infants and older adults; an enveloped negative‑sense RNA virus in the Pneumoviridae family; transmitted via respiratory droplets and close contact; diagnosed by PCR or antigen testing; management is supportive, with targeted monoclonal antibody prophylaxis for high‑risk infants as a preventive measure.

syncytial.definition: Relating to a syncytium; a multinucleated cytoplasmic mass formed by the fusion of multiple cells, with several nuclei sharing a common cytoplasm.

parainfluenza.definition: A group of enveloped RNA viruses (types 1–4) in the Paramyxoviridae family that cause acute respiratory infections, especially croup in children; spread by respiratory droplets and contact; symptoms include cough, runny nose, fever, and sometimes wheezing; usually self-limited.

rhinovirus.definition: A nonenveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus of the Picornaviridae family that causes the common cold; it has many serotypes (A, B, and C) and replicates best at cooler temperatures in the nasopharynx, transmitted by respiratory droplets and contact with contaminated surfaces.

cystic.definition: Relating to or characterized by the presence of cysts; having a sac-like cavity that is typically filled with fluid, air, or semi-solid material.

pertussis.definition: A highly contagious bacterial respiratory infection caused by Bordetella pertussis, characterized by paroxysmal coughing with an inspiratory whoop and posttussive emesis; most severe in unvaccinated infants; transmitted by respiratory droplets; preventable by vaccination; treated with macrolide antibiotics.

bronchopneumonia.definition: Patchy, peribronchial inflammation and consolidation centered on the bronchi that extends into the adjacent alveoli, producing multifocal or bilateral patchy infiltrates rather than a single lobar consolidation.

respiratory_failure.definition: A syndrome in which the lungs cannot sustain adequate gas exchange, causing hypoxemia (low arterial oxygen) and/or hypercapnia (elevated arterial CO2), often with acidemia; it may be acute or chronic and frequently requires ventilatory support.

cor.definition: A Latin noun meaning “heart”; used as a root in medical terminology to denote heart-related anatomy or function, but it is not used as a standalone medical term.

pulmonale.definition: Relating to the lungs; pertaining to pulmonary structures or diseases.

expectorants.definition: A class of medicines that helps loosen and thin mucus in the airways, making it easier to cough up; used to relieve productive coughs by improving mucus clearance.

ribavirin.definition: A broad-spectrum antiviral nucleoside analogue of guanosine that inhibits viral RNA synthesis and replication; used for certain severe viral infections (notably severe RSV in infants via inhalation and historically for hepatitis C in combination with pegylated interferon); adverse effects include hemolytic anemia and teratogenicity.

empyema.definition: An accumulation of pus within a preformed anatomical space, most commonly the pleural cavity, due to infection; typically treated with antibiotics and drainage.

bronchoscopy.definition: An endoscopic procedure that uses a bronchoscope to visualize the airways and lungs, often for diagnosis or treatment; it may include sampling (biopsy, brushings, lavage) and removal of obstructions, using a flexible or rigid scope under local anesthesia with sedation.

bronchioalveolar.definition: Relating to the bronchioles (small airways) and the alveoli (air sacs) of the lungs.

goblet.definition: A secretory epithelial cell in mucous membranes that produces and secretes mucus (mucin), helping to lubricate and protect the lining; most common in the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts.

cells.definition: The basic building block of all living organisms.

mucous.definition: Relating to mucus; describing a secretion produced by mucous membranes or the membranes themselves that produce mucus (as in mucous membranes lining the respiratory, digestive, and urogenital tracts).

glands.definition: Glands are organs that produce and secrete substances; endocrine glands release hormones directly into the bloodstream, while exocrine glands secrete through ducts onto epithelial surfaces (e.g., enzymes, mucus). Some glands have both endocrine and exocrine functions.

adenocarcinoma of the lung.definition: A malignant neoplasm of the lung arising from glandular (mucin-producing) cells, typically located peripherally; the most common type of non-small cell lung cancer.

bronchoalveolar carcinoma.definition: An outdated term for a lung adenocarcinoma that grows along preexisting alveolar walls (lepidic growth) without stromal invasion; in modern classifications it is reclassified as adenocarcinoma in situ (if no invasion) or as lepidic-predominant invasive adenocarcinoma, and it may present radiographically as a ground-glass nodule or pneumonia-like consolidation.

bronchogenic adenocarcinoma.definition: Bronchogenic adenocarcinoma is a primary lung cancer of glandular (adenocarcinoma) differentiation arising from the bronchial or distal airway epithelium; it is a type of non-small cell lung cancer, often located peripherally and may produce mucin.

bronchogenic cyst.definition: A congenital, benign cystic lesion of the mediastinum or lung that arises from abnormal budding of the tracheobronchial (bronchial) tree during embryogenesis; typically lined by ciliated respiratory epithelium with cartilage in the wall; may become infected or enlarge to cause compression; treated with complete surgical excision.

bronchopulmonary dysplasia.definition: A chronic lung disease of infancy, most often in preterm infants, caused by prolonged oxygen exposure and mechanical ventilation, resulting in arrested alveolar development with inflammation and fibrosis of the airways; characterized by ongoing respiratory support or oxygen dependence at 36 weeks postmenstrual age (severity categorized as mild, moderate, or severe).

bronchoscope.definition: A flexible or rigid endoscope used to visualize the tracheobronchial tree; inserted through the mouth or nose into the airways to diagnose and treat conditions, including obtaining biopsies or samples, suctioning, and removing obstructions.

fiberoptic bronchoscopy.definition: An endoscopic diagnostic and therapeutic procedure in which a flexible fiberoptic bronchoscope is passed through the nose or mouth into the airways to visualize the tracheobronchial tree, obtain tissue or fluid samples, and perform interventions (e.g., suctioning, biopsy, BAL, or foreign body removal).

bronchospirometry.definition: A procedure that combines bronchoscopy with spirometry to assess ventilatory function and airway mechanics during bronchoscopic assessment.

bronchography.definition: A radiographic examination of the bronchi obtained by introducing a radiopaque contrast medium into the tracheobronchial tree, typically via bronchoscopy, to outline bronchial anatomy and detect disease such as bronchiectasis, stenosis, or obstruction; largely replaced by CT.

bronchopleural fistula.definition: An abnormal connection between a bronchus and the pleural space that allows air to pass from the airway into the pleural cavity, causing a persistent air leak; commonly occurs after thoracic surgery (e.g., pneumonectomy) or trauma/infection and may lead to pneumothorax and empyema.

bronchotracheal.definition: Relating to the bronchi and the trachea; pertaining to the airway passages of the respiratory tract formed by the trachea and its divisions into the bronchi.

bronchovesicular.definition: Breath sounds heard over the central airways (main bronchi) with intermediate pitch and intensity; inspiratory and expiratory phases are approximately equal in duration, blending features of bronchial and vesicular sounds.

isoetharine.definition: A short-acting inhaled beta-2 adrenergic agonist bronchodilator used to relieve acute bronchospasm; relaxes airway smooth muscle, with usage now largely superseded by newer agents.

methylxanthines.definition: A class of methylated xanthine alkaloids (e.g., caffeine, theobromine, theophylline) that act as central nervous system stimulants and bronchodilators by inhibiting phosphodiesterase enzymes (raising cAMP) and antagonizing adenosine receptors; they have a narrow therapeutic index and have been used for their bronchodilatory effects.

bronchodilation.definition: The widening of the airways in the lungs due to relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle, increasing airflow by decreasing airway resistance.

bronchoconstriction.definition: Narrowing of the airways caused by contraction of the smooth muscle in the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to reduced airflow and difficulty breathing; commonly seen in asthma and allergic reactions.

mucopurulent.definition: Relating to or consisting of mucus and pus; describing a discharge that contains both mucus and pus, typically due to bacterial infection.

clubbing.definition: A painless enlargement of the distal digits with increased nail curvature and soft-tissue thickening at the nail beds, often with loss of the normal diamond-shaped window between the nails (Schamroth sign); commonly associated with chronic hypoxemia from cardiopulmonary disease.

peripheral cyanosis.definition: Blue discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes in the extremities (e.g., fingers, toes, nail beds) due to increased deoxygenated hemoglobin from reduced peripheral perfusion or vasoconstriction; arterial oxygen saturation is often near normal, distinguishing it from central cyanosis.

catarrhal pneumonia.definition: A form of pneumonia characterized by catarrh (inflammation with increased mucus production) of the bronchial and bronchiolar mucosa, with an accompanying exudative inflammatory response in the surrounding lung; historically used to describe bronchopneumonia with mucopurulent sputum, often due to viral infections.

interstitial pneumonia.definition: Inflammation of the lung interstitium (the tissue surrounding the air sacs), characterized by thickening of the alveolar septa and diffuse interstitial infiltrates, often with dry cough and shortness of breath; causes include viral or atypical infections, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, drug reactions, and autoimmune diseases.

mycoplasma pneumoniae.definition: A small, cell-wall–deficient bacterium that colonizes the respiratory tract and is a common cause of atypical ("walking") pneumonia, especially in children and young adults; spread by respiratory droplets; beta-lactam antibiotics are ineffective; treatment typically includes macrolides, doxycycline, or fluoroquinolones.

staphylococcus pyogenes.definition: There is no recognized bacterial species by this name; it is likely a misnomer for either Staphylococcus aureus (a common cause of skin infections, pneumonia, and sepsis) or Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus, which causes strep throat and various infections).

respiratory syncytial virus.definition: An enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA virus in the Pneumoviridae family that causes acute respiratory tract infections, most notably bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants and young children; transmitted by respiratory droplets and close contact; management is supportive.

whooping cough.definition: A highly contagious bacterial infection of the respiratory tract caused by Bordetella pertussis, characterized by prolonged coughing fits that can be followed by a high-pitched inspiratory sound (a whoop).

influenza vaccine.definition: A vaccine that protects against influenza by exposing the immune system to inactivated or attenuated influenza virus antigens (often hemagglutinin), updated yearly to match circulating strains; administered by injection (inactivated) or nasal spray (live attenuated) to reduce the risk of influenza illness and its complications.

pneumonia vaccine.definition: A vaccine designed to prevent pneumonia caused by specific pathogens, most commonly Streptococcus pneumoniae; includes pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (e.g., PCV13/PCV15/PCV20) and pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23). These vaccines reduce the risk of pneumococcal pneumonia and other invasive pneumococcal diseases and are recommended for certain age groups and risk factors.

pneumococcal vaccine.definition: A vaccine that protects against infections caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae; includes pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (e.g., PCV13, PCV15, PCV20) and the pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23), and is used to prevent pneumococcal pneumonia, meningitis, and other invasive pneumococcal diseases in at-risk individuals.

pulmonary hypertension.definition: A condition characterized by elevated pressure in the pulmonary arterial system, defined at rest as mean pulmonary arterial pressure ≥25 mmHg (measured by right heart catheterization); it increases right ventricular workload and can be idiopathic or secondary to left heart disease, lung disease, thromboembolism, or systemic conditions.

cor pulmonale.definition: Right-sided heart failure due to chronic pulmonary hypertension from lung disease or pulmonary vascular disorders, often with right ventricular hypertrophy and dilation.

lung abscess.definition: A localized collection of pus within the lung parenchyma caused by a necrotizing infection, leading to a cavitary lesion that often contains an air-fluid level; commonly associated with aspiration and anaerobic bacterial infection.

pathogens.definition: Biological agents capable of causing disease in a susceptible host; examples include bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites, and prions. They invade or colonize tissues, replicate, and damage cells or trigger harmful host immune responses.

lymph node biopsy.definition: A procedure in which a lymph node (or part of it) is removed and examined under a microscope to diagnose conditions causing lymphadenopathy, including infections, inflammatory diseases, and cancers such as lymphoma or metastasis; it can be performed as an excisional, incisional, core-needle, or fine-needle aspiration biopsy, sometimes under image guidance.

exploratory surgery.definition: A surgical procedure to directly examine the interior of the body to determine the cause of symptoms or diagnose disease when noninvasive tests are inconclusive; it may include biopsy or immediate treatment.

tracheobronchial.definition: Relating to the trachea and the bronchi; the central airways of the respiratory tract, including the trachea and its major branching passages within the lungs.

bronchiolar.definition: Relating to the bronchioles, the small airways in the lungs that connect the bronchi to the alveoli.

bronchiole.definition: A small airway in the respiratory system that connects to the alveoli (air sacs); a branch of the bronchial tubes.

brow lift.definition: A surgical cosmetic procedure to elevate the eyebrows and smooth the forehead by lifting and repositioning brow tissues; also called a forehead lift or browplasty, with approaches including coronal, endoscopic, and temporal (lateral) techniques.

brudzinski's sign.definition: A clinical sign of meningeal irritation where passive flexion of the neck leads to involuntary flexion of the hips and knees.

forehead lift.definition: A cosmetic surgical procedure to raise the eyebrows and tighten the forehead by repositioning the skin and underlying tissues, reducing forehead wrinkles and brow sagging; commonly performed with incisions behind the hairline (coronal), at the hairline (pretrichial/endoscopic brow lift), or similar approaches.

brown-adson forceps.definition: Atraumatic tissue forceps with fine, interdigitating teeth (usually two rows) at the tips to grip delicate tissue with minimal crush injury; used during surgery for fine tissue handling.

adson-brown forceps.definition: A delicate tissue forceps with multiple fine teeth at the tips (typically two rows) that distributes pressure over a larger area to provide an atraumatic grip of delicate tissue during suturing or manipulation.

brown fat.definition: A type of adipose tissue rich in mitochondria and iron-containing cytochromes that generates heat by non-shivering thermogenesis through uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1)–mediated oxidation of fatty acids; primarily present in newborns and in smaller depots in adults.

brown recluse spider.definition: A venomous spider of the genus Loxosceles (Loxosceles reclusa) native to the United States; its bite can cause a necrotic skin lesion and, rarely, systemic effects such as fever or hemolysis.

brown recluse spider bite.definition: An envenomation from a Loxosceles species spider bite; most cases cause localized pain, redness, and swelling and heal without complication. A minority develop necrotic skin ulcers due to venom components such as sphingomyelinase D. Systemic symptoms are uncommon. Management is supportive with wound care and analgesia; antibiotics if secondary infection is suspected; seek care for enlarging ulcers or systemic signs.

necrotic lesion.definition: An area of tissue death (necrosis) within a lesion, where the affected tissue is nonviable; often due to ischemia, infection, or toxic injury and may appear devitalized (darkened) with surrounding inflammation.

brown-séquard's syndrome.definition: A hemisection or unilateral injury of the spinal cord causing ipsilateral motor weakness and loss of dorsal-column modalities (vibration and proprioception) below the level of injury, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation beginning a few segments below the lesion; may have ipsilateral UMN signs below the lesion and at the level of the lesion.

organotherapy.definition: An historical therapeutic approach that uses preparations derived from animal or human organs (organ extracts) to treat disease, based on the belief that organs contain specific healing substances; it is now largely obsolete and not supported by robust modern evidence.

brucella melitensis.definition: A Gram-negative, facultative intracellular bacterium that causes brucellosis in humans, typically acquired from infected goats or sheep via contact or ingestion of unpasteurized dairy; presents with fever, sweats, malaise, and hepatosplenomegaly.

brucella suis.definition: A gram-negative, facultatively intracellular bacterium of the Brucella genus that primarily infects pigs (swine) and can cause zoonotic brucellosis in humans.

brucella canis.definition: A species of Gram-negative, nonmotile bacteria that infects dogs, causing canine brucellosis with reproductive disease (abortion, infertility, epididymo-orchitis) and which can be transmitted to humans (rarely) via contact with infected reproductive fluids or tissues; diagnosed by serology and culture.

muscle pain.definition: Pain or tenderness in a muscle.

joint pain.definition: A symptom characterized by pain, aching, or tenderness in one or more joints, often with stiffness and reduced mobility; it can result from inflammation (as in arthritis), injury, overuse, infection, or systemic diseases and may be acute or chronic.

orchiepididymitis.definition: Inflammation of the testicle (orchitis) and the epididymis (epididymo-orchitis), usually due to infection; presents with acute scrotal pain, swelling, and tenderness; commonly caused by sexually transmitted infections in younger men and by urinary tract pathogens in older men, and may affect one or both testicles.

cyprus fever.definition: Not a recognized medical term; there is no standard clinical definition for this name. It may be a misnomer or a regional/colloquial reference to fever associated with another condition. If you can provide context or alternate spelling, I can help identify the likely condition.

malta fever.definition: A historical name for brucellosis, a zoonotic bacterial infection caused by Brucella species (most often Brucella melitensis), transmitted from infected animals or unpasteurized dairy products, presenting with undulating fever, sweats, malaise, and musculoskeletal pain.

mediterranean fever.definition: A hereditary autoinflammatory syndrome characterized by recurrent fevers and attacks of serosal inflammation (peritonitis, pleuritis, arthritis), most common in people of Mediterranean descent; usually due to mutations in the MEFV gene encoding pyrin.

undulant fever.definition: A fever that waxes and wanes in an undulating pattern, classically seen with brucellosis (Brucella infection); may be accompanied by night sweats, malaise, arthralgias, fatigue, and hepatosplenomegaly.

gibraltar fever.definition: An acute febrile rickettsial illness caused by infection with Rickettsia conorii, transmitted by tick bites (often Rhipicephalus sanguineus) in the Mediterranean region; typically presents with sudden fever, headache, myalgias, a maculopapular rash, and often an inoculation eschar at the bite site, and responds to doxycycline.

rock fever.definition: Not a recognized medical term; there is no formal medical definition for it in standard dictionaries. If used informally, it may describe a climber’s strong urge to climb.

marseilles fever.definition: A historical, non-specific label for a febrile illness observed in Marseille; not a current or clearly defined medical diagnosis.

bruch's disease.definition: No widely recognized medical condition by that name. It may be a misnomer for Bruch's membrane–related changes in the eye, most commonly seen in age-related macular degeneration, where drusen and sclerosis of Bruch's membrane contribute to retinal pigment epithelium dysfunction and progressive central vision loss. If you meant a different term, please specify and I can define that.

meige's syndrome.definition: A focal cranial dystonia consisting of concurrent blepharospasm (involuntary eyelid closure) and oromandibular dystonia (involuntary jaw, tongue, and lower facial movements).

brugia.definition: A genus of parasitic nematodes that cause human lymphatic filariasis; the principal disease-causing species include malayi and timori, transmitted by mosquitoes; adults inhabit the lymphatic system and can lead to lymphedema and elephantiasis, with microfilariae circulating in peripheral blood in a nocturnal pattern.

filariasis.definition: A parasitic disease caused by threadlike filarial nematodes transmitted by mosquitoes; it primarily damages the lymphatic system, leading to lymphedema and swelling (often progressing to elephantiasis), hydrocele, and, in some forms, tropical pulmonary eosinophilia.

bruxism.definition: A condition characterized by repetitive clenching or grinding of the teeth, typically during sleep or while awake.

bruxomania.definition: An outdated or rarely used term for compulsive grinding or clenching of the teeth (bruxism), typically occurring during sleep or periods of stress, which can lead to dental wear, jaw pain, and temporomandibular disorders.

bryant's traction.definition: A skin traction for pediatric femur fractures in which both legs are extended and suspended vertically, with weights attached to the ankles to provide longitudinal traction along the femur.

buck's traction.definition: A skin traction technique for proximal femur/hip fractures in which a padded band or boot around the thigh is attached to external weights to exert gentle longitudinal traction, primarily to relieve muscle spasm and align the fracture as a temporary measure before definitive treatment.

brunnstrom hemiplegia.definition: A staged framework describing post-stroke hemiplegia progression, in which motor recovery evolves from flaccidity to voluntary, coordinated movement through a series of stages (commonly I–VI, sometimes VII) marked by the appearance and evolution of abnormal synergy patterns and spasticity, used to assess prognosis and guide rehabilitation.

brush biopsy.definition: A minimally invasive cytology sampling technique in which a cytology brush is used to collect surface epithelial cells from a lesion for microscopic examination to detect malignant or premalignant changes; not a substitute for a definitive scalpel biopsy when histology is required.

brush border.definition: The apical surface of absorptive epithelial cells, covered by densely packed microvilli (the microvillous border), which increases surface area for absorption and contains membrane-bound digestive enzymes (e.g., disaccharidases in the small intestine).

brushfield's spots.definition: Small, white to yellow-white specks on the peripheral iris, especially near the iris–sclera margin; a common ocular finding in Down syndrome. They are benign, nonprogressive, and typically asymptomatic, present from birth or early childhood and not affecting vision.

bruton’s agammaglobulinemia.definition: A primary X-linked immunodeficiency caused by BTK gene mutations that impair B-cell maturation, resulting in absent or very low circulating B cells and immunoglobulins and leading to recurrent bacterial infections; typically presents in infancy and is treated with immunoglobulin replacement therapy.

buboes.definition: A swollen, tender lymph node, usually in the groin, armpit, or neck, caused by infection; historically associated with bubonic plague.

bubo.definition: A swollen, inflamed lymph node, typically in the groin, armpit, or neck, caused by local infection; historically associated with bubonic plague.

bubonic plague.definition: An acute zoonotic infection caused by Yersinia pestis, transmitted to humans by infected fleas from rodents; it typically presents with sudden fever, malaise, and painful lymphadenopathy (buboes), usually in the groin, axilla, or neck, and can progress to septicemia or pneumonic plague if not treated.

black death.definition: A historic plague pandemic caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, transmitted by fleas on rodents; typically presents with fever and swollen lymph nodes (buboes) and can also cause septicemic or pneumonic forms with high mortality.

plague.definition: A disease caused by a germ (bacteria) carried by rats and the fleas that live on them.

yersinia pestis.definition: A Gram-negative, nonmotile, facultatively anaerobic bacillus that causes plague in humans and animals; transmitted chiefly by fleas from infected rodents and can present as bubonic, septicemic, or pneumonic plague.

plague vaccine.definition: A vaccine designed to elicit active immunity against plague (Yersinia pestis) by presenting plague-specific antigens to the immune system; historically including killed or attenuated whole-cell vaccines and subunit vaccines (e.g., F1 and LcrV antigens), but there is no widely used human plague vaccine in routine use and development continues.

bubble-diffusion humidifier.definition: An airway humidifier that humidifies inspired gas by forcing it through submerged outlets to create bubbles in a water reservoir; water vapor diffuses into the gas as it bubbles, delivering humidified (and often warmed) gas to the patient. Commonly used with oxygen therapy or anesthesia; potential drawbacks include bacterial contamination risk and variable humidification at higher flow rates.

bubble goniometer.definition: A goniometer that uses a spirit-level bubble to indicate alignment with the joint axis; the centered bubble corresponds to a specific angle on the scale, enabling measurement of a patient’s range of motion during rehabilitation.

bubble oxygenator.definition: An older cardiopulmonary bypass oxygenator in which blood is exposed directly to oxygen gas bubbles to facilitate gas exchange; has been largely superseded by membrane oxygenators due to higher hemolysis and risk of microemboli.

bucardia.definition: A slower-than-normal heart rate, typically less than 60 beats per minute in adults; may be a normal finding in trained athletes or indicate conduction system disease, hypothyroidism, electrolyte disturbances, or medication effects.

buccal administration.definition: Delivery of a drug via the buccal mucosa (the inside of the cheek) by placing it against the inner cheek to dissolve and absorb directly into the systemic circulation, thereby bypassing gastrointestinal absorption and hepatic first-pass metabolism.

buccal artery.definition: A small arterial branch that supplies the buccal region of the cheek, including the buccinator muscle and buccal mucosa; typically a branch of the maxillary artery (the buccal branch).

buccal fat pad.definition: An encapsulated pad of fat in the cheek (buccal region) between the buccinator and masseter muscles that cushions the muscles during chewing; it can be surgically reduced or removed for cosmetic facial contouring.

buccal fentanyl.definition: A fentanyl formulation intended for buccal administration (absorbed through the buccal mucosa between the cheek and gum) to provide rapid systemic analgesia for breakthrough pain in opioid-tolerant patients; available as buccal tablets or films.

buccal mucosa.definition: The mucous membrane lining the inner cheek of the oral cavity; a part of the lining mucosa composed of non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium with a lamina propria containing minor salivary glands.

buccal nerve.definition: A sensory branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3) that supplies sensation to the cheek skin, cheek mucosa, and buccal gingiva.

buccal splint.definition: A dental device attached to the buccal (cheek-side) surfaces of teeth to immobilize one or more teeth or a dental arch segment for healing after trauma or surgical repositioning.

buccal vestibule.definition: The buccal vestibule is the space inside the mouth between the buccal mucosa (cheek lining) and the teeth and gingiva, forming the cheek-side recess of the oral cavity.

buccal frenum.definition: A band of mucous membrane and connective tissue that attaches the inner cheek mucosa to the gingiva near the teeth; a tight attachment can contribute to gingival recession or a diastema.

buccal notch.definition: A small indentation or groove on the buccal (cheek-facing) surface of a bone or tooth, serving as an anatomic landmark or site of muscular attachment.

buccal flange.definition: Extension of a denture along the buccal vestibule that borders the buccal mucosa and buccinator muscle; this denture border provides stability, retention, and cheek support and helps define facial contour.

buccal gingivae.definition: Gingival tissue on the buccal (cheek) aspect of the teeth; the portion of the gum adjacent to the cheek, extending from the free gingival margin to the mucogingival junction.

mandibular nerve.definition: A mixed division of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V3) that exits the skull via the foramen ovale; supplies motor innervation to the muscles of mastication and sensory innervation to the lower face, mandible, and oral mucosa, with branches including the inferior alveolar, lingual, and buccal (long buccal) nerves.

superior pharyngeal constrictor.definition: A circular muscle of the pharynx that forms part of the pharyngeal constrictor group. It originates from the pterygoid hamulus and the pterygomandibular raphe (and adjacent mandible) and inserts into the median pharyngeal raphe; its contraction constricts the upper pharynx to propel the bolus downward during swallowing. Innervation: pharyngeal plexus (primarily CN X, with contributions from CN IX).

lateral pterygoid.definition: A muscle of mastication with two heads that originates from the sphenoid bone (lateral pterygoid plate and greater wing) and inserts on the pterygoid fovea of the mandible and the articular disc; it protrudes and depresses the mandible, facilitating jaw opening and side-to-side movements, innervated by the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve.

buccolingualmasticatory triad.definition: A conceptual description of the integrated function of the buccal (cheek-side) and lingual (tongue-side) aspects of the dentition with the masticatory system (jaw muscles and temporomandibular joints) during chewing, shaping occlusal contacts and bite force.

linguoocclusion.definition: An oral pattern describing the contact and pressure of the tongue against the teeth that can influence dental occlusion, often involving tongue thrust or habitual tongue pressure against the teeth.

dyskinesia.definition: Abnormal, involuntary movements arising from dysfunction of the extrapyramidal motor system; they can be choreiform, athetotic, or dystonic in nature and are often a medication-induced side effect of dopamine-modulating therapies (e.g., antipsychotics, long-term levodopa).

gingivae.definition: The gums: the mucosal tissues surrounding and protecting the teeth, attaching to the teeth at the gingival margin and to the underlying alveolar bone, and comprising the free (marginal) and attached gingiva.

occlusal.definition: To chew or grind the surface of your back teeth.

occlusion.definition: The closing or blocking of a hollow organ or body part.

buccogingival.definition: Relating to or involving both the buccal (cheek-facing) aspect and the gingival (gum) tissue; describing a location or direction toward the cheek and gums in dental anatomy.

buccopharyngeal.definition: Relating to the cheek (buccal) and the pharynx; describing structures located between the oral cavity and the pharynx.

budesonide.definition: A glucocorticoid corticosteroid with anti-inflammatory effects, used in inhaled form for asthma and COPD, as a nasal spray for allergic rhinitis, and in oral or rectal forms for inflammatory bowel disease; designed for local action with extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism to minimize systemic exposure.

fascia.definition: A sheet or band of connective tissue, primarily collagen, that envelops, separates, and binds together muscles and other internal structures; it forms superficial and deep layers and helps compartmentalize the body and transmit mechanical forces.

pharyngeal membrane.definition: An embryologic, transient membrane formed by the juxtaposition of endoderm from a pharyngeal pouch with ectoderm of the corresponding pharyngeal groove, with a core of mesenchyme; the first pharyngeal membrane contributes to the tympanic membrane.

buccula.definition: A small cheek; a diminutive form of bucca (cheek) used in anatomical terminology to denote a diminutive cheek region.

bucket-handle fracture.definition: A vertical longitudinal tear of the knee’s meniscus with the inner fragment displaced into the joint, creating a bucket-handle appearance on imaging and often causing mechanical symptoms such as locking or clicking.

buck's fascia.definition: A deep fibrous envelope surrounding the penile erectile tissues (the corpora cavernosa and corpus spongiosum), forming the deep penile fascia.

buck's skin traction.definition: A temporary skin traction for proximal femur fractures (e.g., femoral neck/hip fractures) in which adhesive straps or a padded boot are applied to the leg and connected to a weight via a pulley to produce gentle longitudinal traction and hip extension, immobilizing the limb and relieving pain until definitive fixation.

buckwheat allergy.definition: A food allergy to buckwheat caused by an IgE-mediated immune reaction to buckwheat proteins, producing immediate hypersensitivity symptoms such as hives, swelling, wheezing, abdominal pain, or anaphylaxis after ingestion.

buclizine.definition: An oral, first‑generation antihistamine with antiemetic properties (piperazine derivative) used to prevent nausea and vomiting, especially due to motion sickness; it works by blocking histamine H1 receptors in the vestibular apparatus and vomiting center. Common side effects include drowsiness and dry mouth.

budd-chiari syndrome.definition: Obstruction of hepatic venous outflow (commonly from hepatic vein thrombosis) causing hepatic congestion with hepatomegaly, ascites, abdominal pain, and liver dysfunction; treated with anticoagulation, management of ascites, and possibly hepatic venous interventions or liver transplantation in severe cases.

buerger's disease.definition: A rare, nonatherosclerotic inflammatory disease of small- to medium-sized arteries and veins in the limbs, characterized by segmental thrombosing vasculitis; strongly associated with tobacco use and presenting with ischemia, claudication, ulcers, and possible gangrene. Smoking cessation is the primary treatment.

buerger's postural exercises.definition: A sequence of leg postures (leg elevation followed by a dependent/dangling position) designed to improve arterial blood flow to the lower extremities and aid healing of ischemic ulcers in peripheral vascular disease.

buffalo hump.definition: A dorsocervical fat pad; a localized accumulation of fat at the base of the neck (posterior neck), forming a hump often associated with Cushing syndrome, long-term corticosteroid use, obesity, or lipodystrophy.

buffy coat.definition: A thin layer of white blood cells (leukocytes) and platelets that forms between the plasma and erythrocytes after centrifugation of anticoagulated blood.

buffy coat transfusion.definition: A transfusion of the buffy coat—the leukocyte- and platelet-rich layer that lies between plasma and packed red cells after centrifugation of whole blood—to deliver donor leukocytes (and platelets) to a recipient, historically used to treat severe neutropenia or refractory infection but now largely obsolete due to risks of transfusion reactions and alloimmunization and typically replaced by leukoreduced products.

bulbar.definition: Relating to the medulla oblongata or the lower brainstem; used to describe muscles innervated by cranial nerves IX–XII or disorders affecting those nerves.

bulbar ataxia.definition: A form of ataxia resulting from degeneration or dysfunction of the bulbar (lower brainstem) motor pathways and cranial nerve nuclei, leading to dysarthria and dysphagia with accompanying limb and gait ataxia.

bulbar myelitis.definition: An inflammatory condition affecting the bulbar region of the brainstem (medulla oblongata) and/or adjacent spinal cord segments, typically presenting with bulbar (cranial nerve) dysfunction such as dysarthria and dysphagia, and may be accompanied by limb weakness.

bulbar palsy.definition: Lower motor neuron weakness of the bulbar (cranial nerve IX–XII) muscles due to damage to the brainstem nuclei or their fibers, causing dysarthria, dysphagia, tongue atrophy with fasciculations, palate weakness with nasal regurgitation, and hyporeflexia; often seen in motor neuron disease or brainstem lesions, and distinguished from pseudobulbar palsy (UMN bulbar involvement).

bulbar paralysis.definition: A lower motor neuron palsy of the bulbar cranial nerves (IX–XII) due to degeneration or damage of the medullary bulbar nuclei or their axons, causing weakness or paralysis of the tongue, pharynx, larynx, and soft palate with dysarthria, dysphagia, diminished gag and swallowing reflex, and sometimes fasciculations. It is distinguished from pseudobulbar palsy (an upper motor neuron bulbar syndrome).

bulbar poliomyelitis.definition: A paralytic form of poliomyelitis in which the brainstem (bulbar region) is affected, causing cranial nerve palsies with dysphagia, dysarthria, facial weakness, diminished gag reflex, and often respiratory paralysis due to weakness of bulbar and respiratory muscles.

bulbiform.definition: Having the shape of a bulb; bulb-shaped.

bulbocavernosus.definition: A paired superficial perineal muscle that surrounds the bulb of the penis in males and the bulbs of the vestibule in females; it arises from the perineal body and inserts into the corpus spongiosum (males) or vestibular bulbs (females), and it functions to compress the urethra and assist in erection and ejaculation.

bulbospongiosus.definition: A paired superficial perineal muscle of the perineum that surrounds the bulb of the penis in males (and the vestibular bulbs in females); contraction compresses these bulbs and the urethra, aiding erection and ejaculation in males and narrowing the vaginal opening in females.

cowper's gland.definition: Two small exocrine glands in the deep perineal pouch (bulbourethral glands) that secrete clear mucus (pre-ejaculate) into the penile urethra during sexual arousal to lubricate the urethra and neutralize residual urine acidity; the secretions typically do not contain sperm.

bulbous.definition: Having the shape of a bulb; rounded and swollen. Used to describe a structure, lesion, or tissue that is bulb-shaped or enlarged in a bulb-like manner.

bulb syringe.definition: A squeezable rubber or silicone bulb with a narrow application tip used to aspirate liquids or mucus by releasing and creating negative pressure; commonly used to clear nasal passages in infants.

bulbus oculi.definition: The eyeball—the globe of the eye; the spherical sensory organ within the orbit containing the cornea, lens, retina, and the aqueous and vitreous humors.

bulimia.definition: A mental health eating disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by compensatory behaviors to prevent weight gain (such as self-induced vomiting, laxative or diuretic use, fasting, or excessive exercise), often accompanied by an intense fear of gaining weight and distorted body image.

bulk cathartic.definition: A laxative that increases stool bulk by absorbing water and/or providing insoluble fiber, which stretches the bowel and stimulates peristalsis to facilitate defecation.

bullae.definition: A large fluid-filled blister on the skin or mucous membranes (>1 cm in diameter), caused by separation of epidermal layers from each other or from the dermis.

bullous.definition: Relating to or characterized by the presence of bullae — large, fluid-filled blisters on the skin or mucous membranes (usually ≥1 cm in diameter).

bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythro.definition: A rare genetic form of congenital ichthyosis marked by widespread erythroderma at birth with fragile bullae that rupture easily, followed by thick, adherent scales; part of the epidermolytic ichthyosis spectrum, usually due to keratin gene mutations (commonly KRT1 or KRT10) with autosomal dominant inheritance (though autosomal recessive cases exist).

bullous disease.definition: Any disease that produces bullae (large water-filled blisters) on the skin or mucous membranes, caused by separation of epidermal layers at the dermal-epidermal junction or within the epidermis (as seen in conditions like pemphigoid and pemphigus).

bullous emphysema.definition: A form of emphysema characterized by the development of large air-filled spaces (bullae) in the lung due to destruction of alveolar walls; these bullae can compress nearby lung tissue and rupture, increasing the risk of pneumothorax. Often associated with smoking-related COPD; management includes smoking cessation and COPD treatment, with bullectomy considered in selected cases.

bullous impetigo.definition: A contagious superficial skin infection, typically caused by Staphylococcus aureus, that produces large, flaccid bullae which rupture easily and leave thin honey-colored crusts; most common in infants and young children.

bullous myringitis.definition: A painful inflammatory condition of the tympanic membrane marked by the formation of vesicles or bullae on the drum; presents with severe ear pain and may be associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection, sometimes occurring with acute otitis media. Treatment focuses on analgesia and antibiotics if an infectious etiology is suspected.

bullous pemphigoid.definition: An autoimmune subepidermal blistering disorder in older adults characterized by tense, fluid-filled bullae on normal-appearing or inflamed skin (and sometimes mucous membranes), caused by autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins BP180 (type XVII collagen) and BP230 in the basement membrane zone, with a negative Nikolsky sign.

bullseye rash.definition: A skin lesion often seen in early Lyme disease, consisting of a gradually expanding circular red patch with central clearing (bull's-eye appearance); may be warm or painless and may be accompanied by fatigue, fever, or flu-like symptoms.

erythema migrans.definition: A slowly expanding annular erythematous rash that typically appears at the site of a tick bite in early Lyme borreliosis, often with central clearing (bull's-eye) and may be accompanied by mild constitutional symptoms; multiple lesions can occur.

bumetanide.definition: A potent loop diuretic that inhibits the Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, increasing excretion of sodium, chloride, and water; used to treat edema from heart failure, liver cirrhosis, or kidney disease, and to help manage hypertension.

bun.definition: A blood test that measures the amount of urea nitrogen in the blood, used to assess kidney function and hydration status.

bundle.definition: A bundle is a group of fibers (such as nerve fibers or muscle fibers) bound together by connective tissue to form a functional unit; in the heart, it can refer to conducting pathways such as the Bundle of His.

bundle branch.definition: One of the two main divisions of the His-Purkinje conduction system in the heart, transmitting electrical impulses from the AV node to the ventricles; the right bundle branch conducts to the right ventricle and the left bundle branch conducts to the left ventricle (via its fascicles).

left bundle branch block.definition: A conduction abnormality resulting from impaired conduction in the left bundle branch, causing delayed and dyssynchronous activation of the left ventricle; it typically produces a widened QRS complex (usually ≥120 ms) on ECG with characteristic changes in lateral leads, and is often associated with underlying heart disease rather than being a disease itself.

right bundle branch block.definition: Delay or blockage of electrical conduction through the right bundle branch of the heart's conduction system, leading to asynchronous ventricular activation and a widened QRS complex (≥120 ms) with an rsR' pattern in the right precordial leads (V1–V2) and a wide S wave in leads I and V6 on ECG.

bundle of his.definition: A collection of specialized conduction fibers in the heart that transmits electrical impulses from the atrioventricular node to the ventricles, dividing into the right and left bundle branches to coordinate ventricular contraction.

atrioventricular bundle.definition: A conduction pathway in the heart that transmits impulses from the atrioventricular node to the ventricles, through a bundle of specialized fibers in the interventricular septum that divides into the right and left bundle branches as part of the His–Purkinje system.

intraventricular septum.definition: Wall between the left and right ventricles of the heart, consisting of a muscular portion and a small membranous portion; it separates the ventricles and contains parts of the heart's conduction system (e.g., the bundle of His).

purkinje fibers.definition: A network of specialized conducting fibers in the subendocardial region of the ventricles that rapidly transmit impulses from the bundle of His to the ventricular myocardium, enabling synchronized ventricular depolarization and contraction; part of the His-Purkinje system.

seasonal allergic rhinitis.definition: A type I hypersensitivity reaction of the nasal mucosa to inhaled environmental allergens (most commonly pollen) causing sneezing, itching, rhinorrhea, and nasal congestion; symptoms are seasonal and may be accompanied by itchy, watery eyes.

perennial allergic rhinitis.definition: A form of allergic rhinitis in which nasal symptoms (congestion, runny nose, sneezing, itching) persist for most of the year—typically for at least 4 weeks—due to IgE-mediated sensitivity to perennial indoor allergens such as dust mites, animal dander, molds, or cockroaches.

perennial nonallergic rhinitis.definition: A chronic rhinitis characterized by year-round nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, sneezing, and postnasal drainage lasting at least 12 weeks, in the absence of allergic sensitization or infectious causes; symptoms are often triggerable by irritants (eg, smoke, strong odors) or weather changes and are attributed to vasomotor or neural dysregulation of the nasal mucosa.

epidermolytic hyperkeratosis.definition: A histopathologic pattern of the skin characterized by epidermolytic degeneration of keratinocytes in the stratum spinosum with marked hyperkeratosis, showing perinuclear vacuolization and clumped keratohyalin granules (often due to keratin gene mutations and seen in certain ichthyoses).

ichthyosiform erythroderma.definition: Generalized erythroderma with ichthyosis-like scaling; a red, scaly skin phenotype often present at birth or in infancy and seen in congenital ichthyosis syndromes (e.g., Netherton syndrome) due to defects in skin barrier function.

granulocyte transfusion.definition: A transfusion of donor granulocytes (primarily neutrophils) administered intravenously to a neutropenic patient with a severe or refractory infection, aiming to provide immediate, short-term innate immune defense when the patient’s own neutrophil production is inadequate and antibiotic therapy is insufficient.

postural exercises.definition: Exercises designed to improve upright alignment and the neuromuscular control of the spine and trunk, typically by strengthening the core and back muscles, stretching tight anterior muscles (e.g., chest, hip flexors), and training postural awareness to maintain proper posture during daily activities.

hepatic vein occlusion.definition: Occlusion of the hepatic veins or hepatic venous outflow, blocking drainage of blood from the liver and causing hepatic congestion, hepatomegaly, ascites, and potential liver dysfunction (as seen in Budd-Chiari syndrome).

growth plate.definition: A cartilaginous region near the ends of long bones in children and adolescents where bone lengthening occurs during growth.

penile reflex.definition: A reflexive erection of the penis elicited by tactile stimulation (e.g., of the glans or perineum), mediated by sacral parasympathetic pathways (S2–S4) via the pelvic nerves; it is a spinal reflex that can be used to assess autonomic/sacral function.

bulbospongiosus reflex.definition: A perineal reflex in which stimulation of the perineum or glans penis elicits contraction of the bulbospongiosus muscle, mediated by the pudendal nerve (S2–S4) and used to assess sacral spinal cord or pudendal nerve integrity.

accelerator urinae.definition: A diuretic; an agent that increases the production and excretion of urine by the kidneys, thereby promoting urination.

ejaculator urinae.definition: A nonstandard term; most closely, the urethra—the passage that conveys urine from the bladder to the exterior; in males, it also serves as part of the reproductive tract during ejaculation.

bunionectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to correct a bunion (hallux valgus) by removing the bony bump and realigning the first metatarsophalangeal joint, often with osteotomy and fixation.

bunion.definition: A bump of bone or tissue that forms at the big toe joint, causing inflammation and considerable pain.

bunionette.definition: A small, painful bony bump that forms on the outside of the foot, at the base of the small toe.

bunnell.definition: An eponym in medicine; by itself it does not define a single procedure, but refers to several techniques named after a physician named Bunnell. The exact meaning depends on the specific Bunnell technique being referenced.

bunsen.definition: A small gas-fired laboratory burner that provides a controllable flame for heating substances, typically fueled by natural gas or propane and used in medical and scientific laboratories.

bunyamwera.definition: A mosquito-borne enveloped negative-sense RNA arbovirus, prototype member of the Orthobunyavirus genus; causes Bunyamwera fever, a typically mild febrile illness in humans.

california.definition: Not a medical term; no medical definition.

rift.definition: A narrow opening or split in tissue or bone; a fissure or cleft that results from trauma, disease, or developmental anomaly.

valley.definition: A shallow depression or groove within an organ or tissue; in anatomy, a small valley‑like space between structures (for example, a groove between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis).

melioidosis.definition: An infectious disease caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, a soil- and water-associated gram-negative bacterium found in tropical regions (notably Southeast Asia and northern Australia). It presents variably as pneumonia, abscesses, or septicemia and may be acute, chronic, or latent.

burkholderia.definition: A genus of Gram-negative, non-spore-forming rods in the Burkholderiaceae family; environmental bacteria with several species that are opportunistic human pathogens, including B. cepacia complex (in cystic fibrosis and immunocompromised patients), B. pseudomallei (melioidosis), and B. mallei (glanders).

cepacia.definition: A Gram-negative, nonfermenting bacterium within the Burkholderia cepacia complex; an environmental organism that acts as an opportunistic pathogen, causing respiratory infections (notably in cystic fibrosis and other chronic lung diseases) and, less commonly, bacteremia; often resistant to multiple antibiotics and associated with cepacia syndrome (necrotizing pneumonia with septicemia).

mallei.definition: Plural form of malleus, the hammer-shaped bone in the middle ear that transmits sound vibrations from the tympanic membrane to the incus (one of the auditory ossicles).

pickettii.definition: An environmental, Gram-negative, nonfermenting bacillus that can cause opportunistic infections in immunocompromised individuals and in healthcare settings, often linked to contaminated water or sterile fluids; previously classified as Pseudomonas pickettii.

pseudomallei.definition: A Gram-negative, motile, aerobic bacterium of the genus Burkholderia that causes melioidosis; commonly found in soil and surface water in tropical regions and can cause pneumonia, abscesses, septicemia, and disseminated infection.

caudal.definition: Towards the bottom of the body, away from the head.

peripheral.definition: Situated away from the center; referring to the outer parts of the body or to the peripheral nervous system.

sympathetic.definition: Relating to the sympathetic nervous system, the autonomic nervous system division that mediates rapid fight-or-flight responses, such as increased heart rate and blood pressure, bronchodilation, pupil dilation, and reduced digestive activity.

buprenorphine.definition: A semi-synthetic opioid analgesic and partial μ-opioid receptor agonist used to treat pain and opioid use disorder; it has a ceiling effect on respiratory depression and is commonly given sublingually in tablet or film form.

opioid.definition: Any narcotic, natural or synthetic, that behaves in the body like an opium-derived drug.

arrest.definition: An abrupt cessation of a vital physiological function, most commonly referring to the heart stopping effectively (cardiac arrest) and leading to loss of effective circulation; it can also denote cessation of breathing (respiratory arrest) or other halted biological processes.

osteolytic.definition: Relating to or causing osteolysis (bone resorption); a destructive process in which bone tissue is resorbed, often producing radiolucent lesions on imaging.

lesion.definition: A sore or any part of your skin that looks different from the rest.

curlings.definition: A stress-related duodenal ulcer that occurs after major burns or trauma, due to hypovolemia and splanchnic ischemia leading to mucosal injury; may present with upper GI bleeding and typically develops within the first week after injury.

septic.definition: Relating to sepsis or an infection; infected with pathogenic microorganisms, typically bacteria.

epstein-barr-virus.definition: An enveloped double-stranded DNA herpesvirus of the genus Lymphocryptovirus in the family Herpesviridae; it infects B lymphocytes (via the CD21 receptor), is transmitted primarily through saliva, can cause infectious mononucleosis, and persists for life in latent form, being associated with Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder.

burkitt.definition: An aggressive B‑cell non‑Hodgkin lymphoma driven by MYC gene translocations (most often t(8;14)); causes rapid tumor growth, with endemic African cases often involving the jaw and sporadic cases the abdomen; highly chemosensitive to intensive combination chemotherapy with CNS prophylaxis.

african.definition: Relating to the continent of Africa or its inhabitants; a person from Africa.

glanders.definition: Glanders is a zoonotic infectious disease caused by Burkholderia mallei, primarily affecting horses and other equids; in humans it can cause cutaneous nodules (farcy) or severe pneumonia and septicemia, acquired by contact with infected animals or contaminated materials.

paralytic.definition: Relating to paralysis; causing paralysis by blocking neuromuscular transmission; used of agents that induce temporary skeletal muscle paralysis, such as during anesthesia.

burr holes.definition: Small openings drilled into the skull using a high-speed drill to access the cranial cavity or relieve intracranial pressure, commonly used for draining hematomas or as a preliminary step before a craniotomy.

burn.definition: A tissue injury caused by exposure to heat (thermal), chemicals, electricity, or radiation that damages cells and triggers inflammation; severity is determined by the depth of tissue involvement (superficial, partial-thickness, full-thickness) and the extent of body surface area affected.

germicidal.definition: Capable of destroying or inactivating microorganisms, including bacteria, viruses, and fungi; used to describe agents or procedures that kill or neutralize germs.

bacteriostatic.definition: An antimicrobial agent that inhibits the growth and replication of bacteria, rather than killing them directly; the infection is then cleared by the host's immune response.

porcine heterograft.definition: A graft from pig tissue transplanted into another species (a xenograft), used for surgical tissue replacement with immunologic rejection being a major consideration.

artificial skin.definition: A biomaterial-based skin substitute used to cover wounds, providing a protective barrier, maintaining moisture, and promoting tissue regeneration; it may be temporary or permanent and is used in burn care and extensive skin loss.

skin graft.definition: A surgical procedure in which skin is transplanted from a donor site to a recipient site to cover a wound or defect; grafts can be autograft (from the patient's own body), allograft (from another person), or xenograft (from another species), and may be split-thickness or full-thickness.

craniotomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which a portion of the skull (a bone flap) is temporarily removed to access the brain, typically to treat injury, tumor, or other brain pathology, or to relieve intracranial pressure.

third-degree burn.definition: A full-thickness burn that destroys both the epidermis and dermis (and may extend into subcutaneous tissue), producing a dry, leathery eschar, often painless due to nerve destruction, and typically requiring surgical intervention such as debridement and skin grafting.
