bursectomy.definition: Removal of a bursa by surgery, typically to treat chronic bursitis or infection, or to gain access to underlying structures.

intra-bursal injection.definition: Injection of medication directly into a synovial bursa, a fluid-filled sac that cushions a joint, typically to treat bursitis or inflammation; commonly uses corticosteroids and/or local anesthetics.

adrenocorticosteroid.definition: A corticosteroid hormone produced by the adrenal cortex; includes glucocorticoids (e.g., cortisol) and mineralocorticoids (e.g., aldosterone); synthetic analogs (e.g., prednisone, dexamethasone) are used for anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects and to regulate electrolyte balance.

immobilization.definition: An intervention that restricts movement of a body part to promote healing after injury or surgery and to stabilize fractures or soft-tissue injuries; accomplished with devices such as casts, splints, braces, or external fixation.

calcium deposits.definition: An accumulation of calcium salts in soft tissues where they are not ordinarily present. It occurs in two main contexts: dystrophic calcification—calcium deposition in damaged or necrotic tissue with normal serum calcium; and metastatic calcification—calcium deposition in otherwise normal tissues due to elevated calcium or phosphate levels in the blood.

housemaid’s knee.definition: Inflammation of the prepatellar bursa in front of the kneecap, usually due to prolonged kneeling or trauma, causing swelling, pain, and tenderness over the knee.

miner’s elbow.definition: A tendinopathy of the common extensor tendon origin at the lateral epicondyle of the humerus (lateral epicondylitis) caused by repetitive wrist extension and gripping, presenting with lateral elbow pain and tenderness at the lateral epicondyle, worsened by forearm use.

weaver’s bottom.definition: A historical term for hemorrhoids (piles) — dilated veins of the anal canal — typically arising from prolonged sitting and straining, historically common among weavers. Symptoms may include anal discomfort, itching, and bright red blood with defecation.

rheumatism.definition: Pain and stiffness of soft tissues in and around joints.

burst fracture.definition: A vertebral body fracture caused by a high-energy axial load that results in comminution (multiple fragments) of the vertebral body with retropulsion of bone fragments into the spinal canal, potentially causing spinal canal compromise and neurologic injury.

burton’s line.definition: A bluish-black line along the gingival margin seen in chronic lead poisoning, due to deposition of lead sulfide formed when lead reacts with hydrogen sulfide produced by oral bacteria.

blue line.definition: A bluish-black line along the gum margin seen in chronic lead poisoning, caused by deposition of lead sulfide in the gingival crevices; often correlates with elevated blood lead levels.

buruli ulcer.definition: A chronic skin infection caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans that begins as a painless nodule or plaque and progresses to a large ulcer with undermined edges; commonly affects tropical regions and is associated with aquatic environments; treated with a rifampin-containing antibiotic regimen (often with another agent) and, if needed, surgical debridement.

mycobacterium ulcerans.definition: A slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium that causes Buruli ulcer, a necrotizing skin and soft-tissue infection; it produces the toxin mycolactone, leading to tissue destruction, and is found in aquatic environments in tropical regions (notably West Africa and parts of Australia); treatment typically involves a combination of antibiotics (eg, rifampin with clarithromycin or streptomycin) and sometimes surgical debridement.

byssinosis.definition: A work-related occupational lung disease caused by inhalation of cotton dust (and other vegetable dust) in inadequately ventilated environments, resulting in bronchitic symptoms such as cough, wheeze, chest tightness, and shortness of breath, often worse at the start of the workweek (Monday fever).

blood transfusions.definition: A medical procedure in which blood or blood components (red blood cells, plasma, platelets) are intravenously transfused from a donor to a recipient to replace blood loss or correct deficiencies; compatibility testing (ABO/Rh typing and crossmatching) is typically performed beforehand.

steroid therapy.definition: The medical use of corticosteroids to reduce inflammation and suppress the immune response, delivered systemically (oral or intravenous) or locally (injections, inhaled, topical, etc.) for conditions such as autoimmune diseases, allergies, asthma, and transplant rejection.

antipyretics.definition: A drug or drugs used to reduce fever by acting on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center, typically by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis; examples include acetaminophen (paracetamol), ibuprofen, and aspirin.

contractures.definition: A permanent shortening and tightening of soft tissues around a joint (such as muscles, tendons, ligaments, fascia, or joint capsule) resulting in reduced range of motion and fixed deformity; commonly occurs after injury, burns, prolonged immobilization, or neuromuscular disorders.

nurse.definition: A healthcare professional trained and licensed to provide direct patient care, monitor health status, administer medications and therapies, perform procedures under supervision, educate patients, and coordinate care with other clinicians.

wound care.definition: Care and management of wounds to promote healing and prevent complications, including cleansing and debridement when indicated, appropriate dressing to maintain a moist wound environment, infection prevention, pain control, and ongoing assessment for signs of infection or delayed healing while addressing contributing factors such as nutrition and comorbidities.

plastic surgery.definition: A surgical specialty that repairs, reconstructs, or alters body tissues to restore form and function, encompassing both reconstructive and cosmetic (aesthetic) procedures.

rehabilitation.definition: The process of restoring a person’s health and functional abilities after illness, injury, or surgery through targeted therapies, training, and support to maximize independence.

aluminum sulfate.definition: An inorganic aluminum salt used topically as an astringent and styptic to stop minor bleeding and contract tissue, and also used as a coagulant in water purification.

topical astringent.definition: A substance applied to skin or mucous membranes that causes protein precipitation and tissue contraction, leading to drying, tightening, and reduction of secretions or minor bleeding.

antiseptic.definition: Substances used on wounds to prevent or treat infection; they kill or slow the growth of disease-causing organisms, such as bacteria, on the surface of the body.

butyrophenone.definition: A class of potent dopamine D2 receptor antagonist antipsychotic drugs (also used as antiemetics), exemplified by haloperidol; used to treat schizophrenia and other psychoses and to suppress severe nausea/vomiting; commonly associated with extrapyramidal symptoms.

haloperidol.definition: A high-potency typical (first-generation) antipsychotic that antagonizes dopamine D2 receptors; used to treat schizophrenia and other psychoses, severe agitation, delirium, and sometimes nausea and vomiting; adverse effects include extrapyramidal symptoms and tardive dyskinesia.

droperidol.definition: A potent antiemetic and antipsychotic of the butyrophenone class; a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist used to prevent postoperative nausea and vomiting and to provide sedation; carries a risk of QT interval prolongation and torsades de pointes, leading to restricted use due to cardiac safety concerns.

Alternatively, I can suggest similar or more common eponymous maneuvers if you provide the related area (e.g., obstetrics, cardiology, neurology).

patellar reflex.definition: A stretch reflex elicited by tapping the patellar tendon just below the kneecap, causing contraction of the quadriceps muscle and extension of the knee; mediated by the femoral nerve (L2–L4) and used to assess the integrity of the L2–L4 spinal segments.

quadriceps.definition: A group of muscles on the front of the top part of the leg or thigh.

tics.definition: Sudden, rapid, recurrent, nonrhythmic movements or vocalizations that occur involuntarily; they can be motor or vocal and may wax and wane in frequency.

coprolalia.definition: Involuntary utterance of obscene, profane, or socially inappropriate words or phrases, typically seen as a vocal tic in Tourette syndrome and related tic disorders.

huntington’s disease.definition: An autosomal-dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene on chromosome 4, characterized by chorea, psychiatric changes, and progressive cognitive decline leading to dementia.

neuroleptanesthesia.definition: An anesthetic state produced by combining a neuroleptic (antipsychotic) drug with a potent analgesic, yielding marked analgesia, diminished responsiveness to painful stimuli, and reduced movement (often a cataleptic/sedated state) with little spontaneous activity, allowing surgery without full general anesthesia.

butorphanol tartrate.definition: A synthetic mixed opioid analgesic; acts as a kappa receptor agonist and mu receptor antagonist/partial agonist, used for short-term relief of moderate to severe pain; supplied as the tartrate salt for injectable or intranasal use.

butorphanol.definition: A synthetic opioid analgesic with mixed agonist–antagonist activity—primarily a kappa-opioid receptor agonist and mu-opioid receptor antagonist/partial agonist—for moderate to severe pain; can cause sedation, nausea, and a ceiling effect for respiratory depression, and may precipitate withdrawal in opioid-dependent individuals.

butoconazole nitrate.definition: An azole antifungal agent used topically to treat superficial fungal infections by inhibiting fungal cytochrome P450–dependent 14-α-demethylase, thereby blocking ergosterol synthesis and disrupting fungal cell membranes.

candida.definition: A genus of yeasts (fungi) that are part of the normal human microbiota on mucous membranes and skin but can cause opportunistic infections, ranging from mucocutaneous candidiasis (oral thrush, vaginal candidiasis) to invasive candidiasis and candidemia in immunocompromised individuals.

vulvovaginal infection.definition: A clinical syndrome of inflammation of the vulva and vagina caused by infection with organisms such as Candida species (yeast), bacteria associated with bacterial vaginosis, or the protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis, typically presenting with itching, abnormal discharge, and sometimes odor or irritation.

giant condyloma.definition: A very large, exophytic, wart-like lesion of the anogenital skin and mucosa caused by HPV infection (condylomata acuminata), most commonly HPV types 6 and 11; histologically benign but locally invasive and capable of malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma; typically treated with wide surgical excision and close follow-up due to high recurrence; also known as Buschke-Löwenstein tumor.

condyloma.definition: Benign, soft, wart-like growths on moist skin or mucous membranes, most often in the genital or anal region; usually caused by human papillomavirus infection (genital warts, commonly HPV types 6 and 11).

bursa of fabricius.definition: A lymphoid organ in birds, a dorsal diverticulum of the cloaca; the primary site of maturation for B lymphocytes (B cells), essential for antibody production; analogous to bone marrow in mammals.

prepatellar bursa.definition: A small fluid-filled sac located anterior to the kneecap, between the patella and the skin, that reduces friction during knee movement; inflammation of this bursa is called prepatellar bursitis.

olecranon bursa.definition: A small fluid-filled sac located over the elbow’s olecranon that cushions friction between the skin and the underlying bone during movement; it can become inflamed (olecranon bursitis) due to trauma, pressure, infection, or inflammatory conditions.

bursal abscess.definition: A localized purulent infection of a synovial-lined bursa in which pus accumulates within the bursa (septic bursitis with abscess formation), causing swelling, warmth, and tenderness; often due to Staphylococcus aureus and treated with drainage or aspiration plus targeted antibiotics.

bursa-equivalent tissue.definition: A structure functioning like a bursa by providing a lubricated, friction-reducing space between moving tissues (typically a synovial-lined cushion), such as between a tendon and bone, when a true bursa is absent but similar cushion tissue exists.

byler’s disease.definition: An infantile form of progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis (PFIC type I) caused by ATP8B1 gene mutations, presenting with cholestasis, pruritus, fat malabsorption, and progressive liver disease leading to cirrhosis.

distal renal tubular acidosis.definition: A defect in distal tubule/collecting duct acid secretion, usually at the alpha-intercalated cells, causing impaired urinary acidification and a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with an inappropriately high urine pH (>5.5), often accompanied by hypokalemia and nephrocalcinosis or nephrolithiasis.

autosomal-dominant.definition: A pattern of inheritance in which a single copy of a mutant autosomal gene is sufficient to cause the disorder; typically seen in every generation with equal affection of males and females, and each child of an affected individual has a 50% chance of inheriting the trait.

athlete’s foot.definition: A foot infection caused by fungus; symptoms include cracking and peeling skin and itchiness. Also known as tinea pedis.

jock itch.definition: A red, itchy rash that appears in warm, damp areas, like your inner thighs. It is caused by a germ (a fungus). Also called tinea cruris.

ringworm.definition: A red rash in the shape of a circle, caused by a germ (a fungus). It is not caused by a worm.

butisol sodium.definition: The sodium salt of the barbiturate butabarbital, a CNS depressant used as a sedative/hypnotic for insomnia; it potentiates GABA-A–mediated inhibition and carries risks of sedation, dependence, and respiratory depression.

butabarbital.definition: A barbiturate drug used as a sedative and hypnotic; a CNS depressant that enhances GABA-A receptor activity, producing sedation and sleep, with potential for dependence and respiratory depression.

butabarbital sodium.definition: A barbiturate sedative-hypnotic; the sodium salt of butabarbital, a central nervous system depressant used historically to treat anxiety, agitation, and insomnia. It acts by potentiating GABA-A receptor–mediated inhibition, and can cause drowsiness, dependence, tolerance, and respiratory depression; overdose can be fatal.

butenafine.definition: A topical antifungal agent of the allylamine class used to treat dermatophyte skin infections (e.g., tinea pedis, tinea cruris, tinea corporis); it inhibits fungal squalene epoxidase, disrupting ergosterol synthesis in the fungal cell membrane.

cabg.definition: Surgery to improve blood flow to the heart by diverting blood around a blocked coronary artery, typically using a graft from another vessel.

cadaveric donor transplantation.definition: A transplantation in which an organ or tissue is donated from a deceased person (cadaver) and transplanted into a recipient.

cadaveric renal transplant.definition: A kidney transplant performed using a donor kidney recovered from a deceased person (cadaver) rather than from a living donor; the transplanted kidney is placed into a recipient with kidney failure and requires lifelong immunosuppression to prevent rejection.

cadmium poisoning.definition: Cadmium poisoning is toxicity due to exposure to cadmium, a toxic heavy metal. Chronic exposure—often occupational inhalation or ingestion and cigarette smoke—accumulates in the kidneys and bones, causing proximal renal tubular dysfunction (proteinuria, phosphate wasting) and osteomalacia/osteoporosis (Itai‑itai disease); acute high-dose inhalation can cause pneumonitis, and cadmium is a recognized human carcinogen, especially for the lung, with a long biological half-life in renal tissue.

cadmium nephropathy.definition: Kidney damage from chronic cadmium exposure, chiefly proximal tubular injury with Fanconi-type dysfunction (glycosuria with normoglycemia, aminoaciduria, phosphate wasting), which can progress to chronic kidney disease; exposure is typically occupational or environmental, and management focuses on removing exposure and providing supportive renal care.

caisson disease.definition: A form of decompression sickness caused by rapid ascent from a high-pressure environment, leading to nitrogen gas bubbles forming in blood and tissues and causing joint/muscle pain, neurologic symptoms, cutaneous signs, and sometimes respiratory or circulatory problems; treated with hyperbaric oxygen therapy and careful recompression.

ca125.definition: A high‑molecular‑weight glycoprotein (MUC16) used as a tumor marker primarily to monitor ovarian cancer therapy and detect recurrence; elevated levels can occur with benign gynecologic conditions and other malignancies, and it is not suitable as a general screening test.

ca19-9.definition: A blood-based tumor marker used mainly to monitor pancreatic and biliary cancers; it is a carbohydrate antigen produced by pancreatic and biliary epithelium. Levels correlate with tumor burden and treatment response but are not specific and can be elevated in benign liver/biliary disease; a subset of individuals do not produce it at all, limiting its value for screening.

ca15-3.definition: A serum tumor marker (MUC1-containing glycoprotein) used to monitor breast cancer treatment response and detect recurrence; not sufficiently sensitive or specific for diagnosis or screening.

ca27-29.definition: A serum tumor marker used primarily to monitor breast cancer; it detects a mucin-like glycoprotein derived from MUC1 and generally correlates with disease burden and response to therapy. It is not specific for breast cancer and is not recommended for screening; elevations can occur with benign breast conditions, liver disease, or other cancers.

cafe-au-lait spot.definition: A flat, uniformly pigmented macule (light brown to coffee-colored) present from birth or early childhood, caused by increased melanin in the epidermis; often benign but can be associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 when multiple.

neurofibromatosis.definition: A hereditary genetic disorder characterized by the development of multiple benign tumors along peripheral nerves (neurofibromas), often with skin findings such as café-au-lait spots and axillary/inguinal freckling; two major forms (NF1 and NF2) differ by mutation and clinical features and may include skeletal abnormalities and learning difficulties.

loa loa.definition: A parasitic infection caused by a filarial nematode transmitted by Chrysops (deer flies); it causes loiasis, characterized by transient Calabar swellings and migration of adult worms through subcutaneous tissues, sometimes across the conjunctiva of the eye.

loiasis.definition: A parasitic infection caused by a filarial nematode transmitted by deerflies (Chrysops spp.), characterized by transient subcutaneous Calabar swellings and possible migration of the worm across the conjunctiva; diagnosed by daytime peripheral blood microfilariae and/or visualization of the adult worm; treated with diethylcarbamazine (with consideration of adjunctive therapies in certain infections).

c1 inhibitor.definition: A plasma serine protease inhibitor (serpin) that regulates the classical pathway of complement activation by inhibiting C1r and C1s, and also inhibits the kallikrein–kinin system; deficiency or dysfunction leads to hereditary angioedema.

c1q nephropathy.definition: An uncommon glomerular disease defined by dominant or codominant C1q deposition in the glomerulus (primarily mesangial) on immunofluorescence, with little or no accompanying immunoglobulins, in the absence of systemic lupus erythematosus; biopsy histology is variable (often mesangial proliferative or focal segmental glomerulosclerosis) and clinically it typically presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria.

c3 nephritic factor.definition: An autoantibody (usually IgG) that stabilizes the alternative-pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb), preventing its decay and causing continuous activation of the complement cascade with consumption of C3, associated with C3 glomerulopathy (e.g., dense deposit disease and MPGN type II).

caffey's disease.definition: A self-limited pediatric bone disorder characterized by periosteal new bone formation (hyperostosis) with swelling and tenderness of affected sites, most commonly the mandible and clavicle, presenting in infancy with irritability and fever and resolving spontaneously over months to a few years.

caffey's syndrome.definition: A rare, self-limited inflammatory bone disorder of infancy characterized by periosteal new bone formation (hyperostosis) with swelling and tenderness, often involving the mandible and clavicles and other long bones; patients present with fever and irritability; radiographs show cortical thickening; the condition typically resolves spontaneously over months to a few years.

caffeine.definition: A central nervous system stimulant of the xanthine class found in coffee, tea, cocoa, and some foods; it blocks adenosine receptors in the brain, increasing alertness and reducing fatigue.

caffeine breath test.definition: A noninvasive diagnostic test in which a labeled caffeine dose is ingested and the exhaled breath is collected over time to measure labeled CO2, reflecting hepatic caffeine metabolism by cytochrome P450 1A2.

caffeinism.definition: A syndrome produced by excessive caffeine intake, marked by nervousness, anxiety, insomnia, restlessness, tachycardia, tremor, headaches, and gastrointestinal upset; may involve tolerance and withdrawal symptoms when caffeine use is reduced or stopped.

cafergot.definition: A brand-name combination medication containing ergotamine tartrate and caffeine used to treat acute migraine headaches; it acts by constricting cerebral blood vessels and reducing migraine-related neurogenic inflammation.

ergotamine.definition: An ergot alkaloid used to treat acute migraine attacks; it causes cerebral and systemic vasoconstriction by acting on serotonin (5-HT1B/1D) and α-adrenergic receptors, typically given as ergotamine tartrate; adverse effects include nausea, paresthesias, and risk of ergotism; contraindicated in pregnancy and in vascular diseases or significant hepatic/renal impairment.

lactation mastitis.definition: An infection and inflammation of the breast tissue occurring during lactation, typically due to milk stasis and/or bacterial infection (often Staphylococcus aureus), presenting with localized breast pain, redness, warmth, swelling, and sometimes fever; managed with continued breastfeeding or pumping, supportive care, and antibiotics if bacterial infection is suspected.

second-look laparotomies.definition: A planned repeat exploratory abdominal operation after initial cancer treatment (often chemotherapy or cytoreductive surgery) to assess the extent of residual disease and guide further therapy.

calcaneal apophysitis.definition: An overuse injury of the calcaneal growth plate in skeletally immature individuals, causing posterior heel pain that worsens with activity and is often related to traction from the Achilles tendon; managed with rest, ice, NSAIDs, heel elevation or padding, activity modification, and physical therapy.

calcaneal spur.definition: A bony outgrowth from the heel bone (calcaneus), typically on the inferior aspect, that can cause heel pain and is often associated with plantar fasciitis; commonly seen on X-ray.

calcaneal tuberosity.definition: The large posterior-inferior bony prominence of the heel bone (calcaneus) where the Achilles tendon inserts.

calcaneodynia.definition: Pain in the heel bone (calcaneus); a symptom that can arise from conditions such as plantar fasciitis, Achilles tendinopathy, heel spur, fracture, or other heel disorders.

calcarine fissure.definition: A deep groove on the medial surface of the occipital lobe that marks the boundary between the cuneus above and the lingual gyrus below and contains the primary visual cortex (V1, Brodmann area 17).

calcarine sulcus.definition: A deep groove on the medial surface of the occipital lobe that marks the boundary between the cuneus (superior) and lingual gyrus (inferior) and contains the primary visual cortex (V1).

calcar pedis.definition: A spur-like bony projection from the plantar aspect of the calcaneus (heel bone).

hippocampus.definition: A seahorse-shaped brain structure in the medial temporal lobe, part of the limbic system, essential for encoding, forming, and consolidating new explicit (declarative) memories and for spatial navigation.

cervical nerves.definition: Eight pairs of spinal nerves (C1–C8) arising from the cervical portion of the spinal cord; they provide motor and sensory innervation to the neck, shoulders, and upper limbs and exit the spinal canal through the intervertebral foramina (C1–C7 exit above their vertebrae; C8 exits below C7 between C7 and T1).

cervical vertebrae.definition: Seven cervical vertebrae (C1–C7) form the neck portion of the spine; they support the head, protect the spinal cord, and allow a wide range of head movement. The first two vertebrae (atlas and axis) are specialized for nodding and rotation, and cervical vertebrae have transverse foramina for the vertebral arteries.

kidney transplant.definition: A surgical procedure in which a healthy donor kidney is placed into a person with kidney failure and connected to the recipient’s blood vessels and urinary tract; lifelong immunosuppressive medications are typically required to prevent rejection.

immune complex glomerulonephritis.definition: Glomerulonephritis caused by deposition of antigen–antibody immune complexes in the glomeruli, leading to complement activation and inflammatory injury; commonly occurs after infection or in autoimmune diseases.

mesangial tissue.definition: A component of the renal glomerulus composed of mesangial cells and mesangial matrix located between glomerular capillary loops; it provides structural support, modulates filtration surface area by contraction, and participates in phagocytosis and turnover of extracellular matrix, helping clear immune complexes.

glomerular capillary walls.definition: Three-layer filtration barrier comprising fenestrated endothelium, the glomerular basement membrane, and visceral epithelial (podocyte) foot processes with slit diaphragms; collectively they restrict passage of blood cells and large proteins while allowing water and small solutes to pass.

hyperprolactinemia.definition: Elevated levels of prolactin in the blood (serum prolactin above the normal range), often due to a pituitary tumor (prolactinoma) or other medical conditions and medications; it can cause galactorrhea, menstrual irregularities, infertility, and sexual dysfunction.

dopamine receptor agonist.definition: A drug that directly activates dopamine receptors (D1–D5), mimicking the action of dopamine; used to treat conditions caused by dopamine deficiency, most notably Parkinson disease and restless legs syndrome.

cabergoline.definition: An ergot-derived dopamine D2 receptor agonist used to treat hyperprolactinemia and prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas by inhibiting prolactin secretion; can shrink tumors and restore gonadal function. Administered orally with a long half-life; common side effects include nausea, dizziness, fatigue, and headaches; long-term use has been associated with valvular heart disease in some patients.

pancreatic cancer.definition: A malignant tumor arising from pancreatic tissue, most often pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, characterized by aggressive growth and late diagnosis with a poor prognosis. Risk factors include smoking, chronic pancreatitis, obesity, diabetes, and inherited genetic syndromes; common presentations are weight loss, upper abdominal or back pain, and jaundice when the tumor blocks the common bile duct.

hepatobiliary cancer.definition: Malignant tumors originating in the liver or biliary tract (including hepatocellular carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma—both intrahepatic and extrahepatic—and gallbladder cancer); collectively, cancers of the hepatobiliary system.

colorectal cancer.definition: A malignant tumor of the colon or rectum, most commonly an adenocarcinoma, often arising from preexisting polyps; diagnosed by colonoscopic biopsy and staged for treatment based on the extent of local invasion and metastasis.

tumor marker.definition: A biological molecule (often a protein) that can be measured in blood, urine, or tissue and whose levels may be elevated in cancer; used to help diagnose cancer, monitor treatment, and detect recurrence.

wright stain.definition: A polychromatic Romanowsky-type stain used for staining peripheral blood smears; it combines eosin (an acidic dye) and methylene blue (a basic dye) to differentiate blood cell types, staining cytoplasm pink to orange and nuclei blue to purple.

postmortem graft.definition: A graft obtained from a deceased donor (cadaveric graft) for transplantation, used to replace diseased or damaged tissue in a recipient; includes organs, tissues, or skin harvested after death rather than from the patient.

allogeneic transplantation.definition: Transplantation in which the donor is another genetically non-identical member of the same species (not an identical twin), such as a bone marrow or organ transplant; requires immunosuppression to prevent rejection and may cause graft-versus-host disease.

metastasis.definition: The spread of cancer cells from the primary site to another part of the body.

metastatic calcification.definition: Deposition of calcium salts in normal (non-damaged) tissues due to systemic hypercalcemia or hyperphosphatemia (elevated calcium-phosphate product), often affecting kidneys, lungs, gastric mucosa, and vasculature.

calcific aortic disease.definition: A degenerative process characterized by calcification and thickening of the aortic valve leaflets, leading to reduced valve opening (aortic stenosis); it ranges from valve sclerosis to progressive stenosis and is most common in older adults.

calcific aortic stenosis.definition: Degenerative calcification and thickening of the aortic valve cusps that produces fixed obstruction to left ventricular outflow, typically related to age-related changes (or a bicuspid valve); leads to symptoms such as angina, exertional dyspnea, and syncope, and may cause left ventricular hypertrophy and heart failure.

calcinosis.definition: The abnormal deposition of calcium salts (usually calcium phosphate) in soft tissues, most commonly the skin and subcutaneous tissue, often associated with tissue injury or metabolic disturbances; it may be dystrophic, metastatic, idiopathic, or iatrogenic.

calcinosis cutis.definition: Deposition of calcium salts in the skin and subcutaneous tissues, forming hard nodules or plaques; often due to dystrophic calcification in damaged tissue, but can also occur with metabolic disturbances (e.g., hypercalcemia/hyperphosphatemia) or renal failure.

calcified fetus.definition: A fetus whose tissues have undergone calcification, typically following intrauterine fetal death, resulting in radiopaque deposits detectable by imaging or at autopsy.

lithopedion.definition: A rare condition in which a dead fetus remains in the mother's abdomen and becomes calcified (stone-like), typically after an abdominal or ectopic pregnancy, to protect the mother from infection.

calcitonin.definition: A hormone that can stimulate bone growth and is sometimes used to treat osteoporosis.

calcitonin test.definition: A blood test that measures the level of calcitonin in the serum, used as a tumor marker for medullary thyroid carcinoma and to screen or monitor associated conditions; sometimes performed with stimulation (e.g., secretin or calcium) to provoke calcitonin release when basal levels are inconclusive.

salmon calcitonin.definition: A peptide hormone derived from salmon used as a medication to inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, thereby lowering serum calcium; indicated for osteoporosis, Paget disease, and hypercalcemia, and generally more potent and longer-acting than human calcitonin, administered intranasally or by injection.

thyrocalcitonin.definition: A peptide hormone secreted by the thyroid's parafollicular (C) cells that lowers blood calcium levels by inhibiting osteoclast-mediated bone resorption and increasing renal calcium excretion; another name for calcitonin.

calcimar.definition: A synthetic analogue of ACTH (cosyntropin), consisting of the first 24 amino acids of ACTH; used in ACTH stimulation testing to stimulate adrenal cortisol production and evaluate adrenal insufficiency.

calciferol.definition: A fat-soluble vitamin essential for calcium and phosphorus absorption and bone mineralization; includes ergocalciferol (D2) and cholecalciferol (D3); synthesized in skin under ultraviolet light and obtained from the diet; activated in the liver and kidney to active metabolites.

ergocalciferol.definition: A fat-soluble form of vitamin D (vitamin D2) obtained from fungi; used as a dietary supplement to prevent or treat vitamin D deficiency. It is converted in the liver to 25-hydroxyvitamin D and then to the active form, promoting intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate for bone mineralization.

ergosterol.definition: A sterol component of fungal cell membranes, analogous to cholesterol in animals, that maintains membrane integrity and fluidity; fungi synthesize ergosterol instead of cholesterol, making it a common target of antifungal drugs. It is also a provitamin D2 that is converted to vitamin D2 (ergocalciferol) upon UV irradiation.

cholecalciferol.definition: A fat-soluble vitamin (vitamin D3) produced in the skin on UVB exposure and obtained from diet or supplements; it is converted in the liver to calcidiol and in the kidney to calcitriol, the active hormone that regulates calcium and phosphate homeostasis and bone mineralization.

calcifediol.definition: A liver-derived form of vitamin D, specifically 25-hydroxycholecalciferol; the major circulating metabolite used to assess vitamin D status, and it is further hydroxylated in the kidney to the active hormone calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D).

vitamin d.definition: A hormone that plays a key role in ensuring the absorption of calcium from the intestines.

vitamin d2.definition: A fat-soluble form of vitamin D (ergocalciferol) derived from fungal/plant sterols and produced by UV irradiation of ergosterol; used as a dietary supplement and in fortification. After ingestion it is hydroxylated in the liver to 25-hydroxyvitamin D2 and then to the active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D2; generally less potent than vitamin D3 in raising serum 25(OH)D levels.

viosterol.definition: A historical term for a sterol precursor of vitamin D, typically ergosterol; exposure to ultraviolet light converts it to vitamin D2 (ergocalciferol).

osteomalacia.definition: A condition in which bones are soft and weak, usually due to a lack of vitamin D or an inability of the body to use vitamin D properly.

parathyroid hormone.definition: A hormone that controls levels of calcium and phosphorous in the blood and influences bone loss and growth.

renal osteodystrophy.definition: A spectrum of bone disorders that occur in chronic kidney disease due to disturbances in mineral metabolism (calcium, phosphate, vitamin D) and secondary hyperparathyroidism, resulting in abnormal bone turnover, defective mineralization, and increased fracture risk.

hyperphosphatemia.definition: An abnormally high concentration of phosphate in the blood (serum phosphate), most often due to reduced renal excretion in kidney disease; can also result from excessive phosphate intake, hypoparathyroidism, or rapid cell breakdown.

vitamin d toxicity.definition: Hypercalcemia due to excessive vitamin D intake (hypervitaminosis D), typically from prolonged high-dose supplementation; it results in increased intestinal calcium absorption and renal calcium reabsorption, causing elevated serum calcium and potential nephrocalcinosis or soft-tissue calcification. Common symptoms include nausea, vomiting, anorexia, weakness, polyuria, and polydipsia.

malabsorption syndrome.definition: An umbrella term for disorders in which the small intestine cannot adequately absorb nutrients, leading to chronic diarrhea, weight loss, steatorrhea, and nutritional deficiencies due to mucosal disease, pancreatic insufficiency, bile/acidity disorders, bacterial overgrowth, or post-surgical changes.

renal toxicity.definition: Kidney damage caused by exposure to drugs, chemicals, or other toxins, leading to impaired renal function (e.g., acute kidney injury or chronic kidney disease). Mechanisms include tubular necrosis, interstitial nephritis, glomerular injury, or vascular injury.

soft tissue calcification.definition: Abnormal deposition of calcium salts in non-bony (soft) tissues, often occurring in damaged or necrotic tissue (dystrophic calcification) and/or with systemic disturbances of calcium and phosphate metabolism (metastatic calcification).

calcitriol.definition: The hormonally active metabolite of vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3) produced in the kidney by 1-alpha-hydroxylase; it binds the vitamin D receptor to increase intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate, promote bone mineralization, and modulate parathyroid hormone.

calcium sulfate.definition: An inorganic calcium salt with the formula CaSO4; occurs as dihydrate (gypsum) or anhydrous form and is used in medicine as a resorbable, osteoconductive bone graft substitute.

calcium chloride.definition: A water-soluble calcium salt used therapeutically as a source of calcium to treat hypocalcemia and in certain emergency settings; typically administered intravenously (or intraosseously) with caution for venous irritation and tissue necrosis if extravasation occurs.

calcium gluconate.definition: A calcium salt of gluconic acid used as a calcium supplement to prevent or treat hypocalcemia; it can be given orally or intravenously. In emergency settings, IV calcium salts are used to stabilize cardiac membranes in hyperkalemia or calcium channel blocker overdose.

calcium citrate.definition: A calcium salt of citric acid used as a dietary calcium supplement to prevent or treat calcium deficiency; it provides elemental calcium and is more readily absorbed than calcium carbonate, particularly in individuals with reduced gastric acidity, and can be taken with or without meals.

calcium phosphate.definition: A family of inorganic salts composed of calcium ions (Ca2+) and phosphate ions (PO4^3−) with several crystalline forms, such as dicalcium phosphate, tricalcium phosphate, and hydroxyapatite; these compounds form a major part of bone and teeth mineral and are used clinically as calcium supplements or as bone repair materials.

calcium oxide.definition: A white, caustic alkaline oxide of calcium produced by calcining calcium carbonate; it reacts vigorously with water to form calcium hydroxide and is widely used in cement production, metallurgy, and water treatment.

calcium hydroxide.definition: An inorganic compound with the formula Ca(OH)2; a white, caustic base used in dentistry as a pulp-capping material and liner due to its high pH and antimicrobial properties, and it serves as an alkaline agent in various chemical and medical preparations.

lime.definition: A small green to yellow citrus fruit with acidic juice, commonly used as a source of vitamin C.

lime water.definition: A solution of calcium hydroxide in water (Ca(OH)2); clear and colorless, it turns milky on exposure to carbon dioxide due to precipitation of calcium carbonate, used as a qualitative test for CO2.

calcium oxalate.definition: A chemical compound consisting of calcium ions and oxalate (CaC2O4); forms insoluble crystals and is the most common component of kidney stones. It can also appear as crystals in urine.

calcium urate.definition: A calcium salt of uric acid; formed when calcium ions bind to urate (the deprotonated form of uric acid). It can crystallize in urine and may be found in certain urinary stones.

calciuria.definition: The excretion of calcium in the urine; measured as urinary calcium excretion, which may be normal or elevated (hypercalciuria) and can be associated with conditions such as kidney stones, hyperparathyroidism, or vitamin D excess.

calcofluor white stain.definition: A fluorescent dye that binds to polysaccharides such as cellulose and chitin in fungal cell walls, causing fungal elements (yeasts and hyphae) to fluoresce bright blue-white under ultraviolet or blue light, enabling rapid detection of fungal infections in clinical specimens; it is not species-specific and is often used on prepared smears or with KOH clearing to screen for fungi.

calcospherite.definition: A calcified spherical body formed by deposition of calcium salts within tissue; a small, calcified spherule that may be seen microscopically or grossly in various lesions.

calculogenesis.definition: Process by which calculi (stones) form in the body, through nucleation and crystallization of mineral salts (e.g., calcium oxalate, calcium phosphate) within supersaturated fluids, leading to stone growth.

calculous.definition: Relating to calculi (stones); containing, forming, or caused by stones.

calculous pyelonephritis.definition: A kidney infection (pyelonephritis) occurring in the setting of obstructing renal calculi (stones); typically requires antibiotics and relief of the obstruction.

calculous pyonephrosis.definition: An obstructive, purulent infection of the renal collecting system caused by renal calculi blocking urine outflow, resulting in accumulation of pus within the renal pelvis and calyces; a urologic emergency requiring urgent drainage (eg, percutaneous nephrostomy) and antibiotics.

pyonephrosis.definition: A purulent infection of the kidney’s collecting system in which pus accumulates in the renal pelvis and calyces, usually due to urinary tract obstruction, and requiring urgent drainage (e.g., nephrostomy or ureteral stent) and antibiotics.

renal calculus.definition: A hard mineral concretion formed in the kidney from crystallized salts (most often calcium oxalate); it can cause flank pain, hematuria, and urinary obstruction and may pass spontaneously or require medical treatment.

biliary calculus.definition: Stones formed in the biliary tract (usually in the gallbladder or bile ducts), composed of cholesterol, bilirubin salts, or a mixed composition; they may obstruct bile flow and cause biliary colic, cholecystitis, cholangitis, or pancreatitis.

tartar.definition: A crust on your teeth made from plaque that has hardened.

gastrinoma.definition: A gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor, most often located in the pancreas or duodenum, that causes Zollinger-Ellison syndrome with marked hypergastrinemia and gastric acid hypersecretion leading to refractory peptic ulcers.

gastrin.definition: A peptide hormone produced by G cells in the stomach (antrum) that stimulates gastric acid secretion by parietal cells and promotes growth of the gastric mucosa.

medullary carcinoma of the thyroid.definition: Malignant neoplasm of the thyroid arising from parafollicular (C) cells, typically secreting calcitonin; can be sporadic or hereditary (often due to RET mutations in MEN2); histology shows nests or sheets of polygonal to spindle cells with Congo red–positive amyloid in the stroma; treated primarily with surgical resection (usually total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection); prognosis depends on stage and metastasis.

parafollicular cells.definition: Neuroendocrine cells in the thyroid gland that secrete calcitonin in response to elevated calcium levels, helping to lower blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclast activity and promoting calcium excretion in the kidneys.

renal transplantation.definition: A surgical procedure in which a diseased kidney is replaced with a healthy kidney from a living or deceased donor; the transplanted kidney is placed in the recipient’s abdomen and connected to the blood vessels and urinary tract, with lifelong immunosuppressive therapy to prevent graft rejection.

gypsum.definition: A soft sulfate mineral (calcium sulfate dihydrate, CaSO4·2H2O) used to make plaster of Paris for immobilizing fractures and supporting orthopedic casts.

plaster.definition: A rigid immobilization cast applied to a limb or body part to stabilize fractures or soft-tissue injuries during healing; traditionally made from plaster of Paris (calcium sulfate) but now often fiberglass or other synthetic materials.

laxative.definition: A drug or substance that induces bowel movements or makes the stool softer and looser.

central nervous system disturbances.definition: A broad term for abnormal function of the brain or spinal cord, presenting as altered mental status, cognitive or sensory changes, motor deficits, seizures, or autonomic dysfunction.

renal dialysis.definition: A treatment that substitutes for kidney function by filtering waste products and removing excess fluids from the blood when kidneys can no longer do so; it is performed by hemodialysis (blood filtered outside the body through a dialyzer) or peritoneal dialysis (dialysate in the peritoneal cavity absorbs wastes).

bone mineralization.definition: The process by which minerals, primarily calcium and phosphate, are deposited into the organic bone matrix (osteoid) by osteoblasts, forming hydroxyapatite crystals and hardening the bone tissue.

nerve impulses.definition: An electrochemical signal that travels along a neuron as an action potential, produced by rapid changes in membrane ion permeability that cause depolarization and repolarization, enabling rapid transmission of information along neural pathways.

caldwell-luc procedure.definition: A surgical procedure that creates an opening (antrostomy) into the maxillary sinus via a canine fossa approach (gingivobuccal sulcus incision) to drain the sinus and remove polyps or diseased tissue; historically used for chronic maxillary sinusitis and other maxillary sinus disease, but largely replaced by endoscopic sinus surgery.

caldwell-moloy pelvic classification.definition: A radiographic obstetric pelvis classification proposed by Caldwell and Moloy that categorizes the maternal pelvis into four inlet shapes based on pelvic dimensions, used to predict the likelihood of vaginal delivery.

anthropoid pelvis.definition: An oval-shaped pelvic inlet with a longer anteroposterior diameter than the transverse diameter; the sacrum tends to be long, producing a deeper posterior pelvis.

platypelloid pelvis.definition: A pelvic type with a wide transverse (transversely oval) inlet and a shortened anteroposterior diameter, giving a flattened pelvic cavity; also called a flat pelvis, and it may be associated with labor dystocia.

sacrosciatic notch.definition: A notch on the posterior border of the hip bone, formed where the ilium meets the sacrum and ischium; it is converted by the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments into the greater sciatic foramen, through which the sciatic nerve and other structures exit the pelvis.

ischial spines.definition: Two sharp bony projections on the posteromedial aspect of the ischium that form part of the pelvic wall; they serve as obstetric landmarks for assessing the descent and station of the fetal head during labor.

pubic arch.definition: The angle formed by the inferior rami of the pubic bones as they converge at the pubic symphysis; also known as the subpubic angle, typically wider in females than in males.

ischial tuberosities.definition: Two rounded bony prominences on the inferior part of the ischium (the sit bones) that bear weight when seated and serve as attachment sites for the hamstring muscles and ligaments such as the sacrotuberous ligament.

calvaria.definition: The upper domed portion of the skull (the skullcap) formed by the frontal bone, the two parietal bones, and the occipital bone, enclosing the cranial cavity.

fontanels.definition: Soft spots on an infant's skull where the cranial bones have not yet fused; membranous gaps that allow brain growth and skull molding during birth, with the posterior fontanelle typically closing by 2–3 months and the anterior fontanelle by about 18 months (often up to 2 years).

calva.definition: Not a standard medical term; when used, it is usually a nontechnical reference to baldness (alopecia). The anatomically correct term for the skull’s upper portion is calvaria (the skullcap).

perthes disease.definition: An idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children, typically aged 4–8, causing flattening of the femoral head with a limp and limited hip motion; healing occurs with revascularization and remodeling, and management aims to contain the femoral head within the acetabulum using activity modification, physical therapy, bracing, or surgical containment when indicated.

caliceal fornix.definition: The caliceal fornix is the recess or fold at the margin of a renal calyx where the calyx curves around the renal papilla, forming the transition between the calyx and the infundibulum.

renal calyx.definition: Cup-shaped structures of the kidney that collect urine from the renal papillae and drain into the renal pelvis; they are arranged as minor calyces that join to form major calyces.

calyx.definition: A cuplike cavity of the kidney that collects urine from the renal papillae and passes it to the renal pelvis; the minor calyces join to form the major calyces.

calyces.definition: Calyces are cuplike extensions of the renal pelvis in the kidney that collect urine from the renal papillae; minor calyces drain urine from each renal pyramid, and major calyces are formed by the convergence of several minor calyces before draining into the renal pelvis.

supragingival calculus.definition: An hardened deposit of mineralized dental plaque that forms on the crowns of teeth above the gingival margin; composed of calcified plaque with calcium phosphate crystals (e.g., hydroxyapatite) and organic material, it adheres to tooth surfaces and can irritate the gingiva and harbor bacteria; removed by scaling.

subgingival calculus.definition: Mineralized dental plaque that forms below the gingival margin on tooth roots, typically within periodontal pockets, and can contribute to periodontal inflammation and bone loss by harboring bacteria.

serumal calculus.definition:
Not a standard medical term; no formal definition found. It may be a misspelling or confusion with:
- Salivary calculus (dental tartar): mineralized dental plaque that adheres to tooth surfaces, mainly calcium phosphate, formed over time and removed by professional cleaning.
- Urinary calculus (kidney/bladder stone): stone formed from mineral precipitates in the urinary tract (e.g., calcium oxalate, uric acid), which can cause pain and may require treatment to remove.
