dental prosthesis.definition: An artificial device used to replace missing teeth or surrounding oral tissues, restoring function and aesthetics; it can be fixed (e.g., crowns, bridges) or removable (e.g., dentures, partial dentures).

gingival pocket.definition: A false periodontal pocket formed when gingival inflammation causes swelling and enlargement of the gingiva, deepening the gingival sulcus without loss of connective tissue attachment to the tooth root.

periodontal pocket.definition: A pathologic deepening of the gingival sulcus due to inflammatory periodontal disease, in which the junctional epithelium migrates apically with loss of connective tissue attachment and supporting bone, resulting in probing depths greater than normal (typically >3 mm); can be classified as suprabony or infrabony depending on the bone level relative to the crest.

gingival crest.definition: The gingival crest refers to the highest, coronal edge of the gingiva around a tooth—the free gingival margin that forms the gingival sulcus and follows the contour of the tooth.

veneer.definition: A thin, custom-made shell of tooth-colored material (porcelain or composite resin) bonded to the front surface of a tooth to improve its appearance.

periodontal disease.definition: When your gums are red and swollen. Also called gum disease. There are 2 types: gingivitis and periodontitis.

cameron ulcer.definition: A linear gastric mucosal erosion/ulcer at the diaphragmatic hiatus in a large hiatal hernia, caused by mechanical trauma from the herniated stomach, often presenting with occult gastrointestinal bleeding and iron-deficiency anemia.

hiatal hernia.definition: A condition in which part of the stomach herniates through the diaphragmatic esophageal hiatus into the thoracic cavity; the most common form is sliding, in which the gastroesophageal junction and part of the stomach move above the diaphragm, while paraesophageal hernias involve herniation of part of the stomach beside the esophagus with the junction remaining below the diaphragm.

neobladder.definition: A surgically created bladder substitute made from a segment of intestinal tissue (usually ileum or colon), detubularized and formed into a reservoir, then connected to the urethra to store urine and allow voluntary voiding after cystectomy; aims to provide continence and a more normal urination pattern.

ileal neobladder.definition: An orthotopic urinary reservoir created from a detubularized ileal segment and connected to the urethra after cystectomy, designed to store urine and allow voluntary voiding; aims for continence and near-normal voiding but may require intermittent catheterization and carries risks such as mucus production, infection, stone formation, and metabolic disturbances.

cystectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove all or part of the urinary bladder.

calfactant.definition: A bovine-derived natural lung surfactant preparation used intratracheally to treat or prevent neonatal respiratory distress syndrome by reducing alveolar surface tension.

california encephalitis.definition: An arboviral encephalitis caused by California serogroup viruses transmitted by mosquitoes (most commonly La Crosse virus). It typically presents with fever, headache, and malaise, and can progress to encephalitis with confusion, seizures, or coma, especially in children. Incubation is about 1–2 weeks. Diagnosis is by serology or PCR; treatment is supportive. There is no approved specific antiviral therapy or human vaccine. Prevention focuses on mosquito bite avoidance and mosquito control.

encephalomeningitis.definition: Inflammation of both the brain tissue (encephalon) and the meninges surrounding the brain, typically due to infection; presents with features of meningitis and encephalitis (fever, headache, neck stiffness, altered mental status, sometimes seizures) and requires prompt empirical antimicrobial therapy and further diagnostic evaluation.

campimeter.definition: An ophthalmic instrument used to measure the visual field (perimetry) by presenting light stimuli at various locations on a screen while the patient maintains central fixation; used to map peripheral vision and detect field defects (e.g., the Goldmann perimeter).

camphor.definition: A waxy, aromatic terpenoid (C10H16O) that is a bicyclic monoterpene ketone, derived from the camphor tree or synthetically produced; used topically as a rubefacient and mild analgesic/anti-pruritic; inhaled vapors may relieve cough; ingestion or large exposures can be toxic.

camphor poisoning.definition: An acute toxic reaction to camphor from ingestion or exposure to camphor-containing products (e.g., essential oils, camphorated oil, cough remedies), characterized by central nervous system stimulation followed by depression, with symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, agitation, seizures, and potentially coma; can be life-threatening, especially in children; management is supportive, with decontamination if presentation is early.

camphorated oil.definition: A topical preparation in which camphor is dissolved in an oil (traditionally olive oil); used as a mild rubefacient and counterirritant to relieve local muscular or joint pain, and should not be ingested or applied to broken skin.

camphor salicylate.definition: A topical counterirritant containing camphor and a salicylate; used externally to relieve transient minor aches and pains of muscles and joints by causing local irritation and warmth.

campral.definition: A brand-name medication (acamprosate) used to maintain abstinence in alcohol-dependent individuals by reducing relapse risk after withdrawal, likely through modulation of glutamatergic neurotransmission.

camptocormia.definition: A syndrome of marked forward flexion of the thoracolumbar spine (bent-spine syndrome) that worsens with standing or walking and typically improves when lying supine; commonly associated with neuromuscular disorders such as Parkinson disease with dystonia or myopathy.

camptodactyly.definition: An abnormal flexion (bending) contracture of a finger, most commonly at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint, resulting in inability to fully extend the finger. It can be congenital or acquired and may arise from tight flexor tendons or surrounding soft-tissue anomalies.

camptomelia.definition: A congenital deformity where a limb is abnormally bent or curved at birth, resulting from abnormal limb development during fetal growth.

campylobacter.definition: A genus of curved, motile, Gram-negative bacteria that are microaerophilic and commonly cause acute gastroenteritis in humans; the most frequent species involved are jejuni and coli, with transmission mainly through undercooked poultry, unpasteurized dairy, and contaminated water; symptoms include diarrhea (often bloody), abdominal cramps, and fever.

campylobacter enteritis.definition: An acute bacterial enteritis caused by Campylobacter species (most commonly Campylobacter jejuni). It typically presents with fever, abdominal pain, and acute diarrhea that may be bloody, often after ingestion of contaminated food or water (notably undercooked poultry). Most cases are self-limited and managed with supportive care such as hydration; antibiotics (e.g., macrolides like azithromycin) are considered for severe disease or high‑risk individuals.

campylobacter jejuni.definition: A curved, gram-negative, motile, microaerophilic bacterium and a leading cause of bacterial gastroenteritis worldwide. It is commonly transmitted via undercooked poultry or contaminated dairy or water and causes acute diarrhea with abdominal cramps and fever; illness is typically self-limited but may require antibiotics in severe cases, and it has been associated with Guillain–Barré syndrome.

campylobacteriosis.definition: An infectious gastroenteritis caused by Campylobacter species (most often Campylobacter jejuni), usually acquired from contaminated food or water; presents with fever, abdominal cramps, and diarrhea (often bloody); typically self-limited but hydration is important, and rare complications include reactive arthritis and Guillain-Barré syndrome.

helicobacter pylori.definition: A curved, Gram-negative, microaerophilic bacterium that colonizes the stomach and is a major cause of peptic ulcer disease and chronic gastritis, with associations to gastric cancer and MALT lymphoma.

campylobacter pylori.definition: A curved, Gram-negative, microaerophilic bacterium that colonizes the human stomach and is a major cause of chronic gastritis and peptic ulcers; it also increases the risk of gastric cancer and MALT lymphoma. It survives acidic stomach conditions by producing urease, which neutralizes gastric acid. Diagnosis is via urea breath test, stool antigen test, or gastric biopsy with rapid urease test; treatment typically involves a combination of antibiotics with a proton pump inhibitor (often with bismuth).

callosal agenesis.definition: Congenital absence (agenesis) or underdevelopment of the corpus callosum, the large bundle of nerve fibers that connects the two cerebral hemispheres. It can be complete or partial (hypogenesis) and results from disrupted development of commissural tracts in fetal life. Clinical features vary widely, ranging from normal intellect with subtle motor or coordination issues to developmental delay, intellectual disability, seizures, and other brain malformations; diagnosis is typically by MRI.

callosal fissure.definition: A midline groove that marks the separation between the two cerebral hemispheres—the interhemispheric (longitudinal) fissure that contains the corpus callosum.

callosomarginal fissure.definition: A deep groove on the medial surface of the frontal lobe that marks the boundary between the cingulate gyrus and the paracentral lobule near the corpus callosum (the callosal margin).

pericranium.definition: An outer fibrous membrane that covers the cranial bones, constituting the periosteum of the skull (calvaria).

adenocarcinomas.definition: A malignant neoplasm that originates from glandular (epithelial) tissue and forms glandular or acinar structures, often producing mucin; it can arise in many organs with glandular cells (e.g., colon, lung, breast, pancreas, stomach).

carcinomas.definition: A type of cancer that begins in your skin or the lining of an organ.

cervical cancer.definition: A malignant neoplasm of the cervix (the lower part of the uterus), most commonly arising from persistent infection with high‑risk human papillomavirus (HPV); often presents with abnormal vaginal bleeding or discharge; screening with Pap testing and HPV testing; prevented by HPV vaccination and early detection.

endometrial cancer.definition: Endometrial cancer is a malignant tumor arising from the endometrium (the lining of the uterus), most commonly an endometrioid adenocarcinoma; it typically presents with abnormal uterine bleeding, especially in postmenopausal women, and is diagnosed by endometrial biopsy or curettage. Treatment usually involves surgical hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and lymph node assessment, with adjuvant radiotherapy or chemotherapy based on stage and histology.

uterine cancer.definition: Cancer that develops in the uterus (womb). The most common type is endometrial cancer, which starts in the lining of the uterus.

carcinoids.definition: Slow-growing neuroendocrine tumors arising from enterochromaffin cells, most often in the gastrointestinal tract or lungs; may secrete serotonin, causing carcinoid syndrome (flushing, diarrhea, wheezing, and right‑sided heart lesions).

small intestine cancer.definition: A malignant neoplasm arising from the tissues of the small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, or ileum). It is uncommon and can be adenocarcinoma, neuroendocrine tumor, gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST), or lymphoma.

polyp.definition: An abnormal, noncancerous growth that protrudes from mucous membranes, like those found in the sinuses and colon lining.

polyps.definition: A growth that protrudes from a mucous membrane into the lumen of a hollow organ; most are benign, but some types (notably colorectal adenomatous polyps) can be precancerous and require removal and surveillance.

metastases.definition: The spread of malignant cells from a primary tumor to distant sites, where they establish new malignant growths (secondary tumors) that resemble the primary tumor; typically occurs via lymphatic or hematogenous (blood-borne) routes.

staging.definition: The process of determining how far cancer has progressed. Staging is often used to determine the best course of treatment.

tnm.definition: A cancer staging system that describes the extent of cancer using three components: T for the size/extent of the primary tumor, N for regional lymph node involvement, and M for distant metastasis. Each component is assigned a value to determine the overall stage and guide treatment and prognosis.

immunosuppressive.definition: Describes something that suppresses or weakens the immune response, commonly referring to drugs or agents that reduce immune activity to prevent transplant rejection or treat autoimmune diseases.

canavanine.definition: An arginine analog and non-proteinogenic amino acid found in seeds of certain legumes (notably Canavalia species, such as jack bean); it can be misincorporated into proteins in place of arginine, causing defective proteins and toxicity, and is used in research to study arginine metabolism and protein synthesis.

candesartan.definition: A selective angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB) used to treat hypertension and heart failure; it antagonizes the AT1 receptor, reducing vasoconstriction and aldosterone-mediated fluid retention. The active drug candesartan is formed from the prodrug candesartan cilexetil administered orally.

psa.definition: Abbreviation for prostate-specific antigen, a protein produced by the prostate. Elevated levels may indicate the presence of cancer, benign prostatic hyperplasia, or prostatitis.

rectal exam.definition: A manual digital examination of the rectum performed by a clinician inserting a lubricated, gloved finger into the anal canal to assess anal sphincter tone, rectal walls for tenderness, masses, or lesions, and to check for bleeding or other abnormalities; in males it may evaluate the prostate.

colonoscopy.definition: Looks at the inside of the large intestine using a flexible tube with a tiny camera at the end.

sigmoidoscopy.definition: Internal examination of the rectum and sigmoid colon using a flexible viewing tube inserted through the anus.

ct colonography.definition: A noninvasive radiologic test that uses CT scanning to produce 2D and 3D images of the colon after bowel preparation and insufflation with air or CO2, used to screen for colorectal polyps and cancer (virtual colonoscopy).

virtual colonoscopy.definition: A noninvasive imaging method that uses CT scanning to create detailed 2D and 3D images of the colon after bowel preparation and intraluminal gas insufflation, used to screen for polyps and colorectal cancer; if polyps are detected, conventional colonoscopy is typically performed for biopsy or removal.

fecal occult blood test.definition: A noninvasive screening test that detects hidden (occult) blood in stool, used to screen for colorectal cancer and investigate gastrointestinal bleeding; commonly guaiac-based FOBT or a fecal immunochemical test (FIT).

gfobt.definition: A noninvasive screening test for colorectal cancer that detects hidden blood in stool using a guaiac-based chemical reaction; performed on stool samples (often multiple specimens). A positive result typically leads to diagnostic colonoscopy; dietary restrictions or medications can affect accuracy.

fecal immunochemical test.definition: A noninvasive colorectal cancer screening test that uses antibodies to detect human hemoglobin in stool; more specific for lower GI bleeding than guaiac-based tests and generally requires no dietary changes.

fit.definition:
A sudden attack or convulsion, typically an epileptic seizure.
As an adjective, being in good physical condition or healthy; suitable for a particular purpose.

stool dna test.definition: A noninvasive colorectal cancer screening test that analyzes stool DNA for genetic and epigenetic markers associated with colorectal cancer and precancerous polyps, detecting neoplastic changes without the need for colonoscopy.

sdna.definition: Single-stranded DNA: a molecule of deoxyribonucleic acid composed of a single polynucleotide chain, lacking the paired complementary strand found in double-stranded DNA; it can fold into secondary structures and is used in various molecular biology techniques such as primer design and hybridization.

mammograms.definition: X-ray images of the breast used to screen for and diagnose breast disease, especially breast cancer; screening is performed in asymptomatic women to detect tumors or calcifications, while diagnostic imaging evaluates a known abnormality or symptoms.

clinical breast exam.definition: A physical examination of the breasts performed by a clinician to detect abnormalities, typically involving inspection of the breasts and nipples and palpation of the breast tissue and regional lymph nodes for lumps, skin changes, nipple discharge, or other signs of disease.

cbe.definition: A physical examination of the breasts performed by a clinician to detect lumps or other abnormalities, commonly used for breast cancer screening or diagnostic evaluation.

breast self-exam.definition: A self-examination method in which a person palpates their own breasts and underarm area to detect lumps, thickening, or changes in size, shape, skin, or nipples, typically performed monthly to aid in detecting breast abnormalities early.

bse.definition: A progressive neurodegenerative prion disease of cattle causing sponge-like changes in the brain; commonly known as mad cow disease. A method by which a person examines their own breasts for lumps, thickening, discharge, or other changes to detect possible breast cancer.

pap test.definition: An screening test for cervical cancer in which cells are collected from the cervix and examined microscopically to detect precancerous changes, infection, or cancer; commonly known as a Pap smear.

hpv.definition: A group of viruses that can cause warts on the skin or mucous membranes and are linked to an increased risk of certain cancers; vaccines are available to prevent infection.

rectal.definition: Relating to the rectum, the final section of the large intestine that extends from the sigmoid colon to the anal canal.

endometrial biopsy.definition: A procedure to obtain a small sample of the endometrial lining for microscopic examination, typically performed with a pipette or curette to evaluate abnormal uterine bleeding, infertility, or suspected endometrial pathology.

tympanic cavity.definition: A small air-filled space in the petrous part of the temporal bone that forms the middle ear; it contains the auditory ossicles (malleus, incus, and stapes) and communicates with the nasopharynx via the pharyngotympanic (Eustachian) tube, while being separated from the external ear by the tympanic membrane.

chorda tympani.definition: Branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) that passes through the tympanic cavity; carries taste fibers from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the submandibular ganglion, stimulating the submandibular and sublingual glands.

canaliculus.definition: A small channel or duct within a tissue or organ; in anatomy it refers to tiny canals such as the lacrimal canaliculi that drain tears from the puncta to the lacrimal sac, or to microscopic bone canaliculi that connect lacunae to each other and to blood vessels.

canaliculi.definition: Small channels or ducts in tissues; in bone they connect lacunae and allow exchange of nutrients and wastes between osteocytes, and in the liver they are the narrow bile ducts between hepatocytes.

schlemm's canal.definition: A circular drainage system in the eye located where the clear cornea, white sclera, and colored iris meet to form an angle.

haversian canal.definition: A central channel in each osteon of compact bone that houses blood vessels and nerves; runs longitudinally through the bone, is surrounded by concentric lamellae, and communicates with the periosteum and other osteons via Volkmann's canals.

inguinal rings.definition: A pair of openings at the margins of the inguinal canal: the deep (internal) inguinal ring, an opening in the transversalis fascia just above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament; and the superficial (external) inguinal ring, a triangular opening in the external oblique aponeurosis just above and medial to the pubic tubercle. Through these rings pass the spermatic cord and vessels (in males) or the round ligament of the uterus (in females).

canalicular.definition: Relating to a canaliculus, a small channel or duct within a tissue or organ; for example, the lacrimal canaliculi are tiny ducts that drain tears from the eyelids into the lacrimal sac.

mycotic endocarditis.definition: An infection of the heart’s endocardial surfaces (usually the valves) caused by fungal organisms, most often Candida or Aspergillus; presents with fever, a new or changing murmur, signs of embolization, and septic phenomena, and has high mortality despite treatment. Managed with systemic antifungal therapy and often surgical valve intervention.

endocardial candidiasis.definition: A Candida fungal infection of the heart's endocardial surface presenting as infectious endocarditis with vegetations on the valves; occurs in the setting of candidemia or immunosuppression and is treated with systemic antifungal therapy, often with surgical intervention.

candida glabrata.definition: A yeast species that is part of the normal human microbiota and can cause opportunistic infections ranging from mucosal candidiasis to invasive candidiasis, particularly in immunocompromised individuals; it is less virulent than Candida albicans but often demonstrates reduced susceptibility to azole antifungals (notably fluconazole).

torulopsis glabrata.definition: A yeast species now classified as Candida glabrata; an opportunistic fungal pathogen that can cause mucosal and invasive candidiasis, especially in immunocompromised or hospitalized individuals, and may have reduced susceptibility to fluconazole.

candida guilliermondii.definition: A yeast species that is an opportunistic human pathogen, capable of causing superficial infections (e.g., nail or skin infections) and, in immunocompromised individuals, invasive disease such as fungemia; antifungal susceptibility varies, with possible reduced susceptibility to fluconazole.

cutaneous candidiasis.definition: A superficial fungal infection of the skin caused by Candida species (most commonly Candida albicans), presenting as erythematous, macerated plaques with satellite vesicles or pustules, often in warm, moist intertriginous areas; treated with topical antifungals, with systemic therapy for extensive or refractory disease.

candidemia.definition: The presence of Candida species in the bloodstream, causing a systemic fungal infection (fungemia); usually diagnosed by positive blood cultures and treated with antifungal therapy and removal of infection sources such as central venous catheters.

pulmonary candidiasis.definition: Fungal infection of the lungs caused by Candida species (most commonly Candida albicans), typically in immunocompromised patients; can range from colonization to invasive pneumonia, and confirmation often requires histologic evidence of tissue invasion or culture from sterile sites.

candida kefyr.definition: An opportunistic yeast species in the genus Candida (formerly Torulopsis kefyr); can cause candidiasis and invasive infections in immunocompromised individuals and is commonly associated with dairy environments.

candida pseudotropicalis.definition: An older name for a non-albicans Candida species that is an opportunistic yeast pathogen capable of causing mucosal and invasive candidiasis, particularly in immunocompromised individuals.

candida krusei.definition: A species of non‑albicans yeast that can cause opportunistic fungal infections in humans, particularly in immunocompromised individuals; it is intrinsically resistant to fluconazole and may require alternative antifungal therapy.

candida lusitaniae.definition: A yeast species in the genus Candida that causes opportunistic infections in humans, including candidemia and invasive candidiasis, particularly in immunocompromised or hospitalized patients; it is notable for variable antifungal susceptibility and a tendency to develop resistance to amphotericin B.

candidal vaginitis.definition: Inflammation of the vagina caused by overgrowth of Candida species (most commonly Candida albicans), typically presenting with intense itching and burning and a thick, white, cottage-cheese–like discharge, often with vulvar erythema.

candidal vulvovaginitis.definition: A fungal infection of the vulva and vagina caused predominantly by Candida species (most commonly Candida albicans), presenting with vulvar itching and irritation and thick, white, curd-like vaginal discharge; vaginal pH is typically normal (<4.5). Diagnosis is by clinical features and/or microscopy or culture; treatment is antifungal therapy (topical azoles such as clotrimazole or miconazole, or a single oral dose of fluconazole).

vulvovaginal candidiasis.definition: A common fungal infection of the vagina and vulva caused by Candida species (most often Candida albicans), characterized by itching, irritation, and a thick, white discharge; diagnosed by clinical features and/or microscopy/culture, and treated with antifungal therapy.

candidosis.definition: A fungal infection caused by Candida species (most often Candida albicans) that affects the skin and mucous membranes (such as the mouth and genital tract) and can become invasive in people with weakened immunity.

intravascular catheters.definition: A flexible tube inserted into a blood vessel (vein or artery) to deliver medications or fluids, withdraw blood, or monitor pressures; used for intravenous therapy, nutrition support, hemodialysis access, and central venous or arterial access.

candiru fever.definition: A colloquial, nonstandard term for fever allegedly caused by the candiru fish invading the urinary tract; not a medically recognized syndrome, and fever should be evaluated for more typical causes (eg, urinary tract infection or other infections) with a relevant exposure history.

phlebotomus fever.definition: A mild, self-limited febrile illness transmitted by Phlebotomus sandflies and caused by phleboviruses; it features sudden onset of fever, malaise, headache, and myalgia (often with photophobia), and typically resolves within a few days.

nasal cannula.definition: A lightweight plastic tubing with two small prongs inserted into the nostrils to deliver supplemental oxygen from an external source; commonly used for low-to-moderate oxygen needs and can deliver humidified gas at flow rates typically 1–6 L/min.

cannulation.definition: The insertion of a cannula (a slender tubular instrument) into a vein or other vessel to allow administration of fluids or medications, withdrawal of blood, or monitoring.

cantor tube.definition: Definition not found in standard medical dictionaries. It may be a misspelling or a very obscure term. If you can provide context (medical specialty, condition, or alternative spellings), I can help identify or define the correct term. If you meant a common device like a catheter or cannula, I can define those.

capillary bed.definition: An extensive network of capillaries within a tissue that provides the site for gas, nutrient, and waste exchange between the blood and surrounding interstitial fluid; supplied by arterioles and drained by venules, with flow regulated by precapillary sphincters.

capillary angioma.definition: A benign vascular tumor consisting of proliferation of capillary-sized blood vessels; typically present at birth or in infancy as a bright red, raised lesion (strawberry hemangioma) and often enlarges in the first year before gradually involuting over years.

capillary hemangioma.definition: Benign vascular tumor of infancy characterized by proliferating capillary-sized vessels; commonly presents as a bright red, raised skin lesion (strawberry hemangioma) that enlarges during the first months of life and typically involutes over several years.

capillary fragility.definition: An increased tendency of small blood vessels to rupture or leak, resulting in easy bruising, petechiae, or ecchymosis; associated with aging, vitamin C deficiency (scurvy), certain connective tissue disorders, or medications that affect vessel walls.

cherry angioma.definition: A benign, common cutaneous vascular lesion characterized by a cluster of dilated capillaries in the dermis, presenting as a small, bright red, dome-shaped papule (typically 1–5 mm) most often on the trunk of middle-aged and older adults; no treatment is needed unless for cosmetic reasons or if it bleeds.

nevus vascularis.definition: A benign congenital vascular lesion consisting of dilated superficial capillaries in the skin or mucosa, appearing as a red or violaceous patch or papule.

strawberry hemangioma.definition: A benign vascular tumor of infancy (infantile hemangioma) that appears as a bright red, raised skin lesion (strawberry-colored) shortly after birth, typically grows rapidly over the first months and involutes gradually over years.

strawberry mark.definition: A benign vascular tumor of infancy that presents as a bright red, raised skin lesion, typically appearing in the first weeks of life, often enlarging during infancy and usually involuting over several years.

nevus flammeus.definition: A capillary malformation present at birth, appearing as a flat, well-demarcated pink to purplish-red patch on the skin that typically persists and may darken or enlarge with age; commonly called a port-wine stain; usually benign but can be associated with Sturge–Weber syndrome when located on the face.

capillary action.definition: The movement of a liquid through narrow spaces (such as capillaries or porous tissues) driven by adhesive forces between the liquid and the surface and cohesive forces within the liquid, allowing spontaneous rise or wicking against gravity.

capillarity.definition: The ability of a liquid to flow in narrow spaces (such as capillary tubes or porous tissues) due to adhesive forces between the liquid and the solid surface and cohesive forces within the liquid, producing capillary action.

canthus.definition: The corner of the eye where the upper and lower eyelids meet; there are medial (inner) canthus and lateral (outer) canthus.

canthi.definition: The corners of the eye where the upper and lower eyelids meet; the medial canthus lies near the nose and the lateral canthus near the temple.

cantholysis.definition: Division or cutting of the canthal tendon (typically the lateral canthal tendon), a surgical maneuver to release eyelid tethering or to facilitate exposure/decompression of the orbit during eyelid surgery or trauma.

canthotomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which the lateral canthal tendon is incised to decompress the orbit, typically performed emergently to treat acute orbital compartment syndrome (often from retrobulbar hemorrhage) to prevent optic nerve injury.

canthoplasty.definition: A surgical procedure to reconstruct or tighten the canthus (the corner where the upper and lower eyelids meet), usually to correct eyelid malposition such as entropion or ectropion or to restore eyelid stability; can be performed medially or laterally.

canthorraphy.definition: A surgical procedure in which the canthus (the corner of the eyelid) is sutured to approximate and tighten the eyelid margins, typically to correct eyelid laxity or malposition.

palpebral fissure.definition: The opening between the upper and lower eyelids—the space through which the eye is visible, defined by the eyelid margins when the eye is open.

lacrimal duct.definition: A tear drainage duct that conveys tears from the lacrimal sac into the nasal cavity, forming part of the nasolacrimal tear drainage system.

capgras syndrome.definition: A delusional misidentification syndrome in which a person believes a close relative or familiar person has been replaced by an identical impostor, despite evidence to the contrary; commonly seen in schizophrenia, dementia, brain injury, or other neuropsychiatric disorders.

canker sore.definition: A small, shallow, noncontagious ulcer that develops on the soft tissues inside the mouth (an aphthous ulcer). It typically has a white or yellow center with a red border and usually heals within 1–2 weeks; triggers can include minor trauma, stress, nutritional deficiencies, or immune-related factors.

chancre.definition: A painless, indurated ulcer at the site of Treponema pallidum infection; the primary lesion of syphilis, typically firm with a clean base and well-defined border, usually appearing about 3 weeks after exposure and healing spontaneously within 3–6 weeks.

capastat.definition: A brand-name antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections; the specific active ingredient and approved indications vary by formulation and country.

capd.definition: A form of peritoneal dialysis in which dialysis solution is infused into and drained from the peritoneal cavity manually by the patient, usually several times daily, allowing waste products and excess fluid to diffuse across the peritoneal membrane.

capecitabine.definition: An oral prodrug of 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) that is converted to 5-FU in tumor tissue; a pyrimidine analog used as chemotherapy for colorectal cancer, breast cancer, and gastric cancer.

mepenzolate bromide.definition: A muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist (anticholinergic) used as a gastrointestinal antisecretory and antispasmodic agent to treat peptic ulcers by reducing gastric acid secretion and GI motility.

cannabinol.definition: A cannabinoid formed by the oxidation/degradation of THC, typically found in aged cannabis; it is weakly psychoactive, acts as a low-affinity agonist at CB1 and CB2 receptors, and has been explored for sedative, analgesic, and anti-inflammatory effects, though evidence is limited.

cannabidiol.definition: A non-psychoactive cannabinoid found in Cannabis sativa and Cannabis indica; it does not produce a high and is studied for potential therapeutic effects, including anti-seizure, anxiolytic, analgesic, and anti-inflammatory properties. A prescription formulation is approved for certain seizure disorders (e.g., Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, Dravet syndrome, and tuberous sclerosis complex).

cannabigerol.definition: A non-psychoactive cannabinoid found in cannabis; the biosynthetic precursor to the major cannabinoids THCA, CBDA, and CBCA (in the plant, the acidic precursor decarboxylates to yield this neutral compound). It has been investigated for potential anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antimicrobial, and neuroprotective effects, but clinical evidence remains limited and largely preclinical.

cannabicyclol.definition: A minor phytocannabinoid found in cannabis; a non-psychoactive, bicyclic cannabinoid present in small amounts; limited data exist on its pharmacology and therapeutic potential.

tetrahydrocannabinol.definition: Principal psychoactive constituent of cannabis; a phytocannabinoid that activates CB1 receptors in the brain, producing psychoactive effects, with additional actions on pain, appetite, and nausea.

thc.definition: A principal psychoactive constituent of cannabis; a cannabinoid that acts mainly as a partial agonist at CB1 receptors in the central nervous system, producing euphoria, analgesia, appetite stimulation, altered perception, and impairment of memory and psychomotor function. Common effects include tachycardia, dry mouth, red eyes, and cognitive impairment, with risk of dependence and psychiatric symptoms with heavy or prolonged use; medically, it is used for pain relief, chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, and appetite stimulation in wasting syndromes, but carries potential adverse effects and misuse risk.

cannabinoids.definition: Chemical compounds that interact with the endocannabinoid system by binding to cannabinoid receptors (CB1 and CB2). They include plant-derived cannabinoids (e.g., THC, CBD), endogenous cannabinoids (anandamide, 2-AG), and synthetic cannabinoids, influencing pain, inflammation, mood, appetite, and other physiological processes.

capillaria.definition: A genus of parasitic nematodes (threadworms) in the family Capillariidae that infect humans and animals, causing capillariasis of the intestine or liver (e.g., Capillaria philippinensis, Capillaria hepatica).

capillaria philippinensis.definition: A parasitic nematode that infects the human small intestine, causing intestinal capillariasis; transmission occurs by consuming raw or undercooked freshwater fish containing larvae; presents with chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, and malabsorption; diagnosed by identification of characteristic eggs or adult worms in stool or intestinal tissue; treated with antiparasitic agents such as albendazole or mebendazole.

capillariasis.definition: A parasitic infection caused by nematodes of the genus Capillaria; most commonly refers to intestinal capillariasis caused by Capillaria philippinensis, with chronic diarrhea and malabsorption (often after eating raw/undercooked fish), and there is also hepatic capillariasis caused by Capillaria hepatica, presenting with hepatomegaly and granulomatous liver lesions.

capillaria hepatica.definition: A hepatic nematode parasite of rodents; adults reside in the liver and deposit eggs in hepatic tissue, where they embryonate and are released into the environment after the host dies. Humans and other animals can become infected by ingesting embryonated eggs, causing hepatic capillariasis (granulomatous hepatitis). Also known as Calodium hepaticum.

capillaria aerophila.definition: A parasitic nematode (lungworm) that infects the trachea and bronchi of dogs, cats, and wild carnivores, causing pulmonary disease; transmitted by ingestion of embryonated eggs in contaminated environments; zoonotic infections are rare.

caplan's syndrome.definition: A syndrome in which rheumatoid arthritis coexists with pneumoconiosis and is marked by multiple, well-defined intrapulmonary nodules (rheumatoid nodules) seen on chest imaging, most commonly in coal workers; these nodules are typically noninfectious.

end-tidal.definition: Pertaining to the concentration of a gas at the end of an exhaled breath; specifically, end-tidal CO2 is the level of carbon dioxide at the end of expiration, measured by capnography to monitor ventilation.

capnography.definition: Continuous monitoring of the concentration or partial pressure of carbon dioxide in exhaled breath, typically displayed as a capnograph waveform and reported as end-tidal CO2, used to assess ventilation and airway status.

capnogram.definition: A graphical representation of the concentration of carbon dioxide in exhaled air over time, obtained by capnography, used to assess ventilation and detect respiratory and circulatory problems.

capnometry.definition: Measurement of the concentration or partial pressure of carbon dioxide in exhaled air, typically obtained with infrared sensors; used to monitor ventilation and assess respiratory status (often reported as end-tidal CO2).

captopril.definition: A short-acting oral angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor that reduces production of angiotensin II, leading to vasodilation and decreased aldosterone-mediated sodium and water retention; used to treat hypertension and heart failure (and to improve outcomes after myocardial infarction).

capoten.definition: A brand-name angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor used to treat hypertension and congestive heart failure and to improve survival after myocardial infarction; it inhibits ACE, lowering angiotensin II and aldosterone to cause vasodilation; common adverse effects include cough and risk of angioedema.

capsulectomy.definition: The surgical removal of a fibrous capsule that forms around a prosthetic implant (most commonly a breast implant), typically performed to treat capsular contracture, implant failure, or infection; it may be partial (subtotal) or complete (total capsulectomy).

bowman's capsule.definition: A double-walled, cup-shaped structure at the start of the nephron that surrounds the glomerulus; it receives filtrate from the glomerular capillaries and forms Bowman's space, with visceral and parietal layers.

capsulitis.definition: Inflammation of the joint capsule, the fibrous envelope surrounding a synovial joint, causing pain and reduced range of motion; when it involves the shoulder, it can present as painful stiffness often described as frozen shoulder.

capsuloplasty.definition: A surgical procedure to repair, tighten, or reconstruct a joint capsule to restore stability and reduce laxity or prevent dislocations.

capsulorrhaphy.definition: A surgical procedure to tighten or reinforce a joint capsule by suturing and shortening its lax edges, thereby reducing instability and preventing recurrent dislocations (most commonly in the shoulder).

capsulorrexis.definition: A surgical procedure that creates a circular opening in a capsule (most often the anterior lens capsule) to permit removal and replacement of the lens during cataract surgery; typically performed as a continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis.

capsulotomy.definition: A surgical procedure that involves incising a capsule to create an opening, typically to access interior structures or relieve constriction (e.g., lens capsule in ophthalmology or a joint capsule).

capsular.definition: Relating to or forming a capsule; pertaining to the fibrous envelope that surrounds a joint or organ or other structure.

capsuloma.definition: A mass arising from a fibrous capsule surrounding an organ or implanted prosthesis; often due to scar-tissue proliferation or a foreign‑body–induced granulomatous reaction.

capitate.definition: The largest carpal bone (os capitatum) in the center of the wrist, forming part of the distal carpal row; it articulates proximally with the scaphoid and lunate, and distally with the bases of the 2nd–4th metacarpals.

capitate bone.definition: A large carpal bone centrally located in the distal carpal row of the wrist; the largest of the carpal bones and the keystone of the carpal arch, articulating proximally with the scaphoid and lunate and distally with the base of the third metacarpal.

capitulum.definition: A small, rounded eminence on a bone that forms part of a joint by providing a smooth articular surface; in the elbow, the distal humerus has such a surface that articulates with the head of the radius.

caput.definition: Latin for "head"; used in medical terminology to denote the head or structures of the head. For example, caput succedaneum is transient diffuse swelling of a newborn's scalp due to birth‑related pressure, crossing suture lines and usually resolving within a few days.

caput femoris.definition: The rounded proximal end of the femur that articulates with the acetabulum to form the hip joint; it is covered with articular cartilage and connects to the femoral shaft via the femoral neck.

caput fibulae.definition: The rounded proximal end of the fibula (head) that articulates with the lateral condyle of the tibia at the superior tibiofibular joint; serves as an attachment point for muscles, notably the short head of the biceps femoris.

caput humeri.definition: Proximal, rounded articular end of the humerus (the head) that articulates with the glenoid fossa of the scapula to form the shoulder (glenohumeral) joint.

caput mallei.definition: The head of the malleus, one of the auditory ossicles in the middle ear; it articulates with the incus.

caput mandibulae.definition: Rounded articular end of the mandible (the mandibular condyle) that articulates with the temporal bone to form the temporomandibular joint; located at the superior end of the condylar process and covered by articular cartilage.

caput radii.definition: The proximal end of the radius; the rounded head that articulates with the capitellum of the humerus to form part of the elbow joint and with the ulna at the radial notch via the annular ligament to form the proximal radioulnar joint.

caput stapedis.definition: The head of the stapes; the articular end that articulates with the lenticular process of the incus at the incudostapedial joint, forming part of the middle ear ossicular chain that transmits sound to the inner ear.

caput medusae.definition: Dilated, engorged superficial veins around the umbilicus radiating across the abdomen, caused by portal hypertension with collateral flow through the paraumbilical veins; a sign of advanced liver disease.

caput ossis metacarpalis.definition: The head of a metacarpal bone; the rounded distal end that articulates with the proximal phalanx to form the metacarpophalangeal (knuckle) joint.

caput phalangis.definition: Rounded distal end of a finger bone (a phalanx) that articulates with the adjacent bone (another phalanx or a metacarpal) to form a joint, such as the interphalangeal or metacarpophalangeal joint.

caput succedaneum.definition: Diffuse scalp edema of a newborn due to pressure during vaginal delivery; it crosses suture lines and typically resolves spontaneously within a few days without treatment.

carabelli.definition: An accessory cusp on the mesiolingual (palatal) surface of the maxillary first permanent molar, a common dental morphological variation.

carabelli cusp.definition: An accessory cusp or tubercle on the mesiolingual (palatal) surface of the maxillary first molar, near the cingulum; a common dental anatomical variation (Carabelli trait).

carafate.definition: An oral brand-name mucosal protectant (the generic drug sucralfate) that coats stomach and duodenal ulcers to shield them from acid, pepsin, and bile; minimally absorbed and used to treat and prevent peptic ulcers and gastritis; dosing should be spaced from other medications to avoid interactions.

sucralfate.definition: A medication that adheres to ulcerated or irritated gastric and duodenal mucosa, forming a protective viscous barrier against acid, pepsin, and bile; it is an aluminum-sucrose complex with minimal systemic absorption and is used to treat and prevent gastric and duodenal ulcers (and sometimes GERD).

caramiphen.definition: That term is not found in standard medical dictionaries. Please check the spelling or provide context (drug class, condition, or brand). If you meant another term such as carbamazepine or cariprazine, I can define that.

carapace.definition: The hard, protective dorsal shell or shield of certain animals—most notably turtles and crustaceans—formed by fused plates of the exoskeleton and serving as structural protection.

carbamate.definition: A chemical compound derived from carbamic acid that contains the carbamate functional group (-O-CO-NR2); carbamates are esters or salts of carbamic acid and include substances used as pesticides and reversible cholinesterase inhibitors.

carbamoylphosphate.definition: A high-energy phosphorylated carbamate formed from bicarbonate, ammonia, and ATP; it donates the carbamoyl group in the urea cycle (via CPS1) and in pyrimidine biosynthesis (via CPS2).

carbamide peroxide.definition: A chemical compound formed from urea and hydrogen peroxide that releases hydrogen peroxide in solution; used as a whitening agent in dentistry and as an earwax-softening (cerumenolytic) product.

carbaminohemoglobin.definition: A reversible form of hemoglobin in which carbon dioxide binds to the N-terminal amino groups of the globin chains to form HbCO2, aiding CO2 transport from tissues to the lungs and decreasing hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen (Bohr effect).

carbamino compound.definition: A compound in which carbon dioxide is bound to an amino group, forming a carbamino adduct; this binding is typically reversible and commonly occurs on plasma proteins and hemoglobin to aid CO2 transport.

carbamate kinase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the transfer of a phosphate from carbamoyl phosphate to ADP, producing ATP and the carbamate ion (which rapidly hydrolyzes to ammonia and carbon dioxide); part of the bacterial arginine deiminase pathway for ATP generation.

carbamazepine.definition: An anticonvulsant and mood stabilizer used to treat partial and generalized seizures, trigeminal neuralgia, and bipolar disorder. It acts by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels, stabilizing hyperexcited neuronal membranes, and reducing repetitive firing.

cephalhematoma.definition: A subperiosteal hematoma of the newborn's skull, typically caused by birth trauma, in which blood collects beneath the periosteum between the skull bone and periosteum; it is confined by cranial sutures (does not cross them), appears as a firm scalp swelling within hours to days after birth, and usually resolves spontaneously over weeks. Distinguishing feature: it does not cross suture lines (unlike caput succedaneum).

molding.definition: In obstetrics, molding is the temporary overlap and shaping of the fetal skull bones at birth as the head passes through the birth canal, allowing adaption to the pelvis; it typically resolves within days after delivery.

acapnia.definition: A decreased level of carbon dioxide in the blood (hypocapnia), usually caused by hyperventilation, which can lead to respiratory alkalosis.

capnia.definition: The concentration of carbon dioxide in the blood, reflecting the balance between CO2 production and elimination; abnormalities include hypercapnia (elevated CO2) and hypocapnia (reduced CO2).

lens capsule.definition: A thick, transparent basement membrane surrounding the crystalline lens, secreted by the lens epithelium and forming the capsule that envelops the lens.

phacoemulsification.definition: A method of cataract removal. It uses ultrasound waves to break up the clouded lens of the eye so it can be suctioned out with a needle.

cataract.definition: A clouding of the eye's natural lens that leads to progressive, painless vision loss; commonly age-related; treated with surgical removal of the cloudy lens, usually with implantation of an artificial intraocular lens.

glenohumeral.definition: Relating to the shoulder joint where the head of the humerus articulates with the glenoid fossa of the scapula; a ball-and-socket joint that allows a wide range of motion and is stabilized by the rotator cuff muscles and associated ligaments.

glenoid cavity.definition: An articular depression on the lateral aspect of the scapula that articulates with the head of the humerus to form the shoulder joint; deepened by the glenoid labrum and lined with hyaline cartilage.

scaphoid.definition: A boat-shaped carpal bone in the wrist’s proximal row on the thumb (radial) side; it articulates proximally with the radius and with the lunate and distal carpal bones, and is prone to avascular necrosis after fracture due to retrograde blood supply.

lunate.definition: A crescent-shaped carpal bone in the proximal row of the wrist, positioned between the scaphoid and triquetrum, and articulating with the distal radius and adjacent carpals.

carbetapentane.definition: An antitussive (cough suppressant) used to reduce coughing; commonly included in combination cough medicines.

clotting.definition: The process of blood coagulation that forms a clot to stop bleeding, involving platelet aggregation (primary hemostasis) and a coagulation cascade that converts fibrinogen to fibrin to stabilize the plug.

antitussive.definition: A drug that suppresses coughing by acting on the cough reflex center in the brain (medulla), reducing the urge to cough; includes opioids like codeine and non-opioids like dextromethorphan.

carbidopa.definition: A peripheral aromatic L‑amino acid decarboxylase (AADC) inhibitor used with levodopa to treat Parkinson disease; it prevents peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine, increasing central availability of levodopa and reducing peripheral adverse effects.

dopa decarboxylase inhibitor.definition: A drug that inhibits the enzyme dopa decarboxylase (AADC), preventing peripheral conversion of L-DOPA to dopamine and thereby increasing central availability of L-DOPA while reducing peripheral side effects.

cardiac irregularity.definition: An irregular heartbeat or heart rhythm (arrhythmia); may be too fast (tachycardia), too slow (bradycardia), or irregular, and can range from benign to potentially dangerous.

malignant melanoma.definition: A malignant neoplasm arising from melanocytes, most commonly in the skin, characterized by uncontrolled proliferation of pigment-producing cells with potential for local invasion and distant metastasis; it often presents as a new or changing pigmented lesion.

carbinoxamine maleate.definition: A salt form (maleate) of carbinoxamine, a first‑generation antihistamine that antagonizes histamine H1 receptors to relieve allergic symptoms (e.g., rhinitis, urticaria); commonly causes sedation and anticholinergic side effects.

skin reactions.definition: A group of cutaneous responses to contact or systemic stimuli, such as allergens, irritants, infections, medications, or environmental factors, typically presenting with redness (erythema), itching (pruritus), swelling (edema), rash, urticaria (hives), vesicles, or other surface changes.

carbolic acid.definition: A toxic, caustic phenol used as an antiseptic and disinfectant; corrosive to skin and mucous membranes and hazardous if ingested or inhaled.

phenol.definition: A toxic, caustic aromatic compound with a hydroxyl group on a benzene ring; historically used as an antiseptic and disinfectant and as a chemical precursor for phenolic resins and plastics.

phenol poisoning.definition: An acute toxic condition resulting from exposure to phenol (carbolic acid) or phenol-containing products, via ingestion, inhalation, or dermal absorption, causing caustic injury to skin and mucous membranes and systemic toxicity (including CNS depression, hypotension, and hepatic/renal injury).

carbon-11.definition: A radioactive isotope of carbon (carbon-11) with a half-life of about 20.3 minutes that decays by positron emission to boron-11; used as a PET radiotracer to image metabolic processes and receptor binding in vivo.

carbon-13.definition: A stable, non-radioactive isotope of carbon with mass number 13 (6 protons, 7 neutrons) used as a tracer in metabolic studies and in 13C nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy.

carbon-14.definition: A radioactive isotope with 6 protons and 8 neutrons (mass number 14). It is formed in the atmosphere by cosmic-ray interactions and decays by beta emission to a nitrogen isotope, with a half-life of about 5,730 years. It is used in radiometric dating of formerly living material and as a tracer in biomedical research.

carbon dioxide tension.definition: Partial pressure of carbon dioxide; the pressure exerted by CO2 in a gas or liquid, typically referring to the CO2 tension in arterial blood (PaCO2) or alveolar air (PACO2) and used to assess ventilatory status.

carbon dioxide content test.definition: A laboratory measurement of the amount of carbon dioxide present in a sample (usually blood), typically reported as mmol/L or mEq/L; in clinical practice it reflects the total CO2 content (primarily bicarbonate with dissolved CO2) and is used to assess acid–base balance.

carbonate dehydratase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the reversible hydration of carbon dioxide to carbonic acid (CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ HCO3− + H+), essential for CO2 transport in blood and acid–base balance (commonly known as carbonic anhydrase).

carbon dioxide narcosis.definition: CNS depression due to hypercapnia (elevated arterial CO2), typically from hypoventilation or impaired gas exchange, presenting with headache, dizziness, confusion or drowsiness, and potentially progressing to coma in severe cases.

carbon dioxide poisoning.definition: Hypercapnia due to inhalation of air with excessive carbon dioxide or due to hypoventilation, causing respiratory acidosis and impaired tissue oxygenation; symptoms range from headache and dizziness to confusion, dyspnea, and, in severe cases, loss of consciousness or death. Management includes removing exposure, providing supplemental oxygen, and ventilatory support as needed.

nauheim bath.definition: A hydrotherapy treatment involving immersion in a warm, mineral-rich carbonated bath (from Nauheim, Germany), traditionally used for cardiovascular conditions to improve circulation and autonomic function.

carbon dioxide bath.definition: A balneotherapy treatment in which bathwater is enriched with dissolved carbon dioxide; absorption through the skin causes cutaneous vasodilation and increased peripheral blood flow, which may relieve pain and improve symptoms in conditions related to poor circulation or rheumatic disease.

castellani's paint.definition: A rapid, dye-based staining solution used in microbiology to visualize fungal elements in clinical specimens; applied as a thin layer on a smear, it stains fungal cell walls and spores to improve contrast for light microscopy (commonly used for detecting Candida and other yeasts/filamentous fungi).

ziehl's stain.definition: An acid-fast staining technique used to detect acid-fast bacilli (notably Mycobacterium species) in clinical specimens. It uses carbol fuchsin as the primary stain with heat to penetrate the waxy cell wall, followed by decolorization with acid-alcohol and counterstaining (usually methylene blue); acid-fast organisms retain the red color, while non–acid-fast cells appear blue.

acid-fast stain.definition: A differential staining technique used to detect acid-fast bacteria (e.g., Mycobacterium, Nocardia) in clinical specimens. Organisms with mycolic acid–rich cell walls retain the red carbol fuchsin dye after acid-alcohol decolorization and counterstain blue, appearing red against a blue background; commonly performed by Ziehl-Neelsen or Kinyoun methods.

kinyoun stain.definition: A cold acid-fast staining technique (a modified Ziehl-Neelsen) that uses a concentrated carbol fuchsin with phenol as the primary stain and a milder decolorizer, allowing acid-fast organisms (e.g., Mycobacterium) to retain the red stain while non–acid-fast elements are counterstained blue.

carbohydrate.definition: The sugars and starches in food that provide the body with most of its fuel. Carbohydrates are one of three primary nutrients along with fats and proteins.

carbohydrates.definition: A class of organic compounds composed of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen (often with the general formula (CH2O)n) that provide a primary energy source for the body; includes sugars, starches, glycogen, and dietary fiber; digestible carbohydrates are broken down to glucose, while most dietary fiber is not fully digested.

carbohydrate loading.definition: A strategy used by endurance athletes to maximize glycogen stores in liver and muscle by increasing carbohydrate intake while tapering training in the days before a prolonged event. Typically involves high carbohydrate intake (about 7–12 g/kg/day) for 1–4 days.

carbohydrate intolerance.definition: A condition in which the body cannot properly digest or absorb carbohydrates, typically due to deficiency of intestinal enzymes (most commonly lactase, causing lactose intolerance) or other malabsorption disorders, resulting in symptoms such as bloating, abdominal pain, gas, and diarrhea after consuming carbohydrate-containing foods.

carbohydrate metabolism.definition: Biochemical processes that convert carbohydrates into energy (ATP) and metabolic precursors, primarily via glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation, with glycogen synthesis and breakdown and gluconeogenesis forming key regulatory pathways; regulated by hormones such as insulin and glucagon.

monosaccharides.definition: Simple sugars; the most basic units of carbohydrates that cannot be hydrolyzed into smaller sugars. They include aldoses and ketoses (for example, glucose, fructose, and galactose) and typically contain three to seven carbon atoms. They are the building blocks for disaccharides and polysaccharides.

disaccharides.definition: A class of carbohydrates formed by two monosaccharide units linked by a glycosidic bond; they are hydrolyzed to two monosaccharides and include examples such as sucrose (glucose–fructose), lactose (glucose–galactose), and maltose (glucose–glucose).

polysaccharides.definition: Polysaccharides are large carbohydrate polymers formed by linkage of many monosaccharide units via glycosidic bonds; they serve mainly as energy storage (e.g., starch, glycogen) or structural materials (e.g., cellulose, chitin) in living organisms.

starch.definition: A storage polysaccharide of plants composed of glucose units, existing as amylose (linear) and amylopectin (branched) linked by α-1,4- and α-1,6-glycosidic bonds. It serves as the primary energy reserve in plants and is digestible by humans via salivary and pancreatic amylase to maltose and glucose.

glycogen.definition: A large, highly branched polysaccharide of glucose that serves as the body's main storage form of glucose, primarily in the liver (to maintain blood glucose) and in skeletal muscle (to supply energy during activity). It is synthesized by glycogen synthase and broken down by glycogen phosphorylase during glycogenolysis.

fructose.definition: A kind of sugar in fruit and honey.

galactose.definition: A simple monosaccharide hexose sugar that is a component of lactose; metabolized via the Leloir pathway to glucose-1-phosphate and other metabolites; used for energy production and as a precursor in biosynthetic pathways; found in milk and dairy products; defects in its metabolism cause galactosemia.

sucrose.definition: A non-reducing disaccharide composed of glucose and fructose (table sugar); derived from sugar cane or sugar beets; hydrolyzed in the small intestine to glucose and fructose.

lactose.definition: A sugar found in milk and dairy products.

maltose.definition: A disaccharide of two α-D-glucose units linked by an α-1,4-glycosidic bond; produced by the hydrolysis of starch and digested by intestinal maltase to yield two glucose molecules; it is a reducing sugar.

corn syrup.definition: A viscous sweetener produced by hydrolyzing corn (maize) starch to yield a syrup rich in glucose; used as a sweetener and thickener in processed foods.

table sugar.definition: A disaccharide composed of glucose and fructose; the principal refined sugar used as a sweetener in foods, derived commercially from sugar cane or sugar beets; it provides calories but little or no essential nutrients and hydrolyzes to glucose and fructose in the body.

glycolysis.definition: Glycolysis is the cytosolic metabolic pathway that converts one molecule of glucose into two molecules of pyruvate, producing a net gain of two ATP and two NADH, and does not require oxygen; it consists of ten enzyme-catalyzed steps divided into an energy-investment phase and an energy-yielding phase.

glycogenesis.definition: The metabolic process of converting glucose to glycogen for storage, primarily in liver and skeletal muscle, catalyzed by glycogen synthase and regulated by insulin.

citric acid cycle.definition: A sequence of enzyme-catalyzed reactions in the mitochondrial matrix that oxidizes acetyl-CoA to CO2, generating NADH and FADH2 for ATP production via the electron transport chain. It starts when acetyl-CoA combines with oxaloacetate to form citrate and ends with the regeneration of oxaloacetate for another turn.

electron transport.definition: Transfer of electrons through a series of membrane-bound carrier molecules, releasing energy that pumps protons across a membrane and drives ATP synthesis via ATP synthase.

oxidative phosphorylation.definition: The mitochondrial energy-producing process in which electrons are transferred through the respiratory chain, creating a proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane that drives ATP synthase to convert ADP and inorganic phosphate into ATP; oxygen serves as the final electron acceptor.

alveolar hypoventilation.definition: A condition in which alveolar ventilation is insufficient to meet metabolic needs, leading to hypercapnia (elevated arterial CO2) and often hypoxemia; caused by reduced breathing (e.g., CNS depression, neuromuscular weakness, chest wall restriction, or obesity-related hypoventilation).

ventilation-perfusion abnormalities.definition: A mismatch between the air reaching the alveoli (ventilation) and the blood flow in the pulmonary capillaries (perfusion) that impairs gas exchange; described as V/Q mismatch, with regions of high V/Q (ventilation predominates) or low V/Q (perfusion predominates) seen in various lung diseases.

carbon dioxide retention.definition: An elevation of arterial carbon dioxide (hypercapnia) due to inadequate ventilation or impaired alveolar gas exchange, commonly seen in COPD or hypoventilation disorders, often causing respiratory acidosis.

carbuncle.definition: A deep skin infection consisting of a cluster of boils (furuncles) that coalesce and involve several hair follicles and surrounding tissue, typically caused by Staphylococcus aureus; may drain through multiple sinuses.

carbunculosis.definition: An infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue characterized by the formation of a cluster of connected boils (carbuncles), typically caused by Staphylococcus aureus, with tender, inflamed nodules that may discharge pus and be accompanied by fever; treatment may include drainage and antibiotic therapy.

furuncle.definition: A boil; a deep bacterial infection of a hair follicle and surrounding dermis, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus, presenting as a painful, erythematous nodule that may suppurate and drain pus.

asphyxiation.definition: A condition in which oxygen intake is insufficient or carbon dioxide removal is impaired, leading to hypoxia and often hypercapnia, which can result in unconsciousness, organ damage, and death.

carcinoembryonic antigen.definition: A glycoprotein involved in cell adhesion that is normally expressed during fetal development and is low in healthy adults; elevated levels are seen in colorectal cancer and other malignancies (and some benign conditions), and it is used clinically as a tumor marker to monitor treatment response and detect recurrence.

carcinogenesis.definition: The process by which a normal cell becomes cancerous.

carcinogenic.definition: Having the capacity to cause cancer; agents or exposures that can initiate or promote carcinogenesis by damaging DNA, causing mutations, or promoting uncontrolled cell growth.

carcinoid tumor.definition: A slow-growing neuroendocrine tumor arising from enterochromaffin cells, most commonly in the gastrointestinal tract or lungs; it can secrete serotonin and other vasoactive substances, leading to carcinoid syndrome in some cases.

carcinosis.definition: A diffuse metastatic spread of carcinoma cells on serous membranes (especially the peritoneum) with multiple tumor implants and often ascites; a form of carcinomatosis.

carcinosis pleurae.definition: Diffuse malignant seeding of the pleural surfaces by metastatic cancer, causing pleural nodularity and thickening with recurrent pleural effusions and dyspnea.

carcinostatic.definition: An agent or effect that inhibits the growth or progression of cancer, slowing or stopping the proliferation of malignant cells.

carcinolysis.definition: Destruction or dissolution of malignant (cancerous) tissue or cancer cells, typically by cytotoxic therapies or immune mechanisms.

carcinomatous.definition: Relating to carcinoma; consisting of malignant epithelial cells or resembling carcinoma in histology.

carcinoma cutaneum.definition: An obsolete term for malignant skin cancer arising from epidermal keratinocytes, i.e., cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.

carcinoma en cuirasse.definition: A rare form of cutaneous metastasis of breast carcinoma in which malignant cells diffusely infiltrate the chest wall skin, producing diffuse, hardened, leather‑like induration (sclerodermoid plaques) that encase the chest wall—an armor‑like (cuirass) appearance.

carcinoma fibrosum.definition: A malignant epithelial tumor characterized by extensive fibrous desmoplastic stroma, producing a hard, scirrhous mass (historically used to denote scirrhous carcinoma, such as in the breast).

carcinoma gigantocellulare.definition: A malignant epithelial tumor in which the neoplasm is composed predominantly of large multinucleated giant cells; a histologic variant of carcinoma with epithelial origin. Diagnosis is supported by epithelial markers (e.g., cytokeratins) and exclusion of non-epithelial giant cell lesions. Behavior and treatment depend on the tumor’s anatomical site.

carcinoma medullare.definition: A malignant neoplasm arising from the parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid gland, often secreting calcitonin; may be sporadic or associated with MEN2 syndromes.

carcinoma mucocellulare.definition: A malignant epithelial tumor arising from mucin-producing (mucous-secreting) cells, characterized by production of mucin and glandular differentiation; prognosis and treatment depend on the organ of origin.

carcinoma scroti.definition: A malignant neoplasm of the scrotal skin, most commonly squamous cell carcinoma, historically linked to chronic irritation and exposure to soot or tar (as in chimney sweeps); it can invade locally and metastasize to regional lymph nodes, with treatment typically surgical excision and assessment of nodal involvement.

carcinoma spongiosum.definition: A malignant tumor arising from the corpus spongiosum, the spongy erectile tissue surrounding the penile urethra; a very rare form of penile cancer (often of squamous cell histology).

carcinomatosis.definition: A condition characterized by widespread peritoneal spread of malignant tumor cells, with numerous implants on peritoneal surfaces (peritoneal carcinomatosis), commonly arising from ovarian, colorectal, or gastric cancer; often associated with ascites and poor prognosis.

cardia.definition: The region of the stomach surrounding the gastroesophageal (cardiac) junction, i.e., the proximal part of the stomach just below the esophagus.

cardiac action potential.definition: It is the rapid, orchestrated change in the electrical membrane potential of heart muscle cells that triggers coordinated contraction, produced by sequential fluxes of Na+, Ca2+, and K+ through voltage-gated channels and described by phases 0–4 (with a plateau in ventricular/atrial myocytes and automatic pacemaker depolarization in nodal tissue).

cardiac apnea.definition: A form of apnea associated with cardiac disease—most commonly central sleep apnea in heart failure—characterized by pauses in breathing during sleep due to impaired central respiratory control and extended circulatory time, often presenting as Cheyne–Stokes respiration.

cardiac arrhythmia.definition: An umbrella term for any abnormality of heart rhythm due to disordered electrical activity, causing heartbeats that are too fast, too slow, or irregular, and which may cause palpitations, dizziness, syncope, or hemodynamic compromise.

cardiac asthma.definition: An asthma-like wheeze and dyspnea caused by congestive heart failure with pulmonary edema; not true asthma, but due to elevated left-sided pressures causing bronchial/airway edema and obstruction, improving with heart-failure therapy.

cardiac standstill.definition: A complete cessation of cardiac activity, with no electrical activity and no mechanical pumping of the heart, resulting in absent blood circulation and pulse.

cardiopulmonary arrest.definition: A sudden cessation of both cardiac and pulmonary function, resulting in unresponsiveness, absence of a detectable pulse and respirations, and requiring immediate resuscitation (CPR) and advanced life support.

ventricular aneurysm.definition: A localized bulge or dilation of the wall of a ventricle (usually the left ventricle) due to scar tissue after a myocardial infarction, forming a non-contractile outpouching that can impair systolic function and increase the risk of heart failure, arrhythmias, and thromboembolism.

apex cordis.definition: The pointed tip of the heart, formed mainly by the left ventricle, located at the left fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line; it corresponds to the point of maximal impulse (PMI) on chest examination.

kulchitsky-cell carcinoma.definition: An aggressive high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma of the lung (small cell lung cancer) arising from Kulchitsky neuroendocrine cells in the bronchial epithelium; characterized by rapid growth, early metastasis, strong association with smoking, and expression of neuroendocrine markers.

krukenberg’s tumor.definition: A metastatic ovarian tumor consisting of signet-ring cell adenocarcinoma, most commonly originating from gastric (stomach) cancer; it is typically bilateral.

carboxyhemoglobin.definition: An abnormal form of hemoglobin in which carbon monoxide is bound to the heme iron, preventing oxygen binding and greatly reducing oxygen delivery to tissues due to CO's high affinity and a leftward shift of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve.

carboxyhemoglobin test.definition: A blood test that measures the amount of carboxyhemoglobin (hemoglobin bound to carbon monoxide) to assess exposure to carbon monoxide, typically performed by co-oximetry and used in evaluating suspected CO poisoning.

carboxylase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the introduction of a carboxyl group (-COOH) into a substrate (carboxylation), typically using CO2 or bicarbonate as the carbon source; many are biotin-dependent and may require ATP energy.

carboxylation.definition: The introduction of a carboxyl group (-COOH) into a molecule, typically by a carboxylase enzyme using CO2 as the source.

carboxylic acid.definition: An organic compound containing a carboxyl group (-COOH); generally written as R-COOH, where R is an alkyl or other substituent. They are weak acids that dissociate in water to form carboxylate anions.

carboxymethylcellulose.definition: An anionic cellulose derivative in which some hydroxyl groups are substituted with carboxymethyl groups, producing a water-soluble polymer used as a thickener, stabilizer, binder, and suspending agent in foods, cosmetics, and pharmaceuticals; commonly used as the sodium salt (carboxymethylcellulose sodium) in ophthalmic and other formulations.

carboxymethylcellulose calcium.definition: Calcium carboxymethylcellulose is the calcium salt form of carboxymethylcellulose, a cellulose derivative used as a thickener and stabilizer in foods, pharmaceuticals, and cosmetics; it increases viscosity and helps stabilize suspensions and emulsions.

carbon dioxide pressure.definition: Partial pressure of carbon dioxide; the pressure exerted by CO2 within a gas mixture or body compartment, typically expressed as PaCO2 in arterial blood or PACO2 in alveolar gas. It reflects the balance between CO2 production and alveolar ventilation; normal arterial PaCO2 is about 35–45 mmHg (4.7–6.0 kPa). Elevated PaCO2 indicates hypoventilation, while low PaCO2 indicates hyperventilation.

carbon dioxide therapy.definition: Therapy that administers carbon dioxide gas in a controlled manner to elicit physiological responses, typically by subcutaneous or intradermal injection (carboxytherapy) to increase local microcirculation, oxygen delivery, and tissue remodeling for cosmetic or wound-healing purposes; not equivalent to CO2 used for insufflation in surgery.

carbonic anhydrase inhibitor.definition: A drug that inhibits the enzyme carbonic anhydrase, which catalyzes the reversible hydration of carbon dioxide to bicarbonate and protons; by blocking this reaction, it decreases bicarbonate formation, reducing aqueous humor production in the eye and promoting bicarbonate diuresis, and is used to treat glaucoma, altitude sickness, and as a mild diuretic.

carbon monoxide poisoning.definition: An illness caused by inhaling carbon monoxide, a colorless, odorless gas that binds hemoglobin with high affinity to form carboxyhemoglobin, reducing oxygen delivery to tissues and causing tissue hypoxia. Symptoms range from headache, dizziness, and nausea to confusion or loss of consciousness; severe exposure can be fatal. Treatment is 100% oxygen, with hyperbaric oxygen therapy for selected severe cases.

carbon tetrachloride.definition: An organochlorine solvent (CCl4) that is highly hepatotoxic and can cause centrilobular hepatic necrosis via metabolic activation to reactive free radicals; historically used as a solvent and fire-extinguishing agent.

enterobacteriaceae.definition: A large family of Gram-negative, non-spore-forming, facultatively anaerobic bacilli that inhabit the intestinal tract of humans and animals and include genera such as Escherichia, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Proteus, Salmonella, Shigella, and Yersinia; they are commonly associated with enteric and other infections and are typically oxidase-negative with variable lactose fermentation, and many species can be antibiotic-resistant.

pseudomonas.definition: Genus of Gram-negative, aerobic, nonfermentative bacilli found in soil and water; many species are environmental, with Pseudomonas aeruginosa as a common opportunistic human pathogen causing pneumonia, wound and bloodstream infections; oxidase positive and often pigment-producing; notable for biofilm formation and intrinsic antibiotic resistance.

right atrium.definition: The right upper chamber of the heart; it receives partially deoxygenated blood as it returns from the body's tissues and moves it into the right ventricle for distribution to the lungs.

tricuspid stenosis.definition: A narrowing of the tricuspid valve orifice that restricts blood flow from the right atrium to the right ventricle during diastole, causing elevated right atrial pressures and systemic venous congestion (e.g., hepatomegaly, ascites, edema); commonly due to rheumatic disease, carcinoid syndrome, or congenital anomalies, with a diastolic rumble best heard at the left lower sternal border and often intensified by inspiration.

valvular incompetence.definition: A heart-valve dysfunction in which the valve does not close properly, allowing backward blood flow (regurgitation) into the preceding chamber during the cardiac cycle, often due to structural valve disease or annular dilation.

cardiomyopathy.definition: A disease of the heart muscle (myocardium) that impairs its structure and/or function, often leading to heart failure, arrhythmias, or sudden cardiac death; includes primary forms such as dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive, and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy.

myocardium.definition: The middle layer of heart tissue. The muscular myocardium is sandwiched between the outer layer (epicardium) and the inner layer (endocardium).

sinoatrial node.definition: The natural pacemaker of the heart. Located in the right atrium, the sinoatrial node, sometimes called the sinus node, initiates the heart's electrical activity.

av node.definition: Abbreviation for atrioventricular node, a major part of the electrical system in the heart that acts as a gateway between the atria and the ventricles.
