An electrical signal generated by the sinoatrial node (the heart's natural pacemaker) moves through the heart until it reaches the atrioventricular node, a cluster of cells at the bottom of the right atrium. The AV node delays the signal before it is passed to the ventricles. This lets the atria fully contract before the ventricles contract.

his-purkinje system.definition: A network of specialized cardiac conduction fibers that rapidly propagate electrical impulses from the AV node through the bundle of His to the right and left bundle branches and Purkinje fibers, coordinating synchronized ventricular contraction.

purkinje system.definition: A network of specialized conducting cardiac muscle fibers (Purkinje fibers) in the subendocardial ventricles that rapidly transmit electrical impulses from the AV node/bundle of His to the ventricular myocardium, coordinating and synchronizing ventricular contraction.

paroxysmal atrial tachycardia.definition: A sudden-onset, self-terminating episode of a rapid, regular heart rhythm caused by an ectopic atrial focus, producing a narrow-complex tachycardia (typically about 150–250 beats per minute) with P waves that differ from normal sinus rhythm.

sinus tachycardia.definition: An increased heart rate driven by the sinoatrial node with a normal-appearing P waves and regular rhythm, typically exceeding 100 beats per minute in adults; often a physiologic response to exercise, fever, anxiety, or volume depletion, but can occur in conditions such as thyrotoxicosis or heart failure.

sinus bradycardia.definition: Slower-than-normal heart rate (usually under 60 beats per minute) with a normal sinus rhythm; may be physiologic (e.g., in well-trained athletes or during sleep) or pathologic (sinus node dysfunction, increased vagal tone, or drug effects), and can be asymptomatic or cause dizziness, fatigue, or syncope if the rate is too low.

first-degree atrioventricular block.definition: An atrioventricular conduction delay in which atrial impulses are conducted to the ventricles with a consistently prolonged PR interval (typically ≥200 ms in adults) and with no dropped QRS complexes; usually asymptomatic and benign, but can be influenced by autonomic tone or medications and may indicate underlying heart disease.

second-degree atrioventricular block typ.definition: Progressive prolongation of the PR interval on the ECG until a P wave fails to conduct a QRS complex, after which the cycle repeats (a dropped beat) due to AV nodal conduction delay. Usually benign but can be affected by medications or ischemia.

mobitz type i.definition: Second-degree atrioventricular block with progressive PR interval lengthening until a P wave is nonconducted, resulting in a dropped QRS complex; typically at the AV node and often transient.

wenckebach.definition: A form of Mobitz type I (Wenckebach phenomenon) in which the PR interval progressively lengthens with each beat until a P wave is not followed by a QRS complex, after which the cycle repeats; the conduction delay is typically at the AV node.

second-degree atrioventricular block typ.definition: An atrioventricular conduction disorder in which atrial impulses are intermittently not conducted to the ventricles, producing dropped QRS complexes without preceding PR interval prolongation. Typically infranodal (below the AV node, in the His-Purkinje system) with a fixed conduction ratio (often 2:1 or 3:1), it can cause bradycardia and may progress to complete heart block, often requiring permanent pacemaker implantation.

mobitz type ii.definition: A second-degree atrioventricular (AV) block in which atrial impulses are intermittently not conducted to the ventricles without prior PR interval prolongation (dropped QRS complexes without a lengthening PR). Typically due to infranodal conduction disease, can have normal or wide QRS, and carries a high risk of progression to complete heart block often requiring pacemaker therapy.

junctional rhythm.definition: Originating from the atrioventricular (AV) node or proximal His bundle, typically as an escape rhythm when the SA node fails. It usually runs at 40–60 bpm with a narrow QRS complex; P waves are often absent or inverted (retrograde) and may appear before, during, or after the QRS.

premature atrial contractions.definition: An early heartbeat that originates from an atrial ectopic focus outside the SA node, occurring before the next expected beat; it usually has a premature, differently shaped P wave with a normal QRS complex and is typically followed by a noncompensatory pause. PACs are common and usually benign, though they can cause palpitations and may be related to stimulants, electrolyte disturbances, or underlying heart disease.

premature ventricular contractions.definition: A premature heartbeat originating in the ventricles that interrupts the regular rhythm, typically with a wide QRS complex and a compensatory pause; commonly benign but may indicate underlying cardiac disease if frequent or symptomatic.

ectopic pacemaker.definition: An area of heart tissue outside the sinoatrial (SA) node that spontaneously generates impulses, acting as an alternative cardiac pacemaker and potentially overriding the SA node to produce an ectopic rhythm (e.g., atrial or ventricular ectopy).

ectopic focus.definition: A site of cardiac tissue outside the sinoatrial node that autonomously generates electrical impulses, potentially initiating premature beats or other arrhythmias.

synchronized cardioversion.definition: A procedure that delivers a controlled electrical shock to the heart, synchronized to the QRS complex, to terminate a tachyarrhythmia and restore a normal sinus rhythm (using a defibrillator in synchronized mode; used for unstable SVT, atrial fibrillation/flutter with rapid rate, or VT with a pulse).

cardioversion.definition: The use of an electrical shock to stop an abnormal heart rhythm (an arrhythmia) and restore a normal one (sinus rhythm). Cardioversion can be external, using pads applied to the chest, or internal, from a pacemaker-like device called an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD).

adenosine.definition: An endogenous purine nucleoside formed by adenine linked to ribose; a component of ATP, ADP, and AMP, acting as a signaling molecule; pharmacologically used to acutely terminate certain paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardias by transient AV nodal blockade.

verapamil.definition: A calcium channel blocker (phenylalkylamine) used to treat hypertension, angina, and certain arrhythmias by inhibiting L-type calcium channels in cardiac and vascular smooth muscle, which reduces heart rate, slows AV nodal conduction, and decreases myocardial contractility.

nadolol.definition: A nonselective beta-adrenergic blocker (beta-1 and beta-2 antagonist) used to treat hypertension and angina; also used to prevent variceal bleeding in cirrhosis by lowering portal hypertension.

procainamide.definition: A class IA antiarrhythmic agent that blocks fast sodium channels, slowing conduction and prolonging the cardiac action potential and QT interval; used to treat atrial and ventricular tachyarrhythmias; adverse effects include hypotension, drug-induced lupus erythematosus with long-term use, and hematologic abnormalities.

bretylium.definition: A class III antiarrhythmic agent formerly used for intravenous treatment of refractory ventricular tachyarrhythmias; it prolongs the cardiac action potential by blocking potassium channels and inhibits norepinephrine release from sympathetic nerve terminals, with potential side effects including hypotension and bradycardia; now rarely used.

catecholamines.definition: Biologically active amines derived from the amino acid tyrosine; include dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine; function as neurotransmitters and hormones to regulate cardiovascular function, metabolism, and CNS activity.

nicotine.definition: Potent natural alkaloid found primarily in tobacco that acts as an agonist at neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the brain and autonomic ganglia, producing stimulant effects and reinforcement of drug-taking behavior; it is highly addictive.

hypovolemia.definition: Decreased intravascular (plasma) volume due to fluid loss or fluid shifting, resulting in reduced venous return to the heart and potential systemic hypoperfusion.

thyrotoxicosis.definition: The presence of too much thyroid hormone in the body. This may be caused by an overproductive thyroid, inflammation of the thyroid, or taking too much thyroid hormone.

mitral valve disease.definition: A spectrum of disorders affecting the heart's mitral valve, causing abnormal blood flow between the left atrium and left ventricle. The main subtypes are mitral regurgitation (backflow into the left atrium during systole) and mitral stenosis (narrowing that impedes flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle). Common etiologies include rheumatic heart disease, degenerative valve changes, infective endocarditis, and ischemic heart disease.

pulmonary embolism.definition: A sudden blockage of a pulmonary artery or its branches by a blood clot.

embolization.definition: A minimally invasive procedure in which an embolic agent is introduced into a blood vessel to occlude blood flow to a targeted area, used to stop bleeding or to cut off blood supply to a lesion such as a tumor.

coronary artery.definition: Blood vessel that carries oxygen-rich blood to the heart muscle.

lightheadedness.definition: A transient, non-rotational sensation of dizziness or wooziness, often described as feeling faint or like one might pass out; typically due to temporary reduction in cerebral perfusion or oxygen delivery, and may be caused by dehydration, hypovolemia, orthostatic hypotension, anemia, hypoglycemia, hyperventilation, medications, or vasovagal reactions.

cardiac fibrosis.definition: Excessive deposition of extracellular matrix proteins, especially collagen, in the heart tissue, causing stiffening of the myocardium and impaired diastolic filling; can be replacement fibrosis after cardiomyocyte death or diffuse interstitial fibrosis, potentially disrupting electrical conduction and contributing to heart failure and arrhythmias.

heart block.definition: A delay or complete interruption of electrical conduction from the atria to the ventricles through the AV node and surrounding pathways, producing bradycardia; it can be first-degree, second-degree (Mobitz I or II), or third-degree (complete) and may cause dizziness, syncope, or heart failure, with management ranging from observation to pacemaker depending on severity.

av bundle.definition: A collection of specialized conducting fibers in the heart that transmits electrical impulses from the atrioventricular node to the ventricles, traveling through the interventricular septum and dividing into the right and left bundle branches to coordinate ventricular contraction. Also known as the bundle of His.

left bundle branch.definition: A component of the heart's conduction system that runs within the left side of the interventricular septum and divides into the anterior and posterior fascicles to transmit electrical impulses from the His bundle to the left ventricle.

right bundle branch.definition: A component of the heart's conduction system that carries electrical impulses from the His bundle to the right ventricle, enabling rapid and coordinated activation of the right ventricular myocardium as it courses along the interventricular septum; disruption of this pathway can result in impaired right ventricular conduction.

cardiac conduction defect.definition: A disturbance of the heart's electrical conduction system that slows or blocks impulse transmission through the atrioventricular node, His-Purkinje system, or other pathways, potentially causing bradycardia or varying degrees of heart block; can be congenital or acquired.

glycosides.definition: A class of chemical compounds in which a sugar moiety is covalently linked to a non-sugar moiety (the aglycone) via a glycosidic bond; hydrolysis yields the sugar and the aglycone. They are common in plants and include cardiac glycosides and cyanogenic glycosides.

inamrinone.definition: A phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor with inotropic and vasodilatory effects used in acute decompensated heart failure to increase cardiac output by raising intracellular cAMP in cardiac myocytes, enhancing calcium influx and contractility while dilating vascular smooth muscle; adverse effects include arrhythmias, hypotension, and thrombocytopenia.

dobutamine.definition: A synthetic β1-adrenergic agonist given intravenously to increase myocardial contractility and cardiac output in acute heart failure, cardiogenic shock, or during dobutamine stress testing.

cardiogenic shock.definition: A life-threatening condition in which the heart’s pumping ability is so reduced that tissue perfusion is inadequate, causing sustained hypotension and signs of end-organ hypoperfusion (often due to severe left ventricular dysfunction from myocardial infarction or acute decompensated heart failure).

cardiac cycle.definition: An interval from the beginning of one heartbeat to the beginning of the next, comprising atrial systole, ventricular systole with ejection, and diastole (ventricular filling); it reflects the coordinated electrical and mechanical activity of the heart that changes chamber pressures and volumes.

depolarization.definition: Depolarization is a change in a cell's membrane potential toward a less negative value (toward zero or positive), usually caused by inward sodium (and sometimes calcium) currents; it brings the cell closer to the threshold for triggering an action potential.

hypertrophy.definition: An increase in the size of an organ or tissue caused by enlargement of its constituent cells, rather than by an increase in cell number; can be physiological (adaptive) or pathological.

heart murmur.definition: An abnormal sound heard during the heartbeat, produced by turbulent blood flow within the heart or great vessels, usually detected with a stethoscope; murmurs can be innocent (physiologic) or due to structural valve problems such as stenosis or regurgitation, and are described by timing (systolic or diastolic), intensity, pitch, and quality.

systolic murmur.definition: A heart murmur heard during the systolic phase of the cardiac cycle (from S1 to S2) caused by turbulent blood flow across a valve or great vessel; it can be an ejection (crescendo-decrescendo) murmur or holosystolic and may be benign or indicate valvular or structural heart disease.

diastolic murmur.definition: A heart murmur heard during the diastolic phase of the cardiac cycle (between S2 and the next S1); it can be early, mid, or late in diastole and is usually due to turbulent flow across the heart valves (e.g., aortic or pulmonic regurgitation, mitral or tricuspid stenosis, or high-flow states).

ectopic heartbeats.definition: A premature heartbeat arising from an ectopic focus outside the heart’s normal pacemaker (sinoatrial node). It may be atrial (PAC) or ventricular (PVC) in origin and often presents as a skipped or extra beat. In healthy people they are usually benign, but frequent or symptomatic ectopic beats can be associated with underlying heart disease, electrolyte disturbances, stimulant use, or ischemia and are typically evaluated with ECG.

pulse deficit.definition: The difference between the heart rate measured at the apex (auscultated) and the pulse rate felt at a peripheral site (usually the radial artery); a positive deficit indicates that some heartbeats do not produce a palpable peripheral pulse, often seen with arrhythmias like atrial fibrillation or reduced stroke volume.

pacing.definition: Delivery of timed electrical impulses to the heart to regulate heart rate and rhythm, usually via an implanted pacemaker or external electrical stimulator.

pericardial tamponade.definition: A life-threatening condition in which accumulation of fluid or blood in the pericardial sac increases intrapericardial pressure and compresses the heart, impairing diastolic filling and reducing cardiac output; commonly presents with hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure, muffled heart sounds, tachycardia, and may show pulsus paradoxus, requiring urgent pericardiocentesis or surgical drainage.

pericardial friction rub.definition: An abnormal high-pitched, scratching or grating sound heard on auscultation of the heart, caused by inflammation of the pericardial surfaces rubbing together (pericarditis). Best heard with the patient leaning forward, at the left lower sternal border, often during both systole and diastole, and may lessen or disappear when the patient holds their breath.

pulsus paradoxus.definition: An exaggerated drop in systolic blood pressure during inspiration (typically >10 mmHg), caused by increased intrathoracic pressure reducing venous return and left ventricular filling; classically seen in cardiac tamponade and also in severe asthma/COPD or constrictive pericarditis.

pericardial sac.definition: A double-walled fibroserous sac that encloses the heart and great vessels, consisting of an outer fibrous pericardium and an inner serous pericardium (parietal and visceral layers); the potential space between the serous layers, the pericardial cavity, contains a small amount of lubricating fluid and helps reduce friction, while anchoring the heart within the mediastinum.

left atrial pressure.definition: Pressure within the left atrium of the heart, representing left-sided preload and filling pressures; normally about 6–12 mmHg mean, with elevations indicating increased left-sided filling pressures from volume overload, diastolic dysfunction, or mitral valve disease; often estimated indirectly by pulmonary capillary wedge pressure or measured directly with invasive monitoring.

pulmonary wedge pressure.definition: A pressure measurement obtained by occluding a small branch of the pulmonary artery with a balloon-tipped catheter; it estimates left atrial pressure and left-sided preload. Normal values are about 6–12 mmHg; elevations indicate left-sided heart failure or volume overload, while low values suggest hypovolemia.

thallium-201.definition: A radiopharmaceutical used in nuclear cardiology for myocardial perfusion imaging; a potassium analogue taken up by viable myocardium via Na+/K+-ATPase, enabling assessment of regional blood flow and tissue viability with stress/rest imaging and redistribution over several hours.

gamma camera.definition: A nuclear medicine imaging device that detects gamma rays emitted by radiopharmaceuticals in the patient and converts them into electrical signals to create two-dimensional functional images; it typically uses a scintillation crystal (often NaI(Tl)) with photomultiplier tubes and a collimator.

positron camera.definition: A device used in positron emission tomography to detect coincident 511-keV gamma photons produced by positron annihilation, enabling reconstruction of metabolic activity by localizing the line of response between detector elements arranged around the patient.

rectilinear scanner.definition: A nuclear medicine imaging device that detects gamma radiation from radiopharmaceuticals using a flat, rectangular detector array that scans the patient in straight-line sweeps to form a two‑dimensional image of tracer distribution; largely obsolete today, having been supplanted by gamma cameras and SPECT.

radionuclide imaging.definition: A nuclear medicine imaging technique that uses radiopharmaceuticals administered to a patient to visualize and measure the function, perfusion, or metabolism of organs or tissues by detecting the radiation emitted from the tracer with gamma cameras, SPECT, or PET.

gated cardiac blood pool scan.definition: A nuclear medicine test (radionuclide ventriculography) using ECG-gated imaging of labeled red blood cells to quantify left ventricular systolic function, including ejection fraction and volumes, and to assess regional wall motion.

myocardial imaging.definition: Imaging of the heart muscle to assess perfusion, viability, and function, commonly performed with nuclear techniques (myocardial perfusion imaging using SPECT or PET) and sometimes MRI or CT.

myocardial perfusion.definition: The blood flow to the heart muscle (myocardium) through the coronary circulation, delivering oxygen and nutrients; it is commonly quantified as myocardial blood flow (ml/min/g) and assessed with perfusion imaging or stress testing.

stroke volume.definition: The amount of blood pumped out of the left ventricle with each heartbeat, usually expressed in milliliters per beat; calculated as end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume.

heart rate.definition: The number of heartbeats per minute, a basic measure of cardiovascular activity. Resting values in healthy adults are typically about 60–100 beats per minute and can vary with age, fitness, body position, and autonomic tone.

cardiac index.definition: An index of cardiac output adjusted for body surface area, expressed as liters per minute per square meter (L/min/m^2); it equals cardiac output divided by body surface area, with typical values about 2.5–4.0 L/min/m^2.

ventricles.definition: Plural of ventricle. In the heart, one of the two lower chambers that receives blood from the atria and pumps it to the arteries; in the brain, one of the interconnected cavities that produce and contain cerebrospinal fluid.

atria.definition: The upper chambers of the heart. There are two of these—the right atrium and the left atrium.

atrial contraction.definition: The active phase of atrial systole in which the atria contract to push a final bolus of blood into the ventricles through the mitral and tricuspid valves, contributing to ventricular filling just before ventricular systole.

ventricular contraction.definition: Phase of the cardiac cycle in which the ventricles contract (ventricular systole), generating high intraventricular pressure that opens the aortic and pulmonary valves and ejects blood into the aorta and pulmonary artery.

coronary artery perfusion.definition: Flow of blood through the coronary arteries to the myocardium, delivering oxygen and nutrients required for the heart muscle's metabolism.

einthoven's triangle.definition: An imaginary triangle on the body formed by the three limb electrode positions (right arm, left arm, left leg) used in standard ECG to define the limb leads; itunderpins Einthoven's law (Lead I + Lead III = Lead II).

cardiac reflex.definition: A reflex circuit that regulates heart rate and cardiac output in response to sensory input (such as changes in blood pressure or venous return) via autonomic pathways; key examples include the baroreceptor reflex and the Bainbridge reflex.

hepatic cirrhosis.definition: A chronic liver disease in which irreversible fibrosis and nodular regeneration distort liver architecture, leading to progressive loss of hepatic function and complications such as portal hypertension, ascites, and variceal bleeding.

infarction.definition: The process of tissue becoming injured or dying because there wasn't enough blood flowing there.

chest x-ray.definition: A radiographic imaging study of the chest obtained with ionizing radiation to evaluate the lungs, heart, and mediastinal structures; typically performed in PA or AP and lateral views to detect findings such as pneumonia, edema, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, or masses.

exercise stress test.definition: A cardiac evaluation in which the patient performs incremental physical activity (usually on a treadmill or stationary bike) while monitoring heart rate, blood pressure, ECG, and symptoms to detect ischemia or abnormal cardiac responses; often used to assess chest pain, functional capacity, and prognosis, and may include imaging (stress echocardiography or nuclear perfusion imaging) to improve diagnostic accuracy.

cardiac rehabilitation.definition: A structured, multidisciplinary program after a cardiovascular event or procedure that combines supervised exercise, education on heart-healthy lifestyle and risk-factor management, and psychosocial support to improve functional capacity and reduce recurrent cardiac events.

cardiac nerves.definition: Autonomic nerves supplying the heart, comprising sympathetic fibers that increase heart rate and contractility and parasympathetic (vagal) fibers that slow heart rate, forming the cardiac plexus around the heart.

cardiogram.definition: A graphic record of the heart's electrical activity obtained via electrocardiography (ECG/EKG), used to assess heart rate, rhythm, and conduction; it typically displays P waves, QRS complexes, and T waves.

cardiotonic.definition: A substance that increases the strength of the heart's contractions (positive inotropy), thereby increasing cardiac output; commonly used to support or treat heart failure or shock.

pericardial.definition: Relating to the pericardium, the double-walled sac that encloses the heart.

pericardiocentesis.definition: A procedure in which a needle or catheter is inserted into the pericardial sac to aspirate fluid, performed to relieve cardiac tamponade or to obtain pericardial fluid for diagnostic analysis.

tamponade.definition: An accumulation of fluid or other material in a closed space that compresses surrounding tissues or organs and impairs function. In the heart, it refers to fluid buildup in the pericardial sac that compresses the heart, limits ventricular filling, and reduces cardiac output.

ligation.definition: A surgical tying off or constricting of a vessel, duct, or other tubular structure to stop flow or passage; in molecular biology, the enzymatic joining of two DNA ends by a DNA ligase.

cardiography.definition: The recording and analysis of the heart's activity, most often by electrocardiography, producing a tracing of the heart's electrical activity (rhythm and conduction).

cardiovascular.definition: Having to do with your heart and blood vessels.

cardiospasm.definition: Spasm (hypertonicity) of the lower esophageal (cardiac) sphincter causing functional obstruction at the gastroesophageal junction and dysphagia; an older term often used for esophageal achalasia.

cardioplegia.definition: Temporarily stopping the heart during heart surgery.

cardioprotectant.definition: A substance or intervention that reduces myocardial injury during ischemia and reperfusion or other cardiac stress, thereby protecting heart tissue and preserving cardiac function.

resuscitation.definition: The process of reviving a person who is not breathing or whose heart is not beating using techniques such as artificial respiration and heart massage.

cardioangiography.definition: A radiographic imaging technique in which an iodinated contrast agent is injected into the heart or its vessels to visualize the cardiac chambers and coronary arteries, allowing assessment of anatomy and blood flow for diagnosing heart disease or congenital abnormalities.

cardiobacterium.definition: A genus of fastidious, Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacteria in the HACEK group; members are part of normal oropharyngeal flora and are a known cause of subacute endocarditis, particularly in individuals with preexisting cardiac conditions.

esophagogastroplasty.definition: A surgical procedure to repair or reconstruct the esophagus and stomach, typically to restore continuity of the alimentary tract or to reshape/create a connection between the esophagus and stomach.

regurgitation.definition: When something, like blood or food, leaks back through a valve in the wrong direction.

cardiotachometer.definition: A device that measures heart rate, typically used in physiological or clinical contexts to quantify the tempo of the heartbeat.

tachometer.definition: An instrument that measures the rotational speed of a shaft or engine, typically displayed as revolutions per minute (RPM).

cardiothoracic.definition: Relating to the heart and the thoracic (chest) cavity; pertaining to the heart and other structures in the chest.

precordium.definition: The part of the chest wall that overlies the heart; the anterior region of the thorax where cardiac activity is palpated or auscultated.

cardiasthenia.definition: Weakness or reduced tone of the cardia (lower esophageal sphincter) at the gastroesophageal junction, which can contribute to gastroesophageal reflux and related esophageal symptoms.

hernia.definition: A protrusion of an organ or tissue through an abnormal opening or weakened area in the wall that normally contains it, most often abdominal contents through the inguinal or umbilical regions; hernias can be reducible, incarcerated, or strangulated.

hiatal.definition: Relating to the diaphragmatic hiatus—the opening in the diaphragm through which the esophagus passes.

engagement.definition: In obstetrics, the fetal presenting part passes through the pelvic inlet into the true pelvis, usually when the widest diameter of the part (often the biparietal diameter) crosses the pelvic brim; this marks the fetus's descent into the pelvis and readiness for labor.

descent.definition: The downward movement or migration of a body part from its normal position; in anatomy, the process by which an organ or structure descends to its usual location (for example, the normal descent of the testes from the abdomen into the scrotum during development).

expulsion.definition: The act of forcing out or discharging contents from a body cavity or organ; in obstetrics, the birth (delivery) of a fetus and, often, the placenta.

anteroposterior.definition: Relating to or directed from the front (anterior) to the back (posterior) of the body; along the anterior-posterior axis.

heart sounds.definition: Sounds produced by the beating heart heard with a stethoscope; the normal sequence includes S1 (closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the start of systole) and S2 (closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the end of systole), with possible additional sounds such as S3 or S4 in certain conditions.

murmurs.definition: An abnormal sound heard during auscultation of the heart caused by turbulent blood flow through the heart or great vessels, often due to valvular disease or other hemodynamic disturbances; typically categorized as systolic, diastolic, or continuous, and as innocent (benign) or pathologic.

breath sounds.definition: Audible respiratory noises heard with a stethoscope during chest auscultation, reflecting airflow through the airways and lung tissue; normal sounds are vesicular, while abnormal findings include crackles, wheezes, rhonchi, and pleural friction rub.

rubs.definition: High-pitched, scratchy auscultatory sounds produced when inflamed serous membranes (such as the pericardium or pleura) slide against each other during respiration or the cardiac cycle; they indicate serous membrane inflammation, most commonly pericarditis or pleuritis.

capillary refill time.definition: Capillary refill time is the time required for color to return to a blanched capillary bed (typically a fingernail bed) after firm pressure is applied. It is a quick bedside measure of peripheral perfusion; normal is usually under 2 seconds (often up to 3 seconds in infants); prolongation suggests reduced perfusion from dehydration, shock, hypothermia, or vasoconstriction.

turgor.definition: Pressure of the fluid contents inside a cell against the cell wall, giving plant cells rigidity. Clinically, it also refers to the skin's elasticity and fullness, assessed by pinching to gauge hydration.

lesions.definition: A localized area of tissue alteration or damage resulting from disease, injury, infection, or other pathology; any focal abnormality in tissue structure or function, such as a wound, ulcer, nodule, scar, or tumor.

level of consciousness.definition: Clinical measure of a patient’s arousal and awareness, ranging from full alertness to coma; assessed by responsiveness to stimuli and orientation to person, place, and time, often using scales such as AVPU or the Glasgow Coma Scale.

reflexes.definition: An involuntary, automatic response to a stimulus, mediated by a reflex arc that connects a sensory receptor to an effector (often a muscle or gland) without conscious brain input.

neurological signs.definition: Objective findings on neurological examination indicating abnormal nervous system function; examples include motor weakness, sensory loss, abnormal reflexes, cranial nerve deficits, and ataxia.

occlusive vascular disease.definition: A condition characterized by narrowing or blockage of arteries, leading to reduced blood flow and tissue ischemia; most often due to atherosclerosis with possible contributions from thrombosis or embolism.

lung disorders.definition: Lung disorders are diseases or conditions that affect the lungs’ structure or function, causing impaired gas exchange or airflow. They may involve the airways (e.g., asthma, COPD), the lung parenchyma (e.g., pneumonia, interstitial lung disease), the pleura (e.g., pleural effusion, pneumothorax), or the pulmonary vasculature (e.g., pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension); they can be acute or chronic and commonly present with cough, shortness of breath, wheeze, or chest pain.

kidney disorders.definition: A broad category of diseases that affect kidney structure or function, impairing filtration of waste, regulation of fluid and electrolyte balance, and maintenance of acid-base homeostasis; includes acute and chronic kidney injury, glomerular and tubular diseases, kidney stones, infections, and congenital disorders.

antihypertensives.definition: Medications used to lower and control high blood pressure.

coronary arteriogram.definition: A radiographic image of the coronary arteries obtained after injection of iodinated contrast dye through a catheter, used to evaluate for abnormalities such as stenosis or occlusion (coronary artery disease) and to guide treatment.

arterial wedge pressure.definition: A measurement used to estimate left atrial pressure by wedging a balloon-tipped catheter in a branch of the pulmonary artery; known as the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP).

clotting profiles.definition: An evaluation comprising multiple coagulation tests used to assess the blood’s ability to form clots. It typically includes prothrombin time (PT) with INR, activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), fibrinogen level, and platelet count, with additional tests such as thrombin time, D-dimer, and specific factor assays as needed. It helps diagnose bleeding or clotting disorders, monitor anticoagulant therapy, and screen for coagulopathies; reference ranges vary by laboratory method.

serum cholesterol.definition: Cholesterol content in the blood serum, carried by lipoproteins and used as a biomarker of cardiovascular risk; typically reported as total cholesterol and by fractions such as LDL-C and HDL-C.

triglycerides.definition: The most common type of fat in your body. If you have a high level, it can increase the chance that you will develop heart diseases.

lactic acid dehydrogenase.definition: Una enzima que cataliza la conversión reversible entre piruvato y lactato, facilitando la regeneración de NAD+ a partir de NADH durante la glucólisis cuando la oxigenación es limitada. Existen cinco isoenzimas con distribución tisular específica (predominantemente en corazón, músculo, hígado y eritrocitos); la elevación de sus niveles en sangre es un marcador inespecífico de daño tisular.

electrocardiographic tracings.definition: The graphic recording of the heart's electrical activity produced by an electrocardiograph, showing deflections corresponding to atrial depolarization (P wave), ventricular depolarization (QRS complex), and ventricular repolarization (T wave); used to evaluate heart rhythm, rate, conduction intervals, and evidence of ischemia or infarction.

medications.definition: A substance or preparation used to diagnose, treat, cure, prevent, or alleviate symptoms of disease; typically a pharmacologic agent administered to patients.

cardiovascular reflex.definition: A physiologic autonomic reflex that helps regulate cardiovascular function—altering heart rate, contractility, and vascular tone—in response to sensory input such as changes in arterial pressure or blood gas levels; the baroreceptor reflex is the classic example.

cardiovascular shunt.definition: An abnormal or physiologic conduit that diverts blood from the arterial to the venous circulation, bypassing the normal capillary beds; it can be congenital (e.g., intracardiac septal defects causing left-to-right or right-to-left shunts) or acquired (e.g., arteriovenous fistulas), and may alter oxygenation and cardiac workload depending on the direction and magnitude of flow.

cardiovascular system.definition: A system comprising the heart and a closed network of blood vessels (arteries, veins, and capillaries) that circulates blood throughout the body, delivering oxygen and nutrients to tissues and removing carbon dioxide and other wastes; it also helps regulate blood pressure and systemic circulation.

cardiovascular technologist.definition: A healthcare professional who performs cardiovascular diagnostic tests and imaging and assists with procedures in the cardiac catheterization laboratory, including echocardiography, electrocardiography, and vascular studies, under physician supervision.

sinus rhythm.definition: The heart's normal rate and rhythm.

carditis.definition: Inflammation of the heart, which may affect any cardiac structure—most commonly the myocardium (myocarditis), the pericardium (pericarditis), or the endocardium/valves (endocarditis).

cardizem.definition: A brand-name calcium channel blocker (benzothiazepine) that inhibits L-type calcium channels, slowing AV nodal conduction and reducing myocardial contractility; used to treat hypertension, chronic stable angina, vasospastic angina, and to control ventricular rate in certain supraventricular tachyarrhythmias.

calcium channel blocker.definition: A drug that inhibits voltage-gated calcium channels in cardiac and smooth muscle, reducing calcium influx; leading to vasodilation, decreased myocardial contractility, and slowed conduction in the heart; used to treat hypertension, angina, and some arrhythmias.

meprobamate.definition: A carbamate derivative with anxiolytic and sedative properties; it acts as a central nervous system depressant by enhancing GABAergic transmission to reduce anxiety and tension.

carina.definition: A keel-shaped ridge at the bifurcation of the trachea into the right and left main bronchi; an anatomical landmark that is highly sensitive to irritants, often provoking coughing.

carinae.definition: A keel-shaped ridge of cartilage at the lower end of the trachea where it bifurcates into the right and left main bronchi; a sensitive area that triggers coughing when irritated.

caroticotympanic canaliculi.definition: Small bony passages in the petrous temporal bone that connect the carotid canal to the tympanic cavity, transmitting the caroticotympanic arteries (branches of the internal carotid) and accompanying sympathetic fibers to the middle ear.

caroticotympanic nerves.definition: Small postganglionic sympathetic nerves from the internal carotid plexus that enter the tympanic cavity via the tympanic canal and join the tympanic plexus, supplying the mucosa and blood vessels of the middle ear.

carotid body tumor.definition: A paraganglioma (glomus tumor) arising from the carotid body at the bifurcation of the common carotid artery; a usually benign, highly vascular tumor of chemoreceptor (paraganglionic) cells, presenting as a slow-growing, painless lateral neck mass and may cause pulsation, bruit, or cranial nerve symptoms if enlarged. Imaging typically shows splaying of the internal and external carotid arteries.

carotid bruit.definition: An abnormal sound heard with a stethoscope over the carotid artery, indicating turbulent blood flow and an increased risk of stroke.

carotid artery.definition: One of two major blood vessels found on either side of the neck. The carotid arteries supply blood to the brain.

carotid artery duplex scanning.definition: A noninvasive imaging test that uses duplex ultrasonography (B-mode imaging with Doppler) to visualize the carotid arteries and evaluate blood flow, used to detect atherosclerotic plaque and quantify carotid stenosis.

carotid arch.definition: In embryology, the carotid arch (the third aortic arch) is a pharyngeal arch artery that forms the common carotid arteries and the proximal portions of the internal carotid arteries.

carotenoid.definition: A class of fat-soluble pigments found in plants and some microorganisms; they are tetraterpenoid compounds with conjugated double bonds that give red, orange, and yellow colors, function as antioxidants, and in animals can be converted to vitamin A. They are subdivided into hydrocarbon carotene types and oxygen-containing derivatives (xanthophylls).

carotenemia.definition: Benign condition marked by yellow-orange skin discoloration due to elevated serum carotene from excessive intake of carotene-rich foods; sclerae are normal and liver function is not affected.

carotene.definition: A hydrocarbon pigment of the carotenoid family found in plants and some animals; a provitamin A carotenoid that the body converts to retinol (vitamin A).

carminative.definition: An herb said to expel gas from the digestive system, easing stomach discomfort.

carisoprodol.definition: A centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant prescribed for short-term relief of acute musculoskeletal pain and muscle spasms; it is a prodrug of meprobamate and has sedative effects.

bcnu.definition: A nitrosourea-class alkylating chemotherapy agent used to treat brain tumors and some lymphomas; it crosses the blood-brain barrier and alkylates DNA, causing cross-linking and cancer cell death.

carnitine.definition: A naturally occurring zwitterionic quaternary ammonium compound that acts as a key carrier of long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria for beta-oxidation, enabling fatty acid metabolism; synthesized in the liver and kidney from lysine and methionine and obtained in the diet (notably red meat and dairy).

carnitine palmitoyltransferase deficienc.definition: A group of inherited metabolic disorders caused by deficiency of the carnitine palmitoyltransferase enzymes (CPT1 or CPT2) that transport long‑chain fatty acids into mitochondria for beta‑oxidation, leading to impaired fatty acid oxidation and episodes of hypoketotic hypoglycemia, hepatopathy, myopathy, or cardiomyopathy depending on the enzyme affected.

carnitine palmityltransferase deficiency.definition: A genetic disorder of mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation caused by defective activity of the carnitine palmitoyltransferase enzymes (CPT I or CPT II) that transport long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria for beta-oxidation; impaired transport reduces fat-derived energy production, with CPT I deficiency typically presenting as hypoketotic hypoglycemia and liver disease, and CPT II deficiency presenting as exercise-induced myopathy and rhabdomyolysis.

levocarnitine.definition: A naturally occurring enantiomer of carnitine (the active form, L-carnitine) that participates in mitochondrial beta-oxidation by transporting long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondrial matrix; used clinically as a supplement to treat primary or secondary carnitine deficiency and certain metabolic disorders.

carnitor.definition: A brand-name form of L-carnitine, a quaternary ammonium compound that facilitates transport of long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria for beta-oxidation; used as a dietary supplement or therapeutic agent in carnitine deficiency and certain metabolic disorders.

carnosine.definition: A dipeptide consisting of beta-alanine and histidine linked by a peptide bond; abundant in skeletal muscle and brain; functions as an intracellular pH buffer and antioxidant.

carnosinemia.definition: A rare inherited metabolic disorder characterized by elevated levels of the dipeptide carnosine in blood (and often urine) due to deficient activity of serum carnosinase (CNDP1), typically caused by CNDP1 gene mutations.

carob.definition: Edible pods of a Mediterranean legume tree; when roasted and ground, they are used as a caffeine-free cocoa substitute and provide dietary fiber and polyphenols.

c-arm.definition: An imaging device used in radiology and surgery that combines an X-ray source and an image receptor mounted on a curved, C-shaped frame; enables real-time fluoroscopic imaging from multiple angles to guide procedures such as implant placement or bone realignment.

carotid duplex scanning.definition: A noninvasive ultrasound test that combines B-mode imaging and Doppler flow assessment to evaluate the carotid arteries for plaque, stenosis, and flow abnormalities, helping assess stroke risk.

carpal tunnel syndrome.definition: Injury to a nerve in your wrist that happens when you do the same motion over and over again.

auscultation for carotid bruits.definition: A physical examination technique in which a clinician places a stethoscope over the carotid arteries in the neck to listen for bruits—abnormal, turbulent blood-flow sounds that may indicate carotid artery stenosis or atherosclerotic disease.

carotid bruits.definition: An abnormal, often whooshing sound heard over the carotid artery during auscultation with a stethoscope, indicating turbulent blood flow usually due to carotid artery stenosis (atherosclerosis).

extracranial carotid artery.definition: Portions of the carotid arterial system located in the neck outside the cranial cavity, comprising the common carotid arteries and the extracranial segments of the internal and external carotid arteries; these vessels supply the head and neck and give rise to branches that perfuse the brain and facial structures.

occlusive disease.definition: A condition in which a vessel or duct becomes blocked (occluded), typically due to atherosclerotic plaque, thrombosis, or embolism, resulting in reduced or absent blood flow (ischemia) to the affected tissue.

speech defect.definition: An abnormality of speech production or fluency that reduces intelligibility, encompassing articulation disorders, stuttering (fluency disorder), dysarthria, and apraxia of speech.

visual defect.definition: An impairment of vision due to disease or abnormality of the eye, optic nerve, or visual pathways, resulting in reduced visual acuity, visual field loss, or other visual dysfunction.

carotid endarterectomy.definition: Surgery to remove fatty plaque buildup from the carotid artery and restore blood flow to the brain.

tunica media.definition: The middle layer of a blood vessel wall, consisting primarily of smooth muscle cells with elastic fibers; it regulates vessel diameter via vasoconstriction and vasodilation, contributing to blood pressure and flow (thicker in arteries, thinner in veins).

carotid plexus.definition: A network of postganglionic sympathetic fibers surrounding the internal and external carotid arteries in the head and neck, derived from the superior cervical ganglion; it supplies vasomotor innervation to head vessels and perivascular structures, including facial sweat glands.

common carotid plexus.definition: A periarterial sympathetic nerve plexus surrounding the common carotid artery, formed by postganglionic sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion; it accompanies the artery and gives rise to the internal and external carotid nerve plexuses, regulating vascular tone in the head and neck.

external carotid plexus.definition: A periarterial network of postganglionic sympathetic fibers surrounding the external carotid artery and its branches, derived from the superior cervical ganglion, providing vasomotor (and glandular) sympathetic innervation to the head and neck structures such as facial vessels and salivary/sweat glands.

internal carotid plexus.definition: A periarterial sympathetic nerve plexus surrounding the internal carotid artery as it traverses the skull, formed by postganglionic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion; it accompanies the artery, provides vasomotor innervation to its branches, and contributes sympathetic fibers to the deep petrosal nerve (nerve of the pterygoid canal).

carotid pulse.definition: The pulse felt over the carotid artery in the neck, produced by the surge of blood with each left-ventricular systole; used to assess heart rate, rhythm, and perfusion to the brain.

carotid sheath.definition: A fascial sleeve of the deep cervical fascia in the neck that surrounds the common carotid artery (and its internal carotid segment), the internal jugular vein, and the vagus nerve, along with accompanying sympathetic fibers and lymphatics; it extends from the base of the skull to the superior mediastinum.

carotid sinus massage.definition: A bedside procedure in which gentle, one-sided pressure is applied to the carotid sinus to stimulate baroreceptors, causing reflex bradycardia and slowed AV nodal conduction; used to terminate certain paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardias and to evaluate carotid sinus hypersensitivity; performed with monitoring and with contraindications including carotid bruit, known carotid stenosis, recent stroke or TIA, or neck trauma.

carotid sinus reflex.definition: A baroreceptor reflex originating from carotid sinus stretch receptors that maintains short-term blood pressure by adjusting heart rate and vascular tone in response to arterial pressure changes; afferent signals travel via CN IX to the medulla, and efferent output via CN X and sympathetic pathways modulates heart rate and vessel tone (decreasing HR and causing vasodilation when BP rises).

carotid sinus syndrome.definition: A condition in which carotid sinus stimulation elicits an exaggerated baroreceptor response causing bradycardia and/or hypotension, leading to syncope or near-syncope.

carotidynia.definition: A unilateral, self-limited pain syndrome involving the carotid artery region, presenting with tenderness over the carotid bifurcation and ipsilateral head or neck pain; symptoms usually last hours to days and vascular imaging is typically noncontributory.

carpal.definition: Relating to the carpus, the set of eight small bones that form the wrist.

carpo.definition: A combining form meaning wrist or carpus; used in anatomical terms to denote the wrist region (e.g., carpometacarpal, carpopedal).

archicarp.definition: Not a recognized medical term in standard dictionaries. If you meant a botanical term or a different spelling (e.g., an archaic/carpect-related term), please provide context.

pericarp.definition: The part of a fruit that develops from the wall of the ovary and surrounds the seed, often subdivided into exocarp (outer skin), mesocarp (flesh), and endocarp (inner layer).

carpus.definition: The set of eight small bones that form the wrist, arranged in two rows, connecting the forearm to the hand (proximal row: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform; distal row: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate).

radiocarpal.definition: Relating to the radius and the carpal bones; the radiocarpal joint is the wrist joint formed by the articulation of the distal radius with the proximal row of carpal bones (primarily the scaphoid and lunate, with the triquetrum variably involved).

carpal arch.definition: An arch formed by the carpal bones across the wrist (the transverse carpal arch), creating a curved, concave palmar surface and reinforced by the flexor retinaculum, contributing to the roof of the carpal tunnel.

triquetrum.definition: A small, triangular carpal bone in the proximal row of the wrist on the ulnar side, located between the lunate and pisiform; it articulates with the lunate, pisiform, and distally with the hamate and capitate.

pisiform.definition: A small pea-shaped carpal bone in the proximal row; a sesamoid bone within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon that articulates with the triquetrum and increases the tendon's mechanical advantage.

trapezium.definition: A small, irregular carpal bone on the radial (thumb) side of the wrist, located in the distal carpal row. It articulates with the scaphoid proximally, with the trapezoid medially, and with the base of the first metacarpal distally, forming the saddle-shaped first carpometacarpal joint that enables thumb movement.

trapezoid.definition: A small carpal bone of the distal row in the wrist (os trapezoideum), located between the trapezium and capitate, and articulating with the base of the second metacarpal.

hamate.definition: A carpal bone of the wrist; wedge-shaped and located in the distal row on the ulnar side, with a hook-like projection (hamulus) on its palmar surface, and it articulates with the capitate and the bases of the 4th and 5th metacarpals.

wrist.definition: The joint between the distal radius (and ulna via the articular disc) and the carpal bones of the hand; the radiocarpal and midcarpal joints permit movements such as flexion, extension, and radial and ulnar deviation.

dorsal ligament.definition: A ligament located on the posterior (dorsal) aspect of a joint, connecting bones to stabilize the joint and limit excessive movement.

radiate ligament.definition: A ligament whose fibers radiate outward from a single central attachment to encircle or anchor the surrounding bone or joint capsule, forming a fan- or spoke-like arrangement that helps distribute tension and stabilize the joint.

transverse ligament.definition: Do you mean the transverse ligament of the atlas (a stabilizing band of the cruciform ligament in the neck) or the transverse carpal ligament (flexor retinaculum of the wrist)?

volar ligament.definition: A ligament on the volar (palmar) aspect of a joint that binds adjacent bones and provides anterior stability, helping to prevent hyperextension and guide joint motion (as seen in the wrist and hand).

flexor retinaculum.definition: A thick fibrous band spanning the palmar aspect of the wrist, forming the roof of the carpal tunnel and retaining the flexor tendons (and the median nerve) within the tunnel.

flexor digitorum profundus.definition: A deep forearm flexor muscle that flexes the distal phalanges of digits 2–5, primarily at the distal interphalangeal joints; it arises from the anterior ulna and interosseous membrane and inserts on the distal phalanges, with innervation from the median nerve (anterior interosseous branch) for digits 2–3 and the ulnar nerve for digits 4–5.

flexor digitorum superficialis.definition: A muscle of the superficial flexor group in the forearm; it splits into four tendons inserting on the sides of the middle phalanges of digits 2–5, and it flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints (with additional flexion at the metacarpophalangeal joints and wrist). Innervation is by the median nerve.

flexor pollicis longus.definition: A forearm muscle in the deep anterior compartment that flexes the distal phalanx of the thumb; originates from the radius and interosseous membrane and inserts on the distal phalanx of the thumb, enabling flexion of the thumb's interphalangeal joint and aiding flexion at the MCP and carpometacarpal joints. Innervated by the anterior interosseous nerve (a branch of the median nerve).

carpal tunnel release.definition: A surgical procedure to relieve pressure on the median nerve at the wrist by cutting the transverse carpal ligament, thereby decompressing the carpal tunnel; commonly performed as open or endoscopic release.

volar carpal ligament.definition: A fibrous band on the volar (palmar) aspect of the wrist that spans and connects the carpal bones, forming part of the wrist's palmar ligaments and helping stabilize the radiocarpal joint.

carpenter’s syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal recessive congenital disorder (acrocephalopolysyndactyly type II) caused by mutations in RAB23, characterized by craniosynostosis with acrocephaly, polysyndactyly of the hands and feet (often with syndactyly), brachydactyly, and distinctive facial features; may be associated with other congenital anomalies.

acrocephalopolysyndactyly.definition: A congenital craniofacial-skeletal syndrome characterized by craniosynostosis with acrocephaly and syndactyly of the hands and feet (often polysyndactyly), most commonly due to GLI3 mutations (Greig cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome) and typically inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.

noack’s syndrome.definition: I can’t find a reliable definition for Noack’s syndrome in standard medical references. It may be a misspelling or a term used in a specific subfield. Could you share the context (specialty, source, or where you encountered the term) or confirm the spelling? I’ll define it once I have that.

sakati-nyhan syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder described by Sakati and Nyhan, characterized by congenital hypoparathyroidism with hypocalcemia in infancy, along with growth retardation and developmental delay (intellectual disability), often with distinctive facial/dysmorphic features.

goodman’s syndrome.definition: Not a widely recognized medical condition in standard references; it may be a misspelling or confusion with a well-known autoimmune disorder characterized by antibodies against the glomerular basement membrane, leading to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage.

carpometacarpal joint.definition: A set of joints between the distal carpal bones and the bases of the metacarpal bones; the thumb joint is a saddle articulation between the trapezium and the first metacarpal, while the 2nd–5th joints are plane joints that permit limited gliding and contribute to hand grasp and finger movement.

distal carpal row.definition: The distal carpal row is the four bones at the distal end of the carpus—trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and hamate—that form the distal row of wrist bones and articulate with the bases of the 2nd–5th metacarpals and with the proximal row of carpal bones.

metacarpals.definition: The bones in the middle of the hand, where the palm is.

carpopedal.definition: Relating to the carpus (wrist) and the foot (pedal); used to describe anatomical features or conditions affecting the wrists and feet, notably carpopedal spasm.

carpopedal spasm.definition: A painful, involuntary contraction of the muscles of the hands and feet (tetany), usually due to hypocalcemia or other disturbances of calcium homeostasis; may be accompanied by paresthesias and a positive Trousseau sign.

tetany.definition: A clinical syndrome of neuromuscular irritability causing intermittent muscle cramps and spasms (often with numbness/tingling and carpopedal spasm), typically due to low ionized calcium (hypocalcemia) or other electrolyte/acid–base disturbances such as hypomagnesemia or alkalosis.

carrel-lindbergh pump.definition: An early external pulsatile blood pump used to provide temporary circulatory support in experimental heart surgery and early extracorporeal bypass circuits; developed by Alexis Carrel and Charles Lindbergh, typically driven pneumatically.

lindbergh pump.definition: Not a standard medical term; no widely accepted definition in current medical references. If you have context or alternative spelling, I can help refine.

carrión’s disease.definition: A vector-borne infection caused by Bartonella bacilliformis transmitted by sandflies in the Andean region of South America; it classically has two phases: Oroya fever (acute febrile illness with bacteremia and severe hemolytic anemia) and verruga peruana (chronic angioproliferative skin lesions).

carroll quantitative test of upper extre.word: carroll quantitative test of upper extremity function
carroll quantitative test of upper extre.definition: A standardized, objective scoring system that quantifies upper-extremity motor function through a series of timed and/or scored tasks, measuring strength, coordination, and dexterity to yield numerical scores for assessing impairment and recovery.

upper extremity function.definition: The ability of the upper limb (shoulder girdle through hand) to perform coordinated motor tasks, including gross movements (reaching, lifting, rotating) and fine motor skills (grasping and manipulating objects), supported by sensory perception and neuromotor control.

carrying angle.definition: The angle formed between the humerus and ulna at full elbow extension, reflecting the forearm’s natural valgus alignment relative to the upper arm; typically about 5–15 degrees in adults (varies by sex), with larger values called cubitus valgus and smaller values cubitus varus.

carteolol.definition: A nonselective beta-adrenergic blocker used as an ophthalmic drop to lower intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension; it has intrinsic sympathomimetic activity.

carteolol hydrochloride.definition: An ophthalmic nonselective beta-adrenergic antagonist with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity that reduces intraocular pressure by decreasing aqueous humor formation; used to treat open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension.

carvedilol.definition: An oral, nonselective beta-adrenergic blocker with alpha-1–blocking (vasodilatory) activity used to treat hypertension and heart failure; it reduces heart rate, blood pressure, and afterload.

alpha-/beta-adrenergic blocker.definition: A drug that nonselectively blocks both alpha-adrenergic and beta-adrenergic receptors, reducing sympathetic stimulation of the heart and vasculature; used to treat hypertension and certain cardiovascular conditions (e.g., labetalol, carvedilol).

cartilage.definition: The smooth covering on the end of your bones.

cartilage graft.definition: A graft consisting of cartilage tissue transplanted from one site to another to replace or augment damaged or missing cartilage; most commonly autologous (from the patient) such as septal, auricular, or costal cartilage, and used to provide structural support and contour in reconstructive procedures.

cartilage-hair hypoplasia.definition: A rare autosomal recessive skeletal dysplasia characterized by metaphyseal chondrodysplasia with disproportionate short stature and sparse hair (hypotrichosis), often accompanied by cellular and humoral immunodeficiency that increases susceptibility to infections and certain malignancies; caused by biallelic mutations in the RMRP gene.

cartilaginous skeleton.definition: A skeleton composed primarily of cartilage rather than bone; in development, the fetal vertebrate skeleton is initially cartilaginous and is later replaced by bone through endochondral ossification.

cartos.definition: Not found as a standard medical term in trusted dictionaries. Could you share context (area of medicine, disease, or procedure) or check the spelling? It might be a brand name/acronym used in a specific specialty (e.g., a mapping system in cardiology) or a typo of another term related to cartilage or anatomy. If you provide a bit more context, I can give a precise definition.

caruncle.definition: A small, fleshy eminence or projection on a mucocutaneous surface; for example, the lacrimal caruncle is a small pink mass at the inner corner of the eye, containing skin, glands (sebaceous and sweat), and conjunctival tissue.

caruncula hymenales.definition: Small, fleshy mucosal projections on the vaginal vestibule at or near the hymen, representing residual hymenal tissue; a benign, usually asymptomatic variation that may be single or multiple and can bleed if irritated.

hymenal tag.definition: A small, benign projection of hymenal tissue at the hymenal rim (a mucosal tag) representing a normal anatomic variant; typically asymptomatic and not indicative of sexual activity.

hymen.definition: Thin mucous membrane that partially covers the vaginal opening and typically has a small opening to allow menstrual flow. It varies widely in size, thickness, and perforation; it may be present or absent and is not a reliable indicator of sexual activity.

caseous necrosis.definition: A form of tissue necrosis in which dead cells are degraded to a soft, white, cheese-like material; it features granular, amorphous eosinophilic debris surrounded by a granulomatous inflammatory response, most commonly associated with tuberculosis and certain fungal infections.

caseation.definition: A type of tissue necrosis in which the dead tissue has a soft, white, cheese-like (caseous) appearance, typically seen in granulomatous inflammation such as tuberculosis; the center is acellular and eosinophilic, surrounded by macrophages (epithelioid cells) and lymphocytes.

caseous abscess.definition: A tuberculous-related abscess in which the pus contains caseous (cheese-like) necrotic material produced by granulomatous inflammation; the cavity is typically surrounded by granulomatous tissue and often encapsulated by fibrous tissue.

case fatality rate.definition: The proportion of individuals diagnosed with a disease who die from it within a defined time period, usually expressed as a percentage; calculated as (deaths due to the disease / diagnosed cases) × 100.

case finding.definition: The identification of individuals with a disease who have not yet been diagnosed, typically through targeted testing or evaluation prompted by symptoms, risk factors, or exposure, rather than routine screening of an asymptomatic population.

case history.definition: A detailed narrative of a patient’s health background and current problem, obtained by history taking, including present illness, past medical and surgical history, medications and allergies, and family and social history, to guide diagnosis and management.

case management.definition: Someone who helps people who are sick to get the help they need.

crohn’s disease.definition: Chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by long-lasting inflammation of the digestive tract, usually transmural and segmental, most often involving the terminal ileum and colon.

gallstones.definition: Formed when the fluid that helps to digest fat hardens. When the stones block the flow of bile, it can be very painful.

castration.definition: Surgical removal of the gonads (most commonly the testes in males), resulting in sterilization and loss of gonadal hormone production.

bicalutamide.definition: A non-steroidal antiandrogen (androgen receptor antagonist) used in the treatment of prostate cancer; it blocks androgen actions by inhibiting the androgen receptor.

castleman disease.definition: A rare lymphoproliferative disorder characterized by noncancerous growth of lymphoid tissue with distinctive histology (hyaline-vascular or plasma-cell type). It exists in a localized unicentric form, usually curable by surgical excision, and a systemic multicentric form associated with inflammatory symptoms and HHV-8 infection (often with elevated IL-6) that requires systemic therapy.

castor oil.definition: A vegetable oil extracted from the seeds of the castor bean (Ricinus communis), composed mainly of triglycerides of ricinoleic acid; used medically as a stimulant laxative and, topically, as an emollient in cosmetics. Ingestion can cause abdominal cramping and diarrhea.

clonidine.definition: A centrally acting α2-adrenergic agonist that reduces sympathetic outflow from the CNS, lowering blood pressure; also used for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) management in some regimens and to alleviate opioid withdrawal symptoms. Common adverse effects include sedation, bradycardia, dry mouth, and rebound hypertension if withdrawn abruptly.

intraocular lens.definition: An artificial lens implanted inside the eye to replace the natural crystalline lens, typically after cataract extraction, to restore focusing and vision (usually placed in the posterior chamber behind the iris).

extracapsular.definition: Outside the capsule; located or occurring beyond the capsule that surrounds a structure. In ophthalmology, extracapsular cataract extraction is a technique in which the lens contents are removed while the posterior capsule is left intact.

retrobulbar anesthesia.definition: An ocular regional anesthesia in which local anesthetic is injected into the retrobulbar space behind the eyeball to produce anesthesia and akinesia of the eye for ocular surgery.

mydriatic.definition: A type of drug that widens the pupil.

ophthalmia.definition: An inflammation of the eye, especially the conjunctiva; commonly referred to as conjunctivitis.

catarrh.definition: Inflammation of a mucous membrane, especially in the nose or throat, with excessive mucus production and discharge.

catatonia.definition: Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome defined by prominent abnormalities of motor behavior and responsiveness, including stupor or agitation, mutism, negativism, muscular rigidity or waxy flexibility, posturing, and echolalia or echopraxia; it occurs in mood disorders, schizophrenia-spectrum disorders, and various medical conditions and is treatable with benzodiazepines or electroconvulsive therapy.

narcolepsy.definition: A sleep disorder that causes extreme sleepiness and uncontrollable sleep attacks, making a person fall asleep at inappropriate times during the day.

cataplexy.definition: Sudden paralysis of some or all muscles brought on by laughter, anger, fright, or strong emotions; a hallmark of narcolepsy.

catalepsy.definition: A state of stupor with marked muscular rigidity and diminished responsiveness, in which the person can hold an imposed posture (waxy flexibility); commonly seen in catatonia and can be drug-induced or associated with certain neurological or psychiatric disorders.

hysteria.definition: An outdated, non-specific diagnosis for a wide range of physical and emotional symptoms historically attributed to disturbances of the uterus; in modern medicine these presentations are described as somatic symptom disorders or conversion/functional neurological symptom disorders.

oophorectomy.definition: A surgery to remove one or both ovaries. Often treatment for ovarian cancer.

testicles.definition: The testicles are the paired male gonads located in the scrotum; they produce sperm through the seminiferous tubules and secrete testosterone.

gonads.definition: Primary reproductive organs that produce gametes and secrete sex hormones; in females, ovaries; in males, testes.

sterility.definition: Sterility refers to (1) the inability to reproduce or conceive (infertility) and, in microbiology, the complete absence of viable microorganisms, ensuring asepsis.

orchidectomy.definition: The surgical removal of one or both testes; also known as orchiectomy. Performed for conditions such as testicular cancer or irreparable trauma, or as part of hormone-suppressive therapy; it results in infertility and decreased testosterone production.

dentures.definition: Fake teeth made to replace your own teeth. They can replace all of your teeth or just a few. Also called false teeth.

prostheses.definition: An artificial device that substitutes for a missing body part to restore function and/or appearance.

tubules.definition: Small, elongated tube-like structures that transport or modify fluids or substances within organs; usually lined by epithelium and involved in processes such as reabsorption and secretion in the kidneys.

lymph.definition: Clear, colorless interstitial fluid that drains into lymphatic vessels; it contains immune cells (primarily lymphocytes), proteins, fats, and waste products, and it circulates through lymph nodes to help immune defense, fat absorption, and return of excess fluid to the bloodstream.

tissue.definition: A group of cells that are specialized to do a certain job and are joined together to form a body structure, such as muscle or kidney.

foley-catheter.definition: A flexible indwelling urinary catheter inserted through the urethra into the bladder and secured by an inflatable retention balloon; used to drain urine and monitor urinary output.

catheter-ablation.definition: An electrophysiology procedure in which a flexible catheter is threaded through blood vessels into the heart to destroy or disable arrhythmogenic tissue by delivering energy (commonly radiofrequency or cryothermal energy), creating scar tissue to interrupt abnormal electrical circuits and restore normal rhythm or conduction.

cathexis.definition: In psychoanalytic theory, the investment of mental or emotional energy (libido) into a person, object, or idea; the attachment of psychic energy to a mental representation.

cathode.definition: An electrode where reduction occurs in an electrochemical cell; electrons enter the electrode from the external circuit. In galvanic (voltaic) cells it is the positive electrode; in electrolytic cells it is the negative electrode.

cathode-ray.definition: A stream of electrons emitted by a heated cathode and traveling through a vacuum, forming the electron beam used in cathode-ray tubes; deflected by electric and magnetic fields to create images or signals.

cathode-ray-tube.definition: A vacuum tube in which a heated cathode emits electrons that are deflected by electric and magnetic fields to strike a phosphor-coated screen, producing visible images; commonly used in old television sets, computer monitors, and oscilloscopes.

cation-exchange-resin.definition: A polymeric resin with fixed negatively charged groups that exchanges bound cations in solution for other cations, enabling removal or replacement of metal ions (e.g., in water softening or ion-exchange chromatography).

catling.definition: No widely recognized medical definition. If encountered, it may be a misspelling or dialect term, or in veterinary usage could refer to a young cat (kitten), not a human medical condition. If you had a different term in mind (e.g., catalepsy, catheter), please specify.

catoptric.definition: Relating to the reflection of light by mirrors; in optics, describing systems or devices that form images by reflection rather than by refraction.

cowpox.definition: Zoonotic orthopoxvirus infection acquired from cattle; in humans it causes a localized vesicular-pustular lesion at the inoculation site and is usually mild and self-limiting.

cat-scratch-fever.definition: A bacterial infection caused by Bartonella henselae transmitted through cat scratches or bites, typically presenting with regional lymphadenopathy near the entry site, often with a papule or pustule at the scratch and mild fever, malaise, or headache; usually self-limited in otherwise healthy individuals, with supportive care and antibiotics (e.g., azithromycin) considered in selected cases.

cat-scratch-disease.definition: A zoonotic infection caused by Bartonella henselae transmitted to humans through cat scratches or bites, presenting with an inoculation papule or pustule at the site and tender regional lymphadenopathy; usually self-limited in healthy individuals.

cat-eye-amaurosis.definition: Transient, painless loss or obscuration of vision in one eye due to temporary retinal ischemia, typically lasting seconds to minutes and resolving completely; most often caused by embolic or hemodynamic disturbances from carotid artery disease and serves as a warning sign for potential cerebrovascular events.

leukocoria.definition: A white or pale reflection from the retina seen in the pupil (instead of the normal red reflex) on examination or photography; can indicate serious intraocular conditions such as retinoblastoma and requires urgent ophthalmologic evaluation.

cri-du-chat-syndrome.definition: A chromosomal disorder caused by deletion of part of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-), typically presenting with a distinctive high-pitched cat-like cry in infancy, growth retardation, facial dysmorphism, and developmental delay.

chromosome-5p-syndrome.definition: A chromosomal disorder caused by deletion of part of the short arm (p arm) of chromosome 5 (5p-). Classic features include growth delay, intellectual disability, microcephaly, facial dysmorphism, and a distinctive high-pitched, cat‑like cry in infancy, reflecting loss of genes in the 5p region (notably around 5p15.2).

microcephaly.definition: A birth defect where the baby’s head is smaller in comparison to babies of the same sex and age. These babies often have smaller brains that might not have developed properly.

moon-face.definition: A rounded, plethoric facial appearance with fullness of the cheeks and periorbital region, typically due to fat redistribution and edema from hypercortisolism (Cushing syndrome) or prolonged corticosteroid therapy.

hypotonic.definition: Having a lower osmolality than plasma or intracellular fluid; a hypotonic solution or state draws water into cells, potentially causing cell swelling.

heart-defects.definition: A congenital heart defect is a structural abnormality of the heart or great vessels present at birth, resulting from abnormal heart development during fetal life; it can involve the heart walls, valves, or connections between chambers and vessels and may affect blood flow.

heart-abnormalities.definition: A broad term for any condition causing abnormal structure or function of the heart, whether present at birth (congenital) or acquired, including structural defects, valvular disease, cardiomyopathies, arrhythmias, and coronary abnormalities, which may impair the heart's ability to pump blood effectively.

mental-retardation.definition: A generalized neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by significant limitations in intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior, with onset during the developmental period.

low-birth-weight.definition: A birth weight less than 2,500 grams (5 pounds, 8 ounces) at birth, irrespective of gestational age.

low-set-ears.definition: A congenital feature in which the ears are positioned lower on the head than normal; may be associated with various genetic syndromes and congenital anomalies.

anal-atresia.definition: A congenital malformation in which the anal opening is absent or blocked (imperforate anus), typically part of anorectal malformations; often requires surgical repair.

cauda-equina.definition: A bundle of nerve roots that look like a horse’s tail, located at the end of the spinal cord.

caudal-eminence.definition: A mass of undifferentiated, pluripotent cells at the caudal end of the developing embryo (the tail bud) that persists during embryogenesis and contributes to the formation of the posterior body, including the lower spinal cord and related tail structures, via secondary neurulation.

caudal-ligaments.definition: A fibrous band of connective tissue located at the caudal (tail-end) aspect of an anatomical region; its primary function is to stabilize tissues or joints and restrict movement toward the caudal direction. The specific ligaments referred to as “caudal ligaments” vary by region and species.

caudal-retinaculum.definition: A posterior fibrous band that anchors and guides tendons as they pass over a joint, preventing bowstringing and helping maintain tendon alignment.

caudal-regression-syndrome.definition: A rare congenital disorder defined by underdevelopment or absence of the lower spine (primarily the sacrum, and sometimes the lumbar spine), with a spectrum from sacral hypoplasia to complete sacral agenesis, frequently accompanied by lower limb deformities and associated malformations of the genitourinary, anorectal, and spinal systems; often linked to maternal diabetes and thought to result from disrupted development of the caudal mesoderm early in embryogenesis.
