caudal-anesthesia.definition: Caudal anesthesia is a regional technique in which local anesthetic is injected into the caudal epidural space via the sacral hiatus to produce anesthesia and analgesia of the lower abdomen, pelvis, and lower extremities; it is commonly used in pediatric patients for surgeries below the umbilicus and for postoperative pain relief.

caudate-nucleus.definition: A C-shaped subcortical structure of the basal ganglia in the telencephalon, part of the dorsal striatum with the putamen; it receives cortical input and helps regulate voluntary movement, procedural learning, and reward-related behavior.

caudate-lobe.definition: A small lobe of the liver on the visceral (posterior) surface, situated between the inferior vena cava and the porta hepatis; it is anatomically distinct (often called segment I in the Couinaud system) and comprises the caudate process and the papillary process, with separate vascular and biliary drainage but functioning as part of the liver.

caudate-process.definition: A small posterior projection (processus caudatus) of the caudate lobe of the liver, extending toward the left on the liver’s posterior surface between the inferior vena cava and the left lobe.

cauliflower-ear.definition: A deformity of the external ear caused by repeated blunt trauma that forms a subperichondrial hematoma, disrupting cartilage nutrition and leading to fibrous overgrowth that thickens and deforms the ear into a cauliflower‑like shape; commonly seen in wrestlers and boxers.

caumesthesia.definition: A burning, painful abnormal sensation (dysesthesia), often described as a heat-like burning feel, typically arising from nerve injury or neuropathic conditions.

caumesthetic.definition: Not a recognized medical term in standard dictionaries; if encountered, it would refer to an abnormal thermal sensation—altered perception of temperature, such as heightened sensitivity to warmth (thermal hyperesthesia) or a misspelling of thermoesthesia.

causalgia.definition: Intense, long-lasting burning pain usually caused by damage to a peripheral nerve.

catecholamine.definition: A class of monoamine neurotransmitters and hormones derived from tyrosine, including epinephrine (adrenaline), norepinephrine (noradrenaline), and dopamine; they are produced in the adrenal medulla and sympathetic neurons and act on adrenergic receptors to regulate cardiovascular function, metabolism, and CNS activity.

dopa.definition: 3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine (DOPA) is an amino acid that serves as the immediate precursor to dopamine in catecholamine synthesis; the pharmacologic form L-DOPA is used to treat Parkinson disease by increasing brain dopamine levels.

comt.definition: An enzyme that inactivates catecholamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine) by methylating the catechol ring, using S-adenosyl-L-methionine as the methyl donor; exists in soluble and membrane-bound forms and is encoded by the COMT gene.

catechol-o-methyltransferase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the O-methylation (inactivation) of catecholamines—dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine—as well as other catechol substrates; exists in soluble and membrane-bound forms and is targeted by inhibitors to enhance dopaminergic therapy in Parkinson disease.

coprogogue.definition: A substance that promotes the evacuation of feces; an intestinal stimulant or laxative.

cat-eye-syndrome.definition: A rare congenital chromosomal disorder caused by an extra small supernumerary marker chromosome derived from chromosome 22, resulting in partial tetrasomy of 22q11.2; it is characterized by iris and/or chorioretinal colobomas that give a distinctive cat-eye appearance, often with anal atresia, preauricular pits or tags, ear anomalies, and other congenital malformations such as heart or renal defects.

inferior-vena-cava.definition: A large vein that returns deoxygenated blood from the lower body to the right atrium of the heart; it begins at the union of the common iliac veins, ascends through the abdomen to pass through the diaphragm, and receives blood from pelvic and abdominal organs (e.g., renal and hepatic veins).

lateral-ventricle.definition: A pair of C-shaped, cerebrospinal fluid–filled cavities within each cerebral hemisphere that form the lateral part of the ventricular system; they produce CSF via the choroid plexus and communicate with the third ventricle through the foramina of Monro.

notochord.definition: A flexible rod-like embryonic structure derived from mesoderm that provides axial support and signals to pattern surrounding tissues; in humans it largely regresses, with remnants forming the nucleus pulposus of intervertebral discs.

somites.definition: A segmental block of paraxial mesoderm along the developing neural tube in the embryo that differentiates into the sclerotome (vertebrae and ribs), the myotome (axial skeletal muscles), and the dermatome/dermomyotome (dermis of the dorsal skin and muscle precursors).

tail-bud.definition: A mass of undifferentiated, multipotent progenitor cells located at the caudal end of the developing embryo that drives posterior body elongation by giving rise to neural and mesodermal tissues (via neuromesodermal progenitors) and contributes to the formation of the tail, caudal neural tube, notochord, and vertebral structures.

epidural-space.definition: The potential space between the dura mater and the surrounding periosteum of the vertebral canal, containing fat and a venous plexus; commonly accessed for epidural anesthesia.

dural-puncture.definition: A puncture of the dura mater, the tough outer membrane of the meninges surrounding the brain and spinal cord, typically performed to access cerebrospinal fluid for diagnostic or anesthetic purposes; may cause CSF leakage and post-dural puncture headache.

regional-anesthesia.definition: A technique that blocks sensation in a defined region of the body by injecting local anesthetic near target nerves or the spinal cord (neuraxial or peripheral nerve blocks), enabling surgery without general anesthesia and often providing postoperative analgesia.

intravenous-catheter.definition: A flexible tube inserted into a vein to administer intravenous fluids or medications and to draw blood; commonly a peripheral IV catheter used for short-term IV therapy.

intrauterine-catheter.definition: A slender, flexible tube passed through the cervix into the uterine cavity to deliver substances or fluids (eg, during intrauterine insemination) or to obtain uterine samples.

pediatric-anesthesia.definition: A subspecialty of anesthesiology that provides perioperative care for infants, children, and adolescents, including anesthesia administration, airway management, intraoperative monitoring, analgesia, and postoperative recovery, with attention to pediatric physiology, pharmacology, and safety needs.

bartonella.definition: A genus of small, Gram-negative, facultatively intracellular bacteria transmitted by arthropod vectors; causes diseases such as cat-scratch disease, trench fever, bacillary angiomatosis, and endocarditis in immunocompromised hosts.

pustules.definition: A small, raised skin lesion filled with pus (purulent material), usually less than 1 cm in diameter, caused by infection or inflammation of the epidermis or hair follicles (e.g., acne, folliculitis, impetigo).

lymph-nodes.definition: Glands that contain white blood cells that help protect you against germs.

peristalsis.definition: Wavelike movement of intestinal muscles that propels food through the digestive tract.

defecation.definition: The expulsion of feces from the rectum through the anus, typically following rectal distension and coordinated relaxation of the internal and external anal sphincters.

osmotic-forces.definition: The tendency of water to move across a semipermeable membrane from a region of lower solute concentration to higher solute concentration, driven by differences in osmotic pressure; in physiology this is often described as oncotic (colloid osmotic) pressure pulling fluid into capillaries.

sodium-sulfate.definition: An inorganic salt (Na2SO4) that acts as an osmotic laxative; when ingested in sufficient amounts, it draws water into the colon to induce a bowel movement; historically known as Glauber's salt (the decahydrate); excessive use can cause dehydration and electrolyte disturbances and it is not commonly used in modern medicine.

magnesium-sulfate.definition: An inorganic salt consisting of magnesium cations (Mg2+) and sulfate anions (SO4^2−); used medically as an electrolyte replenisher, with parenteral use for preventing seizures in preeclampsia/eclampsia and for certain arrhythmias, and oral use as a laxative.

magnesium-hydroxide.definition: A poorly soluble inorganic base (formula Mg(OH)2) used medically as an antacid to neutralize stomach acid and as an osmotic laxative (milk of magnesia) to increase water content in the intestine.

sodium-biphosphate.definition: A sodium salt of phosphoric acid containing two phosphate units (a diphosphate); used as a food additive, buffering agent, and sometimes a leavening agent. Common forms include disodium phosphate (Na2HPO4) and sodium acid pyrophosphate (Na2H2P2O7).

sodium-acid-pyrophosphate.definition: An inorganic salt of pyrophosphoric acid (formula Na2H2P2O7) used as a leavening acid in baking powders; it reacts with sodium bicarbonate to release carbon dioxide, aiding dough rise, and is typically a slow-acting acidulant in food formulations.

sodium-bicarbonate.definition: An inorganic compound (sodium hydrogen carbonate) with formula NaHCO3 that acts as a buffering agent; used medically as an antacid to relieve heartburn and indigestion, and in certain conditions to treat metabolic acidosis or to alkalinize urine.

phenolphthalein.definition: A pH indicator chemical that is colorless in acidic solutions and turns pink to fuchsia in basic solutions (transition around pH 8.2–10); commonly used in acid–base titrations. Historically used as a laxative, but not recommended due to safety concerns.

dehydrocholic-acid.definition: A bile acid derivative formed by dehydrogenation (loss of hydrogen) of cholic acid, resulting in an unsaturated derivative that is a component of bile.

aloe.definition: A genus of succulent plants; the gel from Aloe vera is used topically for burns, wounds, and skin irritation, while the leaf’s yellow latex (aloin) has stimulant laxative properties; internal use can cause adverse effects and should be used with medical supervision.

colocynth.definition: A plant (Citrullus colocynthis); its dried fruit pulp is a potent laxative/purgative used historically in traditional medicine, but it is highly toxic and can cause severe diarrhea, dehydration, electrolyte disturbances, and abdominal pain; unsafe for self-use.

croton-oil.definition: A highly irritant fixed oil from the seeds of Croton tiglium; historically used as a very potent purgative (laxative) and topical irritant, containing phorbol esters, and now largely obsolete except for limited research use.

podophyllum.definition: A genus of perennial rhizomatous herbs in the Berberidaceae family; the rhizomes contain podophyllotoxin, a cytotoxic lignan used to produce anticancer drugs (e.g., etoposide, teniposide) and, as podophyllin resin, is used topically to treat anogenital warts.

senna.definition: An herbal stimulant laxative derived from Cassia species (senna) containing sennosides that stimulate colonic peristalsis and increase stool water content, producing bowel movements—typically within 6–12 hours after ingestion; used to treat constipation, with potential cramps, diarrhea, dehydration, and electrolyte disturbances on prolonged use.

hypnotic-drugs.definition: Medications that promote sleep by depressing central nervous system activity; used to treat insomnia and, in some cases, for sedative premedication. They include benzodiazepines, non-benzodiazepine “Z-drugs” (e.g., zolpidem, zaleplon, eszopiclone), and older barbiturates, and they carry risks such as tolerance, dependence, daytime drowsiness, cognitive impairment, and potential respiratory depression, especially with other depressants or in the elderly.

hypnosis.definition: A therapeutic technique in which a practitioner guides a person into a focused, relaxed state of heightened suggestibility to influence perceptions, feelings, or behaviors.

vitreous-humor.definition: The clear, gel-like substance that fills the space behind the lens of the eye and supports the shape of the rear portion of the eye.

cavernous sinus.definition: Paired dural venous sinuses located on either side of the sella turcica at the base of the skull; they drain blood from the brain and face and transmit the internal carotid artery and cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2, and VI, draining ultimately into the superior and inferior petrosal sinuses.

cavernous sinus thrombosis.definition: A life-threatening thrombotic occlusion of the cavernous sinus, usually due to infection spreading from facial, orbital, or sinus sources, presenting with fever, headache, periorbital edema, and cranial nerve palsies (III, IV, V1, V2, VI) with possible ophthalmoplegia, proptosis, and risk of meningitis or intracranial spread.

cavernous lymphangioma.definition: A benign congenital lymphatic malformation composed of dilated, cavernous lymphatic channels forming a soft, compressible mass, most often located in the head and neck of children; may be superficial or deep and can enlarge with infection or hemorrhage.

cavernoma.definition: A vascular malformation of the brain or spinal cord composed of clusters of dilated, thin-walled capillary-like vessels with little intervening neural tissue, often prone to hemorrhage; also called a cavernous angioma or cavernous malformation.

cavernous nerve.definition: A parasympathetic autonomic nerve that supplies the erectile tissue of the penis (corpora cavernosa) and clitoris, arising from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) and traveling with the cavernous arteries to mediate erection via nitric oxide–mediated relaxation of cavernosal smooth muscle.

corpus cavernosum.definition: Sponge-like tissue in the penis that fills with blood during sexual arousal, causing an erection.

clitoris.definition: A female erectile organ composed of highly innervated erectile tissue that becomes engorged with blood during sexual arousal; located at the anterior junction of the labia minora; includes the glans, hood (prepuce), body, and internal crura; its primary function is sexual sensation and arousal.

erectile tissue.definition: A vascular tissue that becomes engorged with blood under arousal to produce an erection; in the penis it consists of the corpora cavernosa and corpus spongiosum, and similar erectile bodies are present in the clitoris.

dura mater.definition: An outermost, tough fibrous membrane that envelops the brain and spinal cord; it is part of the meninges and is double-layered in the skull (periosteal and meningeal), forming dural folds and surrounding the dural venous sinuses, continuing as the spinal dura.

ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve.definition: A purely sensory first division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve that exits via the superior orbital fissure and supplies sensation to the orbit, cornea, conjunctiva, upper eyelid, forehead, and scalp; its main branches are nasociliary, frontal, and lacrimal nerves, and it carries afferent input for the corneal reflex.

maxillary division of trigeminal nerve.definition: Purely sensory division of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V2) that provides somatic sensation to the midface (lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip, lateral nose) and the maxillary teeth, palate, and nasal mucosa; exits the skull via the foramen rotundum.

diaphragma sellae.definition: A fold of dura mater forming the roof of the sella turcica (hypophyseal fossa), perforated by the pituitary stalk (infundibulum), thereby separating the pituitary gland from the hypothalamus above.

cavernous sinus syndrome.definition: A clinical syndrome due to pathology affecting the cavernous sinus, characterized by multiple cranial nerve deficits—primarily III, IV, and VI with involvement of the V1 and V2 sensory branches—leading to ophthalmoplegia with diplopia and ptosis, facial numbness in V1/V2 distributions, and often a reduced corneal reflex; may include proptosis and chemosis and is caused by processes such as cavernous sinus thrombosis, tumors, aneurysms, infection, or inflammatory conditions.

optic disc.definition: The region at the retina where ganglion cell axons converge to form the optic nerve; it contains no photoreceptors and corresponds to the physiologic blind spot, with the central retinal arteries and veins passing through.

cecal.definition: Relating to the cecum, the pouch-like beginning section of the large intestine at the ileocecal junction.

cecitis.definition: Inflammation of the cecum, the beginning portion of the large intestine.

typhlitis.definition: An inflammation of the cecum, most often seen in neutropenic or immunocompromised patients (neutropenic enterocolitis); presents with fever, abdominal pain and distention and can progress to bowel necrosis or perforation.

cecal artery.definition: Small arterial branches that supply the cecum; typically two (anterior and posterior) arising from the ileocolic artery, a branch of the superior mesenteric artery.

cecostomy.definition: A surgical creation of an opening (stoma) from the abdominal wall into the cecum to allow drainage of intestinal contents or administration of irrigation solutions, typically via a cecostomy tube, for bowel management or decompression.

ileocecostomy.definition: A surgical procedure that creates a direct opening between the ileum and the cecum (an ileocecal ostomy) to divert or drain intestinal contents.

ceocoileostomy.definition: A surgical procedure that creates a connection or stoma between the cecum and ileum to divert intestinal contents, effectively bypassing a portion of the colon (not a commonly used term).

nasointestinal tube.definition: A feeding tube inserted through the nose that extends into the small intestine (duodenum or jejunum) to deliver enteral nutrition or drain intestinal contents, bypassing the stomach to reduce aspiration risk or when gastric feeding is not tolerated.

orbital edema.definition: Swelling of the tissues around the eye due to fluid accumulation in the orbit or periorbital tissues, often related to inflammation, allergy, infection, trauma, or systemic edema.

pharyngeal edema.definition: Swelling of the pharyngeal mucosa and surrounding tissues due to inflammation or infection, leading to throat fullness and possible difficulty swallowing or airway compromise in severe cases.

circulatory shock.definition: A life-threatening condition characterized by inadequate tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery due to failure of the circulatory system to meet metabolic demand, leading to cellular hypoxia and progressive organ dysfunction; commonly subclassified as hypovolemic, cardiogenic, distributive (eg, septic), or obstructive shock.

esophageal perforation.definition: A full-thickness rupture of the esophagus that allows contents to leak into the mediastinum or pleural spaces; commonly caused by instrumentation or trauma, or spontaneously (Boerhaave syndrome), and represents a medical emergency.

anticoagulants.definition: These types of drugs, also called blood thinners, help prevent blood clots from forming or getting bigger. Blood clots can cause blockages in arteries or veins, heart attacks or strokes. There are different names for these drugs, including warfarin and dabigatran.

clostridium difficile.definition: A Gram-positive, spore-forming, obligate anaerobic bacterium that causes antibiotic-associated diarrhea and colitis, often after recent antibiotic use; it produces toxins A and B that damage the colonic mucosa and can lead to pseudomembranous colitis.

cefaclor.definition: A second-generation cephalosporin antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins. It treats a range of infections caused by susceptible organisms, including some respiratory, skin, and ear infections, with activity against certain Gram-positive cocci and some Gram-negative bacteria. It is administered orally, and common adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset and hypersensitivity reactions.

ceclor.definition: A second-generation cephalosporin antibiotic used to treat various bacterial infections (e.g., otitis media, sinusitis, bronchitis, pneumonia, skin and urinary tract infections). It works by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis through binding to penicillin‑binding proteins, leading to bacterial lysis. Common adverse effects include allergic reactions, diarrhea, and rash; use with caution in patients with penicillin allergy.

cedax.definition: A cephalosporin antibiotic used to treat various bacterial infections; it inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin‑binding proteins.

ceenu.definition: No widely recognized medical definition for that term. It may be a misspelling or a brand name. Please provide context (body system, condition) or check the spelling, and I can help locate the closest term.

cephalosporin antibiotic.definition: A class of beta-lactam antibiotics that inhibit bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins, leading to bacterial cell death; bactericidal and broadly active, with expanding Gram-negative coverage across generations, commonly used to treat skin/soft tissue, respiratory, urinary tract, and intra-abdominal infections; cross-reactivity with penicillins can occur.

caustic.definition: Capable of burning or corroding organic tissue on contact; a caustic substance causes chemical burns and tissue destruction, typically a strong acid or base (alkali).

caustic poisoning.definition: Injury from exposure to caustic, corrosive substances (usually strong acids or alkalis), most often by ingestion, causing chemical burns of the mucosa of the mouth, esophagus, and stomach and potentially life-threatening complications such as perforation or airway injury.

caustics.definition: Substances that burn, dissolve, or destroy living tissue through a chemical reaction; used medically for chemical cautery or tissue destruction (often including strong acids, bases, or other caustic agents such as silver nitrate).

hydrofluoric acid.definition: A solution of hydrogen fluoride in water; a highly corrosive, toxic weak acid that readily penetrates skin and tissues, causing deep chemical burns and systemic fluoride toxicity (notably hypocalcemia).

nitric acid.definition: A colorless, highly corrosive mineral acid (HNO3) that is a strong oxidizing agent used in chemical synthesis, etching, and the manufacture of fertilizers, explosives, and other chemicals.

sulfuric acid.definition: An extremely corrosive strong mineral acid with the chemical formula H2SO4; a powerful dehydrating agent and oxidizer used in chemical manufacturing and refinement; exposure can cause severe skin and eye burns and respiratory irritation.

cauterization.definition: Destruction or coagulation of tissue by applying heat, cold, electrical current, or chemicals to stop bleeding or remove or seal diseased or unwanted tissue.

cauterize.definition: To burn tissue to stop bleeding.

cautery knife.definition: A heated surgical blade used to cut tissue while simultaneously coagulating blood vessels to reduce bleeding; commonly powered by electricity as electrocautery.

cavogram.definition: A radiographic examination obtained after injecting contrast material into a body cavity to visualize its interior and outline its borders for diagnosis of abnormalities such as leaks or structural defects.

cavosurface.definition: The boundary or junction between a prepared dental cavity and the external surface of the tooth (the interface where cavity walls meet the tooth surface, typically enamel or dentin).

cavosurface bevel.definition: A bevel formed at the cavosurface margin of a tooth preparation, typically on enamel, to increase the enamel surface area available for bonding, improve marginal seal, and enhance esthetics by helping the restoration blend with the tooth.

cavosurface angle.definition: The angle formed between the cavosurface margin of a dental cavity prep and the external surface of the tooth (enamel/dentin).

cavity preparation.definition: In dentistry, the process of removing decayed tooth tissue and shaping the remaining tooth to receive a dental restoration, creating proper margins and retention while preserving as much healthy tooth structure as possible.

continuous arteriovenous hemofiltration.definition: A form of continuous renal replacement therapy in which arterial blood is driven through a hemofilter (by the patient’s arterial pressure) and the resulting ultrafiltrate is removed and returned to the venous circulation, providing continuous convective clearance without an external blood pump.

cd4.definition: A transmembrane glycoprotein receptor expressed primarily on CD4+ T lymphocytes (helper T cells); acts as a co-receptor for MHC class II and is the principal entry receptor exploited by HIV; clinically used as a marker of helper T‑cell counts in HIV infection.

cd8.definition: A transmembrane glycoprotein co-receptor on cytotoxic T lymphocytes that binds MHC class I–presented antigens and enhances T-cell receptor signaling; commonly used as a marker for CD8+ T cells.

cd4 count.definition: An absolute count of CD4+ T lymphocytes per microliter of blood, reflecting immune system strength and primarily used to monitor HIV infection and guide prophylaxis and antiretroviral therapy decisions. Normal range is about 500–1,500 cells/µL; counts below 200 cells/µL indicate high risk for AIDS-defining opportunistic infections.

cd8 count.definition: A laboratory measurement of the number or proportion of CD8-positive T lymphocytes in peripheral blood, typically reported as an absolute count (cells per microliter) or as a percentage of total lymphocytes; used to assess cellular immunity and monitor immune status in conditions such as HIV infection or immunodeficiency.

cd4/cd8 count.definition: Peripheral blood counts of CD4+ helper T lymphocytes and CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes, typically measured by flow cytometry; used to assess immune status and monitor conditions such as HIV infection.

cd4 t lymphocytes.definition: A subset of T lymphocytes that express the CD4 receptor and function as helper T cells, coordinating the immune response by secreting cytokines to activate B cells, cytotoxic T cells, and macrophages, and recognizing antigens presented by MHC class II molecules on antigen-presenting cells.

cd8 t lymphocytes.definition: Cytotoxic T cells that express the CD8 co-receptor; they recognize peptides presented by MHC class I molecules on infected or malignant cells and kill these targets primarily through perforin- and granzyme-mediated apoptosis, with Fas–FasL pathways contributing, and they form memory cells after activation as part of adaptive cellular immunity.

t lymphocytes.definition: A type of lymphocyte that matures in the thymus and mediates cell‑mediated immunity; they recognize antigens presented by MHC molecules and differentiate into helper (CD4+), cytotoxic (CD8+), regulatory, and memory T cells, enabling direct killing of infected cells, activation of other immune cells, and immune regulation.

helper t cells.definition: A subset of CD4+ T lymphocytes that coordinate the adaptive immune response by secreting cytokines to activate B cells, cytotoxic T cells, and macrophages; they recognize antigens presented by MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells and differentiate into functionally distinct subsets (e.g., Th1, Th2, Th17, Tfh, and Treg).

cytotoxic t cell.definition: A CD8+ T lymphocyte that kills virus-infected and malignant cells by recognizing intracellular antigenic peptides presented on MHC class I molecules and inducing target cell death via perforin/granzyme exocytosis and Fas-FasL interactions.

interleukin-2.definition: A cytokine produced by activated T lymphocytes that promotes the growth, differentiation, and survival of T cells and natural killer (NK) cells; it signals via the IL-2 receptor and activates the JAK-STAT pathway, and high-dose IL-2 is used clinically in immunotherapy for certain cancers.

gp120.definition: A surface glycoprotein of the HIV-1 envelope, produced from the gp160 precursor, that binds the CD4 receptor on host T cells and interacts with CCR5 or CXCR4 co-receptors to enable viral attachment and entry.

monoclonal antibodies.definition: Monoclonal antibodies are identical antibodies produced from a single cloned B cell line that bind to one specific antigen epitope; they are manufactured as therapeutic or diagnostic agents to target particular molecules or cells in diseases such as cancer, autoimmune disorders, and infections.

ladd's syndrome.definition: A congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract in which the midgut fails to rotate properly during development, causing abnormal fixation and an increased risk of midgut volvulus or duodenal obstruction; treated surgically with the Ladd’s procedure, which detorses the bowel, divides Ladd’s bands, and broadens the mesentery to lessen future volvulus risk.

cefadroxil.definition: A first-generation oral cephalosporin antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin‑binding proteins, resulting in bactericidal activity against many gram-positive cocci and some gram-negative bacteria.

cefotaxime.definition: A broad-spectrum third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic used to treat serious bacterial infections caused by susceptible gram-positive cocci and gram-negative bacilli; administered intravenously or intramuscularly; it inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins, producing bactericidal activity.

cefadyl.definition: A brand-name cephalosporin antibiotic (cefadroxil) used to treat certain bacterial infections by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis; commonly prescribed for skin and soft tissue infections, throat infections, and urinary tract infections.

cephamandole nafate.definition: A salt form of cefamandole (cefamandole nafate), a second‑generation cephalosporin antibiotic used systemically to treat susceptible bacterial infections by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis; the nafate salt improves solubility for parenteral administration.

cefdinir.definition: A third‑generation oral cephalosporin antibiotic used to treat various bacterial infections (e.g., sinusitis, acute otitis media, pneumonia, bronchitis, and skin infections). It inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin‑binding proteins; taken by mouth as capsules or suspension, with absorption increased by meals and iron-containing preparations potentially reducing absorption (separate dosing).

cefepime.definition: A parenteral fourth-generation cephalosporin antibiotic that is bactericidal by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis through binding to penicillin‑binding proteins; it has broad-spectrum activity against Gram-positive cocci and many Gram-negative bacilli (including Pseudomonas) and is used for serious infections such as pneumonia, complicated urinary tract infections, intra‑abdominal infections, skin and soft‑tissue infections, febrile neutropenia, and meningitis.

cefepime hydrochloride.definition: Cefepime hydrochloride is the hydrochloride salt of cefepime, a broad-spectrum, fourth-generation cephalosporin antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins and is used to treat serious infections caused by susceptible Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, typically administered intravenously or intramuscularly.

cefotetan disodium.definition: Disodium salt of a second-generation cephalosporin antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins; active against certain Gram-negative and anaerobic bacteria; used for intra-abdominal and gynecologic infections and for surgical prophylaxis; may cause hypersensitivity, GI upset, and a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.

cefoxitin.definition: A second-generation cephalosporin antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins. It has good activity against many gram-negative bacteria and anaerobes (notably Bacteroides fragilis) and is used for intra-abdominal and gynecologic infections and for surgical prophylaxis; given IV or IM with limited activity against Pseudomonas and MRSA.

ceftazidime.definition: Third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic with broad-spectrum activity against Gram-negative bacteria, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa; it inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins. It is administered parenterally (intravenous or intramuscular) for serious infections such as pneumonia, meningitis, sepsis, and intra-abdominal infections.

ceftibuten.definition: A third-generation oral cephalosporin antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins, used to treat various susceptible infections such as otitis media, sinusitis, pharyngitis/tonsillitis, bronchitis, and urinary tract infections.

ceftizoxime.definition: Third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic given by injection (parenteral) that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins, with broad activity against many Gram-negative bacteria and some Gram-positive cocci; used for serious infections; adverse effects can include hypersensitivity and diarrhea.

celecoxib.definition: A selective COX-2–inhibiting nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to relieve pain and inflammation; inhibits cyclooxygenase-2 to reduce prostaglandin synthesis.

celestone.definition: A brand-name corticosteroid containing betamethasone, a potent synthetic glucocorticoid used to reduce inflammation and suppress immune responses; available in injectable formulations and used for severe inflammatory or autoimmune conditions and to promote fetal lung maturation in preterm labor.

celexa.definition: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) antidepressant used to treat major depressive disorder; increases serotonin levels in the brain by inhibiting its reuptake at the synaptic cleft. (generic name: citalopram)

cefobid.definition: A parenteral third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic (cefoperazone), with broad-spectrum activity against many Gram-negative bacteria and some Gram-positive bacteria; often given with sulbactam to broaden coverage against beta-lactamase–producing organisms and anaerobes; used for serious infections such as intra-abdominal, gynecologic, and respiratory tract infections.

cefoperazone.definition: A parenteral third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic with broad-spectrum activity against many Gram-negative bacteria; often combined with the beta-lactamase inhibitor sulbactam to extend activity against beta-lactamase–producing organisms and anaerobes.

cefoperazone sodium.definition: An injectable (parenteral) third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic supplied as the sodium salt; it is bactericidal by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis through binding to penicillin-binding proteins, used to treat serious infections caused by susceptible Gram-negative and some Gram-positive bacteria.

cefotaxime sodium.definition: A sodium salt form of cefotaxime, a third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic given IV or IM; it inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin‑binding proteins, providing broad-spectrum activity against many Gram-negative bacteria and some Gram‑positive cocci for serious infections (e.g., meningitis, septicemia, pneumonia, intra‑abdominal or gynecologic infections).

cefotan disodium.definition: A parenteral cephalosporin antibiotic (cephamycin) with activity against many Gram-negative bacteria and anaerobes; given IV/IM for intra‑abdominal and gynecologic infections and perioperative prophylaxis; can cause a disulfiram‑like reaction with alcohol and may cause hypoprothrombinemia, requiring monitoring of coagulation and vitamin K status, especially in renal impairment.

carcinoma of the cecum.definition: A malignant epithelial neoplasm arising from the mucosa of the cecum (the proximal part of the large intestine), most commonly an adenocarcinoma; a form of colorectal cancer.

celiac sprue.definition: An autoimmune gluten-sensitive enteropathy in genetically susceptible individuals (often HLA-DQ2/DQ8) causing small intestinal villous atrophy and malabsorption, with symptoms such as diarrhea and weight loss that improve on a gluten-free diet.

gluten-induced enteropathy.definition: An autoimmune small intestinal enteropathy triggered by gluten in genetically susceptible individuals; characterized by villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, leading to malabsorption and symptoms such as chronic diarrhea and weight loss; typically improves with a strict gluten-free diet (also known as celiac disease).

abdominal distention.definition: Abdominal distention is abnormal enlargement of the abdomen due to accumulation of gas in the bowel, excess fluid in the peritoneal cavity (ascites), or a mass/enlarged organ.

celiac ganglion.definition: A prevertebral sympathetic ganglion located around the celiac trunk in the upper abdomen; part of the celiac plexus; receives preganglionic fibers from the greater splanchnic nerves and provides postganglionic sympathetic innervation to foregut organs (stomach, liver, spleen, pancreas, and proximal duodenum).

celiac plexus.definition: A network of nerves in the upper abdomen; medication is sometimes injected here as part of a therapy to ease pain called a nerve block.

celiacoduodenal part.definition: A foregut-derived segment of the duodenum—the proximal (superior) portion near the stomach—supplied by branches of the celiac trunk, principally the gastroduodenal artery and its superior pancreaticoduodenal branches.

celiac rickets.definition: Rickets due to malabsorption from celiac disease; gluten-induced intestinal damage reduces absorption of calcium, phosphate, and vitamin D, causing defective bone mineralization in children, which improves with a gluten-free diet and vitamin D/calcium supplementation.

solar plexus.definition: A network of autonomic nerves in the upper abdomen around the origin of the celiac artery (the celiac/solar plexus); it provides sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation to the abdominal viscera, including the stomach, liver, spleen, pancreas, and intestines.

celioscope.definition: An endoscope used for celioscopy to visualize the abdominal (peritoneal) cavity; an early instrument for abdominal visualization, a predecessor to the laparoscope.

haemophilus parainfluenzae.definition: A small, Gram-negative coccobacillus of the oropharyngeal flora; an opportunistic pathogen that can cause infections such as endocarditis, meningitis, sinusitis, otitis, and bacteremia, and is part of the HACEK group of fastidious organisms.

morganella catarrhalis.definition: A Gram-negative, oxidase-positive diplococcus that colonizes the upper respiratory tract and is a common cause of otitis media and sinusitis in children, and bronchitis or pneumonia in adults; many strains produce beta-lactamase, contributing to penicillin resistance; typically treated with beta-lactamase–stable antibiotics such as amoxicillin-clavulanate or certain cephalosporins.

streptococcus pyogenes.definition: A gram-positive, beta-hemolytic bacterium of group A Streptococcus; a common human pathogen. It causes diseases ranging from pharyngitis and impetigo to cellulitis, necrotizing fasciitis, rheumatic fever, and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Transmission is via respiratory droplets or direct contact; treatment typically includes penicillin or other beta-lactam antibiotics.

bacterial septicemia.definition: Systemic infection caused by viable bacteria in the bloodstream (bacteremia) that elicits a systemic inflammatory response and may progress to septic shock and organ dysfunction; commonly presents with fever, chills, tachycardia, and hypotension.

lower respiratory tract.definition: The portion of the respiratory system below the larynx that includes the trachea, the main and segmental bronchi, bronchioles, and the lungs (alveolar regions); responsible for air conduction, conditioning and humidifying inhaled air, and gas exchange.

urinary tract.definition: Part of the body that produces and excretes urine. It consists of the kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra.

skin.definition: The outer protective covering of the body, comprising the epidermis and dermis (and underlying subcutaneous tissue); it serves as a barrier to pathogens and fluid loss, helps regulate body temperature, and provides sensation.

reproductive organs.definition: Organs involved in producing offspring, including the gonads (ovaries and testes) that form gametes, and the reproductive tract and associated glands and external genitalia that transport, fertilize, support pregnancy, and enable birth.

surgical prophylaxis.definition: Surgical prophylaxis refers to preventive measures taken to reduce the risk of infection around the time of surgery, most notably perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis given before incision to prevent surgical site infection, along with strict aseptic technique, antisepsis, and proper wound care.

coronary bypass operations.definition: An operation to restore blood flow to the heart by grafting vessels to bypass blocked coronary arteries, usually using a segment of saphenous vein or internal thoracic artery, thereby improving myocardial perfusion and relieving angina.

intramuscular injection.definition: An intramuscular injection is the administration of a medication directly into a muscle using a needle and syringe, typically at a 90-degree angle, to achieve rapid systemic absorption; common sites are the deltoid, gluteus maximus, and vastus lateralis, with site and volume adjusted for patient age and muscle mass.

superinfection.definition: An infection that develops during treatment for another infection, usually due to a different microorganism that exploits disruption of the normal flora (often after broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy).

injection site.definition: The location on the body where a medication is administered by injection, including the skin and underlying tissues at a specific anatomical site (e.g., intramuscular, subcutaneous, or intradermal).

lymphocytosis.definition: An elevated lymphocyte count in the peripheral blood, usually defined as an absolute lymphocyte count above the laboratory’s upper reference limit; most often seen with viral infections but can occur in certain lymphoproliferative disorders and other conditions.

pancytopenia.definition: Pancytopenia is a reduction in all three major blood cell types—red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets—in the peripheral blood, typically due to impaired bone marrow production, increased destruction, or sequestration, and it can lead to anemia, infection risk, and bleeding.

coombs test.definition: Serologic test using anti-human globulin to detect antibodies or complement bound to red blood cells (direct Coombs test) or free antibodies in serum that react with red cells (indirect Coombs test).

lactic dehydrogenase.definition: Una enzima que cataliza la conversión reversible de lactato a piruvato, con la concomitante oxidación-reducción del NADH/NAD+. Se encuentra en el citosol de muchas células y presenta varias isoenzimas con distribución tisular; la elevación de sus niveles en sangre puede indicar daño tisular, hemólisis o enfermedad hepática, cardíaca o muscular.

gluten.definition: A group of storage proteins found in wheat and related grains that give dough its elasticity; in susceptible individuals, ingestion can trigger autoimmune or inflammatory reactions, most notably celiac disease.

enteropathy.definition: A disease of the intestine, especially the small intestine; a broad term for disorders affecting intestinal mucosa and function, often associated with malabsorption and diarrhea.

sprue.definition: A chronic malabsorption syndrome of the small intestine, most commonly referring to gluten-sensitive enteropathy (celiac disease); immune-mediated mucosal damage to the villi in response to gluten leads to diarrhea, weight loss, and steatorrhea, managed with a gluten-free diet.

acute bacterial otitis media.definition: An acute infection of the middle ear with sudden ear pain and middle-ear effusion, usually caused by bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae, or Moraxella catarrhalis.

acute bacterial exacerbation of chronic.word: acute bacterial exacerbation of chronic bronchitis
acute bacterial exacerbation of chronic.definition: An acute, infection-related worsening of chronic bronchitis, characterized by a rapid increase in dyspnea, cough, and sputum production with sputum purulence, often due to bacterial pathogens (e.g., Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, Streptococcus pneumoniae) and frequently treated with antibiotics.

cytotoxic t lymphocytes.definition: CD8+ T cells that recognize peptides presented by MHC class I on infected or malignant cells and kill those targets primarily through perforin/granzyme–mediated cytotoxicity, and also via Fas-FasL–induced apoptosis.

natural killer cells.definition: A type of white blood cell of the immune system. These cells destroy other cells that fail to display the right chemical flags signaling that they are normal cells.

delayed hypersensitivity.definition: A type IV (delayed-type) cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction in which sensitized T lymphocytes recognize an antigen and release cytokines that recruit and activate macrophages, causing localized inflammation; the reaction typically develops 24–72 hours after exposure (examples include the tuberculin skin test and contact dermatitis).

type iv hypersensitivity.definition: A delayed-type, cell-mediated immune reaction in which sensitized T lymphocytes (primarily CD4+ Th1 cells, with CD8+ T cells also involved) recognize antigen and release cytokines that activate macrophages, leading to tissue inflammation and damage a day or two after exposure; not antibody-mediated (examples include contact dermatitis, tuberculin skin test reaction, and granulomatous diseases).

hypersensitivity reaction.definition: An inappropriate or exaggerated immune response to a normally harmless antigen, resulting in tissue injury or disease. Traditionally classified into four types (I–IV): Type I is IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity; Type II is antibody-mediated cytotoxic reactions; Type III is immune complex–mediated diseases; Type IV is delayed-type cell-mediated reactions.

cell-mediated immunity.definition: A type of immune response mounted against viruses, certain types of parasites, and perhaps cancer cells.

cellular immunity.definition: An arm of the adaptive immune system mediated by T lymphocytes that recognizes and destroys infected or malignant cells without antibodies; it relies on antigen presentation via MHC molecules and includes helper, cytotoxic, and regulatory T cells (as well as memory T cells).

humoral immunity.definition: An aspect of the adaptive immune response mediated by B lymphocytes and secreted antibodies that neutralizes extracellular pathogens and toxins, promotes opsonization, and activates the complement system.

antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotox.definition: An immune mechanism in which effector cells recognize and kill antibody-coated target cells through Fc receptors (most commonly NK cells via FcγRIII), triggering release of cytotoxic granules (perforin/granzymes) and target cell lysis; other Fc receptor–bearing cells (e.g., macrophages, neutrophils) can also contribute.

cell-mediated cytotoxicity.definition: A component of the cell-mediated immune response in which cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CD8+ T cells) and natural killer cells recognize and destroy virus-infected or abnormal cells, primarily by releasing perforin and granzymes to induce apoptosis or by engaging death receptors, without the involvement of antibodies.

graft rejection.definition: Graft rejection is an immune-mediated destruction of a transplanted organ or tissue by the recipient’s immune system, which recognizes the graft as foreign and mounts a response that injures or destroys it. It can be hyperacute (minutes–hours, due to preformed antibodies), acute (weeks–months, largely T-cell– or antibody-mediated), or chronic (months–years, with progressive graft dysfunction).

redness.definition: Localized reddening of the skin or mucous membranes caused by increased blood flow from vasodilation of superficial capillaries, typically in response to inflammation, irritation, injury, or infection.

swelling.definition: An abnormal increase in the size of a body part due to fluid accumulation in the interstitial tissues (edema) or accumulation of other material; commonly caused by inflammation, injury, or impaired venous or lymphatic drainage.

paneth cells.definition: A specialized secretory cell located at the base of the crypts of Lieberkühn in the small intestine (most prominent in the duodenum), characterized by eosinophilic apical granules; it secretes antimicrobial peptides such as alpha-defensins (cryptdins), lysozyme, and phospholipase A2, contributing to innate immunity, shaping the gut microbiota, and supporting the intestinal stem cell niche.

mitochondria.definition: Small structures within cells that break down nutrients and generate energy for the cell. Known as the power producers or energy factories of cells.

golgi bodies.definition: A membrane-bound organelle in eukaryotic cells consisting of flattened sacs (cisternae) that modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and lipids for secretion or delivery to other organelles.

plasma membrane.definition: A cellular membrane that surrounds the cytoplasm, formed by a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins, separating the intracellular space from the extracellular environment. It is selectively permeable and regulates the movement of ions and molecules, and participates in signaling and cell recognition.

cell membrane.definition: A phospholipid bilayer that encloses the cell, forming its boundary and regulating the movement of substances into and out of the cell; contains embedded proteins and other molecules and participates in signaling, cell recognition, and adhesion. Described by the fluid mosaic model.

periodontal ligament fibers.definition: Collagen fiber bundles within the periodontal ligament that connect the cementum of the tooth to the surrounding alveolar bone, anchoring the tooth in its socket and distributing occlusal forces.

alveolar fibers.definition: Bundles of collagenous connective tissue in the periodontal ligament that attach the tooth root cementum to the surrounding alveolar bone, forming the principal tooth-supporting fibers (alveolar crest, horizontal, oblique, apical, and interradicular) that resist tooth movement and absorb masticatory loads.

enucleation.definition: The surgical removal of an entire organ or mass in an intact form, preserving surrounding tissues; in ophthalmology, specifically the removal of the eyeball (globe).

cementoblast.definition: A cell that forms cementum, the mineralized tissue covering the tooth root; derived from the dental follicle and responsible for cementogenesis.

cementoblastoma.definition: A rare benign odontogenic tumor originating from cementoblasts in the tooth root, producing cementum-like tissue that fuses to the root and forms a radiopaque mass typically with a radiolucent rim; it often causes jaw expansion and tooth displacement and is usually treated by surgical excision with extraction of the involved tooth.

cementoma.definition: An older term for a benign fibro-osseous jaw lesion in which fibrous tissue contains cementum-like calcifications; commonly used for periapical cemental dysplasia around tooth roots or for cemento-ossifying fibromas; today, more specific diagnoses are preferred.

cementum-producing tumor.definition: A benign odontogenic tumor in which cementum-like material is produced by neoplastic cementoblasts, typically arising from a tooth root and often fused to it; radiographically seen as a radiopaque mass with a surrounding radiolucent border and may cause root resorption; treated by surgical excision, usually with extraction of the involved tooth.

odontogenic tumor.definition: A neoplasm arising from tissues involved in tooth development (odontogenesis), usually within the jaw, derived from odontogenic epithelium and/or odontogenic ectomesenchyme; it can be benign or malignant.

centesis.definition: A surgical puncture of a body cavity or organ to remove fluid or air or to obtain a sample for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes.

coelom.definition: A true body cavity in coelomate animals, lined by mesoderm, that houses and supports the internal organs and allows organ movement; formed during embryogenesis by schizocoely or enterocoely.

celothelioma.definition: A malignant tumor of mesothelial cells lining serous membranes (most commonly the pleura and peritoneum), typically associated with asbestos exposure.

cementifying fibroma.definition: A benign odontogenic fibro-osseous lesion of the jaw composed of fibrous connective tissue with cementum-like calcifications; typically slow-growing and well-circumscribed, usually treated by surgical excision.

cement base.definition: A dental restorative material placed as a barrier on the dentin or pulp chamber floor beneath a restoration to protect the pulp, provide thermal insulation, and support the final restoration; commonly calcium hydroxide, zinc oxide–eugenol, or glass ionomer bases.

cementation.definition: The process of attaching a dental prosthesis (such as a crown, veneer, or bridge) to prepared tooth structure or an implant using a luting cement that hardens to secure the restoration.

cell-surface marker.definition: A molecule expressed on the surface of a cell (often a protein or glycoprotein) that can be used to identify and distinguish cell types, lineages, or functional states; commonly detected with antibodies (e.g., CD markers in immunophenotyping).

auditory hair cells.definition: A type of sensory cell in the cochlea of the inner ear that detects sound by deflection of apical stereocilia, transducing mechanical vibrations into neural signals; includes inner hair cells (primary auditory transducers) and outer hair cells (mechanical amplifiers).

cell of corti.definition: A cell located in the organ of Corti in the cochlea; the organ contains inner and outer hair cells and supporting cells that together transduce mechanical sound vibrations into neural signals.

lysozyme.definition: An enzyme (muramidase) that hydrolyzes the β(1→4) glycosidic linkages between N-acetylmuramic acid and N-acetylglucosamine in peptidoglycan, causing lysis of bacterial cell walls; found in secretions such as tears, saliva, mucus, and egg white, and part of the innate immune system.

femoral head.definition: The rounded proximal end of the thigh bone that articulates with the acetabulum of the pelvis to form the hip joint; it is covered by articular cartilage and connected to the shaft via the femoral neck.

hip joint.definition: A ball-and-socket synovial joint between the head of the femur and the acetabulum of the pelvis; the primary weight-bearing joint of the lower limb, permitting flexion/extension, abduction/adduction, and internal/external rotation (with circumduction), stabilized by a strong capsule, ligaments (iliofemoral, pubofemoral, ischiofemoral), and the acetabular labrum.

central amaurosis.definition: Sudden loss or severe reduction of central vision in one eye due to acute dysfunction of the retina or optic nerve, typically painless and resulting from ischemic or inflammatory macular/optic processes (e.g., retinal artery occlusion, macular infarction, or optic neuritis).

central deafness.definition: Hearing loss caused by damage to the brain's central auditory pathways (beyond the inner ear), with preserved peripheral hearing, leading to impaired processing or interpretation of sounds (especially speech).

central sleep apnea.definition: A disorder in which breathing repeatedly stops during sleep, because the brain doesn’t properly signal the muscles that control breathing.

idiopathic central hypoventilation.definition: A very rare disorder in which automatic control of breathing is impaired, causing inadequate ventilation and elevated carbon dioxide levels (hypercapnia), particularly during sleep, with no identifiable underlying pulmonary, neuromuscular, or cardiac disease and often reduced ventilatory response to hypercapnia.

central nervous system syndrome.definition: A non-specific clinical syndrome indicating dysfunction of the central nervous system (brain and/or spinal cord), typically presenting with altered consciousness or cognition, focal neurological deficits, seizures, coma, or autonomic instability; caused by a wide range of etiologies such as infection, inflammation, trauma, ischemic or hemorrhagic events, tumors, metabolic derangements, or toxin exposure.

central placenta previa.definition: A placenta previa in which the placenta covers the internal cervical os centrally, typically equivalent to complete placenta previa.

central core disease.definition: An inherited congenital myopathy characterized by central, well-demarcated cores within type I muscle fibers that lack oxidative enzyme activity and mitochondria on biopsy; most commonly due to RYR1 mutations and often associated with hypotonia, proximal weakness, and malignant hyperthermia susceptibility.

shy-magee syndrome.definition: A progressive neurodegenerative disorder (a form of multiple system atrophy) characterized by autonomic failure (e.g., orthostatic hypotension, urinary incontinence) with parkinsonian features and often cerebellar signs.

centracinar emphysema.definition: A form of emphysema in which destruction and enlargement of the central portions of the acinus (around the respiratory bronchioles) occur, typically in the upper lung zones, with relative sparing of the peripheral alveoli and often associated with smoking.

centrilobular emphysema.definition: A smoking-related pattern of emphysema in which destruction and enlargement of airspaces occur predominantly around the respiratory bronchioles in the centrilobular region of the acinus, with relative sparing of the peripheral alveoli; most prominent in the upper lung zones and contributing to progressive airflow limitation in COPD.

centriacinar emphysema.definition: A form of emphysema in which destruction and enlargement of the central (proximal) parts of the acini, especially around the respiratory bronchioles, predominate, with relative sparing of the distal alveoli; most commonly affects the upper lung zones and is strongly associated with smoking.

enchondrosarcoma.definition: An intramedullary malignant tumor producing cartilage, arising within bone (often from a preexisting enchondroma), most commonly affecting the small bones of the hands and feet; treated primarily with wide surgical resection.

central chondrosarcoma.definition: A malignant cartilage-producing tumor that originates within the medullary cavity (intramedullary) of a bone, rather than at the bone surface.

spinal cord tumor.definition: A neoplasm arising within the spinal canal, originating from the spinal cord itself (intramedullary) or from surrounding meninges or nerve roots (extramedullary); it can compress or invade the spinal cord and cause pain, weakness, sensory changes, and autonomic symptoms. Diagnosis is typically by MRI with contrast; management depends on histology and may include surgical resection with radiotherapy or chemotherapy.

central nervous system tumor.definition: A neoplasm arising in the brain or spinal cord (the central nervous system); it may be primary (originating in CNS tissues) or metastatic (spread to the CNS from another site) and can be benign or malignant, often presenting with neurologic symptoms due to mass effect, invasion, or edema.

central canal.definition: A CSF-filled channel that runs longitudinally through the center of the spinal cord; it is the adult remnant of the neural tube lumen and is lined by ependymal cells, continuous with the brain's ventricular system.

cerebrum.definition: A large region of the brain comprising two cerebral hemispheres responsible for higher brain functions (conscious thought, sensation, perception, memory, language, and voluntary movement); it contains the cerebral cortex and underlying white matter with subcortical nuclei.

frontal lobe.definition: Front portion of the cerebral cortex located anterior to the central sulcus; it governs voluntary movement (via the primary motor cortex) and higher cognitive functions such as planning, decision-making, attention, language production (Broca's area), and aspects of personality and social behavior.

parietal lobe.definition: Part of the brain. It plays a role in sensory processes, like pain and touch, and language.

occipital lobe.definition: The region in the back of the brain responsible for visual processing.

central lobe.definition: Not a formally recognized brain lobe; the brain contains four lobes—frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital—separated by major sulci, with the central sulcus marking the boundary between the frontal and parietal lobes. If used, the term may refer informally to the central region around the central sulcus rather than a distinct lobe.

island of reil.definition: A portion of the cerebral cortex buried within the lateral sulcus (the insular cortex); it participates in gustation, autonomic regulation, interoception, emotion, and the integration of sensory information.

lateral sulcus.definition: A prominent deep groove on the lateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere (Sylvian fissure) that separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes; it contains the insula.

central sulcus.definition: A prominent fissure on the lateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere that separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe and demarcates the boundary between the primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus) and the primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus); also known as the fissure of Rolando.

vena cava.definition: A large vein that returns deoxygenated blood from the systemic circulation to the right atrium of the heart; consists of the superior vena cava and the inferior vena cava.

central venous catheter.definition: A catheter placed into a large central vein (such as the internal jugular, subclavian, or femoral vein) to provide reliable access for administration of medications, fluids, parenteral nutrition, blood sampling, and for central venous pressure monitoring or dialysis; it can be short-term or long-term.

central line.definition: A catheter inserted into a large central vein (e.g., internal jugular, subclavian, or femoral) with the tip in or near the cavoatrial junction, used for reliable venous access to administer medications, fluids, blood products, and parenteral nutrition, and for hemodynamic monitoring (central venous pressure); includes PICC lines, tunneled catheters, and implanted ports.

central venous oxygen saturation.definition: The percentage of oxygen-saturated hemoglobin in venous blood returned to the right heart from the central venous circulation (typically via a central venous catheter), reflecting the balance between systemic oxygen delivery and oxygen consumption; normal resting values are about 65–75% in adults, with lower values suggesting increased tissue extraction or reduced delivery.

cvso2.definition: An estimate of the oxygen saturation of blood in the central venous circulation, reflecting the balance between systemic oxygen delivery and tissue oxygen consumption. It is typically about 65–75% in healthy adults and is used to assess adequacy of tissue perfusion, often measured from blood drawn via a central venous catheter.

subarachnoid space.definition: Space inside the brain where cerebrospinal fluid circulates.

csf.definition: A clear, colorless fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord within the meninges and ventricular system; it provides buoyant support, cushions neural tissue, maintains intracranial pressure, and enables exchange of nutrients and waste between blood and the CNS. It is produced mainly by the choroid plexus in the brain’s ventricles and reabsorbed into the venous system via arachnoid granulations; normal adult volume is about 125–150 mL with production around 500 mL per day.

neuroglia.definition: Non-neuronal cells of the nervous system that support, nourish, and protect neurons; they maintain the extracellular environment, form myelin (oligodendrocytes in the CNS and Schwann cells in the PNS), regulate synaptic function, and participate in immune defense and repair after injury.

gray matter.definition: A region of the central nervous system composed mainly of neuronal cell bodies, their dendrites, and unmyelinated axons with supporting glial cells; it appears gray in color due to relatively low myelin content and contrasts with white matter, which contains many myelinated axons. It includes areas such as the cerebral cortex, deep brain nuclei, and spinal cord horns.

white matter.definition: The inner portion of the brain, composed primarily of axons, each surrounded by a myelin sheath that insulates the nerve fibers (and appears white). Messages are sent between different regions of the brain (gray matter) via these nerve fibers.

myelinated nerve fibers.definition: Axons wrapped in a myelin sheath formed by Schwann cells (PNS) or oligodendrocytes (CNS); this insulation increases the speed of action potential conduction via saltatory conduction at the nodes of Ranvier.

filum terminale.definition: A slender filament of pia mater extending from the tip of the conus medullaris to the coccyx, anchoring the spinal cord within the vertebral column. It consists of the filum terminale internum (within the dural sac) and the filum terminale externum (outside the dural sac, blending with the coccygeal ligament). It is mainly connective tissue with pia mater, contains no neural elements, and helps stabilize the spinal cord.

symphysis pubis.definition: A fibrocartilaginous joint at the anterior pelvis where the left and right pubic bones meet; it includes an interpubic disc, is reinforced by ligaments, and allows limited movement to absorb load and maintain pelvic stability; hormonal changes in pregnancy can loosen its ligaments, increasing mobility.

central ray.definition: In radiology, the central ray is the central axis of the X-ray beam—the imaginary line from the X-ray tube to the image receptor that passes through the center of the imaged area; it is typically directed perpendicular to the image receptor to establish projection and minimize distortion.

central nervous system stimulant.definition: A drug that increases activity in the brain and spinal cord, elevating alertness, attention, and wakefulness, typically by increasing synaptic dopamine and norepinephrine (and sometimes other monoamines).

pentobarbital.definition: A short-acting barbiturate CNS depressant used as a sedative-hypnotic and anticonvulsant; commonly used for induction of anesthesia and, in some jurisdictions, euthanasia; it potentiates GABA-A receptor–mediated chloride influx, producing CNS depression; adverse effects include respiratory depression, hypotension, and dependence.

secobarbital.definition: A short-acting barbiturate sedative-hypnotic used for short-term treatment of insomnia and for preoperative sedation; depresses CNS activity by potentiating GABA-A–mediated chloride influx, with risks of sedation, respiratory depression, dependence, and withdrawal, and is largely replaced by benzodiazepines and other hypnotics.

glutethimide.definition: A sedative-hypnotic central nervous system depressant formerly used to treat insomnia; a non-barbiturate hypnotic with potential for tolerance, dependence, and abuse, with marked risks when combined with alcohol or other CNS depressants.

methylprylon.definition: A sedative-hypnotic CNS depressant formerly used to treat insomnia; acts as a CNS depressant (GABAergic) to promote sleep; adverse effects include drowsiness, impaired coordination, and risk of tolerance, dependence, and withdrawal; its use is largely obsolete due to safety concerns.

methaqualone.definition: A sedative-hypnotic central nervous system depressant, a quinazolinone derivative formerly prescribed for insomnia and marketed as Quaalude; widely abused for its euphoric and sedative effects, with high potential for dependence and overdose, now tightly controlled or illegal in most countries.

deanol acetamidobenzoate.definition: A chemical compound likely formed as a salt or ester of Deanol (dimethylaminoethanol) with acetamidobenzoic acid; used in some cosmetic formulations, with no widely recognized medical indications or proven therapeutic efficacy.

centrax.definition: Definition not found in standard medical dictionaries. Could you confirm the spelling or provide context (drug, device, condition)? If you meant a brand name or acronym, I can help clarify with that context.

prazepam.definition: A long-acting benzodiazepine anxiolytic used to treat anxiety disorders; it is a prodrug that is metabolized to the active metabolite nordazepam (desmethyldiazepam), with sedative and muscle-relaxant effects and a risk of dependence.

doxapram.definition: A central nervous system and respiratory stimulant used to counteract respiratory depression and neonatal apnea; it increases ventilation by stimulating carotid body and central chemoreceptors to raise respiratory drive.

central nervous system depressant.definition: Substance that slows brain activity by enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission or inhibiting excitatory signaling, resulting in drowsiness, reduced alertness, cognitive and motor impairment, and at higher doses, respiratory depression; examples include alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, and some opioids.

diuresis.definition: Increased production and excretion of urine by the kidneys, resulting in elevated urine output; can be physiologic or induced by drugs or conditions (eg, osmotic diuresis or diuretic use).

central scotoma.definition: A blind spot or markedly reduced vision in the center of the visual field (the macula/fovea), reflecting macular or optic nerve/retinal dysfunction and resulting in decreased central visual acuity.

centrosome.definition: An organelle that serves as the cell's main microtubule organizing center, organizing spindle fibers during cell division; in animal cells it consists of a pair of centrioles surrounded by pericentriolar material.

centrioles.definition: Pair of cylindrical microtubule-based organelles in the cytoplasm of many eukaryotic cells; arranged perpendicularly near the nucleus as part of the centrosome; organize spindle fiber formation during cell division and serve as basal bodies for the formation of cilia and flagella; replicate once per cell cycle.

centromere.definition: The region of a chromosome where sister chromatids are held together after DNA replication and where kinetochores assemble to attach chromosomes to spindle microtubules during mitosis and meiosis.

kinetochore.definition: A protein complex located at the centromere of a chromosome that assembles during cell division to attach the chromosome to spindle microtubules, enabling proper alignment and segregation during mitosis and meiosis.

centrosphere.definition: Not a standard medical term; when used, it may describe the pericentrosomal region surrounding the centrosome in a cell, which contains material important for microtubule nucleation and organization during cell division.

centrocecal.definition: Pertaining to the center of the retina and the physiological blind spot (optic disc); used to describe a visual field defect that encompasses both central vision and the blind spot.

centrocinesia.definition: Definition not found in standard medical dictionaries. Could you share context or check the spelling? If you meant related terms such as akinesia (loss of movement), bradykinesia (slowness of movement), or dyskinesia (involuntary movements), I can define those.

centrosclerosis.definition: Hardening (sclerosis) of the central portion of a tissue or organ; a nonspecific term used to describe central fibrotic changes rather than a named disease.

centrum.definition: A central, weight-bearing portion of a vertebra; the vertebral body that forms the main anterior mass of the bone and supports the body's weight, articulating with adjacent vertebrae.

metacentric.definition: Describing a chromosome whose centromere is located near the middle, resulting in two arms of approximately equal length.

submetacentric.definition: Describes a chromosome whose centromere is off-center, producing two unequal arms: a shorter short arm (p) and a longer long arm (q).

telocentric.definition: Having the centromere at the terminal end of a chromosome, producing essentially a single (long) arm with no short arm.

centromeric.definition: Relating to the centromere of a chromosome; describing the region around the centromere, including centromeric chromatin and proteins involved in chromosome segregation during cell division.

cephalalgia.definition: Headache; pain located in the head or upper neck, which may be a primary disorder (migraine, tension-type, cluster) or a secondary symptom of another condition.

cephalea.definition: Pain in the region of the head; a common symptom that can be primary (e.g., migraine, tension-type, cluster) or secondary to another condition.

cephalaledema.definition: Not a standard medical term. Etymologically, it would refer to edema of the head—swelling from fluid accumulation in the scalp or cranial tissues; if brain swelling is intended, the correct term is cerebral edema.

cephalad.definition: Toward the head; directed toward the head end of the body (opposite of caudad).

cephalic.definition: Relating to the head; toward the head end of the body.

cephalometric.definition: Relating to the measurement of the head, especially the skull and face, using radiographs; cephalometry is the radiographic analysis of craniofacial dimensions and relationships, commonly used in orthodontics and maxillofacial surgery to assess growth and treatment outcomes.

cephalometric radiograph.definition: A radiographic image of the head, typically a lateral view (lateral cephalogram), used to analyze craniofacial morphology and skeletal–dental relationships for diagnosis and treatment planning in orthodontics and craniofacial surgery.

cephalometric tracing.definition: A method of analyzing craniofacial morphology by identifying and tracing standardized anatomical landmarks on a cephalometric radiograph (usually a lateral skull X-ray) to obtain measurements of skeletal and dental relationships for orthodontic diagnosis, treatment planning, and growth assessment.

cephalometry.definition: Measurement and analysis of craniofacial dimensions and relationships using standardized radiographs (cephalometric radiographs) to assess skeletal jaw relationships, growth, and treatment effects.

cephalogram.definition: A radiographic image of the skull used for cephalometric analysis, typically a lateral view to assess craniofacial relationships and occlusion.

cephalocentesis.definition: A historical obstetric procedure in which the fetal skull is punctured to drain intracranial contents (often cerebrospinal fluid) to reduce head size and facilitate vaginal delivery; now obsolete and unsafe.

cephalogenesis.definition: The development and formation of the head (cephalic region) during embryonic growth, including the brain, skull, and facial structures.

cephalocaudal.definition: Relating to the pattern of growth or development that proceeds from the head toward the tail; in development, structures near the head develop before those farther from the head.

cephalopagus.definition: A form of conjoined twinning in which the two individuals are fused at the head and upper body, usually sharing the upper thorax and possibly abdominal organs, resulting in two heads emerging from a single torso.

cephalopelvic.definition: Relating to the fetal head and the maternal pelvis; used in obstetrics to describe how well the baby's head fits through the birth canal, a mismatch that can impede delivery (cephalopelvic disproportion).

cephalopelvic disproportion.definition: A condition in which the fetus cannot pass through the maternal pelvis during labor because the fetal size (head or body) exceeds the dimensions of the pelvis, often due to a small or contracted pelvis or a large/malpositioned fetus; commonly results in labor dystocia and may necessitate cesarean delivery.

cpd.definition: Structured, ongoing education and training activities undertaken by healthcare professionals to maintain, update, and enhance their clinical knowledge, skills, and competencies.

cephalopelvimetry.definition: An obstetric measurement used to assess whether the fetal head can pass through the maternal pelvis by estimating pelvic dimensions and fetal head size; historically performed with X-ray pelvimetry, now mainly with ultrasound to evaluate cephalopelvic disproportion and guide delivery planning.

cephalophlebitis.definition: Inflammation of a vein in the head (a form of phlebitis).

cephalothin.definition: A first-generation cephalosporin antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins; active mainly against Gram-positive cocci and some Gram-negative rods; administered parenterally (IM/IV); used to treat or prevent infections caused by susceptible organisms; limited activity against MRSA and anaerobes; may have cross-sensitivity with penicillins.

cephalothoracoiliopagus.definition: A rare form of conjoined twinning in which two fetuses are fused at the head, chest, and pelvis, producing a single body with shared cephalic, thoracic, and pelvic structures.

cerclage.definition: A surgical procedure in obstetrics in which a suture or tape is placed around the cervix to reinforce it and prevent cervical dilation and preterm birth in cervical insufficiency; it can be performed transcervically or via an abdominal approach.

cercaria.definition: A free-swimming larval stage of trematodes that emerges from the snail intermediate host; it swims in water and may infect the definitive host by penetrating the skin or encyst as a metacercaria.

cercariae.definition: Free-swimming larval stage of certain trematodes released from the snail intermediate host; they possess a tail and are the infective form for the definitive host, typically penetrating the skin (as in Schistosoma spp.) or encysting as metacercariae in the environment.

chlonorchis.definition: A genus of parasitic liver flukes (trematodes) that inhabit the biliary ducts of humans and other mammals; infection (clonorchiasis) is acquired by ingesting raw or undercooked freshwater fish containing encysted metacercariae and can cause biliary inflammation, obstruction, and an increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma.
