paragonimus.definition: A genus of parasitic flatworms (trematodes) that cause paragonimiasis; humans acquire infection by eating undercooked freshwater crustaceans, and adult parasites inhabit the lungs, producing cough, chest pain, and sometimes hemoptysis.

fasciolopsis.definition: A genus of intestinal trematodes (flukes) that infect humans and pigs; the most notable species, Fasciolopsis buski, causes fasciolopsiasis, acquired by ingesting metacercariae on aquatic plants and presenting with abdominal pain, diarrhea, and malabsorption (can be severe in heavy infections).

fasciola.definition: A genus of parasitic flatworms (trematodes) that are liver flukes; they infect the livers of various mammals (especially ruminants) and can cause fascioliasis in humans.

fasciola hepatica.definition: A parasitic trematode (liver fluke) that infects the liver and biliary ducts of humans and other mammals; acquired by ingestion of metacercariae on aquatic vegetation, it migrates to the bile ducts, causing fascioliasis with fever, right upper quadrant pain, hepatomegaly, eosinophilia, and biliary obstruction.

pelvimetry.definition: The measurement of the dimensions of the maternal pelvis to assess its capacity for vaginal delivery, often to predict cephalopelvic disproportion and guide delivery planning; it can be performed clinically or radiographically.

craniopagus.definition: A type of conjoined twins in which two individuals are fused at the skull (the head); they may share portions of the skull, dura mater, brain tissue, and major venous sinuses, making surgical separation highly complex and often not feasible.

synadelphus.definition: An obscure or archaic term describing congenital fusion of two anatomical structures that are normally separate.

congenital erythropoietic porphyria.definition: An extremely rare autosomal recessive disorder of heme biosynthesis caused by deficiency of uroporphyrinogen III synthase (UROS), leading to accumulation of type I porphyrins (uroporphyrin I and coproporphyrin I) in erythrocytes and tissues. It presents with severe cutaneous photosensitivity from infancy, blistering and scarring of sun-exposed skin, erythrodontia (red-discolored teeth), and may be associated with hemolytic anemia. (Also known as Gunther disease.)

farber's disease.definition: A rare autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of the enzyme acid ceramidase (ASAH1), leading to ceramide accumulation in tissues; characterized by painful joint contractures, subcutaneous nodules, hoarseness, progressive neurodegeneration, hepatosplenomegaly, and typically fatal in infancy or early childhood. Also known as Farber lipogranulomatosis.

ceramidase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of ceramide to sphingosine and a free fatty acid, thereby regulating cellular levels of ceramide and sphingosine; exists in multiple isoforms (acid, neutral, and alkaline ceramidases) with different subcellular localizations and pH optima.

ceramidase deficiency.definition: Deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme acid ceramidase (ASAH1) leading to accumulation of ceramide; a lysosomal storage disorder (Farber disease) characterized by painful joint contractures, subcutaneous nodules, hoarseness, hepatosplenomegaly, and developmental delay.

denture prosthetics.definition: The branch of dentistry focused on the design, fabrication, fitting, and management of artificial dentures (complete or partial) to replace missing teeth and restore chewing function, speech, and aesthetics.

denture.definition: Removable dental prosthesis designed to replace missing teeth and surrounding oral tissues; it can be a full-arch appliance or a removable partial that attaches to remaining teeth.

mandibular condyles.definition: Two rounded articular processes at the upper ends of the mandible; each condyle articulates with the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone (via an intervening articular disc) to form the temporomandibular joint, enabling hinge and gliding movements of the jaw.

glabella.definition: The smooth area of the forehead on the frontal bone between the two superciliary arches (above the nasal root), serving as an anatomical landmark.

occiput.definition: The back part of the skull; the region formed by the occipital bone at the posterior aspect of the cranium.

sinciput.definition: The front part of the skull; the forehead region (anterior aspect of the skull).

opisthocranion.definition: The most posterior point on the external contour of the skull used as a cephalometric landmark to measure cranial length.

supramastoid crest.definition: A small bony ridge on the temporal bone, located just above the mastoid process.

centrum semiovale.definition: An area of subcortical white matter in each cerebral hemisphere, just beneath the cerebral cortex and above the lateral ventricles, containing projection fibers (including corona radiata from the internal capsule) and long association tracts that connect different cortical regions (e.g., the superior longitudinal fasciculus).

paranuclear body.definition: A small cytoplasmic inclusion located immediately adjacent to the nucleus; a descriptive term used in histology and pathology to denote material or structures in the perinuclear region, without implying a specific, universally defined organelle.

paranuclear.definition: Situated near or surrounding the cell nucleus; describing structures located in the perinuclear region, often noted as a perinuclear halo around the nucleus (e.g., the Golgi apparatus adjacent to the nucleus in plasma cells).

chromosome.definition: A threadlike structure, found in the nucleus of each cell, that carries almost all of a cell’s genes.

chromatids.definition: One of the two identical copies of a chromosome that are produced during DNA replication and held together at the centromere; these sister chromatids are separated during cell division (anaphase of mitosis or meiosis II) to become independent chromosomes.

mitosis.definition: A fundamental process of cell division in which a parent cell's replicated chromosomes are evenly separated into two genetically identical daughter nuclei, typically followed by cytokinesis to produce two separate diploid daughter cells.

cerebral edema.definition: An abnormal accumulation of excess fluid within brain tissue, causing swelling and increased intracranial pressure; it can arise from cytotoxic edema (cell swelling), vasogenic edema (extracellular fluid from blood–brain barrier disruption), or interstitial edema (CSF transudation).

cerebral amyloid angiopathy.definition: A cerebral small-vessel disease in which beta-amyloid deposits accumulate in the walls of cortical and leptomeningeal arteries, weakening vessels and increasing the risk of lobar intracerebral hemorrhage and cerebral microbleeds; often linked to aging and Alzheimer's disease.

cerebral angiography.definition: An invasive imaging procedure used to make detailed x-ray pictures of the blood vessels in the brain; dye is injected into the carotid arteries to highlight the blood vessels on x-rays.

cerebral anoxia.definition: A complete lack of oxygen to the brain, usually from cessation of blood flow or severe hypoxemia, causing rapid loss of consciousness and risking irreversible brain injury or death if not promptly restored.

cerebral arteriovenous malformation.definition: A congenital vascular anomaly of the brain characterized by a tangled nidus of abnormal arteries and veins that connect directly without an intervening capillary bed, producing high-flow arteriovenous shunting and an elevated risk of intracranial hemorrhage, seizures, or neurological deficits.

cerebral artery.definition: A blood vessel that supplies oxygenated blood to brain tissue; cerebral arteries arise from the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems and include the anterior, middle, and posterior cerebral arteries that perfuse the cerebral hemispheres.

cerebral blood flow.definition: The volume of arterial blood reaching brain tissue per unit time, typically about 50 mL per 100 g of brain tissue per minute at rest, maintained by cerebral autoregulation to keep stable perfusion despite changes in systemic blood pressure.

cerebral cavity.definition: A system of interconnected, cerebrospinal fluid–filled cavities within the brain (the cerebral ventricles), including the lateral ventricles, third ventricle, and fourth ventricle; they are lined by ependymal cells and participate in the production, circulation, and storage of cerebrospinal fluid.

cranial cavity.definition: The space inside the skull that contains the brain, the meninges, and cerebrospinal fluid; bounded by the cranial bones and continuous with the vertebral (spinal) canal, traditionally subdivided into anterior, middle, and posterior cranial fossae.

cerebral compression.definition: Abnormal pressure on brain tissue within the skull caused by swelling, a mass effect, hemorrhage, or external forces, which can reduce cerebral perfusion and risk brain herniation.

cerebral cortex.definition: The part of the brain involved in all forms of conscious experience, including thought, language, and memory.

cerebral falx.definition: A sickle-shaped fold of dura mater that descends within the longitudinal fissure between the cerebral hemispheres, separating them. It attaches anteriorly to the crista galli and posteriorly to the internal occipital protuberance and tentorium cerebelli, and contains the superior sagittal sinus along its superior border, with the inferior sagittal sinus running along its inferior border.

cerebral fossa.definition: A shallow depression on the base of the skull that houses portions of the brain; collectively these are the cranial fossae (anterior, middle, and posterior).

cerebral gigantism.definition: A historic term for a congenital overgrowth syndrome characterized by excessive body and head growth (macrocephaly), distinctive facial features, and developmental delay; the condition is now generally known as Sotos syndrome.

cerebral gyrus.definition: A ridge or convolution on the surface of the cerebrum formed by the folding of the cerebral cortex (gray matter); gyri are separated by grooves called sulci.

cerebral infarction.definition: A type of stroke caused when a blood vessel that supplies blood to the brain is blocked by a blood clot.

cerebral lobes.definition: The four major subdivisions of the cerebrum—frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital—separated by major sulci; each lobe supports distinct functions: frontal in motor planning and higher cognition, parietal in somatosensory processing and spatial reasoning, temporal in auditory processing and memory, and occipital in visual processing.

cerebral localization.definition: The principle that specific neurological functions are mediated by distinct brain regions, so damage to a particular area produces predictable, focal deficits corresponding to that region.

cerebral nerves.definition: Not a standard anatomical term. The closest concept is the cranial nerves—twelve pairs of peripheral nerves that arise from the brain and brainstem and provide sensory and motor innervation to the head and neck.

cerebral hemisphere.definition: One of the two symmetrical halves of the brain's cerebrum (left and right), separated by the longitudinal fissure and connected by the corpus callosum; each hemisphere processes sensory information and motor commands to the opposite side of the body and supports higher cognitive functions, language, and perception.

subarachnoid.definition: Relating to the subarachnoid space, the cerebrospinal fluid–filled interval between the arachnoid mater and the pia mater surrounding the brain and spinal cord.

subarachnoid hemorrhage.definition: A hemorrhagic stroke that occurs when a blood vessel on the surface of the brain bursts and bleeds into the space between the brain and the skull; usually caused by an aneurysm or other blood vessel malformation.

extradural.definition: Situated outside the dura mater; relating to the space between the dura mater and the surrounding skull (cranium) or vertebral canal.

subdural.definition: Situated beneath the dura mater, the outermost protective covering of the brain.

brain herniation.definition: A pathologic displacement of brain tissue due to raised intracranial pressure, causing herniation of brain structures across intracranial partitions (e.g., the falx, tentorium, or foramen magnum) and potentially compressing the brainstem with severe neurological deterioration or death.

hemorrhagic stroke.definition: A type of stroke caused by rupture of a blood vessel with bleeding either inside the brain tissue (intracerebral hemorrhage) or into the surrounding subarachnoid space (subarachnoid hemorrhage).

sotos syndrome.definition: An autosomal dominant overgrowth syndrome (often due to NSD1 gene mutations) characterized by prenatal and postnatal overgrowth with macrocephaly, a distinctive facial appearance (long face, prominent jaw, high forehead), hypotonia in infancy, and developmental delay or intellectual disability; seizures and autism spectrum features may occur.

von hippel-lindau disease.definition: An autosomal dominant genetic disorder due to mutations in the VHL tumor suppressor gene, causing multiple highly vascular tumors and cysts, especially retinal and CNS hemangioblastomas, clear cell renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors.

hemangioblastoma.definition: A benign, highly vascular central nervous system tumor typically arising in the cerebellum or retina; composed of lipid-rich stromal cells with an abundant capillary network; often associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease and frequently cystic with a mural nodule, potentially causing hydrocephalus or focal neurological symptoms.

cerebellar hemangioblastoma.definition: A benign, highly vascular tumor of the cerebellum (posterior fossa), typically cystic with a mural nodule; composed of lipid-rich stromal cells and an extensive capillary network; often associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease and commonly treated by surgical resection.

angioblastoma.definition: A benign vascular neoplasm arising from angioblasts (vascular precursor cells), characterized by proliferation of capillaries embedded in a stromal matrix; frequently described as a hemangioblastoma when occurring in the central nervous system.

cerebellar cortex.definition: Thin outer layer of gray matter covering the cerebellum, consisting of molecular, Purkinje, and granular layers; contains Purkinje cells and integrates input from mossy and climbing fibers to refine and coordinate movement, balance, and motor learning via inhibitory output to the deep cerebellar nuclei.

cerebellar artery.definition: A blood vessel that supplies the cerebellum; specifically, any of the three main cerebellar arteries—the superior cerebellar artery, anterior inferior cerebellar artery, and posterior inferior cerebellar artery—that typically arise from the basilar or vertebral arteries and perfuse the cerebellar hemispheres and vermis, with connections to brainstem vessels.

dentate nucleus.definition: A large deep cerebellar nucleus located in each cerebellar hemisphere; it receives inhibitory input from Purkinje cells and projects excitatory output via the superior cerebellar peduncle to the contralateral thalamus (ventral lateral nucleus) and red nucleus, coordinating planning and execution of smooth, voluntary limb movements.

red nucleus.definition: A midbrain nucleus in the tegmentum, richly pigmented with iron giving a reddish appearance; it is the origin of the rubrospinal tract and functions as part of the extrapyramidal motor system to influence limb movement by relaying signals from the cerebellum and motor cortex to the spinal cord.

pontine nuclei.definition: A group of large neurons in the ventral pons that receive input from the cerebral cortex (corticopontine fibers) and relay signals to the cerebellum via the middle cerebellar peduncle, forming part of the cortico-ponto-cerebellar pathway that coordinates voluntary movement.

vermis.definition: The median, worm-like portion of the cerebellum that connects the two hemispheres and is involved in coordination of movement, posture, and gait.

cerebellar notch.definition: A term not widely used in standard anatomy; it usually refers to the tentorial notch (incisura tentoris), the opening in the tentorium cerebelli that allows the brainstem to pass from the posterior to the middle cranial fossa.

tentorium cerebelli.definition: A sheet-like fold of dura mater that spans horizontally across the posterior cranial fossa, separating the cerebellum from the inferior occipital lobes and forming the tentorial notch (an opening) for the brainstem; it also provides attachment for surrounding dural structures.

falx cerebelli.definition: A small dural fold in the posterior cranial fossa that descends between the cerebellar hemispheres to separate them; it is a sickle-shaped fold of dura mater attached to the internal occipital crest and the tentorium cerebelli, often containing small venous channels along its margins.

falx cerebri.definition: A crescent-shaped fold of dura mater that projects into the longitudinal fissure between the cerebral hemispheres, attaching anteriorly to the crista galli and posteriorly to the internal occipital crest; it partitions the two hemispheres and contains the superior sagittal sinus along its superior border and the inferior sagittal sinus along its inferior edge.

cerebellar gait.definition: A gait ataxia due to cerebellar dysfunction, characterized by a wide-based, unsteady, irregular stepping pattern with veering and a tendency to fall toward the side of the lesion, often with impaired tandem walking.

monoplegia.definition: Paralysis of one limb (arm or leg), usually due to a focal lesion of the brain or spinal cord or a peripheral nerve injury affecting that limb.

diplegia.definition: Paralysis or marked weakness affecting corresponding parts on both sides of the body, most commonly the legs; a form of cerebral palsy characterized by bilateral leg involvement.

tetraplegia.definition: Paralysis or severe loss of motor and sensory function in all four limbs due to damage to the cervical spinal cord.

scissors gait.definition: A gait abnormality in which the legs cross each other or come together with each step due to spastic hip adductors, producing a scissors-like, or scissoring, motion (commonly seen in cerebral palsy).

cerebellar tremor.definition: An intention tremor caused by cerebellar dysfunction, characterized by a low-frequency tremor that increases in amplitude with purposeful movement and worsens as the limb approaches a target, often with ataxia and dysmetria.

opisthotonos.definition: A severe, sustained backward arching of the head, neck, and spine due to intense tonic contractions of the back and neck muscles, typically seen in tetanus and other severe CNS irritative conditions.

prognathism.definition: A condition in which the jaw projects forward relative to the skull, typically involving the mandible, resulting in a protruding lower facial profile.

antimongoloid slant.definition: An outdated, pejorative descriptor for the downward-slanting orientation of the palpebral fissures (eyelid openings); historically used to describe certain populations. Modern clinical usage describes eyelid fissure orientation as downslanting (or upslanting) without racial labeling.

little's disease.definition: Definition not found in standard medical references. “Little's disease” is not a current, widely accepted medical term; it may be an outdated or nonstandard name. If you can share the context (organ system, symptoms, time period, or a source), I can provide a precise definition or suggest the modern term it corresponds to.

corticopontine.definition: A projection pathway from the cerebral cortex to the pontine nuclei in the brainstem; part of the cortico-pontine system that relays cortical information to the cerebellum via the pontine nuclei and pontocerebellar fibers.

cerebral perfusion pressure.definition: A pressure gradient that sustains cerebral blood flow; CPP equals mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure (CPP = MAP − ICP). In adults, maintaining CPP around 60–70 mmHg helps ensure adequate cerebral perfusion, accounting for autoregulation and clinical context.

cpp.definition: An arterial-pressure parameter that governs cerebral blood flow; calculated as mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure (MAP − ICP). Typical adult target is about 60–70 mmHg, with goals tailored to the patient.

mean systemic arterial blood pressure.definition: The average pressure in the systemic arterial circulation during a single cardiac cycle, reflecting organ perfusion; commonly estimated as diastolic blood pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure (MAP ≈ DBP + 1/3(SBP − DBP)) in mmHg.

cerebral sulci.definition: Grooves on the surface of the brain’s cerebral cortex that separate the gyri; they are shallow grooves (fissures are deeper), and together with the gyri form the folded cortex and increase cortical surface area.

sulci.definition: Grooves or furrows on a surface (such as bones or the cerebral cortex), often housing vessels or nerves; in neuroanatomy, the grooves between the gyri of the cerebral cortex.

cerebral thrombosis.definition: A blockage of a brain artery caused by a thrombus that forms in situ within the cerebral vasculature, leading to focal brain ischemia (ischemic stroke).

cva.definition: A sudden loss of brain function caused by an acute disturbance of blood supply to the brain, typically due to ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke.

central vertigo.definition: Vertigo due to a central nervous system lesion, typically in the brainstem or cerebellum, often with accompanying focal neurologic signs (ataxia, dysarthria, limb weakness or sensory loss); nystagmus is usually vertical or gaze-evoked, non-fatigable, and not suppressed by visual fixation, and the dizziness may be persistent.

cerebral vertigo.definition: Vertigo due to central nervous system pathology (brainstem or cerebellar origin), typically with accompanying neurological signs (ataxia, diplopia, dysarthria) and central-type nystagmus (often vertical or direction-changing), as opposed to peripheral vertigo from the inner ear.

cerebral vomiting.definition: Vomiting driven by central nervous system pathology (neurogenic vomiting) rather than gastrointestinal causes, typically due to increased intracranial pressure or brainstem lesions; may be accompanied by headache, altered consciousness, and papilledema, and warrants evaluation for intracranial disease.

cerebriform carcinoma.definition: An epithelial cancer with a brain‑like (cerebriform) convoluted surface or pattern; the term is uncommon and may represent a context‑specific or misused designation rather than a standard histopathologic entity.

medullary carcinoma.definition: Malignant tumor with medullary differentiation; most commonly a thyroid cancer arising from calcitonin-producing parafollicular C cells (medullary thyroid carcinoma), often secreting calcitonin and containing amyloid-like extracellular material on histology.

cerebromeningitis.definition: Inflammation of both the brain parenchyma (encephalitis) and the meninges (meningitis), typically due to infection; also called meningoencephalitis.

cerebroatrophic hyperammonemia.definition: Brain atrophy associated with elevated blood ammonia levels (hyperammonemia), typically due to severe liver disease or inborn errors of nitrogen metabolism, and often contributing to hepatic encephalopathy and neurocognitive impairment.

rett syndrome.definition: A rare X-linked dominant neurodevelopmental disorder caused by MECP2 mutations, primarily in females, characterized by initial normal development followed by regression with loss of purposeful hand use and speech, hand stereotypies (often wringing), gait abnormalities, severe intellectual disability, autistic-like features, seizures, and decelerating head growth.

cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis.definition: A rare autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by CYP27A1 mutations leading to defective bile acid synthesis and accumulation of cholestanol and cholesterol in tissues (notably brain and tendons), causing neurologic symptoms such as ataxia and cognitive decline and tendon xanthomas; treatable with chenodeoxycholic acid.

van bogaert’s disease.definition: Not found in standard medical references; likely a misspelling or extremely obscure term. If you can provide context (medical specialty, region) or an alternate spelling, I can help with an accurate definition.

cerebroretinal angiomatosis.definition: Congenital vascular malformation of the brain characterized by leptomeningeal angiomatosis with concurrent retinal and choroidal vascular abnormalities, most notably seen in Sturge–Weber syndrome.

cerebroside.definition: A neutral glycosphingolipid consisting of ceramide bound to a single sugar (galactose or glucose); a major structural component of myelin in nervous tissue and of cell membranes, contributing to membrane stability and cell recognition.

cerebroside sulfatase.definition: A lysosomal enzyme that removes the 3-O-sulfate group from sulfatides (sulfatide), catalyzing its hydrolysis to galactosylceramide and free sulfate; deficiency leads to sulfatide accumulation and causes metachromatic leukodystrophy.

cerebrospinal axis.definition: Not a standard medical term. If used, it likely refers to the neuraxis—the central nervous system’s longitudinal axis from the medulla oblongata through the brainstem and cerebral hemispheres down the spinal cord, used to describe the orientation of CNS structures.

cerebrospinal fever.definition: A historical term for meningitis, an infection and inflammation of the meninges surrounding the brain and spinal cord, typically presenting with fever and meningeal signs; most commonly refers to meningococcal meningitis.

cisterna magna.definition: A large cerebrospinal fluid–filled subarachnoid space in the posterior cranial fossa, located between the medulla oblongata and the inferior surface of the cerebellum; also called the cerebellomedullary cistern.

choroid plexus.definition: A highly vascularized network of specialized ependymal cells within the brain ventricles that produces cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and contributes to the blood-CSF barrier.

arachnoid villi.definition: Small protrusions of the arachnoid membrane that extend into the dural venous sinuses (chiefly the superior sagittal sinus) and reabsorb cerebrospinal fluid into the venous bloodstream, functioning as one-way valves for CSF drainage.

foramen of magendie.definition: A median opening in the fourth ventricle that allows cerebrospinal fluid to exit the ventricular system into the subarachnoid space.

foramen of luschka.definition: Two lateral openings of the fourth ventricle that allow cerebrospinal fluid to exit into the subarachnoid space, contributing to CSF circulation (lateral apertures of the fourth ventricle).

lateral ventricle.definition: One of a pair of C-shaped, cerebrospinal fluid–filled cavities within each cerebral hemisphere that produces CSF via its choroid plexus and communicates with the third ventricle through the foramina of Monro.

third ventricle.definition: A narrow, midline cerebrospinal fluid–filled cavity of the diencephalon, between the two thalami, that communicates with the lateral ventricles via the foramina of Monro and with the fourth ventricle via the cerebral aqueduct; bounded laterally by the thalami and inferiorly by the hypothalamus.

superior sagittal sinus.definition: An intracranial dural venous sinus that runs along the superior edge of the falx cerebri, collecting venous blood from cerebral veins and CSF via arachnoid granulations, and draining posteriorly into the confluence of sinuses.

foramen of monro.definition: An opening (interventricular foramen) that connects each lateral ventricle to the third ventricle, allowing cerebrospinal fluid to pass from the lateral ventricles into the third ventricle.

basal skull fracture.definition: Fracture at the base of the skull, involving bones at the skull base (often temporal, sphenoid, ethmoid, or occipital); may cause cerebrospinal fluid leakage from the nose or ears, cranial nerve injuries, and signs such as raccoon eyes or Battle sign, with risk of intracranial injury; diagnosed by CT and managed according to complications, sometimes requiring surgical intervention.

cerebrospinal rhinorrhea.definition: Leakage of cerebrospinal fluid from the nose due to a skull base or dura mater defect, typically after trauma or surgery; presents as clear, watery nasal discharge and requires evaluation to prevent meningitis.

rhinorrhea.definition: Nasal discharge from the nose due to inflammation of the nasal mucosa, typically clear and watery; a common symptom of infections, allergies, or irritants.

meningococcal meningitis.definition: A bacterial meningitis caused by Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus), transmitted via respiratory droplets. It typically presents with fever, headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia and can progress rapidly to septicemia with a purpuric rash; requires prompt IV antibiotics and is preventable by vaccination. Close contacts may require chemoprophylaxis.

korsakoff’s psychosis.definition: An acquired memory disorder caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, typically from chronic alcohol use, characterized by Severe impairment of new learning (anterograde amnesia) with confabulation and relatively preserved older memories; often accompanied by disorientation and other cognitive changes, and considered part of Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome.

cerebropathia psychia toxemia.definition: An older term for a brain disorder (toxic encephalopathy) characterized by mental changes caused by circulating toxins in the blood; not a single disease but a description used for conditions like uremic, hepatic, septic, or obstetric toxemia that affect the brain.

metachromatic leukodystrophy.definition: A lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of the enzyme arylsulfatase A (ARSA), leading to accumulation of sulfatides in lysosomes and progressive demyelination of the central and peripheral nervous systems.

gaucher’s disease.definition: Gaucher disease is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient activity of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase, leading to accumulation of glucocerebroside in macrophages (Gaucher cells) and resulting in hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, thrombocytopenia, bone disease, and, in types 2 and 3, neurologic involvement.

imiglucerase.definition: A recombinant form of the human lysosomal enzyme beta-glucocerebrosidase used as enzyme replacement therapy for Gaucher disease; it catalyzes the hydrolysis of glucocerebroside to glucose and ceramide in lysosomes.

beta-glucocerebrosidase.definition: A lysosomal hydrolase that catalyzes the hydrolysis of glucosylceramide (glucocerebroside) to glucose and ceramide; also known as glucocerebrosidase. Deficiency causes Gaucher disease; encoded by the GBA gene.

cerezyme.definition: A recombinant enzyme replacement therapy for Gaucher disease, containing imiglucerase (human beta-glucocerebrosidase) that substitutes the deficient lysosomal enzyme to reduce glucocerebroside buildup in macrophages; administered by IV infusion.

cerubidine.definition: A chemotherapy drug (anthracycline) used to treat certain leukemias; daunorubicin intercalates DNA and inhibits topoisomerase II, generating free radicals. Administered intravenously; major toxicities include myelosuppression and dose-dependent cardiotoxicity.

daunorubicin hydrochloride.definition: A cytotoxic chemotherapy agent of the anthracycline class; the hydrochloride salt of daunorubicin that intercalates DNA and inhibits topoisomerase II, leading to DNA breaks and inhibition of cell replication.

ceruminolytic agent.definition: A substance or preparation used to soften and dissolve cerumen (earwax) to facilitate its removal from the ear canal, often containing carbamide peroxide.

ceruloplasmin.definition: A copper-containing plasma protein produced by the liver that functions as a multicopper oxidase (ferroxidase), oxidizing Fe2+ to Fe3+ to enable iron binding by transferrin; it carries most circulating copper and acts as an acute-phase reactant.

wilson’s disease.definition: An autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, leading to impaired biliary copper excretion and accumulation of copper in the liver, brain, and other tissues; clinically, it presents with hepatic disease, neurologic/psychiatric symptoms, and Kayser–Fleischer rings, and is treated with copper chelators or zinc to reduce copper load.

peroxisomes.definition: A small, membrane-bound organelle in eukaryotic cells that contains enzymes for beta-oxidation of fatty acids and for detoxifying hydrogen peroxide (via catalase); also involved in lipid metabolism, including plasmalogen synthesis.

absence of peroxisomes.definition: A cellular state in which peroxisomes are absent or nonfunctional, usually due to defects in peroxisome biogenesis (such as Zellweger spectrum disorders), resulting in impaired beta-oxidation of very long‑chain fatty acids and accumulation of certain lipids, with multi‑organ disease.

zellweger’s syndrome.definition: A severe congenital peroxisome biogenesis disorder caused by biallelic PEX gene mutations, leading to defective peroxisome formation with accumulation of very long‑chain fatty acids and reduced plasmalogens; features include hypotonia, craniofacial dysmorphism, brain abnormalities, hepatic dysfunction, and profound developmental impairment, usually resulting in death in infancy.

eeg.definition: A test that records the brain's electrical activity using electrodes placed on the scalp (or, rarely, intracranially) to assess brain function; commonly used to diagnose and monitor epilepsy and other neurological conditions.

neonatal respiratory distress.definition: A clinical syndrome of abnormal respiration in a newborn, typically presenting with tachypnea, chest retractions, nasal flaring, grunting, and sometimes cyanosis. It results from impaired gas exchange due to various etiologies—most notably surfactant-deficiency (neonatal respiratory distress syndrome)—and also including transient tachypnea of the newborn, pneumonia/sepsis, or meconium aspiration; management is supportive and directed at the underlying cause.

hypotonia.definition: Decreased muscle tone with reduced resistance to passive movement, resulting in a floppy or soft posture; can arise from disorders of the central or peripheral nervous system, neuromuscular junction, or muscles, and may be congenital or acquired.

polycystic kidneys.definition: An inherited disorder in which multiple fluid-filled cysts develop in the kidneys, causing enlargement and progressive loss of renal function; most commonly autosomal dominant transmission, with a rarer autosomal recessive form presenting in infancy. Associated features may include hypertension, flank pain, hematuria, and liver cysts.

glossoptosis.definition: Downward and posterior displacement of the tongue that can cause airway obstruction, commonly seen in Pierre Robin sequence and often associated with micrognathia and cleft palate.

palatal defects.definition: Congenital or acquired abnormalities of the palate (hard and/or soft) resulting in a defect or gap that communicates between the oral and nasal cavities; commonly includes cleft palate and can impair feeding, swallowing, and speech (examples: submucous cleft palate, palatal fistula).

costovertebral abnormalities.definition: Abnormalities of the costovertebral joints—the rib–vertebra articulations (including the costovertebral and costotransverse joints)—encompassing congenital malformations, degenerative or inflammatory changes, trauma, or other pathologic processes that can cause chest wall pain, restricted rib movement, or thoracic cage deformities.

ceruminoma.definition: A tumor of the ceruminous glands of the external auditory canal (ear canal); these tumors can be benign (ceruminous adenoma) or malignant (ceruminous adenocarcinoma), and are usually treated with complete surgical excision.

ceruminosis.definition: A condition characterized by excessive accumulation or impaction of cerumen (earwax) in the external auditory canal, which can cause conductive hearing loss, a sense of fullness, otalgia, tinnitus, and sometimes secondary infection.

ceruminous.definition: Relating to ceruminous glands, the modified apocrine glands of the external ear canal that secrete cerumen (earwax).

cervical.definition: Relating to the neck (cervical region) or to the cervix of the uterus; used to describe structures such as the cervical spine or the cervix uteri.

cervicectomy.definition: The surgical removal of the cervix (the lower part of the uterus), often performed to treat cervical disease; it can be done with the uterus preserved (fertility-sparing) or as part of a hysterectomy.

cervicobrachial.definition: Relating to the neck (cervical region) and the upper limb (brachial); it typically describes pain, numbness, or weakness radiating from the neck into the arm due to cervical nerve root or brachial plexus irritation.

os.definition: A bone; the Latin term for bone used in anatomy to denote a single bone of the skeleton.

disk.definition: A flat, round plate or structure; in anatomy, the intervertebral disk is the fibrocartilaginous cushion between adjacent vertebrae that absorbs shock and allows movement.

dysplasia.definition: Abnormal growth or development of cells within a tissue, characterized by disordered maturation and variation in size, shape, and organization; often used to describe precancerous changes in epithelium that may progress to neoplasia.

erosion.definition: A shallow, superficial loss of the epidermis resulting from rupture or sloughing (often moist and healing without scarring; deeper tissue loss constitutes an ulcer).

papillomavirus.definition: A nonenveloped double-stranded DNA virus of the Papillomaviridae family that infects epithelial cells of the skin and mucous membranes, causing benign warts; some types (high-risk HPVs) are associated with malignant transformation, notably cervical cancer.

papanicolaou.definition: A cervical cancer screening test that collects cells from the cervix for microscopic examination to detect cervical cancer and precancerous lesions; also known as the Pap smear and named after Georgios Papanikolaou.

nabothian.definition: Relating to the mucous-secreting glands of the cervix; describes small mucus-filled cysts that form when these glands become blocked.

conization.definition: A surgical procedure in which a cone-shaped piece of cervical tissue is removed for biopsy or treatment of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia or early cervical cancer; commonly performed by cold-knife conization, loop electrosurgical excision (LEEP), or laser conization.

cone.definition: A photoreceptor cell in the retina responsible for color vision and high-acuity central vision, most densely packed in the fovea and functioning best in bright light.

radium.definition: A highly radioactive alkaline-earth metal (element 88) that was historically used in radiotherapy and luminous paints; exposure poses serious health hazards due to radiation.

implantation.definition: The attachment and embedding of a fertilized ovum into the endometrium, initiating pregnancy; in broader medical use, it can also refer to the surgical placement of a device or tissue into the body.

colposcopy.definition: An examination of the cervix, vagina, and vulva using a colposcope (a magnified, illuminated instrument) after applying acetic acid (and sometimes Lugol's iodine) to highlight abnormal epithelium, with directed biopsies taken if suspicious lesions are seen to diagnose cervical intraepithelial neoplasia or cancer.

colposcopic.definition: Relating to colposcopy; pertaining to or performed with a colposcope to examine the cervix, vagina, and vulva for signs of disease, such as cervical dysplasia.

cytology.definition: The branch of biology that studies the structure, function, and chemistry of cells; in medicine, the examination of individual cells or cell samples from tissues or body fluids to diagnose disease, especially cancer.

cytologic.definition: Relating to cytology, the branch of pathology dealing with the structure and function of cells.

insitu.definition: Describes something located in its original place; confined to its tissue of origin without invasion into neighboring tissues or crossing the basement membrane. In oncology, it refers to pre-invasive lesions that have not invaded underlying tissues.

squamous.definition: Relating to or consisting of flat, scale-like epithelial cells; used to describe epithelium that is made up of flattened cells, such as the outer layer of the skin and the linings of the mouth and esophagus.

paraaortic.definition: Situated beside or near the aorta; used to describe tissues or lymph nodes located adjacent to the abdominal aorta.

leep.definition: A procedure in which a thin, electrically heated wire loop is used to excise and remove abnormal cervical tissue (typically cervical intraepithelial neoplasia or dysplasia), usually performed on an outpatient basis under local anesthesia.

cap.definition: A small gelatin-shell oral dosage form containing a medication, designed to dissolve in the stomach or intestine to release the drug.

endocervix.definition: The inner portion of the cervix forming the endocervical canal, lined by simple columnar epithelium and containing endocervical glands, extending from the internal os to the external os.

endocervical.definition: Relating to the endocervix, the mucous membrane lining the cervical canal of the uterus.

speculum.definition: A medical instrument with hinged blades that are inserted closed and then opened to dilate and hold open a body cavity (most commonly the vagina) to permit visual inspection and access for examination or procedure.

swab.definition: A small, sterile, absorbent pad or stick (often cotton-tipped on a plastic or wooden handle) used to collect a specimen from a body surface for laboratory testing; also the act of collecting such a specimen by wiping the surface.

sperm.definition: The sex cell produced by males.

horner.definition: Disruption of the sympathetic nerve pathways supplying the eye and face, producing ptosis (drooping eyelid), miosis (constricted pupil), and often facial anhidrosis; may result from lesions along the oculosympathetic tract (e.g., carotid artery dissection, apical lung tumor) or other etiologies.

cervicalspine.definition: The part of the spine located in the neck and consisting of the top seven vertebrae.

spine.definition: Protects your spinal cord and allows you to stand and bend. Also known as backbone.

vertebral.definition: Relating to a vertebra or to the vertebral column (the spine).

plexus.definition: A network or braid of intersecting nerves, blood vessels, or lymphatic vessels.

brachial.definition: Relating to the arm, especially the upper arm.

cervicaldisk.definition: A fibrocartilaginous cushion between adjacent cervical vertebral bodies that absorbs shock and enables motion; degeneration, herniation, or bulging can compress cervical nerve roots or the spinal cord.

cervicalradiculopathy.definition: A pinched nerve, causing sharp pain, tingling, and numbness in the areas served by the nerve.

cervicalcanal.definition: An anatomical passage through the cervix that connects the uterine cavity to the vagina; lined by mucous-secreting endocervical epithelium and containing cervical glands, with its lumen bounded by the internal and external os.

headtraction.definition: A method of applying a controlled pulling force to the skull to align or stabilize the cervical spine or reduce craniovertebral injuries, usually accomplished with a halo ring or skull pins (halo traction).

triangle.definition: A polygon with three straight sides and three interior angles. In anatomy, a triangular region bounded by specific landmarks or muscles (e.g., the triangle of auscultation on the back).

cesarean.definition: A surgical delivery in which a baby is delivered through incisions in the mother's abdomen and uterus.

postmortem.definition: Occurring after death; in medical use, the examination of a body after death to determine the cause of death (an autopsy).

section.definition: A thin slice of tissue cut from a specimen for microscopic examination; also the act of cutting or a portion cut from a structure.

coccygeal.definition: Pertaining to the coccyx (tailbone), the small bone at the base of the spine; used to describe the tailbone region or its nerves.

lumbar.definition: Relating to the lower back; the lumbar region of the spine between the thoracic and sacral regions, typically consisting of five lumbar vertebrae (L1–L5).

sacral.definition: Relating to the sacrum, the large triangular bone at the base of the spine formed by the fusion of five sacral vertebrae; used to describe the region between the lumbar spine and the coccyx.

humanimmunodeficiencyvirus.definition: An enveloped RNA retrovirus that infects and depletes CD4+ T lymphocytes, causing progressive immune deficiency; transmitted via blood, semen, vaginal secretions, breast milk, and mother-to-child transmission; without treatment, infection progresses to Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS), increasing the risk of opportunistic infections and certain cancers. Antiretroviral therapy can suppress viral replication and preserve immune function.

cervicalcancer.definition: Cancer that begins in the cervix, the lower part of the uterus that opens into the vagina. It most commonly arises after persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), often developing from precancerous cervical cell changes detectable by screening.

cervicalpolyp.definition: A benign, usually pedunculated growth arising from the endocervical canal of the cervix, often presenting with vaginal discharge or light bleeding; typically removed with a simple polypectomy or avulsion and examined histologically to exclude malignancy.

genitalwart.definition: Genital warts are soft, wart-like growths on the genital or anal area caused by infection with human papillomavirus (HPV), most commonly types 6 or 11; they are sexually transmitted and may be treated with topical agents, cryotherapy, or other procedures.

cervicoplasty.definition: A surgical procedure to repair or reconstruct the cervix (the neck of the uterus), often performed to correct cervical deformities or damage from trauma or previous procedures and to restore cervical function.

cervicothoracic.definition: Relating to the region where the cervical (neck) and thoracic (upper back) portions of the spine meet, at the cervicothoracic junction (approximately the C7–T1 level).

cervicotomy.definition: A surgical incision into the neck to expose cervical structures (e.g., thyroid, larynx, trachea, esophagus, or cervical lymph nodes) for diagnostic or therapeutic procedures.

cervicouterine.definition: Relating to both the cervix and the uterus; describing structures or regions at the cervix–uterine junction, such as where the cervical canal meets the uterine cavity.

cervicovaginitis.definition: Inflammation of both the cervix and the vagina, typically presenting with vaginal discharge and irritation; causes include infections (eg, Candida, Trichomonas, bacterial vaginosis–associated organisms) and noninfectious irritants, with treatment aimed at the underlying etiology.

cervicovesical.definition: Relating to the cervix of the uterus and the urinary bladder.

supravaginal.definition: Anatomical term meaning located above the vagina.

parametrium.definition: A fibrous and fatty connective tissue region adjacent to the cervix and uterus, extending to the pelvic sidewalls within the broad ligament; it contains the uterine and vaginal vessels, lymphatics, and autonomic nerves and helps anchor and support the uterus via the cardinal (transverse cervical) ligaments.

uterinearteries.definition: Arteries supplying the uterus; branches of the internal iliac arteries that travel in the broad ligament to the uterus and give rise to arcuate arteries in the myometrium and radial arteries that form the straight and spiral arteries of the endometrium, with anastomoses to the ovarian arteries.

effacement.definition: A process in which a tissue or organ becomes thinner and shorter; in obstetrics, the cervix thins and shortens as labor approaches, enabling it to dilate.

cervicodynia.definition: Neck pain localized to the cervical region, often due to strain or cervical spine disorders (such as degenerative changes, disc disease, facet arthropathy) or nerve irritation; may be acute or chronic.

cervicogenic.definition: Relating to or arising from the cervical spine (neck); used to describe pain or disorders that originate in the neck, sometimes radiating to the head or shoulders.

dorsalgia.definition: Pain located in the back (the dorsal region); a symptom that may arise from musculoskeletal strain, spinal conditions, or referred visceral pain.

cervicogenicheadache.definition: Headache related to neck problems. Also called cervical headache.

cervicolabial.definition: Not a standard medical term. If interpreted literally, cervicolabial would mean relating to both the cervix and the labia (the external genital lip tissues); it could be used to describe findings or anatomy involving both regions, though this usage is uncommon.

stellateganglion.definition: A fused inferior cervical and first thoracic sympathetic ganglion in the cervicothoracic region that provides sympathetic innervation to the face, neck, and upper limb (located near the C7–T1 level); it can be blocked or ablated to treat pain and vasomotor disorders such as complex regional pain syndrome and vasospasm.

cestode.definition: A tapeworm; a parasitic flatworm of the class Cestoda that resides in the vertebrate intestine, characterized by a scolex for attachment, a chain of proglottids, lacks a digestive system, and absorbs nutrients through its tegument.

cestodiasis.definition: Infection with tapeworms (cestodes), usually affecting the intestines, acquired by ingesting tapeworm eggs or larvae in undercooked meat or contaminated food, treated with antihelminthic medications such as praziquantel or albendazole.

cestoid.definition: Pertaining to cestodes (tapeworms), parasitic flatworms that inhabit the digestive tract of vertebrates and absorb nutrients through their tegument.

cetuximab.definition: A chimeric monoclonal antibody that binds the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) on tumor cells, inhibiting ligand binding and downstream signaling; used in the treatment of certain cancers such as metastatic colorectal cancer and squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck.

irinotecan.definition: A chemotherapy drug, a semi-synthetic camptothecin analogue that inhibits topoisomerase I; administered intravenously as a prodrug converted to the active metabolite SN-38, and used to treat colorectal cancer and other malignancies.

epidermalgrowthfactorreceptor.definition: An extracellular, transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase that binds epidermal growth factor; ligand binding induces dimerization and autophosphorylation, activating downstream signaling (RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT) that promotes cell proliferation and survival; overexpression or mutation is associated with several cancers.

metastaticcolorectalcarcinoma.definition: A colorectal adenocarcinoma that has spread from the primary site in the colon or rectum to distant organs (most commonly the liver or lungs) via blood or lymphatic routes.

dryskin.definition: A condition in which the skin lacks adequate moisture, leading to dry, rough, flaky, and sometimes itchy skin; commonly due to environmental factors, excessive washing or hot water, aging, and impaired skin barrier; managed with regular emollients, gentle cleansers, avoiding irritants, and protection from further moisture loss.

toxicepidermalnecrolysis.definition: A life-threatening adverse drug reaction characterized by widespread epidermal necrosis with full-thickness skin detachment and mucous membrane involvement, typically affecting more than 30% of body surface area; belongs to the Stevens–Johnson syndrome spectrum and often presents with a positive Nikolsky sign.

renalfailure.definition: Kidney failure is the loss of kidney function, resulting in an inability to adequately filter waste from the blood and to regulate fluids, electrolytes, and acid–base balance; it can be acute (sudden) or chronic (progressive and usually irreversible).

interstitiallungdisease.definition: A broad group of diseases characterized by inflammation and/or fibrosis of the lung interstitium, causing progressive dyspnea and dry cough with impaired gas exchange; includes idiopathic forms (such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis) and numerous secondary forms from environmental exposures, autoimmune diseases, or medications.

pulmonaryembolus.definition: An obstruction of the pulmonary arterial system by a thrombus or other embolic material (most often a venous thrombus that traveled from the legs), leading to impaired pulmonary blood flow and gas exchange with symptoms such as sudden onset dyspnea and chest pain.

mouthulceration.definition: Ulceration of the oral mucosa characterized by painful open sores inside the mouth; causes include local trauma, aphthous stomatitis (canker sores), infections, medications, nutritional deficiencies, and certain systemic diseases; management is usually supportive with topical analgesics or antiseptics and treatment of any underlying cause.

abdominalpain.definition: Pain or discomfort localized to the abdomen, arising from abdominal organs (eg, GI tract, liver, pancreas, kidneys), the abdominal wall, or less commonly referred from other areas. It can be acute or chronic and varies in location, quality, and intensity. Evaluation focuses on onset, duration, associated symptoms, and red flags for serious illness.

cellulitis.definition: An infection of your skin and the cells underneath.

cysts.definition: Pus or other liquid under your skin.

backpain.definition: Pain localized to the back (thoracic or lumbar) that may result from musculoskeletal strain, disc or joint degeneration, nerve compression, or referred pain; most episodes are nonspecific, self-limited, and improve with time and conservative care, but persistent, progressive, or associated symptoms (fever, weight loss, numbness, weakness, or bowel/bladder changes) require medical evaluation.

peripheraledema.definition: A swelling of the limbs (typically the feet and ankles) due to excess fluid accumulating in the interstitial space; usually caused by conditions that impair venous return or fluid balance, such as heart failure, liver or kidney disease, venous insufficiency, or lymphatic obstruction; may be pitting or non-pitting.

cetirizine.definition: A second-generation oral antihistamine that acts as a selective peripheral H1 receptor antagonist. It is used to relieve symptoms of allergic rhinitis and chronic urticaria, and it has less sedative potential than first-generation antihistamines due to limited ability to cross the blood–brain barrier.

cetylalcohol.definition: A long-chain fatty alcohol (hexadecanol, C16H33OH) derived from natural fats (such as coconut or palm oil) and used in cosmetics as an emollient, thickener, and stabilizer to improve texture and viscosity of creams and lotions.

cetylpalmitate.definition: A wax ester derived from cetyl alcohol and palmitic acid; used in cosmetics as an emollient and thickener to soften the skin and improve texture and slip.

cetylpyridiniumchloride.definition: A cationic quaternary ammonium compound with antiseptic and antimicrobial properties, commonly used in oral care products (mouthwashes, rinses, and lozenges) to reduce plaque and gingivitis, and as a topical disinfectant in various products.

cevimeline.definition: A muscarinic receptor agonist used to treat xerostomia (dry mouth), especially in Sjögren's syndrome; it stimulates salivary and lacrimal gland secretion by activating M3 receptors.

sjogrenssyndrome.definition: A disease the glands that make tears and saliva don't work well. This makes your eyes and mouth dry.

cysticfibrosis.definition: A hereditary autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene that impair chloride transport, leading to thick mucus in the lungs and digestive tract and causing recurrent respiratory infections and pancreatic insufficiency.

chaddockreflex.definition: A Babinski-like plantar reflex produced by stroking the lateral aspect of the foot (from heel toward the little toe); the big toe extends with fanning of the other toes, indicating upper motor neuron dysfunction of the corticospinal tract.

babinskireflex.definition: A plantar reflex in which stroking the lateral sole causes extension of the big toe (dorsiflexion) and fanning of the other toes; normal in healthy infants but in adults indicates corticospinal (upper motor neuron) tract dysfunction.

oppenheimreflex.definition: An upper motor neuron sign similar to Babinski, produced by stroking the anterior edge of the tibia from knee to ankle; it causes dorsiflexion of the great toe with fanning of the other toes, indicating corticospinal tract dysfunction.

babinskisreflex.definition: Stroking the lateral sole elicits dorsiflexion of the big toe with fanning of the other toes; a positive sign indicates an upper motor neuron lesion in adults, while a similar response can be normal in infants up to about 1–2 years.

chaddocksign.definition: A Babinski‑like plantar reflex produced by stroking the lateral aspect of the foot (around the lateral malleolus), causing dorsiflexion of the great toe with fanning of the other toes; indicates an upper motor neuron (corticospinal tract) lesion.

pyramidaltractdisease.definition: A condition in which pathology affects the pyramidal tracts (corticospinal and corticobulbar pathways), producing upper motor neuron signs such as spastic weakness, increased muscle tone, hyperreflexia, clonus, and Babinski sign.

typhoidfever.definition: A systemic infection caused by Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi, transmitted through ingestion of food or water contaminated with feces; presents with prolonged high fever, malaise, abdominal pain, headache, and sometimes rose spots; can lead to serious complications such as intestinal hemorrhage or perforation; treated with appropriate antibiotics and preventable by vaccination and improved sanitation.

chadwick's sign.definition: A bluish-purple discoloration of the cervix, vagina, and vulva caused by increased pelvic vascularity in early pregnancy, usually detectable by about 6–8 weeks gestation.

vaginal mucosa.definition: The mucous membrane lining the vagina, formed by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium over a vascular lamina propria; it provides a protective barrier and lubrication and is estrogen-responsive in thickness and keratinization.

cervical mucosa.definition: The mucous membrane lining the cervix (cervix uteri), comprising nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium in the ectocervix and mucus-secreting simple columnar epithelium in the endocervical canal, forming the cervical canal and producing cervical mucus.

trypanosoma cruzi.definition: A flagellated protozoan parasite transmitted by triatomine bugs (kissing bugs) that causes American trypanosomiasis (Chagas disease), with an acute febrile illness and potential chronic cardiomyopathy and gastrointestinal manifestations such as megaesophagus or megacolon.

romana sign.definition: Unilateral periorbital edema with swelling around the eye (often with conjunctival injection) that occurs after inoculation of Trypanosoma cruzi via the conjunctiva; a classic sign of acute Chagas disease.

enlarged spleen.definition: An abnormal enlargement of the spleen, typically defined as a spleen exceeding normal size on imaging (often >12 cm in length) or palpable below the left costal margin; causes include infections, liver disease with portal hypertension, hematologic disorders, malignancy, and infiltrative or inflammatory conditions.

dilatation of esophagus.definition: An abnormal enlargement of the esophageal lumen (megaesophagus) due to impaired esophageal motility or distal outflow obstruction, often with food stasis and possible regurgitation.

dilatation of colon.definition: Abnormal enlargement or widening of the colon (colonic dilatation), usually from distention due to accumulation of gas and fluid when colonic motility is reduced or there is obstructive or inflammatory process; can be seen in megacolon or toxic megacolon.

nifurtimox.definition: A nitrofuran antiparasitic used to treat Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis) caused by Trypanosoma cruzi; activated within the parasite to form reactive nitro radicals that damage macromolecules and kill the parasite. Common adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset and central nervous system symptoms.

benznidazole.definition: A nitroimidazole antiparasitic agent used to treat Trypanosoma cruzi infection (Chagas disease). It is a prodrug activated by parasite nitroreductases, generating reactive metabolites that damage parasite DNA and proteins, leading to parasite death.

brazilian trypanosomiasis.definition: An infection caused by the protozoan parasite Trypanosoma cruzi (American trypanosomiasis/Chagas disease), transmitted mainly by triatomine bugs and endemic in Brazil. The acute phase is often mild or febrile and may present with Romaña sign (periorbital swelling); chronic infection can cause cardiomyopathy, heart failure, and gastrointestinal megasyndromes such as megacolon or megaesophagus. Transmission can also occur congenitally, via blood transfusion or organ transplantation, or by ingesting contaminated food.

chagas-cruz disease.definition: Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis) is a tropical parasitic infection caused by the protozoan Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted primarily by triatomine bugs; the acute phase is usually mild or asymptomatic, while chronic infection can cause cardiomyopathy, megacolon, and megaesophagus, and antiparasitic treatment (benznidazole or nifurtimox) is most effective in the acute or early chronic phase.

cruz trypanosomiasis.definition: An infection caused by the protozoan Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted primarily by triatomine (kissing) bugs and, less commonly, congenitally, by blood transfusion, organ transplantation, or ingestion of contaminated food. The acute phase is often mild or asymptomatic, while the chronic phase can lead to cardiomyopathy, heart failure, arrhythmias, megacolon, and megaesophagus; acute infection may present with Romana’s sign.

south american trypanosomiasis.definition: A parasitic disease caused by the protozoan Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted mainly by triatomine (kissing) bugs. It has an acute phase that is often mild and a chronic phase that can lead to cardiomyopathy, heart rhythm abnormalities, and gastrointestinal megasyndromes (megacolon, megaesophagus); transmission can also occur congenitally, via blood transfusion, organ transplantation, or ingestion of contaminated food.

chagres fever.definition: A historical term for yellow fever, an acute viral hemorrhagic fever transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes; presents with sudden fever, headache, back pain, and sometimes jaundice and bleeding; incubation ~3–6 days; prevented by vaccination; no specific antiviral therapy.

panama fever.definition: A historical term for malaria acquired in Panama, especially during the canal-building era; caused by Plasmodium species and transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes, presenting with recurrent fever, chills, headache, and malaise.

phlebotomus.definition: A genus of Old World sandflies (phlebotomine flies) in the family Psychodidae; small blood-feeding insects that serve as vectors for Leishmania parasites causing leishmaniasis.

muscle pains.definition: Pain or tenderness in a muscle.

giddiness.definition: A nonspecific sensation of lightheadedness or unsteadiness, sometimes with vertigo (a spinning sensation).

chancroid.definition: A sexually transmitted bacterial infection caused by Haemophilus ducreyi, characterized by painful genital ulcers with ragged borders and tender inguinal lymphadenopathy.

haemophilus ducreyi.definition: A Gram-negative, fastidious, pleomorphic coccobacillus that causes chancroid (soft chancre), a sexually transmitted infection characterized by painful genital ulcers and tender inguinal lymphadenopathy.

treponema pallidum.definition: A slender, helical, Gram-negative–like spirochete bacterium and the etiologic agent of syphilis; transmitted sexually or perinatally; difficult to culture in standard media and diagnosed by serology or dark-field microscopy.

lymphogranuloma venereum.definition: A sexually transmitted infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1–L3, presenting initially as a transient genital or anorectal ulcer followed by painful inguinal/femoral lymphadenopathy (buboes); anorectal LGV may cause proctitis with discharge, bleeding, and tenesmus.

intradermal skin test.definition: A diagnostic procedure in which a small amount of antigen is injected into the dermis to elicit a localized immune response, assessed by the size of induration (wheal) after 48–72 hours; used for tuberculin skin testing and certain allergy evaluations.

venereal ulcer.definition: An ulcer of the genital region arising from a sexually transmitted infection; most classically the painless chancre of primary syphilis, though historically the term has been used for other venereal ulcers such as chancroid.

chantix.definition: A prescription smoking cessation medication (varenicline) that acts as a selective partial agonist at the α4β2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, reducing nicotine withdrawal symptoms and blocking the rewarding effects of nicotine; used to help people quit smoking.

varenicline.definition: A prescription smoking-cessation medication that acts as a selective partial agonist at brain alpha-4 beta-2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, reducing nicotine withdrawal symptoms and blocking nicotine’s rewarding effects.

chaotic atrial tachycardia.definition: A rapid atrial tachyarrhythmia caused by multiple ectopic atrial foci, resulting in disorganized atrial activity with an irregular ventricular rhythm; P waves show multiple morphologies (usually at least three distinct forms) and PR intervals are irregular, commonly occurring in structural heart disease or pulmonary/Electrolyte disturbances, and often considered synonymous with multifocal atrial tachycardia.

multifocal atrial tachycardia.definition: An atrial tachycardia with irregular rhythm and at least three different P‑wave morphologies, arising from multiple ectopic atrial foci; QRS complexes are typically normal in duration and the rate is usually >100 bpm.

chaparral.definition: An herbal supplement derived from the leaves and resin of the creosote bush (Larrea tridentata); used in traditional medicine for various ailments, but with little evidence of benefit and a risk of severe liver toxicity, attributed in part to nordihydroguaiaretic acid (NDGA).

chamaemelum nobile.definition: A perennial flowering plant (Roman chamomile) whose flowers are used medicinally in herbal remedies, commonly as tea or essential oil for digestive upset, mild inflammatory conditions, and gentle calming/sleep support.

chamomile.definition: An herb (Matricaria chamomilla or Chamaemelum nobile) whose dried flowers are used as a mild sedative and anti-inflammatory remedy; commonly consumed as tea for insomnia and digestive upset; may cause allergic reactions in people with ragweed or Asteraceae allergies and can interact with certain medications.

magnesium.definition: A vital divalent mineral (Mg2+) that serves as a cofactor for hundreds of enzymatic reactions and is essential for energy production, protein synthesis, nerve and muscle function, and bone health. Deficiency can cause neuromuscular irritability and cardiac arrhythmias; clinically administered as magnesium salts (e.g., magnesium sulfate) for supplementation and certain medical indications such as preeclampsia.

intravenous fluid.definition: Sterile fluid solution given directly into a vein to restore intravascular volume and electrolyte balance; includes crystalloids (e.g., normal saline, lactated Ringer's) and colloids, used for hydration, resuscitation, and maintenance or perioperative fluid management.

chalice cell.definition: A mucus-secreting unicellular epithelial cell found in mucous membranes; it has a goblet- or chalice-shaped appearance, with a narrow base and an expanded apical region packed with mucin-containing granules.

chalasia.definition: Relaxation or dilation of a smooth muscle or sphincter.

esophageal.definition: Relating to the esophagus, the muscular tube that transports food and liquids from the pharynx to the stomach through peristaltic contractions.

chamberlain's line.definition: A radiographic line drawn on a lateral skull radiograph from the posterior edge of the hard palate to the opisthion (posterior margin of the foramen magnum), used to assess basilar invagination or craniovertebral junction alignment; if the odontoid tip projects above this line, basilar invagination is suspected.

chamberlen forceps.definition: A historic obstetric instrument—an early type of vaginal delivery forceps developed by the Chamberlen family in the 17th century, used to grasp and guide the fetal head during birth; largely superseded by modern forceps.

chamfer.definition: A finishing line used in dental crown preparations characterized by a shallow, sloped bevel at the margin to create a smooth, rounded edge for seating the restoration.

crown restoration.definition: A dental restoration in which a prepared tooth is covered by a crown (cap) to restore its size, strength, and appearance; the crown encases the visible portion of the tooth and is cemented in place, with materials including metal, porcelain-fused-to-metal, all-ceramic, or resin.

charcot-bouchard aneurysm.definition: A small hypertensive microaneurysm of a penetrating cerebral artery that, when ruptured, causes intraparenchymal intracerebral hemorrhage—most often in the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, or cerebellum.

charcot-leyden crystal.definition: An eosinophil-derived crystalline protein (galectin-10) that forms hexagonal bipyramidal crystals in mucus, sputum, or tissue during eosinophilic inflammation; commonly associated with asthma and parasitic infections and indicates eosinophil activation but is not disease-specific.

charcot-marie-tooth disease.definition: An inherited motor and sensory peripheral neuropathy characterized by slowly progressive distal weakness and atrophy, sensory loss, and decreased reflexes, often with pes cavus foot deformities, typically beginning in adolescence or early adulthood (demyelinating or axonal subtypes).

charcot's fever.definition: Not a standard term in modern medicine; historically used to describe fever seen in association with Charcot joints (neuropathic arthropathy), but it has no accepted current medical definition.

charcot's foot.definition: A progressive neuropathic arthropathy of the foot and ankle due to peripheral neuropathy (most commonly diabetes), characterized by loss of protective sensation and autonomic dysfunction leading to inflammation, bone resorption, and joint destruction; results in swelling, deformity (often rocker-bottom foot), instability, and a high risk of ulcers and amputation.

polypeptide chain.definition: A polymer of amino acids linked by peptide bonds, forming a single linear chain that can fold into a functional protein; proteins typically consist of one or more polypeptide chains.

membrane channels.definition: Integral membrane proteins that form hydrophilic pores in the lipid bilayer, permitting selective diffusion of ions and small molecules down their electrochemical gradients. Many are gated (voltage-gated, ligand-gated, mechanically gated, or leak channels) and are essential for electrical signaling, osmotic regulation, and various cellular processes.

chalicosis.definition: A pneumoconiosis caused by inhalation of chalk or lime dust (calcium carbonate), characterized by nodular interstitial fibrosis of the lungs in workers exposed to calcareous dust.

chalazion.definition: A chronic, sterile granulomatous inflammation of a meibomian gland in the eyelid, due to duct obstruction, presenting as a painless eyelid lump.

hordeolum.definition: A painful, acute infection of the eyelid margin involving an eyelash follicle or meibomian gland, most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

sty.definition: An acute infection of an eyelash follicle or eyelid gland at the lid margin, presenting as a painful, red, swollen lump (hordeolum), most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus; usually managed with warm compresses, lid hygiene, and, if indicated, topical antibiotics.

charcot's joint.definition: A progressive, neurogenic arthropathy caused by peripheral neuropathy with loss of protective sensation, leading to repeated trauma, joint destruction, dislocation, and deformity—most commonly affecting the foot and ankle in diabetes.

cheilectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove dorsal bone spurs (osteophytes) and a portion of the dorsal articular surface of the first metatarsophalangeal joint to relieve impingement and improve range of motion, most commonly performed for hallux rigidus.

neuropathic joint disease.definition: Progressive degenerative and deforming arthritis caused by loss of protective sensation (peripheral neuropathy), leading to repeated unnoticed trauma, inflammation, osteolysis, and rapid joint destruction with instability; commonly affects the foot and ankle and is known as Charcot joint or neuropathic arthropathy.

charcot's triad.definition: Fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain, a classic triad seen in acute cholangitis.

intention tremor.definition: A kinetic tremor that worsens as the limb approaches a target during purposeful movement, typically due to cerebellar dysfunction; it is usually absent at rest.

scanning speech.definition: A dysarthric speech pattern typical of cerebellar disease in which speech is slow and segmented, with irregular timing and pauses between syllables; syllables are pronounced with equal, stressed emphasis, giving a “scanned” or staccato rhythm.

charge association.definition: A congenital condition historically described as a nonrandom association of multiple anomalies, classically including coloboma, congenital heart defects, choanal atresia, growth retardation or developmental delay, genital anomalies, and ear anomalies/deafness; largely now referred to as CHARGE syndrome, often due to CHD7 gene mutations with variable expression.

coloboma.definition: A congenital defect due to failure of the embryonic choroidal fissure to close, resulting in missing tissue in ocular structures (most commonly the iris, but it can involve the retina, choroid, or optic nerve), often presenting as a notch or keyhole-shaped pupil.

heart anomaly.definition: An abnormality of the heart's structure or function, which may be congenital or acquired, including malformations of the chambers or valves, septal defects, or abnormalities of the great vessels, potentially affecting blood flow or rhythm.

choanal atresia.definition: A congenital condition in which the internal nasal openings (choanae) are blocked by bone or membranous tissue, due to failure of recanalization during development; can be unilateral or bilateral, with bilateral cases causing significant neonatal respiratory distress.

retardation.definition: The act or condition of slowing, delaying, or reducing the rate of progress, development, or function.

genital anomalies.definition: Genital anomalies are congenital or developmental abnormalities of the genital organs (external and/or internal reproductive structures) that result in atypical anatomy or function; they may be present at birth or develop later and can affect males, females, or present as ambiguous genitalia.

ear anomalies.definition: Congenital malformations of the external ear (pinna) resulting from abnormal embryologic development, ranging from minor variants such as preauricular tags or pits to more severe defects like microtia or anotia, and may be associated with canal abnormalities and hearing impairment.

charge-coupled device.definition: A solid-state imaging sensor consisting of an array of photosensitive pixels that convert incoming light into electrical charge; the charge is serially transferred through the array to a readout register and converted to a voltage signal, producing a digital image.

charge-coupled image sensor.definition: A solid-state digital image sensor in which incoming light is converted into electrical charges at photosensitive sites; these charge packets are moved across the chip by clocked electrodes to a readout register and then converted to a voltage signal for image formation.

intraoral sensor.definition: A digital radiography detector placed inside the mouth to capture intraoral dental X-ray images; it converts X-ray photons into an electronic signal for display on a computer, enabling bitewing and periapical radiographs. Common forms include solid-state CCD/CMOS sensors and wireless or wired detectors.

charley horse.definition: An abrupt, involuntary contraction of a muscle (a muscle cramp), most commonly in the calf, thigh, or foot, causing sudden sharp pain and a temporary inability to relax the involved muscle.

chauffeur's fracture.definition: An intra-articular distal radius fracture with avulsion of the radial styloid (radial styloid fragment), typically caused by forced dorsiflexion/extension of the wrist from a direct impact with a steering wheel.

chaussier's areola.definition: A historical anatomical term for the pigmented circular area surrounding the nipple of the breast (the areola); not commonly used in modern texts.

chédiak-higashi syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal recessive lysosomal trafficking disorder caused by mutations in the LYST gene, leading to defective lysosome formation and impaired phagocytic function; clinically characterized by oculocutaneous albinism, recurrent pyogenic infections, giant granules in leukocytes, impaired pathogen killing, and progressive neurologic deterioration (often with bleeding diathesis).

cheek.definition: A fleshy region of the face on each side between the eye and the ear; the buccal region that contains skin, subcutaneous fat, and the buccinator muscle.

cheekbone.definition: A paired facial bone that forms the prominence of the cheek (malar eminence) and part of the orbit; it articulates with the maxilla, frontal bone, sphenoid, and temporal bone.

cheilorrhaphy.definition: Surgical suturing of the lip; repair of a lip wound or deformity (lip reconstruction).

cheiloplasty.definition: Surgical repair or reconstruction of the lips, performed to correct deformities from trauma, disease, or congenital conditions (such as cleft lip); may involve tissue rearrangement and vermilion reconstruction.

cheiloangioscopy.definition: Endoscopic visualization of the blood vessels in the lips to assess lip vasculature and vascular lesions.
