cheilocarcinoma.definition: A malignant tumor of the lip, most often squamous cell carcinoma arising from the lip mucosa (usually the lower lip); presents as a non-healing ulcer or indurated lesion and is associated with sun exposure and tobacco use, treated with surgical excision (often Mohs surgery) and/or radiotherapy.

cheilocarcinomata.definition: Malignant neoplasms arising from the epithelium of the lip (most often squamous cell carcinomas), typically on the lower lip; associated with sun exposure and tobacco use; present as nonhealing ulcers or firm, indurated masses; treated with surgical excision (including Mohs micrographic surgery), radiation therapy, or a combination.

cheirognostic.definition: Relating to palmistry; the practice of predicting a person’s health, character, or future from the lines and features of the hand.

cheiromegaly.definition: Enlargement of the hand, especially the palm and fingers, typically due to excess growth hormone as seen in acromegaly or gigantism.

cheiroplasty.definition: A surgical procedure to repair or reconstruct the hand, often to correct deformities or restore function after injury or congenital abnormalities.

chelate.definition: A chemical complex in which a metal ion is bound by a multidentate ligand at two or more donor sites, forming a ring-like, more stable complex.

chelating agent.definition: A substance that binds metal ions to form stable, soluble complexes (chelates), thereby increasing their solubility and enabling their removal from the body or a system; used in the treatment of heavy metal poisoning and in various industrial and medical applications.

chelation.definition: A treatment that removes lead from your body if your blood lead levels are very high.

chelation therapy.definition: A medical treatment in which a chelating agent binds to metals in the body to form water-soluble complexes that are excreted in urine or bile, used mainly to treat heavy metal poisoning and related metal overload conditions.

cheloid.definition: A benign scar that grows beyond the boundaries of a skin injury due to excessive collagen formation during healing; typically raised, firm, and may be pink, red, or darker, and can be itchy or tender with a tendency to recur after removal.

keloidosis.definition: A condition characterized by abnormal, excessive scar formation after skin injury, with raised, firm scars (keloids) that extend beyond the wound boundaries due to overproduction of collagen.

chemabrasion.definition: A cosmetic procedure that combines chemical exfoliation with mechanical dermabrasion to remove damaged skin layers and stimulate dermal remodeling, typically used to treat scarring, deep wrinkles, and pigmentary changes; carries risks of scarring, infection, pigment alteration, and requires skilled supervision.

chemical indicator.definition: A reagent that produces a measurable signal (often a color change) in response to a specific chemical condition, analyte, or reaction, used to indicate presence, amount, or completion of a process.

chemical mediator.definition: A molecule released by cells that influences the function of other cells, coordinating physiological or inflammatory responses (examples include cytokines, histamine, prostaglandins, and leukotrienes).

chemical peel.definition: A chemical solution applied to the skin to cause it to blister and peel, revealing a new layer of skin; treatment is used to improve the appearance of the skin, reducing lines, wrinkles, age spots, and other problems.

alpha-hydroxy acid.definition: A class of water-soluble organic acids in which a hydroxyl group is on the carbon next to the carboxyl group; used in dermatology and cosmetics for chemical exfoliation of the stratum corneum by loosening intercellular bonds between keratinocytes, improving skin texture, tone, and hydration. Common examples include glycolic acid and lactic acid.

glycolic acid.definition: A simple alpha-hydroxy acid derived from sugar cane that serves as an exfoliant by promoting desquamation of the stratum corneum; used in skincare products and chemical peels in various concentrations; may cause irritation and photosensitivity.

retinol.definition: Vitamin A, an important vitamin in how well you see and grow.

jessner's solution.definition: A chemical peel solution consisting of resorcinol, salicylic acid, and lactic acid (typically 14% each) dissolved in an alcoholic solvent, used to produce superficial to medium-depth skin exfoliation.

beta hydroxy acid.definition: A class of organic carboxylic acids in which a hydroxyl group is attached to the beta carbon relative to the carboxyl group; in dermatology, BHAs (notably salicylic acid) are oil-soluble keratolytic exfoliants that penetrate pores to help unclog hair follicles.

tissue culture.definition: The growth and maintenance of cells, tissues, or organs outside the body under sterile conditions in a nutrient medium (in vitro).

antimicrobial drugs.definition: Agents that kill or inhibit the growth of microorganisms (bacteria, fungi, viruses, and parasites) and are used to treat infectious diseases. They include antibiotics, antifungals, antivirals, and antiparasitic drugs, and can be bactericidal or bacteriostatic depending on the drug and organism.

chemical peritonitis.definition: Inflammation of the peritoneum caused by chemical irritation from noninfectious substances (e.g., bile, pancreatic enzymes, gastric contents, urine, or irritants) in the peritoneal cavity; typically aseptic, though secondary infection can occur.

chemoprevention.definition: Using drugs or chemicals to prevent cancer.

chemoprophylaxis.definition: Administration of a medication to prevent infection or disease in people at risk, given before or after exposure to a pathogen to reduce the likelihood of disease.

chemoprotectant.definition: A substance administered to protect normal tissues from the toxic effects of chemotherapy or radiation, thereby reducing treatment-related toxicity; mechanisms include radical scavenging, DNA repair support, or metabolic rescue of healthy cells.

chemoradiotherapy.definition: A cancer treatment that combines chemotherapy with radiation therapy, usually given concurrently, with chemotherapy acting as a radiosensitizer to enhance tumor kill and address potential systemic disease.

chemoreceptor.definition: An afferent sensory receptor that responds to chemical changes in body fluids (notably oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH) and relays signals to regulate respiration and other autonomic reflexes.

chemoreflex.definition: An autonomic reflex initiated by stimulation of peripheral and central chemoreceptors in response to changes in blood gas composition (notably CO2, O2, and pH), producing adjustments in ventilation and, to a lesser extent, cardiovascular activity to restore arterial gas levels.

chemoresistance.definition: A phenomenon in which cancer cells become resistant to the cytotoxic effects of chemotherapy, either innately or during treatment, through mechanisms such as increased drug efflux, drug inactivation, target alteration, enhanced DNA repair, evasion of apoptosis, and changes in the tumor microenvironment.

chemosis.definition: Edema of the conjunctiva producing swelling of the conjunctival tissue, often with a gelatinous, translucent appearance; commonly due to allergic conjunctivitis, irritation, or inflammation.

conjunctival edema.definition: Swelling of the conjunctiva due to fluid accumulation in the ocular surface tissue, often referred to as chemosis; commonly caused by inflammation from allergy, infection, irritation, or trauma.

bright's disease.definition: A historical term for nephritis—an inflammatory kidney disease, typically glomerulonephritis—characterized by edema and proteinuria (albuminuria), often with hypertension; today this umbrella label is replaced by specific diagnoses such as acute or chronic glomerulonephritis.

chemical sympathectomy.definition: A procedure in which a chemical neurolytic agent (e.g., phenol or alcohol) is injected to destroy or block sympathetic nerve fibers in a targeted region, producing denervation of sympathetic outflow and relief of sympathetically maintained pain or vasospastic symptoms.

chemical restraint.definition: A pharmacologic intervention in which medications are used to restrict a patient’s movement or behavior, usually to prevent harm or facilitate care in agitated or violent individuals; intended as a safety measure, not a therapeutic treatment, and should be time-limited with appropriate monitoring and safeguards.

chemical shift.definition: In NMR spectroscopy, chemical shift is the resonance frequency of a nucleus relative to a standard reference (usually tetramethylsilane, TMS) caused by the shielding or deshielding effects of surrounding electrons; it is measured in parts per million (ppm) and reflects the chemical environment of the nucleus.

chemical shift artifacts.definition: An MRI artifact caused by the difference in resonance frequencies between fat and water protons, which displaces fat relative to water along the frequency-encoding direction at fat–water interfaces, producing bright and/or dark bands and misregistration; it is reduced by increasing bandwidth, using fat suppression, or acquiring in-phase imaging.

interleukin-8.definition: A proinflammatory chemokine of the CXC family (CXCL8) that acts as a key neutrophil chemoattractant and activator, produced by macrophages, epithelial and other cells in response to inflammatory stimuli; signals through CXCR1 and CXCR2 to recruit neutrophils to sites of infection or injury.

cytokine.definition: Small secreted signaling proteins produced by immune and other cells that regulate immunity, inflammation, and hematopoiesis by binding to specific receptors on target cells; they include interleukins, interferons, chemokines, and tumor necrosis factors.

chemokinesis.definition: A non-directional increase or decrease in the rate of cell movement in response to a chemical stimulus, as opposed to directed movement toward or away from the chemical source.

chemokine.definition: A small secreted cytokine that directs the chemotactic movement of leukocytes by binding to chemokine receptors, coordinating immune cell trafficking during development, homeostasis, and inflammation.

chemotaxis.definition: Directed movement of cells or organisms along a chemical gradient, typically toward higher concentrations of a chemoattractant (positive chemotaxis) or away from it (negative chemotaxis).

chemosurgery.definition: A surgical technique in which a chemical agent is applied to tissue to destroy diseased cells, enabling their precise removal in layers while preserving surrounding healthy tissue; historically associated with Mohs micrographic surgery.

chemotherapeutic agent.definition: A chemical substance used in cancer treatment to kill or inhibit the growth of malignant cells, often by disrupting DNA replication or cell division.

chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.definition: A common adverse effect of cytotoxic chemotherapy characterized by nausea and vomiting, typically occurring acutely within 24 hours of treatment, or in delayed, breakthrough, or anticipatory phases.

iodine-131.definition: A radioactive isotope of iodine with a half-life of about 8 days; it emits beta particles and gamma rays and is used therapeutically to ablate thyroid tissue in hyperthyroidism and thyroid cancer, typically administered orally and concentrated in the thyroid.

thyroid cancer.definition: Malignant tumor of the thyroid gland, most commonly papillary thyroid carcinoma; arises from thyroid follicular cells (or parafollicular C cells in medullary carcinoma) and typically presents as a neck mass. Diagnosis is through cytology and imaging; treatment usually involves thyroidectomy with or without radioactive iodine, depending on histology and stage; prognosis varies by subtype and stage.

phosphorus-32.definition: A radioactive isotope of phosphorus with mass number 32 that decays by beta-minus emission to sulfur-32 (half-life about 14.3 days); used as a radiopharmaceutical in certain hematologic conditions and as a radiolabel for nucleic acids in research.

polycythemia vera.definition: A chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by clonal erythroid proliferation (often with a JAK2 mutation) leading to increased red blood cell mass and hematocrit, typically with low erythropoietin levels and an elevated risk of thrombosis; management focuses on reducing red cell mass (phlebotomy), aspirin, and cytoreductive therapy in high-risk patients.

peritoneal ascites.definition: An abnormal accumulation of fluid within the peritoneal cavity (the abdominal space), typically caused by portal hypertension from liver disease, malignancy, infection (peritonitis), heart failure, or hypoalbuminemia.

radioactive gold.definition: A radioactive isotope of gold used in medicine for radiotherapy and sometimes diagnostic imaging; it decays by beta emission with accompanying gamma rays and is used in sealed brachytherapy sources or radiolabeled compounds to deliver targeted radiation.

disseminated carcinoma.definition: Disseminated carcinoma refers to cancer cells that have spread from a primary tumor to distant sites, producing multiple metastatic deposits in various organs or tissues; spread usually occurs via lymphatic or hematogenous routes and indicates advanced, systemic disease.

esophagitis.definition: Inflammation of the esophagus, most commonly due to acid reflux (GERD) but also caused by infections, medication-induced injury, or eosinophilic/allergic processes.

rib fracture.definition: A crack or break in a rib, typically from blunt chest trauma. Presents with localized chest pain worsened by deep breathing or coughing; diagnosed by chest radiography or CT. Management focuses on pain control and pulmonary hygiene; most fractures heal in about 6 weeks. Complications may include pneumothorax, hemothorax, pulmonary contusion, or, in severe cases, flail chest.

rib cartilage.definition: Hyaline cartilage that connects the anterior ends of the ribs to the sternum (true ribs) or to the cartilage above (false ribs), enabling elasticity and expansion of the thoracic cage during breathing.

muscle strain.definition: An injury to muscle fibers (and sometimes the adjacent tendon) caused by overstretching or tearing, typically from a sudden overload or overuse, presenting with sudden pain, weakness, swelling, and limited range of motion; severity is graded from I to III.

barrel chest.definition: An abnormal chest shape with an increased anterior-posterior diameter, giving a rounded, barrel-like appearance; commonly due to chronic lung hyperinflation (often from emphysema/COPD), with reduced inspiratory capacity and prolonged expiration.

flail chest.definition: A severe chest wall injury in which a segment of the thoracic cage moves paradoxically (inward on inspiration, outward on expiration) due to multiple adjacent rib fractures (typically three or more) or a sternum fracture, causing impaired ventilation and often accompanied by pulmonary contusion.

funnel chest.definition: A congenital chest wall deformity in which the sternum and adjacent cartilages grow inward, producing a sunken, funnel-shaped chest; may be asymptomatic or cause cardiopulmonary compression, with treatment ranging from observation or bracing for mild cases to surgical repair (e.g., Nuss or Ravitch procedures) for severe cases.

pigeon breast.definition: A chest wall deformity in which the sternum and adjacent costal cartilages protrude anteriorly, producing a birdlike or pigeon‑chest appearance; it often begins in adolescence and may be associated with connective tissue disorders. Management ranges from observation to external bracing or surgical correction in selected cases.

mammary.definition: Relating to the mammary glands, the milk-producing glands of the breast.

presternal.definition: Pertaining to the area in front of the sternum; located anterior to the sternum.

inframammary.definition: Relating to or located beneath the breast; the region under the breast.

midscapular line.definition: A vertical line on the back that runs through the midpoint of the scapula, parallel to the spine, used as an anatomical landmark to describe posterior chest regions.

right midscapular line.definition: A vertical line on the right posterior thorax that parallels the spine and passes through the midpoint of the scapula, used as a surface landmark to describe the location of underlying structures on the back.

left midscapular line.definition: A vertical anatomical reference line on the left posterior chest wall that runs through the mid-scapular region and is used as a surface landmark for examination and localization (e.g., auscultation, imaging, or procedures).

chest.definition: Anatomical region of the upper trunk between the neck and abdomen, containing the rib cage and the primary organs of breathing and circulation, especially the heart and lungs, along with major vessels and nerves.

thoracic cage.definition: The thoracic cage is the bony and cartilaginous framework of the chest wall, consisting of the sternum, ribs and costal cartilages, and thoracic vertebrae; it encloses and protects the heart and lungs and participates in respiration by expanding and contracting.

parietal pleura.definition: The outer layer of the pleura that lines the thoracic cavity (costal), the superior surface of the diaphragm (diaphragmatic), and the mediastinal surfaces; a serous membrane that secretes pleural fluid to lubricate the lungs and is innervated by somatic nerves.

visceral pleura.definition: The serous membrane that covers the surface of the lungs, forming the inner layer of the pleura and extending into the lung fissures; it secretes pleural fluid to lubricate respiration and is adherent to the lung tissue.

chest tube.definition: A flexible plastic tube inserted through the chest wall into the pleural space to drain air, blood, or other fluid and permit lung re-expansion; commonly used for pneumothorax, hemothorax, and pleural effusion.

chest drainage.definition: A procedure in which a thoracostomy tube (chest tube) is inserted into the pleural space to remove air, blood, or other fluid and to re-expand a collapsed lung; the tube is connected to a drainage system (often with an underwater seal and sometimes suction).

percussion.definition: A physical examination technique in which tapping on the body with the fingers produces sounds and vibrations to assess the size, density, and borders of underlying structures and to distinguish air-filled from solid or fluid-filled tissues.

cupping.definition: An indentation in the optic disc that grows abnormally large with glaucoma.

occipital encephalocele.definition: A congenital neural tube defect characterized by herniation of brain tissue and meninges through a defect in the occipital portion of the skull (posterior cranial region), forming a sac that protrudes externally.

syringomyelia.definition: A disorder characterized by the formation of a syrinx, a fluid-filled cavity within the spinal cord, which can expand and disrupt crossing spinal-cord fibers. This leads to progressive loss of pain and temperature sensation in a cape-like distribution over the shoulders and arms, along with weakness, muscle atrophy, scoliosis, and sometimes autonomic dysfunction; it is often associated with Chiari I malformation or prior spinal cord injury.

myelomeningocele.definition: A neural tube defect in which the spinal cord and meninges protrude through a defect in the vertebral arch (spina bifida aperta), usually in the lumbosacral region.

tonsillar herniation.definition: Downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum, a form of brain herniation often associated with Chiari malformation or raised intracranial pressure, which can compress the brainstem and upper cervical spinal cord.

chiasm.definition: An X-shaped crosspoint in anatomy; most commonly the optic chiasm, the region where the optic nerve fibers from each eye cross to the opposite side of the brain.

chiasma.definition: A cross-shaped region where homologous chromosomes exchange genetic material during meiosis (the crossing-over point); also used for any crossing of two structures, notably the optic chiasm where retinal fibers cross to the opposite side.

chiasmata.definition: A site where homologous chromosomes exchange genetic material during meiosis I, formed by crossing over between non-sister chromatids; it appears as an X-shaped structure linking the homologs during prophase I.

chiasmapexy.definition: A neurosurgical procedure to anchor the optic chiasm in its normal position, typically to treat or prevent downward displacement or compression of the chiasm.

chiari malformation.definition: A condition in which downward herniation of brain tissue—most commonly the cerebellar tonsils—extends through the foramen magnum into the upper spinal canal, often causing headaches, neck pain, dizziness, and other neurologic symptoms; management ranges from observation to surgical posterior fossa decompression.

chiari-frommel syndrome.definition: A postpartum condition characterized by galactorrhea and amenorrhea due to hyperprolactinemia from lactotroph hyperplasia of the anterior pituitary, often resolving after lactation and sometimes mistaken for a prolactin-secreting pituitary tumor.

chiari's syndrome.definition: An historic term for hindbrain herniation in which cerebellar tissue (typically the tonsils) descends below the foramen magnum, often with headaches and brainstem/cervical symptoms, and commonly classified into several types based on extent and associated anomalies.

infantile cerebral sphingolipidosis.definition: An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder (Krabbe disease) caused by galactocerebrosidase (GALC) deficiency, leading to accumulation of galactosphingolipids in the brain (notably psychosine) and resulting in rapid demyelination with progressive neurodegeneration beginning in infancy.

senile angioma.definition: A small, benign vascular skin lesion of dilated capillaries that presents as a bright red to purple papule, typically 1–3 mm in diameter; commonly known as a cherry angioma and more frequent with aging.

de morgan's spots.definition: Retinal hemorrhages with pale centers seen on fundoscopic exam, typically occurring in systemic infections (e.g., infective endocarditis) and certain hematologic conditions such as leukemia or severe anemia.

cherry red spot.definition: A fundoscopic sign in which the fovea appears red against a pale, opaque-appearing retina; results from widespread retinal whitening (edema/ischemia) with preserved choroidal color at the fovea, most classically seen in central retinal artery occlusion and also in certain lysosomal storage diseases (e.g., Tay–Sachs, Niemann–Pick).

cherubism.definition: A rare, inherited (usually autosomal dominant) fibro-osseous jaw disorder that presents in early childhood with bilateral, symmetrical expansion of the mandible and maxilla due to fibrous tissue replacement of bone; it gives a cherubic facial appearance and lesions commonly stabilize or regress after puberty.

cholesterol gallstones.definition: An accumulation of cholesterol crystals in the gallbladder due to bile supersaturation with cholesterol, forming yellow-green, typically radiolucent stones that can cause biliary colic, cholecystitis, or pancreatitis when they obstruct bile ducts; the most common type of gallstone.

chenodeoxycholic acid.definition: A primary bile acid synthesized in the liver from cholesterol; one of the two main primary bile acids in humans (the other being cholic acid), secreted into bile and typically conjugated with glycine or taurine to aid fat digestion; historically used to dissolve cholesterol gallstones but can be hepatotoxic at high doses.

ursodeoxycholic acid.definition: A hydrophilic bile acid used therapeutically to dissolve cholesterol gallstones and treat certain cholestatic liver diseases (e.g., primary biliary cholangitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis); it alters bile composition to reduce cholesterol saturation and protect bile duct cells, improving bile flow.

cherophobia.definition: An irrational fear or aversion to happiness or positive emotion, often leading to avoidance of joyful experiences; not formally recognized as a distinct clinical disorder in major diagnostic manuals.

dyschezia.definition: Difficult or painful defecation, often with straining and a sensation of incomplete evacuation; may reflect anorectal disorders or pelvic floor dysfunction.

hematochezia.definition: Passing of fresh blood through the anus, usually with defecation; typically indicates lower gastrointestinal bleeding but can occur with a brisk upper gastrointestinal bleed.

osmotic diarrhea.definition: A form of diarrhea caused by ingestion of osmotically active substances that are not absorbed in the small intestine, leading to water drawn into the bowel and watery stools; it typically improves with fasting and cessation of the offending agent (e.g., lactose in lactose intolerance, sorbitol, nonabsorbable laxatives).

varicella-zoster-virus.definition: A DNA herpesvirus of the Herpesviridae family that causes primary varicella (chickenpox) and reactivation as herpes zoster (shingles); it establishes latency in sensory ganglia and is transmitted via respiratory droplets or direct contact with vesicular fluid.

herpes-zoster-virus.definition: A human herpesvirus of the Herpesviridae family that causes primary varicella (chickenpox) and establishes latency in sensory ganglia, reactivating later as herpes zoster (shingles); transmitted by respiratory droplets or contact with vesicle fluid; an enveloped double-stranded DNA virus.

vesicles.definition: A small, fluid-filled elevation of the skin or mucous membranes, typically less than 5 mm in diameter, formed by separation of epidermal layers with accumulation of serous fluid; seen in conditions such as herpes infections, varicella, contact dermatitis, and other blistering diseases.

vesicular.definition: Blisters or small bumps on your skin filled with fluid.

macules.definition: A flat, circumscribed area of color change on the skin or mucous membranes that is not raised or depressed, typically less than 1 cm in diameter; if larger than 1 cm, it is called a patch.

papules.definition: A small, raised, solid skin lesion, usually less than 1 cm in diameter, that is palpable and not filled with fluid.

laryngeal-vesicles.definition: Small fluid-filled blisters on the mucous membrane of the larynx (voice box), typically arising from viral infection, irritation, or inflammatory injury; may cause hoarseness or throat discomfort.

antipruritics.definition: Substances or medications that relieve itching (pruritus) by blocking itch signaling, reducing skin inflammation, or numbing the skin; used topically or systemically. Examples include antihistamines, topical corticosteroids, topical anesthetics (e.g., pramoxine), calamine, menthol/camphor preparations, and capsaicin.

calamine-lotion.definition: A topical astringent and antipruritic preparation containing calamine (a zinc oxide–ferric oxide compound) used to relieve itching and mild irritation from minor skin conditions such as insect bites, poison ivy/oak/sumac exposure, and sunburn.

baking-soda-paste.definition: A topical paste composed of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) mixed with water or another liquid; used informally to soothe mild skin irritations, itching, or to neutralize acids on the skin. It is not a medically approved treatment and can cause skin irritation or chemical burns if applied to broken skin or used in excess.

neomycin-bacitracin.definition: A topical antibiotic ointment combo of neomycin and bacitracin used to prevent or treat minor skin infections; it inhibits bacterial protein synthesis (neomycin) and cell wall synthesis (bacitracin).

systemic-antibiotics.definition: Antibiotics that, after absorption, reach therapeutic concentrations in the bloodstream and throughout the body to treat infections at distant sites; typically administered orally or by injection, as opposed to topical antibiotics.

zoster-immune-globulin.definition: A preparation of human immunoglobulin containing antibodies against varicella-zoster virus, administered after exposure to provide passive immunity and reduce the risk or severity of varicella in high‑risk individuals (e.g., newborns, pregnant women, and the immunocompromised).

varicella-zoster-immune-globulin.definition: A human-derived immunoglobulin preparation containing antibodies against varicella-zoster virus, used for passive post-exposure prophylaxis to provide temporary immunity and prevent or lessen varicella in high-risk individuals after exposure (typically given intramuscularly).

immune-globulin.definition: A large family of glycoprotein antibodies produced by plasma cells; they recognize and bind specific antigens, neutralize pathogens, and mark them for attack by other immune cells; they circulate in blood and body fluids, including IgA, IgD, IgE, IgG, and IgM.

immune-serum-globulin.definition: A preparation of antibodies (immunoglobulins) derived from the serum of immune individuals, used to provide passive immunity by supplying ready-made antibodies against specific pathogens.

zoster-immune-plasma.definition: A plasma-derived preparation containing high-titer antibodies to varicella-zoster virus, used as passive immunization after exposure to prevent or lessen varicella infection in susceptible or high-risk individuals.

organ-transplantation.definition: A surgical procedure in which a diseased or failing organ is replaced with a healthy organ from a donor (living or deceased), typically requiring lifelong immunosuppressive therapy to prevent rejection.

cell-mediated-immunity.definition: A form of adaptive immunity mediated by T lymphocytes rather than antibodies; cytotoxic T cells (CD8+) kill infected or abnormal cells, while helper T cells (CD4+) activate macrophages and coordinate other immune responses, including delayed-type hypersensitivity and defense against intracellular pathogens.

abscesses.definition: Caused by an infection; a pocket of pus. You can get them anywhere in your body.

hemorrhagic-varicella.definition: An uncommon, severe variant of varicella (chickenpox) in which vesicular lesions hemorrhage and mucosal or visceral bleeding occurs, often due to accompanying coagulopathy (disseminated intravascular coagulation); associated with high mortality in immunocompromised patients.

reyes-syndrome.definition: An acute pediatric neurohepatic syndrome characterized by encephalopathy (often with cerebral edema) and fatty liver (microvesicular steatosis) following a viral illness, strongly associated with aspirin use; presents with vomiting, lethargy or confusion, can progress to seizures and coma, and requires urgent medical management.

pernicious-anemia.definition: A form of anemia in which red blood cells enlarge and decrease in size due to an inability to properly absorb vitamin B12.

intrinsic-factor.definition: A glycoprotein secreted by gastric parietal cells that binds vitamin B12 (cobalamin) and facilitates its absorption in the terminal ileum.

pepsinogen.definition: The inactive precursor (zymogen) of the stomach enzyme pepsin, produced by gastric chief cells; activated to pepsin in the acidic gastric lumen to aid in protein digestion.

gastric-glands.definition: Glands in the mucosa of the stomach that secrete gastric juice into the lumen; they include parietal cells producing hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, chief cells producing pepsinogen, mucus-secreting cells, and enteroendocrine cells that secrete hormones.

pineal-body.definition: A small endocrine gland in the brain, part of the epithalamus, that secretes melatonin to regulate sleep-wake cycles and circadian rhythms.

parathyroid-glands.definition: Glands responsible for releasing a hormone that controls calcium levels and influences bone loss and growth.

vitamin-b12.definition: A water-soluble B vitamin (cobalamin) essential for DNA synthesis, red blood cell formation, and maintenance of the myelin sheath and nervous system. It acts as a cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl‑CoA mutase; absorbed in the terminal ileum with intrinsic factor and stored mainly in the liver. Deficiency can cause megaloblastic anemia and neurological abnormalities.

chiclero-ulcer.definition: A chronic, painless ulcer of the external ear (pinna) caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans infection; classically described among chicle (gum) harvesters in Central America and often with destruction of ear cartilage.

american-leishmaniasis.definition: A group of leishmanial infections caused by New World (American) Leishmania species transmitted by phlebotomine sandflies, presenting mainly as cutaneous disease, with possible mucocutaneous or visceral forms.

leishmania-mexicana.definition: A protozoan parasite species of the genus Leishmania that causes cutaneous leishmaniasis in the Americas; transmitted by phlebotomine (sandfly) vectors.

chido-rodgers-blood-group.definition: A minor human blood group system defined by two antigens, Chido (Ch) and Rodgers (Rg), located on the C4 component of the complement pathway; antibodies against these antigens can cause alloimmune transfusion reactions or hemolytic disease of the newborn.

blood-group.definition: A classification of blood based on the presence or absence of specific antigens on red blood cells (notably the ABO and Rh systems); used to determine compatibility for blood transfusions.

c4.definition: The fourth cervical vertebra of the spine; one of the seven vertebrae forming the cervical (neck) portion of the vertebral column, articulating with adjacent vertebrae and helping protect the spinal cord.

chief-cell.definition: A gastric gland cell that secretes pepsinogen, the inactive zymogen of pepsin; activation to pepsin occurs in the acidic gastric lumen, enabling protein digestion.

zymogenic-cell.definition: A gastric chief cell in the fundic glands of the stomach that secretes pepsinogen, the inactive zymogen form of the digestive enzyme pepsin.

chilblain.definition: A non-freezing cold injury causing itchy, red to purple, swollen patches on acral areas (toes, fingers, ears, nose) after exposure to damp, cold conditions; due to an abnormal vascular response to cold, typically improving with warming and protection, and may blister or ulcerate in severe cases.

chilblains.definition: Chilblains (perniosis) are an inflammatory skin condition caused by an abnormal vascular response to cold exposure, most often affecting acral sites (toes, fingers, ears, nose). They present after damp, cold conditions as pruritic, erythematous to violaceous papules or plaques, sometimes with swelling or a burning sensation; they typically improve with rewarming and dry warmth but can recur in cold weather.

chilblain-lupus-erythematosus.definition: A form of chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus presenting with chilblain-like lesions on acral sites (e.g., fingers, toes) triggered by cold exposure; it may resemble perniosis and can be associated with systemic lupus erythematosus.

discoid-lupus-erythematosus.definition: A chronic cutaneous form of lupus mellitus presenting with well-defined, erythematous, scaly plaques that may show follicular plugging and progress to atrophy and scarring or pigment change, most often on sun-exposed areas of the face and scalp; systemic involvement is uncommon but can occur in some cases.

childhood disintegrative disorder.definition: An extremely rare pervasive developmental disorder in which a child, after normal development for the first 2 years (often longer), experiences a significant loss of previously acquired language, social, play, and sometimes motor skills, with ensuing impairments in adaptive functioning; onset typically after age 2. In DSM-5 it is not a separate diagnosis and is encompassed by autism spectrum disorder with a history of regression.

pervasive developmental disorders.definition: A group of neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by persistent deficits in social communication and interaction across contexts, plus restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities, with onset in early development and varying in severity; historically included autistic disorder, Asperger syndrome, PDD-NOS, Rett syndrome, and childhood disintegrative disorder (DSM-5 now classifies these under Autism Spectrum Disorder with varying specifiers).

developmental delay.definition: A condition in which a child fails to reach age-expected milestones in one or more developmental domains (e.g., gross motor, fine motor, language, cognitive, social/personal, or adaptive skills) and performs below typical age norms, often defined as a score or milestone well below the expected percentile or standard deviation for age.

mental impairment.definition: A reduction or limitation in cognitive functioning that affects memory, attention, learning, reasoning, judgment, or daily functioning, resulting from developmental, acquired, or degenerative brain conditions.

juvenile myxedema.definition: A pediatric form of hypothyroidism presenting with generalized nonpitting edema of the skin and subcutaneous tissues (myxedema), coarse facial features, dry skin, growth retardation, and often developmental delay; caused by thyroid hormone deficiency and treated with thyroid hormone replacement.

chlamydia.definition: Caused by a germ (a bacteria) that is passed during oral or genital sex from one person to another.

chlamydia trachomatis.definition: An obligate intracellular, Gram-negative bacterium that causes human infections, notably the sexually transmitted infection chlamydia (cervicitis, urethritis, pelvic inflammatory disease) and ocular trachoma; it alternates between infectious elementary bodies and replicating reticulate bodies within host cells.

chilomastix.definition: A genus of flagellated intestinal protozoa; the best-known human species inhabits the large intestine and is generally nonpathogenic, often asymptomatic. Transmission occurs via ingestion of cysts in contaminated water or food; diagnosis is by stool microscopy showing characteristic pear-shaped cysts and slender trophozoites.

chilomastix mesnili.definition: A nonpathogenic flagellated protozoan parasite of the human large intestine (cecum/colon); detected in stool as lemon-shaped cysts and, when present, pear-shaped trophozoites; infection is usually asymptomatic and acquired by ingestion of cysts in contaminated water or food.

puerperal fever.definition: A postpartum infection presenting with fever after delivery, most often due to endometritis (infection of the uterine lining) and may involve surrounding tissues. Historically known as childbed fever.

prenatal care.definition: Prenatal care is the ongoing medical care and education provided to a pregnant person from conception through delivery, including regular visits, maternal and fetal screening, risk assessment, management of health conditions, and counseling on nutrition, lifestyle, and birth planning to promote maternal and fetal health and prevent complications.

delivery.definition: The act of giving birth; the process by which a fetus is expelled from the uterus through the birth canal.

graft-versus-host disease.definition: An immune-mediated complication of allogeneic transplantation in which donor T cells attack recipient tissues, most commonly the skin, liver, and gastrointestinal tract; it can be acute or chronic.

child-pugh classification.definition: An ordinal scoring system used to assess prognosis and disease severity in chronic liver disease, especially cirrhosis. It combines five variables—serum bilirubin, serum albumin, prothrombin time/international normalized ratio (INR), ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy—each scored 1 to 3; total scores range from 5 to 15, with higher scores indicating worse liver function (Class A: 5–6, Class B: 7–9, Class C: 10–15).

scrotal cancer.definition: A malignant tumor of the scrotal skin; most often squamous cell carcinoma, historically linked to chronic irritation and exposure to soot or tar (as seen in chimney sweeps).

monosodium glutamate.definition: A flavor enhancer consisting of the sodium salt of the amino acid glutamic acid; used to intensify savory (umami) taste in foods.

chinese restaurant syndrome.definition: A reported cluster of symptoms—including headache, flushing, sweating, facial pressure or tightness, numbness or tingling, chest pain, and sometimes nausea—that some people experience after consuming monosodium glutamate (MSG) in food, historically linked to meals of Chinese cuisine; evidence for a causal link is inconsistent, and MSG is generally considered safe for most people.

aconite.definition: A highly poisonous perennial plant genus (Aconitum) containing potent alkaloids such as aconitine; exposure can cause numbness and tingling around the mouth, nausea, vomiting, hypotension, arrhythmias, and potentially fatal cardiotoxicity and respiratory failure. Historically used as a poison and, in some traditional medicines, in extremely dilute preparations.

ginseng.definition: Roots of Panax species (most notably Panax ginseng and Panax quinquefolius) used in traditional medicine as an adaptogenic tonic; contains ginsenosides; claimed to enhance energy, stamina, and immune function, but clinical evidence is limited and mixed; adverse effects can include insomnia, headaches, digestive upset, and it may interact with anticoagulants and stimulant medications.

chinese herbal medicine.definition: A traditional system of medicine originating in China that uses combinations of herbs (and sometimes minerals or animal products) to restore balance and treat illness, with formulas tailored to an individual's pattern of disharmony and prepared as decoctions, pills, powders, or granules.

birth.definition: The process of delivering a fetus from the uterus, culminating in the newborn's exit from the mother's body (parturition).

perihepatitis.definition: Inflammation of the peritoneal surface surrounding the liver (the liver capsule/Glisson’s capsule), often in the setting of pelvic inflammatory disease, causing right upper quadrant abdominal pain and sometimes leading to perihepatic adhesions between the liver capsule and the anterior abdominal wall.

eye.definition: An organ of vision that detects light and converts it into neural signals that the brain interprets as visual images; in humans it comprises the cornea, iris, pupil, lens, retina, vitreous body, and optic nerve.

trachoma.definition: A chronic infectious keratoconjunctivitis caused by ocular infection with Chlamydia trachomatis (commonly serovars A–C), characterized by recurrent follicular conjunctivitis, conjunctival scarring and pannus formation, progression to eyelid trichiasis and corneal opacification with potential blindness; transmitted by direct contact with eye/nasal secretions, fomites and flies; a leading cause of preventable blindness in underserved populations; targeted by the SAFE strategy (Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial cleanliness, Environmental improvements).

chlamydia psittaci.definition: A gram-negative, obligate intracellular bacterium of the genus Chlamydia that causes psittacosis (ornithosis) in humans, usually acquired from birds and presenting with fever, headache, myalgia, and atypical pneumonia.

chlamydia pneumoniae.definition: An obligate intracellular bacterium of the genus Chlamydia that causes atypical pneumonia and other upper and lower respiratory tract infections; transmitted person-to-person via respiratory droplets.

taiwan acute respiratory disease.definition: An informal, non-specific term for an acute respiratory illness observed in Taiwan; not a distinct disease entity in modern medical nomenclature. It typically presents with sudden onset of fever and upper or lower respiratory symptoms; etiologies are usually viral (e.g., influenza, RSV, rhinovirus) with possible bacterial complications; management is supportive and guided by standard infectious-disease practices.

upper respiratory tract infections.definition: An infection of the nose, sinuses, pharynx, and often the larynx; usually viral in origin and self-limited, presenting with nasal discharge or congestion, sore throat, cough, and sometimes fever.

lower respiratory tract infections.definition: An infection involving the airways and structures below the larynx (trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, and lungs), typically presenting with cough and dyspnea; includes conditions such as acute bronchitis, bronchiolitis, and pneumonia and can be caused by viral or bacterial pathogens.

community acquired pneumonias.definition: A pneumonia acquired outside of hospital or long-term care facilities, typically presenting with fever, cough and dyspnea, and radiographic evidence of a new infiltrate; most commonly caused by community pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and atypical organisms.

incubation period.definition: The time between when a person is infected and the first signs of sickness.

gram’s stain.definition: A differential staining technique used to classify bacteria into Gram-positive and Gram-negative groups based on cell wall structure. It uses a primary crystal violet stain, iodine mordant, decolorizer, and a counterstain (usually safranin). Thick peptidoglycan retains the violet-iodine complex and appears purple; thin-walled cells with an outer membrane lose the violet and appear pink or red after counterstaining.

endocervical discharge.definition: Discharge from the endocervical canal; may be normal cervical mucus or purulent discharge indicating cervicitis or infection.

urethral discharge.definition: An abnormal discharge from the urethra, typically purulent or mucopurulent, caused by urethritis from infection (most often sexually transmitted pathogens such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis), often with dysuria or irritation.

ofloxacin.definition: A fluoroquinolone antibiotic that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, used to treat a variety of susceptible bacterial infections; available in oral and ophthalmic formulations.

psittacosis.definition: A zoonotic infectious disease caused by Chlamydia psittaci, transmitted to humans from infected birds (notably psittacine birds) via inhalation of dried secretions; presents with fever, headache, myalgias, and often an atypical pneumonia, and is typically treated with tetracyclines (e.g., doxycycline) or macrolides.

primary atypical pneumonia.definition: An infection of the respiratory tract caused by atypical organisms (most often Mycoplasma pneumoniae) that produces a relatively mild illness with insidious onset of fever, malaise, sore throat, and a persistent dry cough, and with diffuse interstitial or peribronchial infiltrates on chest radiographs rather than a lobar consolidation.

rales.definition: Abnormal lung sounds that might be a sign of fluid buildup or congestion in the lungs.

chlamydia test.definition: A laboratory test to detect infection with the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis, most commonly a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) on urine or swab specimens (cervical, vaginal, urethral, or pharyngeal); used for screening and diagnosing chlamydia.

pneumoniae pneumonia.definition: An infection in one or both lungs.

chocolate cyst.definition: A benign ovarian cyst resulting from endometriosis, in which ectopic endometrial tissue within the ovary forms a cyst filled with old, dark brown blood (an endometrioma).

choanae.definition: Two posterior openings of the nasal cavities that lead into the nasopharynx (internal nares).

gray syndrome.definition: A potentially fatal adverse drug reaction in neonates exposed to chloramphenicol, caused by immature hepatic glucuronidation leading to drug accumulation; characterized by pallid/gray skin, cyanosis, hypotension, hypothermia, poor feeding, vomiting, and lethargy.

chloromycetin.definition: A broad‑spectrum antibiotic that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit; used for serious infections when other antibiotics are not effective, but can cause dose‑dependent bone marrow suppression and rare, fatal aplastic anemia, so its use is restricted in many settings.

chloroprocaine.definition: A short-acting ester local anesthetic that is rapidly hydrolyzed by plasma cholinesterases, resulting in a brief duration of anesthesia suitable for infiltration and regional blocks.

retinal.definition: Relating to the retina, the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye. In biochemistry, retinal (retinaldehyde) is the aldehyde form of vitamin A that participates in vision by forming rhodopsin.

extrapyramidal.definition: Pertaining to motor pathways outside the corticospinal (pyramidal) tract, chiefly involving basal ganglia circuitry that regulate automatic movement and posture; dysfunction or pharmacologic blockade of these pathways can cause movement disorders such as dystonia, akathisia, and parkinsonism.

choana.definition: The posterior openings of the nasal cavity that communicate with the nasopharynx; the two internal nares (left and right) forming the posterior nasal apertures.

choking.definition: An acute airway obstruction caused by a blockage (typically a foreign body or swelling) that results in partial or complete inability to breathe, speak, or cough effectively.

agents.definition: A substance or factor that produces a biological, chemical, or pharmacologic effect; in medicine, the term includes drugs (pharmacologic agents), infectious agents such as bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites, and other substances used to diagnose, treat, or study disease.

bromine.definition: A chemical element and halogen (Br, atomic number 35). It is a reddish-brown liquid at room temperature and is toxic; historically used in bromide sedatives and topical antiseptics, but now limited due to safety concerns.

osmium tetroxide.definition: A highly toxic, volatile inorganic compound used as a tissue fixative and lipid stain in histology and electron microscopy; it oxidizes unsaturated lipids and provides membrane contrast.

phosphine.definition: A highly toxic, colorless, flammable gas (chemical formula PH3) that inhibits mitochondrial respiration by inhibiting cytochrome c oxidase; inhalation exposure causes severe respiratory and systemic toxicity, potentially leading to hypoxia, metabolic acidosis, arrhythmias, and shock, with management being supportive and no specific antidote.

phosphorus.definition: An essential dietary mineral and chemical element that occurs in the body mainly as inorganic phosphate; critical for bone and tooth mineralization, energy metabolism (ATP), nucleic acid synthesis, and cell signaling; homeostasis is maintained by intestinal absorption and renal excretion and is regulated by parathyroid hormone and vitamin D; abnormal serum levels include hypophosphatemia and hyperphosphatemia.

cytotoxicity.definition: The quality or state of being toxic to cells, causing cell damage or death; it can describe toxic substances or the ability of certain immune cells (e.g., cytotoxic T cells or natural killer cells) to kill target cells.

respiratory distress.definition: A clinical state of increased work of breathing with impaired gas exchange, often presenting with tachypnea and dyspnea accompanied by use of accessory muscles, chest retractions, nasal flaring (especially in infants/children), grunting, and, if severe, cyanosis or hypoxemia; may progress to respiratory failure if not treated.

cholagogue.definition: A substance that causes the gallbladder to squeeze, increasing the discharge of bile.

cholangiocarcinoma.definition: A malignant neoplasm arising from the epithelial cells lining the bile ducts (cholangiocytes), occurring in intrahepatic or extrahepatic bile ducts.

cholangiocellular carcinoma.definition: A malignant neoplasm arising from the biliary epithelium (cholangiocytes) lining the bile ducts, which can originate in intrahepatic or extrahepatic ducts.

liver flukes.definition: Liver flukes are parasitic trematodes (flatworms) that infect the biliary ducts or liver tissue of humans and other mammals. Infections such as fascioliasis, clonorchiasis, and opisthorchiasis occur after ingestion of metacercariae in contaminated water or undercooked aquatic organisms and can cause biliary obstruction, cholangitis, and hepatobiliary disease.

histological evaluation.definition: A microscopic assessment of tissue samples after fixation and staining, performed by a pathologist to evaluate tissue architecture and cellular morphology for diagnosis, grading, or staging of disease.

cholangiogram.definition: A radiographic imaging study of the biliary tree produced after injection of contrast material to visualize the bile ducts, used to assess obstruction, stones, or leaks.

radiopaque contrast medium.definition: A substance that absorbs X-rays and is used to enhance visualization of body structures on radiologic imaging by increasing the radiodensity of organs, vessels, or lumens (commonly iodine-based agents or barium sulfate suspensions given orally, rectally, or by injection).

iodinated contrast medium.definition: A water-soluble radiopaque contrast agent containing iodine, used to enhance visualization of blood vessels and tissues during radiologic imaging (e.g., CT, angiography, fluoroscopy); administered by intravenous or intra-arterial injection and available in ionic (high-osmolality) and nonionic (low-osmolality) formulations.

indwelling t-tube.definition: A T-shaped biliary drainage catheter placed in the common bile duct after biliary tract surgery to drain bile externally and allow postoperative cholangiography; left indwelling for days to weeks until the ductal tract matures and removal is safe.

percutaneous transhepatic cholangiograph.definition: A radiologic imaging procedure in which a needle or catheter is inserted through the skin into the liver to inject contrast dye into the biliary ducts, allowing fluoroscopic visualization of the intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts to diagnose obstruction, stones, strictures, or leaks (and potentially to enable drainage or guide therapy).

biliary tract.definition: A network of ducts that drains bile from the liver and gallbladder into the duodenum; it includes intrahepatic bile ducts, the hepatic ducts forming the common hepatic duct, the cystic duct, the common bile duct, and the gallbladder as a reservoir.

biliary system.definition: A network of ducts and the gallbladder that stores, concentrates, and transports bile produced by the liver to the duodenum; it includes intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts (hepatic ducts, common hepatic duct, cystic duct, and common bile duct) and the gallbladder.

t-tube.definition: A T-tube is a T-shaped biliary drainage tube inserted into the common bile duct via choledochotomy to drain bile externally and allow postoperative cholangiography; it helps prevent bile leakage and maintain duct patency during healing.

endoscopic retrograde cholangiography.definition: A procedure combining endoscopy with fluoroscopy to visualize the biliary and pancreatic ducts by injecting contrast material via the ampulla of Vater, enabling diagnostic imaging and therapeutic interventions such as stone extraction, stent placement, and sphincterotomy.

ampulla of vater.definition: A dilated portion of the biliary and pancreatic ducts where the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct unite and drain into the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla, surrounded by the sphincter of Oddi.

duodenoscope.definition: A specialized endoscope, typically a flexible, side-viewing instrument used to examine the duodenum and perform endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), enabling visualization of the ampulla of Vater and cannulation of the bile and pancreatic ducts.

intravenous cholangiography.definition: An imaging procedure in which intravenously administered iodinated contrast is excreted into the bile, allowing radiographic visualization of the biliary tree to assess obstruction, stones, or leaks (largely obsolete, now replaced by MRCP/ERCP).

hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid scan.definition: A nuclear medicine imaging study using a hepatobiliary radiotracer (usually Tc-99m mebrofenin or disofenin) to evaluate liver uptake and excretion into the biliary system, allowing assessment of gallbladder function, biliary patency, and bowel excretion; commonly used to diagnose acute cholecystitis, biliary obstruction, bile leaks, and other hepatobiliary disorders.

cholecystokinin.definition: A hormone that signals the gallbladder to contract, releasing bile, and causes the pancreas to release enzymes used in digestion.

cholecystagogue.definition: A substance that stimulates the gallbladder to contract and release bile into the duodenum.

cholecystalgia.definition: Pain located in the gallbladder region (right upper quadrant), typically due to gallbladder disease such as biliary colic from gallstones or cholecystitis; often episodic and may be provoked by fatty meals.

cholecystogram.definition: An oral radiographic study of the gallbladder in which a radiopaque contrast agent is ingested to visualize the gallbladder on X-ray and assess its filling and emptying (historically used; now largely replaced by ultrasound and hepatobiliary scintigraphy).

cholecystography.definition: A radiographic imaging study of the gallbladder that uses a radiopaque contrast agent to visualize its filling and drainage; historically performed after oral ingestion or intravenous administration, primarily to detect gallstones and assess biliary function, but largely replaced by ultrasound and hepatobiliary scintigraphy.

cholecystoduodenostomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which the gallbladder is anastomosed to the duodenum to drain bile directly into the intestine, bypassing an obstructed biliary outflow.

cholecystojejunostomy.definition: A surgical anastomosis between the gallbladder and the jejunum to drain bile directly into the small intestine, bypassing obstruction of the common bile duct or hepatic ducts.

lithotripsy.definition: A procedure that breaks urinary tract stones (such as kidney or ureteral stones) into small fragments to be passed in the urine or removed, typically using shock waves (extracorporeal lithotripsy) or endoscopic/laser energy.

ursodiol.definition: A bile acid used to dissolve small cholesterol gallstones and to treat cholestatic liver diseases; it is a hydrophilic bile acid.

methyl tert-butyl.definition: A volatile organic ether used as a gasoline oxygenate and solvent; it consists of a methyl group attached to an oxygen atom connected to a tert-butyl group and is a common environmental contaminant in water due to fuel leaks.

stent placement.definition: A procedure in which a stent—a small, expandable mesh tube—is inserted into a narrowed or blocked vessel or duct (most commonly a coronary artery) via a catheter and then expanded to hold the lumen open, restoring blood flow or drainage; stents may be bare-metal or drug-eluting.

sphincterotomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which a sphincter muscle is incised to widen a constricted duct or channel and relieve obstruction, commonly performed as an endoscopic biliary sphincterotomy or as an anal sphincterotomy for fissures.

ductal stones.definition: A calcified concretion that forms within a duct (e.g., biliary or pancreatic duct), causing obstruction and potential complications such as cholestasis, cholangitis, or pancreatitis.

laparoscopic cholecystectomy.definition: A minimally invasive surgical procedure to remove the gallbladder through small abdominal incisions using a laparoscope, commonly performed for symptomatic gallstones or biliary disease.

murphy's sign.definition: A clinical sign of acute cholecystitis in which deep palpation of the right upper quadrant during inspiration induces sudden cessation of inhalation due to gallbladder tenderness.

antispasmodics.definition: Drugs that reduce or prevent involuntary smooth-muscle contractions to relieve cramping and pain in conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome, bladder or menstrual cramps.

gastric decompression.definition: A medical procedure to relieve gastric distension by removing air and gastric contents, usually accomplished with a nasogastric or orogastric tube connected to suction.

fiberoptic.definition: Relating to or using fiber optics; devices that transmit light through thin flexible fibers for illumination and imaging in medical procedures (e.g., a fiberoptic endoscope).

roentgenographic.definition: Relating to roentgenography; radiographic imaging obtained using X-rays to visualize internal structures.

cholecystolithiasis.definition: The presence of gallstones within the gallbladder, which may cause biliary colic or inflammation (cholecystitis).

cholecystolithotomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which gallstones are removed from the gallbladder by incising the gallbladder wall and extracting the stones.

cholecystolithotripsy.definition: Fragmentation of gallstones within the gallbladder into smaller pieces using lithotripsy to facilitate passage or removal.

cholescintigraphy.definition: A nuclear medicine imaging study of the hepatobiliary system in which a radiotracer (usually technetium-99m–labeled HIDA) is injected intravenously to visualize hepatic uptake, biliary excretion, gallbladder filling and ejection, and biliary tree patency, aiding diagnosis of conditions such as acute cholecystitis, biliary obstruction, or bile leaks.

cholecystosonography.definition: A noninvasive ultrasound examination of the gallbladder used to visualize stones, inflammation (cholecystitis), sludge or polyps, and wall thickening or bile duct dilation.

choledochal.definition: Relating to the common bile duct, the duct that carries bile from the liver to the small intestine.

choledochojejunostomy.definition: A surgical procedure that creates an anastomosis between the common bile duct and the jejunum to drain bile, bypassing a blockage or injury in the biliary tract.

choledocholith.definition: A stone located in the common bile duct that can obstruct bile flow and cause jaundice, cholangitis, or pancreatitis.

choledocholithotomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove a stone from the common bile duct by incising the duct and extracting the stone.

choledocholithotripsy.definition: Fragmentation of stones within the common bile duct to permit removal, usually by endoscopic lithotripsy during ERCP or by percutaneous approaches.

choledocholitis.definition: Inflammation of the common bile duct (the duct that carries bile from the liver to the duodenum), usually due to infection or obstruction.

cholera.definition: An acute diarrheal illness caused by infection with a toxin-producing bacterium transmitted via contaminated water or food, characterized by sudden, profuse watery stools and rapid dehydration; managed with prompt rehydration and electrolyte replacement, with antibiotics in severe cases and preventive measures such as safe water, sanitation, and vaccination where appropriate.

carbachol.definition: A synthetic carbamate cholinergic agonist that nonselectively stimulates muscarinic and nicotinic acetylcholine receptors; resistant to acetylcholinesterase; used in ophthalmology to induce miosis and to lower intraocular pressure in glaucoma (often administered topically).

methacholine.definition: Direct-acting muscarinic (cholinergic) agonist used primarily for bronchial challenge testing to assess airway hyperresponsiveness; inhaled methacholine induces dose-dependent bronchoconstriction in susceptible individuals, aiding in the diagnosis of asthma.

biliary_colic.definition: A sudden, episodic pain in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium caused by transient obstruction of the cystic duct by gallstones, typically lasting 30 minutes to several hours and often triggered by fatty meals; usually without fever or ongoing inflammation.

wolmans_disease.definition: A rare autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of lysosomal acid lipase, leading to accumulation of cholesteryl esters and triglycerides in tissues; presents in infancy with failure to thrive, vomiting, diarrhea, hepatosplenomegaly, and often adrenal gland calcifications, with rapid progression and high mortality if untreated.

cholesterolemia.definition: Abnormal levels of cholesterol in the bloodstream; commonly refers to elevated cholesterol (hypercholesterolemia).

hypercholesterolemia.definition: A condition characterized by chronically elevated cholesterol levels in the blood, especially LDL cholesterol, which increases the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; it can be inherited (familial hypercholesterolemia) or acquired.

cholesterolosis.definition: An asymptomatic, benign condition of the gallbladder mucosa characterized by accumulation of cholesterol-laden macrophages in thelamina propria, producing cholesterol polyps and sometimes a “strawberry” appearance of the mucosa.

cholesteryl_ester_storage_disease.definition: A lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient lysosomal acid lipase activity, leading to accumulation of cholesteryl esters and triglycerides in lysosomes, particularly in liver and macrophages; presents with hepatomegaly, dyslipidemia, and hepatic steatosis, with onset ranging from childhood to adulthood.

steatorrhea.definition: Excretion of abnormally large amounts of fat in the stool due to fat malabsorption; stools are bulky, pale or clay-colored, greasy/oily, foul-smelling, and may float. Often due to pancreatic insufficiency or intestinal malabsorption.

otitis_media.definition: Ear infection, often in the middle ear.

cholesteatoma.definition: A keratinizing squamous epithelium–lined cyst in the middle ear or mastoid that accumulates keratin debris and expands, often eroding surrounding bone; typically arises from chronic otitis media and is treated surgically.

ossicles.definition: Three small auditory bones in the middle ear—the malleus (hammer), incus (anvil), and stapes (stirrup)—that transmit and amplify sound vibrations from the tympanic membrane to the inner ear.

middle_ear.definition: An air-filled cavity in the temporal bone of the skull between the tympanic membrane (eardrum) and the inner ear; it contains the auditory ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) which transmit sound vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear, and communicates with the nasopharynx via the Eustachian tube to equalize pressure.

chondroectodermal dysplasia.definition: A rare autosomal recessive skeletal dysplasia presenting with congenital chondrodysplasia causing limb shortening, polydactyly, ectodermal dysplasia features (dental anomalies, nail/hair abnormalities), and commonly congenital heart defects.

ellis-van creveld syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by chondrodysplasia with short limbs, postaxial polydactyly, ectodermal dysplasia (dental, nail, and hair abnormalities), and congenital heart defects (most commonly atrioventricular canal defect).

cholografin.definition: An iodinated, water-soluble radiographic contrast agent used to opacify the biliary ducts during cholangiography, typically administered intravenously or directly into the biliary system to visualize the biliary tree.

iodipamide.definition: A water-soluble iodinated radiographic contrast agent used to enhance X-ray images in diagnostic radiology, commonly for intravenous urography and angiography.

chololithiasis.definition: Presence or formation of stones within the biliary tract (bile ducts and/or gallbladder), which can cause biliary obstruction, biliary colic, jaundice, pancreatitis, or cholangitis.

dextrothyroxine sodium.definition: A synthetic dextrorotatory isomer of thyroxine (T4) in the sodium salt form; a thyroid hormone analogue with little physiologic activity, historically investigated as a lipid-lowering agent but now rarely used due to cardiovascular adverse effects.

cholylglycine.definition: A conjugated bile acid (glycocholate) formed in the liver by conjugating cholic acid with glycine; functions as a bile salt to aid fat digestion and is excreted in bile.

glycocholic acid.definition: A conjugated bile acid formed in the liver by amidation of cholic acid with glycine; secreted into bile to emulsify fats and aid lipid digestion, and subsequently reabsorbed in the ileum as part of the enterohepatic circulation.

cholyltaurine.definition: A bile acid formed by conjugating cholic acid with taurine, producing a more water-soluble molecule that aids in emulsifying and digesting fats; also known as taurocholic acid.

taurocholic acid.definition: A bile salt produced by conjugating cholic acid with taurine; a detergent-like molecule secreted in bile that emulsifies dietary fats to aid lipid digestion, typically existing as its sodium or other salt form in bile.

pseudogout.definition: Arthritis caused by crystals of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate in the joints. Also known as calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate disease.

chondrocarcinoma.definition: A malignant tumor arising from cartilaginous tissue or chondrocytes; a cartilaginous sarcoma.

chondroclast.definition: An osteoclast-like cell that resorbs cartilage matrix, especially calcified cartilage at growth plates during endochondral bone formation.

chondroclastic.definition: Relating to chondroclasts, cells that resorb cartilage (especially calcified cartilage) during endochondral bone formation and remodeling; the action is analogous to osteoclast-mediated bone resorption.

chondrocostal.definition: Relating to the cartilage of a rib; pertaining to costal cartilage or to the joints between a rib and its costal cartilage.

chondrodysplasia.definition: A congenital disorder characterized by abnormal development of cartilage, particularly at the growth plates, leading to skeletal dysplasia and abnormal bone growth; commonly results in disproportionate short stature and limb deformities.

chondrodysplasia punctata.definition: A group of inherited skeletal dysplasias characterized by punctate (stippled) calcifications of the epiphyses and other cartilaginous structures on radiographs in infancy, often with limb shortening and variable extra-skeletal anomalies; etiologies include defects in cholesterol biosynthesis or peroxisomal function.

conradi-hunermann form.definition: An X-linked dominant form of chondrodysplasia punctata (CDPX2) caused by mutations in the EBP gene involved in cholesterol biosynthesis; characterized in infancy by asymmetric skin abnormalities along Blaschko lines (ichthyosiform patches) and punctate calcifications of developing cartilage (epiphyses), often with rhizomelic limb shortening and other skeletal anomalies.

chondrodystrophia calcificans congenita.definition: A rare congenital skeletal dysplasia characterized by abnormal cartilage development (chondrodystrophy) with calcification of cartilaginous structures, resulting in skeletal anomalies.

chondrodystrophy.definition: A congenital disorder of cartilage development, particularly endochondral cartilage, resulting in skeletal dysplasia and short stature (dwarfism).

chondrodystrophic myotonia.definition: A rare congenital condition in which skeletal dysplasia (chondrodystrophy) is accompanied by myotonia (delayed relaxation of voluntary muscles after contraction).

chondroendothelioma.definition: A rare neoplasm characterized by cartilaginous (chondroid) differentiation with endothelial/vascular components; a nonstandard term whose exact histogenesis and diagnostic criteria vary across reports.

chondroendotheliomata.definition: A rare neoplasm consisting of cartilaginous (chondroid) tissue intermingled with endothelial (vascular) components; a mixed chondroid-vascular tumor.

chondroangioma.definition: A benign lesion consisting of cartilage tissue with an abnormal network of blood vessels.

chondroblast.definition: A cell that forms cartilage by secreting the extracellular matrix and differentiates into a chondrocyte.

codman’s tumor.definition: A malignant bone tumor (osteosarcoma) arising from osteoblasts that produces malignant osteoid; most often affects the metaphyses of long bones in children and young adults, with radiographs showing subperiosteal new bone such as Codman’s triangle.

chondroblastoma.definition: A rare benign bone tumor originating from chondroblasts (cartilage-forming cells), most commonly arising in the epiphysis of long bones in adolescents; it often presents with joint pain and can be locally aggressive.

chondroid.definition: Resembling cartilage; cartilage-like tissue or matrix, especially as seen in certain neoplasms where the stroma mimics cartilage.

chondroid lipoma.definition: A rare benign soft-tissue tumor composed of mature adipose tissue intermixed with a chondroid (cartilaginous) matrix and myxoid stroma, sometimes containing lipoblast-like cells; it is typically treated with complete surgical excision and has an excellent prognosis.

chondrolipoma.definition: A benign soft-tissue tumor consisting of mature adipose tissue with cartilaginous differentiation; a variant of lipoma.

chondroma.definition: A benign neoplasm consisting of mature cartilage tissue; typically arises within bone (in the medullary cavity) but can also occur in soft tissues.

enchondroma.definition: A benign cartilaginous tumor that develops within the medullary cavity of a bone, most often in the small bones of the hands and feet; typically slow-growing and radiographically shows an intramedullary lucent lesion with endosteal scalloping, and may be solitary or part of enchondromatosis (Ollier disease) or Maffucci syndrome; treatment ranges from observation to curettage with bone grafting if symptomatic or fractured.

ecchondroma.definition: A benign cartilaginous tumor arising within the medullary cavity of bone, most often in small bones of the hands and feet. It typically presents as a slow-growing, often asymptomatic lesion and appears as a well-defined intramedullary lytic area with calcifications on X-ray. Management ranges from observation to curettage with bone grafting if symptomatic or fracture risk is present.

hyaloenchondroma.definition: A benign cartilaginous tumor arising from hyaline cartilage within bone (an enchondroma); most often occurring in the small bones of the hands and feet, typically asymptomatic but may cause pain, deformity, or fracture, with management ranging from observation to curettage and bone grafting if needed.

osteochondroma.definition: A benign cartilage-capped bony outgrowth (exostosis) that arises from the metaphysis of a long bone and is continuous with the cortex and medullary cavity; typically presents in childhood or adolescence and may be solitary or part of hereditary multiple exostoses; usually painless but can cause deformity or mechanical symptoms, with a rare risk of malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma.

chondromatosis.definition: A condition characterized by the proliferation of cartilaginous nodules, typically arising from the synovial membrane within a joint (synovial chondromatosis) and potentially becoming loose bodies; it can also refer to multiple enchondromas within bone (enchondromatosis, Ollier disease).

synovial chondroma.definition: A benign cartilaginous tumor arising from the synovial membrane (lining of a joint, tendon sheath, or bursa), typically presenting as a solitary cartilage nodule within or adjacent to a joint; composed of mature hyaline cartilage and may cause swelling or limited motion, with treatment usually by surgical excision or synovectomy. It is distinguished from synovial chondromatosis, which involves multiple cartilaginous nodules.

chondromatous.definition: Of or relating to cartilage; composed of or resembling cartilaginous tissue.

chondromyxofibroma.definition: A rare benign bone tumor consisting of a lobulated mix of chondroid (cartilaginous) and myxoid matrix with fibrous stroma, most often arising in the metaphysis of long bones in adolescents and young adults.

chondromyxoid fibroma.definition: A rare benign bone tumor consisting of lobulated chondroid (cartilaginous) and myxoid stroma with benign-appearing chondrocyte-like cells, typically arising in the metaphysis of long bones in adolescents and young adults; it is locally aggressive with a risk of recurrence after curettage but does not metastasize.

chondrophyte.definition: A cartilaginous outgrowth or spur from a bone or joint surface, composed primarily of cartilage rather than bone.

chondroplasia.definition: Abnormal formation or growth of cartilage, leading to skeletal abnormalities; it can be congenital or inherited.

chondroplast.definition: A surgical procedure to repair or reshape damaged cartilage, typically performed to treat focal cartilage defects in a joint.

chondroplasty.definition: A surgical procedure to repair or smooth damaged articular cartilage in a joint, typically performed arthroscopically by shaving or debriding irregular cartilage surfaces to restore a smoother joint surface and relieve pain.

chondrosarcomata.definition: A malignant cartilaginous tumor; a malignant mesenchymal neoplasm that produces cartilage matrix, typically arising in bone (often pelvis, femur, or humerus) in adults; grows slowly but can invade locally and metastasize (often to the lungs); treated primarily by wide surgical excision, with limited responsiveness to chemotherapy or radiotherapy; may arise de novo or from preexisting cartilaginous lesions (secondary chondrosarcoma).

chondrosarcomatosis.definition: A rare condition characterized by the presence of multiple malignant cartilaginous tumors (chondrosarcomas) arising in bone or soft tissue.

chondrosarcomatous.definition: Resembling chondrosarcoma; showing malignant cartilage-forming differentiation within a tumor.

chondrosis.definition: A degenerative condition of cartilage, especially articular cartilage, characterized by deterioration, softening, or erosion of the cartilage.

chondrosternal joint.definition: An articulation between a costal cartilage and the sternum (sternocostal/chondrosternal joint). The first sternocostal joint is a primary cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis) with the manubrium, while ribs 2–7 form synovial plane joints with the sternum, allowing small gliding movements during respiration.

chondrotomy.definition: A surgical procedure involving an incision into cartilage, typically to relieve constriction or gain access to underlying structures.

chop.definition: A multi-agent chemotherapy regimen used to treat non-Hodgkin lymphoma (and some other cancers), consisting of cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone.

chorda.definition: Latin for "cord" or "string." In anatomy it refers to a cord-like structure, such as a nerve tract or the embryonic notochord (notochord), a flexible rod that serves as the primitive axial support.

chordae tendineae.definition: Tendinous cords that connect the papillary muscles to the leaflets of the atrioventricular valves (mitral and tricuspid), preventing valve prolapse during ventricular systole by maintaining leaflet tension.

chordal.definition: Relating to a cord or cordlike structure; in anatomy, used to describe cordlike structures such as the chordae tendineae (the heart strings) or related embryologic structures.
