chorditis.definition: A nonstandard term indicating inflammation of a cord‑like structure; not widely used in modern medicine. When used, it should specify the exact cord involved (for example, inflammation of the vocal cords, i.e., laryngitis, or another cord-like structure).

chorditis nodosa.definition: A chronic inflammatory condition of the laryngeal vocal cords characterized by nodular inflammatory lesions on the true vocal folds, causing hoarseness and altered voice quality.

chordoid.definition: Pertaining to a histologic pattern in which cells are arranged in cords or strands, typically within a myxoid or mucinous stroma.

chordoma.definition: A rare malignant tumor arising from residual notochordal cells along the axial skeleton (most often at the skull base/clivus or sacrum), locally aggressive with potential for recurrence and metastasis; treatment typically involves surgical resection and radiotherapy.

chordotomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which a portion of the spinal cord is destroyed or lesioned to relieve intractable pain, typically by interrupting the pain-conducting spinothalamic tract.

chorea.definition: An involuntary, irregular, brief, dancing-like jerky movement that flows from one body part to another, often affecting the face and limbs; seen in Huntington disease, Sydenham chorea, and other basal ganglia disorders.

chorea gravidarum.definition: A form of chorea that begins during pregnancy, characterized by involuntary, rapid, irregular, dance-like movements of the face, limbs, and trunk, usually transient and resolving after delivery.

chorea minor.definition: An involuntary, irregular, dancing movement disorder that occurs in children as part of acute rheumatic fever after streptococcal infection; also known as Sydenham chorea. Movements affect the face, tongue, and limbs and are often accompanied by hypotonia and emotional lability, typically self-limiting over weeks to months.

choreic.definition: Relating to chorea; characterized by involuntary, rapid, irregular, dance-like movements.

choreiform.definition: Relating to chorea or resembling chorea; describing involuntary, irregular, jerky, dance-like movements.

choreoacanthocytosis.definition: A rare autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder in the neuroacanthocytosis spectrum caused by VPS13A mutations, characterized by chorea, orofacial dyskinesias, psychiatric and cognitive impairment, and acanthocytosis (spur cells) on peripheral blood smear.

choreoathetoid cerebral palsy.definition: A dyskinetic form of cerebral palsy characterized by involuntary, irregular, writhing movements (athetoid) often combined with choreiform, rapid movements, resulting in abnormal postures and fluctuating muscle tone and impaired voluntary movement. Typically due to damage to the basal ganglia or related motor pathways.

choreoathetosis.definition: Choreoathetosis is a hyperkinetic movement disorder characterized by a mixture of chorea (quick, irregular, dance-like movements) and athetosis (slow, writhing, twisting movements), typically due to dysfunction of the basal ganglia.

chorioadenoma.definition: An invasive hydatidiform mole; a gestational trophoblastic neoplasm in which molar villi invade the myometrium, often following a hydatidiform mole.

chorioadenomata.definition: A form of gestational trophoblastic disease in which placental villous tissue and trophoblast invade the myometrium, typically arising from a hydatidiform mole and behaving like an invasive mole.

chorioadenoma destruens.definition: An invasive form of gestational trophoblastic disease arising from a molar pregnancy, in which hydropic chorionic villi invade the myometrium; historically called an invasive mole and may persist after evacuation or metastasize.

chorioamnionic.definition: Pertaining to the chorion and amnion, the fetal membranes that enclose the amniotic cavity.

chorioamnionitis.definition: An infection and inflammation of the chorion and amnion (the fetal membranes) usually caused by ascending bacteria during pregnancy or labor, typically presenting with maternal fever and uterine tenderness (often with fetal tachycardia and/or foul-smelling amniotic fluid).

prosencephalon.definition: An embryonic forebrain (the anterior primary brain vesicle) that develops into the telencephalon (cerebral hemispheres) and diencephalon (thalamus, hypothalamus, and related structures).

mesencephalon.definition: Midbrain; the portion of the brainstem between the pons and the diencephalon. It contains the cerebral aqueduct and key structures such as the cerebral peduncles, tectum (superior and inferior colliculi), red nucleus, substantia nigra, and oculomotor nerve nuclei; it participates in motor control and visual and auditory reflexes.

rhombencephalon.definition: The hindbrain; the embryonic region of the developing neural tube that forms the metencephalon (which becomes the pons and cerebellum) and the myelencephalon (which becomes the medulla oblongata).

alar plate.definition: The dorsal region of the developing neural tube that differentiates into sensory interneurons and sensory nuclei, forming the dorsal horn of the spinal cord and related sensory structures; it gives rise to the pathways for somatic and visceral sensation.

basal plate.definition: Forming the ventral (motor) portion of the developing neural tube, the basal plate gives rise to motor neurons and the ventral gray matter of the spinal cord; its dorsal counterpart is the alar plate, which forms sensory structures.

chordencephalon.definition: An archaic term used in historical embryology to refer to the developing brain region during early neural development; not used in contemporary anatomy.

chordencephalic.definition: Relating to the brain and spinal cord; pertaining to the central nervous system.

notochordal canal.definition: A temporary embryologic canal within the developing notochord that briefly connects the primitive gut (endoderm) with the neural tube region and typically closes as development proceeds.

notochordal tissue.definition: A rod-shaped embryonic structure derived from mesoderm that provides axial support and emits developmental signals; in humans it largely regresses, with remnants forming the nucleus pulposus of intervertebral discs.

lipoblasts.definition: Immature adipocytes derived from mesenchymal cells; they contain multiple cytoplasmic lipid vacuoles that indent or displace the nucleus (scalloped appearance) and serve as precursors to mature fat cells, seen in developing adipose tissue and in liposarcoma.

perichondrial bone.definition: Bone formed in the perichondrium, the connective tissue envelope around cartilage, by surface ossification around a cartilaginous model; it differs from bone formed by endochondral replacement of cartilage.

left atrium.definition: The left upper chamber of the heart.

tricuspid valve.definition: A three-flap valve that sits between the right atrium and the right ventricle.

aortic semilunar valve.definition: A three-cusped semilunar valve at the left ventricle outflow tract that opens during systole to permit ejection of blood into the aorta and closes during diastole to prevent backflow into the ventricle; one of the two semilunar heart valves.

pulmonary semilunar valve.definition: A semilunar heart valve between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk, consisting of three cusps; it opens during systole to allow blood into the pulmonary artery and closes during diastole to prevent backflow into the right ventricle.

interventricular septum.definition: A muscular and membranous partition between the right and left ventricles of the heart that prevents mixing of blood between the two chambers.

papillary muscle.definition: Muscular projections from the walls of the ventricles that attach to the leaflets of the atrioventricular valves (mitral and tricuspid) via chordae tendineae; their contraction prevents valve prolapse during systole.

descending aorta.definition: A major segment of the aorta that descends from the aortic arch through the thorax and abdomen, giving off branches to the chest and abdominal organs; it is divided into the thoracic (descending thoracic) aorta and the abdominal aorta after passing through the diaphragm.

left pulmonary artery.definition: A branch of the pulmonary trunk that carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the left lung for oxygenation; it courses to the left lung and divides into the left superior and left inferior lobar arteries.

branches of left pulmonary vein.definition: Two main veins draining the left lung—left superior pulmonary vein and left inferior pulmonary vein—that return oxygenated blood to the left atrium; each main vein collects blood from the corresponding lobes via segmental/tributary veins (near the hilum) and may have subdividing branches.

sella.definition: A saddle-shaped depression in the sphenoid bone of the skull (the hypophyseal fossa) that houses the pituitary gland.

chorionic.definition: Relating to the chorion, the outer fetal membrane that forms part of the placenta.

chorioblastoma.definition: An obsolete or nonstandard term with no widely accepted modern definition; not used in current medical nomenclature, and if encountered its meaning is unclear and does not correspond to a specific recognized tumor.

chorioepithelioma.definition: A malignant tumor of trophoblastic tissue arising from the chorionic epithelium of the placenta; a form of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia characterized by rapid growth and early metastatic spread, often with markedly elevated hCG.

choriocele.definition: An abnormal sac-like protrusion of the fetal chorionic membranes through a defect in the uterus (uterine wall), i.e., herniation of the chorion.

choriogenesis.definition: The formation and development of the chorion, the outer fetal membrane that contributes to placental formation, arising from the trophoblast and extraembryonic mesoderm.

choriogonadotropin.definition: A glycoprotein hormone produced by placental trophoblasts (human chorionic gonadotropin, hCG) that stimulates the corpus luteum to produce progesterone in early pregnancy; LH-like activity.

choriomeningitis.definition: Inflammation of the meninges (the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord) with concurrent inflammation of the choroid plexus; usually caused by infection (often viral, as in lymphocytic choriomeningitis).

chorioretinitis.definition: An inflammation of the choroid and retina of the eye, usually due to infection or inflammatory disease, which can impair vision.

chorioretinopathy.definition: A disease process affecting both the choroid and retina of the eye, describing combined pathological changes in these tissues (such as inflammation, degeneration, edema, or scarring) that can impair vision.

choroidal.definition: Relating to the choroid, the vascular layer of the eye between the retina and the sclera that supplies blood to the outer retina.

choroideremia.definition: An X-linked recessive inherited retinal dystrophy caused by CHM mutations, leading to progressive degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium, photoreceptors, and choroid; typically presents in childhood or adolescence with night blindness and peripheral vision loss, progressing to central vision loss in many affected males, while female carriers may have mild or no symptoms.

choroiditis.definition: Inflammation of the choroid, the vascular layer of the eye between the retina and sclera; a form of uveitis that can be infectious or noninfectious and may cause blurred vision, floaters, photophobia, and eye pain.

choroidocyclitis.definition: Inflammation of the choroid and the ciliary body of the eye (the posterior part of the uveal tract), a form of uveitis.

plexectomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which a nerve plexus is removed or excised.

chromaffin.definition: Relating to cells that stain with chromium salts (chromaffin reaction) due to catecholamine-containing granules; these cells are primarily in the adrenal medulla and paraganglia and synthesize and secrete catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine) in response to stress.

chromaffinoma.definition: A neoplasm arising from chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla or sympathetic paraganglia, often secreting catecholamines; when located in the adrenal gland it is commonly called pheochromocytoma. May be benign or malignant and typically presents with symptoms of catecholamine excess (e.g., episodic hypertension, headaches, sweating, palpitations); treatment is surgical resection with appropriate perioperative catecholamine blockade.

paraganglion.definition: A small cluster of neuroendocrine cells derived from neural crest, located outside the adrenal glands and forming part of the peripheral autonomic nervous system; these tissues can function as chemoreceptors (as in the carotid body) and may secrete catecholamines.

paraganglia.definition: Small clusters of neuroendocrine cells derived from neural crest that accompany the autonomic nervous system; located along the sympathetic chain and in the head and neck, with sympathetic paraganglia containing chromaffin cells that secrete catecholamines and parasympathetic paraganglia being non-chromaffin and typically nonsecretory.

chromatid.definition: One of the two identical copies of a replicated chromosome, held together at the centromere; these copies separate during anaphase of mitosis or meiosis II to become independent chromosomes.

chromatin.definition: A complex of DNA and proteins (histones) that packages genetic material in the nucleus; exists in a less condensed form (euchromatin) that is typically transcriptionally active and a more condensed form (heterochromatin) that is usually transcriptionally inactive.

deletion.definition: A genetic alteration in which a portion of a chromosome is deleted, resulting in the loss of one or more genes; can be inherited or arise de novo and may cause developmental abnormalities or disease depending on the genes affected.

villus.definition: A finger-like projection of the mucous membrane lining the small intestine that increases surface area for nutrient absorption; each villus contains a network of capillaries and a central lacteal, and is lined by absorptive enterocytes with microvilli.

sampling.definition: The process of selecting a representative subset of individuals, items, or specimens from a larger population for measurement, analysis, or testing in order to estimate characteristics of the whole population; in clinical practice, it also refers to obtaining a specimen (e.g., blood, tissue) for laboratory examination.

cvs.definition:
- A prenatal diagnostic procedure in which a small sample of placental tissue is collected for genetic or chromosomal analysis, typically performed in early pregnancy (about 10–13 weeks).
- The cardiovascular system: the organ system comprising the heart and blood vessels that circulates blood to supply oxygen and nutrients to tissues and remove wastes.

cord.definition: A long, slender, rope-like anatomical structure in the body that connects parts or carries substances, such as transmitting neural signals or transporting blood.

cryptorchidism.definition: A condition in which one or both testes fail to descend into the scrotum, typically remaining in the abdomen or inguinal canal; it is usually present at birth and, if not corrected, can impair fertility and increase the risk of testicular cancer, with treatment commonly involving orchiopexy in infancy or early childhood.

hypogonadism.definition: A condition in which the gonads produce insufficient sex hormones and often have impaired gamete production, arising from primary gonadal failure or secondary hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction.

follicle-stimulating.definition: A gonadotropin hormone produced by the anterior pituitary that stimulates growth and maturation of ovarian follicles (and estrogen production) in females, and promotes spermatogenesis in males.

luteinizing.definition: Relating to luteinization; the process by which ovarian follicle cells are transformed into the corpus luteum, typically under the influence of luteinizing hormone.

thyroid-stimulating.definition: Pertaining to stimulation of the thyroid gland; substances or processes that increase thyroid hormone production by acting on the thyroid.

gamete.definition: The egg (from women) or sperm (from men) that together can form the beginning of human life.

transfer.definition: A process in a healthcare setting involving moving a patient, specimen, or equipment from one location or level of care to another, typically requiring handoff communication, accompanying documentation, and appropriate monitoring or safety measures.

fertilization.definition: Process by which a sperm cell fuses with an oocyte to form a zygote, restoring the diploid chromosome number and beginning embryonic development.

oocytes.definition: Oocytes are the female germ cells in the ovaries; immature egg cells that mature by meiosis to become ova capable of fertilization.

trophoblast.definition: An outer-layer cell population of the early embryo (blastocyst) that contributes to the placenta; it differentiates into cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast, invades the uterine lining to establish implantation, and facilitates nutrient exchange while secreting hormones such as human chorionic gonadotropin.

trophoblastic.definition: Relating to trophoblasts, the outer cell layer of the blastocyst that contributes to the placenta and is involved in implantation and placental development.

hemorrhagic.definition: Relating to or caused by hemorrhage (bleeding); characterized by or involving bleeding.

necrotic.definition: Relating to tissue that has died; the death of cells or tissue in a living organism, typically due to injury, insufficient blood supply (ischemia), infection, or toxins.

chromatography.definition: A laboratory technique for separating components of a mixture by passing it through a system with a stationary phase and a moving (mobile) phase, causing components to travel at different speeds and be collected for analysis and quantification.

chromomere.definition: A bead-like, densely staining segment of a chromosome formed by localized chromatin condensation, most clearly visible on polytene chromosomes and during early mitosis.

chromatopsia.definition: A disturbance of color vision in which colors are perceived abnormally, with distorted hues or impaired color discrimination, potentially due to retinal/cone dysfunction, optic pathway disease, or cortical pathology, and sometimes drug or toxin effects.

chromatosis.definition: An abnormal coloration of tissue or skin due to pigment deposition or pigmentary changes; a descriptive term rather than a specific disease.

chromaturia.definition: Discoloration of urine due to pigments or metabolites excreted in the urine (e.g., blood pigments, bilirubin, porphyrins, or myoglobin) or certain drugs, producing colors other than the normal pale yellow.

chromophobe.definition: A cell or tissue that stains poorly with standard histologic dyes (e.g., hematoxylin and eosin), typically appearing pale; in pituitary histology it refers to nonsecretory chromophobe cells that stain weakly due to lack of secretory granules.

chromophobe adenoma.definition: A pituitary adenoma characterized by tumor cells that stain poorly with standard histologic stains (chromophobe cells), typically nonfunctional and presenting with mass effects rather than hormone excess.

chromophobia.definition: An irrational fear of colors, classified as a specific phobia, causing anxiety and avoidance of colored stimuli or environments.

chromophobic.definition: Describing cells or tissues that do not take up color readily with standard histological stains (e.g., hematoxylin and eosin), appearing pale or weakly stained compared with surrounding structures.

chromoblastomycosis.definition: A chronic fungal infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue caused by pigmented dematiaceous fungi acquired through traumatic inoculation, presenting with verrucous lesions (often on the legs) and histology showing muriform (sclerotic) bodies.

chromomycosis.definition: A chronic subcutaneous fungal infection caused by pigmented (dematiaceous) fungi, acquired by traumatic inoculation, presenting as slowly enlarging verrucous lesions on the skin (typically the lower limbs); histology shows sclerotic bodies, often called "copper pennies."

chromocenter.definition: An interphase nuclear structure in which pericentromeric heterochromatin from multiple chromosomes aggregates into a single dense cluster, rich in repetitive DNA and often visible as a bright spot with DNA staining.

chromocystoscopy.definition: An endoscopic procedure in which a chromogenic dye is instilled into the bladder to color the mucosa and highlight abnormal lesions, aiding detection of urothelial pathology such as bladder cancer.

cystochromoscopy.definition: A cystoscopic technique in which a chromophore dye is instilled into the bladder to enhance mucosal visualization during cystoscopy, helping detect bladder lesions such as tumors or carcinoma in situ.

chromonema.definition: A threadlike form of chromatin observed during the early stages of mitosis as chromosomes condense; it represents the chromosome before full condensation into a discrete, rod-shaped structure.

chromonemata.definition: Threadlike chromatin fibers that comprise a chromosome during meiotic prophase, representing elongated chromatin that condenses to form the paired sister chromatids; visible as filamentous chromosomes before full condensation.

chromoneme.definition: A subunit of chromatin described as a repeating, bead‑like segment along the threadlike chromatin fiber of a chromosome during cell division; used in some older cytogenetic descriptions and not widely used in modern terminology.

chromosomal.definition: Relating to chromosomes, the threadlike structures in cell nuclei that carry genetic material (DNA); used to describe inheritance patterns and abnormalities in chromosome number or structure.

chromosomal aberration.definition: A change in chromosome number or structure, such as aneuploidy or structural rearrangements (deletions, duplications, inversions, translocations), which can cause genetic disorders.

klinefelter syndrome.definition: An aneuploidy in males in which an extra X chromosome is present (most commonly 47,XXY) due to nondisjunction, causing hypogonadism and infertility, tall stature, gynecomastia, small testes, and often learning or language difficulties; managed with testosterone replacement therapy and supportive educational or fertility interventions.

philadelphia chromosome.definition: A reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 (t(9;22)(q34;q11)) that creates the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene, producing a constitutively active tyrosine kinase that drives chronic myeloid leukemia.

philadelphia chromosomes.definition: Reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 (t(9;22)(q34;q11)) that creates the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene with constitutive tyrosine kinase activity; a hallmark of chronic myeloid leukemia and also seen in some cases of acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

karyotype.definition: A karyotype is the number, size, and appearance of an organism's chromosomes as observed in a cell, usually by arranging chromosomes into a karyogram. In humans, the normal karyotype consists of 46 chromosomes (22 autosome pairs and 2 sex chromosomes).

meiosis.definition: Meiosis is a specialized form of cell division that reduces the chromosome number by half to produce four genetically diverse haploid gametes from a single diploid germ cell, via two sequential divisions (meiosis I and meiosis II) following a round of DNA replication, with recombination and independent assortment of chromosomes contributing to genetic variation.

interphase.definition: An interval of the cell cycle between mitotic divisions during which the cell grows, replicates its DNA, and prepares for mitosis; chromosomes are decondensed and metabolic activity is high (G1, S, and G2 phases).

prophase.definition: The first stage of cell division in which chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes, the nucleolus disappears, the mitotic spindle forms outside the nucleus, and the nuclear envelope begins to break down, preparing chromosomes for alignment and separation.

glomerular filtration rate.definition: The volume of filtrate produced by all kidney glomeruli per minute, reflecting overall kidney function; usually expressed in milliliters per minute and estimated from serum creatinine, age, sex, and race (eGFR).

edetate.definition: A salt of ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) used as a chelating agent to bind metal ions; common forms include disodium edetate and calcium disodium edetate.

edetic acid.definition: An organic chelating agent that binds metal ions to form stable complexes; used to treat heavy metal poisoning and as a chelating agent in laboratory settings (also used as a food preservative and as an anticoagulant in blood collection).

chromium.definition: A trace mineral that is an essential micronutrient required in small amounts for normal carbohydrate, fat, and protein metabolism; it functions as a cofactor in insulin signaling and glucose uptake. Deficiency is rare; chromium supplementation is controversial and not routinely recommended for diabetes; high doses can be toxic.

chromium-51.definition: Radioactive chromium isotope (51Cr) used in nuclear medicine to label red blood cells for determining red cell survival and total blood volume; emits gamma radiation detectable by scintigraphy.

catgut.definition: An absorbable suture material made from collagen derived from the connective tissue of animal intestines (typically sheep or cattle); commonly called catgut, though it is not derived from cats.

color blindness.definition: Color vision deficiency is a condition in which a person has difficulty distinguishing colors due to abnormalities in the retinal cone photoreceptors, most commonly an inherited deficiency affecting red and green cones (often X‑linked); blue–yellow deficiencies and complete color blindness occur less commonly. It typically does not affect visual acuity or peripheral vision.

chromium trioxide.definition: A highly toxic inorganic compound with the formula CrO3; a hexavalent chromium compound that acts as a strong oxidizer and is used in chrome plating and oxidation processes; exposure (especially inhalation) can cause severe irritation and lung injury and is carcinogenic to humans.

gene.definition: A basic unit of heredity consisting of a specific sequence of DNA (or RNA in some viruses) that encodes the information to produce a functional product, usually a protein or RNA molecule.

chromosome walking.definition: A molecular genetics technique used to localize and clone a gene by progressively sequencing overlapping DNA clones that extend from a known sequence along the chromosome, moving from the known region into adjacent, previously unknown DNA.

chromotherapy.definition: An alternative therapy that claims exposure to specific colors (often via colored light) can influence physiological or psychological states; there is little robust evidence supporting its therapeutic efficacy.

chromotrope.definition: Not a standard term in medical dictionaries. A colorant or staining dye used in microscopy to impart color to cellular components for visualization; in some contexts it may refer to a specific dye used for highlighting parasites or other structures.

chromotropic.definition: Relating to or causing a color change; colorimetric or color-sensitive, typically describing substances or reactions that change color in response to a chemical or physiological stimulus.

chronaxy.definition: The minimum duration of an electrical stimulus of twice the rheobase required to excite a nerve or muscle fiber; a measure of tissue excitability.

electroneuromyography.definition: A diagnostic test that combines nerve conduction studies and needle electromyography to evaluate the function of peripheral nerves and the muscles they innervate, measuring conduction velocity, amplitude, and muscle electrical activity to diagnose neuromuscular disorders.

portal inflammation.definition: Inflammation confined to the portal tracts of the liver (the portal triads), characterized by infiltration of inflammatory cells—usually lymphocytes and plasma cells—in histologic sections; commonly seen in hepatitis and chronic liver disease.

parenchyma.definition: Functional tissue of an organ comprising the cells that perform the organ's primary tasks, as opposed to the supporting connective tissue (stroma).

viral infections.definition: Infections caused by viruses that invade host cells and hijack cellular machinery to replicate, producing a range of illnesses that vary by virus and tissue involved; transmission occurs through respiratory, fecal-oral, bloodborne, or vector routes and outcomes can be from asymptomatic to severe; prevention includes vaccination and, when available, antiviral therapy.

autoimmune reactions.definition: An immune response directed against the body's own tissues, arising from loss of self-tolerance by B and T lymphocytes; often mediated by autoantibodies or autoreactive T cells, leading to inflammation and tissue injury.

korsakoff psychosis.definition: A chronic amnestic neuropsychiatric disorder due to thiamine deficiency (often from chronic alcohol misuse), characterized by severe anterograde amnesia with variable retrograde memory loss, prominent confabulation, and impaired new learning, with relatively preserved language and social function early in the course.

detoxification.definition: The process of removing toxins from the body, typically by metabolic transformation (primarily in the liver) and excretion (via the kidneys and bile); in addiction medicine, it also refers to medically supervised withdrawal and stabilization from a toxic or addictive substance.

chronic appendicitis.definition: A recurrent or persistent inflammation of the vermiform appendix causing intermittent right lower quadrant abdominal pain over an extended period; symptoms may be mild and nonspecific, and diagnosis is often made after excluding other causes; management may include interval appendectomy if symptoms recur.

bacterial prostatitis.definition: An infection and inflammation of the prostate gland caused by bacteria, presenting as acute or chronic prostatitis with urinary symptoms and pelvic or perineal pain; treated with prolonged antibiotics that penetrate the prostate (commonly fluoroquinolones or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole).

calcific pancreatitis.definition: A form of chronic pancreatitis characterized by calcifications within the pancreatic tissue and/or ducts, reflecting long-standing inflammatory damage; imaging typically shows pancreatic calcifications, and patients may develop pancreatic exocrine and endocrine insufficiency.

pancreatitis with calcification.definition: Chronic inflammation of the pancreas accompanied by calcifications in the pancreatic tissue or ducts, typically arising from long-standing injury (often alcohol-related). Imaging usually shows pancreatic calcifications and the condition presents with persistent abdominal pain and progressive loss of pancreatic exocrine and endocrine function, leading to malabsorption and diabetes. Management includes pain control, pancreatic enzyme replacement, addressing underlying risk factors, and, if needed, endoscopic or surgical interventions.

chronic carrier.definition: An asymptomatic person who harbors a pathogenic organism after an acute infection and can transmit it to others for an extended period, sometimes for life.

chronic cholecystitis.definition: A long-standing inflammation of the gallbladder, usually due to gallstones or recurrent episodes of acute cholecystitis, resulting in thickening and fibrosis of the gallbladder wall with persistent or intermittent right upper quadrant pain and impaired gallbladder function.

huntingtons disease.definition: A hereditary neurodegenerative disorder caused by an autosomal dominant CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene on chromosome 4, leading to progressive motor dysfunction (chorea), cognitive decline, and psychiatric symptoms; onset typically in mid-adulthood; there is no cure; management is supportive and symptom-based.

cystic mastitis.definition: A benign breast condition in which cysts develop within the breast tissue, commonly as part of fibrocystic changes; it presents with tender, palpable lumps that may fluctuate with the menstrual cycle and is not an infectious inflammatory process.

fibrocystic disease.definition: A common benign breast condition characterized by proliferation of fibrous tissue and the formation of cysts, causing bilateral lumpiness and sometimes cyclic tenderness or pain that fluctuates with the menstrual cycle.

dieting syndrome.definition: An informal term for the constellation of adverse health effects that arise from prolonged or extreme caloric restriction, including malnutrition, electrolyte disturbances, hypoglycemia, fatigue, dizziness, cognitive impairment, and hormonal/metabolic disturbances.

chronic disease.definition: A disease or condition that persists for a long time (usually at least 3 months), may develop slowly or recur, and requires ongoing medical care, management, or rehabilitation; it is typically not rapidly curable and may limit daily activities.

endarteritis deformans.definition: A chronic inflammatory disease of medium- and small-sized arteries characterized by endarteritis with thickening and deformity of the vessel walls, leading to luminal narrowing or occlusion.

valvular endocarditis.definition: An infection of the heart’s endocardial surface that predominantly involves a valve, producing vegetations on the valve leaflets and causing valvular dysfunction; usually due to bacteria (infective endocarditis) or fungi after bacteremia, and can be acute or subacute with risk of systemic embolization.

chronic fatigue syndrome.definition: A serious, long-term illness that affects many body systems. It is also called myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS).

cidp.definition: A chronic autoimmune inflammatory disorder of the peripheral nervous system characterized by immune-mediated demyelination of peripheral nerves, leading to slowly progressive or relapsing symmetric weakness and sensory loss over at least 8 weeks; diagnosis is supported by electrophysiologic evidence of demyelination and elevated CSF protein with normal cell count, and it often responds to immunotherapy.

chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyn.definition: A chronic autoimmune inflammatory neuropathy in which the peripheral nerves are demyelinated, causing progressive or relapsing symmetric weakness and sensory loss, typically lasting at least 8 weeks; diagnosed by demyelinating features on nerve conduction studies and elevated CSF protein with a normal cell count, and treated with corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), or plasma exchange.

guillain barre syndrome.definition: A rapid-onset, immune-mediated inflammatory polyneuropathy of the peripheral nerves, typically triggered by infection, presenting with symmetric, ascending weakness and hyporeflexia or areflexia; sensory symptoms and autonomic dysfunction may occur, and it can progress to respiratory failure. Treatment includes plasmapheresis or intravenous immunoglobulin, with most patients gradually recovering over weeks to months.

chronic glomerulonephritis.definition: A chronic inflammatory disease of the kidney's glomeruli with long-standing or progressive hematuria and proteinuria, hypertension, and declining renal function due to glomerular scarring (glomerulosclerosis) and immune-mediated injury; often represents the end stage of various glomerulonephritides rather than a single disease.

postinfectious glomerulonephritis.definition: An immune complex–mediated glomerulonephritis that follows a preceding infection (most commonly group A streptococcal pharyngitis or impetigo) and presents with acute nephritic syndrome (hematuria, edema, hypertension, and typically proteinuria), often with transient low complement levels (especially C3).

subacute glomerulonephritis.definition: An inflammatory disease of the kidney glomeruli with a slower, subacute onset compared with acute nephritic syndromes, typically immune-mediated, presenting with hematuria and proteinuria, variable edema and hypertension, and potential progressive renal dysfunction over weeks to months.

urates.definition: Salts of uric acid (most commonly monosodium urate), formed when uric acid is deprotonated and binds to a cation (e.g., Na+, K+); these salts can crystallize in tissues (as in gout) or be excreted in urine.

chronic granulocytic leukemia.definition: A myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by clonal expansion of granulocytic precursors (primarily neutrophils) in the bone marrow and peripheral blood, typically driven by the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene (Philadelphia chromosome); presents with marked leukocytosis, left-shifted granulopoiesis, splenomegaly, and may progress from a chronic phase to accelerated and blast phases if untreated.

chronic myelocytic leukemia.definition: A myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene from the Philadelphia chromosome, causing clonal expansion of mature granulocytes (primarily neutrophils) and marked leukocytosis in blood and bone marrow; it typically progresses from a chronic phase to accelerated and blast phases and is treated with BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g., imatinib).

chronic granulomatous disease.definition: A genetic primary immunodeficiency due to defects in the NADPH oxidase complex of phagocytes, causing defective respiratory burst and impaired killing of certain catalase-positive bacteria and fungi; presents with recurrent infections and granuloma formation.

myeloperoxidase.definition: A heme-containing peroxidase enzyme in neutrophil azurophilic granules that catalyzes the production of hypochlorous acid from hydrogen peroxide and chloride, contributing to microbial killing during the respiratory burst.

hepatitis c.definition: Caused by a germ (a virus) that affects your liver. It can be a short-term disease or it can last for a long time.

hepatitis d.definition: Caused by a germ (a virus) that affects your liver. It is only found in people who also have hepatitis B.

hepatitis e.definition: A viral infection of the liver caused by the hepatitis E virus; transmitted primarily through ingestion of water contaminated with feces. It is usually self-limited but can be severe in pregnant women and in people with weakened immune systems.

hyperplastic rhinitis.definition: A chronic inflammatory disease of the nasal mucosa with thickening from hyperplasia of the mucosal lining and submucosal glands, goblet cell proliferation, and edema, leading to nasal obstruction and rhinorrhea; historically referred to as hypertrophic rhinitis.

hyperplastic sinusitis.definition: A form of chronic rhinosinusitis in which the sinus mucosa undergoes hyperplasia (increased mucosal cell mass), resulting in thickened mucosa and often nasal polyps; presents with chronic nasal obstruction, facial pressure, and discharge, and is managed with intranasal corticosteroids, saline irrigation, and, if needed, endoscopic sinus surgery.

polyp formation.definition: The development of a polyp, a localized mucosal tissue growth that protrudes into a lumen or cavity; it results from abnormal mucosal proliferation and can be inflammatory, hyperplastic, hamartomatous, or neoplastic, with adenomatous polyps carrying potential for malignant progression.

mucous membranes.definition: Moist, protective linings of body cavities that open to the exterior, composed of epithelium overlying a connective tissue layer (lamina propria). They secrete mucus to lubricate and protect surfaces and line the respiratory, gastrointestinal, urinary, and reproductive tracts.

sinuses.definition: Air-filled cavities within certain skull bones connected to the nasal cavity; the major examples are frontal, maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid spaces. They help lighten the skull, humidify and warm inhaled air, contribute to voice resonance, and drain mucus.

chronic hypertrophic rhinitis.definition: A chronic inflammatory nasal mucosal disease characterized by marked hypertrophy and edema of the turbinates (predominantly the inferior turbinates), leading to persistent nasal obstruction, discharge, crusting, and sometimes epistaxis.

panacinar emphysema.definition: Diffuse emphysema with uniform destruction of the entire acinus (air sacs) distal to the terminal bronchioles, due to protease–antiprotease imbalance, classically linked to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and often presenting earlier with basal predominance.

hypertrophic emphysema.definition: An outdated or nonstandard term; not a widely recognized entity in modern pulmonology. Emphysema is defined by permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles with destruction of alveolar walls, not by hypertrophy of tissue.

chronic hypoxia.definition: A persistent deficiency of oxygen delivery to tissues, typically due to sustained hypoxemia from chronic lung or circulatory disease, leading to adaptive responses (e.g., polycythemia, pulmonary hypertension) and potential organ dysfunction over time.

right ventricular heart failure.definition: A condition in which the right ventricle fails to pump blood effectively into the pulmonary circulation, leading to systemic venous congestion with signs such as peripheral edema, ascites, hepatomegaly, and jugular venous distension.

pneumococcal infections.definition: Caused by a specific germ (a bacteria). Includes diseases like ear and sinus infections, pneumonia, and meningitis.

atrovent.definition: An inhaled short-acting anticholinergic bronchodilator (ipratropium bromide) that blocks muscarinic receptors in airway smooth muscle to relieve bronchospasm in COPD and sometimes asthma.

adrenergics.definition: Drugs that stimulate adrenergic receptors (α- and β-adrenergic receptors), producing effects of the sympathetic nervous system; they include endogenous catecholamines (e.g., epinephrine, norepinephrine) and synthetic sympathomimetics.

pursed-lip breathing.definition: A breathing technique that involves inhaling through the nose and exhaling slowly through pursed lips to prolong expiration, increase airway pressure, and reduce the work of breathing (commonly taught for COPD and dyspnea management).

low-flow oxygen.definition: Delivery of supplemental oxygen at low flow rates (typically via a nasal cannula or simple mask) that provides a variable inspired oxygen concentration depending on the flow and the patient’s breathing pattern; contrasts with high-flow oxygen therapies.

pulmonary function test.definition: A set of noninvasive tests that measure how well the lungs take in and release air and how effectively oxygen passes into the blood, typically including spirometry, lung volumes, and diffusion capacity (DLCO) to evaluate, diagnose, and monitor respiratory diseases.

chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.definition: A primary immunodeficiency presenting with chronic or recurrent Candida infections of the skin, nails, and mucous membranes due to impaired T-cell–mediated immunity, often presenting in childhood and sometimes associated with autoimmune endocrinopathies or IL-17 pathway/STAT1 defects.

candidal infection.definition: A fungal infection caused by Candida species (most commonly Candida albicans) affecting skin and mucous membranes, typically presenting as mucocutaneous candidiasis (e.g., oral thrush, vulvovaginal candidiasis, diaper dermatitis); in immunocompromised individuals it can become invasive, causing candidemia and end-organ disease.

moeller's glossitis.definition: A historical term for an inflammatory condition of the tongue (glossitis); in modern practice it is not widely recognized as a distinct entity, and glossitis generally presents with tongue redness, swelling, pain or burning, and may result from nutritional deficiencies, infections, irritants, or autoimmune processes.

lingual papillitis.definition: A benign, self-limited inflammatory condition of the tongue marked by sudden onset of small, painful papules on the tongue surface (often involving the fungiform papillae on the anterior dorsum), typically resolving within a few days to two weeks with symptomatic care.

guillain-barré syndrome.definition: An acute autoimmune inflammatory polyneuropathy causing rapidly progressive, symmetrical weakness and areflexia, usually following a preceding infection, due to immune-mediated damage to the peripheral nerves. Most patients recover with supportive care, and treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin or plasmapheresis can hasten recovery.

demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy.definition: A syndrome in which autoimmune-mediated demyelination affects multiple peripheral nerves and their nerve roots, causing rapidly developing weakness and sensory abnormalities with decreased or absent reflexes; often inflammatory, with acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (Guillain-Barré syndrome) as a prototypical form.

intestinal ischemia.definition: A condition in which insufficient blood flow to the intestines causes intestinal hypoperfusion and tissue injury; it can be acute (often due to embolic/thrombotic mesenteric ischemia or nonocclusive hypoperfusion) or chronic (typically from atherosclerotic mesenteric arterial disease with postprandial pain and weight loss).

intestinal angina.definition: Postprandial abdominal pain due to chronic mesenteric ischemia from atherosclerotic narrowing of the mesenteric arteries, often with weight loss as patients avoid eating.

intractable pain.definition: A chronic pain syndrome that remains inadequately controlled despite adequate trials of standard analgesic therapies and best-practice management.

leg ulcer.definition: A leg ulcer is a chronic wound on the leg that fails to heal within several weeks (often defined as 6 weeks), most commonly caused by venous insufficiency and venous hypertension, but it can also result from arterial insufficiency, neuropathy, or other vascular disorders.

varicose veins.definition: Swollen, twisted veins that you can see just under your skin.

deep venous insufficiency.definition: Impaired drainage of venous blood through the deep venous system of the lower extremities, leading to venous hypertension and chronic venous insufficiency; commonly due to deep vein valvular incompetence or obstruction (e.g., post-thrombotic changes), with edema, aching, skin changes, and risk of venous ulcers.

arterial disease.definition: Any disease of the arteries that reduces or disrupts blood flow to tissues or organs, commonly due to atherosclerosis but also arising from vasculitis, aneurysm, dissection, or thrombotic/occlusive processes.

chronic lymphocytic leukemia.definition: An overproduction of lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell, that crowds out other blood cells; a chronic leukemia that usually progresses slowly.

cll.definition: A slowly progressive leukemia characterized by clonal expansion of mature-appearing B lymphocytes that are functionally incompetent, causing persistent lymphocytosis and involvement of blood, bone marrow, and lymphoid tissues; most common in older adults and may present with fatigue, anemia, infections, lymphadenopathy, or splenomegaly.

iron deficiency.definition: Iron deficiency is a condition in which the body's iron stores are depleted due to reduced intake, impaired absorption, increased demand, or blood loss, leading to impaired hemoglobin synthesis and often progressing to iron deficiency anemia if prolonged.

chronic pancreatitis.definition: A long-standing inflammatory disease of the pancreas characterized by irreversible fibrosis and progressive loss of exocrine and endocrine function, usually after repeated episodes of acute pancreatitis; presents with persistent abdominal pain, malabsorption, and sometimes diabetes.

chronic pain.definition: Pain that persists after an injury has healed or a disease is over.

chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hyperte.definition: A form of pulmonary hypertension caused by chronic obstruction of the pulmonary arteries from organized thromboemboli, leading to increased pulmonary vascular resistance and right-sided heart failure; categorized as WHO Group 4.

chronic progressive myelopathy.definition: A spinal cord disorder in which neurological function deteriorates gradually over months to years due to ongoing injury or compression of the spinal cord, producing progressive motor weakness, sensory loss, hyperreflexia, gait disturbance, and possible autonomic symptoms (e.g., bowel/bladder dysfunction).

htlv-1-associated myelopathy.definition: A chronic, progressive inflammatory-demyelinating disease of the spinal cord caused by infection with human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1), presenting with spastic weakness and sensory loss in the legs and bladder dysfunction from thoracic spinal cord involvement.

tropical spastic paraparesis.definition: A chronic, progressive myelopathy due to human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) infection, characterized by spastic weakness and stiffness of the legs (paraparesis), gait disturbance, lower-extremity sensory abnormalities, hyperreflexia, and bladder dysfunction, typically seen in HTLV-1–endemic regions.

chronic purulent synovitis.definition: A long-standing infection of the synovial membrane with pus formation in the joint space, causing persistent swelling, pain, warmth, and restricted motion, and risking cartilage and bone destruction if not treated.

reflex sympathetic dystrophy.definition: A chronic pain syndrome—often after an injury—characterized by severe, disproportionate limb pain with autonomic changes (swelling, temperature and color differences), allodynia/hyperalgesia, and reduced range of motion; now called complex regional pain syndrome type I (CRPS I).

chronic regional pain syndrome.definition: A chronic pain condition typically affecting a limb after injury, characterized by ongoing, disproportionate pain with sensory, autonomic, and motor changes such as swelling, color and temperature changes, sweating abnormalities, and reduced range of motion; it is divided into Type I (no confirmed nerve injury) and Type II (confirmed nerve injury).

immune rejection.definition: A process in which the recipient's immune system recognizes donor antigens as foreign in a transplanted organ or tissue and mounts an immune response that damages or destroys the graft.

chronic rejection.definition: A gradual, chronic loss of function of a transplanted organ due to ongoing immune-mediated injury, typically occurring months to years after transplantation, characterized by vascular intimal hyperplasia (allograft vasculopathy) and interstitial fibrosis leading to graft failure.

hepatic function.definition: The liver’s functional activities, including metabolism of nutrients, detoxification and clearance of drugs and toxins, bile production for digestion, synthesis of plasma proteins (such as albumin and clotting factors), and storage of vitamins and glycogen.

miconazole.definition: An azole antifungal medication used topically or vaginally to treat superficial fungal infections (e.g., dermatophyte infections and vulvovaginal candidiasis); it inhibits fungal ergosterol synthesis by blocking the cytochrome P450 enzyme 14-α-demethylase.

thymosin.definition: A thymic peptide hormone involved in the development and differentiation of T lymphocytes, produced by the thymus and contributing to immune modulation.

levamisole.definition: A synthetic immunomodulatory drug (an imidazothiazole) that enhances cell-mediated immunity by stimulating T-lymphocytes, used to treat certain parasitic worm infections and, in some regimens, as adjuvant therapy for colorectal cancer.

transfer factor.definition: A dialyzable fraction of leukocyte extracts containing factors that can transfer cell-mediated (T-cell–driven) immunity from an immune donor to a non-immune recipient, enabling a specific response to particular antigens; it does not transfer antibodies.

fetal thymus transplantation.definition: Transplantation of fetal thymic tissue into a recipient to establish a thymic microenvironment that supports thymopoiesis and the development of T lymphocytes, typically used to treat athymia such as complete DiGeorge syndrome.

bcr/abl1 mutation.definition: A fusion gene produced by the Philadelphia chromosome translocation t(9;22)(q34;q11) that fuses BCR to ABL1, generating an unregulated tyrosine kinase that drives malignant transformation in certain leukemias (most notably chronic myeloid leukemia); it is a therapeutic target for tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib.

alkylating agent.definition: A class of cytotoxic drugs that covalently transfer alkyl groups to nucleophilic targets (primarily DNA), causing cross-linking and strand breaks that inhibit replication and transcription and lead to cell death.

nephrotoxin.definition: A substance capable of causing kidney injury (nephrotoxicity) by damaging renal cells or impairing renal function; exposure can occur via medications, contrast agents, metals, or other toxins.

chronic myeloid leukemia.definition: Occurs when there are too many of a type of white blood cell (granulocytes) that crowd out other types of blood cells. Chronic leukemias grow slowly. Also called CML.

splenomyelogenous leukemia.definition: A historical or nonstandard term for leukemia in which malignant hematopoietic cells prominently involve the spleen and bone marrow, often with splenomegaly; not a widely used modern diagnostic term.

tuberculous mastitis.definition: Breast infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, leading to granulomatous inflammation of the breast tissue; often presents as a lump with possible suppuration and sinus formation, usually secondary to a TB focus elsewhere, and treated with standard anti-tuberculous chemotherapy (often 6–9 months) with surgical drainage or excision as needed.

digeorge's syndrome.definition: A genetic disorder caused by a microdeletion on chromosome 22 at q11.2, leading to variable features such as congenital heart defects, thymic hypoplasia with T-cell immunodeficiency, hypocalcemia from parathyroid aplasia, palatal abnormalities, facial dysmorphism, and developmental delays.

ataxia-telangiectasia.definition: A rare autosomal recessive neurodegenerative and immunodeficiency disorder caused by mutations in the ATM gene, resulting in defective DNA repair; features include progressive cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasia, immune deficiency with recurrent infections, elevated alpha-fetoprotein, and increased cancer risk.

severe combined immunodeficiency disease.definition: An inherited primary immunodeficiency characterized by defective development and function of T lymphocytes, with accompanying impairment of B-cell–mediated immunity (and often NK-cell function), leading to severe, recurrent infections beginning in infancy; without definitive therapy such as hematopoietic stem cell transplantation or gene therapy, prognosis is poor.

pigmented purpura.definition: A spectrum of chronic, benign skin conditions characterized by capillaritis with extravasation of erythrocytes and deposition of hemosiderin, presenting as slowly enlarging reddish-brown patches and petechiae—most often on the lower legs; usually asymptomatic or mildly pruritic and without systemic symptoms, with a relapsing course.

lichen aureus.definition: A localized form of pigmented purpuric dermatosis presenting as a solitary, golden-brown to orange-yellow patch (often on the lower leg), caused by capillaritis with erythrocyte extravasation and hemosiderin deposition; usually asymptomatic or mildly pruritic and tends to be benign and self-limited.

pigmented purpuric lichenoid dermatitis.definition: Chronic pigmented purpuric dermatosis presenting as violaceous patches or papules, usually on the lower extremities, due to capillaritis with erythrocyte extravasation and hemosiderin deposition. Histology shows a superficial lichenoid (interface) lymphocytic infiltrate with erythrocyte leakage. Etiology is unknown; the condition is usually benign and can be persistent, with treatment ranging from topical corticosteroids to observational management.

purpura annularis telangiectodes.definition: A benign, chronic pigmented purpuric dermatosis presenting as annular reddish-brown patches with superficial telangiectasias on the lower limbs; caused by capillaritis with extravasation of red blood cells, usually asymptomatic or mildly pruritic.

schamberg disease.definition: A chronic pigmented purpuric dermatosis presenting as reddish-brown, nonpalpable purpura on the lower legs due to capillary fragility with extravasation of red blood cells and hemosiderin deposition; benign and usually asymptomatic; etiology unknown; management is primarily observation, with topical therapies or compression in select cases.

cystinosis.definition: An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by CTNS gene mutations that impair cystinosin function, leading to accumulation of cystine in lysosomes and widespread tissue damage; classically presents in infancy with renal Fanconi syndrome and may involve multiple organ systems, treated with cysteamine to reduce lysosomal cystine levels.

chrysotherapy.definition: A treatment for inflammatory rheumatic diseases employing gold compounds (gold salts), such as aurothioglucose or auranofin; it was once commonly used for rheumatoid arthritis but is now rarely employed due to limited efficacy and notable adverse effects.

cicatricial pemphigoid.definition: A chronic autoimmune blistering disease characterized by subepidermal blisters of mucous membranes that heal with scarring, potentially causing adhesions and functional impairment; mediated by autoantibodies against components of the basement membrane zone.

systemic necrotizing vasculitis.definition: A pattern of systemic inflammation in which small- to medium-sized blood vessels undergo necrotizing inflammation, causing tissue ischemia and multi-organ dysfunction; commonly encompasses ANCA-associated vasculitides (eg, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis) and polyarteritis nodosa.

granulomatous reactions.definition: A chronic inflammatory response characterized by granuloma formation—aggregates of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells) with possible multinucleated giant cells, usually surrounded by lymphocytes. This reaction occurs in response to persistent irritants such as certain infections (e.g., Mycobacterium tuberculosis, fungi), foreign bodies, or immune-mediated diseases (e.g., sarcoidosis). Granulomas may be caseating or noncaseating depending on the underlying cause.

vasculitis.definition: When an artery, vein, or capillary gets swollen (inflamed).

chvostek sign.definition: A clinical sign of hypocalcemia in which tapping the facial nerve anterior to the ear elicits twitching of facial muscles (notably around the mouth and nose), reflecting increased neuromuscular excitability and tetany.

chvostek-weiss sign.definition: An involuntary contraction of facial muscles triggered by tapping the facial nerve anterior to the ear, reflecting neuromuscular hyperexcitability commonly due to hypocalcemia.

chyle.definition: A milky lymphatic fluid formed in the small intestine during fat absorption, containing emulsified dietary lipids packaged as chylomicrons and transported via the intestinal lymphatics to the thoracic duct.

chylous ascites.definition: A condition in which lymphatic fluid (chyle) accumulates in the peritoneal cavity due to disruption or obstruction of abdominal lymphatics, producing milky ascitic fluid with high triglyceride content and chylomicrons; commonly caused by malignancy (e.g., lymphoma), trauma or surgical injury, cirrhosis, or infections.

chylomediastinum.definition: A condition in which chyle, a milky lymphatic fluid rich in triglycerides, leaks into or accumulates within the mediastinal space—usually from injury to the thoracic duct or lymphatic vessels, often after trauma or thoracic surgery.

chylomicron.definition: A fat globule that ferries triglyceride from the intestine to the liver and fat tissue.

chylomicrons.definition: A lipoprotein particle formed in the intestinal mucosa that transports dietary triglycerides and cholesterol from the gut to peripheral tissues via the lymphatic system; it is the largest and least dense lipoprotein, rich in triglycerides, and is converted to chylomicron remnants after lipoprotein lipase activity.

chylemia.definition: Presence of chyle (lipid-rich lymph) in the bloodstream, usually due to abnormal lymphatic-venous communication (e.g., thoracic duct injury or lymphatic-venous fistula), leading to lipemic, milky blood.

chylothorax.definition: A pleural effusion consisting of chyle (lymphatic fluid rich in triglycerides) that leaks into the pleural space due to disruption or obstruction of the thoracic duct or its tributaries, often from trauma or thoracic surgery and sometimes from malignancy or congenital lymphatic abnormalities. The fluid is typically milky and rich in triglycerides and contains chylomicrons.

chylous.definition: Relating to chyle, the milky lymphatic fluid formed in the small intestine during fat absorption; chylous describes material or effusions containing chyle.

chylocele.definition: A cystic collection of chyle (milky lymph) due to leakage or obstruction of lymphatic vessels, yielding a chyle-filled sac, often presenting as a scrotal swelling in infants.

chyluria.definition: A condition in which lymphatic fluid (chyle) leaks into the urinary tract through an abnormal lymphatic-urinary connection, producing milky, triglyceride-rich urine and often associated with lymphatic obstruction or filarial infection.

chymase.definition: A chymotrypsin-like serine protease stored in mast cell granules (especially connective tissue-type mast cells) that cleaves peptide bonds after aromatic residues and, in many tissues, converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, contributing to local vasoconstriction, inflammation, and tissue remodeling.

chyme.definition: A nearly liquid mass of partly digested food and digestive juices; found in the stomach and intestine.

chymopapain.definition: An enzyme, specifically a cysteine protease, derived from papaya latex (Carica papaya) used in chemonucleolysis to digest and dissolve the nucleus pulposus of a herniated intervertebral disc.

rennin.definition: An enzyme produced by the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney that cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, initiating the hormonal cascade that regulates blood pressure and fluid balance.

chymosin.definition: A proteolytic enzyme (rennin) produced in the stomachs of young ruminants that coagulates milk by cleaving κ-casein, forming the cheese curd; used in cheese production (and now also produced recombinantly).

chymotrypsin.definition: Pancreatic serine protease that digests dietary proteins by hydrolyzing peptide bonds on the carboxyl side of aromatic amino acids (phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan); secreted as chymotrypsinogen and activated to chymotrypsin in the small intestine; optimal activity at near-neutral to slightly alkaline pH.

chymotrypsinogen.definition: A pancreatic zymogen; the inactive precursor of the digestive enzyme chymotrypsin, activated to chymotrypsin by trypsin in the small intestine.

cinacalcet.definition: A calcimimetic oral medication that increases the sensitivity of the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells to extracellular calcium, thereby suppressing parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion; used to treat secondary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease and to manage severe hypercalcemia due to parathyroid carcinoma.

cimetidine.definition: A histamine H2-receptor antagonist (an H2 blocker) that reduces gastric acid secretion by blocking H2 receptors on gastric parietal cells; used to treat peptic ulcers, GERD, and other acid-peptic disorders; may cause antiandrogenic effects and drug interactions via cytochrome P450 inhibition.

tadalafil.definition: A selective phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) inhibitor used to treat erectile dysfunction; also approved for benign prostatic hyperplasia and for pulmonary arterial hypertension.

cibophobia.definition: An irrational or excessive fear of food or eating that leads to avoidance of meals and potential weight loss; a form of specific phobia that may require psychological therapy such as cognitive-behavioral therapy.

cicatrix.definition: A scar formed when normal tissue is replaced by fibrous connective tissue during the healing of a wound.

cicatricial alopecia.definition: A group of inflammatory hair disorders that can cause irreversible damage to the follicle that results in permanent hair loss and scarring. Also known as scarring alopecia.

cicatricial entropion.definition: Inward turning of the eyelid margin caused by scar formation (cicatrization) of the palpebral conjunctiva and/or tarsal structures, pulling the lid toward the globe and causing lash contact with the cornea and ocular surface irritation; often due to burns or cicatrizing conjunctival diseases (e.g., ocular cicatricial pemphigoid, Stevens–Johnson syndrome).

stenosis.definition: Abnormal narrowing of a canal or passage in the body, such as a blood vessel, airway, or spinal canal, that can impede flow.

ciclopirox.definition: A synthetic antifungal agent (hydroxypyridone) used topically to treat fungal infections of the skin and nails; it chelates polyvalent cations, inhibiting metal-dependent enzymes and disrupting fungal energy metabolism and growth.

cicutism.definition: Poisoning from cicutoxin-containing hemlock (Cicuta species); causes central nervous system excitation with seizures and autonomic instability, and can be fatal.

cytomegalic inclusion disease.definition: A congenital cytomegalovirus infection characterized by enlarged cells (cytomegaly) with intranuclear inclusion bodies in infected tissues; in newborns it can cause hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, microcephaly, chorioretinitis, growth restriction, and sensorineural hearing loss.

cytomegalovirus retinitis.definition: An infection of the retina caused by cytomegalovirus, usually in people with severely weakened immune systems (e.g., AIDS or transplant recipients). It causes necrotizing retinitis with retinal hemorrhages (often described as a “pizza pie” appearance) and can lead to progressive vision loss if untreated; managed with antiviral therapy such as ganciclovir or valganciclovir, and may require intravitreal injections or other antivirals.

epistaxis.definition: A nosebleed; bleeding from the nasal mucosa, most often from the anterior septum (Kiesselbach's plexus) due to trauma, dryness, or irritation.

conjunctival hemorrhage.definition: Bleeding beneath the conjunctiva from rupture of a small conjunctival vessel, producing a bright red patch on the white of the eye; typically painless, without discharge or vision change, and resolves spontaneously over 1–3 weeks, often after minor trauma or a sudden rise in venous pressure (coughing, sneezing, vomiting).

gastroesophageal reflux disease.definition: A chronic condition in which reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus causes troublesome symptoms (typically heartburn and acid regurgitation) and/or complications such as esophagitis, esophageal stricture, or Barrett’s esophagus.

duodenal ulcers.definition: An ulceration of the mucosa of the duodenum (the first part of the small intestine), a form of peptic ulcer disease most often caused by Helicobacter pylori infection or NSAID use. It typically presents with episodic epigastric pain that may be relieved by meals, and can lead to complications such as gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, or gastric outlet obstruction.

parathyroid carcinoma.definition: A rare malignant tumor of the parathyroid gland that typically causes primary hyperparathyroidism due to excess parathyroid hormone secretion; it may invade surrounding tissues and metastasize; definitive treatment is en bloc surgical excision of the tumor (often with the ipsilateral thyroid lobe).

secondary hyperparathyroidism.definition: An adaptive overproduction of parathyroid hormone in response to chronic hypocalcemia and/or impaired vitamin D metabolism, most commonly due to chronic kidney disease, resulting in elevated PTH with low or normal calcium and renal bone disease (renal osteodystrophy).

ciliary artery.definition: Arteries that supply the eye’s ciliary body and iris; they include the short posterior ciliary arteries and the long posterior ciliary arteries (from the ophthalmic artery) that form the arterial circle of the iris and nourish the ciliary processes and iris.

ciliary canal.definition: A small canal located within the ciliary body of the eye.

ciliary disc.definition: Not a standard anatomical term; if used, it may refer to a disc-shaped region at the base of a cilium where the basal body attaches to the cell and organizes the microtubule cytoskeleton, anchoring the cilium to the cell.

ciliary ganglion.definition: A small parasympathetic ganglion in the posterior orbit, near the optic nerve, associated with the oculomotor nerve (CN III). It receives preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the Edinger–Westphal nucleus via CN III and synapses there; postganglionic fibers travel with the short ciliary nerves to innervate the sphincter pupillae (pupillary constriction) and the ciliary muscle (accommodation). Sympathetic fibers pass through without synapsing.

ciliary gland.definition: Small apocrine sweat glands located at the eyelid margin near the eyelashes; they secrete sweat to help lubricate and protect the lid margin.

ciliary margin.definition: The peripheral border of the ciliary body, i.e., the anterior edge from which the ciliary processes arise, marking the boundary between the ciliary body and the iris/sclera.

ciliary movement.definition: Coordinated beating of motile cilia on epithelial surfaces, generating directed fluid flow (such as mucus clearance) or propelling cells, powered by dynein-driven sliding of ciliary microtubules.

ciliary mucous transport.definition: Movement of mucus across the mucosal surfaces driven by the coordinated beating of cilia, transporting mucus toward the pharynx to clear inhaled particles and pathogens (mucociliary clearance).

ciliary muscle.definition: A smooth muscle in the ciliary body of the eye that adjusts lens shape to enable accommodation: contraction rounds the lens for near vision by reducing zonular tension, while relaxation allows the lens to flatten for distance vision.

ciliary process.definition: A fold of the ciliary body containing the ciliary epithelium that secretes aqueous humor.

ciliary reflex.definition: A reflex causing contraction of the ciliary muscle, relaxing the zonular fibers and increasing lens curvature to focus on a near object; it is part of the near (accommodation) reflex and is often accompanied by convergence of the eyes and pupil constriction.

ciliary ring.definition: A circular portion of the ciliary body surrounding the lens; contains the ciliary muscle and ciliary processes, forming part of the uvea and involved in accommodation and production of aqueous humor.

ciliary zone.definition: An anatomical region of the eye—the portion of the sclera overlying and surrounding the ciliary body, extending from near the limbus toward the ora serrata; it is the scleral area where the ciliary body attaches.

lacteals.definition: Specialized lymphatic capillaries in the villi of the small intestine that absorb dietary fats and fat-soluble vitamins, transporting chyle to the thoracic duct.

pecquets cistern.definition: A dilated sac at the inferior end of the thoracic duct formed by the convergence of the intestinal trunk and lumbar lymphatic trunks; it is the origin of the thoracic duct and lies in the retroperitoneum anterior to the L1–L2 vertebrae.

balantidium coli.definition: A large, ciliated protozoan parasite that inhabits the large intestine of humans and pigs and is the etiologic agent of balantidiasis; transmitted by ingestion of cysts in contaminated water or food.

ciguatera.definition: A foodborne illness caused by ciguatoxins from marine dinoflagellates that bioaccumulate in reef fish; ingestion presents with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea followed by neurologic symptoms (paresthesias, temperature-related dysesthesia such as hot–cold reversal), myalgias, dizziness, and can persist for days to months; treatment is supportive.

ciguatoxin.definition: A potent marine neurotoxin produced by certain dinoflagellates (notably Gambierdiscus spp.) that bioaccumulates in reef fish and activates voltage-gated sodium channels, causing ciguatera fish poisoning.

cilostazol.definition: A selective phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor with antiplatelet and vasodilatory effects used to treat intermittent claudication in peripheral arterial disease. It increases intracellular cyclic AMP in platelets and vascular smooth muscle, inhibiting platelet aggregation and causing vasodilation. Contraindicated in heart failure; common adverse effects include headache, diarrhea, and palpitations.

bedbug.definition: A small, flat, reddish-brown parasitic insect that feeds on human blood, usually at night; bites can cause itching and welts; commonly found in beds and furniture; infestations require pest-control measures; not known to transmit diseases to humans.

cinchona.definition: A genus of tropical evergreen trees and shrubs in the Rubiaceae family, native to the Andean region of South America; the bark yields cinchona alkaloids, chiefly quinine, historically used to prevent and treat malaria.

cinchonine.definition: An alkaloid isolated from Cinchona bark; one of the cinchona alkaloids, closely related to quinine.

cinchonism.definition: A toxicity syndrome from excessive quinine (cinchona alkaloids) intake, characterized by tinnitus, hearing loss, headache, vertigo, visual disturbances, nausea, and sometimes flushing and delirium; symptoms typically resolve after stopping quinine.

cin cervical intraepithelial neoplasia.definition: Premalignant lesion of the cervix characterized by dysplastic squamous epithelium confined to the epithelium with no invasion through the basement membrane. Graded 1–3 by severity (CIN 1 = mild, CIN 2 = moderate, CIN 3 = severe dysplasia or carcinoma in situ). Often associated with persistent infection by high‑risk human papillomavirus; progression to invasive cervical cancer is possible if untreated.

cineangiogram.definition: A radiographic study in which a contrast agent is injected and a sequence of cine X-ray frames is captured to visualize blood vessels and assess patency, anatomy, and blood flow (commonly used for coronary arteries).

cineangiocardiogram.definition: A diagnostic imaging technique that uses rapid-sequence X-ray (cine) imaging after injection of radiopaque contrast into the heart or its vessels to visualize cardiac chambers and blood flow, enabling assessment of chamber function, valvular activity, and vascular anatomy.

cineangiography.definition: A radiographic technique using rapid-sequence X-ray imaging with intravascular contrast to visualize the dynamic flow of blood through vessels and cardiac chambers.

cinefluorography.definition: A radiographic technique that records fluoroscopic imaging as a rapid sequence on film to produce a motion picture for evaluating dynamic physiological processes.

cineradiography.definition: A radiographic technique that records a rapid sequence of X-ray images to visualize motion of internal structures (cine radiography or cine fluoroscopy).

cineangiograph.definition: Radiographic imaging technique that records moving images of blood vessels after contrast injection to visualize blood flow and vessel anatomy, enabling assessment of patency, stenosis, and other vascular abnormalities.

cineroentgenofluorography.definition: A dynamic radiographic technique that records rapid cine sequences during fluoroscopy to visualize and assess movement of internal structures in real time.

cineangiocardiography.definition: A radiographic technique in which iodinated contrast is injected and rapid-sequence X-ray (cine) imaging is used to visualize the beating heart and great vessels, allowing assessment of cardiac chambers, valves, and blood flow.

kinesia.definition: Movement; the act or ability to move, especially as it relates to the initiation, speed, and quality of voluntary movements in clinical contexts (e.g., bradykinesia, akinesia, dyskinesia).

cingulate.definition: Relating to the cingulate gyrus or cingulate sulcus of the brain; a curved cortical region on the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere that is part of the limbic system involved in emotion, behavior, and memory.

cingulate_gyrus.definition: A fold of the medial cerebral cortex located just above the corpus callosum on the brain’s inner surface; part of the limbic system involved in emotion formation and processing, learning, and memory, with anterior portions related to emotion and autonomic regulation and posterior portions to memory and attention.

cingulotomy.definition: A neurosurgical procedure in which a lesion is made in the anterior cingulate cortex (cingulate gyrus) to disrupt fronto-limbic circuits; it has been used for treatment-resistant obsessive-compulsive disorder and, less commonly, major depressive disorder or chronic pain.

cingulectomy.definition: Removal of the cingulate gyrus, the medial portion of the cerebral cortex involved in emotion and behavior.

circumflex.definition: An adjective meaning curved around or encircling; in anatomy, used to describe vessels or structures that wrap around a region to supply or encircle it.

liver_biopsy.definition: A procedure to obtain a small sample of liver tissue for histologic examination, usually by percutaneous needle biopsy, to diagnose liver disease, assess its severity, and monitor treatment; risks include bleeding, pain, and infection.

alkaline_phosphatase.definition: An enzyme that hydrolyzes phosphate esters at alkaline pH; produced by liver, bile ducts, bone, and other tissues; clinically used as a biomarker for hepatobiliary and bone disease; serum levels rise in cholestasis and increased bone turnover.

alanine_aminotransferase.definition: An intracellular liver enzyme (a transaminase) that transfers the amino group from alanine to α-ketoglutarate, forming pyruvate and glutamate; elevated serum levels indicate hepatocellular injury and are used to assess liver disease.

nosebleeds.definition: Bleeding from the nasal mucosa (epistaxis), most commonly from the anterior nasal septum (Kiesselbach’s area), usually caused by dryness or minor trauma and typically self-limited; posterior epistaxis is less common and can be more serious.

spider_angiomas.definition: A small, benign vascular lesion with a central arteriolar feeder and radiating fine capillaries that blanch on pressure; commonly appears on the face, neck, or upper chest and may be associated with increased estrogen states or liver disease, often regressing spontaneously.
