factor ix.definition: A vitamin K–dependent coagulation protein produced by the liver; a serine protease zymogen that is activated to IXa and, within the intrinsic tenase complex, converts Factor X to Xa, facilitating thrombin generation. Deficiency causes hemophilia B (Christmas disease).

coagulation time.definition: The time required for blood to form a clot after a procoagulant trigger is added; an overall measure of hemostasis reflecting platelet function and plasma coagulation factors.

coagulation necrosis.definition: A form of necrosis in which the tissue architecture is preserved for some time after cell death because protein denaturation inhibits proteolysis; typically resulting from ischemic or hypoxic injury in solid organs, with cells showing eosinophilic cytoplasm and loss of nuclei while outlines are maintained (“ghost cells”), followed by inflammation and eventual scar formation.

avascular necrosis.definition: Death of bone tissue due to loss of blood supply (ischemia), leading to bone collapse and joint dysfunction, most often affecting the femoral head.

ischemic necrosis.definition: Tissue death caused by prolonged inadequate blood supply (ischemia), leading to hypoxia and irreversible cell injury; in most solid organs this presents as coagulative necrosis.

coagulopathy.definition: A disorder of hemostasis in which the blood's ability to clot is impaired, causing excessive bleeding or easy bruising; due to defects in coagulation factors, platelets, or their regulation, and can be inherited or acquired.

coal worker's pneumoconiosis.definition: A form of occupational lung disease caused by chronic inhalation of coal dust, leading to inflammation and fibrotic nodules in the lungs (often called “black lung”); may progress to progressive massive fibrosis with worsening dyspnea and reduced lung function.

notching.definition: An indentation or groove formed in a body structure; in radiology, indentation of the lower rib margins can indicate collateral vessels associated with coarctation of the aorta.

coarctation of the aorta.definition: A congenital narrowing of the aorta, typically at the aortic isthmus just distal to the left subclavian artery, causing obstruction to systemic blood flow; presents with upper-extremity hypertension and diminished femoral pulses, and is treated with surgical repair or endovascular angioplasty/stenting.

aortic rupture.definition: A rupture of the aorta causing massive internal bleeding and usually rapid circulatory collapse, most commonly due to rupture of an aortic aneurysm or acute aortic dissection.

infective endocarditis.definition: An infection of the endocardial surface of the heart (most often the heart valves) caused by bacteria or fungi, characterized by vegetations on valves and clinical features such as fever and a new or changing heart murmur; diagnosed by blood cultures and echocardiography and treated with prolonged intravenous antibiotics, with surgery sometimes required.

fainting.definition: A brief, self-limited loss of consciousness and postural tone due to transient cerebral hypoperfusion, with spontaneous recovery.

fibrin.definition: A fibrous protein formed by the enzymatic conversion of soluble fibrinogen to fibrin by thrombin during blood coagulation; it polymerizes and cross-links to form an insoluble fibrin mesh that stabilizes a blood clot.

hemarthrosis.definition: Bleeding into a joint space, usually after trauma or in individuals with a bleeding disorder, causing swelling, warmth, pain, and reduced range of motion, most commonly affecting the knee.

clinical nurse specialist.definition: A clinical nurse specialist is an advanced practice registered nurse who has expert knowledge in a defined area of nursing (such as a patient population, setting, or disease). They provide direct patient care, expert consultation to other clinicians, education for patients and staff, and leadership in quality improvement, research, and evidence-based practice within a clinical setting.

photocoagulation.definition: Use of a laser to seal off blood vessels.

electrocoagulation.definition: Coagulation of tissue by means of a high-frequency electrical current, producing heat that denatures proteins and seals blood vessels to achieve hemostasis; used in electrosurgical procedures for cutting or stopping bleeding.

electrocautery.definition: A surgical method in which heat produced by electrical energy is applied to tissue to cut or coagulate it, typically via a heated instrument or through tissue with an electrosurgical device to achieve hemostasis.

central neurogenic hyperventilation.definition: A pattern of sustained, rapid, deep breathing caused by injury or dysfunction of central nervous system respiratory centers (typically brainstem injury), leading to marked hyperventilation and hypocapnia; not attributable to metabolic or primary pulmonary disease.

coats disease.definition: A rare, nonhereditary retinal vascular disorder of childhood characterized by unilateral telangiectatic and aneurysmal retinal vessels with lipid-rich exudation, which can progress to exudative retinal detachment.

coats retinitis.definition: A unilateral retinal vascular disorder, typically presenting in childhood, characterized by abnormal dilated retinal capillaries (telangiectasia) and aneurysmal vessels with lipid-rich exudation in the retina, which can progress to exudative retinal detachment; treated with laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy to the abnormal vessels.

exudative retinopathy.definition: A retinal vascular disorder characterized by leakage of fluid and lipids from damaged retinal vessels, leading to lipid-rich hard exudates in the retina and often macular edema with vision loss; it occurs in conditions that disrupt the blood-retinal barrier, such as diabetic or hypertensive retinopathy.

cobalamin.definition: A water-soluble vitamin containing cobalt (vitamin B12); a cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, essential for DNA synthesis and normal neurological function; deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neuropathy.

cobalt.definition: A trace element that forms the central atom of vitamin B12 (cobalamin); essential for DNA synthesis, red blood cell formation, and nervous system function through B12-dependent reactions; deficiency leads to megaloblastic anemia and neuropathy, and chronic excess exposure can cause cobalt toxicity (e.g., cardiomyopathy, thyroid dysfunction, pneumonitis).

cobalt-60.definition: A radioactive isotope of cobalt that emits high-energy gamma rays (1.17 and 1.33 MeV) and beta particles; used as a gamma radiation source in radiotherapy and industrial radiography; decays to nickel-60 with a half-life of about 5.27 years.

cobalt poisoning.definition: Toxicity due to excessive cobalt exposure (cobaltism), from inhalation, ingestion, or release from implants; features include cardiomyopathy and heart failure, thyroid dysfunction (often hypothyroidism), polycythemia, peripheral neuropathy, and dermatitis; diagnosed by elevated cobalt levels in blood or urine; treatment involves removing exposure and managing symptoms, with chelation in severe cases.

hard metal disease.definition: An occupational pneumoconiosis caused by inhalation of cobalt-containing hard metal dust (often from tungsten carbide), leading to progressive interstitial lung disease with cough and dyspnea; management focuses on eliminating exposure and treating respiratory symptoms.

cobb collar.definition: I can’t find a standard medical definition for “Cobb collar.” Could you share more context or confirm the spelling (e.g., Cobb’s collar vs Cobb collar) and the anatomical area or specialty (dermatology, ENT, cardiology, etc.)? With that, I can give you a precise definition or explanation.

cobra venom.definition: A potent venom produced by cobras (genus Naja and related species), a complex mixture of neurotoxins and cytotoxins that disrupt neuromuscular transmission and damage tissues; delivered via fangs to immobilize prey or defend the snake, and capable of causing paralysis, respiratory failure, and local tissue necrosis in humans.

cobra venom solution.definition: A laboratory preparation in which cobra venom is dissolved in sterile saline or buffer at a defined concentration for research, toxin characterization, pharmacology studies, or antivenom production; cobra venom contains neurotoxins and other components that disrupt neuromuscular transmission.

cocaine hydrochloride.definition: A water-soluble salt form of cocaine produced with hydrochloric acid; used medically as a topical local anesthetic and vasoconstrictor in certain procedures, but also a potent central nervous system stimulant with high abuse potential and risk of cardiovascular toxicity.

cocaine hydrochloride poisoning.definition: Acute poisoning from cocaine exposure (the hydrochloride salt), a potent central and peripheral nervous system stimulant that causes marked sympathetic activation, presenting with agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, mydriasis, diaphoresis, chest pain, arrhythmias, seizures, and potential fatal complications such as myocardial ischemia, stroke, or hyperthermic collapse.

coccidia.definition: A group of intracellular, spore-forming protozoan parasites (apicomplexans) that infect the intestinal tract of animals, producing oocysts shed in feces and causing coccidiosis.

coccidioides.definition: A genus of dimorphic fungi (including Coccidioides immitis and Coccidioides posadasii) that causes coccidioidomycosis; it grows in soil as mold producing arthroconidia, and in human tissue forms large spherules containing endospores.

coccidioides immitis.definition: A pathogenic dimorphic fungus that causes coccidioidomycosis (Valley Fever) after inhalation of arthroconidia; endemic to arid regions of the Americas; clinical presentation ranges from asymptomatic or mild pneumonia to disseminated disease.

coccidioides posadasii.definition: A dimorphic fungal species of the genus Coccidioides; one of two species (with C. immitis) that cause coccidioidomycosis (Valley fever) in humans and animals. Found in arid regions of the Americas; infection occurs by inhalation of airborne arthroconidia, which develop into tissue-stage spherules containing endospores.

coccidioidomycosis.definition: A dimorphic fungal infection caused by Coccidioides immitis or Coccidioides posadasii, typically presenting as a Valley fever pulmonary illness and, less commonly, disseminating to skin, bones, and meninges.

coccidiosis.definition: A parasitic disease of the intestinal tract caused by coccidian protozoa (coccidia), typically presenting with diarrhea and abdominal cramps; transmitted by ingesting sporulated oocysts in contaminated food or water.

coccyalgia.definition: Pain in the coccyx region (tailbone), often due to trauma, prolonged sitting, childbirth, or degenerative changes; typically worsened by sitting or rising from a seated position.

coccygeal vertebra.definition: A vertebra of the coccyx (tailbone); a small, rudimentary vertebra at the distal end of the spinal column, typically 3–5 that fuse to form the coccyx.

coccyges.definition: A pair of small triangular muscles of the pelvic floor (coccygeus/ischiococcygeus) that originate from the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament and insert on the coccyx and lower sacrum; they support pelvic viscera and assist in flexing and stabilizing the coccyx.

coccygeus.definition: A muscle of the pelvic floor that originates from the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament and inserts on the coccyx and lower sacrum; it helps support pelvic viscera and assists in moving the coccyx anteriorly.

coccygodynia.definition: A condition characterized by localized pain in the coccyx (tailbone), typically following trauma or prolonged sitting, with tenderness over the coccyx.

coccygeal cornu.definition: A small horn-like projection on the coccyx; one of a pair that articulate with the sacral cornua to form the sacrococcygeal joint.

cochlear.definition: Relating to the cochlea, the spiral-shaped organ in the inner ear that transduces sound vibrations into neural signals via hair cells.

cochlear canal.definition: The spiral-shaped bony canal within the cochlea of the inner ear, forming part of the osseous labyrinth and housing the perilymph surrounding the membranous cochlear structures involved in hearing.

cochlear implant.definition: A small electronic device that is implanted in the inner ear to restore some hearing to a deaf person.

cochlear prosthesis.definition: An implantable medical device that bypasses damaged cochlear hair cells by converting sound into electrical impulses and delivering them via an implanted electrode array to stimulate the auditory nerve, enabling perception of sound in individuals with severe to profound sensorineural hearing loss; it consists of an external speech processor and transmitter and an internal receiver/stimulator with an electrode array.

cochlear toxicity.definition: Toxic injury to the cochlea causing sensorineural hearing loss, often from ototoxic substances (e.g., aminoglycoside antibiotics, platinum-based chemotherapy, loop diuretics) that damage cochlear hair cells, supporting cells, stria vascularis, or spiral ganglion neurons; typically bilateral and dose- or exposure-related.

cochlear window.definition: An opening at the base of the cochlea covered by a flexible membrane that allows movement of cochlear fluids to relieve pressure changes produced by sound vibrations at the oval window (the round window, fenestra rotunda).

cochleovestibular.definition: Relating to the cochlea and vestibular apparatus of the inner ear; pertaining to both hearing (cochlear) and balance (vestibular) functions.

cockayne syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal recessive disorder with growth failure, microcephaly, photosensitivity, and progressive neurologic deterioration due to defects in transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair (typically mutations in ERCC6/ERCC8).

cockscomb papilloma.definition: A benign epithelial tumor (papilloma) occurring on the comb of a bird (cock’s comb), typically presenting as a cauliflower‑like, pedunculated growth and often associated with papillomavirus infection in birds.

synapse.definition: The junction between two neurons, across which chemical neurotransmitters carry messages.

euphoria.definition: A subjective mood state of elated, exaggerated happiness and well-being, often with increased energy and decreased judgment; can occur in mania, stimulant intoxication, or as a drug effect.

paranoia.definition: Irrational, persistent mistrust and suspicion of others' motives or actions, often accompanied by delusions of persecution and interpreting others' behavior as hostile or threatening; commonly seen in certain psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia with persecutory features or delusional disorder.

presynaptic axon.definition: An axonal segment that conducts action potentials toward a synapse and ends in a nerve terminal, where neurotransmitter-containing vesicles are released into the synaptic cleft in response to Ca2+-triggered vesicle fusion.

postsynaptic dendrite.definition: A portion of a neuron's dendrite that receives neurotransmitter signals from a presynaptic neuron at a synapse; it contains neurotransmitter receptors and postsynaptic densities and integrates inputs to generate postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs or IPSPs).

dopamine receptor.definition: A cell-surface receptor that binds dopamine and transduces its signal by activating intracellular G protein–coupled signaling pathways; there are five subtypes (D1–D5) grouped into D1-like (D1, D5) and D2-like (D2, D3, D4) families, which modulate cyclic AMP and other second-messenger systems to influence neuronal activity.

dopamine transporter.definition: A presynaptic membrane transporter that reuptakes dopamine from the synaptic cleft into the presynaptic neuron via sodium- and chloride-dependent transport, thereby terminating dopaminergic signaling and regulating dopamine availability; a major target of psychostimulants such as cocaine and amphetamine.

catecholamine transporter.definition: A presynaptic membrane transporter that reuptakes catecholamines (primarily dopamine and norepinephrine) from the synaptic cleft into the presynaptic neuron, terminating their signaling; these transporters are targets of various psychostimulants and antidepressants and belong to the SLC6 family.

sympathetic neuron target cell interface.definition: An autonomic neuroeffector junction between a postganglionic sympathetic neuron and its target cell (e.g., smooth muscle or gland), where neurotransmitter release—primarily norepinephrine—from sympathetic varicosities activates adrenergic receptors on the target cell; some fibers also release acetylcholine at eccrine sweat glands, acting on muscarinic receptors.

myocardial infarct.definition: Death of heart muscle tissue resulting from prolonged ischemia caused by occlusion of a coronary artery, typically due to thrombosis on a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque; commonly called a heart attack.

cerebral infarct.definition: An area of brain tissue death due to ischemia from reduced blood flow, typically caused by occlusion of a cerebral artery, and associated with ischemic stroke.

desert fever.definition: An infection caused by inhalation of arthroconidia from the dimorphic fungi Coccidioides immitis or Coccidioides posadasii, occurring in arid desert regions; it typically presents with fever and flu-like respiratory symptoms (cough, chest pain, fatigue), may be asymptomatic, and can rarely disseminate to skin, bone, or meninges.

desert rheumatism.definition: A non-specific, informal term used to describe rheumatic-like musculoskeletal symptoms observed in people exposed to desert environments; it is not a recognized medical diagnosis with formal criteria.

san joaquin fever.definition: A fungal infection caused by inhalation of spores of Coccidioides species (C. immitis or C. posadasii), endemic to arid regions of the southwestern United States including the San Joaquin Valley. It commonly presents with fever, cough, and chest pain; most infections are self-limited but can progress to pneumonia or disseminated disease (such as meningitis) and may be associated with erythema nodosum.

valley fever.definition: A disease caused by a mold that lives in hot, dry places.

guanethidine.definition: A drug that blocks norepinephrine release from postganglionic sympathetic neurons (adrenergic neuron blocker), used historically for hypertension; it lowers blood pressure but has significant orthostatic hypotension and other adverse effects, and is now largely obsolete.

normochromic anemia.definition: Anemia in which red blood cells have normal hemoglobin content per cell (normochromic), often with normal cell size, with a reduced red cell mass due to decreased production or increased loss rather than decreased hemoglobin per cell.

normocytic anemia.definition: Anemia in which the average size of red blood cells is normal (mean corpuscular volume about 80–100 fL) despite reduced red cell mass; often described as normochromic, and arising from causes such as acute blood loss, anemia of chronic disease, renal failure, bone marrow suppression, or hemolysis.

60co.definition: A radioactive isotope of cobalt used as a gamma-ray source in external beam radiotherapy and sterilization of medical equipment; it decays to nickel-60.

nerve deafness.definition: A type of hearing loss caused by damage to the inner ear (cochlea) or the auditory nerve (vestibulocochlear nerve), resulting in impaired perception and discrimination of sounds and usually permanent.

exophthalmia.definition: Abnormal protrusion of one or both eyeballs from the orbital socket, typically due to increased orbital contents (edema, inflammation, or infiltration), most classically seen in Graves disease.

mydriasis.definition: Pupil dilation; enlargement of the pupil, typically due to sympathetic activation of the iris dilator muscle or pharmacologic blockade of the parasympathetic constrictor mechanism (and can occur in low light or with certain drugs).

peripheral vascular collapse.definition: An acute failure of the peripheral circulation due to severe hypotension or vasodilation, resulting in diminished or absent distal pulses and signs of systemic hypoperfusion (e.g., cool, clammy extremities).

isospora belli.definition: A coccidian intestinal protozoan parasite that causes isosporiasis, typically presenting with prolonged watery diarrhea and malabsorption, especially in immunocompromised individuals; transmitted by ingestion of sporulated oocysts in contaminated food or water; diagnosed by stool examination for oocysts; treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

isospora hominis.definition: A protozoan intestinal parasite that causes isosporiasis in humans; transmission occurs by ingesting sporulated oocysts in contaminated food or water, leading to prolonged watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and weight loss, particularly in immunocompromised individuals; diagnosed by stool examination for characteristic oocysts (often acid-fast positive) and treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

oocysts.definition: A thick-walled, spore-like cyst produced by certain intracellular protozoan parasites (coccidia) during their life cycle; shed in the feces and, upon sporulation, contains sporozoites that infect the next host; serves as the environmentally resistant, infectious stage.

pulmonary infection.definition: An infection of the lungs (pulmonary parenchyma) caused by bacteria, viruses, fungi, or other pathogens, resulting in inflammation and symptoms such as cough, fever, dyspnea, and chest pain; pneumonia is the most common manifestation.

erythema nodosum.definition: A hypersensitivity-driven inflammatory condition of the subcutaneous fat (panniculitis) presenting as tender, erythematous nodules on the shins, often with fever and malaise; commonly associated with infections, medications, pregnancy, or systemic inflammatory diseases and typically resolving over weeks with supportive care.

arthrospores.definition: A type of asexual fungal spore produced by fragmentation of a hypha at septa, yielding free, thick-walled conidia that facilitate dispersal.

mycelium.definition: The vegetative, feeding stage of a fungus, consisting of a network of thread-like hyphae that grow through and within a substrate to absorb nutrients; may give rise to fruiting bodies such as mushrooms.

spherule.definition: A thick-walled, spherical reproductive structure formed by certain pathogenic fungi (notably Coccidioides spp.) in tissue, containing numerous endospores that are released when the spherule ruptures.

codeine.definition: An opioid analgesic and antitussive that is a prodrug of morphine, activated by CYP2D6 metabolism; used for mild to moderate pain and cough suppression; risks include dependence, respiratory depression, constipation, and sedation.

codeine phosphate.definition: An opioid analgesic salt formed from codeine and phosphoric acid; used to relieve moderate to severe pain and to suppress coughing, often supplied in combination preparations, and regulated due to risks of dependence and respiratory depression.

codeine sulfate.definition: A salt form of codeine used as an analgesic and antitussive; an opioid that acts as a mu-opioid receptor agonist to relieve mild-to-moderate pain and suppress coughing; metabolized to morphine in the body via CYP2D6 and carries risks such as respiratory depression, sedation, constipation, tolerance, and dependence.

opium.definition: Dried latex from the seed capsules of Papaver somniferum containing multiple alkaloids, chiefly morphine, used as a potent opioid analgesic; historically used as a narcotic for pain and cough but associated with dependence and tightly regulated.

benztropine.definition: A central-acting antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) medication used to treat Parkinson disease symptoms such as tremor and rigidity and to alleviate drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms; it works by blocking acetylcholine activity in the basal ganglia.

cogentin.definition: A brand-name anticholinergic medication (benztropine) used to treat Parkinson disease symptoms and drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms; it works by blocking central muscarinic acetylcholine receptors to reduce tremor and rigidity.

cognex.definition: A brand-name acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (Tacrine) formerly used to treat mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease; increases central acetylcholine by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, but limited by hepatotoxicity and largely replaced by safer agents.

tacrine.definition: A reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used in the treatment of mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease; increases brain acetylcholine levels by preventing breakdown, but its use is limited by a risk of hepatotoxicity and it has largely been supplanted by newer cholinesterase inhibitors.

coenzyme q.definition: A lipid-soluble cofactor of the mitochondrial electron transport chain that functions as an electron carrier, transferring electrons from Complexes I and II to Complex III to drive ATP synthesis; it also acts as an antioxidant in its reduced form (ubiquinol).

coenzyme q10.definition: A lipid-soluble cofactor (ubiquinone/ubiquinol) that participates in the mitochondrial electron transport chain to generate ATP and acts as an antioxidant; it is synthesized in the body and obtained from the diet, and is available as a dietary supplement.

ubiquinone.definition: A lipid-soluble coenzyme that participates in mitochondrial electron transport and ATP production by shuttling electrons between complexes I/II and III, and also acts as an intracellular antioxidant. Also known as CoQ10.

coffee-ground vomitus.definition: Vomitus that is brown, granular, and resembles ground coffee, caused by partially digested blood from an upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage; the color results from gastric acid altering hemoglobin (forming hematin) in the blood.

vomitus.definition: The material ejected from the stomach through the mouth during vomiting (emesis); it typically consists of partially digested food, gastric secretions, and mucus, and may vary in color and content depending on the underlying cause.

coffin-lowry syndrome.definition: A rare X-linked genetic disorder caused by mutations in the RPS6KA3 gene encoding ribosomal S6 kinase 2 (RSK2), characterized by severe intellectual disability, distinctive coarse facial features, growth retardation, and skeletal anomalies.

coffin-siris syndrome.definition: A rare genetic disorder of neurodevelopment with developmental delay/intellectual disability, distinctive facial features, sparse scalp hair, and hypoplasia or absence of the fifth fingernails and distal phalanges (often with broad thumbs and toes); most commonly caused by mutations in SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling complex genes, particularly ARID1B.

cogan's oculomotor apraxia.definition: A congenital oculomotor disorder in which a person has difficulty initiating voluntary saccadic eye movements (especially horizontal), often compensating with head thrusts; smooth pursuit and the vestibulo-ocular reflex are preserved, and the condition is typically nonprogressive.

cogan's syndrome.definition: A rare autoimmune inflammatory syndrome characterized by noninfectious ocular inflammation—most often interstitial keratitis—and vestibulocochlear symptoms (sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo); without syphilis, it may involve other organ systems and is treated with corticosteroids and immunosuppressants.

codman's exercise.definition: A passive shoulder range-of-motion exercise in which the patient leans forward with the arm hanging and lets the arm swing (pendulum) in small circles or pendular movements, using body momentum rather than active muscle contraction to promote glenohumeral joint mobility during rehabilitation.

codman's tumor.definition: A solitary bone lesion due to Langerhans cell histiocytosis (eosinophilic granuloma), classically involving the skull in children.

cod-liver oil.definition: A dietary supplement derived from cod liver oil, rich in vitamins A and D and omega-3 fatty acids; historically used to prevent vitamin A and D deficiencies and rickets and for general nutritional support; excessive intake can cause toxicity of vitamins A or D.

pleural.definition: Relating to the pleura, the serous membranes surrounding the lungs and lining the chest cavity.

coelomic.definition: Relating to the coelom, the true, fluid-filled body cavity lined by mesoderm in many animals.

coelenterata.definition: An obsolete zoological grouping for diploblastic, radially symmetric animals (mainly Cnidaria; sometimes including Ctenophora) characterized by a blind gastrovascular cavity, no true coelom, and a diffuse nerve net.

coelosomy.definition: Not a standard medical term; no widely accepted definition in medical dictionaries. It may be a misspelling of coelostomy (creation of an opening into a body cavity) or colostomy (surgical creation of a stoma from the colon to the abdominal surface).

brain lesion.definition: A localized area of damaged or abnormal brain tissue resulting from injury or disease, which may disrupt neural function in the affected region. It is detected by imaging (e.g., MRI or CT) and can result from stroke, tumor, infection, trauma, demyelinating disease, or other etiologies; its significance depends on location and cause.

oculomotor.definition: Relating to the movement of the eye; specifically, the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III) innervates most extraocular muscles and the levator palpebrae superioris, and carries parasympathetic fibers to the pupil for constriction and to the lens for accommodation.

somatic cavity.definition: The somatic cavity is the portion of the intraembryonic coelom that lies adjacent to the body wall and is lined by the somatic (parietal) mesoderm; it forms the parietal serosa and contributes to the body-wall–associated cavities (such as the pleural, pericardial, and peritoneal spaces).

opiate.definition: Any painkilling drug such as morphine or codeine derived from the opium poppy.

colchicine.definition: A microtubule inhibitor that binds tubulin to prevent microtubule polymerization, thereby reducing neutrophil chemotaxis and inflammatory responses; used to treat acute gout attacks and prevent gout flares, and to treat familial Mediterranean fever.

probenecid.definition: A uricosuric medication that inhibits the reabsorption of uric acid in the renal proximal tubules, increasing urinary uric acid excretion; used to treat gout and to prolong the effect of certain antibiotics by reducing their renal clearance.

colesevelam.definition: A bile acid sequestrant that binds bile acids in the intestine and prevents their reabsorption, leading to increased conversion of cholesterol to bile acids and reduced LDL cholesterol; used to treat hyperlipidemia.

docusate.definition: A stool-softening laxative (emollient) that acts as a surfactant to decrease surface tension, allowing water and fat to mix into stool to soften it; used to relieve constipation and reduce straining.

colectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove all or part of the colon (large intestine); the remaining bowel is usually reconnected (anastomosis) to restore continuity, or a stoma may be formed.

trigone.definition: A triangular area on the interior of the bladder delineated by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice; its mucosa is smooth and relatively insensitive to distension.

ureteroneocystostomy.definition: An operation in which a ureter is surgically reimplanted into the urinary bladder to create a new ureter–bladder connection, typically to correct vesicoureteral reflux or relieve ureteral obstruction.

cold-pressor-test.definition: A procedure in which the hand is immersed in ice-cold water (typically 0–4°C) for a defined period to provoke a sympathetic autonomic response; cardiovascular measurements (e.g., heart rate, blood pressure) and pain perception are monitored to assess autonomic function or pain tolerance.

parkinsons.definition: A movement disorder that occurs when the brain does not produce enough of a chemical.

frostbite.definition: When your body is injured because of severe cold, most often on hands, feet, ears, and nose.

xanthoma.definition: A yellow, lipid-laden deposit in the skin or on a tendon.

ldl-c.definition: Cholesterol carried by low-density lipoprotein particles in the blood; a primary measure of atherogenic cholesterol used to assess cardiovascular risk. Higher levels are associated with increased risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and guide lipid-lowering therapy.

colfosceril.definition: A synthetic phospholipid (L-α-dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) used as a component of artificial pulmonary surfactant in the treatment of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

pulmonary surfactant.definition: A lipoprotein–lipid complex secreted by type II pneumocytes that coats the alveoli, reducing surface tension at the air–liquid interface to prevent alveolar collapse and maintain lung compliance; major lipid component is dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) and it contains surfactant proteins SP-A, SP-B, SP-C, and SP-D.

neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.definition: A respiratory failure of the newborn caused by surfactant deficiency in the immature lung, leading to alveolar collapse, decreased lung compliance, and hypoxemia; often treated with exogenous surfactant and assisted ventilation.

intratracheal administration.definition: Delivery of a drug directly into the trachea (usually via an endotracheal tube) for rapid onset, either to affect the airways locally or to achieve systemic absorption, commonly used in emergency resuscitation when other routes are unavailable.

infantile colic.definition: A benign, self-limited condition of infancy defined by recurrent, prolonged, inconsolable crying in an otherwise healthy, well-fed infant, usually beginning in the first weeks of life and resolving by 3–4 months; episodes may be accompanied by fussiness and abdominal discomfort, with no underlying medical illness detected.

renal colic.definition: An acute, severe, intermittent flank or groin pain caused by obstruction of the urinary tract (usually a ureteral stone) with associated symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, hematuria, and sweating.

colistin.definition: An antibiotic of the polymyxin class (polymyxin E) used as a last-resort treatment for severe infections caused by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria; it disrupts the bacterial outer membrane by binding to lipopolysaccharides and is associated with nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity; administered as colistin sulfate or as the prodrug colistimethate sodium.

colistimethate sodium.definition: A prodrug form of colistin (polymyxin E) used as an antibiotic for severe infections caused by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria; in vivo it is hydrolyzed to the active drug colistin and is typically given by IV, IM, or inhalation, with nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity as notable adverse effects.

neurotoxicity.definition: Nervous-system toxicity from exposure to chemicals or other agents, causing structural or functional damage to neurons or glial cells and resulting in neurological symptoms such as cognitive impairment, sensory or motor deficits, autonomic dysfunction, seizures, or neuropathic pain.

crohn's disease.definition: A chronic inflammatory disease of the gastrointestinal tract that can affect any part of it, causing abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and fatigue.

collagen.definition: A fibrous protein that is the main component of connective tissue in the body.

collagenase.definition: An enzyme that breaks down collagen.

debridement.definition: Removal of dead, damaged, or infected tissue and foreign material from a wound to promote healing and reduce the risk of infection; it can be performed surgically, mechanically, enzymatically, or autolytically.

decubitus ulcers.definition: A pressure-induced skin and soft-tissue injury over a bony prominence caused by prolonged immobilization or pressure, leading to ischemia and tissue necrosis; commonly called a bedsore and staged by depth (I–IV).

peyronie's disease.definition: Fibrous plaque formation in the tunica albuginea of the penis, causing penile curvature and deformity, often with painful erections and sometimes erectile dysfunction.

dupuytren's disease.definition: A benign fibromatosis of the palmar fascia causing progressive thickening and shortening (cord formation) that leads to fixed flexion contractures of one or more fingers, typically the ring and little fingers.

collagen disease.definition: A historical, non-specific label for autoimmune or inflammatory diseases affecting connective tissue and collagen; not a precise modern diagnosis, with specific conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus and scleroderma now classified separately.

collagen vascular disease.definition: An umbrella, non-specific term for autoimmune disorders that affect connective tissue (collagen) and small blood vessels, causing systemic inflammation in skin, joints, muscles, and internal organs; includes conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus, scleroderma (systemic sclerosis), polymyositis/dermatomyositis, rheumatoid arthritis, and mixed connective tissue disease.

collagen injection.definition: An injectable dermal filler procedure in which collagen protein is injected into the dermal or subcutaneous tissue to restore volume, fill wrinkles, or contour tissues; collagen can be derived from bovine or human sources; allergy testing may be required; effects are temporary, lasting months.

collagenoblast.definition: A collagenoblast is a cell that synthesizes collagen fibers for the extracellular matrix; in connective tissue, this role is typically fulfilled by fibroblasts.

collagenous colitis.definition: A form of microscopic colitis characterized by chronic non-bloody watery diarrhea; diagnosis is histologic, with a thickened subepithelial collagen band in the colonic mucosa on biopsy, while the colon typically appears normal on endoscopy.

collagenous fiber.definition: A primary extracellular matrix fiber composed mainly of collagen; thick, eosinophilic bundles that confer high tensile strength to connective tissues and are relatively inelastic.

collagen shield.definition: A biodegradable, collagen-based corneal patch used as a temporary protective bandage over the ocular surface to promote healing of corneal epithelial defects after injury or surgery; applied to the cornea and typically dissolves as healing occurs.

colles' fascia.definition: Membranous layer of the superficial perineal fascia in the perineum; continuous with Scarpa’s fascia of the abdomen and with the dartos fascia of the penis/scrotum; attaches to the posterior edge of the perineal membrane and to the ischiopubic rami, forming the inferior boundary of the superficial perineal pouch and helping contain urinary extravasation in urethral injury.

colles' fracture.definition: A fracture of the distal radius with dorsal (posterior) displacement of the distal fragment, typically caused by a fall on an outstretched hand; classically produces a dinner-fork deformity and may be associated with an ulnar styloid fracture, occurring more often in older adults with osteoporosis.

coliform.definition: A broad group of Gram-negative, non-spore-forming, lactose-fermenting bacilli that are normally present in the intestines of humans and other warm-blooded animals; they are used as indicator organisms to detect fecal contamination in water and food safety testing.

coloenteritis.definition: Inflammation of both the colon and the small intestine, usually as part of gastroenteritis; presents with acute diarrhea and abdominal cramps, often with fever, and results from infectious etiologies (bacterial, viral, or parasitic) or other causes such as inflammatory or ischemic disease.

colon hydrotherapy.definition: A procedure in which water is introduced into the large intestine via the rectum to flush out fecal matter; marketed as a detoxifying cleanse, but there is little evidence of benefit and it carries risks such as dehydration, electrolyte disturbances, infection, and bowel perforation.

polyarteritis nodosa.definition: Systemic necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries causing aneurysm formation and thrombosis with organ ischemia, classically affecting the kidneys, skin, peripheral nerves, and gastrointestinal tract; lungs are typically spared; pathology shows transmural inflammation with fibrinoid necrosis; often associated with hepatitis B infection; treated with corticosteroids and immunosuppressants; prognosis depends on severity and treatment response.

necrotizing vasculitis.definition: Inflammation of blood vessel walls with necrosis (often fibrinoid necrosis) of the vessel wall, leading to vessel destruction and potential ischemia or hemorrhage; typically affects small- to medium-sized arteries and arterioles and is seen in various systemic vasculitides and immune complex–mediated processes.

relapsing polychondritis.definition: A rare autoimmune disorder characterized by episodic inflammatory destruction of cartilaginous tissues—most commonly the ears, nose, and respiratory tract—with relapsing-remitting episodes; may involve eyes, joints, skin, and the cardiovascular system, and can lead to deformity and airway compromise.

connective tissue disease.definition: A broad group of autoimmune diseases that affect connective tissues (skin, joints, muscles, blood vessels, and related structures), often with circulating autoantibodies; examples include systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), polymyositis/dermatomyositis, and mixed connective tissue disease.

collateral circulation.definition: A system of minor arteries, known as collaterals, that can serve as an alternate blood supply to the heart when a major coronary artery is blocked.

collateral fissure.definition: An anatomical groove on the inferior surface of the brain that lies between the lingual gyrus and the fusiform gyrus, forming part of the boundary between the occipital and temporal lobes.

collateral innervation.definition: Collateral innervation refers to the innervation of a structure by collateral branches or anastomoses from nearby nerves, providing secondary or redundant neural supply in addition to the primary nerve supply.

collateral ligaments (interphalangeal jo.definition: One of a pair of fibrous ligaments on the medial and lateral sides of each interphalangeal joint in the toes; they connect adjacent phalanges and stabilize the joint by limiting sideways (medial–lateral) movement.

Lateral stabilizing bands on the sides of each finger’s interphalangeal joints (proximal and distal). They limit sideways (varus/valgus) movement and tighten with flexion, providing stability to the PIP and DIP joints.

collateral ligaments of the metacarpopha.word: collateral ligaments of the metacarpophalangeal joints
collateral ligaments of the metacarpopha.definition: A pair of strong fibrous bands on the sides of each metacarpophalangeal joint (radial and ulnar collateral ligaments) that stabilize the joint by limiting lateral (abduction/adduction) movement of the finger and anchoring the proximal phalanx to the metacarpal head.

collateral ligaments of the metatarsopha.word: collateral ligaments of the metatarsophalangeal joints
collateral ligaments of the metatarsopha.definition: Medial and lateral ligaments that reinforce the metatarsophalangeal joint capsule by connecting the metatarsal head to the base of the proximal phalanx on each side; they stabilize the toe and limit abduction and adduction, and are taut in flexion.

collateral pulp canal.definition: A small secondary canal branching from the main root canal within a tooth, extending laterally toward the periodontal ligament; also called a lateral or accessory canal, it may contain pulp tissue and provides a pathway between the pulp chamber and the periradicular tissues.

collateral ventilation.definition: Collateral ventilation is the ventilation of alveoli through alternative interalveolar and interbronchiolar pathways (pores of Kohn, canals of Lambert, and channels of Martin) that bypass obstructed airways.

collateral vessel.definition: A small blood vessel that provides an alternative route for blood flow around a blocked or narrowed vessel, forming collateral circulation; it may be a pre-existing connection that enlarges or a newly formed vessel.

collecting system.definition: An anatomic component of the kidney comprising the minor calyces, major calyces, and renal pelvis; it collects urine produced by the nephrons and funnels it into the ureter.

collecting tubule.definition: A segment of the nephron that collects urine from distal tubules and channels it into the collecting ducts, located in the renal cortex and medulla; its epithelium participates in electrolyte and water balance under hormonal control.

bowmans capsule.definition: A cup-shaped structure that surrounds the glomerulus in the nephron; part of the renal corpuscle, consisting of an outer parietal layer of simple squamous epithelium and an inner visceral layer of podocytes, forming Bowman's space where filtrate collects before entering the renal tubule.

oncotic pressure.definition: An osmotic pressure created by plasma proteins, especially albumin, that pulls water from the interstitial space into capillaries, helping to maintain intravascular volume and fluid balance.

colloid osmotic pressure.definition: The osmotic pressure exerted by plasma proteins (primarily albumin) in the blood that pulls water from the interstitial space back into the capillaries, opposing capillary hydrostatic pressure and helping to maintain intravascular volume.

colloid cyst.definition: An intracranial, benign, epithelium-lined cyst in the anterior roof of the third ventricle near the foramen of Monro, filled with gelatinous material. It can obstruct CSF flow, causing hydrocephalus and symptoms such as headache, nausea, cognitive or gait disturbances, and in rare cases sudden deterioration.

colloid bath.definition: A therapeutic bath in which finely dispersed colloidal particles are suspended in water, forming a stable suspension used to soothe the skin and/or aid in delivery of topical medications (e.g., colloidal oatmeal baths, colloidal silver baths).

colloid sulfur.definition: A topical preparation in which finely dispersed elemental sulfur is suspended as a colloid in an ointment base (commonly petrolatum), used for its keratolytic and mildly antimicrobial properties in dermatologic conditions.

colloid suspension.definition: A heterogeneous mixture in which finely divided particles (the colloidal dispersed phase) are dispersed in a continuous medium; the particles are in the colloidal size range (roughly 1 nanometer to 1 micrometer) and remain suspended rather than dissolving, often exhibiting the Tyndall effect.

colobomatous.definition: Pertaining to a congenital ocular defect characterized by a gap or notch in the iris, retina, choroid, or optic nerve, caused by failure of the embryonic fissure to close during development.

colobomas.definition: A congenital defect in which normal tissue in or around the eye is missing, producing a gap or notch in structures such as the iris, retina, choroid, or optic nerve, due to failure of the embryonic fissure to close during development.

harlequin fetus.definition: A rare congenital keratinization disorder caused by ABCA12 mutations, presenting at birth with severe generalized hyperkeratosis and thick, plate-like scales that cover the body, producing a characteristic harlequin appearance with deep fissures and often facial involvement.

collodion baby.definition: Neonate with a tight, parchment-like membrane covering the skin at birth (collodion membrane), usually an early manifestation of congenital ichthyosis; the membrane may fissure and peel, risking dehydration, temperature instability, and infection until the skin barrier and epidermal function mature.

collarbone.definition: A slender, S-shaped bone of the shoulder girdle that connects the sternum to the scapula; it acts as a strut to hold the arm away from the thorax and transmits loads from the upper limb to the axial skeleton. It forms the sternoclavicular joint medially and the acromioclavicular joint laterally; its middle third lies just beneath the skin and is a common fracture site.

corrigan's pulse.definition: A rapid, forceful pulse with a brisk upstroke and abrupt collapse, seen in aortic regurgitation due to a widened pulse pressure; also called a water-hammer pulse.

intestinal toxemia.definition: A systemic toxic state arising from absorption of toxins produced by intestinal bacteria, typically due to bacterial overgrowth, mucosal damage, or increased intestinal permeability.

regional enteritis.definition: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by transmural, granulomatous inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract, most often the terminal ileum, with skip lesions and complications such as fistulas and strictures; commonly presents with abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss. Also known as Crohn disease.

cecal volvulus.definition: A twisting of the cecum around its mesentery causing large-bowel obstruction; often due to an abnormally mobile or unfixed cecum, and it may progress to ischemia if not promptly treated.

sigmoid volvulus.definition: A twisting of the sigmoid colon around its mesentery that causes large-bowel obstruction and may lead to ischemia or perforation; often treated with endoscopic detorsion in stable patients, followed by surgical resection to prevent recurrence.

transverse colon volvulus.definition: An uncommon form of large-bowel volvulus in which the transverse colon twists around its mesentery, causing mechanical obstruction that can progress to bowel ischemia if not relieved; presents with acute abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and obstipation, and is treated with endoscopic detorsion if viable or surgical resection for necrotic or recurrent cases.

volvulus.definition: A twisting of a loop of intestine around its mesentery, causing intestinal obstruction and potential bowel ischemia; most often occurs with the sigmoid colon in adults and the midgut in neonates, presenting with acute abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and obstipation; urgent management with detorsion and, if needed, surgical resection.

colonic fistula.definition: An abnormal passage (fistula) between the colon and another surface or organ (e.g., skin, bladder, vagina, or another loop of bowel) through which colonic contents can pass.

coloproctectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove the colon and rectum. Also known as proctocolectomy.

coloproctitis.definition: Inflammation of both the colon and the rectum (the distal large bowel), often presenting with diarrhea, rectal bleeding, and urgency; etiologies include infection, inflammatory bowel disease, ischemia, and radiation.

colorectitis.definition: Inflammation of the colorectum (the colon and rectum).

rectocolitis.definition: Inflammation of the mucosa of the rectum and colon (the distal large intestine), often presenting with diarrhea and rectal bleeding; can be due to inflammatory bowel disease (e.g., ulcerative colitis), infection, ischemia, radiation, or chemical injury, with variable extent and severity.

melena.definition: Black, tarry stools that are foul-smelling, caused by digestion of blood as it passes through the gastrointestinal tract; typically indicates bleeding from an upper gastrointestinal source (esophagus, stomach, or proximal small intestine).

digital rectal examination.definition: A physical examination in which a clinician inserts a lubricated, gloved finger into the rectum to palpate the anal canal and rectum for masses, hemorrhoids, bleeding, tenderness, and to assess anal sphincter tone; in males, it also assesses the prostate's size, shape, and consistency.

proctosigmoidoscopic examination.definition: An endoscopic procedure in which a proctoscope or sigmoidoscope is inserted through the anus to visualize the rectum and sigmoid colon (distal colon), often performed to evaluate bleeding, pain, diarrhea, or inflammatory/neoplastic disease, and may include biopsy or therapeutic intervention.

sigmoidoscope.definition: A flexible or rigid endoscope used to visualize the sigmoid colon via the rectum, for diagnostic examination and biopsy (sigmoidoscopy) and sometimes treatment of distal colon diseases.

colonoscope.definition: A flexible endoscope used to visualize the colon and rectum through the anus; it allows biopsy, polypectomy, and other therapeutic interventions.

colonography.definition: An imaging study of the colon used to detect polyps, masses, or inflammatory disease; typically performed after insufflation of the colon with gas, and commonly using CT colonography (virtual colonoscopy) or fluoroscopic barium enema methods.

loop colostomy.definition: A temporary ostomy in which a loop of colon is brought to the abdominal surface and opened to form a stoma with proximal and distal lumens for fecal diversion; the loop is typically supported with a bridge and later reversed.

double-barreled colostomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which the colon is divided and both ends are brought out to the abdominal wall as two adjacent stomas; the proximal stoma drains feces while the distal stoma (mucous fistula) drains mucus, typically used to divert stool temporarily to allow healing of a distal colorectal anastomosis.

colostomy irrigation.definition: An outpatient technique in which warm water is introduced into the colon through a stoma using an irrigation device (cone/catheter) to flush stool and regulate evacuation on a scheduled basis, reducing leakage and increasing stool control.

enterostomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which a segment of bowel is brought to the surface of the abdomen to create a temporary or permanent opening (stoma) for diversion and drainage of intestinal contents.

stoma.definition: A surgically created opening between an internal hollow organ (commonly the bowel or urinary tract) and the external skin, enabling diversion of waste or drainage away from the normal route.

colostomate.definition: A person who has had a colostomy—a surgically created opening (stoma) from the colon to the abdominal wall to divert stool.

colotomy.definition: A surgical incision into the colon to gain access to its lumen, typically to relieve obstruction, drain contents, obtain biopsies, or facilitate other colorectal procedures.

colovaginal fistula.definition: An abnormal fistulous tract between the colon (usually the sigmoid colon) and the vagina, allowing fecal material to pass into the vagina and causing feculent vaginal discharge and recurrent infections; commonly acquired after pelvic surgery, diverticulitis, Crohn disease, or radiation therapy.

vesicocolonic fistula.definition: An abnormal communication between the urinary bladder and the colon, allowing passage of urine and fecal material between these organs; commonly due to diverticular disease or colorectal pathology and often presenting with pneumaturia and fecaluria.

colovesical fistula.definition: An abnormal communication between the colon (usually the sigmoid) and the urinary bladder, allowing fecal matter and gas to pass into the bladder; most commonly caused by diverticular disease and presents with pneumaturia and fecaluria, often requiring surgical resection of the involved colon and repair of the bladder.

colpocystitis.definition: Simultaneous inflammation of the vaginal mucosa and the urinary bladder, typically due to infection; presents with vaginal irritation or discharge plus urinary symptoms such as dysuria, frequency, or urgency. Management targets the underlying infection with appropriate antibiotics and supportive care.

colpalgia.definition: Vaginal pain; pain in the vaginal area, usually a symptom stemming from infections, irritation, trauma, or other gynecologic conditions.

colpitis.definition: Inflammation of the vaginal mucosa (vagina), commonly due to infection (such as Candida, bacterial vaginosis, or Trichomonas) or irritation/allergic factors, typically presenting with itching, discharge, burning, and vaginal soreness.

colpectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove all or part of the vagina (vaginal tissue); also called vaginectomy.

fap.definition: An autosomal dominant hereditary syndrome characterized by hundreds to thousands of adenomatous polyps in the colon and rectum, usually starting in adolescence; nearly 100% risk of colorectal cancer without intervention; caused by germline mutations in the APC gene; managed with intensive colonoscopic surveillance and often prophylactic colectomy; may have extracolonic features such as desmoid tumors and osteomas.

hnpcc.definition: A hereditary cancer syndrome caused by germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair genes (most often MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, or EPCAM deletions), resulting in a high lifetime risk of colorectal cancer and several other cancers; tumors often show microsatellite instability and loss of mismatch repair, with autosomal-dominant inheritance.

familial adenomatous polyposis.definition: An autosomal-dominant hereditary syndrome caused by APC gene mutations, characterized by hundreds to thousands of colorectal adenomatous polyps with near‑certain progression to colorectal cancer if untreated; managed by intensive polyp surveillance and often prophylactic colectomy, with possible extraintestinal features such as desmoid tumors and duodenal polyps.

neomycin.definition: An aminoglycoside antibiotic produced by Streptomyces fradiae that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit; used topically in combination preparations for skin infections and, historically, for bowel decontamination; systemic exposure carries a risk of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

ileocecal sphincter.definition: A circular smooth muscle component surrounding the ileocecal valve that regulates passage of chyme from the terminal ileum into the cecum and prevents backflow from the large intestine.

splenic flexure.definition: The bend between the transverse colon and the descending colon near the spleen in the left upper quadrant; marks the transition from transverse to descending colon and is relatively fixed by peritoneal attachments (e.g., splenocolic and phrenicocolic ligaments).

teniae coli.definition: Three longitudinal bands of smooth muscle on the wall of the colon that run the length of the organ; they contract to form sacculations (haustra) and help shorten the colon during peristalsis.

epiploic appendages.definition: Small, fat-filled peritoneal pouches that hang from the colon (appendices epiploicae); these peritoneal outpouchings are derived from the greater omentum and attached along the teniae coli, and they can become inflamed or infarcted (epiploic appendagitis), sometimes mimicking appendicitis or diverticulitis.

colpocystocele.definition: A prolapse in which the bladder protrudes into the vagina through the anterior vaginal wall due to weakness of the pelvic floor support.

prolapse.definition: A condition in which an organ or other body part drops from its normal position.

colpohysterectomy.definition: A hysterectomy performed through the vagina; removal of the uterus (and usually the cervix) via the vaginal route, without an abdominal incision.

colporrhaphy.definition: A surgical repair of the vaginal wall to correct pelvic organ prolapse, typically by tightening and reinforcing the vaginal fascia (anterior colporrhaphy for cystocele and posterior colporrhaphy for rectocele).

colposcope.definition: An optical magnification instrument with illumination used to inspect the cervix, vagina, and vulva in detail during gynecologic evaluation, to identify abnormal epithelium and guide biopsies.

cervical dysplasia.definition: A premalignant condition in which abnormal, precancerous changes occur in the squamous epithelium of the cervix, most commonly due to persistent infection with high‑risk human papillomavirus; graded from mild (CIN 1) to severe (CIN 3), detected by Pap smear or biopsy, and not cancer but increases the risk of invasive cervical cancer if untreated.

colpotomy.definition: A surgical incision into the vaginal wall, usually through the posterior fornix, to gain access to the peritoneal cavity for gynecologic procedures.

columella.definition: A fleshy nasal tissue that separates the two nostrils at the lower part of the nose; formed by cartilage and surrounding soft tissue and providing support to the nasal tip.

column.definition: A vertical supporting structure in the body; in anatomy, the spinal column (vertebral column) is a segmented series of vertebrae from the base of the skull to the pelvis that protects the spinal cord and supports the body's weight.

columnar cell.definition: An epithelial cell that is tall and slender (column-shaped), taller than wide, typically with the nucleus near the base; it forms columnar epithelium and functions in absorption or secretion, often with microvilli or cilia depending on the tissue.

columnar epithelium.definition: A type of epithelial tissue composed of tall, column-shaped cells. It can be simple (single layer) or pseudostratified; specialized for absorption and secretion, often bearing apical microvilli (as in the small intestine) or cilia (as in the respiratory tract).

column chromatography.definition: A laboratory separation method in which a mixture is passed through a column packed with a solid adsorbent (stationary phase); components separate based on their differing affinities for the stationary phase versus the mobile phase, allowing collection of purified fractions.

colymycin m.definition: A polymyxin-class antibiotic used against multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria; it binds to lipopolysaccharides and disrupts the bacterial outer membrane, leading to cell death; its use is limited by nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity.

colymycin s.definition: A polypeptide antibiotic used to treat serious infections caused by susceptible Gram-negative bacteria; it disrupts the bacterial outer membrane by binding to lipopolysaccharides, causing cell lysis. Typically reserved for multidrug-resistant infections due to nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity; available as the sulfate salt in various systemic, inhalational, or topical formulations.

hydrocortisone.definition: A glucocorticoid corticosteroid used pharmaceutically for its anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects; available topically, orally, or by injection, and used for adrenal insufficiency replacement as well as a wide range of inflammatory, autoimmune, and allergic conditions.

combitube.definition: An emergency airway device with two lumens and cuffs that is blindly inserted through the mouth and can ventilate the patient via either the tracheal or the esophageal route, used when endotracheal intubation is difficult or not possible.

esophageal obturator airway.definition: A historical emergency airway device consisting of an inflatable tube inserted into the mouth and advanced into the esophagus, with the distal cuff inflated to occlude the esophagus and reduce gastric inflation during resuscitation; largely obsolete due to aspiration risk and inferior ventilation compared with modern airways.

lamivudine.definition: A nucleoside analogue reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) used to treat HIV-1 infection and chronic hepatitis B; it inhibits viral DNA synthesis after intracellular phosphorylation to its active triphosphate form.

combivir.definition: A fixed-dose combination antiretroviral medication containing zidovudine (AZT) and lamivudine (3TC), used to treat HIV-1 infection in combination with other antiretrovirals.

subacute combined degeneration of the sp.word: subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
subacute combined degeneration of the sp.definition: Dem ye lination of the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts of the spinal cord caused by vitamin B12 deficiency, producing combined posterior column (sensory) and motor tract (weakness, spasticity) dysfunction with ataxia; commonly due to pernicious anemia or malabsorption; treated with vitamin B12 replacement.

brain ischemia.definition: Brain ischemia is a condition in which inadequate blood flow to brain tissue deprives neurons of oxygen and glucose, causing cellular injury or death and potentially leading to stroke or transient neurological deficits; it can result from arterial occlusion, hypoperfusion, or cerebral vasospasm.

glasgow coma scale.definition: A clinical scale used to assess level of consciousness in patients with acute brain injury, based on three responses: eye opening, verbal response, and motor activity. Scores range from 3 (deep coma) to 15 (fully awake), with lower scores indicating greater impairment and guiding prognosis and management.

comedo.definition: A clogged hair follicle filled with keratinous debris and sebum; when the opening is open, it appears as a blackhead (open comedo), and when closed, as a whitehead (closed comedo).

comedocarcinoma.definition: High-grade ductal carcinoma in situ of the breast characterized by malignant cells filling ducts with central necrosis (comedonecrosis) and calcifications; a noninvasive precursor lesion that may progress to invasive ductal carcinoma if untreated.

comedogenicity.definition: The tendency of a substance to promote the formation of comedones (clogged hair follicles), often by blocking pores; used to describe cosmetics or skincare ingredients likely to provoke acne.

comedomastitis.definition: Inflammation of a clogged pilosebaceous pore, a lesion seen in acne; presents with localized redness and tenderness around the blocked pore and may progress to a papule, pustule, or abscess.

comfrey.definition: An herb (Symphytum officinale) traditionally used topically for wound healing and inflammation; it contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids that can cause serious liver toxicity if ingested, so internal use is not recommended, and topical use should avoid broken skin.

common cold.definition: An acute viral infection of the upper respiratory tract, most commonly caused by rhinoviruses, presenting with nasal congestion, runny nose, sore throat, sneezing, and cough; typically self-limited within 7–10 days, transmitted by respiratory droplets and contact with contaminated surfaces; management is supportive and antibiotics are not indicated unless a bacterial complication develops.

common hepatic artery.definition: A branch of the celiac trunk that supplies the liver, typically dividing into the proper hepatic artery and the gastroduodenal artery and running within the hepatoduodenal ligament.

common fibular nerve.definition: A branch of the sciatic nerve (L4–S2) that winds around the fibular neck and divides into the superficial and deep peroneal nerves; it supplies motor innervation to the muscles of the anterior and lateral compartments of the leg and sensory innervation to much of the dorsum of the foot (with the deep branch supplying the first web space); injury can cause foot drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot.

intraductal neoplasm.definition: A neoplasm arising from the ductal epithelium and growing within the lumen or wall of a duct; it may be benign or malignant and can cause ductal obstruction or discharge.

mammary duct.definition: A duct in the breast that carries milk from the mammary lobules to the nipple; part of the lactiferous duct system.

single-cell gel electrophoresis.definition: A method to measure DNA strand breaks in individual cells by embedding cells in agarose on a slide, lysing to form nucleoids, and applying electrophoresis; damaged DNA migrates away from the nucleus, creating a comet-like tail whose length and DNA content reflect the extent of DNA damage.

comet assay.definition: A sensitive technique for measuring DNA damage in individual cells. Cells are embedded in agarose on a slide, lysed, and subjected to electrophoresis; damaged DNA migrates out of the nucleus to form a "comet" tail, with tail length and intensity reflecting the amount of DNA strand breaks (alkaline version detects single- and double-strand breaks and alkali-labile sites; neutral version emphasizes double-strand breaks).

iliac artery.definition: One of the two large arteries arising from the bifurcation of the abdominal aorta; each common iliac artery supplies the pelvis and lower limb and divides into the internal iliac artery (pelvic organs and gluteal region) and the external iliac artery (which becomes the femoral artery in the thigh).

right common iliac artery.definition: A terminal branch of the abdominal aorta that arises at the aortic bifurcation, runs to the right side of the pelvis, and divides into the right external iliac artery (continuing as the femoral artery) and the right internal iliac artery (supplying pelvic organs and walls).

left common iliac artery.definition: One of the two terminal branches of the abdominal aorta; it descends into the left pelvis and bifurcates at the pelvic brim into the left external iliac artery (continuing as the femoral artery) and the left internal iliac artery, supplying the lower limb (via the external) and pelvic organs/gluteal region (via the internal).

external iliac artery.definition: A pelvic artery arising from the bifurcation of the common iliac artery; it courses along the pelvic brim, passes beneath the inguinal ligament to become the femoral artery, and supplies the lower abdominal wall and the lower limb via branches such as the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac arteries.

iliac vein.definition: One of the veins in the iliac (pelvic) region. The external iliac vein drains the lower limb and continues as the femoral vein, while the internal iliac vein drains pelvic organs; the common iliac veins are formed by the union of the internal and external iliac veins and drain into the inferior vena cava.

iliolumbar vein.definition: A deep pelvic and retroperitoneal vein that drains the iliacus and adjacent posterior abdominal wall, accompanying the iliolumbar artery and typically draining into the common iliac vein (variations include drainage into the internal iliac vein or via the ascending lumbar system into the IVC).

lateral sacral vein.definition: A vein draining the lateral sacral region and sacral canal, forming part of the sacral venous plexus and typically draining into the internal iliac vein.

middle sacral vein.definition: A small vein that runs with the middle sacral artery along the sacrum and drains the posterior sacral venous plexus, typically emptying into the left common iliac vein (variations exist).

sacroiliac articulation.definition: A weight-bearing joint between the sacrum and the ilium of the pelvis; a strong synovial (plane) joint with irregular articular surfaces, reinforced by the anterior and posterior sacroiliac ligaments and the interosseous sacroiliac ligament, allowing only limited gliding and rotation (nutation and counternutation) to transfer load from the spine to the pelvis.

common iliac node.definition: A lymph node situated along the common iliac vessels near their bifurcation; receives lymph from the internal and external iliac nodes and drains to the lumbar (para-aortic) nodes.

external iliac node.definition: A lymph node along the external iliac vessels in the pelvis that filters lymph from the lower limb and lower abdominal wall and drains into the common iliac lymph nodes.

internal iliac node.definition: A lymph node located along the internal iliac (hypogastric) arteries in the pelvis that drains lymph from pelvic organs (e.g., bladder, uterus, cervix, rectum) and perineal regions; part of the pelvic/iliac lymphatic drainage pathway.

lateral aortic nodes.definition: Retroperitoneal lymph nodes located along the lateral aspect of the abdominal aorta, forming part of the paraaortic (lumbar) node group. They drain lymph from retroperitoneal structures such as the kidneys, adrenal glands, gonads, ureters, and parts of the posterior abdominal wall, and drain into the lumbar trunks and cisterna chyli (ultimately the thoracic duct).

coagulation pathway.definition: An enzymatic cascade that converts soluble fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin to form a stable blood clot; initiated by vascular injury via the extrinsic pathway (tissue factor–VIIa) and/or the intrinsic pathway (contact activation), both converging on activation of factor X to Xa and thrombin formation.

common pathway of coagulation.definition: The convergent part of the coagulation cascade where factor Xa, in complex with factor Va on a phospholipid surface and calcium, converts prothrombin to thrombin; thrombin then cleaves fibrinogen to fibrin, forming a stable fibrin clot. This pathway integrates the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways.

intrinsic pathway of coagulation.definition: A coagulation pathway initiated by contact activation of factor XII on negatively charged surfaces, sequentially activating factors XI and IX (with VIII as a cofactor) to form the intrinsic tenase (IXa–VIIIa), which activates factor X and leads to thrombin generation and fibrin formation.

extrinsic pathway of coagulation.definition: A pathway of the coagulation cascade initiated by exposure of tissue factor (thromboplastin) from damaged tissue; tissue factor binds factor VIIa to form the TF–VIIa complex, which activates factor X to Xa, leading to thrombin generation and fibrin clot formation; it is faster and is assessed by the prothrombin time (PT).

factor x.definition: A vitamin K–dependent coagulation factor produced by the liver; it is activated to a serine protease that, with cofactor Va and calcium on phospholipid surfaces, converts prothrombin to thrombin in the coagulation cascade.

factor v.definition: A vitamin K–dependent plasma glycoprotein that acts as a nonenzymatic cofactor for Factor Xa in the prothrombinase complex, promoting the conversion of prothrombin to thrombin on phospholipid surfaces; activated to Factor Va by thrombin; deficiency causes a rare bleeding disorder; a common inherited mutation (Factor V Leiden) impairs inactivation by activated protein C and increases risk of venous thrombosis.

fibrin clot.definition: A blood clot whose structural framework is fibrin; formed during coagulation when thrombin converts fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin, which traps platelets and red blood cells and is stabilized by cross-linking via factor XIII.

periorbita.definition: Thin fibrous membrane lining the orbital cavity—the orbital periosteum. It lines the bones of the orbit, is continuous with the cranial periosteum, and forms the inner boundary enveloping the orbital contents.

optic canal.definition: A short bony passage in the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone that transmits the optic nerve (CN II) and the ophthalmic artery from the cranial cavity into the orbit.

superior orbital fissure.definition: A bony opening in the posterior orbital wall (between the greater and lesser sphenoid wings) that connects the orbit to the middle cranial fossa; it transmits cranial nerves III (oculomotor), IV (trochlear), V1 (ophthalmic nerve), and VI (abducens), along with the superior ophthalmic vein (and accompanying sympathetic fibers).

bony orbit.definition: A conical cavity in the skull that houses the eyeball and its adnexa; formed by seven bones (frontal, maxilla, zygomatic, sphenoid, ethmoid, lacrimal, and palatine).

rectus muscles.definition: Muscles whose fibers run parallel to a straight axis of the body; the term “rectus” denotes straight. These muscles typically have a longitudinal orientation and insert along a straight line, contributing to flexion or stabilization of the trunk or limb. Examples include the rectus abdominis (flexes the trunk) and the rectus femoris (part of the quadriceps, extends the knee and flexes the hip).

common tendinous ring.definition: A fibrous ring at the posterior orbit (annulus tendineus communis oculi, also called the annulus of Zinn) that serves as the common origin for the four rectus extraocular muscles.

communicating hydrocephalus.definition: Enlargement of the ventricular system due to impaired absorption of CSF at the arachnoid granulations, with CSF flow between the ventricles and subarachnoid space still intact (no intraventricular obstruction).

ventricular system.definition: A network of interconnected cavities within the brain and spinal cord that contain cerebrospinal fluid (CSF); it includes the lateral ventricles, third and fourth ventricles, the cerebral aqueduct and foramina, and the central canal, and it is involved in CSF production, circulation, and drainage.

communicable disease.definition: Any disease caused by bacteria, viruses, or other pathogens that is spread from person to person.

communicability period.definition: The time frame during which an infected person can transmit the infectious agent to others; it may begin before symptom onset and continues until the person is no longer contagious—duration varies by disease and individual.

community-acquired infection.definition: An infection contracted outside of a hospital or other healthcare setting, typically defined as one present on admission or developing within 48 hours of admission, not acquired during hospitalization.

infectious disease.definition: A disease caused by pathogenic microorganisms (bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites) that can be transmitted from an infected person, animal, or environment to susceptible individuals, leading to illness.

contagious disease.definition: An infectious disease that can be transmitted from one person to another via direct contact, respiratory droplets, contaminated surfaces or objects (fomites), or vectors.

cvid.definition: A primary humoral immunodeficiency characterized by low serum immunoglobulins (usually IgG, often with IgA and/or IgM deficiency) and impaired specific antibody responses, due to defective B‑cell maturation; presents with recurrent sinopulmonary and gastrointestinal infections, and may be associated with autoimmunity, lymphoproliferation, and increased cancer risk. Treated with immunoglobulin replacement therapy.

antibody production.definition: Antibody production is the process by which B lymphocytes, after recognizing an antigen and receiving signals from helper T cells, differentiate into plasma cells that secrete specific antibodies (immunoglobulins) into the circulation to neutralize pathogens and mark them for attack; it is the humoral component of the adaptive immune response.

t lymphocyte.definition: A type of white blood cell that is produced in the bone marrow and is part of the body’s immune system. Also called a T cell.

autoimmune disorders.definition: A group of conditions in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the body’s own tissues due to loss of self-tolerance, often involving autoantibodies and autoreactive T cells; they can be organ-specific or systemic, with symptoms varying by the tissues involved.

commotio cordis.definition: A sudden cardiac arrest caused by a blunt, non-penetrating chest impact (usually to the precordium) that triggers ventricular fibrillation without structural heart damage, often occurring in young athletes and requiring immediate defibrillation.
