conglomerate silicosis.definition: An advanced form of chronic silicosis in which numerous silicotic nodules coalesce to form large conglomerate masses in the lungs (often termed progressive massive fibrosis), leading to extensive pulmonary fibrosis and respiratory impairment; caused by prolonged exposure to crystalline silica and associated with an increased risk of tuberculosis.

silicosis.definition: A chronic occupational lung disease caused by inhalation of crystalline silica dust, leading to progressive fibrosis of the lungs (silicotic nodules), reduced lung function, and increased risk of tuberculosis; exposure is common in mining, quarrying, sandblasting, and stone cutting.

right ventricular hypertrophy.definition: An increase in the size and thickness of the right ventricular myocardium due to chronic pressure or volume overload, commonly from pulmonary hypertension or right-sided heart disease.

pulmonary fibrosis.definition: A disease that occurs when your lung tissues are scarred and don't work as well.

murine typhus.definition: A flea-borne rickettsial infection caused by Rickettsia typhi, transmitted to humans by rat fleas (primarily Xenopsylla cheopis); presents with fever, headache, myalgia, and sometimes rash; usually mild to moderate and effectively treated with doxycycline.

congolese red fever.definition: No widely recognized medical term by that name exists. It appears to be a nonstandard or outdated/local label for a febrile illness with a red rash seen in the Congo region, and is not specific. Differential diagnoses would include common tropical fevers such as malaria, typhus, dengue, typhoid fever, measles, and scarlet fever, among others. If you have a source or context, I can help clarify further.

conidiobolus coronatus.definition: An environmental fungus in the order Entomophthorales that causes conidiobolomycosis, a rare chronic infection of subcutaneous facial tissues (rhinofacial region), acquired from soil or decaying vegetation via inhalation or inoculation of conidia, typically occurring in tropical and subtropical regions.

conivaptan.definition: An intravenous nonpeptide vasopressin receptor antagonist that blocks V1A and V2 receptors, used to treat hyponatremia by promoting free water excretion (aquaresis).

euvolemia.definition: A state of normal body fluid volume (normovolemia), with preserved intravascular and interstitial fluid compartments and adequate tissue perfusion; no edema or dehydration.

pollakiuria.definition: Abnormally frequent daytime urination with small-volume voids, most often in children; typically benign and self-limited, possibly related to bladder overactivity or behavioral factors, and distinguished from polyuria (increased urine production) and nocturia (nighttime urination).

injection site reaction.definition: A localized inflammatory reaction at the site of a parenteral injection, characterized by redness, swelling, warmth, and pain (often with itching or a tender lump) that is usually mild and self-limited, resolving within hours to days.

hypomagnesia.definition: Low magnesium level in the blood; caused by inadequate intake, malabsorption, increased renal or GI losses, chronic alcohol use, or certain medications; can cause neuromuscular symptoms (tremor, cramps, tetany, seizures), mental status changes, and cardiac arrhythmias; diagnosed by serum magnesium below the normal range; treated with magnesium supplementation and by addressing the underlying cause.

conjoined twins.definition: A pair of genetically identical twins whose bodies are physically connected due to incomplete splitting of the embryo after fertilization, resulting in shared tissues or organs depending on the fusion site.

siamese twins.definition: A rare form of monozygotic twinning in which two genetically identical individuals are born physically joined to each other, typically due to incomplete division of a single fertilized egg; the site and extent of fusion can involve skin, bone, or internal organs, influencing treatment options and prognosis.

conjoined family therapy.definition: A form of family therapy in which multiple family members participate in joint sessions with a therapist to examine and alter patterns of communication, interaction, and roles within the family, with the aim of improving cohesion, problem-solving, and overall functioning.

psycho-therapy.definition: An evidence-based treatment for mental illness and emotional distress in which a trained therapist uses structured talking or behavioral techniques to help individuals understand and modify problematic thoughts, feelings, and behaviors.

conjugation.definition: Direct transfer of genetic material between two bacterial cells through cell-to-cell contact, usually via a conjugative pilus, enabling transfer of plasmids (e.g., F plasmid) or chromosomal DNA.

conjugon.definition: Not a standard medical term; there is no widely recognized definition in reputable medical dictionaries. If you meant conjugation, it is the process by which genetic material is transferred between bacterial cells through direct contact, typically via a pilus, often involving a conjugative plasmid.

conjunctival burn.definition: An injury to the conjunctival mucosa of the eye caused by chemical or thermal exposure, resulting in irritation, redness, tearing, and pain, with possible involvement of the cornea.

conjunctival fornix.definition: A cul-de-sac formed where the palpebral conjunctiva reflects onto the bulbar conjunctiva at the upper and lower edges of the eyelids, creating the conjunctival sac (fornices).

inferior conjunctival fornix.definition: An inferior recess of the conjunctival sac created by the reflection of bulbar conjunctiva onto the palpebral conjunctiva of the lower eyelid, located between the globe and the lower lid and serving as a tear reservoir.

superior conjunctival fornix.definition: The upper cul-de-sac of the conjunctival sac, formed where the palpebral conjunctiva of the upper eyelid reflects onto the bulbar conjunctiva over the anterior surface of the eyeball; it is the deepest recess of the superior conjunctival sac.

conjunctival reflex.definition: A protective reflex causing blinking in response to irritation or stimulation of the conjunctiva, mediated by trigeminal nerve (afferent) input and facial nerve (efferent) output.

corneal reflex.definition: An involuntary blinking response to stimulation of the cornea, mediated by the trigeminal nerve (afferent limb) and the facial nerve (efferent limb) to the orbicularis oculi, serving to protect the eye.

limbus.definition: The border between the cornea and the white of the eye.

conjunctival test.definition: A diagnostic ophthalmology test in which a suspected allergen or irritant is applied to the conjunctiva to provoke a reaction, allowing assessment of conjunctival inflammation and ocular allergy (often referred to as the conjunctival allergen provocation test).

pinkeye.definition: An infection around your eyes. Also called conjunctivitis.

ophthalmia neonatorum.definition: A purulent conjunctivitis occurring in a newborn within the first month of life, usually caused by vertical transmission of Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis during delivery; without treatment it can lead to corneal involvement and serious eye infection.

fibrocartilage.definition: A tough, dense type of cartilage that contains abundant collagen fibers (predominantly type I) and a relatively low proteoglycan content, giving it high tensile strength; it provides support and is found in structures like intervertebral discs, the pubic symphysis, menisci of the knee, and the temporomandibular joint disc.

concentric rings.definition: Multiple circular layers sharing the same center; in anatomy, the concentric lamellae of an osteon surround the central Haversian canal in compact bone.

laminae.definition: Thin plate or layer of tissue; in anatomy, one of the thin bony plates forming a structure—most commonly the laminae of the vertebral arch that form the posterior boundary of the vertebral canal.

diagonal conjugate.definition: An obstetric measurement: the distance from the inferior border of the pubic symphysis to the sacral promontory, measured via vaginal examination; used to estimate the obstetric (true) conjugate of the pelvic inlet.

true conjugate.definition: The anteroposterior diameter of the pelvic inlet, measured from the sacral promontory to the upper border of the pubic symphysis.

conjugate pelvis.definition: An obstetric dimension of the pelvis describing the shortest anteroposterior diameter of the pelvic inlet, extending from the sacral promontory to the posterior aspect of the pubic symphysis; it is the narrowest passage for the fetal head during vaginal delivery and is often estimated clinically via the diagonal conjugate (from the lower pubic symphysis to the sacral promontory).

conjugata.definition: The conjugate (conjugate diameter) is the pelvic inlet's anteroposterior (AP) diameter; specifically, the true conjugate is the AP distance from the sacral promontory to the upper border of the pubic symphysis.

conjugated bilirubin.definition: Bilirubin that has been conjugated in the liver with glucuronic acid, making it water-soluble and ready for excretion in bile.

conjugated estrogen.definition: A mixture of estrogenic hormones (primarily estrone sulfate and related sulfated estrogens) derived from the urine of pregnant mares, used for estrogen replacement therapy in menopause and related hypoestrogenic states.

estrone.definition: An endogenous estrogen steroid hormone that is weaker than estradiol; produced mainly by adipose tissue (via aromatization of androgens such as androstenedione) with contributions from the ovaries and adrenal glands; one of the three major human estrogens and the predominant circulating estrogen after menopause, acting through estrogen receptors to maintain reproductive tissues, bone density, and metabolism.

equilin.definition: An estrogenic steroid derived from the urine of pregnant mares; one of the estrogens in conjugated equine estrogens used in hormone replacement therapy; acts as an estrogen receptor agonist.

17-alpha-dihydroequilin.definition: A steroidal estrogen; a dihydro derivative of the horse estrogen equilin, one of the estrogenic components of conjugated equine estrogens (e.g., Premarin) used in hormone replacement therapy.

postmenopausal vasomotor symptoms.definition: Episodes of sudden warmth (hot flashes) with sweating and flushing, sometimes accompanied by palpitations or anxiety, occurring after menopause due to estrogen withdrawal and dysregulation of hypothalamic thermoregulation. They commonly manifest as hot flashes and night sweats and can persist for months to years.

hot flashes.definition: A sudden, transient sensation of warmth, often most intense in the face, neck, and chest, accompanied by sweating and flushing; commonly due to menopause-related estrogen withdrawal but can occur with other hormonal changes, medications, or medical conditions.

atrophic vaginitis.definition: A thinning and inflammation of the vaginal mucosa due to decreased estrogen (hypoestrogenism), commonly occurring after menopause, leading to dryness, irritation, itching, burning, and dyspareunia.

female hypogonadism.definition: A condition in which ovarian function is diminished or absent, resulting in reduced estrogen production and often amenorrhea and infertility; it can be primary (ovarian failure with high gonadotropins) or secondary (hypothalamic or pituitary dysfunction with low gonadotropins).

primary ovarian failure.definition: An condition in which the ovaries permanently stop functioning before age 40, causing cessation of menses, infertility, hypoestrogenism, and elevated gonadotropins (especially FSH) with low circulating estrogen.

palliation.definition: Relief of symptoms and suffering associated with a serious illness without attempting to cure the underlying disease, with the aim of improving quality of life for the patient.

advanced prostatic carcinoma.definition: Prostate cancer that has spread beyond the prostate gland or become locally invasive, typically presenting as metastatic disease (most commonly to bone) and not curable with local therapy alone. Management focuses on systemic treatment (e.g., androgen-deprivation therapy, androgen receptor pathway inhibitors, chemotherapy) and palliation.

metastatic breast cancer.definition: Breast cancer that has spread from the original tumor in the breast to distant parts of the body (most commonly bone, liver, lung, or brain); it is considered stage IV disease and is typically treated with systemic therapies rather than local treatments alone.

thromboembolic disorders.definition: A broad category of disorders in which abnormal clot formation within blood vessels (thrombosis) leads to vessel obstruction; when clots detach they become emboli that travel to distant sites (e.g., lungs, brain, limbs) causing ischemia and organ injury, and they include venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism) and arterial thromboembolism.

topical agents.definition: A substance formulated for application to the skin or mucous membranes to exert a local effect—such as delivering a drug, providing moisture, protection, or antisepsis—typically available as creams, ointments, gels, lotions, or solutions.

conjugated estrogens.definition: A mixture of estrogenic compounds, primarily estrone sulfate and other conjugated estrogens derived from the urine of pregnant mares, used as hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms and related conditions.

thromboembolism.definition: Obstruction of a blood vessel by an embolus formed from a thrombus that has dislodged and traveled through the circulation to occlude a distant vessel.

vulvar atrophy.definition: A thinning and drying of the vulvar skin and mucosa due to estrogen deficiency (most often in menopause), resulting in fragility, irritation, itching, and dyspareunia.

vaginal atrophy.definition: Vaginal atrophy is thinning, drying, and inflammation of the vaginal epithelium caused by decreased estrogen levels (most commonly after menopause), leading to symptoms such as vaginal dryness, irritation, itching, dyspareunia, and urinary symptoms.

connective tissue.definition: A group of tissues in the body that provide internal support and bind other tissues in the body, including bone, cartilage, tendons, and ligaments.

cartilage tissue.definition: A resilient, avascular connective tissue consisting of chondrocytes within an extracellular matrix rich in collagen (primarily type II) and proteoglycans; it provides flexible support, cushions joints, and enables smooth movement. It exists in hyaline, fibrocartilage, and elastic forms.

dense connective tissue.definition: A type of connective tissue with densely packed collagen fibers, little ground substance, and few cells, providing high tensile strength. It includes dense regular tissue in tendons and ligaments (parallel collagen fibers) and dense irregular tissue in the dermis and organ capsules, and is poorly vascularized.

fibrous tissue.definition: A type of connective tissue composed mainly of collagen fibers with sparse cellularity, produced by fibroblasts, that provides tensile strength and structural support to soft tissues and organs.

loose connective tissue.definition: A connective tissue proper with a loose, irregular mesh of collagen and elastic fibers in a viscous extracellular matrix, containing various cells (fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells, adipocytes) and abundant blood vessels; it supports and binds tissues, nourishes epithelia, and provides a reservoir for interstitial fluid.

collagenous.definition: Of or relating to collagen; consisting of collagen or containing collagen fibers.

elastic.definition: Capable of being stretched and then returning to its original shape; describes tissues or materials that recoil after deformation due to elastin.

matrix.definition: A noncellular extracellular framework surrounding cells, made of proteins and polysaccharides (notably collagen and proteoglycans), that provides structural support to tissues and mediates cell adhesion and signaling.

ground substance.definition: A viscous, hydrated gel component of the extracellular matrix in connective tissues that fills the space around cells and fibers; composed mainly of water, glycosaminoglycans, proteoglycans, and glycoproteins; it provides diffusion pathways for nutrients and waste, resists compression, and helps cushion and lubricate tissues.

intercellular material.definition: Intercellular material (extracellular matrix) is the noncellular substance between cells in tissues, composed of fibrous proteins (primarily collagen and elastin), glycosaminoglycans and proteoglycans, and adhesive glycoproteins; it provides structural support, facilitates cell adhesion and signaling, and regulates diffusion of nutrients and waste.

coracoclavicular ligament.definition: A ligamentous connection between the coracoid process of the scapula and the clavicle, comprising the conoid and trapezoid ligaments; it stabilizes the acromioclavicular joint.

gap junction.definition: A specialized intercellular channel formed by connexin proteins that directly connects adjacent cells, allowing ions and small molecules to pass between their cytoplasm and enabling electrical and metabolic coupling.

connexin.definition: A family of transmembrane proteins that assemble into hexameric connexons to form gap junction channels between adjacent cells, enabling direct intercellular transport of ions and small molecules for rapid cell-to-cell communication.

connexon.definition: A hexameric hemichannel formed by six connexin subunits; when two such hemichannels from adjacent cells align, they form a gap junction channel that directly connects the cytoplasm of the two cells, allowing ions and small molecules to pass and enabling intercellular electrical and metabolic communication.

aldosterone-secreting adenoma.definition: A unilateral adrenal cortical tumor that autonomously overproduces aldosterone, causing primary hyperaldosteronism with hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and suppressed renin activity; often curable by surgical removal.

hypokalemic alkalosis.definition: A metabolic alkalosis characterized by low serum potassium (hypokalemia), usually due to potassium and hydrogen ion loss (e.g., diuretic use, vomiting/NG suction, or mineralocorticoid excess), with elevated bicarbonate and alkalemic pH; treatment targets potassium repletion and addressing the underlying cause.

potassium depletion.definition: Potassium depletion: A reduction in total body potassium stores due to ongoing losses (renal, gastrointestinal, or sweating) or inadequate intake, often with low serum potassium (hypokalemia); may cause weakness, muscle cramps, arrhythmias, and other neuromuscular or cardiovascular symptoms, and is treated with potassium replacement and by addressing the underlying loss.

hypervolemia.definition: An abnormal increase in circulating blood volume and total body water (extracellular fluid) due to fluid overload; commonly caused by kidney failure, heart failure, liver cirrhosis, or excessive fluid administration, and can lead to edema, hypertension, and pulmonary or systemic congestion.

diverticulosis.definition: Occurs when small pouches form and push outward through weak spots in the wall of your colon.

mucosal ulcers.definition: A lesion characterized by a break or loss of the mucous membrane (epithelium) with exposure of underlying tissue; caused by inflammation, infection, trauma, ischemia, or chemical/immune injury and can occur on any mucosal surface (such as the mouth, GI tract, or genitourinary tract).

fecal impaction.definition: A large, hardened mass of stool that becomes stuck in the rectum or colon, preventing passage of stool and often resulting from severe constipation; may require manual disimpaction, enemas, or laxatives.

enemas.definition: A procedure in which liquid is introduced into the rectum via the anus to soften stool and stimulate evacuation, cleanse the bowel, or administer medications; commonly saline, phosphate, or oil-based solutions.

laxatives.definition: A substance or medication that relieves constipation by increasing stool frequency, volume, or softness and by accelerating bowel movement; laxatives act via bulk-forming, osmotic, stimulant, stool-softening, or lubricating mechanisms.

constipation/impaction.definition:
- A condition characterized by infrequent or difficult bowel movements, often with hard stools, straining, and a sense of incomplete evacuation; commonly due to low fiber intake, inadequate fluids, immobility, medications, or impaired colonic motility.

- A severe form of constipation in which a mass of dry, hardened stool becomes lodged in the rectum or colon and cannot be passed; may cause abdominal pain, distention, and overflow diarrhea; requires disimpaction and treatment of underlying causes.

valsalva maneuver.definition: A physiologic maneuver in which a person forcibly exhales against a closed glottis, markedly raising intrathoracic pressure; this increases vagal tone to slow the heart rate and can terminate certain tachyarrhythmias (notably SVT) and is used to assess autonomic function.

conradi-hunermann syndrome.definition: An X-linked dominant disorder of cholesterol biosynthesis caused by EBP gene mutations, characterized by chondrodysplasia punctata with epiphyseal stippling, ichthyosis-like skin changes, mosaic skin and hair findings, and skeletal dysplasia.

warfarin.definition: A type of blood thinner. It helps prevent clots from forming or getting bigger. Blood clots can cause blockages in arteries or veins, heart attacks or strokes.

warfarin sodium.definition: A salt form of an oral anticoagulant that is a vitamin K antagonist; inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing synthesis of vitamin K–dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, used to prevent and treat thromboembolic disorders; requires careful INR monitoring and dose adjustment.

constant region.definition: In immunoglobulins, the constant region is the portion of the antibody composed of the constant domains of the heavy and light chains that is relatively nonvariable between antibodies of the same isotype; it determines the antibody class and mediates effector functions (e.g., binding to Fc receptors and activating complement), while the variable region forms the antigen-binding sites.

variable region.definition: In immunology, the portion of an antibody or T-cell receptor that varies among different molecules and determines antigen specificity; it contains the antigen-binding site and is encoded by rearranged gene segments (V, D, J for heavy chains; V and J for light chains).

immunoglobulin constant region.definition: Part of the immunoglobulin heavy-chain structure consisting of conserved constant domains; it determines the antibody class (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, IgE) and mediates effector functions by interacting with Fc receptors on immune cells and with the complement system, differentiating it from the variable (antigen-binding) region.

lemniscal system.definition: A sensory pathway (the dorsal column–medial lemniscus system) that transmits fine touch, vibration, proprioception, and two-point discrimination from the body to the brain. It travels via the dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus) to the medulla, crosses to form the medial lemniscus, and projects to the ventral posterior nucleus of the thalamus and onward to the somatosensory cortex.

joint receptors.definition: Mechanoreceptors located in synovial joints—primarily in the joint capsule and supporting ligaments—that respond to mechanical deformation such as changes in joint angle, tension, pressure, and vibration to provide proprioceptive information about joint position and movement.

continuous positive pressure ventilation.definition: A mode of respiratory support in which positive airway pressure is supplied continuously throughout the entire breathing cycle to support ventilation and gas exchange; it can be delivered noninvasively (e.g., via a mask) or invasively via an endotracheal/tracheostomy tube.

constant pressure generator.definition: A device or circuit that maintains a fixed, regulated pressure within a closed system, regardless of changes in flow, typically achieved by a regulator or feedback control to offset pressure fluctuations (e.g., constant airway pressure in respiratory support or constant pressure in vascular/experimental setups).

constriction ring.definition: A ring-shaped device placed around a body part to apply constriction, typically to restrict blood flow or lymphatic drainage; used as a tourniquet to control bleeding or, in penile implants, to maintain erection by limiting venous outflow.

retraction ring.definition: A ring-shaped surgical instrument used to retract tissue by encircling a wound or area and applying traction to hold tissue out of the operative field, providing circumferential exposure around the incision or cavity.

constrictive cardiomyopathy.definition: A rare cardiomyopathy characterized by a stiff, noncompliant ventricular myocardium that limits diastolic filling, leading to diastolic heart failure with preserved systolic function; it can mimic constrictive pericarditis.

restrictive cardiomyopathy.definition: A disease of the heart muscle in which the ventricles are abnormally stiff and noncompliant, leading to impaired diastolic filling and diastolic heart failure with relatively preserved systolic function; often due to infiltrative, fibrotic, or storage disorders and elevated filling pressures.

constructional apraxia.definition: A neuropsychological disorder characterized by an inability to plan and execute tasks requiring visuospatial construction, such as drawing, copying figures, or assembling objects, despite preserved motor function and comprehension; typically due to parietal lobe damage (often right-sided) affecting visuospatial processing.

right hemisphere.definition: The right cerebral hemisphere is the right half of the brain responsible for visuospatial processing, pattern and face recognition, emotion and prosody, and other nonverbal aspects of cognition; it mainly controls movement on the left side of the body, while language functions are typically localized to the left hemisphere.

contact dermatitis.definition: A rash or skin irritation that results when skin contacts an allergen or irritating substance.

contact lens.definition: A small, curved lens placed on the surface of the eye (usually the cornea) to correct refractive errors or for cosmetic/therapeutic purposes; made of soft hydrogel or silicone hydrogel or rigid gas-permeable material and worn under professional guidance with proper hygiene.

allergic contact dermatitis.definition: A delayed-type (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction of the skin to a contact allergen in a sensitized individual, causing pruritic, erythematous, vesicular or crusted eczematous dermatitis at the site of contact.

nickel dermatitis.definition: An allergic contact dermatitis caused by sensitivity to nickel (a type IV hypersensitivity reaction) characterized by a pruritic, eczematous eruption at sites of nickel exposure (e.g., earrings, jewelry); diagnosed by history and nickel patch testing; managed by avoiding nickel-containing items and using topical corticosteroids for flares.

patch testing.definition: Patch testing is a dermatologic diagnostic procedure in which small patches containing suspected contact allergens are applied to the skin (usually the back) under occlusion for about 48 hours and then evaluated at 48–96 hours to detect delayed-type (type IV) hypersensitivity reactions.

topical corticosteroids.definition: An anti-inflammatory medication formulated for topical (skin) use to reduce inflammation, itching, and immune responses in dermatologic conditions; commonly applied as creams, ointments, lotions, foams, or gels, with potential local adverse effects such as skin thinning and, with extensive use, systemic effects.

systemic corticosteroids.definition: Corticosteroids administered systemically (by mouth, injection, or infusion) that exert anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects throughout the body; used to treat a wide range of inflammatory, allergic, and autoimmune conditions.

atopic dermatitis.definition: A long-lasting itchy red rash caused by a skin reaction.

poison ivy.definition: A plant-induced allergic contact dermatitis caused by urushiol oil in Toxicodendron species; presents as a pruritic, erythematous, vesicular rash at contact sites, often arranged in linear streaks from brushing against vegetation.

hmwk.definition: An assignment given to students to complete outside of class to reinforce material learned; commonly used to practice skills or review concepts. Not a medical term.

high-molecular-weight kininogen.definition: A large plasma glycoprotein that serves as a cofactor in the intrinsic coagulation pathway and as the precursor to bradykinin in the kallikrein–kinin system; it binds prekallikrein and factor XII and is cleaved to release bradykinin.

fitzgerald factor.definition: A historical name for prekallikrein, a plasma zymogen in the kallikrein–kinin system that is activated to kallikrein and participates in contact activation of coagulation and the production of bradykinin.

prekallekrein.definition: A circulating serine protease zymogen that is the inactive precursor of plasma kallikrein; activated by factor XIIa in the contact pathway, it then cleaves high-molecular-weight kininogen to bradykinin and amplifies the coagulation–inflammation axis.

factor xii.definition: An inactive serine protease zymogen produced by the liver (also known as Hageman factor) that, upon contact with negatively charged surfaces, is activated to XIIa to initiate the intrinsic coagulation pathway by activating factor XI and prekallikrein, and to participate in the kallikrein–kinin system; deficiency prolongs the aPTT but does not cause clinically significant bleeding.

nipple valve.definition: No widely recognized anatomical valve is located at the nipple. Milk flow is regulated by hormonal signals and contraction of myoepithelial cells around lactiferous ducts rather than by a true valvular structure; if used in device terminology, the phrase may refer to a one-way valve in a nipple prosthesis or feeding bottle to regulate flow and prevent backflow.

continent ileostomy.definition: A surgically constructed ileal reservoir (pouch) made from a segment of ileum to store fecal output after ileostomy; it includes a continence mechanism (such as a nipple or intussuscepted valve) to prevent leakage and is emptied at intervals by intermittent catheterization through a catheterizable stoma.

ileostomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which the end of the ileum is brought through the abdominal wall to form a stoma, diverting intestinal contents away from the colon into an external pouch; it can be temporary or permanent and is used after colectomy or in certain inflammatory bowel diseases.

continent urostomy.definition: A continent urinary diversion in which a segment of intestine is fashioned into a reservoir that stores urine, with a catheterizable stoma allowing intermittent emptying; continence between catheterizations is maintained by a valve mechanism, enabling drainage without an external collection bag.

indiana pouch.definition: A continent urinary reservoir created from a detubularized ileal segment (ileal pouch) used after bladder removal to store urine, drained intermittently via a catheterizable stoma.

kock’s pouch.definition: A continent urinary reservoir created from a segment of ileum (often forming an ileal pouch) after cystectomy, with a catheterizable stoma and a continence mechanism (typically a nipple valve) to prevent leakage, requiring intermittent self-catheterization.

ileal reservoir.definition: A surgically constructed pouch made from ileal tissue to store urine as part of a urinary diversion, usually continent and drained intermittently via catheter through a stoma or occasionally through the urethra.

stoma cap.definition: A small, closed ostomy pouch worn over a stoma for short-term use when drainage is minimal, serving as a temporary alternative to a drainable ostomy bag.

continuous bladder irrigation.definition: A procedure in which sterile irrigation solution is continuously pumped into the bladder through a catheter while urine is drained, to prevent clot formation and maintain unobstructed urinary flow, typically after urologic surgery or in gross hematuria.

ccpd.definition: An automated peritoneal dialysis modality in which a cycler machine automatically performs multiple peritoneal dialysis exchanges during the night, delivering and draining dialysate to the peritoneal cavity to achieve continuous solute clearance and fluid removal for patients with kidney failure.

contagion.definition: The transmission of an infectious disease from an infected person or source to a susceptible person, usually through direct contact, respiratory droplets, or contact with contaminated surfaces; diseases that spread readily by these means are described as contagious.

ecthyma contagiosum.definition: A self-limited zoonotic skin infection caused by the Orf virus (parapoxvirus) transmitted from sheep or goats to humans, presenting as a papulonodular lesion on exposed skin (usually hands) that progresses to vesicular and crusted stages and typically resolves in several weeks; management is supportive with wound care; no specific antiviral therapy; prevention includes protective gloves and avoiding contact with infected animals.

orf.definition: A zoonotic viral infection caused by the Orf virus (a parapoxvirus) that primarily infects sheep and goats; in humans it causes a self-limited papular/pustular skin lesion at the contact site (often on the hands) that typically heals over several weeks, without specific treatment. Also known as contagious ecthyma.

pustular dermatitis.definition: A dermatitis defined by the appearance of small, pus-filled pustules on inflamed skin; it is a descriptive term for several conditions with pustules, including infectious, inflammatory, or drug-related etiologies.

pox virus.definition: Large, enveloped double-stranded DNA virus of the family Poxviridae that replicates in the cytoplasm and causes pox diseases such as smallpox, molluscum contagiosum, cowpox, and monkeypox; virions are brick-shaped and the genome is large and complex.

contamination.definition: The presence or introduction of unwanted microorganisms or foreign material on or into a substance, surface, wound, or specimen, compromising sterility and potentially leading to infection or erroneous results.

contaminated culture.definition: A culture that has been contaminated by extraneous microorganisms, leading to unreliable or uninterpretable results because organisms other than the intended pathogen are growing.

continuous mandatory ventilation.definition: A mode of mechanical ventilation in which the ventilator provides all breaths at a fixed rate and tidal volume (or pressure) with no patient-initiated breaths; complete ventilatory support.

assist-control mode.definition: A mode of mechanical ventilation in which every breath—whether patient-triggered or time-triggered—is delivered with a preset tidal volume (or inspiratory pressure), providing full ventilatory support and ensuring a minimum minute ventilation.

continuous murmur.definition: A heart murmur heard throughout the entire cardiac cycle (systole and diastole) with no gap, classically described as a machinery-like murmur best heard at the left infraclavicular area and most often due to patent ductus arteriosus.

cervical venous hum.definition: A benign, low‑frequency, continuous murmur heard over the neck (usually at the right supraclavicular region) caused by turbulent flow in the internal jugular veins; common in children and young people, and it typically changes with posture and disappears with compression of the jugular veins or turning the head.

systole.definition: The brief period during which the heart contracts during a normal heartbeat, pumping blood into the aorta and the pulmonary artery.

diastole.definition: The phase of the cardiac cycle during which the ventricles relax and fill with blood after systole.

negative chest wall pressure.definition: The subatmospheric pressure in the thoracic cavity generated during inspiration by respiratory muscle contraction, enabling chest wall expansion and inflow of air into the lungs.

transpulmonary pressure.definition: Alveolar (intra-alveolar) pressure minus pleural pressure; the distending pressure across the lung wall that keeps the lungs inflated.

continuous passive motion.definition: A rehabilitative technique in which a motorized device moves a joint through a prescribed, continuous, passive range of motion, with no active muscle contraction by the patient, to maintain or improve joint mobility and prevent stiffness after surgery or injury.

cpap.definition: An abbreviation for continuous positive airway pressure, a therapy for obstructive sleep apnea in which a machine delivers a continuous stream of air that prevents the collapse of the airway during sleep.

sleep apnea.definition: A sleep disorder characterized by repeated episodes of partial or complete obstruction of the upper airway during sleep, causing breathing pauses lasting at least 10 seconds and often leading to daytime sleepiness.

hood.definition: A fold of skin or other tissue that partially covers and protects an underlying organ or opening; common examples include the clitoral hood over the clitoris and the foreskin (prepuce) over the glans penis.

continuous regional anesthesia.definition: A regional anesthesia technique in which a local anesthetic is continuously infused or repeatedly administered via a catheter placed near a peripheral nerve or nerve plexus (or in the neuraxial space) to provide ongoing regional anesthesia and extended postoperative analgesia beyond a single-shot block.

epidural anesthesia.definition: A regional anesthesia technique wherein a local anesthetic (often with an opioid) is injected into the epidural space surrounding the spinal cord to block nerve signals and produce anesthesia or analgesia of the lower body; can be given as a single injection or via a catheter for continuous infusion, commonly used for labor analgesia and lower-extremity or abdominal surgeries.

indwelling catheter.definition: A catheter that is left in place inside the body for an extended period to allow ongoing drainage of urine from the bladder (e.g., a Foley catheter).

intrauterine system.definition: A small, T-shaped hormonal intrauterine device inserted into the uterus that releases levonorgestrel to provide long-acting reversible contraception for about 3–5 years.

levonorgestrel intrauterine system.definition: A small, flexible, T-shaped intrauterine device that locally releases levonorgestrel to provide long-acting reversible contraception for several years; it thickens cervical mucus, thins the endometrium, and often suppresses ovulation, and may reduce menstrual bleeding and pain.

mirena.definition: A brand of levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) that provides long-acting reversible contraception for up to about 5 years and can reduce heavy menstrual bleeding.

copper-releasing intrauterine device.definition: A nonhormonal, long-acting intrauterine device that releases copper ions into the uterine cavity, producing a local inflammatory reaction that is toxic to sperm and impairs fertilization (and may prevent implantation); it provides contraception for up to about 10 years after insertion.

subdermal contraceptive implants.definition: A long-acting reversible contraceptive consisting of a small flexible rod implanted subcutaneously in the upper arm, which releases etonogestrel continuously for up to about 3 years to prevent pregnancy by suppressing ovulation, thickening cervical mucus, and thinning the endometrium.

progestin-only pill.definition: An oral contraceptive containing only a synthetic progestin (no estrogen) that mainly thickens cervical mucus and thins the endometrium to prevent pregnancy; ovulation suppression may occur in some users. Requires near-daily dosing with a strict time window and is commonly chosen by breastfeeding women.

depo-provera.definition: A long-acting progestin-only injectable contraceptive (medroxyprogesterone acetate) given by intramuscular injection every 12 weeks to prevent pregnancy; it works by suppressing ovulation, thickening cervical mucus, and thinning the endometrium. Common side effects include irregular or absent menses, weight gain, and decreased bone mineral density with long-term use; fertility return may be delayed after stopping.

ortho evra.definition: A transdermal combined hormonal contraceptive patch that delivers ethinyl estradiol and norelgestromin through the skin to prevent pregnancy; worn on the skin for seven days per patch, typically replaced for three consecutive weeks with a patch-free week.

norelgestromin.definition: A synthetic progestin used in some combined hormonal contraceptives; it suppresses ovulation, thickens cervical mucus, and thins the endometrium to prevent pregnancy.

levonorgestrel.definition: A synthetic progestin used in contraception to suppress ovulation, thicken cervical mucus, and thin the endometrium, thereby preventing pregnancy. It is used in various forms, including oral contraceptives, emergency contraception, and levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine systems.

nuvaring.definition: A flexible vaginal ring that delivers the combined hormones etonogestrel (a progestin) and ethinyl estradiol to prevent pregnancy; it is worn in the vagina for 3 weeks, then removed for a 1-week ring-free interval during which withdrawal bleeding may occur.

etonogestrel.definition: A synthetic progestin used in hormonal contraception; the active metabolite of desogestrel, delivered via subdermal implant (and in some vaginal ring formulations) to prevent pregnancy by suppressing ovulation, thickening cervical mucus, and thinning the endometrium.

emergency contraception.definition: An intervention to prevent pregnancy after unprotected intercourse or contraceptive failure; it includes progestin-only pills (levonorgestrel), ulipristal acetate, and copper IUD, and works mainly by delaying ovulation and/or preventing fertilization; it is not an abortion.

contraceptive diaphragm.definition: A dome-shaped silicone or latex cup inserted into the vagina to cover the cervix and prevent sperm from entering the uterus; a barrier method of contraception used with spermicide, typically reusable and requiring proper fitting.

cervical cap.definition: A small silicone cap that fits over the cervix to block sperm from entering the uterus; a barrier method used with spermicide and requiring clinician fitting to determine the proper size; inserted before intercourse and left in place for at least 6 hours after sex, up to a maximum of about 48 hours; reusable with proper cleaning.

condom.definition: A thin, disposable barrier worn over the erect penis during sexual activity to prevent semen from entering the partner and to reduce the risk of pregnancy and transmission of many sexually transmitted infections; most commonly made of latex, polyurethane, or lambskin.

spermicidal jelly.definition: A vaginal gel containing a spermicide (most commonly nonoxynol-9) that kills or immobilizes sperm, used to prevent fertilization when inserted into the vagina before intercourse.

spermicidal foam.definition: A vaginal foam containing a spermicide (typically nonoxynol-9) that kills or immobilizes sperm; inserted before intercourse as a chemical form of contraception and effective for a limited time, requiring reapplication with each act of intercourse.

spermicidal cream.definition: A topical contraceptive cream containing a chemical spermicide (commonly nonoxynol-9) that is applied inside the vagina prior to intercourse to immobilize or kill sperm; used to reduce pregnancy risk but provides only modest protection and does not protect against sexually transmitted infections; may cause vaginal irritation.

nonoxynol-9.definition: A nonionic surfactant used as a spermicide; it disrupts sperm cell membranes to render sperm nonfunctional. It is formulated in vaginal spermicides (foams, gels, films). It does not protect against HIV or other sexually transmitted infections, and frequent use can irritate vaginal mucosa, potentially increasing infection risk.

progesterone-like compounds.definition: Compounds that mimic the effects of the hormone progesterone by binding to progesterone receptors and activating progestational pathways; includes natural progesterone and synthetic analogs (progestins) used in contraception and hormone therapy.

gonadotropins.definition: Hormones that stimulate the gonads (ovaries or testes). The primary human examples are follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH), produced by the anterior pituitary, regulating gametogenesis and sex steroid production.

anterior pituitary gland.definition: Endocrine portion of the pituitary gland (adenohypophysis) that synthesizes and secretes hormones such as growth hormone (GH), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), prolactin (PRL), and the gonadotropins luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH); its activity is regulated by hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones via the hypophyseal portal system.

ovarian cysts.definition: Fluid-filled sacs that develop on or within the ovaries. Most are benign and functional (such as follicular or corpus luteum cysts) and resolve spontaneously, but larger, persistent, or complex cysts can cause pelvic pain or pressure and may require ultrasound evaluation and, if indicated, medical or surgical management.

contraception.definition: The intentional use of methods or devices to prevent pregnancy by inhibiting ovulation, fertilization, or implantation, or by preventing sperm from reaching the egg; includes hormonal options (pills, injections, implants, patches), barrier methods (condoms, diaphragms), intrauterine devices, sterilization, emergency contraception, and fertility-awareness methods.

sterilization.definition: Medical procedure for women (having your tubes tied, also called tubal ligation) or men (vasectomy) that permanently prevents pregnancy. Also means "clean" when applied to medical instruments.

toxic shock syndrome.definition: Life-threatening systemic illness caused by toxin-producing strains of Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes, presenting with sudden fever, hypotension or shock, diffuse erythroderma, and multisystem dysfunction; desquamation of the skin may occur during recovery. Requires urgent antimicrobial therapy and intensive supportive care.

sexually transmitted diseases.definition: Any infection transmitted primarily through sexual contact (vaginal, anal, or oral), caused by bacteria, viruses, or parasites; common examples include gonorrhea, chlamydia, syphilis, HIV, human papillomavirus (HPV), herpes simplex virus, hepatitis B, and trichomoniasis.

stds.definition: Illnesses transmitted from one person to another through sexual contact, caused by bacteria, parasites, or viruses; there are many types, including chlamydia and gonorrhea.

vaginal discharge.definition: Secretions from the vagina and cervix that lubricate, cleanse, and protect the vaginal tract; normal discharge is typically clear to white, mild-smelling, and varies with hormonal status and the menstrual cycle. Abnormal discharge may be colored, foul-smelling, or associated with itching or irritation, and can indicate infection or other conditions.

leukorrhea.definition: A vaginal discharge that is white or off-white, typically thin to thick and nonirritating; often a normal mucus secreted by cervical glands that can vary with hormonal changes. If accompanied by foul odor, itching, irritation, or color change, it may indicate infection or other pathology.

breast tenderness.definition: Pain, soreness, or tenderness in one or both breasts, typically mild and temporary. It most often arises from hormonal fluctuations during the menstrual cycle but can also occur with pregnancy, lactation, menopause, certain medications, fibrocystic breast changes, infection, or injury; most cases are benign and resolve on their own.

ectopic pregnancy.definition: When the fertilized egg does not grow in the womb.

expulsion rate.definition: A measure of how quickly contents are expelled from a body cavity or organ, typically expressed as a quantity per unit time (e.g., mL per hour) or as a proportion over a defined interval; used in contexts such as labor or evacuation of contents.

nulliparous.definition: A woman who has never given birth to a child.

weight gain.definition: An increase in body weight relative to baseline, typically due to increases in body fat, water, or lean tissue; may result from caloric surplus, fluid retention, medications, hormonal changes, or certain diseases.

uterine os.definition: The opening between the uterine cavity and the cervical canal, known as the internal os of the cervix (ostium internum).

cervical os.definition: The openings of the cervical canal: the internal os (the opening between the cervical canal and the uterine cavity) and the external os (the opening between the cervical canal and the vagina).

tub bath.definition: A bath taken in a tub in which the body is immersed in water for cleansing, relaxation, or hydrotherapy.

medicated tub bath.definition: A therapeutic bath in which a medicated solution is added to bathwater to treat skin conditions or irritation, typically used to reduce itching, inflammation, and to soften or cleanse the skin (examples include colloidal oatmeal, Burow's solution, or antiseptics).

therapeutic bath.definition: A bath used as medical therapy to relieve symptoms or promote healing, typically performed with controlled water temperature and immersion time and, when indicated, additives (e.g., minerals, medicated solutions) as part of hydrotherapy.

resting tremor.definition: A tremor occurring in a limb when the muscles are relaxed (at rest) and diminishing with voluntary movement; commonly seen in Parkinson disease.

pill-rolling tremor.definition: An at-rest tremor characteristic of Parkinson disease: a rhythmic, slow tremor of the fingers or hand, often described as rolling a pill between the thumb and index finger, that occurs at rest and improves with movement.

febrile reaction.definition: An abnormal rise in body temperature, typically defined as fever above 38°C (100.4°F), occurring in response to infection, inflammation, or immune-mediated stimuli, often with chills, sweating, malaise, and tachycardia.

rapid pulse.definition: A rapid heart rate (tachycardia), defined as a resting heart rate above about 100 beats per minute in adults; may be a normal physiologic response (e.g., exercise, fever, stress) or due to cardiac or systemic conditions, and can be sinus tachycardia or another arrhythmia.

weak pulse.definition: A pulse that is faint and barely palpable, with reduced amplitude (often described as thready), reflecting decreased cardiac output or poor peripheral perfusion; common in dehydration, shock, significant blood loss, heart failure, or severe arrhythmias.

fitting.definition: A sudden attack or convulsion, especially an epileptic seizure.

pubic.definition: Relating to the pubis, the anterior portion of the pelvic bone; pertaining to the pubic region.

symphysis.definition: A cartilaginous joint in which the adjacent bones are joined by a fibrocartilage pad, allowing limited movement (amphiarthrosis).

fornix.definition:
- Brain anatomy: A C-shaped bundle of white-matter fibers in the brain that connects the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies, forming part of the limbic system and memory circuit.

- Female reproductive anatomy: A recess around the cervix in the upper vagina, consisting of the anterior and posterior fornices (and lateral fornices).

spermicide.definition: A chemical agent that kills or immobilizes sperm to prevent fertilization; used as a method of contraception, often formulated as a gel, foam, film, or suppository (commonly containing nonoxynol-9).

jelly.definition: Semisolid, gelatinous material with a soft, jelly-like consistency; used descriptively in medicine to describe tissues or fluids that have a jelly-like texture.

intrauterine.definition: Located within the uterus; occurring or situated in the uterine cavity.

device.definition: A medical device is an instrument, apparatus, implant, software, or similar article intended for use in diagnosing, preventing, monitoring, treating, or alleviating disease or for modifying the structure or function of the body; it is not a drug.

oral.definition: Relating to the mouth; of or pertaining to the oral cavity, or to administration of substances by mouth.

hyperstimulation.definition: Excessive stimulation of a biological system by hormones, drugs, or other stimuli, leading to an amplified or potentially harmful response. In clinical contexts, this often refers to an overreaction of the ovaries to fertility drugs, causing ovarian enlargement and fluid shifts.

follicles.definition: Any of several small sac-like structures in tissues from which secretions, cells, or products develop; for example, a hair follicle in the skin that produces hair, an ovarian follicle that contains a developing oocyte, and lymphoid follicles that are aggregates of immune cells.

oocyte.definition: An immature female gamete (egg cell) in the ovary that develops through meiosis to become a mature ovum capable of fertilization.

previa.definition: A pregnancy complication in which the placenta implants in the lower uterine segment near or covering the cervix, causing painless vaginal bleeding in the second or third trimester; often managed with cesarean delivery.

insufficiency.definition: A failure or impairment of an organ or body system to perform its normal physiological function, often due to disease, injury, or aging.

stimulation.definition: The process of provoking activity in a tissue, organ, or neural pathway by external input (electrical, chemical, mechanical, or sensory) to elicit or modulate a response.

labor.definition: The process of a baby being born, from early pain to delivery of the baby.

inlet.definition: An opening or entrance into a body cavity or tubular structure; in anatomy, the entry region to a cavity (for example, the thoracic inlet is the superior opening of the thoracic cavity).

midpelvic.definition: Pertaining to the middle portion of the pelvis, between the pelvic inlet and the pelvic outlet; in obstetrics, the midpelvis is the region of the pelvic canal where descent is assessed and where midpelvic arrest may occur.

outlet.definition: An opening or passage by which something exits a hollow organ or body; a channel (duct, pore, orifice) through which fluids, gases, or other substances are discharged.

fetal.definition: Relating to a fetus; the developing unborn offspring during gestation.

rate.definition: The frequency or speed of a physiological process, expressed per unit time; for example, the number of heartbeats per minute or the number of breaths per minute.

central.definition: Located at or near the center; in anatomy, relating to the central nervous system or to the central/midline region of a structure, as opposed to peripheral.

pressure.definition: The force exerted per unit area on or within a surface; in physiology, the force of a fluid against the walls of a body space or vessel (e.g., arterial blood pushing against arterial walls).

infusion.definition: To put fluids or drugs directly into your blood.

acute.definition: An illness or symptom that begins suddenly or lasts a short time. It can also be an intense flare-up of an illness.

radiopaque.definition: Describes substances that do not transmit X-rays well, appearing white or light on radiographs because they attenuate X-ray beams more than surrounding tissues (examples include bone, metal, and iodinated contrast media).

radiolucent.definition: A substance or tissue that allows X-rays to pass through with little attenuation, appearing dark on radiographs; contrasts with radiopaque tissues.

barium.definition: A chemical element (Ba) with atomic number 56; in medicine, a radiopaque contrast agent, typically barium sulfate, used to image the gastrointestinal tract on X-ray or fluoroscopy.

conus medullaris.definition: A tapered cone-shaped end of the spinal cord that typically terminates at the L1–L2 vertebral level in adults; below it, the nerve roots descend as the cauda equina within the lumbar cistern.

bruise.definition: A closed soft-tissue injury caused by blunt trauma in which small blood vessels are damaged and blood leaks into surrounding tissues, producing localized skin discoloration that changes color as it heals.

convalescence.definition: The period of recovery after illness or medical treatment during which strength, health, and normal functioning are gradually restored.

convalescent.definition: Relating to the period of recovery after illness or injury; recovering health and strength; a person who is recovering.

convection.definition: Convection is the transfer of heat or dissolved substances by the bulk motion of a fluid (gas or liquid), rather than by molecular contact (conduction) or radiation.

convergence.definition: The inward turning of both eyes toward the nose to maintain single binocular vision when viewing a near object; produced by contraction of the medial rectus muscles and coordinated with accommodation and pupillary constriction as part of the near reflex.

convergent evolution.definition: The independent evolution of similar traits in different lineages due to similar environmental pressures, leading to analogous structures or functions.

convergent nystagmus.definition: An involuntary rhythmic eye movement elicited by convergence of the eyes when focusing on a near object.

convergent squint.definition: A form of strabismus in which one or both eyes turn inward toward the nose (medial deviation); commonly referred to as esotropia.

conversion.definition: A psychiatric condition in which psychological distress is converted into neurological or sensory symptoms (e.g., weakness, abnormal movement, numbness, blindness, or seizures) that lack an identifiable organic cause.

conversion disorder.definition: A mental health condition in which neurological symptoms—such as weakness or paralysis, abnormal movements, non-epileptic seizures, sensory loss, or blindness—develop that are not explained by medical disease and are believed to arise from psychological factors or distress rather than intentional behavior.

conversion hysteria.definition: A historical diagnosis for neurological symptoms such as weakness, paralysis, blindness, or seizures that are not explained by medical disease and are thought to arise from psychological factors; today this condition is called conversion disorder or functional neurological symptom disorder.

conversion reaction.definition: A neuropsychiatric disorder in which one or more neurological symptoms (such as weakness, abnormal movement, sensory loss, vision/hearing changes, or seizures) cannot be explained by medical disease and are believed to arise from psychological factors converting emotional distress into physical symptoms; in modern classification, this is termed functional neurological symptom disorder.

somatoform disorder.definition: A historical DSM-IV umbrella term for disorders in which one or more physical symptoms are not fully explained by a medical condition and are accompanied by excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviors regarding the symptoms (now largely encompassed by somatic symptom disorder and related diagnoses).

conversion dysphonia.definition: A functional (psychogenic) voice disorder characterized by loss or alteration of voice without organic laryngeal pathology, often precipitated by psychological stress, with normal laryngoscopic findings; management includes voice therapy and addressing underlying psychosocial factors.

convulsion.definition: Movements that you can't control caused by unusual activity in your brain. Also called a fit or seizure.

convulsive seizure.definition: A convulsive seizure is a generalized seizure characterized by loss of consciousness with tonic (stiffening) followed by clonic (rhythmic jerking) motor activity, sometimes accompanied by incontinence, tongue biting, and a postictal recovery period.

convulsive syncope.definition: Transient loss of consciousness due to brief cerebral hypoperfusion, accompanied by short-lived generalized convulsive movements; not an epileptic seizure, as the convulsions occur with syncope and resolve rapidly once perfusion returns, often with a preceding prodrome and a vasovagal or orthostatic trigger.

convulsive tic.definition: A motor tic involving sudden, brief, repetitive, sometimes forceful contractions of a muscle group, which may resemble a convulsion but occurs in tic disorders and can be temporarily suppressed with effort.

hemifacial spasm.definition: A neuromuscular disorder characterized by involuntary, unilateral contractions of the facial muscles on one side, typically caused by irritation or compression of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) as it exits the brainstem or along its course, often starting around the eyelid and potentially spreading to the cheek and mouth.

gilles de la tourette's syndrome.definition: A neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic, with onset in childhood (before age 18), tics persisting for more than a year and waxing and waning in severity; commonly associated with ADHD and obsessive-compulsive disorder.

cook catheter.definition: A flexible tube inserted into a body lumen or cavity to drain fluids, deliver medications or contrast, or provide access for diagnostic or therapeutic procedures.

cooley's anemia.definition: A severe form of beta-thalassemia (beta-thalassemia major) due to defective beta-globin synthesis, causing chronic, severe microcytic anemia in infancy with hepatosplenomegaly and skeletal changes from extramedullary hematopoiesis; requires lifelong blood transfusions and iron chelation therapy.

coolidge tube.definition: A vacuum X-ray tube with a heated cathode (thermionic emission) and a target anode, developed by William D. Coolidge; the standard hot-cathode X-ray tube used in diagnostic radiography, providing stable output and longer life than Crookes tubes.

cooling.definition: A medical process of lowering the body or tissue temperature to a predefined target, often to reduce metabolic demand and limit injury from ischemia or inflammation; achieved via external cooling (e.g., cooling blankets) or internal/endovascular cooling (therapeutic hypothermia/targeted temperature management).

cooling rate.definition: A rate at which a body or material loses heat, expressed as the change in temperature over time (dT/dt), typically negative during cooling; determined by heat transfer with the surroundings, tissue properties, and blood flow.

cooper's ligament.definition: Fibrous connective tissue septa within the breast that extend from the dermis to the pectoral fascia, providing structural support and helping suspend the breast tissue.

pectineal ligament.definition: A thick fibrous band along the pectineal line of the pubis, extending from the lacunar ligament to the pectineal line; it reinforces the posterior wall of the femoral canal (Cooper's ligament).

coordinated movement.definition: The smooth, accurate, and well-timed execution of voluntary movements achieved through integrated motor planning, sensory feedback, and coordinated activation of multiple muscle groups, mediated by cerebellar and cortical motor pathways.

coordinated reflex.definition: A reflex whose motor response is integrated with voluntary motor control to produce smooth, coordinated movement rather than a simple, isolated reflex action.

co-oximeter.definition: A co-oximeter is a spectrophotometric device that measures multiple hemoglobin species (oxyhemoglobin, deoxyhemoglobin, carboxyhemoglobin, methemoglobin) in blood to determine true oxygen saturation and detect dyshemoglobinemias, typically as part of a blood gas analyzer.

cope loop catheter.definition: A catheter with a loop-shaped distal tip used in interventional procedures to engage, snare, or retrieve tissue or foreign bodies and to facilitate cannulation or mapping; specific applications vary by device and specialty.

copp.definition: A multi-agent chemotherapy regimen used to treat Hodgkin lymphoma, consisting of cyclophosphamide, vincristine, procarbazine, and prednisone.

copper.definition: An essential trace element that acts as a cofactor for multiple enzymes (e.g., ceruloplasmin, lysyl oxidase, dopamine beta-hydroxylase) and is important for iron metabolism, connective tissue formation, and nervous system function; deficiency can cause anemia and neutropenia, while excess leads to copper toxicity (as in Wilson disease).

wilson's disease.definition: An autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism due to ATP7B mutations causing impaired biliary copper excretion and copper accumulation in the liver, brain, and other tissues; clinically characterized by hepatic disease and neuropsychiatric symptoms, often with Kayser–Fleischer rings in the cornea.

chronic extrahepatic biliary tract obstr.definition: A persistent obstruction of bile flow in the extrahepatic biliary tract (outside the liver), typically involving the common bile duct or common hepatic duct, usually due to stones, stricture, or tumor, leading to cholestasis with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and potential progressive liver damage and biliary complications if untreated.

copper gluconate.definition: A copper(II) salt of gluconic acid used as a dietary supplement to prevent or treat copper deficiency; it provides copper, an essential trace element required for various enzymatic processes, iron metabolism, and connective tissue formation.

copperhead.definition: A venomous pit viper native to eastern North America; envenomation typically causes intense local pain and swelling, tissue damage, and may include systemic symptoms; treatment is supportive care and antivenom for significant bites.

cordarone.definition: A broad-spectrum antiarrhythmic agent (amiodarone) used to treat and prevent life-threatening ventricular and atrial tachyarrhythmias; it prolongs the cardiac action potential and refractoriness by blocking multiple ion channels and has a very long half-life with potential toxicities requiring regular monitoring.

cord blood transplantation.definition: A hematopoietic stem cell transplant using stem cells derived from a stored umbilical cord blood unit, performed allogeneically to reconstitute the recipient's bone marrow after conditioning with chemotherapy or radiation. Advantages include rapid availability and less stringent HLA matching; limitations include limited cell dose, slower engraftment, and higher early graft failure or infection risk, sometimes requiring two cord blood units in adults.

cordiform.definition: Heart-shaped; having the form or outline of a heart.

corditis.definition: Inflammation of a cord, most often the umbilical cord (funisitis), usually due to infection and sometimes associated with chorioamnionitis.

cord presentation.definition: A situation in which the umbilical cord lies at the internal cervical os with the fetal presenting part not yet engaged, i.e., the cord lies between the cervix and the presenting part; it increases the risk of cord prolapse if membranes rupture.

cordran.definition: Brand name for flurandrenolide, a topical corticosteroid used to treat inflammatory skin conditions (e.g., dermatitis, eczema); available in cream, ointment, solution, and medicated tape.

core temperature.definition: The temperature of the body's internal organs and deep tissues, maintained by hypothalamic thermoregulation within a narrow range—approximately 36.5–37.5°C (97.7–99.5°F) in adults.

corgard.definition: A nonselective beta-adrenergic blocker (beta-blocker) used to treat hypertension, angina, and certain arrhythmias; it reduces heart rate, contractility, and blood pressure by blocking beta receptors and can cause bronchospasm and mask hypoglycemia; contraindicated in asthma or severe bradycardia.

coracoacromial.definition: Relating to the coracoid process and the acromion of the scapula; used to describe structures between them, notably the coracoacromial ligament that spans from the coracoid to the acromion.

coracoid process.definition: A hook-shaped bony projection on the anterior surface of the scapula near the superior border, serving as an attachment for the pectoralis minor, short head of biceps brachii, and coracobrachialis, and as an attachment point for the coracoclavicular ligaments.

coracobrachialis muscle.definition: A small muscle of the anterior upper arm that originates from the coracoid process of the scapula and inserts on the medial surface of the humerus; it flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder joint and is innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C7).

coral snake.definition: A venomous New World elapid snake of the genus Micrurus, typically with red, yellow/white, and black banding; its venom is neurotoxic and can cause progressive paralysis, requiring urgent medical evaluation and antivenom as indicated.

coprolith.definition: A concretion of fecal matter in the gastrointestinal tract; commonly a calcified mass known as a fecalith.

coprology.definition: The study and analysis of feces (stool) for diagnostic purposes, including macroscopic and microscopic examination, and tests for parasites, occult blood, fat, infections, and malabsorption.

coproporphyria.definition: A type of porphyria caused by deficiency of the enzyme coproporphyrinogen oxidase (CPOX) in the heme biosynthesis pathway, resulting in accumulation of coproporphyrinogen and coproporphyrin in tissues and urine; it presents with intermittent neurovisceral attacks (abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, hypertension) and may be associated with skin photosensitivity.

copula.definition: An embryologic median tongue swelling from the second pharyngeal arch that overgrows the tuberculum impar to form the posterior (base) part of the tongue; it is later overlaid by the hypopharyngeal eminence.

copulation.definition: The act of sexual intercourse; mating between two organisms, especially animals; in humans, the act of sexual union.

coq.definition: A fat-soluble coenzyme involved in mitochondrial energy production (ATP) via the electron transport chain; also acts as an antioxidant. It exists in oxidized (ubiquinone) and reduced (ubiquinol) forms and is synthesized in the body with dietary sources such as meat and fish.

hydrocele.definition: A fluid-filled sac around the testicle within the tunica vaginalis, causing painless swelling of the scrotum; it results from accumulation of serous fluid and may be congenital or acquired.

varicocele.definition: A dilation of the pampiniform venous plexus within the scrotum (varicocele), typically left-sided, resembling varicose veins; may cause scrotal pain, testicular atrophy, and infertility; diagnosed by physical examination and Doppler ultrasound; treatment ranges from observation to surgical ligation or percutaneous embolization.

seminiferous tubules.definition: Coiled tubules within the testes where spermatogenesis occurs; the walls are lined by Sertoli cells and germ cells (spermatogenic epithelium), producing spermatozoa that mature and are released into the lumen for onward transport to the rete testis.

gyri.definition: Ridges on the cerebral cortex that form the brain's folded surface, located between sulci, and that increase the cortical surface area.

anisocoria.definition: Unequal pupil sizes; a condition in which the diameters of the pupils differ between the two eyes, which can be a normal physiological variation or due to ocular, neurologic, or pharmacologic causes.

diplocoria.definition: A rare congenital anomaly in which two pupils are present in one eye (a duplicated pupil), resulting from abnormal iris development; it can occur with other anterior segment anomalies such as coloboma or persistent pupillary membrane and may impair vision.

platycoria.definition: A rare ophthalmologic condition in which the pupil is abnormally flattened or nonround in shape, typically reflecting iris or anterior-segment abnormalities.

corectopia.definition: An abnormal displacement of the pupil from the center of the iris, producing an eccentric (off-center) pupil; it can be congenital or acquired and may be due to iris abnormalities, trauma, inflammation, or synechiae.

hereditary coproporphyria.definition: A rare autosomal dominant disorder of heme biosynthesis caused by deficiency of coproporphyrinogen oxidase, resulting in accumulation of coproporphyrin and other porphyrin precursors and episodic acute neurovisceral attacks; photosensitivity may be variable. Diagnosis is by elevated urinary coproporphyrin and CPOX gene mutations; management focuses on trigger avoidance and hemin therapy during attacks, with prophylaxis or transplantation considered in severe cases.

porphyrins.definition: A class of heterocyclic macrocyclic compounds made of four pyrrole rings connected by methine bridges to form the porphyrin ring; these molecules commonly coordinate a central metal ion and form the core of heme and chlorophyll.

methemoglobin.definition: An oxidized form of hemoglobin in which the iron in the heme is ferric (Fe3+) instead of ferrous (Fe2+), reducing its ability to bind and release oxygen to tissues; elevated levels impair tissue oxygen delivery.

reduced hemoglobin.definition: A lower-than-normal concentration of hemoglobin in the blood, resulting in reduced oxygen-carrying capacity; commonly due to iron deficiency, chronic disease, or blood loss.

sulfonamides.definition: A class of synthetic antimicrobial agents that act as competitive inhibitors of the bacterial enzyme dihydropteroate synthase in the folate synthesis pathway, functioning as PABA analogs to block production of dihydrofolic acid and tetrahydrofolate; they are generally bacteriostatic and are often used with trimethoprim (co-trimethoprim) for various infections.

hepatolenticular degeneration.definition: A genetic disorder of copper metabolism due to ATP7B mutations that causes excessive copper accumulation in the liver and brain, often with Kayser–Fleischer rings in the cornea, leading to hepatic disease and neuropsychiatric symptoms; treated with copper chelators and zinc with dietary copper restriction.

copper deficiency.definition: A state of copper deficiency due to inadequate intake, malabsorption, or excessive zinc that impairs copper-dependent enzymes (eg, ceruloplasmin, lysyl oxidase) and presents with microcytic anemia and neutropenia, neurologic symptoms such as gait disturbance and sensory neuropathy, and bone or connective tissue abnormalities.

fanconi's anemia.definition: A rare inherited bone marrow failure syndrome characterized by pancytopenia and congenital abnormalities, caused by defects in DNA repair genes that lead to increased chromosomal breakage; usually autosomal recessive and associated with higher cancer risk (notably leukemia).

cori cycle.definition: A metabolic pathway in which lactate produced by anaerobic glycolysis in exercising muscle is transported to the liver, converted to glucose by gluconeogenesis, and released back into the bloodstream to be reused by tissues; this process regenerates NAD+ and helps maintain blood glucose during strenuous exercise.

cori's disease.definition: Glycogen storage disease type III caused by deficiency of the debranching enzyme (alpha-1,6-glucosidase/4-α-glucanotransferase) in liver and muscle, leading to accumulation of limit dextrin–like structures in the cytosol and presenting with fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly; historically called Cori disease (Forbes disease).

glycogen storage disease type iii.definition: An autosomal recessive glycogen storage disease caused by deficiency of the glycogen debranching enzyme (AGL), resulting in impaired glycogenolysis and accumulation of abnormal glycogen in the liver (and in muscle in type IIIa); presents with fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, growth retardation, and hyperlipidemia, with muscle weakness or cardiomyopathy possible in IIIa; managed by avoiding fasting with regular carbohydrate intake (e.g., cornstarch).
