phencyclidine_hydrochloride.definition: A salt form of a synthetic dissociative anesthetic and NMDA receptor antagonist (PCP); illicitly used as a hallucinogen, producing dissociation, perceptual distortion, analgesia, and autonomic instability; overdose may cause severe agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, seizures, and psychosis; management is supportive with benzodiazepines for agitation.

jarisch.definition: A transient, febrile reaction that begins within hours of starting antibiotics for certain spirochetal infections (most commonly syphilis), caused by release of endotoxins from killed organisms; features fever with chills/rigors, headache, myalgias, and sometimes tachycardia or hypotension; self-limited and typically resolves within 24 hours, with supportive care while continuing therapy.

herxheimer.definition: A transient febrile reaction occurring after starting antibiotic therapy for spirochetal infections, caused by release of endotoxins from dying bacteria; symptoms include fever, chills, rigors, headache, myalgias, and sometimes tachycardia or hypotension, typically within 24 hours and self-limited.

grapefruit.definition: A large citrus fruit (Citrus × paradisi) with yellow-orange rind and segmented flesh; grapefruit juice contains furanocoumarins that inhibit intestinal cytochrome P450 3A4, increasing the bioavailability of certain medications and potentially causing drug toxicity.

juice.definition: A liquid contained in plant or animal tissue; in nutrition, a beverage derived from pressed fruit or vegetables, primarily water with sugars, vitamins, and minerals.

hepatopathy.definition: Any disease or abnormal condition of the liver.

teratogenesis.definition: The process by which congenital malformations (birth defects) arise in a developing fetus, usually due to exposure to teratogenic agents (such as certain drugs, infections, or chemicals) during critical periods of organ development.

thalidomide.definition: An immunomodulatory and anti-angiogenic prescription medication with anti-inflammatory effects; originally developed as a sedative and antiemetic for pregnant women but proven to be highly teratogenic, causing birth defects and fetal loss; now used under strict controls to treat multiple myeloma and certain inflammatory/skin conditions.

drospirenone.definition: A synthetic progestin (a fourth-generation progestin) used in combined hormonal contraceptives; it has antimineralocorticoid and antiandrogenic properties, contributing to effects such as reduced water retention and acne in some regimens.

drotrecogin.definition: A recombinant activated form of human protein C used as an anticoagulant and anti-inflammatory agent in the treatment of severe sepsis; it was marketed as drotrecogin alfa (activated) but was withdrawn after trials showed no mortality benefit and an increased risk of serious bleeding.

alfa.definition: The first letter of the Greek alphabet; used in medicine to denote the first or primary form, such as alpha-adrenergic receptors or alpha waves.

thrombolytic.definition: A thrombolytic is a drug that dissolves blood clots by converting plasminogen to plasmin, which degrades fibrin; used to treat acute thrombotic conditions such as myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, and pulmonary embolism.

organ.definition: A structurally distinct body part composed of multiple tissue types that performs a specific physiological function or set of functions, typically forming part of an organ system.

ptosis.definition: A drooping of the eyelid attributed to weakened muscles.

duplex.definition: An imaging test that combines B-mode ultrasound with Doppler flow analysis to visualize blood vessels and assess blood flow direction and velocity.

system.definition: An organized group of organs and tissues that work together to perform a specific physiological function in the body.

tendon.definition: A type of tissue that connects muscle to bone.

fentanyl.definition: A highly potent synthetic opioid analgesic that binds to mu-opioid receptors in the central nervous system to relieve severe pain; it is about 50–100 times more potent than morphine and is available in various formulations (injectable, transdermal patch, lozenge, nasal spray) but carries a high risk of respiratory depression, overdose, and dependence.

suctioning.definition: The act of removing secretions, fluids, or other material from a body cavity or airway using suction (via a suction catheter or device); commonly performed to clear the airway or drain fluids.

media.definition: Plural of medium; a substance that provides nutrients for growing cells or microorganisms in culture; in ophthalmology, the transparent structures of the eye through which light passes to reach the retina.

drug-resistant.definition: Describing organisms or cells that show reduced or no susceptibility to a medication that would normally be effective, meaning the drug does not adequately treat or kill them.

drug resistance.definition: A reduced or absent therapeutic response to a drug despite adequate dosing, typically due to genetic, metabolic, or cellular adaptations that diminish the drug's effectiveness (e.g., antimicrobial resistance or altered drug targets).

pneumococcal conjugate vaccine.definition: A vaccine in which pneumococcal polysaccharide antigens from multiple Streptococcus pneumoniae serotypes are conjugated to a carrier protein to enhance immunogenicity, producing a T-cell–dependent immune response that protects against invasive pneumococcal disease and other pneumococcal infections; examples include PCV13 and PCV20.

dubin-johnson syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by defective canalicular excretion of conjugated bilirubin due to mutations in ABCC2 (MRP2), leading to chronic conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with a typically benign course and a pigmented liver.

dry eye syndrome.definition: A multifactorial disease of the tears and ocular surface characterized by tear film instability and hyperosmolarity, often due to reduced tear production or increased tear evaporation, leading to ocular surface inflammation and damage with symptoms such as dryness, burning, grittiness, and fluctuating vision.

sjögren’s syndrome.definition: A chronic autoimmune condition in which lymphocytes attack exocrine glands, most notably the lacrimal and salivary glands, causing persistent dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and dry mouth (xerostomia); it can occur alone (primary) or with other autoimmune diseases (secondary) and is often associated with autoantibodies such as anti-SSA (Ro) and anti-SSB (La).

age-related macular degeneration.definition: A potentially blinding condition that destroys sharp central vision.

drusen.definition: An accumulation of lipid-rich extracellular debris between the retinal pigment epithelium and Bruch's membrane, seen as yellow‑white spots; associated with aging and age-related macular degeneration, with hard drusen being small and discrete and soft drusen larger and confluent, carrying higher risk of geographic atrophy or neovascular AMD.

duane's syndrome.definition: A congenital eye movement disorder caused by misdevelopment of the sixth cranial nerve with aberrant innervation of the lateral rectus by oculomotor nerve fibers, leading to limited horizontal gaze (often limited abduction, and sometimes adduction), globe retraction, and narrowing of the palpebral fissure on attempted adduction; subtypes describe the pattern of movement limitation.

duchenne-aran disease.definition: Probably a misspelling of Duchenne muscular dystrophy: an X-linked recessive genetic disorder caused by mutations in the DMD gene encoding dystrophin, leading to progressive proximal muscle weakness beginning in early childhood, calf pseudohypertrophy, and eventual cardiopulmonary complications.

duchenne-erb paralysis.definition: An injury to the upper brachial plexus (C5–C6) causing paralysis or weakness of shoulder and elbow muscles, resulting in a characteristic “waiter’s tip” posture (arm adducted and internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated); often due to birth trauma or traction injuries to the neck.

winged scapulae.definition: A clinical sign in which the medial border of the scapula protrudes posteriorly away from the thoracic wall (scapular winging), most often due to weakness or paralysis of the serratus anterior muscle from long thoracic nerve injury; may also result from dysfunction of the trapezius or rhomboid muscles.

cardiac murmur.definition: An abnormal heart sound produced by turbulent blood flow within the heart or great vessels, usually detected with a stethoscope; it can be innocent (physiologic) or due to pathology such as valvular disease (stenosis or regurgitation), congenital or acquired heart defects, or high-output states. It is described by timing (systolic or diastolic), location, intensity, pitch/quality, and radiation.

acellular pertussis.definition: A vaccine consisting of purified, inactivated components of Bordetella pertussis (for example, pertussis toxin, filamentous hemagglutinin, pertactin, and fimbriae) rather than whole bacterial cells, used to immunize against pertussis with fewer adverse reactions than whole-cell vaccines.

d-tubocurarine.definition: A nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent (curare alkaloid) that competitively inhibits nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction to produce skeletal muscle paralysis, used to facilitate intubation and surgery; historically associated with histamine release causing hypotension and bronchospasm, and largely replaced by newer agents.

delayed-type hypersensitivity.definition: Type IV hypersensitivity reaction driven by sensitized T lymphocytes, not antibodies; occurs 24–72 hours after exposure, with cytokine-mediated recruitment and activation of macrophages leading to tissue inflammation and damage (e.g., contact dermatitis, tuberculin skin test).

dual-energy absorptiometry.definition: A radiographic technique that uses two different X-ray energy levels to differentiate bone from soft tissue and quantify bone mineral density, used to diagnose osteoporosis and assess fracture risk.

dubois formula.definition: A formula to estimate body surface area (in square meters) from weight and height: BSA = 0.007184 × (weight in kg)^0.425 × (height in cm)^0.725.

dubowitz assessment.definition: An neonatal gestational age assessment that estimates a newborn’s gestational age by scoring 10 physical maturity signs and 10 neuromuscular maturity signs (developed by Dubowitz and colleagues).

transposon.definition: A DNA sequence that can change its position within the genome, potentially disrupting or altering genes; moves either by a cut-and-paste mechanism (DNA transposons) or by a copy-and-paste mechanism via an RNA intermediate (retrotransposons).

plasmid.definition: A small, circular, double-stranded DNA molecule that replicates independently of the host's chromosomal DNA, usually found in bacteria; it often carries accessory genes (such as antibiotic resistance) and is used as a cloning vector in molecular biology.

beta-lactam.definition: An antibiotic class containing a four-membered lactam ring in its chemical structure; they kill bacteria by inhibiting cell-wall synthesis through binding to penicillin-binding proteins, leading to cell lysis; includes penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, and monobactams; can be inactivated by lactamase enzymes.

antibiotic resistance.definition: Antibiotic resistance is the ability of a microorganism to survive and multiply despite exposure to an antibiotic that would normally prevent its growth or kill it. It arises through genetic mutations or acquisition of resistance genes and can spread between organisms, leading to reduced treatment effectiveness, longer illnesses, and greater risk of transmission.

intrinsic resistance.definition: Natural, inherent resistance of a microorganism to a given antimicrobial agent, due to intrinsic structural or physiological traits (such as cell wall permeability, efflux mechanisms, or absence of the drug target), and not acquired through mutation or gene transfer.

alveolitis.definition: Inflammation of the alveolar tissue, especially the tooth socket after extraction (alveolar osteitis or dry socket), marked by severe pain, disruption of the blood clot, exposed bone, and often foul odor.

pigment.definition: A coloring substance present in cells or tissues that imparts color; in humans, the principal pigment of the skin, hair, and eyes is melanin.

dry cough.definition: An unproductive cough that yields little or no sputum; a nonproductive cough often due to viral infections, environmental irritants, allergies, asthma, gastroesophageal reflux, or certain medications (e.g., ACE inhibitors). Duration classifies it as acute (<3 weeks), subacute (3–8 weeks), or chronic (>8 weeks).

toxoids.definition: An inactivated or detoxified toxin used in vaccines to provoke an antibody response against the toxin without causing disease.

pseudohypertrophic muscular dystrophy.definition: An inherited X-linked recessive muscular dystrophy caused by mutations in the dystrophin gene, leading to absent or defective dystrophin; presents with progressive proximal muscle weakness and calf pseudohypertrophy beginning in early childhood, with Gowers' sign and eventual loss of ambulation; cardiopulmonary complications are common.

ductus venosus.definition: A fetal vessel that shunts oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein directly to the inferior vena cava, bypassing hepatic circulation; it closes after birth to form the ligamentum venosum.

umbilical vein.definition: A fetal vessel that carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the developing fetus; in the liver it bypasses hepatic sinusoids via the ductus venosus to the inferior vena cava, and after birth it becomes the ligamentum teres hepatis (round ligament).

duodenal atresia.definition: A congenital obstruction of the duodenum caused by failure of recanalization during embryonic development, typically presenting in newborns with bilious vomiting and proximal distention, and treated by surgical bypass of the obstructed segment (most commonly duodeno-duodenostomy).

duodenal bulb.definition: The first, dilated portion of the duodenum immediately distal to the pylorus (the duodenal cap; bulbus duodeni); a short intraperitoneal segment that marks the stomach–small intestine transition and is a common site of peptic ulcers.

duodenal digestion.definition: Chemical digestion that occurs in the duodenum, the proximal part of the small intestine, where chyme mixes with pancreatic juice (amylase, proteases, lipase), bile, and intestinal brush-border enzymes; bicarbonate neutralizes gastric acid and enables breakdown of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats for absorption.

duodenal mesentery.definition: Peritoneal fold that suspends the intraperitoneal portion of the duodenum (the superior part) from the posterior abdominal wall; part of the dorsal mesentery, containing vessels, nerves, and lymphatics supplying the duodenum.

duodenal switch.definition: A bariatric procedure that combines a restrictive sleeve gastrectomy with a long intestinal bypass (biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch), rearranging the small intestine so most of its length is bypassed to markedly reduce nutrient absorption and produce substantial weight loss; requires lifelong nutritional monitoring and supplementation due to malabsorption.

duodenectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove part or all of the duodenum, the first portion of the small intestine, typically followed by reconstruction to restore continuity of the gastrointestinal tract.

duodenitis.definition: Inflammation of the duodenum, the first portion of the small intestine. It can be acute or chronic and is commonly due to infection (notably Helicobacter pylori), NSAID use, peptic disease, or inflammatory bowel disease; symptoms typically include epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Diagnosis and treatment focus on the underlying cause, with approaches such as antibiotic therapy for H. pylori, acid suppression, and avoidance of offending medications.

duodenojejunal flexure.definition: The sharp bend where the duodenum ends and the jejunum begins, typically at about the L2 vertebral level in the left upper abdomen; maintained by the suspensory (ligament of Treitz) and marks the foregut–midgut transition.

duodenography.definition: Radiographic imaging of the duodenum after administration of contrast material to delineate the duodenal lumen, used to detect ulcers, diverticula, strictures, and other duodenal abnormalities.

hypotonic duodenography.definition: A radiographic examination of the duodenum in which contrast material is introduced and the duodenal smooth muscle is pharmacologically relaxed to reduce peristalsis, producing a static image that allows better delineation of the duodenal mucosa and folds (used to detect ulcers, diverticula, and other mucosal lesions; historically more common but largely replaced by modern imaging).

duodenohepatic.definition: Relating to the duodenum and the liver; pertaining to anatomical structures or relationships involving both organs.

duodenocolic.definition: Relating to the duodenum and the colon; involving or connecting these two parts of the gastrointestinal tract.

duodenogastric reflux.definition: Reflux of duodenal contents (bile and pancreatic secretions) into the stomach (and sometimes the esophagus), usually due to pyloric or gastric outlet dysfunction or postoperative anatomic changes, causing gastritis and dyspepsia.

duodenogastroesophageal reflux.definition: Backward flow of duodenal contents—bile and pancreatic secretions—into the stomach and then into the esophagus, usually due to pyloric or gastroesophageal junction dysfunction, which can cause gastritis and esophagitis and reflux symptoms.

wirsung.definition: A major pancreatic duct that runs through the pancreas, draining pancreatic exocrine secretions into the duodenum via the major duodenal papilla (ampulla of Vater).

superior mesenteric vein.definition: A major tributary of the hepatic portal system that drains blood from the small intestine (jejunum and ileum), as well as parts of the large intestine (cecum, ascending and part of the transverse colon) and the pancreatic head; it joins the splenic vein behind the neck of the pancreas to form the hepatic portal vein.

right kidney.definition: One of the two bean-shaped kidneys in the retroperitoneal space on the right side of the upper abdomen; it filters blood to form urine, regulates fluid and electrolyte balance and acid-base homeostasis, and secretes hormones such as erythropoietin; it lies slightly lower than the left kidney due to the liver.

dukes' classification.definition: A historical staging system for colorectal cancer that classifies tumors by extent of invasion and spread: A—tumor confined to the mucosa; B—tumor invades through the muscularis propria into the bowel wall; C—regional lymph node metastasis; D—distant metastasis.

colorectal tumors.definition: Neoplasms arising in the colon or rectum; they can be benign (e.g., adenomatous or hyperplastic polyps) or malignant (colorectal carcinoma), with many cancers evolving from adenomatous polyps over time.

dupuytren's contracture.definition: A benign fibromatosis of the palmar fascia characterized by thickening with cords and nodules that progressively limit finger extension, producing flexion contractures of the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, most often in the ring and little fingers.

galeazzi's fracture.definition: A fracture of the distal third of the radius with dislocation or disruption of the distal radioulnar joint.

rivinus' duct.definition: A series of small excretory ducts of the sublingual salivary gland that drain saliva into the floor of the mouth along the sublingual folds.

sublingual duct.definition: The major excretory duct of the sublingual gland that opens into the floor of the mouth, typically at the sublingual caruncle; it drains saliva from the sublingual gland and is also known as the duct of Bartholin.

dural venous sinuses.definition: Endothelium-lined venous channels between the layers of the dura mater in the brain that collect venous blood and cerebrospinal fluid (via arachnoid granulations) and drain into the internal jugular veins; they are valveless and include major sinuses such as the superior sagittal, straight, transverse, and sigmoid.

dura.definition: The tough outermost layer of the meninges that envelops the brain and spinal cord; a dense fibrous membrane that provides protection and forms dural folds such as the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli.

duroziez murmur.definition: A diastolic murmur heard over the femoral artery when the artery is lightly compressed with the stethoscope, associated with aortic regurgitation.

tick-borne relapsing fever.definition: A vector-borne illness caused by Borrelia spirochetes transmitted to humans by Ornithodoros soft ticks, characterized by recurrent febrile episodes due to antigenic variation of the spirochete.

borrelia duttonii.definition: A spirochete bacterium that is the etiologic agent of East African tick-borne relapsing fever; transmitted by soft ticks of the genus Ornithodoros, causing relapsing febrile episodes with headaches and myalgias.

dulcolax.definition: A stimulant laxative (bisacodyl) used to treat constipation and to evacuate the bowel before medical procedures; it stimulates colonic peristalsis to promote stool passage, with oral onset typically 6–12 hours and rectal onset 15–60 minutes.

dutasteride.definition: A medication that inhibits both isoforms of the enzyme 5-alpha-reductase, lowering dihydrotestosterone (DHT) levels; used to treat benign prostatic hyperplasia and, in some contexts, male-pattern hair loss.

durabolin.definition: A long-acting injectable anabolic‑androgenic steroid containing nandrolone decanoate; used medically for testosterone replacement in hypogonadism and for certain wasting conditions. It promotes protein synthesis and muscle growth but can cause androgenic side effects and suppression of endogenous testosterone, and it is sometimes misused for performance enhancement.

duverneys fracture.definition: An isolated fracture of the iliac wing (iliac ala) of the pelvis, typically a stable, non-displacing injury with no disruption of the pelvic ring or acetabulum, usually due to blunt trauma.

anterior superior spine.definition: A bony prominence on the pelvis at the anterior end of the iliac crest; a palpable landmark that serves as the origin of the sartorius muscle and as the attachment site for the inguinal ligament.

bethanechol chloride.definition: A direct-acting muscarinic cholinergic agonist (quaternary ammonium) that increases smooth muscle tone and motility in the bladder and GI tract; used to treat postoperative ileus and urinary retention.

tapeworm infection.definition: An infection caused by intestinal tapeworms (cestodes) acquired by ingesting undercooked meat or fish containing larval cysts; adults reside in the small intestine and may cause mild abdominal symptoms or nutritional deficiencies, diagnosed by stool examination and treated with antihelminthic medications such as praziquantel or albendazole.

hymenolepis nana.definition: A small intestinal cestode parasite (the dwarf tapeworm) that infects humans and animals; transmitted by ingestion of embryonated eggs from contaminated food or water and capable of autoinfection; often asymptomatic or causes mild abdominal symptoms.

whipple's disease.definition: A rare chronic systemic infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei, characterized by malabsorption with weight loss, diarrhea, arthralgias, fever, and lymphadenopathy; diagnostic hallmark is PAS-positive foamy macrophages in the intestinal lamina propria with confirmation by PCR for T. whipplei; treated with prolonged antibiotic therapy (initial IV therapy followed by oral antibiotics).

d-xylose.definition: A five-carbon aldose sugar used in the D-xylose absorption test to evaluate small intestinal mucosal absorption. It is absorbed in the proximal small intestine without requiring pancreatic enzymes and is excreted in the urine; reduced absorption suggests mucosal damage (e.g., celiac disease) rather than pancreatic insufficiency.

d-xylose absorption test.definition: A diagnostic test of proximal small intestinal absorption in which a patient ingests a dose of D-xylose and the amount recovered in urine (typically over 5 hours) is measured; reduced urinary excretion indicates impaired intestinal mucosal absorption (e.g., mucosal disease like celiac disease), whereas normal excretion suggests intact mucosa (pancreatic causes unlikely).

d-xylose breath test.definition: A diagnostic test of small‑intestinal carbohydrate absorption in which a dose of D‑xylose (often labeled) is ingested and the amount of labeled CO2 exhaled in the breath is measured; reduced exhaled label indicates malabsorption due to mucosal disease, whereas a normal result suggests pancreatic insufficiency or intact mucosa.

dysautonomia.definition: An umbrella term for disorders of the autonomic nervous system, which regulates involuntary bodily functions such as heart rate, blood pressure, digestion, temperature regulation, and sweating. It causes impaired autonomic responses, commonly with orthostatic intolerance (dizziness or fainting on standing), abnormal heart rate or blood pressure, digestive or bladder dysfunction, and abnormal sweating. It can be primary (genetic) or secondary to other diseases (e.g., diabetes, autoimmune disorders, Parkinson disease, amyloidosis).

riley-day syndrome.definition: A congenital autosomal recessive autonomic neuropathy caused by IKBKAP gene mutations (familial dysautonomia), most common in Ashkenazi Jewish individuals, characterized by dysautonomia with alacrima (reduced tear production), insensitivity to pain and temperature, labile blood pressure with orthostatic hypotension, abnormal sweating, dysphagia, and growth/feeding difficulties.

dysbarism.definition: Illness caused by changes in ambient barometric pressure, leading to gas bubble formation and tissue injury; it includes decompression sickness (the bends), arterial gas embolism, and barotrauma of air-containing spaces, typically after rapid ascent or descent in diving or aviation.

dysbasia.definition: Difficulty walking or an abnormal gait resulting from neuromuscular or neurologic impairment; may reflect cerebellar dysfunction, sensory ataxia, vestibular disturbance, or motor pathway disorders.

dysbetalipoproteinemia.definition: A hereditary disorder of lipoprotein metabolism (Type III hyperlipoproteinemia) caused by defective uptake of chylomicron and VLDL remnants due to APOE2/E2 genotype, leading to accumulation of beta-VLDL remnants with elevated cholesterol and triglycerides and an increased risk of premature atherosclerosis; palmar xanthomas may be present.

dyscholia.definition: An old or seldom-used term for a dysphoric or melancholic mood—an abnormal, distressed affect characterized by unhappiness or low spirits; largely obsolete in modern psychiatric nomenclature.

dyschondroplasia.definition: An abnormal development of cartilage due to defective chondrogenesis, resulting in skeletal dysplasia with abnormal bone growth.

dyscrastic fracture.definition: A fracture that occurs because the bone is weakened by an underlying systemic disease (dyscrasia), i.e., a pathologic fracture due to abnormal bone integrity from a blood- or marrow-related disorder.

dysdiadochokinesia.definition: An inability or difficulty performing rapid, alternating movements (e.g., pronation–supination of the hands or rapid tapping), typically due to cerebellar dysfunction.

dysacusis.definition: An abnormal perception of sound in which auditory signals are perceived with distorted quality (e.g., altered pitch, timbre, or loudness), often occurring with sensorineural hearing loss or cochlear dysfunction.

dysadrenia.definition: Not a recognized medical term; there is no standard definition in contemporary medical dictionaries. If you meant a similar term (e.g., dysadrenalism or adrenal dysfunction), I can define that.

dysaesthesia.definition: An abnormal, unpleasant sensation, such as burning, tingling, itching, or electric-shock-like feelings, produced by sensory nerve dysfunction or damage; it can be spontaneous or provoked by stimulation.

dysarthrosis.definition: Abnormal development or formation of one or more joints.

dynamic ileus.definition: A non-obstructive impairment of intestinal motility (paralytic ileus) characterized by reduced or absent peristalsis, leading to abdominal distension, gas and fluid accumulation, nausea or vomiting, and failure to pass stool or flatus; commonly occurs after abdominal surgery or with opioids, electrolyte disturbances, or inflammation.

dynamic imaging.definition: An imaging approach that captures a series of images over time to visualize motion and dynamic physiological processes in tissues or organs, enabling assessment of function (e.g., dynamic MRI, cine CT, fluoroscopy, dynamic ultrasound).

dynamic orthosis.definition: An orthopedic device that permits controlled movement of a joint by applying adjustable external forces (springs, elastic bands, or hinges) to assist or resist motion during rehabilitation, while providing alignment and support.

dynamic retinoscopy.definition: An eye examination technique in which retinoscopy is performed with active accommodation (typically by having the patient view a near target) to evaluate the accommodative response and refractive error under dynamic, accommodating conditions.

dynamic spatial reconstructor.definition: A computer-based imaging method that reconstructs three-dimensional, time-resolved models of moving anatomy from a series of two-dimensional images, enabling visualization of motion over a cycle (for example, the beating heart).

dwyer cable instrumentation.definition: A brand-associated term referring to cable-based instrumentation systems from Dwyer Instruments, used to connect sensors and transducers to monitoring readouts in laboratory or process settings.

dicloxacillin sodium.definition: A penicillinase-resistant penicillin antibiotic in the sodium salt form; used to treat infections caused by penicillinase-producing Staphylococcus aureus and susceptible streptococci, including skin and soft tissue and some respiratory infections; not effective against MRSA or most Gram-negative bacteria.

dyrenium.definition: A brand-name potassium-sparing diuretic (triamterene) that inhibits epithelial sodium channels in the distal nephron, increasing sodium and water excretion while conserving potassium; used for edema and hypertension, often combined with a thiazide diuretic.

triamterene.definition: A potassium-sparing diuretic that inhibits epithelial sodium channels in the distal nephron, increasing sodium and water excretion while reducing potassium loss; used to treat hypertension and edema, often prescribed with a thiazide diuretic.

cephalodynia.definition: Pain occurring in the head; a headache.

gastrodynia.definition: Pain in the stomach; stomach ache.

dynode.definition: An electrode in a vacuum tube (notably a photomultiplier tube) that, upon impact by incident electrons, emits secondary electrons, producing electron multiplication and amplification of an electrical signal; used in radiation detectors and imaging equipment.

dynorphin.definition: Endogenous opioid peptides derived from prodynorphin that preferentially activate κ-opioid receptors; they modulate pain, stress responses, mood, and addiction.

dyphylline.definition: A methylxanthine bronchodilator previously used to treat bronchospasm in asthma and COPD; it inhibits phosphodiesterase, increasing intracellular cAMP and producing bronchodilation, with a narrow therapeutic index and potential adverse effects such as tachycardia, tremor, and GI upset.

gi distress.definition: A non-specific collection of gastrointestinal symptoms indicating irritation or dysfunction of the GI tract, commonly including abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, bloating, and indigestion; may result from infection, inflammation, obstruction, functional disorders, medications, or other systemic illness.

hyperadrenocorticism.definition: A disorder of chronic excess cortisol exposure, typically due to endogenous overproduction from ACTH-secreting pituitary adenomas (Cushing disease) or cortisol-producing adrenal tumors, or from prolonged exogenous corticosteroid therapy.

hypoadrenalism.definition: A condition characterized by insufficient production of adrenal cortex hormones (primarily cortisol, and often aldosterone), due to primary adrenal failure or secondary/tertiary suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis.

hypoadrenocorticism.definition: A condition of adrenal insufficiency due to inadequate cortisol production by the adrenal cortex, typically from primary adrenal gland failure or secondary (pituitary/ACTH) deficiency; may include mineralocorticoid deficiency in primary disease and presents with fatigue, weakness, nausea, weight loss, hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and risk of adrenal crisis.

pancreatic dysfunction.definition: A broad term for impaired pancreatic function, including reduced exocrine enzyme secretion causing maldigestion and steatorrhea, and/or diminished endocrine hormone production leading to glucose intolerance or diabetes.

biliary dysfunction.definition: Abnormal functioning of the biliary system, leading to impaired production, flow, or storage of bile. It can result from obstruction (such as gallstones or biliary strictures), cholestasis, inflammation, infection, or gallbladder disease.

rh incompatibility.definition: A condition that occurs when you are pregnant if you have Rh-negative blood and your baby has Rh-positive blood.

dyseidetic.definition: A deficit in visual memory or imagery, characterized by an inability to form or recall vivid, detailed mental pictures (the opposite of eidetic imagery).

dyskinetic.definition: Relating to dyskinesia; involving involuntary, abnormal, often jerky or writhing movements.

dysmetria.definition: A cerebellar dysfunction manifested as an inability to judge the distance or range of a movement, causing overshooting (hypermetria) or undershooting (hypometria) of a target.

dyslexic.definition: Relating to dyslexia; a learning disorder characterized by difficulties with accurate and fluent word recognition and poor spelling/decoding, typically due to phonological processing deficits.

dysenteric.definition: Relating to dysentery; describing or causing inflammation of the colon, typically with abdominal cramps and frequent stools that contain blood and mucus.

shigella.definition: Genus of Gram-negative, nonmotile, rod-shaped bacteria in the Enterobacteriaceae family that causes bacillary dysentery (bloody diarrhea) via invasion of the colonic mucosa and fecal-oral transmission; comprises four species (dysenteriae, flexneri, boydii, sonnei); infection typically presents with abrupt fever, abdominal cramps, and acute diarrhea with mucus and blood; some strains produce Shiga toxin, which can precipitate severe complications such as hemolytic-uremic syndrome; management focuses on rehydration and electrolyte replacement; antibiotics are reserved for certain cases or outbreaks due to resistance concerns.

entamoeba.definition: A genus of unicellular parasitic protozoa (amoebae) that inhabit the intestinal tract of humans and many animals; some species are pathogenic and can invade the intestinal mucosa, causing amebiasis and, in some cases, liver abscesses.

histolytica.definition: A protozoan parasite (Entamoeba histolytica) that infects humans, causing amebiasis; transmitted via ingestion of cysts in contaminated food or water; it can invade the colonic mucosa causing dysentery and may form liver abscesses.

amebic.definition: Relating to or caused by amoebae (primarily Entamoeba histolytica); used to describe infections such as amebic dysentery or amebic liver abscess.

exotoxin.definition: A highly potent protein toxin secreted by certain bacteria into the surrounding environment; it damages host cells by specific mechanisms (e.g., A-B toxins, superantigens, or membrane-disrupting toxins) and is usually heat-labile. It is distinct from endotoxins, which are lipopolysaccharide components released upon bacterial lysis, and many such toxins can be neutralized by antitoxins and converted into toxoids for vaccines.

dysergia.definition: Impaired coordination of muscle action due to faulty neuromuscular integration, resulting in abnormal, uncoordinated movement.

dysesthesia.definition: An unpleasant or abnormal sensation (such as burning, itching, tingling, or electric-shock feelings) that is often caused by nerve injury or neuropathic conditions and may be spontaneous or evoked by stimuli.

dysfibrogenemia.definition: Abnormal level of fibrinogen in the blood (a clotting factor), which may be elevated or reduced and can reflect liver disease, inflammatory states, or consumption in coagulopathies.

dysfunctional.definition: Not functioning normally or properly; describing impaired or abnormal physiological, anatomical, or behavioral function of an organ, tissue, or system.

dysgammaglobulinemia.definition: A disturbance of the serum gamma globulin (immunoglobulin) fraction, reflecting abnormal antibody production or regulation; may present as decreased, increased, or imbalanced immunoglobulin levels and is often detected by serum protein electrophoresis showing an abnormal gamma region.

dysgenesis.definition: Abnormal development of an organ or tissue during embryogenesis, resulting in malformation or defective formation of that structure. It is used when the organ is present but improperly formed, and is distinct from agenesis (complete absence) and hypoplasia (incomplete development).

gonadal.definition: Relating to the gonads (the ovaries or testes), the primary reproductive organs that produce gametes (eggs or sperm) and the associated sex hormones.

dysgenic.definition: Relating to abnormal or defective development of tissue or an organ, typically due to dysgenesis during embryonic formation.

dysgenics.definition: A historical/controversial concept describing a proposed decline in the genetic quality or fitness of a population due to the accumulation of deleterious alleles, often discussed in the context of eugenics; not a formal medical term.

dysgenitalism.definition: Abnormal development of the gonads and/or genitalia resulting from defective embryologic differentiation or hormonal signaling, often encompassing gonadal dysgenesis and related genital malformations.

dysgerminoma.definition: A malignant germ cell tumor of the ovary arising from primordial germ cells; the ovarian counterpart of seminoma, most often occurring in young women and typically radiosensitive and chemosensitive.

dysgerminomas.definition: A malignant germ cell tumor of the ovary that is the ovarian counterpart of seminoma; typically affects adolescents and young women; composed of large, uniform cells with clear cytoplasm and central nuclei; often positive for placental alkaline phosphatase; radiosensitive and chemosensitive, with a favorable prognosis when treated with surgery and platinum‑based chemotherapy; may be bilateral in a subset.

dysgeusia.definition: A distortion or alteration of taste perception, in which ordinary tastes are perceived as abnormal (e.g., metallic, foul, or salty), often caused by medications, infections, nutritional deficiencies, or nerve injury.

dysglandular.definition: Pertaining to glandular tissue that is abnormally developed or arranged, with disorganized glandular architecture.

dysgnathia.definition: An abnormal development or alignment of the jaw (maxilla and/or mandible), resulting in malocclusion and facial disharmony; can be congenital or acquired.

dysgnathic.definition: Relating to an abnormal relationship or alignment of the jaws (maxilla and mandible), often due to skeletal jaw deformity and resulting in malocclusion.

dysgraphia.definition: A neurodevelopmental learning disability characterized by difficulties with handwriting and the cognitive production of written text, resulting in illegible or inefficient handwriting, poor spelling, and disorganized or error-prone written expression; it can occur alone or with other learning or attention disorders.

dyshidrosis.definition: Dyshidrosis, or dyshidrotic eczema, is a form of hand eczema marked by sudden outbreaks of small, fluid-filled vesicles on the palms and sides of the fingers (and sometimes the soles), often with itching or burning and possible cracking as it resolves.

dyskeratosis.definition: Abnormal, premature keratinization of epithelial cells with disordered keratinocyte maturation, resulting in keratotic lesions on the skin and mucous membranes.

congenita.definition: Relating to a condition that is present at birth; congenital.

dysmorphogenesis.definition: Abnormal development of form and structure during embryogenesis, resulting in congenital malformations; a defect in morphogenesis due to disrupted cellular signaling, tissue interactions, or environmental factors.

dysmorphophobia.definition: A mental health condition characterized by excessive preoccupation with perceived flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear minor to others, causing significant distress or impairment and often accompanied by repetitive behaviors such as mirror checking, excessive grooming, or camouflaging; commonly diagnosed as body dysmorphic disorder.

dysmyelination.definition: Defective formation or maturation of the myelin sheath, leading to structurally abnormal or insufficient myelin (often due to genetic defects in myelin-forming cells), not loss of existing myelin.

dysorexia.definition: An abnormal or disordered appetite, characterized by aversion to food or a diminished desire to eat, leading to reduced food intake.

epiphysealis.definition: Relating to the epiphysis, the end portion of a long bone that grows separately from the shaft and contains the growth plate.

hemimelica.definition: Relating to hemimelia; a congenital deficiency of a limb, characterized by partial absence or underdevelopment of part of a limb (longitudinal limb deficiency).

dysplastic.definition: Relating to dysplasia; showing abnormal development or maturation of cells within a tissue, often with disorganized tissue architecture and cellular atypia, and potentially a precursor to cancer.

nevi.definition: Benign pigmented skin lesions formed by nests of nevus cells (moles); they can be flat or raised and vary in color, usually harmless, but any lesion that changes in size, shape, color, or becomes new should be evaluated for melanoma.

dysphasia.definition: An impairment of language function due to brain injury or disease, characterized by difficulties in speaking, understanding, reading, or writing; commonly resulting from stroke or other neurologic illness.

dyspnoea.definition: A subjective sensation of breathing discomfort or breathlessness (air hunger) that varies in intensity and can be caused by cardiopulmonary disorders, anemia, deconditioning, or anxiety; it is a symptom, not a disease.

dyspneal.definition: Relating to the sensation of breathlessness; the experience of shortness of breath or difficult, labored breathing.

dyspneic.definition: Relating to dyspnea; experiencing or presenting with shortness of breath; having difficult or labored breathing.

dysraphia.definition: A congenital neural tube defect caused by failure of the neural folds to fuse during early embryonic development, resulting in incomplete closure of the spine or skull (neural-tube closure defect).

dysraphic.definition: Relating to dysraphism; a congenital malformation of the spine or spinal cord due to incomplete neural tube closure during embryonic development.

dysreflexia.definition: An acute, potentially life-threatening syndrome in people with spinal cord injury (usually above T6) caused by unregulated autonomic reflex activity below the level of injury, leading to sudden, severe hypertension often with headache, flushing or sweating above the lesion, and bradycardia; precipitated by triggers such as bladder distension or bowel impaction; requires prompt removal of the triggering stimulus and measures to lower blood pressure.

arnoldchiari.definition: A congenital condition in which downward herniation of cerebellar tissue (often including the brainstem) through the foramen magnum occurs, commonly associated with hydrocephalus and spinal myelomeningocele (classic Arnold–Chiari II malformation).

dermatome.definition: A defined region of skin supplied by sensory fibers from a single dorsal (spinal) nerve root, used to map spinal nerve function and localize neurological lesions.

tenesmus.definition: A painful, urgent sensation to defecate accompanied by a persistent feeling of incomplete evacuation, often due to rectal inflammation or distal colorectal disease.

laparoscopy.definition: A type of small surgery where a tiny tube with a camera is put into a small cut in the stomach to look at organs.

hormones.definition: Chemical messengers produced by endocrine glands or neuroendocrine cells, released into the bloodstream to travel to distant target tissues. They regulate physiology and behavior by binding to specific receptors, and include peptide, steroid, and amino acid–derived hormones; they coordinate processes such as metabolism, growth, development, reproduction, and homeostasis.

oralcontraceptives.definition: Pills taken by mouth to prevent pregnancy, typically containing estrogen and progestin or progestin alone; they prevent ovulation, thicken cervical mucus, and thin the endometrium, with possible non-contraceptive benefits and risks such as thromboembolism in certain individuals.

contraceptives.definition: A group of methods, devices, or agents used to prevent pregnancy by preventing fertilization or implantation; includes hormonal methods (e.g., pills, patches, injections, rings), barrier methods (e.g., condoms, diaphragms), intrauterine devices, sterilization, fertility‑awareness methods, and emergency contraception.

narcotics.definition: A class of drugs that dull the senses and relieve pain; most commonly referring to opioids (e.g., morphine, codeine, heroin) that can cause analgesia, sedation, and dependence and are regulated as controlled substances.

antiprostaglandin.definition: A substance that inhibits the synthesis or action of prostaglandins (i.e., a prostaglandin antagonist), such as NSAIDs that reduce prostaglandin production or agents that block prostaglandin receptors.

seminoma.definition: A malignant germ cell tumor of the testis originating from the seminiferous tubules; the most common testicular cancer in young men, typically presenting as a painless testicular mass and usually highly curable with orchiectomy and appropriate adjuvant therapy.

embryoma.definition: An embryonic-type tumor composed of primitive embryonal cells resembling early developmental tissue; a historical, non-specific term for neoplasms of embryonal appearance that is now replaced by more precise names such as blastoma or embryonal carcinoma depending on the tissue of origin.

fanconi.definition:
- A rare inherited bone marrow failure syndrome caused by defects in DNA repair, leading to pancytopenia, congenital anomalies, and an increased risk of leukemia and other cancers.
- A proximal renal tubulopathy characterized by urinary loss of glucose, bicarbonate, phosphate, and amino acids, resulting in metabolic acidosis and electrolyte disturbances; can be inherited or acquired.

vaginismus.definition: Spasms of the muscles around the vaginal opening that prevent penile penetration.

lipoproteins.definition: Lipoproteins are spherical particles composed of lipids (such as triglycerides and cholesterol esters) surrounded by a shell of phospholipids and proteins (apolipoproteins) that enable the transport of hydrophobic lipids through the aqueous bloodstream and lymph; they are classified by density into chylomicrons, VLDL, IDL, LDL, and HDL.

dyslipidemia.definition: Abnormal levels of lipids in the blood, typically meaning elevated LDL cholesterol and/or triglycerides and/or low HDL cholesterol, which increases the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

hypolipoproteinemia.definition: A condition characterized by abnormally low levels of circulating lipoproteins in the blood (e.g., low cholesterol and triglyceride levels), typically due to genetic defects in lipoprotein synthesis or transport or to certain acquired states.

hyperpigmentation.definition: A condition in which areas of skin become darker than the surrounding skin due to increased melanin production or deposition, commonly following sun exposure, inflammation or injury (post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation), hormonal changes (melasma), aging, or certain medications.

depigmentation.definition: Loss or reduction of skin color due to loss or dysfunction of pigment-producing cells (melanocytes) or decreased melanin production.

leukokeratosis.definition: A white patch on mucosa or skin caused by thickening of the keratin layer (hyperkeratosis); a descriptive, non-specific finding that may result from chronic irritation or friction and is not by itself a diagnosis.

mucosal.definition: Relating to a mucous membrane; the moist lining of cavities and channels that open to the exterior (e.g., respiratory, digestive, and genitourinary tracts) that secretes mucus.

nail.definition: A hard, keratinized plate on the dorsal distal aspect of digits, produced by the nail matrix and resting on the nail bed; it protects the fingertip and aids in object manipulation.

dystrophin-glycoprotein complex.definition: A multiprotein transmembrane complex that links the intracellular actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular basement membrane, stabilizing the muscle cell membrane during contraction and participating in signaling. It comprises dystrophin, dystroglycan (alpha and beta), sarcoglycans, sarcospan, and associated proteins; defects in its components cause dystrophinopathies such as Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy.

duchenne muscular dystrophy.definition: An X-linked recessive neuromuscular disorder caused by mutations in the DMD gene encoding dystrophin, leading to progressive proximal skeletal muscle weakness and wasting, calf pseudohypertrophy, a positive Gowers sign, and loss of ambulation typically in adolescence, with cardiopulmonary complications as major causes of morbidity and mortality.

dystrophin.definition: A large cytoskeletal protein that links actin filaments to the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex in the sarcolemma, stabilizing the muscle cell membrane during contraction; mutations in the DMD gene cause Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy.

dystrophic.definition: Relating to dystrophy; describing tissue degeneration or wasting due to abnormal development or loss of function, often progressive.

dysregulation.definition: Impaired regulation of a biological system or process, resulting in instability or inappropriate responses; commonly used to describe dysregulation of immune, endocrine, autonomic, or emotional processes.

affective disorders.definition: Affective disorders are psychiatric conditions characterized by disturbances of mood (affect), including depressive, manic, or hypomanic episodes, such as major depressive disorder and bipolar disorder.

dysrhythmia.definition: A disorder of the heart's electrical activity causing an abnormal heart rhythm or rate, which may be irregular, too fast (tachyarrhythmia), or too slow (bradyarrhythmia), and can range from benign to life-threatening.

dyssebacea.definition: Abnormal function of the sebaceous glands causing altered sebum production and related skin changes (e.g., oily or dry skin and acne).

dyssynergia.definition: A loss or impairment of coordinated muscle activity; discoordination between muscles that normally contract and relax together (e.g., pelvic floor/anal sphincters during defecation or detrusor and external sphincter during urination).

dystaxia.definition: Impaired or abnormal coordination of voluntary movements, resulting in clumsiness and lack of smooth, precise motor control, often due to cerebellar or proprioceptive dysfunction.

dysthymia.definition: A chronic depressive disorder characterized by a depressed mood most of the day, for most days, for at least 2 years in adults (1 year in children), with at least two accompanying symptoms such as poor appetite or overeating, insomnia or hypersomnia, low energy, low self-esteem, poor concentration, or feelings of hopelessness; the symptoms are milder than major depressive episodes but persistent and impair functioning.

dysthymic disorder.definition: A chronic mood disorder with a depressed mood most of the day for most days, lasting at least 2 years in adults (1 year in children/adolescents), plus at least two additional symptoms of major depressive disorder; typically milder than major depression but persistent and may include episodes of major depressive disorder (double depression).

dysthyroid orbitopathy.definition: An autoimmune inflammatory disorder of the orbit associated with Graves disease, characterized by inflammation and enlargement of orbital tissues and extraocular muscles, leading to proptosis, diplopia, lid retraction, and exposure keratopathy.

graves' disease.definition: An autoimmune thyroid disorder in which autoantibodies stimulate the TSH receptor, causing excess thyroid hormone production (hyperthyroidism) and typically diffuse goiter, often with ophthalmopathy and occasionally pretibial myxedema; management includes antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine, or thyroidectomy.

dystonia musculorum deformans.definition: A form of dystonia characterized by sustained, involuntary muscle contractions that produce twisting and abnormal postures, typically starting in childhood and often progressing; falls within the spectrum of early-onset generalized (torsion) dystonia.

autosomal dominant.definition: A pattern of inheritance in which a single pathogenic allele on an autosome is sufficient to produce the phenotype; affected individuals typically have an affected parent, and each child has a 50% chance of inheriting the condition; males and females are affected in equal proportions.

muscle-relaxing drugs.definition: Medications that reduce skeletal muscle tone and spasms, used to relieve acute musculoskeletal pain and chronic spasticity from neurological conditions. They act centrally to depress CNS activity (e.g., baclofen, tizanidine, cyclobenzaprine) or directly on muscle (e.g., dantrolene); botulinum toxin provides focal relaxation when injected.

dystonic.definition: Relating to dystonia; describing or causing involuntary, sustained or intermittent muscle contractions that produce twisting movements or abnormal postures.

dystrophic calcification.definition: Deposition of calcium salts in necrotic or degenerated tissues in the setting of normal serum calcium and phosphate levels, typically at sites of tissue injury such as infarcts, atherosclerotic plaques, or granulomas.

vitreous.definition: A clear, gel-like substance that fills the vitreous chamber of the eye, occupying most of the globe's volume. It is avascular and consists of a collagen–hyaluronan matrix that helps maintain the retina's position against the choroid and transmits light; with aging it can liquefy (syneresis) leading to floaters or posterior vitreous detachment.

eales' disease.definition: An idiopathic inflammatory occlusive retinal vasculopathy of young adults characterized by peripheral retinal vasculitis with areas of nonperfusion, progressive retinal neovascularization, and recurrent vitreous hemorrhages, often bilateral and without systemic involvement.

east african sleeping sickness.definition: A form of human African trypanosomiasis caused by Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense transmitted by tsetse flies in East Africa; it presents with an acute febrile illness and lymphadenopathy and can rapidly progress to central nervous system involvement with sleep disturbances and neuropsychiatric symptoms if untreated.

eating disorders.definition: A group of psychiatric disorders characterized by disordered eating patterns and preoccupation with body weight or shape that impair physical health, psychological well-being, and functioning; includes anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, and binge-eating disorder, along with other specified feeding or eating disorders.

bulimia nervosa.definition: An eating disorder defined by recurrent binge-eating episodes followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviors (such as self-induced vomiting, laxative misuse, fasting, or excessive exercise) to prevent weight gain, accompanied by an undue emphasis on body weight or shape in self-evaluation.

binge eating.definition: Recurrent episodes of eating an unusually large amount of food in a short period (e.g., within 2 hours) with a sense of loss of control, often followed by distress or guilt, and not regularly followed by compensatory behaviors such as purging.

ecc.definition:
Early Childhood Caries: a pattern of tooth decay in children under 6 years, defined by decayed, missing, or filled primary teeth; risk factors include frequent sugary exposures and inadequate oral hygiene.

Emergency Cardiovascular Care: guidelines and training for resuscitation, including CPR, defibrillation, airway management, and post-arrest care.

early childhood caries.definition: When the teeth of young children get holes in them. Also called ECC.

dental caries.definition: Holes in your teeth. Also called cavities or tooth decay.

bottle mouth caries.definition: A form of early childhood caries caused by prolonged nocturnal exposure of young children's teeth to fermentable carbohydrates in bottle contents (often milk or juice), leading to rapid decay of the maxillary incisors and other primary teeth.

streptococcus mutans.definition: A Gram-positive, facultatively anaerobic bacterium that is a primary etiologic agent of dental caries; it colonizes tooth surfaces in dental plaque and ferments fermentable sugars to lactic acid, leading to enamel demineralization.

pica.definition: Eating something that is not food, like dirt or clay.

oral cavity.definition: The entry portion of the digestive tract (the mouth), bounded anteriorly by the lips and cheeks and posteriorly by the oropharynx, containing the teeth, gums, tongue, and hard and soft palate; it functions in ingestion, chewing, swallowing, speech, and taste.

mycoplasma pneumonia.definition: An atypical pneumonia caused by a small, cell-wall–deficient bacterium; typically affects adolescents and young adults and presents with gradual fever, malaise, sore throat, and a persistent dry cough. Chest imaging often shows patchy interstitial infiltrates. Transmitted by respiratory droplets; diagnosed by serology or PCR; treated with macrolide antibiotics (e.g., azithromycin) or doxycycline; usually mild and self-limited.

eaton agent pneumonia.definition: There is no recognized medical term "Eaton agent pneumonia." Could you check the spelling or provide more context (e.g., related symptoms, organism, or associated condition)? If you meant a different term (for example, Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, a paraneoplastic autoimmune disorder often linked to small cell lung cancer), I can provide a concise definition.

eaton-lambert syndrome.definition: An autoimmune presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder caused by antibodies against P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels, leading to reduced acetylcholine release and proximal muscle weakness with autonomic symptoms; commonly associated with small cell lung cancer, and characterized by strength improvement with continued use (facilitation) and an incremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation.

ebola hemorrhagic fever.definition: A viral hemorrhagic fever caused by Ebola virus (a member of the Filoviridae family). It typically begins with abrupt fever, malaise, myalgias, and headache, followed by gastrointestinal symptoms and, in severe cases, hemorrhagic manifestations; transmission occurs through contact with infected bodily fluids or contaminated objects, and fruit bats are suspected natural reservoirs.

marburg virus disease.definition: A severe, often fatal hemorrhagic fever caused by a filovirus transmitted to humans from fruit bats and through contact with infected bodily fluids or contaminated materials. Incubation is typically 2–21 days; early symptoms include fever, malaise, and headache, with progression to vomiting, diarrhea, rash, organ dysfunction, and bleeding; management is supportive, and there is no widely available specific antiviral therapy or approved vaccine.

ebv.definition: A double-stranded DNA herpesvirus that infects B lymphocytes and epithelial cells; spread mainly via saliva; etiologic agent of infectious mononucleosis and associated with various malignancies such as Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease.

ebstein's anomaly.definition: A congenital heart defect in which the septal and posterior leaflets of the tricuspid valve are displaced toward the apex, producing atrialization of part of the right ventricle and significant tricuspid regurgitation with an enlarged right atrium and a small functional right ventricle.

ebp.definition: A systematic approach to clinical decision-making that combines the best available research evidence with clinical expertise and patient preferences to improve patient outcomes.

ebner's glands.definition: Small, purely serous minor salivary glands located in the submucosa at the base of the tongue around the circumvallate (and nearby foliate) papillae; they secrete a watery serous fluid containing lingual lipase that cleanses the taste bud area and aids initial fat digestion.

eccentric contraction.definition: A type of muscle contraction in which the muscle lengthens while contracting, producing force as it controls or decelerates a movement (e.g., lowering a weight); opposite of a concentric contraction.

eccentric exercise.definition: A form of resistance training in which the muscle produces force while lengthening under load (eccentric contraction), such as the lowering phase of a movement; it is effective for increasing strength and promoting tendon adaptation.

eccentric implantation.definition: An implantation occurring off-center relative to the intended central location or axis of the structure involved.

ear.definition: The organ of hearing and balance in humans and many animals, comprising the outer, middle, and inner structures; it collects sound waves, converts them into neural signals, and helps maintain equilibrium.

earache.definition: Pain in one or both ears (otalgia) that may be caused by inflammation or infection of the ear or surrounding structures, most commonly otitis media or otitis externa, but also by earwax blockage, sinus or dental problems, TMJ disorders, or referred pain; evaluation is recommended to determine the cause and appropriate treatment.

otodynia.definition: Pain in the ear, a common symptom caused by local ear disorders such as infections, wax buildup, or a perforated eardrum, and sometimes by referred pain from nearby structures such as the jaw or throat.

eardrops.definition: A liquid preparation applied into the ear canal to treat or prevent ear conditions; formulations may include antibiotics, antifungals, corticosteroids, analgesics, or ceruminolytic agents, and are used for otitis externa, otitis media, or cerumen removal.

ear speculum.definition: An otoscopic instrument—typically a funnel-shaped tip used with an otoscope to dilate the external auditory canal and allow visualization of the tympanic membrane during ear examination.

otoscope.definition: A handheld instrument with a light and magnifying lens used to examine the ear canal and tympanic membrane (eardrum).

eardrum.definition: Thin, cone-shaped membrane that separates the external auditory canal from the middle ear; it vibrates in response to sound waves and transmits those vibrations to the auditory ossicles, enabling hearing, while also protecting the middle ear and helping maintain air-pressure balance.

ear oximeter.definition: A noninvasive sensor placed on the ear (typically the earlobe) that estimates arterial oxygen saturation (SpO2) and pulse rate by emitting light and detecting its absorption.

ear thermometry.definition: Measurement of body temperature by inserting an ear (tympanic) thermometer into the ear canal, which detects infrared energy from the tympanic membrane to estimate core temperature.

tympanic membrane thermometer.definition: A device that measures core body temperature by detecting infrared radiation from the tympanic membrane (eardrum) through the ear canal; commonly called an infrared ear thermometer.

vestibular apparatus.definition: The inner-ear sensory system responsible for balance and spatial orientation; it includes the vestibule (utricle and saccule) and the three semicircular canals, whose hair cells transduce linear and angular head movements into neural signals conveyed by the vestibular nerve.

x-ray pelvimetry.definition: Radiographic assessment of the maternal pelvis where X-ray images are used to measure pelvic dimensions (eg, obstetric/conjugate diameters, inlet and outlet) to estimate the risk of cephalopelvic disproportion and the likelihood of vaginal delivery; involves ionizing radiation and is largely obsolete in modern obstetric practice.

fetal presentation.definition: The part of the fetus that enters the birth canal first during labor, determined by fetal position; common presentations are cephalic (head first), breech (buttocks or feet first), or shoulder.

ophthalmopathy.definition: A disease of the eye or orbit; in clinical practice, commonly denotes inflammatory or autoimmune involvement of orbital tissues, most notably Graves’ ophthalmopathy (thyroid eye disease).

orbitopathy.definition: Inflammation and/or enlargement of the tissues within the eye socket (orbit), particularly the extraocular muscles and orbital fat, often referring to Graves' ophthalmopathy (thyroid-associated orbitopathy); may cause eyeball protrusion, eyelid retraction, diplopia, and, in severe cases, optic neuropathy.

circumvallate papillae.definition: A row of large, dome-shaped lingual papillae on the dorsum of the tongue, located just anterior to the sulcus terminalis and arranged in an inverted V; each is surrounded by a trench (moat) containing taste buds on its lateral walls and drained by von Ebner's glands.

sarcolemma.definition: A membrane that covers the muscle fiber and ties the end of it to a tendon.

sarcoglycans.definition: A family of single-pass transmembrane glycoproteins that are components of the dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex at the muscle cell membrane, linking the cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix; mutations in sarcoglycan genes cause limb-girdle muscular dystrophies.

dystroglycans.definition: A family of transmembrane glycoproteins that are part of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex, linking the extracellular matrix to the cytoskeleton. It includes alpha-dystroglycan, an extracellular, heavily glycosylated receptor that binds laminin and other ECM ligands, and beta-dystroglycan, a membrane-spanning partner that associates with dystrophin.

sarcospan.definition: A small, four-pass (tetraspanin-like) transmembrane protein that is a component of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex in skeletal and cardiac muscle; it links the cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix at the sarcolemma and helps stabilize the DGC.

syntrophins.definition: A family of PDZ-domain–containing cytoplasmic adaptor proteins that bind the dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex and scaffold signaling molecules (including ion channels and nitric oxide synthase) at the plasma membrane.

dystrobrevin.definition: A protein component of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex in muscle that acts as an adaptor linking the actin cytoskeleton to the sarcolemma and extracellular matrix; exists as alpha- and beta-dystrobrevin isoforms and interacts with dystrophin and syntrophins to help stabilize membranes and participate in signaling.

actin cytoskeleton.definition: A dynamic network of actin filaments (F-actin) beneath the plasma membrane that provides structural support and shape, generates contractile forces, and drives cell movement, division, and intracellular trafficking through regulated polymerization/depolymerization and interactions with actin-binding proteins and myosin.

extracellular matrix.definition: A complex network of proteins and polysaccharides outside cells in tissues, composed mainly of collagen, elastin, proteoglycans with glycosaminoglycans, and glycoproteins. It provides structural support, forms a hydrated gel, and regulates cell adhesion, migration, proliferation, and differentiation; it is continually remodeled by enzymes such as matrix metalloproteinases.

ecchondrosis.definition: A degenerative disorder of cartilage, especially articular cartilage, in which the cartilage becomes softened and roughened, leading to fissures, loss of smooth joint surfaces, and possible pain and reduced mobility.

ecchymoma.definition: A subcutaneous hematoma (bruise) from trauma, in which blood leaks from ruptured vessels into surrounding tissue, producing discoloration of the skin that changes color as it resolves.

ecchymotic.definition: Relating to ecchymosis; characterized by skin bruising due to subcutaneous bleeding, typically appearing as purplish patches.

eccrine gland.definition: A type of sweat gland that is a simple coiled tubular gland distributed over most of the body; it secretes a watery, relatively odorless sweat directly onto the skin surface through a pore, mainly for thermoregulation, and is innervated by sympathetic cholinergic nerves, producing a hypotonic secretion with electrolytes.

exocrine.definition: Relating to glands that secrete their products through ducts onto an epithelial surface or into a body cavity, rather than into the bloodstream.

echoencephalogram.definition: A diagnostic imaging technique in which ultrasound waves are transmitted through the skull to visualize intracranial structures, primarily to assess ventricular size and midline shift; largely supplanted by CT and MRI.

echoencephalography.definition: An imaging test that uses ultrasound to visualize intracranial structures by transmitting high‑frequency sound waves through the skull (often via an open fontanelle in infants) and recording echoes to assess ventricular size and midline shift; largely supplanted by CT and MRI.

echoencephalographic.definition: A diagnostic imaging method using ultrasound to visualize brain structures and estimate ventricular size by measuring echoes, historically used to detect hydrocephalus and midline brain shifts (often performed through the skull or fontanelle in infants; now largely replaced by CT/MRI).

echoplanar imaging.definition: A rapid MRI technique that acquires almost all of k-space after a single RF excitation by rapidly switching gradients to generate a train of gradient echoes, enabling very fast image acquisition. It is widely used for functional MRI and diffusion imaging due to high temporal resolution, but it is susceptible to geometric distortion and susceptibility artifacts.

echo-planar imaging.definition: A rapid MRI sequence that collects most or all k-space data in a single shot (or a few shots) after one excitation using a fast gradient-echo readout, enabling fast imaging such as functional MRI and diffusion MRI but with high susceptibility- and distortion-related artifacts.

echopraxia.definition: Involuntary, automatic imitation of another's movements or actions, occurring without conscious intent; the motor equivalent of echolalia, often seen in certain psychiatric or neurological conditions such as schizophrenia, catatonia, or frontal lobe disorders.

echoradiography.definition: A noninvasive imaging modality that uses high-frequency sound waves (ultrasound) to visualize internal organs and tissues in real time; when used for the heart, it is specifically called echocardiography.

echovirus.definition: A group of non-polio enteroviruses (genus Enterovirus, family Picornaviridae) that are positive-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses with multiple serotypes (historically echoviruses 1–9 and 11–27). They commonly cause aseptic meningitis, febrile illness, gastroenteritis, and occasionally myocarditis or other focal infections; transmission is primarily via the fecal–oral and respiratory routes.

echinacea.definition: A genus of North American flowering plants in the daisy family (Asteraceae); used in herbal medicine to support immune function and to treat or prevent colds, though clinical evidence of benefit is limited and some individuals may have allergic reactions or interact with certain medications.

echinococcus.definition: A genus of small tapeworms (cestodes) that cause echinococcosis in humans; species such as E. granulosus and E. multilocularis use canids as definitive hosts and form larval cysts (hydatid cysts) in the liver and lungs after ingesting eggs.

echinocyte.definition: A red blood cell with numerous evenly spaced projections (spicules) on its surface, giving a burr-like (crenated) appearance; seen in uremia, liver disease, electrolyte disturbances, certain anemias, and as a smear artifact; also called burr cell.

eclampsia.definition: A life-threatening complication of pregnancy characterized by new-onset generalized tonic-clonic seizures in a woman with preeclampsia (hypertension with proteinuria or signs of organ dysfunction), typically occurring in the third trimester or early postpartum, requiring urgent stabilization, magnesium sulfate, blood pressure control, and prompt delivery.

erythema chronicum migrans.definition: An expanding, ring-shaped red rash at the site of a Borrelia burgdorferi tick bite and the hallmark early cutaneous manifestation of Lyme disease; it often shows central clearing, may be warm to touch, and is typically treated with doxycycline or amoxicillin.

ecm.definition: An extracellular network of macromolecules secreted by cells that forms a scaffold outside the cell, providing structural support to tissues and regulating cell adhesion, migration, proliferation, and differentiation; components include collagen, elastin, proteoglycans, and glycoproteins.

ectasia.definition: An abnormal dilation or distention of a hollow organ, vessel, or duct, resulting from stretching or weakening of its wall; enlargement beyond normal size.

esophagectasia.definition: Dilation or enlargement of the esophagus; a radiologic or anatomic finding that can occur with esophageal obstruction or motility disorders, and is not a disease in itself.

lymphectasia.definition: Dilation or distension of lymphatic vessels; enlargement of lymphatic channels, often due to obstruction or congenital malformation.

pharyngectasia.definition: Abnormal dilation or enlargement of the pharynx (the muscular tube behind the nasal and oral cavities that leads to the esophagus and larynx).

esophageal varices.definition: Enlarged submucosal veins in the lower esophagus due to portal hypertension (most commonly from cirrhosis), which can rupture and cause life-threatening upper GI bleeding.

eck's fistula.definition: I can’t locate a standard medical definition for this term in reputable dictionaries. Please verify the spelling or provide context (anatomical site or condition) so I can give an accurate definition. In general, a fistula is an abnormal, epithelial-lined tract that connects two surfaces (e.g., organ to skin or between two organs), often due to inflammation, infection, or trauma.

ectodermal.definition: Relating to the ectoderm, the outermost embryonic germ layer; it gives rise to the epidermis and nervous system.

ectodermoid.definition: Of or derived from the ectoderm; resembling ectodermal tissue in origin or histology.

ectomorph.definition: A body type in the somatotype framework characterized by a slender, linear physique with a narrow frame, small bone structure, low body fat, and a tendency to have difficulty gaining weight or muscle.

hydatid disease.definition: Parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of Echinococcus tapeworms (most commonly E. granulosus) that forms hydatid cysts in organs such as the liver and lungs; acquired by ingesting eggs from infected canids, and treated with surgery or percutaneous drainage and antiparasitic therapy (e.g., albendazole).

hydatidosis.definition: A zoonotic parasitic disease caused by larval infection with Echinococcus tapeworms (most often E. granulosus), characterized by development of hydatid cysts in organs—primarily the liver and lungs—in humans who ingest eggs shed in the feces of definitive hosts; cysts can grow slowly and rupture, causing complications, and treatment includes surgery or percutaneous drainage and antiparasitic therapy (e.g., albendazole).

benzimidazole.definition: A bicyclic heteroaromatic compound formed by fusion of a benzene ring with an imidazole ring; a common pharmacophore scaffold in medicinal chemistry.

puncture.definition: A wound or opening produced by piercing with a sharp instrument, creating a tract through tissue; can be intentional (e.g., needle puncture) or accidental.

reaspiration.definition: The act of performing an aspiration again; a second attempt to withdraw fluid, air, or tissue from a body cavity or lesion using suction (e.g., with a needle, catheter, or syringe).

petechial hemorrhages.definition: Small (usually <2 mm) nonblanching capillary hemorrhages in the skin or mucous membranes caused by extravasation of blood from dermal capillaries; commonly seen with thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction, vasculitis, infection, or trauma.

retinal detachment.definition: When part of your eye pulls away from its normal position.

lens opacity.definition: Opacity of the crystalline lens causing decreased vision and glare; most commonly age-related (cataract) but can be congenital or due to trauma, inflammation, or systemic diseases; treatment is surgical removal of the cloudy lens.

iritis.definition: Inflammation of the iris (the colored part of the eye), a form of anterior uveitis. It typically presents with a red, painful, light-sensitive eye and blurred vision; treatment usually involves topical corticosteroid eye drops and pupil-dilating (cycloplegic) drops under medical supervision, with evaluation for underlying causes as needed.

uveitis.definition: Inflammation of the pigmented part of the eye (the iris); may seriously affect vision.

retinal hemorrhages.definition: Bleeding from retinal vessels into the retinal tissue, seen as red to dark patches on fundoscopic exam; typically seen as dot-and-blot (intraretinal) or flame-shaped hemorrhages, and associated with retinal vascular diseases, hypertension, diabetes, vein occlusions, trauma, or hematologic disorders.
