hypofibrinogenemia.definition: A reduced level of fibrinogen (factor I) in the blood, leading to impaired formation of a stable fibrin clot and increased bleeding risk; can be congenital or acquired (e.g., DIC, liver disease, massive transfusion), with plasma fibrinogen below the normal reference range (often <150–200 mg/dL).

midline structures.definition: Structures located along the body’s midline—the sagittal plane that divides the body into left and right halves—or centrally positioned anatomical elements.

atrial tumors.definition: Neoplasms arising in the atrial chambers of the heart; they can be primary (most commonly benign atrial myxomas, often in the left atrium) or malignant, and may cause obstruction to blood flow, embolic events, arrhythmias, or constitutional symptoms.

prosthetic valve.definition: A surgically implanted artificial heart valve used to replace a diseased native valve, restoring unidirectional blood flow; it can be mechanical (durable) or bioprosthetic (tissue).

valve function.definition: Regulates fluid flow by opening to permit forward movement and closing to prevent backflow, thereby maintaining unidirectional flow and appropriate pressure within a conduit (e.g., the heart, vessels, or airways).

ventricular septum.definition: The wall between the left and right ventricles of the heart, consisting of a muscular portion and a small membranous portion, that separates the two ventricular chambers and prevents mixing of blood between them.

ventricular chambers.definition: The two lower chambers of the heart (the right and left ventricles) that receive blood from the atria and pump it out of the heart: the right ventricle sends deoxygenated blood to the lungs via the pulmonary artery, and the left ventricle sends oxygenated blood to the body via the aorta. The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall than the right.

pregnancy-induced hypertension.definition: A new-onset elevation of blood pressure arising after about 20 weeks' gestation in a previously normotensive pregnant person, typically defined as systolic ≥140 mmHg or diastolic ≥90 mmHg on two occasions, without proteinuria or other features of preeclampsia (and may progress to preeclampsia if proteinuria or organ dysfunction develops).

magnesium sulfate.definition: A chemical salt of magnesium and sulfate (MgSO4). In medicine, it is used as an electrolyte supplement to treat magnesium deficiency, as an osmotic laxative (oral), and, when given intravenously, to prevent seizures in preeclampsia/eclampsia and to treat certain arrhythmias such as torsades de pointes.

antihypertensive medications.definition: Drugs used to lower blood pressure in individuals with hypertension, by decreasing plasma volume, dilating systemic arteries, or reducing cardiac output; major classes include diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers, alpha-blockers, and vasodilators.

parenteral administration.definition: Administration of a substance by routes other than the alimentary tract, most commonly by injection through the skin or mucous membranes (e.g., intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous, intradermal). It is used when oral administration is ineffective or contraindicated or when rapid systemic effect is required.

echolalia.definition: The automatic repetition of words or phrases heard from others, either immediately after hearing them or after a delay; often seen in autism spectrum disorder and other neurological conditions, and can be nonfunctional or, in some cases, serve communicative purposes.

echo speech.definition: A phenomenon in which a person involuntarily repeats words or phrases spoken by others, either immediately after hearing them or after a delay; commonly seen in autism spectrum disorders, certain language disorders, dementia, and after brain injury.

scotoma.definition: A blank spot in the visual field that is sometimes evident during the aura of a migraine headache.

solar maculopathy.definition: A form of retinal injury from direct solar exposure causing photochemical damage to the photoreceptors and retinal pigment epithelium in the fovea, leading to impaired central vision and metamorphopsia; typically occurs after sun-gazing or viewing a solar eclipse, and recovery may occur over weeks to months with variable outcome.

solar retinopathy.definition: Photochemical injury to the retina, typically the macula, caused by direct solar exposure (e.g., during a solar eclipse), resulting in acute, painless central vision loss and often permanent macular defects due to damage to the outer retina and retinal pigment epithelium.

echothiophate iodide.definition: An organophosphate acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used topically in the eye to induce miosis (pupil constriction) by increasing acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors; long-acting agent formerly used to treat chronic open-angle glaucoma to improve aqueous humor outflow.

lobectomy.definition: An operation to remove one lobe of an organ, most commonly a lobe of the lung, to treat cancer or localized disease; can be performed via open surgery or minimally invasive approaches (VATS/robotic).

ectrosyndactyly.definition: Congenital limb malformation in which digits are missing or severely underdeveloped (split-hand/foot) with fusion or webbing of adjacent digits (syndactyly), often seen in ectodermal dysplasia–related syndromes.

ectrosyndactylia.definition: Not a standard medical term; no definition found in major dictionaries. It may be a misspelling of ectrodactyly, a congenital limb malformation with missing or underdeveloped central digits giving a lobster-claw appearance, often with syndactyly and sometimes seen in ectodermal dysplasia syndromes (e.g., EEC syndrome).

ectoparasite.definition: A parasite that lives on the exterior of the host (skin, fur, or feathers) and derives nutrients from the host, typically by feeding on blood or tissue fluids.

ectopia.definition: Displacement or malposition of an organ or body part from its normal location, arising from congenital developmental anomaly or acquired factors.

extrasystole.definition: A premature heartbeat arising from an ectopic focus in the atria or ventricles, occurring earlier than the next expected beat and often followed by a pause; commonly benign but may be associated with cardiac disease or palpitations.

ectopic beat.definition: A premature heartbeat that originates from an ectopic focus outside the sinoatrial node, occurring earlier than the expected normal beat (e.g., a premature atrial contraction or premature ventricular contraction).

ectopic rhythm.definition: A cardiac rhythm that originates from an ectopic pacemaker outside the sinoatrial node (e.g., ectopic atrial, junctional, or ventricular rhythm) rather than the SA node.

ectopic tachycardia.definition: A tachycardia originating from an ectopic focus outside the sinoatrial node, typically arising in atrial or ventricular tissue and producing a rapid heart rate.

ectopic teratism.definition: A germ cell tumor located in an abnormal (extragonadal) site outside the ovaries or testes, typically containing tissues from more than one embryonic germ layer; it can be benign or malignant.

ectopic testis.definition: A testis located outside the scrotum in an abnormal position due to descent along an aberrant (ectopic) pathway, commonly in sites such as the perineum, thigh, pubic or suprapubic region.

ectopic kidney.definition: A congenital anomaly in which a kidney is located outside its normal position (most commonly in the pelvis) due to abnormal ascent during embryologic development; it may be asymptomatic or predispose to infection, obstruction, or hydronephrosis.

abdominal ectopic kidney.definition: A congenital anomaly in which a kidney resides in the abdomen instead of its normal retroperitoneal flank position, due to failure of ascent during embryologic development; often supplied by aberrant renal vessels and may be asymptomatic or associated with hydronephrosis, obstruction, stones, or infection.

lumbar ectopic kidney.definition: A kidney located in the lumbar (flank) region due to failed or incomplete ascent during embryologic development; a form of renal ectopia often with abnormal rotation and anomalous blood supply, and it may be asymptomatic but can be associated with obstruction, hydronephrosis, stones, or infections.

pelvic ectopic kidney.definition: A congenital kidney that fails to ascend from the pelvic region during fetal development and remains located in the pelvis, often with anomalous blood supply and potential for hydronephrosis or urinary tract complications.

thoracic ectopic kidney.definition: A congenital renal ectopia where the kidney lies in the thoracic cavity above the diaphragm, usually due to abnormal ascent or diaphragmatic development; often unilateral and asymptomatic with preserved function, commonly found incidentally on chest imaging; may be associated with diaphragmatic hernia or diaphragmatic eventration.

crossed fused ectopic kidneys.definition: A rare congenital anomaly in which both kidneys lie on the same side of the body and are fused, usually at the lower poles; the contralateral kidney may be absent or located on the same side. It results from abnormal ascent and fusion of the renal primordia during embryonic development and may be asymptomatic or present with hydronephrosis, infections, stones, or obstruction.

ectoplasm.definition: The clear, outer layer of cytoplasm in certain amoeboid cells, more gel-like and less granular than the inner endoplasm; it forms the cell cortex and pseudopods and participates in locomotion.

ectopy.definition: Displacement or presence of tissue or an organ outside its normal anatomical location; it can be congenital or acquired, with tissue functioning in an abnormal site (e.g., implantation outside the uterus in an ectopic pregnancy).

ectotoxin.definition: An externally released toxin produced by an organism (often secreted by bacteria) that harms the host, as opposed to endotoxins which are part of the organism’s cell structure and released upon lysis.

entropion.definition: An inward turning of the eyelid margin toward the eyeball (usually the lower lid), causing the eyelashes to rub against the cornea and conjunctiva with irritation and risk of corneal damage.

ectromelia.definition: A congenital limb reduction defect in which part of a limb is absent or underdeveloped, typically with the proximal portion present and a deficiency of distal segments.

hemimelia.definition: A congenital deficiency or absence of part of a limb on one side, resulting in partial absence or underdevelopment (hypoplasia) of the bones on that limb segment.

phocomelia.definition: A congenital limb malformation in which the proximal segments of one or more limbs are absent or underdeveloped, causing the hands or feet to attach close to the trunk (often with a flipper-like appearance).

ectromelus.definition: A congenital limb malformation involving partial or complete absence or severe underdevelopment of a limb, present at birth.

ectodermal dysplasia-clefting syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal-dominant genetic syndrome characterized by ectodermal dysplasia features (such as hypohidrosis, hypodontia or anodontia, sparse hair, and nail anomalies), ectrodactyly (split hand/foot malformation), and cleft lip and/or palate, most commonly due to TP63 gene mutations.

eec syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal-dominant genetic syndrome defined by the triad of ectrodactyly (split-hand/foot malformation), ectodermal dysplasia (affecting hair, teeth, nails, and sweat glands), and orofacial clefts (cleft lip and/or palate), usually due to TP63 gene mutations.

ectrogenic.definition: Not a standard medical term; used to denote a factor or condition arising from outside the body (exogenous) rather than from within the organism.

ectrogeny.definition: The development of an organism, especially a fetus, outside the parent's body, typically in an artificial gestational environment.

ectrogenic teratism.definition: A process by which congenital malformations are produced by external (exogenous) factors acting on the developing embryo during gestation (teratogenesis due to exogenous agents such as drugs, infections, or chemicals).

dextrocardia.definition: A congenital condition in which the heart is located on the right side of the chest; it may occur in isolation or as part of situs inversus, where the thoracic and abdominal organs are mirrored.

palatine teeth.definition: An obsolete or nonstandard term that may refer to the upper (maxillary) teeth or to the palatal surfaces of teeth—the surfaces facing the palate.

sinus node.definition: A specialized group of heart cells in the right atrium that generate the electrical impulses that cause the heart muscle to contract. Also called the heart's natural pacemaker.

pacemaker catheter.definition: A temporary transvenous catheter equipped with an electrode at its tip that delivers electrical pacing to the heart to maintain heart rate, often used during emergencies or prior to permanent pacemaker implantation.

premature heartbeat.definition: An early heartbeat caused by ectopic electrical activity in the atria or ventricles; a premature atrial or ventricular contraction that interrupts the normal rhythm and is usually benign, though frequent episodes or symptoms may indicate an underlying condition.

paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.definition: An acquired clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder caused by somatic mutations in PIGA leading to deficiency of GPI-anchored proteins (CD55 and CD59) on red blood cells, resulting in complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinuria, and a high risk of thrombosis.

meningococcal infection.definition: An invasive infection caused by Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus) that typically presents as meningitis and/or meningococcemia; it can progress rapidly to septic shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation. It is transmitted via respiratory droplets, and prompt antibiotic treatment plus public health measures (including prophylaxis for close contacts) and vaccination can prevent disease.

eczema herpeticum.definition: An acute, widespread herpes simplex virus infection of skin that occurs on areas of eczema or atopic dermatitis, characterized by sudden eruption of painful vesicles that rupture to form punched-out erosions, often with fever and malaise; can be complicated by bacterial superinfection or systemic illness and is treated with antiviral therapy (eg, acyclovir), often intravenously in severe cases.

kaposi's varicelliform eruption.definition: A disseminated herpes simplex virus infection in individuals with preexisting skin barrier defects (most commonly atopic dermatitis), presenting as a widespread vesiculopustular eruption resembling varicella and often with fever; requires systemic antiviral therapy.

eczema marginatum.definition: An annular (ring-shaped) form of eczema characterized by well-defined circular plaques with inflamed, scaly margins and central clearing; a chronic, pruritic condition often classified as discoid (nummular) eczema.

eczematous.definition: Relating to eczema; describing dermatitis with itchy, inflamed, red, and often scaly skin.

eczopiclone.definition: A nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic used to treat insomnia; acts as a GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulator to promote sleep onset and maintenance. Typically taken orally at bedtime; common adverse effects include daytime drowsiness, dizziness, and a bitter or metallic taste; has potential for dependence and next-day impairment; commonly classified as a schedule IV controlled substance.

edrophonium test.definition: A diagnostic pharmacologic test for myasthenia gravis in which a short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor is administered to transiently increase acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction; a short-lived improvement in muscle strength supports the diagnosis.

hypercalcemic crisis.definition: A life-threatening manifestation of severe hypercalcemia, typically with serum calcium exceeding about 14 mg/dL (3.5 mmol/L), presenting with dehydration, neuropsychiatric changes, gastrointestinal symptoms, renal impairment, and possible cardiac arrhythmias; requires urgent hospitalization and rapid calcium-lowering therapy.

ventricular arrhythmia.definition: Abnormal heart rhythm that starts in the lower chambers of the heart; this rhythm disturbance can occur as a complication of a heart attack and impairs the heart's pumping ability.

edetate calcium disodium.definition: A calcium salt of EDTA used as a chelating agent to treat heavy metal poisoning (notably lead). It binds divalent and some trivalent metal ions to form water-soluble chelates excreted in urine; administered parenterally, with potential adverse effects including hypocalcemia and nephrotoxicity.

edta.definition: A chelating agent (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) that binds metal ions (especially Ca2+ and Mg2+); used medically in chelation therapy for heavy metal poisoning and in clinical labs as an anticoagulant in certain blood collection tubes, and widely used as a sequestrant/stabilizer in foods and cosmetics.

ethacrynic acid.definition: A loop diuretic that inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, increasing excretion of Na+, Cl−, K+, and water; used to treat edema and hypertension; non-sulfonamide, with potential ototoxicity.

edecrin.definition: A potent loop diuretic (ethacrynic acid) that inhibits the Na+-K+-2Cl− cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, increasing excretion of sodium, chloride, and water; used to treat edema from heart failure, liver cirrhosis, or kidney disease, especially in patients with sulfonamide allergy; may cause ototoxicity and electrolyte disturbances.

loop diuretic.definition: A diuretic that inhibits the Na+-K+-2Cl− cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, increasing excretion of sodium, chloride, and water; used to treat edema and hypertension; adverse effects include dehydration and hypokalemia.

ethylene dibromide.definition: A colorless, oily, highly toxic halogenated hydrocarbon (1,2-dibromoethane) formerly used as a soil fumigant and pesticide; exposure can cause gastrointestinal symptoms, neurologic effects, liver/kidney toxicity, and it is carcinogenic, with its use now heavily restricted or banned in many countries.

electrodynograph.definition: A recording method/instrument that measures the time-varying electrical activity of muscles or nerves during movement, used in electrodiagnostic assessments.

endothelial-derived relaxing factor.definition: Substance released by vascular endothelium that causes relaxation of adjacent smooth muscle and vasodilation; nitric oxide is the principal endothelium-derived relaxing factor, acting by activating soluble guanylate cyclase in smooth muscle to raise cyclic GMP.

nitric oxide.definition: A compound produced by the endothelium (the lining of the interior walls of arteries) that helps widen blood vessels and counteract high blood pressure. Also called endothelium-derived relaxing factor.

kidney damage.definition: Impaired structure or function of the kidneys that reduces their ability to filter waste from the blood and regulate fluids, electrolytes, and acid-base balance. It can be acute (sudden) or chronic (progressive) and results from injury, ischemia, infection, inflammation, toxins (nephrotoxic drugs or substances), or obstruction; signs include elevated serum creatinine, reduced glomerular filtration rate, proteinuria, edema, and electrolyte disturbances.

edema of glottis.definition: Swelling of the mucosa and vocal cords at the glottic opening of the larynx, narrowing the glottic aperture and potentially causing hoarseness and airway obstruction; commonly due to inflammation, infection, allergic reaction, trauma, or reflux.

laryngeal edema.definition: Swelling of the mucosa and submucosa of the larynx (voice box), usually from inflammation or fluid leakage, causing narrowing of the laryngeal airway and symptoms such as hoarseness, throat discomfort, stridor, and dyspnea; can result from infection, allergic reactions (angioedema), trauma, irritants, or reflux and may be life-threatening if airway obstruction develops.

varicosities.definition: A condition of dilated, tortuous superficial veins most often in the legs, arising from venous valve incompetence and increased venous pressure; commonly causes aching, swelling, heaviness, and cosmetic concerns, and may progress with chronic venous insufficiency.

edsall's disease.definition: Definition not found in standard medical references; it may be a misspelling or an obscure term. Please confirm the spelling or provide context (e.g., related symptoms or specialties) so I can help define the intended condition.

efferent nerve.definition: Nerve fibers that carry motor commands from the central nervous system to effectors such as muscles or glands; they conduct impulses away from the CNS and form the motor (efferent) pathway, in contrast to the sensory (afferent) pathway.

heat cramp.definition: A painful involuntary muscle spasm during or after strenuous exercise in hot environments, caused by dehydration and electrolyte depletion (primarily sodium); managed with rest, hydration with electrolytes, and gradual cooling.

ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid.definition: A hexadentate chelating agent that binds metal ions (especially Ca2+ and Mg2+), used medically for chelation therapy in heavy-metal poisoning and, in salt forms, as an anticoagulant in blood collection tubes.

edwards' syndrome.definition: Chromosomal disorder due to an extra copy of chromosome 18 (trisomy 18); characterized by multiple congenital malformations and severe intellectual disability, often with distinctive facial features, clenched hands with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, micrognathia, and heart/kidney anomalies. Most affected infants die within the first year of life.

trisomy 18.definition: An aneuploidy caused by an extra copy of chromosome 18, resulting in Edwards syndrome with multiple severe congenital anomalies and developmental delay; most affected neonates have low birth weight and growth restriction, characteristic facial features, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, and congenital heart defects; prognosis is poor, with high mortality in infancy.

hypopigmentation.definition: A reduction in skin color due to decreased melanin production or loss of melanocytes, resulting in lighter patches of skin.

scanty hair.definition: Sparse hair density; a descriptive finding of unusually low hair quantity or coverage in a region (e.g., the scalp), which can be a normal variant or associated with conditions causing hair loss such as alopecia, telogen effluvium, nutritional deficiencies, or endocrine disorders.

absence of lashes.definition: Loss or absence of eyelashes on the eyelids; may be partial or complete and can result from inflammatory, infectious, autoimmune, traumatic, or congenital factors, and is commonly seen with conditions like blepharitis or alopecia areata.

nail dysplasia.definition: Abnormal development or malformation of the nails, resulting in irregular nail plate growth, shape, thickness, or texture; it can be congenital or acquired and may occur as an isolated finding or as part of ectodermal or systemic disorders.

ectrodactyly-ectodermal-dysplasia-clefti.definition: An autosomal dominant genetic syndrome caused by TP63 mutations, characterized by ectrodactyly (split-hand/foot malformations), ectodermal dysplasia (hair, teeth, nails, and skin abnormalities), and orofacial clefting (lip/palate).

electroencephalograph.definition: A device that records the brain's electrical activity by placing electrodes on the scalp or directly on the brain surface, producing a continuous trace of brain waves for diagnostic and research purposes.

eelworm.definition: An informal term for slender, eel‑shaped nematodes (roundworms); used for various parasitic or free‑living nematodes, not a precise taxonomic group.

nematode.definition: A phylum of unsegmented, cylindrical roundworms with a pseudocoelom and a tough cuticle; they have a complete digestive tract and lack a circulatory system, including many free-living and parasitic species.

ears.definition: Pair of organs on the sides of the head responsible for hearing and balance; each ear includes an external ear that collects sound, a middle ear with the tympanic membrane and ossicles that transmit vibrations, and an inner ear (cochlea and vestibular apparatus) that converts sound to neural signals and helps maintain balance.

nose.definition: External organ on the face composed of bone and cartilage that conducts air to the nasal cavities, houses the olfactory system, and conditions inspired air by warming, humidifying, and filtering it; also contributes to voice resonance.

enterohemorrhagic escherichia coli.definition: Shiga toxin–producing Escherichia coli (EHEC or STEC), an enteric pathovar that causes hemorrhagic colitis and can lead to hemolytic uremic syndrome; commonly transmitted through contaminated food (notably undercooked ground beef), water, or person-to-person contact; management is supportive, and antibiotics are typically avoided.

ehec.definition: An enterohemorrhagic strain of Escherichia coli that produces Shiga toxin and can cause hemorrhagic colitis and hemolytic-uremic syndrome; usually acquired through consumption of contaminated food or water.

ehrlichia.definition: A genus of obligate intracellular, gram-negative bacteria in the family Anaplasmataceae, transmitted by ixodid ticks; causes a tick-borne rickettsial infection presenting with fever, headache, malaise, and sometimes leukopenia or thrombocytopenia; diagnosed by PCR or serology; treated with doxycycline.

ehrlichiosis.definition: Tick-borne bacterial infection caused by Ehrlichia species (most commonly Ehrlichia chaffeensis) presenting with fever, malaise, headache, and myalgias; leukopenia and thrombocytopenia are common; rash occurs variably; diagnosed by serology or PCR; treated with doxycycline.

ehrlichia chaffeensis.definition: A gram-negative, obligate intracellular bacterium of the genus Ehrlichia that causes human monocytic ehrlichiosis; transmitted by tick bites (notably the lone-star tick, Amblyomma americanum) and infects monocytes.

ehrlichia equi.definition: A Gram-negative, obligate intracellular bacterium of the Anaplasmataceae family that infects neutrophils and causes ehrlichiosis; historically known as Ehrlichia equi and now generally classified as Anaplasma phagocytophilum, the agent of granulocytic anaplasmosis transmitted by Ixodes ticks.

human monocytic ehrlichiosis.definition: A tick-borne bacterial infection caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis; presents with fever, headache, malaise, and myalgias, often with leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated liver enzymes; diagnosed by serology or PCR; treated with doxycycline.

human granulocytic ehrlichiosis.definition: A tick-borne bacterial infection caused by Anaplasma phagocytophilum that infects neutrophils; transmitted by Ixodes ticks; presents with fever, headache, myalgias, malaise, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated liver enzymes; historically known as human granulocytic ehrlichiosis.

egyptian ophthalmia.definition: A historical term for trachoma, a chronic contagious conjunctivitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, characterized by follicular conjunctival inflammation, scarring of the conjunctiva and cornea, and potential blindness; historically prevalent in Egypt.

electrohemodynamics.definition: The study of how electrical fields and currents interact with blood flow in the circulatory system, including the effects of electrical stimulation on hemodynamics.

effective half-life.definition: An effective half-life is the time required for the amount or activity of a radiopharmaceutical in the body to decline by half when both radioactive decay (physical half-life) and biological clearance act together. It is Teff = ln(2)/(λphys+λbiol) = 1/(1/Tphys + 1/Tbiol) = (Tphys × Tbiol)/(Tphys+Tbiol).

effective atomic number.definition: An energy-dependent estimate of the average atomic number of a material that characterizes its X-ray attenuation, used to compare tissues or contrast agents in medical imaging.

effective dose.definition: An index used in radiological protection to estimate the overall risk from ionizing radiation by summing, across all tissues, the tissue-weighted equivalent doses; the result is expressed in sieverts.

effective dose equivalent limit.definition: An exposure cap defined in terms of effective dose: the maximum average amount of ionizing radiation a person may receive in a given period, calculated by summing tissue-specific absorbed doses weighted by tissue sensitivity factors, and expressed in sieverts (or rem). It is used to limit stochastic health risks and varies by context (e.g., occupational vs. public).

effective compliance.definition: An overall measure of how easily a structure expands under pressure; the change in volume per unit pressure, reflecting the combined elastic properties of the tissue and any resistive constraints. In respiratory physiology, effective compliance represents the net distensibility of the lung–chest wall system and is often estimated as tidal volume divided by the driving pressure (for example, PIP minus PEEP or Pplat minus PEEP) during ventilation.

effective osmotic pressure.definition: The portion of osmotic pressure produced by impermeant (non-diffusible) solutes; it is the actual driving force for water movement across a semipermeable membrane, since permeant solutes equilibrate and do not sustain the gradient.

effective radiating area.definition: In diagnostic ultrasound, the portion of the transducer face that actively emits acoustic energy; the effective emitting aperture is usually smaller than the physical element size due to backing and damping, and it is used to estimate the beam area and acoustic intensity at a given depth, affecting lateral resolution.

effective refractory period.definition: The interval after an action potential during which a new stimulus cannot produce a propagating action potential; it ends when enough voltage-gated sodium channels have recovered to permit a propagated impulse.

effector.definition: A structure that executes a response to a stimulus, such as a muscle or gland in a reflex arc; in immunology, a cell that actively carries out an immune response (for example an effector T cell or effector B cell).

effector cell.definition: A mature immune cell that actively mediates the immune response by performing its effector functions—such as killing infected cells (cytotoxic T cells or NK cells), helping other immune cells (helper T cells), or secreting antibodies (plasma cells)—as opposed to naïve or memory lymphocytes.

efferent.definition: Carrying away from the center or from a specific structure; in neuroanatomy, describing motor pathways that transmit impulses from the central nervous system to muscles or glands.

efferent duct.definition: A duct (one of the ductuli efferentes) that carries sperm from the rete testis to the epididymis, reabsorbs most of the luminal fluid, and helps move sperm along.

efferent pathway.definition: A neural pathway that carries impulses away from the central nervous system to an effector organ (such as a muscle or gland); also called a motor pathway.

effleurage.definition: A massage technique involving light, slow gliding strokes over the skin, usually performed with the palms or fingertips to warm tissues, promote relaxation, and enhance venous and lymphatic circulation.

effusion.definition: An abnormal accumulation of fluid in a body cavity or tissue space, or leakage of fluid from vessels into surrounding tissues (e.g., pleural effusion, pericardial effusion).

effort syndrome.definition: An historical term for exertional angina: chest pain or discomfort caused by myocardial ischemia during physical activity, usually due to obstructive coronary artery disease, typically relieved by rest or nitroglycerin.

effort thrombosis.definition: An upper-extremity deep vein thrombosis precipitated by strenuous or repetitive arm activity, usually involving the subclavian or axillary vein; commonly known as Paget-Schroetter syndrome.

effraction.definition: A fracture; a traumatic disruption or break of a bone.

eglandulous.definition: Lacking glands; devoid of glandular tissue.

ego.definition: In psychoanalytic theory, the ego is the part of the psyche that mediates among the id's instinctual desires, the moral constraints of the superego, and external reality, operating on the reality principle to regulate judgment, planning, and problem-solving.

ego-dystonic.definition: Thoughts, impulses, or behaviors that are distressing and perceived as inconsistent with one’s self-concept or values; the person recognizes them as unwanted or foreign.

ego-dystonic homosexuality.definition: A historical, now-obsolete concept describing distress caused by one’s same-sex attractions that are inconsistent with self-image or values; it implied a psychiatric disorder, but contemporary psychiatry views sexual orientation as not a mental illness.

ego-alien.definition: A phenomenological description of experiences in which thoughts, impulses, or other aspects of the mental life are felt as external or not belonging to the self; a disturbance of selfhood commonly described in psychotic disorders (e.g., delusions of alien control or thought insertion).

ego-analysis.definition: A form of psychoanalytic therapy within ego psychology that emphasizes the ego’s adaptive, reality-testing functions—such as defense mechanisms, coping, and self-regulation—over drive-focused interpretation, with the goal of strengthening ego functioning and improving overall functioning.

ego boundary.definition: The psychological boundary that delineates the self from others, defining one’s thoughts, feelings, and identity and enabling autonomy and appropriate interpersonal distance. Healthy boundaries are flexible and clear; porous boundaries lead to enmeshment, while overly rigid boundaries lead to detachment.

egocentric.definition: Relating to or centered on the self; self-centered; in psychology, the inability to differentiate one's own perspective from that of others.

ego-defense mechanism.definition: A psychological strategy, often unconscious, by which the ego protects itself from anxiety and internal conflict by distorting or denying reality; common defense mechanisms include repression, denial, projection, rationalization, and displacement.

ego ideal.definition: A component of the superego in Freudian psychoanalysis representing the internalized ideal self; the set of standards for self-evaluation that one strives to attain, producing pride when met and guilt when not.

ego-integrity.definition: A late-life psychosocial state characterized by a sense of wholeness and fulfillment from one’s life, acceptance of past experiences, and readiness to face death; when not achieved, it may lead to despair.

egoism.definition: A self-centered tendency to prioritize one's own interests and needs over those of others; in psychology, related to egocentrism or narcissistic traits; not a specific medical diagnosis.

egoist.definition: A person who acts primarily in their own self-interest, prioritizing their own needs over those of others; in psychology, an egoist is someone with a self-centered orientation and motivation by personal gain rather than altruism. It is not a formal psychiatric diagnosis.

egotism.definition: Excessive preoccupation with oneself; self-centeredness and an inflated sense of one’s own importance or abilities; not a formal medical diagnosis but a personality trait or behavior pattern.

egotist.definition: A person who is excessively self-centered and preoccupied with their own interests and self-image; often vain and lacking consideration for others’ needs (narcissistic traits).

egotistic.definition: Characterized by an excessive focus on oneself and one's own needs or desires, often with little regard for others; self-centered or egocentric.

ego-libido.definition: Ego-libido is the portion of psychic energy (libido) that is invested in the ego, representing narcissistic or self‑focused energy used for self-preservation and self‑enhancement rather than directed toward external objects or relationships.

egomania.definition: A pathological preoccupation with oneself and one’s own importance, typically accompanied by grandiose fantasies, self-absorption, and a lack of empathy; historically used to describe extreme narcissistic or megalomaniacal traits but not a formal DSM-5 diagnosis.

egophony.definition: An abnormal auscultatory finding in which the spoken “ee” vowel is heard as an “ay” sound over a region of the chest, typically due to underlying lung consolidation such as lobar pneumonia or atelectasis.

ego strength.definition: The ego's capacity to regulate impulses, maintain reality testing, and cope with stress using adaptive defenses and mature coping strategies.

ego-syntonic.definition: Thoughts, impulses, or behaviors that are in harmony with a person’s self-concept and goals, perceived as acceptable and aligned with their identity, and not distressing or unwanted.

paget-schroetter's syndrome.definition: A primary upper-extremity deep vein thrombosis of the axillary or subclavian vein caused by thoracic outlet compression, typically occurring in young, physically active individuals after repetitive overhead activity (effort thrombosis).

trypanosoma brucei.definition: Flagellated protozoan parasite of the genus Trypanosoma; the causative agent of African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) in humans and nagana in animals, transmitted by the bite of an infected tsetse fly (Glossina spp.); subspecies such as T. b. gambiense and T. b. rhodesiense infect humans.

plaque psoriasis.definition: A common chronic autoimmune skin disease characterized by well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with silvery scales, most often on the elbows, knees, scalp, and trunk; may be itchy and can be associated with nail changes or psoriatic arthritis.

antiretroviral agents.definition: Medications used to treat HIV and other retroviral infections by inhibiting viral replication at multiple stages of the viral life cycle (entry, reverse transcription, integration, and maturation), typically given in combination as antiretroviral therapy to suppress viral load and prevent disease progression.

esophagogastroduodenoscopy.definition: A procedure using a flexible endoscope inserted through the mouth to visualize the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum, often with biopsies or therapeutic interventions.

epidermal growth factor.definition: An extracellular polypeptide growth factor that binds to the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) to stimulate cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival; it activates receptor tyrosine kinase signaling (e.g., MAPK/ERK, PI3K/AKT) and plays a key role in development and wound healing.

efudex.definition: Topical anticancer cream containing 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) used to treat actinic keratoses and some superficial skin cancers; it disrupts DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing skin cells, causing cell death and a local inflammatory reaction (redness, peeling, crusting).

electronic fetal monitor.definition: An electronic device used during pregnancy and labor to continuously record the fetal heart rate and uterine contractions, enabling assessment of fetal well-being and detection of potential distress.

electronic infusion device.definition: A programmable pump that delivers intravenous or other infusions at a controlled rate and volume, using electronic monitoring and alarms to ensure accurate dosing and detect occlusions, air, or pump malfunctions.

omega-3 fatty acid.definition: Omega-3 fatty acids are polyunsaturated fatty acids with the first double bond located at the third carbon from the end of the carbon chain (the omega end); key examples include alpha-linolenic acid (ALA), eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA).

eicosanoic acid.definition: A saturated long-chain fatty acid with 20 carbon atoms (C20:0); commonly known as arachidic acid.

arachidic acid.definition: A saturated long-chain fatty acid with 20 carbon atoms (C20:0); a straight-chain carboxylic acid found in some animal fats and plant waxes; chemical formula C20H40O2.

eicosapentaenoic acid.definition: A long-chain omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (20:5 n-3) derived mainly from fish oils; it modulates inflammation and is used as a dietary supplement to lower triglycerides and support cardiovascular health.

meningoencephalitic stage.definition: The late CNS-involved stage of African sleeping sickness (trypanosomiasis) in which Trypanosoma parasites invade the central nervous system, causing meningoencephalitis with sleep disturbances, neuropsychiatric changes, motor abnormalities, and progressive neurological decline; CSF often shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein, with detectable parasites.

costochondral junctions.definition: The joints between a rib and its costal cartilage; a primary (hyaline) cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis) that permits growth in children and allows only minimal movement in adults.

fractured ribs.definition: An injury in which one or more ribs are cracked or broken, typically from blunt chest trauma; presents with focal chest wall pain and tenderness that worsens with deep breathing or coughing, and may be complicated by pneumothorax or lung contusion; most fractures heal with conservative management over several weeks.

neurocirculatory asthenia.definition: An historical term for a functional syndrome of fatigue with autonomic (neurocirculatory) symptoms—such as tachycardia, palpitations, chest discomfort, shortness of breath, dizziness, and fainting—in the absence of identifiable cardiac disease; often regarded as neurasthenia or autonomic nervous system dysregulation.

cervical effacement.definition: Thinning and shortening of the cervix in preparation for labor, described as a percent effacement (0% to 100%), with 100% indicating a fully effaced, paper-thin cervix.

station.definition: An obstetric measure of how far the fetal presenting part has descended through the maternal pelvis during labor, expressed relative to the ischial spines (0 at the spinal level; negative values above; positive values below, typically −5 to +5).

vaginal examination.definition: A manual internal pelvic examination in which the clinician inserts one or more fingers into the vagina to palpate the cervix and pelvic organs (e.g., uterus, ovaries) to assess tenderness, size, position, and any masses; in pregnancy, to evaluate cervical dilation/effacement and fetal status.

congestive heart disease.definition: A chronic condition in which the heart's pumping action is insufficient to meet the body's needs, leading to congestion and fluid buildup in the lungs, abdomen, and legs, with symptoms such as shortness of breath, fatigue, and edema.

transudate.definition: An ultrafiltrate of plasma produced by noninflammatory disturbances of capillary filtration (e.g., increased hydrostatic pressure or decreased oncotic pressure), resulting in fluid with low protein content and few cells; seen in edema and effusions from conditions such as congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, and nephrotic syndrome.

eighth cranial nerve.definition: A purely sensory cranial nerve (CN VIII) that transmits hearing information from the cochlea and balance information from the vestibular apparatus to the brain; composed of the cochlear and vestibular divisions and traveling through the internal acoustic meatus to the pontomedullary junction to connect with the cochlear and vestibular nuclei.

einthoven's formula.definition: An ECG relation stating that the three standard limb-lead potentials satisfy Lead II = Lead I + Lead III (i.e., Lead I plus Lead III equals Lead II), reflecting the geometry of the heart’s electrical axis (Einthoven’s triangle).

eisenmenger's complex.definition: A congenital heart defect with a long-standing large left-to-right shunt (most often VSD, PDA, or ASD) that leads to progressive pulmonary vascular remodeling and pulmonary hypertension, ultimately reversing the shunt to right-to-left with cyanosis and clubbing; the syndrome includes both the underlying defect and its secondary pulmonary vascular disease.

eisenmenger's syndrome.definition: An advanced complication of certain congenital heart defects with a long-standing left-to-right shunt (e.g., VSD, ASD, PDA) in which progressive remodeling of the pulmonary vasculature causes severe pulmonary hypertension that reverses the shunt to right-to-left, producing cyanosis, hypoxemia, and secondary polycythemia.

aortic root.definition: The portion of the aorta that originates at the left ventricular outflow tract and extends to the sinotubular junction; it includes the aortic valve annulus and cusps, the sinuses of Valsalva, and the origins of the coronary arteries.

ejection fraction.definition: The percentage of blood ejected from a ventricle (usually the left ventricle) with each heartbeat, calculated as (stroke volume / end-diastolic volume) × 100; normal range is about 55–70%, and a reduced value indicates impaired systolic function.

ejection murmur.definition: A systolic murmur caused by turbulent blood flow as the ventricle ejects blood through a semilunar valve or outflow tract; usually a crescendo-decrescendo murmur best heard at the right upper sternal border, sometimes radiating to the carotids (as in aortic stenosis) or to the left upper sternal border (as in pulmonic stenosis).

ejection period.definition: The portion of the cardiac cycle during which the ventricles actively eject blood into the aorta and pulmonary artery, from the opening to the closing of the semilunar valves.

ejection click.definition: A brief, high-pitched sound heard early in systole, produced by the sudden opening of a semilunar valve (usually aortic or pulmonic) and rapid cuspal separation; often seen with valvular stenosis or congenital valve abnormalities and best heard at the base of the heart.

ejection sound.definition: A brief, high-pitched extra heart sound heard in early systole, produced by the abrupt opening of a noncompliant semilunar valve (usually aortic or pulmonic) as blood is ejected into the outflow tract.

ekbom's syndrome.definition: A fixed, false belief of being infested with parasites on the skin despite normal medical evaluation, often with tactile sensations of crawling (formication) and self-inflicted skin lesions; considered a somatic delusional disorder and typically treated with antipsychotic therapy and psychiatric evaluation.

restless legs syndrome.definition: Achy or unpleasant feelings in the legs associated with a need to move. Most prominent at night, making it hard to fall asleep or stay asleep.

ekc.definition:
- A highly contagious infection of the eye caused by adenovirus, affecting the conjunctiva (and sometimes the cornea), with redness, tearing, and discharge; outbreaks occur in communities; typically managed with supportive care and ophthalmology consultation if vision is affected.

- A chronic inflammatory skin condition with itchy, red, scaly patches, often on flexural areas; managed with regular moisturizers and topical anti-inflammatory therapy.

epidemic keratoconjunctivitis.definition: An acute, highly contagious conjunctival infection caused by adenoviruses, marked by red eye with mucopurulent discharge, tearing, foreign‑body sensation, and sometimes preauricular lymphadenopathy, with possible keratopathy (subepithelial corneal infiltrates) that can occur in outbreaks and persist for weeks; management is supportive and focused on hygiene and symptom relief; no proven antiviral therapy.

ekg.definition: A test that records the electrical activity of the heart to measure heart rate and rhythm; also known as an electrocardiogram (ECG).

elapid.definition: A member of a family of venomous snakes that includes cobras, kraits, mambas, and sea snakes; they have front-fanged venom delivery and typically neurotoxic venom.

elaprase.definition: An enzyme replacement therapy consisting of recombinant human iduronate-2-sulfatase (IDS) used to treat mucopolysaccharidosis type II (Hunter syndrome) by replacing deficient lysosomal enzyme to degrade glycosaminoglycans (e.g., heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate); administered by intravenous infusion.

idursulfase.definition: A recombinant form of the human enzyme iduronate-2-sulfatase used as enzyme replacement therapy for mucopolysaccharidosis type II (Hunter syndrome).

elase.definition: Not a standard medical term. If you meant elastase, it is a serine protease that degrades elastin, produced by neutrophils and some bacteria, and plays a role in tissue remodeling and inflammatory damage.

elastase.definition: A serine protease that cleaves elastin, produced by neutrophils and pancreatic acinar cells; involved in tissue remodeling and inflammatory processes.

elastic-band fixation.definition: An orthopedic or surgical technique in which elastic bands are looped around tissue or bone fragments to hold them in proper alignment under continuous gentle traction, typically as a temporary measure to stabilize structures during healing or before definitive fixation.

elastic traction.definition: A method of applying a low, continuous pulling force to a limb or body part using elastic material (such as rubber bands or elastic cords) rather than rigid weights or pins, used to aid alignment or stabilization of fractures or dislocations.

elastin.definition: A highly elastic extracellular matrix protein that forms elastic fibers in connective tissue, enabling tissues to stretch and recoil; it is cross-linked by desmosine and isodesmosine and produced mainly by fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells.

elastofibroma.definition: Benign, slow-growing fibrous tumor of elastic tissue most commonly located beneath the inferior angle of the scapula; composed of thickened elastic fibers intermingled with collagen and fibroblasts. Typically affects elderly women and may be painful with shoulder movement or cause snapping/scapular motion; management ranges from observation to surgical excision if symptomatic.

elastomer.definition: A polymer with rubber-like elasticity that can undergo large reversible deformations and return to its original shape after stress; it is soft, viscoelastic, and commonly used in medical devices and components (such as silicone elastomers).

elastomeric.definition: Relating to elastomers; a rubbery polymer that can be stretched and then return to its original shape after removal of stress.

elastic stocking.definition: An elastic stocking is close-fitting hosiery that applies graduated compression to the leg to improve venous return, reduce edema, and help prevent venous thromboembolism; used for venous insufficiency, edema, and varicose veins, and contraindicated in significant peripheral arterial disease.

elastic tissue.definition: A type of connective tissue characterized by abundant elastic fibers (elastin) that allow tissues to stretch and recoil; commonly found in the dermis, walls of large arteries, lungs, and certain ligaments.

elastic recoil.definition: The tendency of the lungs to return to their resting volume after being stretched during inspiration, due to elastic fibers in the lung parenchyma and the surface tension of the alveolar lining; it drives passive expiration and is opposed by the outward recoil of the chest wall.

elastic cartilage.definition: A type of cartilage whose extracellular matrix contains a dense network of elastic fibers (with type II collagen), giving it flexible, resilient support; it contains chondrocytes in lacunae, is surrounded by perichondrium, and is found in structures requiring bending, such as the external ear (pinna) and epiglottis.

yellow cartilage.definition: A type of cartilage rich in elastic fibers (elastin) in its matrix, giving it a yellowish color and high elasticity; it provides flexible support and shape, found in structures such as the external ear (pinna) and the epiglottis.

white fibrocartilage.definition: A tough type of cartilage with a dense, collagen-rich extracellular matrix (predominantly type I) and chondrocytes in lacunae; it combines cartilage and dense connective tissue properties to resist compression, tension, and shear, and is found in load-bearing structures such as intervertebral discs, menisci, and the pubic symphysis. It typically appears white due to its collagen content and is relatively avascular, healing poorly.

elbow reflex.definition: An upper-limb deep tendon reflex elicited at the elbow, typically the triceps reflex, produced by tapping the triceps tendon near the olecranon to cause elbow extension; it assesses the integrity of the C7–C8 nerve roots and triceps motor neurons.

elbow jerk.definition: A deep tendon reflex elicited by tapping the triceps tendon just above the olecranon, causing contraction of the triceps with elbow extension; tests integrity of the C7–C8 nerve roots.

medial epicondyle.definition: A bony prominence on the medial side of the distal humerus at the elbow, where the common flexor tendon attaches; serves as the attachment site for forearm flexor muscles and as a landmark for the ulnar nerve.

elbow bone.definition: The long bone of the upper limb that extends from the shoulder to the elbow; it forms the elbow joint with the forearm bones (radius and ulna) at its distal end and serves as the main lever for arm movement.

elder abuse.definition: The intentional or neglectful harm, exploitation, or deprivation of an older adult by someone in a trusted relationship, resulting in physical, emotional, financial, or sexual harm or neglect.

elder abuse signs.definition: Physical, emotional, or financial indicators suggesting an older adult is being harmed, neglected, or exploited by a caregiver or other person; common signs include unexplained injuries or bruising; signs of neglect such as poor hygiene, malnutrition, or dehydration; untreated medical issues; fear or withdrawal around a caregiver; social isolation; and unusual changes in finances or loss of possessions.

physical abuse.definition: A deliberate use of physical force by one person against another that results in or has the potential to cause bodily injury, pain, or impairment (e.g., hitting, slapping, punching, kicking, burning, or otherwise harming).

sexual abuse.definition: Any sexual activity or exposure imposed on a person without their valid consent or when they cannot consent (such as a minor or vulnerable adult), including non-consensual sexual contact, coercion, exploitation, or forcing exposure to sexual acts or materials.

emotional abuse.definition: An intentional pattern of non-physical mistreatment that harms a person’s emotional well-being and self-esteem through behaviors such as constant criticism, humiliation, intimidation, manipulation, gaslighting, threats, and controlling or isolating actions; a form of abuse that can contribute to anxiety, depression, and other mental health problems.

neglect signs.definition: Neuropsychological syndrome in which a person fails to attend to or respond to stimuli on one side of space, typically opposite a brain lesion, due to diminished attention or awareness rather than sensory or motor loss.

nasal congestion.definition: Blockage or stuffiness of the nasal passages due to swelling of the nasal mucosa and increased mucus production, commonly caused by viral infections, allergic rhinitis, or irritants.

chronic congestion.definition: Persistent nasal obstruction or fullness lasting more than 12 weeks, usually due to chronic inflammation of the nasal mucosa or sinuses (eg, chronic rhinitis or chronic rhinosinusitis), and may be accompanied by nasal discharge, postnasal drip, facial pressure, and reduced sense of smell.

ejaculation.definition: Ejaculation is the ejection of semen from the male reproductive tract, usually at orgasm, produced by a two-phase process: emission of seminal fluids into the posterior urethra from the seminal vesicles and prostate, followed by rhythmic contractions of pelvic floor muscles that propel semen through the urethra and out of the penis.

ejaculate.definition: The semen discharged from the male reproductive tract during ejaculation, consisting of spermatozoa and seminal fluids produced by the testes, seminal vesicles, and prostate, expelled through the urethra at orgasm.

ejaculatory duct.definition: A paired duct formed by the junction of the ductus deferens and the duct of the seminal vesicle; it traverses the prostate and opens into the prostatic urethra, conveying sperm-containing fluid from the vas deferens and seminal vesicles into the urethra during ejaculation.

aortic valve stenosis.definition: A narrowing of the aortic valve opening that restricts blood flow from the left ventricle to the aorta, usually due to calcific degeneration or a congenital valve abnormality; it increases left ventricular afterload and can cause chest pain, fainting, and shortness of breath, potentially progressing to heart failure if untreated.

aortic dilation.definition: An abnormal enlargement of the aorta beyond its normal diameter, which may be focal (aneurysm) or diffuse (ectasia), due to weakening or degeneration of the vessel wall; detectable on imaging and associated with an increased risk of rupture or dissection.

semilunar valves.definition: Two heart valves with crescent-shaped cusps that separate the ventricles from the great arteries: the aortic valve (left ventricle to aorta) and the pulmonary valve (right ventricle to pulmonary artery). They open when ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure to eject blood and close during diastole to prevent backflow into the ventricles.

systolic click.definition: A high-pitched, midsystolic click heard best at the apex, caused by sudden prolapse and tensing of the mitral valve leaflets into the left atrium during systole (mitral valve prolapse).

septal defect.definition: A hole in the wall (septum) separating the heart's chambers, most often an atrial septal defect or a ventricular septal defect, causing abnormal shunting of blood between chambers.

fibrinolysin.definition: A proteolytic enzyme that dissolves fibrin clots; the active enzyme of the fibrinolytic system (plasmin), produced from plasminogen by activators such as tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) or streptokinase.

desoxyribonuclease.definition: An enzyme that cleaves deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) by hydrolyzing phosphodiester bonds, thereby degrading DNA.

seminal vesicles.definition: Structures surrounding the prostate gland involved in storing secretions made by the gland.

ductus deferens.definition: A muscular tube of the male reproductive tract that transports sperm from the epididymis to the ejaculatory ducts during ejaculation; also known as the vas deferens, it ascends from the scrotum through the inguinal canal into the pelvis and joins with the duct from the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct.

antiembolism hose.definition: A type of calibrated elastic stockings that apply graduated compression to the legs to improve venous blood flow and help prevent venous thromboembolism (e.g., deep vein thrombosis) in immobilized or postoperative patients.

medication overdose.definition: A medication overdose is the intake of a drug in an amount greater than the recommended therapeutic dose, producing toxic effects that may range from mild to life-threatening; it can be accidental or intentional and requires prompt medical evaluation and treatment.

prescription drugs.definition: Medications that require a clinician’s prescription to be dispensed, regulated due to safety concerns, potential for adverse effects or interactions, and typically used under medical supervision.

nasomandibular fixation.definition: An immobilization technique that fixes the mandible to the maxilla via the nasal region, typically using wires or fixation devices, to prevent jaw movement during healing after mandibular fractures or during orthognathic procedures; effectively a form of intermaxillary fixation.

maxillomandibular fixation.definition: An immobilization of the upper and lower jaws to stabilize the occlusion and facial fracture segments, achieved by intermaxillary fixation with wires, arch bars, or elastics during healing or after orthognathic surgery.

bougie.definition: A slender cylindrical dilator or guide instrument, often flexible, used to dilate a constricted body passage or to facilitate insertion of other instruments (e.g., esophageal or urethral dilation, guide for intubation).

elastic bougie.definition: A flexible, elastic dilator made of rubber used to progressively dilate a narrowed lumen (such as the esophagus or urethra) during dilatation procedures by gradual insertion.

primigravida.definition: A woman who is pregnant for the first time.

osteogenesis.definition: Bone formation process in which osteoblasts produce osteoid that is mineralized to form bone; occurs through intramembranous ossification and endochondral ossification, underlying skeletal development, growth, and fracture healing.

bedsores.definition: A localized injury to the skin and underlying tissue caused by prolonged pressure (often with shear), typically over a bony prominence in immobilized or bedridden individuals; also called a pressure ulcer.

polypharmacy.definition: The use of multiple medications by a patient, typically five or more concurrently, often to treat multiple chronic conditions; associated with increased risk of adverse drug events, drug–drug interactions, and medication mismanagement.

hydroquinone.definition: A topical depigmenting agent that inhibits tyrosinase, reducing melanin production in the skin; used to treat hyperpigmentation such as melasma, lentigines, and age spots; available in various concentrations (e.g., 2% OTC, higher with prescription); possible adverse effects include irritation and, with prolonged use, ochronosis.

cathodes.definition: An electrode in an electrochemical system at which reduction occurs; in biomedical contexts it is the electrode through which current enters the tissue (often the negative electrode in stimulation setups).

nonunion.definition: A fracture that fails to heal within the expected time despite appropriate treatment, evidenced by a persistent fracture line and lack of progressive callus formation or consolidation on serial imaging, often with ongoing pain or instability.

malleolus.definition: A bony prominence on the distal end of a leg bone that forms part of the ankle joint—specifically, the medial malleolus from the tibia and the lateral malleolus from the fibula.

pseudarthrosis.definition: A nonunion of a fracture in which fibrous or cartilaginous tissue forms a false joint between the bone ends, allowing some movement at the site and often causing pain and instability.

imperfecta.definition: A genetic or developmental disorder in which tissue formation is defective, leading to structural abnormalities or weakness of the affected tissues.

electroconvulsive.definition: Relating to or producing convulsions by electrical stimulation of the brain; in medical use, referring to the procedure that induces a controlled generalized seizure under anesthesia for treatment of certain psychiatric disorders.

electroshock.definition: A procedure in which a controlled brief electrical current is delivered to the brain to induce a generalized seizure, usually under anesthesia with a muscle relaxant; used primarily to treat severe depression and other refractory psychiatric conditions.

hypovolemic.definition: Relating to a decreased volume of circulating blood in the vascular system (hypovolemia), typically due to hemorrhage, severe dehydration, or substantial fluid loss, which can lead to reduced tissue perfusion and shock.

spinal.definition: Relating to the spine (the vertebral column) or the spinal cord.

electroanesthesia.definition: An historical or experimental method of analgesia or anesthesia produced by electrical stimulation of nerves or the nervous system, aiming to temporarily abolish sensation.

electrodermal.definition: Relating to the electrical properties of the skin, particularly changes in skin conductance (galvanic skin response) that occur with sweating and autonomic arousal.

hyperhidrosis.definition: Excessive sweating beyond what is needed to regulate body temperature, typically affecting focal areas (palms, soles, axillae, face) or generalized. It can be primary (idiopathic) with no identifiable cause or secondary to medical conditions or medications.

transcutaneous.definition: Through or across the skin; pertaining to or involving the skin, often referring to methods that act on or measure across the skin without an incision.

electrode.definition: A conductor used to make contact with the body to deliver electrical energy to, or sense electrical activity from, biological tissue for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes (e.g., ECG leads, defibrillator pads, neural stimulators).

electrodes.definition: A conductor or pad that interfaces with body tissue to detect electrical signals or deliver electrical stimulation; used for monitoring bioelectrical activity (e.g., ECG, EEG, EMG) and for therapeutic stimulation (e.g., pacing, defibrillation, neuromodulation).

electrodesiccation.definition: A procedure in electrosurgery in which high-frequency electrical current is delivered through a contact electrode to tissue, causing rapid desiccation (drying) and coagulation of proteins, thereby destroying the tissue. Used to treat superficial cutaneous lesions with minimal bleeding.

diathermy.definition: Diathermy is a medical technique that uses high‑frequency electrical currents to generate heat within body tissues, applied for therapeutic deep heating or, in surgical settings, to cut or coagulate tissue and achieve hemostasis.

electroanalgesia.definition: A method of pain relief achieved by applying electrical stimulation to nerves or tissues to modulate pain signals or activate endogenous analgesic mechanisms; commonly implemented via transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) or electroacupuncture.

electrosurgery.definition: A surgical technique that uses high‑frequency electrical current to cut tissue and coagulate blood vessels, providing hemostasis; energy is delivered via an active electrode with a return path (monopolar) or between two electrodes (bipolar).

electrodiagnosis.definition: A diagnostic approach that uses electrical measurements to assess the function of the nervous system, nerves, and muscles, typically via nerve conduction studies and electromyography (EMG).

nerves.definition: Bundles of axons enclosed by connective tissue that transmit electrical impulses between the central nervous system and peripheral tissues, enabling sensory input, motor output, and autonomic regulation.

muscles.definition: The soft tissues that help you move and enable your body to work properly. They are in your arms and legs, but also in your stomach and heart.

electrodynamics.definition: Branch of physics that studies how electric charges in motion and changing electric and magnetic fields interact, including the generation and propagation of electromagnetic waves, as described by Maxwell's equations.

encephalography.definition: A radiographic examination of the brain in which contrast material or air is introduced into the ventricular system or subarachnoid space to outline brain structures; historically used to diagnose intracranial lesions but largely supplanted by CT/MRI.

electroencephalographic.definition: Relating to electroencephalography, the recording of the brain's electrical activity via scalp electrodes, used to assess brain function and diagnose conditions such as epilepsy and sleep disorders.

electrogram.definition: A recording of the electrical activity of a tissue (most often the heart) obtained with electrodes, used to assess conduction, timing of depolarization, and arrhythmias.

emg.definition: A diagnostic procedure that assesses the health of muscles and the nerves that control them by recording the electrical activity of skeletal muscles, typically using needle electrodes (and sometimes surface electrodes) and often performed with nerve conduction studies.

laryngectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove all or part of the larynx (voice box), typically to treat laryngeal cancer; it results in a permanent tracheostomy and loss of natural voice, with possible rehabilitation options such as esophageal speech, an electrolarynx, or a tracheoesophageal puncture.

electrolarynx.definition: An electronic voice-synthesis device, typically worn against the neck, that generates a periodic vibrating sound which is shaped by the lips and oral cavity to produce speech; used to restore vocalization after laryngectomy or in cases of severe laryngeal impairment; voice is usually monotone with fixed pitch.

homeostasis.definition: An organism's tendency to maintain a relatively constant internal environment through regulatory processes and feedback mechanisms that counteract external and internal changes (e.g., temperature, pH, glucose, fluid balance).

hypermagnesemia.definition: A condition characterized by an elevated level of magnesium in the blood (serum magnesium above the normal upper limit, typically >2.5 mg/dL or >1.0 mmol/L), often due to renal failure or excessive magnesium intake; can cause neuromuscular and cardiac depression.

disorders.definition: A disorder is an abnormality of function in a part of the body or mind; a disturbance of normal physiological or psychological processes that often presents as illness or pathology.

neurosurgery.definition: A surgical specialty focused on diagnosing and treating disorders of the nervous system (brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves) through operative and nonoperative means, including procedures such as tumor removal, vascular repair, and spinal stabilization.

epicardium.definition: Visceral layer of the serous pericardium that covers the outer surface of the heart; a thin membrane of mesothelial cells and connective tissue that is part of the heart wall and continuous with the parietal pericardium at the great vessels.

electromagnetic.definition: Relating to electric and magnetic fields and their interactions; in medicine, describes electromagnetic fields or radiation produced by devices or procedures (e.g., MRI, diathermy, transcranial magnetic stimulation) and the safety considerations of exposure.

electromyographic.definition: Relating to electromyography; pertaining to the recording and analysis of the electrical activity produced by skeletal muscles to evaluate muscle function and nerve innervation.

biofeedback.definition: An treatment that helps people learn to gain control over normally unconscious body functions, such as breathing and heart rates.

floor.definition: Anatomical bottom boundary or base of a body cavity or hollow organ, forming its inferior limit and providing structural support; examples include the floor of the mouth.

incontinence.definition: A condition characterized by the involuntary loss of bladder or bowel control, resulting in leakage of urine and/or stool.

fecal.definition: Relating to feces; the solid waste excreted by the digestive tract.

injury.definition: A physical harm or damage to the body's tissues or organs resulting from an external force or energy, leading to pain, dysfunction, or disability.

cerebral.definition: Of or relating to the cerebrum, the principal part of the brain; pertaining to brain tissue or brain function.

electrodiagnostic.definition: Tests that measure the electrical activity of nerves and muscles to diagnose neuromuscular disorders, typically including nerve conduction studies and electromyography (EMG), and sometimes evoked potentials.

electroneurography.definition: A neurophysiologic test that evaluates peripheral nerve function by delivering an electrical stimulus to a nerve and recording the resulting action potentials, measuring conduction velocity, latency, and amplitude to identify nerve injuries or neuropathies.

electromyoneurography.definition: A diagnostic test that combines nerve conduction studies with electromyography to assess the electrical activity of muscles and the nerves that control them, used to evaluate neuromuscular disorders and nerve injuries.

elephantiasis.definition: A condition of extreme swelling of a limb or other body part caused by chronic obstruction of lymphatic drainage, most often due to lymphatic filariasis from parasitic worms; it leads to thickened, fibrotic skin and tissue with potential disfigurement and secondary infections.

eletriptan.definition: A selective serotonin 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonist used for the acute treatment of migraine; it causes cranial vasoconstriction and inhibits release of vasoactive neuropeptides such as CGRP.

elixophyllin.definition: A brand name for theophylline, a methylxanthine bronchodilator used to prevent and relieve symptoms of asthma and COPD. It inhibits phosphodiesterase enzymes and antagonizes adenosine receptors, increasing intracellular cAMP and relaxing airway smooth muscle. It has a narrow therapeutic index and requires monitoring; common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, palpitations, jitters, and insomnia, with interactions (e.g., certain antibiotics, caffeine) that can raise toxicity risk.

obstetric.definition: Relating to pregnancy and childbirth; the branch of medicine that deals with the care of women during pregnancy, labor, and the postpartum period.

electrosleep.definition: A historical noninvasive therapy that used mild electrical currents applied to the scalp or temples to induce sleep; largely abandoned due to inconsistent efficacy and safety concerns.

electrotherapy.definition: Therapeutic use of electrical energy to produce physiological effects in the body, such as nerve or muscle stimulation, pain relief, tissue healing, or bone growth, delivered by external or implanted electrical devices.

electroporation.definition: A technique that uses brief, high-voltage electrical pulses to transiently permeabilize the cell membrane, creating pores that allow extracellular molecules (e.g., DNA, RNA, drugs) to enter the cell; used for transfection, gene therapy, and electrochemotherapy.

electroresection.definition: A surgical procedure in which tissue is cut away using electrical energy, typically with a specialized instrument (e.g., a resection loop), providing simultaneous coagulation to reduce bleeding.

intrapartum.definition: During labor and delivery; the period from the onset of true labor (regular contractions with cervical changes) to the delivery of the baby.

ep.definition: An abbreviation with several medical meanings; most commonly denotes epithelium (the cellular lining of organs and body surfaces) or epidermis (the outer skin layer); it may also refer to electrophysiology in cardiology.

psg.definition: A comprehensive sleep study that records multiple physiological parameters during sleep—brain activity, eye movements, muscle tone, heart rate, respiratory effort and airflow, and oxygen saturation—to diagnose sleep disorders.

embolectomy.definition: A surgical or endovascular procedure to remove an embolus from a blocked blood vessel to restore blood flow, often using techniques such as a Fogarty catheter or catheter-based thrombectomy.

embolotherapy.definition: An interventional radiology procedure in which embolic material is injected through a catheter to occlude blood vessels feeding a target area, thereby reducing blood flow to the area for purposes such as stopping hemorrhage or shrinking tumors.

embololysis.definition: Dissolution of an embolus within a blood vessel, usually achieved by thrombolytic (clot-dissolving) therapy to restore perfusion.

embolismic?.definition: Relating to embolism or to an embolus; caused by or resulting from the lodging of an embolus in a blood vessel, leading to obstruction of blood flow.

embolic gangrene.definition: An ischemic form of gangrene caused by an embolus occluding an arterial supply, abruptly cutting off blood flow to a region (typically a limb) and leading to tissue necrosis, which may progress from dry to wet gangrene if infection ensues.

embolic necrosis.definition: Necrosis caused by occlusion of a blood vessel by an embolus, leading to ischemia and infarction of the supplied tissue. Emboli may be thrombotic, fat, air, or tumor fragments.

embolic thrombosis.definition: A thrombus that has dislodged from its site of formation and travels through the bloodstream to occlude a distant vessel; i.e., a thrombus-derived embolus causing embolic occlusion.

elliptocyte.definition: An abnormally elongated, oval-shaped red blood cell seen on a peripheral smear, characteristic of elliptocytosis and often due to defects in the red blood cell membrane skeleton (eg, spectrin/ankyrin deficiencies).

elliptocytic anemia.definition: An inherited (and sometimes acquired) red blood cell disorder in which peripheral blood smear shows predominantly elliptically shaped erythrocytes (elliptocytes); caused by defects in erythrocyte membrane proteins that reduce cell deformability and increase hemolysis, with a clinical spectrum from mild to severe anemia.

hereditary elliptocytosis.definition: An inherited disorder of red blood cell membrane caused by defects in cytoskeletal proteins (notably spectrin and related proteins) leading to elliptically shaped erythrocytes and variable hemolytic anemia; most cases are autosomal dominant.

ovalocytosis.definition: An abnormality in which red blood cells are oval-shaped (ovalocytes) instead of the normal disc shape, observed on peripheral blood smear.

congenital nonspherocytic hemolytic anem.definition: An inherited hemolytic anemia caused by defects in red blood cell glycolytic enzymes (most often pyruvate kinase deficiency) leading to reduced ATP, red cell membrane instability, and premature destruction of red cells from birth, with chronic hemolysis and reticulocytosis and typically without spherocytes on blood smear.

spherocytic anemia.definition: A hemolytic anemia characterized by circulating abnormally spherical red blood cells (spherocytes) on the peripheral smear, usually due to red cell membrane defects (eg, hereditary spherocytosis) or immune-mediated destruction, which reduces red cell deformability and shortens their lifespan.

pyruvate kinase deficiency.definition: An autosomal recessive deficiency of erythrocyte pyruvate kinase due to PKLR gene mutations, causing impaired glycolysis and ATP depletion in red blood cells and resulting in chronic non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia; clinically can include jaundice, splenomegaly, and pigment gallstones; management is supportive (folate, transfusions) with splenectomy in selected cases.

embden-meyerhof pathway.definition: A cytosolic metabolic pathway that converts glucose to two molecules of pyruvate, generating a net of 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose and providing intermediates for biosynthesis.
