embryonal carcinoma.definition: Malignant germ cell tumor composed of primitive, embryonal-like cells; a nonseminomatous testicular cancer (often part of a mixed germ cell tumor) that is typically aggressive and capable of early spread, with tumor markers variably elevated depending on the differentiation and presence of other components.

embryonal leukemia.definition: An historic or nonstandard label for an acute leukemia in which the malignant blasts resemble embryonal hematopoietic precursors; it is not considered a distinct entity in modern classifications and cases are categorized as ALL or AML based on lineage markers and genetics.

embryonal adenomyosarcoma.definition: Not a widely recognized medical term; in theory, it would describe a malignant uterine tumor composed of embryonal (primitive) mesenchymal cells with gland-forming epithelial components, i.e., a high-grade neoplasm with both sarcomatous and glandular elements. Definitive classification requires histopathologic evaluation.

embryonal adenosarcoma.definition: Not a recognized term in standard medical literature. If referring to adenosarcoma, it is a rare uterine tumor composed of benign-appearing glandular epithelium with a malignant stromal (mesenchymal) component; it often presents with abnormal uterine bleeding. Management is typically surgical (often hysterectomy), and prognosis depends on factors like sarcomatous overgrowth and invasion.

embryomata.definition: Plural form referring to a tumor composed of embryonal tissue with immature, primitive-appearing cells; historically used for embryonic-type neoplasms in infancy or childhood. The term is largely obsolete and such lesions are now described with modern terminology as embryonal tumors or blastomas.

wilms tumor.definition: A malignant kidney tumor of childhood (nephroblastoma) arising from embryonal renal tissue; typically presents as a painless abdominal mass and may be associated with hypertension or hematuria. Management usually includes surgical removal (nephrectomy) with chemotherapy, and sometimes radiotherapy; prognosis is favorable with modern multimodal therapy.

embryopathy.definition: An abnormal development of the embryo, usually referring to congenital malformations caused by teratogenic factors during embryogenesis (early pregnancy).

rubella embryopathy.definition: Fetal anomalies caused by maternal rubella infection during pregnancy (congenital rubella syndrome), commonly including ocular defects (cataracts, microphthalmia), sensorineural deafness, congenital heart disease (e.g., patent ductus arteriosus, pulmonary stenosis), microcephaly, and growth retardation; severity depends on gestational age at infection.

embryo transfer.definition: An assisted reproductive technology procedure in which one or more embryos created outside the body (typically by IVF or ICSI) are placed into the uterus to achieve pregnancy; embryos may be fresh or frozen-thawed and the transfer is usually performed transcervically with a catheter (often under ultrasound guidance).

embryogenesis.definition: The process by which a fertilized egg develops into an embryo, encompassing cleavage (cell division), differentiation, morphogenesis, gastrulation, and organogenesis to establish the basic body plan.

embryonic.definition: Relating to an embryo; occurring in the early stages of development, before organ formation.

embryonic disk.definition: Bilaminar germ disc formed from the inner cell mass of the blastocyst; composed of the epiblast and hypoblast, located between the amniotic cavity and the yolk sac, and serving as the embryonic precursor that gives rise to all three germ layers during gastrulation.

embryoblast.definition: Inner cell mass of the blastocyst that gives rise to the embryo proper; it differentiates into the epiblast and hypoblast layers.

germ disk.definition: The bilaminar region of the early embryo formed from the inner cell mass, consisting of the epiblast and hypoblast; during gastrulation it gives rise to the three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm).

germinal area.definition: An anatomic area in the developing brain along the walls of the lateral ventricles rich in neural precursor cells that give rise to neurons and glial cells; it is highly vascular and particularly susceptible to hemorrhage in premature infants.

embryotomy.definition: An obsolete obstetric procedure in which the fetus is dismembered within the uterus and removed in pieces to facilitate delivery when vaginal delivery is not possible or the fetus is nonviable.

embryotroph.definition: Nutrition supplied to the developing embryo by maternal tissues and secretions (historically termed histotroph) during early development, before the placenta provides direct nutrient transfer.

histotroph.definition: A nutritive secretion from the uterine endometrium (uterine glands) that bathes and nourishes the developing embryo before placental nutrition is established; often described as uterine milk and rich in proteins, amino acids, sugars, lipids, and growth factors.

embryonic rest.definition: A residual island of embryonic tissue that persists in a tissue after normal development; these rests consist of embryonic cells and are usually dormant, but may occasionally give rise to developmental anomalies or, rarely, neoplasms if they proliferate.

embryo rest.definition: Not a standard medical term; it usually denotes a pause or cessation of embryonic development during early development (embryonic arrest), in which cell division and progression halt, often due to genetic abnormalities or unfavorable conditions.

elspar.definition: A brand-name form of L-asparaginase, an enzyme used in chemotherapy to deplete asparagine, thereby inhibiting protein synthesis in leukemic cells and aiding treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

emcyt.definition: An anticancer agent consisting of estramustine phosphate; an estrogen-linked alkylating compound used to treat metastatic prostate cancer, which disrupts microtubule function and inhibits cell division.

estramustine phosphate sodium.definition: A chemotherapy agent; the sodium salt of estramustine phosphate, an estrogen‑linked alkylating antineoplastic used mainly for metastatic prostate cancer; acts as a prodrug that releases estramustine, which disrupts microtubule function by binding tubulin and inhibits mitosis (with accompanying estrogenic effects).

emetine.definition: An alkaloid derived from ipecac, used historically to induce vomiting (an emetic) and as an antiamoebic agent; its use is now limited due to significant cardiotoxicity.

emedastine.definition: A topical ophthalmic antihistamine (H1 receptor antagonist) used to relieve itching and other symptoms of allergic conjunctivitis.

emedastine difumarate.definition: An ophthalmic antihistamine (H1 receptor antagonist) used to treat allergic conjunctivitis; it blocks histamine receptors and stabilizes mast cells, reducing ocular itching, redness, and other allergic symptoms, typically given as eye drops.

emend.definition: To correct or amend; to rectify an error in a manuscript, text, or record.

benzquinamide hydrochloride.definition: An organic compound that forms a hydrochloride salt; there is limited public information about its pharmacology, indications, or clinical use, and it is not a commonly used pharmaceutical.

apomorphine hydrochloride.definition: A potent non-ergoline dopamine receptor agonist; the hydrochloride salt of apomorphine, used to rapidly relieve “off” episodes in Parkinson disease, typically administered by subcutaneous injection and often given with antiemetic pretreatment due to nausea and hypotension risks.

emery-dreifuss syndrome.definition: An inherited muscular dystrophy characterized by early contractures of the elbows and ankles, proximal muscle weakness and wasting, and a risk of cardiomyopathy or conduction defects; inheritance can be X-linked or autosomal dominant/recessive, commonly due to mutations in genes such as EMD (emerin) and LMNA.

cardiac conduction disorders.definition: A group of disorders affecting the heart's electrical conduction system, causing impaired generation or propagation of impulses through the SA node, AV node, or His-Purkinje pathways, leading to bradycardia, pauses, blocks, or other rhythm disturbances.

cord clamp.definition: A sterile device applied to the umbilical cord shortly after birth to compress and seal the umbilical vessels, preventing blood flow between the infant and the placenta once the cord is cut.

vaginal introitus.definition: The external opening of the vagina into the vulvar vestibule; the vaginal orifice that leads into the vaginal canal.

electrical defibrillation.definition: A medical procedure in which a controlled electrical shock is delivered to the heart to terminate life-threatening arrhythmias (most commonly ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia) and to restore a normal cardiac rhythm; shocks may be delivered externally via pads or internally via an implanted device.

emetic.definition: A substance that induces vomiting; used to evacuate the stomach in poisoning or overdose, acting by irritation of the stomach lining or stimulation of the vomiting center.

emetic agent.definition: A substance that induces vomiting, typically by stimulating the vomiting center or chemoreceptor trigger zone in the brain or by irritating the stomach, in order to remove ingested toxins.

emesis gravidarum.definition: Vomiting that occurs during pregnancy, especially in the first trimester; usually mild and self-limited, but can be severe (hyperemesis gravidarum) with dehydration and weight loss.

postcoital contraceptive.definition: An emergency method of contraception used after unprotected intercourse or contraceptive failure to prevent pregnancy, typically involving hormonal regimens (eg, levonorgestrel or ulipristal acetate) or the insertion of a copper intrauterine device.

bloody show.definition: A small amount of blood-tinged vaginal discharge that occurs when the mucus plug is expelled from the cervix in late pregnancy, often signaling that labor is approaching.

emetical.definition: Relating to vomiting or to an emetic; capable of inducing vomiting.

ipecac.definition: A plant-derived emetic once used to induce vomiting after poisoning; typically as syrup containing emetine and cephaeline, but routine use is no longer recommended due to unreliable efficacy and risks such as aspiration and cardiotoxicity.

hematemetic.definition: Relating to the vomiting of blood; usually due to upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

hyperemetic.definition: Relating to or characterized by extreme vomiting; severe, often intractable vomiting.

emetrol.definition: An over-the-counter antiemetic comprising a phosphorated carbohydrate solution used to relieve nausea and vomiting; it contains phosphoric acid along with glucose and fructose.

orthophosphoric_acid.definition: A colorless, corrosive mineral acid with the formula H3PO4; a weak, triprotic acid that dissociates in water to H2PO4−, HPO4^2−, and PO4^3−. It is used as a laboratory reagent, as a food acidity regulator (E338), and in dentistry to etch enamel; in the body it contributes to the phosphate buffering system.

beckwith_wiedemann_syndrome.definition: A congenital overgrowth syndrome characterized by neonatal macrosomia and macroglossia, hemihyperplasia, omphalocele or other abdominal wall defects, and visceromegaly, often with neonatal hypoglycemia. It carries an increased risk of embryonal tumors, most notably Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma. The syndrome typically results from dysregulation of imprinted genes on chromosome 11p15.5 due to abnormal DNA methylation or paternal uniparental disomy.

umbilical_hernia.definition: A protrusion of intra-abdominal contents through a weakness in the abdominal wall at the umbilicus, typically containing omentum or small intestine; most are congenital in infants but can occur in adults with increased intra-abdominal pressure.

exomphalos.definition: A congenital anterior abdominal wall defect (omphalocele) in which abdominal viscera herniate through the umbilicus into a sac, covered by amnion and peritoneum, due to failure of the midgut to return to the abdomen during embryogenesis.

dysplasia_of_renal_medulla.definition: A congenital or developmental disorder in which the renal medulla is abnormally formed, with disorganized tubules and collecting ducts often accompanied by scarring or cysts, leading to impaired concentrating ability and potential progression to chronic kidney disease.

adrenal_cortex.definition: Outer portion of the adrenal gland that synthesizes corticosteroid hormones: mineralocorticoids (e.g., aldosterone), glucocorticoids (e.g., cortisol), and androgens; organized into three zones—zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata, and zona reticularis—and regulated mainly by ACTH and the renin-angiotensin system (especially for aldosterone).

emissary_veins.definition: Small, valveless veins that traverse skull foramina to connect extracranial veins (such as scalp and diploic veins) with intracranial dural venous sinuses (e.g., superior sagittal, cavernous, or transverse sinuses). They provide collateral venous channels between the external and internal cranial venous systems and can transmit infection from scalp to brain.

dura_mater.definition: Outermost of the three meninges enveloping the brain and spinal cord; a dense fibrous membrane that in the skull has an outer periosteal layer and an inner meningeal layer, forms dural folds (e.g., falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli) and houses the dural venous sinuses; it is separated from the arachnoid by the subdural space and continues as the dural sac around the spinal cord.

anastomoses.definition: A connection between two previously separate hollow or tubular structures (e.g., blood vessels, lymphatics, or intestinal segments) that permits flow or communication between them; can be congenital or surgically created.

emission_computed_tomography.definition: A nuclear medicine imaging technique that reconstructs three-dimensional images of radiotracer distribution by detecting photons emitted from within the body, typically using single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) or positron emission tomography (PET).

positron.definition: A positively charged antiparticle of the electron with the same mass; it annihilates with an electron to produce two 511 keV gamma photons, a principle used in positron emission tomography (PET).

gamma_ray.definition: A form of high-energy ionizing electromagnetic radiation emitted by atomic nuclei during radioactive decay or nuclear transitions; highly penetrating with energies typically ranging from about 100 keV to several MeV, and used in certain medical imaging and radiotherapy applications.

detectors.definition: A device that detects a physiological, chemical, or physical signal and converts it into a measurable electrical, optical, or digital readout; used in medical diagnostics and monitoring (for example, radiation-detection devices in imaging, biosensors, and sensor-based monitoring systems).

cross_sectional_image.definition: A two-dimensional image of a plane cut through the body, produced by tomographic imaging (e.g., CT or MRI), showing anatomy and any pathology in that slice.

emmetropia.definition: A normal refractive state in which the eye focuses distant objects' parallel rays precisely on the retina, so no corrective lenses are needed.

emmetropic.definition: A normal refractive state of the eye in which light from distant objects is focused on the retina with the eye in a relaxed position, requiring no corrective lenses for distance vision.

hyperopia.definition: When you can see clearly far away, but not close up. Also called farsightedness.

emmets_operation.definition: An historical eponym describing a surgical procedure named after the practitioner Emmet; the exact technique, indications, and steps differ across specialties, and the term is not commonly used in contemporary practice. If you can share the medical field or context (e.g., dentistry, orthopedics), I can provide a more precise definition.

emollient.definition: A substance (such as a cream, lotion, ointment, or oil) that softens and moisturizes the skin by forming an occlusive layer to reduce moisture loss; used to treat dry, rough, or irritated skin.

emollient_bath.definition: A bath in which an emollient (e.g., bath oil) is added to bathwater to moisturize and soften the skin, reducing dryness and improving skin barrier function; commonly used for dry or irritated skin such as eczema.

emotional_abuse.definition: A pattern of nonphysical acts by someone aimed at controlling, demeaning, or isolating another person, damaging their emotional or psychological well-being. It includes verbal insults, humiliation, threats, manipulation, gaslighting, and social or geographic isolation, and can lead to anxiety, depression, and low self-esteem.

emotional_deprivation.definition: An absence of sufficient emotional nourishment—such as warmth, attention, and consistent supportive caregiving—during critical developmental periods, which can disrupt healthy emotional development and attachment, and increase risk for mood, anxiety, and behavioral problems.

emotional_diarrhea.definition: A colloquial, nonmedical term for diarrhea that is triggered or worsened by emotional distress or anxiety; not a formal diagnosis. If diarrhea is persistent or accompanied by other symptoms, evaluation for infectious, inflammatory, malabsorptive, or functional bowel disorders is advised.

eccrine_sweat_glands.definition: Eccrine sweat glands are small, simple, coiled tubular glands distributed widely across the skin that secrete a watery, hypotonic sweat directly onto the surface through a duct, primarily for thermoregulation and minor waste excretion; their secretory portion lies in the dermis and is regulated by sympathetic cholinergic innervation.

emotional_lability.definition: Rapid, involuntary changes in affect or mood, with exaggerated or inappropriate emotional responses to stimuli; commonly seen in neurological disorders (e.g., after stroke or brain injury) and can be part of pseudobulbar affect.

emotional_needs.definition: The psychological and social requirements essential for emotional well-being, including affection, safety, belonging, respect, and the opportunity to express emotions; when unmet, they can contribute to distress and mental health issues.

emotional_response.definition: A mental and physiological reaction to a stimulus or situation, involving the subjective experience of an emotion, outward expressive behavior, and autonomic arousal mediated by the limbic system.

emotional_support.definition: Non-professional social support provided by others (e.g., family, friends, caregivers) that aims to alleviate emotional distress and promote coping by offering empathy, reassurance, active listening, and encouragement; it complements but does not replace professional mental health or medical care.

emphysematous_abscess.definition: A localized abscess in which gas-forming organisms produce gas within the purulent collection, leading to intralesional gas visible on imaging; it is more common in diabetics and other immunocompromised hosts and typically requires antibiotics with drainage when feasible.

emphysematous_chest.definition: Gas within the chest tissues, most often seen as subcutaneous emphysema of the chest wall or air in the mediastinum, caused by trauma, thoracic surgery, or infection with gas-forming organisms; a finding that can signal injury or infection and may require urgent assessment.

emphysematous_gastritis.definition: A uncommon, life-threatening infection of the gastric wall caused by gas-forming organisms that leads to intramural gas and gastric necrosis; commonly presents with severe abdominal pain and sepsis and has a high mortality, requiring broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and urgent surgical evaluation (often debridement or gastrectomy).

emphysematous_pyelitis.definition: A gas-forming infection of the renal collecting system in which gas is present within the renal pelvis and calyces, typically due to gas-forming bacteria in diabetics or obstructive uropathy; unlike emphysematous pyelonephritis, it does not involve the renal parenchyma.

centriacinar_emphysema.definition: A form of emphysema in which destruction and enlargement predominantly affect the central (proximal) parts of the acinus—the respiratory bronchioles—with relative sparing of the distal alveoli; strongly associated with smoking and typically more prominent in the upper lung zones.

distal_acinar_emphysema.definition: An emphysematous change limited to the distal part of the acinus (alveolar ducts and sacs), causing enlargement and destruction of distal airspaces, most prominent in subpleural regions near the pleura, often with subpleural blebs and potential spontaneous pneumothorax; less strongly linked to smoking than centrilobular emphysema.

panacinar_emphysema.definition: A form of emphysema in which the alveolar walls are uniformly destroyed throughout the acinus (from respiratory bronchioles to alveolar ducts and sacs), leading to enlarged air spaces; typically greatest in the lung bases and strongly associated with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

barrel_chest.definition: An increased anterior-posterior diameter of the chest giving a round, barrel-shaped appearance, commonly due to chronic lung hyperinflation (eg, emphysema/COPD); a physical exam finding rather than a disease.

oxygen_therapy.definition: An medical treatment that delivers supplemental oxygen to patients with hypoxemia or risk of low blood oxygen, to improve arterial oxygenation and tissue oxygen delivery, typically via nasal cannula, face mask, or other devices and guided by target SpO2 or PaO2.

mechanical_ventilation.definition: A method of providing artificial ventilation using a mechanical ventilator to deliver breaths to the lungs, supporting or replacing spontaneous breathing; can be invasive (via endotracheal or tracheostomy tube) or noninvasive (via a mask or similar interface).

chronic_bronchitis.definition: A form of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease defined clinically by a productive cough with sputum lasting at least 3 months in each of two consecutive years, due to chronic bronchial inflammation and mucus hypersecretion (goblet cell hyperplasia), most commonly from long-term tobacco smoke exposure.

whooping_cough.definition: A highly contagious bacterial respiratory infection caused by Bordetella pertussis, characterized by severe paroxysmal coughing spells often accompanied by an inspiratory whoop; preventable by vaccination and treated with macrolide antibiotics.

strychnine.definition: A highly toxic alkaloid derived from the seeds of Strychnos nux-vomica; it acts as an antagonist of glycine receptors in the central nervous system, causing disinhibition of motor neurons and leading to severe, painful generalized convulsions and, if untreated, death from asphyxia. It has historical use as a pesticide and has no accepted therapeutic use due to toxicity.

alpha_1_antitrypsin.definition: A liver-produced serine protease inhibitor that protects lung tissue by inhibiting neutrophil elastase and other proteases. Deficiency from SERPINA1 gene variants leads to low circulating levels and predisposes to early-onset panacinar emphysema and, in some individuals, liver disease from accumulation of misfolded protein.

leukocyte_collagenase.definition: A zinc-dependent matrix metalloproteinase produced by neutrophils (leukocytes) that cleaves native collagen types I, II, and III, participating in inflammatory tissue remodeling (neutrophil collagenase, MMP-8).

pneumoencephalography.definition: A historical neuroradiologic procedure in which air is injected into the cerebral ventricles (via lumbar puncture or direct ventricular puncture) to displace cerebrospinal fluid and delineate the ventricular system on X-ray imaging; largely obsolete due to risks and the availability of CT and MRI.

computed_axial_tomography.definition: A medical imaging technique that uses rotating X-ray beams and computer reconstruction to produce cross-sectional (axial) images of the body, typically arranged as a series of slices and used for diagnostic evaluation.

cerebrospinal_fluid.definition: The clear, colorless fluid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord, providing buoyant protection, chemical stability, and removal of metabolic waste; it circulates within the ventricles and subarachnoid space and is reabsorbed into the venous system.

pituitary_gland.definition: Controls other glands (like the thyroid) and also how you grow.

sella_turcica.definition: A saddle-shaped depression in the sphenoid bone at the base of the skull that houses the pituitary gland (in the hypophyseal fossa); bounded anteriorly by the tuberculum sellae and posteriorly by the dorsum sellae.

empty_follicle_syndrome.definition: A rare complication of assisted reproductive technology in which no oocytes are retrieved from mature ovarian follicles after appropriate stimulation and ovulation triggering, despite ultrasound-confirmed follicular development. It can be categorized as false (due to laboratory or timing errors) or true (intrinsic ovarian/oocyte failure).

empty_sella_syndrome.definition: A condition in which the sella turcica is filled with cerebrospinal fluid, giving an "empty" appearance on imaging and often flattening the pituitary gland; it can be incidental but may be associated with headaches or pituitary hormone deficiencies, with primary (diaphragma sellae defect) and secondary (post-surgical/radiation) forms.

emprosthotonos.definition: A rare dystonic movement disorder characterized by sustained, involuntary flexion of the trunk (often with neck flexion) producing a forward-bent posture; the opposite of opisthotonos, which causes backward arching. It can occur in acute dystonias, tetanus, or drug-induced movement disorders.

lacerated_perineum.definition: A tear of the perineum—the region between the vaginal opening and the anus—caused by trauma or childbirth, ranging from superficial skin lacerations to deep injuries involving underlying perineal muscles and, in severe cases, the anal sphincter or rectal mucosa.

uterine_cervix.definition: The lower, narrow portion of the uterus that connects the uterine cavity to the vagina. It comprises the endocervical canal lined by glandular columnar epithelium and the ectocervix lined by stratified squamous epithelium, with an internal os and an external os; it produces cervical mucus, acts as a barrier to pathogens, and dilates during labor.

emtricitabine.definition: An antiretroviral medication that is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI); a fluorinated cytidine analog that inhibits HIV-1 reverse transcriptase by incorporating into viral DNA and causing chain termination, used in combination regimens for HIV-1 treatment and for PrEP when given with tenofovir.

eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome.definition: An uncommon systemic hypersensitivity syndrome marked by persistent eosinophilia and severe muscle pain (myalgia), often with fever, skin changes, edema, and fatigue; historically linked to contaminated L-tryptophan supplements.

arthroempyema.definition: A purulent infection of a joint with accumulation of pus within the synovial cavity (septic arthritis with intra-articular empyema).

pneumoempyema.definition: A pleural empyema in which gas is present in the pleural space, typically due to infection with gas-forming organisms or a fistulous communication with the bronchial tree.

typhloempyema.definition: Pus accumulation within the cecum (the first part of the large intestine) due to a purulent inflammatory process.

enalapril.definition: An angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor used to treat hypertension and heart failure; it is a prodrug converted to the active metabolite enalaprilat, which lowers angiotensin II–mediated vasoconstriction and aldosterone secretion.

enalapril maleate.definition: A salt form of an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor; it is a prodrug converted to an active metabolite that inhibits ACE, reducing angiotensin II–mediated vasoconstriction and aldosterone secretion to treat hypertension and heart failure.

angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.definition: A drug used to treat high blood pressure and congestive heart failure; it inhibits the production of angiotensin II, lowering blood pressure and reducing the heart's workload.

mucoid.definition: Relating to mucus; having a mucus-like appearance or consistency, often thick and viscous.

purulent.definition: Relating to or containing pus; suppurative.

central cyanosis.definition: Bluish discoloration of the lips, tongue, and central mucous membranes due to increased deoxygenated hemoglobin in arterial blood, reflecting systemic hypoxemia.

chest radiography.definition: An imaging study that uses X-rays to produce pictures of the chest, allowing visualization of the lungs, heart, mediastinum, and pleural spaces; typically obtained in frontal (PA or AP) and lateral views to evaluate for pneumonia, edema, effusion, pneumothorax, tumors, or other thoracic pathology.

hyperinflation.definition: An abnormal increase in lung volumes caused by air trapping (incomplete expiration), leading to elevated total lung capacity and residual volume; commonly seen in obstructive lung diseases such as COPD, emphysema, and asthma.

blebs.definition: A small, fluid-filled bubble on the skin or mucous membranes (a vesicle or blister); in cell biology, a temporary bulge of the plasma membrane and cytoplasm that can form during apoptosis or cell movement.

congested lung fields.definition: Radiologic description of increased lung markings on chest imaging, suggesting pulmonary edema or vascular congestion from fluid overload (often due to heart failure); can also reflect infection or inflammatory processes and is not a diagnosis by itself.

bronchial markings.definition: Radiographic appearance of the bronchi on chest imaging, characterized by thickened or prominent peribronchial markings; commonly indicates airway inflammation or infection (e.g., bronchitis, bronchiolitis) or other inflammatory airway disease.

arterial blood gas analysis.definition: A test that measures oxygen and carbon dioxide levels in arterial blood, along with pH and bicarbonate, to assess acid–base balance and gas exchange; used to diagnose and manage respiratory and metabolic disorders and to guide therapy.

right axis deviation.definition: An electrocardiographic finding in which the mean frontal-plane QRS axis is shifted to the right (typically +90° to +180°), seen with right ventricular hypertrophy, pulmonary hypertension or COPD, and sometimes as a normal variant.

atrial arrhythmias.definition: A group of heart rhythm disorders that originate in the atria, causing abnormal atrial activation and an irregular or rapid heart rhythm; includes atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, and focal atrial tachycardias.

total lung capacity.definition: Maximum amount of air the lungs can contain after a maximal inspiratory effort; the sum of vital capacity and residual volume (about 4–6 liters in healthy adults).

static lung compliance.definition: Change in lung volume per unit change in transpulmonary pressure under no-flow (static) conditions; reflects the elastic properties of the lung and is typically measured with an inspiratory hold, often estimated as Vt divided by (Pplat − PEEP) on mechanical ventilation.

postinfectious encephalitis.definition: An inflammatory, immune-mediated encephalitis that develops after a viral or other infection, typically within days to weeks, due to an autoimmune attack on CNS tissue; presents with confusion or altered consciousness, fever, seizures, and focal neurologic deficits, often with demyelinating lesions on MRI and inflammatory CSF. Treated with immunotherapy (e.g., high‑dose corticosteroids, IVIG, plasmapheresis) with variable prognosis.

encephalomyocarditis.definition: A viral disease caused by encephalomyocarditis virus (EMCV), a picornavirus of the Cardiovirus genus; it classically causes concurrent inflammation of the brain (encephalitis) and heart muscle (myocarditis) in various animal species, especially pigs and rodents. In humans, EMCV infection is rare and usually mild but can be associated with myocarditis or febrile illness.

encephalogram.definition: A radiographic image or tracing of the brain obtained by encephalography; an older cranial-imaging technique that used contrast material or air to outline brain structures and is largely obsolete today.

posterior fossa.definition: The posterior fossa is the region at the base of the skull that houses the cerebellum, brainstem (pons and medulla), and the fourth ventricle.

encephalon.definition: The brain—the organ within the skull comprising the cerebrum, cerebellum, and brainstem; the central nervous system responsible for processing sensory information, enabling cognition and thought, and regulating bodily functions.

encephalalgia.definition: Pain perceived in the head; historically used to denote headache; in reality headaches arise from pain in the meninges, skull, blood vessels, and other structures surrounding the brain, not from the brain tissue itself.

rhinencephalia.definition: A congenital malformation characterized by hypoplasia or agenesis of the olfactory portion of the forebrain (olfactory bulbs, tracts and related rhinencephalic structures), resulting in impaired olfactory function and often associated with other forebrain anomalies.

encephalodysplasia.definition: A developmental brain malformation defined by abnormal formation and organization of brain tissue, usually due to disrupted neuronal proliferation, migration, or differentiation (a nonstandard/historic term for cerebral dysplasia).

encephaloid carcinoma.definition: An archaic term for a malignant epithelial tumor (carcinoma) in which the tumor cells are poorly differentiated and have a brain-like (encephaloid) appearance; historically used to describe aggressive undifferentiated carcinomas, but it is not a current standard diagnostic term.

encephalomeningocele.definition: Congenital herniation of brain tissue and meninges through a defect in the skull, forming a sac (a cranial neural tube defect).

encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis.definition: A nonfamilial neurocutaneous disorder characterized by a facial port-wine stain in the trigeminal distribution and ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas, leading to seizures, cognitive impairment, and motor deficits; imaging shows tram-track intracranial calcifications and leptomeningeal enhancement (Sturge-Weber syndrome).

sturge-weber syndrome.definition: A neurocutaneous vascular disorder (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) characterized by a facial port-wine stain in the trigeminal nerve distribution and ipsilateral leptomeningeal capillary-venous malformations, which can cause seizures, hemiparesis, cognitive impairment, visual loss, and glaucoma; imaging may show tram-track intracranial calcifications.

epidemic encephalitis.definition: An acute inflammatory disease of the brain that occurs in epidemic outbreaks, usually caused by a viral infection, characterized by fever, headache, altered consciousness, seizures, and possibly focal neurologic deficits or coma.

encephalitis neonatorum.definition: An historical term for inflammation of the brain in a newborn caused by infection (perinatal or congenital), typically presenting with poor feeding, irritability, seizures, lethargy, and fever; nowadays described as neonatal encephalitis or neonatal meningitis/meningoencephalitis depending on CNS involvement, with etiologies including herpes simplex virus and various bacterial pathogens.

encephalitis periaxialis diffusa.definition: A diffuse, nonfocal inflammatory process of the brain parenchyma; historically used to denote widespread inflammatory involvement rather than localized lesions, with etiologies including infectious or inflammatory (autoimmune) processes.

enamel hypocalcification.definition: A qualitative defect of dental enamel caused by insufficient mineralization during tooth development, yielding chalky, opaque white patches that are softer and more prone to caries.

enamel niche.definition: Not a standard dental term; it would refer to a small depression or recess in the enamel surface, representing a localized enamel defect (such as a pit) rather than a normal anatomical feature.

enamel organ.definition: The dental organ of the tooth germ that forms enamel by differentiating into ameloblasts; a component of the developing tooth consisting of inner enamel epithelium, stellate reticulum, and stratum intermedium.

hydroxyapatite.definition: A calcium phosphate mineral (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) that is the principal inorganic component of bone and tooth enamel; biocompatible and osteoconductive, widely used as a bone graft substitute and as coatings for dental and orthopedic implants.

fluorapatite.definition: Calcium phosphate mineral in which fluoride ions substitute for hydroxide in the hydroxyapatite lattice; a fluoride-substituted form of hydroxyapatite found in bone and dental enamel, more resistant to acid dissolution than hydroxyapatite.

tooth crown.definition: The portion of a tooth that is visible above the gum line, covered by enamel; in restorative dentistry, a crown is a cap placed over a tooth to restore its shape, size, strength, and function.

enchondromatosis.definition: Multiple enchondromas (benign cartilaginous tumors within the medullary cavity of bones), typically in the small bones of the hands and feet, causing deformities and fractures; a nonhereditary skeletal disorder also known as Ollier disease (may be associated with Maffucci syndrome when soft tissue hemangiomas are present).

enchondrosis.definition: A disorder characterized by abnormal development or formation of cartilage, often referring to cartilaginous tissue anomalies within bone such as enchondromas or other cartilaginous growths.

ollier's disease.definition: A nonhereditary skeletal disorder characterized by multiple enchondromas (benign cartilaginous tumors) within bones, typically in an asymmetric pattern, causing deformities and limb shortening; there is a risk of malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma.

maffucci's syndrome.definition: A nonhereditary disorder characterized by multiple enchondromas (benign cartilaginous bone tumors) accompanied by soft-tissue hemangiomas (venous malformations), typically presenting in early childhood with limb deformities and an increased risk of malignant transformation of enchondromas to chondrosarcoma.

pleurisy.definition: Inflammation of the pleura, the thin membranes surrounding the lungs and lining the chest cavity.

endarteritis.definition: Inflammation of the intima, the inner lining of an artery, which can cause thickening of the vessel wall and narrowing of the arterial lumen; it can be caused by infection or immune-mediated processes (e.g., syphilitic endarteritis of the vasa vasorum).

endarteritis obliterans.definition: A chronic inflammatory process of small- to medium-sized arteries characterized by endarteritis with intimal proliferation that leads to progressive luminal narrowing and obliteration, classically seen in tertiary syphilis (syphilitic endarteritis obliterans).

libman-sacks endocarditis.definition: A form of nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis with sterile, immune-mediated vegetations on the heart valve leaflets (most often the mitral and aortic valves), seen in systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid syndrome; these vegetations may cause valvular regurgitation and systemic emboli.

subacute bacterial endocarditis.definition: An infection of the heart’s endocardial surface (usually the valves) caused by less virulent bacteria, most commonly viridans group streptococci, with a gradual, weeks‑long onset of fever, fatigue, and weight loss; often a new or changing heart murmur and possible embolic phenomena, occurring in people with preexisting valvular disease or congenital heart defects.

endocardial cushion defect.definition: A congenital heart defect caused by failure of the endocardial cushions to fuse, resulting in a primum-type atrial septal defect with involvement of the AV septum and often a common AV valve; may be partial or complete and is frequently associated with Down syndrome.

endocardial cushions.definition: Two thickened masses of endocardial-derived mesenchyme in the embryonic heart's atrioventricular canal that proliferate and fuse to form the atrioventricular septum and the mitral and tricuspid valves; they arise by endothelial-to-mesenchymal transformation of the endocardium and contribute to the membranous portions of the septa. Defects can lead to AV canal defects.

endocardial fibroelastosis.definition: A rare form of cardiomyopathy in which the endocardium of the ventricles becomes thickened by fibrous and elastic tissue, leading to restrictive (diastolic) ventricular filling and heart failure, most often presenting in infancy and frequently involving the left ventricle.

endocardial murmur.definition: Not a standard term. A heart murmur is a sound produced by turbulent blood flow within the heart, usually across a valve or within a chamber. If "endocardial murmur" is used, it would imply intracardiac (endocardial) turbulence rather than a valvular lesion, but this terminology is not commonly employed.

endocervicitis.definition: Inflammation of the endocervical canal—the inner mucous-lined portion of the cervix that extends into the uterus—usually due to infection, commonly caused by pathogens such as Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

endochondral.definition: A process of bone formation in which a hyaline cartilage template is progressively replaced by bone tissue, generating most bones of the skeleton (especially long bones) during fetal development and postnatal growth.

endochondral bone.definition: Bone that forms through endochondral ossification, in which a hyaline cartilage model is gradually replaced by bone tissue, producing most long bones and the axial skeleton with primary ossification in the diaphysis, secondary centers in the epiphyses, and growth at the epiphyseal plates.

endocrine diabetes mellitus.definition: A form of diabetes mellitus caused by an underlying endocrine disorder that impairs insulin secretion or action (secondary diabetes due to conditions such as acromegaly or Cushing syndrome).

endocrine gland.definition: A ductless gland that releases hormones directly into the bloodstream to regulate metabolism, growth, and other body functions.

langerhans.definition: A dendritic cell of the epidermis that functions as an antigen-presenting cell to T cells, initiating cutaneous immune responses; characterized by Birbeck granules and expression of CD1a and Langerin (CD207).

suprarenal glands.definition: A pair of endocrine glands located on the superior poles of the kidneys; they consist of the adrenal cortex and adrenal medulla and secrete corticosteroids (including aldosterone and cortisol), and catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine) to regulate metabolism, electrolyte balance, vascular tone, and the body's stress response.

end-diastolic pressure.definition: Pressure in a ventricle at the end of diastole (just before contraction); reflects preload and ventricular compliance and is used to assess filling pressures and diastolic function.

endometrial.definition: Relating to the endometrium, the mucous membrane lining the uterus that thickens during the menstrual cycle and is shed during menstruation if pregnancy does not occur.

endodermal.definition: Pertaining to the endoderm, the innermost of the three primary germ layers in the embryo; it forms the epithelium of the digestive and respiratory tracts and gives rise to associated glands such as the liver and pancreas.

endodontia.definition: The branch of dentistry concerned with the study and treatment of diseases of the dental pulp and surrounding periradicular tissues; its common procedures include root canal therapy.

endodontology.definition: A branch of dentistry dealing with the study and treatment of the dental pulp and the root canal–related tissues, including diagnosis, prevention, and management of pulpal and periapical diseases (e.g., root canal therapy).

pulpodontia.definition: A nonstandard term likely referring to disease or pathology of the dental pulp (the soft tissue inside a tooth), such as pulpitis or pulpal degeneration; not a widely recognized term in current dental/medical dictionaries.

endodontist.definition: A dentist who treats diseases in the soft tissue (dental pulp) in your teeth.

endogenous.definition: Produced within the body; arising from internal physiological processes rather than from external sources.

hypertriglyceridemia.definition: An elevation of triglycerides in the bloodstream, usually defined as fasting plasma triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL; it can be primary (genetic lipoprotein disorders) or secondary to conditions such as diabetes, obesity, alcohol use, or certain medications, and it increases the risk of pancreatitis and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

endorphin.definition: Endogenous opioid neuropeptides produced by the central nervous system and pituitary that activate opioid receptors to modulate pain and produce analgesia and euphoria.

uric.definition: Pertaining to uric acid, a nitrogenous waste product produced from purine metabolism.

acid.definition: A substance that donates hydrogen ions (protons) in aqueous solution, thereby lowering pH; in clinical contexts, gastric acid (primarily hydrochloric acid) aids digestion and maintains stomach acidity.

endointoxication.definition: A historical term for systemic poisoning caused by endogenous toxins produced within the body (often by gut bacteria) and absorbed from the intestines—autointoxication; largely discredited in modern medicine.

endolymph.definition: The potassium-rich fluid within the membranous labyrinth of the inner ear, produced by the stria vascularis, that bathes hair cells and is essential for auditory and vestibular transduction.

endolymphatic.definition: Relating to endolymph, the potassium-rich fluid contained within the membranous labyrinth of the inner ear.

pap.definition: A cytology-based screening test for cervical cancer in which cells collected from the cervix are stained (usually with the Papanicolaou stain) and examined microscopically to detect precancerous or cancerous changes; also known as a Pap smear.

progestogen.definition: Any hormone having the same effect as progesterone in the body; refers to both natural progesterone and synthetic progestin.

adenoacanthomas.definition: A rare benign adnexal skin tumor characterized by mixed differentiation with gland-like (adeno) structures and squamous (acanthomatous) components.

fibroids.definition: Common, noncancerous growths of the uterus that occur in women of reproductive age.

postmenopausal.definition: Relating to the period after menopause, defined clinically as no menstrual periods for 12 consecutive months and corresponding decreased ovarian estrogen production.

perimenopausal.definition: Relating to the transitional period before menopause, during which menstrual cycles become irregular and ovarian estrogen production declines, often with vasomotor symptoms.

myometrium.definition: Thick middle muscular layer of the uterus composed of smooth muscle fibers; it contracts during childbirth to expel the fetus and also contributes to menstrual contractions, lying between the endometrium (inner lining) and the serosa (outer covering).

parietal.definition: Relating to the walls of a body cavity; in anatomy, used to describe structures that form the outer boundary of a cavity, such as the bones forming the sides and roof of the skull.

rectosigmoid.definition: Relating to the rectum and sigmoid colon; the rectosigmoid region is the distal portion of the large intestine where the sigmoid colon transitions to the rectum.

yolk.definition: Yellow, nutrient-rich portion of an ovum that provides fats, proteins, and other nutrients to nourish the developing embryo in egg-laying animals.

tympanic.definition: Relating to the tympanum (the eardrum) or the middle ear; pertaining to the eardrum.

gonococci.definition: Gram-negative diplococci of the genus Neisseria, the etiologic agents of gonorrhea; they commonly infect mucous membranes of the genitourinary tract, rectum, and pharynx, and are transmitted sexually.

streptococci.definition: Genus of Gram-positive cocci that typically occur in chains and are facultatively anaerobic; many species are normal human flora of the oropharynx and skin, while others are pathogens. They are classified by Lancefield group antigens (A, B, C, G, etc.) and by hemolysis pattern (α, β, or γ). Clinically important species include β-hemolytic Group A and Group B organisms, which cause infections such as pharyngitis, skin infections, neonatal sepsis, pneumonia, and meningitis.

menstrual.definition: Relating to menstruation—the monthly process in which the endometrium is shed and vaginal bleeding occurs when pregnancy does not occur.

ovulatory.definition: Relating to ovulation; the release of a mature oocyte from the ovary during the menstrual cycle.

endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreato.definition: An endoscopic procedure that combines endoscopy and fluoroscopy to diagnose and treat disorders of the biliary and pancreatic ductal systems, typically involving cannulation of the ampulla of Vater, injection of contrast to obtain radiographic images, and potential therapeutic interventions such as sphincterotomy, stone extraction, stricture dilation, or stent placement.

ercp.definition: An endoscopic procedure that uses fluorescence/fluoroscopy to visualize and treat the biliary and pancreatic ductal systems; a scope is passed to the duodenum, contrast dye is injected into the ducts, and X-ray imaging guides diagnosis and therapy (e.g., removal of bile duct stones, stent placement, sphincterotomy).

abdominoscopy.definition: Endoscopic examination of the abdominal cavity performed by introducing a scope through the abdominal wall to visualize abdominal organs; a historical term largely superseded by laparoscopy.

gastroscopy.definition: A procedure in which a flexible endoscope is inserted through the mouth to visualize the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum, allowing biopsy and therapeutic interventions.

otoscopy.definition: Otoscopy is the clinical examination of the external auditory canal and tympanic membrane performed with an otoscope to assess ear health and identify infections, effusions, injuries, or other ear pathology.

vaginoscopy.definition: An endoscopic examination of the vagina using a vaginoscope to visualize the vaginal mucosa and cervix, allowing evaluation of discharge, trauma, foreign bodies, or congenital anomalies; can be performed without a traditional speculum in certain patients (e.g., children or uncooperative patients).

endotoxin.definition: A heat-stable lipopolysaccharide component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria (specifically the lipid A portion) that, when released, activates the host innate immune response via TLR4, causing fever and potentially septic shock.

endotoxin shock.definition: A form of septic shock caused by endotoxins (lipopolysaccharide) from Gram-negative bacteria, triggering a systemic inflammatory response with vasodilation, capillary leakage, hypotension, and potential organ dysfunction; management includes prompt antibiotics, aggressive IV fluid resuscitation, and vasopressor support.

septic shock.definition: A subset of sepsis characterized by persistent hypotension requiring vasopressor therapy to maintain a mean arterial pressure ≥65 mmHg and a serum lactate level >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation, reflecting circulatory, cellular, and metabolic dysfunction.

endothelial cell.definition: Flattened cell that lines the interior surface of blood and lymphatic vessels and the heart, forming the endothelium; it regulates vascular permeability, blood flow, coagulation, and immune/inflammatory responses.

edrf.definition: A vasodilatory factor released by the vascular endothelium that induces relaxation of adjacent smooth muscle and vasodilation, primarily via nitric oxide–mediated activation of soluble guanylate cyclase and increased cyclic GMP.

endothelin.definition: A family of potent vasoconstrictor peptides produced mainly by endothelial cells (principally endothelin-1) that regulate vascular tone and blood pressure by binding to endothelin receptors on vascular smooth muscle; involved in cardiovascular and renal pathophysiology and targeted by endothelin receptor antagonists in conditions such as pulmonary arterial hypertension.

et-1.definition: 21-amino-acid peptide produced mainly by endothelial cells; a potent vasoconstrictor and mitogen for vascular smooth muscle that signals through endothelin receptors ET_A and ET_B to regulate vascular tone and contribute to conditions such as pulmonary arterial hypertension.

et-2.definition: A potent vasoconstrictive peptide of the endothelin family produced by endothelial and other cells; encoded by the EDN2 gene; involved in regulation of vascular tone and blood pressure and implicated in various physiological and pathophysiological processes.

et-3.definition: Endothelin-3 is a 21‑amino‑acid peptide in the endothelin family produced mainly by endothelial cells; it acts as a potent vasoconstrictor and signals through endothelin receptors (primarily ETB) to regulate vascular tone and the development of neural crest–derived tissues, including the enteric nervous system. It is encoded by the EDN3 gene.

endothelioma.definition: A tumor arising from endothelial cells that line blood vessels and lymphatic channels; it can be benign or malignant depending on histology and behavior. Modern terminology uses more specific classifications (e.g., hemangioma for benign vascular tumors, hemangioendothelioma for intermediate-grade lesions, and angiosarcoma for malignant tumors).

hemendothelioma.definition: A rare vascular tumor arising from endothelial cells with intermediate malignant potential, lying between benign hemangiomas and malignant angiosarcomas; it can involve soft tissue, liver, bone, or lung, and its behavior and prognosis vary by site and histologic subtype.

lymphendothelioma.definition: A rare vascular neoplasm arising from the endothelial lining of lymphatic vessels.

endosteal.definition: Relating to the endosteum, the thin membranous lining of the inner surface of bone and the medullary cavity.

endosteal hyperostosis.definition: An uncommon genetic skeletal disorder characterized by excessive bone formation along the inner surface of bones (the endosteum), causing osteosclerosis and thickening of cortical bone; features range from asymptomatic radiographic findings to bone pain, stiffness, and deformities.

van buchem's syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal recessive osteosclerotic bone dysplasia caused by deletion of a regulatory region of the SOST gene, leading to decreased sclerostin and excessive bone formation; characterized by diffuse skull and facial bone thickening, possible nerve compression and dental crowding, typically with normal intellect and without syndactyly.

endosteal implant.definition: A dental implant type surgically embedded into the jawbone (alveolar bone) to serve as an anchor for a prosthetic tooth; typically a titanium screw or blade that osseointegrates with the bone and supports crowns, bridges, or dentures.

dental implant.definition: A fake tooth that is put into your jaw bone.

basal bone.definition: The base of the skull; the floor of the cranial cavity that supports the brain, formed by portions of the occipital, sphenoid, temporal, and ethmoid bones.

orthodontic appliances.definition: Devices used in orthodontics to move and align teeth and influence jaw growth by applying controlled forces to teeth and supporting tissues; includes fixed appliances (braces with brackets and wires), removable appliances (retainers, aligners, space maintainers), and functional devices (expanders, headgear).

fracture fixation.definition: Fracture fixation is the stabilization of fractured bone fragments to preserve proper alignment and allow healing, typically achieved by surgical means using internal or external hardware (eg, plates, screws, intramedullary nails, pins, external fixators); nonoperative immobilization with casts or splints can also serve to stabilize a fracture when appropriate.

endoskeletal prosthesis.definition: An artificial limb in which the load-bearing framework is internal—a central pylon inside soft tissue—with a removable cosmetic outer shell (often silicone). Joints and components attach to the internal skeleton rather than to a load-bearing external shell.

endoskeleton.definition: An internal skeleton made of bone and/or cartilage within the body that provides structural support, protects internal organs, and acts as a lever system for muscles (bone marrow resides in the bones).

endplate.definition: Endplate refers to a terminal tissue boundary: (1) the thin hyaline cartilage layer (vertebral endplate) that separates an intervertebral disc from the adjacent vertebral body and permits nutrient diffusion; (2) the postsynaptic region of the neuromuscular junction (motor endplate) on the muscle fiber where acetylcholine receptors cluster to receive nerve impulses.

motor end plate.definition: Post-synaptic region of a skeletal muscle fiber at the neuromuscular junction; the specialized area of the sarcolemma opposite the motor neuron terminal rich in acetylcholine receptors (nicotinic) within junctional folds. When acetylcholine is released, it binds these receptors to generate an end-plate potential that triggers a muscle action potential and contraction.

myoneural junction.definition: Synapse between a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fiber where acetylcholine is released to stimulate depolarization of the muscle cell and trigger contraction.

ach.definition: Neurotransmitter used at cholinergic synapses; mediates transmission at the neuromuscular junction and in parasympathetic pathways; synthesized from choline and acetyl-CoA by choline acetyltransferase and degraded by acetylcholinesterase.

acetylcholine receptors.definition: Acetylcholine receptors are proteins that bind acetylcholine to trigger cellular responses; they include nicotinic receptors (ligand-gated ion channels at neuromuscular junctions and in the CNS) and muscarinic receptors (G protein–coupled receptors mediating slower, modulatory cholinergic effects in heart, smooth muscle, glands, and brain).

synaptic cleft.definition: A narrow extracellular gap (~20–40 nm) between the presynaptic and postsynaptic membranes at a chemical synapse, across which neurotransmitters are released and diffuse to bind receptors on the postsynaptic cell to propagate the neural signal.

end-tidal capnography.definition: A noninvasive monitoring modality that measures the concentration (or partial pressure) of carbon dioxide in the gas exhaled at the end of expiration (end-tidal CO2, EtCO2) and displays it as a capnogram; used to assess ventilation, confirm airway placement, and guide resuscitation.

end-tidal co2.definition: Partial pressure or concentration of carbon dioxide at the end of an exhaled breath, measured noninvasively by capnography; reflects alveolar CO2 and is used to monitor ventilation and verify airway placement. Normal range is about 35–45 mmHg.

end-tidal co2 determination.definition: Noninvasive measurement of the carbon dioxide concentration at the end of expiration, typically by capnography, reflecting alveolar CO2 and used to assess ventilation, verify airway placement, and monitor respiratory status.

endotracheal extubation.definition: The removal of an endotracheal tube from the trachea after the patient has regained sufficient spontaneous breathing and airway protective reflexes, usually after meeting extubation/readiness criteria or completing a spontaneous breathing trial.

endotracheal anesthesia.definition: An anesthesia technique in which an endotracheal tube is inserted to secure the airway and allow controlled ventilation, with anesthesia maintained using inhaled anesthetics and/or intravenous agents during surgery.

laryngeal mask airway.definition: A supraglottic airway device consisting of an inflatable mask that sits over the laryngeal inlet and is connected to a ventilation tube; it seals around the glottis to permit ventilation during anesthesia or rescue airway management, without endotracheal intubation.

supraglottic airway.definition: A ventilation device placed above the glottis that seals around the laryngeal inlet to permit breathing support without endotracheal intubation; commonly used in anesthesia and emergency airway management (examples include the laryngeal mask airway and the i-gel).

mainstem bronchi.definition: Two principal airways that originate from the distal trachea and enter the lungs (right and left mainstem bronchi); they conduct air into the lungs and divide into the lobar (secondary) bronchi.

volume respirator.definition: A mechanical ventilator that delivers a predetermined tidal volume with each inspiration; the inspiratory phase ends when the set volume is reached, providing a fixed amount of air per breath while airway pressure varies with lung compliance and resistance.

positive-pressure ventilation.definition: Delivery of air or oxygen to the lungs by applying positive pressure during the inspiratory phase, typically using a ventilator; can be invasive (endotracheal or tracheostomy tube) or noninvasive (mask), used to support or replace spontaneous breathing.

end-stage disease.definition: An advanced, typically irreversible stage of a disease in which curative treatment is no longer feasible or beneficial, with progressive symptoms and functional decline, for which care emphasizes comfort and quality of life (palliative/end-of-life care).

enduron.definition: Not a widely recognized medical term; it may be a brand name or a misspelling. Please provide context or check spelling to allow an accurate definition.

methyclothiazide.definition: A thiazide-like diuretic used to treat hypertension and edema; inhibits NaCl reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule, increasing excretion of sodium and water; can cause hypokalemia and metabolic disturbances; contraindicated in anuria.

deserpidine.definition: An antihypertensive alkaloid that depletes monoamine neurotransmitters from sympathetic nerve endings, thereby reducing sympathetic tone and lowering blood pressure; historically used but now largely obsolete due to adverse effects.

gastric ulcer.definition: A gastric ulcer is a peptic ulcer in the stomach characterized by a break or erosion of the gastric mucosa, often forming a crater, usually due to an imbalance between mucosal defenses and aggressive factors such as Helicobacter pylori infection or NSAID use.

gastric ulcers.definition: A peptic ulcer occurring in the lining of the stomach (gastric mucosa), usually due to Helicobacter pylori infection or NSAID use, presenting with epigastric pain and carrying risks of bleeding or perforation.

benign strictures.definition: Noncancerous narrowing of a tubular organ (such as the esophagus, biliary tract, or ureter) caused by scar tissue or inflammation, which may lead to obstruction; distinguished from malignant strictures by the absence of cancerous tissue.

ampullary stenosis.definition: A narrowing at the ampulla of Vater (the major duodenal papilla) where the bile and pancreatic ducts drain into the duodenum, leading to impaired drainage and potential obstructive jaundice, cholangitis, or pancreatitis.

malignant tumors.definition: Occurs when new cells grow rapidly, creating a growth or tumor, rather than simply replacing old cells with new ones. Malignant tumors are cancer. Also called malignant neoplasms.

pancreatic ducts.definition: The pancreatic ducts are a network of channels that carry pancreatic juice—digestive enzymes and bicarbonate-rich fluid—from the exocrine pancreas to the duodenum. The main pancreatic duct (duct of Wirsung) runs the length of the pancreas and typically joins the common bile duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater) at the major duodenal papilla; the smaller accessory duct (duct of Santorini) drains at the minor duodenal papilla.

endothelial myeloma.definition: Not a recognized medical term; no standard definition exists. It may be a misnomer for a plasma cell neoplasm (multiple myeloma) or a vascular endothelial tumor, but there is no entity specifically called “endothelial myeloma.”

enkephalin.definition: An endogenous opioid peptide that functions as a neurotransmitter/neuromodulator to suppress pain signaling; two main forms, met-enkephalin and leu-enkephalin, are short pentapeptides derived from proenkephalin and preferentially bind delta opioid receptors.

enervation.definition: The loss or interruption of nerve supply to a muscle or body part, resulting in diminished function or atrophy.

enflurane.definition: An inhaled volatile anesthetic agent (a halogenated ether) formerly used to induce and maintain general anesthesia; largely replaced by sevoflurane, desflurane, and isoflurane due to risks of epileptiform activity and hepatic toxicity.

enfuvirtide.definition: A fusion inhibitor antiretroviral for HIV-1 that binds gp41 and blocks fusion of the viral envelope with the host cell membrane, thereby inhibiting viral entry; administered by subcutaneous injection (typically 90 mg twice daily).

amebic-dysentery.definition: An invasive intestinal infection caused by Entamoeba histolytica, presenting with bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and colitis; transmitted by ingestion of cysts in contaminated food or water; treated with a tissue amebicide (e.g., metronidazole or tinidazole) followed by a luminal agent (e.g., paromomycin or iodoquinol) to eradicate cysts.

entamoeba-histolytica.definition: A pathogenic intestinal protozoan parasite that causes amebiasis, including amebic dysentery and liver abscess; acquired by ingesting cysts in contaminated food or water; treated with a tissue-active agent (metronidazole or tinidazole) followed by a luminal agent (paromomycin or iodoquinol) to eradicate cysts.

entamoeba-coli.definition: A nonpathogenic amoebic protozoan of the human large intestine; a commensal Entamoeba species detected in stool that does not invade tissue or cause disease, often distinguished from the pathogenic E. histolytica by its lack of tissue invasion and cysts typically with up to eight nuclei.

entamoeba-gingivalis.definition: A non–cyst-forming amoeboid protozoan that inhabits the human oral cavity, especially the gingival crevice; trophozoites feed on bacteria and debris; its presence is associated with gingivitis and periodontitis in some cases, but its role as a pathogen is not proven.

entacapone.definition: An oral catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) inhibitor used with levodopa (often with carbidopa) to treat Parkinson disease by blocking peripheral levodopa metabolism, thereby increasing and prolonging dopamine levels and reducing wearing-off.

enteral-feeding.definition: Delivery of nutritionally complete or partial nourishment directly into the stomach or small intestine via a feeding tube (e.g., nasogastric, orogastric, gastrostomy, or nasojejunal) when oral intake is insufficient or unsafe; uses the gastrointestinal tract and can be provided continuously or intermittently.

enteral-nutrition.definition: Delivery of nutrition directly into the gastrointestinal tract to meet caloric and nutrient needs when oral intake is insufficient or unsafe, using specially formulated formulas administered via feeding routes such as nasogastric, gastrostomy, or jejunostomy tubes.

enteric-infection.definition: An infection of the intestinal tract caused by pathogenic microorganisms (bacteria, viruses, or parasites) that invade and multiply in the GI mucosa, typically causing diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and sometimes fever; usually transmitted via the fecal-oral route through contaminated food or water.

enteric-fever.definition: A systemic febrile illness caused by Salmonella enterica serovars Typhi and Paratyphi (typhoid and paratyphoid fever), transmitted via the fecal-oral route. It presents with prolonged fever, malaise, abdominal pain, and sometimes rose spots or hepatosplenomegaly; diagnosis is by blood culture and treatment with appropriate antibiotics.

typhoid-fever.definition: A systemic infection caused by Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi, acquired via ingestion of contaminated food or water; presents with prolonged high fever, malaise, abdominal pain, headache, loss of appetite, and sometimes rose-colored spots on the trunk; can lead to serious complications such as intestinal perforation or hemorrhage if untreated; treated with targeted antibiotics and preventable by vaccination and improved sanitation.

enterectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove a portion of the small intestine.

enteric-coating.definition: A pH-sensitive coating applied to oral tablets or capsules that resists dissolution in the acidic stomach and dissolves in the higher pH of the small intestine, to protect the drug from stomach acid or to achieve intestinal release.

echo-virus.definition: An echovirus is a member of the enterovirus genus (nonpolio picornaviruses) historically termed “enteric cytopathic human orphan virus.” These nonenveloped, positive-sense RNA viruses are transmitted mainly by the fecal–oral route and can cause illnesses ranging from mild fever or gastroenteritis to aseptic meningitis and, rarely, more severe disease.

antiretrovirals.definition: Medications used to treat HIV infection by inhibiting replication of the virus at various stages of its life cycle, usually given in combination to suppress viral load and preserve immune function; they include nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), protease inhibitors (PIs), integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs), and entry/fusion inhibitors.

enoxacin.definition: A fluoroquinolone antibiotic that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, blocking bacterial DNA replication; previously used for various infections such as UTIs and gonorrhea but now less commonly employed due to safety and resistance concerns.

enoximone.definition: An intravenous phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor used as an inodilator in acute heart failure to increase myocardial contractility and cause vasodilation by raising intracellular cAMP; used for short-term hemodynamic support.

myocardial-infarction.definition: Occurs when the flow of blood to the heart is stopped by a blood clot or a spasm of an artery. Also called a heart attack or MI.

unstable-angina.definition: Chest pain that occurs or worsens in frequency, severity, or duration when a person is at rest or engaging in mild activity.

pulmonary-embolism.definition: A sudden blockage of a pulmonary artery or its branches by a blood clot, most often arising from a deep vein thrombosis in the legs.

deep-venous-thrombosis.definition: A condition characterized by the formation of a blood clot (thrombus) in a deep vein, most often in the legs, causing leg swelling and pain; it can detach and travel to the lungs, causing a potentially life-threatening pulmonary embolism.

renal-failure.definition: An impairment of kidney function in which the kidneys cannot adequately filter waste products from the blood, leading to buildup of urea and creatinine, electrolyte and fluid imbalances, and, in severe cases, uremia; it may be acute or chronic and can progress to end-stage renal disease requiring dialysis or transplantation.

lactic-acidosis.definition: A rare but potentially lethal condition in which blood lactic acid levels increase.

guillain-barre-syndrome.definition: An acute autoimmune inflammatory polyneuropathy causing rapidly progressive, symmetric limb weakness with areflexia, often after a gastrointestinal or respiratory infection; due to immune-mediated demyelination (and sometimes axonal damage) of peripheral nerves; diagnosed by clinical features with CSF albuminocytologic dissociation and abnormal nerve conduction studies; treated with intravenous immunoglobulin or plasmapheresis and supportive care; most patients recover, though some have persistent deficits and autonomic dysfunction can occur.

guillainbarresyndrome.definition: An acute autoimmune inflammatory polyneuropathy causing rapidly progressive, symmetrical weakness and areflexia, typically triggered by an infection; may lead to respiratory failure and autonomic instability; treated with plasmapheresis or intravenous immunoglobulin, with variable recovery over weeks to months.

abdominal-distress.definition: Subjective discomfort or pain in the abdomen, often with associated symptoms such as nausea, bloating, cramping, or tenderness, that may arise from various gastrointestinal or abdominal conditions.

abdominal-pain.definition: Discomfort or pain located anywhere in the abdomen, which may be acute or chronic and can arise from disorders of abdominal organs (stomach, intestines, liver, pancreas, kidneys, gallbladder) or from the abdominal wall; evaluation focuses on onset, location, quality, duration, intensity, radiation, and associated symptoms.

back-pain.definition: Discomfort or pain located in the back (cervical to lumbar) that can be acute or chronic; commonly due to musculoskeletal strain, disc problems, or arthritis, but may also reflect nerve compression or other spine conditions. Symptoms may be localized or radiate to the limbs.

hypokinesia.definition: Decreased amplitude and speed of voluntary movements; reduced spontaneous movement commonly observed in Parkinsonian syndromes.

hyperkinesia.definition: An abnormally increased amount of movement, either excessive voluntary movements or involuntary motor activity, seen in certain neurological disorders or due to drug effects.

orthostatic-hypotension.definition: A sudden drop in blood pressure upon standing or getting out of bed, causing dizziness.

protein-energy-malnutrition.definition: A form of malnutrition caused by insufficient protein and energy (calorie) intake, resulting in wasting and/or edema; includes marasmus (severe wasting), kwashiorkor (edema with fatty liver), and mixed PEM.

protein-energy.definition: Relating to the intake and metabolism of dietary protein and calories (energy); used to describe nutritional adequacy or disorders resulting from insufficient protein and energy intake (protein-energy malnutrition).

biparietal-diameter.definition: The maximum transverse width of the fetal skull measured on ultrasound in the axial view at the level of the thalami and cavum septi pellucidi; used to estimate gestational age and monitor fetal growth, with head shape variations (brachycephaly/dolichocephaly) potentially affecting the measurement.

ischial-spines.definition: One of two bony projections on the posterior border of the ischium; palpable pelvic landmarks used to estimate pelvic width, with the distance between them (the interspinous or interischial diameter) aiding pelvimetry.

midpelvis.definition: The middle portion of the true pelvis, between the pelvic inlet (superior border) and the pelvic outlet (inferior border); bounded anteriorly by the pubic symphysis, posteriorly by the sacrum, and laterally by the ischial spines.

xiphoid-process.definition: The small cartilaginous projection at the inferior end of the sternum (breastbone) that ossifies with age; serves as an attachment for the diaphragm and abdominal muscles and is a key landmark for chest compressions in CPR.

ensiform-cartilage.definition: The cartilaginous portion of the xiphoid process of the sternum; the lowest part of the sternum that is initially cartilage in infancy and ossifies with age, serving as an attachment for parts of the diaphragm and abdominal muscles and as an anatomical landmark.

posterior-horn.definition: A region of the spinal cord's gray matter on the posterior (dorsal) side that contains sensory interneurons and receives afferent input from the dorsal roots, processing somatic and visceral sensory information.

spinal-cord.definition: A cylindrical bundle of nervous tissue that extends from the medulla oblongata to the lower back within the vertebral column; it conducts sensory information from the body to the brain, transmits motor commands from the brain to the body, and mediates reflexes. It comprises white matter tracts surrounding gray matter.

gray-matter.definition: Gray matter refers to regions of the nervous system composed mainly of neuronal cell bodies, dendrites, unmyelinated axons, glial cells, and capillaries; it appears gray due to the absence of myelin and is the site of synaptic processing and integration (e.g., cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, spinal dorsal horns).

pituitary-gland.definition: Controls other glands (like the thyroid) and also how you grow.

ent.definition: Abbreviation for the medical specialty that diagnoses and treats disorders of the ears, nose, and throat; also known as otolaryngology.

nasoduodenal.definition: Relating to the nose and the duodenum; used to describe a nasoduodenal tube, a feeding tube inserted through the nostril into the duodenum.

nasojejunal.definition: Relating to a feeding tube inserted through the nose that extends into the jejunum, used to deliver enteral nutrition directly to the small intestine.

esophagostomy.definition: A surgical procedure that creates a stoma from the esophagus to the skin (often in the neck) to divert esophageal secretions or provide access for feeding when the esophagus is obstructed or nonfunctional.

gastrostomy.definition: A surgical procedure that creates an opening (stoma) from the abdominal wall into the stomach to allow direct access for feeding, drainage, or decompression, typically with placement of a gastrostomy tube (often via endoscopic, percutaneous, or surgical methods).

jejunostomy.definition: A surgical procedure that creates an opening (stoma) between the jejunum and the abdominal wall to provide direct access for enteral feeding or drainage.

enophthalmos.definition: Posterior displacement of the eyeball within the orbit, producing a sunken appearance of the eye; often due to orbital trauma with fat loss, scarring, or orbital diseases.

enteroclysis.definition: A radiographic procedure in which contrast material is infused directly into the small intestine via a nasoduodenal or enteric catheter, with fluoroscopic visualization to evaluate small-bowel anatomy and motility.

typhoid.definition: An acute systemic febrile illness caused by infection with Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi, usually transmitted via ingestion of contaminated food or water; characterized by prolonged fever, malaise, abdominal pain, and sometimes rose-colored spots; untreated infection can lead to serious complications, but it is treatable with appropriate antibiotics and preventable by vaccination and improvements in sanitation.
