enterocolitis.definition: Inflammation of the small intestine and the colon (simultaneous enteritis and colitis), which can result from infections, ischemia, inflammatory bowel disease, or antibiotic-associated changes.

enterobacter.definition: A genus of Gram-negative, rod-shaped, facultatively anaerobic bacteria in the family Enterobacteriaceae; many species are part of the normal intestinal flora, but some are opportunistic pathogens causing infections such as urinary tract infections, pneumonia, wound infections, and sepsis, especially in hospitalized or immunocompromised patients.

cloacae.definition: A common posterior cavity or opening through which the digestive, urinary, and reproductive tracts discharge in certain animals (e.g., birds, reptiles, amphibians, monotremes); in humans, it refers to the embryonic cloaca that divides to form the anorectal canal and the urogenital sinus.

aerobacter.definition: A historical, now obsolete genus of Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacteria in the Enterobacteriaceae family; the species previously placed in Aerobacter (such as Aerobacter aerogenes) have been reclassified into Enterobacter and related genera.

aerogenes.definition: A historical name for a Gram-negative, lactose-fermenting, non-spore-forming rod in the Enterobacteriaceae family; formerly classified as Enterobacter aerogenes (also called Aerobacter aerogenes), an opportunistic pathogen associated with nosocomial infections.

escherichia.definition: A genus of Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacteria in the Enterobacteriaceae family; many species inhabit the intestinal tract of humans and animals, with the best-known species being a common gut bacterium that ranges from harmless commensals to pathogenic strains causing gastroenteritis, urinary tract infections, and sepsis.

coli.definition: A Gram-negative, facultatively anaerobic, rod-shaped bacterium in the genus Escherichia; a normal inhabitant of the human and animal gut, but certain strains can cause gastroenteritis, urinary tract infections, neonatal meningitis, and other invasive diseases.

salmonella.definition: A group of germs (bacteria) that can be found in raw foods and sometimes in pets that can make you very sick.

enterococcemia.definition: A bloodstream infection caused by Enterococcus species (most commonly E. faecalis or E. faecium), often arising from urinary tract or intra‑abdominal sources and frequently associated with nosocomial bacteremia and complications such as endocarditis.

enterococcus.definition: Genus of gram-positive, catalase-negative cocci that are facultative anaerobes; part of the normal gastrointestinal flora but can cause opportunistic infections such as urinary tract infections, bacteremia, endocarditis, and intra-abdominal infections. Common species include Enterococcus faecalis and Enterococcus faecium, often resistant to multiple antibiotics (notably vancomycin in VRE).

enterococci.definition: A genus of Gram-positive cocci that grow in pairs or short chains, are facultative anaerobes and part of the normal human intestinal flora; they can cause opportunistic infections (e.g., urinary tract infections, bacteremia, endocarditis) and are notable for intrinsic resistance to many antibiotics, with some strains vancomycin-resistant (VRE).

faecalis.definition: Latin adjective meaning "of feces" or "fecal"; used in scientific names to indicate isolation from fecal material, and by itself does not denote a disease or a specific organism.

faecium.definition: A species of Gram-positive cocci in the genus Enterococcus; part of the normal intestinal flora but can cause nosocomial infections, including urinary tract infections, bacteremia, and endocarditis. Some strains are resistant to multiple antibiotics, notably vancomycin (vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus).

vancomycin-resistant.definition: Describing bacteria that have acquired resistance to vancomycin, typically by altering the cell wall target to reduce drug binding (eg, replacing D-Ala-D-Ala with D-Ala-D-Lac or D-Ala-D-Ser), often via van gene clusters (eg, vanA, vanB), as seen in vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE).

otitis.definition: Inflammation of any part of the ear, most commonly referring to otitis media (middle ear infection) or otitis externa (ear canal infection).

enteroenterostomy.definition: A surgical connection between two segments of the intestine (usually the small bowel) created to restore continuity after resection or to bypass a diseased or obstructed segment.

enterogastritis.definition: Inflammation of both the stomach and the small intestine (gastritis and enteritis), often presenting with nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea; may be caused by infection, toxins, medications, or immune-mediated processes.

enteroglucagon.definition: A glucagon-like peptide produced by enteroendocrine L cells in the small intestine from proglucagon; collectively referred to as enteroglucagon, including glicentin and other glucagon-derived fragments involved in gut function and glucose regulation.

glicentin.definition: A peptide hormone produced by intestinal L cells from proglucagon; it is a relatively large proglucagon-derived peptide that includes part of the glucagon sequence, and its exact physiological role remains not fully understood.

oxyntomodulin.definition: A gut-derived peptide hormone produced by intestinal L-cells from proglucagon; a 37‑amino‑acid glucagon‑like peptide that acts as a dual agonist of the glucagon receptor and GLP‑1 receptor, promoting satiety, slowing gastric emptying, and influencing energy and glucose metabolism.

enterhepatic.definition: Relating to the intestine and liver; used to describe processes that move substances between the gut and liver, such as the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids and certain drugs.

enterokinase.definition: A brush-border serine protease of the duodenum that activates pancreatic trypsinogen to trypsin by cleaving after a lysine in the activation peptide (recognizing the DDDDK sequence).

enterolith.definition: A stone formed within the lumen of the gastrointestinal tract from the precipitation of minerals around a nidus in areas of intestinal stasis (often associated with diverticular disease or other motility/obstruction-related conditions); it can cause obstruction.

enterolithiasis.definition: Formation of stone-like concretions within the lumen of the intestine (enteroliths); stones form often due to intestinal stasis or abnormal contents and may be associated with diverticular disease, strictures, or Crohn disease, potentially causing obstruction or abdominal pain.

enterocele.definition: A pelvic floor prolapse in which loops of small intestine (or the peritoneal sac containing them) herniate through a defect in the posterior vaginal wall into the vagina, often via the rectovaginal septum or cul-de-sac.

enterochromaffin.definition: Of or relating to enterochromaffin cells of the gastrointestinal mucosa; neuroendocrine cells that synthesize and secrete serotonin (5-HT).

enterocutaneous.definition: Relating to an abnormal connection between the intestinal tract and the skin.

enterovesical.definition: Relating to the intestine and the urinary bladder; used to describe a connection between these two organs, such as an abnormal fistula between the bowel and bladder.

vesicoenteric.definition: Relating to an abnormal communication between the urinary bladder and the intestinal tract, often due to fistula formation, which may cause symptoms such as pneumaturia and fecaluria.

echo.definition: A noninvasive ultrasound imaging test of the heart used to visualize cardiac anatomy and assess function, including chamber sizes, valves, wall motion, and blood flow (often with Doppler).

enteroviruses.definition: Small, nonenveloped, icosahedral, positive-sense RNA viruses in the family Picornaviridae. They primarily replicate in the gastrointestinal tract but can cause a wide spectrum of disease, from mild febrile illness and gastroenteritis to aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, myocarditis, respiratory infections, or hand-foot-and-mouth disease. Transmission is mainly fecal-oral, with respiratory spread possible in some infections; notable members include polioviruses, coxsackieviruses, echoviruses, and other related viruses.

enteroviral.definition: Relating to enteroviruses, a group of nonenveloped, positive-sense RNA viruses in the family Picornaviridae (genus Enterovirus) that commonly infect the gastrointestinal tract and can cause a range of illnesses from mild febrile disease to aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, myocarditis, and hand-foot-and-mouth disease.

enthesitis.definition: Inflammation at the enthesis, the site where a tendon, ligament, or joint capsule inserts into bone; it commonly causes focal tenderness at tendon insertions and is characteristic of seronegative spondyloarthropathies.

enthesopathy.definition: Enthesopathy is a disorder of the enthesis, the site where a tendon, ligament, or joint capsule attaches to bone, characterized by pain and structural changes at the attachment, often due to inflammatory enthesitis or degenerative changes.

entodermal.definition: Relating to the endoderm, the innermost embryonic germ layer that forms the lining of the gut and its derivatives, including parts of the respiratory and digestive tracts.

basidiobolus.definition: A genus of environmental fungi in the order Entomophthorales; Basidiobolus ranarum is the species most commonly associated with human basidiobolomycosis, a rare subcutaneous fungal infection.

ranarum.definition: Not a recognized clinical term; it may be a misspelling or a Latin genitive form meaning “of the frogs,” which has no medical definition. If you have a context or a related term, I can help pinpoint the intended term.

entopic.definition: Located in its normal place; not displaced from its usual anatomical position.

entropy.definition: A thermodynamic quantity that measures the degree of disorder or randomness of a system and the dispersal of energy at the molecular level. In spontaneous processes, total entropy tends to increase; in biological contexts, higher entropy corresponds to greater molecular disorder and energy dissipation.

enucleator.definition: A surgical instrument used to remove an organ or mass in enucleation by grasping and gently separating it from surrounding tissues, usually preserving the organ's capsule.

envenomation.definition: The injection of venom into a person by a venomous animal (e.g., snake, spider, scorpion, cone snail) resulting in local injury and possible systemic toxic effects.

uranium.definition: A radioactive chemical element (symbol U, atomic number 92); a heavy metal with radiotoxicity and nephrotoxicity; not biologically essential; exposure may cause radiation injury and kidney damage.

vinylchloride.definition: A colorless, flammable gas used to manufacture polyvinyl chloride (PVC); chronic exposure is an occupational carcinogen linked to hepatic angiosarcoma, and acute exposure can cause CNS effects such as dizziness, headaches, and confusion.

ionizing.definition: Capable of removing electrons from atoms or molecules, producing ions; describes high-energy radiation (ionizing radiation) such as X-rays and gamma rays that can ionize tissue and cause cellular damage.

radiation.definition: Energy in the form of particles or waves, such as x-rays and gamma rays. Radiation is often used to help make a diagnosis, as in x-rays, or as a treatment for cancer.

ultraviolet.definition: An electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths shorter than visible light, roughly 10–400 nanometers; in medicine, UV radiation is used for phototherapy and sterilization, but overexposure causes DNA damage, sunburn, skin aging, and cancer risk. It is subdivided into UVA (315–400 nm), UVB (280–315 nm), and UVC (100–280 nm).

x-rays.definition: A picture of the inside of your body, using small amounts of radiation.

coal.definition: A combustible sedimentary rock mainly composed of carbon, formed from ancient plant material and used as fuel; inhalation of coal dust can cause coal workers’ pneumoconiosis (black lung disease) and other pulmonary problems.

cigarette.definition: A small cylinder of finely cut tobacco wrapped in paper (often with a filter) designed to be lit and smoked, delivering nicotine and numerous toxicants; smoking cigarettes is associated with nicotine dependence and increased risk of cancer, cardiovascular disease, and respiratory disease.

cellophane.definition: A thin, transparent film made from regenerated cellulose used for wrapping and packaging; non-toxic and widely used for food packaging.

parasitic.definition: Relating to or caused by a parasite; living on or in a host from which it derives nutrients at the host’s expense.

enterobius.definition: A genus of small parasitic nematodes (pinworms) that inhabit the intestinal tract of vertebrates; in humans, the most common species causes enterobiasis (pinworm infection), transmitted by the fecal-oral route and frequently presenting with perianal itching.

vermicularis.definition: A Latin adjective meaning worm-like or worm-shaped; used to describe organisms or structures that resemble a worm. It is the species epithet of the pinworm, a small intestinal nematode parasite that causes enterobiasis.

oxyuriasis.definition: A parasitic infection of the large intestine caused by Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm), characterized by nocturnal perianal itching; transmitted by ingesting eggs from contaminated hands or surfaces; treated with albendazole, mebendazole, or pyrantel pamoate.

pinworm.definition: Small, white nematode parasite that infects humans, most often children. It causes enterobiasis, with nocturnal perianal itching from female worms laying eggs around the anus; transmission is fecal-oral via eggs on hands or surfaces. Diagnosis is typically by perianal cellophane-tape test. Treatment is a course of antihelminthic medication (e.g., albendazole or mebendazole), and household contacts may require treatment to prevent reinfection.

intestine.definition: A long, tubular portion of the digestive tract extending from the stomach to the anus, consisting of the small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum) where most nutrient digestion and absorption occur, and the large intestine (cecum, colon, rectum) where water absorption and feces formation occur.

ostomy.definition: A surgical procedure that creates an opening (stoma) from an internal organ to the body’s surface to divert and discharge waste (feces or urine).

nosocomial.definition: An infection that you catch in the hospital.

eosinophil.definition: A white blood cell of the granulocyte family with a bilobed nucleus and cytoplasmic granules that stain with eosin; it defends against parasitic infections and participates in allergic inflammation by releasing cytotoxic proteins and inflammatory mediators.

eosinophilic.definition: Relating to eosinophils; describing tissue with eosinophil infiltration or cells that stain readily with eosin dye (pink/red on routine histology).

cantonensis.definition: A parasitic nematode (rat lungworm) whose larvae can infect humans, causing eosinophilic meningitis after ingestion of larvae in contaminated snails, slugs, or produce.

gnathostoma.definition: A genus of parasitic nematodes (family Gnathostomatidae) that infect humans and other vertebrates, causing gnathostomiasis.

spinigerum.definition: A parasitic nematode species that causes gnathostomiasis in humans; humans acquire infection by consuming raw or undercooked fish, amphibians, or reptiles containing infective larvae, which migrate through tissues and can cause migratory subcutaneous swellings and, rarely, severe visceral or neurological disease.

subtilis.definition: A Gram-positive, rod-shaped, endospore-forming bacterium of the genus Bacillus, commonly found in soil; generally nonpathogenic in healthy individuals but can be an opportunistic pathogen; widely used as a model organism in microbiology and in industrial enzyme production.

alcalase.definition: A commercial protease enzyme (subtilisin-like serine protease) derived from Bacillus licheniformis, used industrially to hydrolyze proteins in detergents and food processing; optimally active under alkaline conditions and thermostable.

enzyme.definition: A biological catalyst, usually a protein, that accelerates a specific chemical reaction in living organisms by lowering the activation energy; it is not consumed in the reaction and is often substrate-specific, sometimes requiring cofactors or coenzymes.

triphosphate.definition: A molecule consisting of a nucleoside bound to three phosphate groups, containing high-energy phosphoanhydride bonds; nucleoside triphosphates (e.g., ATP, GTP) serve as cellular energy carriers and as substrates for polymerization.

enzymatic.definition: Relating to enzymes; occurring or produced by enzymes, or catalyzed by enzymes in biochemical reactions.

substrate.definition: A molecule that binds to the active site of an enzyme and is converted into products; the reactant in an enzymatic biochemical reaction.

elisa.definition: Plate-based immunoassay that detects and quantifies a target analyte by antigen–antibody binding and a labeled enzyme that converts a substrate to produce a colorimetric, fluorescent, or luminescent signal proportional to the analyte concentration. Formats include direct, indirect, sandwich, and competitive variants.

radioimmunoassay.definition: Radioimmunoassay is an in vitro assay that uses radiolabeled antigen or antibody to measure very small concentrations of a substance (often a hormone or drug) in a biological sample. It relies on competitive binding: a fixed amount of radiolabeled antigen competes with the unlabeled antigen in the sample for a limited amount of antibody; the bound fraction is separated and its radioactivity measured to determine the unknown concentration.

fixation.definition: The stabilization and immobilization of a structure—most commonly a fracture or joint—to allow healing (often with implants or external devices); it can also refer to the preservation of biological tissue by chemical fixation.

glutaraldehyde.definition: A potent dialdehyde chemical used as a high-level disinfectant and chemical sterilant for heat‑sensitive medical instruments; it inactivates microorganisms by cross‑linking proteins and nucleic acids.

fluorometry.definition: An analytical technique that measures the intensity of light emitted by a sample after it is excited by light, used to quantify fluorescent molecules or labeled biomolecules and to study molecular interactions.

photometry.definition: Measurement of visible light as perceived by the human eye, quantifying brightness through luminous flux (lumens), illuminance (lux), and luminous intensity (candela); it is distinguished from radiometry, which measures radiant energy regardless of eye sensitivity.

ependymal.definition: Relating to the ependyma; ependymal cells line the brain’s ventricular system (ventricles) and the spinal cord’s central canal, forming a simple ciliated epithelium that helps circulate cerebrospinal fluid.

ependyma.definition: Thin, single-layer neuroepithelium lining the brain's ventricular system and the spinal cord's central canal; formed by ependymal cells, it lines the ventricles and helps circulate cerebrospinal fluid, with some regions contributing to CSF production.

ependymitis.definition: Inflammation of the ependymal lining of the brain's ventricular system (and the spinal cord’s central canal), typically due to infection or inflammatory disease, which can contribute to ventriculitis and hydrocephalus.

ependymoblastoma.definition: A rare, highly malignant embryonal tumor of the central nervous system, typically occurring in infancy or early childhood, composed of undifferentiated blastemal cells with ependymal differentiation and often multilayered rosettes; historically called ependymoblastoma but now regarded as part of embryonal tumor with multilayered rosettes (ETMR), frequently with amplification of the C19MC microRNA cluster and a poor prognosis.

ependymoma.definition: A glial tumor arising from ependymal cells lining the ventricular system of the brain or the spinal canal; it can obstruct CSF flow and cause hydrocephalus, and is typically treated with surgical resection, sometimes followed by radiotherapy.

ependymocytoma.definition: A neoplasm arising from ependymal cells lining the brain ventricles and spinal canal; an ependymal tumor that may cause hydrocephalus and is usually treated with surgical resection, with radiotherapy for higher-grade disease.

epicardial.definition: Relating to the epicardium, the outermost layer of the heart wall that covers the heart; it is the visceral layer of the serous pericardium.

epicondyle.definition: A bony prominence above a condyle on a long bone that serves as an attachment site for muscles and ligaments.

epicondylar.definition: Relating to an epicondyle, a rounded projection above a bone’s condyle (most commonly the humerus at the elbow) where ligaments and tendons attach.

epicondylitis.definition: Inflammation or degeneration of the tendinous insertions of the forearm muscles at the elbow, typically due to overuse; includes lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) and medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow).

epicranial.definition: Relating to the epicranium—the scalp and the skull cap; the tissues covering the skull, including the galea aponeurotica.

galea.definition: A tough fibrous layer of the scalp that covers the top of the skull; a flat aponeurosis connecting the frontal and occipital muscle bellies and lying between the skin/ connective tissue and the pericranium.

epicanthus.definition: A fold of skin on the upper eyelid at the inner corner of the eye (medial canthus) that covers the medial aspect of the eye.

epicanthal.definition: Relating to the vertical fold of skin at the inner corner of the upper eyelid that covers the medial canthus.

epicanthic.definition: Relating to the epicanthus; describing an epicanthal fold of skin at the inner corner of the eye that can cover part of the medial canthus.

epicostal.definition: Pertaining to a rib; located on or over the rib (on the external surface of a rib rather than between ribs).

epaxial.definition: Muscles of the back that develop from the epaxial portion of the somite and lie dorsal to the vertebral column; they include the intrinsic back muscles (e.g., erector spinae, transversospinales) and are innervated by the dorsal rami of spinal nerves.

obturator.definition: An adjective meaning to close or obstruct a passage. In anatomy, describing structures related to the pelvic foramen and the muscles and nerve that pass through or arise from it.

extraocular.definition: Pertaining to structures outside the eyeball; relating to the extraocular muscles that move the eye.

epec.definition: A diarrheagenic Escherichia coli pathotype that causes watery diarrhea by attaching to intestinal mucosa and effacing microvilli via a type III secretion system; commonly transmitted through contaminated food or water.

occipitofrontalis.definition: A muscle of facial expression consisting of the frontal and occipital bellies connected by the galea aponeurotica; it elevates the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead and retracts the scalp.

temporoparietalis.definition: A thin muscle of the temporal region that overlies the temporalis muscle; in many mammals it aids ear movement (pinna), but in humans it is typically vestigial with little functional significance.

shulman.definition: Not a recognized medical term; commonly a surname with no standard medical definition.

myeloencephalitis.definition: Inflammation of both the spinal cord and the brain (involving myelitis and encephalitis), typically caused by infectious, autoimmune, or parainfectious processes, leading to combined central nervous system dysfunction.

intolerance.definition: In medicine, intolerance is an adverse reaction to a substance (such as a drug or food) that occurs because the body cannot adequately tolerate or metabolize it, typically non–immune mediated.

bovine.definition: Relating to cattle; pertaining to cows or bulls.

porcine.definition: Relating to pigs; derived from pigs; used to describe pig anatomy, tissues, organs, or products (e.g., pig heart valves).

pathogenic.definition: Capable of causing disease; used to describe agents (such as bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites) that can induce illness.

organisms.definition: A living, organized unit capable of growth, metabolism, response to stimuli, and reproduction; can be unicellular or multicellular and is composed of one or more cells.

benign.definition: Something that isn't harmful or is not cancer.

epicritic.definition: Relating to finely discriminative somatic sensation (e.g., fine touch, vibration, proprioception) as opposed to crude, nociceptive, or temperature sensations; in neurophysiology, the epicritic pathway is carried by the dorsal-column–medial‑lemniscus system.

epidermal nevus.definition: A benign congenital proliferation of epidermal keratinocytes producing hyperkeratotic, warty plaques that follow Blaschko lines; typically present at birth or in early childhood and may be isolated or part of epidermal nevus syndrome with multisystem anomalies.

ep epithelial nevus.definition: A congenital, non-melanocytic hamartoma of the epidermis due to overgrowth of keratinocytes, presenting as a hyperkeratotic plaque or patch (often verrucous) that may follow Blaschko lines; typically present at birth or in early childhood and usually benign, though it can be part of epidermal nevus syndromes when associated with systemic abnormalities.

epidermolysis bullosa.definition: An inherited skin disorder characterized by extreme fragility of the skin and mucous membranes with blistering after minor trauma, due to mutations in genes encoding structural proteins that mediate epidermal–dermal adhesion (e.g., keratins, laminin-332, type VII collagen), with a spectrum of severity across subtypes.

epidermomycosis.definition: A superficial fungal infection of the epidermis (outer skin layer), typically caused by dermatophytes or yeasts, resulting in pruritic, erythematous, scaling plaques without deep dermal involvement.

epidermophytosis.definition: A fungal infection of the epidermis caused by dermatophyte fungi (classically Epidermophyton species), producing scaly, pruritic patches on the skin (tinea).

epididymitis.definition: Inflammation of the epididymis, the coiled duct at the back of the testicle that stores and transports sperm; usually due to infection, presenting with acute unilateral scrotal pain and swelling (often with fever), and treated with antibiotics targeting likely pathogens plus supportive care.

epididymoorchitis.definition: Inflammation of the epididymis and the testis, usually due to infection; presents with acute or subacute scrotal pain and swelling, often with fever, dysuria, or urethral discharge; treated with targeted antibiotics and supportive care.

epididymovesiculography.definition: A radiographic procedure in which contrast medium is injected into the epididymal ducts (and often the ejaculatory ducts) to visualize the epididymis, vas deferens, and seminal vesicles and to evaluate for obstructive pathology.

epidural abscess.definition: A collection of pus in the epidural space (between the dura mater and the vertebral bones), usually due to bacterial infection, that can compress the spinal cord or nerve roots; presents with back or neck pain, fever, and neurologic deficits, andRequires urgent antimicrobial therapy with surgical drainage if needed.

epidural hematoma.definition: Blood collection between the skull and the dura mater, typically caused by traumatic rupture of a meningeal artery; presents with rapid neurological decline and requires urgent CT imaging and neurosurgical evacuation.

epidural space.definition: In the spinal canal, the epidural space is the potential space between the dura mater and the periosteum of the vertebral canal, containing fat and a venous plexus; it is the site where epidural anesthesia is administered.

epidural catheter.definition: A flexible tube inserted into the epidural space around the spinal cord (commonly via the lumbar region) to deliver local anesthetics and/or opioids for regional anesthesia or continuous analgesia during labor or postoperative pain control.

epiglottic vallecula.definition: A shallow depression in the mucosa of the oropharynx located between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis; one of the valleculae, used as a landmark during laryngoscopy and intubation.

keratoconjunctivitis.definition: Inflammation involving both the cornea and the conjunctiva of the eye, typically presenting with redness, irritation, tearing, discharge, and sensitivity to light; it can be allergic, infectious, or irritant in origin and may be acute or chronic.

epidemic cerebrospinal meningitis.definition: An outbreak of acute bacterial meningitis affecting many people in a defined area over a short period, most often due to Neisseria meningitidis; transmitted person-to-person by respiratory droplets; presents with fever, headache, neck stiffness, and altered mental status; managed with antibiotics and public health interventions.

japanese encephalitis.definition: An acute viral infection of the central nervous system caused by a mosquito-borne flavivirus transmitted primarily by Culex species; endemic in Asia and parts of the western Pacific. It typically starts with fever, headache, and vomiting, and can progress to altered consciousness, seizures, or coma in severe cases. Survivors may have long-term neurological deficits; vaccination is available for prevention, and there is no proven specific antiviral therapy beyond supportive care.

von economo's encephalitis.definition: An historical inflammatory brain disease described by Constantin von Economo, typically beginning with an influenza‑like prodrome followed by a prolonged somnolent state, oculomotor disturbances, and later movement disorders and neuropsychiatric symptoms; many survivors developed chronic sequelae such as Parkinsonian features, with the exact cause remaining unknown.

epidemic hemorrhagic fever.definition: A rodent-borne viral illness caused by hantaviruses, presenting with abrupt fever and malaise followed by hemorrhagic manifestations and renal involvement; transmitted via inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta, with incubation of about 1–2 weeks and a spectrum from mild illness to severe, potentially fatal disease.

devil's grip.definition: A historical term for sudden, severe, cramping abdominal pain (colic), typically due to spasms of the gastrointestinal or urinary tracts.

epidemic myalgia.definition: A viral illness, typically due to Coxsackie B virus, characterized by abrupt, severe focal chest or upper abdominal pain (pleurodynia) often with fever and malaise, occurring in outbreaks and resolving with supportive care.

epidemic myositis.definition: An acute, outbreak-associated inflammatory myopathy, often in children, triggered by a viral infection, presenting with sudden, severe muscle pain (tender calves commonly) and mild proximal weakness; serum CK may be elevated, and most cases resolve spontaneously within days to weeks with supportive care.

parotitis.definition: Inflammation of the parotid gland (the largest salivary gland located near the ear), typically due to infection or obstruction; presents with swelling and tenderness in the preauricular region, and may be viral (e.g., mumps) or bacterial, acute or chronic.

european typhus.definition: A form of epidemic (louse-borne) typhus caused by the intracellular bacterium Rickettsia prowazekii, transmitted by the body louse (Pediculus humanus corporis). It presents with abrupt onset of high fever, severe headache, myalgias, and a trunk-predominant maculopapular rash that often spreads to the limbs; complications such as delirium, pneumonia, or encephalitis can occur if untreated. Treatment is with doxycycline or other tetracyclines; prevention focuses on lice control and improved hygiene, with historical outbreaks in Europe during wars and famines.

jail fever.definition: An historical term for epidemic typhus fever occurring in overcrowded prisons; caused by the bacterium Rickettsia prowazekii and transmitted by body lice; characteristically presents with sudden high fever, severe headache and myalgias, often with a maculopapular rash; can be severe or fatal without treatment.

louse-borne typhus.definition: An infectious disease (epidemic typhus) caused by the bacterium Rickettsia prowazekii, transmitted to humans by the body louse (Pediculus humanus corporis). It typically presents with abrupt high fever, severe headache, myalgias, and a maculopapular rash that begins on the trunk and spreads outward; can be severe and lead to delirium or systemic complications. Treated with doxycycline; prevention by delousing.

brill-zinsser disease.definition: A recrudescence (reactivation) of latent syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum, occurring years after the initial infection, typically presenting with a secondary-syphilis–type illness (fever, malaise, and a generalized skin eruption) and treated with standard syphilis therapy (e.g., benzathine penicillin).

norwalk virus.definition: Non-enveloped, single-stranded positive-sense RNA virus of the Caliciviridae family that causes acute gastroenteritis; abrupt onset of vomiting and watery diarrhea with abdominal cramps and nausea, usually lasting 1–3 days; highly contagious and spread via contaminated food or water, person-to-person contact, and contaminated surfaces; diagnosis is usually clinical, with confirmation by RT-PCR; treatment is supportive (rehydration, electrolyte management, antiemetics); no specific antiviral therapy; prevention focuses on hand hygiene, isolation of the ill, and surface disinfection.

epigastric reflex.definition: An abdominal superficial reflex in which gentle stroking of the epigastric region evokes contraction of the upper abdominal wall muscles, used to assess the integrity of the abdominal nerve pathways and corticospinal tract.

epigastric node.definition: A lymph node located in the epigastric region of the abdomen; part of the abdominal lymphatic system, filtering lymph from the skin and subcutaneous tissues of the upper anterior abdominal wall and communicating with other nearby lymph node groups.

epigastric sensation.definition: A sensation localized to the epigastric region (the upper central abdomen beneath the sternum), which may include pain, discomfort, fullness, burning, or pressure and can be related to gastric or esophageal conditions.

epigastrium.definition: The upper central region of the abdomen, located just below the sternum, that overlies the stomach and portions of the liver and pancreas.

pilar cyst.definition: A benign, keratin-filled skin cyst that originates from the outer root sheath of a hair follicle (most often on the scalp), lined by stratified squamous epithelium with trichilemmal keratinization.

sebaceous cyst.definition: A benign subcutaneous cyst arising from blockage of a sebaceous gland or hair follicle, lined by stratified squamous epithelium and filled with keratinous material; commonly referred to as an epidermoid cyst.

epidermal inclusion cyst.definition: A benign cutaneous cyst formed by epidermal cells implanted into the dermis, lined by stratified squamous epithelium and filled with keratin; presents as a slow-growing, mobile subcutaneous nodule often with a central punctum and may become inflamed or infected.

epidermoid cyst.definition: A benign cutaneous cyst formed by epidermal elements implanted into the dermis, lined by stratified squamous epithelium and filled with keratin; presents as a slow-growing, movable subcutaneous nodule, often with a central punctum, and may become inflamed if infected.

epidermoid carcinoma.definition: A malignant neoplasm arising from squamous epithelial cells (epidermal keratinocytes); a form of squamous cell carcinoma commonly arising in skin or mucous membranes, characterized by invasive growth and potential for metastasis.

two-point discrimination.definition: The minimum distance at which two simultaneous tactile stimuli applied to the skin are perceived as two distinct points; a measure of tactile acuity that varies by body region and is influenced by age and nerve function.

stereognosis.definition: The ability to recognize objects by touch alone, without visual input, by integrating tactile and proprioceptive information.

proprioception.definition: The ability to sense the position of one’s body in space, in relation to other objects.

epilating forceps.definition: A small pair of forceps with fine tips used to grasp and pull hair from the follicle (epilation) for hair removal in dermatologic or minor surgical procedures.

epilation.definition: The removal of hair from the body by pulling it out from the root, typically by waxing, plucking, or threading (as opposed to shaving or chemical depilatories).

epileptic.definition: Relating to epilepsy; a person who has epilepsy.

klebsiella pneumoniae.definition: A Gram-negative, encapsulated, non-motile rod-shaped bacterium of the Enterobacteriaceae family that ferments lactose; a common cause of pneumonia and other infections, especially in healthcare settings, and often associated with antibiotic resistance.

neisseria meningitides.definition: A gram-negative, encapsulated diplococcus bacterium that colonizes the human nasopharynx and can invade the bloodstream and meninges, causing meningococcal meningitis and meningococcemia; transmitted by respiratory droplets and vaccine-preventable, with several serogroups (including A, B, C, W, and Y).

varicella zoster.definition: An HHV-3 herpesvirus that causes initial varicella (chickenpox) and can remain latent in dorsal root ganglia, reactivating later to cause herpes zoster (shingles). Transmission is via respiratory droplets or contact with vesicular fluid.

bronchial spasm.definition: A sudden constriction of the smooth muscle in the walls of the bronchi, leading to narrowing of the airways and symptoms such as wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath; commonly triggered by asthma, allergic reactions, respiratory infections, or irritants, and usually reversible with bronchodilator therapy.

partial seizures.definition: A seizure that starts in a localized region of one cerebral hemisphere (focal onset). It may remain confined with preserved consciousness (simple partial) or involve impaired consciousness (complex partial); it can secondarily generalize to a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure.

simple partial.definition: A focal onset seizure in which consciousness remains intact during the event; symptoms arise from the involved cortex and may include unilateral motor jerking or stiffening, sensory phenomena (tingling, numbness), autonomic changes, or brief psychic experiences—awareness is preserved, distinguishing it from seizures with impaired consciousness.

complex partial.definition: A type of focal (partial) seizure that begins in a localized area of the brain and causes impaired consciousness or awareness during the event, often with automatisms (such as lip-smacking or fidgeting), confusion, and postictal amnesia.

generalized seizures.definition: Seizures that begin simultaneously in both cerebral hemispheres, leading to impaired consciousness and bilateral, widespread motor and/or autonomic symptoms (including generalized tonic–clonic, absence, myoclonic, clonic, tonic, and atonic seizures).

tonic-clonic seizure.definition: A generalized seizure characterized by an initial tonic stiffening of the body followed by clonic jerking, usually with loss of consciousness and postictal confusion; duration typically 1–3 minutes.

atonic.definition: Lacking normal muscle tone; floppy or relaxed, with reduced resistance to passive movement. It can refer to muscles or to an organ that has lost its tonicity (e.g., uterine atony).

myoclonic.definition: Relating to myoclonus; characterized by brief, involuntary, shock-like jerks of a muscle or group of muscles, which can occur spontaneously or in response to stimulus and may be seen in various neurological disorders.

ictus.definition: The onset of a sudden neurological attack, most commonly the clinical onset of an epileptic seizure.

salter fracture.definition: A fracture through the growth plate (physis) of a developing bone, typically in children, classified into five patterns (types I–V) depending on which parts of the physis, metaphysis, and/or epiphysis are involved; these injuries can disrupt normal bone growth.

epiphyseal fracture.definition: A fracture through the epiphysis, the end portion of a long bone that articulates at a joint; in children it can involve the growth plate (physis) and may affect future bone growth.

epiphyseal plate.definition: A zone of hyaline cartilage between the epiphysis and metaphysis of a long bone in children and adolescents that enables longitudinal bone growth by endochondral ossification; it gradually ossifies to form the epiphyseal line when growth ceases.

epiphysis cerebri.definition: A small endocrine gland in the brain that secretes melatonin and helps regulate circadian rhythms.

epiphysitis.definition: A condition characterized by inflammation of the epiphysis, the end portion of a long bone near a joint (typically involving the growth plate in children).

epipial.definition: Relating to or situated upon the pia mater, the delicate innermost membrane of the meninges surrounding the brain and spinal cord.

epiploic appendage.definition: Small, fat-filled peritoneal pouches projecting from the serosal surface of the colon, attached by a narrow pedicle and scattered along the taeniae coli.

epiploic appendix.definition: Small fat-filled peritoneal outpouchings of the serosal surface of the colon, typically along the taenia coli.

epiploic foramen.definition: An opening in the peritoneal cavity that connects the greater sac to the lesser sac (omental bursa); it is bounded anteriorly by the hepatoduodenal ligament containing the portal triad, posteriorly by the inferior vena cava and right crus of the diaphragm, superiorly by the caudate lobe of the liver, and inferiorly by the first part of the duodenum.

omental foramen.definition: An opening between the greater and lesser sacs of the peritoneal cavity that allows communication between them. It is bounded anteriorly by the hepatoduodenal ligament (containing the portal triad), posteriorly by the inferior vena cava and the right crus of the diaphragm, superiorly by the caudate lobe of the liver, and inferiorly by the first part of the duodenum.

epipygus.definition: An anatomical term historically used to designate a projection or pad at the buttocks, i.e., a prominence in the gluteal/epipygial region.

pygomelus.definition: Definition not found in standard medical dictionaries. It may be a misspelling or an obscure term. If you can provide context (anatomy, disease, or the source), I can help identify the intended term or offer a definition.

epiretinal membrane.definition: A thin fibrocellular membrane on the inner surface of the retina (often the macula) that contracts and distorts retinal architecture, causing metamorphopsia and reduced central vision; it can be idiopathic or secondary to retinal disease.

retinal pigment epithelium.definition: A monolayer of melanin-containing epithelial cells between the neural retina and the choroid that absorbs stray light, phagocytoses shed photoreceptor outer segments, supports the visual cycle and retinal metabolism, and forms the outer blood-retina barrier via tight junctions.

epirubicin.definition: A chemotherapy agent in the anthracycline class that intercalates DNA and inhibits topoisomerase II, leading to DNA strand breaks and cancer cell death; used to treat breast cancer and other solid tumors; usually given intravenously; adverse effects include myelosuppression and dose-dependent cardiotoxicity.

episcleritis.definition: An inflammation of the episclera—the thin vascular layer between the conjunctiva and sclera—characterized by acute redness and mild eye discomfort, with vision typically preserved. It is usually idiopathic or associated with systemic inflammatory diseases and often resolves spontaneously within 1–3 weeks; management includes lubricating drops and, if needed, topical NSAIDs or short courses of topical corticosteroids for persistent or nodular cases.

episcope.definition: A device used to visually inspect the surface of an organ or tissue, typically by illumination and magnification; an older or obscure term not commonly used today.

episiotomy.definition: A surgical incision made in the perineum during childbirth to enlarge the vaginal opening and facilitate delivery.

mediolateral episiotomy.definition: A surgical incision of the perineum made from the posterior vaginal opening and extended laterally away from the midline toward the perineal skin (typically at about a 45-degree angle) to enlarge the vaginal outlet during childbirth.

midline episiotomy.definition: A surgical incision made in the perineum during vaginal delivery, extending vertically from the vaginal opening toward the anus along the midline to enlarge the vaginal outlet; it is repaired with sutures after delivery.

episioplasty.definition: A surgical procedure to repair, reconstruct, or tighten the perineal tissues (the area between the vaginal opening and the anus), typically after childbirth to repair episiotomy or perineal tears and improve function or contour.

episome.definition: A genetic element, usually a plasmid or viral genome, that can either replicate independently as extrachromosomal DNA or become integrated into the host’s chromosome and replicate as part of it.

epispadias.definition: A rare congenital anomaly in which the urethral opening is on the dorsal (upper) aspect of the penis in males, or near the clitoris in females, rather than at the glans tip; often associated with urinary incontinence and penile curvature and may occur as part of the exstrophy–epispadias complex.

rectocele.definition: A weakening of the vaginal wall that allows the rectum to bulge into the vagina.

uterine prolapse.definition: Happens when the womb (uterus) falls down and presses on the vaginal area.

vaginal sulcus.definition: A groove or furrow in the vaginal mucosa; note that “vaginal sulcus” is not a widely standardized anatomical term and may be used variably in different contexts.

febrile neutropenia.definition: An infectious complication of neutropenia characterized by fever (typically ≥38.3°C orally or ≥38.0°C sustained) in a patient with an absolute neutrophil count <500 cells/µL (or expected to fall below 500), requiring urgent evaluation and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics.

intracranial infection.definition: An infection within the skull involving intracranial structures such as the meninges, brain parenchyma, or ventricular system, including conditions like meningitis, encephalitis, and brain abscess.

cerebral trauma.definition: An injury to the brain resulting from an external mechanical force to the head or neck, causing temporary or permanent impairment of cognitive, physical, and/or behavioral functioning; includes both open and closed head injuries and is classified as traumatic brain injury (TBI).

vascular disturbances.definition: An abnormality of the blood vessels that disrupts normal blood flow and tissue perfusion, including vasospasm, thrombosis or occlusion, hemorrhage, aneurysm, and inflammatory or degenerative vessel-disease processes.

extrasystoles.definition: An ectopic heartbeat that occurs earlier than the next expected beat, interrupting the regular rhythm; can be atrial (premature atrial contraction) or ventricular (premature ventricular contraction) in origin. Usually benign in healthy individuals but may be associated with electrolyte disturbances, stimulants, ischemia, or structural heart disease when frequent or symptomatic.

glial cells.definition: Non-neuronal cells in the nervous system that provide support and protection for neurons, regulate the extracellular environment, participate in myelination (CNS: oligodendrocytes; PNS: Schwann cells), and contribute to immune defense and synaptic modulation.

epistasis.definition: A genetic interaction in which the phenotype produced by one gene is masked or modified by alleles at a second gene (a different locus).

epistropheus.definition: The axis—the second cervical vertebra (C2) of the spine—characterized by the odontoid process (dens) that projects upward to articulate with the atlas (C1) and enables head rotation.

epithelioma.definition: A tumor arising from epithelial cells; historically used to denote a malignant epithelial tumor (carcinoma), though the term is largely obsolete in modern practice.

epitheliofibril.definition: A slender filament associated with epithelial tissue; typically refers to cytokeratin intermediate filaments within epithelial cells.

tonofibril.definition: A bundle of keratin intermediate filaments in epithelial cells that anchors at desmosomes and connects to the cytoskeleton, providing mechanical strength and resistance to shear.

epithelioblastoma.definition: Not a standard term in current practice; likely refers to a malignant, high-grade astrocytic brain tumor (WHO grade IV) also known as glioblastoma multiforme. It is the most aggressive primary brain tumor in adults, characterized by rapid growth, necrosis, and microvascular proliferation, often presenting with headaches, focal neurologic deficits, or seizures; treatment typically combines maximal safe surgical resection with radiotherapy and chemotherapy (e.g., temozolomide), but prognosis is poor.

trichoepithelioma.definition: A benign adnexal skin tumor arising from hair follicle germinative cells; presents as small, firm, skin-colored or pink papules or nodules on the face, may be solitary or multiple, and can clinically and histologically resemble basal cell carcinoma.

epizootic.definition: A disease that is common in animals.

epoophoron.definition: A vestigial remnant of the Wolffian (mesonephric) duct in females, consisting of a few small tubules in the broad ligament near the ovary and fallopian tube; typically nonfunctional and of little clinical significance.

parovarium.definition: A vestigial structure in the female reproductive tract, comprising remnants of the Wolffian (mesonephric) ducts near the ovary within the broad ligament; consists of small tubules (epoophoron/paroophoron remnants) and has no significant function in adults.

epoprostenol.definition: An intravenous prostacyclin analog and potent vasodilator that inhibits platelet aggregation; used to treat pulmonary arterial hypertension, administered as a continuous IV infusion due to a short half-life, with adverse effects including flushing, jaw pain, headache, hypotension, and risk of catheter-related complications.

eplerenone.definition: A selective mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) receptor antagonist used as a potassium-sparing diuretic to treat hypertension and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction; it blocks aldosterone receptors in the distal nephron, reducing sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion.

eprosartan.definition: An angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB) used to treat hypertension; it competitively blocks the AT1 receptor, reducing vasoconstriction and aldosterone secretion to lower blood pressure.

electrophysiological.definition: Relating to the electrical properties or activity of biological tissues; used to describe recordings or studies of electrical signals in nerves, muscles, or the heart.

epsdt.definition: A U.S. Medicaid program requirement mandating states to provide comprehensive preventive and health services for children under 21, including periodic screening examinations, diagnostic assessments, and any medically necessary treatment to address identifiable health conditions.

nasopharyngeal.definition: Relating to the nasopharynx, the upper part of the pharynx behind the nasal cavity, extending from the posterior nares to the soft palate.

central_nervous_system_lymphoma.definition: A lymphoma arising within the central nervous system (brain, spinal cord, meninges), either as primary CNS lymphoma (most often diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma) or as secondary involvement from systemic lymphoma; typically treated with high‑dose methotrexate–based chemotherapy, with radiotherapy used selectively.

posttransplantation.definition: Relating to the period following an organ, tissue, or cell transplantation; occurring after transplantation and involving follow-up care, immunosuppressive therapy management, and potential complications.

leukoplakia.definition: A white patch or plaque on mucous membranes (most often the oral mucosa) that cannot be rubbed off and cannot be explained by another diagnosable condition; it is considered a potentially premalignant lesion, often associated with tobacco or alcohol use and chronic irritation, and may require biopsy to assess for dysplasia or malignancy.

vasodilator.definition: A substance or condition that causes blood vessels to open wider and increase the flow of blood.

antiplatelet.definition: A substance or drug that inhibits platelet activation and aggregation, thereby reducing thrombus (clot) formation.

silver_nitrate.definition: An inorganic compound with the formula AgNO3; a topical caustic agent used to cauterize tissue and as an antiseptic with antimicrobial properties. It can cause chemical burns on skin and mucous membranes, and prolonged exposure can lead to argyria (bluish-gray skin discoloration).

packing.definition: Placement of sterile material into a wound or body cavity to absorb drainage, apply pressure to control bleeding, fill dead space, and facilitate healing.

carotid.definition: Relating to the carotid arteries, the pair of major vessels in the neck that supply blood to the brain, face, and neck; the term may also refer to nearby structures such as the carotid sinus or carotid body.

metaphase.definition: A stage of cell division where duplicated chromosomes align at the cell's equatorial plane (metaphase plate) and attach to spindle microtubules via kinetochores in readiness for separation in anaphase.

subthalamus.definition: A small, lens-shaped structure of the diencephalon, located ventral to the thalamus and containing the subthalamic nucleus; part of the basal ganglia circuitry that modulates voluntary movement.

habenula.definition: A pair of small nuclei in the epithalamus (medial and lateral habenula) near the thalamus; involved in processing aversive/negative reward signals and modulating monoaminergic neurotransmission (dopamine and serotonin), thereby influencing mood, motivation, and decision-making.

nasal.definition: Things that are related to the nose.

ergometry.definition: Measurement of work output and metabolic response during physical activity, typically assessed with an ergometer (e.g., bicycle or treadmill) to evaluate fitness or cardiovascular function.

erb-duchenne-paralysis.definition: An injury to the upper trunk (C5–C6) of the brachial plexus causing paralysis of the proximal arm muscles (deltoid, supraspinatus, biceps), typically from traction on the neck during birth or shoulder trauma; presents with a "waiter's tip" posture—adducted and internally rotated arm, extended elbow, and pronated forearm.

erbs-palsy.definition: An obstetric brachial plexus injury affecting the C5–C6 nerve roots, causing paralysis or marked weakness of the shoulder and elbow muscles (e.g., deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps) and producing a characteristic “waiter’s tip” posture of the arm; typically due to traction on the neck during difficult delivery and often improves with time.

erbs-point.definition: A landmark on the left chest, at the third intercostal space near the sternal border, used as a standard auscultation point to hear heart sounds and murmurs.

endoscopic-retrograde-cholangiopancreato.definition: A procedure that uses endoscopy and fluoroscopic guidance to diagnose and treat biliary and pancreatic duct disorders by injecting contrast into the ducts and performing interventions (e.g., stone removal, stenting).

erectile-dysfunction.definition: An ongoing inability to achieve or maintain an erection sufficient for satisfactory sexual activity, due to vascular, neurogenic, hormonal, anatomical, or psychogenic factors.

erection.definition: Physiologic process in which the penis becomes firm and enlarged due to relaxation of smooth muscle in the erectile tissues and engorgement with blood (corpora cavernosa and corpus spongiosum), typically triggered by sexual arousal and mediated by nitric oxide–dependent vasodilation of penile arteries and venous occlusion.

erector-spinae.definition: Group of deep intrinsic back muscles that run longitudinally along the spine and function to extend the vertebral column and maintain an upright posture; comprises the iliocostalis, longissimus, and spinalis. They originate from the sacrum, iliac crest, and lumbar spinous processes and insert on ribs, vertebrae, and the skull, innervated by the dorsal rami of spinal nerves.

ergot.definition: A fungus (Claviceps purpurea) that infects cereal grains such as rye, producing potent alkaloids (ergot alkaloids) used medically to induce uterine contractions and control postpartum bleeding; ingestion of contaminated grain can cause ergotism.

ergotamine-tartrate.definition: A vasoconstrictive ergot alkaloid used to treat acute migraine headaches by constricting cranial blood vessels; commonly administered in combination with caffeine.

ergonovine-maleate.definition: An ergot alkaloid vasoconstrictor used in obstetrics to induce or augment uterine contractions and to treat postpartum hemorrhage by promoting sustained uterine contraction.

ergometrine.definition: A vasoconstrictive ergot alkaloid that stimulates uterine smooth muscle to induce or augment contractions, used as an oxytocic to prevent or treat postpartum hemorrhage.

ergometrine-maleate.definition: A vasoconstrictive ergot alkaloid used as a uterotonic to prevent or treat postpartum hemorrhage by increasing uterine tone and contractions; administered intramuscularly or intravenously after delivery; also known as methylergonovine maleate.

ergotism.definition: Poisoning from ergot alkaloids produced by the fungus Claviceps purpurea contaminating grain; presents in two principal forms: vasoconstrictive (causing painful, cold extremities and possible gangrene) and convulsive (seizures, diarrhea, paresthesias, and psychiatric symptoms).

ergotherapy.definition: A form of rehabilitation focused on enabling individuals to perform daily activities and meaningful tasks, including work, by improving physical, cognitive, and psychosocial functioning through purposeful activities and adaptations, typically provided by an occupational therapist.

ertapenem.definition: A broad-spectrum carbapenem antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins, leading to bactericidal activity; administered intravenously or intramuscularly, with activity against many Gram-negative bacteria and some Gram-positive cocci and anaerobes, but limited activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter species.

erlotinib.definition: An oral epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitor used to treat certain cancers, notably advanced non–small cell lung cancer and pancreatic cancer; it blocks EGFR signaling to inhibit tumor cell proliferation.

dihydroergotamine.definition: A semi-synthetic ergot alkaloid used for the acute treatment of migraine attacks; it acts as a vasoconstrictor, narrowing dilated cranial blood vessels.

eruptive-xanthoma.definition: Small, yellow-orange papules with erythematous bases that erupt abruptly, typically on the buttocks, shoulders, and extensor surfaces; caused by severe hypertriglyceridemia with lipid-laden macrophage deposition in the dermis, and often indicates an underlying lipid disorder and risk of pancreatitis; lesions improve as triglyceride levels are lowered.

erysipelas.definition: An acute bacterial infection of the superficial dermis and lymphatics, typically caused by beta-hemolytic streptococci, presenting as a sharply demarcated, raised, erythematous, and tender plaque, often with fever; managed with systemic antibiotics.

nephrotic-syndrome.definition: Symptoms that indicate kidney damage, resulting from a problem with the kidneys’ filters (called glomeruli). It is caused by a variety of diseases, most commonly diabetes and lupus. Also called nephrosis.

postpartum-hemorrhage.definition: Excessive blood loss after childbirth, usually defined as ≥500 mL after vaginal delivery or ≥1000 mL after cesarean delivery, occurring within 24 hours of birth and potentially leading to hypovolemia.

uterine-atony.definition: A failure of the uterus to contract adequately after delivery, resulting in continued bleeding and postpartum hemorrhage; it is the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage.

fetal-death.definition: The death of a fetus during pregnancy, typically defined as intrauterine fetal demise occurring after about 20 weeks of gestation (or a fetal weight around 500 grams), resulting in a stillbirth.

gastroesophageal.definition: Relating to the stomach and the esophagus, especially the region where they meet (the gastroesophageal junction).

aphthous-ulcers.definition: Recurrent, noncontagious, shallow ulcers of the oral mucosa (often on non-keratinized surfaces) that are painful and usually heal spontaneously within 1–2 weeks; they can be categorized as minor, major, or herpetiform.

external-carotid.definition: A major neck artery that arises from the common carotid and supplies the face and neck; it gives branches including the superior thyroid, ascending pharyngeal, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, maxillary, and superficial temporal arteries, and terminates by dividing into the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries.

cervical-nerve-roots.definition: The dorsal (sensory) and ventral (motor) roots of the eight cervical spinal nerves (C1–C8) that exit the spinal canal through the intervertebral foramina; C1–C7 exit above their vertebrae and C8 exits between C7 and T1, supplying the neck and upper limb.

brachial-plexus.definition: A network of nerves that are rooted at the cervical spine and provide sensation and movement to the shoulder and arm.

biceps.definition: A two-headed muscle of the upper arm that flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm; the long head originates from the supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula and the short head from the coracoid process, inserting on the radial tuberosity and bicipital aponeurosis; innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C6).

sacrospinalis.definition: A group of intrinsic back muscles (the erector spinae) including the spinalis, longissimus, and iliocostalis; it extends and stabilizes the vertebral column and maintains posture, running longitudinally along the back from the sacrum to the skull.

erogenous.definition: Relating to or capable of arousing sexual desire or excitement.

erotogenic.definition: Relating to or capable of eliciting sexual arousal; stimuli or body areas that provoke erotic arousal (erogenous zones).

erysipeloid.definition: A localized cutaneous infection caused by Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, typically acquired from handling fish, meat, or animal products. It presents as a well-defined, violaceous, swollen plaque on the hands or fingers and may imitate erysipelas; treated with antibiotics such as penicillin or doxycycline.

multiforme.definition: Having many forms or appearances; in medicine, used to describe lesions or manifestations that vary in shape, size, or pattern (as in erythema multiforme, a hypersensitivity reaction with target-like skin lesions).

erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae.definition: A gram-positive, non-spore-forming, nonmotile slender rod bacterium that is a zoonotic pathogen, causing erysipeloid in humans after occupational exposure to fish, meat, or poultry, and less commonly septicemia or endocarditis; in animals it causes erysipelas and septicemia, especially in pigs.

fish-handler's disease.definition: A cutaneous infection caused by Mycobacterium marinum acquired from aquatic exposure (e.g., handling fish or aquarium injuries); presents as chronic nodules or plaques that may spread along lymphatic channels (sporotrichoid pattern). Diagnosis is by culture or PCR from tissue; treatment typically requires a multi-drug antibiotic regimen for several months.

erythema marginatum.definition: A nonpruritic, ring-shaped (annular) erythematous rash with central clearing that expands and fades; commonly seen on the trunk and proximal limbs and classically associated with acute rheumatic fever (a major Jones criterion).

acute rheumatic fever.definition: An inflammatory, immune-mediated sequela of infection with group A Streptococcus (usually pharyngitis) that can involve the heart (pancarditis), joints (migratory polyarthritis), brain (Sydenham chorea), skin (erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules), and other tissues; most common in children and adolescents and diagnosed by Jones criteria.

plaque toxic epidermal necrolysis.definition: A life-threatening severe cutaneous adverse reaction most often drug-induced, characterized by widespread epidermal necrosis and skin detachment (typically involving ≥30% of body surface area), mucosal involvement, and a positive Nikolsky sign; requires immediate withdrawal of the offending agent and intensive supportive care, often in a burn unit or ICU.

toxic epidermal necrolysis.definition: A rare, life-threatening drug reaction featuring widespread keratinocyte death with epidermal detachment over a large body surface area (classically >30%), mucous membrane involvement, and systemic illness; considered the most severe form of the Stevens-Johnson syndrome spectrum and requires aggressive supportive care in specialized units.

erythema neonatorum.definition: A neonatal erythematous eruption appearing in the first days of life; historically used as a blanket term for various non-specific, usually benign skin rashes of the newborn.

neonatal pustular melanosis.definition: A benign, self-limited newborn dermatosis presenting at birth or within the first days of life with superficial pustules that rupture easily to leave hyperpigmented macules; lesions are sterile, often on the face, trunk, and extremities, and spontaneously resolve over weeks to months.

erythema perstans.definition: A persistent redness of the skin that remains for an extended period, typically due to ongoing capillary dilation or inflammatory skin processes; it is not, by itself, a specific diagnosis.

erythematous pemphigus.definition: A form of pemphigus presenting with erythematous, sometimes scaly plaques and occasional blisters; an autoimmune blistering disorder in which IgG autoantibodies target desmogleins (desmoglein-1 and/or desmoglein-3), causing acantholysis; diagnosed by histology showing acantholysis and direct immunofluorescence with intercellular IgG in the epidermis; treated with systemic corticosteroids and immunosuppressants.

pemphigus erythematosus.definition: A rare autoimmune blistering disease that represents an overlap between pemphigus and lupus erythematosus. It typically presents with erythematous, crusted facial lesions and superficial blisters from acantholysis; autoantibodies target desmoglein cadherins (primarily desmoglein‑1) with intercellular IgG on immunofluorescence, and it is treated with systemic immunosuppression similar to other pemphigus forms.

erythemogenic.definition: Producing erythema (skin redness); capable of inducing redness of the skin by causing vasodilation and/or inflammatory reactions.

erythralgia.definition: Pain in an area that is red, typically due to inflammation; a rare or historical term denoting erythema-related pain.

erythrasma.definition: A superficial bacterial skin infection caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum, typically in intertriginous areas (groin, axillae). It presents as well-defined, reddish-brown patches that may show coral-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp and is treated with topical or oral antibiotics (commonly macrolides).

erythremia.definition: An abnormal increase in red blood cell mass (polycythemia) causing a ruddy complexion and increased blood viscosity; can be primary (polycythemia vera) or secondary to hypoxia or elevated erythropoietin.

erythroblast.definition: An immature red blood cell precursor in the bone marrow that matures through stages and ejects its nucleus to form a reticulocyte, which then becomes a mature red blood cell.

erythroblastoma.definition: A tumor composed primarily of erythroblasts (immature erythroid precursors), representing a hematopoietic neoplasm of the erythroid lineage (often extramedullary).

erythroblastosis.definition: Presence of immature red blood cell precursors (erythroblasts) in the peripheral blood, indicating stressed or accelerated erythropoiesis; can occur in severe anemia or marrow disorders and, in the fetus/newborn, refers to hemolytic disease of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis) due to Rh incompatibility.

erythroblastosis fetalis.definition: A hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn caused by maternal IgG antibodies (most commonly anti-D) that cross the placenta and destroy fetal red blood cells, leading to fetal anemia, hydrops fetalis, and neonatal jaundice or kernicterus.

erythrochromia.definition: Red discoloration of tissue or mucosa due to increased blood flow or vascular congestion (hyperemia); a descriptive finding rather than a specific disease.

esr.definition: A blood test that measures inflammation by the rate at which red blood cells settle in a sample; also known as the erythrocyte sedimentation rate.

erythrocytopenia.definition: A decreased number of erythrocytes (red blood cells) in the circulating blood, resulting in reduced oxygen-carrying capacity and often contributing to anemia.

erythrocytosis.definition: An increase in the red blood cell mass in the circulation, usually reflected by elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit; it can be absolute (increased red cell production, as in polycythemia vera or secondary erythrocytosis) or relative (hemoconcentration from plasma volume loss).

erythroderma.definition: Generalized redness of the skin involving most of the body surface area (typically ≥90%), usually with diffuse scaling and pruritus; a syndrome caused by a variety of underlying conditions such as inflammatory dermatoses (e.g., psoriasis, eczema), drug reactions, or cutaneous lymphoma.

erythroderma desquamativum.definition: A clinical syndrome of widespread diffuse red (erythematous) skin with shedding of the superficial epidermis (desquamation), typically arising from severe inflammatory dermatoses, drug reactions, or infectious processes.

erythrogenesis.definition: The production and maturation of red blood cells (erythrocytes) from erythroid progenitors in the bone marrow, i.e., erythropoiesis, regulated by erythropoietin.

erythropoiesis.definition: The production and maturation of red blood cells from hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow, regulated by erythropoietin in response to hypoxia, culminating in the release of reticulocytes into the bloodstream.

erythropoietin test.definition: Measurement of erythropoietin concentration in serum or plasma; used to evaluate the cause of anemia or polycythemia by determining whether red blood cell production is appropriately stimulated by erythropoietin, often to distinguish renal or marrow disorders from other causes.

erythrovirus.definition: A genus of small, nonenveloped, single-stranded DNA viruses in the Parvoviridae family. Its best known member infects human erythroid progenitor cells and can cause erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) in children and transient aplastic crises in individuals with hemolytic disorders.

escharotomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which incisions are made through burned eschar to relieve constrictive pressure and restore perfusion, typically to prevent vascular compromise or respiratory compromise in circumferential full-thickness burns.

escharonodulaire.definition: A lesion featuring an eschar (necrotic, crusted tissue) with nodular components.

e. coli.definition: A Gram-negative, facultatively anaerobic, lactose-fermenting bacterium that normally inhabits the intestines of humans and animals; most strains are harmless, but certain pathogenic strains can cause gastroenteritis, urinary tract infections, and neonatal meningitis.

hemolytic disease of the fetus and newbo.word: hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
hemolytic disease of the fetus and newbo.definition: A condition in which maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta and destroy fetal red blood cells, usually due to Rh(D) incompatibility (anti-D) and less commonly ABO incompatibility, leading to fetal anemia and hyperbilirubinemia, which can cause hydrops fetalis and fetal or neonatal death.

hdfn.definition: A condition in which maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta and destroy fetal red blood cells, causing fetal anemia and hyperbilirubinemia; can lead to hydrops fetalis and fetal death; most commonly due to Rh incompatibility or ABO incompatibility.

abo blood groups.definition: An ABO blood group system classifying blood by the presence or absence of A and B antigens on red blood cells; types are A, B, AB, and O (the latter lacking both antigens but with the H antigen present). Plasma contains antibodies against the antigens not present on an individual's red cells (e.g., anti-A or anti-B), which is critical for safe transfusion and transplantation.

hydrops fetalis.definition: A severe fetal condition defined by the accumulation of fluid in at least two fetal compartments (eg, edema, pleural or pericardial effusions, ascites), often due to immune (eg, Rh incompatibility) or nonimmune causes, with high perinatal mortality.

erythrocyte reinfusion.definition: Reinfusion of the patient’s own red blood cells after collection and processing (such as via intraoperative blood salvage) back into the circulation to reduce the need for donor (allogeneic) transfusion.

tick bite.definition: A bite from a tick, a small blood-feeding arachnid; while most bites are harmless, some ticks can transmit pathogens that cause illnesses such as Lyme disease and other tick-borne diseases.

esmarch's bandage.definition: An elastic or rubberized limb bandage used to exsanguinate a limb by wrapping from distal to proximal, pushing blood toward the body to create a bloodless field for surgical procedures (often applied before a tourniquet).

eskalith.definition: A brand-name medication containing lithium carbonate, used as a mood stabilizer to treat and prevent manic and depressive episodes in bipolar disorder.

escobar's syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal recessive fetal akinesia syndrome presenting with multiple congenital joint contractures (arthrogryposis multiplex congenita), often with chest-wall restriction and infancy respiratory insufficiency; commonly due to mutations in nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunit genes (e.g., CHRNG).

escitalopram.definition: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor antidepressant (SSRI) consisting of the S-enantiomer of citalopram; it increases serotonin levels in the synaptic cleft by inhibiting serotonin reuptake and is approved for the treatment of major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder.

escalith.definition: Brand name for lithium carbonate, a mood stabilizer used to treat and prevent manic and depressive episodes in bipolar disorder; requires regular monitoring of serum lithium levels due to a narrow therapeutic index.

bowen's disease.definition: A form of squamous cell carcinoma in situ (intraepidermal squamous cell carcinoma) of the skin, presenting as a persistent, slowly enlarging, well-defined red, scaly or crusted patch or plaque on sun-exposed areas; it is precancerous and may progress to invasive squamous cell carcinoma if untreated.

toxic erythema of the newborn.definition: A common, benign neonatal eruption characterized by sudden onset of erythematous papules, vesicles, or pustules (often on the trunk and proximal limbs) appearing in the first days of life and resolving spontaneously within several days to two weeks; lesions may show eosinophilic infiltrates on pathology, and no treatment is required.

intertrigo.definition: An inflammatory dermatitis of skin folds (intertriginous areas) due to friction, moisture, and maceration, often complicated by secondary infection (commonly Candida albicans or bacteria).

nodules.definition: A nodule is a small, solid, circumscribed mass of tissue that is larger than a papule and distinct from surrounding tissue; it can occur in the skin or in other organs and may be benign or malignant.

target lesions.definition: A skin lesion with three concentric zones: a central dark or necrotic core, a pale or edematous middle zone, and a peripheral erythematous outer ring, giving a bull's-eye or iris appearance; classically seen in erythema multiforme and certain drug reactions.

blistering.definition: Formation of vesicles or bullae on the skin or mucous membranes; typically results from friction, burns, chemical injury, infection, or inflammatory/autoimmune skin diseases.

detachment.definition: Separation or disengagement of a structure from its normal attachments or supporting tissue, such as the retina from the underlying tissue, the placenta from the uterine wall, or a tissue layer peeling away after injury or disease.

pruritic.definition: Relating to itching; producing or characterized by an itchy sensation.

esophagectomy.definition: A surgical operation in which all or part of the esophagus is removed, usually for esophageal cancer or other severe esophageal disease, with reconstruction of the digestive tract (commonly using a portion of the stomach or colon) to restore continuity.

oesophagus.definition: The tube that carries food and liquids from your mouth to your stomach.

esogastritis.definition: Inflammation of the esophagus and stomach (concomitant esophagitis and gastritis).

esomeprazole.definition: A proton pump inhibitor that irreversibly inhibits the hydrogen-potassium ATPase (the proton pump) in gastric parietal cells, reducing gastric acid secretion; the S-enantiomer of omeprazole. Used to treat gastroesophageal reflux disease, erosive esophagitis, ulcers, and to prevent NSAID-induced ulcers, often in combination with antibiotics for H. pylori eradication.

esophageal atresia.definition: A congenital disorder in which the esophagus does not form a continuous passage from the mouth to the stomach, typically with a blind-ended upper segment and often with a fistula between the trachea and esophagus (tracheoesophageal fistula).

thoracotomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which an incision is made through the chest wall to access the thoracic cavity and its organs (most often the lungs or heart) for operative, diagnostic, or therapeutic purposes.

plummer-vinson syndrome.definition: A rare condition characterized by iron-deficiency anemia, dysphagia due to esophageal webs (often postcricoid), and atrophic glossitis; also known as sideropenic dysphagia.
