facetectomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which one or more facet joints of the spine are removed to decompress neural structures, usually to treat foraminal or central stenosis; can be partial or complete, with complete removal sometimes necessitating spinal fusion to maintain stability.

zygapophyseal joint.definition: A synovial plane joint between the superior articular process of one vertebra and the inferior articular process of the vertebra above, forming the spine's facet joints; it permits gliding motions and contributes to stability, and is innervated by the medial branches of the dorsal rami.

bells palsy.definition: An acute, unilateral peripheral facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) palsy causing sudden weakness or paralysis of the facial muscles on the affected side; commonly idiopathic and presumed inflammatory, with most patients recovering within weeks to months.

moebius syndrome.definition: A rare congenital, non-progressive neurological disorder characterized by bilateral facial nerve (CN VII) palsy causing facial weakness or paralysis and often concurrent abducens nerve (CN VI) palsy leading to limited eye movements; may be associated with feeding difficulties in infancy, speech impairment, and sometimes limb anomalies or other cranial nerve palsies.

facial palsy.definition: Weakness or paralysis of the facial muscles due to dysfunction of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) or its central pathways, resulting in asymmetric facial movement and impaired eye closure or mouth movement; can be peripheral (e.g., Bell palsy) or central in origin.

facial paralysis.definition: Weakness or loss of voluntary movement of the facial muscles caused by impairment of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII); commonly presents with drooping on one side of the face and difficulty closing the eye or smiling, and can result from Bell palsy, stroke, trauma, or infection.

facial tic.definition: An involuntary, brief, repetitive movement of facial muscles (e.g., blinking, grimacing, nose or lip movements) often driven by an urge, suppressible for short periods, and characteristic of tic disorders such as Tourette syndrome.

tic douloureux.definition: Pain from a disorder of the trigeminal nerve, the chief sensory nerve of the face. Also called trigeminal neuralgia.

digastric.definition: Relating to having two bellies; in anatomy, the digastric muscle has an anterior and a posterior belly joined by an intermediate tendon, and it functions to elevate the hyoid bone during swallowing and assist in opening the mouth by depressing the mandible.

stylohyoid.definition: A slender neck muscle that originates from the styloid process of the temporal bone and inserts into the body of the hyoid bone; it elevates the hyoid bone during swallowing and is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII).

nasal mucous membranes.definition: The mucous membranes lining the nasal cavity, composed of pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells and a supportive lamina propria; they secrete mucus to humidify and trap particles, warm inspired air, and aid in olfaction.

pterygopalatine ganglion.definition: A parasympathetic ganglion in the pterygopalatine fossa that receives preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the greater petrosal nerve via the nerve of the pterygoid canal and distributes postganglionic fibers with branches of the maxillary nerve (V2) to innervate lacrimal, nasal, palatine, and pharyngeal glands.

trigeminal ganglion.definition: A sensory ganglion of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) located in Meckel's cave; it contains the cell bodies of the primary sensory neurons for somatic sensation of the face and head and gives rise to the ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2), and mandibular (V3) divisions.

geniculate ganglion.definition: A sensory ganglion of the facial nerve (CN VII) located in the temporal bone at the genu of the facial nerve; it contains the cell bodies of taste fibers from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (via the chorda tympani) and general somatic sensation from parts of the external ear, and it gives rise to the chorda tympani and greater petrosal nerves.

facial vein.definition: A superficial vein of the face that drains facial tissues; it begins at the angular vein near the nose/eye, courses down the cheek, and typically drains into the internal jugular vein (via the common facial vein).

facial bones.definition: The bones that form the face, totaling 14, including the two maxillae, two zygomatic bones, two nasal bones, two lacrimal bones, two palatine bones, two inferior nasal conchae, the vomer, and the mandible; they provide the facial framework and protect the entrances to the respiratory and digestive tracts.

facial hemiplegia.definition: Paralysis of the muscles on one side of the face, due to disruption of the facial motor pathways (central or peripheral); central lesions often spare the forehead, while peripheral (facial nerve) palsy involves all ipsilateral facial muscles.

facial nerve paralysis.definition: Paralysis of the muscles innervated by the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) due to damage or dysfunction of the nerve along its course, resulting in weakness or loss of voluntary facial movement on the affected side, often with an inability to close the eye and drooping of the mouth corner.

facial perception.definition: The cognitive and neural process by which the brain interprets facial features to recognize individuals and infer social information, such as emotional expression and intent; it relies on specialized face-processing networks and can be impaired in prosopagnosia.

facial vision.definition: Not a standard medical term; when used, it may refer to the ability to recognize faces (facial recognition) or to the portion of the visual field occupied by viewing a face, but there is no formal clinical definition in ophthalmology or neurology.

tissue factor.definition: A transmembrane glycoprotein that acts as the cellular cofactor for coagulation factor VIIa, initiating the extrinsic pathway of blood coagulation by forming a TF–VIIa complex that activates factor X to Xa.

proconvertin.definition: Vitamin K–dependent coagulation factor IX; a serine protease zymogen of the intrinsic pathway. When activated to IXa, it forms the intrinsic tenase complex with factor VIIIa to activate factor X to Xa; deficiency causes hemophilia B. Also known as plasma thromboplastin component or Christmas factor.

proaccelerin.definition: A non-enzymatic coagulation cofactor in the prothrombinase complex that, with Factor Xa and calcium, accelerates the conversion of prothrombin to thrombin; produced by the liver and not vitamin K–dependent; deficiency leads to bleeding.

stuart-prower factor.definition: A vitamin K–dependent coagulation factor that is activated to the enzyme Xa; it participates in the prothrombinase complex (with Factor V, calcium, and phospholipid) to convert prothrombin to thrombin, activated by the tissue factor–VIIa complex (extrinsic pathway) or by the intrinsic tenase complex.

christmas factor.definition: A coagulation factor in the intrinsic pathway of blood coagulation (Factor IX); deficiency causes Hemophilia B.

factor v leiden.definition: An inherited mutation in the F5 gene (G1691A) that causes resistance to activated protein C, leading to an increased risk of venous thromboembolism (e.g., deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism).

venous thrombosis.definition: Formation of a blood clot (thrombus) within a vein, most commonly in the deep veins of the legs (deep vein thrombosis); the clot can obstruct venous return and may detach, traveling to the lungs (pulmonary embolism).

factor ii.definition: A vitamin K–dependent proenzyme produced by the liver; it is activated to thrombin in the coagulation cascade, which then converts fibrinogen to fibrin to form a blood clot.

intravascular coagulation.definition: Pathological activation of the coagulation system within blood vessels, leading to intravascular fibrin clot formation that can obstruct microcirculation; ongoing activation may consume platelets and clotting factors, increasing the risk of bleeding.

factor vii.definition: Vitamin K–dependent coagulation protein produced by the liver that participates in the extrinsic pathway by forming a complex with tissue factor to activate factor X to Xa; deficiency or inhibition (e.g., warfarin) prolongs the prothrombin time and can cause bleeding. Levels reflect vitamin K status and are influenced by anticoagulants.

factor xi.definition: An intrinsic pathway coagulation zymogen produced by the liver; when activated to XIa, it proteolytically activates factor IX to IXa, aiding thrombin generation; activation can occur via factor XIIa or thrombin, and deficiency causes a mild-to-moderate bleeding disorder (hemophilia C) inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.

factor xiii.definition: A coagulation factor (fibrin-stabilizing factor) that, when activated to Factor XIIIa by thrombin and calcium, cross-links fibrin to stabilize the clot; deficiency leads to impaired clot stability and a tendency to bleed.

hageman factor.definition: A plasma serine protease that initiates the intrinsic coagulation pathway via contact activation; it activates kallikrein and factor XI, and its deficiency prolongs the aPTT but typically does not cause bleeding.

rosenthal disease.definition: An outdated or inconsistent term used in historical medical literature to refer to various, unrelated conditions; it is not a currently recognized diagnosis and lacks a single, agreed-upon definition. If you can provide the specific context (system, era, or source), I can clarify its intended meaning in that usage.

prekallikrein.definition: An inactive plasma zymogen that is the precursor of the serine protease plasma kallikrein; activated by factor XIIa to kallikrein, which cleaves high‑molecular‑weight kininogen to release bradykinin, contributing to inflammation and vasodilation; deficiency often prolongs the aPTT but does not cause a bleeding tendency.

high molecular weight kininogen.definition: A large plasma glycoprotein (~85 kDa) that serves as a precursor to bradykinin in the kallikrein–kinin system; it functions as a cofactor for activation of factor XII and prekallikrein on negatively charged surfaces and is cleaved by kallikrein to release bradykinin, a potent vasodilator (synthesized by the liver).

factor xa.definition: A serine protease enzyme in the coagulation cascade that converts prothrombin to thrombin, promoting fibrin formation and clot development; part of the common pathway and a target of direct oral anticoagulants such as rivaroxaban, apixaban, and edoxaban.

fallopian canal.definition: Also known as the facial canal; a bony canal within the petrous part of the temporal bone that houses the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) as it courses from the internal auditory meatus to the stylomastoid foramen, comprising the labyrinthine, tympanic, and mastoid segments.

fallot’s syndrome.definition: A congenital cyanotic heart defect classically with four anatomic features—ventricular septal defect, pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, and an overriding aorta—leading to a right-to-left shunt and variable cyanosis.

midforceps operation.definition: An obstetric delivery performed with obstetric forceps applied at the midpelvic level to facilitate vaginal delivery when the fetal head is high in the pelvis and cannot be delivered by spontaneous descent or low-forceps methods.

false pelvis.definition: The portion of the pelvic cavity located above the pelvic brim, bounded by the iliac crests; it is part of the abdomen and contains abdominal viscera, not the true (lesser) pelvis.

faget's sign.definition: Fever with relative bradycardia (pulse–temperature dissociation): heart rate is slower than expected for the degree of fever; classically seen in typhoid fever (and occasionally described in dengue and other infections).

blackwater fever.definition: A severe complication of malaria (most often falciparum) characterized by intravascular hemolysis with hemoglobinuria (dark urine), accompanied by fever, anemia, and sometimes jaundice; historically associated with quinine therapy but can occur with other antimalarials.

tinea nigra.definition: A superficial fungal infection of the stratum corneum caused by Hortaea werneckii, presenting as dark brown to black, well-defined macules on the palms or soles; more common in tropical climates and treatable with topical antifungals.

fimbriae.definition: Finger‑like surface projections. In bacteria, they are short hair‑like appendages that mediate adhesion to host cells and surfaces (and can promote biofilm formation); in the female reproductive tract, the fimbriae at the end of the fallopian tube are fringe‑like projections that help capture the ovum.

isthmus.definition: A narrow, constricted region that connects two larger parts of an organ or structure; used to describe, for example, the connecting zone between the lobes of the thyroid gland or the region between the body and cervix of the uterus.

mesosalpinx.definition: A portion of the broad ligament of the uterus that encloses and supports the fallopian (uterine) tube, forming the upper border of the broad ligament and containing the tubal vessels.

ovarian ligament.definition: A fibromuscular band extending from the ovary to the uterus (near the uterine horn), anchoring the ovary to the uterus; derived from the gubernaculum and located in the mesovarium part of the broad ligament.

broad ligament.definition: A large double layer of peritoneum that extends from the sides of the uterus to the lateral pelvic walls, forming the mesometrium, mesovarium, and mesosalpinx; it supports the uterus and contains the vessels, nerves, and lymphatics to the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries.

oviduct.definition: The oviduct is the muscular tube in the female reproductive tract that transports the ovulated oocyte from the ovary to the uterus; in humans it is the fallopian tube, where fertilization may occur.

tubal ligation.definition: A type of surgery that prevents a woman from getting pregnant. Also called "getting your tubes tied."

uterine tube.definition: A pair of slender muscular tubes that extend from the uterus to the ovaries; they capture the ovulated oocyte with fimbriae, provide the site of fertilization, and transport the egg or embryo to the uterus via ciliary action and muscular contractions.

falx inguinalis.definition: A fibrous band formed by the fusion of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses, reinforcing the posterior wall of the inguinal canal.

falx ligmentosa.definition: A sickle-shaped peritoneal fold that attaches the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm; contains the ligamentum teres hepatis at its inferior edge.

medullary cystic disease.definition: An inherited tubulointerstitial kidney disease characterized by cysts in the medullary region of the kidneys and progressive renal failure, typically presenting in adolescence or adulthood with impaired urine concentrating ability and polyuria; most cases are autosomal dominant and linked to MUC1 or UMOD mutations.

werdnig-hoffmann disease.definition: A congenital, rapidly progressive form of spinal muscular atrophy (type I) caused by degeneration of anterior horn cells in the spinal cord, leading to severe hypotonia and progressive symmetric muscle weakness in infancy, often with poor feeding and early respiratory failure.

morquio’s disease.definition: A lysosomal storage disorder (mucopolysaccharidosis type IV) caused by deficiency of N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase (GALNS), or in Morquio B, beta-galactosidase, leading to accumulation of keratan sulfate and chondroitin-6-sulfate; it is characterized by severe skeletal dysplasia, short stature, joint abnormalities, and typically normal intellect.

pelizaeus-merzbacher disease.definition: A rare X-linked leukodystrophy caused by mutations or duplications in the PLP1 gene, leading to defective CNS myelin formation (hypomyelination); it typically presents in infancy with nystagmus and hypotonia, followed by developmental delay, spasticity, and ataxia, with MRI showing diffuse hypomyelination.

spinal muscular atrophy.definition: A genetic neuromuscular disorder caused by SMN1 gene mutation/deletion, leading to degeneration of motor neurons in the spinal cord and brainstem and resulting in progressive proximal muscle weakness and atrophy, often with respiratory failure; inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.

gilbert’s syndrome.definition: A common, benign inherited disorder of bilirubin metabolism caused by reduced activity of hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1), leading to mild, intermittent unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia; jaundice may occur with fasting, illness, or stress, but liver function is otherwise normal and no treatment is required.

gardner’s syndrome.definition: An autosomal dominant variant of familial adenomatous polyposis characterized by multiple colorectal polyps plus extracolonic features such as osteomas of the skull/jaw, dental abnormalities (supernumerary teeth, odontomas), epidermoid cysts, and desmoid tumors, usually due to an APC gene mutation.

familial mediterranean fever.definition: A hereditary autoinflammatory disorder characterized by recurrent febrile episodes with serositis (commonly peritonitis, pleuritis, and arthritis) due to MEFV gene mutations; autosomal recessive, often managed with colchicine to prevent attacks and amyloidosis.

benign paroxysmal peritonitis.definition: A self-limited, paroxysmal abdominal pain syndrome characterized by transient peritoneal irritation causing acute abdominal symptoms that resolve without evidence of infection or lasting inflammation.

periodic peritonitis.definition: Recurrent, self-limited episodes of inflammation of the peritoneum, presenting with acute abdominal pain and tenderness, fever, and signs of peritoneal irritation, with complete or near-complete resolution between episodes.

recurrent polyserositis.definition: Repeated episodes of inflammation of two or more serous membranes (pleura, peritoneum, and/or pericardium) with recurrent serous effusions, commonly seen in autoinflammatory syndromes such as familial Mediterranean fever.

periodic fever.definition: A pattern of fever that recurs at intervals, with asymptomatic periods between episodes. The episodes may last hours to days and can be accompanied by symptoms such as sore throat, abdominal pain, rash, or lymphadenopathy, depending on the underlying autoinflammatory syndrome.

traps.definition: A large superficial back muscle with three regions (upper, middle, lower) that elevates, retracts, and depresses the scapula, upwardly rotates the scapula, and helps extend the neck; it stabilizes the shoulder girdle during arm movements.

polyposis.definition: The presence of multiple polyps on mucosal surfaces (most often the colon); it can be sporadic or inherited, as seen in familial adenomatous polyposis and other polyposis syndromes.

colon cancer.definition: A malignant neoplasm that originates in the lining of the colon (large intestine), commonly referred to as colorectal cancer; it often develops from preexisting polyps and can invade surrounding tissue and metastasize.

proctocolectomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which the rectum and all or part of the colon are removed.

pseudocyesis.definition: A false belief of being pregnant, accompanied by signs and symptoms of pregnancy (such as amenorrhea, abdominal enlargement, breast changes, nausea) despite no actual gestation; often considered a psychosomatic condition linked to emotional or psychosocial factors and may improve with psychiatric evaluation and counseling.

false labor.definition: Contractions that resemble labor but are irregular and do not cause progressive cervical dilation or effacement; they usually resolve with rest, hydration, or a change in activity and do not indicate imminent delivery.

pseudoanorexia.definition: A nonstandard term used to describe feigned or simulated anorexia nervosa symptoms; essentially false reporting or display of loss of appetite or intentional food avoidance, not a recognized medical diagnosis.

pseudoarthrosis.definition: Failure of fracture healing (nonunion) characterized by formation of a mobile, false joint at the fracture site, with fibrous or cartilaginous tissue instead of mature bone bridging the gap.

false suture.definition: I couldn’t locate a standard medical definition for “false suture.” Could you share the context (e.g., skull anatomy, dental/surgical sutures, imaging terms) or the source where you saw it? With context, I can provide a precise definition.

sutura plana.definition: A cranial suture with smooth, flat, non-interdigitated margins between adjacent skull bones.

sutura squamosa.definition: A cranial suture between the squamous part of the temporal bone and the parietal bone; a fibrous joint that typically fuses with age.

glottis spuria.definition: Not a standard medical term; no formal definition exists. If encountered, it may imply a nonanatomic or false glottal opening, but there is no established clinical entity by this name.

rima respiatoria.definition: Espacio de la vía aérea por donde pasa el aire durante la respiración; es la abertura entre las cuerdas vocales (glotis) de la laringe, cuyo tamaño se regula por los músculos laríngeos y cambia entre la inspiración/espiración y la fonación.

rima vestibule.definition: The opening between the vestibular folds (false vocal cords) in the larynx; the upper opening of the laryngeal cavity whose size varies with movement of the vestibular folds.

vocal cord.definition: A fold of mucous membrane within the larynx that vibrates as air passes through the glottis to produce voice; there are two such folds (the vocal folds) that adduct to form the closed glottis during phonation.

ventricular ligament.definition: Not a standard anatomical term; there is no widely recognized structure by this name. In the heart, the ventricles are supported by the fibrous skeleton and valve annuli, with chordae tendineae to papillary muscles, rather than a distinct ligament. If you intended another term (e.g., a ductus/arterial remnant or a brain ventricle structure), please specify.

false glottis.definition: The space in the larynx bounded by the vestibular (false) vocal folds, lying above the true vocal cords; essentially the supraglottic portion of the glottic area.

pseudoneuroma.definition: A non-neoplastic lesion that mimics a neuroma, typically arising from scar tissue or regenerating nerve fibers at a site of nerve injury or surgery, and not a true nerve tumor.

ostertag.definition: Parasitic nematode that infects the abomasum (stomach) of cattle and other ruminants; causes ostertagiasis, presenting with weight loss, diarrhea, and reduced productivity.

apgar.definition: Apgar score is a rapid, standardized scoring system used to evaluate a newborn's physical condition immediately after birth (typically at 1 and 5 minutes). It assesses five criteria—heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, reflex irritability, and color—each scored 0, 1, or 2, for a total of 0 to 10; higher scores indicate better condition. Scores of 7–10 are usually normal, while lower scores suggest distress and may require intervention.

dysmelia.definition: A congenital limb abnormality caused by defective development in utero, resulting in partial or complete absence or deformity of one or more limbs.

congenital.definition: Present at birth; arising during fetal development; may be genetic or due to intrauterine factors; encompasses structural defects and functional disorders.

breaks.definition: Fractures are breaks or cracks in bones or other hard tissues, typically caused by trauma or disease; they are categorized as closed (skin intact) or open (bone exposed through a wound) and are treated with immobilization, reduction (realigning the bone), and often surgery if needed.

stress-ulcer.definition: A gastric or duodenal mucosal ulcer that develops in the setting of severe illness or physiological stress (such as trauma, sepsis, or major surgery) due to stress-related mucosal ischemia; typically shallow erosions of the gastric/duodenal mucosa with potential for GI bleeding.

famotidine.definition: A histamine-2 receptor antagonist that reduces gastric acid secretion by blocking H2 receptors on parietal cells; used to treat peptic ulcers, GERD, and other acid-related disorders.

famciclovir.definition: An oral antiviral prodrug of penciclovir; after ingestion it is converted to penciclovir, which inhibits viral DNA synthesis and is used to treat infections caused by herpes simplex virus and varicella-zoster virus (e.g., herpes zoster, genital herpes, and cold sores).

famvir.definition: A prodrug of penciclovir; an antiviral purine nucleoside analog that, after activation in infected cells, inhibits viral DNA polymerase and viral DNA synthesis. Used to treat acute herpes zoster and recurrent herpes simplex infections (genital herpes and cold sores).

fanconi's syndrome.definition: A generalized proximal tubule dysfunction resulting in renal wasting of glucose, amino acids, phosphate, and bicarbonate, causing glycosuria with normoglycemia, aminoaciduria, hypophosphatemia, and a proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis; it can be inherited or acquired (eg, by drugs or toxins).

renal tubular dysfunction.definition: A disorder of the kidneys in which the renal tubules fail to reabsorb or secrete substances properly, leading to urinary losses of electrolytes and solutes (such as bicarbonate, phosphate, glucose, and amino acids) and often impaired urine concentration; it can occur as part of Fanconi syndrome or in various acquired or inherited tubulopathies.

phosphaturia.definition: Urinary excretion of phosphate; abnormally high phosphate loss in the urine, often due to renal phosphate wasting or proximal tubular dysfunction.

bicarbonate wasting.definition: Renal loss of bicarbonate in the urine due to impaired proximal tubule reabsorption (or bicarbonate diuresis), resulting in a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.

autosomal-recessive disorder.definition: An inherited genetic disorder caused by pathogenic variants in both copies of a gene on an autosome. The disease manifests when two mutated alleles are present (homozygous or compound heterozygous), while carriers with one mutated allele are typically asymptomatic. Each child of two carrier parents has a 25% chance of being affected.

heavy metal poisoning.definition: A toxic condition produced by exposure to elevated levels of heavy metals (such as lead, mercury, arsenic, and cadmium) that accumulate in the body and cause multisystem organ injury; clinical features depend on the metal but commonly include abdominal pain, neurodevelopmental or cognitive impairment, neuropathy, anemia, renal dysfunction, and skin or mucous membrane changes; management involves eliminating exposure and using chelation therapy for certain metals, with supportive care as needed.

vitamin d deficiency.definition: An insufficient level of circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D, usually due to inadequate intake, limited sun exposure, or malabsorption, resulting in impaired calcium and phosphate homeostasis and bone mineralization (rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults).

fansidar.definition: A fixed-dose combination antimalarial comprising sulfadoxine and pyrimethamine; it inhibits folate synthesis in malaria parasites (sulfadoxine blocks dihydropteroate synthase and pyrimethamine inhibits dihydrofolate reductase) and is used to treat and prevent falciparum malaria, though resistance and risk of serious adverse reactions limit its use.

pyrimethamine.definition: A dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor used as an antiprotozoal and antimalarial agent; it blocks folate metabolism and inhibits DNA synthesis in parasites.

sulfadoxine.definition: A long-acting sulfonamide antimetabolite that inhibits dihydropteroate synthase in the folate synthesis pathway, used in combination with pyrimethamine (e.g., sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine) for the treatment or prevention of malaria.

farber lipogranulomatosis.definition: A rare autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of acid ceramidase (ASAH1), leading to ceramide accumulation; characterized by painful subcutaneous nodules with lipogranulomas, progressive joint contractures, hoarseness, hepatosplenomegaly, and neurodevelopmental delay, with prognosis often severe in infancy.

ceramide.definition: A lipid molecule consisting of a fatty acid linked to a sphingosine backbone via an amide bond; a central component of sphingolipids in cell membranes, particularly abundant in the skin, and a bioactive signaling molecule involved in processes such as apoptosis, cell differentiation, and inflammation.

desquamating dermatitis.definition: A nonspecific inflammatory skin condition in which the epidermis sheds or peels (desquamates) extensively, typically with redness, scaling, and itching.

foam cell infiltration.definition: Accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages within tissues, most often in the arterial intima, caused by uptake of modified lipoproteins (notably oxidized LDL) by macrophages; this lipid-rich macrophage population contributes to atherosclerotic plaque formation.

granulomatous reaction.definition: A chronic granulomatous inflammatory response featuring granulomas—organized aggregates of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells) often with multinucleated giant cells, surrounded by lymphocytes and fibroblasts—typically in reaction to persistent antigens such as mycobacterial or fungal infections, foreign bodies, or certain immune-mediated conditions.

psychomotor retardation.definition: A slowing of physical movement and speech, with slowed thinking and reduced spontaneous activity, often seen in severe depression and other neuropsychiatric or neurologic disorders.

lanugo.definition: Fine, soft hair that grows all over the body of a fetus and is typically shed before birth.

squamous cells.definition: Flat, scale-like epithelial cells that line many surfaces and cavities; they form squamous epithelium (keratinized in the skin and non-keratinized in areas like the mouth, esophagus, and vagina) and function as a protective barrier.

intestinal obstruction.definition: A blockage that prevents the normal passage of intestinal contents through the small or large intestine, due to mechanical obstruction (e.g., adhesions, hernias, tumors, volvulus) or functional ileus. It commonly presents with abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and inability to pass gas or stool.

far eastern hemorrhagic fever.definition: Hantavirus-associated viral hemorrhagic fever presenting with abrupt fever, hemorrhagic manifestations, and renal dysfunction (renal syndrome), historically described in eastern Asia.

febrile phase.definition: A stage of illness in which fever is present, caused by pyrogenic cytokines that raise the hypothalamic set point, often with systemic symptoms such as malaise, chills, and sweating.

hypotensive phase.definition: A period of abnormally low blood pressure (hypotension) resulting in reduced blood flow to organs, commonly seen in shock, severe dehydration, hemorrhage, sepsis, or adverse drug effects.

oliguric phase.definition: An early stage of acute kidney injury in which urine output falls markedly (oliguria, commonly <400 mL/day in adults), leading to accumulation of nitrogenous wastes (azotemia) and disturbances of fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance.

polyuric phase.definition: Phase of acute kidney injury—often following a period of reduced urine output—characterized by a sudden and marked increase in urine volume as tubular function returns; urine is typically dilute due to impaired concentrating ability, and patients may develop dehydration and electrolyte losses until renal recovery completes.

hypotensive shock.definition: An acute circulatory failure with insufficient tissue perfusion due to reduced effective blood flow, resulting in hypotension and organ dysfunction; it is typically associated with low blood pressure (e.g., systolic <90 mmHg or mean arterial pressure <65 mmHg) and requires urgent resuscitation.

urea nitrogen.definition: A measure of the amount of nitrogen in the blood that comes from urea, a waste product of protein metabolism; used to assess kidney function and hydration status.

farmer's lung.definition: A hypersensitivity pneumonitis (extrinsic allergic alveolitis) caused by inhalation of moldy hay, straw, or grain—often thermophilic actinomycetes or fungal spores. It triggers an immune‑mediated inflammatory reaction in the lungs, typically presenting with fever, cough, and dyspnea after exposure, and can progress to chronic interstitial fibrosis with ongoing exposure.

fasciotomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which fascia is incised to relieve elevated pressure within a muscle compartment, commonly to treat compartment syndrome and prevent ischemic injury.

fasciitis.definition: Inflammation of the fascia, the fibrous connective tissue that surrounds and separates muscles and other structures; can result from overuse, injury, or infection; a common localized example is inflammation of the plantar fascia of the foot.

fasciodesis.definition: A surgical procedure in which fascial tissue is fused or anchored to another structure (often bone or fascia) to create fixation or restriction of motion, effectively tethering or stabilizing tissue.

fascioliasis.definition: A parasitic liver infection caused by ingestion of encysted metacercariae of liver flukes (primarily Fasciola hepatica or Fasciola gigantica); it typically presents with fever and right upper quadrant pain during the migratory phase, followed by biliary obstruction, jaundice, and eosinophilia in the chronic phase.

fasciola gigantica.definition: A large trematode liver fluke that infects the biliary ducts of humans and ruminants, causing fascioliasis; transmitted by ingestion of metacercariae on aquatic plants after snail-mediated development; endemic in tropical regions; treated with triclabendazole.

fasciolopsis buski.definition: A large intestinal fluke (trematode) that infects humans after ingestion of metacercariae on aquatic plants; causes fasciolopsiasis with symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, anorexia, and weight loss, and is endemic to parts of Asia.

fasciolopsiasis.definition: An infection of the human intestine caused by the trematode Fasciolopsis buski, acquired by ingesting raw or undercooked aquatic vegetation contaminated with metacercariae; it causes gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and malabsorption, and heavy infections can lead to intestinal obstruction.

fascioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy.definition: A hereditary muscular dystrophy characterized by progressive weakness of facial muscles, scapular stabilizers, and proximal upper-extremity muscles, often with scapular winging and reduced facial expressiveness; typically autosomal dominant, with two main genetic forms (FSHD1 due to D4Z4 contraction on chromosome 4q35 and FSHD2 due to SMCHD1 mutations).

landouzy-dejerine muscular dystrophy.definition: A historical name for facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD), an inherited dystrophy characterized by early weakness of facial muscles and scapular winging, with progression to proximal shoulder and arm (and often leg) muscles.

fascicle.definition: A fascicle is a small bundle of fibers, typically a bundle of skeletal muscle fibers encased by perimysium (a subdivision of a muscle). In the nervous system, it can also refer to a bundle of nerve fibers (axons) within a nerve, surrounded by perineurium.

fasciculus.definition: An anatomical bundle of fibers—either muscle fibers within a skeletal muscle or axons within a nerve or CNS tract.

fascicular neuroma.definition: Benign lesion of a peripheral nerve involving disorganized proliferation of nerve fibers within a nerve fascicle, typically seen after nerve injury (traumatic neuroma), causing focal nerve enlargement and possible neuropathic pain.

medullated neuroma.definition: A neuroma in which the constituent axons are myelinated, i.e., a nerve growth composed mainly of medullated (myelinated) fibers.

fascicular twitching.definition: A spontaneous, involuntary contraction of muscle fibers supplied by a single motor neuron, typically visible as a fine, brief twitch under the skin (fasciculation).

fasciculation.definition: An involuntary, spontaneous contraction of a small group of muscle fibers within a single motor unit, visible as a fine twitch under the skin; typically benign but can be seen with neuromuscular disorders when persistent or widespread.

fascia lata.definition: A thick, fibrous layer of connective tissue that forms the deep fascia of the thigh, enclosing the thigh muscles, extending from the inguinal ligament to the knee, and thickening laterally to form the iliotibial tract.

fascia bulbi.definition: A fibrous fascial envelope surrounding the eyeball, forming Tenon's capsule; a loose connective tissue sheath that encases the globe and the extraocular muscles, separating them from orbital fat and extending from the limbus anteriorly to the optic nerve posteriorly, blending with the conjunctiva anteriorly and with the orbital periosteum posteriorly.

piriform fascia.definition: A fascial sheath enveloping the piriformis muscle in the gluteal region, forming the deep investing fascia of the muscle and continuous with the sacral fascia; helps delineate the boundary of the greater sciatic foramen and separate the piriformis from adjacent structures.

tenon's capsule.definition: A thin fibrous fascial sheath that envelops the eyeball, separating the globe from orbital fat and the extraocular muscles; extends from the anterior conjunctival fornix to the posterior sclera, where it blends with the sclera and provides a potential space for globe movement.

perineurium.definition: A dense connective tissue sheath around each fascicle of nerve fibers in a peripheral nerve, formed by concentric layers of specialized perineurial cells that create a diffusion barrier and provide mechanical protection.

fast-acting.definition: Relating to a medication or treatment that begins to exert its effects quickly after administration, with a rapid onset of action.

short-acting.definition: A drug that begins to work quickly after administration and has a brief duration of action, often requiring more frequent dosing to maintain therapeutic effect.

c-fibers.definition: Unmyelinated, small-diameter sensory nerve fibers that conduct impulses slowly and mediate dull, diffuse, long-lasting pain; they are polymodal nociceptors that respond to chemical, thermal, and mechanical noxious stimuli.

reticular activating system.definition: A neural network in the brainstem (reticular formation) that regulates wakefulness and arousal by activating the cerebral cortex; essential for consciousness, alertness, and attention, and it helps control sleep–wake cycles.

sodium channel.definition: A transmembrane protein that forms a pore in the cell membrane and selectively conducts Na+ ions, enabling initiation and propagation of action potentials; many are voltage-gated and open in response to membrane depolarization.

voltage-gated channel.definition: A transmembrane ion channel that opens or closes in response to changes in membrane voltage, allowing selective passage of ions (e.g., Na+, K+, Ca2+) and enabling generation of action potentials.

fastigial.definition: Relating to a midline cerebellar structure; a deep cerebellar nucleus located in the vermis that coordinates posture and stabilizes gaze via vestibular pathways.

posture.definition: The position in which the body is held, especially the alignment of the head, spine, pelvis, and limbs while standing, sitting, or lying, reflecting the balance of musculoskeletal forces; abnormal posture can contribute to discomfort or injury.

equilibrium.definition: When things are in balance or a calm state of mind.

fastigium.definition: An apex or peak; the median highest point of a structure; in anatomy, used to denote the highest or most median point of a structure.

zollinger-ellison syndrome.definition: A condition caused by a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma) that leads to excessive gastric acid production and recurrent, refractory peptic ulcers, often with diarrhea; most commonly located in the pancreas or duodenum and may occur with MEN1.

g-cell hyperplasia.definition: An increase in the number of gastrin-secreting cells in the gastric antrum, leading to hypergastrinemia.

fasting.definition: Voluntary abstention from all or some caloric intake for a defined period, often to prepare for medical testing or procedures or as part of a dietary regimen; typically water is allowed unless specified otherwise, with common durations for lab tests around 8–12 hours.

neutron therapy.definition: A form of external-beam radiotherapy that uses fast neutrons as the delivering radiation, which have high linear energy transfer and can be more biologically effective at killing tumor cells (especially some radioresistant cancers) but also cause greater damage to surrounding normal tissue; usage is limited to specialized centers.

soft tissue sarcoma.definition: An uncommon type of cancer in tissues like muscles, tendons, and blood vessels.

fast-twitch.definition: Type II skeletal muscle fibers that contract rapidly and generate high force but fatigue quickly; they rely primarily on anaerobic metabolism and are suited for short, explosive movements.

adipose.definition: Adipose tissue, a loose connective tissue composed mainly of adipocytes that store energy as triglycerides; it provides insulation and padding and functions as an endocrine organ by secreting adipokines.

hibernoma.definition: Benign tumor arising from brown adipose tissue, presenting as a slow-growing, painless subcutaneous mass (often in the neck, supraclavicular region, or upper trunk) of young to middle-aged adults. Histology shows multivacuolated adipocytes with abundant mitochondria; imaging may reveal metabolic activity. Treatment is complete surgical excision with an excellent prognosis and rare recurrence.

fat embolism.definition: A fat embolism is the lodging of fat droplets in the body's microcirculation after trauma (most often long-bone or soft-tissue injury), which can cause pulmonary, neurologic, and dermatologic symptoms; when it leads to systemic illness, it is called fat embolism syndrome, typically developing 24–72 hours after injury and managed with supportive care (oxygenation and hemodynamic stabilization).

fat necrosis.definition: Death of adipose tissue due to trauma or enzymatic injury (e.g., pancreatitis), characterized by adipocyte destruction, an inflammatory response with macrophages, and often oil cysts or saponification.

fatty liver.definition: A condition characterized by abnormal accumulation of fat in liver cells (hepatic steatosis), often defined as fat making up more than 5% of liver weight; it may be alcohol-related (alcoholic fatty liver disease) or nonalcoholic, and can range from asymptomatic to progressive liver damage such as steatohepatitis, fibrosis, or cirrhosis.

kwashiorkor.definition: A form of severe protein-energy malnutrition resulting from deficient dietary protein in the setting of adequate or near-adequate caloric intake, typically in young children after weaning; it is characterized by edema (often with fatty liver), hepatomegaly, irritability, anorexia, dermatosis, hair changes, and hypoalbuminemia.

radiographic.definition: Relating to radiography (X-ray imaging); produced by or seen on radiographs.

bone fracture.definition: A fracture is a break in the continuity of a bone, typically due to trauma or a pathologic process, which may be displaced or non-displaced; diagnosed by imaging and treated with immobilization, and, if needed, reduction and stabilization or surgical repair.

stress fracture.definition: A hairline crack in a bone that usually occurs from overuse; left untreated, this may lead to displacement of the bones.

axillae.definition: The axillae are the bilateral armpit regions—the pyramidal spaces beneath the shoulder that contain the axillary vessels and nerves (including the brachial plexus), lymph nodes, and surrounding fat, serving as a passageway for neurovascular structures to the upper limb.

fauces.definition: A narrow passage at the back of the mouth leading to the oropharynx, bounded by the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches (the faucial pillars); the space between them is the isthmus of the fauces.

glossopalatine.definition: Relating to the tongue and palate; used to describe anatomical structures or relations between the tongue and the palate.

pharyngopalatine.definition: Relating to the pharynx and the palate; pertaining to structures that involve both, such as the palatopharyngeal arch.

oropharyngeal isthmus.definition: An opening between the mouth and the oropharynx, bounded by the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches (the faucial arches) and containing the palatine tonsil; the roof is formed by the soft palate and the floor by the tongue.

prostration.definition: Extreme physical weakness or exhaustion with an inability to sit or stand, often accompanied by collapse or lying motionless.

augmentation.definition: An increase in size, amount, intensity, or effectiveness of a body part or physiological function; used to describe procedures that enlarge tissue or organs or to enhance function.

favism.definition: An acute hemolytic anemia precipitated by ingestion of fava beans in individuals with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, due to oxidative compounds in the beans.

acute hemolytic anemia.definition: A rapid-onset hemolytic anemia due to sudden destruction of circulating red blood cells, usually intravascular, often from immune-mediated reactions (e.g., ABO-incompatible transfusion) or other acute triggers.

favus.definition: A chronic dermatophyte infection of the scalp (a form of tinea capitis) caused by Trichophyton schoenleinii, characterized by yellow cup-shaped crusts (scutula), patchy alopecia, and potential scarring.

febrile agglutinins test.definition: A historical serologic test in which serum from a febrile patient is mixed with a standardized antigen (often red blood cells or bacteria) to detect agglutinins—antibodies that cause clumping; a positive result suggests circulating antibodies and recent or current infection with that antigen.

cold agglutinins test.definition: A laboratory test that detects cold agglutinins, IgM autoantibodies that bind red blood cells at low temperatures and cause agglutination; used to evaluate autoimmune hemolytic anemia and related infections (e.g., Mycoplasma pneumoniae), typically via an indirect antiglobulin (Coombs) assay with titer/thermal amplitude assessment.

febrile delirium.definition: An acute confusional state (delirium) occurring in the setting of fever or systemic infection, characterized by fluctuating attention and consciousness, disorientation, perceptual disturbances, and either agitation or lethargy, usually resolving with fever control and treatment of the underlying infection.

febrile seizure.definition: A convulsive event that occurs in a child with fever, not due to an established central nervous system infection or other neurologic disorder; most occur between 6 months and 5 years of age, are generalized and brief (usually <15 minutes), and may occur once within 24 hours.

febrile state.definition: A febrile state is a condition characterized by fever—an elevation of core body temperature above the normal range (generally >38°C/100.4°F)—often due to infection or inflammation.

fecalith.definition: A hard, stone-like mass of feces formed in the colon or rectum; in the appendix, it can obstruct the lumen and contribute to appendicitis.

fecal softener.definition: An emollient laxative that softens stool by increasing water content and lubricating the stool surface, easing passage; commonly used to prevent or treat constipation and reduce straining (e.g., docusate salts).

feces.definition: Solid or semisolid digestive waste excreted through the anus, formed in the colon and composed of indigestible material, bacteria, mucus, shed intestinal cells, and water; commonly known as stool.

fecal fistula.definition: An abnormal tract that connects the intestinal lumen to another surface or cavity (such as skin, bladder, or vagina), allowing fecal matter to drain through the fistulous tract.

obstipation.definition: Severe constipation characterized by the inability to pass stool or gas, often persisting despite effort and suggesting possible bowel obstruction or markedly reduced bowel motility requiring evaluation.

fecal fat test.definition: Quantitative stool test that measures the amount of fat excreted in the stool over a defined collection period (usually 24–72 hours) to assess fat malabsorption; used to evaluate conditions such as pancreatic insufficiency, celiac disease, and other causes of steatorrhea.

fecundation.definition: Fertilization; the union of a male gamete (sperm) with a female gamete (ovum) to form a zygote.

fecundity.definition: The biological capacity to reproduce; the potential to conceive and bear offspring.

felty's syndrome.definition: A complication of long-standing rheumatoid arthritis characterized by neutropenia and splenomegaly, with increased susceptibility to infections.

hypersplenism.definition: A condition in which the spleen is overactive, causing excessive sequestration and destruction of circulating blood cells (red cells, white cells, and platelets) and resulting cytopenias, typically associated with splenomegaly.

felon.definition: A purulent infection of the volar fingertip pulp (the pad at the tip of the finger), usually after a penetrating injury, causing severe fingertip pain and swelling and potentially forming an abscess or spreading to underlying structures if untreated.

female catheterization.definition: Insertion of a urinary catheter through the female urethra into the bladder to drain urine, commonly performed for urinary retention or voiding difficulties, to obtain sterile urine samples, or to monitor urine output in medical or surgical patients.

tube feeding.definition: An enteral nutrition method in which a feeding tube delivers nutritionally complete formulas directly into the gastrointestinal tract when oral intake is insufficient or unsafe; tubes may be placed nasally (e.g., nasogastric, nasoenteric) or via the abdominal wall (e.g., gastrostomy, jejunostomy) to deliver formulas to the stomach or small intestine.

feeding tube.definition: A tube placed into the gastrointestinal tract to deliver nutrients, fluids, and medications directly when oral intake is inadequate or unsafe; commonly inserted nasogastrically or orogastrically for short-term use or surgically placed as a gastrostomy or jejunostomy tube for long-term feeding.

parenteral nutrition.definition: A method of providing nutrition intravenously, bypassing the gastrointestinal tract, used when oral or enteral nutrition is not possible; it delivers a complete or partial blend of amino acids, carbohydrates, lipids, electrolytes, vitamins, and trace elements via central or peripheral venous access.

felbamate.definition: An oral carbamate anticonvulsant used as add-on therapy for partial-onset seizures in refractory epilepsy; it exerts anticonvulsant effects via NMDA receptor antagonism and GABAergic modulation, among other mechanisms; rare but serious adverse effects include aplastic anemia and severe hepatic toxicity.

piroxicam.definition: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that inhibits cyclooxygenase enzymes (COX-1 and COX-2), reducing prostaglandin synthesis to relieve pain and inflammation.

feldene.definition: A brand-name nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) containing the anti-inflammatory agent piroxicam, used to relieve pain and inflammation in arthritis such as osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis; it is a non-selective COX inhibitor and can cause gastrointestinal irritation, ulcers/bleeding, and renal impairment.

majora.definition: Two outer folds of skin and subcutaneous tissue of the female external genitalia that enclose and protect the openings of the vagina and urethra; they are typically covered with pubic hair on their outer surfaces and are homologous to the male scrotum.

hymenal.definition: Relating to the hymen, the thin membrane that partially covers the vaginal opening in females.

bacteriological.definition: Relating to bacteriology, the science that studies bacteria, including their classification, physiology, detection, culture, and role in health and disease.

sensitivity.definition: In diagnostic testing, the ability of a test to correctly identify people who actually have the disease; the proportion of diseased individuals who yield positive results; high sensitivity reduces false negatives.

indwelling.definition: Remaining inside the body for an extended period; describes a device or object left in place within a body cavity or duct to allow ongoing access or drainage.

asepsis.definition: Absence of pathogenic microorganisms; the practices used to prevent infection by eliminating or preventing contamination with microorganisms (e.g., sterile technique, antisepsis, disinfection, and sterilization).

trichomoniasis.definition: A sexually transmitted disease caused by a parasite; also called trich.

discharge.definition: Going home or leaving the hospital.

polycystic.definition: Having multiple cysts; characterized by the presence of more than one cyst.

fenofibrate.definition: A fibric acid derivative lipid-lowering agent that activates peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPAR-α) to decrease triglycerides and increase HDL cholesterol; used to treat hypertriglyceridemia and mixed dyslipidemia.

human.definition: A member of the species Homo sapiens; a bipedal primate with a highly developed brain capable of complex language, abstract thought, problem solving, and culture.

basal.definition: Relating to the base or bottom; located at the base of a structure; in histology, describing the deepest layer of epithelium that rests on the basement membrane.

metabolic.definition: Relating to metabolism, the chemical processes by which the body converts food into energy and the molecules needed for growth, repair, and maintenance.

function.definition: The normal physiological activity of a body part or system, and the role it plays in maintaining homeostasis and health.

cold.definition: A common viral upper respiratory infection (acute nasopharyngitis) caused most often by rhinoviruses; presents with nasal congestion, runny nose, sore throat, cough, and malaise, sometimes fever; usually self-limited within 7–10 days; managed with supportive care; antibiotics are not routinely indicated.

knife.definition: A sharp-edged cutting instrument used in surgical procedures to incise or dissect tissue; a scalpel is a common form.

insufflation.definition: Introduction of gas (typically carbon dioxide) into a body cavity or hollow organ to distend it, enabling visualization or access during diagnostic or surgical procedures.

saphenous.definition: Relating to the saphenous vein, especially the great (long) saphenous vein of the leg.

longus.definition: A Latin adjective meaning "long"; used in anatomical naming to denote a long muscle or tendon, typically contrasted with brevis ("short").

trochanter.definition: A large bony prominence on the proximal femur that serves as a major muscle attachment site; there are two— the greater trochanter (a large lateral projection) and the lesser trochanter (a smaller posteromedial projection) near the hip joint.

window.definition: In diagnostic imaging, a window is a display setting that defines the range of CT numbers (densities) shown as grayscale; adjusting the window width controls contrast and the window level adjusts brightness to optimize visualization of different tissues.

fenestra.definition: An opening or window in a bone or membrane; in anatomy, commonly the openings of the inner ear (oval window and round window) that transmit vibrations from the middle ear to the inner ear.

fenestrae.definition: An opening or window in a bone or membrane; in anatomy, the natural openings of the inner ear (the oval window or fenestra vestibuli/ovalis and the round window or fenestra cochleae/rotunda) that permit transmission of sound vibrations to the inner-ear fluids.

rotunda.definition: A round or circular opening or cavity; in cranial anatomy, a circular opening in the sphenoid bone that transmits the maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve (V2).

fenestration.definition: An opening or window-like passage in a structure; a surgical procedure that creates such an opening in bone or a membrane to connect compartments, drain fluid, or relieve obstruction.

fenestrated.definition: Having small openings (fenestrae) in the endothelial lining that permit rapid exchange of small molecules between blood and surrounding tissue; a feature of fenestrated capillaries found in the kidneys, endocrine glands, and intestinal mucosa.

fenoprofen.definition: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) of the propionic acid class that provides analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects by nonselectively inhibiting cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2) enzymes; used to treat mild to moderate pain and inflammatory conditions such as arthritis.

ferrous sulfate.definition: A salt of iron in the +2 oxidation state used as an oral iron supplement to treat or prevent iron deficiency anemia.

st-t wave changes.definition: Abnormalities of the ST segment and T wave on an electrocardiogram (ECG), such as ST-segment elevation or depression and T-wave inversion, which can reflect myocardial ischemia or infarction, ventricular strain, electrolyte disturbances, pericarditis, or other cardiac or systemic conditions; interpretation depends on lead location and clinical context.

nonsteroidal antiinflammatory agent.definition: A medication that reduces inflammation, pain, and fever by inhibiting cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes and thereby decreasing prostaglandin synthesis; not a corticosteroid. Common examples include ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin, and celecoxib.

renal dysfunction.definition: Impaired kidney function with reduced ability to filter waste and regulate fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance; may be acute or chronic.

upper gi disease.definition: A broad category of disorders affecting the upper gastrointestinal tract—the esophagus, stomach, and proximal duodenum—encompassing inflammatory, functional, peptic, neoplastic, and vascular conditions that commonly cause symptoms such as heartburn, dysphagia, epigastric pain, nausea/vomiting, GI bleeding, or obstruction.

gastric ulceration.definition: A localized break or crater in the stomach lining (gastric mucosa) resulting from disruption of mucosal defenses by stomach acid and enzymes; commonly associated with Helicobacter pylori infection or NSAID use and may cause epigastric pain or bleeding.

duodenal ulceration.definition: An ulcerative lesion of the duodenal mucosa (the first portion of the small intestine) caused by an imbalance between mucosal defenses and gastric acid, most often due to Helicobacter pylori infection or NSAID use; can cause epigastric pain and may lead to complications such as bleeding or perforation.

fenoterol.definition: Selective beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonist inhaled bronchodilator used to relieve bronchospasm in asthma and COPD; a short-acting beta-2 agonist that relaxes airway smooth muscle.

reversible bronchospasm.definition: An episodic constriction of the bronchi (airways) that reduces airflow but is reversible, typically with bronchodilator therapy or spontaneously; commonly seen in asthma and exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, due to smooth muscle constriction often with inflammation.

fentanyl citrate.definition: A citrate salt of fentanyl, a highly potent synthetic opioid analgesic used for anesthesia and treatment of severe pain; it is a mu-opioid receptor agonist with a high risk of respiratory depression and overdose.

drug dependence.definition: A state of physiological and/or psychological reliance on a drug, typically with tolerance to its effects, withdrawal symptoms if use is reduced or stopped, and compulsive drug-seeking and continued use despite adverse consequences.

respiratory depression.definition: A decrease in the rate and/or depth of breathing due to suppression of the central respiratory drive, resulting in hypoventilation and impaired gas exchange (hypoxemia and hypercapnia); commonly caused by opioids or other central nervous system depressants, as well as neurological injury or disorders.

laryngospasm.definition: A sudden involuntary constriction of the laryngeal (glottic) muscles, causing partial or complete airway obstruction by closure of the vocal cords; commonly occurs during anesthesia emergence or airway irritation and may present with inspiratory stridor and hypoxemia.

fenugreek.definition: An annual herb (Trigonella foenum-graecum) whose dried seeds are used as a spice and in traditional medicine; commonly used as a galactagogue to promote lactation and for digestive complaints. It contains soluble fiber and steroidal saponins; may cause GI upset, diarrhea, or hypoglycemia and can interact with antidiabetic medications and anticoagulants; should be avoided in pregnancy due to potential uterotonic effects.

loss of appetite.definition: Decreased or absent desire to eat; a common symptom that can arise from illness, medications, infection, pain, psychological factors, or metabolic/endocrine disorders, and may lead to reduced caloric intake and weight loss.

skin inflammation.definition: When your skin swells and is itchy. Also called eczema.

water retention.definition: An accumulation of excess fluid in the body's tissues or cavities (edema), typically presenting as swelling in the legs, ankles, or feet; caused by impaired fluid balance from kidney, heart, or liver disease, venous insufficiency, hormonal changes, medications, or prolonged immobility.

high cholesterol.definition: An elevated level of cholesterol in the bloodstream, especially low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, that increases the risk of atherosclerosis and cardiovascular disease. It can result from genetic factors, diet, obesity, inactivity, and other conditions, and is commonly managed with lifestyle changes and medications such as statins.

high blood glucose.definition: A condition in which the concentration of glucose in the blood is higher than normal, typically due to insufficient insulin action or insulin deficiency (as in diabetes) or as a temporary response to illness or stress. Chronic hyperglycemia can lead to vascular and organ complications.

calcium oxalate stones.definition: A type of kidney stone composed primarily of calcium oxalate crystals; the most common form of nephrolithiasis, formed when urine is supersaturated with calcium and oxalate, often linked to low urine volume or factors increasing calcium or oxalate in urine.

ferritin.definition: An intracellular iron-storage protein that sequesters iron in a soluble, readily mobilizable form; serum ferritin reflects body iron stores but can be elevated with inflammation or infection.

ferritin test.definition: A blood test that measures ferritin, the iron-storage protein, to estimate the body's iron stores and help diagnose iron deficiency or iron overload.

ferrous gluconate.definition: An iron supplement in which ferrous ions are bound to gluconate; used to treat or prevent iron deficiency anemia by supplying elemental iron, often better tolerated than ferrous sulfate, with possible GI side effects.

iron supplement.definition: A dietary supplement containing elemental iron used orally to prevent or treat iron deficiency anemia by replenishing iron stores; common formulations include ferrous sulfate, ferrous gluconate, and ferrous fumarate.

feosol.definition: A brand-name oral iron supplement used to prevent or treat iron deficiency anemia; it contains ferrous iron (usually ferrous sulfate) and is absorbed in the small intestine. Common adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset and dark stools.

ferguson’s reflex.definition: A neuroendocrine reflex in labor whereby stimulation or dilation of the cervix triggers the posterior pituitary to release oxytocin, increasing uterine contractions and promoting labor.

fermentative dyspepsia.definition: An historical or older term for dyspepsia attributed to fermentation of ingested carbohydrates in the stomach, causing gas, bloating, belching, and epigastric discomfort after meals in the absence of an organic cause.

fertilization membrane.definition: A protective envelope that forms around an egg after fertilization, derived from the egg’s zona pellucida or vitelline envelope, which hardens to block entry by additional sperm (polyspermy).

fertizin.definition: Definition not found for "fertizin." Please confirm spelling or provide context (e.g., drug, condition).

festal.definition: Relating to digestion; used to describe digestive enzymes or supplements that aid digestion (e.g., pancreatic enzyme preparations containing amylase, protease, and lipase).

festinant.definition: An adjective describing a gait that becomes progressively faster and shorter in amplitude, with a forward-leaning trunk, resulting in a shuffling, hurried walk commonly seen in parkinsonism.

festinating gait.definition: A gait pattern characterized by small, rapid, shuffling steps with a forward-leaning trunk that tends to accelerate; commonly seen in Parkinson disease (parkinsonism) and other neurodegenerative disorders.

fetal abortion.definition: Termination of a pregnancy before the fetus is viable (typically before about 20 weeks' gestation); most often refers to spontaneous miscarriage, though it can also denote induced abortion.

fetal activity determination.definition: Assessment of fetal movements and activity to evaluate fetal well-being, typically via maternal perception of kicks (kick counts) and, if indicated, objective testing such as nonstress testing or a biophysical profile.

fetal advocate.definition: An individual who represents the fetus's interests in obstetric care decisions, particularly when fetal well-being or viability conflicts with maternal autonomy, and who may assist in mediating between the patient, family, and healthcare providers to incorporate fetal considerations into treatment planning.

fetal age.definition: The age of the developing fetus, typically expressed as gestational age in weeks from the first day of the last menstrual period; it roughly equals time since conception (fetal age) plus about two weeks, so about 38 weeks from fertilization or ~40 weeks from LMP.

fetal alcohol syndrome.definition: A congenital disorder caused by prenatal exposure to alcohol during pregnancy, characterized by growth deficiency, distinctive facial features (e.g., smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, short palpebral fissures), and central nervous system abnormalities that lead to cognitive, behavioral, and neurodevelopmental problems.

fetal alcohol effects.definition: An outdated term for the range of neurodevelopmental and behavioral problems in a child caused by prenatal alcohol exposure, typically without the facial features of fetal alcohol syndrome; these effects are now encompassed under fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASD).

fetal alveoli.definition: The primitive air sacs of the developing lung during fetal life, forming in the saccular stage; they are fluid-filled and not yet capable of gas exchange, and mature into functional alveoli after birth with postnatal aeration.

fetal distress.definition: A clinical situation in which the fetus is not adequately oxygenated or perfused, usually indicated by abnormal fetal heart rate patterns (e.g., tachycardia or bradycardia, reduced variability, late or variable decelerations) or other signs of fetal hypoxia, requiring urgent assessment and possible intervention to prevent fetal injury.

fetal attitude.definition: The posture of the fetus in the uterus, especially the degree of flexion of the head and the alignment of the spine and limbs; the normal attitude is complete flexion of the head with the chin tucked to the chest.

fetal biophysical profile.definition: An ultrasound-based prenatal assessment of fetal well-being that combines five components—fetal breathing movements, gross body movements, fetal tone, amniotic fluid volume, and a nonstress test (electronic fetal heart-rate reactivity)—with each component scored 0 or 2 for a maximum total of 10; a normal score indicates adequate fetal oxygenation, while a low score may prompt closer monitoring or delivery planning.

fetal bradycardia.definition: Baseline fetal heart rate less than 110 beats per minute for at least 10 minutes on fetal monitoring; may indicate fetal hypoxia or other pathology and requires prompt evaluation and management to identify and treat reversible causes.

fetal circulation.definition: The pattern of blood flow in the fetus in which oxygenated blood from the placenta reaches the fetus and is shunted away from the nonfunctioning lungs and liver via the ductus venosus, foramen ovale, and ductus arteriosus, directing blood into the systemic circulation; after birth, these shunts close to establish normal postnatal circulation.

nonstress test.definition: A nonstress test is a noninvasive obstetric test that monitors fetal heart rate (FHR) for spontaneous accelerations in response to fetal movements using external monitoring; a reactive result shows at least two accelerations of the FHR (usually 15 bpm or more, lasting about 15 seconds) within a 20- to 40-minute period, indicating fetal well‑being, while a nonreactive result may prompt further testing such as a contraction stress test or biophysical profile.

oogenesis.definition: The production and development of female gametes (ova) in the ovaries, beginning with the formation of primary oocytes during fetal life, arresting in meiosis I until puberty, and, during each cycle, a subset of follicles resume meiosis to form a secondary oocyte and polar bodies, with meiosis II completing only upon fertilization to yield a haploid ovum.

spermatogenesis.definition: Spermatogenesis is the process by which male germ cells in the seminiferous tubules of the testes develop into mature haploid spermatozoa, comprising spermatogonial mitosis, meiosis of primary and secondary spermatocytes, and spermiogenesis, and is hormonally regulated by FSH and testosterone.

uteroplacental insufficiency.definition: An obstetric condition characterized by inadequate uteroplacental blood flow, resulting in insufficient delivery of oxygen and nutrients to the fetus and increased risk of fetal growth restriction, hypoxia, and adverse perinatal outcomes.

umbilical arteries.definition: Two arteries in fetal circulation that carry deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta via the umbilical cord; they arise from the internal iliac arteries and, after birth, become fibrous cords known as the medial umbilical ligaments.

portal sinus.definition: Not a standard anatomical term; there is no widely recognized structure named "portal sinus" in human anatomy—the portal venous system comprises the portal vein and its intrahepatic branches delivering blood to hepatic sinusoids.

spermatozoon.definition: A mature male gamete produced by the testes that is motile and haploid, containing a nucleus with paternal DNA, a cap-like acrosome that assists penetration of the egg, a midpiece packed with mitochondria for energy, and a tail (flagellum) enabling locomotion.

vitelline membrane.definition: A membranous envelope surrounding the yolk sac in early embryogenesis; derived from extraembryonic endoderm and mesoderm, and involved in early nutrient transfer before placental circulation.

pronucleus.definition: A haploid nucleus of a gamete formed after fertilization and before the fusion of the two pronuclei; the paternal pronucleus derives from sperm DNA and the maternal pronucleus from oocyte DNA, they replicate and then fuse to form the diploid zygotic nucleus.

meiotic.definition: Relating to meiosis, the two-stage cell division that reduces the chromosome number by half to form haploid gametes.

external fertilization.definition: Fertilization that occurs outside the body, when eggs and sperm are released into the surrounding medium (usually water) and unite there, often with synchronized gamete release and minimal parental care.

cross-fertilization.definition: Fertilization by gametes from different individuals; in plants, pollen from a different plant fertilizes the ovule, producing genetically diverse offspring.

internal fertilization.definition: Fertilization that occurs inside the body, typically within the female reproductive tract after mating, as opposed to external fertilization that occurs outside the body.

fertilized ovum.definition: A diploid cell formed when a sperm fertilizes an ovum; it contains genetic material from both parents and marks the beginning of embryonic development, undergoing rapid mitotic divisions (cleavage).

amniotic fluid volume.definition: Quantity of amniotic fluid surrounding the fetus in the amniotic sac; it increases with gestational age and is typically about 800–1000 mL at term. Abnormal volumes include oligohydramnios (low) and polyhydramnios (high).

late decelerations.definition: A gradual decrease in fetal heart rate that begins after the onset of a uterine contraction and returns to baseline after the contraction ends, indicating uteroplacental insufficiency and possible fetal hypoxia.

electronic fetal monitoring.definition: A method of continuously monitoring a fetus during labor by recording the fetal heart rate and uterine contractions using external sensors (or internal devices), producing a cardiotocogram to assess fetal well-being and detect signs of distress.

alkalotic.definition: Relating to or characterized by alkalosis; having an excess of base (alkali) in body fluids, resulting in elevated blood pH.

acidotic.definition: Relating to acidosis; in a state of abnormally low pH in body fluids, indicating increased acidity.

narcotic antagonist.definition: A drug that blocks the effects of opioids by competitively binding to opioid receptors (primarily mu), reversing opioid effects; used in overdose treatment and in management of opioid dependence. Examples include naloxone and naltrexone.

millirad.definition: A unit of absorbed ionizing radiation dose equal to one thousandth of a rad; equal to 0.001 rad, which is 1×10^-5 Gy (10 μGy).

milliroentgens.definition: A thousandth of a roentgen; a historical unit of exposure that expresses the amount of ionization produced by X-ray or gamma radiation in dry air; not a unit of absorbed dose and is rarely used in modern practice.

fetal face syndrome.definition: A nonstandard term referring to dysmorphic facial features observed in a fetus, typically associated with congenital disorders such as fetal alcohol spectrum disorders or chromosomal/genetic syndromes. It is not a specific, widely accepted medical diagnosis.

robinow syndrome.definition: A rare genetic disorder characterized by mesomelic limb shortening, distinctive facial features, and skeletal abnormalities, often with genital and dental anomalies; caused by mutations in WNT signaling pathway genes (most commonly ROR2 in autosomal recessive cases; autosomal dominant forms involve DVL1 or DVL3).

fetal fibronectin test.definition: A laboratory immunoassay that detects fetal fibronectin, a glycoprotein produced by fetal membranes, in cervicovaginal secretions (typically from 22 to 34 weeks gestation) to help predict imminent preterm birth. A negative result has a high negative predictive value for delivery within the next 7–14 days, while a positive result indicates increased risk but does not confirm preterm birth; used to guide management in women with suspected preterm labor.

maternal-fetal hypotension.definition: An abnormally low maternal blood pressure during pregnancy or labor, which can reduce uteroplacental blood flow and fetal oxygen delivery, potentially leading to fetal distress if not corrected.

fetal oxygen saturation monitoring.definition: Measurement of the oxygen saturation of fetal arterial blood to assess fetal oxygenation and well-being during labor or high-risk pregnancy, typically achieved with a fetal pulse oximeter placed on the fetal presenting part; abnormal readings may prompt obstetric interventions to prevent fetal hypoxia.

fetal scalp blood ph test.definition: An intrapartum diagnostic test in which a small amount of fetal scalp blood is drawn and the pH is measured to assess fetal acid–base status; a low pH indicates fetal acidosis and possible hypoxia, while a normal or higher pH is reassuring and may guide management decisions about continuing labor or expediting delivery.
