fetal membranes.definition: Two extraembryonic membranes—the amnion and the chorion—that surround the developing fetus and the amniotic cavity, containing amniotic fluid and protecting the fetus; they contribute to placental formation, and rupture of membranes occurs at labor.

microchimerism.definition: The presence of a small population of genetically distinct cells or DNA within one person, derived from another genetically different individual (e.g., fetal cells in a mother after pregnancy or maternal cells in a fetus, or donor cells after transplantation).

fetal mortality rate.definition: The number of fetal deaths after a specified gestational age per 1,000 total births (live births plus fetal deaths) in a defined population.

fetal movements.definition: Movements of the fetus within the uterus, typically felt by the pregnant person starting in the second trimester (around 18–20 weeks gestation), used as a rough indicator of fetal well-being; a decrease or absence may indicate fetal distress and warrant medical assessment.

fetal tachycardia.definition: A sustained fetal heart rate greater than 160 beats per minute for at least 10 minutes.

fetal viability.definition: The ability of a fetus to survive outside the uterus with medical support, generally possible from about 24 weeks of gestation, though viability depends on fetal weight, organ maturity, and the quality of neonatal care.

viable infant.definition: An infant born at a gestational age and with physiologic maturity sufficient to have a reasonable chance of survival outside the uterus with medical care; the threshold is commonly cited around 24 weeks of gestation, with survival improving with greater gestational age and higher birth weight.

feticide.definition: The intentional killing of a fetus, usually before birth; used in obstetric and legal contexts to describe fetal death caused by an action or omission.

fetochorionic.definition: Relating to the fetus and the chorion (the outer fetal membrane that forms part of the placenta).

fetofetal transfusion.definition: A pathological transfer of blood from one fetus to its co-twin through placental vascular connections in monochorionic pregnancies, causing donor hypovolemia/anemia and recipient hypervolemia/polycythemia, and often manifesting as twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome.

fetoglobulins.definition: A class of immunoglobulins present in fetal blood, produced by the fetus, representing the fetal humoral immune components and distinct from maternal antibodies.

roentgenography.definition: A radiographic imaging technique that uses X-ray (Roentgen) radiation to visualize internal body structures; historically known as X-ray imaging.

fetology.definition: The branch of obstetrics concerned with the fetus in utero, including fetal development, assessment, and management during pregnancy.

fetometry.definition: Measurement of fetal size and growth (fetal biometric assessment), usually by obstetric ultrasound, to estimate gestational age and fetal weight.

fetoplacental.definition: Relating to the fetus and its placenta; pertaining to the fetal-placental unit, including the exchange of nutrients, oxygen, and waste between mother and fetus.

fetoprotein.definition: A glycoprotein produced mainly by the fetal liver and yolk sac; in pregnancy, abnormal levels can indicate neural tube defects or multiple gestations, and in adults it serves as a tumor marker for hepatocellular carcinoma and certain germ cell tumors.

fetoscope.definition: A slender endoscope used to visualize the fetus in the uterus during prenatal procedures or fetal surgery; inserted through the maternal abdomen or cervix into the amniotic cavity.

fetoscopy.definition: An in utero endoscopic procedure in which a fetoscope is inserted into the uterus to directly visualize the fetus for diagnosis or, in some cases, fetal surgical intervention.

fetotoxic.definition: Toxic to the fetus; capable of causing fetal harm (such as growth restriction, congenital anomalies, or fetal death) when exposure occurs during pregnancy.

fetus acardiacus.definition: Acardiac fetus is a nonviable monochorionic twin that lacks a functional heart and most of the body, and is perfused by the normal twin through placental vessel connections (a component of twin reversed arterial perfusion, TRAP).

fetus acardius.definition: A malformed twin in a monochorionic pregnancy that lacks a functional heart and is perfused by the normal twin through placental vascular connections (twin reversed arterial perfusion), effectively acting as a parasitic, nonviable co-twin.

fetus amorphus.definition: A nonviable conceptus with no organized embryonic tissue or recognizable fetal form; essentially an undeveloped embryo, often described in very early pregnancy loss or molar pregnancies.

fetus anideus.definition: Not found in standard medical dictionaries; it may be a misspelling or obscure term. Please confirm the spelling or provide context, and I can define the intended term (e.g., if you meant "fetus anencephalus" or another fetal condition).

fetus in fetu.definition: An extremely rare congenital condition in which a malformed, parasitic twin is located inside the body of its sibling, usually within the abdomen or retroperitoneum, containing disorganized tissues and sometimes rudimentary vertebral and organ structures; it is thought to arise from failed twinning and is treated with surgical removal.

fetus papyraceus.definition: A dead co-twin in a multifetal pregnancy that becomes flattened and mummified, producing a parchment-like (papyraceous) appearance due to intrauterine death and compression by the surviving fetus.

fetus sanguinolentis.definition: A historical Latin descriptor meaning “bloody fetus” used to denote an unborn fetus that is blood-stained or shows evidence of intrauterine hemorrhage; it is not a standard term in modern obstetrics.

fev.definition: The volume of air forcibly exhaled from the lungs after a maximal inhalation, typically measured over a fixed time (most often 1 second as FEV1) and used with FVC to assess pulmonary function and airway obstruction.

fevc.definition: Not a standard medical term; there is no universally accepted definition in medical dictionaries. If you meant a pulmonary function measure, the standard terms are forced vital capacity (FVC) and forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1).

fever blister.definition: An infectious sore around the mouth caused by the herpes simplex virus (usually HSV-1); also known as a cold sore.

fetor hepaticus.definition: A distinctive musty, sweet odor of the breath seen in advanced liver failure and hepatic encephalopathy, caused by accumulation of volatile sulfur-containing compounds (notably dimethyl sulfide) due to reduced hepatic metabolism and portosystemic shunting.

fetor oris.definition: Fetor oris is foul-smelling breath originating from the mouth, typically due to bacterial production of volatile sulfur compounds on the tongue and dental surfaces; commonly associated with poor oral hygiene, dental disease, and dry mouth, but can indicate systemic illness in some cases.

fetal stage.definition: From about week 9 of gestation until birth, this stage involves rapid growth and maturation of tissues and organs that were formed during the embryonic phase, with increasing functional maturation and body size.

embryatrics.definition: The branch of medicine focused on the care, health, and development of embryos and fetuses during pregnancy, including prenatal diagnosis and fetal therapy.

prenatal diagnosis.definition: Prenatal diagnosis is the detection and assessment during pregnancy of fetal genetic, chromosomal, or structural abnormalities, using tests such as ultrasound, maternal serum screening, and invasive procedures like amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling to inform management and decision-making.

teratogenic influences.definition: Factors (agents, exposures, or conditions) during pregnancy that can cause congenital malformations or developmental abnormalities in the fetus, often by interfering with fetal organogenesis (typically in the first trimester).

paper-doll fetus.definition: A deceased fetus in a multiple pregnancy that becomes crushed and mummified into a parchment-like, paper-thin mass within the uterus, typically after early intrauterine demise of one twin; the surviving co-twin may be affected by shared placental circulation.

quartan malaria.definition: A form of malaria caused by Plasmodium malariae, characterized by fever spikes at roughly 72-hour intervals (every third day) with associated chills, sweats, and malaise.

remittent fever.definition: A fever pattern in which the body temperature remains above normal for several days, with continual daily fluctuations but not returning to baseline.

septic fever.definition: Fever due to sepsis; a systemic inflammatory response to infection, typically with elevated temperature and accompanying signs such as tachycardia, tachypnea, leukocytosis, and potential organ dysfunction.

tertian malaria.definition: A form of malaria caused by Plasmodium vivax or Plasmodium ovale, characterized by fever paroxysms occurring every 48 hours (every other day) and relapses due to dormant liver-stage parasites (hypnozoites).

herpes simplex virus 1.definition: Double-stranded DNA virus of the Herpesviridae family that commonly causes oral herpes (cold sores) and other mucocutaneous infections; it establishes lifelong latency in sensory ganglia (most often the trigeminal ganglion) with periodic reactivation causing vesicular lesions; transmitted via close contact with infected secretions; no cure exists, but antiviral therapy (e.g., acyclovir, valacyclovir) can shorten and prevent outbreaks.

abnormal facies.definition: Facial features that deviate from normal and are characteristic of a specific disease or syndrome, often used as clues in clinical diagnosis.

hydantoin.definition: A five-membered heterocyclic ring containing two adjacent carbonyl groups (the 2,4-imidazolidinedione scaffold); a cyclic urea framework used as the core structure in many anticonvulsant drugs and related medicinal compounds.

hydantoin syndrome.definition: A teratogenic congenital syndrome caused by in utero exposure to hydantoin anticonvulsants (most notably phenytoin) during pregnancy, characterized by growth retardation, microcephaly, craniofacial and limb anomalies, and cognitive impairment.

hydantoin derivatives.definition: A class of anticonvulsant drugs derived from hydantoin (imidazolidinedione) in which substituents are placed at the 5-position of the ring; they stabilize neuronal membranes by slowing inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels and are used to treat various seizures (examples include phenytoin, fosphenytoin, mephenytoin, ethotoin, and primidone).

neural crest tumors.definition: A group of neoplasms arising from neural crest–derived cells—the embryonic cells that migrate to form the peripheral nervous system, adrenal medulla, melanocytes, and related tissues; these tumors can be benign or malignant and include neuroblastoma, ganglioneuroma, pheochromocytoma, paraganglioma, medullary thyroid carcinoma, and melanoma.

hemoglobin f.definition: A form of hemoglobin produced during fetal development, composed of two alpha and two gamma chains (α2γ2). It has a higher affinity for oxygen than adult hemoglobin, enabling efficient placental transfer; levels decline after birth to less than about 1% of total hemoglobin.

fetal hemoglobin test.definition: A test that measures the amount or percentage of fetal hemoglobin (HbF) in a blood sample, typically by electrophoresis or HPLC, used to help diagnose and monitor inherited anemias such as beta-thalassemia and hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin, and to assess sickle cell disease severity or treatment response.

roentgen fetometry.definition: A historical radiographic method for estimating gestational age and fetal size by measuring fetal skeletal dimensions on in utero X-ray images; largely obsolete due to fetal radiation exposure and replaced by ultrasound.

fetal lie.definition: The orientation of the fetus within the uterus, describing the alignment of the fetus's long axis relative to the mother's long axis; commonly longitudinal (head or buttocks presenting), transverse, or oblique.

fetal position.definition: The orientation of the fetus within the uterus relative to the mother's pelvis, defined by the presenting part (usually the head), the left-right position, and whether the presenting part is directed anterior, posterior, or transverse to the pelvis (e.g., LOA = left occipitoanterior).

presenting part.definition: In obstetrics, the fetal part that lies closest to and presents first at the birth canal during labor; most commonly the occiput (head) in cephalic presentation.

mentum.definition: The chin; the forward projection of the anterior mandible (mental eminence) on the lower face.

vertex.definition: Anatomy: the highest point of the skull; the crown or most superior point of the head. In obstetrics: the fetal head presenting first, with the occiput oriented toward the maternal pelvis (vertex presentation).

brow.definition: The eyebrow: the paired strip of hair-covered skin and underlying tissue above the eye, overlying the frontal bone’s superciliary (supraorbital) arch; helps shield the eye from sweat and debris and plays a role in facial expression.

chin.definition: The anterior, inferior part of the mandible that forms the protruding lower facial region; the mental eminence (menton) of the jaw.

occiput posterior.definition: A fetal position in which the occipital bone of the fetal head is oriented toward the mother's posterior pelvis (the back of the head toward the mother's back), often associated with back labor and longer labor, and may rotate to a more anterior position during delivery.

breech presentation.definition: A fetal presentation in which the buttocks or feet are positioned to deliver first through the birth canal, instead of the head; includes frank breech (buttocks presenting with legs extended), complete breech (buttocks presenting with knees flexed), and footling breech (one or both feet presenting).

frank breech.definition: A breech presentation in which the fetal buttocks present first with the legs extended upward toward the head (hips flexed, knees extended), so the feet are near the face.

complete breech.definition: An obstetric breech presentation in which the fetus's buttocks are the presenting part with both hips and knees flexed (the legs are folded at both joints).

incomplete breech.definition: A breech presentation in which one or both feet are presenting first at delivery (footling breech, including single-footling and double-footling variants).

single/sole? breech.definition: A birth presentation in which the fetus is delivered buttocks, feet, or knees first through the birth canal rather than head first.

single footling breech.definition: A breech presentation in which one fetal foot presents first into the birth canal, with the other leg flexed at the knee (a type of incomplete breech).

double footling breech.definition: A breech presentation in which both feet are the presenting parts at the cervix, so that both feet protrude first ahead of the buttocks.

shoulder presentation.definition: A fetal presentation in which the fetus lies transversely in the uterus with the shoulder as the presenting part entering the birth canal, rather than the head or buttocks; an uncommon obstetric presentation that often necessitates cesarean delivery.

compound presentation.definition: An obstetric presentation in which the presenting part at the cervix consists of two fetal parts simultaneously, most often the head accompanied by a hand or arm (e.g., cephalic with a hand).

feverfew.definition: An herb (Tanacetum parthenium) used in traditional medicine to prevent migraine headaches; contains sesquiterpene lactones such as parthenolide; adverse effects may include mouth ulcers, GI upset, and skin reactions, and it can interact with anticoagulants.

cluster headaches.definition: A short-lived, extremely painful headache that occurs repeatedly over a period of a few weeks or months and then disappears for months or years.

migraine prophylaxis.definition: A preventive treatment strategy aimed at reducing the frequency, duration, and severity of migraine attacks, typically implemented with daily medications (such as beta-blockers, anticonvulsants, antidepressants, or CGRP-targeted therapies) and lifestyle modifications for patients with frequent or disabling migraines.

fuo.definition: A fever higher than 38.3°C (101°F) that persists or recurs for several weeks without an identifiable source after appropriate initial diagnostic workup.

febrile illness.definition: An illness characterized by fever (pyrexia), usually due to infection or inflammation, and often accompanied by systemic symptoms such as malaise, chills, or sweats.

hyperemic.definition: Increased blood flow to a tissue, causing redness and warmth due to dilation of arterioles; can be physiological or inflammatory.

restlessness.definition: A subjective feeling of inner agitation or discomfort with a compelling urge to move, often accompanied by observable fidgeting, pacing, or inability to sit still; it can occur with anxiety, pain, withdrawal, delirium, or medication effects such as akathisia.

sedative.definition: A drug that you take to make you feel calm or less anxious.

cooling tub bath.definition: A hydrotherapy treatment in which a patient is immersed in cool water in a tub to rapidly lower core body temperature, typically used for fever management, heat-related illness, or hyperthermia, with ongoing monitoring of temperature and cardiovascular status.

cold wet sheet.definition: A historical fever-reduction therapy in which a large sheet soaked in cold water is wrapped around the patient, sometimes followed by blankets to promote evaporative cooling and lower core body temperature; it can cause shivering, dehydration, and electrolyte disturbances.

ice packs.definition: A bag or pouch containing a substance that freezes or remains cold, used to apply cold therapy to an injured or inflamed area; it helps reduce swelling, inflammation, and pain by cooling tissue and causing vasoconstriction. Typically applied for short periods (about 15–20 minutes) with a cloth barrier to protect the skin.

nic.definition: Neonatal intensive care, specialized medical care for ill or premature newborns, typically provided in a neonatal intensive care unit. If you meant another term such as nicotinic or nicotinic acid, let me know.

fevre-languepin syndrome.definition: Not found in standard medical references; likely a misspelling or an extremely obscure eponym. If you can provide context (affected system, key symptoms, or a source), I can help locate a correct term and its definition.

popliteal pterygium syndrome.definition: A rare congenital syndrome characterized by webbing of the popliteal fossa behind the knees (popliteal pterygium) and a spectrum of craniofacial, limb, and genital anomalies, often including orofacial clefts and lower-lip pits; typically inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with variable expressivity and mutations in IRF6 identified in many cases. Sometimes described in its more severe form as Bartsocas–Papas syndrome.

fexofenadine.definition: A selective peripheral H1 histamine receptor antagonist (second-generation antihistamine) used to treat symptoms of allergic rhinitis and chronic idiopathic urticaria; it is non-sedating due to limited penetration of the central nervous system.

hepatic disease.definition: A broad term for any disease that affects the liver, impairing its structure or function. Examples include hepatitis, fatty liver disease (steatosis), cirrhosis, cholestasis, and hepatocellular failure.

premature infants.definition: A baby born before 37 completed weeks of gestation (preterm); often has immature organ systems and is at increased risk of complications such as respiratory distress syndrome and feeding difficulties.

urinary frequency.definition: Routinely needing to urinate more than eight times during the day or more than twice at night.

dry nose.definition: Nasal mucosal dryness is a lack of moisture in the lining of the nose, often due to dry air, dehydration, aging, or medications; it can cause crusting, irritation, itching, and nosebleeds.

free fatty acid.definition: A fatty acid that is not esterified to glycerol; released from adipose triglycerides during lipolysis and circulating in the blood primarily bound to albumin; used as an energy substrate by tissues via beta-oxidation and can participate in cellular signaling.

f factor.definition: A fertility plasmid is a circular DNA molecule in bacteria that carries the genes required for conjugation, including the tra region and the sex pilus. Its presence enables a donor cell (F+) to transfer the plasmid to a recipient cell (F−) during conjugation, and when integrated into the chromosome it forms an Hfr (high-frequency recombination) strain.

18f-fdg.definition: A radiotracer for positron emission tomography consisting of 2-deoxy-2-[18F]fluoro-D-glucose; a glucose analogue that is taken up by cells and phosphorylated but not further metabolized, becoming trapped, allowing visualization of tissues with high glycolytic activity (e.g., many cancers, brain, and heart).

fg syndrome.definition: An X‑linked intellectual disability syndrome characterized by distinctive facial features and genital anomalies in males, with variable developmental delay.

fgt.definition: An anatomical tract of the female reproductive system comprising the internal and external organs through which ova and sperm are transported, fertilization occurs, and gestation takes place (includes the uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries, vagina, and external genitalia).

fhr.definition: The heart rate of a fetus, typically assessed during pregnancy and labor; normal range is approximately 110–160 beats per minute.

fhs.definition: The audible heartbeat of a fetus detected via auscultation (e.g., with a Doppler or fetoscope), used to assess fetal well-being.

fi.definition: Not found as a standalone medical term. Please provide context or the full term that “fi” stands for (e.g., FI as fecal incontinence, fluorescence imaging, or fetal intervention).

fiberoptic colonoscope.definition: A flexible endoscope that uses fiber-optic bundles to illuminate and image the interior of the colon, used to perform colonoscopy for visualization of the colon mucosa, biopsy, and therapeutic interventions.

fiberoptic duodenoscope.definition: A flexible endoscope with a fiber-optic illumination and viewing system used to examine the duodenum and to perform instrumentation, most commonly during endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP).

fees.definition: A charge for medical services; the amount billed by a provider for a service or procedure, commonly associated with fee-for-service payment models that reimburse for each service performed.

fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swal.definition: A bedside procedure in which a flexible endoscope is inserted through the nose to visualize the laryngopharynx during swallowing, allowing assessment of swallow safety and efficiency, including penetration or aspiration and post-swallow residue (often with colored bolus).

fibroadenoma.definition: A benign breast tumor composed of fibrous stroma and glandular epithelium; typically a small, well-circumscribed, mobile, firm, painless lump in premenopausal women, often estrogen-responsive and may enlarge during pregnancy.

fibroadenomata.definition: Benign breast tumors composed of fibrous stroma and glandular epithelium; typically present as well-circumscribed, mobile, painless lumps in premenopausal women and may be solitary or multiple, often hormone-responsive and potentially enlarging during pregnancy. Management ranges from observation to biopsy or surgical excision if needed to exclude malignancy or symptoms.

fibroangioma.definition: A benign lesion made up of fibrous connective tissue with a prominent vascular component (fibrovascular tissue), often presenting as a soft, reddish nodule.

fibroblast.definition: A connective tissue cell that synthesizes and remodels the extracellular matrix, including collagen and glycoproteins, and plays a key role in tissue maintenance and wound healing.

fibroblastoma.definition: A benign soft-tissue tumor composed mainly of mature, spindle-shaped fibroblasts; typically a well-circumscribed, slow-growing lesion in dermal or subcutaneous tissue, usually treated by complete surgical excision with a low risk of recurrence.

fibrocarcinoma.definition: An epithelial malignant tumor in which carcinoma cells are embedded in dense fibrous (desmoplastic) stroma; essentially a carcinoma with prominent fibrous tissue.

fibrocartilaginous.definition: Relating to a tough, load-bearing connective tissue that blends fibrous tissue with cartilage and contains abundant collagen and chondrocytes; it provides tensile strength and shock absorption in joints such as intervertebral discs and knee menisci.

fibrocartilaginous joint.definition: A joint in which the bones are joined by fibrocartilage, providing limited movement (an amphiarthrosis); examples include the pubic symphysis and the intervertebral discs between vertebral bodies.

fibrochondritis.definition: Inflammation of fibrocartilage (the fibrous cartilage at joints such as the costal cartilage of the ribs), presenting as localized chest wall pain; generally self‑limited and treated with NSAIDs and rest.

fibrochondroma.definition: A rare benign tumor composed of fibrous connective tissue with islands of mature cartilage; a mixed fibrous‑cartilaginous lesion within the spectrum of chondromas, usually slow-growing and well circumscribed, arising in bone or soft tissue. Treatment is surgical excision with an excellent prognosis; malignant transformation is rare.

fibrocyst.definition: A benign breast condition characterized by fibrous tissue proliferation and cyst formation, resulting in lumpy, often tender breasts that vary with the menstrual cycle; not malignant but can mimic breast cancer.

fibrocystic.definition: Relating to benign breast changes characterized by fibrous tissue and cyst formation; typically causes lumpiness and tenderness of the breasts, often cycling with the menstrual period.

fibrocystic disease of the breast.definition: A benign breast condition characterized by nodular, lumpy tissue with cyclic breast pain and the formation of fluid-filled cysts and fibrous tissue; symptoms typically fluctuate with the menstrual cycle and it does not increase the risk of breast cancer.

fibrocyte.definition: A relatively quiescent connective-tissue cell derived from a fibroblast that maintains the extracellular matrix; during tissue repair it can become activated and differentiate into a fibroblast or myofibroblast to synthesize collagen.

fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva.definition: A rare genetic disorder in which soft tissues progressively ossify, forming bone within muscles, tendons, and ligaments, leading to increasing immobility and disability; caused by activating mutations in the ACVR1 gene, often with congenital malformations of the great toes.

fibroelastic membrane.definition: A thin layer of connective tissue containing both collagen and abundant elastic fibers, produced by fibroblasts, giving the membrane both strength and elasticity.

fibroelastic tissue.definition: A connective tissue characterized by a matrix rich in elastic fibers (elastin) interwoven with collagen; produced by fibroblasts, it provides both structural support and elasticity, e.g., in ligaments, arterial walls, and certain fasciae.

fibroepithelial papilloma.definition: A benign lesion composed of fibrous connective tissue with an overlying epithelium that forms papillary projections; typically a small, soft, pedunculated growth on skin or mucous membranes (often called a fibroepithelial polyp or skin tag).

fibroepithelial polyp.definition: A benign, pedunculated skin lesion composed of fibrous stroma with overlying epidermis; commonly known as a skin tag.

fibroepithelioma.definition: A variant of basal cell carcinoma characterized by fibrous stroma with anastomosing cords of basaloid cells; typically appears as a pinkish or flesh-colored plaque on the trunk or extremities.

fibrofolliculoma.definition: A benign cutaneous hamartoma composed of follicular structures embedded in fibrous stroma; typically presents as small, skin-colored papules on the face, neck, or trunk and may be associated with Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome.

fibrinogenopenia.definition: A deficiency or marked reduction of fibrinogen (factor I) in the blood, leading to impaired formation of fibrin and a tendency to bleeding. It can be congenital (hypofibrinogenemia or afibrinogenemia) or acquired from liver disease, disseminated intravascular coagulation, massive transfusion, or other consumptive coagulopathies.

fibrinogenous.definition: Describing a substance or process that promotes or results in the formation of fibrin, the insoluble protein that forms the mesh of a blood clot during coagulation.

fibrinogen test.definition: A blood test that measures the concentration of fibrinogen, a liver-produced plasma protein essential for blood clot formation; used to evaluate coagulation status, with low levels suggesting bleeding risk (e.g., in liver disease or DIC) and high levels suggesting inflammation or pregnancy.

fibrinokinase.definition: A fibrin-degrading enzyme that promotes fibrinolysis by dissolving the fibrin mesh of blood clots; plasmin is the primary endogenous enzyme activated from plasminogen by activators such as tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) or streptokinase.

fibrinopeptide.definition: A small peptide released from fibrinogen during blood coagulation when thrombin cleaves fibrinogen to form fibrin; the two main forms are fibrinopeptide A and fibrinopeptide B, cleaved from the Aα and Bβ chains, respectively, as fibrin is formed.

fibrinoscopy.definition: Endoscopic examination used to visualize fibrin-containing exudates or fibrin deposits on mucosal surfaces or within a body cavity.

fibrinous pericarditis.definition: A form of acute pericarditis in which a fibrinous exudate accumulates on the pericardial surfaces, producing a rough or shaggy “bread‑and‑butter” appearance and a pericardial friction rub; often associated with uremia, viral infections, post‑myocardial infarction (Dressler syndrome), rheumatic fever, or autoimmune diseases.

fibrin-stabilizing factor.definition: A plasma transglutaminase that cross-links fibrin strands to stabilize the clot; activated by thrombin in the presence of calcium.

fibroblastic.definition: Relating to fibroblasts, the connective-tissue cells that synthesize collagen and extracellular matrix; describing cells with spindle-shaped, fibroblast-like morphology.

megalencephaly.definition: An abnormal enlargement of the brain, usually accompanied by an increased head size, resulting from overgrowth of brain tissue; it can be isolated or part of genetic or developmental syndromes and may be associated with developmental delay, seizures, or other neurologic findings.

imperforate anus.definition: A congenital condition in which the anal opening is absent or blocked because the anorectal canal failed to develop or recanalize, often with fistulas to the urinary or genital tract and requiring surgical repair to create a patent anus.

congenital hypotonia.definition: Decreased muscle tone present at birth or in early infancy due to abnormalities of the central nervous system, peripheral nerves, neuromuscular junction, or muscles, resulting in a floppy infant with poor head control and delayed motor milestones.

short stature.definition: A height significantly below the average for age and sex, typically defined as more than two standard deviations below the mean on growth charts (roughly below the 2nd or 3rd percentile), due to genetic, nutritional, endocrine, or chronic illness factors.

skeletal anomalies.definition: Skeletal anomalies are abnormalities of bone structure or formation, including congenital malformations, abnormal bone growth or mineralization, variations in bone size or number, and deformities or misalignments of the skeleton.

congenital cardiac defects.definition: Heart and/or great-vessel abnormalities present at birth due to abnormal fetal development, including septal defects, valve or outflow tract anomalies, and patent ductus arteriosus; they range in severity and may require medical management, catheter-based procedures, or surgery.

fibrocystic disease of the pancreas.definition: A rare benign pancreatic condition in which pancreatic tissue becomes fibrotic with multiple cystic dilations of the ducts, leading to a firm, scarred pancreas and potentially causing abdominal pain and impaired exocrine pancreatic function.

fetal hydantoin syndrome.definition: A pattern of congenital anomalies in offspring exposed in utero to hydantoin anticonvulsants (most notably phenytoin) during pregnancy, characterized by growth retardation and microcephaly, craniofacial anomalies (e.g., broad nasal bridge, hypertelorism, ptosis, short palpebral fissures), limb defects such as hypoplastic nails and distal phalanges, and sometimes cleft lip/palate or cardiac defects.

fibrogliosis.definition: A reactive process in the central nervous system characterized by proliferation and hypertrophy of astrocytes and deposition of fibrous scar tissue at sites of injury, forming a dense glial scar that can impede regeneration.

fibromyalgia.definition: A chronic condition that causes pain all over your body, fatigue, and other symptoms.

fibroid.definition: A benign tumor of smooth muscle cells and fibrous connective tissue, most commonly arising from the uterus (uterine leiomyoma).

fibroidectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove uterine fibroids (leiomyomas) while preserving the uterus, typically performed via abdominal, laparoscopic, or vaginal approaches.

fibromyoma.definition: A benign neoplasm composed of fibrous tissue and smooth muscle cells, most commonly referring to a uterine fibroid (leiomyoma) arising from the myometrium.

fibromyomectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove fibromyomas (benign tumors composed of fibrous tissue and smooth muscle), usually uterine fibroids, while preserving the uterus.

fibromyositis.definition: An inflammatory condition of muscle tissue and its surrounding fascia (fibrous connective tissue) causing muscle pain and tenderness; the term is largely historical and not a specific modern diagnosis.

fibromatosis.definition: A group of benign fibroblastic proliferations in soft tissues that are locally infiltrative and can recur after treatment; they do not metastasize, but may be locally aggressive, with desmoid-type fibromatosis being the best-known form.

fibromuscular dysplasia.definition: A noninflammatory, nonatherosclerotic arteriopathy characterized by segmental arterial stenosis with alternating areas of dilation (the “string of beads”), most often affecting renal and carotid arteries and presenting with renovascular hypertension or neurovascular symptoms.

fibrolipoma.definition: A benign lipomatous tumor in which mature adipose tissue is interspersed with dense fibrous connective tissue (fibrous stroma); a variant of lipoma. It is typically slow-growing and painless, usually located in subcutaneous tissues of the trunk or limbs, with adipocytes separated by band-like fibrous tissue on histology.

lipofibroma.definition: A benign soft-tissue lesion consisting of mature adipose tissue intermingled with fibrous connective tissue (a fibrolipoma variant); typically presents as a slow-growing, well-circumscribed subcutaneous mass and is usually treated by local excision with an excellent prognosis.

fibrous hamartoma.definition: A benign soft-tissue lesion of infancy characterized by a disorganized mixture of dense fibrous tissue, mature adipose tissue, and primitive neural elements; typically presents as a subcutaneous or intramuscular mass in the first year of life and is treated with complete surgical excision, with an excellent prognosis and rare recurrence.

fibrous histiocytoma.definition: A benign skin tumor comprised of spindle-shaped fibroblasts and histiocyte-like cells in a storiform pattern, commonly presenting as a small, firm, painless, pigmented or skin-colored nodule on the extremities.

dermatofibroma.definition: A common benign skin lesion (benign fibrous histiocytoma) composed of fibroblasts and histiocytes in the dermis, typically presenting as a small, firm, skin-colored to red-brown papule or nodule on the extremities, usually asymptomatic.

gingival hyperplasia.definition: An overgrowth of the gingival tissue (gum tissue) leading to enlargement of the gums, often due to chronic inflammation from dental plaque or medication-induced fibrous hyperplasia (e.g., phenytoin, cyclosporine, certain calcium channel blockers); may present as swollen, firm gums that can cover part of the teeth.

gingival enlargement.definition: An overgrowth of the gingival tissues (gums) resulting in enlarged, bulky gums that may cover part of the teeth; commonly caused by plaque-induced inflammation, drug-induced gingival hyperplasia (e.g., phenytoin, cyclosporine, calcium channel blockers), hormonal changes, or hereditary gingival fibromatosis.

phenytoin hyperplasia.definition: Gingival overgrowth associated with phenytoin use (phenytoin-induced gingival hyperplasia): enlargement of the gingival tissues, often fibrous and inflamed, that can cover tooth crowns; commonly linked to poor oral hygiene and prolonged therapy, and managed with meticulous plaque control, dental cleaning, possible drug adjustment, and surgical reduction in severe cases.

fibrous thyroiditis.definition: A rare chronic inflammatory thyroid disease in which extensive fibrous tissue replaces the thyroid parenchyma, often extending into surrounding neck structures, producing a hard, painless goiter with possible compressive symptoms and frequently associated with hypothyroidism as part of IgG4-related disease.

ligneous thyroiditis.definition: A very rare inflammatory thyroid condition in which the thyroid develops ligneous (wood‑like) fibrous pseudomembranes or masses, consisting of dense fibrin‑rich material with chronic inflammatory cells.

riedel's thyroiditis.definition: A rare, IgG4-related fibrosing inflammatory disease in which the thyroid parenchyma is replaced by dense fibrous tissue that extends into surrounding neck structures, producing a hard, painless, fixed thyroid with potential compressive symptoms (dysphagia, dyspnea, hoarseness); biopsy shows extensive fibrosis with inflammatory infiltrates, and management often involves corticosteroids or other immunosuppressants, with limited surgical intervention due to fibrous invasion.

cafe-au-lait.definition: A flat, uniformly pigmented birthmark (macule) that is light to dark brown in color, usually present at birth or in early childhood; caused by increased melanin in the epidermis and typically benign, though multiple lesions can be seen in neurofibromatosis type 1.

café-au-lait.definition: A flat, uniformly pigmented macule or patch of light to medium brown skin, typically present at birth or appearing in early childhood; color resembles coffee with milk and the lesion is non-raised. Usually benign, though multiple lesions can be seen in certain genetic conditions (e.g., neurofibromatosis type 1) when numerous and larger.

albright's syndrome.definition: A mosaic genetic disorder caused by postzygotic activating mutations in the GNAS1 gene, leading to constitutive Gsα signaling with fibrous dysplasia of bone (often polyostotic), café-au-lait skin patches with irregular borders, and various endocrinopathies such as precocious puberty, hyperthyroidism, or Cushing syndrome.

precocious puberty.definition: A condition in which puberty starts earlier than normal, before age 8 in girls or before age 9 in boys, with early development of secondary sexual characteristics and accelerated growth.

polyostotic.definition: Describing a condition that affects more than one bone.

monostotic.definition: Affected in only one bone; localized involvement of a single bone, as opposed to disease affecting multiple bones (polyostotic).

fibroplasia.definition: The formation and proliferation of fibrous connective tissue, primarily by fibroblasts with collagen deposition, as part of wound healing and scar formation; it can also refer to replacement of normal tissue by dense fibrous tissue in response to injury or chronic inflammation.

fibrosarcomas.definition: Malignant tumor of fibroblasts arising from fibrous connective tissue; a type of soft tissue sarcoma that can invade locally and metastasize, typically treated with wide surgical excision, often with adjuvant radiotherapy or chemotherapy.

fibrosarcomata.definition: A malignant soft tissue tumor of fibroblastic origin composed of spindle-shaped cells that produce collagen, typically showing a herringbone histologic pattern.

fibrothorax.definition: Fibrothorax is fibrous thickening of the pleural space that encases the lung, causing restrictive expansion and reduced lung volumes, usually after an inflammatory pleural process such as empyema or pleuritis.

pleural membranes.definition: Two layered serous membranes that encase the lungs and line the thoracic cavity: the visceral pleura covers the lungs, the parietal pleura lines the chest wall and diaphragm; the pleural cavity between contains lubricating pleural fluid that minimizes friction during breathing.

fibrous joint.definition: A joint in which adjacent bones are joined by dense fibrous connective tissue, with little or no movement and no joint cavity; includes sutures, syndesmoses, and gomphoses.

syndesmosis.definition: A fibrous joint in which two adjacent bones are bound by a ligament or interosseous membrane, allowing little to no movement; a typical example is the distal tibiofibular joint between the tibia and fibula.

sutura.definition: A seam or line of junction between bones, especially the fibrous joints between skull bones; in surgery, a stitch or material used to close a wound.

gomphosis.definition: A fibrous peg-in-socket joint between a tooth and its alveolar socket, stabilized by the periodontal ligament; an immovable (synarthrotic) joint.

synarthrosis.definition: An immovable joint between bones, held together by fibrous or cartilaginous tissue.

cafe-au-lait patches.definition: Flat, uniformly pigmented skin macules or patches (light to dark brown) due to increased melanin in the epidermis; commonly present at birth or in early childhood. Usually benign, but multiple lesions (typically six or more) can indicate neurofibromatosis type 1, with size thresholds of >5 mm in children or >15 mm in postpubertal individuals.

fibrous hamartoma of infancy.definition: A benign, slowly enlarging subcutaneous soft-tissue lesion of infancy composed of a disorganized admixture of fibrous tissue, immature mesenchymal/fibroblastic elements, and adipose tissue; typically presents as a painless mass in the trunk or proximal limbs during the first years of life. Treatment is complete surgical excision, with an excellent prognosis and rare recurrences.

infancy.definition: The period of early life from birth through the first year of age (roughly 0–12 months), during which rapid physical and neurological development occurs and the child is dependent on caregivers.

fibular.definition: Relating to the fibula, the slender bone of the lower leg located on the lateral side; it runs parallel to the tibia and serves mainly as a site for muscle attachment and ankle stability.

fibularis brevis.definition: A muscle of the lateral compartment of the leg that originates from the distal two-thirds of the fibula and inserts on the tuberosity of the base of the fifth metatarsal; it everts the foot and assists in plantarflexion of the ankle. Innervation: superficial peroneal (fibular) nerve.

fibularis longus.definition: A muscle in the lateral compartment of the leg that originates from the head and shaft of the fibula, runs behind the lateral malleolus, and inserts on the plantar aspect of the base of the first metatarsal and the medial cuneiform; it everts and plantarflexes the foot and helps maintain the transverse arch, innervated by the superficial fibular (peroneal) nerve.

fibularis tertius.definition: A small muscle of the anterior compartment of the leg that dorsiflexes and everts the foot; it originates from the distal fibula and interosseous membrane and inserts on the base of the fifth metatarsal, innervated by the deep peroneal nerve, and is variably present in individuals.

fibular notch.definition: A notch on the distal tibia on the lateral side that accommodates the distal end of the fibula, forming part of the inferior tibiofibular joint of the ankle.

fick.definition: Fick's law of diffusion: the rate of diffusion of a substance across a barrier is proportional to the concentration gradient, with the proportionality constant being the diffusion coefficient; commonly expressed as J = -D dC/dx (diffusion flux per unit area).

fick's law.definition: A principle of diffusion stating that the rate (flux) of a solute moving through a medium is proportional to the diffusion coefficient, the surface area, and the concentration gradient, and inversely proportional to the distance over which diffusion occurs; commonly expressed as J = -D(dC/dx) for one-dimensional steady-state diffusion.

fick's principle.definition: The rate at which a substance is taken up (or released) by an organ equals the organ’s blood flow multiplied by the arteriovenous concentration difference of that substance; for oxygen, VO2 = Q × (CaO2 − CvO2), where CaO2 is arterial oxygen content and CvO2 is venous oxygen content.

figlu.definition: A metabolite formed in histidine catabolism; its urinary excretion increases after a histidine load and indicates folate (tetrahydrofolate) deficiency or impaired THF metabolism.

figo.definition: An international professional organization of gynecology and obstetrics that develops standardized guidelines and staging systems for gynecologic cancers and obstetric care.

figo staging.definition: A cancer staging framework developed by the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) to describe the extent of gynecologic cancer spread, assigning stages I through IV (with subcategories) based on local invasion, regional lymph node involvement, and distant metastasis; it complements or maps to the TNM classification and is updated periodically for different cancer types.

field fever.definition: A nonstandard term with no formal medical definition; it is sometimes used to describe fever occurring in outdoor or field settings and is not a specific syndrome. If used, it implies evaluation for an underlying infectious or environmental cause (e.g., travel- or field-acquired infections or heat-related illness).

leptospira grippotyphosa.definition: A pathogenic spirochete of the genus Leptospira (Leptospira interrogans serovar Grippotyphosa) that causes leptospirosis in humans and animals; transmitted via contact with water or soil contaminated with urine from infected animals, with reservoirs including rodents and other wildlife.

canefield fever.definition: Historical name for dengue fever observed among Allied personnel at Canefield, New Guinea during World War II; a viral, mosquito-borne illness causing sudden high fever with severe myalgias, headache, retro-orbital pain, and sometimes rash.

harvest fever.definition: Not a recognized medical term. A colloquial or historical phrase for febrile illness observed during the harvest season, without a specific disease meaning; evaluation should follow standard fever workup and consider regional exposure risks. Causes vary by geography and exposure and can include zoonotic infections (e.g., leptospirosis, brucellosis), vector-borne diseases, malaria in endemic areas, heat-related illness, or other seasonal febrile illnesses.If you have a specific region or context, I can tailor the differential.

7-day fever.definition: A fever that lasts seven consecutive days; a persistent fever that may indicate ongoing infection, inflammatory, or malignant processes and typically warrants clinical evaluation.

dracunculus medinensis.definition: A parasitic nematode that causes guinea worm disease (dracunculiasis); transmitted by drinking water containing copepods infected with its larvae; the adult female migrates to the skin and emerges through the surface, causing a painful ulcer and releasing larvae.

fibrovascular proliferation.definition: A histologic process in which fibrous connective tissue proliferates with accompanying neovascularization; a fibrovascular scar tissue that can contract and distort surrounding tissue.

avascular fibrous tissue.definition: Fibrous connective tissue with little to no blood vessels; composed predominantly of densely packed collagen fibers and relies on diffusion from surrounding vessels for nutrients, resulting in slower healing. Common in tendons, ligaments, and fascia.

biopsies.definition: Biopsies are medical procedures in which small samples of tissue are removed from the body for laboratory examination, typically under a microscope, to diagnose disease or assess pathology and guide treatment.

microfilariae.definition: The microscopic larval stage of filarial nematodes that circulates in the blood or resides in the skin of the mammalian host and is transmitted to arthropod vectors (such as mosquitoes or blackflies) during a blood meal.

mansonella.definition: A genus of filarial nematodes that cause mansonelliasis in humans; transmitted by biting arthropods (various Culicoides or Simulium species); microfilariae circulate in blood or skin, and infections are often asymptomatic or mild.

onchocerca.definition: Genus of parasitic nematodes; Onchocerca volvulus causes onchocerciasis (river blindness). Transmitted by bites of Simulium blackflies; adults inhabit subcutaneous nodules and release microfilariae that disseminate to skin and eyes, causing dermatitis and potentially irreversible blindness.

wuchereria.definition: A genus of filarial nematodes that are human parasites causing lymphatic filariasis; transmitted by mosquitoes; adults reside in the lymphatic system and microfilariae circulate in the peripheral blood; infection can lead to lymphatic obstruction, lymphedema, and elephantiasis; diagnosed by microfilariae in blood or circulating filarial antigens; treated with antifilarial medications (e.g., diethylcarbamazine, ivermectin, albendazole) and measures to reduce transmission.

ivermectin.definition: A broad-spectrum antiparasitic medication (a macrocyclic lactone) used to treat infections caused by various nematodes and ectoparasites, including Onchocerca volvulus (river blindness), Strongyloides stercoralis, other intestinal worms, scabies, and lice; it acts by binding to glutamate-gated chloride channels in the nervous system of invertebrates, causing paralysis and death of the parasite.

antihelminthic.definition: A drug used to treat infections caused by parasitic worms (helminths) by killing the parasites or inhibiting their growth.

helminth.definition: A parasitic worm, typically referring to nematodes (roundworms), cestodes (tapeworms), and trematodes (flukes) that live in or on a vertebrate host and may cause disease.

worm burden.definition: The number of parasitic worms (helminths) present in a host, reflecting the intensity of infection and often correlating with morbidity; typically assessed by worm counts or by detecting eggs, larvae, or antigens in stool, urine, or tissue samples.

filarial worms.definition: Parasitic, thread-like nematodes of the superfamily Filarioidea that inhabit humans (often in lymphatic vessels or subcutaneous tissues) and are transmitted by arthropod vectors; adults produce microfilariae that circulate in blood or skin and cause diseases such as lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis, and loiasis.

filarioidea.definition: A superfamily of parasitic nematodes (filarial worms) that infect vertebrate hosts and are transmitted by arthropod vectors; they cause filarial diseases such as lymphatic filariasis and onchocerciasis.

filoviridae.definition: A family of enveloped, filamentous, negative-sense RNA viruses that includes Ebola and Marburg viruses; causes severe hemorrhagic fever in humans and nonhuman primates, with transmission mainly through contact with infected bodily fluids and bats thought to serve as reservoirs.

filovirus.definition: A member of the Filoviridae family of enveloped, filamentous, negative-sense RNA viruses that cause severe viral hemorrhagic fever in humans and nonhuman primates (examples include Ebola and Marburg viruses).

ebola.definition: A very serious illness that causes fever and bleeding. Also called Ebola hemorrhagic fever or Ebola virus disease.

marburg.definition: A viral hemorrhagic fever caused by a filovirus; transmission occurs through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person or contaminated objects, and the natural reservoir is believed to be fruit bats. Incubation is about 2–21 days; initial symptoms include fever, malaise, headache, and myalgia, which may progress to severe hemorrhagic manifestations, shock, and multiorgan failure. There is no widely available specific antiviral treatment; care is supportive and focuses on infection control and supportive laboratory monitoring.

hemorrhagic fevers.definition: A group of viral infections characterized by fever and hemorrhagic manifestations due to vascular damage and coagulopathy; caused by diverse virus families (including arenaviruses, filoviruses, bunyaviruses, and flaviviruses), and may lead to shock and organ failure.

filiform bougie.definition: A slender, flexible dilator used to probe a narrowed lumen (such as the urethra or esophagus) and to guide subsequent dilation or introduction of larger instruments.

filiform catheter.definition: A very slender, threadlike catheter used to guide other catheters or devices through narrow or tortuous passages, often to facilitate cannulation or exchange of catheters.

filiform papilla.definition: Slender, threadlike or conical projections on the dorsal surface of the tongue; the most numerous papillae, lacking taste buds, and primarily providing a rough surface for mechanical manipulation of food (not for taste).

filiform warts.definition: A form of HPV-related skin wart characterized by slender, thread-like projections on the face (often around the lips or eyes); lesions are soft, flesh-colored and can spread by contact.

filling.definition: A dental restoration placed into a prepared tooth cavity to replace missing tooth tissue and restore contour, function, and aesthetics after decay or damage; commonly made of amalgam, composite resin, or other restorative materials.

endodontic therapy.definition: A dental procedure to treat infection or inflammation of the dental pulp by removing the pulp, cleaning and disinfecting the root canal system, filling the canals, and sealing the tooth, usually followed by restoration to preserve the tooth.

thyroid biopsy.definition: A procedure to obtain a tissue sample from the thyroid gland for cytological or histological examination, most commonly performed as an ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy to evaluate nodules for malignancy or other thyroid disease.

fine-needle aspiration.definition: A minimally invasive diagnostic procedure in which a thin needle is inserted into a lump or mass to aspirate cells or fluid for cytologic examination, often performed under imaging guidance to evaluate tumors or lesions (e.g., thyroid nodules, breast lumps).

goniometer.definition: An instrument used to measure angles, particularly the range of motion of a joint, typically consisting of two arms with a protractor-scale.

finger-nose test.definition: A cerebellar function test in which the patient repeatedly touches their nose and a moving target (usually the examiner's finger) with the same finger, assessing the accuracy and smoothness of voluntary movement; dysmetria or tremor during the task suggests cerebellar dysfunction.

finger-stick.definition: A method of obtaining a small capillary blood sample by pricking the fingertip with a lancet, typically used for point-of-care tests such as blood glucose measurement.

finger-sweep.definition: A procedure in which a clinician uses a gloved finger to palpate for and remove a visible foreign body from the throat or airway; it should not be performed blindly, as it can push the object deeper or cause injury.

finger-percussion.definition: A clinical percussion technique in which the examiner taps the surface of the body with a finger (commonly the tip of one finger placed on the area while another finger strikes it) to produce sounds that help distinguish air-filled from fluid- or solid-containing areas.

butalbital.definition: A short- to intermediate-acting barbiturate CNS depressant used in combination analgesic preparations (e.g., with acetaminophen or aspirin and caffeine) to treat tension-type headaches; it provides sedative effects but carries risks of dependence, withdrawal, and CNS/respiratory depression, especially when taken with alcohol or other depressants.

finasteride.definition: A 5-alpha reductase inhibitor that blocks the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT); used orally to treat benign prostatic hyperplasia and androgenetic alopecia in men (brand names include Proscar and Propecia).

benign prostatic hyperplasia.definition: Noncancerous enlargement of the prostate gland that occurs with aging in men and can cause lower urinary tract symptoms.

film-screen mammography.definition: A conventional mammography technique in which breast X-ray images are recorded on radiographic film via a screen-film cassette with intensifying screens and then chemically developed to produce a hard-copy image; largely replaced by digital mammography.

fimbriae tubae.definition: Fingerlike projections at the infundibulum (ovarian end) of the fallopian tube that capture the ovum after ovulation and guide it into the tube; they are lined with ciliated epithelium to help transport the egg toward the uterus.

fimbria ovarica.definition: Finger-like projections at the distal end of the fallopian tube that surround the ovary and capture the ovulated oocyte, guiding it into the fallopian tube.

fimbrial tubal pregnancy.definition: An ectopic (tubal) pregnancy in which implantation occurs at the fimbrial end of the fallopian tube (the distal end near the ovary); a rare form of tubal ectopic pregnancy.

epithelial cells.definition: They are cells that line the surfaces and cavities of the body and its organs, forming epithelial tissue. They are tightly joined and polarized, with distinct apical and basal surfaces, and rest on a basement membrane. They are avascular and receive nutrients by diffusion from underlying connective tissue. Their functions include protection, selective absorption and secretion, and sensation; they are classified by shape (squamous, cuboidal, columnar) and by layering (simple, stratified, pseudostratified, transitional).

fimbria hippocampi.definition: White matter tract along the medial edge of the hippocampus, consisting of hippocampal efferent axons; it continues posteriorly to become the fornix, carrying output from the hippocampus.

alveus.definition: A sheet of white-matter fibers on the surface of the hippocampus composed of axons from hippocampal neurons; its fibers converge to form the fimbria and, as the fornix, project to subcortical targets.

posterior pillar of the fornix.definition: A longitudinal fiber bundle (pillar) of the fornix forming the posterior limb, consisting of hippocampal efferent fibers that extend toward subcortical targets (notably the mammillary bodies) as part of the limbic system.

lymphatics.definition: An extensive network of lymphatic vessels and tissues that drains interstitial fluid as lymph, filters it through lymph nodes, transports immune cells, and assists in the absorption of dietary fats via intestinal lacteals, returning lymph to the venous circulation.

embryonated eggs.definition: An egg that contains a developed embryonic larva inside the eggshell; formed when fertilized eggs undergo embryonation under suitable environmental conditions, and such eggs are typically infective to a host when ingested (as with many intestinal helminths).

prelarvae.definition: An immature developmental form preceding the larval stage in the life cycle of certain parasites; it develops from an egg and gives rise to a larva, often being non-feeding and morphologically distinct from the larva.

gerstmann's syndrome.definition: A rare acquired neuropsychological syndrome due to damage to the dominant parietal cortex (usually the left angular gyrus), characterized by finger agnosia, agraphia, acalculia, and left–right disorientation.

finger agnosia.definition: An impairment of tactile-kinesthetic finger recognition, causing difficulty identifying, naming, or distinguishing an individual finger, or localizing fingers on command—often seen with dominant parietal lobe injury as part of Gerstmann syndrome.

organic hemiplegia.definition: Paralysis of one side of the body due to a definite structural lesion in the brain (an organic brain disorder), such as a cerebrovascular accident, tumor, or traumatic brain injury, as opposed to functional or psychogenic paralysis.

patency.definition: The condition of being open and unobstructed; the degree to which a hollow organ or vessel (such as a blood vessel or duct) remains open.

olfactory.definition: Relating to the sense of smell; pertaining to the olfactory system, including the olfactory epithelium, olfactory bulb, and olfactory nerve (cranial nerve I).

vesiculation.definition: The formation of vesicles (small fluid-filled blisters) on the skin or mucous membranes, due to separation of tissue layers or accumulation of fluid—the process of vesicle formation.

tetraodon.definition: A genus of freshwater pufferfish in the family Tetraodontidae; several species contain tetrodotoxin in their tissues, making them poisonous if consumed.

b12.definition: A water-soluble vitamin essential for DNA synthesis, red blood cell formation, and neurological function; absorption requires intrinsic factor, and deficiency can cause megaloblastic anemia and neuropathy.

intestinal.definition: Relating to the intestines; pertaining to the digestive tract between the stomach and the anus.

chlamydial.definition: Relating to Chlamydia, a genus of obligate intracellular bacteria that cause infections such as nongonococcal urethritis, cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, conjunctivitis, and pneumonia; the term describes diseases or organisms associated with these bacteria.

fistulotomy.definition: A surgical procedure to treat an anal fistula by laying open the fistulous tract along its length to allow drainage and healing from the inside out.

fistulectomy.definition: Excision of a fistulous tract and any surrounding inflamed tissue; a surgical procedure that removes the fistula completely, typically resulting in a wound that heals by secondary intention.

torticollis.definition: A condition in which the head is tilted to one side and rotated, due to contraction or shortening of the neck muscles (most often the sternocleidomastoid); it can be congenital (muscular torticollis) or acquired from muscle spasm, trauma, or cervical dystonia.

phagocyte.definition: A cell capable of phagocytosis; it engulfs and digests foreign particles, bacteria, and cellular debris as part of the immune response (examples include neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages, and dendritic cells).

marrow.definition: Soft tissue inside bone cavities that produces blood cells (red marrow) and stores fat (yellow marrow); located mainly in the medullary cavities, with red marrow predominant in the axial skeleton and at the ends of long bones in children, and red marrow decreasing with age as yellow marrow increases.

fitz-hugh–curtis.definition: A form of perihepatitis associated with pelvic inflammatory disease, most commonly caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis, characterized by right upper quadrant abdominal pain and violin-string adhesions between the liver capsule and the peritoneum.

giardia.definition: A genus of flagellated protozoan parasites that infect the small intestine of humans and other animals, causing giardiasis; transmitted by ingestion of cysts in contaminated water or food.

trichomonas.definition: A genus of flagellated, anaerobic parasitic protozoa; the most clinically relevant species, Trichomonas vaginalis, infects the human urogenital tract and causes trichomoniasis, a common sexually transmitted infection.

trypanosoma.definition: A genus of parasitic, flagellated protozoa that infect vertebrates; transmitted by blood-sucking insects (tsetse flies or triatomine bugs); causes diseases such as African sleeping sickness and Chagas disease.

protozoon.definition: A single-celled, eukaryotic microorganism classified among the protists; historically described as animal-like and typically heterotrophic, occurring as free-living or parasitic forms.

flagellum.definition: A slender, thread-like appendage that projects from the cell surface and enables locomotion; in prokaryotes it rotates to propel the cell, while in many eukaryotes it moves in a whip-like fashion to move the cell.

flagella.definition: Long, whip-like cellular appendages that enable movement of certain cells. In bacteria they rotate to propel the cell; in eukaryotes (such as sperm) they beat in a whip-like motion.

flagyl.definition: A nitroimidazole antibiotic/antiprotozoal used to treat anaerobic bacterial infections and protozoal infections; it is activated in anaerobic conditions and inhibits nucleic acid synthesis.

hemothorax.definition: A collection of blood in the pleural space (between the lung and chest wall), usually due to chest trauma or rupture of intrathoracic vessels, causing dyspnea and chest pain; treated with drainage (chest tube) and stabilization of bleeding.

respiratory arrest.definition: Sudden cessation of breathing (apnea) with no effective ventilation, leading to hypoxia; a medical emergency requiring immediate resuscitation (airway management and ventilation, with CPR if there is no pulse).

positive pressure.definition: Pressure greater than the surrounding atmospheric pressure; in medicine, it refers to gas or fluid pressure that exceeds ambient pressure, such as the pressure applied to the airways during positive-pressure ventilation.

bilevel positive pressure.definition: A noninvasive ventilation mode delivering two pressures: a higher inspiratory pressure to assist breathing and a lower expiratory pressure to keep airways open, reducing the work of breathing.

flap reconstruction.definition: A surgical technique in reconstructive surgery in which tissue (skin, fat, muscle, or bone) with an intact blood supply is mobilized from one site to another to repair a defect; it may be a local/pedicled flap or a free flap requiring microvascular anastomosis.

skin flap.definition: A surgical piece of skin and subcutaneous tissue with its own blood supply that is moved from one site to another to cover a wound or defect; unlike a graft, it maintains its vascular supply during transfer.

denture base.definition: The portion of a removable denture that rests on the oral mucosa and to which the artificial teeth are attached; it is typically made of acrylic resin and molded to fit the edentulous ridges and palate, providing support, retention, and stability.

rib.definition: A bone in the chest that acts as a cage for the heart and lungs.

nostrils.definition: External openings of the nasal cavity that allow air to enter and exit the nose; lined with respiratory mucosa and hairs and bordered by the nasal alae.

flaring.definition: An abrupt worsening or escalation of symptoms in a chronic disease (a flare-up); in pediatrics, it can also refer to widening of the nostrils during breathing as a sign of respiratory distress.

flame photometry.definition: An atomic emission spectroscopy method in which a liquid sample is introduced into a flame to atomize its elements; the excited atoms emit light at characteristic wavelengths, and the emission intensity is proportional to the concentration of specific metal ions (classically sodium and potassium) in the sample.

flea.definition: A small, wingless ectoparasitic insect of the order Siphonaptera that feeds on the blood of mammals or birds; laterally compressed body with powerful hind legs for jumping; can transmit diseases such as plague and murine typhus.

flea bite.definition: A bite by a flea, typically presenting as a small, itchy red bump on the skin; bites may be scratched and flea exposure should be controlled to prevent infestation and potential transmission of infections such as plague or murine typhus.

flea-borne typhus.definition: An infection caused by Rickettsia typhi transmitted to humans by fleas (primarily rat fleas such as Xenopsylla cheopis) that infest rodents; it presents as a febrile illness with headache and myalgias, often with a maculopapular rash, and is typically mild to moderate in severity; treated with doxycycline.

flecainide.definition: A class IC antiarrhythmic that blocks fast sodium channels to slow conduction in cardiac tissue; used to maintain sinus rhythm in selected supraventricular tachyarrhythmias (e.g., paroxysmal atrial fibrillation) but carries a risk of proarrhythmia and is contraindicated in patients with structural heart disease.

flecainide acetate.definition: An antiarrhythmic medication (class Ic) used to treat and prevent certain tachyarrhythmias, especially atrial fibrillation or flutter, by blocking fast sodium channels and slowing conduction in the heart. It can cause proarrhythmia and is contraindicated in patients with structural heart disease, ischemic heart disease, or a history of myocardial infarction.

flavivirus.definition: Enveloped, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses in the family Flaviviridae; most are arthropod-borne (mosquitoes or ticks) and include dengue, Zika, West Nile, yellow fever, Japanese encephalitis, and tick-borne encephalitis viruses.

flavocoxid.definition: A proprietary mixture of flavonoids marketed as an anti-inflammatory agent for osteoarthritis; it inhibits both cyclooxygenase (COX) and 5-lipoxygenase (5-LOX) pathways, reducing downstream inflammatory mediators.

flavoxate.definition: A urinary antispasmodic (antimuscarinic) agent used to treat bladder spasm–related symptoms such as urgency, frequency, and dysuria by inhibiting muscarinic receptors in the detrusor muscle.

flavoxate hydrochloride.definition: A urinary antispasmodic (antimuscarinic) agent—the hydrochloride salt of flavoxate that inhibits muscarinic receptors in the bladder to relieve smooth muscle spasms and symptoms of overactive bladder (urgency, frequency, urge incontinence).

flavone.definition: A simple member of the flavonoid family, defined by a 2-phenylchromen-4-one skeleton (2-phenyl-1-benzopyran-4-one); a polyphenolic plant metabolite commonly found as a pale-yellow crystalline solid and serving as the core structure for related flavonoids.

flavonoid.definition: A class of plant-derived polyphenolic compounds with antioxidant activity, found in many fruits, vegetables, and beverages; includes subgroups such as flavonols, flavones, flavanones, anthocyanidins, and isoflavones, and is studied for potential health benefits.

flavoprotein.definition: A protein that contains a flavin cofactor (FMN or FAD) bound as a prosthetic group and participates in oxidation–reduction reactions, acting as a redox coenzyme in a variety of enzymes.

supraventricular tachycardia.definition: An abnormally fast heartbeat originating in heart tissue above the ventricles.

second-degree atrioventricular block.definition: An arrhythmia in which some atrial impulses are blocked at the atrioventricular (AV) node so that not every P wave is followed by a QRS complex, causing intermittent dropped beats. There are two main types: Mobitz type I (Wenckebach), with progressively lengthening PR intervals until a beat is dropped; and Mobitz type II, with fixed PR intervals and sudden dropped QRS complexes.

third-degree atrioventricular block.definition: A complete atrioventricular block in which no atrial impulses are conducted to the ventricles, resulting in AV dissociation with independent atrial and ventricular rhythms. The ventricles beat via a below-the-block escape rhythm, typically at a slow rate; symptoms can include bradycardia, dizziness, or syncope, and permanent pacemaker therapy is often required.

cyp3a.definition: A subfamily of cytochrome P450 enzymes that metabolizes a wide range of drugs and endogenous compounds; includes CYP3A4 and CYP3A5, mainly expressed in liver and intestines, with activity readily inhibited or induced by various drugs, affecting drug metabolism.

cyp2d6.definition: A gene encoding the cytochrome P450 2D6 enzyme, a major hepatic drug-metabolizing enzyme that oxidizes many drugs; highly polymorphic, resulting in variable metabolizer phenotypes (poor, intermediate, extensive, and ultrarapid) that affect drug response.

isoelectric electroencephalogram.definition: An EEG pattern with essentially no detectable cerebral electrical activity across the recording leads, producing a flat tracing; indicates profound suppression of brain activity and may be seen in deep coma or brain death, among other contexts, and requires clinical correlation.

central nervous system depression.definition: A decrease in brain function producing reduced level of consciousness and responsiveness, often caused by central nervous system depressant drugs (eg, alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, opioids) or metabolic/structural brain disturbances; ranges from drowsiness and disorientation to stupor or coma, and may include slowed respiration and depressed reflexes.
