friedman curve.definition: An obstetric labor-progress diagram introduced by Emanuel Friedman that plots cervical dilation over time to describe normal labor progress, delineating latent and active phases and typical dilation rates (about 1.2 cm/hour for nulliparas and ~1.5 cm/hour for multiparas) to identify protraction or arrest of labor.

friedman's test.definition: A nonparametric statistical test used to detect differences in treatments across related samples (repeated measures). It ranks data within blocks across treatments and tests the null hypothesis that the related samples come from the same distribution; it is the nonparametric analogue of the one-way repeated-measures ANOVA.

froment's sign.definition: A clinical sign of ulnar nerve palsy where, during a pinch test, the thumb flexes at the interphalangeal joint due to compensation by the flexor pollicis longus, indicating weakness of the adductor pollicis.

frontonasal dysplasia.definition: A rare congenital craniofacial syndrome caused by abnormal development of the frontonasal prominence during embryogenesis, resulting in midline facial anomalies such as hypertelorism (increased distance between the eyes) with a broad nasal root, nasal/nasofrontal defects, and often a median facial cleft; severity and associated features vary.

frontoethmoidal suture.definition: A fibrous joint between the frontal bone and the ethmoid bone of the skull; a cranial suture located at the anterior cranial fossa near the nasal/orbital region that typically ossifies with age.

frontal lobectomy.definition: A neurosurgical procedure in which part or all of the frontal lobe is removed or functionally disconnected, usually to treat intractable epilepsy or a frontal lobe tumor; the extent and location determine potential neurological or cognitive effects.

frontal nerve.definition: A purely sensory branch of the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve that travels in the orbit to supply the forehead and scalp, and divides into the supratrochlear and supraorbital nerves.

supraorbital nerve.definition: A sensory branch of the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve that exits the skull via the supraorbital foramen/notch and supplies cutaneous sensation to the forehead and anterior scalp up to the vertex, including the upper eyelid; may give a meningeal branch to the dura mater.

supratrochlear nerve.definition: A sensory branch of the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve; supplies cutaneous sensation to the medial forehead and upper eyelid, exiting the orbit above the trochlea of the superior oblique muscle.

frontal plane.definition: An anatomical plane that divides the body into anterior (front) and posterior (back) portions; it runs vertically from left to right and is perpendicular to the sagittal plane (also called the coronal plane).

frontal pole.definition: An anatomical term for the most anterior part of the frontal lobe (the frontal pole), the rostral end of the frontal cortex associated with higher-order cognitive functions.

frontal section.definition: A coronal (frontal) plane or section that divides the body or an organ into anterior (front) and posterior (back) portions; a vertical plane parallel to the forehead.

frontal vein.definition: A superficial vein of the forehead that drains blood from the forehead and frontal scalp; it communicates with the supratrochlear and supraorbital veins and typically drains into the angular vein, then into the facial vein.

frontal crest.definition: A vertical bony ridge on the inner surface of the frontal bone along the midline, serving as the attachment site for the falx cerebri (the dural fold).

frontocortical aphasia.definition: A language disorder caused by injury to the frontal and adjacent frontocortical language networks (typically in the dominant hemisphere), presenting with nonfluent, effortful speech and agrammatism, relatively preserved comprehension, impaired repetition, and often accompanying speech motor planning difficulties such as apraxia of speech.

fronto-temporal dementia.definition: A neurodegenerative disorder marked by progressive atrophy of the frontal and temporal lobes, causing early changes in behavior and personality or language, with memory relatively preserved early on and a gradual decline.

frontal lobe dementia.definition: A neurodegenerative disorder in which progressive degeneration of the frontal lobes leads to early changes in personality, behavior, and executive function, often with later or concurrent language or motor symptoms; tends to present at a younger age than Alzheimer’s disease.

frontal lobe syndrome.definition: A syndrome of cognitive, behavioral, and personality changes due to damage to the frontal lobes, characterized by dysexecutive deficits (impaired planning, problem-solving, working memory, cognitive flexibility), disinhibition or apathy, impaired social judgment, perseveration, and variable motor signs.

interocclusal distance.definition: Vertical distance between the upper and lower occlusal surfaces when the jaw is in its physiologic rest position (the freeway space), typically about 2–4 mm.

sagittal plane.definition: A vertical anatomical plane that divides the body or an organ into left and right portions; when it runs along the midline and creates equal left and right halves, it is the midsagittal (median) plane.

ethmoidal air cell.definition: Air-filled cavities within the ethmoid bone that form part of the paranasal sinuses; they are subdivided into anterior, middle, and posterior groups and are lined by respiratory mucosa, draining into the nasal cavity (anterior and middle cells into the middle meatus, posterior cells into the superior meatus).

sphenoidal sinus.definition: An air-filled paranasal sinus located within the sphenoid bone behind the nasal cavity; lined with mucosa and communicating with the nasal cavity (via the sphenoidal ostium) and draining into the nasal cavity, with size that varies among individuals and potential involvement in sphenoid sinusitis.

ethmoidofrontal suture.definition: An immovable fibrous joint between the ethmoid and frontal bones of the skull.

frontonasal duct.definition: A slender bony channel that connects the frontal sinus to the nasal cavity, allowing drainage of mucus from the frontal sinus into the middle meatus (via the frontonasal ostium).

orbital plate.definition: A bony portion that forms part of the wall of the orbit (eye socket); the orbital surface of a skull bone that contributes to the orbital cavity and supports ocular structures.

nasal spine.definition: A pointed bony projection on the anterior inferior border of the nasal aperture formed by the maxilla; an anatomical landmark used in radiographic and surgical planning and contributing to the shape of the piriform aperture.

interocclusal gap.definition: The vertical distance between the opposing dentition when the jaw is in a relaxed, non-occluding rest position (freeway space), typically about 2–4 mm.

angular vein.definition: A facial vein formed at the medial canthus by the union of the supratrochlear and supraorbital veins; it courses obliquely down the side of the nose and drains into the facial vein, with communications to the ophthalmic veins.

superficial temporal vein.definition: A vein of the scalp that runs with the superficial temporal artery in the temple region; it drains blood from the lateral scalp and temple and empties into the retromandibular vein.

superciliary arches.definition: The paired bony ridges on the frontal bone just above the eye sockets, forming the superior margins of the orbits (eyebrow ridges) and serving as attachment points for forehead/eyebrow muscles.

middle meatus.definition: A groove in the lateral wall of the nasal cavity beneath the middle turbinate that serves as the drainage pathway for the maxillary sinus and the anterior ethmoidal air cells (frontal sinus drainage reaches this area via the frontonasal duct/infundibulum).

greater sublingual duct.definition: The main duct of the sublingual salivary gland that drains saliva into the oral cavity, typically opening at the sublingual caruncle on the floor of the mouth; also known as Bartholin's duct (ductus sublingualis major).

lesser sublingual ducts.definition: Small excretory ducts of the sublingual gland that drain mucous secretions, opening along the sublingual folds on the floor of the mouth (the ducts of Rivinus).

deep lingual artery.definition: A branch of the lingual artery that runs anteriorly to the apex of the tongue, supplying the tongue’s mucosa and intrinsic muscles (and giving branches to the sublingual region).

deep lingual vein.definition: A vein on the underside of the tongue that drains the deep portions of the tongue; it drains into the lingual vein, which ultimately empties into the internal jugular vein.

sublingual caruncle.definition: A small mucosal papilla on the floor of the mouth on each side of the lingual frenulum, serving as the opening site for the ducts of the submandibular glands (Wharton's ducts) and, to a lesser extent, the sublingual gland ducts.

front-tap.definition: Not a standard medical term; there is no established definition in medical dictionaries.

reflex.definition: An involuntary, rapid motor response to a stimulus mediated by a neural circuit that carries the signal from a sensory receptor through a sensory neuron to the central nervous system and back via a motor neuron to an effector muscle.

cleft.definition: A fissure or gap in a body structure resulting from incomplete fusion or separation during development; commonly used to describe congenital defects such as those of the lip or palate.

median.definition: Situated in the middle; in anatomy, the median plane (midsagittal plane) is the vertical plane that divides the body into equal left and right halves.

facial.definition: Relating to the face; a skin-care treatment for the face involving cleansing, exfoliation, massage, and application of masks or serums.

iatrogenic.definition: Originating as a result of medical care; an adverse condition or complication caused by a medical procedure, treatment, or diagnostic intervention.

ethyl.definition: An alkyl substituent consisting of two carbon atoms (–CH2–CH3) derived from ethane; represented by the formula C2H5. Used in chemical nomenclature to indicate the presence of a two-carbon substituent; in medical contexts, when combined with 'alcohol' it denotes ethanol.

spray.definition: A medicinal preparation in which a liquid drug is atomized into a fine aerosol or mist and expelled through a nozzle for administration to mucosal surfaces or by inhalation (commonly nasal or throat sprays).

immersion.definition: Submergence of the body or a body part completely in a liquid, typically water, for therapeutic, diagnostic, cleansing, or absorptive purposes.

manifestations.definition: Signs, symptoms, or other observable features that indicate the presence or course of a disease or condition; the outward expression of an underlying pathology.

rewarming.definition: The medical process of restoring a hypothermic patient's core body temperature to normal, using passive warming (e.g., blankets, a warm environment) and/or active warming methods (external warming devices, warmed intravenous fluids or gases, or invasive internal warming).

expanders.definition: A device implanted under the skin that is gradually inflated to stretch surrounding tissue, creating extra skin or soft tissue for later reconstruction.

whirlpool.definition: A hydrotherapy modality in which a body part is immersed in warm water that is agitated to create a swirling effect; used to cleanse wounds, debride tissue, reduce edema, relieve pain, and promote circulation and healing.

sympathectomy.definition: A surgical procedure that interrupts or destroys portions of the sympathetic nervous system to reduce sympathetic outflow to a target area, commonly performed to treat hyperhidrosis and certain vascular or pain disorders.

constrictive.definition: Tending to constrict or cause constriction; causing narrowing or compression of a body part, vessel, or lumen.

wet.definition: Covered with or saturated with liquid; in clinical use, describing tissue or wounds that are moist or exuding fluid.

clothing.definition: A garment worn on the body, typically made of fabric, designed to cover and protect the skin, regulate temperature, and provide modesty and comfort; in medical contexts, it refers to protective clinical attire (e.g., gowns, scrubs) worn to reduce contamination and protect patients and staff.

insulated.definition: Covered or shielded by an insulating material that prevents the transfer of heat, electricity, or sound; in neurophysiology, describes a nerve fiber wrapped in myelin, which increases conduction velocity.

immobilized.definition: Made unable to move; movement restricted to promote healing or reduce pain, typically achieved with casts, splints, braces, or other devices that hold a limb or body part steady.

digits.definition: One of the fingers or toes; the terminal segments of the hand or foot composed of phalanges and their joints.

extremities.definition: The limbs of the body—the upper and lower extremities (arms and legs), including the hands and feet.

fructoseintolerance.definition: Fructose intolerance is the condition of adverse symptoms after consuming fructose, most commonly due to fructose malabsorption (impaired absorption in the small intestine), but it can also refer to hereditary fructose intolerance, a rare autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by aldolase B deficiency that leads to hypoglycemia and liver injury after fructose intake.

fructosemia.definition: Presence of fructose in the blood.

fructosuria.definition: The presence of fructose in the urine, most commonly due to essential fructosuria from hepatic fructokinase deficiency, a benign and usually asymptomatic condition.

fructokinase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the ATP-dependent phosphorylation of fructose to fructose-1-phosphate, initiating fructose metabolism (fructolysis) primarily in the liver and kidney; it bypasses the PFK-1 regulatory step of glycolysis.

fructosamine.definition: A measure of glycated serum proteins (primarily albumin) formed by nonenzymatic reaction with glucose; it reflects average blood glucose over the previous 2–3 weeks and is used to monitor short-term glycemic control, especially when HbA1c is unreliable.

levulose.definition: A monosaccharide (ketohexose) found in fruits and honey; commonly called fructose; the sweetest natural sugar, absorbed in the small intestine and largely metabolized in the liver.

glycerolized.definition: Treated with or preserved in glycerol (glycerin), commonly to protect tissues from dehydration and decay or to serve as a cryoprotectant during preservation.

cryopreserved.definition: Preserved by cooling to extremely low temperatures (typically in liquid nitrogen) to halt biological activity and preserve the viability of cells, tissues, or other biological samples for future use.

frozen.definition: Preserved by freezing at very low temperatures (cryopreservation) to halt biological activity and maintain tissue or sample integrity for later analysis; commonly used for frozen-section intraoperative pathology.

fucosidosis.definition: An ultra-rare autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of the enzyme alpha-L-fucosidase, leading to accumulation of fucose-containing glycoproteins and glycolipids in multiple tissues; clinical features typically include developmental delay or regression, progressive neurologic deterioration, coarse facial features, skeletal abnormalities (dysostosis multiplex), hepatosplenomegaly, recurrent infections, and angiokeratomas.

lysosomal.definition: Relating to lysosomes, which are membrane-bound organelles containing hydrolytic enzymes that digest waste materials, cellular debris, and damaged organelles.

storage.definition: The retention or accumulation of substances within cells or tissues for later use, often as an energy reserve (e.g., glycogen in liver and muscle, lipid stores in adipose tissue).

fucoside.definition: A glycoside in which the sugar moiety is fucose (a 6-deoxyhexose); a compound in which a fucose residue is linked by a glycosidic bond to an aglycone.

fudr.definition: A chemotherapy drug (brand name FUDR); floxuridine, a pyrimidine analog used to treat cancer (often via hepatic arterial infusion); it inhibits DNA synthesis by blocking thymidylate synthase.

fukuyama.definition: A congenital muscular dystrophy caused by defective glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan (a component of the dystroglycan complex), typically due to mutations in the FKTN (fukutin) gene, leading to severe hypotonia at birth, muscle weakness, and brain malformations such as cobblestone lissencephaly; inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern and part of the dystroglycanopathy group.

duchenne.definition: A severe X-linked recessive muscular dystrophy caused by mutations in the DMD gene encoding dystrophin; it leads to progressive proximal muscle weakness beginning in early childhood, calf pseudohypertrophy, and often cardiopulmonary complications with reduced life expectancy.

fulcrum.definition: Pivot point or fixed support around which a lever rotates, allowing force to be transferred or amplified; in medical contexts, it can also refer to the point of stabilization used for instruments or tissues.

fulgurate.definition: To destroy or ablate tissue by electric current or electrical spark (fulguration), a method used to destroy tissue or coagulate tissue during surgical procedures.

full-arch.definition: Replacement or restoration of all teeth in one dental arch (upper or lower), typically using a complete denture or an implant-supported prosthesis that spans the entire arch.

complete.definition: Fully developed or entire; not partial. In medicine, describes a condition or lesion that involves the entire structure or extent, such as a complete fracture (bone broken through its entire cross-section) or a complete blood count (a test measuring all major blood components).

molar.definition: A large tooth at the back of the mouth with a broad, flat surface and multiple cusps, specialized for grinding and chewing food.

arch.definition: An arched or curved anatomical structure. In the foot, the medial and lateral longitudinal arches and the transverse arch form a curved framework that distributes weight and absorbs shock; in vascular anatomy, an arch is a curved segment of a vessel, most notably the aortic arch, connecting the ascending and descending aorta.

methyl.definition: A one-carbon substituent consisting of a carbon bonded to three hydrogens (–CH3); the methyl group, the simplest alkyl group, used to modify molecules in organic chemistry and biochemistry (e.g., methylation).

methacrylate.definition: An ester of methacrylic acid; a vinyl monomer used to form polymers (e.g., polymethyl methacrylate) upon polymerization, and widely used in dental resins, bone cements, and various coatings and adhesives.

full-liquid.definition: A diet consisting of liquids and foods that are liquid at room or body temperature, including clear liquids plus opaque liquids such as milk, dairy products, strained soups, yogurt, custards, ice cream, pudding, and fruit juice; used as a transitional diet when swallowing solids is unsafe or after certain surgeries.

diet.definition: The usual pattern of foods and beverages consumed by an individual; or a prescribed or medically supervised set of foods for health, weight management, or disease treatment.

liquid.definition: A substance that flows readily, has a definite volume but no fixed shape; in medicine, a liquid is a fluid dosage form in which a drug is dissolved or dispersed (e.g., solutions, syrups, suspensions) for administration.

fta-abs.definition: A treponemal-specific serologic test for syphilis that detects antibodies to Treponema pallidum using indirect immunofluorescence; used to confirm syphilis after a positive non-treponemal screening test and typically remains positive for life.

fluorescent.definition: Relating to fluorescence; emitting visible light when illuminated by ultraviolet or other excitation light.

treponemal.definition: Relating to Treponema, a genus of spiral-shaped bacteria; in clinical practice, used to describe tests that detect antibodies against Treponema pallidum, the causative agent of syphilis.

nitroblue.definition: A blue tetrazolium salt used in a colorimetric assay to assess neutrophil respiratory burst; it is reduced by superoxide produced by NADPH oxidase to an insoluble blue formazan, allowing visualization and measurement of phagocyte oxidative activity.

tetrazolium.definition: A heterocyclic organic compound with a five-membered ring containing four nitrogen atoms; its salts are used as redox indicators in biochemical assays and are reduced to colored formazan dyes in tests such as cell viability assays.

a1c.definition: A blood test that measures the percentage of glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) to reflect average blood glucose over the past 2–3 months; used to diagnose and monitor diabetes. Normal is below 5.7%, prediabetes is 5.7–6.4%, and diabetes is diagnosed at 6.5% or higher.

merrf.definition: A mitochondrial disorder characterized by myoclonic seizures and epilepsy, often with ataxia and weakness; muscle biopsy shows ragged-red fibers; caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA (most commonly MT-TK), with maternal inheritance.

full-thickness graft.definition: A skin graft that includes the full thickness of the epidermis and dermis transplanted to a prepared recipient bed; provides durable coverage and superior cosmetic match but requires a well-vascularized bed and donor-site closure primarily.

flatfoot.definition: A condition in which the medial longitudinal arch of the foot is abnormally low or absent, so the sole is flat on weight-bearing (pes planus); it can be flexible or rigid and may be asymptomatic or associated with foot, ankle, or knee pain.

hepatic parenchyma.definition: The functional tissue of the liver, composed primarily of hepatocytes arranged in lobules with a network of sinusoids, responsible for metabolism, detoxification, protein synthesis, bile production, and storage.

fulvestrant.definition: A selective estrogen receptor degrader (SERD) used in the treatment of hormone receptor–positive breast cancer; binds the estrogen receptor and promotes its degradation, thereby blocking estrogen signaling and inhibiting tumor growth. Administered by intramuscular injection.

advanced breast carcinoma.definition: A breast cancer at an advanced stage (locally advanced or metastatic) with spread beyond the breast to regional lymph nodes or distant organs; management is typically systemic (chemotherapy, hormonal therapy, or targeted therapy) with palliative care as appropriate.

estrogen receptor-positive.definition: A cancer whose cells express estrogen receptors, meaning estrogen can promote its growth; such tumors often respond to hormonal (endocrine) therapy.

fulvicin.definition: A brand name for griseofulvin, a systemic antifungal used to treat dermatophyte infections of hair, skin, and nails; inhibits fungal mitosis by binding to tubulin; induces hepatic enzymes, with potential drug interactions; teratogenic and photosensitive; best absorbed with fatty meals.

fumigate.definition: To disinfect or sterilize a space or object by exposing it to fumigants—volatile chemical vapors or gases—to kill pests, microorganisms, or other unwanted organisms.

fungal abscess.definition: A localized collection of pus in tissue or an organ caused by fungal infection, often seen in immunocompromised patients; commonly due to organisms such as Candida, Aspergillus, or Cryptococcus; management typically includes systemic antifungal therapy and drainage when feasible.

fungal infection.definition: An infection caused by fungi (such as dermatophytes, yeasts, or molds) that invades or colonizes body tissues, commonly affecting the skin, nails, or mucous membranes, and can be superficial or invasive, particularly in immunocompromised individuals.

fungal pneumonia.definition: A lung infection caused by fungi, typically occurring in people with weakened immune systems. Common causes include Pneumocystis jirovecii, Aspergillus species, Histoplasma, Coccidioides, and Blastomyces. Symptoms often include fever, cough, and shortness of breath, with chest imaging showing diffuse interstitial or nodular infiltrates. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion plus microbiologic testing of respiratory samples, and treatment depends on the organism and severity, usually involving antifungal therapy and supportive care.

blastomyces dermatitidis.definition: A thermally dimorphic fungal pathogen that causes blastomycosis; in the environment it grows as mold with conidia, while in human tissue it appears as yeast with broad-based budding. Infection is acquired by inhalation and can present as pulmonary disease with possible dissemination to skin and bone; endemic to parts of eastern and central North America.

histoplasma capsulatum.definition: A dimorphic fungal pathogen that causes histoplasmosis; environmental mold form becomes yeast in tissue, acquired by inhalation of microconidia from soil enriched with bird or bat guano; infection ranges from asymptomatic or mild pulmonary illness to acute or disseminated disease, especially in immunocompromised individuals.

fungemia.definition: Presence of viable fungi in the bloodstream, usually diagnosed by positive blood cultures; can lead to disseminated fungal infection and sepsis.

fungiform papilla.definition: Mushroom-shaped projections on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue that house taste buds; they are innervated by the chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve.

fungus.definition: An organism that belongs to the kingdom Fungi; a eukaryotic, absorptive heterotroph that can be unicellular (yeasts) or multicellular (molds, mushrooms), reproducing by spores; some species cause fungal infections.

pectus excavatum.definition: A congenital chest-wall deformity in which the sternum is depressed, producing a sunken or funnel-shaped chest that may compress the heart and lungs; severity varies and treatment ranges from observation to surgical correction (e.g., Nuss or Ravitch procedures).

fever of unknown origin.definition: A fever ≥38.3°C (101°F) on several occasions for at least three weeks with no diagnosis established after a structured diagnostic evaluation.

nitrofurantoin.definition: Nitrofurantoin is an oral nitrofuran antibiotic used to treat and prevent uncomplicated lower urinary tract infections. It concentrates in urine and is active against many urinary pathogens, with bacteriostatic or bactericidal effects depending on organism and concentration. Common adverse effects include GI upset; serious risks—especially with prolonged use—include pulmonary toxicity, hepatic injury, and peripheral neuropathy. It is contraindicated in significant renal impairment and near the end of pregnancy, and in newborns under 1 month.

furadantin.definition: A nitrofurantoin antibiotic used to treat and prevent uncomplicated lower urinary tract infections; it concentrates in urine and is active against common uropathogens; given orally, with contraindications including significant renal impairment and late-pregnancy.

furazolidone.definition: An oral nitrofuran antimicrobial agent formerly used to treat certain bacterial and protozoal diarrheas; its use has declined due to safety concerns and the availability of safer alternatives.

giardiasis.definition: A disease caused by a bug (the parasite Giardia intestinalis) that lives in the ground, food, and water.

undescended testicle.definition: A congenital condition in which one or both testes fail to descend into the scrotum, typically remaining in the abdomen or inguinal canal along the normal descent pathway.

funiculus.definition: A cordlike structure; in neuroanatomy, a bundle of nerve fibers (axons) in the spinal cord's white matter, comprising the anterior, lateral, and posterior funiculi.

funicular hernia.definition: An obsolete term for an indirect inguinal hernia in which the hernial sac is aligned along the spermatic cord (the funiculus) within the inguinal canal, typically not extending into the scrotum.

funiculopexy.definition: A surgical procedure in which the spermatic cord (funiculus) is anchored to adjacent tissue (commonly the scrotal wall) to prevent torsion or stabilize a malpositioned testis.

fundus.definition: In anatomy, the fundus is the portion of a hollow organ that is opposite the opening (the organ's base or dome); for example, the fundus of the stomach is its dome-shaped upper part, and the fundus of the uterus is the portion above the openings of the fallopian tubes.

fundus of the gallbladder.definition: The rounded, distal end of the gallbladder that projects anteriorly and inferiorly from the liver, furthest from the cystic duct.

fundus of the stomach.definition: The dome-shaped, superior portion of the stomach, located to the left of the cardia beneath the left hemidiaphragm; serves as a reservoir for swallowed air and undigested food and contains fundic (gastric) glands.

fundic gastritis.definition: Inflammation of the mucosa of the gastric fundus (the proximal stomach); a pattern of chronic gastritis affecting the fundic glands, which can be associated with autoimmune gastritis and mucosal atrophy.

gastric fundus.definition: The upper, dome-shaped portion of the stomach located above the gastroesophageal junction and to the left; it acts as a reservoir for swallowed food and air and contains the stomach’s rugae.

fundoplication.definition: A surgical procedure to treat gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) or hiatal hernia by wrapping the stomach’s fundus around the lower esophagus to reinforce the lower esophageal sphincter; most commonly performed laparoscopically, with variants including a 360-degree complete wrap (Nissen) and partial wraps such as 270-degree (Toupet) or 180-degree (Dor).

nissen fundoplication.definition: A surgical procedure to treat GERD and hiatal hernia by wrapping the stomach fundus 360 degrees around the lower esophagus to reinforce the lower esophageal sphincter and prevent reflux, usually performed laparoscopically.

fundoscopy.definition: A procedure to inspect the interior of the eye, especially the retina, optic disc, macula, and retinal vessels, typically performed with an ophthalmoscope (direct or indirect) and often after pupil dilation.

ophthalmoscopy.definition: An examination of the interior of the eye, particularly the retina and optic disc, using an ophthalmoscope (direct or indirect) to detect eye disease and assess systemic conditions.

funduscope.definition: An instrument used to visualize the fundus of the eye (the retina), including the optic disc and macula, for ophthalmologic examination and detection of retinal disease.

funduscopy.definition: An examination of the interior surface of the eye (the fundus) using ophthalmoscopy to view the retina, optic disc, macula, and posterior pole.

electrolyte depletion.definition: A deficiency of one or more essential electrolytes (eg, sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate) in the body's extracellular fluids, usually due to losses (vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, diuresis), third-space losses, or insufficient intake; it disrupts fluid balance and electrolyte-dependent processes, leading to neuromuscular symptoms and potential cardiovascular or acid–base disturbances.

functional dyspepsia.definition: A chronic upper abdominal dyspeptic syndrome characterized by postprandial fullness, early satiety, epigastric pain, or epigastric burning, in the absence of an identifiable organic disease after standard evaluation.

functional bowel syndrome.definition: A functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by chronic or recurrent abdominal pain or discomfort associated with altered bowel habits (diarrhea, constipation, or both) in the absence of an identifiable structural or biochemical abnormality after evaluation.

functional imaging.definition: Imaging techniques that visualize or quantify physiological function—such as blood flow, metabolism, or neural activity—rather than tissue structure, used to assess organ function and brain activity (e.g., functional MRI, PET, and SPECT).

functional magnetic resonance imaging.definition: A noninvasive neuroimaging technique that uses MRI to detect brain activity by measuring changes in blood flow and oxygenation (the BOLD signal), producing maps of functional brain activity during tasks or at rest.

fmri.definition: A functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) technique that measures brain activity by detecting changes in blood flow and oxygenation (the BOLD signal) that occur in response to neural activity; it maps functional brain areas.

functional murmur.definition: A heart murmur heard in the absence of structural heart disease, caused by normal or increased blood flow across a normal valve; typically a soft systolic murmur (grades I–II/VI) heard best at the left upper or left sternal border in healthy children or young adults, and it is not indicative of cardiac pathology.

physiological murmur.definition: A benign heart murmur caused by normal blood flow across a structurally normal heart and great vessels; not indicative of heart disease.

dynamic splint.definition: A splint that applies a continuous, adjustable external force to a joint to produce passive or assisted movement, promoting tissue lengthening and improving range of motion after injury or surgery.

hand.definition: Distal portion of the upper limb from the wrist to the fingertips, including the palm, dorsum, and digits; composed of the carpal, metacarpal, and phalangeal bones with joints, muscles, nerves (median, ulnar, radial), and arteries enabling grasping and fine motor function.

proximal interphalangeal joints.definition: Joints between the proximal and middle phalanges of digits 2–5, forming hinge joints that allow flexion and extension of the fingers; stabilized by collateral ligaments and the volar plate.

interphalangeal joints.definition: Joints between the phalanges of the fingers and toes; they are hinge-type synovial joints allowing flexion and extension. The fingers typically have proximal and distal interphalangeal joints, while the thumb has a single interphalangeal joint.

functional position of the hand.definition: The posture of the hand used for most daily function, with the wrist in slight extension (about 20–30°), the metacarpophalangeal joints flexed about 60–70°, the proximal interphalangeal joints flexed about 30–45°, the distal interphalangeal joints in slight flexion, and the thumb in opposition with some abduction.

fundal height.definition: Clinical measurement of the size of the uterus during pregnancy, obtained by measuring the distance from the pubic symphysis to the uterine fundus with a tape measure; the result in centimeters roughly corresponds to gestational age in weeks.

distal esophagus.definition: The lower portion of the esophagus closest to the stomach, beginning at the gastroesophageal (lower esophageal) junction and extending upward a short distance, lying just above the diaphragm.

cardiac orifice.definition: Opening at the proximal stomach where the esophagus meets the stomach (the gastroesophageal junction), guarded by the lower esophageal sphincter to regulate entry and prevent reflux.

fundus of the uterus.definition: The rounded, superior portion of the uterus, extending above the openings of the fallopian tubes and opposite the cervix.

furunculosis.definition: A recurrent or localized infection of hair follicles and surrounding skin causing painful boils (furuncles) and abscesses, most often due to Staphylococcus aureus.

boils.definition: A boil (furuncle) is a localized skin infection of a hair follicle or adjacent sebaceous gland, presenting as a painful, red, swollen lump that may form a purulent center and drain pus; most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

fusiform.definition: Spindle-shaped; widest in the middle and tapered toward both ends.

lithiasis.definition: The formation or presence of calculi (stones) within an organ or duct, such as kidney stones or gallstones.

gallium.definition: A chemical element (Ga), atomic number 31; a soft, silvery metal. In medicine, gallium is used as a radiopharmaceutical for imaging infections and tumors (e.g., gallium-67 citrate scans and gallium-68 PET tracers).

gabapentin.definition: A structural analogue of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) that acts as an anticonvulsant and analgesic by binding to the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels; used to treat partial-onset seizures and neuropathic pain.

gamma-aminobutyric acid.definition: A major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system that reduces neuronal excitability by activating GABA receptors (mainly GABA-A and GABA-B). It is synthesized from glutamate by glutamic acid decarboxylase.

g6pd.definition: An enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway that catalyzes the oxidation of glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphoglucono-δ-lactone, generating NADPH and protecting cells from oxidative damage.

glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase.definition: A cytosolic enzyme that catalyzes the first step of the pentose phosphate pathway, oxidizing glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphoglucono-δ-lactone while reducing NADP+ to NADPH; NADPH provides reducing power for biosynthetic reactions and helps protect red blood cells from oxidative damage. Deficiency predisposes to hemolytic anemia under oxidative stress.

krabbe disease.definition: A lysosomal storage disorder caused by autosomal recessive deficiency of the enzyme galactocerebrosidase (GALC), leading to accumulation of psychosine and other lipids with progressive demyelination of the central and peripheral nervous systems; also known as globoid cell leukodystrophy, it typically presents in infancy with irritability, feeding difficulties, developmental delay, and rapid neurological decline.

globoid leukodystrophy.definition: A rare autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder (Krabbe disease) caused by deficient galactocerebrosidase (GALC) activity, leading to accumulation of psychosine and galactocerebroside with widespread CNS and PNS demyelination and formation of globoid cells; typically presents in infancy with irritability, fever episodes, developmental regression, hypertonia/spasticity, and optic atrophy.

galactosuria.definition: The presence of galactose in the urine, typically due to impaired galactose metabolism (eg, hereditary galactosemia such as galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase deficiency or galactokinase deficiency) or transient neonatal immaturity.

lipidosis.definition: An intracellular accumulation of lipids (primarily triglycerides) within cells due to disrupted lipid metabolism or transport, often described as fatty change in tissues such as the liver (hepatic lipidosis) but can affect other organs.

scan.definition: A medical imaging procedure that uses imaging technology (such as X-ray, ultrasound, CT, or MRI) to visualize internal body structures for diagnostic assessment.

total body scanning.definition: An imaging approach that surveys the entire body for signs of disease or injury, typically using whole-body modalities such as PET-CT, whole-body CT, or whole-body MRI. It is used selectively (e.g., cancer staging/restaging, metastatic work-up, or polytrauma assessment) and protocols vary; it is not a routine screening test for asymptomatic individuals.

radionuclide.definition: An unstable radioactive isotope whose nucleus decays, emitting ionizing radiation; used in clinical imaging or therapy (radiopharmaceuticals).

benign tumor.definition: A noncancerous growth of cells that remains localized, does not invade surrounding tissues, and does not spread to distant sites (no metastasis).

malignant tumor.definition: Occurs when new cells grow rapidly, creating a growth or tumor, rather than simply replacing old cells with new ones. Malignant tumors are cancer. Also called malignant neoplasms.

metastatic tumor.definition: A malignant neoplasm that has spread from its primary site to distant sites in the body via lymphatic or hematogenous routes, forming secondary tumors that resemble the original cancer.

gallop.definition: An abnormal extra heart sound heard on auscultation, producing a triple cadence (S3 or S4). An S3 (ventricular) occurs after S2 during rapid ventricular filling and can indicate volume overload or heart failure; an S4 (atrial) occurs before S1 and suggests a stiff ventricle from hypertrophy or ischemia.

acute pancreatitis.definition: A sudden inflammatory condition of the pancreas presenting with acute epigastric pain often radiating to the back, nausea and vomiting, and elevated pancreatic enzymes (amylase and/or lipase) or characteristic imaging findings; commonly caused by gallstones or alcohol use and treated with supportive care (IV fluids, pain control) and management of the underlying cause.

gallstone pancreatitis.definition: An episode of acute pancreatitis caused by obstruction of the pancreatic duct by a gallstone, leading to pancreatic inflammation; management includes supportive care and removal of the obstruction (often via ERCP) with cholecystectomy to prevent recurrence.

mucopolysaccharidosis vi.definition: An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of the enzyme arylsulfatase B, leading to accumulation of dermatan sulfate with multisystemic involvement including skeletal dysplasia (dysostosis multiplex), short stature, joint stiffness, coarse facial features, corneal clouding, hepatosplenomegaly, and valvular heart disease; treatable with enzyme replacement therapy using galsulfase.

maroteaux-lamy syndrome.definition: A lysosomal storage disorder (MPS type VI) due to deficient arylsulfatase B, causing dermatan sulfate accumulation with skeletal dysostosis multiplex, short stature, joint stiffness, corneal clouding, and hepatosplenomegaly; inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.

galsulfase.definition: A recombinant human enzyme used as enzyme replacement therapy for mucopolysaccharidosis type VI (Maroteaux-Lamy syndrome), providing arylsulfatase B activity to break down dermatan sulfate in lysosomes.

galvanic cautery.definition: A cautery method that uses direct current (galvanic current) to destroy tissue and achieve hemostasis by electrochemical injury and heating at the active electrode.

galvanic electric stimulation.definition: A form of electrical stimulation that uses direct current (DC) delivered through skin electrodes to activate nerves or muscles and to influence tissue healing; it delivers a constant polarity (anode or cathode) and causes electrochemical effects at the electrode–tissue interface, and is used in physical therapy and wound care.

transcutaneous electric nerve stimulatio.definition: The use of low-voltage electrical current (through electrodes placed on the skin) to provide pain-suppressing stimulation.

galvanic skin response.definition: A measure of the skin's electrical conductance that increases with eccrine sweat gland activity driven by sympathetic arousal; used as an index of autonomic arousal in psychophysiology and sometimes in lie-detection testing.

galvanometer.definition: A device for detecting and measuring small electrical currents by deflecting a magnetized coil in a magnetic field; historically used in physiology and clinical electrodiagnosis to monitor bioelectric potentials such as nerve and muscle activity.

galveston orientation and amnesia test.definition: A bedside cognitive assessment used after traumatic brain injury to quantify a person’s orientation to person, place, and time and their amnesia for events surrounding the injury; it yields a score that helps determine the onset and duration of post-traumatic amnesia and monitor recovery.

posttraumatic amnesia.definition: A transient period after a traumatic brain injury during which the patient is disoriented and unable to form new memories (anterograde amnesia), with impaired recall of events surrounding the injury; PTA ends when reliable orientation and memory for ongoing events return.

west african sleeping sickness.definition: A form of human African trypanosomiasis caused by Trypanosoma brucei gambiense, transmitted by tsetse flies; it is typically a chronic infection that begins with fever, lymphadenopathy, and pruritus, and progresses to central nervous system involvement with sleep disturbances, behavioral changes, and dementia if untreated.

gamma interferon.definition: A cytokine produced primarily by activated T lymphocytes and natural killer cells that acts as a type II interferon; it activates macrophages, enhances antigen presentation and phagocytic activity, promotes Th1 differentiation, and mediates antiviral, immunoregulatory, and antitumor responses.

gamma knife.definition: A type of stereotactic radiosurgery that uses multiple converging gamma-ray beams from cobalt-60 sources to deliver a high dose of radiation precisely to a brain lesion, typically in a single session and without an open surgical incision.

stereotactic radiosurgery.definition: A noninvasive form of radiation therapy that delivers a highly precise, high-dose of radiation to a small target in the brain or body in a single treatment session or a few fractions, using stereotactic imaging guidance to spare surrounding tissue.

gamma radiation.definition: High-energy electromagnetic radiation consisting of photons emitted by atomic nuclei during radioactive decay or nuclear transitions; highly penetrating and used in medicine for radiotherapy and nuclear imaging.

gammopathy.definition: A condition involving abnormal amounts or types of gamma globulins (immunoglobulins) in the blood; commonly polyclonal gammopathy from chronic inflammation or monoclonal gammopathy from a clonal plasma cell disorder (e.g., MGUS, multiple myeloma).

monoclonal gammopathy.definition: A condition characterized by the presence of a monoclonal immunoglobulin (M protein) produced by a single clone of plasma cells or B lymphocytes, typically detected as an M-spike on serum protein electrophoresis; it may be benign (MGUS) or associated with malignant gammopathies such as multiple myeloma or Waldenström macroglobulinemia.

polyclonal gammopathy.definition: An elevation of the serum gamma globulin fraction due to polyclonal expansion of many B-cell clones producing diverse immunoglobulins, typically seen in chronic inflammation, infection, autoimmune disease, or liver disease; distinguishes from monoclonal gammopathy, which arises from a single clone producing a single immunoglobulin.

bence jones protein.definition: Free monoclonal immunoglobulin light chain (κ or λ) excreted in urine, produced by clonal plasma cells; commonly associated with multiple myeloma and other plasma cell disorders.

gamma-glutamyltransferase.definition: An enzyme that participates in the gamma-glutamyl cycle by transferring gamma-glutamyl groups between amino acids and glutathione; clinically, its serum activity is used as a marker of cholestasis and hepatobiliary disease and is often elevated in biliary obstruction, alcoholic liver disease, and hepatocellular injury.

gamma-glutamyltransferase test.definition: A blood test that measures the level of a liver enzyme in the blood to assess biliary tract and liver function; elevated levels suggest cholestasis or liver disease and are typically interpreted with other liver-function tests.

biliary obstruction.definition: Blockage of the bile ducts that impedes bile flow from the liver to the duodenum, causing cholestasis and often jaundice; causes include gallstones, biliary strictures, tumors, and inflammatory conditions such as cholangitis or pancreatitis.

liver disorders.definition: Any condition that impairs the liver's structure or function, including inflammatory, infectious, metabolic, toxic, or neoplastic diseases, resulting in impaired metabolism and detoxification, reduced bile production, and diminished synthetic functions such as clotting factors and albumin.

liver carcinoma.definition: A malignant neoplasm arising in the liver; the most common primary liver cancer is hepatocellular carcinoma, arising from hepatocytes (other primary hepatic cancers include intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma). Risk factors include chronic hepatitis B or C infection, cirrhosis, and aflatoxin exposure. Diagnosis relies on imaging and often biopsy; treatment depends on stage and may include surgical resection, liver transplantation, locoregional therapies, or systemic therapy.

gallbladder disorders.definition: A group of diseases affecting the gallbladder, the organ that stores and concentrates bile. Common conditions include gallstones (cholelithiasis), gallbladder inflammation (cholecystitis), biliary dyskinesia (functional gallbladder disorder), gallbladder polyps, and gallbladder cancer; symptoms typically include right upper-quadrant pain after meals, nausea, and vomiting, with potential complications such as biliary obstruction, pancreatitis, and cholangitis.

gallbladder obstruction.definition: Obstruction of the gallbladder outflow, usually by a gallstone in the cystic duct, causing bile stasis and gallbladder distension, and potentially biliary colic or acute calculous cholecystitis.

growth hormone releasing hormone.definition: A hypothalamic peptide that stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete growth hormone by binding to the GHRH receptor on somatotroph cells; its action is inhibited by somatostatin.

ganglia.definition: A cluster of nerve cell bodies in the peripheral nervous system; also refers to a benign cystic swelling near a joint or tendon (ganglion cyst).

ganglioneuroma.definition: A benign, slow-growing tumor of neural crest–derived cells of the sympathetic nervous system, composed of mature ganglion cells with Schwannian stroma and little to no immature neuroblasts. It often arises in the adrenal medulla or paravertebral sympathetic ganglia, typically in children. Treatment is complete surgical excision, with an excellent prognosis and rare recurrence.

gangliocytoma.definition: A rare, benign CNS tumor consisting mainly of mature ganglion cells with no or minimal neoplastic glial component; a low-grade neuronal tumor often associated with epilepsy.

ganglionic neuroma.definition: A benign tumor arising from autonomic ganglia, composed of mature ganglion cells with Schwannian stroma; typically slow-growing and nonfunctional.

ganglionic blockade.definition: Pharmacologic inhibition of transmission at autonomic ganglia by antagonists of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, blocking postganglionic sympathetic and parasympathetic activity.

ganglionic blocking agent.definition: A drug that blocks transmission in autonomic ganglia by antagonizing nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, causing simultaneous inhibition of sympathetic and parasympathetic output; historically used to manage severe hypertension but largely obsolete due to significant side effects.

mecamylamine.definition: A ganglion-blocking agent that antagonizes nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at autonomic ganglia; historically used to treat severe hypertension but largely abandoned due to significant autonomic side effects such as orthostatic hypotension.

nicotinic neuronal receptors.definition: A type of nicotinic acetylcholine receptor in the nervous system that forms a pentameric, ligand-gated ion channel activated by acetylcholine (and nicotine); composed of various α and β subunits (e.g., α4β2, α7) and permeable to Na+, K+, and Ca2+, mediating fast excitatory neurotransmission and modulation of neurotransmitter release in the central and peripheral nervous systems.

coronary insufficiency.definition: An older term for insufficient blood flow to the heart muscle (myocardial ischemia) due to reduced coronary perfusion, usually from partial obstruction of the coronary arteries; manifests as angina or fatigue and can progress to myocardial infarction if perfusion becomes severely reduced.

cerebrovascular insufficiency.definition: A condition in which the brain does not receive adequate blood flow (cerebral hypoperfusion), leading to cerebral ischemia and potential neurological deficits, including transient symptoms or stroke, typically due to carotid/vertebral artery disease, hypotension, or embolic/thrombotic events.

renal insufficiency.definition: A reduction in kidney function with impaired filtration and excretion, resulting in the buildup of waste products (such as urea and creatinine) and disturbances of fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance; may be acute or chronic.

paralytic ileus.definition: Temporary loss of intestinal peristalsis resulting in a functional (non-mechanical) bowel obstruction, characterized by abdominal distension, pain, nausea/vomiting, and inability to pass gas or stools, with decreased or absent bowel sounds; commonly occurs after surgery or with electrolyte disturbances, medications (notably opioids), infection, or trauma, and usually resolves as motility returns.

visual disturbances.definition: Any alteration in vision, including blurred vision, flashes or sparkles (photopsia), floaters, blind spots (scotomas), double vision (diplopia), halos, or partial/complete vision loss; it can be temporary or persistent and may result from ocular, vascular, or neurological disorders.

heartburn.definition: A burning sensation behind the breastbone caused by reflux of stomach acid into the esophagus, commonly related to gastroesophageal reflux disease; symptoms often worsen after meals or when lying down.

intravenous injection.definition: Administration of a medication or fluid directly into a vein through a needle or cannula, producing rapid systemic effects; can be given as a bolus (IV push) or as an ongoing infusion.

neural crest.definition: A transient multipotent embryonic cell population that arises at the border of the neural tube during neurulation, migrates throughout the embryo, and differentiates into diverse derivatives including peripheral neurons and glia, melanocytes, craniofacial cartilage and bone, odontoblasts, smooth muscle, and adrenal medulla chromaffin cells.

ganglion impar.definition: A single midline sympathetic ganglion located anterior to the coccyx at the sacrococcygeal junction, formed by the fusion of the bilateral inferior ganglia of the sympathetic chain; it provides postganglionic sympathetic innervation to the perineum, distal rectum/anal canal, and external genitalia and is a target for ganglion impar blockade in certain pain syndromes.

ganglionar neuroma.definition: A benign tumor of neural crest origin composed of mature ganglion cells within Schwannian stroma; a well-differentiated end of neuroblastic tumors that typically arises along the sympathetic nervous system (e.g., posterior mediastinum, retroperitoneum, adrenal gland) and presents in children or young adults as a slow-growing, usually nonfunctional mass. Treatment is surgical excision with an excellent prognosis.

ganglionitis.definition: Inflammation of a ganglion (a cluster of nerve cell bodies in the peripheral nervous system), which may cause localized pain, swelling, and neurologic symptoms in the distribution of the affected nerve; etiologies include infectious, autoimmune, or inflammatory processes.

gardnerella vaginalis.definition: A Gram-variable, facultatively anaerobic bacterium that colonizes the human vagina and is the principal etiologic agent associated with bacterial vaginosis; it forms biofilms and disrupts the normal Lactobacillus-dominated flora.

ganglioside.definition: A complex glycosphingolipid component of animal cell membranes, especially abundant in neurons, containing one or more sialic acid residues; comprises a ceramide lipid anchor linked to an oligosaccharide with sialic acid and participates in cell–cell recognition and signaling. Abnormalities can lead to lysosomal storage diseases known as gangliosidoses (e.g., GM1 and GM2).

gangliosidosis.definition: A group of inherited lysosomal storage disorders caused by deficient enzymes that degrade gangliosides, leading to accumulation of GM1 or GM2 gangliosides in neurons and progressive neurodegeneration.

gangliosidosis type i.definition: An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by beta-galactosidase deficiency (GLB1) leading to accumulation of GM1 ganglioside in lysosomes; the infantile-onset form is characterized by hepatosplenomegaly, skeletal abnormalities (dysostosis multiplex) with coarse facial features, hypotonia and progressive neurodegeneration with developmental delay, often resulting in early death in early childhood.

gangliosidosis type ii.definition: Autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of hexosaminidases A and B (usually due to HEXB mutations), leading to accumulation of GM2 ganglioside in neurons and visceral tissues with infancy-onset neurodegeneration and hepatosplenomegaly.

sandhoff’s disease.definition: An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder (GM2 gangliosidosis) due to deficiency of both beta-hexosaminidases A and B, leading to GM2 ganglioside accumulation in neurons and early infancy–onset neurodegeneration with hypotonia, seizures, vision loss, and hepatosplenomegaly.

dry gangrene.definition: Ischemic necrosis of tissue due to loss of blood supply, typically in an extremity, leading to dry, shriveled, darkened (often black) tissue with a clear line of demarcation and little early infection.

moist gangrene.definition: A rapidly spreading form of gangrene in which infected, necrotic tissue becomes soft and moist due to edema and pus; follows vascular compromise with bacterial infection, producing a foul odor and discharge and carrying a high risk of sepsis, requiring urgent debridement, antibiotics, and measures to restore blood flow.

gangrenous appendicitis.definition: A severe form of acute appendicitis in which the appendix tissue becomes necrotic (gangrenous) due to ischemia, often with perforation and peritoneal infection.

gangrenous necrosis.definition: A form of tissue necrosis caused by severe ischemia, often with superimposed infection, leading to gangrene; dry gangrene features dry, shriveled, black tissue from prolonged ischemia, while wet or gas gangrene involves rapidly spreading infection with foul odor and gas production.

gangrenous stomatitis.definition: A rapidly progressive necrotizing infection of the oral mucosa and surrounding facial tissues, typically in malnourished children, beginning as gingivitis and advancing to gangrenous necrosis with tissue destruction; historically referred to as noma. Requires urgent broad-spectrum antibiotics, nutritional support, and often surgical debridement.

noma.definition: Noma (cancrum oris) is a rapidly progressive necrotizing infection of the orofacial region that begins as necrotizing gingivitis and advances to widespread soft-tissue and bone destruction of the mouth and face, primarily affecting malnourished children in resource-limited settings; without prompt treatment, it carries a high mortality rate.

gangrenous vulvitis.definition: A severe, necrotizing infection of the vulva causing tissue death (gangrene); it presents with rapidly progressive vulvar necrosis, edema, often severe pain, foul discharge, and systemic illness, and requires urgent surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics.

vulvitis.definition: Inflammation of the vulva, the external female genitalia, typically due to infection (eg, candidiasis or bacterial vulvitis) or dermatitis/irritants, presenting with itching, redness, swelling, burning, and sometimes discharge.

ganirelix.definition: A synthetic gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) antagonist that competitively blocks GnRH receptors, suppressing pituitary secretion of LH and FSH; used to prevent a premature LH surge during controlled ovarian stimulation in assisted reproductive technologies (such as IVF).

garamycin.definition: Brand-name aminoglycoside antibiotic (gentamicin) used to treat serious gram-negative infections; inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit, usually given IV or IM (with topical/ophthalmic formulations available); adverse effects include nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

gantrisin.definition: A brand-name sulfonamide antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections.

sulfamethoxazole.definition: A sulfonamide antibiotic that inhibits bacterial folic acid synthesis by competitively blocking dihydropteroate synthase; commonly used in combination with trimethoprim (as trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) to treat or prevent a variety of infections, including urinary tract infections, otitis media, bronchitis, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, and certain gastrointestinal infections.

sulfisoxazole.definition: A sulfonamide antibiotic that inhibits bacterial folic acid synthesis by competitively blocking dihydropteroate synthase; it is bacteriostatic and has been used to treat urinary tract infections and other bacterial infections, sometimes in combination with erythromycin for pediatric otitis media.

gardner-wells tongs.definition: A skull traction device in which two pins are inserted into the skull and linked to a traction apparatus to apply controlled longitudinal traction to the cervical spine, used to immobilize and/or reduce cervical spine fractures or dislocations.

gargle.definition: To rinse the mouth and throat by holding a liquid in the mouth, tilting the head back, and allowing the liquid to bubble or swirl in the throat before spitting it out, often with antiseptic or saline solutions.

gars.definition: Glycyl-tRNA synthetase; an enzyme that adds glycine to its corresponding tRNA-Gly during cytoplasmic protein translation. Mutations in the gene encoding this enzyme (GARS1) are associated with hereditary neuropathies such as Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease type 2D and distal hereditary motor neuropathy.
