gartner’s cyst.definition: A benign vaginal wall cyst arising from embryologic remnants of the Wolffian (mesonephric) ducts in the lateral upper vagina; usually asymptomatic but may present as a palpable vaginal mass; management is observation or surgical excision if symptomatic.

gartner’s duct.definition: A vestigial remnant of the Wolffian (mesonephric) duct in females, typically located in the lateral vaginal wall; may give rise to a Gartner duct cyst.

gas chromatography.definition: A technique for separating and analyzing volatile compounds by passing a vaporized sample through a column containing a stationary phase, carried by an inert gas; components migrate at different rates due to varying interactions with the stationary phase, enabling qualitative identification and quantitative measurement with a detector.

gas embolism.definition: A blockage of a blood vessel caused by gas bubbles (usually air or inert gas) in the circulation, leading to impaired blood flow and tissue injury; can occur with rapid decompression, trauma, or medical procedures, and is treated with high-flow oxygen and, in select cases, hyperbaric oxygen therapy.

gastric antral vascular ectasia.definition: A condition in which dilated, ectatic blood vessels in the gastric antrum cause chronic gastrointestinal bleeding and iron-deficiency anemia; endoscopically has a characteristic red, stripe-like “watermelon” appearance; treated mainly with endoscopic coagulation or ablation (commonly argon plasma coagulation) and management of anemia.

gastric analysis.definition: A diagnostic procedure in which stomach contents are aspirated (typically via a nasogastric tube) and analyzed for volume and acidity (pH), and sometimes enzyme content or total acid output, to assess gastric secretory function.

gastroenterostomy.definition: A surgical procedure that creates an anastomosis between the stomach and a segment of the small intestine (typically the jejunum) to bypass the duodenum, usually to relieve gastric outlet obstruction or other upper GI obstructions.

gastric acid pump inhibitor.definition: A class of medications that irreversibly inhibits the gastric H+/K+-ATPase (the proton pump) in gastric parietal cells, leading to a substantial and prolonged reduction of gastric acid secretion; used to treat GERD, peptic ulcers, erosive esophagitis, and other acid-related disorders (examples include omeprazole, esomeprazole, pantoprazole, lansoprazole, rabeprazole, and dexlansoprazole).

proton pump inhibitor.definition: An acid-suppressing drug class that irreversibly inhibits the H+/K+-ATPase proton pump in gastric parietal cells, blocking the final step of gastric acid secretion; used to treat GERD, erosive esophagitis, peptic ulcers, gastritis, and to support H. pylori eradication therapy.

vitamin b12 deficiency.definition: An insufficient amount of vitamin B12 (cobalamin) in the body that impairs DNA synthesis, leading to megaloblastic anemia and neurologic symptoms; causes include inadequate dietary intake, malabsorption (eg, pernicious anemia, gastritis, ileal disease), vegan diets, and certain medications; treated with vitamin B12 replacement and management of underlying causes.

folic acid deficiency.definition: A deficiency of folate (vitamin B9) that impairs DNA synthesis, causing megaloblastic anemia and increasing the risk of neural tube defects during fetal development.

dumping syndrome.definition:
Dumping syndrome is a constellation of gastrointestinal and systemic symptoms caused by rapid emptying of hyperosmolar gastric contents into the small intestine, typically after gastric surgery. It includes:
- Early dumping: within about 30 minutes of a meal, with cramping, diarrhea, nausea, bloating, flushing, and tachycardia.
- Late dumping: 1–3 hours after a meal, with hypoglycemia symptoms such as weakness, dizziness, and confusion due to excessive insulin release.

gastrectasia.definition: A dilation or distention of the stomach—enlargement of the gastric cavity—often due to gas or fluid accumulation or impaired gastric emptying; can occur with obstruction, gastroparesis, or other gastric motility disorders.

body.definition: The physical form of a living organism, comprising all tissues and organs organized into organ systems.

mesenteric arteries.definition: Arteries that supply the intestines via the mesentery; principally the superior mesenteric artery and inferior mesenteric artery arising from the abdominal aorta, with a network of branches perfusing the midgut (distal duodenum to proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon) and hindgut (distal transverse colon to the upper anal canal).

ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.definition: A potentially life-threatening complication of ovulation induction or assisted reproductive technology characterized by enlarged ovaries and increased vascular permeability, leading to third-space fluid accumulation (ascites, sometimes pleural effusions), hemoconcentration, electrolyte disturbances, and risk of thromboembolism; symptoms range from mild abdominal discomfort to severe weight gain, shortness of breath, and organ dysfunction.

gonadotropin-releasing hormone antagonis.definition: A medication that competitively blocks GnRH receptors in the anterior pituitary, suppressing LH and FSH secretion to prevent premature ovulation and control ovarian stimulation in fertility treatment; onset is rapid and effect is reversible.

lennox-gastaut syndrome.definition: A severe childhood-onset epilepsy characterized by multiple seizure types (including tonic, atonic, and absence seizures), cognitive and behavioral impairment, and a characteristic EEG with slow spike-and-wave discharges; often treatment-resistant and requiring multiple antiepileptic drugs.

hemolytic uremic syndrome.definition: A microangiopathic illness presenting with hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury, most commonly after infection with Shiga toxin–producing bacteria; caused by endothelial injury leading to thrombotic microangiopathy, with management largely supportive.

gastric distension.definition: The enlargement of the stomach due to accumulation of gas, air, or fluid, leading to abdominal distension and often discomfort; may result from aerophagia, gastric outlet obstruction, ileus, or gastroparesis.

gastric resection.definition: A surgical procedure in which part or all of the stomach is removed (partial or total gastrectomy), usually for gastric cancer or severe peptic disease, with reconstruction to restore continuity of the alimentary tract (e.g., gastroduodenostomy or gastrojejunostomy).

watermelon stomach.definition: A gastric mucosal vascular ectasia of the antrum that causes chronic gastrointestinal bleeding and iron-deficiency anemia; on endoscopy it appears as parallel red stripes across the antrum, giving a watermelon rind pattern.

leiomyosarcomas.definition: A malignant tumor of smooth muscle cells, a type of soft tissue sarcoma that can arise in any organ containing smooth muscle, most commonly the uterus, retroperitoneum, or gastrointestinal tract; histology shows spindle-shaped cells with smooth muscle differentiation.

gastric lymphoma.definition: A malignant neoplasm of lymphoid tissue in the stomach, most often a primary gastric non-Hodgkin lymphoma, frequently of the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) type and commonly linked to Helicobacter pylori infection; presents with upper GI symptoms (e.g., epigastric pain, weight loss) and its management depends on histology and stage (e.g., H. pylori eradication for MALT lymphoma, systemic chemotherapy or radiotherapy for other subtypes).

gastric dumping syndrome.definition: A condition that occurs after rapid gastric emptying into the small intestine—usually following gastric surgery (eg, gastrectomy or gastric bypass)—causing a range of symptoms that appear after meals, including early dumping (nausea, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, flushing, tachycardia, dizziness within 10–30 minutes) and late dumping (hypoglycemia with weakness, sweating, confusion, and palpitation 1–3 hours after eating) due to osmotic shifts and hormonal changes.

acute gastritis.definition: A sudden inflammation of the gastric mucosa causing epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and sometimes bleeding; commonly due to irritants such as NSAIDs or alcohol, infection, ischemia, or stress, and typically resolves with removal of the irritant and supportive care.

chronic gastritis.definition: Chronic gastritis is long-standing inflammation of the stomach lining (gastric mucosa), often with mucosal atrophy and possible intestinal metaplasia. It can be autoimmune (type A), Helicobacter pylori–associated (type B), or chemical/other (type C). Symptoms range from none to epigastric pain, nausea, or bloating; diagnosis is by endoscopy with gastric biopsies; treatment targets the underlying cause (e.g., H. pylori eradication, acid suppression, avoidance of NSAIDs).

hemorrhagic gastritis.definition: Inflammation of the gastric mucosa with bleeding from the mucosa; an acute, erosive form of gastritis often caused by NSAIDs, alcohol, severe physiologic stress, infection, or ischemia.

hypertrophic gastritis.definition: A rare disorder in which the gastric mucosa becomes thickened due to foveolar hyperplasia with glandular atrophy, often causing protein-losing gastropathy with hypoalbuminemia and edema, and an increased risk of gastric cancer (classically Menetrier disease).

alkaline reflux gastritis.definition: Inflammation of the stomach lining caused by reflux of alkaline duodenogastric contents (bile and pancreatic secretions) into the stomach, often after gastric surgery that disrupts pyloric function or gastric emptying.

gastric fistula.definition: An abnormal conduit from the stomach to another organ or to the body surface, permitting gastric contents to drain externally or into adjacent tissues (e.g., gastrocutaneous fistula or gastroenteric fistula).

pyloric sphincter.definition: A muscular valve at the lower end of the stomach that opens to the duodenum.

esophageal ulcer.definition: A mucosal ulceration of the esophagus—an open sore in the esophageal lining—caused by reflux-related damage, infections (e.g., Candida, CMV, HSV), pill- or caustic-induced injury, or radiation; commonly presents with odynophagia (painful swallowing), chest pain, and sometimes dysphagia or bleeding.

fundic glands.definition: Gastric glands in the fundus and body of the stomach that secrete gastric juice, mainly acid (hydrochloric acid) and pepsinogen, via parietal and chief cells, with mucus-secreting cells lining the glands.

cardiac glands.definition: Cardiac glands are the mucus-secreting simple tubular glands located in the cardia (proximal stomach) that produce protective mucus (often with bicarbonate) to shield the mucosa at the gastroesophageal junction from gastric acid.

pyloric glands.definition: Mucous-secreting glands in the mucosa of the pyloric region (antrum) of the stomach that produce protective mucus (and bicarbonate), helping to shield the mucosa from gastric acid.

gastric pits.definition: Tubular invaginations of the gastric mucosa that extend from the lumen into the lamina propria and form the openings to the gastric glands; lined by surface mucous cells.

left gastric artery.definition: A branch of the celiac trunk that runs along the lesser curvature of the stomach, supplying the stomach’s lesser curvature and giving esophageal branches; it anastomoses with the right gastric artery.

hepatic node.definition: A lymph node located in or around the liver region that receives lymph from hepatic tissue; part of the hepatic lymphatic network, usually along the portal triad or porta hepatis, and typically drains to the celiac lymph nodes; enlargement may reflect hepatic disease, biliary pathology, or metastasis.

pancreatico-lienal node.definition: A lymph node in the abdominal lymphatic system, in the pancreaticosplenic (pancreatico-splenic) lymph node group, located near the pancreas and spleen; it drains lymph from the pancreas (especially the body/tail) and spleen and channels it to neighboring nodes (often toward the celiac lymph nodes).

gastric nodes.definition: A group of lymph nodes that drain lymph from the stomach, located along the stomach's arteries (left and right gastric; left and right gastro-omental/gastroepiploic nodes) and the pyloric region, ultimately draining into the celiac lymph node basin.

superior gastric node.definition: An abdominal lymph node located near the lesser curvature of the stomach, part of the gastric lymphatic drainage; it receives lymph from the proximal stomach and drains to the celiac lymph node group.

inferior gastric node.definition: A lymph node along the inferior border of the stomach, part of the perigastric (gastric) lymph node group; it drains lymph from the distal stomach and communicates with the celiac lymph node basin.

levin tube.definition: A single-lumen nasogastric tube used for gastric decompression and drainage by suction; inserted through the nose into the stomach and typically has side holes near the distal end.

gastroscope.definition: A flexible endoscope designed for visualization of the stomach during upper gastrointestinal endoscopy (gastroscopy), often with channels for biopsy and therapeutic interventions.

gastroduodenoscopy.definition: A procedure that uses a flexible endoscope to visualize and evaluate the stomach and duodenum, often allowing biopsies, polypectomy, and other therapeutic interventions.

gastroduodenostomy.definition: A surgical connection between the stomach and the duodenum, typically performed after distal gastrectomy to restore continuity of the GI tract (often referred to as a Billroth I procedure).

gastroduodenitis.definition: Inflammation of the stomach and the duodenum (gastroduodenal region), often due to infection (e.g., Helicobacter pylori), NSAID use, or other irritants; it can be acute or chronic and commonly causes upper abdominal (epigastric) pain, nausea, and sometimes vomiting.

gastroenterology.definition: The study of diseases of the stomach and intestines.

gastroenterologist.definition: A doctor who treats problems with your stomach and related organs.

gerd.definition: A chronic condition in which stomach contents frequently reflux into the esophagus, causing symptoms such as heartburn and regurgitation, typically due to lower esophageal sphincter dysfunction; it can lead to esophagitis or complications like strictures or Barrett's esophagus and is managed with lifestyle measures and acid-suppressive therapy.

gastroesophagitis.definition: Inflammation of the stomach and the esophagus, commonly due to reflux of gastric contents (acid) at the gastroesophageal junction; may also result from infection or irritation.

gastric bypass.definition: A bariatric surgical procedure (most commonly Roux-en-Y gastric bypass) in which a small upper stomach pouch is created and connected to the mid-small intestine, bypassing most of the stomach and duodenum to reduce food intake and nutrient absorption, promoting weight loss and improvement of obesity-related conditions. Risks include leakage, infection, vitamin deficiencies, dumping syndrome, and other surgical complications.

gastric banding.definition: An adjustable bariatric procedure in which a silicone band is placed around the upper stomach to create a small pouch, restricting food intake; the band’s tightness is adjustable via a subcutaneous port to control weight loss.

gastric restriction.definition: A mechanism in obesity treatment that decreases the stomach’s capacity, limiting meal size and promoting early satiety to reduce total caloric intake.

gastric partitioning.definition: A surgical procedure in which the stomach is divided to create a small proximal pouch and a larger distal remnant, thereby restricting food intake and promoting weight loss.

gastrocolic omentum.definition: The portion of the greater omentum that extends from the stomach to the transverse colon, anchoring the stomach to the colon and containing fat and peritoneal tissue.

occult blood in stool.definition: Blood that is present in the stool but not visible to the eye, detected by a fecal occult blood test or fecal immunochemical test; it can indicate bleeding anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract and may be due to conditions such as hemorrhoids, ulcers, polyps, inflammatory bowel disease, or colorectal cancer.

stool cultures.definition: A laboratory test in which a stool sample is cultured on selective media to isolate and identify pathogenic bacteria that cause gastrointestinal infection, guiding diagnosis and treatment.

rectal cultures.definition: A laboratory test in which a specimen obtained from the rectum (usually a swab or stool sample) is cultured to grow and identify bacteria or other pathogens, often to diagnose lower gastrointestinal infections or to screen for carriage of specific organisms to guide treatment and infection control.

cytological studies.definition: The diagnostic examination of cells and cellular material under a microscope to detect disease, typically obtained from body fluids, scrapings, or tissue aspirates (e.g., Pap test, fine-needle aspiration cytology).

exfoliated tumor cells.definition: Malignant cells that have detached from a primary or metastatic tumor and are shed into surrounding body fluids or surfaces, where they can be collected and examined cytologically to diagnose or monitor cancer (e.g., in sputum, urine, pleural or ascitic fluid).

upper gi series.definition: A fluoroscopic radiographic study of the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum performed after ingestion of a barium-based contrast agent to visualize anatomy and motility; used to diagnose ulcers, inflammation, obstruction, strictures, tumors, hiatal hernia, and gastroesophageal reflux.

mallory-weiss syndrome.definition: A mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction caused by forceful retching or vomiting, leading to nonvariceal upper GI bleeding; commonly linked to heavy alcohol use; diagnosed by endoscopy showing longitudinal mucosal lacerations at the GE junction; usually self-limited and managed with supportive care, with endoscopic hemostasis or acid suppression if bleeding persists.

gastrin test.definition: A blood test that measures fasting serum gastrin levels to evaluate excessive gastrin production, commonly used to help diagnose gastrin-secreting tumors (gastrinomas) such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome; a secretin stimulation test may be used to confirm gastrinoma, and results can be influenced by medications (e.g., proton pump inhibitors) or renal function.

gastrin-releasing peptide.definition: Gastrin-releasing peptide is a bombesin-like neuropeptide encoded by the GRP gene that stimulates gastrin secretion from gastric G cells and acts on bombesin receptors, participating in gut–brain signaling and potentially promoting growth in certain cancers.

gip.definition: A peptide hormone secreted by K cells of the duodenum and jejunum that stimulates insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells in a glucose-dependent manner in response to oral glucose; formerly known as gastric inhibitory peptide.

gastric inhibitory polypeptide.definition: A peptide hormone produced by K cells in the duodenum and proximal jejunum in response to nutrient ingestion (especially glucose and fat); it stimulates insulin release from pancreatic beta cells in a glucose-dependent manner and inhibits gastric acid secretion, slowing gastric emptying.

smoked fish.definition: Fish that has been preserved and flavored by exposure to smoke from wood or other combustibles; hot smoking cooks the fish, while cold smoking preserves it without cooking; proper handling and refrigeration are essential to prevent foodborne illness.

salted fish.definition: A preserved fish product produced by curing with salt to inhibit microbial growth and extend shelf life; often desalinated before use. It is typically high in sodium and, if not properly stored, can spoil or develop histamine-related toxicity in susceptible species.

achlorhydria.definition: A condition in which the stomach produces little or no acid. This can affect digestion, cause stomach pain, and keep the body from absorbing vitamins and nutrients.

gastroparesis.definition: When the stomach muscle is paralyzed. Also called paralyzed stomach.

gastroesophageal reflux scan.definition: A nuclear medicine study in which the patient ingests a radiolabeled meal and dynamic gamma-camera imaging is used to detect reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus, allowing evaluation of gastroesophageal reflux and esophageal clearance, especially in infants and children.

lactose_intolerance.definition: Means that you cannot digest food with lactose, a type of sugar found in milk and milk products.

anaphylactic_shock.definition: A life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction triggered by an allergen, in which widespread release of mediators from mast cells and basophils causes rapid airway edema, bronchospasm, vasodilation, and increased vascular permeability leading to hypotension and shock; it often presents with respiratory symptoms (wheezing, throat tightness), skin signs (hives, angioedema), and gastrointestinal symptoms, and requires immediate treatment with intramuscular epinephrine, airway support, and fluids.

food_allergy.definition: An immune-mediated adverse reaction to a specific food protein, most often IgE-mediated, triggered by ingestion and potentially causing skin, gastrointestinal, and respiratory symptoms, up to life-threatening anaphylaxis.

respiratory_distress.definition: An acute clinical state characterized by increased work of breathing and inadequate ventilation or oxygenation, typically with rapid breathing, shortness of breath, nasal flaring, chest-wall retractions, use of accessory muscles, tachycardia, and sometimes cyanosis or hypoxemia.

mallory-weiss_syndrome.definition: A nonvariceal upper gastrointestinal bleed caused by longitudinal mucosal tears at the gastroesophageal junction after forceful retching or vomiting; presents with hematemesis and is typically self-limited with supportive care.

ulcerative_colitis.definition: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by continuous mucosal inflammation of the colon, starting in the rectum and extending proximally, leading to symptoms such as bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and urgency. The disease is limited to the colon and typically involves non-transmural inflammation; management includes aminosalicylates, corticosteroids for flares, immunomodulators or biologic therapies, and often colectomy in severe cases.

small_bowel.definition: The portion of the gastrointestinal tract between the stomach and the ileocecal valve, comprising the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum; the major site of digestion and absorption of nutrients, electrolytes, and vitamins.

gastrointestinal_bleeding.definition: An emergency characterized by bleeding from any part of the gastrointestinal tract (from the esophagus to the anus), presenting with signs such as hematemesis, melena, or hematochezia. Causes vary by location and include peptic ulcers, gastritis, esophageal or gastric varices, diverticulosis, hemorrhoids, angiodysplasia, inflammatory bowel disease, tumors, and other lesions; management focuses on hemodynamic stabilization and identifying and treating the source.

coffee-ground_vomitus.definition: A vomitus with a dark, granular appearance resembling coffee grounds, resulting from partially digested blood in the stomach and often indicating upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

hepatobiliary_iminodiacetic_acid_scan.definition: A nuclear medicine imaging study in which a radiotracer (typically technetium-99m labeled iminodiacetic acid) is injected and sequential images track hepatic uptake, biliary excretion, gallbladder filling and contraction, and bile flow into the small intestine to evaluate the hepatobiliary system and diagnose biliary obstruction, cholecystitis, or bile leaks.

percutaneous_transhepatic_cholangiograph.definition: A radiologic procedure in which contrast material is injected into the biliary tree through a needle inserted via the skin and liver (percutaneous transhepatic approach) to visualize the bile ducts under fluoroscopy, used to evaluate biliary obstruction or leaks and to guide drainage or stenting.

endoscopic_retrograde_cholangiopancreato.definition: A procedure in which an endoscope is passed via the mouth to the duodenum to access the biliary and pancreatic ducts; contrast dye is injected and fluoroscopy is used to visualize these ducts for diagnosis and treatment, including stone extraction, sphincterotomy, and stent placement.

magnetic_resonance_cholangiopancreatogra.definition: An MRI-based, noninvasive imaging technique that visualizes the biliary and pancreatic ducts using heavily T2-weighted sequences to detect stones, strictures, dilatation, or congenital anomalies without ionizing radiation.

cholangiopancreatography.definition: A diagnostic imaging study used to visualize the biliary and pancreatic ductal systems, typically using contrast; commonly performed by ERCP (endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography) or MRCP (magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography).

gastrointestinal_tract.definition: A continuous tube from the mouth to the anus that ingests, digests, and absorbs nutrients and water, and eliminates waste; comprising the esophagus, stomach, and small and large intestines.

upper_gi_series.definition: A radiographic study of the upper gastrointestinal tract (esophagus, stomach, and duodenum) performed after ingestion of radiopaque contrast (usually barium) to visualize anatomy and function under fluoroscopy; used to diagnose structural abnormalities and motility disorders.

barium_enema.definition: An imaging study in which radiopaque barium contrast is introduced into the colon via the rectum to outline the large intestine on X-ray or fluoroscopy, used to evaluate abnormalities such as polyps, diverticula, cancers, or inflammatory bowel disease; a double-contrast (air–barium) technique may be used to improve mucosal detail.

enteral_feeding.definition: Delivery of nutrition directly into the gastrointestinal tract through a tube (such as nasogastric, orogastric, gastrostomy, or jejunostomy feeding) when oral intake is insufficient or unsafe.

gastrostomy_feeding.definition: Delivery of nutrition directly into the stomach through a gastrostomy tube (for example, a PEG tube), bypassing the mouth and esophagus; used for long-term enteral feeding when oral intake is unsafe or inadequate.

gatifloxacin.definition: A fourth-generation fluoroquinolone antibiotic that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; used for various infections but withdrawn in many markets due to safety concerns such as dysglycemia and QT interval prolongation.

metoclopramide.definition: A medication that acts as a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist with antiemetic effects in the chemoreceptor trigger zone and prokinetic effects on the stomach, facilitating gastric emptying; used for nausea and vomiting (including postoperative and chemotherapy-induced) and gastroparesis; may cause extrapyramidal symptoms and tardive dyskinesia with long-term use.

cisapride.definition: A prokinetic agent that stimulates gastrointestinal motility by agonizing serotonin 5-HT4 receptors, increasing acetylcholine release and promoting gastric emptying (and often increasing lower esophageal sphincter tone); historically used for gastroparesis and GERD but largely withdrawn or restricted in many countries due to risk of QT interval prolongation and torsades de pointes.

proton_pump_inhibitors.definition: A class of medications that irreversibly inhibits the hydrogen-potassium ATPase (proton pump) in gastric parietal cells, thereby dramatically reducing gastric acid secretion; used to treat gastroesophageal reflux disease, peptic ulcers, and other acid-related disorders.

antacids.definition: A substance or preparation that neutralizes stomach acid to relieve heartburn, indigestion, and acid reflux; commonly contains aluminum hydroxide, magnesium hydroxide, calcium carbonate, or sodium bicarbonate.

antidiarrheals.definition: Medications that reduce diarrhea by slowing intestinal motility, increasing stool absorption, or decreasing intestinal secretions; examples include opioid‑receptor agonists (such as loperamide and diphenoxylate) and adsorbents or antisecretory agents (such as bismuth subsalicylate).

antiemetics.definition: A class of medications used to prevent or relieve nausea and vomiting.

tranquilizers.definition: An informal, historically used term for drugs that produce a calming or sedating effect. It encompassed major tranquilizers (antipsychotics) that help control psychotic symptoms and minor tranquilizers (anxiolytics/sedatives) that reduce anxiety and promote sleep; the term is outdated and imprecise, with modern practice naming drugs by class and mechanism (e.g., antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, sedatives).

diabetes_mellitus.definition: A group of metabolic disorders characterized by chronic hyperglycemia due to defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or both; includes type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, and gestational diabetes.

liver_cirrhosis.definition: A chronic, irreversible liver disease characterized by diffuse hepatic fibrosis with regenerative nodules, causing distortion of hepatic architecture and progressive loss of liver function, often with portal hypertension. It results from long-standing liver injury (e.g., chronic alcohol use, viral hepatitis, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease).

alzheimers_disease.definition: A progressive brain disease that causes memory loss, impaired thinking, and personality changes.

spider_angioma.definition: A small, bright red, blanchable cutaneous lesion consisting of a central arteriole with radiating telangiectatic capillaries (spider-like); commonly seen on the face, neck, or upper chest and associated with increased estrogen states (e.g., pregnancy) or liver disease.

palmar_erythema.definition: Diffuse redness of the palms caused by dilation of superficial hand vessels; commonly seen with increased estrogen states (e.g., pregnancy) and liver disease (cirrhosis), but can occur with autoimmune conditions, hyperthyroidism, or certain medications; typically symmetric and may blanch with pressure.

gastrointestinal_allergy.definition: An umbrella term for immune-mediated adverse reactions to foods that primarily involve the gastrointestinal tract, causing symptoms such as vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, or blood in stool; can be IgE-mediated or non-IgE-mediated and includes disorders like food protein–induced enterocolitis syndrome and eosinophilic gastrointestinal diseases.

gastrointestinal_series.definition: A radiologic examination of the gastrointestinal tract in which radiopaque contrast (usually barium) is ingested or administered to outline the esophagus, stomach, and intestines on X-ray, used to evaluate anatomy and function; includes upper GI series (barium swallow) and lower GI series (barium enema).

gastroschisis.definition: A congenital defect in which the infant's abdominal contents (usually the intestines) protrude through a hole in the abdominal wall, typically to the right of the umbilicus, and are not covered by a protective sac.

gastromalacia.definition: Softening of the stomach tissue (gastric wall or mucosa); a historical term referring to degenerative or inflammatory changes of the stomach, not a commonly used modern diagnosis.

gastromegaly.definition: Enlargement of the stomach; a descriptive term for an abnormally large stomach, which may result from distension, thickening of the gastric wall, or mass effect, rather than a specific diagnosis.

gastropericardial_fistula.definition: An abnormal communication between the stomach and the pericardial sac, typically arising from gastric ulceration, trauma, or erosion from malignancy or prior surgery, allowing gastric contents and air to enter the pericardial space and potentially causing pericarditis, pneumopericardium, effusion, mediastinitis, and sepsis.

gastroplasty.definition: A surgical procedure to reduce stomach capacity and alter gastric anatomy to promote weight loss, typically by creating a smaller gastric pouch or rearranging the stomach.

gaucher's disease.definition: A lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient activity of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase, leading to accumulation of glucocerebroside within macrophages and lipid‑laden cells. Clinically, it causes hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and bone disease; neuronopathic forms (types 2 and 3) may involve the central nervous system. It is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.

glucosylceramide lipidosis.definition: A lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient glucocerebrosidase activity, resulting in accumulation of glucosylceramide in macrophages and reticuloendothelial tissues, leading to hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, bone abnormalities, and, in some variants, neurologic involvement.

reticulum cell hyperplasia.definition: Proliferation of the reticular (fibroblastic) cells that form the stromal framework of lymphoid and hematopoietic tissues, resulting in an expanded reticular network often as a reactive response to infection or inflammation.

bone marrow smear.definition: A microscopic slide prepared from a bone marrow aspirate, stained and examined to evaluate marrow cellularity, hematopoietic cell morphology and maturation, and the presence of abnormal cells or infiltrates.

limb-girdle muscular dystrophy.definition: A group of hereditary muscular dystrophies characterized by progressive weakness and wasting of proximal muscles, especially the hip and shoulder girdle regions, with onset typically in adolescence or adulthood; caused by mutations in a variety of genes and inherited in autosomal dominant or recessive patterns.

huntington disease.definition: An autosomal dominant, progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG-repeat expansion in the HTT gene, leading to degeneration of neurons in the caudate and cortex and presenting with choreiform movements, psychiatric symptoms, and cognitive decline.

myotonic dystrophy.definition: A genetic muscular dystrophy characterized by myotonia (delayed relaxation of muscles after contraction) and progressive muscle weakness; mainly two forms, DM1 and DM2, caused by nucleotide repeat expansions, with possible systemic features such as cataracts, cardiac conduction defects, endocrine problems, and respiratory involvement.

macular degeneration.definition: An eye disease that destroys your sharp, central vision, which helps with seeing clearly and reading and driving.

hereditary amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.definition: A familial form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis characterized by inherited genetic mutations (most often autosomal dominant) that cause progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons, leading to muscle weakness, atrophy, and spasticity; it accounts for a minority of ALS cases (about 5–10%).

non-small-cell lung cancer.definition: Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is a broad category of primary lung cancers that are not small cell carcinoma; the major histologic subtypes are adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma. NSCLC accounts for about 85% of lung cancers and generally has a slower progression than small cell lung cancer. Treatment is stage- and molecular-feature-driven and may include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy.

gemcitabine.definition: A nucleoside analog (2',2'-difluorodeoxycytidine) used as chemotherapy; an antimetabolite that inhibits DNA synthesis by inhibiting ribonucleotide reductase and by incorporating into DNA, causing chain termination and cell death.

gefitinib.definition: An oral epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitor used to treat certain non–small cell lung cancers with activating EGFR mutations; it blocks EGFR tyrosine kinase activity, inhibiting signaling and reducing tumor cell proliferation.

gemtuzumab ozogamicin.definition: An antibody-drug conjugate consisting of a monoclonal antibody against CD33 linked to the cytotoxic agent calicheamicin (ozogamicin); it binds CD33-positive leukemic cells and delivers the toxin to cause DNA double-strand breaks and cell death, used in the treatment of acute myeloid leukemia.

mucinous carcinoma.definition: A histologic subtype of cancer in which malignant epithelial cells produce large amounts of extracellular mucin, forming pools in which the tumor cells are embedded; it occurs in several organs (e.g., breast, colon, ovary) and prognosis and management depend on the site and tumor grade.

gelatin sponge.definition: An sterile, absorbable gelatin-based hemostatic sponge that, when applied to a bleeding site, swells on contact with blood to provide a scaffold for clot formation and is gradually resorbed by the body.

gelatin film.definition: A thin, flexible sheet formed from gelatin, a protein derived from collagen, used as a film-forming material in pharmaceuticals and food for coatings, edible films, or wound dressings; it is typically water-soluble and swells or dissolves upon hydration.

gelatin.definition: A protein derived from collagen by hydrolysis, typically obtained from animal connective tissues; it dissolves in hot water and forms a gel upon cooling, and is used as a gelling/thickening agent in foods, pharmaceuticals, and laboratory media.

gelatinous carcinoma.definition: A malignant tumor characterized by abundant extracellular mucin that gives a gelatinous, jelly-like gross appearance; histology typically shows tumor cells dispersed in large pools of mucin, aligning with a mucinous (colloid) adenocarcinoma pattern or, in some cases, signet-ring cell morphology depending on the organ and cellular features.

gel diffusion.definition: Movement of solute molecules through a gel matrix (such as agarose or polyacrylamide) from regions of higher to lower concentration due to passive diffusion, often used in gel-based assays to separate macromolecules.

gel filtration.definition: A chromatography technique (size-exclusion chromatography) that separates solute molecules in a liquid by their size as they pass through a column packed with porous beads; larger molecules are excluded from the beads and elute first, while smaller molecules enter the pores and elute later.

gelfoam.definition: A resorbable gelatin sponge used as a local hemostatic agent in surgery; it swells on contact with blood to provide a scaffold for clot formation and is gradually absorbed over weeks.

gell-coombs classification.definition: A framework that categorizes hypersensitivity reactions into four main types (I–IV) by their underlying immunologic mechanisms and timing: Type I—IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity; Type II—antibody-dependent cytotoxic reactions; Type III—immune complex–mediated reactions; Type IV—delayed-type, T-cell–mediated hypersensitivity.

gellhorn pessary.definition: A vaginal pessary used to support pelvic organs in prolapse; it is a ring-shaped device with a post or stem that passes through the vaginal fornix to anchor the device, providing more stable support for moderate-to-severe uterine or vaginal prolapse.

guthrie's bacterial inhibition assay.definition: An early neonatal screening test for phenylketonuria in which a blood spot on filter paper is placed on agar seeded with Bacillus subtilis and containing a growth inhibitor; phenylalanine from the blood diffuses into the medium and permits bacterial growth, with colony counts reflecting phenylalanine concentration.

gadolinium.definition: An element in the periodic table, a silver-white lanthanide metal (atomic number 64). In medicine, it is used in contrast agents for magnetic resonance imaging to enhance tissue contrast by shortening the T1 relaxation time of nearby water protons, and it is chelated to reduce toxicity.

gestational diabetes mellitus.definition: A form of glucose intolerance with onset or first recognition during pregnancy, due to inadequate insulin secretion in the setting of increased insulin resistance, resulting in maternal hyperglycemia.

glial cell line-derived neurotrophic fac.definition: A secreted neurotrophic factor produced by glial cells that promotes survival, maintenance, and growth of neurons—especially midbrain dopaminergic neurons—by signaling through a receptor complex of GFRα1 and RET tyrosine kinase; a member of the GDNF family of ligands.

geriatric depression scale.definition: A brief self-report screening tool used to identify depressive symptoms in older adults; typically comprises 30 yes/no items (with a 15-item short form available); higher scores reflect more severe depressive symptoms; widely used in clinical and research settings to screen for depression and monitor changes over time.

germanium.definition: A metalloid chemical element (Ge) with atomic number 32; not essential for human nutrition, and some germanium compounds marketed as supplements have been linked to kidney toxicity and are not proven to treat disease.

nasogastric feeding.definition: Delivery of nutrition directly into the stomach through a nasogastric tube, used when oral intake is unsafe or insufficient; a form of enteral feeding.

low fowler's position.definition: A semi-reclined position where the patient lies supine with the head of the bed elevated about 15–30 degrees.

postural drainage.definition: A chest physiotherapy technique that uses gravity—via specific body positions—to drain bronchial secretions from particular lung segments into the central airways for expectoration, often performed with percussion or vibration.

apneic spells.definition: Episodes of transient cessation of breathing (apnea), typically lasting 20 seconds or longer, or shorter pauses accompanied by cyanosis, pallor, or bradycardia. They can be central, obstructive, or mixed in origin and are common in infants, often reflecting immaturity of respiratory control (apnea of prematurity) or signaling an underlying condition.

gastric tube.definition: A flexible tube inserted through the nose or mouth into the stomach to drain gastric contents or to deliver nutrition and medications.

geiger-muller counter.definition: A handheld radiation detector that uses a Geiger–Müller tube filled with inert gas and biased at high voltage; when ionizing radiation enters the tube, it ionizes the gas and produces an electrical pulse that is counted to indicate radioactivity levels.

generalized anxiety disorder.definition: Chronic condition characterized by excessive, difficult-to-control worry about multiple domains for at least 6 months, accompanied by symptoms such as restlessness, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance, causing clinically significant distress or impairment; not attributable to substances, another medical condition, or another mental disorder.

generalized peritonitis.definition: Diffuse inflammation of the peritoneum involving most or all of the peritoneal cavity, typically due to perforation of a viscus or widespread infection, presenting with acute, diffuse abdominal pain and peritoneal signs (guarding, rigidity), fever, leukocytosis, and possible sepsis; a surgical emergency.

general paresis.definition: A form of neurosyphilis in which Treponema pallidum infection causes chronic brain inflammation, leading to progressive cognitive decline with psychiatric and neurologic symptoms in late-stage syphilis; it is treatable with penicillin.

paretic dementia.definition: Not a recognized medical term; there is no formal dementia syndrome by this name. If used, it likely reflects a misnomer or informal reference to dementia with motor impairment (e.g., Parkinsonian dementia or vascular dementia), and standard diagnostic terminology should be used.

syphilitic meningingoencephalitis.definition: An inflammatory neurosyphilis condition in which Treponema pallidum infection causes inflammation of the meninges and adjacent brain tissue (meningoencephalitis), typically presenting with headaches, fever, altered mental status, seizures, or focal neurologic deficits; diagnosed by CSF pleocytosis with positive syphilis serology and treated with high-dose intravenous penicillin G.

anxiety state.definition: A transient emotional condition characterized by heightened worry and apprehension, accompanied by autonomic arousal (e.g., increased heart rate, tremor, sweating) in response to a perceived threat or stressor; it fluctuates with the situation and time, unlike a stable trait anxiety.

pupillary dilation.definition: Enlargement of the pupil due to contraction of the iris dilator (radial) muscle under sympathetic stimulation (mydriasis); increases light intake and can occur in dim light, during stress, or with certain medications.

gastric wall.definition: The wall of the stomach, formed by four main layers—the mucosa (gastric epithelium with glands), submucosa, muscularis externa (three smooth muscle layers: inner oblique, middle circular, outer longitudinal), and serosa—protects the stomach, secretes mucus, acid, and enzymes, and coordinates peristaltic mixing and gastric emptying.

cortical neurons.definition: Neurons located in the cerebral cortex; the major cortical cells are pyramidal neurons (excitatory, glutamatergic) and diverse interneurons (inhibitory, GABAergic) that form local and long-range circuits and mediate processing of sensory information, perception, cognition, and motor planning.

gene therapy.definition: An experimental medical approach that introduces or alters genetic material within a patient's cells to treat or prevent disease by correcting defects, silencing faulty genes, or augmenting gene function; delivery is usually via viral or nonviral vectors or gene-editing tools, and can be performed in vivo or ex vivo.

somatic-cell gene therapy.definition: A form of gene therapy in which therapeutic genes are delivered to somatic (non-reproductive) cells to treat or prevent disease; the genetic modifications are not heritable and cannot be passed to offspring.

termination of pregnancy.definition: The ending of a pregnancy before birth, which can be spontaneous (miscarriage) or induced (abortion), achieved through medical or surgical means.

genioglossus.definition: A broad, fan-shaped extrinsic tongue muscle that originates from the mental spine of the mandible and inserts into the tongue; its contraction protrudes the tongue (with posterior fibers aiding protrusion and anterior fibers depressing the tongue). Innervated by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).

geniohyoideus.definition: A narrow neck muscle that originates from the inferior mental spine of the mandible and inserts into the body of the hyoid bone; it elevates and moves the hyoid bone anteriorly during swallowing, and, with the hyoid fixed, can assist in depressing the mandible. Innervation is via C1 fibers carried by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).

hypoglossal.definition: Situated beneath the tongue; relating to the tongue.

hyoid.definition: A small U-shaped bone at the top of the neck, underneath the jaw.

genitals.definition: The external organs of the reproductive system; in common usage, it may refer to the external genitalia (penis and scrotum in males; vulva, including the labia and clitoris, in females) or to the reproductive organs of either sex as a whole.

minora.definition: Latin for "smaller" or "lesser"; in anatomy, the inner, smaller folds of the vulva that surround the openings of the vagina and urethra.

geographic.definition: Relating to geography; in medical usage, describing a pattern of distribution or borders that are irregular and map-like (e.g., geographic tongue).

migrans.definition: A Latin adjective meaning migratory or moving; used in medical terms to denote signs that move or spread over time (for example, a rash that gradually enlarges and changes location).

migratory.definition: Relating to symptoms that move from one location to another over time; in clinical use, it describes manifestations that change location, such as pain that shifts between joints.

areata.definition: Patchy; localized to discrete areas with well-defined margins, describing involvement limited to certain areas rather than diffusely.

prader-willi.definition: A genetic imprinting disorder caused by loss of paternal gene expression on chromosome 15q11-q13 (often due to paternal deletion or maternal uniparental disomy) that presents with infantile hypotonia and feeding problems, followed by hyperphagia leading to obesity, along with short stature, hypogonadism, developmental delay, and behavioral problems.

angelman.definition: A genetic neurodevelopmental disorder caused by loss of function of the maternally inherited UBE3A gene on chromosome 15q11-q13, most often due to a maternal deletion but also caused by paternal uniparental disomy, imprinting defects, or UBE3A mutations. It presents in infancy with developmental delay, severe speech impairment, ataxia, seizures, and a characteristic happy demeanor with frequent laughter; intellectual disability is typically profound. Management is multidisciplinary and supportive (epilepsy control, physical and occupational therapy, communication therapy).

tay-sachs.definition: An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by HEXA gene mutations that produce beta-hexosaminidase A deficiency, leading to GM2 ganglioside accumulation in neurons and progressive neurodegeneration beginning in infancy, with symptoms such as hypotonia, developmental delay, seizures, and vision loss (often with a cherry-red spot on the retina).

gardasil.definition: A preventive vaccine against human papillomavirus (HPV) infection that protects against multiple HPV types—originally types 6, 11, 16, and 18 (quadrivalent) and, in newer formulations, nine types including 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58 (nonavalent)—reducing the risk of cervical, other anogenital, and oropharyngeal cancers as well as genital warts; administered by injection in a multi-dose schedule.

acuminatum.definition: A Latin adjective meaning tapering to a pointed apex; used to describe structures or lesions that narrow to a sharp point.

verruca.definition: A viral skin lesion caused by human papillomavirus infection, presenting as a rough, keratotic papule or nodule (wart), most commonly on the hands or feet; contagious and can spontaneously resolve over time.

acuminata.definition: The feminine form of the Latin adjective acuminatus, meaning tapering to a point or sharply pointed; used to describe pointed morphological features in anatomy or taxonomy.

zoster.definition: An acute, painful vesicular eruption in a dermatomal distribution caused by reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus.

warts.definition: Growths on the skin caused by infection with human papillomavirus (HPV).

ramsay.definition: Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus affecting the facial nerve within the temporal bone, presenting with ipsilateral facial paralysis and vesicular eruption in the ear canal or auricle.

hunt.definition: Not a recognized medical term; no formal clinical definition exists for this word.

growth-hormone.definition: A peptide hormone produced by the anterior pituitary that stimulates growth and metabolism in tissues, primarily by inducing liver-derived IGF-1; its secretion is regulated by growth hormone-releasing hormone and somatostatin.

podofilox.definition: A topical antimitotic agent derived from the mayapple plant Podophyllum peltatum (podophyllotoxin), used to treat external genital warts and other external anogenital warts caused by HPV; inhibits tubulin polymerization, disrupting mitosis and causing cell death; supplied as 0.5% solution or gel; can cause local irritation and is contraindicated in pregnancy.

trichloracetic.definition: A strong halogenated carboxylic acid in which three chlorine atoms replace hydrogens on the methyl group of acetic acid; used in dermatology as a chemical peel agent and in organic synthesis; it coagulates proteins and causes controlled tissue necrosis at topical concentrations. It is caustic and can cause chemical burns if misused.

geophagia.definition: The compulsive ingestion of earth or soil substances (such as clay, dirt, or chalk), a form of pica; it is sometimes associated with iron-deficiency anemia or pregnancy and can lead to gastrointestinal complications, dental wear, and exposure to toxins or parasites.

gentian.definition: A plant genus in the Gentianaceae family; its dried root (gentian root) is used as a bitter tonic to stimulate appetite and aid digestion, containing bitter compounds such as gentiopicroside and amarogentin.

violet.definition: A purple-blue color; in medicine, used to describe tissue coloration (e.g., bruising) and, as crystal violet, a basic dye used in Gram staining to color bacterial cells.

tegretol.definition: A broad-spectrum anticonvulsant and mood stabilizer (carbamazepine) used to treat partial and generalized seizures, certain neuropathic pains, and bipolar disorder; it works by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels to reduce nerve excitability.

sansert.definition: A brand-name formulation of methysergide, a serotonin 5-HT2 receptor antagonist used as a preventive treatment for migraines; associated with serious fibrotic adverse effects (retroperitoneal, pleural, and cardiac valvular fibrosis) and is now rarely used due to safety concerns.

geotrichosis.definition: A fungal infection caused by Geotrichum species (most commonly Geotrichum candidum), affecting the skin, mucous membranes, or lungs; can be localized or disseminated, especially in immunocompromised individuals.

geotrichum candidum.definition: An environmental, yeast-like filamentous fungus commonly found in soil and dairy environments; it forms white, powdery colonies and produces rectangular arthroconidia along hyphae. It can act as an opportunistic human pathogen causing geotrichosis, but is also used in cheese ripening for rind development.

pharyngeal.definition: Relating to the pharynx, the muscular tube behind the nose and mouth that connects to the esophagus and larynx.

intestinal disorders.definition: A broad category of diseases affecting the intestines (small and/or large bowel), involving abnormalities of motility, absorption, inflammation, infection, obstruction, or neoplasia that produce symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, constipation, bloating, or GI bleeding.

allergic aspergillosis.definition: An IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to colonization by Aspergillus species (most often Aspergillus fumigatus) in the airways, typically in people with asthma or cystic fibrosis, causing chronic bronchial inflammation, wheezing, cough with mucus plugging, eosinophilia, and elevated IgE, and potentially leading to bronchiectasis.

rectal bleeding.definition: Rectal bleeding is the passage of blood from the rectum or anus with bowel movements. It can originate from benign anorectal conditions (eg, hemorrhoids, anal fissures) or from more serious diseases of the colon or rectum (eg, diverticular disease, inflammatory bowel disease, colorectal cancer); the color, amount, and accompanying symptoms guide the need for urgent evaluation.

oral lesions.definition: An oral lesion is any abnormality of the oral mucosa or other tissues in the mouth (lips, tongue, gums, palate, floor of mouth) that alters appearance or function, including ulcers, erosions, vesicles, masses, or discolorations; causes include trauma, infection, inflammatory or autoimmune disease, or neoplasia.

gentian violet.definition: A topical antiseptic dye (crystal violet; a triphenylmethane dye) used on skin and mucous membranes to treat superficial infections, particularly candidiasis; it stains tissues purple and can cause mucosal irritation, with safety concerns and the availability of safer alternatives limiting its use.

potassium iodide.definition: A salt of potassium and iodide that provides iodide for the body, essential for thyroid hormone synthesis; used to prevent iodine deficiency and to block uptake of radioactive iodine by the thyroid after exposure.

arcus juvenilis.definition: A grayish-white arc at the margin of the cornea due to lipid deposition in the peripheral corneal stroma, typically seen in young individuals and often associated with familial or secondary hyperlipidemia; lipid evaluation is recommended.

germicide.definition: A chemical agent that kills microorganisms (germs), including bacteria, viruses, and fungi.

germinal.definition: Relating to a germ cell or to the early developmental stages; used of tissues derived from or forming the germinal epithelium or germ layers in embryology.

germinal cords.definition: In embryology, germinal cords are the early clusters of primordial germ cells within the developing gonad (paired with supporting somatic cells) that later form the seminiferous tubules of the testis or the ovarian cords and eventual follicles of the ovary.

germinal disk.definition: A small disk-shaped region on the surface of a fertilized avian egg (the blastodisk) that contains the embryonic primordium and from which the embryo develops, giving rise to the germ layers (epiblast and hypoblast).

germinal epithelium.definition: An epithelial layer covering the surface of the ovary, derived from the coelomic (mesothelial) lining; historically described in relation to germ cell development, but it does not give rise to germ cells in adults.

germinal infection.definition: Not a standard medical term with a defined meaning; there is no established definition. If used, it would generally refer loosely to an infection caused by germs (microorganisms) at a particular site, but the exact meaning depends on context.

germinal membrane.definition: An historic term for the ovarian surface epithelium (germinal epithelium) that covers the ovary; a layer derived from coelomic epithelium, historically believed to give rise to germ cells.

germinal nucleus.definition: The nucleus of a germ cell—the cell that develops into a gamete (sperm or egg); in developing oocytes, this nucleus is referred to as the germinal vesicle before meiosis begins.

germinal pole.definition: A region at one end of an embryo or oocyte where germ plasm is localized, containing determinants that specify and give rise to primordial germ cells (gametes) during development.

germinal stage.definition: First phase of prenatal development, from fertilization of the ovum to implantation in the uterine lining; the zygote undergoes rapid mitotic divisions (cleavage) to form a morula and then a blastocyst, which implants into the endometrium typically about 6–10 days after fertilization (roughly within the first two weeks).

germination.definition: The process by which a dormant seed or spore resumes growth to form a new plant, initiated by water uptake and favorable conditions, with activation of metabolism and emergence of the embryonic root (radicle) and shoot.

germinoma.definition: A malignant germ cell tumor arising from primordial germ cells, most often in midline brain structures (pineal or suprasellar region); histologically it resembles a seminoma and is highly radiosensitive and chemosensitive.

germ layer.definition: One of the three primary tissue layers formed during gastrulation in the early embryo (ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm) from which all tissues and organs develop.

germ line.definition: The cell lineage that gives rise to gametes (sperm and eggs) and the genetic material within those cells that can be transmitted to offspring; mutations in this lineage are heritable.

germ plasm.definition: A historical term for the hereditary material located in germ cells (gametes) that is transmitted to offspring; proposed by August Weismann, positing that inheritance occurs through the germ line and is distinct from somatic cells.

germ theory.definition: Many diseases are caused by microorganisms—such as bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites—that invade the body, multiply, and cause illness; transmission occurs via contaminated air, water, food, or direct contact.

geriatric.definition: Relating to older adults; pertaining to the medical care and health issues of the elderly.

gerodontics.definition: A branch of dentistry focusing on the prevention, diagnosis, and management of oral health issues in older adults, taking into account age-related changes, systemic diseases, and medication effects.

gerodontia.definition: The branch of dentistry focused on the oral health care of older adults, addressing age-related changes in dentition and tissues and providing prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of dental problems in the elderly.

gerodontology.definition: The branch of dentistry focused on the oral health care of older adults, studying age-related changes in the dentition and oral tissues and providing appropriate dental care for the elderly.

geropsychiatry.definition: A psychiatric subspecialty focused on the mental health care of older adults, including assessment, diagnosis, and treatment of conditions such as dementia, delirium, depression, anxiety, psychosis, and agitation, with attention to age-related cognitive and medical comorbidity and caregiver needs.

gds.definition: A self-report screening questionnaire used to identify depressive symptoms in older adults; typically available in 15- or 30-item versions with yes/no responses; higher scores indicate more severe depressive symptoms; not diagnostic on its own.

gems.definition: An acronym for the Global Enteric Multicenter Study, a multinational research project that investigates the causes and burden of diarrheal diseases in children, aiming to inform prevention, treatment, and policy.

gerbich blood group.definition: An RBC antigen system defined by several antigens on the red cell membrane, mainly on glycophorin C; antibodies to Gerbich antigens (e.g., Ge2, Ge3) can cause hemolytic transfusion reactions and, rarely, hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.

erythrocytic antigens.definition: Antigens located on the membrane of red blood cells that determine blood group specificity (e.g., ABO, Rh) and can provoke antibody responses, leading to transfusion reactions or hemolytic disease of the newborn.
