gametogenesis.definition: The formation and maturation of gametes (sperm and ova) in the gonads, typically by meiosis, producing haploid cells for fertilization (spermatogenesis in males and oogenesis in females).

oogonia.definition: Diploid germ cells of the ovary that proliferate by mitosis during fetal development to form primary oocytes, which then enter meiosis and arrest in prophase I until puberty.

pineal region.definition: An anatomical midline region of the brain surrounding the pineal gland (epithalamus), located just posterior to the third ventricle and between the two thalami; it includes the pineal gland and adjacent structures such as the habenular nuclei and quadrigeminal plate.

transmissible spongiform encephalopathy.definition: A group of fatal, progressive neurodegenerative diseases caused by misfolded prion proteins, characterized by spongiform changes and neuronal loss in the brain with little inflammatory response; can occur sporadically, be inherited, or be acquired through prion exposure (examples include Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease, variant CJD, scrapie, bovine spongiform encephalopathy).

gerstmann-straussler-scheinker syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal-dominant prion disease caused by mutations in the PRNP gene, characterized by early progressive cerebellar ataxia followed by dementia and other neurologic signs, with rapid progression and shortened survival.

neurofibrillary tangles.definition: Twisted strands of proteins that are found inside the dead or dying nerve cells of people with Alzheimer's disease.

hyperreflexia.definition: An abnormally exaggerated deep tendon reflex in response to a stimulus, reflecting upper motor neuron dysfunction; commonly seen with spinal cord or brain lesions (e.g., stroke, multiple sclerosis) and may be accompanied by spasticity and clonus.

endogenous infection.definition: An infection caused by microorganisms that originate from the body’s own flora or latent reservoirs, invading normally sterile sites from within the body rather than being acquired from the external environment.

mixed infection.definition: An infection caused by two or more different pathogens simultaneously, frequently involving bacteria and fungi, which can complicate treatment due to differing antimicrobial susceptibilities.

retrograde infection.definition: An infection that spreads in the reverse direction of normal physiological flow, often from a distal site toward upstream tissues or organs, frequently facilitated by reflux, instrumentation, or obstruction.

secondary infection.definition: An infection that occurs during or after a primary infection, usually caused by an opportunistic pathogen when the host's defenses are weakened or normal flora are disrupted, and that often complicates the initial illness.

giant axonal neuropathy.definition: A rare autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder in which biallelic mutations in the GAN gene cause abnormal accumulation of neurofilaments and other intermediate filaments in neurons, producing giant-caliber axons and progressive axonal neuropathy with motor and sensory impairment (often beginning in childhood).

dens in dente.definition: A developmental dental anomaly in which the enamel organ invaginates into the dental papilla during tooth formation, creating a tooth-like structure within the crown or root of a tooth (dens invaginatus); it most commonly affects maxillary lateral incisors and can predispose to caries, pulpal exposure, and complex endodontic treatment.

gestational hypertension.definition: New-onset hypertension occurring after 20 weeks of gestation in a woman who was previously normotensive, defined as blood pressure ≥140/90 mmHg on at least two occasions at least 4 hours apart, without proteinuria or other signs of end-organ dysfunction; it may progress to preeclampsia and usually resolves after delivery.

gestational psychosis.definition: An acute, rare psychiatric illness that begins during pregnancy or in the early postpartum period, characterized by psychosis (delusions and/or hallucinations), disorganized thinking, and mood disturbance, with risk of harm to self or the fetus; requires urgent psychiatric evaluation and treatment (often hospitalization), typically with antipsychotic therapy and mood stabilization.

gestational sac.definition: An early intrauterine, fluid-filled cavity formed after implantation that surrounds the developing embryo (and later the yolk sac); it is the earliest ultrasound sign of intrauterine pregnancy.

gestation period.definition: The period of intrauterine development during pregnancy, extending from conception to birth; in humans it is typically about 38 weeks from fertilization or about 40 weeks from the first day of the last menstrual period, with full term generally 37–42 weeks.

ghon focus.definition: A small subpleural granulomatous lesion in the lung that arises in primary tuberculosis; the initial focus of infection from hematogenous spread, typically associated with ipsilateral hilar lymphadenopathy to form the Ghon complex.

ghons complex.definition: A primary lesion of pulmonary tuberculosis characterized by a subpleural Ghon focus in the lung coupled with ipsilateral hilar lymphadenopathy; represents a primary TB infection and may calcify over time to form a Ranke complex.

ghost cells.definition: Anucleate keratinocytes with eosinophilic cytoplasm and preserved cell outlines, giving a pale "ghost" appearance; produced by keratinization and seen in lesions such as pilomatricoma and the calcifying odontogenic cyst.

odontodysplasia.definition: A rare, nonhereditary developmental anomaly of dental hard tissues (enamel and dentin) often affecting a region of the jaw, resulting in hypoplastic/dysplastic teeth that erupt poorly or not at all and appear “ghost-like” on radiographs due to thin enamel and dentin and enlarged pulp chambers.

giardia lamblia.definition: A flagellated protozoan parasite of the small intestine that causes giardiasis, typically presenting with diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and malabsorption; transmitted via cysts in contaminated water or food.

infantile acrodermatitis.definition: A rare autosomal recessive zinc malabsorption disorder (infantile acrodermatitis enteropathica) caused by mutations affecting zinc uptake, presenting in infancy with periorificial and acral dermatitis, alopecia, and diarrhea; lifelong zinc supplementation is required.

papular acrodermatitis of childhood.definition: A self-limited pediatric viral exanthem characterized by symmetric, nonfollicular papules or papulovesicles, typically on the face (especially the cheeks), buttocks, and extensor surfaces of the limbs; often associated with hepatitis B or other viral infections and resolving within several weeks.

growth hormone releasing factor.definition: A hypothalamic peptide that stimulates the anterior pituitary to release growth hormone, promoting growth and metabolism; its secretion is inhibited by somatostatin.

growth hormone releasing inhibiting horm.definition: A hypothalamic peptide that inhibits the secretion of growth hormone from the anterior pituitary gland; produced primarily by hypothalamic delta cells (and also by pancreatic delta cells) and acts to suppress GH release.

menetrier disease.definition: A rare acquired hypertrophic gastropathy characterized by diffuse mucosal thickening with giant gastric folds (foveolar hyperplasia) leading to protein-losing gastropathy and hypoalbuminemia; patients may have epigastric pain, weight loss, and edema, and there is an increased risk of gastric cancer; severe cases may require gastrectomy.

giant cell carcinoma.definition: A malignant epithelial tumor characterized by the presence of multinucleated giant tumor cells; it is a descriptive term used for certain carcinomas in which giant cells dominate, and it does not denote a single, uniform disease. Prognosis and treatment depend on the tumor’s anatomical site and other histologic features.

giant cell carcinoma of the bladder.word: giant cell carcinoma of the bladder
giant cell carcinoma of the bladder.definition: A rare histologic variant of urothelial (transitional) carcinoma of the bladder characterized by malignant, pleomorphic giant cells with abundant cytoplasm (often multinucleated) arising within conventional urothelial carcinoma; tumor cells typically express epithelial markers (e.g., cytokeratins) and the neoplasm tends to be aggressive with a poor prognosis.

giant cell hepatitis.definition: A histopathologic pattern in which hepatocytes become enlarged and multinucleated (giant cells), typically seen in neonatal/infantile hepatitis and in various forms of severe liver injury (e.g., viral hepatitis, drug-induced injury, autoimmune hepatitis).

giant cell interstitial pneumonia.definition: Rare histologic pattern of interstitial pneumonia characterized by multinucleated giant cells in the alveolar spaces and interstitium, typically occurring in smokers; described as a smoking-related interstitial pneumonia pattern.

giant cell myeloma.definition: A rare morphologic variant of multiple myeloma in which malignant plasma cells appear as multinucleated giant cells; the disease otherwise shares the clonal plasma-cell proliferation and systemic features of classic myeloma.

giant cell tumor of bone.definition: A usually benign, locally aggressive primary bone neoplasm composed of mononuclear stromal cells intermixed with numerous multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells; it typically involves the epiphysis of long bones in young to middle-aged adults and presents as an expanding lytic lesion, treated with surgical curettage (often with adjuvants) or resection, with a risk of local recurrence and rare pulmonary metastasis.

giant cell sarcoma.definition: Not a widely recognized or defined term in current medical literature; when used, it may describe a malignant mesenchymal tumor containing abundant multinucleated giant cells, but there is no universally accepted diagnostic criteria for this wording.

buschke-loewenstein tumor.definition: A giant, exophytic tumor of the anogenital region (giant condyloma acuminatum) caused by human papillomavirus infection (often HPV types 6 and 11); histologically benign but locally aggressive and capable of malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma. Treatment typically involves wide local excision or Mohs micrographic surgery, with close follow-up due to high recurrence risk.

giant follicular lymphoma.definition: Descriptive rather than a formal entity; it refers to follicular lymphoma with unusually large follicles or large malignant cells within a follicular pattern. It is a B‑cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (typical FL immunophenotype: CD20+, CD10+, BCL6+, often BCL2+; commonly with the t(14;18) translocation), usually indolent but capable of transforming to diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma.

symmers disease.definition: A form of hepatic periportal fibrosis seen in chronic Schistosoma mansoni infection, also known as pipestem fibrosis; it is characterized by thickening of the portal tracts that can cause presinusoidal portal hypertension.

giant peristaltic contractions.definition: A very large-amplitude, propagating contraction of the gastrointestinal smooth muscle that moves a bolus along the tract; stronger and longer-lasting than ordinary peristalsis and can involve long segments of intestine.

gianturco coil.definition: A helical stainless steel vascular embolization coil used endovascularly to occlude blood vessels and promote thrombosis, commonly used to treat aneurysms and other vascular malformations.

gilbert's syndrome.definition: An inherited, usually benign condition characterized by mild, intermittent unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia due to reduced hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1) activity, often precipitated by fasting or illness, with normal liver function tests and no evidence of liver disease.

gilles de la tourette syndrome.definition: A neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic, persisting for more than a year with onset before age 18; tics wax and wane in intensity and are not due to another medical condition or substance, often associated with ADHD and OCD.

tourette's syndrome.definition: A neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic, with onset before age 18 and persistence for more than a year; tics wax and wane in frequency and severity and may be associated with ADHD and OCD.

gillies operation.definition: A historical facial reconstructive procedure developed by Sir Harold Gillies for repairing severe facial trauma, involving staged tissue rearrangement with local or regional flaps and grafts to restore form and function. Often used for post-traumatic or burn-related facial deformities.

gill-vernet technique.definition: I can’t find a standard medical definition for “Gill-Vernet technique.” Could you specify the medical specialty (e.g., ENT, orthopedics, dentistry) or provide an alternate spelling? I can look for related terms (e.g., “Vernet technique”) or variants to locate the correct definition.

gingival blanching.definition: A pale or white discoloration of the gingival tissue caused by reduced blood flow or vasoconstriction; may occur after exposure to vasoconstrictive agents, cold, or systemic conditions such as dehydration, anemia, or shock; persistent blanching warrants clinical evaluation.

gingival blood supply.definition: Arterial supply to the gingiva from branches of the maxillary and facial arteries (including the superior and inferior alveolar, infraorbital, and mental arteries) that form a dense subepithelial vascular plexus around the teeth to nourish the gingival epithelium and connective tissue.

gingival cavity.definition: Not a standard dental term; if used, it may refer to a cavity-like space within gingival tissue (as in a gingival abscess) or, more accurately, to the gingival sulcus—the natural shallow groove between the tooth and the gingiva, typically 0–3 mm deep in healthy gums.

gingival color.definition: The hue of the gingival tissue (gums); in health it is usually pink or coral-colored, with variation due to pigmentation, thickness, and vascularity. Abnormal colors (red with inflammation, purple/blue from vascular congestion, or dark pigmentation from melanin) can indicate disease or normal physiologic variation.

gingival consistency.definition: The firmness or resiliency of the gingival tissue on palpation, with firm gingiva indicating relative health and soft or edematous gingiva indicating inflammation or edema.

gingival corium.definition: The connective tissue layer (lamina propria) of the gingiva beneath the gingival epithelium, composed of fibroblasts, collagen and elastic fibers, blood vessels, and nerves; it supports the epithelium and helps anchor the gingiva to the underlying bone via gingival fiber bundles.

lamina propria mucosae.definition: A layer of loose connective tissue beneath the epithelium of a mucous membrane (the lamina propria), containing blood vessels, lymphatics, resident immune cells, and sometimes glands, which supports the epithelium and participates in mucosal immune defense.

intraalveolar blood vessels.definition: Small pulmonary capillaries embedded in the walls of the alveoli (alveolar septa) that encircle each alveolus and form the alveolar–capillary membrane for gas exchange between the air in the alveoli and the bloodstream.

periodontal membrane.definition: A dense connective tissue that surrounds the tooth root and attaches it to the surrounding alveolar bone via collagen fiber bundles (the periodontal ligament); part of the periodontium, providing tooth support and containing nerves and blood vessels.

zygomatic arch.definition: A bony arch on the side of the skull formed by the temporal process of the zygomatic bone and the zygomatic process of the temporal bone; it contributes to the cheek prominence and provides attachment for the masseter muscle.

giemsa's stain.definition: A Romanowsky-type polychrome stain used in hematology and cytology to differentiate cellular components; it employs a mixture of methylene blue, eosin, and azure dyes, staining nuclei blue to purple and cytoplasm pink to gray, and is commonly used to examine blood smears for leukocyte differentiation and to detect malaria and other parasites.

gift.definition: A fertility treatment in which eggs and sperm are placed directly into the fallopian tube to fertilize there, bypassing laboratory fertilization.

gibson's murmur.definition: Not a standard term in modern medical references. It doesn’t have a widely accepted definition and may be a misspelling or an outdated eponym. If you can provide context (patient age, symptoms, or the source you saw it in) or an alternate spelling, I can help clarify. If you’d like, I can define common murmur categories (e.g., systolic vs. diastolic, location, radiation).

machinery murmur.definition: A continuous, “machinery-like” murmur best heard at the left infraclavicular area, radiating to the back, associated with patent ductus arteriosus; caused by ongoing blood flow from the aorta to the pulmonary artery during both systole and diastole.

granulomas.definition: A small nodular inflammatory lesion consisting of aggregates of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells), often with multinucleated giant cells, surrounded by lymphocytes; formed in response to chronic inflammation from persistent pathogens, foreign bodies, or immune-mediated processes.

hilar lymph node granulomas.definition: Granulomatous inflammation within the hilar lymph nodes (the nodes at the lung hilum), characterized by aggregates of epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells, often with lymphocytes; commonly seen in sarcoidosis and granulomatous infections (e.g., histoplasmosis, tuberculosis) and associated with hilar lymphadenopathy.

calcifications.definition: Deposition of calcium salts in tissues, often as a result of tissue injury or necrosis (dystrophic calcification) or from elevated calcium levels causing deposition in otherwise normal tissues (metastatic calcification).

primary pulmonary tuberculosis.definition: An initial infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis in a person with no prior exposure, typically involving the lungs; most infections are latent, but active primary pulmonary tuberculosis can present with cough, fever, night sweats, and weight loss.

spindle cells.definition: Elongated, fusiform (spindle-shaped) cells with tapered ends and elongated nuclei, typical of mesenchymal tissues; often seen in spindle cell tumors (sarcomas) with cells arranged in fascicles.

osteoblastic sarcoma.definition: A malignant bone tumor in which malignant osteoblasts produce osteoid (bone matrix); the most common primary bone cancer, typically arising in the metaphyses of long bones in children and young adults, and is aggressive with rapid local destruction and a high risk of lung metastases.

lampbrush chromosomes.definition: A pair of highly extended meiotic chromosomes observed in oocyte diplotene, with a central chromosomal axis and numerous lateral chromatin loops radiating outward, indicating extensive transcription of those regions.

polytene chromosomes.definition: An enlarged chromosome formed when a cell undergoes endoreplication—repeated rounds of DNA replication without cell division—creating many identical sister chromatids that align side by side and appear as a giant, banded chromosome under light microscopy; commonly observed in salivary gland cells of Drosophila and some other species and used for cytogenetic mapping.

giant chromosome.definition: A polytene chromosome produced by endoreduplication (repeated rounds of DNA replication without cell division), resulting in many sister chromatids aligned in register to form a very large, banded chromosome visible under light microscopy (notable in certain tissues like Drosophila salivary glands and used to study chromosome structure and transcriptional activity).

gigantoblast.definition: An abnormally large cell, often referring to a giant multinucleated cell formed by cell fusion or endoreduplication; used in some histopathology descriptions but not a widely standardized term.

gigantochromoblast.definition: Not a standard medical term; it would hypothetically refer to an abnormally large pigment-containing cell, but there is no established clinical entity by this name.

gigantocyte.definition: A very large cell; a type of giant cell, often of macrophage lineage, seen in granulomatous inflammation and related conditions.

neonatal hepatitis.definition: Neonatal hepatitis is inflammation of the liver in a newborn, typically presenting with jaundice and hepatocellular dysfunction in the first weeks of life; etiologies include congenital infections (eg, TORCH pathogens), metabolic disorders (eg, galactosemia, hereditary tyrosinemia), drug exposure, and idiopathic causes, with histology showing hepatocellular injury and often cholestasis.

gingival sulcus.definition: A shallow groove between the tooth and the free gingiva, bordered apically by the junctional epithelium and coronally by the free gingival margin; lined by sulcular epithelium and typically 0–3 mm deep in health.

junctional epithelium.definition: A specialized, non‑keratinized stratified squamous epithelium that attaches to tooth enamel via a basal lamina and hemidesmosomes, lines the gingival sulcus, and forms the biologic seal between the tooth and surrounding periodontal connective tissue; it has rapid turnover and relatively permeable intercellular junctions.

gingival cyst.definition: A benign developmental cyst of the gingival mucosa arising from remnants of the dental lamina; presents as a small, painless gingival swelling and is treated by surgical excision (gingival cysts of the newborn often resolve spontaneously; in adults they are rare).

odontogenic cyst.definition: A cyst that arises from odontogenic epithelium and other tooth-forming tissues in the jaws, usually lined by stratified squamous epithelium and containing fluid; can be inflammatory (e.g., radicular or residual) or developmental (e.g., dentigerous, keratocyst).

lateral periodontal cyst.definition: A developmental odontogenic cyst arising along the lateral aspect of a tooth root, usually in the mandibular canine–premolar region, in a tooth that is typically vital; radiographs show a well-defined, often small, unilocular radiolucency adjacent to the root, and treatment is surgical enucleation with a favorable prognosis.

interdental papilla.definition: The portion of the gingiva that fills the interdental space between two adjacent teeth, extending from the gingival margin to the contact point; a pyramidal or knife-edged projection that helps seal the embrasure and protect the underlying periodontal structures.

pregnancy epulis.definition: A benign gingival lesion that occurs during pregnancy, presenting as a rapidly enlarging, highly vascular mass on the gums that often bleeds easily; histologically it is a pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) and it may regress after delivery. Also known as granuloma gravidarum or pregnancy tumor.

gingival hypertrophy.definition: Abnormal enlargement of the gum tissue (gingiva), typically due to chronic inflammation or medication‑induced fibrous overgrowth, and can be influenced by plaque, hormonal changes, or systemic conditions.

gingivectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove or reshape gum tissue.

gingivoplasty.definition: A surgical procedure to reshape or contour the gingival tissue around the teeth to improve gum-line contour and aesthetics, and to facilitate better oral hygiene; often performed after periodontal treatment.

gingival festoon.definition: A scalloped, wave-like contour of the free gingival margin around adjacent teeth, giving a festooned (undulating) gingival margin.

mccall's festoon.definition: A pendulous fold of tissue beneath the lower eyelid due to edema or skin laxity, giving a festooned (folded) appearance around the eye.

gingivostomatitis.definition: Gingivostomatitis is inflammation of the gingiva (gums) and the oral mucosa, presenting with painful swelling, redness, and often ulcers or vesicles; most commonly caused by primary herpes simplex virus infection in children (acute herpetic gingivostomatitis), but it can also result from bacterial infections or other viral etiologies; treatment is supportive (hydration, analgesia) and targets the underlying cause (antivirals for HSV when indicated).

cerebral degeneration.definition: Progressive loss of brain tissue and function due to degenerative processes (such as neurodegenerative diseases, vascular injury, metabolic or inflammatory conditions), leading to cognitive, motor, and behavioral decline.

infectious mononucleosis.definition: An acute viral illness caused by Epstein-Barr virus, presenting with fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, and fatigue; commonly transmitted via saliva and usually self-limited over 2–4 weeks, diagnosed by heterophile antibody tests or EBV serology and managed with supportive care.

glandular fever.definition: An infectious mononucleosis caused primarily by the Epstein-Barr virus; characterized by fever, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes, fatigue, and sometimes an enlarged spleen, and transmitted mainly through saliva.

gipoma.definition: Not a recognized term. A benign tumor of adipose tissue: a soft, painless, slow-growing, encapsulated lesion composed of mature fat cells and usually mobile under the skin.

glatiramer.definition: A disease-modifying therapy for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis. It is a synthetic random copolymer of the amino acids tyrosine, glutamic acid, alanine, and lysine that mimics myelin basic protein and modulates the immune response by acting as a decoy for autoreactive T cells, thereby reducing inflammatory demyelination. Administered by subcutaneous injection.

ginkgo.definition: Leaf extract from a Chinese tree used as an herbal supplement with claimed cognitive benefits; evidence for efficacy is inconsistent; can inhibit platelet aggregation and increase bleeding risk, especially with anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents; adverse effects include GI upset, headache, dizziness, and allergic reactions; use with caution in pregnancy and when taking blood thinners.

glands of moll.definition: Modified apocrine sweat glands located at the eyelid margin near the base of the eyelashes; they secrete via ducts that open on the lid margin.

zeis.definition: Sebaceous glands associated with the eyelash follicles on the eyelid margin; they secrete sebum to lubricate the eyelashes and can become inflamed in conditions such as an external hordeolum (stye).

glans.definition: The rounded, highly innervated head at the distal end of certain erectile organs, most commonly the penis (glans penis) or the clitoris (glans clitoridis); it is the terminal portion of the erectile tissue and is highly sensitive to touch.

glabrous.definition: Hairless; having a smooth, non-hairy skin surface.

glasgow outcome scale.definition: A scale used to categorize the functional outcome after brain injury into five categories: death, persistent vegetative state, severe disability, moderate disability, and good recovery. An extended version (GOS-E) expands to eight categories.

glandular epithelium.definition: A type of epithelial tissue specialized for secretion, composed of secretory cells that form glands or line secretory ducts; may be unicellular or multicellular, producing substances such as enzymes, mucus, hormones, or other secretions.

glandular tissue.definition: Glandular tissue is the functional (parenchymal) tissue of glands made up of secretory cells that produce and release substances—such as enzymes, hormones, or mucus—either into ducts (exocrine glands) or into the bloodstream (endocrine glands).

glenohumeral joint.definition: A ball-and-socket synovial joint between the head of the humerus and the glenoid cavity of the scapula; the most mobile joint in the body, allowing flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation, and circumduction, stabilized by the glenoid labrum, joint capsule, ligaments, and the rotator cuff muscles.

hypertonia.definition: An increased, often abnormal, muscle tone causing greater resistance to passive stretch; typically due to central nervous system dysfunction (often upper motor neuron lesions) and may present as spasticity, rigidity, or dystonia.

speech disorder.definition: A communication disorder characterized by difficulties with producing, coordinating, or controlling speech sounds, voice, or fluency, resulting in reduced intelligibility. It can involve articulation/phonological disorders, stuttering (fluency disorder), apraxia of speech, or dysarthria, and may be developmental or acquired.

ocular pain.definition: Discomfort, aching, or pain arising from the eye or surrounding structures; a symptom that can be described as a sharp, burning, or gritty sensation in or around the eye, often worsened by eye movement or bright light and may be accompanied by redness, tearing, discharge, or changes in vision.

urinary urgency.definition: A sudden, compelling urge to urinate that is difficult to defer, often followed by involuntary leakage (urge incontinence); commonly associated with overactive bladder and other lower urinary tract disorders.

vaginal moniliasis.definition: A fungal infection of the vagina caused by Candida species (most commonly Candida albicans), characterized by vaginal itching and irritation with a thick, white discharge; also known as candidal vaginitis.

acute angle-closure glaucoma.definition: A sudden, painful, unilateral rise in intraocular pressure caused by abrupt closure of the anterior chamber angle, blocking aqueous humor outflow; presents with severe eye pain, headache, halos, nausea/vomiting, conjunctival injection, decreased vision, and a mid-dilated nonreactive pupil. It is an ophthalmic emergency requiring rapid IOP reduction and definitive treatment with laser peripheral iridotomy or surgical iridectomy.

primary open-angle glaucoma.definition: A chronic, progressive optic neuropathy of unknown cause characterized by retinal ganglion cell death with cupping of the optic disc and corresponding peripheral visual field loss, in the setting of an open anterior chamber angle and typically elevated intraocular pressure (which may be normal in some cases).

peripheral visual field loss.definition: Loss of vision in the peripheral (side) part of the visual field, with intact central vision; can be partial or complete and may affect one or both eyes, commonly due to glaucoma, optic neuropathies, retinal disease, or brain/occipital lesions; detected by visual field testing (perimetry).

trabecular meshwork.definition: A system of fine, mesh-like tissue in the anterior chamber of the eye through which aqueous humor drains; located in the angle where the clear cornea, white sclera, and colored iris join.

tonometry.definition: A glaucoma screening test that measures pressure inside the eye.

glycerol.definition: A simple polyol (1,2,3-propanetriol); a colorless, viscous, sweet-tasting liquid that is miscible with water and used as a solvent and humectant in pharmaceutical preparations; when ingested, it can act as an osmotic laxative and is metabolized to glycerol-3-phosphate that enters glycolysis.

alpha-agonists.definition: Drugs that activate alpha-adrenergic receptors (alpha-1 and/or alpha-2) of the sympathetic nervous system, causing responses such as vasoconstriction and increased blood pressure; effects vary by receptor subtype and can include pupil dilation, reduced nasal secretions, or decreased sympathetic outflow.

topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors.definition: Eye drops that inhibit carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary body, reducing bicarbonate production and aqueous humor formation to lower intraocular pressure in glaucoma or ocular hypertension.

prostaglandin analogs.definition: Compounds that mimic the actions of endogenous prostaglandins by activating prostaglandin receptors; synthetic or natural prostaglandins used therapeutically to induce labor or cervical ripening, reduce intraocular pressure in glaucoma, and protect the gastric mucosa.

iridectomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which a portion of the iris is removed to create or enlarge an opening between the anterior and posterior chambers of the eye, enabling drainage of aqueous humor and reducing intraocular pressure, most often to treat or prevent angle-closure glaucoma.

glaucomatocyclitic crisis.definition: A recurrent unilateral condition characterized by sudden, markedly elevated intraocular pressure during attacks with mild anterior chamber inflammation (cyclitis); a form of hypertensive uveitis also known as Posner-Schlossman syndrome.

posner-schlossman syndrome.definition: Recurrent unilateral ocular inflammatory syndrome with abrupt, markedly elevated intraocular pressure and only mild anterior uveitis (often with keratic precipitates and corneal edema); attacks are typically self-limited over days to weeks, but repeated episodes can risk optic nerve damage. Treated with intraocular pressure–lowering agents and anti-inflammatory drops; antimicrobial/antiviral therapy may be considered if a viral etiology (e.g., CMV) is suspected.

halos.definition: A perceptual phenomenon in which rings or circles appear around bright light sources; commonly due to corneal edema, cataracts, dry eye, or refractive/lens problems, and may be accompanied by glare and decreased night vision.

corneal edema.definition: Swelling of the cornea due to excess fluid in the stroma (and sometimes the epithelium) from endothelial dysfunction or impaired fluid regulation; causes blurred vision and halos around lights with a cloudy, hazy cornea.

glaucoma consummatum.definition: An antiquated term likely referring to advanced or terminal glaucoma, i.e., a fulminant form with progressive, irreversible optic nerve damage and substantial vision loss, often with markedly elevated intraocular pressure; not used in current practice as a formal subtype.

absolute glaucoma.definition: An end-stage form of glaucoma characterized by no light perception (complete loss of vision) and sustained very high intraocular pressure with irreversible optic neuropathy; the eye has no potential for useful vision and is often painful.

glenoid fossa.definition: A shallow articular socket on the lateral scapula (glenoid cavity) that articulates with the head of the humerus to form the shoulder joint; it is lined with hyaline cartilage and rimmed by the fibrocartilaginous glenoid labrum to deepen the socket.

glenoid labrum.definition: A fibrocartilaginous rim surrounding the glenoid cavity of the scapula that deepens the socket and stabilizes the shoulder by providing a margin for the joint capsule and ligaments (the superior portion also serves as the attachment for the biceps tendon).

glenoid.definition: The shallow articular cavity on the lateral aspect of the scapula that articulates with the head of the humerus to form the glenohumeral (shoulder) joint; rimmed by the glenoid labrum.

glenohumeral ligaments.definition: Intrinsic capsular ligaments of the shoulder joint (superior, middle, and inferior glenohumeral ligaments) that reinforce the anterior capsule to stabilize the humeral head against the glenoid and limit excessive translation, especially during abduction and external rotation; the inferior ligaments form an anterior and posterior band with an axillary pouch.

superior glenohumeral ligament.definition: A ligament of the glenohumeral joint that extends from the superior glenoid rim/labrum to the humeral head (often blending with the coracohumeral ligament); it tightens with arm adduction to help stabilize the shoulder, contributing to anterior and superior stability within the rotator interval.

medial glenohumeral ligament.definition: A ligament of the shoulder that reinforces the anterior capsule of the glenohumeral joint, extending from the anterior glenoid rim to the humeral neck (near the lesser tubercle) and aiding anterior stability by limiting forward translation and external rotation of the humerus.

inferior glenohumeral ligament.definition: A thickened part of the inferior capsule of the glenohumeral joint, consisting of anterior and posterior bands with an inferior (axillary) pouch; it provides primary restraint against inferior translation of the humeral head, especially when the arm is abducted.

acromiocoracoid ligament.definition: A ligament that connects the acromion to the coracoid process of the scapula, forming part of the coracoacromial arch and helping to limit upward displacement of the humeral head.

tendon of long head of biceps brachii.word: tendon of long head of biceps brachii
tendon of long head of biceps brachii.definition: The tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii is the portion of the biceps muscle that originates from the supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, passes through the glenohumeral joint in the intertubercular groove of the humerus, and blends with the distal tendon inserting on the radial tuberosity, contributing to elbow flexion and forearm supination and helping stabilize the shoulder joint.

subscapularis muscle.definition: A muscle of the rotator cuff that originates on the anterior surface of the scapula and inserts on the lesser tubercle of the humerus; it medially rotates and adducts the arm and helps stabilize the glenohumeral joint. Innervation: upper and lower subscapular nerves (C5–C6, sometimes C7).

subdeltoid bursa.definition: A fluid-filled lubricating sac in the shoulder, located beneath the deltoid muscle between the deltoid and the glenohumeral joint capsule (often continuous with the subacromial bursa), whose function is to reduce friction during arm movement.

glomerular endothelium.definition: Fenestrated endothelial cells lining the glomerular capillaries, forming the blood-facing component of the glomerular filtration barrier; these fenestrations allow rapid passage of water and small solutes while restricting large proteins, and they interact with the glomerular basement membrane and podocytes to regulate filtration.

gfr.definition: Volume of filtrate produced by the kidneys’ glomeruli per minute; a standard measure of overall kidney function, usually reported as mL/min/1.73 m² and commonly estimated from serum creatinine (eGFR) using equations such as CKD-EPI or MDRD. Normal roughly 90–120 mL/min/1.73 m²; lower values indicate reduced renal function and CKD staging.

glomerular disease.definition: A broad category of kidney diseases characterized by primary or secondary injury to the glomeruli—the kidney’s filtering units—leading to disruption of the glomerular filtration barrier with clinical features such as proteinuria (often nephrotic-range), hematuria, and impaired kidney function (often with edema and hypertension).

glomerulopathy.definition: A disease of the kidney's glomeruli (the filtering units) characterized by structural or functional abnormalities of the glomerular capillary walls, often presenting with proteinuria and impaired kidney function; encompasses noninflammatory glomerular diseases.

glomerular proteinuria.definition: Proteinuria due to damage to the glomerular filtration barrier that increases permeability to plasma proteins, allowing leakage of mainly albumin into the urine; typically of glomerular (not tubular) origin and often nonselective.

globin.definition: A family of soluble, heme-containing globular proteins that bind oxygen and participate in its transport or storage; examples include the subunits of hemoglobin and myoglobin.

methemoglobinuria.definition: Excretion of methemoglobin in the urine, resulting in dark brown to chocolate-colored urine; reflects oxidation of hemoglobin to the ferric form (methemoglobin), often related to oxidative drug or chemical exposure and may accompany methemoglobinemia.

globulinuria.definition: The presence of globulin proteins (non-albumin serum proteins such as immunoglobulins) in the urine; a form of proteinuria in which globulins predominate, often indicating increased glomerular permeability or overflow of immunoglobulins.

globus hystericus.definition: A sensation of a lump or constriction in the throat without any detectable structural obstruction, often linked to anxiety or gastroesophageal reflux, with a typically normal ENT examination.

globose nucleus.definition: A deep cerebellar nucleus; the globose nucleus is the medial component of the interposed nucleus within the cerebellar hemisphere. It receives inhibitory input from Purkinje cells and sends excitatory projections to the red nucleus and ventrolateral thalamus, contributing to the coordination and control of limb movements.

globule.definition: A small rounded particle or droplet; a tiny spherical inclusion found in cells, tissues, or body fluids, such as a lipid (fat) droplet.

gdnf.definition: A secreted neurotrophic factor of the GDNF family that promotes survival and maintenance of certain neurons, especially dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, via signaling through the GFRα1 co-receptor and the RET tyrosine kinase receptor.

gliadin.definition: A class of alcohol-soluble storage proteins in gluten, found in wheat and related grains; a prolamin rich in glutamine and proline that constitutes the immunogenic fraction of gluten and is relatively resistant to digestion.

endomysial antibodies.definition: IgA autoantibodies directed against endomysial connective tissue; a highly specific serologic marker for celiac disease detected by indirect immunofluorescence, indicating gluten-sensitive enteropathy.

gliadin antibodies.definition: Antibodies directed against gliadin, a gluten-derived protein; historically used to screen for celiac disease (antigliadin antibodies), but they are less specific and sensitive than newer tests such as anti-tissue transglutaminase and anti-endomysial antibodies.

glioblastoma multiforme.definition: An aggressive, Grade IV primary brain tumor of astrocytic origin characterized by rapid growth, diffuse infiltration, necrosis, and microvascular proliferation; the most common and deadly adult brain tumor, typically treated with maximal safe surgical resection followed by radiotherapy and temozolomide chemotherapy, with a poor overall prognosis.

gliomata.definition: A group of glial-cell tumors arising from the supportive cells of the brain and spinal cord; gliomata are the plural of glioma and include subtypes such as astrocytomas, oligodendrogliomas, and ependymomas. They are typically infiltrative and graded by malignancy (commonly I–IV), with prognosis and treatment depending on the tumor type and grade; management often involves surgical resection, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy.

gliosarcoma.definition: A rare, high-grade primary brain tumor with two malignant components: glial (usually astrocytic) tissue and a malignant mesenchymal (sarcomatous) component, representing a biphasic variant of glioblastoma.

glioneuroma.definition: A rare, benign neoplasm consisting primarily of mature glial cells with little to no cellular atypia; it is usually slow-growing and treated by surgical excision.

glia.definition: Non-neuronal cells of the nervous system that support and protect neurons by maintaining the extracellular environment, providing nutrients, forming myelin, modulating synaptic activity, and aiding in injury repair (e.g., astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and microglia in the CNS; Schwann cells in the PNS).

glial.definition: Relating to the non-neuronal cells of the nervous system that provide support and nourishment to neurons, insulate axons via myelination, maintain homeostasis, and contribute to immune defense.

galactosylceramide lipidosis.definition: A lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of the enzyme galactocerebrosidase (GALC), leading to accumulation of galactosylceramide and psychosine in oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells with progressive demyelination of the central and peripheral nervous systems; typically presents in infancy with irritability, feeding difficulties, developmental delay, stiffness, and optic atrophy.

glomangiomas.definition: A benign vascular tumor arising from the glomus body, characterized by proliferation of glomus cells around dilated vascular channels; typically presents as a small, painful nodule on the fingers or under the nails and can be solitary or multiple (glomangiomatosis).

glomangiomata.definition: A benign vascular tumor arising from glomus bodies in the dermis, characterized by proliferating glomus cells surrounding dilated vascular channels; often presents as painful nodules and may occur as multiple lesions (glomangiomata), frequently in the subungual or subcutaneous regions.

glomus.definition: An arteriovenous shunt in the dermis consisting of glomus cells around a small vessel, regulating skin blood flow and temperature; a glomus tumor is a benign paraganglioma arising from these cells.

global assessment of functioning.definition: A clinician-rated scale that assigns a single score from 0 to 100 to reflect an individual's overall level of psychological, social, and occupational functioning; higher scores indicate better functioning. It was used in DSM-IV as a global measure of functioning, but in DSM-5 has been largely replaced by the WHODAS 2.0.

global assessment of functioning (gaf).definition: An overall clinician-rated scale (0–100) of a person’s psychological, social, and occupational functioning; higher scores indicate better functioning and lower scores indicate greater impairment. It originated in DSM-IV and has largely been replaced by WHODAS 2.0 in DSM-5.

global aphasia.definition: A severe impairment of all language modalities (speaking, understanding, reading, and writing) due to extensive damage to the language-dominant hemisphere, most often from a large left-hemisphere stroke; patients have markedly reduced spontaneous speech, poor comprehension, and little ability to repeat.

mixed aphasia.definition: An aphasia in which several language abilities—speech fluency, comprehension, naming, and often repetition—are impaired simultaneously, typically from a large left-hemisphere lesion affecting multiple language areas.

inulin.definition: A non-digestible plant polysaccharide (fructan) composed of β(2→1) linked fructose units; not absorbed or metabolized in humans, used as dietary fiber and, clinically, as a marker of glomerular filtration rate since it is freely filtered by the kidney and neither reabsorbed nor secreted.

creatinine clearance.definition: A measure of kidney function quantifying the amount of plasma cleared of creatinine per minute by the kidneys; it approximates glomerular filtration rate and is usually calculated from urine creatinine, urine volume, and plasma creatinine (often via formulas such as Cockcroft–Gault or MDRD) and reported in mL/min.

rhomboidea.definition: Shaped like a rhombus; an adjective used to describe anatomical structures that have a rhomboid (diamond) shape.

mediana.definition: Relating to the middle; in anatomy, the midline plane (midsagittal plane) that divides the body into equal left and right halves, or to structures located along or near that midline.

glomerulosclerosis.definition: A pathologic process characterized by scarring (sclerosis) of the glomeruli—the kidney’s filtration units—resulting in impaired filtration, often with proteinuria, and possible progression to chronic kidney disease; it can be focal or diffuse.

glomerulotubular.definition: Relating to both the glomerulus and the renal tubule; describes the functional interaction between glomerular filtration and tubular reabsorption (e.g., glomerulotubular balance).

balance.definition: The ability to maintain upright position and stable body orientation by integrating sensory information from the vestibular system, vision, and somatosensory inputs; essential for steady gait and preventing falls.

reabsorption.definition: The movement of substances from a filtrate or lumen back into the circulatory system, enabling the body to reclaim water, ions, and nutrients; in the kidney, it refers to the renal tubules reclaiming filtered substances from tubular fluid into the peritubular capillaries.

proximal.definition: Something that is closer to the center of the body.

filtration.definition: A process by which a liquid passes through a semipermeable membrane under pressure, allowing water and small solutes to cross while retaining larger particles; in physiology, the filtration of plasma through glomerular capillaries into Bowman's capsule.

glomustumor.definition: A benign vascular tumor arising from glomus bodies in the dermis, usually subungual, characterized by intense, paroxysmal pain, point tenderness, and cold sensitivity; treated by surgical excision.

glossectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove all or part of the tongue, typically performed to treat tongue cancer.

glossodynia.definition: Painful burning sensation of the tongue without visible mucosal disease; a chronic, often idiopathic tongue pain that may be part of burning mouth syndrome and can be linked to neuropathic, nutritional, or hormonal factors.

glossalgia.definition: Pain, burning, or discomfort of the tongue; a term often used synonymously with glossodynia, which can be idiopathic or related to neuropathic, inflammatory, infectious, nutritional, or systemic factors.

glossoplasty.definition: A surgical repair or reconstruction of the tongue to restore its form or function, typically after trauma, congenital deformities, or tumor resection.

glossopyrosis.definition: A burning sensation of the tongue (often called burning tongue syndrome), typically without visible mucosal abnormalities; may be idiopathic or related to nutritional deficiencies, dry mouth, neuropathy, diabetes, or certain medications.

glossorrhaphy.definition: Surgical suturing of the tongue to repair a laceration or other injury.

glossotrichia.definition: An oral condition in which the filiform papillae on the dorsum of the tongue become elongated and hypertrophied, giving a hairy or fuzzy appearance (lingua pilosa); color can range from white to brown or black and it is usually reversible with improved hygiene and removal of contributing factors such as dry mouth, tobacco use, or certain medications.

glottides.definition: Plural form of the opening between the vocal folds in the larynx; this opening governs airflow during breathing and voice production and helps protect the airway during swallowing.

glottidis.definition: Genitive singular form of glottis; the opening between the vocal cords in the larynx through which air passes.

glossoepiglottic.definition: Relating to the tongue and the epiglottis; describes the mucosal folds that connect the posterior tongue to the epiglottis, forming the vallecula.

hyoglossal.definition: Relating to the tongue and the hyoid bone; most often used to describe the hyoglossus muscle that extends from the hyoid bone to the side of the tongue and depresses the tongue.

glossopathy.definition: A disease or disorder of the tongue; a broad term for tongue pathology not specifying the exact condition.

glossopexy.definition: A surgical procedure in which the tongue is fixed in place by suturing it to the floor of the mouth or mandible to prevent tongue displacement (glossoptosis) and relieve airway obstruction, commonly used in Pierre Robin sequence.

glossopharyngeal.definition: Relating to the glossopharyngeal nerve (the ninth cranial nerve), a mixed nerve that provides sensory innervation to the oropharynx and posterior tongue, taste from the posterior tongue, sensory input from the carotid body and sinus; motor to the stylopharyngeus muscle; and parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland.

glossopharyngealnerve.definition: A mixed cranial nerve (CN IX) that provides sensory and special sensory innervation to the posterior third of the tongue and oropharynx (including taste from the posterior tongue); carries visceral sensory input from the carotid body and sinus; supplies motor fibers to the stylopharyngeus; and carries parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland via the otic ganglion.

glossopharyngealneuralgia.definition: A neuropathic pain syndrome involving the glossopharyngeal nerve, characterized by sudden, severe, lancinating pain in the throat, base of the tongue, tonsillar region, or ear, often triggered by swallowing, chewing, or talking; typically unilateral and may result from vascular compression or demyelination, with treatment including anticonvulsants and, in refractory cases, surgical decompression or nerve intervention.

stylopharyngeus.definition: A pharyngeal muscle that originates from the styloid process of the temporal bone and inserts into the lateral pharyngeal wall; it elevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing and is innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

palatine.definition: Relating to the palate (the roof of the mouth); in anatomy, describing structures in that region, including the bones that form the hard palate.

tonsil.definition: One of the paired masses of lymphoid tissue at the back of the throat (palatine tonsil) that forms part of Waldeyer’s ring; they trap pathogens and initiate immune responses, and can become enlarged or inflamed in tonsillitis.

circumvallate.definition: An anatomical term meaning surrounded by a wall or border; in practice, referring to circumvallate papillae of the tongue—large, dome-shaped taste papillae arranged in a V near the sulcus terminalis, each with a surrounding trench (moat) containing taste buds.

papillae.definition: A small nipple-like projection of tissue; in anatomy, it refers to projections such as dermal papillae (projections of the dermis into the epidermis containing capillaries and nerve endings) and taste papillae on the tongue (which house taste buds).

glucose6phosphate.definition: A phosphorylated form of glucose (phosphate on carbon 6) that serves as a central metabolic intermediate in glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway, and glycogen metabolism; in the liver it can be dephosphorylated to glucose for release into the bloodstream.

glucose6phosphatedehydrogenase.definition: An enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway that oxidizes glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphoglucono-δ-lactone while reducing NADP+ to NADPH; provides reducing power for biosynthesis and protects red blood cells from oxidative damage. Deficiency causes a hereditary X-linked hemolytic anemia triggered by oxidative stress.

gluconeogenesis.definition: A metabolic pathway that synthesizes glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors (notably lactate, glycerol, and glucogenic amino acids), primarily in the liver (and to a lesser extent the kidney), during fasting or carbohydrate restriction, by bypassing the irreversible steps of glycolysis to maintain circulating glucose levels; regulated by hormones such as glucagon and cortisol.

glyconeogenesis.definition: A metabolic pathway that generates glucose from non-carbohydrate substrates (such as lactate, glycerol, and glucogenic amino acids), predominantly in the liver and to a lesser extent in the kidneys, activated during fasting or low-carbohydrate states.

glucosetolerancetest.definition: A diagnostic test in which a person ingests a standard glucose solution after fasting and blood glucose is measured at intervals (commonly at 0 and 2 hours) to assess glucose metabolism; used to diagnose diabetes mellitus, impaired glucose tolerance, and gestational diabetes.

glucosuria.definition: The presence of glucose in the urine, typically because blood glucose exceeds the kidney’s ability to reabsorb it (renal threshold ~180 mg/dL), though it can also occur with proximal tubule dysfunction or certain medications.

glucagonoma.definition: A rare pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor arising from alpha cells that overproduces glucagon, leading to hyperglucagonemia and a syndrome of diabetes/hyperglycemia, necrolytic migratory erythema, weight loss, stomatitis and cheilitis, anemia, and sometimes thromboembolism.

glucagonomasyndrome.definition: A paraneoplastic syndrome caused by a glucagon-secreting pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, characterized most notably by necrolytic migratory erythema, weight loss, diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance, stomatitis or cheilitis, glossitis, anemia, and sometimes diarrhea or venous thrombosis.

glucagontest.definition: A provocative diagnostic test in which glucagon is administered to stimulate release of growth hormone (and sometimes cortisol) from the pituitary–adrenal axis, used to assess growth hormone reserve and diagnose GH deficiency in children and adults; involves serial blood sampling over several hours after injection, with possible side effects including nausea, vomiting, and abdominal discomfort.

diabetesmellitus.definition: A group of metabolic disorders characterized by chronic hyperglycemia due to defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or both; includes type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, and gestational diabetes, with risk of microvascular and macrovascular complications if untreated.

pancreaticinsufficiency.definition: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency is the failure of the pancreas to produce or deliver adequate digestive enzymes (lipase, amylase, proteases) and bicarbonate, leading to maldigestion and malabsorption—most notably fat malabsorption (steatorrhea)—and weight loss; commonly caused by chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, pancreatic duct obstruction, or pancreatic resection.

glycogenolysis.definition: Glycogenolysis is the metabolic process of breaking down glycogen into glucose-1-phosphate (and ultimately free glucose), primarily in the liver and skeletal muscle, to raise blood glucose; it is catalyzed by glycogen phosphorylase and debranching enzymes and stimulated by hormones such as glucagon and epinephrine.

hexokinase.definition: A cytosolic enzyme that catalyzes the phosphorylation of glucose (and other hexoses) to glucose-6-phosphate using ATP, initiating glycolysis; exists in several isoforms (HK1–HK4) with tissue-specific distribution and is inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate in most tissues.

bronzing.definition: Bronzing: a bronze-brown discoloration of the skin due to increased melanin production or iron deposition, as seen in conditions such as Addison disease or hemochromatosis.

adrenocorticotropic.definition: Pertaining to stimulation of the adrenal cortex; specifically, a pituitary hormone that stimulates the adrenal cortex to synthesize and secrete glucocorticoids (e.g., cortisol).

prednisolone.definition: A synthetic glucocorticoid corticosteroid with potent anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects used to treat inflammatory and autoimmune conditions; available in oral, injectable, or topical forms.

methylprednisolone.definition: A synthetic glucocorticoid corticosteroid with potent anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects; it decreases inflammatory mediator production and modulates immune responses, used in a wide range of conditions such as allergic reactions, asthma, inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, and MS relapses. It can be given orally, intravenously, or intramuscularly.

glucogenesis.definition: The formation of glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors (such as lactate, glycerol, and certain amino acids), predominantly in the liver and to a lesser extent in the kidney; the process is commonly known as gluconeogenesis.

glp1.definition: A peptide hormone produced by intestinal L cells that acts as an incretin, stimulating glucose-dependent insulin secretion, inhibiting glucagon release, slowing gastric emptying, and reducing appetite.

glucagonlikepeptide1.definition: An incretin hormone produced by enteroendocrine L-cells in the gut that enhances insulin secretion in a glucose-dependent manner, inhibits glucagon release, slows gastric emptying, and promotes satiety.

parotid.definition: Relating to the parotid gland, the largest salivary gland located in the cheek near the ear; it secretes saliva via the parotid duct.

parotidgland.definition: A major paired salivary gland located in the cheek just anterior to the ear; it secretes serous saliva via Stensen's duct into the oral cavity and is the largest of the salivary glands.

glucophage.definition: A brand-name oral antidiabetic medication (metformin) used to treat type 2 diabetes; it lowers hepatic glucose production and improves insulin sensitivity, and is also used to manage polycystic ovary syndrome.

glucosegalactosemalabsorption.definition: A rare congenital disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in SLC5A1, encoding the intestinal sodium-glucose cotransporter SGLT1, leading to defective absorption of glucose and galactose in the small intestine and resulting in severe osmotic diarrhea and dehydration in infancy; management requires strict avoidance of glucose and galactose (often with fructose-based formulas) and proper rehydration/electrolyte support.

glycocholic.definition: Pertaining to glycocholic acid, a conjugated bile acid formed by conjugation of cholic acid with glycine; a component of bile involved in fat digestion.

glucosyl.definition: A glucosyl group is a glucose moiety attached to another molecule through a glycosidic bond, typically at the anomeric carbon (C1) of glucose. Used to describe glucose residues in glycosides and glycoconjugates.

glucosuric.definition: Relating to the presence of glucose in the urine (glucosuria).

glucotrol.definition: A brand-name oral antidiabetic medication of the sulfonylurea class that stimulates pancreatic insulin release to lower blood glucose in type 2 diabetes; used with diet and exercise; may cause hypoglycemia; contraindicated in type 1 diabetes and diabetic ketoacidosis; use with caution in hepatic or renal impairment and in the elderly.

glipizide.definition: A second-generation oral sulfonylurea antidiabetic medication that increases pancreatic insulin secretion by closing ATP‑sensitive potassium channels in beta cells; indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus; can cause hypoglycemia and weight gain and is typically taken with meals.

toluene.definition: A colorless, volatile aromatic hydrocarbon solvent (methylbenzene; formula C7H8) used in paints, coatings, inks, and adhesives; inhalation or dermal exposure can cause central nervous system depression and dizziness, and chronic exposure may lead to renal tubular acidosis, nephrotoxicity, and potential liver injury.

glue sniffing.definition: Inhalation of volatile solvents found in glues or adhesives to achieve a short-lived intoxicating effect, typically by sniffing or huffing; acute effects include dizziness, euphoria, slurred speech, and impaired coordination, while chronic use can lead to brain injury, peripheral neuropathy, liver and kidney damage, and risk of sudden death.

glutamate.definition: An acidic amino acid, the anionic form of glutamic acid, that acts as the principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system; it activates ionotropic receptors (AMPA, NMDA, kainate) and metabotropic receptors; synthesized in neurons from glutamine by glutaminase; essential for fast excitatory synaptic transmission, synaptic plasticity, and cerebral metabolism; also encountered in foods as various salts.

glutamic acid decarboxylase.definition: An enzyme, pyridoxal phosphate–dependent, that catalyzes the decarboxylation of glutamate to gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system; two major neuronal isoforms, GAD65 and GAD67, differ in localization and regulation.

insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus.definition: A form of diabetes mellitus caused by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, resulting in absolute insulin deficiency and requiring lifelong insulin therapy.

glutamic acidemia.definition: A biochemical state defined by an abnormally elevated concentration of glutamic acid (glutamate) in the plasma, reflecting disturbance of amino acid metabolism or excretion (as seen with liver or kidney disease or certain inborn errors of metabolism); it is not a single, distinct disease.

glutamic acid hydrochloride.definition: A hydrochloride salt of the amino acid glutamic acid (L-glutamic acid monohydrochloride); a water-soluble form used to supply glutamate in pharmaceutical and biochemical contexts. In solution it dissociates to give protonated glutamic acid and chloride ions.

hypoacidity.definition: Decreased production of gastric hydrochloric acid in the stomach (hypochlorhydria), resulting in a higher-than-normal gastric pH and impaired digestion and absorption of nutrients such as iron, calcium, and vitamin B12.

systemic acidosis.definition: A body-wide acid–base disorder in which the arterial pH is below normal due to an excess of hydrogen ions or a loss of bicarbonate, reflecting a disturbance that affects the whole organism; it can be metabolic (increased acid production or bicarbonate loss) or respiratory (CO2 retention from hypoventilation).

glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the transfer of an amino group from aspartate to alpha-ketoglutarate to form oxaloacetate and glutamate; found in liver, heart, skeletal muscle, and other tissues, and measured in blood as a marker of tissue injury (particularly hepatocellular injury or myocardial damage).

glutamic pyruvic transaminase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the transfer of an amino group from L-alanine to α-ketoglutarate, producing pyruvate and L-glutamate; predominantly located in the liver and widely used clinically as a marker of hepatocellular injury (elevated levels indicate liver damage). Also known as alanine aminotransferase (ALT).

glutargin.definition: Not found in standard medical dictionaries; likely a brand-name drug (often from Russia) that combines arginine and glutamate (or their salts). Exact composition and indications vary by country. If you can share the country or an alternative spelling, I can give a more precise definition.

glutaric aciduria.definition: An autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by deficiency of the mitochondrial enzyme glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase, leading to accumulation of glutaric and 3-hydroxyglutaric acids and brain injury, typically presenting in infancy with macrocephaly and a risk of dystonia after febrile illness.

glutathione.definition: A tripeptide antioxidant formed from glutamate, cysteine, and glycine; the major intracellular thiol that buffers oxidative stress and participates in detoxification, existing in reduced (GSH) and oxidized (GSSG) forms.

gluteal.definition: Relating to the buttocks or the gluteal region; pertaining to the gluteal muscles (gluteus maximus, medius, and minimus).

gluteal fold.definition: A skin crease at the junction of the buttock and the posterior thigh, marking the inferior boundary of the gluteal region.

gluteal reflex.definition: Not a standard clinical reflex; there is no widely recognized reflex arc or routinely tested response in the gluteal region during neurological examination. Any gluteal muscle contraction in response to stimulation would not be part of a formal, validated reflex test.

gluteal region.definition: The gluteal region is the posterior aspect of the hip/buttock area of the pelvis, containing the gluteal muscles (gluteus maximus, medius, and minimus) and surrounding fascia and fat; bounded superiorly by the iliac crests and inferiorly by the gluteal folds.

gluteal tuberosity.definition: A roughened area on the posterior aspect of the proximal femur that serves as the insertion site for the gluteus maximus.

gluteus minimus.definition: A small, deep gluteal muscle located beneath the gluteus medius; it abducts and medially rotates the thigh and helps stabilize the pelvis during walking. Innervation: superior gluteal nerve.

von gierke's disease.definition: A glycogen storage disease (type I) caused by deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase, leading to impaired glucose release from the liver during fasting; presents with severe fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, and increased glycogen storage in liver and kidneys.

pompe's disease.definition: A rare inherited lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of the enzyme acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA), leading to glycogen buildup in lysosomes of muscle and heart tissue; infantile-onset disease presents with cardiomyopathy and hypotonia, while later-onset forms cause progressive skeletal muscle weakness and respiratory failure. Treated with enzyme replacement therapy and supportive care.

mcardle's disease.definition: A glycogen storage disease (type V) caused by autosomal recessive deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase (myophosphorylase), leading to impaired glycogenolysis in skeletal muscle. It presents with exercise-induced muscle cramps, weakness, and myoglobinuria after strenuous activity, with little or no rise in blood lactate during exercise and a compensatory “second wind” with continued activity.
