gullet.definition: The esophagus; a muscular tube that transports swallowed food and liquids from the pharynx to the stomach by coordinated peristaltic contractions.

gumboil.definition: A localized purulent swelling of the gingiva caused by drainage from a dental abscess, often presenting as a painful lump that may discharge pus via a sinus tract and typically related to a necrotic tooth pulp or chronic periodontal infection.

gumma.definition: A soft, necrotizing granulomatous lesion of tertiary (late) syphilis that may ulcerate and destroy surrounding tissues.

gurgle.definition: A bubbling or splashing sound produced by the movement of gas and fluid within a hollow organ, most commonly heard in the abdomen as audible bowel sounds (borborygmi).

gurney.definition: A wheeled stretcher used to transport patients, typically in hospitals and ambulances.

gurry.definition: An archaic or dialect term referring to fish offal or spoiled fish used as bait; not a recognized term in modern medical terminology.

gustation.definition: The sense of taste; the sensory perception produced by taste receptor cells in taste buds (primarily on the tongue) in response to tastants, enabling perception of the five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami.

gustatory.definition: Relating to the sense of taste; pertaining to taste perception.

gustatory hallucination.definition: A false perception of taste in the absence of a taste stimulus, often described as a persistent or episodic metallic, bitter, or sweet taste; associated with temporal lobe dysfunction, seizures, delirium, migraines, or psychosis.

gustatory organ.definition: An organ responsible for the sense of taste; the tongue contains taste buds on its papillae that detect tastants and transduce them into neural signals.

gustatory papilla.definition: Any of the tongue papillae that contain taste buds and mediate taste; primarily fungiform, circumvallate, and foliate papillae, while filiform papillae lack taste buds.

gut.definition: The gastrointestinal tract—the alimentary canal from the esophagus to the anus, including the stomach and intestines—responsible for digestion, nutrient absorption, and waste elimination; colloquially used to refer to the intestines.

gut-associated lymphoid tissue.definition: An integral component of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue in the gastrointestinal tract, comprising organized lymphoid structures (such as Peyer’s patches and the appendix) and diffuse lymphoid tissue in the lamina propria; it contains immune cells (B and T lymphocytes, dendritic cells) and M cells that sample luminal antigens to initiate mucosal immune responses and drive secretory IgA production.

peyers patches.definition: Aggregates of lymphoid tissue in the ileum, part of gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT), consisting of lymphoid follicles with germinal centers; overlying M cells sample luminal antigens and deliver them to immune cells, initiating mucosal immune responses and IgA production.

guthrie bacterial inhibition assay.definition: A neonatal screening test for phenylketonuria using a phenylalanine–auxotrophic Bacillus subtilis on a growth-inhibitor medium; dried blood from a heel-prick provides phenylalanine, which overcomes the inhibition and allows bacterial growth, with the extent of growth indicating phenylalanine levels.

guthrie test.definition: A historical newborn screening test for phenylketonuria that uses a dried blood spot on filter paper and a bacterial inhibition assay to detect elevated phenylalanine levels; a positive result prompts confirmatory testing.

treponema.definition: A genus of slender, spiral-shaped, motile, Gram-negative bacteria (spirochetes) with periplasmic flagella; several species cause human treponematoses such as syphilis, yaws, pinta, and bejel.

intravenous immunoglobulins.definition: An intravenous preparation of pooled IgG antibodies derived from thousands of donor plasmas, administered to replace or augment humoral immunity and to modulate immune responses in a range of immunodeficiency and autoimmune/inflammatory disorders.

nerve conduction velocity.definition: A measure of the speed at which an electrical impulse travels along a peripheral nerve, usually expressed in meters per second; obtained during nerve conduction studies by stimulating the nerve and recording the evoked response at a distant site; influenced by myelin integrity, axon diameter, temperature, and age; used to evaluate peripheral neuropathies and distinguish demyelinating from axonal processes.

central venous line.definition: A catheter inserted into a large central vein (e.g., internal jugular, subclavian, or femoral) with its tip in the lower superior vena cava near the cavoatrial junction, used for central venous access to administer medications and fluids, parenteral nutrition, monitor hemodynamics, and obtain blood samples.

gastric feeding tube.definition: A tube inserted into the stomach to provide enteral nutrition and medications, usually placed through the nose or mouth (nasogastric/orogastric) for short-term use or via a gastrostomy for long-term feeding.

intravenous catheter.definition: A flexible tube inserted into a vein to deliver intravenous fluids or medications and to obtain blood samples; used for short- or long-term venous access.

bradyarrhythmias.definition: Slower-than-normal heart rhythms resulting from impaired impulse formation or conduction within the cardiac electrical system, typically defined as a resting heart rate below 60 beats per minute in adults; includes sinus bradycardia and various degrees of atrioventricular block, and may be asymptomatic or cause dizziness, fatigue, or syncope.

ventilator.definition: Machine that inflates the lungs with oxygen.

partial denture.definition: A removable dental prosthesis designed to replace one or more missing teeth in a jaw, anchored to the remaining natural teeth and sometimes to the mucosa, and held in place with clasps or precision attachments.

abutment teeth.definition: Natural teeth that act as anchors to support a dental prosthesis (such as a fixed bridge or removable partial denture); these teeth are typically crowned to provide retention, stability, and load distribution for the prosthesis.

centric relation.definition: The maxillomandibular relationship in which the condyles articulate anterior-superiorly against the articular eminences with the discs properly interposed, independent of tooth contact.

alveolar processes.definition: The thickened ridges of bone in the maxilla and mandible that form the tooth sockets (alveoli) and support the teeth, providing attachment for the periodontal ligaments.

labia majora.definition: A pair of large, fatty skin folds that form the outer aspect of the female vulva and protect the openings of the vagina and urethra.

hyperphenylalaninemia.definition: An abnormal elevation of the amino acid phenylalanine in the blood, most commonly due to defective phenylalanine hydroxylase activity or impaired BH4 cofactor function, as seen in phenylketonuria and related metabolic disorders.

bacillus subtilis.definition: A Gram-positive, rod-shaped, endospore-forming bacterium commonly found in soil; typically nonpathogenic but can be opportunistic in immunocompromised individuals and is widely used as a model organism in microbiology and biotechnology.

gutta-percha.definition: A natural polymer derived from the latex of Palaquium gutta trees, used in dentistry as a root canal filling material; it is heated to become pliable and then compacted, and it hardens to seal the canal when used with sealer.

gutta-percha point.definition: A cone-shaped, flexible filling material made from gutta-percha used to obturate (seal) a cleaned and shaped root canal in endodontic therapy.

endodontic sealer.definition: A cement-like material used in root canal obturation to seal the root canal system by filling gaps, irregularities, and dentinal tubules, thereby preventing bacterial leakage and periapical inflammation; it is placed with gutta-percha and sets to form a fluid-tight seal. Types include zinc oxide eugenol, epoxy resin, and calcium silicate-based sealers.

dental imaging.definition: Imaging techniques used to visualize teeth, their supporting bone, and surrounding soft tissues for diagnosis, treatment planning, and follow-up. Common modalities include intraoral radiographs (bitewing and periapical), panoramic radiography, and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT); advanced applications may use MRI or ultrasound in select cases.

periodontal pockets.definition: Pathologic deepening of the gingival sulcus caused by inflammatory destruction of the supporting periodontal structures (migration of the junctional epithelium, loss of periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone resorption), creating a space between tooth and gum that harbors bacteria; clinically, probing depths greater than about 3 mm indicate a pocket. Pockets can be classified as suprabony or infrabony based on the base of the pocket relative to the crest of the alveolar bone.

guttate psoriasis.definition: A form of psoriasis characterized by numerous small, drop-like salmon-pink to red papules with fine scaling, often preceded by a streptococcal throat infection, most commonly affecting the trunk and proximal limbs; lesions may resolve spontaneously within weeks to months.

pustular psoriasis.definition: An inflammatory skin condition marked by sterile pustules arising on erythematous skin; it can present as generalized pustular disease with widespread noninfectious pustules and systemic symptoms, or as localized pustules on the hands and feet (palmoplantar variant).

streptococcal pharyngitis.definition: An acute infection of the pharynx caused by group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes). It typically presents with sudden sore throat, fever, tonsillar exudates, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and usually no cough; diagnosed by rapid antigen detection test or throat culture, and treated with appropriate antibiotics (eg, penicillin or amoxicillin).

beta-hemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis.definition: An acute pharyngitis caused by beta-hemolytic streptococci, most commonly group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes); typically presents with sore throat, fever, tonsillar exudates, and tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, often without cough, and is diagnosed by rapid antigen testing or throat culture and treated with appropriate antibiotics.

angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.definition: Therapy using medications that inhibit the angiotensin-converting enzyme, thereby reducing angiotensin II production and aldosterone-mediated vasoconstriction and sodium retention. This results in vasodilation, lower blood pressure, and decreased cardiac workload; it protects cardiac and renal function and is used to treat hypertension, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, post‑myocardial infarction, and proteinuric kidney disease such as diabetic nephropathy. Common adverse effects include cough, hyperkalemia, and rarely angioedema; contraindicated in pregnancy and requires monitoring of renal function and electrolytes.

hiv-associated dementia.definition: A severe neurocognitive disorder caused by HIV infection of the central nervous system, characterized by substantial deficits in memory, attention, processing speed, and executive function, along with motor dysfunction and behavioral changes, leading to impairment in daily functioning; historically known as AIDS dementia complex.

hacek.definition: An acronym for a group of fastidious Gram-negative bacteria (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, and Kingella) that are a common cause of infective endocarditis.

eikenella.definition: A genus of Gram-negative, non-spore-forming, facultatively anaerobic bacilli in the Neisseriaceae family; part of the normal human oral flora and an opportunistic pathogen associated with bite wound infections and periodontitis, known for corroding culture media.

kingella.definition: A genus of Gram-negative, oxidase-positive, nonmotile coccobacilli in the family Neisseriaceae. They commonly inhabit the oropharynx and can be associated with invasive infections (notably septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, bacteremia, and endocarditis), particularly in children; identification is often challenging and may require culture on enriched media and molecular methods.

haemangioma.definition: A benign vascular tumor formed by an abnormal proliferation of blood vessels.

haemarthrosis.definition: Bleeding into a joint cavity, typically after trauma or in patients with a bleeding disorder, causing joint swelling, pain, warmth, and reduced range of motion; can lead to cartilage damage if recurrent.

hematocytoblast.definition: A primitive hematopoietic stem cell in the bone marrow that differentiates into all formed elements of blood (red cells, white cells, and platelets).

hematology.definition: The branch of medicine that studies blood, the hematopoietic system, and blood disorders, including laboratory analysis of blood cells, coagulation, and related diseases.

hematomyelia.definition: Bleeding into the spinal cord parenchyma (intramedullary hemorrhage), often presenting with acute back or neck pain and rapid onset of motor and sensory deficits; can result from trauma, spinal vascular malformations, tumors, or anticoagulation.

haematocele.definition: A collection of blood within a preexisting cavity or sac; in the scrotum, blood within the tunica vaginalis around the testis, typically following trauma or surgery.

haemochromatosis.definition: An iron-overload disorder caused by excessive intestinal iron absorption and progressive deposition of iron in tissues (especially the liver, heart, and pancreas); may lead to liver cirrhosis, diabetes, cardiomyopathy, and skin hyperpigmentation; commonly due to mutations in iron-regulation genes (most often HFE); treated with regular phlebotomy and, if necessary, iron chelation.

hemochromatosis.definition: A genetic or acquired disorder characterized by excessive absorption of dietary iron, leading to iron overload with deposition in tissues (especially liver, heart, and pancreas) and causing liver disease, diabetes mellitus, and cardiomyopathy; treated primarily with therapeutic phlebotomy, with iron chelation if phlebotomy is contraindicated.

haemoconcentration.definition: A relative increase in the concentration of blood cells and plasma proteins in the blood due to a decrease in circulating plasma volume.

hemoconcentration.definition: Relative increase in the concentration of blood cells and plasma proteins in the circulating blood caused by a reduction in plasma volume, typically from dehydration or fluid loss; often evidenced by elevated hematocrit and hemoglobin.

haemodialysis.definition: A procedure to remove waste products and excess fluids from the blood when the kidneys cannot adequately perform these functions, by circulating blood through an artificial kidney (dialyser) in a dialysis machine and returning it to the body.

heme.definition: An iron-containing porphyrin prosthetic group (iron protoporphyrin IX) that forms the prosthetic component of several proteins, notably hemoglobin and myoglobin, enabling reversible oxygen binding and supporting electron transfer in cytochromes.

gynecologist.definition: A doctor who helps women stay healthy treats diseases of the womb and related organs.

gynecologic.definition: Relating to gynecology; pertaining to the female reproductive system and its medical care.

gynecological.definition: Relating to gynecology, the medical specialty concerned with the health of the female reproductive system and its disorders.

gynaecoid.definition: Relating to the gynecoid pelvis; the female-type pelvic shape with a rounded inlet and wide subpubic angle, regarded as the most favorable for vaginal delivery.

gynaecology.definition: The medical specialty concerned with the health of the female reproductive system, including the uterus, ovaries, vagina, and related structures, and with the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of disorders affecting these organs.

gynaecomastia.definition: A benign enlargement of male breast glandular tissue caused by an imbalance between estrogen and androgen activity on breast tissue; it can be physiological (neonatal, pubertal, older age) or due to drugs, systemic disease, or endocrine disorders.

gynephobia.definition: An irrational, persistent fear of women that leads to avoidance, distress, or impairment in social, occupational, or other functioning; a type of specific phobia (also referred to as gynophobia).

gynandrous.definition: Having both male and female reproductive organs; in botany, describing a flower that contains both stamens (androecium) and pistils (gynoecium), i.e., hermaphroditic.

gynogamone.definition: Not a standard medical term; conceptually, a hypothetical substance that would influence female gamete formation or fertilization (oogenesis or gamete function).

gyrase.definition: A bacterial enzyme that is a type II topoisomerase; it introduces negative supercoils into double-stranded DNA and relieves torsional strain during replication and transcription, using ATP energy; a target of fluoroquinolone antibiotics.

gyromagnetic ratio.definition: A proportionality constant relating a particle's magnetic moment to its angular momentum (μ = γ J). It determines the spin's Larmor precession in a magnetic field, with angular frequency ω0 = γ B0; commonly expressed in rad s−1 T−1 (or Hz T−1).

habermann disease.definition: A rare neutrophilic dermatosis characterized by recurrent, sterile subcorneal pustules on the trunk and intertriginous areas, often with a relapsing course; histology shows subcorneal neutrophilic pustules with minimal epidermal change.

mucha habermann disease.definition: An acute/subacute inflammatory skin condition in the pityriasis lichenoides spectrum, presenting with crops of small red papules that rapidly become vesicular or necrotic crusted lesions, often varioliform (pox-like); typically self-limited but may relapse.

haas method.definition: I can’t locate a standard medical definition for “Haas method.” This term appears in different fields and may refer to a technique named after someone in a specific specialty. Could you specify the medical field or provide a source citation (e.g., dentistry, orthopedics, psychology)? I can then give you a precise definition.

gxt.definition: A cardiopulmonary stress test in which exercise intensity is progressively increased to evaluate cardiovascular response and exercise tolerance, typically performed on a treadmill or stationary bike with monitoring of ECG, blood pressure, heart rate, and symptoms.

gray.definition:
- A color between black and white; in medical descriptions, tissues rich in neuron cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers—such as the gray matter of the brain and spinal cord—often appear this color.
- In neuroanatomy, the portion of the central nervous system consisting mainly of neuronal cell bodies, dendrites, and unmyelinated axons, which contrasts with white matter that contains myelinated axons.

haemodilution.definition: Dilution of blood constituents caused by an increase in plasma volume, resulting in a fall in hematocrit and hemoglobin concentration; it can occur with intravenous fluid administration or during procedures such as cardiopulmonary bypass, and is sometimes used clinically to reduce blood viscosity and perioperative blood loss.

haemofiltration.definition: Renal replacement therapy that removes water and solutes by convective clearance across a semipermeable membrane, with replacement fluid added to restore volume and solute balance; commonly performed as continuous renal replacement therapy for acute kidney injury, especially in critically ill patients.

haemoglobinometer.definition: A device for measuring the concentration of hemoglobin in a blood sample, typically by colorimetric or photometric analysis to estimate the Hb level.

haemoglobinopathy.definition: An inherited group of disorders affecting the hemoglobin molecule, due to qualitative (structural) defects or quantitative (production) defects of globin chains, resulting in anemia and related complications.

haemoglobinuria.definition: The presence of free hemoglobin in the urine, typically due to intravascular haemolysis; urine is often dark or tea-colored, and dipstick may be positive for blood with few or no red blood cells on microscopy.

haemolysin.definition: A toxin that lyses red blood cells, causing hemolysis; produced by certain bacteria and some other organisms, often acting by forming pores in the erythrocyte membrane or by enzymatic disruption of membrane components.

haemolysis.definition: The rupture or destruction of red blood cells, resulting in the release of hemoglobin into the blood plasma (intravascular hemolysis) or clearance by macrophages in the spleen (extravascular hemolysis).

haemolytic.definition: Relating to or causing the destruction of red blood cells (hemolysis).

haemoperfusion.definition: A procedure in which blood is circulated through an adsorbent cartridge (such as charcoal or resin) to remove toxins or drugs from the bloodstream, usually used in cases of poisoning or overdose and sometimes for inflammatory mediators.

haemopericardium.definition: The accumulation of blood in the pericardial sac, usually from trauma or rupture of a cardiac or great vessel, potentially causing cardiac tamponade.

haemoperitoneum.definition: The presence of blood within the peritoneal cavity, usually from intra-abdominal hemorrhage due to trauma, ruptured organs, ectopic pregnancy, or postoperative bleeding; may cause acute abdominal symptoms and signs of hypovolemia, often requiring urgent evaluation and intervention.

haemophilia.definition: A genetic bleeding disorder caused by deficiency or dysfunction of coagulation factors, most commonly factor VIII (hemophilia A) or factor IX (hemophilia B), leading to prolonged bleeding after injury or surgery. It is X-linked recessive, predominantly affecting males, with severity determined by remaining factor activity; treatment includes factor replacement therapy and, for mild cases, desmopressin.

haemolyticus.definition: Relating to or causing hemolysis—the destruction of red blood cells.

ducreyi.definition: A species epithet used in the binomial name of a Gram-negative, facultatively anaerobic bacterium that causes chancroid, a sexually transmitted infection characterized by painful genital ulcers.

haemoptysis.definition: Coughing up blood or blood-streaked sputum from the lower respiratory tract (bronchial tree), commonly due to infection, inflammation, malignancy, or vascular causes; requires evaluation to identify source and underlying etiology.

haemorrhage.definition: The escape of blood from the circulatory system, either externally (visible bleeding) or internally (into tissues or body cavities), due to rupture or injury of blood vessels or impaired hemostasis.

haemorrhagic.definition: Relating to hemorrhage; characterized by bleeding or a tendency to bleed.

haemorrhoid.definition: A swollen vein in the lower rectum or anal canal; a common anorectal vascular condition that can be internal or external, often presenting with painless rectal bleeding, itching, and discomfort.

hemorrhoid.definition: A swollen vein in the lower rectum or anus caused by dilation of the venous cushions in that area; it can be internal (above the dentate line) or external (below) and may cause bleeding, itching, or discomfort.

haemorrhoidectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove hemorrhoids by excising hemorrhoidal tissue from the anal canal; typically used for symptomatic or prolapsed internal hemorrhoids and performed with either open or closed techniques under anesthesia. Also known as hemorrhoid removal.

hemorrhoidectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove hemorrhoids by excising the swollen anal cushions (hemorrhoidal tissue) from the anorectal region, typically performed for symptomatic internal or external hemorrhoids.

haemosiderin.definition: An iron-storage pigment formed from ferritin by partial degradation; an insoluble ferric iron–containing pigment that accumulates in macrophages during iron overload or after hemorrhage (stains with Prussian blue).

hemosiderin.definition: An iron-storage pigment consisting of aggregated ferritin that stores iron in tissues; formed during hemoglobin breakdown and commonly seen after hemorrhage or iron overload.

haemostasis.definition: The physiological process of stopping bleeding after vascular injury, involving platelet plug formation and coagulation to form a stable fibrin clot, followed by clot retraction and fibrinolysis.

haemostatic.definition: Relating to stopping bleeding; an agent that promotes the body's clotting processes to achieve haemostasis.

haemothorax.definition: Blood in the pleural cavity (the space between the visceral and parietal pleura), typically caused by thoracic trauma or rupture of intrathoracic vessels, leading to chest pain, dyspnea, and reduced breath sounds; large collections may cause hypovolemia and respiratory distress.

halcinonide.definition: A potent synthetic topical corticosteroid used to treat inflammatory skin conditions (e.g., eczema, dermatitis, psoriasis) by reducing inflammation, itching, and redness.

halcion.definition: A short-acting benzodiazepine hypnotic (triazolam) used for short-term treatment of insomnia; it enhances GABA-A receptor activity, has rapid onset, and carries risks of daytime drowsiness, anterograde amnesia, cognitive/psychomotor impairment, dependence, and withdrawal; not recommended for long-term use.

haldol.definition: A potent first-generation antipsychotic (dopamine D2 receptor antagonist) used to treat schizophrenia and other psychoses; also used for acute agitation, delirium, and certain motor disorders; available orally, intramuscularly, or intravenously; carries a high risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and QT interval prolongation.

half-life.definition: The time required for the amount of a substance in the body or its concentration to decrease by 50%, due to elimination or decay.

half-normal.definition: An absolute value of a zero-mean normal random variable; a one-sided, positively skewed distribution used to model nonnegative measurements or statistics derived from symmetric measurement errors. It is a special case of the folded normal distribution with mu = 0 (PDF ∝ exp(-x^2/(2σ^2)) for x ≥ 0).

epstein-barr.definition: An enveloped double-stranded DNA herpesvirus that primarily infects B lymphocytes and epithelial cells; transmitted mainly through saliva; causes infectious mononucleosis and is associated with several malignancies; establishes lifelong latent infection in B cells.

haglund.definition: A bony enlargement of the posterior aspect of the calcaneus (heel bone) that irritates the retrocalcaneal bursa and Achilles tendon, causing painful posterior heel impingement.

haglund's.definition: A bony enlargement at the posterior superior aspect of the calcaneus (heel bone) that can irritate the retrocalcaneal bursa and Achilles tendon, causing posterior heel pain; commonly called a pump bump.

deformity.definition: Something that is not a normal shape or is oddly shaped.

hailey-hailey.definition: An autosomal-dominant genetic skin disorder (also called familial benign chronic pemphigus) characterized by recurrent vesicular and crusted erosions in intertriginous areas due to acantholysis of epidermal keratinocytes from mutations in ATP2A2 encoding the SERCA2 calcium pump.

hairline.definition: A very fine fracture line in a bone that is typically nondisplaced and may be difficult to detect on X-ray.

hairy-cell.definition: A rare chronic B-cell leukemia characterized by malignant B lymphocytes with hair-like cytoplasmic projections; presents with fatigue, infections, splenomegaly, and cytopenias; bone marrow aspiration often yields a dry tap; immunophenotype commonly includes CD11c, CD25, and CD103; frequently harbors the BRAF V600E mutation; first-line therapy typically involves purine analogs such as cladribine or pentostatin with high response rates.

catagen.definition: The transition phase of the hair-growth cycle.

stratum.definition: A layer or bed of tissue; a defined sheet of cells within a tissue or organ (for example, one of the epidermal layers).

corneum.definition: The outermost layer of the epidermis composed of dead, flattened keratinocytes (corneocytes) filled with keratin; forms the protective barrier and reduces transepidermal water loss.

arrector.definition: A small smooth muscle attached to a hair follicle that contracts to erect the hair, causing goosebumps in response to cold, fear, or other stimuli.

pili.definition: Hair-like keratinized filaments that grow from hair follicles in humans and animals. In microbiology, pili are slender protein appendages on bacterial surfaces that mediate adhesion to surfaces and, in some cases, DNA transfer during conjugation.

achilles.definition: A thick band of connective tissue that attaches the calf muscles to the heel bone (calcaneus), enabling plantarflexion of the foot; also known as the calcaneal tendon. Common injuries include tendinopathy and rupture.

subacute.definition: A disease or condition that progresses slower than an acute condition but faster than a chronic condition.

tetracyclines.definition: A class of broad-spectrum antibiotics that reversibly binds the 30S ribosomal subunit to inhibit bacterial protein synthesis, effective against many Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and atypical pathogens; generally bacteriostatic and subject to chelation with divalent cations, which can reduce absorption, with adverse effects including teeth discoloration in children and photosensitivity.

hallux varus.definition: A deformity in which the great toe deviates medially (toward the midline) at the first metatarsophalangeal joint; it can be congenital or acquired (often after bunion surgery or trauma) and may be associated with soft-tissue imbalance or joint instability.

hallux valgus.definition: A deformity of the first metatarsophalangeal joint characterized by lateral deviation of the great toe and medial deviation of the first metatarsal, commonly with a bunion and often with pain or shoe irritation.

halobetasol.definition: A very potent topical corticosteroid used to treat inflammatory and itchy skin conditions (e.g., plaque psoriasis, dermatitis) by reducing inflammation and immune responses in the skin; due to its high potency, it is prescribed for short courses under medical supervision.

halofantrine.definition: A synthetic antimalarial drug used to treat malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum; acts as a blood schizonticide but is associated with serious cardiotoxicity, including QT interval prolongation, and is rarely used as first-line therapy due to safety concerns.

halotestin.definition: An oral, potent androgenic–anabolic steroid (fluoxymesterone) used to treat male hypogonadism and historically advanced breast cancer in women; it acts by activating androgen receptors to promote male secondary sexual characteristics and protein synthesis, but carries risks of liver toxicity, virilization, and various androgenic side effects.

halogenoderma.definition: Halogenoderma is a skin eruption caused by exposure to halogen-containing compounds (most often iodine or bromine), presenting as acneiform or pustular lesions that may ulcerate or form vegetating plaques, typically resolving after withdrawal of the halogen source.

halo nevus.definition: A benign melanocytic nevus (mole) that is surrounded by a circular area of depigmented skin (halo) due to an autoimmune reaction against melanocytes; the central lesion and halo may regress over time and it’s most common in children and young adults.

halo sign.definition: A radiologic sign on chest CT characterized by a nodular lesion surrounded by a halo of ground-glass opacity, most often associated with angioinvasive fungal infections such as invasive aspergillosis in immunocompromised patients.

pseudoparkinsonism.definition: A reversible extrapyramidal syndrome that mimics Parkinson disease, caused by dopamine receptor blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway—most commonly from antipsychotic or antiemetic drugs. It presents with tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, and slowed movements, and typically improves after reducing or stopping the offending medication.

akathisia.definition: An extrapyramidal side effect characterized by a subjective inner sense of restlessness and an inability to sit still, often manifested by pacing, fidgeting, or repetitive movements, commonly caused by dopamine-blocking medications such as antipsychotics.

hand-schüller-christian disease.definition: A form of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (histiocytosis X) in children presenting with the classic triad of skull bone lesions, diabetes insipidus, and exophthalmos; a chronic disseminated variant of LCH.

hamman-rich syndrome.definition: An idiopathic, rapidly progressive interstitial pneumonia presenting with abrupt onset dyspnea and hypoxemia, diffuse bilateral interstitial and alveolar infiltrates on imaging, and swift progression to respiratory failure; histology typically shows diffuse alveolar damage.

pneumomediastinum.definition: Presence of air or gas within the mediastinal space of the chest. It can be spontaneous or due to trauma, esophageal or tracheal injury, pulmonary barotrauma, or medical procedures; patients may have chest pain, dyspnea, or subcutaneous emphysema, and it is diagnosed by imaging showing mediastinal air.
