If you meant a prefix meaning "half," like hemi-, related concepts include half of a structure (e.g., half of the chest or spine) or unilateral conditions (e.g., weakness on one side).

hemiterata.definition: Not a standard medical term in major dictionaries; likely a misspelling or an extremely uncommon word. Please share context or the intended spelling to provide an accurate definition.

hemithorax.definition: One half of the thoracic cavity, extending from the mediastinum to the chest wall and from the diaphragm to the thoracic inlet; it contains one lung and its pleural cavity along with associated structures on that side.

hemithyroidectomy.definition: A surgical procedure that removes one lobe of the thyroid gland, leaving the other lobe intact; typically performed for unilateral thyroid nodules, goiter, or thyroid cancer.

hemisphere.definition: One half of a sphere or of a paired organ; in neuroanatomy, the left or right cerebral hemisphere of the brain.

hemispherectomy.definition: An operation that removes or functionally disconnects one cerebral hemisphere to treat severe, drug-resistant epilepsy originating from that side; the anatomical variant involves removal, while the functional variant disconnects neural connections, typically performed in children and carrying risks to motor, language, and cognitive function depending on the hemisphere involved.

hemisomus.definition: Not a recognized medical term; there is no standard definition or diagnosis by this name.

hemipagus.definition: A type of heteropagus (parasitic) twin in which only part of one fetus is developed and attached to the normally formed twin (autosite), often presenting as a partial body or limb mass that cannot survive independently.

reticuloendothelial.definition: A network of phagocytic cells (primarily monocytes/macrophages) in tissues such as liver, spleen, lymph nodes, and bone marrow that remove debris, senescent cells, and pathogens.

bone_marrow.definition: The tissue inside some of your larger bones where blood cells are made.

spinal_fusion.definition: A procedure to attach two or more vertebrae with a bone graft in order to eliminate motion and relieve pain.

thyroid_gland.definition: A two-lobed gland located in the front of the neck below the larynx (voice box). It secretes hormones that help regulate the body's metabolism and calcium balance.

mandibular_tooth.definition: A tooth situated in the mandible (lower jaw); one of the teeth of the permanent dentition, including incisors, canines, premolars, or molars.

hemizygote.definition: Having only one allele at a given gene locus in a diploid organism; in humans, males are hemizygous for X-linked genes because they have only one X chromosome.

hemizygosity.definition: A state in which only one copy of a gene at a given locus is present in a normally diploid organism; for example, males are hemizygous for X-linked genes because they have only one X chromosome, and deletions or monosomy can also create hemizygosity.

hemizygotic.definition: Having only one allele at a gene locus in a diploid organism; the second allele is missing or inactivated (e.g., males are hemizygous for X-linked genes because they have only one X chromosome).

hemizygous.definition: Having only one allele at a gene locus; in humans, males have only a single X chromosome and a single copy of X-linked genes, so these genes are expressed from one allele.

hemlock.definition: A highly poisonous plant whose alkaloids, notably coniine, depress the central and peripheral nervous systems, causing numbness, weakness, ataxia, and potentially fatal respiratory paralysis; historically used as a poison.

coniine.definition: An alkaloid toxin from poison hemlock (Conium maculatum) that acts as a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonist, causing initial excitation followed by flaccid paralysis and potentially fatal respiratory failure.

hemoagglutination.definition: Clumping of red blood cells caused by antibodies binding to surface antigens (or to viral antigens), producing visible agglutination and used in serologic testing such as blood typing and viral detection assays.

hemobilinuria.definition: The presence of hemoglobin-derived bile pigments (hemobilin) in the urine, typically resulting from intravascular hemolysis with excess heme catabolism and excretion of pigment into the urine.

hemoblastic.definition: Pertaining to hemoblasts, primitive hematopoietic precursor cells from which blood cells originate.

hemoclip.definition: A small surgical clip, usually made of stainless steel or titanium, applied with a clip applier to occlude a blood vessel or seal a duct, thereby achieving hemostasis during surgery or endoscopic procedures; typically left in place as a permanent implant.

hemocyanin.definition: A copper-containing respiratory pigment used by many mollusks and arthropods to transport oxygen in the hemolymph; it is blue when bound to oxygen due to binuclear copper centers and is not found in vertebrates.

hemocyte.definition: A circulating immune cell of invertebrates found in the hemolymph that mediates innate defense against pathogens, primarily by phagocytosis and encapsulation; functionally analogous to vertebrate leukocytes.

hematocytology.definition: The study of blood cells, including their development (hematopoiesis), structure, function, and disorders of erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets; a subfield of hematology.

hemodiafiltration.definition: A renal replacement therapy that combines diffusion and convection to remove solutes and excess fluid from the blood across a semipermeable membrane, typically performed continuously (continuous hemodiafiltration) in critically ill patients.

hemofiltration.definition: A renal replacement therapy that uses convection to remove plasma water and solutes across a semipermeable filter, with replacement fluid infused to maintain volume and electrolyte balance; commonly performed as continuous hemofiltration in CRRT for acute kidney injury.

hemoglobinopathy.definition: A group of inherited disorders characterized by abnormal hemoglobin molecules, either from structural variants or deficient synthesis of globin chains, causing abnormal red blood cells and usually anemia.

mellitus.definition: Latin for "honey-sweet"; in medical terminology, used to denote sweetness, notably referenced in the historical description of sweet-tasting urine in diabetes.

phlebotomies.definition: Procedures in which blood is drawn from a vein, typically using a needle and collection device, for laboratory testing or therapeutic blood removal.

protamine.definition: A positively charged protein used clinically to neutralize heparin anticoagulation by forming a stable complex, thereby reversing heparin's effects during or after procedures.

heinz.definition: A red blood cell inclusion consisting of precipitated, denatured hemoglobin seen on supravital staining; forms under oxidative stress (e.g., G6PD deficiency, unstable hemoglobins) and may be removed by splenic macrophages, resulting in bite cells.

microcytosis.definition: A finding of smaller-than-normal red blood cells, reflected by a low mean corpuscular volume (MCV) on a CBC; microcytosis is commonly due to iron deficiency anemia, thalassemia, or sideroblastic anemia.

hypochromia.definition: A reduced hemoglobin content in red blood cells, causing them to appear paler on a blood smear (hypochromic cells) and typically associated with a low MCHC; commonly seen in iron deficiency anemia and other hypochromic anemias.

siderosis.definition: A deposition of iron in tissues, most commonly in the lungs, caused by inhalation of iron oxide dust; a form of pneumoconiosis characterized by iron-laden macrophages and typically minimal clinical symptoms.

bart's.definition: Do you mean Barth syndrome (Barth’s syndrome) or Bartter syndrome? I can provide a concise definition for either.

gower.definition: A clinical sign of proximal muscle weakness (typically hip girdle) in which the patient rises from a supine position by using the hands to push up on the thighs and climb to standing, commonly seen in Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

gower-1.definition: Definition not found in standard medical dictionaries. Please provide context (e.g., genetics, diagnostics, or field) to refine the definition.

gower-2.definition: Not a recognized medical term; no standard medical definition exists in reputable medical dictionaries. If you have a specific context or source, please share it for a more precise clarification.

philadelphia.definition: A chromosomal abnormality resulting from a reciprocal translocation between chromosome 9 and chromosome 22 (t(9;22)(q34;q11)) that creates the BCR-ABL fusion gene, producing constitutively active tyrosine kinase; most associated with chronic myelogenous leukemia and some cases of acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

thalassemia trait.definition: Carrier state (heterozygous) for a mutation in the α- or β-globin gene leading to reduced production of one globin chain; usually asymptomatic or with mild microcytic, hypochromic anemia, and in β-thalassemia trait often an elevated HbA2 on electrophoresis.

hbs.definition: A protein on the surface of the hepatitis B virus; its presence in blood indicates active hepatitis B infection (acute or chronic).

hba.definition: The major adult form of hemoglobin, consisting of two alpha and two beta globin chains (α2β2); it is the predominant form of hemoglobin in healthy adults.

hbc.definition: Hepatitis B core antigen; a component of the hepatitis B virus nucleocapsid present in infected cells but not typically detectable in serum, with exposure usually indicated by anti-HBc antibodies. If you meant a different meaning for HBC, please provide context.

hemoglobin sc disease.definition: A form of sickle cell disease caused by inheriting one beta-globin gene with the S mutation and one with the C mutation, resulting in red blood cells containing abnormal hemoglobins S and C; characterized by chronic hemolytic anemia and episodic vaso-occlusive pain, with variable severity and risk of organ complications.

hemoglobin sd disease.definition: A form of sickle cell disease caused by inheriting one HbS allele and one HbD allele (most commonly HbD-Punjab). Red blood cells can sickle under low oxygen, leading to hemolytic anemia and vaso-occlusive crises; the clinical severity is typically similar to sickle cell anemia but can vary.

hemoglobin c disease.definition: An autosomal recessive hemoglobinopathy caused by homozygosity for the HbC mutation in the beta-globin gene (Glu6→Lys), leading to a mild chronic hemolytic anemia with splenomegaly and red blood cells that often appear as target cells; hemoglobin electrophoresis shows predominance of HbC with little or no HbA.

hemoglobin d.definition: An inherited group of beta-globin variants caused by point mutations in the HBB gene, producing structurally abnormal beta chains; most HbD variants are clinically mild or asymptomatic, but when inherited with other hemoglobinopathies (e.g., HbS or beta-thalassemia) they can cause mild to moderate anemia.

sickle cell trait.definition: A genetic carrier state in which a person has one sickle cell gene (HbS) and one normal hemoglobin gene (HbA); individuals are typically asymptomatic and do not have sickle cell disease, though rare sickling can occur under extreme conditions such as severe hypoxia or dehydration, and the trait provides some protection against falciparum malaria.

hemoglobin electrophoresis.definition: A laboratory test in which hemoglobin is separated into its variants by applying an electric field to a supporting medium, allowing detection and quantification of abnormal hemoglobins (e.g., HbS, HbC, HbF) for diagnosing hemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell disease and thalassemias.

zeta chain.definition: A signaling subunit of the T-cell receptor-CD3 complex; a transmembrane glycoprotein encoded by CD247 that associates with other CD3 subunits, contains ITAM motifs, and transduces activation signals upon antigen recognition, essential for T-cell development and function.

gamma chain.definition: A shared signaling subunit of several interleukin receptors (including those for IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, and IL-21) that enables downstream cytokine signaling; encoded by the IL2RG gene; essential for development and function of T cells, B cells, and NK cells; defects cause X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (X-SCID).

beta chain.definition: A component of adult hemoglobin (beta-globin) that pairs with alpha-globin to form the HbA (α2β2) tetramer responsible for oxygen transport; mutations can cause beta-thalassemia and contribute to sickle cell disease.

hemoglobin seattle.definition: An extremely rare variant of hemoglobin with markedly increased oxygen affinity (left-shifted oxygen dissociation curve) due to a beta-globin mutation, resulting in reduced oxygen delivery to tissues and often asymptomatic.

hemolytic jaundice.definition: A jaundice caused by accelerated destruction of red blood cells (hemolysis), resulting in elevated unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin with normal or only mildly elevated direct (conjugated) bilirubin, often accompanied by reticulocytosis and anemia.

icterus gravis neonatorum.definition: A severe neonatal jaundice due to markedly elevated unconjugated bilirubin in a newborn, typically presenting in the first days of life and carrying a risk of bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus) if untreated.

alloimmune hemolytic anemia.definition: Destruction of red blood cells mediated by antibodies formed against alloantigens on donor or fetal red cells, usually after exposure to foreign antigens via transfusion or pregnancy, causing hemolysis and anemia (often with a positive direct antiglobulin test).

blood group antibodies.definition: Antibodies directed against antigens on red blood cells that define the blood group systems (for example, A, B, D, Kell). They may be naturally occurring or formed after exposure to foreign antigens (via transfusion or pregnancy) and can cause agglutination and hemolysis of incompatible red cells, leading to transfusion reactions or hemolytic disease of the newborn.

fetal red cells.definition: Red blood cells produced during fetal development that contain fetal hemoglobin (HbF) and transport oxygen to fetal tissues; they originate in the yolk sac and later in the fetal liver and spleen, and are largely replaced by adult erythrocytes after birth.

vitamin k deficiency.definition: An inadequacy of the fat-soluble vitamin K that impairs hepatic synthesis of vitamin K–dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) and proteins C and S, leading to increased bleeding risk and prolonged coagulation tests. Causes include poor intake or absorption of fats/fat-soluble vitamins, liver disease, biliary obstruction, fat malabsorption, antibiotic use disrupting gut flora, and in newborns with immature gut flora. Treatment is vitamin K replacement and management of the underlying cause.

hemorrhagic disease of newborn.definition: A bleeding disorder in newborns caused by vitamin K deficiency that impairs production of vitamin K–dependent clotting factors, leading to spontaneous or delayed hemorrhages (often intracranial or gastrointestinal); preventable by vitamin K prophylaxis at birth.

fanconi’s syndrome.definition: Fanconi syndrome is a generalized proximal renal tubule dysfunction causing defective reabsorption of filtered substances (glucose, amino acids, phosphate, bicarbonate, and uric acid) by the proximal tubule, leading to glycosuria with normoglycemia, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia with hypophosphatemia, bicarbonaturia with a metabolic acidosis (proximal renal tubular acidosis), and often bone demineralization such as rickets or osteomalacia; it can be inherited or acquired (e.g., due to drugs, toxins, or chronic diseases).

christmas disease.definition: A genetic X-linked recessive bleeding disorder caused by deficiency of coagulation factor IX (factor IX deficiency), also known as Hemophilia B; characterized by impaired coagulation and prolonged bleeding after injury or surgery, and treated with factor IX replacement.

hemolytic antibody.definition: An antibody directed against red blood cell antigens that causes destruction of red blood cells, typically by activating complement or promoting phagocytosis; implicated in transfusion reactions and hemolytic disease of the newborn.

coagulation factor.definition: A protein that participates in the blood coagulation cascade to promote clot formation; it is activated in a proteolytic cascade that leads to the conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin, forming a stable clot. Many coagulation factors are produced by the liver, and several are vitamin K–dependent.

recombinant factor products.definition: Coagulation factors produced by recombinant DNA technology in cell culture, used to replace deficient clotting factors in bleeding disorders; not derived from human plasma and designed to provide standardized dosing (e.g., recombinant factor VIII for hemophilia A and recombinant factor IX for hemophilia B).

plasma-derived factor concentrates.definition: Concentrated clotting factors purified from human plasma, prepared by fractionation to provide specific factors (such as factor VIII or factor IX) for replacement therapy in inherited bleeding disorders.

intramuscular injections.definition: Administration of a medication by injecting it into a skeletal muscle, allowing rapid systemic absorption. Common sites include the deltoid, ventrogluteal, and vastus lateralis muscles; injection volumes and needle length vary by site, medication, and patient.

radiographic examination.definition: An imaging procedure that uses X-rays to visualize internal body structures; radiographs (X-ray images) are captured on film or digital detectors, often with contrast agents to enhance detail.

x-linked recessive.definition: A mode of genetic inheritance in which a mutation on the X chromosome causes disease mainly in males (who have only one X) and in females only if two mutated X chromosomes are present; it is typically transmitted through carrier mothers, with no father-to-son transmission. An affected father passes the mutant allele to all daughters (who become carriers) but to no sons, while carrier females have a 50% chance to pass the mutation to their children, giving sons a 50% chance of being affected and daughters a 50% chance of being carriers.

nocturnal haemoglobinuria.definition: An acquired clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder caused by a somatic PIGA gene mutation leading to loss of glycosylphosphatidylinositol–anchored proteins (especially CD55 and CD59) on red cells and other blood cells; this renders cells susceptible to complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis, causing episodic hemoglobinuria (often more noticeable in the morning), anemia, and a high risk of thrombosis. Diagnosis is by flow cytometry showing deficiency of GPI-anchored proteins; treatment includes complement inhibitors (e.g., eculizumab or ravulizumab) and supportive care.

hemopericardium.definition: A collection of blood in the pericardial sac around the heart, usually from trauma or rupture of cardiac/vascular structures, which can compress the heart and cause cardiac tamponade.

hemoperitoneum.definition: Blood located in the peritoneal cavity; a form of intraabdominal hemorrhage typically due to trauma or rupture of an abdominal organ, which can cause abdominal pain, distension, and signs of hypovolemia.

hemopneumopericardium.definition: A condition in which blood and air occupy the pericardial cavity, typically due to chest trauma or invasive procedures, and which can impede heart filling (cardiac tamponade).

hemopneumothorax.definition: A condition in which both air and blood accumulate in the pleural space, causing partial or complete lung collapse; usually due to chest trauma or pulmonary/pleural injury, and typically treated with chest-tube drainage and management of bleeding.

aspergillus infection.definition: A fungal infection caused by Aspergillus species (most often A. fumigatus) that can present as allergic disease, colonization with a fungus ball, chronic pulmonary infection, or invasive disease—primarily in immunocompromised patients—and may affect the lungs or disseminate to other organs; diagnosed by clinical features plus imaging and microbiologic or antigen testing; treated with antifungal therapy such as voriconazole or isavuconazole.

black measles.definition: A historical term not used in modern medicine; it referred to a severe or hemorrhagic form of measles (rubeola).

hemorrhagic plague.definition: A severe form of plague due to systemic infection with Yersinia pestis, characterized by widespread bleeding (hemorrhages) from multiple sites and often disseminated intravascular coagulation, typically in the setting of septicemia and potential shock.

hemorrhagic pleurisy.definition: Inflammation of the pleural membranes accompanied by a bloody (hemorrhagic) pleural effusion; an exudative fluid accumulation in the pleural space often due to malignancy, tuberculosis, pulmonary embolism, or trauma, and typically presenting with pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath.

hemorrhagic purpura.definition: A term describing non-blanching purplish patches or bruising due to bleeding into the skin from ruptured small vessels, typically due to platelet abnormalities, coagulation factor deficiencies, or vascular fragility/vasculitis.

weil’s disease.definition: A severe form of leptospirosis caused by Leptospira interrogans, characterized by jaundice, acute kidney injury, and hemorrhagic manifestations; often with fever and conjunctival suffusion, acquired from contact with water or soil contaminated by infected animal urine.

hemorrhagic infarct.definition: A red (hemorrhagic) infarct is tissue necrosis that becomes hemorrhagic due to bleeding into the infarcted area, typically from venous occlusion or reperfusion in tissues with dual blood supply or loose parenchyma (e.g., lung, intestine).

hemorrhagic jaundice.definition: A clinical syndrome in which jaundice (yellowing of skin and eyes from elevated bilirubin) occurs with spontaneous bleeding or hemorrhagic manifestations, typically due to liver dysfunction that impairs coagulation factor production and causes coagulopathy.

hemorrhagic lung.definition: Bleeding into the lung parenchyma and/or airways (pulmonary hemorrhage), resulting in blood within the alveoli and airways and impaired gas exchange; causes include vasculitis, infection, coagulopathy, diffuse alveolar hemorrhage syndromes, pulmonary embolism with infarction, and trauma.

hemorrhagic pericarditis.definition: A form of pericarditis characterized by a hemorrhagic (bloody) pericardial effusion due to inflammation, commonly associated with malignancy, tuberculosis, bacterial infection, trauma, or postoperative states; can lead to cardiac tamponade.

hemorrhoidal.definition: Relating to hemorrhoids; pertaining to swollen or inflamed veins in the lower rectum or anus.

rubber band ligation.definition: A minimally invasive procedure in which a small elastic band is placed around the base of an internal hemorrhoid to cut off its blood supply, causing the hemorrhoid to shrink and slough off.

anoscope.definition: A short, rigid (often slightly flexible) tubular instrument used to inspect the anal canal and lower rectum; inserted through the anus to visualize the mucosa, usually with illumination, for diagnostic or minor therapeutic procedures.

jackknife.definition: An operative position in which the patient lies prone with the hips sharply flexed and the buttocks elevated on a support, forming a V-shaped body; used to expose the anal/rectal region and posterior pelvis during anorectal or perineal surgeries.

external hemorrhoids.definition: Swollen veins of the external hemorrhoidal venous plexus located below the dentate (pectinate) line around the anal margin; they are covered by anoderm, typically painful (especially if thrombosed), and can bleed, contrasting with internal hemorrhoids which lie above the line and are usually painless.

internal hemorrhoids.definition: Enlarged submucosal vascular cushions above the dentate line in the anal canal that typically cause painless bright-red rectal bleeding and may prolapse with straining; they are usually not painful due to visceral innervation and are classified by degree of prolapse.

anal skin tag.definition: Benign excess skin at the anal verge (perianal skin tag), often a residual tag after anorectal inflammation such as hemorrhoids or fissures; usually asymptomatic but may cause irritation or hygiene issues and can be excised if symptomatic or for cosmetic reasons.

hemostat.definition: A surgical instrument used to clamp and occlude blood vessels or tissue to control bleeding during procedures; it typically has locking handles and serrated jaws.

vitamin k1.definition: A fat-soluble vitamin (phylloquinone) essential for the gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues on vitamin K–dependent proteins, including the coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X; it supports blood clotting and plays a role in bone metabolism.

heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.definition: A prothrombotic, immune-mediated adverse reaction to heparin in which antibodies form to the heparin–PF4 complex, activating platelets and causing thrombocytopenia with new thrombosis; typically appears 5–14 days after exposure and may occur sooner with re-exposure; management involves stopping heparin and using a non-heparin anticoagulant (eg, a direct thrombin inhibitor or fondaparinux) and avoiding platelet transfusions unless bleeding is life-threatening.

protamine sulfate.definition: An intravenous antidote to unfractionated heparin that binds heparin to form an inactive complex, reversing its anticoagulant effect; used during procedures or in heparin overdose; derived from salmon sperm and can cause hypotension or allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis in those with fish allergies.

gelatin sponges.definition: An absorbable hemostatic agent: a sterile, porous gelatin sponge (often porcine-derived) that swells with blood to form a gel and provide a scaffold for clot formation; gradually resorbed by the body.

microfibrillar collagen.definition: Topical hemostatic material consisting of finely dispersed collagen microfibrils derived from animal sources; when applied to a bleeding surface, it acts as a scaffold to promote platelet adhesion and aggregation, accelerating clot formation and local hemostasis; it is resorbable.

entamoeba histolytica.definition: A pathogenic protozoan parasite transmitted via cysts in contaminated food or water, causing amebiasis; it ranges from asymptomatic colonization to amebic colitis and liver abscess, and is treated with a tissue-active agent (e.g., metronidazole) followed by a luminal amoebicide.

hepatectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove all or part of the liver.

hepaticoduodenostomy.definition: A surgical anastomosis between a hepatic duct and the duodenum to drain bile directly into the duodenum, bypassing distal biliary obstruction or injury; an alternative to hepaticojejunostomy.

hepaticoenterostomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which a connection is created between the liver's biliary system and the small intestine (usually the jejunum) to drain bile, bypassing an obstructed biliary tract.

hepaticolithotomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove stones from the intrahepatic biliary ducts by incising liver tissue to extract calculi.

hepaticolithotripsy.definition: A procedure to fragment intrahepatic biliary stones (stones within the liver’s bile ducts) to enable their removal, typically performed percutaneously or endoscopically using lithotripsy techniques.

hepatic fistula.definition: An abnormal tract or connection between hepatic tissue or the biliary tree and another organ or the body's surface, resulting from infection, inflammation, trauma, or surgery, through which bile or infected material can drain externally or into another hollow viscus.

hepatic insufficiency.definition: Impaired liver function with inadequate metabolic, synthetic, and detoxification capacity, typically from acute liver failure or advanced chronic liver disease, often leading to jaundice, coagulopathy, hypoalbuminemia with edema/ascites, encephalopathy, and impaired drug metabolism.

hepatic ischemia.definition: Inadequate blood flow to the liver resulting in reduced oxygen delivery to hepatocytes, typically from decreased hepatic arterial inflow or portal venous perfusion, causing hepatocellular injury and potentially necrosis; often seen in shock or vascular compromise and affecting the centrilobular (zone 3) region.

portal circulation.definition: A venous system that drains blood from the gastrointestinal tract and spleen via the portal vein to the liver for metabolism and detoxification before entering the systemic circulation.

hepatic veins.definition: Veins that drain deoxygenated blood from the liver into the inferior vena cava; the three major hepatic veins (right, middle, and left) plus smaller tributaries drain the liver parenchyma.

porta hepatis.definition: A transverse fissure on the visceral (inferior) surface of the liver that serves as the hilum, through which the portal triad—the hepatic artery proper, portal vein, and common bile duct—along with accompanying nerves and lymphatics, enter or exit the liver.

hepatic lobes.definition: Two major anatomical divisions of the liver—the right and left lobes—separated by the falciform ligament; two smaller lobes, the caudate and quadrate lobes, lie on the visceral surface and are described as part of the liver’s lobulation.

hepatic nodes.definition: Lymph nodes located in the liver region, typically along the portal triad, that drain lymph from the liver and biliary tract and route it to the celiac and paraaortic lymph node groups.

henle’s fissure.definition: Not a standard anatomical term and has no widely accepted definition in medical references; if encountered, it is likely a misnomer or used in a specific context, possibly referring to other Henle-related structures (e.g., Henle's fiber layer of the retina or the loop of Henle in the kidney).

henle’s loop.definition: A U-shaped portion of the nephron in the kidney that extends into the medulla; it has a descending limb permeable to water and an ascending limb that actively transports ions, thereby creating a hyperosmotic medullary interstitium and enabling concentration of urine.

henoch-schönlein purpura nephritis.definition: IgA-mediated nephritis associated with IgA vasculitis, characterized by deposition of IgA-containing immune complexes in the glomerular mesangium, causing hematuria and proteinuria; histology shows mesangial proliferation with IgA and C3 deposition. Usually affects children; prognosis is generally favorable but can be chronic in some cases.

hepatoblastoma.definition: A malignant liver tumor in early childhood arising from immature hepatocytes (hepatoblasts); the most common primary liver cancer in children, often presenting with an abdominal mass and elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein, treated with chemotherapy and surgical resection.

acute hepatitis.definition: A sudden onset inflammation of the liver of short duration (usually <6 months) that can be caused by viral infection, toxins or drugs, autoimmune disease, or other etiologies; commonly presents with jaundice, fatigue, right upper quadrant pain, and elevated liver enzymes.

viral hepatitis.definition: Inflammation of the liver caused by infection with hepatitis viruses (A, B, C, D, or E). Transmission varies by virus; A and E are typically fecal-oral and usually acute, while B, C, and D can cause chronic infection. Diagnosis is by serology and viral RNA testing; treatment ranges from supportive care for acute cases to antiviral therapy for chronic HBV/HCV, with vaccines available for HAV and HBV.

hepadnavirus.definition: A family of small enveloped hepatotropic DNA viruses with partially double-stranded, circular genomes that replicate through an RNA intermediate using reverse transcription; includes hepatitis B virus.

hepatocyte.definition: A large polygonal liver cell (parenchymal cell) that carries out most hepatic metabolic, synthetic, and detoxification functions, including bile production and glycogen storage.

hepatocytes.definition: Hepatocytes are the principal parenchymal cells of the liver, polygonal in shape and arranged in plates between sinusoids; they carry out most hepatic metabolic functions, including glucose and lipid metabolism, detoxification and drug metabolism, protein synthesis (e.g., albumin and clotting factors), and bile production.

recombinant hepatitis b vaccine.definition: A subunit vaccine created by recombinant DNA technology that contains the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) to induce protective immunity against hepatitis B.

hepatitis b vaccine.definition: A recombinant vaccine that prevents hepatitis B infection by inducing protective antibodies against the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg); given in a multi-dose schedule (commonly 3 doses) and recommended for newborns, children, at-risk adults, and health-care workers.

hepatitis a vaccine.definition: A vaccine that prevents hepatitis A infection by stimulating the immune system to produce antibodies against the hepatitis A virus; it is an inactivated intramuscular vaccine given in a two-dose schedule (typically 0 and 6–12 months) to provide long-term protection.

hbig.definition: A sterile preparation containing high-titer antibodies against the hepatitis B surface antigen, used for passive immunization after exposure to hepatitis B virus to provide immediate, temporary protection (often given with the hepatitis B vaccine for post-exposure prophylaxis).

postexposure prophylaxis.definition: A drug that is given to someone who has been near someone who is sick or may be near someone who is sick to prevent a disease.

hbsab.definition: An antibody to the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg); its presence indicates immunity to hepatitis B, usually after vaccination or recovery from infection.

hbcab.definition: An antibody against the hepatitis B core antigen. Its presence indicates exposure to hepatitis B virus; IgM suggests acute infection, while IgG indicates past infection or immunity. Interpretation typically combines this marker with other HBV serologies (HBsAg and anti-HBs).

hbeag.definition: A viral protein secreted by the hepatitis B virus; its presence correlates with high HBV replication and greater infectivity, while loss of detectable antigen (typically with anti-HBe seroconversion) indicates lower replication and reduced infectivity.

hbeab.definition: An antibody produced against the hepatitis B e antigen; its appearance after seroconversion generally indicates reduced hepatitis B virus replication and lower infectivity, and it may reflect an inactive carrier state, though it does not prove viral clearance.

hcv igg.definition: Hepatitis C virus immunoglobulin G antibodies; a serologic marker indicating exposure to hepatitis C. A positive HCV IgG suggests prior or current infection, but RNA testing is needed to confirm active infection; IgG persists for life.

hepatitis b surface antibody.definition: An antibody directed against the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg); its detectable presence after vaccination or resolution of hepatitis B indicates immunity to hepatitis B.

hepatitis b core antibody.definition: An antibody directed against the hepatitis B core antigen (HBc). It indicates past or current exposure to hepatitis B virus. There are two main isotypes: IgM anti-HBc, which appears in acute or recent infection; and IgG anti-HBc, which persists for life and indicates prior exposure or chronic infection. Anti-HBc is not produced in response to hepatitis B vaccination.

hepatitis b e antigen.definition: A secreted antigen produced by the hepatitis B virus during active replication; its presence in blood indicates high levels of viral replication and increased infectivity, and it is used to assess contagiousness and monitor antiviral therapy.

hepatitis b e antibody.definition: An antibody against the hepatitis B e antigen; its appearance after seroconversion from the e antigen is usually associated with reduced HBV replication and lower infectivity, though replication may persist in some chronic cases with certain viral mutations.

non-a non-b hepatitis.definition: A historical term for viral hepatitis caused by infectious agents other than hepatitis A or hepatitis B, commonly used for post-transfusion hepatitis; most cases were later found to be due to hepatitis C virus, and the label is now obsolete in favor of naming the specific virus.

delta hepatitis.definition: An infection caused by the hepatitis D virus (HDV), a defective RNA virus that requires hepatitis B surface antigen to replicate; it occurs only in people with hepatitis B, as a coinfection or as a superinfection, and it tends to cause more severe hepatitis and faster progression to cirrhosis. Transmitted parenterally (blood-borne); prevention is via hepatitis B vaccination. There is no widely effective specific antiviral therapy; management focuses on treating HBV and liver disease, with pegylated interferon used in some cases.

hepatitis e virus.definition: Small, nonenveloped, positive-sense RNA virus of the Hepeviridae family that causes hepatitis E, typically an acute, self-limited liver infection transmitted fecal-orally via contaminated water; chronic infection can occur in immunocompromised individuals; diagnosed by HEV RNA or anti-HEV antibodies.

hev.definition: A non-enveloped, positive-sense RNA virus of the Hepeviridae family that causes hepatitis E; typically transmitted via the fecal–oral route through contaminated water; infection is usually self-limited in healthy individuals but can be severe in pregnancy and in immunocompromised patients, with supportive management and a vaccine available in some regions.

hepatitis g virus.definition: A positive-sense, single-stranded RNA virus in the Pegivirus genus of the Flaviviridae family. It is transmitted primarily through blood and body fluids; infection is usually asymptomatic and not clearly linked to hepatitis; there is no specific treatment or vaccine; diagnosis relies on molecular detection of viral RNA.

hgv.definition: A positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus in the Flaviviridae family; its association with hepatitis is uncertain and it is not clearly established as a cause of hepatitis; transmitted mainly via blood, with many infections being asymptomatic.

hepatovirus.definition: A genus of nonenveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses in the family Picornaviridae; includes hepatitis A virus and is associated with acute hepatitis, typically transmitted via the fecal–oral route.

hepato-duodenal ligament.definition: A peritoneal fold at the free edge of the lesser omentum that connects the liver to the duodenum, enclosing the portal triad (hepatic artery proper, portal vein, common bile duct) and forming the anterior boundary of the omental (Winslow) foramen.

hepatogastric ligament.definition: A peritoneal fold of the lesser omentum connecting the liver to the lesser curvature of the stomach; contains the left gastric vessels and associated lymphatics.

glisson's capsule.definition: A fibrous capsule surrounding the liver, composed of dense irregular connective tissue; it is continuous with the peritoneum and extends into the porta hepatis, enclosing the branches of the hepatic artery, portal vein, and bile duct as they enter the liver.

hepatolithiasis.definition: Formation or presence of stones within the intrahep hepatic bile ducts, which can cause biliary obstruction, cholestasis, and recurrent cholangitis.

hepatologist.definition: A physician who specializes in diseases of the liver, biliary system, and pancreas, often practicing within gastroenterology, and who diagnoses and treats conditions such as hepatitis, cirrhosis, fatty liver disease, liver cancer, and related disorders.

hepatology.definition: A medical specialty focused on diseases of the liver, including diagnosis, treatment, and monitoring of liver conditions (e.g., hepatitis, fatty liver disease, cirrhosis, liver failure, and liver cancer), as well as biliary tract disorders and liver transplant evaluation.

hepatotoxic.definition: Capable of causing liver injury or toxicity to the liver; describes substances (such as certain drugs or chemicals) that damage hepatic cells and can impair liver function.

hepatotropic.definition: Having an affinity for the liver; describing pathogens, toxins, or drugs that preferentially affect hepatic tissue.

hepatotropic virus.definition: A virus that preferentially infects liver cells (hepatocytes), causing hepatitis; examples include the hepatitis A–E viruses.

hepatocyte growth factor.definition: A cytokine-like growth factor produced by mesenchymal cells that binds to the Met (c-Met) receptor on epithelial and endothelial cells, promoting cell proliferation, motility, morphogenesis, and organ regeneration; also known as scatter factor.

hgf.definition: A growth factor secreted by mesenchymal cells that signals via the MET receptor to promote proliferation, motility, and morphogenesis of epithelial cells; also known as scatter factor.

hepatoerythropoietic porphyria.definition: A rare autosomal recessive porphyria caused by markedly reduced activity of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase in both hepatic and erythroid tissues, leading to accumulation of porphyrins and presenting in infancy with severe cutaneous photosensitivity, blistering, and liver dysfunction.

kayser-fleischer rings.definition: A copper-containing brownish ring at the peripheral cornea (Descemet's membrane) seen on slit-lamp exam, classically associated with Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) and used as a diagnostic clue in patients with neuropsychiatric symptoms.

pityriasis rosea.definition: A common, self-limited inflammatory skin condition characterized by a single herald patch followed by a generalized eruption of oval, salmon-colored, finely scaly plaques on the trunk and proximal limbs, often in a Christmas-tree pattern; etiology is unknown but may involve reactivation of HHV-6 or HHV-7; resolves spontaneously in weeks to a couple of months; management is supportive (emollients, antihistamines for itch, topical steroids if needed).

herbicide.definition: A chemical substance used to kill or suppress unwanted vegetation (weeds); it can be selective (affecting only certain plant species) or non-selective, and may be applied to foliage, soil, or roots. It may act systemically (absorbed and translocated within the plant) or as a contact herbicide that damages only treated tissue.

herbicide poisoning.definition: Toxicity from exposure to herbicides (chemicals used to kill weeds), typically via ingestion, inhalation, or dermal/ocular contact, causing variable symptoms and organ injury depending on the agent (e.g., gastrointestinal, neurological, dermatologic symptoms with potential pulmonary, hepatic, or renal toxicity).

hepatorenal syndrome.definition: A functional kidney failure that occurs in people with advanced liver disease (most often cirrhosis with ascites) caused by marked renal vasoconstriction due to profound splanchnic vasodilation and reduced effective arterial blood volume, with little or no intrinsic renal pathology; diagnosed after excluding other causes of kidney injury and classified as type 1 (rapid progression) or type 2 (slower progression).

hepatobiliary.definition: Relating to the liver and the biliary system (bile ducts and gallbladder); encompassing the anatomy, physiology, and diseases of the liver and biliary tract.

hepatojugular reflux.definition: A clinical sign where firm pressure over the liver (hepatic region) causes a sustained rise in jugular venous pressure for about 10–15 seconds; a positive result indicates elevated right atrial pressure and right‑sided venous congestion, commonly due to congestive heart failure or other right heart dysfunction.

hermaphroditism.definition: A historical and now-outdated term for a condition in which a person has both male and female reproductive organs or gonadal tissue; in humans, the contemporary language is intersex or disorders of sex development (DSD).

heredity.definition: The transmission of genetic material from parents to offspring, resulting in the inheritance of traits and genetic predispositions.

hereditability.definition: A population-level statistic describing the proportion of phenotypic variation in a trait that is attributable to genetic differences under a given environment; it ranges from 0 to 1 (0%–100%) and is not applicable to individuals.

hereditary.definition: Relating to traits or diseases that are transmitted from parents to offspring through genetic inheritance.

ataxia-telangiectasia_syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the ATM gene, characterized by progressive cerebellar ataxia beginning in early childhood, oculocutaneous telangiectasias, immunodeficiency (often IgA deficiency), hypersensitivity to ionizing radiation, elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein, and markedly increased cancer risk, especially lymphoid malignancies.

friedreichs_ataxia.definition: An autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder caused by a GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FXN gene, leading to progressive degeneration of the dorsal columns, spinocerebellar tracts, and peripheral nerves; onset in childhood or adolescence with gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, absent deep-tendon reflexes, pyramidal signs, pes cavus, and commonly diabetes or cardiomyopathy.

amelogenesis_imperfecta.definition: An inherited disorder of enamel formation in which the enamel is defective—thin, soft, or poorly mineralized—leading to pits, discoloration, rapid wear, and dentin sensitivity; with forms including hypoplastic, hypomature, and hypocalcified.

aclasia.definition: Not a standard medical term in common dictionaries. Please confirm the spelling or provide the context (anatomical site or suspected condition) for an accurate definition.

deforming_chondroplasia.definition: A skeletal dysplasia marked by abnormal cartilage development during skeletal growth, leading to bone and limb deformities and often short stature; part of the chondrodysplasias.

dentinogenesis_imperfecta.definition: An autosomal-dominant hereditary disorder of dentin development characterized by abnormal, discolored dentin that gives teeth an opalescent appearance, with rapid wear and fracture; enamel is typically normal, but dentin defects lead to weakened teeth and pulp chamber changes.

opalescent_dentin.definition: An iridescent, pearly translucence of dentin seen under light; a descriptive term in dentistry for dentin whose optical properties are altered by tubule arrangement and mineral content, rather than indicating a separate disease.

protoporphyria.definition: An inherited disorder of heme biosynthesis in which protoporphyrin IX accumulates, most often due to ferrochelatase deficiency (erythropoietic protoporphyria), causing marked photosensitivity with painful skin burning on sun exposure and possible hepatic involvement; diagnosis relies on elevated erythrocyte protoporphyrin and genetic testing.

renal_adysplasia.definition: A congenital abnormality of kidney development in which the renal parenchyma is disorganized and immature, often with cyst formation, producing small, poorly functioning kidneys.

tyrosinemia.definition: A group of inherited metabolic disorders characterized by impaired breakdown of the amino acid tyrosine, leading to elevated tyrosine and its metabolites in blood and urine; caused by deficiencies in hepatic tyrosine catabolic enzymes (most commonly fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase in type I, tyrosine aminotransferase in type II, or p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase in type III) and presenting with variable liver, kidney, ocular, or neurologic features depending on type.

tyrosinaemia.definition: A hereditary metabolic disorder caused by impaired degradation of the amino acid tyrosine, resulting in elevated tyrosine levels in blood and urine and potential liver, kidney, ocular, or neurologic problems depending on the type.

lesch-nyhan_syndrome.definition: A rare X-linked recessive disorder caused by deficiency of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT), leading to excess uric acid production with early motor dysfunction, cognitive impairment, and neurobehavioral features such as self-injurious and aggressive behavior, often accompanied by gout and kidney stones.

olliers_dyschondroplasia.definition: A nonhereditary skeletal disorder characterized by multiple enchondromas (benign cartilaginous tumors within the medullary cavity of bones), typically presenting in childhood with asymmetric multifocal lesions that cause bone deformities and limb-length discrepancies, and an increased risk of malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma.

multiple_exostoses.definition: An autosomal dominant skeletal disorder characterized by the development of multiple osteochondromas (benign cartilage-capped bony outgrowths) near the growth plates of long bones; also known as hereditary multiple exostoses (HME). It can cause limb deformities and restricted movement, with a rare risk of malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma.

nail_patella_syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by mutations in the LMX1B gene, characterized by nail dysplasia, hypoplastic or absent patellae, elbow abnormalities, and the distinctive iliac horns on pelvic radiographs; renal involvement with proteinuria and progressive nephropathy occurs in many individuals.

osteonychodysplasia.definition: A developmental abnormality affecting both bone and nail formation, resulting in malformation of the bones and nail dystrophy, typically involving the distal digits.

essential_tremor.definition: A common, often hereditary movement disorder characterized by a bilateral postural and kinetic tremor of the hands and arms (sometimes the head or voice), worsened with voluntary movement and typically absent at rest; neurologic exam is otherwise normal.

fructose_intolerance.definition: A disorder in which fructose is not properly processed or absorbed, typically due to either hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B deficiency, causing hypoglycemia and liver injury after fructose intake) or fructose malabsorption (impaired intestinal absorption, causing bloating, gas, cramps, and diarrhea after fructose-containing foods).

hemorrhagic_telangiectasia.definition: A genetic vascular disorder (autosomal dominant) characterized by mucocutaneous telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations in the lungs, liver, brain, and gastrointestinal tract, causing recurrent epistaxis and bleeding and potentially AVM-related complications; diagnosed by Curaçao criteria.

osler-weber-rendu_syndrome.definition: A hereditary autosomal dominant vascular disorder characterized by mucocutaneous telangiectasias and visceral arteriovenous malformations (especially in the lungs, liver, and brain), causing recurrent epistaxis, easy bleeding, and iron-deficiency anemia, with potential AVM-related complications. (Also known as hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia.)

rendu-osler-weber_syndrome.definition: An autosomal dominant genetic vascular disorder characterized by mucocutaneous telangiectasias and recurrent epistaxis, with arteriovenous malformations affecting the lungs, liver, and brain.

gargoylism.definition: An archaic term for the coarse, gargoyle-like facial features and skeletal deformities seen in Hurler syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type I) due to glycosaminoglycan accumulation.

familial_amyloidosis.definition: An inherited form of amyloidosis caused by germline mutations in amyloidogenic proteins (most often transthyretin), leading to systemic deposition of misfolded amyloid and progressive organ dysfunction, especially peripheral neuropathy and cardiomyopathy; usually autosomal dominant with variable age of onset.

sickle_cell_anemia.definition: An inherited hemoglobinopathy caused by a mutation in the beta-globin gene that produces hemoglobin S; under low oxygen, HbS polymerizes, causing red blood cells to sickle, leading to chronic hemolytic anemia and recurrent vaso-occlusive crises with potential organ damage; inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.

crouzons_disease.definition: Chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by transmural, segmental inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract, most commonly affecting the terminal ileum and colon with skip lesions; presents with abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and may lead to fistulas, strictures, or abscesses. Management typically includes anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive medications, along with biologic therapies and nutritional support.

hermansky_pudlak_syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by defects in lysosome-related organelle biogenesis, presenting with oculocutaneous albinism and a bleeding diathesis due to platelet dense granule deficiency; may also include granulomatous colitis, pulmonary fibrosis, and other organ involvement.

herpes_simplex.definition: A common DNA virus of the Herpesviridae family (types 1 and 2) that causes mucocutaneous infections, most often oral (HSV-1) and genital (HSV-2); after initial infection it remains latent in sensory ganglia and can reactivate, causing recurrent vesicular lesions, transmitted by close contact.

herpes_genitalis.definition: A sexually transmitted infection caused by herpes simplex virus (usually HSV-2) affecting the genital area, characterized by painful vesicular lesions that may ulcerate, with possible recurrences; transmitted through sexual contact; treated with antiviral medications (e.g., acyclovir, valacyclovir).

herpes_labialis.definition: A contagious viral infection of the lips and surrounding oral skin caused by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), presenting with painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base that crust and heal; reactivations occur with triggers such as stress, fever, or sun exposure.

herpes_menstrualis.definition: A pattern of herpes simplex virus infections in which outbreaks recur in relation to the menstrual cycle, typically around menses, believed to be influenced by hormonal changes; not a distinct disease and is treated with standard antiviral therapy.

valacyclovir.definition: Valacyclovir is an antiviral prodrug of acyclovir that, after oral administration, is converted to acyclovir and inhibits viral DNA synthesis to treat and suppress infections caused by herpes simplex viruses (HSV-1/2) and varicella-zoster virus (VZV).

penciclovir.definition: A topical antiviral agent; an acyclic guanine nucleoside analogue that is phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase and cellular kinases to its active triphosphate form, which inhibits viral DNA polymerase and viral replication; used to treat recurrent herpes simplex infections, especially herpes labialis (cold sores).

tzanck_reaction.definition: A cytologic diagnostic test in which cells scraped from a vesicle or lesion are smeared on a slide and stained to look for characteristic cells; the presence of multinucleated giant cells suggests herpes simplex or varicella-zoster infection, but the test is not specific and cannot distinguish HSV from VZV.

nucleated_giant_cells.definition: Large macrophage-derived cells formed by the fusion of monocytes, containing two or more nuclei; commonly seen in granulomatous inflammation and foreign body reactions, with subtypes such as Langhans-type (peripherally arranged nuclei) and foreign-body giant cells (nuclei scattered).

oral_mucosa.definition: The layer of soft pinkish tissue that lines the interior of the mouth.

nasal_mucosa.definition: The mucous membrane lining the nasal cavity, typically the respiratory mucosa composed of pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells over a lamina propria; it humidifies and warms inspired air, traps particles in mucus, and clears debris via the mucociliary escalator. A small region—the olfactory mucosa—in the superior nasal cavity houses olfactory receptor neurons for the sense of smell.

glossopharyngeal_nerve.definition: A mixed cranial nerve (CN IX) supplying sensory, motor, and parasympathetic fibers: sensory to the oropharynx and posterior tongue (including taste), carotid body/sinus; motor to the stylopharyngeus; parasympathetic to the parotid gland via the otic ganglion; and afferent limb of the gag reflex.

vagus_nerve.definition: A mixed cranial nerve (CN X) that provides parasympathetic innervation to thoracic and most abdominal viscera, carries visceral afferent fibers, and supplies motor innervation to certain pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles, thereby regulating heart rate, airway tone, and gastrointestinal motility and secretions.

medullary_respiratory_center.definition: An area in the medulla oblongata containing the dorsal and ventral respiratory groups that generates the basic inspiratory rhythm and integrates chemoreceptor and higher-center input to regulate respiratory rate and depth.

intratracheal_pressure.definition: The pressure inside the tracheal lumen; the airway pressure within the trachea during respiration or mechanical ventilation, determined by ventilator settings and airway/compliance factors.

pulmonary_inflation.definition: The act of expanding the lungs by drawing air into the airways during inspiration, increasing lung volume and facilitating gas exchange in the alveoli.

herniography.definition: A radiographic examination in which contrast material is injected into the hernial sac to outline the hernia and its contents.

incisional_hernia.definition: A hernia that develops at the site of a prior abdominal surgical incision, caused by weakness or failure of the fascial closure, allowing abdominal contents (commonly small bowel or omentum) to protrude through the incision.

direct_inguinal_hernia.definition: A protrusion of abdominal contents through a weakness in the floor of the inguinal canal (Hesselbach's triangle), medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, through the posterior wall of the canal; typically acquired in older men and has a lower risk of strangulation than indirect inguinal hernias.

indirect_inguinal_hernia.definition: An indirect inguinal hernia is a hernial sac that enters the inguinal canal through the deep (internal) inguinal ring, carrying abdominal contents lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, typically due to a persistent processus vaginalis; it often descends into the scrotum in males and is usually congenital but can present later.

abdominal_hernia.definition: A bulge of abdominal contents through a defect or weakness in the abdominal wall, often at the umbilicus or a prior surgical scar, which may be reducible and carries a risk of incarceration or strangulation requiring surgical repair.

diaphragmatic_hernia.definition: A defect or opening in the diaphragm that allows abdominal organs to protrude into the thoracic cavity; it can be congenital (e.g., Bochdalek or Morgagni hernias) or acquired (traumatic) and may impair respiration.

femoral_hernia.definition: A protrusion of abdominal contents through the femoral canal in the groin, just below the inguinal ligament, typically presenting as a groin or upper-thigh bulge; it has a relatively high risk of incarceration or strangulation and usually requires surgical repair.

hiatal_hernia.definition: A condition in which part of the stomach protrudes through the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm into the thorax, often causing gastroesophageal reflux; the most common form is sliding, in which the gastroesophageal junction and part of the stomach move above the diaphragm, while the paraesophageal (rolling) form involves herniation of part of the stomach beside the esophagus with the junction remaining below the diaphragm.

herniated_disk.definition: Protrusion of the inner gel-like nucleus pulposus through a tear in the outer annulus fibrosus of an intervertebral disc, potentially compressing adjacent nerves and causing back pain with radicular symptoms such as leg pain, numbness, or weakness.

herniated_nucleus_pulposus.definition: A condition in which the soft inner material (nucleus pulposus) of a spinal intervertebral disc protrudes through a tear in the outer disc layer (annulus fibrosus), potentially compressing adjacent nerve roots and causing back pain with radicular symptoms.

ruptured_intervertebral_disk.definition: Protrusion of the nucleus pulposus through a tear in the annulus fibrosus of an intervertebral disk, potentially compressing adjacent nerve roots and causing back pain with radicular symptoms (sciatica). Most common in the lumbar spine; often due to degenerative changes or acute injury. Treatments range from conservative measures (NSAIDs, physical therapy) to surgical discectomy in cases of persistent or progressive neurologic deficits.

slipped_disk.definition: A condition in which the soft inner part of an intervertebral disc protrudes through the outer fibrous ring, potentially irritating or compressing adjacent nerves and causing back pain, leg pain (sciatica), numbness, or weakness.

intervertebral_disk.definition: A fibrocartilaginous cushion between adjacent vertebrae that absorbs compressive forces and allows limited movement; it consists of an outer ring called the annulus fibrosus and an inner gel-like core called the nucleus pulposus.

nucleus_pulposus.definition: The gel-like shock-absorbing central portion of each spinal disc.

annulus_fibrosus.definition: The tough outer covering of the discs in the spine.

lumbar_spine.definition: Lower portion of the vertebral column composed of five lumbar vertebrae (L1–L5) between the thoracic spine and the sacrum; bears most of the body's weight, enables movement of the trunk (flexion, extension, and lateral bending), and contains the lumbar intervertebral discs and accompanying nerve roots.

nerve_root.definition: The portion of a spinal nerve as it emerges from the spinal cord, comprising the dorsal (sensory) root and ventral (motor) root; the dorsal root carries sensory fibers (with cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion) and the ventral root carries motor fibers.

spinal_cord.definition: A cylindrical bundle of nervous tissue within the vertebral canal that transmits motor and sensory information between the brain and the body and coordinates reflexes; it is a part of the central nervous system and is protected by the vertebral column, meninges, and cerebrospinal fluid.

withdrawal.definition: A response to danger or stress characterized by apathy, lethargy, and depression; or the physical or psychological response to a sudden lack of an addictive substance such as alcohol or nicotine.

abstinence_syndrome.definition: A withdrawal syndrome that occurs when a person who is physically dependent on a drug stops or reduces intake, causing autonomic hyperactivity, tremor, anxiety, irritability, nausea/vomiting, insomnia, and agitation; severity and symptoms depend on the substance.

maintenance_therapy.definition: A long-term treatment given after an initial course of therapy to maintain disease remission or control and to prevent relapse or progression.

opium_alkaloids.definition: A group of naturally occurring alkaloids derived from opium (Papaver somniferum), including morphine, codeine, thebaine, noscapine, and papaverine; they act on opioid receptors to produce analgesia and other effects, with risks of dependence, tolerance, and respiratory depression.

iron_deficiency_anemia.definition: A common form of anemia caused by insufficient iron available for hemoglobin synthesis, usually due to inadequate intake, malabsorption, or ongoing blood loss; it results in microcytic, hypochromic red blood cells and low ferritin.

hemorrhagic_familial_angiomatosis.definition: A hereditary condition characterized by numerous vascular lesions (angiomas) that have a propensity to bleed, typically involving the skin and mucous membranes and sometimes internal organs.

herpes simplex encephalitis.definition: A rapidly progressive viral encephalitis caused by herpes simplex virus (most often HSV-1), typically affecting the temporal lobes; it presents with fever, headache, altered mental status, seizures, and focal neurological deficits. Diagnosis is by CSF PCR for HSV DNA and MRI with temporal lobe involvement. Treatment is urgent intravenous acyclovir.

herpes zoster ophthalmicus.definition: Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve, causing shingles affecting the eye and periocular skin; presents with a unilateral vesicular rash on the forehead/eyelids and potential ocular involvement (conjunctivitis, keratitis, uveitis) that can threaten vision, with Hutchinson sign indicating higher risk of eye involvement.

hsv1.definition: An enveloped double-stranded DNA virus of the herpesviridae family (alphaherpesvirus) that commonly causes orolabial herpes (cold sores) and establishes lifelong latency in the trigeminal ganglion with periodic reactivation; transmitted by direct contact with infected secretions.

oral herpes.definition: An infection of the lips and oral mucosa caused primarily by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV‑1), characterized by painful vesicular lesions on the lips or inside the mouth that crust over; it may recur due to latent infection in the trigeminal ganglion and is spread by close contact such as kissing or sharing utensils.

herpes labialis.definition: A recurrent viral infection of the lips and peri-oral skin caused by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), characterized by painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base that crust and heal within 1–2 weeks; highly contagious and often reactivates with triggers such as sun exposure, fever, or stress.

cold sore.definition: A contagious eruption around the lips or perioral skin caused by reactivation of herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1); it typically begins with tingling or itching, then grouped vesicles on an erythematous base that crust over, and it tends to recur.

hsv2.definition: An infection caused by herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2); a lifelong viral infection that typically presents with recurrent painful genital ulcers or vesicles, sometimes accompanied by fever and malaise, and is transmitted mainly through sexual contact. The virus establishes latency in sacral nerve ganglia with episodic reactivations; there is no cure, but antiviral medications can shorten symptoms, reduce recurrences, and lower transmission risk.

crusts.definition: A dried exudate on the surface of the skin or mucous membranes, composed of serum, blood, or pus, typically forming over a healing lesion or ulcer.

herpes simplex keratitis.definition: An ocular infection/inflammation of the cornea caused by herpes simplex virus (most often HSV-1), typically presenting with eye pain, redness, and photophobia, with epithelial disease showing dendritic corneal ulcers on staining; treated with antiviral therapy and, in stromal involvement, corticosteroids under antiviral cover.

herpetic gingivostomatitis.definition: An acute primary infection of the oral mucosa and gingiva caused by herpes simplex virus (usually HSV-1), characterized by fever, irritability, gingival swelling, and clusters of painful vesicles that rupture to form ulcers on the lips, tongue, and other oral surfaces; common in children and typically self-limited within 1–2 weeks; management focuses on hydration, analgesia, and, in select cases, antiviral therapy (eg, acyclovir) started early.

herpetic encephalitis.definition: A viral brain infection caused by herpes simplex virus (usually HSV-1) leading to acute encephalitis, often with temporal lobe involvement; presents with fever, altered mental status, seizures, and focal neurological deficits; diagnosed by CSF HSV PCR and treated urgently with intravenous acyclovir.

simian b virus encephalomyelitis.definition: Encephalomyelitis caused by Macacine herpesvirus 1 (B virus) in nonhuman primates, characterized by inflammation of the brain and spinal cord; zoonotic transmission to humans can occur, often resulting in severe, frequently fatal encephalitis.

herpes zoster virus.definition: An enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus in the Herpesviridae family that causes varicella (chickenpox) as the primary infection and can later reactivate to cause herpes zoster (shingles); it establishes lifelong latency in sensory ganglia and is transmitted primarily via respiratory droplets.

human herpesvirus 6.definition: An enveloped double‑stranded DNA human herpesvirus of the Betaherpesvirinae subfamily (HHV‑6) that infects humans and establishes lifelong latency in monocytes and CD4+ T cells; most commonly acquired in early childhood and causes roseola infantum (exanthem subitum); exists as HHV‑6A and HHV‑6B and is transmitted mainly by saliva, with possible reactivation in immunocompromised individuals and rare neurologic complications.

human herpesvirus 7.definition: A ubiquitous beta-herpesvirus of the Herpesviridae family with double-stranded DNA; acquired mainly in early childhood and establishing lifelong latent infection in CD4+ T lymphocytes, often asymptomatic or presenting with mild febrile illness; reactivation can occur and may be associated with roseola-like rashes or other mild illnesses, but it is generally less pathogenic than HHV-6.

herpesviridae.definition: A family of large enveloped double-stranded DNA viruses with icosahedral capsids and a tegument, which establish lifelong latent infections in hosts and include alpha-, beta-, and gammaherpesviruses (e.g., HSV-1, HSV-2, varicella-zoster virus, CMV, Epstein-Barr virus, Kaposi sarcoma–associated herpesvirus).

postherpetic neuralgia.definition: A chronic neuropathic pain in the area of a previous shingles (herpes zoster) rash that persists after the rash has resolved, often lasting months to years.

corneal ulceration.definition: A defect of the corneal surface (epithelium) that may extend into the stroma (a corneal ulcer), typically due to infection or trauma, presenting with eye pain, redness, tearing or discharge, photophobia, and reduced vision; urgent ophthalmologic evaluation and targeted therapy are required to prevent perforation and scarring.

orbital frontal lobes.definition: Portions of the prefrontal cortex on the ventral surface of the frontal lobes, adjacent to the orbits. They participate in evaluating rewards and punishments, emotion regulation, impulse control, and social behavior; dysfunction can lead to impulsivity and disinhibition.

inferomedial temporal lobe.definition: An anatomical region on the inferior medial surface of the temporal lobe, encompassing limbic structures such as the hippocampus, amygdala, and parahippocampal gyrus; involved in memory and emotion.

gasserian ganglion.definition: A sensory ganglion of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) located in Meckel's cave; it contains the cell bodies of sensory neurons for the face and gives rise to the ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2), and mandibular (V3) divisions.

cranial nerve v.definition: A mixed cranial nerve that provides sensory innervation to the face and motor innervation to the muscles of mastication; it has three divisions (V1 ophthalmic, V2 maxillary, V3 mandibular), with V1 and V2 purely sensory and V3 both sensory and motor. It exits the skull via the superior orbital fissure (V1), foramen rotundum (V2), and foramen ovale (V3) and is derived from the first pharyngeal arch.

ophthalmic branch.definition: A sensory division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1) that supplies sensation to the forehead, scalp, upper eyelid, conjunctiva, cornea, and parts of the nose; it travels through the superior orbital fissure and divides into the frontal, nasociliary, and lacrimal nerves.

external ear canal.definition: A tubular passage that extends from the external opening of the ear to the tympanic membrane, comprising a cartilaginous outer portion and a bony inner portion; it is lined with skin bearing hair and ceruminous glands and functions to conduct sound to the middle ear while protecting it by trapping debris and producing earwax.

hesselbach's hernia.definition: A direct inguinal hernia arising through a weakness in the floor of the inguinal canal (Hesselbach's triangle) medial to the inferior epigastric vessels; typically acquired with age and does not pass through the deep inguinal ring.

inguinal hernia.definition: A protrusion of abdominal contents (most often omentum or bowel) through a weakness in the inguinal canal, presenting as a groin bulge; can be indirect (through the deep inguinal ring) or direct (through Hesselbach's triangle); may be reducible, incarcerated, or strangulated; usually repaired surgically.

direct inguinal hernia.definition: A hernia that protrudes directly through a weakness in the posterior wall of the inguinal canal (Hesselbach's triangle), medial to the inferior epigastric vessels; caused by acquired weakness of the transversalis fascia, more common in older men, and typically does not extend into the scrotum with a relatively low risk of strangulation.

femoral sheath.definition: A fascial sleeve in the femoral triangle that encloses the femoral artery (lateral), femoral vein (middle), and the femoral canal (medial, containing lymphatics and deep inguinal lymph nodes), forming three compartments.

hesselbach's triangle.definition: A triangular area of the anterior abdominal wall in the inguinal region bounded medially by the lateral border of the rectus abdominis, laterally by the inferior epigastric vessels, and inferiorly by the inguinal ligament; its floor is transversalis fascia. It is the site of direct (acquired) inguinal hernias, which protrude medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.

inguinal triangle.definition: An anatomical triangular area of the lower anterior abdominal wall, bounded medially by the lateral border of the rectus abdominis, laterally by the inferior epigastric vessels, and inferiorly by the inguinal ligament; its floor is transversalis fascia. It is the site where direct (acquired) inguinal hernias occur.

glycogen storage disease type vi.definition: A hepatic glycogen storage disease caused by deficiency of liver glycogen phosphorylase, leading to impaired glycogen breakdown with fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly; also known as Hers disease.

glycogen phosphorylase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the phosphorolytic cleavage of α-1,4-glycosidic bonds in glycogen to produce glucose-1-phosphate, the rate-limiting step of glycogenolysis; exists as muscle and liver isoforms and is regulated by phosphorylation and allosteric effectors.

hers disease.definition: I can’t find a recognized medical term “HERS disease” in standard references. Could you please confirm the spelling or provide context (symptoms, body system, or the full term/abbreviation)? If you meant another term (e.g., a specific syndrome or condition), I can define that.

herplex.definition: A brand-name antiviral medication used to treat infections caused by herpes simplex viruses, such as oral or genital herpes.

diazepam.definition: A long-acting benzodiazepine that enhances GABA-A receptor–mediated inhibition, producing anxiolytic, anticonvulsant, sedative, and muscle-relaxant effects; used for anxiety disorders, seizures, alcohol withdrawal, muscle spasm, and procedural sedation; adverse effects include drowsiness, cognitive impairment, amnesia, dependence, tolerance, and respiratory depression, especially with other CNS depressants.

hiccup.definition: A sudden, involuntary contraction (spasm) of the diaphragm and sometimes the intercostal muscles, followed by abrupt closure of the glottis, producing a brief, sharp sound. Also known as singultus; usually self-limited but may indicate underlying irritation or disease if persistent.

sandhoff disease.definition: An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by mutations in HEXA and HEXB that lead to deficiency of β-hexosaminidase A and B and accumulation of GM2 ganglioside in neurons, resulting in progressive neurodegeneration beginning in infancy (often with hepatosplenomegaly).

hunter syndrome.definition: A rare X-linked recessive lysosomal storage disorder (mucopolysaccharidosis type II) caused by deficiency of the enzyme iduronate-2-sulfatase, leading to accumulation of dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate with multisystem involvement (coarse facies, hepatosplenomegaly, airway obstruction, skeletal abnormalities, and often progressive cognitive decline in severe cases).

hib disease.definition: An invasive bacterial infection caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b, potentially presenting as meningitis, epiglottitis, pneumonia, septicemia, or septic arthritis, primarily affecting young children; it is preventable by Hib vaccination.

heterotaxy syndrome.definition: A congenital disorder characterized by abnormal left–right patterning of the thoracoabdominal organs (situs ambiguous), not fitting normal situs solitus or situs inversus; often associated with complex congenital heart disease and visceral/vascular anomalies, typically categorized as polysplenia (left isomerism) or asplenia (right isomerism).

hidradenitis suppurativa.definition: A chronic, relapsing inflammatory skin condition characterized by painful nodules and abscesses that form sinus tracts and scarring in intertriginous areas (most commonly the axillae, groin, and perineal region), often associated with follicular occlusion, obesity, and smoking.

hidradenitis axillaris.definition: A chronic inflammatory skin disorder characterized by recurrent, painful nodules and abscesses in apocrine-gland–bearing skin folds (most commonly the axillae and groin), often with sinus tract formation and scarring.

myositis ossificans.definition: Heterotopic bone formation within skeletal muscle or soft tissues, typically after trauma (traumatic myositis ossificans), causing swelling and progressive stiffness; diagnosed by imaging and usually managed conservatively, with surgical removal reserved for mature lesions if function is impaired.

hexachlorophene.definition: A chlorinated bisphenol antiseptic agent formerly used to reduce microbial growth, especially gram-positive bacteria; it is absorbed through the skin and, at high exposures (notably in infants), can cause serious central nervous system toxicity, leading to regulatory restrictions on its use in consumer products.

hexacosanol.definition: A saturated long-chain fatty alcohol with 26 carbon atoms (hexacosan-1-ol); a primary alcohol found in natural waxes and used as an emollient in cosmetics.

chlorhexidine gluconate.definition: A topical antiseptic formed as the gluconate salt of chlorhexidine; provides broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, yeasts, and some enveloped viruses; used for skin disinfection, preoperative skin prep, wound cleansing, and antiseptic mouthwash; rapid bactericidal action with residual activity; may cause skin irritation or allergic reaction and is not sporicidal.
