intersphincteric groove.definition: A shallow groove along the anal canal that marks the boundary between the internal anal sphincter and the external anal sphincter; it corresponds to the intersphincteric plane, a potential space used to describe fistulous tracts and surgical approaches in anorectal disease.

external anal sphincter.definition: A ring of striated (voluntary) muscle surrounding the distal anal canal that forms part of the anal sphincter complex; it maintains continence through voluntary contraction and is innervated by the inferior rectal nerves from the pudendal nerve.

internal anal sphincter.definition: A thickened ring of smooth muscle at the distal rectum that forms the involuntary anal sphincter, maintaining resting anal tone and continence; it relaxes reflexively during defecation in response to rectal distention and is under autonomic (involuntary) control.

intersection syndrome.definition: A tenosynovitis of the wrist caused by friction where the tendons of the first dorsal extensor compartment (APL, EPB) cross over those of the second dorsal extensor compartment (ECRL, ECRB); presents with tenderness and swelling on the dorsoradial wrist about 4–6 cm proximal to Lister’s tubercle, often due to repetitive wrist extension/flexion (overuse).

interrupted suture.definition: A suturing technique in which each stitch is placed and tied separately, rather than as a continuous running suture; allows precise tissue approximation and easier removal of individual sutures, but is more time-consuming.

intersexuality.definition: A term for a group of congenital conditions in which a person's chromosomal, gonadal, or anatomical sex characteristics do not fit typical binary notions of male or female bodies.

intersex.definition: A person born with a combination of female and male traits.

interneuron.definition: A neuron located entirely within the central nervous system that connects sensory and motor neurons and other interneurons to form neural circuits for information processing; its activity can be excitatory or inhibitory and it does not send signals to the periphery.

internist.definition: A doctor who treats many diseases in adult patients and who also teaches patients good habits to help prevent disease.

internship.definition: A period of supervised practical training following completion of formal education, designed to provide hands-on experience, skills development, and evaluation of competence; in medicine, a year-long clinical training after medical school before entering residency.

os pubis.definition: The pubic bone; one of the three fused components (ilia, ischia, and pubis) that form each hip bone (os coxae). It constitutes the anterior part of the pelvis and articulates with the opposite pubis at the pubic symphysis; its anatomy includes the body (corpus) and the superior and inferior pubic rami.

interspinales.definition: Small muscles between adjacent spinous processes of the vertebrae that aid in extending and stabilizing the vertebral column.

interspinal ligament.definition: A short fibrous band connecting the spinous process of one vertebra to the adjacent vertebra, located in the interspinous space along the posterior spine; it tightens with flexion to limit forward bending and helps stabilize the vertebral column, often blending with the supraspinous ligament.

interspinous.definition: Located between the spinous processes of adjacent vertebrae; refers to the structures in that region, including the ligaments that connect the processes and help limit spinal flexion.

interspinous ligament.definition: A short, fibrous band connecting the adjacent spinous processes of vertebrae, spanning the interspinous space and helping to limit flexion of the spinal column; it blends with the supraspinous ligament.

interstitial cell-stimulating hormone.definition: A gonadotropin produced by the anterior pituitary that stimulates the Leydig cells of the testes to produce testosterone; in humans it is essentially the same as luteinizing hormone (LH).

icsh.definition: An international professional organization that promotes standardization and quality assurance in haematology laboratory testing, developing guidelines, reference materials, and harmonization of hematology methods across laboratories.

painful bladder syndrome.definition: Chronic pelvic or bladder pain with associated urinary symptoms (such as urgency, frequency, or nocturia) lasting six weeks or more, in the absence of an identifiable infection or other cause.

distension of the bladder.definition: Abnormal enlargement of the urinary bladder due to urine accumulation from retention or obstruction, resulting in increased intravesical pressure.

interstitial emphysema.definition: Air within the pulmonary interstitium caused by rupture of alveolar or airway structures, often due to barotrauma or high‑pressure ventilation; may be seen as interstitial lucencies on imaging and can lead to pneumomediastinum or pneumothorax.

uremic pneumonitis.definition: A noninfectious pulmonary complication of advanced kidney failure in which patients develop fever, dyspnea, and diffuse bilateral interstitial/alveolar infiltrates that typically improve with effective dialysis; believed to result from uremic toxins causing inflammation and increased alveolar–capillary permeability.

interstitial fibroid.definition: A benign tumor of smooth muscle cells that develops within the myometrium, the muscular wall of the uterus.

intervillous spaces.definition: Intervillous spaces are the spaces within the placenta between chorionic villi that contain maternal blood; they bathe the villi and facilitate exchange of gases, nutrients, and wastes between maternal and fetal circulations.

intervillous.definition: Relating to the space between the chorionic villi of the placenta; the intervillous space is filled with maternal blood that bathes the villi, allowing maternal–fetal exchange of gases, nutrients, and waste products.

interstitial inflammation.definition: Inflammation of the interstitial tissue (the connective tissue between organ parenchymal cells), typically with inflammatory cell infiltrates (often lymphocytes and macrophages) and edema, which can disrupt tissue architecture and function.

vascular hypersensitivity.definition: An exaggerated immune-mediated reaction of the blood vessels to an antigen or trigger, causing inflammation and injury to the vessel walls (vasculitis); commonly immune complex–mediated (type III) hypersensitivity.

ild.definition: A group of disorders characterized by inflammation and fibrotic scarring of the lung interstitium, causing restrictive lung disease and impaired gas exchange; etiologies include idiopathic forms and secondary causes such as environmental or occupational exposures, autoimmune diseases, and certain drugs; symptoms typically include progressive dyspnea and a dry cough; diagnosis relies on high‑resolution CT and pulmonary function tests; treatment is disease‑specific and may include antifibrotic therapy for idiopathic cases and immunosuppressants for inflammatory subtypes.

interstitial mastitis.definition: Inflammation of the breast interstitium (stroma)—the connective tissue surrounding the ducts and lobules—rather than inflammation confined to the ducts or glandular tissue, often presenting with breast tenderness, swelling, and sometimes fibrotic changes.

ducts of the breast.definition: A network of lactiferous ducts that carry milk from the mammary lobes to the nipple; they branch within the breast and converge toward the nipple, with dilated lactiferous sinuses beneath the areola.

interstitial myositis.definition: An inflammatory myopathy in which inflammatory cells predominantly infiltrate the interstitial connective tissue between muscle fibers (instead of the muscle fibers themselves), often with edema and possible fibrosis, and may be seen in autoimmune conditions.

fibrosa.definition: Relating to or composed of fibrous tissue; a fibrous layer or tunic in anatomy (for example, the fibrous tunic of the eye, consisting of the sclera and cornea).

chronic interstitial nephritis.definition: A long-standing inflammatory and fibrotic process of the kidney interstitium with tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis, causing progressive decline in renal function; etiologies include analgesic nephropathy, chronic infection, autoimmune disease, reflux/obstructive disease, and nephrotoxin exposure.

ureteral obstruction.definition: A mechanical blockage of one or both ureters that prevents urine from passing from the renal pelvis to the bladder, often causing hydronephrosis and flank or groin pain; common causes include ureteral stones, strictures, tumors, or external compression, with persistent obstruction risking renal impairment.

interval health history.definition: An account of changes in a patient’s health since the last visit, including onset, duration, progression or improvement of symptoms, and response to treatments.

interval.definition: A period of time between two events or states; used in medicine to describe the duration between onset of symptoms and evaluation, between treatments, or between follow-up assessments (e.g., interval change on follow-up imaging).

interventional cardiology.definition: Catheter-based treatment of heart disease, primarily percutaneous coronary interventions (angioplasty with stents) to open narrowed coronary arteries, plus other minimally invasive procedures for structural heart disease and select valvular or arrhythmic conditions, performed via vascular access.

interventional.definition: Relating to medical procedures in which instruments are introduced into the body to diagnose or treat disease.

intervertebral ganglion.definition: A dorsal root ganglion located near the intervertebral foramen that contains the cell bodies of sensory neurons of a spinal nerve.

intervertebral fibrocartilage.definition: Fibrocartilaginous tissue between adjacent vertebral bodies forming the intervertebral discs; consists of an outer annulus fibrosus of concentric fibrocartilaginous lamellae surrounding an inner gelatinous nucleus pulposus, providing shock absorption and permitting limited spinal movement.

intervertebral joint.definition: A cartilaginous joint between adjacent vertebral bodies in the spine, consisting of the intervertebral disc and adjacent endplates, allowing limited movement and distributing axial load.

interstitium.definition: The connective tissue framework and the spaces between the cells of a tissue or organ, containing extracellular matrix and interstitial fluid, along with resident cells (e.g., fibroblasts) and microvasculature.

intertransverse ligament.definition: A thin band of connective tissue connecting the transverse processes of adjacent vertebrae, forming part of the spinal ligaments; it limits lateral flexion and helps stabilize the vertebral column.

intertransverse ligaments.definition: A series of thin fibrous ligaments connecting the transverse processes of adjacent vertebrae, forming part of the spinal ligaments; they limit lateral flexion and stabilize the vertebral column.

intertransverse.definition: Situated between the transverse processes of adjacent vertebrae; used to describe structures such as the intertransverse ligaments and intertransverse muscles that connect neighboring transverse processes.

intertrochanteric crest.definition: A bony ridge on the posterior surface of the femur that extends between the greater and lesser trochanters, forming the posterior boundary of the intertrochanteric region.

intertrochanteric fracture.definition: A fracture of the proximal femur that occurs between the greater and lesser trochanters (the intertrochanteric region), typically extracapsular and often resulting from a fall in older adults with osteoporosis; managed surgically with internal fixation or arthroplasty depending on fracture pattern and patient factors.

intertrochanteric line.definition: A line on the anterior aspect of the proximal femur that connects the greater and lesser trochanters, marking the junction between the femoral neck and shaft.

linea aspera.definition: A prominent longitudinal ridge on the posterior surface of the femur shaft, with medial and lateral lips that serve as attachment sites for several thigh muscles (e.g., adductor longus, adductor brevis, adductor magnus, vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, and the short head of the biceps femoris).

intertuberous diameter.definition: Distance between the two ischial tuberosities (the sit bones) of the pelvis, representing the transverse width of the pelvic outlet.

interureteral.definition: Situated between the two ureters; referring to structures or regions that lie between the ureters.

tubal pregnancy.definition: An ectopic pregnancy in which a fertilized egg implants and grows within the fallopian tube (most often the ampulla), outside the uterine cavity; it may rupture and cause life-threatening internal bleeding if not treated.

interstitial tubal pregnancy.definition: An ectopic pregnancy implanted in the intramural (interstitial) portion of the fallopian tube within the myometrium at or near the uterotubal junction; a tubal ectopic that can rupture later and cause life-threatening hemorrhage.

interstitial pregnancy.definition: A type of ectopic pregnancy in which the gestational sac implants in the interstitial (intramural) portion of the fallopian tube as it traverses the myometrium near the uterine cornua; it is surrounded by only a thin myometrial layer and carries a high risk of rupture and life-threatening hemorrhage in the first trimester.

interstitial implantation.definition: A form of brachytherapy in which radioactive sources are implanted directly into the tissue of a tumor (interstitially), delivering a high local radiation dose with rapid fall-off to spare surrounding normal tissue.

pneumocystosis.definition: An opportunistic fungal infection caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii, typically presenting as pneumonia in immunocompromised individuals.

interstitial plasma cell pneumonia.definition: An uncommon histopathologic pattern of interstitial pneumonia defined by predominant infiltration of plasma cells in the lung interstitium.

candidal.definition: Relating to Candida species, a genus of yeasts that can cause opportunistic fungal infections in humans.

silica.definition: A mineral composed of silicon dioxide (SiO2); crystalline forms (quartz, cristobalite, tridymite) that, when inhaled, can cause silicosis and other pneumoconioses.

chlorambucil.definition: An oral nitrogen mustard–type alkylating chemotherapy agent that cross-links DNA, inhibiting DNA replication and causing tumor cell death; used to treat certain lymphoid cancers such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia and some non-Hodgkin lymphomas.

hexamethonium.definition: An autonomic ganglion-blocking agent (nicotinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist) historically used as an antihypertensive; it blocks transmission at autonomic ganglia, reducing sympathetic and parasympathetic outflow, but is largely obsolete due to widespread autonomic side effects.

sjogren's syndrome.definition: A chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by lymphocytic infiltration and destruction of exocrine glands, most commonly the lacrimal and salivary glands, leading to dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and dry mouth (xerostomia); it can be primary or associated with other autoimmune diseases (secondary) and may have systemic manifestations such as fatigue, arthralgia, and vasculitis.

systemic sclerosis.definition: A chronic autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by progressive fibrosis of the skin and internal organs due to excessive collagen deposition, accompanied by vasculopathy and immune dysregulation; commonly presents with Raynaud phenomenon and skin thickening (scleroderma) with variable involvement of the lungs, heart, kidneys, and gastrointestinal tract. It is classified into diffuse and limited cutaneous subtypes.

lumen.definition: The hollow part of a tube, like a blood vessel, or the cavity in a hollow organ.

lacteal.definition: A lymphatic capillary in the core of a villus of the small intestine that absorbs dietary fats (lipids) from digested food and transports chyle via the lymphatic system.

lymphatic.definition: Related to the lymph system, an important part of your immune system (helps to protect you against disease).

apoplexy.definition: A sudden onset of neurological impairment caused by disruption of cerebral blood flow—historically referred to as a stroke, arising from either cerebral hemorrhage or vessel occlusion (ischemia).

intestinal bypass.definition: A surgical procedure in which a portion of the small intestine is bypassed to reduce nutrient and caloric absorption, typically by creating a small stomach pouch and rerouting food to a distal intestinal segment (gastric bypass).

intestinal colic.definition: A cramp-like, intermittent abdominal pain caused by rhythmic contractions of the intestinal smooth muscle, often due to gas, distension, or partial obstruction.

flora.definition: Microorganisms that normally inhabit a body site or environment (such as the human gut or skin), forming a balanced microbial ecosystem that aids digestion, metabolism, and protection against pathogens; disruption can contribute to disease.

enteric infection.definition: An infection of the intestinal tract by pathogenic organisms (bacteria, viruses, or parasites) causing gastroenteritis, characterized by diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, and sometimes fever and dehydration; typically acquired via ingestion of contaminated food or water.

intestinal fluke.definition: A parasitic flatworm (trematode) that inhabits the intestine of humans or animals; infection occurs after ingestion of larvae in undercooked fish or contaminated aquatic foods and can cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, and malabsorption; diagnosed by stool examination for eggs and treated with praziquantel.

heterophyes.definition: A genus of small intestinal flukes (trematodes) in the family Heterophyidae; humans become infected by eating undercooked freshwater fish containing metacercariae, with adults living in the small intestine and causing gastrointestinal symptoms; diagnosis is by stool examination for eggs; treated with praziquantel.

metagonimus.definition: A genus of small intestinal flukes (trematodes) in the family Heterophyidae that can cause metagonimiasis in humans; infection occurs after ingestion of raw or undercooked freshwater fish containing metacercariae, with adult worms residing in the small intestine.

impacted feces.definition: A mass of hardened stool that cannot be passed from the colon or rectum, usually due to severe constipation or reduced bowel motility; it may cause abdominal pain, bloating, and overflow incontinence, and typically requires disimpaction plus laxatives or enemas along with treatment of underlying causes.

pseudoobstruction.definition: Functional intestinal obstruction presenting with signs of obstruction (abdominal distension, pain, nausea/vomiting, obstipation) but without a mechanical blockage on imaging; caused by impaired peristalsis (paralytic ileus) or nonmechanical dilatation of the colon (e.g., Ogilvie syndrome).

strangulation.definition: External constriction of the neck by a hand, ligature, or other device that compresses the airway and/or neck vessels, leading to cerebral hypoxia and potentially unconsciousness or death.

intestinal tract.definition: The portion of the digestive tract consisting of the small and large intestines where digestion continues, most nutrients are absorbed, water is reabsorbed, and waste is formed and moved toward elimination.

pyloric.definition: Relating to the pylorus, the distal portion of the stomach that opens into the duodenum; includes the pyloric sphincter that regulates gastric emptying.

intima.definition: The innermost layer of a blood vessel, consisting of endothelial cells lining the lumen (the vascular endothelium) and a basement membrane.

intimal.definition: Relating to the tunica intima, the innermost lining of a blood vessel or heart chamber.

intimal sclerosis.definition: Thickening and hardening of the tunica intima of arteries due to fibrous tissue deposition and smooth muscle proliferation, leading to reduced elasticity and potential luminal narrowing; a component of arteriosclerotic vascular change often associated with aging and vascular risk factors.

intradialytic hypotension.definition: A drop in blood pressure that occurs during hemodialysis, often defined as a decrease in systolic blood pressure by ≥20 mmHg (or a drop in mean arterial pressure) accompanied by symptoms such as dizziness, nausea, or cramps and requiring treatment (e.g., fluid administration or reduced ultrafiltration).

intradermal test.definition: A diagnostic skin test in which a small amount of antigen is injected into the dermis to elicit a localized immune reaction, typically used for allergy assessment or tuberculin testing.

intradermal testing.definition: A diagnostic procedure in which a small volume of antigen is injected into the dermis to provoke a localized wheal-and-flare reaction, used to assess immediate-type hypersensitivity to medications, venoms, or other substances.

intradiscal electrothermal therapy.definition: A percutaneous procedure in which a temperature-controlled probe is placed into a painful intervertebral disc and heated to around 80–90°C to denature collagen and ablate nociceptive nerve fibers in the annulus, with the goal of sealing annular fissures and reducing discogenic low back pain.

discogenic low back pain.definition: A form of axial low back pain caused by pathology of the intervertebral disc itself (e.g., degeneration, annular tears, or internal disc disruption) rather than nerve root compression; pain is localized to the lumbar region and may be referred to the buttock or thigh.

intraductal carcinoma.definition: A neoplasm arising within the ducts of a gland; in the breast, it most often refers to ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), a noninvasive cancer in which malignant epithelial cells are confined to the ducts and have not invaded the surrounding tissue.

intraductal carcinoma of the salivary gl.word: intraductal carcinoma of the salivary gland
intraductal carcinoma of the salivary gl.definition: A rare, noninvasive malignant epithelial proliferation confined to the ductal system of a salivary gland, analogous to ductal carcinoma in situ of the breast; characterized by malignant cells within ducts with no invasion of surrounding tissue.

intraductal papilloma.definition: A benign papillary tumor arising within a duct (most often in the breast) characterized by a fibrovascular core covered by ductal epithelium with an outer myoepithelial layer; commonly presents with unilateral nipple discharge and is typically treated by local excision.

intradural lipoma.definition: A benign fat-containing lesion confined to the dural sac of the spinal canal (intradural, usually intradural extramedullary), often congenital and associated with spinal dysraphism; it can cause compression of the spinal cord or nerve roots, leading to myelopathy or radiculopathy. MRI typically shows a fat signal that is high on T1 and suppresses with fat-saturation sequences.

intraepidermal carcinoma.definition: A malignant squamous cell neoplasm confined to the epidermis (carcinoma in situ) with no invasion into the dermis.

intraepidermal vesicle.definition: A small fluid-filled blister located within the epidermis, arising from separation between keratinocytes (intraepidermal split), commonly due to acantholysis (as seen in pemphigus vulgaris).

intrafollicular insemination.definition: A fertility procedure in which motile sperm are injected directly into a mature ovarian follicle (typically under ultrasound guidance) with the goal of fertilizing the contained oocyte in situ; largely superseded by IVF/ICSI and now rarely used.

intrafusal muscle fiber.definition: Specialized fibers inside a muscle spindle that detect muscle stretch and the rate of length change; they are innervated by gamma motor neurons, have a noncontractile central region with sensory endings, and have contractile polar ends that adjust spindle tension and sensitivity.

intrahepatic cholestasis.definition: A condition in which bile flow is impaired within the liver, leading to accumulation of bile acids in the liver and blood and typically causing pruritus, jaundice, and cholestatic liver-test abnormalities; causes include pregnancy-associated cholestasis, drug-induced cholestasis, and other hepatocellular disorders.

intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy.definition: A pregnancy-associated cholestatic liver disorder presenting with pruritus and elevated serum bile acids (with or without raised transaminases) that typically begins in the third trimester and resolves after delivery; it increases the risk of fetal distress, preterm birth, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, and stillbirth, and is often treated with ursodeoxycholic acid and careful fetal monitoring.

intraluminal coronary artery stent.definition: An expandable mesh tube placed within a diseased coronary artery during percutaneous coronary intervention to keep the lumen open after angioplasty, supporting the vessel wall and reducing recoil and restenosis; it remains intraluminal and can be bare-metal or drug-eluting.

intramammary abscess.definition: A localized collection of pus within the breast tissue caused by infection, most often secondary to mastitis; it commonly presents as a painful, tender, fluctuant mass and typically requires antibiotics and drainage.

intramembranous ossification.definition: Bone formation that occurs directly from mesenchyme without a cartilage intermediate, forming flat bones of the skull, face, and clavicles; osteoblasts lay down bone matrix that mineralizes into woven bone, which is later remodeled into lamellar bone.

mittelschmerz.definition: Mid-cycle ovulatory pain presenting as unilateral lower abdominal or pelvic discomfort around the time of ovulation, caused by follicular rupture and peritoneal irritation; typically lasts from a few minutes to 1–2 days and is benign.

intramural part of the urethra.definition: That segment of the male urethra that lies within the wall of the urinary bladder at the bladder neck; it is the preprostatic portion just proximal to the prostate.

intramural part of the ureter.definition: The portion of the ureter that runs within the wall of the urinary bladder (the intramural or intravesical segment), traversing the detrusor muscle obliquely to open into the bladder lumen at the ureteric orifice; its oblique course helps prevent vesicoureteral reflux.

intravenous bolus.definition: A single, rapid injection of a drug or fluid directly into the bloodstream via an intravenous line, designed to rapidly achieve therapeutic plasma levels or restore intravascular volume.

bolus.definition: A soft mass of chewed food. Alternatively, a single large dose of a medication given intravenously.

serums.definition: Clear, pale-yellow fluid that remains after blood has clotted; the liquid portion of blood that contains antibodies and other proteins but lacks fibrinogen and other clotting factors; used in serology and diagnostic testing, and in cosmetics refers to a concentrated topical product with active ingredients.

iol.definition: An artificial lens implanted inside the eye to replace the natural crystalline lens, typically after cataract removal; used to restore focus and vision and can be monofocal, multifocal, or toric to correct refractive errors.

intraoperative.definition: Occurring during a surgical procedure; relating to events or actions that take place during the operation.

intraoperative hyperthermia.definition: An abnormal elevation of core body temperature that occurs during surgery, typically defined as a rise above normal baseline (often >38°C/100.4°F), caused by malignant hyperthermia, adverse anesthetic or drug reactions, infection, or extensive tissue injury, and requiring prompt evaluation and treatment.

intraoperative lymphatic mapping.definition: A surgical technique in which a tracer (such as blue dye and/or a radiotracer) is injected near a tumor during surgery to visualize lymphatic drainage and identify sentinel lymph nodes for biopsy to stage cancer.

sentinel node biopsy.definition: A surgical procedure to identify and remove the sentinel lymph node—the first lymph node draining the tumor—for pathological examination to determine if cancer has spread; usually using a radioactive tracer and/or blue dye, and if negative, further lymph node dissection may be avoided.

intraoperative radiotherapy.definition: A procedure in which a single, targeted dose of ionizing radiation is delivered to the tumor bed during surgery, immediately after tumor removal, to eradicate residual cancer cells while minimizing exposure to surrounding healthy tissue.

intraoperative ultrasound.definition: A real-time imaging technique using ultrasound during surgery to visualize tissues, guide instrument placement and resections, assess lesion extent and margins, and evaluate blood flow; performed with a sterile intraoperative ultrasound probe and does not involve ionizing radiation.

syrinx.definition: A fluid-filled cavity or tubular channel within the spinal cord or brainstem; enlargement of this cavity can lead to syringomyelia with neurologic deficits.

syrinxes.definition:
- A fluid-filled cavity or dilation within the spinal cord, which can enlarge and contribute to syringomyelia.
- The avian vocal organ located at the junction of the trachea and primary bronchi, consisting of vibrating membranes and muscles used to produce sound.

intrathoracic goiter.definition: Thyroid enlargement that extends from the neck into the thoracic cavity, usually into the superior mediastinum (retrosternal/intrathoracic goiter); it may be asymptomatic or cause compression of the trachea, esophagus, or great vessels and often requires surgical excision.

intrathoracic kidney.definition: A rare congenital ectopic kidney located in the thoracic cavity, typically due to a diaphragmatic defect or diaphragmatic eventration, often asymptomatic with preserved renal function.

thoracic kidney.definition: Congenital ectopic renal tissue located in the thoracic cavity, resulting from abnormal ascent of the kidney through a diaphragmatic defect; usually unilateral and asymptomatic with preserved renal function, and may be associated with diaphragmatic hernia or diaphragmatic eventration.

intratubal insemination.definition: Direct deposition of prepared sperm into the fallopian tube via a transcervical catheter to achieve fertilization; it is an infrequently used fertility procedure due to higher risks and the availability of IUI and IVF.

intrauterine transfusion.definition: A ultrasound-guided fetal procedure in which donor packed red blood cells are transfused directly into the fetal circulation—most often via the umbilical vein—to treat fetal anemia (commonly due to maternal alloimmunization).

intrauterine insemination.definition: A fertility procedure in which prepared sperm are placed directly into the uterus around the time of ovulation to facilitate fertilization, often using a partner's or donor sperm and sometimes combined with ovulation-inducing medications.

intrauterine growth retardation.definition: A condition in which a fetus fails to reach its growth potential, typically defined as estimated fetal weight below the 10th percentile for gestational age, often due to placental insufficiency, maternal disease, fetal anomalies, or infection.

intrauterine growth curve.definition: A graphical reference that plots fetal size measurements against gestational age to evaluate whether fetal growth is appropriate, identifying patterns such as small-for-gestational-age or fetal growth restriction.

intrauterine catheter.definition: A flexible tube inserted through the cervix into the uterus to deliver substances (most commonly semen during intrauterine insemination) or to measure intrauterine pressure during labor.

iui.definition: An infertility treatment in which prepared sperm is placed directly into the uterus around the time of ovulation to increase the chance of fertilization, often following ovarian stimulation and using partner or donor sperm.

iud.definition: A small, T-shaped contraceptive device inserted into the uterus to prevent pregnancy; it may be copper (nonhormonal) or hormonal (releases progestin) and provides long-acting contraception for several years (typically 3–12 years depending on the type).

copper iud.definition: An intrauterine device (IUD) that is nonhormonal and contains copper; released copper ions create a spermicidal environment in the uterus, impairing sperm motility and viability to prevent fertilization; provides long-acting reversible contraception for up to about 10–12 years (brand dependent) and may cause heavier menstrual bleeding and cramps.

perforation of the uterus.definition: A full-thickness defect in the wall of the uterus (through the myometrium) creating a communication between the uterine cavity and the peritoneal cavity, usually caused by uterine instrumentation or obstetric procedures, and potentially leading to intraperitoneal bleeding, infection, or injury to adjacent organs.

intravascular coagulation test.definition: A set of laboratory tests used to detect and monitor intravascular coagulation disorders (notably disseminated intravascular coagulation). It typically includes platelet count, prothrombin time (PT/INR), activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), fibrinogen level, and markers of fibrin degradation such as D-dimer or fibrin degradation products. These tests assess platelet numbers, coagulation cascade function, and consumption of coagulation factors.

intravascular fluid.definition: Fluid within the vascular system—the plasma portion of extracellular fluid that circulates in blood vessels.

intravenous alimentation.definition: Administration of nutrients directly into the bloodstream via an intravenous route to meet caloric and nutritional needs when the gastrointestinal tract cannot be used for feeding.

intrapleural space.definition: A potential space between the visceral pleura (covering the lungs) and parietal pleura (lining the chest wall) that normally contains a small amount of lubricating pleural fluid and maintains a negative pressure to keep the lungs inflated.

intrapulmonary shunt.definition: A portion of venous blood bypasses alveolar gas exchange by passing through the lungs via intrapulmonary vascular pathways or nonventilated alveoli, resulting in hypoxemia that is incompletely corrected by supplemental oxygen.

intrarenal azotemia.definition: Azotemia due to intrinsic renal parenchymal injury (e.g., acute tubular necrosis, glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis) resulting in reduced glomerular filtration and impaired tubular function; urine studies often show impaired concentrating ability and elevated urinary sodium, with possible urinary casts depending on the underlying pathology.

intrarenal hemodynamics.definition: The regulation of blood flow and pressure within the kidney, including renal perfusion, glomerular capillary pressure, and filtration rate, achieved by adjusting afferent and efferent arteriolar resistance and by intrarenal autoregulatory mechanisms (e.g., myogenic response, tubuloglomerular feedback) and neurohumoral influences.

renal parenchyma.definition: The functional tissue of the kidney, consisting of the renal cortex and medulla and containing the nephrons and collecting ducts responsible for urine formation.

intrapartum hemorrhage.definition: Bleeding from the genital tract that occurs during labor and delivery, most commonly due to placental pathology (e.g., placental abruption, placenta previa) or uterine rupture; can compromise maternal and fetal status and requires urgent evaluation and management.

winged-tip needle.definition: A small, short intravenous needle with two flexible plastic wings on either side that stabilize it against the skin during venipuncture; used for drawing blood or starting IV therapy, typically attached to tubing or a syringe (also known as a butterfly needle).

intravenous push.definition: A method of delivering a medication directly into the bloodstream by rapid injection through an intravenous line or catheter, typically over 1–5 minutes, often followed by a saline flush.

radiopaque contrast material.definition: A substance with high radiodensity used to enhance X-ray imaging by absorbing X-rays, thereby increasing contrast between structures; commonly iodine- or barium-based agents given orally, rectally, or by injection.

radiographic films.definition: Photographic film used in conventional X-ray imaging to record a radiograph; placed in a light-tight cassette with an intensifying screen, exposed to X-rays, and chemically developed to produce a visible image that reflects tissue density and pathology.

drip chamber.definition: A short, transparent chamber in an IV infusion set between the solution bag and the tubing that visually monitors and helps regulate the infusion rate (drops per minute) and traps air bubbles to reduce the risk of air embolism.

iv bag.definition: A sterile plastic bag containing intravenous solution (such as saline or dextrose) used to deliver fluids, electrolytes, medications, or nutrients into a patient’s bloodstream via an IV catheter.

iv tube.definition: A sterile, disposable tube system that connects an IV catheter to an IV fluid source, enabling administration of fluids, medications, or nutrients directly into a vein; includes a drip chamber, roller clamp, and access ports, and must be primed to remove air.

clamp.definition: A surgical instrument with locking jaws used to grasp and occlude tissue or blood vessels to control bleeding.

drop sensor.definition: A device or sensor that detects the presence or formation of liquid drops, used in medical equipment to verify dosing, monitor drip rate, and trigger alarms for occlusion, leakage, or air in the line.

alarm.definition: A warning signal or alert indicating danger or a problem; in physiology, the initial phase of the body's stress response marked by activation of the sympathetic nervous system and rapid release of stress hormones such as adrenaline and cortisol.

gravity.definition: The seriousness or severity of a medical condition, including its potential to cause morbidity or mortality; used to gauge clinical urgency and prognosis.

iv pump.definition: An electronic device that delivers prescribed IV fluids or medications into a patient’s bloodstream at a controlled, programmable flow rate, often with alarms for occlusions or air in the line.

iv controller.definition: A device that regulates the rate and amount of intravenous fluids delivered to a patient, typically via a programmable pump, and provides alarms for occlusion, air in the line, or tubing disconnection.

peristaltic pump.definition: A positive-displacement pump that moves fluid by sequentially occluding a flexible tubing with rollers or cams, pushing the contents forward as the rollers roll along; the fluid contacts only the tubing, enabling sterile, disposable sets and precise flow for medical infusions and laboratory applications.

syringe pump.definition: A device that delivers precise volumes of fluid by advancing a syringe plunger with a motor at a programmed rate, enabling continuous or intermittent infusion of medications or nutrients via intravenous, subcutaneous, or other routes; includes safety alarms for occlusion and flow issues.

fat emulsion.definition: A stable intravenous emulsion of fat droplets (triglyceride-rich oils) used as a source of calories and essential fatty acids in parenteral nutrition.

intravenous fat emulsion.definition: A sterile intravenous lipid emulsion used as part of parenteral nutrition to provide calories and essential fatty acids; typically made from plant oils (such as soybean or safflower) stabilized with an emulsifier (often egg yolk phospholipids) for IV administration.

soybean oil.definition: An edible vegetable oil derived from mature soybean seeds; it is mainly triglycerides of polyunsaturated and monounsaturated fatty acids (notably linoleic and oleic acids) and is used for cooking, food processing, and as a lipid source in parenteral nutrition.

egg-yolk phospholipids.definition: Phospholipids derived from egg yolk, principally phosphatidylcholine (lecithin) and phosphatidylethanolamine, with smaller amounts of phosphatidylinositol and phosphatidylserine; amphipathic molecules that form lipid bilayers and act as emulsifiers, providing choline in the diet.

linoleic acid.definition: An essential polyunsaturated fatty acid of the omega‑6 family (18:2, n‑6) that must be obtained from the diet; a precursor to arachidonic acid and various eicosanoids, and a component of cell membranes.

oleic acid.definition: A monounsaturated fatty acid (cis-9-octadecenoic acid) with 18 carbon atoms; a major component of olive oil and other dietary fats; serves as a source of energy and a structural component of triglycerides and phospholipids; not an essential fatty acid.

palmitic acid.definition: A saturated long-chain fatty acid with 16 carbon atoms (C16:0); a major component of dietary fats and body lipids (e.g., triglycerides and membrane phospholipids).

linolenic acid.definition: An essential omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (18:3 n-3) that cannot be synthesized by humans and must be obtained from the diet. It serves as a precursor to the longer-chain omega-3 fatty acids eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) through desaturation and elongation. Dietary sources include flaxseed, chia seeds, walnuts, and certain vegetable oils such as canola and soybean.

parenteral alimentation.definition: A method of delivering nutrients directly into the bloodstream via intravenous infusion, bypassing the gastrointestinal tract, to provide total or partial nutrition when oral or enteral feeding is not feasible; typically administered through a central venous catheter and may include amino acids, dextrose, lipids, electrolytes, vitamins, and trace elements.

fatty-acid overload.definition: An excess of circulating fatty acids (free fatty acids) that overwhelms storage and oxidation capacity, causing ectopic lipid accumulation and lipotoxic effects in tissues such as liver and muscle, and contributing to insulin resistance and metabolic disease.

hyperlipemia.definition: A condition characterized by elevated levels of lipids (fats), especially cholesterol and triglycerides, in the blood; can be familial or acquired and increases the risk of atherosclerosis and cardiovascular disease.

hepatic damage.definition: Injury to liver tissue that impairs liver function, often resulting from toxins, ischemia, infection, autoimmune or metabolic diseases, and may present with elevated liver enzymes, jaundice, coagulopathy, and reduced synthetic or detoxification capacity.

gastroduodenal ulcer.definition: A peptic ulcer of the stomach or duodenum—an erosion of the mucosa due to gastric acid and pepsin, commonly linked to Helicobacter pylori infection or NSAID use.

intravenous feeding.definition: Administration of nutrients directly into the bloodstream via a vein (parenteral nutrition), used when the gastrointestinal tract cannot absorb nutrients or when oral/enteral feeding is not feasible.

intravenous infusion filter.definition: A sterile inline device placed in an IV infusion line that removes particulate matter (and, in some designs, microorganisms) from the infused solution before it enters the circulation, using a membrane or depth-filter with a defined pore size.

impurities.definition: Substances present in a material or product that are not part of its intended composition; contaminants arising from manufacturing, processing, or storage that may affect safety, purity, or efficacy.

detergents.definition: A class of surfactant chemicals that lower surface tension between liquids and solids, enabling emulsification of fats and oils and disruption of lipid membranes; used for cleaning and disinfection, and in biochemistry and cell biology to solubilize membrane proteins and permeabilize cells.

proteins.definition: They are large, complex biomolecules made of amino acids linked by peptide bonds; they fold into specific three‑dimensional shapes that determine their function. They perform a wide range of cellular roles, including catalysis (enzymes), structural support, transport, signaling, and defense, and are encoded by genes.

extraneous salts.definition: Foreign or unintended salts that are not endogenous to the human body, acting as contaminants in samples or pharmaceutical preparations and potentially altering osmolarity, electrolyte balance, or drug behavior.

microorganisms.definition: Microscopic living organisms, including bacteria, fungi, protozoa, and certain algae; they may be unicellular or multicellular and are too small to be seen without magnification, with roles ranging from pathogens to beneficial symbionts.

particles.definition: Minute pieces of matter; in medical contexts, tiny airborne or suspended units such as dust or droplets that can be inhaled or deposited in tissues.

precipitates.definition: A solid formed in solution when two or more substances react or when solubility is exceeded, which separates from the liquid as an insoluble product.

undissolved drug powders.definition: A solid drug material in a liquid dosage form that has not dissolved; consists of particulate drug that remains suspended or settled rather than forming a true solution, typically due to poor solubility or insufficient dissolution time, and can affect dose uniformity and bioavailability.

infiltration of iv fluid.definition: In IV therapy, infiltration is the accidental leakage of IV fluids into the surrounding subcutaneous tissue, usually due to catheter dislodgement or vein puncture, causing swelling, pallor or cool skin, and often a slowed or stopped infusion.

intraventricular pressure.definition: The pressure inside the brain's ventricular system (cerebrospinal fluid pressure), typically measured through an intraventricular catheter to monitor intracranial pressure and CSF dynamics.

left anterior fascicular block.definition: A conduction disturbance in which the left anterior fascicle of the left bundle branch is blocked or delayed, causing left axis deviation on the ECG with a typically normal QRS duration and often without overt structural heart disease.

posterior fascicular block.definition: A conduction block involving the left bundle branch's posterior fascicle, leading to delayed activation of the posterior/inferior left ventricle and typically causing rightward (right) axis deviation on the electrocardiogram; a rare form of intraventricular conduction delay often seen with other conduction disease.

bifascicular block.definition: An intraventricular conduction abnormality in which two of the three fascicles of the His-Purkinje system are blocked, most commonly right bundle branch block with left anterior fascicular block or with left posterior fascicular block; it widens the QRS and can progress to complete heart block.

intraventricular conduction defect.definition: A non-specific delay in ventricular conduction resulting in a widened QRS complex on ECG; not fitting classic patterns of left- or right-bundle-branch block.

intraventricular hydrocephalus.definition: Obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid flow within the ventricular system causing CSF buildup, ventricular dilation, and increased intracranial pressure; causes include intraventricular hemorrhage, ventricular tumors, and aqueductal stenosis.

intravenous urography.definition: A radiographic examination of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder after intravenous administration of iodinated contrast, with timed X-ray images to visualize anatomy and assess urinary tract function.

descending urography.definition: A radiographic examination of the urinary tract in which iodinated contrast is introduced (commonly intravenously) and serial images are captured as the contrast descends from the renal pelvis through the ureters into the bladder, to evaluate anatomy and excretory function.

renal calyces.definition: A funnel-shaped collecting system in the kidney that receives urine from the renal papillae; minor calyces collect urine from the papillae and drain into major calyces, which join to form the renal pelvis that leads to the ureter.

cathartic.definition: An agent with a strong laxative effect.

void.definition: To urinate; to empty the bladder by passing urine.

residual urine.definition: An amount of urine remaining in the bladder after urination, typically measured as post-void residual (PVR) volume; elevated residual urine suggests urinary retention from obstruction, detrusor underactivity, or neurogenic bladder.

intraventricular sulcus.definition: Not a widely recognized anatomical term; used informally to describe a groove within the brain’s ventricular system, but there is no official sulcus by that name. If seen, it likely refers to internal contours of the ventricles rather than a standard cortical sulcus.

posterior interventricular artery.definition: An artery that runs in the posterior interventricular groove to supply the posterior part of the interventricular septum and the diaphragmatic (inferior) surfaces of the ventricles; it typically originates from the right coronary artery in right-dominant circulation, but can arise from the left circumflex artery in left-dominant circulation.

middle cardiac vein.definition: A vein that drains the posterior aspect of the heart, running in the posterior interventricular sulcus and typically emptying into the coronary sinus; also known as the posterior interventricular vein.

intravesical pressure.definition: The pressure inside the urinary bladder, measured via a catheter during urodynamic testing; it reflects bladder distending pressure and is influenced by abdominal pressure, with detrusor pressure derived by subtracting abdominal pressure (Pdet = Pves − Pabd).

vesical pressure.definition: The pressure within the urinary bladder (intravesical pressure), determined by bladder filling and detrusor muscle tone; used in urodynamic assessments to evaluate bladder function.

intravesical ureterocele.definition: A cystic dilation of the distal ureter that resides entirely within the bladder lumen (intravesical ureterocele), often associated with a duplicated collecting system and potentially causing obstruction or urinary tract infections.

orthotopic.definition: Placed in the normal anatomical position; a transplanted organ or tissue is placed in its original site in the body, as opposed to a heterotopic transplant placed elsewhere.

atrophy of gastric mucosa.definition: Thinning of the stomach lining with loss of gastric glands, typically from chronic gastritis (autoimmune or Helicobacter pylori–related); it reduces acid production and intrinsic factor, and may be accompanied by intestinal metaplasia, increasing the risk of pernicious anemia and gastric cancer.

intrinsic minus hand deformity.definition: Loss or severe weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles (interossei and lumbricals) leading to unopposed extensor/flexor forces and a posture of hyperextended metacarpophalangeal joints with flexed interphalangeal joints (clawing), commonly due to ulnar nerve palsy.

metacarpophalangeal joint hyperextension.definition: Hyperextension of the metacarpophalangeal joints is the extension of the fingers at the knuckles beyond the normal straight position, typically beyond 0 degrees, and can result from ligamentous laxity, injury, or certain deformities.

interphalangeal joint flexion.definition: Bending of the finger at the joints between adjacent phalanges (proximal and distal interphalangeal joints; the thumb’s IP joint), decreasing the angle between the two connected phalanges and producing finger curling.

intrinsic motivation.definition: Motivation that arises from internal factors—such as interest, enjoyment, curiosity, or personal meaning—driving a person to perform an activity for its own sake rather than for external rewards or pressures.

intrinsic muscles.definition: Muscles whose origin and insertion are both within the same organ or region, enabling precise, localized movements within that structure; they contrast with extrinsic muscles, which originate outside the region.

intrinsic muscles of the tongue.definition: Muscles with origins and insertions entirely within the tongue; they modify its shape (curling, shortening, flattening or narrowing) rather than protruding the tongue, and include the superior longitudinal, inferior longitudinal, transverse, and vertical muscles.

superior longitudinal muscle.definition: A thin intrinsic muscle of the tongue, located just beneath the dorsal mucosa and running longitudinally from the root to the apex. Its contraction shortens the tongue and elevates and curls the tip, helping to shape the tongue during speech and swallowing.

inferior longitudinal muscle.definition: An intrinsic tongue muscle that lies on the inferior (underside) surface and runs longitudinally; its contraction shortens the tongue and depresses the tip, assisting in articulation. Innervated by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).

transverse muscle.definition: A muscle whose fibers run transversely (horizontally) across a body region; when contracted, it compresses or tightens that region and helps stabilize the surrounding structures (for example, contributing to trunk stability and intra-abdominal pressure).

vertical muscle.definition: A muscle oriented along the vertical axis; its contraction produces movement in the vertical (upward or downward) direction. In the eye, the vertical rectus muscles—the superior and inferior rectus—control up-and-down gaze.

auto-peep.definition: Intrinsic positive end-expiratory pressure resulting from incomplete expiration and air trapping during mechanical ventilation, causing elevated end-expiratory lung pressure that is not set by the ventilator.

introjection.definition: A psychoanalytic defense mechanism in which external objects (people, their traits or values) are internalized and taken as part of the self.

intromission.definition: The act of inserting or introducing a part of the body into another body cavity or orifice; in human sexuality, commonly the insertion of the penis into the vagina.

intron.definition: A non-coding segment of a eukaryotic gene that is transcribed into pre-mRNA and subsequently removed by RNA splicing, with the remaining exons forming mature mRNA.

intron a.definition: A brand-name recombinant human interferon alfa-2b used as immunotherapy for certain cancers and viral infections.

nasotracheal intubation.definition: A procedure to secure the airway by inserting an endotracheal tube through the nostril into the trachea, typically performed during anesthesia or airway management when oral intubation is not feasible.

invagination.definition: Infolding of a tissue or organ, producing an inward fold that forms a pocket or cavity; used to describe embryologic inward folding (e.g., during gastrulation) and, in gastroenterology, the telescoping of one intestinal segment into another (intussusception).

invasion.definition: An invasion in medicine is the penetration and spread of disease-causing cells or organisms into neighboring tissues, crossing tissue boundaries; in oncology, it denotes malignant cells extending beyond the original tumor into surrounding stroma.

invasive carcinoma.definition: A malignant epithelial tumor in which cancer cells have breached the basement membrane and invaded surrounding tissues (stroma) and often local lymphatics or blood vessels, enabling potential metastasis.

invasive hemodynamic monitoring.definition: A method of directly measuring cardiovascular pressures and flows with intravascular catheters (e.g., arterial line, central venous line, and pulmonary artery catheter) to assess hemodynamics and guide therapy in critically ill or perioperative patients.

invasive mole.definition: A form of gestational trophoblastic disease in which hydropic villi and trophoblastic tissue from a molar pregnancy invade the myometrium, potentially causing uterine perforation and metastasis; represents persistent GTD after evacuation.

invasive procedure.definition: To go into the body through a cut, slit, or puncture.

in vitro.definition: A test or procedure that happens in a laboratory.

in vivo.definition: A test or procedure that happens inside a living body (animal or human).

ivf.definition: A medical procedure for assisted reproduction in which mature eggs are retrieved from the ovaries, fertilized with sperm in a laboratory, and one or more embryos are transferred to the uterus to achieve pregnancy.

in vitro susceptibility testing.definition: A laboratory procedure that determines whether a microorganism is inhibited by various antimicrobial agents by exposing it to those agents in vitro, typically reporting a minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) or a susceptibility category (e.g., susceptible, intermediate, resistant).

radionuclide angiocardiogram.definition: A nuclear medicine imaging study in which a radiotracer is injected and serial gamma camera images of the heart are acquired, typically gated to the ECG, to assess ventricular volumes and function (e.g., left ventricular ejection fraction and regional wall motion).

inulin clearance.definition: An estimate of glomerular filtration rate: the volume of plasma completely cleared of inulin per unit time, since inulin is freely filtered and neither secreted nor reabsorbed by the renal tubules. It is calculated as C_in = (U_in × V) / P_in.

kidney function.definition: The kidneys filter blood to remove waste products and excess fluids, regulate electrolyte and acid-base balance, and perform hormonal functions (erythropoietin and renin) and vitamin D activation.

circulatory overload.definition: A condition characterized by excess intravascular fluid (volume overload) that the heart cannot adequately accommodate, leading to edema and signs of congestive heart failure such as dyspnea and hypertension; commonly due to rapid or excessive IV fluid administration, kidney failure–related fluid retention, or other fluid shifts.

bounding pulse.definition: A bounding pulse is a strong, forceful pulse with a rapid upstroke and quick collapse, reflecting high stroke volume or low vascular resistance (as seen in fever, anemia, hyperthyroidism, pregnancy; can occur with certain cardiac conditions).

venous distention.definition: Dilation of a vein caused by increased venous pressure, most commonly observed as neck vein dilation that reflects elevated central venous pressure.

pulmonary rales.definition: An abnormal lung sound heard on auscultation, described as fine to coarse crackling noises caused by the sudden opening of small airways or alveoli that have been collapsed or filled with fluid; commonly associated with pulmonary edema, pneumonia, atelectasis, or interstitial fibrosis.

anaphylactic reaction.definition: A serious allergic reaction that happens quickly and can be fatal.

apprehension.definition: A feeling of fear, anxiety, or dread about a potential future event or outcome; a sense of impending danger or harm.

tightness of chest.definition: Chest tightness is a subjective sensation of pressure, squeezing, or constriction in the chest. It can result from cardiac causes (eg, angina, heart attack), lung conditions (eg, asthma, bronchospasm, pneumonia), gastrointestinal issues (eg, GERD), anxiety, or musculoskeletal factors. If it’s sudden, severe, or accompanied by shortness of breath, sweating, or radiating pain, seek urgent medical care.

ileocolic valve.definition: A ring-like smooth muscle sphincter at the junction of the ileum and cecum that regulates passage of chyme into the large intestine and prevents backflow from the colon into the ileum.

mecamylamine hydrochloride.definition: Salt form of mecamylamine; a nondepolarizing antagonist of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at autonomic ganglia, functioning as a ganglion blocker to decrease sympathetic outflow and lower blood pressure; historically used for severe hypertension but largely obsolete due to adverse autonomic side effects.

inverse anaphylaxis.definition: Not a recognized medical term; there is no standard medical definition. If you have a source or context, I can help interpret it or suggest related concepts (e.g., anaphylaxis or biphasic/anaphylactoid reactions).

reverse anaphylaxis.definition: Not a standard medical term; it generally refers to the management aimed at reversing the manifestations of anaphylaxis. Immediate treatment is prompt intramuscular epinephrine, plus airway and breathing support (oxygen and bronchodilators as needed) and intravenous fluids; ongoing monitoring and supportive care, with antihistamines or corticosteroids as adjuncts, to prevent relapse (biphasic reaction).

inverse i:e ratio.definition: In ventilation, an inverse I:E ratio is a setting where the inspiratory time exceeds the expiratory time (I:E > 1:1, e.g., 2:1 or 3:1); used to improve alveolar recruitment and oxygenation, but it increases airway pressures and the risk of air trapping and hemodynamic compromise.

marcus gunn syndrome.definition: Congenital ptosis with a synkinetic eyelid movement (jaw-winking), caused by aberrant innervation of the levator palpebrae superioris by the motor branches of the trigeminal nerve, so the eyelid elevates with jaw movement.

inverse marcus gunn syndrome.definition: A rare congenital ptosis syndrome in which eyelid droop worsens with jaw movement (synkinesis between jaw and eyelid muscles), the opposite of the Marcus Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon which causes eyelid elevation with jaw movement.

ide.definition: A suffix used in chemical nomenclature to form names of negative ions or binary compounds (e.g., chloride, oxide, sulfide).

ind.definition: A regulatory status for a drug or biological product that has not yet been approved by the FDA and is being tested in humans; requires an IND submission to authorize clinical trials and ensure safety oversight by the FDA and an Institutional Review Board, with use restricted to investigational purposes.

investigational device exemption.definition: A regulatory mechanism by which the U.S. FDA allows the use of a medical device in a clinical study to collect safety and effectiveness data needed for FDA marketing approval; the process requires IRB approval, informed consent, and reporting of adverse events, and differentiates between significant-risk and non-significant-risk studies (with possible exemptions).

investigational new drug.definition: An experimental drug that has not yet been approved by regulatory authorities for any use and is being studied for safety and efficacy in human clinical trials under a formal regulatory authorization.

investing fascia.definition: The deep fascia that envelops and invests a muscle or group of muscles, forming a sheath around them and helping define their compartment.

invirase.definition: A protease inhibitor antiretroviral medication used in combination therapy to treat HIV-1 infection. It inhibits the HIV-1 protease enzyme, preventing cleavage of the Gag-Pol polyprotein and maturation of infectious virions; often boosted with ritonavir to increase drug levels.

climacteric.definition: The menopausal transition; the period in midlife when ovarian function and estrogen production decline, leading to menopause.

major depressive episode.definition: A period of at least two weeks characterized by depressed mood or markedly diminished interest or pleasure, plus five or more additional symptoms (such as significant changes in weight or appetite, sleep disturbance, psychomotor changes, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt, diminished ability to think or concentrate, and recurrent thoughts of death), causing clinically significant distress or impairment and not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or another medical condition.

aggression.definition: An intentional behavior aimed at harming or intimidating another person or animal, including physical violence and verbal threats; it can be reactive (in response to threat or frustration) or instrumental (to achieve a goal) and may occur in various psychiatric or neurodevelopmental disorders or as a defensive response.

masochism.definition: Masochism is a paraphilic condition in which sexual arousal derives from being subjected to pain, humiliation, or domination; it is considered a disorder when these fantasies, urges, or behaviors cause distress or impairment, or involve non-consenting individuals.

iodinated serum albumin.definition: A radiolabeled form of serum albumin used as a tracer to measure plasma volume and assess capillary or vascular permeability in physiological and clinical studies.

radioiodinated.definition: A compound that has been labeled with a radioactive isotope of iodine (e.g., iodine-123 or iodine-131) for detection by imaging or for delivering targeted radiotherapy.

iodine poisoning.definition: Toxicity from excessive iodine or iodide intake or exposure (iodism). Acute exposure causes metallic taste, burning mouth/throat, stomatitis, salivation, nausea/vomiting/diarrhea, and fever; chronic exposure may lead to thyroid dysfunction (hypo- or hyperthyroidism) and dermatitis/iododerma.

iodism.definition: Toxicity from excessive intake of iodine or iodide, resulting in symptoms such as a metallic taste, stomatitis, salivation, gastrointestinal upset, skin eruptions (iododerma or acneiform eruption), and thyroid dysfunction (iodine-induced hypo- or hyperthyroidism).

iododerma.definition: A rare inflammatory skin eruption triggered by exposure to iodide-containing substances (e.g., iodine, iodinated contrast) presenting as painful papulopustular or nodular lesions that appear within days of exposure and remit after iodide is withdrawn, often due to a hypersensitivity reaction.

iodophor.definition: An antiseptic preparation in which iodine is bound to an organic carrier (commonly povidone) to release iodine slowly, providing broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity for skin disinfection and wound care.

iodopsin.definition: A cone cell photopigment in the retina responsible for color vision; iodopsin comprises cone opsins bound to 11-cis-retinal and exists in three spectral forms corresponding to blue, green, and red cones.

optic neuropathy.definition: Damage to the optic nerve causing visual impairment, often with decreased acuity and color vision and an afferent pupillary defect; etiologies include ischemic, inflammatory/demyelinating, compressive, toxic/metabolic, and infectious processes.

iodotherapy.definition: A treatment using iodine, especially radioactive iodine (such as iodine-131), to destroy or ablate thyroid tissue in conditions like hyperthyroidism and thyroid cancer, typically administered orally and taken up selectively by thyroid cells.

ion exchange chromatography.definition: A chromatography technique that separates molecules based on their net electric charge by passing a sample through a resin with fixed charged groups; molecules bind to the resin according to their charge and are eluted by increasing ionic strength or changing pH, enabling purification of charged biomolecules such as proteins and nucleic acids.

ionization.definition: The process by which a neutral atom or molecule loses or gains electrons, forming positively or negatively charged ions. In medicine, it often refers to the creation of ions in tissue by ionizing radiation, which can generate reactive free radicals.

ion-selective electrode.definition: An ion-selective electrode is a sensor that converts the activity of a specific ion in solution into an electrical potential, allowing quantitative measurement of that ion; it uses a selective membrane or ionophore that responds to that ion, and the potential follows the Nernst equation.

iontophoresis.definition: A noninvasive method of delivering charged drug ions through the skin by applying a mild electric current, which drives ions from a solution or bath into underlying tissues for local or systemic therapy.

iopromide.definition: A nonionic, low-osmolar iodinated contrast agent used to enhance radiographic visualization of vessels and organs during imaging studies such as CT and angiography.

ioversol.definition: A nonionic iodinated radiographic contrast agent used to enhance visualization of vessels and organs during X-ray and CT imaging; administered intravenously or intra-arterially to increase tissue radiodensity.

ioxilan.definition: A nonionic iodinated contrast agent used in radiology to enhance imaging by increasing the visibility of blood vessels and tissues during procedures such as CT scans and angiography; administered intravenously or intra-arterially and excreted by the kidneys.

iowa trumpet.definition: A nonstandard, unrecognized medical term; there is no widely accepted medical definition.

iridotomy.definition: A laser or surgical procedure that creates a small opening in the iris to allow aqueous humor to flow from the posterior to the anterior chamber, reducing intraocular pressure in cases of pupillary block or angle-closure glaucoma.

cataract extraction.definition: Surgical removal of a cloudy crystalline lens (cataract) from the eye, typically by phacoemulsification with aspiration and implantation of an intraocular lens; historically performed as extracapsular or intracapsular cataract extraction.

radiopaque medium.definition: A substance that markedly attenuates X-rays and thus appears white on radiographs, used as a contrast agent to delineate organs or vessels in radiologic studies (commonly iodinated solutions or barium sulfate).

inactivated poliovirus vaccine.definition: A killed (inactivated) poliovirus vaccine containing formalin-inactivated poliovirus serotypes 1, 2, and 3; administered by intramuscular injection to confer systemic immunity against poliomyelitis without causing disease, and requiring multiple doses for lasting protection.

ipsp.definition: A postsynaptic potential that decreases the likelihood of an action potential by hyperpolarizing the postsynaptic membrane or making it harder to reach threshold, typically via inhibitory neurotransmitters (e.g., GABA, glycine) opening Cl− or K+ channels.

interventional radiology.definition: A medical specialty that uses real-time imaging guidance to perform minimally invasive diagnostic and therapeutic procedures, typically percutaneously, such as angiography, catheter-based interventions (e.g., stent placement, embolization), biopsies, and drain placements.

image receptor.definition: An image receptor is the device used to capture and record a radiographic image after X-ray exposure; it converts attenuated X-ray photons into a visible image and may be traditional film or a digital detector (e.g., phosphor storage plate or flat-panel detector).

institutional review board.definition: A committee at research institutions that reviews and approves proposed studies involving human subjects to protect their safety, rights, and welfare by ensuring ethical conduct, informed consent, risk minimization, and regulatory compliance.

iridium.definition: A dense, silvery-white transition metal of the platinum group; not biologically essential; its radioactive isotope is used in certain cancer brachytherapy procedures and in radiography.

iridology.definition: A diagnostic pseudoscience that claims patterns, colors, and other characteristics of the iris reflect a person's systemic health and can indicate medical conditions; it is not supported by credible scientific evidence and is not considered a valid basis for diagnosis.

iridopathy.definition: A disease or pathological condition of the iris (the colored portion of the anterior eye). The term is non-specific and can refer to inflammatory iris disease (iritis/iridocyclitis), iris atrophy, or other iris abnormalities.

iridoplegia.definition: Paralysis of the iris, especially the sphincter pupillae, resulting in a dilated, nonreactive pupil and loss of the pupillary light reflex.

iressa.definition: A brand-name epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitor (gefitinib) used to treat certain cancers, most notably EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer.

desirudin.definition: A recombinant hirudin-derived direct thrombin inhibitor used as an anticoagulant to prevent postoperative deep vein thrombosis in patients undergoing elective hip replacement surgery; it inhibits thrombin (factor IIa) by binding to its active site, preventing the conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin.

irbesartan.definition: An angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB) that selectively blocks AT1 receptors, causing vasodilation and reduced aldosterone secretion; used to treat hypertension and to protect kidney function in type 2 diabetes with nephropathy (diabetic nephropathy).

diabetic nephropathy.definition: A form of chronic kidney disease caused by long-standing diabetes mellitus, characterized by persistent albuminuria (microalbuminuria progressing to proteinuria), a progressive decline in glomerular filtration rate, and hypertension; pathologic features include glomerular basement membrane thickening, mesangial expansion, and nodular glomerulosclerosis. It is a leading cause of end-stage renal disease.

pudendal block.definition: A regional anesthesia in which a local anesthetic is injected near the pudendal nerve to numb the perineum, vulva, lower vagina, and anal region, typically used for childbirth analgesia or perineal procedures such as episiotomy or repair.

iron poisoning.definition: Acute iron poisoning is a potentially life-threatening toxicity resulting from ingestion of excessive iron, usually from iron-containing tablets. It causes initial gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, sometimes bloody stools) and can progress to metabolic acidosis, hepatic injury, coagulopathy, shock, and multiorgan failure; treatment includes supportive care and iron chelation with deferoxamine.

iron dextran.definition: An injectable iron preparation in which iron is bound to dextran; used to treat iron deficiency anemia when oral iron is ineffective or unsuitable, administered intramuscularly or intravenously.
