ferrous fumarate.definition: An oral iron supplement; the ferrous (Fe2+) salt of fumaric acid used to treat or prevent iron deficiency anemia; provides elemental iron.

iron-polysaccharide.definition: An oral iron preparation in which iron is bound to a polysaccharide to form a complex that releases iron slowly, designed to improve gastrointestinal tolerability and provide more gradual iron absorption compared with ferrous salts; used to treat or prevent iron deficiency anemia.

polysaccharide-iron complex.definition: An oral iron supplement in which iron ions are bound to a polysaccharide (a carbohydrate polymer) to form a complex that provides iron for hemoglobin synthesis with reduced gastrointestinal irritation and often slower iron release than standard iron salts.

flatus.definition: Gas produced in the digestive tract and expelled through the anus; commonly known as flatulence.

site irritation.definition: A local inflammatory reaction at a specific site, characterized by redness, warmth, itching, burning, or pain, typically caused by irritation from topical agents, adhesives, dressings, or devices, and not necessarily indicating infection.

normoblast.definition: A nucleated precursor red blood cell (erythroblast) in late erythropoiesis, found in the bone marrow, containing hemoglobin and a condensed nucleus that is expelled to form a reticulocyte.

transferrin.definition: Plasma glycoprotein produced primarily by the liver that binds ferric iron (Fe3+) and transports it through the bloodstream to iron-requiring tissues, playing a central role in iron homeostasis.

serum iron.definition: A laboratory measurement of the amount of circulating iron bound to transferrin in the blood; part of iron studies used to assess iron status and diagnose iron deficiency or overload, and it is influenced by diurnal variation and recent iron intake.

transferrin saturation.definition: A measure of the percentage of transferrin binding sites occupied by iron in the blood; calculated as (serum iron / total iron-binding capacity) × 100; used to assess iron status, with low values suggesting iron deficiency and high values suggesting iron overload or sideroblastic anemia; normal range is roughly 20–50%.

iron overload.definition: Excess iron in the body from increased absorption or chronic transfusions, leading to iron deposition in organs (liver, heart, pancreas, endocrine glands) and progressive organ dysfunction; common in hereditary hemochromatosis or transfusional iron overload; diagnosed by elevated ferritin and transferrin saturation and treated with therapeutic phlebotomy (when feasible) or iron chelation therapy.

iron storage disease.definition: An iron overload disorder characterized by excessive deposition of iron in body tissues (especially the liver, heart, and endocrine organs) due to abnormal iron metabolism. The most common form is hereditary hemochromatosis from increased intestinal iron absorption, with secondary overload from transfusions or iron therapy; if untreated, it can lead to cirrhosis, diabetes, and cardiomyopathy. Management includes phlebotomy and/or iron chelation.

iron level.definition: The amount of iron circulating in the blood, measured as the serum iron concentration. It is used to assess iron status and diagnose iron deficiency or iron overload, and is interpreted alongside ferritin, transferrin saturation, and total iron-binding capacity.

iron transport.definition: Iron transport is the systemic and cellular movement of iron from intestinal absorption to delivery to tissues, primarily via transferrin-bound iron in the plasma; cells acquire iron through transferrin receptor–mediated endocytosis, iron is stored intracellularly as ferritin, and exported by ferroportin. Hepatic hepcidin regulates overall iron homeostasis.

exogenous iron.definition: Iron that originates outside the body (from food or supplements) and is absorbed in the GI tract to contribute to body iron stores and erythropoiesis, as opposed to iron recycled from senescent red blood cells (endogenous iron).

iron encephalopathy.definition: Encephalopathy caused by iron overload or abnormal iron deposition in the brain, leading to progressive neurological dysfunction; commonly seen with systemic iron overload (hemosiderosis) or with disorders of brain iron metabolism such as neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA).

iron-rich food.definition: Foods that provide substantial amounts of dietary iron, a mineral essential for hemoglobin synthesis and oxygen transport in red blood cells. They include heme iron sources from animal products (red meat, poultry, fish) and non-heme iron sources from plants (beans, lentils, fortified cereals, spinach); absorption is enhanced by vitamin C and can be reduced by phytates, polyphenols, and calcium.

oysters.definition: A marine filter-feeding bivalve mollusk of the family Ostreidae with a hinged shell; commonly eaten as seafood, often raw; raw or undercooked oysters can transmit pathogens such as Vibrio species and norovirus, posing health risks.

clams.definition: An edible marine bivalve mollusk with a two-part hinged shell; commonly harvested for food.

lean meat.definition: Meat with relatively low fat content, especially saturated fat, typically from lean cuts; provides high‐quality protein with fewer calories from fat than fattier cuts.

seafood.definition: Edible products from aquatic organisms derived from saltwater or freshwater, including fish, shellfish (mollusks and crustaceans), and sometimes edible aquatic plants; consumed as food.

iron-fortified foods.definition: A food product to which iron has been added or fortified during processing to increase dietary iron intake and help prevent iron deficiency anemia.

leafy green vegetables.definition: A broad group of edible vegetables in which the leaves (and sometimes young stems) are the primary edible portion; typically low in calories and high in dietary fiber, vitamins A, C, and K, folate, and minerals, as well as various phytonutrients; commonly eaten raw or cooked and associated with supportive cardiovascular and overall health.

whole grains.definition: A cereal grain that retains all three components of the kernel—the bran, germ, and endosperm—i.e., is not refined; this preserves more fiber, vitamins, minerals, and phytochemicals than refined grains.

legumes.definition: A family of flowering plants (Fabaceae) whose fruit is a pod that splits along both sides to release seeds; the edible seeds—such as beans, lentils, chickpeas, and peas—are widely used for protein and fiber, and the plants often fix atmospheric nitrogen in root nodules.

oral iron therapy.definition: Administration of iron via the oral route (most commonly ferrous salts such as ferrous sulfate, gluconate, or fumarate) to replenish iron stores and treat iron deficiency anemia; absorption is improved by acid and vitamin C, but can be reduced by calcium, antacids, or certain foods, and adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset and dark stools.

early pregnancy.definition: The initial period of gestation from conception to roughly 12 weeks (end of the first trimester), during which implantation occurs, early embryonic development proceeds, and pregnancy hormone levels (e.g., hCG) rise.

anemias.definition: A condition in which the number or hemoglobin content of red blood cells is insufficient to meet the body's oxygen needs, usually due to decreased production, increased destruction, or blood loss; common types include iron-deficiency anemia, megaloblastic (B12/folate) anemia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, and anemia of chronic disease.

ischemic pain.definition: Pain caused by reduced blood flow (ischemia) to tissue, resulting in tissue hypoxia and accumulation of metabolic byproducts that activate pain receptors; commonly presents as angina with myocardial ischemia or rest pain with peripheral ischemia.

ischemic lumbago.definition: Not a standard medical term; if used, it would refer to lower back pain attributed to ischemia (reduced blood flow) of lumbar structures, a rare and poorly defined cause that warrants evaluation for vascular insufficiency or spinal ischemia.

ischaemic contracture.definition: A permanent shortening of a muscle or muscle group caused by ischaemia, with fibrous replacement of the muscle tissue, leading to a fixed deformity of the affected joint (often after severe injury or compartment syndrome).

ischaemia.definition: A reduction in blood flow to a tissue or organ, leading to insufficient oxygen and nutrient delivery and potential cellular injury or death if circulation is not promptly restored.

irving technique.definition: Not found in standard medical references; there is no widely recognized technique by that exact name. If you can share the medical specialty, context, or correct spelling (e.g., Irvine/Irvine method, or another term), I can help locate or clarify it.

If you meant a well-known esophageal cancer operation involving abdominal and thoracic approaches, I can define that once confirmed.

uterine tubes.definition: Pair of slender channels connecting the ovaries to the uterus; they capture the ovulated oocyte and are the typical site of fertilization. The oocyte is transported to the uterus via rhythmic peristalsis and ciliary beating of the mucosal (ciliated columnar) lining.

isaacs' syndrome.definition: An autoimmune peripheral nerve hyperexcitability syndrome (also known as acquired neuromyotonia) characterized by spontaneous, continuous motor activity in muscles, causing myokymia, cramps, stiffness, and fasciculations; EMG shows continuous motor-unit activity. Often associated with antibodies to voltage-gated potassium channel complexes (e.g., CASPR2). Managed with immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, plasmapheresis) and symptomatic anticonvulsants or analgesics (e.g., carbamazepine, gabapentin).

stiff-man syndrome.definition: A rare autoimmune neurological disorder characterized by progressive stiffness and rigidity of the axial and proximal limb muscles with episodic painful spasms, often triggered by startle or emotional stimuli; commonly associated with antibodies to GAD65; management includes benzodiazepines and baclofen, with immunotherapy (e.g., IVIG, plasmapheresis) for refractory cases.

radiation sickness.definition: An illness caused by exposure to a high dose of ionizing radiation over a short period, leading to damage of rapidly dividing cells. It typically presents in stages: early prodromal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea; a latent period; and a manifest phase with bone marrow suppression (increased infection and bleeding), plus possible GI and neurologic symptoms at higher doses; death may occur with very high exposures.

radioactivity.definition: Spontaneous emission of ionizing radiation (alpha, beta, or gamma rays) from unstable atomic nuclei as they decay toward a more stable configuration.

isotopes.definition: Atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, resulting in different atomic masses; their chemical properties are virtually identical, but some are radioactive and used in medical imaging and therapy.

sulfur dioxide.definition: A colorless, pungent gas produced by the combustion of sulfur-containing materials and certain industrial processes; it is a respiratory irritant that damages mucous membranes and can cause coughing, bronchospasm, and pulmonary edema with high exposure, and it reacts with water to form sulfurous acid.

hydrogen sulfide.definition: A colorless, flammable, and highly toxic gas with a rotten-egg odor (chemical formula H2S); produced by bacterial metabolism and certain industrial processes; at high concentrations it inhibits mitochondrial respiration by blocking cytochrome oxidase, potentially causing death; at lower concentrations it can act as a gasotransmitter involved in neuromodulation and vascular regulation.

nitrogen dioxide.definition: A reddish-brown toxic gas produced by high-temperature combustion (chemical formula NO2); it irritates the eyes, nose, and lungs and can provoke coughing, wheezing, and bronchospasm. It is a component of air pollution (smog) and contributes to atmospheric acid formation.

irrigate.definition: To flush or wash out a wound, surgical site, or body cavity with a steady stream of fluid (often sterile saline) to cleanse, remove debris, or moisten tissues.

irrigator.definition: A device or instrument used to flush a body cavity, wound, or other space with fluid (often sterile saline) to cleanse, remove debris, reduce infection risk, or deliver medications.

irritant.definition: Something that is a bother or a pain.

irritant poison.definition: A substance whose primary toxic effect is local irritation of the skin, eyes, or mucous membranes on contact or inhalation, causing symptoms such as burning, redness, or coughing, rather than causing significant systemic toxicity.

irritable bladder.definition: A nonstandard term for a constellation of urinary symptoms—urge to void, increased daytime frequency, and often urge incontinence—thought to reflect detrusor overactivity or bladder hypersensitivity; it is not a formally defined medical condition and is often used interchangeably with overactive bladder.

ibs.definition: A chronic functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by recurrent abdominal pain or discomfort associated with altered bowel habits (diarrhea, constipation, or both) and no identifiable organic cause; often with bloating and relief of symptoms with defecation; subtypes include IBS-D, IBS-C, and IBS-M.

antidiarrheal.definition: A medication used to treat diarrhea by reducing stool frequency and liquidity, usually by slowing intestinal motility or increasing water and electrolyte absorption in the colon.

ophthalmic.definition: Relating to the eye; pertaining to the anatomy, disorders, or treatment of the eye.

dilator pupillae.definition: A smooth muscle of the iris (radial fibers) that, when stimulated by the sympathetic nervous system, contracts to dilate the pupil (mydriasis), increasing the amount of light entering the eye.

sphincter pupillae.definition: A smooth muscle ring in the iris that constricts the pupil (miosis) in response to light and during accommodation, under parasympathetic control via the oculomotor nerve (CN III) through the ciliary ganglion.

stroma.definition: A supportive tissue framework inside an organ, made up of connective tissue, extracellular matrix, blood vessels, and resident cells that provides structural support and nourishment to the functional (parenchymal) cells; in tumors, it refers to the non-epithelial supportive tissue surrounding the tumor cells.

pectinate ligament.definition: A fibrous, sieve-like tissue in the iridocorneal angle of the eye that forms part of the trabecular meshwork; it consists of delicate beams (pectinate ligaments) extending from the scleral spur toward the cornea to help route aqueous humor into Schlemm's canal.

isoagglutinin.definition: Naturally occurring antibodies directed against isoantigens of the same species—most notably anti-A and anti-B antibodies in humans—that agglutinate red blood cells bearing the corresponding ABO antigens and can cause transfusion reactions.

penumbra.definition: The region around an ischemic brain infarct that is hypoperfused and functionally impaired but still viable and potentially salvageable with timely reperfusion.

ischemic stroke.definition: A type of stroke caused by a blocked blood vessel—usually a thrombus or embolus—that reduces or stops blood flow to part of the brain, causing brain tissue ischemia and, if prolonged, infarction.

ischial spine.definition: A small, pointed bony projection on the posterior border of the ischium, between the greater and lesser sciatic notches, just below the greater sciatic notch. It serves as the attachment for the sacrospinous ligament and as a landmark for locating the pudendal nerve (e.g., during nerve blocks) and helps define the boundaries of the sciatic foramina.

ischiocavernosus.definition: A muscle of the superficial perineal pouch that covers the crura of the penis (in males) or clitoris (in females); it originates from the ischiopubic ramus and ischial tuberosity and inserts on the crus of the penis or clitoris, and its contraction compresses the crus to maintain erection by restricting venous outflow; innervated by the pudendal nerve.

ischioanal fossae.definition: Paired fat-filled spaces in the perineum on either side of the anal canal. Bounded medially by the external anal sphincter and levator ani, laterally by the obturator internus muscle and its fascia, anteriorly by the perineal membrane (inferior fascia of the urogenital diaphragm), and posteriorly by the sacrotuberous ligament and gluteus maximus. Each contains fat and the pudendal neurovascular bundle (pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels) in Alcock’s canal; facilitates expansion of the anal canal and can be a site for infection spread.

ischiococcygeal.definition: Relating to the ischium and coccyx; in anatomy, describing the pelvic floor muscle that extends from the ischial spine to the coccyx and helps support pelvic organs.

ischiofemoral ligament.definition: A strong fibrous band that reinforces the posterior aspect of the hip joint capsule, extending from the ischial part of the acetabular rim to the greater trochanter and femoral neck; it tightens with hip extension to limit internal rotation and prevent hyperextension/posterior dislocation.

iliofemoral ligament.definition: A strong, Y-shaped ligament of the hip joint that extends from the ilium (AIIS and acetabular rim) to the intertrochanteric line of the femur; it reinforces the anterior capsule, is the strongest hip ligament, and primarily resists hyperextension of the hip to help maintain upright posture.

pubofemoral ligament.definition: A thick band of the hip joint capsule that originates from the pubic portion of the acetabular rim and the superior pubic ramus and inserts on the femoral neck; it helps stabilize the joint by limiting abduction and external rotation.

sciatic nerve.definition: A major peripheral nerve of the lower limb formed from the ventral rami of L4–S3; the thickest nerve in the body, it exits the pelvis via the greater sciatic foramen, runs down the posterior thigh, and divides into the tibial and common fibular (peroneal) nerves, supplying motor innervation to most of the posterior thigh and leg muscles and sensory innervation to portions of the leg and foot.

sciatic.definition: Relating to the major nerve that originates in the lower spine and travels through the buttock down the back of the leg; commonly used to describe conditions causing pain along this nerve’s pathway (sciatica).

somatostatinoma.definition: A rare pancreatic or duodenal neuroendocrine tumor that secretes excess somatostatin, producing the somatostatinoma syndrome—diabetes mellitus, steatorrhea, hypochlorhydria, and cholelithiasis (gallstones).

raltegravir.definition: An HIV-1 integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI) antiretroviral drug that blocks the integration of viral DNA into the host genome, thereby inhibiting HIV-1 replication.

ishihara color test.definition: A screening test for color vision deficiency using pseudoisochromatic plates of colored dots; the patient identifies numbers or shapes embedded in the dot patterns to detect red-green color blindness (protanopia/deuteranopia).

ishihara.definition: A color-vision screening test that uses pseudoisochromatic plates composed of colored dots to detect red-green color vision deficiencies.

isolated systolic hypertension.definition: A form of high blood pressure with an elevated systolic pressure (usually ≥140 mmHg) and a normal diastolic pressure (typically <90 mmHg), commonly due to arterial stiffness in older adults and associated with increased cardiovascular risk.

incubator.definition: A device that maintains a controlled, warm environment with regulated humidity and oxygen for the care of premature or ill newborns.

isologous graft.definition: A transplant between genetically identical individuals (e.g., identical twins) or between individuals with identical genotypes; immunologic compatibility is high, with little to no graft rejection.

isometheptene.definition: A vasoconstrictive sympathomimetic agent used to treat acute migraine by constricting cranial and intracranial blood vessels; often used in combination products with other analgesics (e.g., acetaminophen and dichloralphenazone).

isometheptene hydrochloride.definition: A short-acting vasoconstrictive sympathomimetic amine (an alpha-adrenergic agonist) used to treat acute migraine by constricting intracranial blood vessels; often formulated in combination products with other analgesic or sedative agents.

isometheptene mucate.definition: A vasoconstrictor; the mucate salt form of isometheptene used in prescription migraine medications to constrict cranial blood vessels and relieve migraine symptoms.

isometric contraction.definition: A type of muscle contraction in which the muscle generates force without changing length, typically when the external load equals the force produced, resulting in little or no joint movement.

isometric exercise.definition: A type of strength training in which a muscle contracts without changing length or moving a joint, typically against immovable resistance or while holding a static position, producing force and muscle tension without movement.

isoprenaline.definition: Non-selective beta-adrenergic agonist that stimulates beta-1 and beta-2 receptors, increasing heart rate, myocardial contractility, and AV conduction; used to treat bradycardia/heart block and, to a lesser extent, bronchospasm; adverse effects include tachycardia, arrhythmias, and angina.

isophane insulin suspension.definition: An intermediate-acting insulin formulated as a suspension in which insulin is complexed with protamine to delay absorption and extend action; onset about 1–2 hours after injection, peak effect at 4–12 hours, and duration about 14–24 hours.

nph insulin.definition: A form of intermediate-acting human insulin in which protamine is added to slow absorption, providing basal insulin coverage with onset in about 1–2 hours, a peak effect around 4–12 hours, and a duration of roughly 14–24 hours.

isosorbide mononitrate.definition: A nitrate vasodilator (nitric oxide donor) used for the long-term prevention of angina in patients with coronary artery disease; it relaxes vascular smooth muscle, reducing venous return (preload) and myocardial oxygen demand.

isosorbide.definition: A chemical compound derived from sorbitol that serves as the backbone for nitrate vasodilators; its nitrate esters (isosorbide dinitrate and isosorbide mononitrate) are used to treat angina and heart failure by releasing nitric oxide and relaxing vascular smooth muscle.

isoxsuprine hydrochloride.definition: A vasodilator agent that acts as a beta-adrenergic agonist to relax uterine smooth muscle; used as a tocolytic to inhibit preterm labor; can cause tachycardia, hypotension, and flushing.

isradipine.definition: An orally administered dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that inhibits L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle, causing peripheral arteriolar vasodilation and reduced systemic vascular resistance; used to treat hypertension (and sometimes angina).

isordil.definition: A brand name for isosorbide dinitrate, a nitrate vasodilator used to prevent angina by dilating veins and arteries, thereby reducing preload and myocardial oxygen demand.

isotopic tracer.definition: An isotopically labeled molecule (with a stable or radioactive isotope) used to trace the distribution, uptake, metabolism, and excretion of that molecule in biological systems.

isospora.definition: An intracellular protozoan parasite that infects the intestinal epithelium and causes isosporiasis, a diarrheal illness transmitted by ingestion of mature oocysts in contaminated food or water; disease is usually self-limited in healthy individuals but can be chronic and severe in immunocompromised patients.

isosporiasis.definition: An intestinal parasitic infection caused by the coccidian protozoan parasite Cystoisospora belli (formerly Isospora belli), characterized by prolonged or watery diarrhea and malabsorption, especially in immunocompromised individuals; acquired by ingesting sporulated oocysts from contaminated food or water; diagnosed by stool examination for oocysts and treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX).

isovaleric acid.definition: A branched-chain short-chain carboxylic acid (3-methylbutanoic acid; C5H10O2) that is a metabolite in the catabolism of the amino acids leucine.

isovaleric acidemia.definition: An autosomal recessive metabolic disorder due to deficiency of isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase in leucine degradation, leading to accumulation of isovaleric acid and related compounds; characterized by intermittent metabolic crises with vomiting, poor feeding, lethargy, and a distinctive sweaty-foot odor.

isopentoic acid.definition: Five-carbon branched-chain carboxylic acid; the α-methylated isomer of pentanoic acid, also known as 2-methylbutanoic acid or α-methylbutyric acid.

isovolume pressure-flow curve.definition: A plot of pressure versus flow in the heart during the isovolumetric phases of the cardiac cycle, when all valves are closed and the ventricular volume remains essentially constant; during isovolumetric contraction the pressure rises with negligible flow, and during isovolumetric relaxation the pressure falls with negligible flow.

isovolumic contraction.definition: A phase of ventricular systole in which the ventricles contract and pressure rises but no blood is ejected because both the atrioventricular and semilunar valves are closed; ventricular volume remains constant until the aortic/pulmonary valves open.

sarcoptes scabiei.definition: A parasitic mite that burrows into the skin's stratum corneum, causing scabies with intense itching and a papular rash; transmitted through close personal contact; treated with topical scabicides (e.g., permethrin) or oral ivermectin.

tension headache.definition: A headache, usually mild or moderate in intensity, not accompanied by other symptoms; pain is usually felt throughout the head, across the forehead, or in the back of the head. Also known as a muscle-contraction headache.

raynaud’s disease.definition: A disease where the blood vessels in your fingers and toes get narrow when you are cold or stressed. This means that blood can't get to the surface and causes your skin to change color.

buerger’s disease.definition: An inflammatory, nonatherosclerotic vasculitis of small- to medium-sized arteries and veins in the extremities (thromboangiitis obliterans), strongly linked to tobacco use; presents with distal ischemia, claudication, ulcers, and Raynaud phenomenon; management centers on complete tobacco abstinence.

gi reflux.definition: Reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus or proximal gastrointestinal tract, typically due to incompetence or inappropriate relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter, often presenting with heartburn and regurgitation and potentially leading to esophagitis or other complications.

isthmus of gastric gland.definition: The upper, narrow portion of a gastric gland just below the gastric pit, containing progenitor (stem) cells that renew surface mucous cells and give rise to other glandular cells as they migrate down toward the neck and base.

isthmus of thyroid.definition: The narrow central portion of the thyroid gland that unites the two lobes, located in the anterior neck and lying anterior to the trachea.

gastric gland.definition: A gland in the stomach lining (gastric mucosa) that secretes gastric juice into the lumen, comprising acid-secreting parietal cells, enzyme-secreting chief cells, mucus-producing cells, and enteroendocrine cells that regulate digestion.

gastric pit.definition: Shallow indentations in the stomach's mucosa that open onto the luminal surface and lead to the gastric glands; they are lined by mucus-secreting foveolar cells and contain stem cells for epithelial renewal.

nitrogycerin.definition: A nitrate vasodilator used to treat and prevent angina and other ischemic heart conditions. It releases nitric oxide, increasing cyclic GMP and relaxing vascular smooth muscle, with predominant venodilation that decreases preload and myocardial oxygen demand; higher doses can reduce afterload. Routes include sublingual, transdermal, oral, topical, and IV, with common side effects such as headache, flushing, dizziness, and hypotension; contraindicated with phosphodiesterase inhibitors.

dichloralphenazone.definition: A historical fixed-dose combination used as a sedative-hypnotic and analgesic; it combines chloral hydrate with phenazone (antipyrine) to depress the central nervous system for short-term relief of insomnia and mild pain; usage is limited today due to safety concerns.

sulfacetamide sodium.definition: An antimicrobial sulfonamide; the sodium salt of sulfacetamide; used topically (most commonly as an ophthalmic solution) and in dermatologic products to treat bacterial infections of the eye and skin. It inhibits bacterial folic acid synthesis by competitively inhibiting dihydropteroate synthase, producing a bacteriostatic effect.

sulfacetamide.definition: A sulfonamide antibiotic used in ophthalmic solutions and topical preparations to treat bacterial infections (notably conjunctivitis and certain skin infections). It inhibits bacterial folate synthesis by blocking dihydropteroate synthase, producing a bacteriostatic effect. Caution: potential hypersensitivity in individuals with sulfa allergies.

isoptin.definition: Brand-name calcium channel blocker (verapamil) used to treat hypertension, angina, and certain arrhythmias; it inhibits L-type calcium channels in cardiac and smooth muscle, decreasing heart rate and AV nodal conduction and causing vasodilation.

pilocarpine hydrochloride.definition: A direct-acting muscarinic cholinergic agonist (the hydrochloride salt of pilocarpine) that stimulates exocrine secretions and increases aqueous humor outflow to lower intraocular pressure; used to treat xerostomia and to induce miosis in ophthalmic procedures, with potential systemic cholinergic side effects.

homatropine.definition: An ophthalmic antimuscarinic agent (homatropine hydrobromide) used as a mydriatic and cycloplegic; it blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in the iris and ciliary body, producing pupil dilation and temporary paralysis of accommodation; onset about 30–60 minutes with a duration of roughly 1–3 days.

homatropine hydrobromide.definition: A tropane alkaloid antimuscarinic (muscarinic receptor antagonist) used primarily in ophthalmology as a topical mydriatic and cycloplegic to dilate the pupil and temporarily paralyze accommodation for eye examinations or procedures; the hydrobromide salt increases solubility, with effects such as blurred vision and photophobia that typically last about 24–72 hours.

scopolamine hydrobromide.definition: A muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist (anticholinergic) in the hydrobromide salt form; used to prevent motion sickness and postoperative nausea/vomiting and to reduce secretions, with CNS and anticholinergic side effects such as drowsiness, confusion, dry mouth, and blurred vision.

isopto hyoscine.definition: A brand-name ophthalmic solution containing scopolamine (hyoscine) used to dilate the pupil (mydriasis) and paralyze accommodation (cycloplegia) for eye examinations or procedures; it acts as an antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) agent.

itp.definition: An autoimmune disorder characterized by isolated thrombocytopenia due to autoantibody-mediated destruction of platelets, often with normal red blood cell and white blood cell counts. It commonly follows a viral illness in children (acute form) and may be chronic in adults; patients may have mucocutaneous bleeding such as petechiae or purpura. Diagnosis is by exclusion; treatment options include corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, and splenectomy or thrombopoietin receptor agonists for refractory cases.

erlichiosis.definition: A tick-borne bacterial infection caused by Ehrlichia species (most commonly Ehrlichia chaffeensis) transmitted by ixodid ticks; presents with fever, headache, malaise, and myalgias, often with leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated liver enzymes; diagnosed by serology or PCR and typically treated with doxycycline.

babesiosis.definition: A tick-borne malarial-like parasitic infection caused by Babesia species (most commonly Babesia microti) that invades red blood cells, causing fever, chills, fatigue, and hemolytic anemia; transmitted by Ixodes ticks and can be severe in asplenic, elderly, or immunocompromised individuals.

japanese spotted fever.definition: A tick-borne rickettsial infection caused by Rickettsia japonica, occurring mainly in Japan and parts of East Asia. It typically presents with fever, headache, myalgia, a localized inoculation eschar, and a maculopapular or petechial rash; transmitted by Haemaphysalis ticks. Treated with doxycycline; prognosis is generally good with early therapy.

scrub typhus.definition: A mite-borne infectious disease caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi, transmitted by larval trombiculid mites (chiggers); presents with acute febrile illness and often an eschar at the bite site, and can progress to pneumonitis, hepatitis, or meningitis if untreated; treated with doxycycline or azithromycin.

epidemic typhus.definition: A severe febrile illness caused by the bacterium Rickettsia prowazekii, transmitted to humans by the body louse (Pediculus humanus corporis). It presents with abrupt onset fever, severe headache, myalgias, malaise, and a diffuse maculopapular rash that typically starts on the trunk and spreads to the limbs; can be life-threatening if not treated.

japanese b encephalitis.definition: An acute viral encephalitis caused by Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV), a mosquito-borne flavivirus transmitted by Culex species; it ranges from febrile illness to severe encephalitis with fever, headache, vomiting, altered mental status, seizures, and neurologic deficits, and is most prevalent in parts of Asia-Pacific. Prevention relies on vaccination and vector control.

janeway lesion.definition: Painless, erythematous or hemorrhagic macules on the palms and soles seen in infective endocarditis, caused by septic emboli from the infected valve.

jacksonian epilepsy.definition: A focal motor seizure that originates in the primary motor cortex and spreads contiguously to adjacent muscle groups, producing a progressive unilateral jerking (march) from one region (often starting in the face or hand) and may secondarily generalize to a generalized seizure.

marcus gunn's syndrome.definition: A relative afferent pupillary defect due to impaired input from the retina or optic nerve (e.g., optic neuropathy or severe retinal disease); detected by a swinging flashlight test, in which the pupil of the affected eye shows reduced constriction compared with the normal eye.

jarcho-levin syndrome.definition: A rare inherited congenital disorder characterized by segmentation defects of the spine and ribs (vertebral anomalies with rib fusions), leading to a markedly shortened trunk and a constricted thoracic cage, often with respiratory compromise in infancy. It has two main phenotypes: spondylocostal dysostosis and spondylothoracic dysostosis.

spondylothoracic dysplasia.definition: A rare congenital skeletal disorder featuring vertebral segmentation abnormalities and rib/thoracic cage malformations that produce a narrow thorax and can lead to respiratory insufficiency.

jansen's disease.definition: A rare congenital skeletal dysplasia caused by activating mutations in the PTH1R gene, leading to constitutive PTH/PTHrP receptor signaling; it presents in infancy with severe hypercalcemia, short stature with limb shortening, and distinctive metaphyseal flaring and irregularities on radiographs.

jansky-bielschowsky disease.definition: Definition not found in standard medical references; it may be a misspelling or obscure eponym. Please provide alternate spelling, a source, or some clinical context (e.g., specialty or key symptoms) for a precise definition.

crigler-najjar syndrome.definition: An autosomal recessive hepatic disorder caused by mutations in the UGT1A1 gene, leading to deficient or absent hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity and impaired bilirubin conjugation, resulting in marked unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Type I shows near-complete enzyme deficiency with severe early-onset jaundice and kernicterus risk; Type II has partial deficiency and may respond to phenobarbital.

jarisch-herxheimer reaction.definition: A transient febrile reaction that occurs after starting antimicrobial therapy for certain infections (most notably syphilis), caused by rapid lysis of organisms and release of endotoxins with cytokine-mediated symptoms; it typically develops within hours of treatment and resolves within 24 hours; it is not an allergic reaction.

jejunal atresia.definition: A congenital small-intestinal obstruction of the jejunum caused by failure of lumen recanalization during embryonic development, leading to a narrowed or blocked jejunal segment; presents with bilious vomiting and abdominal distension in newborns and is treated with surgical resection of the affected segment and end-to-end anastomosis.

jejunal feeding tube.definition: A tube inserted into the jejunum to deliver enteral nutrition directly into the small intestine, bypassing the stomach; used when gastric feeding is contraindicated or not tolerated (e.g., high aspiration risk, gastroparesis, obstruction, or post-surgical needs).

jejunocecostomy.definition: A surgical anastomosis between the jejunum and the cecum, creating a conduit that allows intestinal contents to pass directly from the jejunum into the cecum, typically to bypass a distal obstruction or re-route intestinal flow.

jejunocolostomy.definition: An anastomosis between the jejunum and the colon; a surgical connection that allows contents to pass from the small intestine into the large intestine, typically performed to restore bowel continuity after resection or bypass diseased segments.

jejunogastric intussusception.definition: A rare postoperative complication in which a loop of jejunum invaginates into the stomach through a gastrojejunostomy, causing acute upper GI obstruction and risking ischemia if not reduced.

jeunoileitis.definition: Inflammation of the jejunum and ileum (the middle and distal portions of the small intestine), commonly seen in Crohn disease, causing abdominal pain, diarrhea, and malabsorption with weight loss.

jejunotomy.definition: A surgical incision into the jejunum (the middle portion of the small intestine), typically performed to access the intestinal lumen for diagnostic, therapeutic, or reparative purposes.

jejunal.definition: Relating to the jejunum, the middle section of the small intestine between the duodenum and ileum.

intravenous transfusion.definition: A procedure in which blood or blood components are delivered directly into a vein via an IV line to replace lost blood volume or improve oxygen-carrying capacity.

iv push.definition: A method of administering a medication by direct injection into a vein through a syringe over a short period, typically 1–5 minutes, usually via an existing IV line or saline lock, followed by flushing with saline.

intravenous pump.definition: A device that delivers intravenous fluids or medications into a patient’s bloodstream at a precisely programmed rate and volume, typically using an electronic or syringe infusion pump with alarms to detect occlusion, air in the line, or completion of therapy.

maxillae.definition: The paired bones forming the upper jaw; they bear the upper teeth and form the floor of the orbit, the lateral walls of the nasal cavity, and the anterior part of the hard palate, each containing a maxillary sinus.

sclerae.definition: The sclerae are the tough, opaque, white outer coat of the eyeball made of dense connective tissue; they provide structural support and shape, protect intraocular contents, and serve as the attachment for extraocular muscles, forming the majority of the globe’s outer surface and continuing posteriorly with the optic nerve.

volar.definition: Relating to the palm side of the hand or the sole of the foot; the volar surface is the palmar (palm) surface of the hand, and in limbs can refer to the anterior surface.

upper arm.definition: The region of the upper limb between the shoulder and the elbow (the brachium); it contains the humerus and the arm muscles (biceps brachii, brachialis, coracobrachialis anteriorly; triceps brachii posteriorly), along with the accompanying neurovascular structures.

palms.definition: The palmar aspect of the hand; the inner surface from the wrist to the fingertips, including the skin, underlying fascia, and neurovascular/tendinous structures that enable grasping.

soles.definition: The undersides of the feet; the plantar (bottom) surfaces that contact the ground.

urethral orifice.definition: An external opening of the urethra through which urine exits the body; in males at the tip of the penis and in females just anterior to the vaginal opening (the external urethral meatus).

jacksonian seizure.definition: A focal motor seizure that begins in a localized region of the motor cortex (often the hand/face area) and propagates contiguously to adjacent regions, producing a progressive “march” of jerking movements and sometimes evolving into a generalized seizure.

macule.definition: A flat, circumscribed skin lesion with color different from surrounding skin, nonpalpable, and measuring less than 1 cm in diameter.

hemorrhagic macule.definition: A flat skin lesion less than 1 cm in diameter caused by leakage of blood into the skin (extravasation), producing a red to purplish patch that does not rise above the skin surface and typically does not blanch with pressure.

cartilaginous joint.definition: A joint in which the bones are firmly connected by cartilage, so that only slight movement is possible.

sutural joint.definition: A fibrous joint between skull bones (a suture) that binds bones with dense connective tissue and permits little or no movement; an immovable joint (synarthrosis) that may ossify with age.

synchondrosis.definition: A cartilaginous joint in which the bones are joined by hyaline cartilage, producing a rigid, immobile joint; it is typically temporary in growing individuals and ossifies with maturation (e.g., the epiphyseal (growth) plate).

amphiarthrosis.definition: A joint that permits only slight, or limited, movement between the articulating bones; most commonly a cartilaginous joint, as seen in the pubic symphysis and the intervertebral joints.

saddle joint.definition: A type of synovial joint with saddle-shaped articular surfaces—each surface is concave in one axis and convex in the other—allowing biaxial movement (flexion–extension and abduction–adduction) with little or no axial rotation; classic example is the first carpometacarpal joint of the thumb.

gliding joint.definition: A type of synovial joint (plane joint) with flat or nearly flat articular surfaces that allows the bones to slide past one another in small, gliding motions, usually in multiple directions; examples include intercarpal and intertarsal joints and facet joints of the spine.

atlantoaxial joint.definition: A joint between the atlas (C1) and axis (C2) in the cervical spine, comprising the median atlantoaxial joint (the dens of C2 pivoting within the anterior arch of C1) and two lateral atlantoaxial joints; its primary function is to allow rotation of the head.

vernet's syndrome.definition: A jugular foramen syndrome with ipsilateral palsy of cranial nerves IX, X, and XI due to a lesion at the jugular foramen or skull base, causing dysphagia, hoarseness, loss of gag reflex, palate weakness, and weakness of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles; commonly due to skull base tumors such as glomus jugulare.

jugular notch.definition: Central shallow depression on the skin at the superior border of the sternum’s manubrium, between the medial ends of the clavicles; an external landmark (suprasternal notch) that roughly corresponds to the level of the second thoracic vertebra (T2).

jugular process.definition: A small bony projection of the occipital bone that forms the posterior boundary of the jugular foramen; with the temporal bone it completes the foramen through which the internal jugular vein and cranial nerves IX–XI pass.

petrous part.definition: A dense, pyramid-shaped portion of the temporal bone that houses the inner ear (the bony labyrinth) and contains the internal acoustic meatus, protecting hearing and balance structures.

squamous part.definition: The thin, fan-shaped, anterior portion of the temporal bone that forms the upper and lateral wall of the skull; it contains the zygomatic process (which articulates with the zygomatic bone) and the mandibular fossa with the articular tubercle, where the mandible articulates with the skull.

inferior petrosal sinus.definition: A dural venous sinus located along the petrous part of the temporal bone that drains venous blood from the cavernous sinus into the internal jugular vein at the jugular foramen.

jugular fossa.definition: A shallow depression on the inferior surface of the petrous part of the temporal bone (skull base) that forms part of the jugular foramen and marks where the sigmoid sinus drains into the internal jugular vein.

manubrium.definition: The broad, superior part of the sternum that articulates with the clavicles and the first costal cartilage, forming the upper portion of the breastbone and joining the body at the sternal angle.

suprasternal notch.definition: A shallow indentation at the superior border of the sternum (the manubrium), located between the clavicles; commonly used as a surface landmark for mediastinal structures.

odontoid process.definition: A tooth-like projection from the body of the axis (C2) that acts as a pivot for rotation of the atlas (C1) and skull, stabilized by the transverse ligament of the atlas.

cerebellar vermis.definition: The midline portion of the cerebellum that unites the two cerebellar hemispheres; it integrates vestibular and proprioceptive information to regulate posture, balance, and trunk- and proximal-limb coordination.

joubert's syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by midbrain-hindbrain malformation with cerebellar vermis hypoplasia and the distinctive "molar tooth sign" on MRI; presents in infancy with hypotonia and abnormal breathing, followed by ataxia, oculomotor abnormalities, and developmental delay, and is often accompanied by multisystem features (kidney, liver, or eye involvement) as part of a ciliopathy.

long bones.definition: Long bones are bones that are longer than they are wide and function as levers for movement; they have a tubular shaft (diaphysis) of compact bone and two enlarged ends (epiphyses) that participate in joints and contain cancellous bone, with growth plates present in children.

radius-ulna articulation.definition: An articulation consisting of the proximal and distal radioulnar joints that connect the radius and ulna, allowing forearm rotation (pronation and supination); stability is provided by the interosseous membrane and surrounding ligaments (annular ligament at the proximal joint and the triangular fibrocartilage complex at the distal joint).

ileoanal anastomosis.definition: A surgical connection between the ileum and the anal canal, typically after colectomy with construction of an ileal pouch to restore intestinal continuity and continence; commonly part of ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA) used for ulcerative colitis or familial adenomatous polyposis.

j-pouch.definition: A surgical procedure in which the terminal ileum is fashioned into a J-shaped reservoir and anastomosed to the anal canal after proctocolectomy, restoring intestinal continuity and continence without a permanent ileostomy; also known as ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA).

polydylism.definition: Definition not found in standard medical dictionaries. Please provide context or confirm the spelling (it may be a misspelling or a very uncommon term).

polydactylism.definition: A congenital condition characterized by the presence of extra fingers or toes; can be preaxial, postaxial, or central, and may occur as an isolated finding or as part of a genetic syndrome.

short-limbed dwarfism.definition: Disproportionate dwarfism in which the limb bones are markedly shorter than the trunk due to defective endochondral bone growth; most commonly caused by achondroplasia.

calcaneal spurs.definition: A bony outgrowth from the heel bone (calcaneus), typically associated with chronic plantar fasciitis, that can cause heel pain and is seen on imaging as a spur projecting from the underside or back of the heel.

trigger finger.definition: A stenosing tenosynovitis of the flexor tendon sheath (usually the A1 pulley) causing locking or catching of a finger or thumb in flexion, often with a painful or audible snap on movement.

jimson weed.definition: A plant (Datura stramonium) containing tropane alkaloids such as atropine, hyoscyamine, and scopolamine; ingestion or exposure can cause anticholinergic toxicity, presenting with delirium or hallucinations, dry skin and mucous membranes, dilated pupils with blurred vision, tachycardia, urinary retention, fever, and decreased bowel motility; treatment is supportive, with consideration of antidotes (e.g., physostigmine) in select cases.

datura stramonium.definition: A poisonous flowering plant of the nightshade family containing tropane alkaloids (atropine, hyoscyamine, and scopolamine) that produce severe anticholinergic toxicity, causing delirium and hallucinations, dry mouth, tachycardia, mydriasis, urinary retention, and potentially fatal outcomes after ingestion.

gutta-percha cones.definition: A flexible, thermoplastic endodontic filling point made of gutta-percha used to obturate (fill and seal) a cleaned root canal, typically with a sealer and placed by condensation or warm obturation to prevent leakage.

lateral condensation.definition: A root canal obturation technique in which a master gutta-percha cone is placed to the working length and additional cones are laterally compacted against the canal walls with a spreader to form a dense seal.

condensation method.definition: Not a standard medical term. If used in a laboratory context, it refers to the physical process of a gas turning into a liquid by cooling or increasing pressure, often to concentrate volatile analytes or collect samples for analysis.

intraarticular fracture.definition: A fracture that extends into the articular (joint) surface, crossing the joint cartilage and potentially disrupting joint congruity, with a higher risk of posttraumatic arthritis if not reduced and aligned.

joint instability.definition: A condition in which a joint cannot maintain normal alignment and movement under physiological loads due to insufficient passive restraints (ligaments, joint capsule, bone geometry) and/or impaired active stabilization (muscles), leading to excessive translational or rotational motion and episodes of pain, giving way, or recurrent subluxation or dislocation.

loose body.definition: A free fragment of bone or cartilage floating within a joint space, often arising after trauma or degenerative joint disease; it can cause mechanical symptoms such as locking, catching, or pain, and is commonly removed surgically (e.g., via arthroscopy).

jet nebulizer.definition: A device that uses compressed gas (air or oxygen) passed through a narrow orifice to convert a liquid medication into a fine aerosol for inhalation, typically delivered via mouthpiece or mask; used to administer bronchodilators, corticosteroids, antibiotics, or saline in respiratory therapy.

endemic goiter.definition: Diffuse enlargement of the thyroid gland occurring in populations with chronic iodine deficiency, typically due to low dietary iodine and preventable with iodized salt or iodine supplementation.

multinodular goiter.definition: An enlargement of the thyroid gland with more than one lump or nodule appearing on the neck.

nontoxic multinodular goiter.definition: A goiter caused by multiple nodules that function independently and do not cause hyperthyroidism; patients are typically euthyroid.

iodine deficiency.definition: An insufficient intake or utilization of iodine leading to impaired synthesis of thyroid hormones (T4 and T3). This can cause goiter and hypothyroidism; in fetal and early postnatal life it may cause cretinism and irreversible neurodevelopmental deficits. It is a major, preventable cause of intellectual disability worldwide.

endemic iodine deficiency.definition: A chronic, population-wide deficiency of dietary iodine due to low environmental iodine, leading to an elevated prevalence of goiter and hypothyroidism; in pregnant women and infants, it can cause cretinism and impaired neurodevelopment.

iodine-induced hyperthyroidism.definition: A form of thyrotoxicosis precipitated by excess iodine exposure in susceptible individuals with autonomous thyroid tissue (e.g., nodular goiter or latent Graves’ disease), due to increased synthesis and release of thyroid hormones (the Jod-Basedow phenomenon).

jod-basedow phenomenon.definition: An iodine-induced hyperthyroidism occurring in patients with autonomous thyroid tissue (e.g., multinodular goiter or latent Graves’ disease) after exposure to excess iodine, causing thyrotoxicosis due to stimulation of autonomous nodules.

basedow.definition: An autoimmune hyperthyroidism (Graves disease) caused by stimulating antibodies to the TSH receptor, leading to diffuse thyroid enlargement and thyrotoxicosis; commonly associated with ophthalmopathy and sometimes pretibial myxedema.

jones criteria.definition: A set of clinical criteria used to diagnose acute rheumatic fever. Major criteria: migratory polyarthritis, carditis, chorea, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules. Minor criteria: fever, arthralgia, elevated acute phase reactants (ESR/CRP), and prolonged PR interval. Diagnosis requires evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection, plus either two major criteria or one major plus two minor criteria (per revised 2015 AHA criteria).

juvenile rheumatoid arthritis.definition: A chronic autoimmune inflammatory arthritis of childhood characterized by persistent joint swelling, pain, and morning stiffness lasting at least six weeks, often with systemic features, and classified into subtypes such as oligoarticular, polyarticular, and systemic.

juvenile-onset diabetes mellitus.definition: A form of diabetes mellitus caused by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, resulting in absolute insulin deficiency and lifelong dependence on exogenous insulin; typically presents in children and adolescents with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, and hyperglycemia.

jra.definition: An inflammatory arthritis of childhood characterized by persistent joint swelling, pain, and stiffness for at least six weeks, which may involve a few joints or many, and can be associated with systemic features such as fever or rash.

judd method.definition: Not found in standard medical dictionaries. Could you share the medical field or a source for the Judd method (or confirm the spelling)? I can look up related variations like "Judd's method" if you provide context.

jugular_pulse.definition: Visible pulsation of the jugular veins in the neck that reflects right atrial and central venous pressure; used to assess preload/volume status and right-sided heart function.

jugular_vein.definition: A major neck vein that drains deoxygenated blood from the head and neck to the heart; it comprises the internal jugular vein (draining intracranial structures and most of the face) and the external jugular vein (draining superficial head and neck regions), both ultimately emptying into the brachiocephalic veins and then the superior vena cava.

diastolic_filling.definition: Ventricular filling during diastole, when the ventricles relax and blood flows from the atria into the ventricles; rapid early filling is followed by slower filling (diastasis), with atrial contraction contributing to final end-diastolic volume.

congestive_heart_failure.definition: When your heart can't pump enough blood. Also called heart failure or CHF.

jugular_trunk.definition: A major lymphatic vessel draining lymph from the head and neck; on the left, it drains into the thoracic duct, and on the right, into the right lymphatic duct.

jugular_tubercle.definition: A small bony prominence on the inferior surface of the occipital bone, just anterior to the jugular foramen, serving as an anatomical skull-base landmark.

jugular_foramen.definition: An opening at the base of the skull formed by the temporal and occipital bones through which the internal jugular vein and cranial nerves IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), and XI (spinal accessory) exit the skull; typically divided into pars nervosa (anterior) and pars vascularis (posterior).

jugular_venous_pressure.definition: An indirect estimate of right atrial pressure obtained by examining the venous pulse in the neck; the height of the venous column above the sternal angle is used, with the patient typically at 30–45 degrees, to assess central venous pressure and fluid status.

jvp.definition: A clinical estimate of central venous pressure derived from the height of the jugular venous pulsation in the neck; reflects right atrial pressure and preload, typically assessed with the patient at about 30–45 degrees. An elevated JVP suggests increased right atrial pressure (e.g., right heart failure, tamponade, constrictive pericarditis), while a normal JVP is a small vertical height above the sternal angle.

venous_pressure.definition: Pressure exerted by blood within the venous system. It is normally low (a few mm Hg) and varies with respiration and blood volume; central venous pressure is the clinical surrogate for right atrial pressure and venous return, typically about 2–8 mm Hg.

sternal_angle.definition: An anatomical landmark at the junction of the manubrium and body of the sternum (the angle of Louis), at the level of the second costal cartilage; it marks the level where the trachea bifurcates into the main bronchi and where the aortic arch begins.

external_jugular_vein.definition: A superficial vein of the neck that drains the scalp and exterior face; it courses superficial to the sternocleidomastoid muscle and drains into the subclavian vein.

internal_jugular_vein.definition: A large venous channel in the neck that drains blood from the brain, face, and neck; it forms at the jugular foramen as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus, courses in the carotid sheath, receives tributaries such as facial, lingual, pharyngeal, and thyroid veins, enlarges at the jugular bulb, and drains into the brachiocephalic vein.

lymphatic_vessels.definition: A network of thin-walled vessels that collect interstitial fluid (lymph) from tissues and transport it to the venous system; they begin as blind-ended lymphatic capillaries, merge into larger collecting vessels with valves, and ultimately drain via the thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct into the subclavian veins.

occipital_bone.definition: The bottom of the back of the skull.

jugum.definition: A Latin term meaning "yoke"; in anatomy, a bridging ridge or projection that connects two parts, such as the jugum sphenoidale in the skull.

gastric_juice.definition: The highly acidic digestive secretion produced by the stomach’s glands, comprising water, mucus, hydrochloric acid, pepsinogen (converted to pepsin), intrinsic factor, and small amounts of enzymes; it acidifies stomach contents and initiates protein digestion.

intestinal_juice.definition: Digestive secretion produced by the mucosal glands of the small intestine; it contains water, mucus, and brush-border enzymes (including enteropeptidase/enterokinase, peptidases, and disaccharidases) that facilitate digestion of carbohydrates and proteins in the intestinal lumen.

pancreatic_juice.definition: Exocrine pancreatic secretions rich in bicarbonate and digestive enzymes (amylase, lipase, proteases such as trypsin and chymotrypsin) released into the duodenum via the pancreatic duct; neutralizes gastric acid and facilitates digestion of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins.

juice_therapy.definition: An unproven dietary regimen that replaces or predominates meals with fruit- and vegetable-based juices for detox or weight loss; there is little high-quality evidence of benefit, and extended use can cause malnutrition, electrolyte disturbances, and other adverse effects.

jumping_disease.definition: A historical term for a rare startle-syndrome in which individuals exhibit exaggerated, involuntary startle responses to sudden stimuli.

gilles_de_la_tourette_syndrome.definition: A chronic neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by multiple motor tics and one or more vocal tics that persist for more than a year, with onset before age 18; tics wax and wane and may be accompanied by comorbid conditions such as ADHD or OCD.

jumping_frenchmen_of_maine_syndrome.definition: An extremely exaggerated startle reaction to unexpected stimuli, typically presenting with abrupt, involuntary motor responses (such as jumping or shouting) and sometimes associated features like echolalia or echopraxia; historically described in French-Canadian lumberjacks in Maine and considered a rare hereditary startle syndrome.

jumping_gene.definition: A transposable element, a DNA sequence that can move to new positions within the genome, potentially disrupting genes or altering gene expression; includes DNA transposons and retrotransposons.

junctional_bigeminy.definition: A rhythm in which a premature junctional contraction occurs on every other beat, producing a bigeminal pattern; junctional beats often lack visible P waves or have inverted P waves and a shortened PR interval.

junctional_epithelium.definition: A specialized non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium that forms the attachment of the gingiva to the tooth surface, lining the gingival sulcus and sealing the area at the cemento-enamel junction; it adheres to enamel via a basement membrane and hemidesmosomes, acts as a barrier to bacterial invasion, and has a rapid turnover (about 4–6 days).

epithelial_cuff.definition: A ring-like boundary of epithelial cells encircling a lesion or foreign body in histological sections, representing reactive epithelial proliferation at the margins.

gingival_cuff.definition: A cuff-like band of gingival tissue surrounding the tooth at the gingival margin, comprising the free gingiva and the attached gingiva, forming the seal around the tooth and protecting the underlying periodontal structures.

junctional_extrasystole.definition: Premature beat arising from the AV junction (near the AV node) that occurs earlier than expected; the QRS is usually narrow, and P waves are often absent or inverted due to retrograde atrial activation, reflecting a premature junctional contraction.

junctional_parenchymal_defect.definition: A localized deficit of functional parenchymal tissue at a junctional area between two anatomical structures; the exact meaning varies by context and organ, and on imaging may reflect atelectasis, scarring, or tissue loss at a junction.

junctional_rhythm.definition: A cardiac rhythm originating from the AV node or below (junctional tissue) as an escape mechanism when the SA node fails; usually 40–60 beats per minute; P waves may be absent, inverted, or occur after the QRS (sometimes buried within the QRS), and the QRS complex is typically narrow.

junctional_tachycardia.definition: Atrioventricular (AV) junctional tachycardia: a fast heart rhythm (typically 100–200 beats per minute) arising from tissue in the AV junction near the AV node, often with absent or retrograde P waves and a narrow QRS, produced by automatic or reentrant impulses.

junctional_nevus.definition: A benign melanocytic nevus in which nevus cells remain confined to the epidermal-dermal (dermoepidermal) junction; typically flat and evenly pigmented, common in children, and may evolve into a compound or intradermal nevus over time.

junctura_cartilaginea.definition: A cartilaginous joint in which bones are united by cartilage (hyaline cartilage in synchondroses or fibrocartilage in symphyses), typically immobile or only slightly movable.

cartilaginous_joint.definition: A cartilaginous joint is a joint in which the bones are joined by cartilage (hyaline cartilage in synchondroses or fibrocartilage in symphyses), lacks a synovial cavity, and allows limited movement (amphiarthrosis).

junctura_fibrosa.definition: A fibrous joint in which bones are joined by dense fibrous connective tissue, allowing little or no movement (synarthrosis); examples include skull sutures, distal tibiofibular syndesmosis, and gomphoses (tooth sockets).

junctura_synovialis.definition: A synovial joint (diarthrosis), a freely movable articulation where bone surfaces are covered with articular cartilage, enclosed by a fibrous capsule lined with synovial membrane and containing synovial fluid within a joint cavity.

juxtaglomerular_apparatus.definition: A functional renal structure in the kidney formed by the macula densa of the distal tubule, the juxtaglomerular (granular) cells of the afferent arteriole, and extraglomerular mesangial cells; it regulates glomerular filtration rate and systemic blood pressure by sensing NaCl delivery and perfusion pressure and modulating renin release (tubuloglomerular feedback).

juxtaglomerular_complex.definition: A functional unit in the kidney comprising the macula densa of the distal tubule, juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole, and extraglomerular mesangial (Lacis) cells; it senses NaCl concentration and blood pressure to regulate glomerular filtration rate and renal perfusion by secreting renin as part of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system.

juxtaglomerular_cells.definition: Specialized smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent (and sometimes efferent) arterioles at the juxtaglomerular apparatus that synthesize, store, and secrete renin; they regulate blood pressure and electrolyte balance via the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system.

juxtaglomerular.definition: Situated adjacent to the glomerulus in the kidney; refers to the specialized renal structure that regulates blood flow and glomerular filtration rate by secreting renin.

epo.definition: An endogenous glycoprotein hormone produced by the kidneys that stimulates red blood cell production in the bone marrow; used medically as an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (epoetin) to treat anemia due to chronic kidney disease or chemotherapy, and may be abused as a performance-enhancing drug.

macula_densa.definition: A group of tall, densely packed epithelial cells in the distal tubule at the juxtaglomerular apparatus that senses NaCl concentration in tubular fluid and modulates glomerular filtration rate via tubuloglomerular feedback, signaling to nearby juxtaglomerular cells to adjust renin release.

afferent_arteriole.definition: A small artery that supplies blood to the glomerulus of a nephron in the kidney; its smooth muscle can constrict or dilate to regulate glomerular filtration rate and renal blood flow.

efferent_arteriole.definition: A small-diameter blood vessel that carries blood away from the glomerulus after filtration, delivering it to the peritubular capillaries or vasa recta; its narrow size helps maintain high glomerular capillary pressure and promote filtration.

proximal_convoluted_tubule.definition: A segment of the nephron immediately after Bowman's capsule; a highly metabolic, brush-border-lined tubule that reabsorbs about 65% of filtered Na+, water, glucose, amino acids, and bicarbonate, and also secretes organic acids and bases; reabsorption is driven by Na+/K+-ATPase and Na+/H+ exchange, with carbonic anhydrase facilitating bicarbonate reclamation.

distal_convoluted_tubule.definition: A segment of the nephron between the thick ascending limb and the collecting duct that reabsorbs sodium and chloride via the Na-Cl cotransporter, is relatively impermeable to water, and regulates electrolyte handling (sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion) under aldosterone, with calcium reabsorption stimulated by parathyroid hormone.

loop_of_henle.definition: A U-shaped segment of the nephron in the kidney that dips into the medulla; the descending limb is permeable to water and concentrates tubular fluid, while the ascending limb actively reabsorbs ions (primarily Na+, Cl−) and is water-impermeable, establishing the medullary osmotic gradient necessary for concentrating urine.

renal_cortex.definition: The outer portion of the kidney, between the renal capsule and the medulla, that contains the glomeruli and proximal and distal tubules; the site of filtration and initial urine formation.

renal_medulla.definition: The innermost portion of the kidney, between the cortex and the renal pelvis, comprising the renal pyramids and surrounding columns; it contains portions of the nephron (loops of Henle and collecting ducts) and the vasa recta, and is essential for concentrating urine.

corticomedullary_border.definition: The boundary between the renal cortex and renal medulla in the kidney; marks the transition from cortex, which contains glomeruli and proximal/distal tubules, to the medulla, which contains loops of Henle and collecting ducts.

juxtamedullary_cortex.definition: The portion of the renal cortex adjacent to the renal medulla, where juxtamedullary nephrons are concentrated and whose long loop of Henle extends into the medulla.

juxtamedullary_glomerulus.definition: A glomerulus of a juxtamedullary nephron; located near the corticomedullary junction, it filters blood and, with its long loop of Henle and vasa recta, contributes to the medullary concentration mechanism enabling urine concentration.

juxtamedullary_nephron.definition: A nephron with a long loop of Henle that extends deep into the medulla, with the glomerulus located near the corticomedullary junction, enabling the production of highly concentrated urine via the countercurrent multiplier system and vasa recta.

visceral_leishmaniasis.definition: A systemic protozoal infection caused by Leishmania donovani complex, transmitted by sandflies, presenting with fever, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, weight loss, and pancytopenia; can be fatal without treatment.

kala_azar.definition: A systemic protozoal infection caused by Leishmania donovani complex transmitted by Phlebotomine sandflies; characterized by prolonged fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, and pancytopenia; untreated, often fatal.

assam_fever.definition: A nonstandard, historical name for a fever observed in the Assam region of India; there is no precise, universally accepted medical definition. The label may have referred to various endemic febrile illnesses (e.g., malaria, typhoid, dengue); accurate diagnosis requires clinical evaluation and appropriate laboratory testing.

black_fever.definition: An often-used name for visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), a protozoan infection transmitted by sandflies; characterized by prolonged fever, weight loss, enlargement of the liver and spleen, anemia, and sometimes darkened skin; without treatment it can be fatal. Diagnosis is by detecting Leishmania parasites in tissue or via PCR, and treatment includes anti-leishmanial medications such as liposomal amphotericin B or miltefosine.

dumdum_fever.definition: An obsolete, nonstandard term not used in modern medicine; historically used to describe a febrile illness following combat wounds, without representing a distinct, recognized disease.

ponos.definition: Not a recognized medical term. If you meant “pons” (the brainstem structure), I can define that.

sodium_antimony_gluconate.definition: An antimonial (pentavalent) compound used systemically to treat leishmaniasis (especially visceral leishmaniasis); administered by intramuscular or intravenous injection and associated with toxicities including pancreatitis, hepatotoxicity, and cardiotoxicity.

blood_transfusion.definition: A medical procedure in which blood or blood components from a donor are transfused intravenously into a patient, usually to replace lost blood or treat anemia, after compatibility testing to reduce reaction risk and with monitoring for adverse reactions.

bed_rest.definition: A prescribed period of immobilization with limited activity, typically in bed, to promote healing after illness or injury.

bone_marrow_suppression.definition: A decrease in bone marrow activity resulting in reduced production of erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets; commonly caused by chemotherapy or radiation and leading to anemia, infection risk, and bleeding.

kanamycin.definition: An aminoglycoside antibiotic produced by Streptomyces kanamyceticus that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of mRNA; used for treating serious infections caused by susceptible bacteria; typically given by intramuscular or intravenous injection; adverse effects include nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

kanamycin_sulfate.definition: A bactericidal aminoglycoside antibiotic—the sulfate salt of kanamycin—that binds to the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of mRNA and inhibition of protein synthesis in susceptible bacteria. Used for serious Gram-negative infections; potential nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity; typically administered parenterally.

aminoglycoside.definition: A class of antibiotics that irreversibly bind to the 30S ribosomal subunit, inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis and causing misreading of mRNA; bactericidal and primarily active against aerobic Gram-negative bacteria, with notable risks including nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

sand_fly.definition: Small hematophagous fly of the subfamily Phlebotominae that transmits Leishmania parasites, causing leishmaniasis; bites primarily at dusk or night in tropical and subtropical regions; infections can be cutaneous, mucocutaneous, or visceral depending on the parasite species.

leishmania_donovani.definition: A protozoan parasite of the species Leishmania donovani that causes visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) in humans; transmitted by female Phlebotomine sandflies and characterized by fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia.

nasopharyngeal_angiofibroma.definition: A benign, highly vascular tumor of the nasopharynx that occurs predominantly in adolescent males, presenting with recurrent epistaxis and nasal obstruction; it is locally aggressive and prone to recurrence, and is typically treated with surgical resection after preoperative embolization, with radiotherapy for unresectable or recurrent disease.

juvenile_alveolar_rhabdomyosarcoma.definition: A malignant soft tissue sarcoma of skeletal muscle differentiation occurring in children, defined by alveolar histology and frequently driven by PAX3-FOXO1 or PAX7-FOXO1 gene fusions; clinically aggressive with a high risk of metastasis, and treated with multimodal therapy including chemotherapy, surgery, and radiation.

juvenile_angiofibroma.definition: A benign, highly vascular nasopharyngeal tumor that almost exclusively affects adolescent males; presents with unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent epistaxis and tends to locally invade surrounding structures; treated with preoperative embolization followed by surgical resection.

juvenile_aponeurotic_fibroma.definition: A rare benign soft-tissue tumor arising from fascia or aponeuroses in children, composed of spindle-shaped fibroblasts within dense collagen; presents as a slow-growing, painless mass and is typically treated with surgical excision, with an excellent prognosis and low recurrence.

juvenile_diabetes_mellitus.definition: A form of diabetes mellitus diagnosed in children and adolescents due to autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, resulting in absolute insulin deficiency and lifelong dependence on insulin therapy.

juvenile_glaucoma.definition: An inherited form of primary glaucoma that presents in youth (adolescence to early adulthood), with elevated intraocular pressure causing progressive optic neuropathy and peripheral visual field loss, typically with an open iridocorneal angle.

juvenile_kyphosis.definition: An excessive forward curvature of the thoracic spine in children and adolescents, most commonly due to Scheuermann's disease; characterized by rigid hyperkyphosis and sometimes back pain, with radiographs often showing anterior wedging of multiple vertebrae; management ranges from observation and physical therapy to bracing, with surgical correction reserved for severe deformities.

scheuermanns_disease.definition: An adolescent-onset structural kyphosis of the thoracic spine caused by anterior wedging of multiple adjacent vertebral bodies (often with Schmorl nodes), resulting in a rigid forward curvature.

juvenile_laryngeal_respiratory_papilloma.definition: A pediatric form of recurrent respiratory papillomatosis in which human papillomavirus types 6 and 11 induce benign papillomas in the larynx (and sometimes lower airways), causing progressive hoarseness and potential airway obstruction; lesions frequently recur, requiring repeated surgical removal.

papillomatosis.definition: A condition defined by multiple papillomas—benign epithelial proliferations forming finger-like projections on skin or mucosal surfaces; it can be localized or widespread and, in certain sites (notably the airway), is associated with human papillomavirus infection (e.g., HPV types 6 and 11 in recurrent respiratory papillomatosis).

juvenile_lentigo.definition: A benign pigmented macule appearing in childhood that remains stable over time and is not caused by sun exposure; a type of lentigo resulting from increased melanocytes in the epidermis.

juvenile_myoclonic_syndrome.definition: A form of idiopathic generalized epilepsy that begins in adolescence, characterized by morning myoclonic jerks (often in the arms), sometimes progressing to generalized tonic-clonic seizures, with EEG showing generalized polyspike-and-wave discharges.

juvenile_myxedema.definition: A pediatric form of hypothyroidism characterized by diffuse nonpitting edema (myxedema) from glycosaminoglycan deposition in the dermis, often with growth retardation and developmental delay; untreated, it can progress to cretinism.

juvenile_onset_diabetes.definition: A form of diabetes mellitus that typically begins in childhood or adolescence, resulting from autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells and leading to absolute insulin deficiency; requires lifelong insulin therapy.

juvenile_periodontitis.definition: A rapidly progressive inflammatory periodontal disease in children and adolescents, marked by fast attachment loss and alveolar bone destruction, commonly involving first molars and incisors; often associated with Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans infection and classified as localized or generalized aggressive periodontitis.
