curandero.definition: A traditional healer in Latin American folk medicine who provides physical and spiritual healing through herbal remedies, rituals, prayer, and other folk practices; typically part of the curanderismo tradition and not a licensed medical professional.

susto.definition: A culture-bound syndrome in Latin American folk medicine attributed to a frightening event or trauma that causes the soul to leave the body; presents with anxiety, insomnia, irritability, fatigue, and somatic complaints.

empacho.definition: A culturally defined gastrointestinal upset (folk illness) seen in Latin American communities, characterized by abdominal pain or discomfort, fullness or distension after eating, poor appetite, and sometimes nausea or vomiting; traditionally attributed to indigestion or a “blocked” stomach, but not a distinct medical disorder in evidence-based medicine.

mal de ojo.definition: A cultural belief that a person’s envious or malevolent gaze can cause harm, illness, or misfortune in someone else; not a medically recognized condition.

latex allergy.definition: An immune-mediated hypersensitivity to proteins in natural rubber latex, most often IgE-mediated, causing reactions that can range from skin irritation or hives to life-threatening anaphylaxis upon exposure; risk is higher with repeated or occupational exposure, and there may be cross-reactivity with certain fruits (e.g., banana, avocado, chestnut, kiwi).

latex fixation test.definition: A serologic test in which small latex beads coated with a specific antigen or antibody are mixed with patient serum; if the corresponding antibody or antigen is present, the beads agglutinate, producing a visible clump and indicating a positive reaction. Historically used for various infections, but largely replaced by more modern immunoassays.

rheumatoid factor.definition: An antibody found in about 85% of people with rheumatoid arthritis; also appears in other diseases and sometimes in healthy people.

latex precautions.definition: Practices to prevent latex exposure and allergic reactions, including using latex-free gloves and products, avoiding latex-containing materials, and implementing latex allergy precautions in healthcare and other settings.

laughing gas.definition: A colorless, odorless nitrous oxide gas used as an inhalational analgesic and mild anesthetic; administered with oxygen for rapid sedation and pain relief during short procedures, with risks including hypoxia if not given with oxygen and the potential for expansion of gas-filled spaces.

internal jugular veins.definition: Paired major neck veins that drain venous blood from the brain, face, and neck; they descend within the carotid sheath, lateral to the common carotid arteries, and drain into the subclavian veins behind the sternoclavicular joints to form the brachiocephalic veins.

frog leg position.definition: A body position in which the patient lies on the back with the hips flexed and abducted, the thighs externally rotated and the knees flexed, with the legs held apart as in a frog’s posture.

sims’ position.definition: A left lateral decubitus position in which the patient lies on the left side with the left leg extended and the right knee and thigh flexed, the right arm flexed and placed in front of the body, and the left arm positioned behind the back (often with a pillow under the pelvis to elevate the buttocks). Used for rectal examinations and certain procedures.

laurence-moon syndrome.definition: Trastorno hereditario poco frecuente caracterizado por retinitis pigmentosa (distro de la retina) con obesidad, hipogonadismo y discapacidad intelectual; históricamente se ha considerado distinto del síndrome de Bardet-Biedl, pero a menudo se ubica dentro del espectro de ciliopatías de Bardet-Biedl y, por lo general, carece de polidactilia.

retinitis pigmentosa.definition: An inherited group of retinal dystrophies characterized by progressive photoreceptor degeneration, particularly rods, causing night blindness and gradual constriction of the visual field with eventual central vision impairment; fundoscopic exam often shows bone-spicule pigmentation and attenuated retinal vessels.

autosomal recessive disorder.definition: An inherited condition due to recessive variants in a gene on a non-sex chromosome, expressed only when two mutant alleles are present (one from each parent); carriers are usually asymptomatic; affects males and females equally; the chance of affected offspring is 25% with each pregnancy when both parents are carriers.

spastic paraplegia.definition: Progressive weakness and spasticity of the lower limbs due to degeneration of the corticospinal tracts; a clinical syndrome that can be hereditary (hereditary spastic paraplegia) or acquired.

laureth-9.definition: An nonionic surfactant formed by ethoxylating lauryl alcohol with nine units of ethylene oxide; used as a cleansing agent and emulsifier in cosmetics and personal care products to reduce surface tension and improve foaming, wetting, and emulsification.

maxillary sinuses.definition: Paired air-filled cavities within the maxillary bones of the skull, the largest of the paranasal sinuses; they are lined with respiratory mucosa and drain into the middle nasal meatus via the maxillary ostia.

lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase.definition: An enzyme in plasma that esterifies free cholesterol on lipoproteins by transferring a fatty acyl group from phosphatidylcholine (lecithin) to cholesterol, forming cholesteryl esters and aiding HDL maturation and reverse cholesterol transport.

lcat deficiency.definition: An inherited disorder caused by deficiency of the enzyme lecithin–cholesterol acyltransferase, resulting in impaired cholesterol esterification and abnormal lipoprotein metabolism, with manifestations including corneal opacities and, in some forms, progressive renal disease.

local cerebral blood flow.definition: The portion of cerebral blood flow that supplies a localized region of brain tissue per unit time, typically expressed as mL of blood per 100 g of brain tissue per minute (mL/100 g/min); it is regulated by cerebral autoregulation and local metabolic demand.

pigmentary retinopathy.definition: Retinal degenerative disorder characterized by photoreceptor loss with retinal pigment epithelium changes, presenting with bone-spicule pigmentation in the mid-to-peripheral retina and progressive nyctalopia with constricted visual fields; commonly used to describe retinitis pigmentosa or RP-like pigmentary changes.

low-density lipoprotein.definition: A lipoprotein that transports cholesterol from the liver to peripheral tissues; high levels are associated with an increased risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and it is commonly referred to as "bad cholesterol."

lead encephalopathy.definition: Encephalopathy resulting from lead poisoning; a neurotoxic brain injury due to elevated lead levels, commonly presenting with irritability, developmental delay or regression, cognitive deficits, seizures, or coma; management includes removing the lead source and chelation therapy when indicated.

lead nephropathy.definition: Kidney damage from lead exposure, typically presenting as a chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis with proximal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi-type syndrome: glycosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia and bicarbonate loss), which can progress to impaired renal function.

lead pipe fracture.definition: A fracture pattern described as a single, straight fracture line through a bone with minimal displacement and little to no angulation or comminution; radiographically it appears as a clean, rigid break.

torus fracture.definition: A pediatric closed fracture in which axial loading causes the outer cortex to buckle (bulge) without a complete cortical break; commonly called a buckle fracture, usually involving the distal radius or tibia and considered a stable fracture treated with immobilization.

lead-pipe rigidity.definition: A type of rigidity in extrapyramidal disease characterized by a uniform, constant resistance to passive movement throughout the entire range of motion, without fluctuations or brief releases (in contrast to cogwheel rigidity).

succimer.definition: A water-soluble chelating agent (dimercaptosuccinic acid) used to treat exposure to heavy metals, notably lead in children; administered orally and forms stable metal complexes that are excreted in urine.

emla cream.definition: A topical local anesthetic cream containing a eutectic mixture of lidocaine 2.5% and prilocaine 2.5% (total 5%) used to numb the skin before injections or minor procedures; applied to intact skin under occlusion for about 30–60 minutes, with caution in infants and those at risk for methemoglobinemia, and not for broken skin or mucous membranes.

fetal development.definition: Prenatal process in which a human organism grows and differentiates from fertilization to birth, including embryogenesis (early organ formation) and subsequent fetal growth and maturation of body systems to achieve viability.

cortical blindness.definition: Loss of vision caused by bilateral damage to the primary visual cortex (occipital lobes) or its pathways, with intact ocular structures and a preserved pupillary light reflex.

abdominal cramping.definition: A symptom characterized by intermittent, painful tightening or contractions of the abdominal muscles (cramp-like pain) that can occur with gas, indigestion, gastroenteritis, irritable bowel syndrome, menstrual cramps, inflammatory bowel disease, or food intolerances; severity varies and may be relieved by bowel movements or passage of gas.

intestinal spasm.definition: A sudden, involuntary contraction of the smooth muscle in the intestines causing cramp-like abdominal pain, often accompanied by bloating, nausea, or changes in bowel movements.

rigidity of abdominal wall.definition: An involuntary, boardlike stiffness of the abdominal wall produced by contraction of the abdominal muscles, usually indicating peritoneal irritation or peritonitis; unlike voluntary guarding, it is not willingly relaxed.

liver damage.definition: Injury to the liver that impairs hepatic function or structure, caused by toxins (including alcohol), drugs, infections, ischemia, autoimmune disease, or metabolic disorders; it can range from mild enzyme elevations to acute liver failure.

lazy leukocyte syndrome.definition: An historical label for an inherited defect causing diminished leukocyte mobility and chemotaxis, leading to recurrent infections; not a precise modern diagnosis and is now described more accurately as impaired leukocyte chemotaxis or phagocyte dysfunction.

angiographic examinations.definition: A radiologic study in which a contrast agent is injected into the bloodstream to visualize blood vessels, typically performed by catheter-based angiography with fluoroscopy or by CT/MR angiography to assess vascular anatomy and pathology.

leak point pressure.definition: The intravesical pressure at the onset of urine leakage during a provocative urodynamic maneuver (such as coughing or Valsalva); used to assess urethral resistance and continence, with lower values suggesting intrinsic sphincter deficiency and higher values indicating stronger urethral closure.

leech therapy.definition: A medical treatment that uses medicinal leeches to relieve venous congestion and improve microcirculation, especially after tissue reattachment or reconstructive surgery. Leech saliva contains anticoagulants (notably hirudin), vasodilators, and enzymes that promote blood flow and tissue perfusion. There is a risk of infection from Aeromonas species, so antibiotic prophylaxis is often recommended and treatment is conducted under medical supervision.

urethral sphincters.definition: Muscular rings that regulate urine flow by constricting the urethra. There are two: an internal (involuntary) urethral sphincter at the bladder neck/proximal urethra, controlled by autonomic nerves to retain urine, and an external (voluntary) urethral sphincter around the mid-to-distal urethra, formed by skeletal muscle and innervated by the pudendal nerve, allowing conscious control of micturition.

leaky gene.definition: A gene variant whose product retains some functional activity despite mutation; the resulting phenotype is partial or milder than a complete loss-of-function, reflecting residual activity.

lean body mass.definition: The total body mass minus all fat; it includes muscles, bones, organs, connective tissue, and body water—the body’s non-fat components.

learning disability.definition: A neurodevelopmental condition marked by persistent difficulties with acquiring and using specific academic skills—most commonly reading, writing, and mathematics—that are below what would be expected for age and education and that cause significant interference with daily functioning, not better explained by intellectual disability, sensory deficits, or inadequate schooling.

attention-deficit disorder.definition: A neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent inattention and distractibility that impair functioning; in DSM-5 it is encompassed under ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation (formerly called attention-deficit disorder).

dyslexia.definition: A neurodevelopmental learning disorder characterized by persistent difficulties with accurate and fluent word recognition, poor decoding and spelling, and often reduced reading comprehension, typically due to deficits in phonological processing, despite normal intelligence and adequate educational opportunities.

leather-bottle stomach.definition: A historical term describing a stomach that is chronically distended and noncompliant, with thickened, rigid walls giving a leathery appearance, typically seen with longstanding gastric outlet obstruction or severe chronic gastritis.

linitis plastica.definition: A form of diffuse gastric adenocarcinoma characterized by diffuse infiltration of the stomach wall by malignant cells (often signet-ring cells), leading to thickening and rigidity of the gastric wall and a “leather bottle” stomach with poor distensibility.

leber's congenital amaurosis.definition: A rare inherited retinal dystrophy causing severe vision loss from birth or early infancy due to dysfunction or degeneration of photoreceptors and/or the retinal pigment epithelium; most cases are autosomal recessive and feature nystagmus, poor visual responsiveness, and markedly reduced or non-detectable electroretinography. It is genetically heterogeneous with multiple implicated genes, and some subtypes have gene-specific therapies.

leber's plexus.definition: A network of autonomic nerves surrounding the hepatic artery/portal triad that provides parasympathetic and sympathetic innervation to the liver and biliary tract.

leboyer method of delivery.definition: A birth method that aims to reduce neonatal stress by delivering the baby in a calm, warm, and minimally stimulating environment with gentle handling, often including immersion in a warmed bath shortly after birth.

le cell.definition: Phagocytic white blood cell (usually a neutrophil or macrophage) that has engulfed the denatured nucleus of another cell, forming a distinctive inclusion; historically observed in lupus erythematosus and used as a diagnostic clue.

lecithin.definition: A group of phospholipids, mainly phosphatidylcholine, that are major constituents of cell membranes and function as emulsifiers; derived from sources such as egg yolk or soy and used as a dietary supplement and food additive.

lecithin-cholesterol acetyltransferase d.definition: A rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficient activity of lecithin–cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT). It disrupts esterification of free cholesterol on lipoproteins, especially HDL, leading to abnormal, cholesterol-rich lipoproteins and reduced cholesteryl esters. Clinically, it can cause corneal opacities (fish-eye appearance); the classic familial form may include hemolytic anemia and nephrotic-range proteinuria with progressive kidney disease, while partial deficiency presents mainly with corneal opacities.

lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio.definition: A test of amniotic fluid that measures the ratio of lecithin (phosphatidylcholine) to sphingomyelin to assess fetal lung maturity; a ratio of about 2:1 or higher indicates mature lungs and a lower risk of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, whereas a lower ratio suggests immature lungs.

lecithoblast.definition: A primitive embryonic cell historically described as producing or accumulating lecithin (a phospholipid) during early development; often associated with yolk-sac structures.

lecithoprotein.definition: A protein bound to lecithin (phosphatidylcholine), forming a lecithin–protein complex; not a widely used or distinct clinical term, and is typically considered part of lipid–protein assemblies such as lipoproteins.

lectin.definition: A protein that binds specifically to certain carbohydrate residues on glycoproteins or glycolipids, mediating carbohydrate-dependent cell–cell interactions and often causing agglutination of cells.

ledercillin vk.definition: An oral penicillin-type antibiotic; the potassium salt of penicillin V. It inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis and is active mainly against susceptible Gram-positive bacteria (e.g., Streptococcus species). Used for mild-to-moderate infections caused by penicillin-susceptible organisms; not effective against beta-lactamase–producing bacteria or MRSA, and should be avoided in penicillin-allergic individuals.

leeuwenhoekia australiensis.definition: A species of bacterium in the genus Leeuwenhoekia, described from an Australian isolate; a microorganism defined by its taxonomic description using genetic (e.g., 16S rRNA) sequence data and phenotypic characteristics (morphology, metabolism, and growth conditions).

left ventricular failure.definition: A condition in which the left ventricle fails to pump enough blood to meet the body’s needs, leading to reduced systemic cardiac output and elevated pressures in the left atrium and pulmonary veins, causing pulmonary congestion and edema. It may present with dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, fatigue, and exercise intolerance; it can be due to systolic dysfunction (reduced ejection fraction) or diastolic dysfunction (preserved ejection fraction) from causes such as ischemic heart disease, hypertension, valvular disease, or cardiomyopathy.

left atrioventricular valve.definition: A valve between the left atrium and left ventricle of the heart that opens to allow blood to pass from the atrium to the ventricle during diastole and closes to prevent backflow during systole; typically has two cusps (anterior and posterior) and is also known as the mitral (or bicuspid) valve.

left innominate vein.definition: The left brachiocephalic (innominate) vein is a major vein of the upper chest formed by the union of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins; it crosses the superior mediastinum obliquely to join the right brachiocephalic vein, forming the superior vena cava.

left common carotid artery.definition: A major artery of the left neck arising from the aortic arch; it ascends to the level of the fourth cervical vertebra and bifurcates into the internal and external carotid arteries, supplying oxygenated blood to the head and neck.

left hepatic duct.definition: A bile duct draining bile from the left lobe of the liver (segments II–IV); it runs in the left hepatoduodenal ligament, is formed by the union of the left sectoral (left lateral and left medial) ducts, and typically joins the right hepatic duct to form the common hepatic duct.

left-to-right shunt.definition: An abnormal flow of blood from the left side of the heart or systemic circulation into the right side or pulmonary circulation through a defect or connection, causing increased pulmonary blood flow and recirculation of oxygenated blood to the lungs; commonly due to defects such as an atrial septal defect (ASD), ventricular septal defect (VSD), or patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).

left heart failure.definition: A condition in which the left ventricle fails to pump blood effectively, leading to increased pressures in the left atrium and pulmonary circulation with pulmonary congestion and symptoms such as dyspnea, orthopnea, and fatigue.

left lymphatic duct.definition: A large lymphatic vessel (the thoracic duct) that collects lymph from the cisterna chyli in the abdomen and ascends to drain into the left venous angle (junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins); it drains lymph from the lower body and the left side of the head, neck, and upper limb (the right side above the diaphragm is drained by the right lymphatic duct).

left ventricular assist device.definition: A mechanical pump that supports the left ventricle by drawing blood from the ventricle and pumping it into the aorta, increasing systemic circulation; used in advanced heart failure as a bridge to transplantation or as destination (long-term) therapy.

corneal opacity.definition: An area of decreased corneal transparency due to scarring, edema, infection, or degenerative changes, which blocks or scatters light entering the eye and leads to reduced visual acuity.

premature atherosclerosis.definition: Atherosclerosis occurring at an unusually young age, characterized by early development of atherosclerotic plaques in arteries and a higher risk of cardiovascular events relative to age; often defined as disease presenting before age 45 in men or before age 50 in women, and associated with genetic lipid disorders (e.g., familial hypercholesterolemia) and conventional risk factors such as smoking, hypertension, diabetes, and obesity.

autosomal-recessive trait.definition: A pattern of inheritance in which a trait or disorder is expressed only when an individual has two copies of the mutant allele on an autosome; heterozygous individuals are carriers and typically unaffected, and males and females are equally affected.

respiratory infection.definition: An infection of the respiratory tract—from the nose and throat to the bronchi and lungs—typically caused by viruses but may be bacterial or fungal, presenting with cough, fever, nasal congestion or discharge, sore throat, and sometimes shortness of breath.

pendular nystagmus.definition: A form of involuntary eye movement in which the eyes oscillate smoothly and rhythmically with equal velocity in opposite directions (pendulum-like), without a distinct fast corrective phase; often seen congenitally and associated with visual impairment or certain neurologic conditions.

electroretinography.definition: An ophthalmic diagnostic test that records the retina's electrical responses to light via surface or corneal electrodes, assessing overall retinal function—primarily photoreceptor (a-wave) and inner retinal (b-wave) activity under dark- and light-adapted conditions.

ciliary region.definition: A portion of the eye's uveal tract consisting of the ciliary body and its processes, located behind the iris; it contains the ciliary muscle and ciliary processes that produce aqueous humor and facilitate accommodation of the lens.

hovius' plexus.definition: Not a widely recognized anatomical term in standard medical references. It may be a misspelling or a term used in a specific text to describe a venous or neural plexus in a particular region. If you can share the location (e.g., orbit, face, skull base) or a source, I can help identify or define the correct structure.

heparin therapy.definition: An anticoagulant treatment that uses heparin (unfractionated or low-molecular-weight) to prevent or treat thrombosis by potentiating antithrombin III and inhibiting thrombin and factor Xa; used for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and treatment, certain arterial clots, and during various procedures; unfractionated heparin often requires aPTT monitoring and carries risks of bleeding and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

lee-white method.definition: A historical coagulation test in which fresh whole blood is placed in a dry glass tube kept at 37°C and the time to spontaneous clot formation is recorded (Lee-White clotting time); used to screen for bleeding disorders and factor deficiencies, but results are variable and the test is largely obsolete today.

left ventricular thrust.definition: A forceful, thrust-like impulse at the apex of the heart felt during systole, representing a hyperdynamic left ventricle; typically seen with left ventricular hypertrophy or dilation and can be associated with conditions such as long-standing hypertension, aortic regurgitation, or high-output states.

breathlessness.definition: A subjective sensation of breathing discomfort, ranging from mild to severe, often described as shortness of breath or air hunger; commonly due to cardiopulmonary disease, anemia, or anxiety.

peripheral vasoconstriction.definition: Contraction of smooth muscle in peripheral arterioles, narrowing peripheral blood vessels and reducing blood flow to the skin and limbs, typically mediated by sympathetic alpha-adrenergic stimulation to help preserve core perfusion and blood pressure during cold exposure, stress, or volume loss.

third heart sound.definition: A low-frequency extra heart sound heard shortly after S2 during early diastole, produced by rapid ventricular filling; best heard with the bell at the apex in the left lateral position; often indicates left ventricular volume overload or reduced ventricular compliance in adults, but can be normal in children and young athletes.

precordial movement.definition: Movement or pulsation of the chest wall over the heart (the precordium) produced by cardiac contractions; most often refers to the apical impulse felt at the point of maximal impulse.

left ventricular veins.definition: Veins draining the left ventricle that collect deoxygenated blood from the ventricular walls and typically drain into the coronary sinus (chiefly via the great cardiac vein), with several small tributaries along the left ventricle.

cardiac veins.definition: Veins draining the heart muscle (myocardium) and returning deoxygenated blood to the right atrium via the coronary sinus; major vessels include the great cardiac vein, middle cardiac vein, and small cardiac veins.

legionellosis.definition: An infectious disease caused by Legionella bacteria acquired by inhalation of aerosolized water or soil from contaminated sources (e.g., cooling towers, showers), ranging from a mild febrile illness (Pontiac fever) to a severe pneumonia (Legionnaires’ disease); not typically transmitted person-to-person.

legionnaires disease.definition: A severe pneumonic illness caused by Legionella bacteria (most commonly Legionella pneumophila) acquired by inhaling aerosolized contaminated water; presents with fever, cough, dyspnea, and often gastrointestinal symptoms; diagnosed by urinary antigen testing or culture and treated with a macrolide or fluoroquinolone antibiotic.

legionnaires disease antibody test.definition: A serologic test for antibodies against Legionella bacteria (the cause of Legionnaires’ disease) in a patient’s blood, used to support diagnosis; commonly done by indirect immunofluorescence or ELISA, but is less useful for acute diagnosis because antibody responses take time to develop and a paired sample showing a rising titer may be required.

leishman-donovan body.definition: An intracellular amastigote form of Leishmania donovani that resides within macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system, seen in visceral leishmaniasis.

leishmania donovani.definition: A protozoan parasite of the genus Leishmania that causes visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) in humans; transmitted by female phlebotomine sandflies.

leishmanin test.definition: An intradermal delayed-type hypersensitivity skin test using Leishmania–derived antigen to detect prior exposure to the parasite; induration is read after 48–72 hours, and a positive reaction indicates previous exposure or infection with a cell-mediated immune response but does not diagnose active disease.

montenegro test.definition: A skin test (leishmanin skin test) that assesses delayed-type hypersensitivity to Leishmania antigens. An intradermal injection is read after 48–72 hours; a positive induration indicates prior exposure or infection with Leishmania spp. and intact cell-mediated immunity, while a negative result may indicate no exposure or anergy, and it is not by itself diagnostic of active disease.

leigh disease.definition: A severe, inherited mitochondrial disorder presenting in infancy or early childhood with subacute neurodegeneration and symmetric brain lesions (often in the basal ganglia and brainstem) due to defects in oxidative phosphorylation; commonly associated with lactic acidosis and mutations in mitochondrial or nuclear DNA encoding respiratory-chain components.

wernicke-korsakoff syndrome.definition: An irreversible state of acute confusion and amnesia that develops in alcoholics as a result of malnutrition-related thiamine deficiency.

leiner's disease.definition: An historically described, severe form of infantile dermatitis (a generalized seborrheic-type eruption) with failure to thrive; thought to reflect nutritional deficiencies (notably biotin and/or essential fatty acids) and typically improves with nutritional supplementation.

lenalidomide.definition: An oral immunomodulatory imide drug (IMiD) derived from thalidomide with antiangiogenic, antiproliferative, and immune‑modulating effects; used to treat several hematologic malignancies, including multiple myeloma, certain lymphomas (e.g., mantle cell and follicular lymphoma), chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma, and myelodysplastic syndromes with 5q deletion.

lemon balm.definition: An aromatic perennial herb of the mint family (Melissa officinalis) used in traditional medicine for anxiety, insomnia, and digestive upset; typically prepared as tea or used as an extract or essential oil; contains essential oils such as citronellal, citral, and linalool.

leucopenia.definition: An abnormally low total white blood cell count in the peripheral blood, typically defined as fewer than about 4,000 cells per microliter (4×10^9/L), due to decreased production, increased destruction, or sequestration, which increases infection risk; it can involve any leukocyte line but is most clinically significant when neutrophils are reduced (neutropenia).

lenegres disease.definition: A rare, life-threatening septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein that follows an oropharyngeal infection (often tonsillitis), usually caused by Fusobacterium necrophorum, with risk of septic emboli to the lungs; managed with broad-spectrum antibiotics and supportive care.

tonic.definition: An agent believed to invigorate a specific body organ.

absence.definition: The lack or nonexistence of a normally present element, such as a body part, function, or condition.

tonic-clonic.definition: A generalized seizure characterized by an initial tonic phase of sustained muscle stiffening and loss of consciousness, followed by a clonic phase of rhythmic jerking movements; often with postictal confusion or drowsiness.

akinetic.definition: Characterized by a marked reduction or absence of voluntary movement; a state of minimal or absent spontaneous motor activity, as seen in certain neurological conditions (e.g., akinetic mutism or parkinsonian syndromes).

gastaut's disease.definition: A severe pediatric-onset epileptic encephalopathy characterized by multiple seizure types (often including atonic or “drop” attacks), cognitive and developmental impairment, and a distinctive EEG with generalized slow spike-and-wave discharges (typically 1.5–2.5 Hz); onset is usually in early childhood and the condition is often resistant to many antiseizure medications.

inherited metabolic abnormalities.definition: A group of genetic disorders in which mutations disrupt one or more metabolic pathways, typically due to defective enzymes or transport proteins, causing abnormal accumulation or deficiency of specific metabolites and a broad range of clinical effects often starting in infancy; inheritance is usually autosomal recessive or X-linked.

postnatal disorders.definition: Conditions that occur in the postpartum period (the puerperium), typically within about the first 6 weeks after delivery, including mental health disorders such as postpartum depression and postpartum psychosis, as well as physical complications like postpartum hemorrhage, infection, and thromboembolism.

lens implant.definition: An artificial intraocular lens implanted in the eye to replace the natural crystalline lens, typically after cataract extraction to restore refractive ability; can be monofocal, multifocal, or toric to correct refractive error.

corneal incision.definition: A surgical cut through the cornea of the eye to access intraocular structures during ophthalmic procedures (most commonly cataract extraction or corneal transplantation); the incision may be partial-thickness (lamellar) or full-thickness depending on the procedure.

eye drops.definition: Sterile ophthalmic solutions or suspensions administered as small volumes by dropping into the conjunctival sac of the eye to moisturize, relieve irritation, or deliver medications (e.g., antibiotics, anti-inflammatory agents, antihistamines).

lente insulin.definition: An historical intermediate-acting insulin preparation consisting of a zinc-insulin suspension designed to slow absorption and provide longer action than regular insulin; used to provide basal insulin coverage but largely replaced by NPH and newer formulations.

intermediate-acting insulin.definition: An insulin formulation with intermediate duration that begins acting in about 1–2 hours, peaks around 4–12 hours, and lasts roughly 16–24 hours (often formulated with protamine to delay absorption, as in NPH).

lenticonus.definition: A localized cone-shaped bulge of the crystalline lens surface (usually the anterior surface) due to thinning of the lens capsule, causing irregular astigmatism and reduced vision. Anterior lenticonus is strongly associated with Alport syndrome; posterior lenticonus refers to a similar bulge of the posterior lens surface, often seen with congenital posterior polar cataracts.

lenticular nucleus.definition: A basal ganglia structure composed of the putamen and globus pallidus; it modulates and regulates voluntary movement through connections with the thalamus and motor cortex.

lentigo.definition: A small, flat, well-defined pigmented macule on the skin caused by localized proliferation of melanocytes; benign and persists, with common types including lentigo simplex and solar lentigo (age spot).

lentigo maligna.definition: A melanoma in situ arising on chronically sun-exposed skin, most often on the face of older adults; a slowly enlarging pigmented macule with atypical melanocytes confined to the epidermis (and adnexal structures) that may progress to invasive melanoma if untreated.

lentigo maligna melanoma.definition: A melanoma that arises from a lentigo maligna lesion on chronically sun-damaged skin (most often the face of older adults); it typically begins with a long in situ/radial growth phase and may invade deeper tissues if not treated.

lentivirus.definition: An enveloped, complex retrovirus genus within the family Retroviridae that causes chronic, lifelong infection by integrating its reverse-transcribed DNA into the host genome; it can infect non-dividing cells and typically has a long incubation period (examples include HIV-1 and HIV-2).

leopard syndrome.definition: An autosomal-dominant disorder in the Noonan syndrome spectrum (Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines) caused by mutations in RAS/MAPK pathway genes; characterized by numerous pigmented lentigines on the skin, cardiac conduction defects or structural heart disease (often pulmonic stenosis), distinctive facial features, short stature, genital abnormalities, and sensorineural deafness.

leopold's maneuver.definition: A systematic abdominal palpation technique used in obstetrics to determine fetal presentation, lie, and position by performing a series of maneuvers to identify the presenting part, fetal back, and engagement in the pelvis.

leptomeningitis.definition: Inflammation of the leptomeninges (the arachnoid and pia mater), typically due to infection in the subarachnoid space.

leptomeninges.definition: The thin membranes comprising the arachnoid mater and pia mater that enclose the brain and spinal cord, forming the inner layer of the meninges and surrounding the subarachnoid space filled with cerebrospinal fluid.

leptomeningeal cyst.definition: A CSF-filled cyst that forms when the leptomeninges (arachnoid membrane) herniate through a skull fracture with a dural tear, causing progressive enlargement—typically in children—and is known as a growing skull fracture.

lepromin test.definition: A skin test using intradermal lepromin antigen (inactivated Mycobacterium leprae) to assess cell-mediated immunity; a positive reaction suggests tuberculoid-type leprosy with stronger immunity, while a negative reaction suggests lepromatous-type leprosy, and it is not diagnostic on its own and is rarely used today.

hansen's disease.definition: A long-term disease caused by a germ (a bacteria) that affects the nerves around the outside of the body, skin, and eyes. Also called leprosy.

lepromatous leprosy.definition: An advanced, multibacillary form of Hansen disease characterized by widespread symmetric skin lesions and nodules with diffuse skin thickening, a high bacillary load with numerous acid-fast bacilli, and extensive nerve involvement due to poor cell-mediated immunity.

tuberculoid leprosy.definition: A paucibacillary form of Hansen’s disease characterized by a strong cell-mediated immune response with few, well-defined hypoesthetic skin patches and corresponding peripheral nerve involvement; bacilli are scarce or absent on skin smears.

leprosarium.definition: A hospital or institution for the treatment and isolation of people with leprosy (Hansen's disease); historically used to segregate patients and provide care, but now largely obsolete with modern outpatient multidrug therapy.

leptospira interrogans.definition: A pathogenic spirochete bacterium of the genus Leptospira that causes leptospirosis in humans and other animals; transmission is typically through contact with water or soil contaminated with urine from infected animals, and disease ranges from mild febrile illness to severe Weil disease with jaundice, renal failure, and hemorrhage.

leptospira agglutinin.definition: An antibody directed against Leptospira species that causes the spirochetes to clump (agglutinate), used in serologic testing (e.g., microscopic agglutination test) to diagnose leptospirosis.

weil's disease.definition: A severe form of leptospirosis caused by Leptospira interrogans, characterized by jaundice, acute kidney injury, and hemorrhagic manifestations; acquired through contact with water or soil contaminated with urine from infected animals.

autumn fever.definition: Not a recognized medical term; when used, it may describe a seasonal influenza-like illness occurring in autumn or autumnal allergic rhinitis (hay fever) due to fall pollen (e.g., ragweed), depending on context.

mud fever.definition: A common inflammatory bacterial skin infection in horses affecting the pasterns, promoted by damp, muddy conditions; presents with crusty scabs, hair loss, and dermatitis.

leptin.definition: A hormone produced by fat cells that acts on the brain to suppress appetite and burn stored fat.

leptodermic.definition: Relating to or characterized by very thin skin; having an abnormally thin epidermis.

leptodactylosis.definition: A medical condition in which the fingers or toes are abnormally slender and elongated.

leptocyte.definition: A thin red blood cell with an increased membrane-to-hemoglobin ratio, resulting in prominent central pallor; a category that includes target cells (codocytes) and stomatocytes, seen in liver disease, certain hemoglobinopathies (e.g., thalassemia), iron deficiency, and after splenectomy.

leptocytosis.definition: An increase in slender, thin red blood cells (leptocytes) seen on a peripheral blood smear; a morphological pattern due to a higher membrane-to-volume ratio of erythrocytes, often seen in iron deficiency, liver disease, or thalassemia.

leptonema.definition: The earliest stage of meiotic prophase I in which replicated chromosomes condense and become visible as long, thread-like structures; each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids, and homologous chromosomes have not yet paired.

parinaud's oculoglandular syndrome.definition: A unilateral granulomatous conjunctivitis with ipsilateral preauricular lymphadenopathy, most commonly caused by Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch disease); may be accompanied by fever and malaise and is typically self-limiting, with treatment directed at the underlying infection.

leptotrichia.definition: A genus of Gram-negative, anaerobic, non-spore-forming, pleomorphic rod bacteria that are part of the normal human oral microbiota and can occasionally cause opportunistic infections such as bacteremia or endocarditis.

leptotrichosis.definition: A bacterial infection caused by Leptotrichia species, a genus of Gram-negative, anaerobic rods that are part of the normal oral and genitourinary flora; it can cause bacteremia, endocarditis, and obstetric infections in susceptible individuals.

leptotrichia conjunctivae.definition: A species of Gram-negative, anaerobic, non-spore-forming bacillus in the genus Leptotrichia; typically part of normal mucosal flora but can be isolated from the conjunctiva as an opportunistic pathogen in conjunctival infections.

leriche's syndrome.definition: Aortoiliac occlusive disease due to obstruction of the distal aorta (often at the aortic bifurcation) and/or proximal iliac arteries, presenting with buttock and thigh claudication, diminished or absent femoral pulses, and often impotence in men.

bypass graft.definition: A surgical graft used to bypass a blocked or narrowed blood vessel, restoring blood flow—most often in the coronary arteries (coronary artery bypass graft) using a vein or artery such as the saphenous vein or internal mammary artery.

aortic bifurcation.definition: The division of the abdominal aorta into the left and right common iliac arteries, typically at the level of the fourth lumbar vertebra (L4).

terminal aorta.definition: The distal portion of the abdominal aorta that ends by bifurcating into the left and right common iliac arteries.

iliac arteries.definition: The paired arteries arising from the common iliac arteries (which originate from the terminal abdominal aorta) that supply the pelvis and lower limbs; they divide into the internal iliac arteries, which perfuse pelvic organs and gluteal regions, and the external iliac arteries, which continue as the femoral arteries to supply the lower extremities.

femoral arteries.definition: Major arteries of the thigh that supply oxygenated blood to the lower limb; each is a continuation of the external iliac artery after crossing under the inguinal ligament, gives off the profunda femoris (deep femoral) as a major branch, and continues distally to become the popliteal artery after passing through the adductor hiatus.

lesser sciatic notch.definition: A notch on the ischium, inferior to the greater sciatic notch, that with the sacrospinous ligament forms the lesser sciatic foramen and transmits the tendon of obturator internus (and its nerve to obturator internus), as well as the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels.

lesser sciatic foramen.definition: A small pelvic passage formed by the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments inferior to the greater sciatic foramen; it transmits the tendon of obturator internus, the nerve to obturator internus, and the internal pudendal vessels with the pudendal nerve as they pass to and from the perineum.

lesser omentum.definition: A peritoneal double layer extending from the liver to the lesser curvature of the stomach and the first part of the duodenum; it forms the hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments and transmits the portal triad (hepatic artery proper, portal vein, and common bile duct) between the liver and foregut.

hepatoduodenal ligament.definition: A peritoneal fold forming the free edge of the lesser omentum, extending from the porta hepatis to the duodenum; it contains the portal triad (hepatic artery proper, portal vein, and common bile duct) and forms the anterior boundary of the omental (epiploic) foramen.

portal fissure.definition: A fissure on the visceral surface of the liver known as the porta hepatis, through which the hepatic triad (portal vein, proper hepatic artery, and common bile duct) enters or exits the liver.

omentum.definition: A fold of peritoneum that connects the stomach to adjacent abdominal organs; the greater omentum hangs from the greater curvature and contains fat and immune tissue, while the lesser omentum connects the stomach and duodenum to the liver.

bacille calmette-guérin vaccine.definition: Live attenuated vaccine derived from Mycobacterium bovis used to prevent tuberculosis; administered intradermally, typically to infants or children in TB-endemic areas; protection against pulmonary TB is variable, but it reduces the risk of severe TB forms in children; contraindicated in severely immunocompromised individuals and in those with active tuberculosis.

wheal.definition: A raised, pruritic, transient swelling of the skin caused by edema in the dermis, typically seen in urticaria (hives) and often with a pale center and red outer border.

pustule.definition: A small, raised, superficial skin lesion that contains pus, typically less than 1 cm in diameter, resulting from localized infection or inflammation (e.g., folliculitis, acne, impetigo).

scale.definition: A thin plate or flake of keratinized skin shed from the epidermis (desquamation); commonly seen in conditions such as psoriasis or eczema.

lichenification.definition: Thickening of the skin with accentuation of normal surface markings (a leathery, rough appearance) due to chronic rubbing or scratching.

scar.definition: A fibrous tissue that replaces normal skin after injury during the wound-healing process; composed mainly of collagen, it lacks normal skin structures and can be flat, depressed, or raised (keloid or hypertrophic scar), often altering texture and color.

hypertrophic scar.definition: A raised scar caused by excessive collagen production during wound healing, confined to the margins of the original wound and not extending beyond it; often follows skin injury or surgery and may improve gradually over months to years, sometimes with itching or stiffness.

decubiti.definition: Localized injury to the skin and underlying tissue, typically over a bony prominence, caused by prolonged pressure (often with shear/friction); commonly called a pressure ulcer or bedsore.

stasis ulcer.definition: A venous leg ulcer caused by chronic venous insufficiency and elevated venous pressure, typically arising at the medial malleolus; commonly associated with edema, skin hyperpigmentation, and lipodermatosclerosis.

seborrheic keratoses.definition: Benign, pigmented epidermal tumors that present as well-demarcated, waxy, “stuck-on” plaques or papules, most commonly on the trunk of older adults; they are noncancerous and usually asymptomatic.

actinic keratoses.definition: Premalignant skin lesion resulting from chronic ultraviolet radiation exposure; typically presents as rough, scaly, red or skin-colored patches on sun-exposed areas (e.g., face, ears, backs of the hands) and may progress to squamous cell carcinoma if not treated.

varicella-zoster.definition: An enveloped double-stranded DNA herpesvirus that causes varicella (chickenpox) as a primary infection and can later reactivate to cause herpes zoster (shingles), with latency in sensory ganglia.

leser-trélat sign.definition: A paraneoplastic phenomenon characterized by the abrupt onset of multiple seborrheic keratoses (benign skin lesions), which may herald or indicate an occult internal malignancy, most commonly gastrointestinal adenocarcinomas; may be associated with pruritus.

lepromin.definition: An extract of killed Mycobacterium leprae used in a skin test to assess cell-mediated immunity to leprosy; a positive reaction suggests tuberculoid forms and a negative reaction suggests lepromatous forms, and it is not used to diagnose leprosy.

lesser trochanter.definition: A small conical projection on the medial/posterior aspect of the proximal femur, just below the femoral neck, that serves as the insertion site for the iliopsoas muscle (tendon).

trochanter minor.definition: A small, conical bony prominence on the proximal femur, located on the posteromedial aspect just below the femoral neck; serves as the insertion site for the iliopsoas muscle (iliacus and psoas major).

psoas major muscle.definition: A large, deep hip flexor of the lumbar region that originates from the vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs of T12–L5 and the transverse processes of L1–L5, and inserts on the lesser trochanter of the femur. It flexes the thigh at the hip and assists in flexing the trunk when the thigh is fixed; innervation is by the ventral rami of L1–L3.

let.definition: The energy deposited by ionizing radiation per unit distance traveled in tissue; higher values indicate more densely ionizing radiation and, for the same absorbed dose, greater localized biological damage (often expressed in keV/μm).

linear energy transfer.definition: The energy deposited by ionizing radiation per unit length of its path through matter, typically expressed in keV per micrometer (keV/μm); higher values indicate denser ionization along the track and greater potential for biological damage.

letairis.definition: A brand-name medication (ambrisentan) that acts as an endothelin receptor antagonist used to treat pulmonary arterial hypertension by blocking endothelin-1–mediated vasoconstriction and vascular remodeling; contraindicated in pregnancy and requires monitoring for liver toxicity.

let-down reflex.definition: A neurohormonal reflex triggered by infant suckling that causes oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary, stimulating contraction of myoepithelial cells around mammary alveoli and milk ejection into the ducts; may be suppressed by maternal stress or fatigue.

milk ejection reflex.definition: A neuroendocrine reflex triggered by nipple stimulation that releases oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, causing contraction of myoepithelial cells around mammary alveoli and milk ejection into the ducts.

lethal allele.definition: An allele that causes death or inviability of an organism, typically when present in two copies (homozygous); recessive lethal alleles are lethal only in homozygotes, while dominant lethal alleles kill in the heterozygous state and are rare.

lethal dose.definition: The amount of a toxin or radiation sufficient to cause death in a defined population; commonly expressed as LD50—the dose that kills 50% of exposed individuals.

median lethal dose.definition: An estimate of acute toxicity: the dose of a substance expected to kill 50% of a defined experimental population (usually laboratory animals) within a specified period after exposure.

lethal equivalent.definition: A unit of genetic load representing the total effect of deleterious recessive alleles on viability; defined as the number of fully recessive lethal mutations that would produce the same reduction in viability if present in homozygous form, typically expressed per haploid genome or per individual. It quantifies the cumulative deleterious mutational burden.

lethality.definition: Capacity to cause death; the potential to be fatal in an individual or population, as seen with diseases, toxins, injuries, or other conditions.

lethargic.definition: When you feel slow or very sleepy.

letrozole.definition: A nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor that lowers estrogen production by inhibiting the aromatase enzyme; used in the treatment of hormone receptor–positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women.

letterer-siwe syndrome.definition: An aggressive, disseminated form of Langerhans cell histiocytosis in infants, presenting with a seborrheic-like rash, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, bone lesions, fever, and cytopenias; historically associated with a poor prognosis.

leukemia cutis.definition: Infiltration of the skin by malignant leukemic cells, producing red to violaceous papules, plaques, or nodules; may precede, accompany, or follow systemic leukemia and is confirmed by skin biopsy showing leukemic blasts.

leukemia inhibitory factor.definition: A cytokine in the interleukin-6 family that signals through gp130-containing receptor complexes to activate JAK/STAT, MAPK, and PI3K pathways; it inhibits differentiation of certain leukemia cell lines and supports survival, and in mouse models helps maintain embryonic stem cell pluripotency in culture. It is produced by multiple cell types (e.g., macrophages, fibroblasts) and has roles in inflammation, hematopoiesis, neural development, and implantation.

leukemic.definition: Relating to leukemia; describing conditions, cells, or processes associated with or resembling leukemia, notably the malignant overproduction of white blood cells in blood and bone marrow.

hairy-cell leukemia.definition: A rare, indolent B‑cell neoplasm characterized by circulating “hairy” lymphocytes with bone marrow infiltration, leading to splenomegaly and cytopenias; commonly associated with a BRAF V600E mutation and primarily treated with purine analogs such as cladribine or pentostatin.

leukemoid reaction.definition: A reactive, exaggerated neutrophilic leukocytosis with a marked left shift that imitates leukemia but results from severe infection, inflammation, major physiologic stress, or certain drugs/toxins; it features a high white blood cell count with neutrophils and immature forms, but lacks clonal chromosomal abnormalities.

leukeran.definition: A brand-name chemotherapy drug (chlorambucil), an oral alkylating nitrogen mustard used to treat certain leukemias (notably chronic lymphocytic leukemia) and lymphomas; it cross-links DNA to inhibit cell replication.

leukocytopenia.definition: A decreased total white blood cell count in the peripheral blood, reducing immune defense and increasing infection risk; can result from bone marrow suppression, drug toxicity, autoimmune destruction, or severe illness, and is typically defined by a WBC count below about 4,000 cells per microliter in adults.

lap.definition: An abbreviation for laparoscopy; a minimally invasive surgical procedure in which operations in the abdomen or pelvis are performed through small incisions using a laparoscope (a camera) and specialized instruments.

leukopoiesis.definition: The production, differentiation, and maturation of white blood cells (leukocytes) from hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow under the influence of cytokines, giving rise to granulocytes, monocytes, and lymphocytes; can be upregulated during infection.

leucopoiesis.definition: The production and development of white blood cells (leukocytes) from hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow, including differentiation into granulocytes, monocytes, and lymphocytes, regulated by cytokines and growth factors.

leukoderma.definition: A condition characterized by patches of skin depigmentation due to loss or dysfunction of melanocytes, resulting in pale or white macules that may be acquired (e.g., vitiligo, postinflammatory leukoderma, chemical leukoderma) or congenital.

leukoencephalopathy.definition: A broad term for diseases that affect the brain's white matter, typically involving demyelination or degeneration of myelinated nerve fibers and leading to neurologic deficits; seen as white-matter abnormalities on imaging and arising from diverse etiologies such as genetic leukodystrophies, inflammatory/infectious processes, metabolic disorders, toxins, or ischemia.

lad.definition: A major coronary artery that runs in the anterior interventricular groove and supplies the anterior wall of the left ventricle; occlusion can result in a large myocardial infarction.

leukocyte migration inhibition factor.definition: A lymphokine produced by sensitized T lymphocytes that inhibits the in vitro migration (chemotaxis) of leukocytes in response to chemotactic stimuli, reflecting cell-mediated immunity (as assessed by migration inhibition assays).

macrophage migration inhibiting factor.definition: A proinflammatory cytokine produced by T cells, macrophages, and other cells that promotes macrophage activation and cytokine release, antagonizes glucocorticoids, and inhibits macrophage migration, thereby regulating innate and adaptive immune responses and contributing to inflammatory diseases.

leukocytogenesis.definition: The production and maturation of white blood cells (leukocytes) from hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow during hematopoiesis.

leukophoresis.definition: A procedure in which white blood cells are selectively removed from the circulating blood by apheresis, typically to treat hyperleukocytosis or to collect leukocytes for transplantation.

leucophoresis.definition: A procedure to remove white blood cells (leukocytes) from the bloodstream, typically by apheresis, used to reduce high leukocyte counts or to collect leukocytes for transplantation.

leukoplakic vulvitis.definition: A vulvar white patch or plaque due to marked epithelial hyperkeratosis (keratinized lesion) on the vulvar mucosa; a premalignant, keratotic condition often linked with chronic inflammatory dermatoses such as lichen sclerosus and with an increased risk of vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia or vulvar squamous cell carcinoma.

leucovorin calcium.definition: A calcium salt form of leucovorin (folinic acid), a reduced form of folic acid used to protect normal cells from methotrexate toxicity (folinic acid rescue) and to enhance the effectiveness of certain chemotherapy regimens such as 5-fluorouracil.

leucovorin rescue.definition: A treatment strategy in which folinic acid (leucovorin) is given after high-dose methotrexate to rescue normal cells from methotrexate-induced inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase, replenishing folate pools and reducing toxicity while preserving the anticancer effects of methotrexate; timing and dosing are critical.

leucinosis.definition: A metabolic disorder characterized by abnormal accumulation of the essential amino acid leucine in blood and tissues due to defective catabolism of branched-chain amino acids (often associated with maple syrup urine disease).

leukocytoclastic vasculitis.definition: Small-vessel vasculitis with neutrophilic inflammation and fragmentation of neutrophil nuclei (leukocytoclasia) in vessel walls, usually presenting with palpable purpura; often immune complex–mediated and associated with infections, drugs, or systemic diseases.

leukocyturia.definition: The presence of white blood cells (leukocytes) in the urine, typically indicating urinary tract inflammation or infection; detected as pyuria on urinalysis.

leukoagglutinin.definition: A substance, typically an antibody, that binds to leukocyte antigens and causes leukocytes to agglutinate (clump together).

leukoagglutinin test.definition: A laboratory assay that detects antibodies directed against leukocytes by causing their agglutination; used to identify anti-leukocyte antibodies that can affect transfusion or transplant compatibility.

monocytes.definition: White blood cells that protect the body from disease by attacking and consuming foreign particles.

myeloblasts.definition: An immature precursor cell of the myeloid lineage in the bone marrow that differentiates into granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) through the granulocytic maturation series; typically large with a high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio and prominent nucleoli.

peripheral blood.definition: Circulating blood in the systemic circulation outside the heart and lungs, consisting of plasma and formed elements (erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets); it is the blood typically sampled from veins for laboratory testing.

white blood cells.definition: A type of blood cell (leukocyte) that protects the body from infection by recognizing and attacking bacteria, viruses, and other foreign invaders; produced in the bone marrow and circulating in the blood, they migrate to tissues as needed and include subtypes such as neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils.

high-dose methotrexate therapy.definition: An intensive chemotherapy regimen in which methotrexate is given at very high intravenous doses, with folinic acid (leucovorin) rescue to protect normal tissues, plus aggressive hydration and urine alkalinization to prevent nephrotoxicity and promote drug clearance, and serial monitoring of blood levels and organ function.

leukosarcoma.definition: A malignant tumor composed of leukocytes or their precursors, representing an extramedullary mass of leukemic cells; the term is rarely used today and such lesions are usually described as myeloid (granulocytic) sarcoma or chloroma.

levator veli palatini.definition: A muscle of the soft palate that elevates the soft palate during swallowing and yawning to close off the nasopharynx; it originates near the auditory (pharyngotympanic) tube and the petrous part of the temporal bone and inserts into the palatine aponeurosis. Innervation: pharyngeal plexus via cranial nerve X.

leukostasis.definition: A medical emergency caused by extreme leukocytosis, usually with high circulating leukemic blasts, that clogs the microvasculature and impairs tissue perfusion, leading to organ dysfunction (most often neurologic symptoms and respiratory distress).

hyperleukocytosis.definition: A hematologic emergency defined by a very high leukocyte count, typically >100,000/µL, with increased risk of leukostasis and end-organ hypoperfusion; most often seen in acute leukemias and myeloproliferative neoplasms.

leukotomy.definition: A historical psychosurgical procedure in which the white matter of the frontal lobes is lesioned or severed to disrupt neural circuits thought to underlie severe psychiatric disorders; also known as leucotomy or frontal lobotomy.

lobotomy.definition: A surgical procedure to sever one or more nerve fibers in the frontal lobe of the brain.

leukotoxin.definition: A toxin produced by certain bacteria that destroys or impairs white blood cells, typically by forming pores in the leukocyte membrane and causing cell lysis, thereby aiding immune evasion.

leukotoxic.definition: Toxic to leukocytes; capable of destroying or impairing the function of white blood cells.

leukovirus.definition: Not a standard term in virology; there is no recognized virus named “leukovirus.” Hypothetically, it would refer to a virus that infects leukocytes (white blood cells) and could affect immune function, but this is not an established classification.

leuprolide acetate.definition: A synthetic gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist that, with continuous administration, suppresses pituitary LH and FSH release, lowering estrogen and testosterone; used for hormone-sensitive conditions such as prostate cancer, endometriosis, uterine fibroids, precocious puberty, and to control ovarian stimulation in assisted reproduction; typically given as injectable depot with potential initial hormone flare.

prostatic cancer.definition: A cancer that arises from the prostate gland; the most common cancer in men; often slow-growing but may be aggressive; diagnosed by PSA testing, digital rectal examination, and biopsy; treated by surgery, radiation therapy, hormone therapy, chemotherapy, or active surveillance depending on stage and grade.

central precocious puberty.definition: A GnRH‑dependent condition in which puberty begins earlier than normal due to premature activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, causing development of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8 in girls and before age 9 in boys, often with accelerated bone age and growth; evaluation may include GnRH stimulation testing and brain imaging as indicated, and treatment can involve GnRH agonists to suppress progression.

urinary obstruction.definition: An obstruction to the flow of urine anywhere along the urinary tract, causing partial or complete urinary retention and potentially hydronephrosis and kidney damage; causes include stones, urethral or ureteral strictures, benign prostatic hyperplasia, tumors, or external compression.

neurological problems.definition: Neurological problems are disorders of the nervous system—comprising the brain, spinal cord, peripheral nerves, and muscles—that cause symptoms such as weakness, numbness or tingling, headaches, seizures, movement or balance problems, vision or speech changes, cognitive or psychiatric symptoms, and autonomic dysfunction.

injection site irritation.definition: Local redness, swelling, pain, warmth, or itching at the site of an injection, caused by a mild inflammatory or irritant reaction to the injected substance or needle, usually self-limiting within a few days.

levalbuterol.definition: A short-acting inhaled beta-2 adrenergic agonist bronchodilator that is the active (R)-enantiomer of albuterol; relieves bronchospasm in asthma and COPD by relaxing airway smooth muscle; rapid onset within minutes with several hours of effect; administered via inhaler or nebulizer.

beta-2-adrenergic agonist.definition: A drug that selectively activates beta-2 adrenergic receptors, increasing intracellular cAMP in smooth muscle to cause relaxation and bronchodilation; used to treat asthma and COPD.

obstructive airway disease.definition: A broad category of respiratory disorders characterized by partial or complete obstruction of the airways, leading to reduced airflow, especially during expiration; commonly includes conditions such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

sympathomimetics.definition: A class of drugs that mimic sympathetic nervous system activity by stimulating adrenergic receptors (alpha and beta), producing effects such as increased heart rate and contractility, bronchodilation, vasoconstriction, and pupil dilation.

irritation of the nose and throat.word: irritation of the nose and throat
irritation of the nose and throat.definition: Irritation of the nose and throat refers to irritation or inflammation of the nasal and pharyngeal mucosa, typically presenting with sneezing, runny or congested nose, itching, sore throat, and cough, often caused by infections, allergies, or irritants such as smoke or pollutants.

dukes' stage c colon cancer.definition: A colon cancer with regional lymph node metastasis but no distant metastasis.

adjuvant treatment.definition: An additional therapy given after the primary treatment (most often after surgical removal of a tumor) to eradicate microscopic residual disease and reduce the risk of cancer recurrence, with the aim of improving survival. It can include chemotherapy, radiotherapy, hormonal therapy, or targeted therapy.

norepinephrine bitartrate.definition: An injectable salt of the catecholamine norepinephrine (noradrenaline) with bitartrate used as a potent vasopressor to treat acute hypotension and shock; it stimulates alpha-1 receptors causing vasoconstriction and beta-1 receptors increasing heart rate and contractility, thereby raising mean arterial pressure.

levarterenol.definition: An obscure or historical sympathomimetic agent that acts as an adrenergic agonist to increase vascular tone and raise blood pressure; used as a vasopressor.

levocardia.definition: The normal left-sided position of the heart in the thoracic cavity, with the apex pointing to the left.

levoclination.definition: Leftward tilting or inclination of a structure (such as a tooth or bone) toward the left side; orientation or angulation toward the left relative to the midline.

levotorsion.definition: Leftward torsion; twisting of a body part around its axis toward the left.

levobetaxolol.definition: An ophthalmic beta-adrenergic receptor blocker (the levo enantiomer of betaxolol) used to lower intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension.

levobunolol.definition: A nonselective topical beta-adrenergic receptor blocker used in ophthalmology to lower intraocular pressure by decreasing aqueous humor formation. It is indicated for open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension.

miller-abbott tube.definition: A long, flexible, weighted, double-lumen enteric tube used to decompress the GI tract in bowel obstruction; one lumen provides suction to drain gas and fluid, while the other lumen allows irrigation or instillation to facilitate advancement of the tube.

gastric intubation.definition: Insertion of a flexible tube through the nose or mouth into the stomach for drainage or decompression, sampling of gastric contents, or administration of nutrients or medications.

gavage feeding.definition: Administration of liquid nourishment or medications through a tube inserted into the stomach (gastric gavage), typically via a nasogastric or orogastric tube, used when oral intake is not possible or insufficient.

levitation.definition: A phenomenon in which a person or object appears to rise or float without physical support; not a medically recognized condition.

levitra.definition: A brand-name erectile dysfunction medication containing vardenafil, a phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitor that increases penile blood flow in response to sexual stimulation; should not be used with nitrates.

vardenafil.definition: A selective phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitor used to treat erectile dysfunction; it enhances erectile response to sexual stimulation by increasing cGMP levels and penile blood flow in the corpora cavernosa; contraindicated with nitrates.

pituitary dwarf.definition: An endocrine disorder characterized by short stature due to insufficient growth hormone production by the pituitary gland during childhood; individuals typically have proportionate body build, delayed bone age, and normal intelligence, and may have other pituitary hormone deficiencies; treated with growth hormone replacement therapy.

anococcygeal raphe.definition: Midline fibrous seam in the posterior perineum that runs from the anus to the coccyx; formed by the fusion of fibers from the external anal sphincter and levator ani, marking the anococcygeal region.

pubococcygeus.definition: A muscle of the pelvic floor, part of the levator ani, extending from the pubic bone to the coccyx; it supports pelvic organs and helps maintain continence by tensing the pelvic floor.

iliococcygeus.definition: A muscle of the pelvic floor (part of the levator ani) that originates from the tendinous arch of the obturator internus and the ischial spine and inserts into the coccyx and the anococcygeal raphe; it supports pelvic viscera and elevates the pelvic floor.

pharyngeal isthmus.definition: The narrow passage that connects the oral cavity to the oropharynx; bounded anteriorly by the soft palate and tongue and posteriorly by the posterior pharyngeal wall, forming the opening from the mouth into the pharynx.

pudendal plexus.definition: A venous network surrounding the pudendal vessels in the perineum (pudendal venous plexus), which drains the perineal region and external genitalia into the internal iliac venous system.

sphincter ani externus.definition: A circular skeletal muscle surrounding the lower anal canal, under voluntary control, whose constriction helps maintain continence by closing the anal opening; innervated by the inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve (S2–S4).

abdominal cancer.definition: A cancer that originates in an organ within the abdominal cavity or in the peritoneum.

retroviridae.definition: A family of enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses that replicate through a DNA intermediate via reverse transcription and integrate into the host genome; includes HIV and HTLV among others.

ribonucleic acid tumor viruses.definition: RNA tumor viruses are RNA viruses that can cause cancer by transforming host cells; most are retroviruses that replicate through a DNA copy made by reverse transcriptase, integrate into the host genome, and often carry or activate oncogenes (v-onc) to drive malignant transformation.

leveen shunt.definition: A ventriculoperitoneal hydrocephalus shunt featuring a LeVeen silicone elastomer valve that regulates cerebrospinal fluid drainage from the ventricles to the peritoneal cavity.

levobupivacaine.definition: A long-acting amide local anesthetic; the pure S(-) enantiomer of bupivacaine used to produce regional anesthesia and analgesia via neuraxial (epidural/spinal) or peripheral nerve blocks and infiltration, with a lower cardiotoxicity risk than the racemic formulation.

lewy bodies.definition: Intracellular eosinophilic inclusions within neurons composed primarily of alpha-synuclein protein, characteristic of certain neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson disease and related dementias.

chronic open-angle glaucoma.definition: A chronic, progressive optic neuropathy characterized by retinal ganglion cell death and cupping of the optic nerve, usually associated with elevated intraocular pressure in eyes with an open anterior chamber angle; commonly presents with gradual, painless loss of peripheral vision and may be asymptomatic in early stages. Treatment aims to lower intraocular pressure to slow vision loss.

severe chronic obstructive pulmonary dis.definition: A stage of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in which airflow obstruction is markedly reduced (typically a post-bronchodilator FEV1 about 30–49% of the predicted value) and is associated with pronounced dyspnea, limited activity, and a higher risk of exacerbations and respiratory complications.

o vert cardiac failure.definition: A clinically evident form of heart failure in which symptoms and signs of impaired cardiac function are present (e.g., dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue, edema) with objective findings such as crackles, elevated jugular venous pressure, or reduced activity tolerance, indicating decompensation.

ocular burning.definition: A burning sensation in the eyes, a common symptom of ocular surface irritation or inflammation; often due to dry eye or environmental irritants, allergies, conjunctivitis, contact lens wear, or eyelid disease, and may be accompanied by redness, itching, or tearing.

ocular stinging.definition: A subjective burning or stinging sensation in one or both eyes caused by irritation of the ocular surface, commonly from dry eye, allergies, contact lens wear, or exposure to irritants or chemicals.

blepharoconjunctivitis.definition: An inflammatory condition in which both the eyelid margins (blepharitis) and the conjunctiva are inflamed, causing red eye with irritation, tearing, and crusting or discharge; etiologies include bacterial infection, seborrheic dermatitis, rosacea, and allergic or irritant conjunctivitis, with treatment focused on eyelid hygiene, lubricants, and targeted anti-inflammatory or antimicrobial therapy.

local and regional anesthesia.definition:
- Loss of sensation in a small, well-defined area produced by applying or injecting a local anesthetic near nerve endings or mucosa, without affecting consciousness.

- Loss of sensation in a larger region of the body produced by injecting anesthetic near major nerves or nerve plexuses (such as spinal, epidural, or peripheral nerve blocks), with the patient typically awake or lightly sedated.

continuous epidural analgesia.definition: A method of providing continuous regional analgesia by infusing local anesthetic (often with an opioid) through an epidural catheter placed in the epidural space, typically for labor or postoperative pain.

severe liver disease.definition: An advanced, often end-stage impairment of liver function due to chronic or acute liver disease, characterized by markedly reduced hepatic synthetic and metabolic capacity, portal hypertension, and complications such as jaundice, coagulopathy, hypoalbuminemia, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy.

children less than 12 years.definition: A pediatric age group comprising individuals from birth up to 11 years of age; these patients are not considered adolescents and require age-appropriate medical care and dosing.

elderly.definition: Relating to or characteristic of older adults, typically aged 65 years or older, who may have increased frailty, chronic medical conditions, and reduced physiological reserve.

loss of consciousness.definition: A transient state of unresponsiveness and lack of wakefulness, in which a person cannot respond to stimuli or be aroused, typically due to temporary impairment of brain function from reduced cerebral perfusion, metabolic disturbance, seizure, or neurologic injury; recovery occurs when the underlying cause resolves.

myocardial depression.definition: A decrease in the contractile function of the myocardium, resulting in reduced stroke volume and cardiac output; can be caused by ischemia, toxins, electrolyte disturbances, or metabolic/critical illness.

shivering.definition: Involuntary rhythmic muscle contractions (shakes) that generate heat in response to cold exposure or fever, as part of the body's thermoregulatory response.

pupil constriction.definition: Contraction of the pupil (pupillary sphincter) leading to a smaller pupil diameter; mediated by parasympathetic stimulation of the iris, typically in bright light or during near focus (accommodation). Opposite of mydriasis.

tissue necrosis.definition: Death of cells and tissue in a localized area due to irreversible cellular injury, most commonly from ischemia or hypoxia, but also caused by infection, toxins, or trauma; the affected tissue becomes nonviable and typically elicits an inflammatory response.

levocabastine.definition: A selective H1 antihistamine used topically for allergic conjunctivitis and rhinitis; it blocks histamine H1 receptors to relieve itching, redness, and discharge, typically as ophthalmic drops (levocabastine hydrochloride) and sometimes a nasal spray.

seasonal allergic conjunctivitis.definition: An IgE-mediated allergic inflammation of the conjunctiva triggered by seasonal pollen exposure, producing itching, redness, tearing, and eyelid swelling, often with concurrent hay-fever symptoms.

primary systemic carnitine deficiency.definition: An autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by mutations in SLC22A5 (encoding the carnitine transporter OCTN2) that impairs renal reabsorption and cellular uptake of carnitine, leading to systemic carnitine deficiency and impaired mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation; clinically, it presents with hypoketotic hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, cardiomyopathy, and muscle weakness, and is treated with lifelong oral L-carnitine supplementation.

hypersensitivity to carnitine.definition: An immune- or immune-mediated adverse reaction to carnitine (e.g., L-carnitine) after exposure, presenting with allergy-like symptoms from mild (rash, urticaria, pruritus) to severe (anaphylaxis); rare and may be IgE-mediated or non–IgE-mediated.
