lower-cervical-cesarean-section.definition: A cesarean delivery in which the uterus is incised in the lower uterine segment (below the fundus and above the cervix), usually with a low transverse (horizontal) incision, to deliver the fetus; the cervix is not incised.

extraperitoneal-cesarean-section.definition: An obstetric procedure in which a cesarean delivery is performed through an extraperitoneal route, preserving the peritoneal cavity by developing a plane superficial to the peritoneum and accessing the lower uterine segment without entering the peritoneal cavity.

low-cholesterol-diet.definition: An eating plan aimed at lowering blood cholesterol by restricting dietary cholesterol and saturated fats, typically limiting high-cholesterol foods (such as eggs, fatty meats, and full-fat dairy) and emphasizing fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, lean proteins, and unsaturated fats to reduce cardiovascular risk.

very-low-density-lipoproteins.definition: Produced by the liver, these lipoprotein particles transport endogenous triglycerides and cholesterol from the liver to peripheral tissues; they are metabolized by lipoprotein lipase to intermediate-density lipoprotein (IDL) and eventually to low-density lipoprotein (LDL). Elevated levels are associated with atherogenic cardiovascular risk.

low-density-lipoprotein.definition: A "bad" kind of fat in your blood that can lead to disease. Also called LDL.

low-density-lipoprotein-receptor-disorde.definition: A genetic disorder caused by mutations in the LDL receptor (LDLR) gene that reduces or abolishes hepatic clearance of low-density lipoprotein particles, leading to markedly elevated plasma LDL cholesterol and accelerated atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (most commonly familial hypercholesterolemia with autosomal dominant inheritance).

familial-hypercholesterolemia.definition: A genetic disorder characterized by markedly elevated low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol from birth due to mutations affecting LDL receptor function, apolipoprotein B, or PCSK9, leading to an increased risk of premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. It is typically inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern; heterozygous forms are common, while homozygous forms are rare and more severe.

lown-ganong-levine-syndrome.definition: An atrioventricular conduction pathway–mediated pre-excitation syndrome in which the PR interval is shortened (typically <120 ms) but the QRS complex remains normal and lacks delta waves; an accessory pathway (often via James fibers) bypasses the AV node, allowing rapid ventricular conduction and predisposing to paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia.

atrioventricular-conduction-system.definition: The part of the heart's electrical conduction system that transmits impulses from the atria to the ventricles, coordinating the timing of ventricular contraction. It includes the AV node and the His–Purkinje conduction pathways (bundle of His, bundle branches, and Purkinje fibers), providing a brief delay to allow atrial emptying.

paroxysmal-atrial-arrhythmias.definition: A group of atrial-origin arrhythmias that begin abruptly and terminate spontaneously, with episodes lasting seconds to hours (typically less than 7 days) and recurring with symptom-free intervals between episodes.

supraventricular-tachycardia.definition: An abnormally fast heartbeat originating in heart tissue above the ventricles.

atrial-flutter.definition: A rapid, regular supraventricular tachycardia caused by a reentrant circuit in the atria, typically with sawtooth flutter waves on ECG and an atrial rate of about 250–350 beats per minute; the ventricular rate depends on AV conduction (often 2:1).

quinidine-sulfate.definition: A salt of quinidine used as a class IA antiarrhythmic agent that blocks fast sodium channels and prolongs the cardiac action potential, employed to treat certain supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias; may cause cinchonism, hypotension, and torsades de pointes.

wolff-parkinson-white-syndrome.definition: A congenital pre-excitation syndrome due to an accessory atrioventricular conduction pathway (most often the bundle of Kent) that bypasses the AV node, causing a shortened PR interval with a delta wave on ECG and predisposes to tachyarrhythmias such as atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia; management ranges from observation to catheter ablation of the accessory pathway.

short-pr-normal-qrs-syndrome.definition: A preexcitation syndrome characterized by a shortened PR interval with a normal QRS duration and absence of delta waves on ECG, due to an accessory atrioventricular conduction pathway (such as James fibers) bypassing the AV node; may be associated with tachyarrhythmias.

lower-esophageal-sphincter.definition: A ring of smooth muscle at the distal esophagus (the gastroesophageal junction) that maintains a high resting pressure to prevent reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus and relaxes transiently during swallowing to allow the passage of food into the stomach.

esophagogastric-junction.definition: Anatomical region where the distal esophagus meets the proximal stomach (the gastroesophageal/esophagogastric junction), including the lower esophageal sphincter; marks the transition from squamous to columnar mucosa (the Z-line) and acts as a barrier to reflux.

lower-motor-neuron-dysarthria.definition: Damage to the lower motor neurons (bulbar system) innervating the speech muscles, causing flaccid dysarthria with weakness, hypotonia, fasciculations, and atrophy of bulbar muscles, often producing breathy or hoarse voice, hypernasality, imprecise articulation, and reduced loudness.

lower-motor-neuron-paralysis.definition: Paralysis or severe weakness caused by damage to the lower motor neurons (anterior horn cells, peripheral motor nerves, or the neuromuscular junction). It produces flaccid paralysis with hypotonia, hyporeflexia or areflexia, and marked muscle atrophy and fasciculations; sensory may be preserved, and unlike upper motor neuron lesions, spasticity and hyperreflexia are absent.

lower-pole-ureter.definition: A segment of the ureter located near the kidney's lower pole that conducts urine from the renal pelvis toward the bladder.

lower-respiratory-tract.definition: The portion of the respiratory tract below the larynx, comprising the trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, and the lungs (alveoli), where air is conducted to the lungs and gas exchange occurs.

lowes-syndrome.definition: A rare X-linked disorder caused by OCRL gene mutations, also known as oculocerebrorenal syndrome, characterized by congenital cataracts (often with glaucoma), renal proximal tubulopathy (Fanconi-type) with aminoaciduria and phosphate wasting, and varying neurologic impairment.

renal-tubular-dysfunction.definition: A disorder in which the renal tubules fail to reabsorb or secrete solutes properly, leading to loss of bicarbonate, phosphate, glucose, amino acids, or water, and to abnormalities in urine concentration and electrolyte balance.

cortical-cataracts.definition: A cataract characterized by opacities in the lens cortex (the outer portion of the lens), typically forming wedge- or spoke-like patterns that radiate from the periphery toward the center, leading to glare and decreased visual acuity.

low-fat-diet.definition: A diet that restricts total fat intake, especially saturated fat, to reduce caloric density and cardiovascular risk; it typically emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins, and low-fat dairy products.

gallbladder-disease.definition: A broad category of disorders affecting the gallbladder, most commonly gallstones (cholelithiasis) and inflammation (cholecystitis). It typically presents with right upper abdominal pain, often after meals, with nausea or vomiting; biliary obstruction can cause jaundice and pancreatitis. Management ranges from pain control and observation to antibiotics for infection and surgical removal of the gallbladder (cholecystectomy) or biliary drainage as needed.

heart-disease.definition: A broad term for diseases that affect the heart’s structure or function, including coronary artery disease, heart failure, arrhythmias, and valvular heart disease, which can impair the heart’s ability to pump blood and supply the body with oxygen.

malabsorption-syndromes.definition: A group of disorders in which the small intestine fails to absorb nutrients adequately, leading to malnutrition and various nutritional deficiencies; caused by mucosal diseases (e.g., celiac disease, Crohn disease), pancreatic insufficiency, bile acid deficiency, infections or overgrowth, and post-surgical changes.

tendinous-xanthomatosis.definition: A form of xanthomatosis with lipid-laden macrophage (foam cell) deposits within tendons, causing firm nodular thickening most often in the Achilles tendon and extensor tendons of the hands; it is strongly associated with familial hyperlipidemia, particularly familial hypercholesterolemia, and may impair tendon function.

hypercholesterolemic-xanthomatosis.definition: A cutaneous and tendinous xanthomatosis associated with marked hypercholesterolemia (often familial hypercholesterolemia), due to deposition of lipid-laden macrophages in the skin and tendons; presents as nodules or plaques such as tuberous xanthomas and xanthelasma and is linked to high LDL cholesterol and premature atherosclerosis.

achilles-tendon.definition: A strong cord of fibrous tissue at the back of the ankle that attaches the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles to the calcaneus (heel bone), enabling plantar flexion of the foot. Also known as the calcaneal tendon; it is commonly affected by tendinopathy or rupture.

extensor-tendons.definition: Tendons on the back (dorsal) aspect of the hand that transmit contraction from forearm extensor muscles to extend the fingers and wrist, including the tendons of extensor digitorum, extensor indicis, and extensor pollicis longus.

coronary-arteries.definition: The arteries that supply oxygenated blood to the heart muscle (myocardium); they arise from the aorta as the left and right coronary arteries and branch to perfuse the myocardium.

ischemic-heart-disease.definition: A condition in which the heart muscle receives insufficient blood supply due to narrowing or blockage of the coronary arteries, most commonly from atherosclerosis, leading to angina, myocardial infarction, and other cardiac complications.

sodium-restricted-diet.definition: A diet that limits sodium (salt) intake to help manage conditions such as hypertension, edema, heart failure, and certain kidney diseases; daily sodium targets vary but are commonly around 1500–2000 mg, achieved by choosing fresh foods and avoiding high-sodium processed items.

low-sodium-diet.definition: A diet that restricts sodium (salt) intake to help control blood pressure and fluid balance; it emphasizes fresh, unprocessed foods and limits added salt and high-sodium processed foods, often targeting about 1500–2300 mg of sodium per day depending on medical guidance.

liver-disease.definition: A broad term for any condition that damages the liver or impairs its ability to perform normal functions (such as metabolism, detoxification, bile production, and protein synthesis), including hepatitis, fatty liver disease, cirrhosis, and liver failure.

kidney-failure.definition: When your kidneys stop working. Also called chronic kidney disease or end stage kidney disease.

renal-disease.definition: A disease affecting the kidneys that impairs their structure or function, including acute kidney injury and chronic kidney disease, and may cause reduced filtration (low GFR), electrolyte and fluid disturbances, and accumulation of waste products.

deep-vein-thrombosis.definition: A blood clot that forms in a vein deep in your body.

low-molecular-weight-heparin.definition: An anticoagulant medication consisting of smaller heparin fragments; it primarily inhibits coagulation factor Xa (via antithrombin III) with little direct effect on thrombin, providing more predictable pharmacokinetics and enabling subcutaneous dosing. Used to prevent and treat venous thromboembolism and for prophylaxis in surgical or medical patients, with a lower risk of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia than unfractionated heparin.

hip-replacements.definition: An operation in which a diseased or damaged hip joint is removed and replaced with artificial components (prosthesis) to relieve pain and restore function; most commonly a total hip replacement (total hip arthroplasty), used for severe arthritis, osteonecrosis, or fractures; may be partial (hemiarthroplasty) in selected cases.

knee-replacements.definition: A surgical procedure in which a diseased or damaged knee joint is replaced with artificial components (prosthetic implants) to relieve pain and restore function.

placenta-previa.definition: A pregnancy complication in which the placenta implants low in the uterus and partially or completely covers the cervical opening, causing painless vaginal bleeding in the second or third trimester and typically requiring cesarean delivery.

lower-uterine-segment.definition: The portion of the uterus between the uterine isthmus and the cervix; it enlarges during pregnancy and becomes relatively thin-walled, and is the common site for lower-segment cesarean incisions.

pelvic-floor.definition: The sling of muscles that support the intestines and bladder, as well as the uterus in women. Weak or damaged pelvic floor muscles can cause incontinence or diminished sexual pleasure, among other problems.

left-bronchi.definition: A main airway that branches from the trachea and enters the left lung; it conducts air to the left lung and divides into the left upper lobe bronchus and left lower lobe bronchus. It is typically longer and more horizontal than the right main bronchus.

right-bronchi.definition: The principal airway that conducts air from the trachea into the right lung; it is shorter, wider, and more vertical than the left main bronchus and quickly divides into the right upper lobe bronchus and the bronchus intermedius, which further give rise to the middle and lower lobe bronchi.

alveolar-sacs.definition: A cluster of alveoli forming the distal end of an alveolar duct; the alveolar sacs share a common opening into the duct and constitute the terminal gas-exchange airspaces of the lung.

alveolar-ducts.definition: A duct in the lung that connects the respiratory bronchioles to the alveolar sacs; part of the gas-exchange region, lined by simple epithelium that transitions from cuboidal to thin squamous cells as it approaches the alveoli; alveoli open into the duct.

bundle-of-his.definition: A collection of specialized conducting fibers that transmits the cardiac impulse from the atrioventricular (AV) node to the ventricles via the right and left bundle branches, enabling synchronized ventricular contraction (part of the His-Purkinje system).

forceps-delivery.definition: An obstetric procedure in which a pair of metal forceps is applied to the fetal head to facilitate vaginal delivery, typically during the second stage when the mother cannot push effectively or fetal distress necessitates faster delivery.

low-forceps.definition: An obstetric instrument used for assisted vaginal delivery when the fetal head is low in the birth canal (low in the pelvis), with the cervix fully dilated and the head engaged; the forceps are applied to provide traction (and rotation if needed) to facilitate delivery.

outlet-forceps.definition: An obstetric instrument used to facilitate vaginal delivery when the fetal head is at the vaginal outlet and the scalp is visible at the perineum, allowing controlled traction to deliver the head.

prophylactic-forceps.definition: A surgical instrument (a type of forceps) used prophylactically during a procedure to grasp and manipulate tissue or remove material, with the aim of preventing complications or facilitating a safer outcome.

high-forceps.definition: An assisted vaginal delivery in which obstetric forceps are applied to the fetal head when it is high in the birth canal (above the pelvic inlet and not yet engaged) to expedite delivery in certain circumstances, such as fetal distress or maternal exhaustion; it carries higher risks than a low-forceps delivery or cesarean section.

mid-forceps.definition: An obstetric instrument used to assist vaginal delivery when the fetal head is at midpelvic level; the blades encircle the head to apply controlled traction and rotation to aid descent and birth, typically by an experienced clinician.

natural-childbirth.definition: A birth conducted with minimal medical intervention, emphasizing nonpharmacologic pain relief and avoiding routine procedures (e.g., induction, augmentation, analgesia, episiotomy, and instrumental delivery) unless medically necessary.

spontaneous-delivery.definition: Delivery that occurs naturally without induction of labor or use of instrumental assistance, typically resulting in a vaginal birth.

obstetric-forceps.definition: A pair of curved, hinged metal instruments used by obstetricians to grasp the fetal head and apply controlled traction to facilitate vaginal delivery when labor is not progressing or when maternal or fetal conditions necessitate expedited birth.

loxapine.definition: A typical antipsychotic (dibenzoxazepine) used to treat schizophrenia and related psychoses; it blocks central dopamine D2 receptors and can cause extrapyramidal symptoms.

ludwig’s angina.definition: Rapidly spreading bilateral cellulitis of the floor of the mouth involving the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces, typically arising from an odontogenic infection (often mandibular molars). It can cause tongue elevation, airway compromise, trismus, drooling, and fever, and requires urgent airway assessment with IV antibiotics and often surgical drainage.

extrapyramidal reactions.definition: A group of drug-induced movement disorders caused by disruption of dopaminergic signaling in the brain’s extrapyramidal (basal ganglia) motor pathways, most commonly from dopamine D2 receptor antagonists such as antipsychotics. They include acute dystonia, akathisia, drug-induced parkinsonism, and tardive dyskinesia.

loxitane.definition: A typical antipsychotic (dibenzoxazepine) used to treat schizophrenia and related psychoses; it acts as a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist and can cause extrapyramidal symptoms, sedation, and other antipsychotic-related effects.

loxophthalmus.definition: Not a recognized medical term; no standard clinical definition. If you can share context or confirm the spelling, I can help interpret possible alternatives.

loxotic.definition: Not a recognized medical term in standard dictionaries; no official definition exists. If you meant a similar term—such as lipotoxic (cell injury due to lipid accumulation) or lytic (causing destruction)—please provide context or the correct spelling for a precise definition.

loxotomy.definition: Not a recognized medical term; no standard definition in reputable medical dictionaries. It may be a misspelling or obsolete. If you can share context or the intended spelling, I can help.

loxosceles.definition: A genus of venomous spiders in the family Sicariidae, including species whose bites can cause dermonecrotic skin lesions (loxoscelism) and, rarely, systemic symptoms.

l. laeta.definition: A species of protozoan parasite in the genus Leishmania; it causes leishmaniasis and is transmitted to humans by phlebotomine sandflies.

l. reclusa.definition: A venomous spider of the genus Loxosceles (brown recluse) found in the central and southern United States; its bite can produce a necrotic skin lesion and, rarely, systemic symptoms such as hemolysis; treatment is supportive with wound care and analgesia, with no widely used antivenom.

spider bite.definition: An injury resulting from a spider’s venomous bite. Most bites cause a minor local reaction— a small puncture wound with redness, swelling, and itching—that resolves with basic wound care. Bites from certain species can produce more severe pain, swelling, tissue damage, or systemic symptoms.

lozenge.definition: A small medicated tablet that dissolves in the mouth to release a local or systemic drug, typically used to treat sore throat or cough.

troche.definition: A small, dissolvable medicated tablet meant to dissolve in the mouth and release a drug for buccal or sublingual absorption.

lysergic acid diethylamide.definition: A potent semi-synthetic hallucinogenic drug in the lysergamide class derived from lysergic acid; it acts primarily as a serotonin 2A receptor agonist to induce profound alterations in perception, mood, and cognition; onset is typically 30–90 minutes after ingestion and effects last about 8–12 hours.

lsd.definition: A potent synthetic psychedelic that profoundly alters perception, mood, and cognition by activating serotonin 5-HT2A receptors; commonly produces visual hallucinations and altered sense of time, with potential for anxiety or paranoia; illegal in many jurisdictions.

lysergide.definition: A potent psychedelic drug of the ergoline class (lysergic acid diethylamide, LSD); a serotonergic hallucinogen that induces profound alterations in perception, mood, and cognition, typically lasting about 6–12 hours.

l-shaped kidney.definition: A rare congenital renal fusion anomaly in which two kidneys fuse to form an L-shaped configuration, typically due to fusion of the lower pole of one kidney with the upper pole of the other, and it may be associated with malrotation, abnormal ureteral course, hydronephrosis, or other urinary tract abnormalities.

l-spine.definition: The lower portion of the spine; it includes the five lumbar vertebrae (L1–L5) and forms the start of the lower back.

long-term care.definition: A range of services and supports intended to meet the ongoing medical, personal, and social care needs of individuals with chronic illness, disability, or aging-related frailty who require assistance with daily activities; provided at home, in community settings, or in long-term care facilities.

luteotropic hormone.definition: A hormone that promotes growth and maintenance of the corpus luteum and stimulates progesterone production; prolactin is the classic luteotropic hormone in humans.

levothyroxine.definition: A synthetic, biologically identical form of the thyroid hormone thyroxine (T4) used as lifelong replacement therapy for hypothyroidism; also used to suppress thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in certain thyroid conditions, including thyroid cancer.

levothyroxine sodium.definition: A man-made version of the thyroid hormone thyroxine.

l-tryptophan.definition: An essential amino acid (the L-enantiomer) required for protein synthesis; a precursor to the neurotransmitter serotonin and the hormone melatonin, and can be converted to niacin in the body. Obtainable from dietary proteins.

lutetium.definition: A chemical element (symbol Lu), a lanthanide metal with atomic number 71; its radioisotope lutetium-177 is used in targeted radiotherapy for certain cancers.

lubb.definition: The first heart sound (S1) produced by closure of the atrioventricular valves (mitral and tricuspid) at the start of ventricular systole; it marks the beginning of systole and is typically a low-frequency, longer-duration sound.

lubb-dupp.definition: An onomatopoeic reference to the two main heart sounds heard with a stethoscope. The first sound (S1) is produced by the closure of the atrioventricular valves (mitral and tricuspid) at the start of ventricular systole; the second sound (S2) is produced by the closure of the semilunar valves (aortic and pulmonary) at the end of systole. Together, they mark the beginning and end of systole and compose the normal cardiac cycle (with possible physiological splitting of S2 during respiration).

lugol’s solution.definition: A solution of elemental iodine in potassium iodide in water (typically about 5% iodine with 10% potassium iodide), used as a topical antiseptic/disinfectant and as a laboratory reagent (e.g., for starch testing).

luetic aortitis.definition: Inflammation of the aorta due to syphilitic infection (Treponema pallidum), typically in tertiary syphilis, characterized by endarteritis of the vasa vasorum with degeneration of the aortic media, leading to dilation or aneurysm formation and often aortic regurgitation.

lufyllin.definition: A methylxanthine bronchodilator used to treat symptoms of asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; it works by inhibiting phosphodiesterase to increase cAMP and by antagonizing adenosine receptors, with a narrow therapeutic index requiring careful dosing and monitoring.

left upper lobe.definition: The superior portion of the left lung, situated above the oblique fissure and separated from the lower lobe; it contains the lingula and is divided into bronchopulmonary segments (commonly apical, posterior, anterior, and lingular segments).

left upper extremity.definition: The left upper extremity is the entire left arm from the shoulder to the hand, including the shoulder girdle, upper limb segments (arm and forearm), wrist, and hand.

lumbar lordosis.definition: An inward curvature of the lumbar (lower back) region of the spine, seen in the sagittal plane as part of normal spinal alignment; excessive curvature is hyperlordosis, while reduced curvature is hypolordosis.

lumbar nerves.definition: A group of spinal nerves arising from the lumbar spinal cord segments (L1–L5) that form the lumbar plexus and provide motor and sensory innervation to the lower back, lower abdomen, groin, thigh, and proximal leg.

lumbar plexus.definition: A network of nerves in the posterior abdominal wall formed by the anterior rami of L1–L4 (occasionally including T12), giving rise to the femoral, obturator, and other nerves that supply the lower abdominal wall, pelvis, and lower limb.

lumbar subarachnoid peritoneostomy.definition: A surgical procedure that diverts cerebrospinal fluid from the lumbar subarachnoid space into the peritoneal cavity, typically via a lumboperitoneal shunt, to treat hydrocephalus or elevated intracranial pressure.

lumbar subarachnoid ureterostomy.definition: A historical urinary diversion in which a ureter is connected to the lumbar subarachnoid space, allowing urine to drain directly into the cerebrospinal fluid rather than the bladder; used in select cases of severe bladder dysfunction but carries high risks (e.g., meningitis, arachnoiditis, infection).

lumbar veins.definition: Veins of the posterior abdominal wall that accompany the lumbar arteries; they drain the lumbar muscles and vertebral venous plexus and typically drain into the inferior vena cava directly or via the ascending lumbar veins and the azygos/hemiazygos venous system.

lumbar vertebra.definition: One of the five vertebrae in the lumbar region of the spine (L1–L5). It has a large, kidney-shaped body; a triangular vertebral foramen; a short, thick spinous process; and superior/inferior articular facets oriented mainly sagittally, with no costal facets, designed for substantial weight bearing and limited rotation.

lumbosacral.definition: Relating to the region of the spine that includes the lumbar (lower back) and sacral (pelvic) areas, i.e., the junction between these sections (typically around the L5–S1 vertebrae).

lumbosacral plexus.definition: A network of ventral rami from the lumbar and sacral spinal nerves (typically L1–S4) that provides motor and sensory innervation to the lower limb and pelvic region; formed by the lumbar and sacral plexuses and giving rise to nerves such as the femoral, obturator, sciatic, tibial, common peroneal, and pudendal.

lumbar spine.definition: The lower portion of the spine that consists of the five lumbar vertebrae, forming the lower back.

luminal.definition: Relating to or situated within a lumen; pertaining to the inside space of a hollow organ or vessel.

lumina.definition: The internal spaces or cavities within tubular structures (such as blood vessels, ducts, or hollow organs) through which fluids or gases pass.

lucentis.definition: A brand-name anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody fragment (ranibizumab) given by intravitreal injection to treat neovascular age-related macular degeneration and other retinal vascular diseases such as diabetic macular edema.

ranibizumab.definition: A humanized monoclonal antibody fragment (Fab) that inhibits vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A); administered by intravitreal injection to treat neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration and other retinal vascular diseases.

lucid interval.definition: A temporary period of regained consciousness and apparent normal function after head trauma, typically followed by rapid neurological deterioration due to expanding intracranial bleeding (classically an epidural hematoma).

lucio’s leprosy phenomenon.definition: A rare necrotizing cutaneous vasculitis seen in diffuse lepromatous leprosy (Lucio leprosy), presenting with widespread ulceronecrotic skin lesions due to destruction of cutaneous vessels by Mycobacterium leprae; distinct from erythema nodosum leprosum.

ludiomil.definition: A tetracyclic antidepressant (maprotiline) used to treat major depressive disorder; it primarily inhibits norepinephrine reuptake and can cause sedation and anticholinergic effects, with a risk of seizures in overdose.

t cell–derived immunoblastic lymphoma.definition: An aggressive high-grade non-Hodgkin lymphoma composed of immunoblasts of T-cell origin, with rapid progression and systemic symptoms; tumor cells express T-cell markers (eg, CD3) on immunophenotyping.

fecal incontinence.definition: Inability to control bowel movements, resulting in involuntary passage of stool or gas from the anus; can be temporary or chronic and may arise from anal sphincter weakness or damage, pelvic floor dysfunction, nerve injury, or changes in stool consistency.

fecal urgency.definition: A sudden, compelling urge to have a bowel movement that is difficult to defer, sometimes resulting in fecal leakage.

fecal retention.definition: A condition in which stool is not evacuated and remains in the colon or rectum, causing infrequent or difficult defecation; often due to constipation, impaired rectal sensation, or pelvic floor dysfunction.

pain in extremities.definition: Pain in the limbs (arms or legs); a symptom that can result from musculoskeletal, vascular, neuropathic, or systemic causes and may be acute or chronic. It varies by location, quality (sharp, dull, throbbing), intensity, timing, and triggering factors; evaluation relies on history, exam, and targeted testing to identify the underlying etiology.

eructation.definition: The act of belching; the expulsion of swallowed air or gas from the stomach through the mouth.

nasopharyngitis.definition: Inflammation of the nasopharynx, usually due to a viral infection; presents with nasal congestion, runny nose, sore throat, sneezing, and sometimes fever, and is typically self-limited.

intracranial tumor.definition: A mass or neoplasm that develops within the skull, arising from brain tissue (parenchyma), meninges, or cranial nerves (primary) or from metastatic spread (secondary); it may be benign or malignant and typically presents with neurologic symptoms due to mass effect or invasion.

cauda equina.definition: A bundle of nerve roots that resembles a horse’s tail, located at the end of the spinal cord.

psoas major.definition: A large, deep hip flexor muscle that originates from the transverse processes, bodies, and intervertebral discs of T12–L5 and inserts on the lesser trochanter of the femur; it flexes the hip and, with the trunk fixed, helps flex or tilt the pelvis, and stabilizes the lumbar spine (forming the iliopsoas with the iliacus).

nuchal ligament.definition: A thick, fibrous band along the posterior neck formed by the expansion of the supraspinous ligament, extending from the external occipital protuberance and superior nuchal line to the spinous processes of C2–C7; it serves as an attachment for neck muscles and helps support the head.

thoracolumbar fascia.definition: A dense fascial sheet in the lower thoracic and lumbar region that envelops the paraspinal muscles (erector spinae and quadratus lumborum). It consists of three layers (anterior, middle, and posterior laminae) that attach to the ribs, transverse processes, iliac crest, and spinous processes, helping stabilize the back and transmit muscular forces between the trunk and limbs.

lumbodorsal fascia.definition: A thick layer of deep fascia in the lower back that envelops the intrinsic back muscles (e.g., erector spinae), forming the posterior portion of the thoracolumbar fascia and attaching to the iliac crest, sacrum, lumbar vertebrae, and lower ribs to help stabilize the back.

paraspinal muscles.definition: Paraspinal muscles are the muscles adjacent to and running alongside the spine that stabilize and move the vertebral column; they include the superficial erector spinae group (iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis) and the deeper transversospinales (semispinalis, multifidus, rotatores) that assist extension, lateral flexion, rotation, and posture.

sacrospinalis muscle.definition: A muscle (or muscle group) of the back, part of the erector spinae, running longitudinally along the spine from the sacral region to the skull and extending and laterally flexing the vertebral column to maintain posture.

ilioinguinal.definition: Relating to the ilium and inguinal region; in anatomy, commonly refers to the ilioinguinal nerve (L1), which provides sensation to the groin and proximal genitalia and motor to the internal oblique and transversus abdominis as it traverses the inguinal region.

genitofemoral.definition: Relating to the genitofemoral nerve, a branch of the lumbar plexus (L1–L2) that divides into genital and femoral branches; the genital branch supplies motor innervation to the cremaster muscle and sensory innervation to the skin of the scrotum or labia majora, while the femoral branch supplies sensory innervation to the skin of the upper anterior thigh.

lateral femoral cutaneous.definition: A pure sensory branch of the lumbar plexus (typically L2–L3) that passes under the inguinal ligament near the anterior superior iliac spine to supply sensation to the skin of the anterolateral thigh; entrapment here can cause meralgia paresthetica.

accessory obturator.definition: An anatomical variant in the obturator region, typically an extra nerve (the accessory obturator nerve) arising from the lumbar plexus that runs with the obturator nerve through the obturator canal to innervate the medial thigh (and sometimes the hip joint), leading to atypical innervation patterns.

lumbar node.definition: A lymph node along the lumbar (para-aortic) lymphatic chain in the posterior abdominal wall, near the aorta and inferior vena cava. It drains lymph from the posterior abdominal wall, kidneys and adrenal glands, gonads, and pelvic viscera, and communicates with other abdominal lymph nodes; it can be a site of metastatic spread from abdominal or pelvic cancers.

preaortic nodes.definition: Abdominal lymph nodes located anterior to the aorta around the origins of the major abdominal arteries (celiac trunk, superior mesenteric artery, and inferior mesenteric artery); they drain lymph from the foregut, midgut, and hindgut and pass it to the intestinal trunk leading to the cisterna chyli.

retroaortic nodes.definition: Lymph nodes located behind the aorta in the retroperitoneum; part of the paraaortic lymphatic chain that drains posterior abdominal structures, and they may enlarge with infection, inflammation, or metastatic disease.

lung biopsy.definition: A procedure in which a small sample of lung tissue is removed for histopathologic examination to diagnose lung disease; samples are obtained via bronchoscopy (transbronchial biopsy) or percutaneous needle biopsy under imaging guidance.

lung transplantation.definition: A surgical procedure in which a diseased lung (or both lungs) is removed and replaced with a healthy donor lung or lungs, performed for end-stage lung disease; typically done as single-lung or bilateral transplantation and requiring lifelong immunosuppression to prevent rejection.

paclitaxel.definition: A chemotherapy agent in the taxane class that stabilizes microtubules, preventing their disassembly and blocking mitosis, leading to cancer cell death. It is given intravenously for various cancers (notably breast and ovarian cancer). Common adverse effects include neutropenia, neuropathy, fatigue, alopecia, and hypersensitivity reactions; premedication is often used to reduce reactions.

carboplatin.definition: A platinum-based chemotherapy agent that forms DNA crosslinks, inhibiting DNA replication and transcription and leading to cancer cell death; used for ovarian cancer (often with paclitaxel) and other cancers; typically given intravenously; main toxicity is myelosuppression (especially thrombocytopenia), with less nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity than cisplatin.

small cell carcinoma.definition: An aggressive neuroendocrine carcinoma most commonly arising in the lung, composed of small cells with scant cytoplasm, ill-defined borders, finely granular chromatin, absent nucleoli, high mitotic rate, and early metastasis; strongly associated with smoking; primarily treated with systemic chemotherapy and radiotherapy, with limited role for surgical resection.

large cell carcinoma.definition: A non–small cell lung carcinoma composed of large, poorly differentiated, polygonal cells with abundant cytoplasm and prominent nuclei, lacking features of squamous or adenocarcinoma differentiation (a diagnosis of exclusion based on histology and immunohistochemistry).

palliative therapy.definition: Treatment aimed at relieving symptoms and improving quality of life for patients with serious, life-limiting illness, without curative intent; it may accompany disease-modifying therapies.

intrathoracic.definition: Situated within the thoracic cavity (the chest); inside the chest, as opposed to outside the thorax.

lung capacity.definition: The maximum amount of air the lungs can contain after a maximal inhalation; the total of all lung volumes (tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume, expiratory reserve volume, and residual volume).

inspiratory capacity.definition: The maximum volume of air that can be inspired after a normal expiration; equal to tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve volume (IC = VT + IRV); typically about 2.5–3.5 L in a healthy adult.

resting expiratory level.definition: The lung volume at which passive inward recoil of the lungs and outward recoil of the chest wall are balanced with no active respiratory muscle contraction, corresponding to the end-expiratory position at zero airway pressure (approximately the functional residual capacity in healthy individuals).

tidal volume.definition: Volume of air inhaled or exhaled in a single normal breath during resting respiration; in a healthy adult it averages about 500 mL (roughly 6–8 mL per kilogram of body weight).

compliance.definition: The extent to which a patient follows prescribed medical advice or treatment (adherence); in physiology, the ease with which a hollow organ or vessel expands in response to pressure.

bronchial washings.definition: A diagnostic procedure in which sterile saline is instilled into the bronchi during bronchoscopy and then aspirated to obtain a sample of bronchial secretions for cytology and microbiology analysis, used to evaluate infections, malignancy, or inflammatory lung diseases.

brushings.definition: A cytologic specimen obtained by brushing a mucosal surface with a small brush to collect epithelial cells for microscopic examination, commonly used for sampling airway, nasal, or gynecologic mucosa to diagnose infection, inflammation, or malignancy.

surfactant.definition: A substance that lowers surface tension at air–liquid interfaces; in the lungs, pulmonary surfactant is a complex mixture of phospholipids and proteins that lines the alveoli to reduce surface tension, preventing alveolar collapse and decreasing the work of breathing.

secondary lobules.definition: The smallest functionally defined unit of the lung parenchyma, delineated by interlobular septa, typically about 1–2.5 cm in diameter, centered on a terminal bronchiole and its accompanying pulmonary artery, and containing several acini.

primary lobules.definition: An uncommon term for the main, first‑order lobular unit of a gland or organ, from which smaller lobular subdivisions may arise; exact meaning and usage vary by organ, and many texts do not use the term.

bronchial arteries.definition: Systemic arteries that arise mainly from the thoracic aorta (often one left and one right) and supply oxygenated blood to the structures of the lung outside the alveoli—primarily the tracheobronchial tree, bronchial walls, supporting tissues, and visceral pleura; they form the bronchial circulation and commonly anastomose with the pulmonary arteries.

bronchial vein.definition: A vein that drains blood from the bronchi as part of the lung's systemic (bronchial) circulation; it accompanies the bronchial arteries and typically drains into the azygos vein on the right or into the left superior intercostal/ accessory hemiazygos veins on the left.

lupus anticoagulant.definition: An antiphospholipid antibody that prolongs phospholipid-dependent clotting tests (e.g., the aPTT) in vitro and is associated with antiphospholipid syndrome and a tendency for thrombotic events in vivo; it is not a true anticoagulant.

lupus band test.definition: A direct immunofluorescence test on a skin biopsy (usually perilesional) showing granular or linear deposits of immunoglobulins (typically IgG, often with IgM and sometimes IgA) and C3 along the dermoepidermal junction, supporting a diagnosis of cutaneous or systemic lupus erythematosus.

lupus vulgaris.definition: A chronic, progressive, paucibacillary form of cutaneous tuberculosis presenting as slowly enlarging plaques that may become atrophic and scarred; commonly affects the face and neck and shows the characteristic “apple‑jelly” color (apple jelly nodules) on diascopy.

lupus pernio.definition: A chronic cutaneous manifestation of sarcoidosis presenting as persistent, indurated, violaceous plaques or nodules—commonly on the nose, cheeks, ears, and fingers—with noncaseating granulomatous inflammation and frequent association with systemic sarcoidosis.

lupoid hepatitis.definition: A form of autoimmune hepatitis occurring in the setting of systemic lupus erythematosus; an immune-mediated chronic liver inflammation characterized by interface hepatitis and lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, often with positive autoantibodies and responsive to immunosuppressive therapy.

ixodes.definition: A genus of hard-bodied ticks (family Ixodidae) that are common ectoparasites and vectors for several pathogens, including Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease), Anaplasma phagocytophilum (anaplasmosis), Babesia microti (babesiosis), and tick-borne encephalitis virus.

tick.definition: A small blood-sucking arachnid that attaches to the skin of vertebrates to feed on blood; many species are vectors for diseases such as Lyme disease, ehrlichiosis, babesiosis, anaplasmosis, and Rocky Mountain spotted fever.

gonadal insufficiency.definition: Impaired function of the gonads (ovaries or testes) with decreased production of gonadal sex steroids (estrogen and/or testosterone) and often reduced gametogenesis; may be primary gonadal failure or secondary/tertiary dysfunction of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.

pituitary insufficiency.definition: A deficiency of pituitary hormones due to impaired pituitary function, resulting in reduced secretion of one or more anterior pituitary hormones (eg, ACTH, TSH, LH/FSH, GH, prolactin); can be partial or panhypopituitarism, leading to secondary adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, gonadal failure, growth impairment, and metabolic disturbances.

luteal phase.definition: The post-ovulatory phase of the menstrual cycle, typically lasting about 14 days, during which the corpus luteum secretes progesterone (and some estrogen) to thicken and maintain the endometrium for potential implantation; if fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates (luteolysis), progesterone falls, and menses begin.

luteal phase deficiency.definition: An inadequate luteal phase characterized by insufficient progesterone production or endometrial maturation to support implantation and maintenance of early pregnancy, often associated with infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss; commonly defined by a short luteal phase or low mid‑luteal progesterone, though its status as a distinct disorder is debated.

luteotropin.definition: A hormone that supports the function or maintenance of the corpus luteum in the ovary, particularly promoting progesterone production; in humans, luteal maintenance is mainly provided by LH (with hCG maintaining the luteum in early pregnancy), though prolactin can have luteotrophic effects in some species.

luvox.definition: An SSRI antidepressant (fluvoxamine) used primarily to treat obsessive-compulsive disorder; it increases serotonin levels in the brain by inhibiting its reuptake and is occasionally used for anxiety disorders. Common side effects include nausea, insomnia or drowsiness, headache, and sexual dysfunction.

lupron.definition: A synthetic gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist that suppresses gonadal hormone production by desensitizing the pituitary; used by injection to treat hormone-sensitive conditions such as prostate cancer, endometriosis, uterine fibroids, and central precocious puberty.

lunesta.definition: A nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic used to treat insomnia; it enhances GABAergic activity at the GABA-A receptor to promote sleep onset and maintain sleep.

luteinizing surge.definition: A rapid, temporary rise in luteinizing hormone (LH) from the anterior pituitary during midcycle, driven by rising estrogen from the dominant ovarian follicle, that triggers ovulation within about 24–36 hours and promotes luteinization of the follicle into the corpus luteum.

lymphangiosarcoma.definition: A rare malignant tumor arising from lymphatic endothelium (a form of angiosarcoma) that typically develops in chronically lymphedematous tissue, most notably after breast cancer treatment; it presents as violaceous skin lesions or nodules on an edematous limb and is aggressive with a high risk of recurrence and metastasis.

lymphangitis.definition: Inflammation of the lymphatic vessels, typically due to a bacterial infection spreading from a nearby skin infection; classically presents with painful, red streaks (lymphangitic streaking) toward regional lymph nodes, often with fever.

lymphoblastic lymphoma.definition: An aggressive high-grade malignant lymphoma composed of precursor lymphoid cells (lymphoblasts), most often of T-cell lineage; commonly presents with a mediastinal mass and generalized lymphadenopathy, especially in children and young adults; biologically resembles T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and is treated with intensive systemic chemotherapy regimens used for ALL.

hodgkin disease.definition: Malignant lymphoma of B-lymphocyte origin, defined pathologically by the presence of Reed-Sternberg cells. Clinically presents as painless lymphadenopathy (often in the neck) with possible systemic symptoms such as fever, night sweats, and weight loss (B symptoms). Diagnosis is by biopsy showing Reed-Sternberg cells; immunophenotype typically CD15 and CD30 positive. Treated with chemotherapy (often ABVD) with or without radiation; prognosis is favorable, especially in early stages.

streptococcal lymphangitis.definition: Inflammation of the lymphatic vessels caused by infection with Streptococcus species (classically group A Streptococcus), typically presenting as tender, red streaks extending from a site of cellulitis along the lymphatic channels.

lymphangioma cavernosum.definition: A benign congenital malformation of the lymphatic system consisting of large, dilated lymphatic channels forming cavernous spaces; a type of lymphangioma that most often presents as a soft, compressible, ill-defined mass in the head and neck of infants or children.

lymphangioma circumscriptum.definition: A benign congenital lymphatic malformation of the skin and subcutaneous tissue, characterized by dilated lymphatic channels in the dermis that form clustered, translucent vesicles (often described as frog-spawn) that may leak clear lymph fluid.

lymphangioma cysticum.definition: A benign congenital malformation of the lymphatic system characterized by large, cystic spaces filled with lymphatic fluid (macrocystic lymphangioma), most commonly presenting as a neck mass (cystic hygroma) in newborns or infants; may require treatment with sclerotherapy or surgical excision.

lymphangioma simplex.definition: A benign congenital malformation of superficial lymphatic vessels characterized by dilated lymphatic channels in the dermis, forming clusters of clear, fluid‑filled vesicles on the skin or mucosa (often present at birth or in early childhood; may leak fluid or become infected; treat options include observation, laser therapy, or excision for symptoms).

lymphangiomata.definition: A benign congenital malformation of the lymphatic vessels characterized by dilated lymphatic channels that form cystic, soft, compressible masses.

lymphangiogram.definition: A radiologic imaging procedure in which a contrast agent is injected into lymphatic vessels (typically in the foot) to visualize lymphatic channels and regional lymph nodes, used to evaluate lymphatic disorders, leaks, or chylous effusions.

lymphangiography.definition: An imaging procedure in which contrast material is injected into the lymphatic vessels (commonly in the foot) to visualize the lymphatic system on radiographs, used to diagnose lymphatic obstruction, leaks, and malformations.

lymphatic capillary.definition: A microscopic, blind-ended lymphatic vessel in tissues that collects interstitial fluid, proteins, lipids, and cells; lined by a single layer of loosely connected endothelial cells with overlapping junctions that form primary valves, allowing unidirectional entry of fluid and anchored to surrounding tissue by filaments.

lymphatic capillary plexus.definition: A network of microscopic lymphatic capillaries in tissues that absorbs interstitial fluid, proteins, and lipids; composed of overlapping endothelial cells forming primary valves, anchored by filaments to surrounding connective tissue, and draining into collecting lymphatic vessels.

lymphatic vasculitis.definition: Inflammation of the lymphatic vessels (lymphatics), typically secondary to infection or inflammatory processes, causing tenderness and swelling along lymphatic channels and sometimes erythematous streaking.

lymphangiectasia.definition: Dilation of lymphatic vessels, which can be primary (congenital) or secondary to obstruction; when involving intestinal lymphatics, it can cause protein-losing enteropathy with hypoalbuminemia and edema.

lymphatic vessel.definition: An elastic, thin-walled conduit of the lymphatic system that transports lymph (interstitial fluid, immune cells, and absorbed fats) from tissues toward the venous circulation, beginning as blind-ended lymphatic capillaries and containing valves to ensure unidirectional flow.

lymph vessel.definition: A thin-walled tube that carries lymph (interstitial fluid and immune cells) from tissues toward the venous circulation; it contains valves to prevent backflow and, in larger vessels, smooth muscle.

lymphadenectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove one or more lymph nodes, typically performed to stage cancer and/or reduce the spread of disease.

malpighian body.definition: The renal corpuscle of a nephron in the kidney, consisting of Bowman's capsule surrounding a glomerulus; the site of blood filtration that forms the initial filtrate (glomerular filtrate) for urine formation.

pyloric region.definition: Distal part of the stomach between the body and the pylorus, including the pyloric antrum and pyloric canal, containing the pyloric sphincter that regulates emptying of stomach contents into the duodenum.

lymphatic follicles.definition: A nodular aggregation of lymphoid tissue rich in B cells, found in lymphoid organs such as lymph nodes, spleen, and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue; primary follicles lack germinal centers, while secondary (germinal) follicles have germinal centers where B cells proliferate and differentiate during an immune response.

lymphocryptovirus.definition: A genus of enveloped double‑stranded DNA herpesviruses in the family Herpesviridae, subfamily Gammaherpesvirinae, that naturally infect primates and primarily target B lymphocytes; Epstein‑Barr virus is the best‑known member. They establish latent infection in B cells and are associated with infectious mononucleosis and various B‑cell lymphomas and other lymphoproliferative diseases, with transmission commonly via saliva.

b lymphocytes.definition: An adaptive immune system lymphocyte that matures in the bone marrow and mediates humoral immunity by recognizing specific antigens via surface immunoglobulin receptors; upon activation they differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells and memory B cells, and can present antigen to helper T cells.

lymphocyte immune globulin.definition: A preparation of antibodies directed against lymphocytes used to deplete lymphocytes and suppress immune responses in transplantation and certain immune-mediated conditions.

antithymocyte.definition: An antibody directed against thymocytes (T lymphocytes), used to deplete T cells in transplantation and other immunosuppressive therapies.

ospa.definition: Outer surface protein A (OspA) is a Borrelia burgdorferi lipoprotein encoded by the ospA gene; a major surface antigen expressed in the tick midgut that helps the bacterium adhere and survive in the vector, with expression downregulated in the mammalian host. Antibodies to OspA have been used in Lyme disease vaccines and can block transmission by ticks.

outer surface protein a.definition: A major outer-surface lipoprotein of Borrelia burgdorferi; expressed on the bacterium's surface, especially in the tick midgut, where it aids adherence and survival in the vector; it is immunogenic and was used as the target in a Lyme disease vaccine.

lyme disease vaccine.definition: A vaccine designed to prevent Lyme disease by inducing immunity to Borrelia burgdorferi, typically by targeting its antigens (for example, outer surface protein A). A human vaccine (LYMErix) was once licensed in the United States but withdrawn in 2002; currently, there is no approved human Lyme disease vaccine, though several candidates are under development.

thiazide diuretics.definition: A class of diuretics that inhibits the Na+-Cl− cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, increasing excretion of sodium and chloride (and water) with a tendency to cause potassium loss; used to treat hypertension and edema (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, indapamide, metolazone).

pelvic tuberculosis.definition: An extrapulmonary form of tuberculosis affecting the female genital tract, most often the fallopian tubes and endometrium, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It may present with chronic pelvic pain, infertility, abnormal uterine bleeding, or pelvic masses and can mimic ovarian or peritoneal disease. Diagnosis is by microbiologic/histologic confirmation (eg, acid-fast bacilli or granulomatous inflammation on biopsy, culture or PCR) and imaging; treated with standard anti-tuberculous therapy for 6–9 months, with surgery reserved for complications.

mesenteric metastases.definition: Spread of malignant cells to the mesentery (the peritoneal fold attaching the intestines) from a primary cancer, resulting in nodular mesenteric implants and potential complications such as bowel obstruction or peritoneal carcinomatosis.

mesenteric node metastases.definition: Metastatic cancer in the mesenteric lymph nodes—the lymph nodes embedded in the mesentery—reflecting lymphatic spread from an intra-abdominal primary tumor, most commonly colorectal cancer.

wheals.definition: A raised, pruritic, well-demarcated swelling of the skin due to superficial dermal edema and capillary dilation; it is transient and typically blanches with pressure, as seen in urticaria (hives).

faintness.definition: A subjective feeling of lightheadedness or weakness, sometimes with dizziness or blurred vision, that may precede fainting (syncope).

lymphoid system.definition: A group of lymphoid tissues and organs—such as bone marrow, thymus, spleen, lymph nodes, and tonsils—that generate and host lymphocytes (B and T cells) and coordinate adaptive immune responses through the lymphatic system.

light-headedness.definition: A feeling of faintness or wooziness, usually described as near-fainting, caused by transiently reduced blood flow to the brain or other reversible factors such as dehydration, orthostatic hypotension, hypoglycemia, anemia, certain medications, or hyperventilation.

postviral encephalopathy.definition: An acute or subacute brain dysfunction that follows a viral illness, presenting with altered mental status (e.g., confusion, lethargy) and sometimes seizures or focal neurologic signs, in the absence of ongoing active infection. Pathogenesis is thought to be immune-mediated or metabolic rather than due to direct viral injury; management is supportive, and prognosis ranges from full recovery to residual deficits.

liver function tests.definition: A panel of blood tests used to assess liver health and function, typically measuring liver enzymes (AST, ALT), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT); bilirubin (total and direct); and markers of synthetic function such as albumin and prothrombin time/INR.

opportunistic infections.definition: An infection that occurs due to a weakened immune system, allowing normally nonpathogenic organisms to cause disease.

lymphocyte transformation.definition: A process by which lymphocytes activate, enlarge into blast cells, and proliferate in response to antigenic or mitogenic stimulation, reflecting an activated cell-mediated immune response.

t memory cells.definition: A subset of T lymphocytes that persists after an initial antigen exposure, enabling a faster, more robust immune response upon re-encounter with the same antigen. They originate during the primary immune response from activated naive T cells and can be long-lived, circulating or residing in tissues. Subsets include central memory, effector memory, and tissue-resident memory cells.

radioactive thymidine.definition: Thymidine labeled with a radioactive isotope (commonly 3H or 14C) used as a tracer to measure DNA synthesis; it is incorporated into newly synthesized DNA during S phase and detected by autoradiography or scintillation counting.

lymphocytic choriomeningitis.definition: A rodent-borne viral infection caused by lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (an arenavirus); commonly presents as aseptic meningitis or meningoencephalitis with fever and headache and lymphocytic pleocytosis in CSF, and can cause congenital infection with hydrocephalus, microcephaly, or ocular abnormalities if acquired during pregnancy.

helicobacter pylori infection.definition: A chronic infection of the stomach caused by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori, which colonizes the gastric mucosa and is a major cause of gastritis and peptic ulcer disease and is associated with an increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma. Diagnosis is typically by urea breath test, stool antigen test, or endoscopic biopsy with histology/rapid urease test; treatment involves antibiotic therapy combined with acid suppression to eradicate the infection.

lymphocytic gastritis.definition: A histopathologic pattern of gastritis defined by prominent intraepithelial lymphocytosis in the gastric surface epithelium with a chronic lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate in the lamina propria; often associated with Helicobacter pylori infection or celiac disease, but can occur in other contexts.

lymphocytic hypophysitis.definition: An autoimmune inflammatory disease of the pituitary gland characterized by lymphocytic infiltration causing pituitary enlargement and varying degrees of hormonal deficiency; it often occurs in the peripartum period and can mimic a pituitary tumor.

lymphoid leukemia.definition: A type of leukemia arising from lymphoid cells (B-, T-, or NK-lineage) with clonal proliferation of malignant lymphocytes or lymphoblasts in the bone marrow and blood; includes acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).

lymphocytic lymphoma.definition: An indolent nodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma composed of small, mature-appearing lymphocytes; historically used for the nodal presentation of chronic lymphocytic leukemia, now usually classified as chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL); presents with painless lymphadenopathy and often marrow involvement, and may progress or transform to a more aggressive lymphoma.

lymphosarcoma.definition: A malignant tumor of lymphoid tissue arising from lymphocytes; an older term for lymphoma.

well-differentiated lymphocytic malignan.definition: An indolent (low‑grade) malignant lymphoma composed predominantly of mature, small lymphocytes; historically called well-differentiated lymphocytic lymphoma and now generally equated with small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), often considered part of the CLL/SLL spectrum (with blood/bone marrow involvement producing CLL).

hashimoto’s disease.definition: An autoimmune thyroiditis in which immune-mediated destruction of the thyroid gland leads to progressive hypothyroidism; commonly associated with anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies and a painless goiter, and occurs more often in women.

lymphocytoma.definition: A localized tumor or lesion composed primarily of lymphocytes; a proliferation of lymphoid tissue.

lymphocytopenia.definition: An abnormally low lymphocyte count in the peripheral blood, reflecting diminished adaptive immune function; typically defined as a count below the laboratory's lower limit of normal (often <1.0 x 10^9/L in adults).

lymphocytotoxic antibody.definition: An antibody directed against lymphocyte surface antigens that destroys these cells by the action of complement (complement-dependent cytotoxicity).

lymphocytotrophic.definition: Having a tropism for lymphocytes; preferentially affecting or infecting lymphocytes.

lymphoepithelioma.definition: A histologic subtype of nasopharyngeal carcinoma consisting of undifferentiated malignant epithelial cells with a prominent lymphoid (lymphocyte-rich) stroma; strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus.

lymphogenesis.definition: The formation and development of lymphocytes (lymphopoiesis) from hematopoietic progenitors, primarily in the bone marrow and thymus, with maturation and differentiation of B and T cells.

lymphogenous leukemia.definition: A leukemia of lymphoid origin—malignant proliferation of lymphoid cells (lymphoblasts in acute lymphoblastic leukemia or mature lymphocytes in chronic lymphocytic leukemia) in the bone marrow and peripheral blood, arising from the lymphoid lineage rather than the myeloid lineage.

lymphogranulomatosis.definition: A sexually transmitted infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1–L3, presenting initially with a transient genital or rectal lesion, followed by tender inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes) that may suppurate; can involve proctitis in anorectal cases.

hodgkin’s disease.definition: A type of cancer that grows in a part of your immune system (your lymph nodes).

lymphadenoma venereum.definition: A sexually transmitted infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1–L3, characterized by an initial often painless genital or rectal lesion followed by painful inguinal and/or femoral lymphadenopathy (buboes), sometimes with proctocolitis in anorectal infections.

lgv.definition: A sexually transmitted infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1–L3, characterized by a transient genital lesion followed by tender inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes), which can progress to proctocolitis in some patients.

aseptic technique.definition: A set of practices used to prevent contamination by microorganisms in medical procedures, including hand hygiene, sterilization of instruments, use of sterile barriers (gloves, gowns, drapes), and proper wound or invasive-line care.

lymphography.definition: A radiographic imaging procedure in which radiopaque contrast is injected into lymphatic vessels or nodes to visualize the lymphatic system, allowing assessment of lymphatic drainage, obstruction, or related abnormalities.

severe combined immunodeficiency.definition: An inherited primary immunodeficiency characterized by markedly reduced or absent T-cell function, with concomitant B- and often NK-cell defects, resulting in severe, recurrent infections beginning in infancy; caused by genetic mutations and often treated with hematopoietic stem cell transplantation or gene therapy.

peyer’s patches.definition: Organized lymphoid follicles in the lamina propria and submucosa of the distal ileum, forming part of the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT); they sample luminal antigens via M cells and initiate mucosal immune responses (including IgA production).

waldeyer’s ring.definition: A ring of lymphoid tissue in the pharynx (nasopharynx and oropharynx) that defends the upper aerodigestive tract, formed by the adenoids (pharyngeal tonsil), tubal tonsils, palatine tonsils, and lingual tonsils.

lymphokine.definition: A cytokine produced by lymphocytes (especially T cells) that modulates or mediates immune responses by signaling to other immune cells.

lymphotoxin.definition: A cytokine of the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) superfamily produced mainly by lymphocytes; it exists as a soluble LT-α (TNF-β) homotrimer and as a membrane-bound LT-α1β2 heterotrimer, signaling through TNF receptors and the LTβ receptor to regulate immune responses, inflammation, and lymphoid tissue development.

migration inhibiting factor.definition: A lymphokine produced by sensitized T lymphocytes that inhibits macrophage migration in response to antigenic stimulation; an early immune cytokine later characterized as regulating macrophage trafficking.

mitogenic factor.definition: A substance that stimulates cell division (mitosis) and proliferation; a mitogen.

lak cells.definition: Antigen-presenting dendritic cells located in the epidermis that capture microbial antigens and migrate to regional lymph nodes to activate naive T cells, initiating adaptive immune responses.

memory cytotoxic thymus-derived lymphocy.definition: Long-lived memory CD8+ T lymphocytes that originate from thymus-derived T cells; after initial antigen exposure they persist and rapidly proliferate and exert cytotoxic effects upon re-exposure to the same antigen.

burkitt’s lymphoma.definition: A highly aggressive B‑cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma driven by MYC gene translocations (most commonly t(8;14)), leading to rapid tumor growth; commonly presents with jaw/facial masses in endemic areas and abdominal involvement in sporadic cases; highly responsive to intensive short‑course chemotherapy.

histiocytic malignant lymphoma.definition: A historical term for a malignant proliferation of histiocyte (macrophage-lineage) cells that can mimic lymphoma clinically and pathologically; not a true lymphoid lymphoma; in modern terminology it corresponds to malignant histiocytosis or histiocytic sarcoma, a rare and aggressive neoplasm of histiocytes.

mixed cell malignant lymphoma.definition: A lymphoma in which the malignant lymphoid cells are heterogeneous, consisting of a mixture of different cell types or sizes (e.g., small and large lymphocytes) rather than a uniform clone. This is not a single formal entity; pathology reports may describe it as mixed cellularity or a mixed histology, with subtype classification based on immunophenotype and molecular features.

lymphoma staging.definition: Process of determining the extent and distribution of lymphoma in the body to guide treatment and prognosis. It most commonly uses the Ann Arbor (Cotswold) staging system, classifying disease into stages I–IV based on the number and location of involved lymph node regions and extranodal sites, with B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss) and bulky disease serving as modifiers; assessment typically involves imaging (CT or PET-CT) and, for some subtypes, bone marrow biopsy.

lymphomatoid granulomatosis.definition: A rare, Epstein-Barr virus–driven B‑cell lymphoproliferative disorder characterized by angiocentric and angiodestructive granulomatous lesions—most often in the lungs—containing EBV‑positive B cells with a reactive T‑cell infiltrate; can involve other organs and may progress to overt lymphoma.

wegener’s granulomatosis.definition: A form of ANCA-associated vasculitis characterized by necrotizing granulomatous inflammation of the upper and lower airways and necrotizing vasculitis of small- to medium-sized vessels, commonly presenting with sinusitis, pulmonary nodules or infiltrates, and glomerulonephritis; often associated with PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA).

waldeyer’s throat ring.definition: A circular assembly of lymphoid tissue in the pharynx that guards the entrance to the respiratory and digestive tracts by sampling inhaled and ingested antigens; it includes the palatine tonsils, pharyngeal (adenoids), lingual tonsils, and tubal tonsils.

lymphoreticular system.definition: A network of lymphoid tissues and reticuloendothelial (phagocytic) cells that filter lymph and blood and mediate immune responses; includes lymph nodes, spleen, thymus, tonsils, and macrophage systems in liver, bone marrow, and other organs.

lymphorrhagia.definition: Abnormal discharge of lymph fluid from a damaged lymphatic vessel or fistula, typically after surgery or trauma.

cystadenolymphoma.definition: A benign salivary gland tumor, most often arising in the parotid, characterized by cystic spaces with papillary epithelial infoldings lined by oncocytic cells and a dense lymphoid stroma containing germinal centers.

adenolymphoma.definition: Benign cystic tumor of the parotid gland characterized by cystic spaces with papillary infoldings lined by oncocytic epithelium and a prominent lymphoid stroma; strongly associated with smoking; also known as Warthin tumor (papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum).

angiolymphoma.definition: A benign vascular lesion of the skin and subcutaneous tissue characterized by proliferation of blood vessels with plump epithelioid endothelial cells and a mixed inflammatory infiltrate rich in eosinophils; not a true lymphoma.

serological blood test.definition: A blood test that detects antibodies to pathogens or antigens in a patient's serum, used to diagnose infections, determine immune status, or monitor exposure.

mycosis fungoides.definition: A malignant cutaneous T-cell lymphoma characterized by clonal proliferation of mature CD4+ helper T cells that predominate in the skin, presenting with patches, plaques, or tumors; often indolent but can progress to erythroderma and systemic involvement (Sezary syndrome). Histology shows epidermotropic atypical T cells and, commonly, Pautrier microabscesses.

bone lesions.definition: A localized area of abnormal bone tissue that appears different from surrounding bone on imaging; it can reflect benign conditions, malignant tumors or metastases, infection, trauma with healing, or metabolic/inflammatory diseases and often requires clinical correlation and possibly further imaging or biopsy to determine the cause.

acquired immunodeficiency syndrome–relat.definition: An aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma that arises in people with AIDS (advanced HIV infection), typically a high-grade B-cell neoplasm (most often diffuse large B-cell lymphoma) that is frequently EBV-associated and often presents with extranodal disease; historically an AIDS-defining illness, with incidence reduced by antiretroviral therapy but still more common in HIV-infected individuals than in the general population.

chemotactic factor.definition: A chemical substance that induces chemotaxis, attracting immune cells to move toward higher concentrations of the substance, typically guiding leukocytes to sites of infection or tissue damage.

irrelevant.definition: Not related or pertinent to the clinical condition, diagnostic question, or management being considered; not useful for diagnosis, prognosis, or treatment decisions.

lymphotrophy.definition: Growth or nourishment of lymphatic tissue; a trophic effect or influence on the lymphatic system.

lymph vessels.definition: Thin-walled, valved vessels of the lymphatic system that transport lymph, the interstitial fluid collected from tissues, toward the venous circulation; they drain lymph through lymph nodes and play a role in immune defense and fat absorption (via intestinal lacteals).
