lysholm method.definition: A questionnaire-based knee function scoring system used to assess outcomes after knee ligament injuries and surgeries (notably ACL reconstruction). It evaluates eight domains—limp, need for support, instability/locking, pain, swelling, climbing stairs, and squatting—with higher scores indicating better knee function; the total score ranges up to 100.

maceration.definition: The softening and breakdown of skin or tissue due to prolonged exposure to moisture, such as wound exudate or urine, resulting in pale, wrinkled, fragile tissue that is more prone to damage and infection.

macrencephaly.definition: An abnormally large brain (megalencephaly), often congenital or developmental in origin and frequently associated with neurodevelopmental delays or seizures; distinct from macrocephaly, which refers to an enlarged head rather than brain size.

macrocephaly.definition: An abnormally large head size, defined as a head circumference more than two standard deviations above the mean for age and sex; it can be benign/familial or associated with underlying conditions such as hydrocephalus, megalencephaly, or certain genetic syndromes.

macroadenoma.definition: A pituitary adenoma larger than 1 centimeter in diameter; may be nonfunctioning or hormonally active, and its size can compress nearby structures (notably the optic chiasm causing visual field defects and headaches). Functional tumors may secrete excess hormones (e.g., prolactin, growth hormone, or ACTH).

macroamylase.definition: A condition in which circulating amylase forms high-molecular-weight complexes with immunoglobulins (most commonly IgG) or other serum proteins, preventing renal clearance and causing a persistent elevation of serum amylase without pancreatitis.

macroamylasemia.definition: A benign condition in which elevated serum amylase is due to the formation of macroamylase—amylase complexed with immunoglobulins (usually IgG)—leading to reduced renal clearance and persistent high serum amylase with low or absent urinary amylase, in the absence of pancreatitis.

macrobiosis.definition: A rare/archaic term meaning life in a macroscopic form—life large enough to be seen with the naked eye—as opposed to microscopic life; not a standard term in contemporary medical terminology.

macrobiotic.definition: Relating to a dietary approach emphasizing whole grains and plant-based foods with limited refined foods and animal products; associated with balancing bodily energies in some traditional beliefs, but with little high-quality evidence of medical benefit and not a substitute for proven therapies.

macroblepharia.definition: An abnormal enlargement of the eyelids (blepharon), usually due to excess eyelid tissue or edema, which may be congenital or acquired and can cause cosmetic concerns or functional eyelid impairment.

macrocephalic.definition: Relating to an abnormally large head; head circumference above the normal range for age and sex, typically above the 97th percentile or more than 2 standard deviations above the mean.

macrocephalous.definition: Having an abnormally large head; characterized by an excessive head circumference for age and sex (often defined as above the 97th percentile).

macrocephalus.definition: An abnormally large head; an enlarged skull or head circumference that is above the normal range for age and sex, often a morphological finding that can be associated with conditions such as hydrocephalus or megalencephaly.

macrocyte.definition: An abnormally large red blood cell, typically with an increased mean corpuscular volume, seen in conditions such as megaloblastic anemia due to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, liver disease, alcoholism, and hypothyroidism.

macrocytosis.definition: Macrocytosis is the presence of abnormally large red blood cells on a peripheral smear, typically with an elevated mean corpuscular volume (MCV > 100 fL); it commonly reflects impaired DNA synthesis (e.g., vitamin B12 or folate deficiency) but can also occur with liver disease, alcoholism, hypothyroidism, or reticulocytosis.

macrodrip.definition: A method of intravenous fluid administration using an infusion set with a larger drop factor (typically 10–20 drops per milliliter) to deliver IV fluids at a faster rate than microdrip systems.

macrodantin.definition: Brand-name nitrofurantoin; an oral antibiotic used to treat and prevent uncomplicated urinary tract infections caused by susceptible bacteria; it concentrates in urine and is not effective for systemic infections.

macrodex.definition: A brand-name intravenous solution containing dextran (typically dextran 40) used as a plasma volume expander to increase circulating blood volume in hypovolemia or during surgery; it can interfere with coagulation and may cause allergic reactions.

macroelement.definition: An essential chemical element required by living organisms in relatively large amounts for normal growth, development, and metabolism; in human nutrition these macroelements include calcium, phosphorus, potassium, magnesium, sulfur, sodium, and chloride, and are contrasted with trace (micro) elements.

macroelements.definition: Elements required by living organisms in relatively large amounts; collectively known as major minerals (macrominerals), they include calcium, phosphorus, potassium, magnesium, sulfur, sodium, and chloride, and are essential for bone formation, fluid balance, nerve and muscle function, and acid-base balance.

macrogamete.definition: The large, nonmotile female gamete produced in oogamous or anisogamous reproduction; it fuses with a smaller, motile male gamete (microgamete) to form a zygote.

macrogametocyte.definition: A mature female gametocyte of Plasmodium species (malaria parasites); a large sexual stage formed in infected red blood cells that is taken up by a mosquito and fertilizes with a microgamete to form a zygote.

macroglobulin.definition: A high-molecular-weight plasma protein that acts as a broad-spectrum protease inhibitor by trapping proteases in covalent complexes; the predominant human form is alpha-2-macroglobulin, produced by the liver.

macroglobulinemia.definition: A monoclonal gammopathy with markedly elevated serum IgM due to clonal B‑cell proliferation (lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma), often causing hyperviscosity and related neurologic, hematologic, and constitutional symptoms.

waldenström's macroglobulinemia.definition: A type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma) characterized by clonal proliferation of lymphoplasmacytic cells in the bone marrow that produce an IgM monoclonal immunoglobulin, often causing hyperviscosity syndrome and cytopenias, with symptoms such as fatigue, anemia, mucosal bleeding, and visual disturbances.

mycobacterium avium complex disease.definition: An infection caused by the Mycobacterium avium complex, a group of non-tuberculous mycobacteria (primarily M. avium and M. intracellulare). It typically presents as chronic pulmonary disease in older adults or as disseminated disease in severely immunocompromised individuals (e.g., advanced HIV/AIDS).

monoclonal antibody.definition: A laboratory-produced antibody derived from a single B-cell clone that binds to a single specific antigen epitope, used for targeted therapy or diagnosis.

minimum alveolar concentration.definition: The alveolar concentration of an inhaled anesthetic at which 50% of patients do not move in response to a standardized noxious stimulus (e.g., a skin incision); a measure of anesthetic potency, with lower MAC indicating greater potency, typically expressed as a percentage of inspired gas at 1 atmosphere.

midupper arm circumference.definition: A measurement of the circumference of the upper arm taken at the midpoint between the acromion and the olecranon, using a non‑stretchable tape; used to assess nutritional status and muscle mass, especially in children and in malnutrition screening; lower values indicate undernutrition or risk of malnutrition.

anopheles.definition: A genus of mosquitoes in the family Culicidae; several species are primary vectors of human malaria, transmitting Plasmodium parasites to humans via female mosquito blood meals.

lysine intolerance.definition: An adverse, nonimmune reaction to ingestion or supplementation of the essential amino acid lysine, typically due to malabsorption or metabolic intolerance rather than an allergy; management involves limiting lysine-containing foods or supplements and addressing any underlying metabolic issues.

lysinemia.definition: A metabolic disorder characterized by abnormally high levels of the essential amino acid lysine in blood and urine, caused by defects in lysine breakdown (catabolism) or transport; may be benign or associated with other aminoacidurias such as lysinuric protein intolerance.

lysine monohydrochloride.definition: A salt form of the essential amino acid lysine created by reacting lysine with hydrochloric acid; used to provide lysine in dietary supplements and nutritional formulations.

lysin.definition: A lytic enzyme produced by some bacteriophages that cleaves bonds in the bacterial peptidoglycan, leading to cell wall rupture and lysis; used in phage therapy research and as antibacterial agents.

lysinuria.definition: The excretion of abnormally high amounts of the amino acid lysine in the urine, typically due to impaired renal reabsorption or a metabolic disorder such as lysinuric protein intolerance.

lysinurea.definition: The presence of lysine in the urine; an aminoaciduria in which excess lysine is excreted in the urine, often seen in lysinuric protein intolerance due to defective transport of dibasic amino acids.

lysate.definition: A solution containing the contents released from cells after lysis (cell membranes disrupted), including proteins, nucleic acids, and other intracellular components; used in biochemical assays and molecular biology workflows.

lysodren.definition: An adrenolytic antineoplastic agent (mitotane) used to treat adrenocortical carcinoma and sometimes refractory Cushing's syndrome; it selectively destroys adrenal cortical cells, suppressing cortisol production and requiring monitoring for adrenal insufficiency and toxicity.

lysogenesis.definition: The process by which a temperate bacteriophage integrates its genome into a host bacterium, establishing a latent lysogenic infection (prophage) that does not immediately lyse the cell and can later be induced to enter the lytic cycle.

lysokinase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the transfer of a phosphate group to lysine residues on substrate molecules; lysine phosphorylation is a relatively rare and not well-established regulatory modification in most contexts, so the term is not widely standardized.

lysotype.definition: A cell type or classification characterized by prominent lysosomes or high lysosomal enzyme activity; used mainly in research to describe lysosome-rich cells and is not a widely standardized clinical term.

synesthesia.definition: A perceptual phenomenon in which stimulation of one sensory modality leads to involuntary experiences in a second modality (for example, hearing sounds that evoke colors).

panic.definition: A sudden, intense surge of fear or dread, often accompanied by autonomic arousal (e.g., rapid heartbeat, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath) and a sense of impending doom; in clinical use, such episodes are called panic attacks and typically peak within minutes.

paranoid behavior.definition: A pattern of unwarranted distrust and suspicion of others' motives, interpreting their actions as malicious or persecutory, often with hypervigilance and defensive or hostile responses; it can occur in several psychiatric conditions (e.g., paranoid personality disorder, delusional disorder persecutory type, schizophrenia) and can impair social and occupational functioning.

psychotic episodes.definition: A period during which a person loses touch with reality, characterized by delusions or hallucinations, disorganized thinking or behavior, and impaired insight or judgment, resulting in distress or functional impairment; can occur in schizophrenia, bipolar disorder with psychotic features, severe depression, substance-induced psychosis, or medical illness.

macrognathia.definition: Abnormally enlarged jaw, typically the mandible, which may be congenital or acquired and can cause facial disproportion and dental malocclusion; may be seen in conditions such as acromegaly or fibrous dysplasia.

macula densa.definition: A group of tall, densely packed cells in the distal tubule of the nephron, located at the juxtaglomerular apparatus where the tubule contacts the afferent arteriole. They sense sodium chloride concentration in the filtrate and initiate tubuloglomerular feedback to modulate glomerular filtration rate and renin release.

macula albida.definition: A flat, non-palpable white patch on the skin or mucous membrane representing hypopigmentation or depigmentation; a descriptive white macule rather than a specific diagnosis.

milk patch.definition: Not a standard medical term. If referring to milk-related allergy testing, standard evaluations include skin prick testing or oral food challenges for cow’s milk protein; patch testing is used for contact dermatitis and is not a routine diagnostic method for milk allergy.

macula atrophica.definition: A degenerative condition of the retina in which the macula—the central area responsible for detailed vision—undergoes atrophy and thinning, causing progressive loss of central vision; often used to describe atrophic changes seen in macular degeneration.

macula cerulea.definition: A bluish discoloration or lesion of the macula, the center of the retina responsible for high-acuity vision; an older or descriptive term rather than a specific disease.

macula solaris.definition: Not a standard term in modern anatomy; likely an obsolete or erroneous reference to the macula lutea, the central retina region responsible for high-acuity, detailed vision.

macular.definition: Relating to the macula, the central region of the retina responsible for high-acuity, detailed central vision.

macular dystrophy.definition: An inherited retinal dystrophy primarily affecting the macula, causing progressive loss of central vision due to degeneration or dysfunction of the macular photoreceptors and supporting retinal pigment epithelium. It encompasses several conditions with variable age of onset and inheritance patterns, such as Stargardt disease and Best disease.

macular rash.definition: A rash in which the lesions are macules—flat, non-palpable, color-changed patches of skin that are level with the surrounding surface, typically less than 1 cm in diameter.

maculopathy.definition: A disease or pathology of the macula, the central portion of the retina responsible for sharp, detailed central vision. Such macular diseases can cause central vision loss or distortion and include conditions like age-related macular degeneration, diabetic macular edema, and macular hole.

macrognathic.definition: Pertaining to macrognathia; having an abnormally large mandible (lower jaw).

macronodular adrenal disease.definition: A bilateral adrenal cortical disorder characterized by macronodular hyperplasia (nodules >1 cm) of the adrenal cortex that autonomously secretes cortisol, producing ACTH-independent Cushing’s syndrome; cortisol secretion may be stimulated by non-ACTH signals due to aberrant hormone receptor expression.

macronucleus.definition: A large, transcriptionally active somatic nucleus of certain ciliates (e.g., Paramecium, Tetrahymena) that governs everyday metabolic and vegetative functions; it is polyploid and divides amitotically, while the micronucleus serves as the germline.

micronucleus.definition: A small extranuclear chromatin-containing body formed from chromosomes or chromosome fragments that fail to be incorporated into the daughter nuclei during cell division; used as a biomarker of genotoxicity and chromosomal damage.

macronutrient.definition: A nutrient required in relatively large amounts by the body to supply energy, support growth and maintenance, and regulate metabolism; the main macronutrients are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, and water.

macroovalocyte.definition: An enlarged, oval-shaped red blood cell (macrocyte) commonly seen in megaloblastic anemias due to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, reflecting impaired DNA synthesis and asynchronous maturation of the nucleus and cytoplasm in erythroid precursors.

macropenis.definition: An abnormally large penis, typically defined as an erect or stretched penile length more than 2.5 standard deviations above the mean for age; may be a benign familial variation or associated with hormonal disorders causing androgen excess or precocious puberty.

macrophage activating factor.definition: A cytokine that enhances the antimicrobial and antigen-presenting functions of macrophages, increasing phagocytosis, microbicidal activity (reactive oxygen and nitrogen species production), and cytokine secretion; the principal activator in humans is interferon-gamma produced by T cells and NK cells.

macroprolactinoma.definition: A prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma larger than 1 cm in diameter (a macroadenoma), causing hyperprolactinemia and potential mass effects such as headaches and visual field defects, along with hypogonadism.

bromocriptine.definition: A dopamine D2 receptor agonist (ergot-derived) used to treat hyperprolactinemia and Parkinson disease; it suppresses prolactin secretion from the pituitary and is also used to suppress lactation and, in some cases, to treat acromegaly.

macropsia.definition: A perceptual distortion in which visual objects appear larger than their actual size; a form of metamorphopsia that can occur with migraines, temporal lobe epilepsy, occipital lobe lesions, or certain drug effects.

macroreentry circuit.definition: A reentrant tachycardia that propagates around a large circuit, typically encircling nonconductive tissue or an anatomical obstacle (such as scar tissue or the annulus), resulting in a sustained rapid heart rate.

bundle branch reentry.definition: A macroreentrant ventricular tachycardia in which the reentry circuit uses the His-Purkinje system, typically involving the bundle branches; activation propagates antegrade down one bundle branch and retrograde up the other, forming a loop around the ventricular septum.

macroscopic.definition: Visible to the naked eye; not requiring magnification.

microscopic.definition: Visible only under a microscope; too small to be seen with the naked eye; pertaining to observations or specimens examined with magnification.

macroshock.definition: An electrical injury caused by exposure to a relatively large external current passing through the body, typically producing painful muscular contractions, respiratory difficulties, burns, and potentially ventricular fibrillation; in contrast to microshock, which involves small currents delivered directly to internal conductors.

macrosis.definition: Not a standard medical term; there is no widely accepted definition. It may be a misspelling or rare usage. If you meant tissue softening, the related term is malacia (softening of a tissue). If you meant moisture-induced softening of skin or tissue, the term is maceration. If you have a specific context, I can help clarify.

macrosomia.definition: A newborn with an excessive size for gestational age, typically defined as birth weight >4,000 g (8 lb 13 oz) or above the 90th percentile for gestational age; often associated with maternal diabetes or obesity and increased risk of delivery complications and birth injuries.

macrostomia.definition: An abnormally wide mouth or oral aperture, a congenital craniofacial anomaly that can occur as an isolated finding or as part of syndromic conditions.

macrotear.definition: Enlargement of the external ear (pinna) beyond the normal size; can be congenital or acquired and may occur as an isolated finding or as part of a broader syndrome, often mainly a cosmetic concern.

madelung's neck.definition: Symmetric accumulation of non-encapsulated adipose tissue around the neck (often extending to the upper trunk), producing a prominent “horse-collar” or buffalo-neck appearance; a benign lipomatosis variant associated with metabolic disturbances and frequently linked to alcohol use, with treatment typically involving liposuction or surgical debulking for cosmetic or functional relief.

mad hatter's disease.definition: Historical term for mercury poisoning (mercurialism) due to occupational exposure (notably in hatmakers); characterized by tremors, irritability and personality changes (erethism), cognitive/sensory disturbances, and gingivitis.

madigan prostatectomy.definition: Not a widely recognized term; in general, a prostatectomy is the surgical removal of the prostate gland, usually for prostate cancer or benign prostatic hyperplasia, with approaches including radical retropubic, perineal, laparoscopic, and robotic-assisted techniques.

perineal prostatectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove the prostate gland through an incision in the perineum, typically performed for localized prostate cancer (radical perineal prostatectomy), sometimes including removal of the seminal vesicles.

madura foot.definition: A chronic subcutaneous infection of the foot caused by certain fungi (eumycetoma) or actinomycete bacteria (actinomycetoma), presenting with painless swelling, multiple draining sinuses, and grain-containing discharge, and may involve underlying bone.

maduromycosis.definition: A chronic subcutaneous fungal infection (a form of eumycetoma) caused by Madurella species, presenting with localized swelling, multiple draining sinuses, and grain-containing discharge.

maedi visna virus.definition: A sheep lentivirus (Retroviridae) causing chronic disease with maedi (progressive interstitial pneumonia) and visna (progressive demyelinating disease of the CNS); transmitted via respiratory secretions and milk/colostrum; lifelong infection with no cure and limited/no vaccine; control via testing and culling.

maedi/visna virus.definition: Maedi–visna virus is a lentivirus in the Retroviridae family that chronically infects sheep, causing Maedi (progressive interstitial pneumonia) and Visna (progressive demyelinating disease of the CNS); transmitted mainly via prolonged close contact and milk, leading to lifelong infection with gradual respiratory or neurological decline.

mafenide acetate.definition: A topical sulfonamide antibiotic used to prevent and treat infection in burn wounds; applied as a cream (mafenide acetate) that penetrates burned eschar and inhibits bacterial folic acid synthesis.

magaldrate.definition: An antacid preparation consisting of aluminum and magnesium salts that neutralizes gastric acid to relieve heartburn, indigestion, and other dyspeptic symptoms.

magendie's law.definition: A principle in neurophysiology stating that the dorsal (posterior) roots of spinal nerves carry sensory (afferent) fibers and the ventral (anterior) roots carry motor (efferent) fibers.

magical thinking.definition: A belief that one's thoughts, words, or actions can influence or cause events in the world despite a lack of causal connection or empirical evidence.

magic-bullet approach.definition: An approach to therapy that aims to selectively target disease-causing organisms or abnormal cells with agents that have minimal toxicity to normal host tissues.

magill forceps.definition: Curved, slender forceps used to facilitate airway management by guiding an endotracheal tube into the trachea during intubation and to retrieve foreign bodies from the oropharynx.

maglinte tube.definition: Definition not found in standard medical dictionaries. Please verify spelling or provide context (field or use) so I can help accurately.

magnesemia.definition: The concentration of magnesium in the blood; a laboratory measure used to assess magnesium status.

milk of magnesia.definition: A suspension of magnesium hydroxide in water used as an osmotic laxative and antacid.

magnesium alginate.definition: A magnesium salt of alginic acid used as an antacid; in gastric acid it forms a viscous, buoyant raft that floats on the stomach contents to act as a barrier and relieve reflux-related symptoms such as heartburn.

magnesium chloride.definition: Magnesium chloride is a chemical compound and the magnesium salt of hydrochloric acid (MgCl2). It is used medically as an oral magnesium supplement to treat or prevent magnesium deficiency and as an electrolyte source in intravenous or other formulations; excessive intake can cause diarrhea, nausea, and hypermagnesemia, especially in those with renal impairment.

magnesium gluconate.definition: A magnesium salt of gluconic acid used as a dietary mineral supplement to prevent or treat magnesium deficiency (hypomagnesemia), typically administered orally.

magnesium lactate.definition: A magnesium salt of lactic acid used as a dietary supplement to provide elemental magnesium for prevention or treatment of magnesium deficiency.

magnesium salicylate.definition: A salt of magnesium and salicylic acid used as an analgesic and antipyretic; it relieves mild pain and fever by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis (COX inhibition) and, like other salicylates, may cause GI irritation and increase bleeding risk.

magnesium silicate.definition: A hydrated magnesium silicate mineral with the chemical formula Mg3Si4O10(OH)2; a soft, greasy powder used medically as talcum powder and as an inert excipient/adsorbent in pharmaceutical preparations.

magnesium test.definition: A laboratory test that measures the concentration of magnesium in the blood (usually serum magnesium) to evaluate magnesium status; used to detect deficiency or excess and to monitor treatment, though serum levels may not reflect total body magnesium.

acute nephritis.definition: An acute inflammatory disease of the kidneys—most often presenting as acute nephritic syndrome—with abrupt onset hematuria (often cola-colored) and red blood cell casts, modest proteinuria, oliguria, edema, and hypertension due to glomerular inflammation (usually immune-mediated, such as post-infectious glomerulonephritis).

toxemia of pregnancy.definition: A pregnancy-related hypertensive disorder presenting after mid-gestation with new-onset hypertension and proteinuria (edema may be present); it is now commonly called preeclampsia, which can progress to eclampsia if untreated.

diabetic acidosis.definition: An acute, life-threatening complication of diabetes caused by insulin deficiency leading to hyperglycemia, a ketone-driven high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, dehydration, and electrolyte disturbances; presents with rapid breathing, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, polyuria, polydipsia, and altered mental status; requires urgent IV fluids, insulin therapy, and electrolyte correction.

renal impairment.definition: A decline in kidney function with reduced glomerular filtration rate and impaired elimination of wastes, leading to accumulation of nitrogenous wastes and disturbances of fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance; can be acute or chronic.

plasmodium ovale.definition: A human malaria parasite of the genus Plasmodium that infects red blood cells and commonly causes benign tertian malaria; transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes and capable of forming dormant liver-stage hypnozoites that can cause relapses.

majocchi's granuloma.definition: A deep fungal infection of hair follicles caused by dermatophytes, characterized by granulomatous perifolliculitis within the dermis; it typically results from extension of superficial dermatophytosis into follicles and is often seen in immunosuppressed individuals or after local corticosteroid use, requiring systemic antifungal therapy rather than topical treatment.

pinta.definition: A chronic infectious skin disease caused by the protozoan parasite Trypanosoma carateum; it produces hypopigmented (depigmented) patches on the skin that can become lighter and may scar, transmitted by direct skin contact, historically found in parts of Central and South America.

meleda disease.definition: A rare autosomal recessive palmoplantar keratoderma characterized by diffuse hyperkeratosis of the palms and soles with transgredient extension to the dorsal surfaces, usually presenting in infancy; caused by mutations in the SLURP1 gene.

delusions.definition: A false, firmly held belief that is not shared by others, not consistent with the person’s cultural background, and persists despite clear evidence to the contrary; commonly seen in psychotic disorders.

abdominal bloating.definition: A subjective sensation of abdominal fullness or swelling, sometimes with visible distension, typically caused by gas accumulation in the gastrointestinal tract, fluid retention, or increased intra-abdominal contents; it can be related to dietary factors, constipation, swallowed air, or functional GI disorders.

microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.definition: A form of hemolytic anemia caused by mechanical fragmentation of red blood cells as they pass through narrowed or thrombotically obstructed microvessels, leading to schistocytes on the peripheral smear and laboratory evidence of intravascular hemolysis; associated with thrombotic microangiopathies such as TTP, HUS, DIC, and malignant hypertension.

nonunion fractures.definition: A fracture that fails to heal within the expected time frame, with a persistent fracture line and no progressive radiographic or clinical union despite adequate time (often beyond 6–9 months). It results from an unfavorable biological or mechanical environment (eg, instability, poor vascular supply, infection, or systemic factors) and often requires surgical intervention to restore stability and stimulate healing.

mainz pouch.definition: A continent catheterizable urinary reservoir fashioned from ileal segments, developed in Mainz, used for urinary diversion after cystectomy and emptied by intermittent self-catheterization.

male catheterization.definition: A procedure in which a urinary catheter is inserted via the male urethra into the bladder to drain urine.

magnetic resonance angiography.definition: A noninvasive imaging method that uses magnetic resonance to visualize blood vessels, often by exploiting blood flow (time-of-flight or phase-contrast techniques) or with gadolinium-based contrast, to evaluate arteries and veins for stenosis, occlusion, aneurysm, or vascular malformations.

magnetic resonance urography.definition: An MRI-based imaging modality of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder that uses heavily T2-weighted sequences to visualize urine-containing structures and, with gadolinium contrast, excretory imaging to assess anatomy and function without ionizing radiation.

contrast agents.definition: A substance used to enhance the visibility of internal structures during medical imaging by increasing radiodensity or altering MRI signal; administered by various routes (IV, oral, rectal, etc.) to delineate anatomy and pathology. Examples include iodinated contrast media for CT and angiography, gadolinium-based agents for MRI, barium sulfate for GI fluoroscopy, and ultrasound microbubble contrast.

open magnetic resonance imaging.definition: An MRI system with an open design (wider bore or open sides) intended to reduce claustrophobia and accommodate patients who are large or claustrophobic; it uses the same principles—strong magnetic field and radiofrequency pulses—to generate detailed internal-body images, but may offer lower signal-to-noise ratio and longer scan times than conventional closed-bore MRI.

open mri.definition: An MRI system with a wide bore or open-frame magnets designed to reduce claustrophobia and improve patient comfort and access; however, it can have lower image resolution and longer scan times compared with conventional closed MRI.

closed magnetic resonance imaging.definition: A diagnostic imaging modality that uses a strong magnetic field and radiofrequency pulses to generate detailed cross-sectional images of body tissues; in a closed MRI, the patient lies inside the narrow bore of the magnet, which typically provides high image quality but can cause claustrophobia.

zeugmatography.definition: Not a widely recognized medical term; there is no established technique or definition by this name. If you can provide context or confirm the spelling, I can help look up the correct term.

maitake.definition: A culinary-medicinal mushroom (Grifola frondosa) used in Asian cuisine and traditional medicine; contains immune-modulating polysaccharides (notably beta-glucans) and has been studied for potential anti-cancer and anti-diabetic effects, though evidence is limited and it is not a proven therapy.

proguanil.definition: An antimalarial prodrug converted to cycloguanil that inhibits plasmodial dihydrofolate reductase, blocking folate synthesis and parasite DNA replication; used for malaria prophylaxis and, in combination with atovaquone (e.g., Malarone), for malaria treatment.

mefloquine.definition: An oral antimalarial medication used for prophylaxis against malaria and for treatment of chloroquine-resistant Plasmodium falciparum infections; a 4-quinoline methanol derivative that can cause neuropsychiatric adverse effects in some patients.

quinine.definition: An alkaloid derived from the Cinchona bark with antimalarial activity; historically the first effective therapy for malaria, but now limited by toxicity and resistance.

primaquine.definition: An 8-aminoquinoline antimalarial used to eradicate dormant liver-stage hypnozoites of Plasmodium vivax and P. ovale (radical cure) and, in some regimens, to prevent transmission by targeting gametocytes; it can cause hemolytic anemia in individuals with G6PD deficiency and is contraindicated in pregnancy, with G6PD testing recommended before use.

malathion.definition: A synthetic organophosphate insecticide that inhibits acetylcholinesterase, causing accumulation of acetylcholine and cholinergic toxicity; used to control insects in agriculture and, in topical formulations, for treating head lice. Exposure can cause muscarinic and nicotinic symptoms and may require treatment with atropine and pralidoxime in severe cases.

parathion.definition: An organophosphate insecticide that inhibits acetylcholinesterase, causing accumulation of acetylcholine and cholinergic toxicity; highly toxic to humans and animals; use is restricted or banned in many countries.

malassezia furfur.definition: A lipophilic, yeast-like fungus that colonizes human skin and hair; a common cause of pityriasis versicolor (tinea versicolor), growing best in lipid-rich environments, and formerly classified as Pityrosporum ovale.

malassezia.definition: A genus of lipophilic yeasts that normally colonize human skin, especially sebaceous areas; they can cause superficial fungal infections such as pityriasis versicolor and are associated with seborrheic dermatitis and folliculitis.

pityrosporum ovale.definition: A lipophilic yeast of the Malassezia genus that colonizes the skin’s outer layers and causes superficial infections such as pityriasis versicolor, typically producing hypo- or hyperpigmented patches on the trunk; diagnosed by microscopy (KOH) showing a spaghetti-and-meatballs pattern.

major histocompatibility antigen.definition: Proteins on the surface of cells that form the major histocompatibility complex and present peptide fragments to T lymphocytes, enabling immune recognition of self versus non-self and influencing tissue compatibility in transplants. In humans they are known as HLA antigens and are categorized into class I (CD8+ T cell presentation of endogenous peptides) and class II (CD4+ T cell presentation of exogenous peptides).

hla complex.definition: A gene cluster on chromosome 6 encoding the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) proteins, which are major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I and II molecules that present peptide antigens to T cells; essential for antigen recognition, immune response, transplant compatibility, and disease susceptibility; highly polymorphic.

esophagomalacia.definition: Softening of the esophageal wall due to degeneration or inflammatory damage, resulting in decreased structural integrity of the esophagus.

tracheomalacia.definition: Softening or weakening of the tracheal cartilage that causes dynamic collapse of the airway lumen, especially during expiration; may be congenital or acquired and can lead to cough, wheeze, stridor, dyspnea, and recurrent respiratory infections.

cardiomalacia.definition: Softening of the heart muscle (myocardium), typically due to degeneration or necrosis of cardiac tissue, resulting in decreased contractile strength; the term is rare and largely archaic in modern use.

malacia.definition: A suffix meaning softening of a tissue; for example osteomalacia (softening of bone) and laryngomalacia (softening of the tissues of the larynx).

tendinomuscular system.definition: The musculoskeletal subsystem comprising skeletal muscles and their attached tendons that contract to produce movement, stabilize joints, and transmit force to bones; controlled by the nervous system through motor innervation.

climacterium.definition: A transitional midlife phase in which gonadal function declines and sex hormone production decreases; in individuals assigned female at birth, this leads to menopause (cessation of menstruation).

balloon.definition: An inflatable, flexible device attached to a catheter, expanded to dilate a constricted vessel or body passage, compress tissue, or occlude a space during medical procedures.

urgency.definition: The sudden and uncontrollable need to urinate or defecate.

nonspecific.definition: Not specific to a single disease or cause; signs, symptoms, or findings that are general and do not point to a particular etiology.

orchitis.definition: Swelling of 1 or both testicles. It is often a side effect of mumps.

gram.definition: A metric unit of mass equal to one-thousandth of a kilogram (0.001 kg); commonly used to measure small masses, including medicines and laboratory specimens.

malloryweiss.definition: A mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction caused by forceful retching or vomiting, leading to upper gastrointestinal bleeding; typically self-limited and managed with supportive care, with endoscopy used for diagnosis or bleeding control if needed.

neurosarcoma.definition: A malignant tumor arising from nerve sheath cells of the peripheral nervous system (usually referred to as a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor, MPNST); it often arises in or near nerves, may develop from a preexisting neurofibroma, and is associated with neurofibromatosis type 1; treatment typically involves wide surgical excision with adjuvant radiotherapy, and chemotherapy in selected cases.

malrotation.definition: An abnormal embryologic rotation and fixation of the intestines, resulting in malposition of the bowel and a predisposition to midgut volvulus and intestinal obstruction.

malrotated.definition: Adjective describing abnormal rotation of the intestines during embryologic development, leading to abnormal fixation and an increased risk of midgut volvulus and intestinal obstruction.

malposition.definition: An abnormal position or misalignment of a body part or medical device; a deviation from its normal anatomical position.

malpractice.definition: Professional negligence by a healthcare provider in which the care given falls below the accepted standard of practice and causes injury or harm to the patient.

malpresentation.definition: Fetal presentation during labor that is not cephalic (head first); most commonly breech (buttocks or feet first) or transverse/shoulder presentations.

malfunction.definition: A failure of a body part, organ, or system to function normally, or a medical device to perform its intended function.

malfeasance.definition: Wrongdoing or illegal conduct by a physician or other healthcare professional, especially actions that cause harm to a patient or violate laws or professional standards.

corpuscle.definition: An extremely small particle or cell; a general histological term for minute structures in tissues, historically applied to red blood cells and to specialized sensory receptors in the skin (e.g., touch and pressure detectors).

malpighian.definition: Relating to the eponymous anatomist; in dermatology, the deepest layer of the epidermis, comprising the stratum basale and stratum spinosum, where proliferating keratinocytes reside and melanocytes are located.

cords.definition: Long, flexible, cord‑like structures composed of connective tissue that connect or support body parts and may contain blood vessels, nerves, or muscle; they function to transmit substances or impulses, or to facilitate vibration in some contexts.

orifice.definition: An opening or hole in a body part; a natural opening into a hollow organ or cavity, such as the mouth or nostril.

sims.definition: A position used for rectal examinations and enemas in which the patient lies on the left side (left lateral decubitus) with the right knee flexed and drawn up toward the chest, and the left arm placed behind the back.

abstinence.definition: The voluntary refraining from engaging in a desired behavior or from the use of a substance, especially sexual activity or alcohol/drug use.

count.definition: Numerical total of a specified cell type or other measurable parameter in a biological sample, usually reported with a unit (for example, white blood cell count per microliter or per liter; platelet count).

degos.definition: An extremely rare, progressive thrombo-obliterative vasculopathy of small- to medium-sized vessels, characterized by porcelain-white atrophic cutaneous papules with a surrounding telangiectatic rim; systemic involvement (notably the gastrointestinal tract and central nervous system) can occur, leading to organ infarction and high mortality in the systemic form.

malunion.definition: Healing of a fracture in an incorrect alignment or position, resulting in deformity or impaired function.

mamillary body.definition: Two small rounded eminences on the inferior surface of the hypothalamus, part of the limbic system; they receive input from the hippocampus via the fornix and project to the thalamus via the mammillothalamic tract, playing a role in memory processing and formation. Lesions can cause memory impairment, such as anterograde amnesia.

mammary glands.definition: A pair of milk-producing glands in the breast; modified sweat glands organized into lobes and lobules that secrete milk through ducts to the nipple during lactation.

mammary papilla.definition: A pigmented projection on the breast that contains the openings of the lactiferous ducts and serves as the outlet for milk; commonly known as the nipple.

mqsa.definition: A U.S. federal law enacted in 1992 to establish minimum quality standards for mammography facilities, including facility accreditation, personnel certification, regular inspections, and ongoing quality assurance programs to ensure accurate and reliable breast imaging.

mammoplasty.definition: A surgical procedure to alter the size, shape, or position of the breast, commonly by augmentation with implants, reduction, or mastopexy (breast lift).

mammothermography.definition: A breast imaging technique that uses infrared thermography to map surface temperature and heat patterns, aiming to detect abnormal vascular activity associated with breast pathology; noninvasive and radiation-free, but not proven to reliably detect breast cancer and not recommended as a stand-alone screening test.

mammotroph.definition: A prolactin-secreting cell (lactotroph) of the anterior pituitary; produces prolactin and is regulated by hypothalamic dopamine (inhibitory) and TRH (stimulatory).

maneuver.definition: A deliberate movement or position of the body or a body part performed by a patient or clinician during examination or treatment to elicit a diagnostic sign, assess function, or facilitate a procedure.

manoeuvre.definition: A deliberate movement or sequence of movements performed by a patient or clinician to provoke a clinical sign, test a diagnosis, or facilitate examination or treatment.

mangafodipir.definition: A manganese-containing MRI contrast agent used to enhance hepatic imaging by shortening T1 relaxation times; administered intravenously and historically used for hepatobiliary MRI but now rarely used due to safety concerns.

manganese.definition: An essential trace element that serves as a cofactor for several enzymes (e.g., MnSOD, pyruvate carboxylase, arginase); important for bone formation, metabolism, and antioxidant defense. Deficiency is rare but can impair growth and skeletal development; excess exposure can cause neurotoxicity (manganism) with Parkinsonian features. Dietary sources include whole grains, nuts, legumes, leafy vegetables, and tea.

mange.definition: A skin disease of animals caused by infestation with parasitic mites (commonly Sarcoptes scabiei or Demodex), causing intense itching, hair loss, and crusted or crusty skin.

maniaphobia.definition: An irrational, persistent fear of insanity or manic states, leading to avoidance of situations associated with mental illness; this is not a widely recognized clinical diagnosis.

maniac.definition: A person experiencing mania—a mood state with an abnormally elevated or irritable mood and markedly increased energy or activity, lasting at least one week (or any duration if hospitalization is required) and accompanied by symptoms such as grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, flight of ideas, distractibility, and risky or increased goal-directed behavior; seen in bipolar disorder.

manic-depressive.definition: An older term for bipolar disorder, a mood disorder with recurrent episodes of mania or hypomania and depressive episodes, often with periods of normal mood in between.

manipulation.definition: The manual movement of a bone or joint by a clinician to restore alignment, reduce dislocation, or improve range of motion.

mannose.definition: A simple monosaccharide (aldohexose) that is the C-2 epimer of glucose; D-mannose is involved in the biosynthesis of glycoproteins and glycopolysaccharides and is found in certain polysaccharides.

mannosidosis.definition: A rare autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme alpha-mannosidase, leading to accumulation of mannose-containing oligosaccharides in tissues; clinical features often include developmental delay, hypotonia, skeletal abnormalities, and recurrent infections.

mantoux test.definition: A tuberculin skin test in which purified protein derivative (PPD) is injected intradermally and induration is measured 48–72 hours later to indicate prior exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis; a positive result suggests latent or active infection, with interpretation affected by risk factors and prior BCG vaccination or non-tuberculous mycobacteria.

mansonella ozzardi.definition: A filarial nematode species that causes mansonelliasis in humans; transmitted by biting Culicoides midges; infections are frequently asymptomatic or cause mild symptoms; diagnosis is by detection of microfilariae in peripheral blood.

mansonella perstans.definition: A human filarial nematode that causes mansonelliasis; transmitted by Culicoides biting midges; adults inhabit serous cavities; microfilariae circulate in peripheral blood; infections are often asymptomatic or mild; diagnosed by finding microfilariae in blood; treated with antiparasitic therapy such as diethylcarbamazine.

mansonellosis.definition: An infection caused by filarial nematodes of the genus Mansonella, transmitted by bites of hematophagous insects in tropical regions; many cases are asymptomatic but can present with pruritus, eosinophilia, fever, and subcutaneous or lymphatic manifestations.

mantle cell lymphoma.definition: A mature B‑cell non‑Hodgkin lymphoma arising from mantle zone B cells; characteristically driven by the t(11;14)(q13;q32) translocation with cyclin D1 overexpression; typically CD5‑positive, occurring in older adults and presenting with generalized lymphadenopathy, often with splenomegaly and bone marrow involvement; usually aggressive in behavior.

mandibular foramen.definition: An opening on the medial aspect of the mandible's ramus through which the inferior alveolar nerve and vessels enter the mandible, supplying the lower teeth.

mandibular process.definition: An embryologic structure: the lower prominence of the first pharyngeal (branchial) arch that develops into the mandible (lower jaw) and related lower facial tissues, largely via intramembranous ossification from neural crest cells.

mandibular ramus.definition: A vertical, posterior extension of the mandible arising from the body, bearing the condylar and coronoid processes; it forms the temporomandibular joint via the condyle and provides attachment for jaw muscles.

mandibular reflex.definition: A monosynaptic stretch reflex of the jaw muscles elicited by tapping the chin, causing the mandible to elevate; tests the motor function of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve and corticobulbar pathways. An exaggerated response suggests upper motor neuron (pseudobulbar) lesions, while a diminished or absent response indicates CN V/ motor nucleus pathology.

retrognathia.definition: A condition in which the lower jaw (mandible) is positioned posteriorly relative to the upper jaw (maxilla), resulting in a receding chin and often associated with Class II malocclusion.

mandibular sling.definition: A surgical technique in which a loop or sling of tissue (such as fascia or tendon) or a synthetic material is anchored to surrounding jaw structures to suspend, support, or reposition the mandible, typically to stabilize the jaw after injury or during reconstructive jaw surgery.

sphenomandibular ligament.definition: A fibrous band of the temporomandibular joint extending from the spine of the sphenoid bone to the lingula of the mandible; an accessory, passive ligament that limits mandibular excursion, particularly excessive opening and protrusion.

mandibular spine.definition: A small projection on the inner (lingual) surface of the mandible at the midline (mental/genial spine); the superior spine provides origin for the genioglossus muscle, and the inferior spine provides origin for the geniohyoid muscle.

mandibular symphysis.definition: Midline fusion point where the left and right halves of the mandible meet; in the adult this junction is typically fused into a single mandible (a synostosis), whereas in infancy it is a fibrous/cartilaginous joint that ossifies with age.

mandibular torus.definition: A benign bony exostosis on the lingual (inner) surface of the mandible, most commonly near the premolar region, often bilateral and asymptomatic.

mandibulofacial dysostosis.definition: A congenital craniofacial disorder (Treacher Collins syndrome) due to neural crest cell maldevelopment, characterized by hypoplasia of the mandible and midface (zygomatic arches), downward-slanting palpebral fissures, ear abnormalities with possible conductive hearing loss, and often cleft palate.

franceschetti syndrome.definition: Congenital craniofacial disorder (mandibulofacial dysostosis) characterized by hypoplasia of the zygomatic arches and mandible, downward-slanting palpebral fissures, micrognathia, ear anomalies with conductive hearing loss, and often cleft palate; typically autosomal dominant with variable expressivity; most cases due to mutations in the TCOF1 gene.

treacher collins syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal-dominant craniofacial syndrome caused by defective neural crest cell migration during embryogenesis, leading to midface hypoplasia (zygomatic/maxillary), micrognathia, downward-slanting palpebral fissures, external ear anomalies with conductive hearing loss, and often cleft palate; commonly due to mutations in TCOF1 with variable expressivity and many de novo cases.

mandol.definition: The lower jawbone; the largest facial bone that forms the lower jaw, houses the lower teeth, and moves at the temporomandibular joints to enable chewing and speech.

interpeduncular space.definition: Anatomical space on the ventral midbrain between the two cerebral peduncles (the interpeduncular fossa/cistern); contains CSF in the cistern and is the region where the oculomotor nerves (CN III) emerge from the brainstem.

gibbus deformity.definition: A sharp, angular kyphotic deformity caused by focal collapse of one or more vertebral bodies, producing a wedge-shaped deformity of the spine (often in the thoracolumbar region), typically due to infection, osteoporosis with compression, trauma, or neoplasm.

microtia.definition: A congenital malformation in which the external ear (pinna) is underdeveloped or absent; commonly unilateral and may be associated with canal stenosis/atresia and middle-ear malformations, often causing conductive hearing loss.

zygomatic arches.definition: Two bony arches on the side of the skull formed where the temporal process of the zygomatic bone meets the zygomatic process of the temporal bone; they create the cheek prominence, contribute to the lateral orbital rim, and separate the temporal fossa above from the infratemporal fossa below, providing attachment for the masseter and other facial muscles.

oligosaccharides.definition: A carbohydrate comprised of a small number of monosaccharide units (typically 3–10) linked by glycosidic bonds; shorter than polysaccharides and commonly found as components of glycoproteins and glycolipids, where they mediate cell recognition and signaling.

upper respiratory.definition: The upper respiratory tract is the portion of the respiratory system that includes the nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, pharynx, and larynx; it conducts, filters, humidifies, and warms inhaled air and aids phonation, while protecting the lower respiratory tract.

gibbus.definition: An abrupt, angular kyphosis of the spine due to wedge-shaped collapse or destruction of one or more vertebral bodies, often seen with spinal tuberculosis or osteoporotic compression.

manubrial.definition: Relating to the manubrium, the broad upper portion of the sternum.

manubriosternal articulation.definition: A secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis) between the manubrium and the body of the sternum, usually united by fibrocartilage and typically ossifying with age, allowing only limited movement during respiration.

xiphisternal articulation.definition: The joint between the xiphoid process and the body of the sternum; typically a cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis) in youth that ossifies with age to a bony synostosis, and is essentially immobile.

manudynamometer.definition: A handheld device that measures the force of a person’s handgrip (grip strength) during maximal contraction, used to assess hand function and monitor changes over time.

manus.definition: An anatomical term for the hand: the distal part of the upper limb from the wrist to the fingertips, including the palm, metacarpals, and phalanges.

scultetus binder.definition: A historical, circumferential pressure dressing used to apply controlled constriction around a limb or stump to control bleeding, reduce edema, and secure dressings after injury or amputation; typically formed from layered cloths wrapped tightly and secured with ties, as described by 17th‑century surgeon Johann Scultetus.

mao.definition: An enzyme in the outer mitochondrial membrane that degrades monoamines (e.g., dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin) by oxidative deamination; exists as MAO-A and MAO-B isoforms with different substrate specificities, and its inhibition increases monoamine levels, used therapeutically in depression and Parkinson’s disease.

monoamine oxidase.definition: An mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the oxidative deamination of monoamines (e.g., dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin) to their corresponding aldehydes, generating hydrogen peroxide; exists as two isoforms, MAO‑A and MAO‑B, with different substrate specificities.

maoi.definition: A class of antidepressants that inhibits the enzyme monoamine oxidase, increasing brain levels of norepinephrine, serotonin, and dopamine; used to treat depressive disorders and certain anxiety conditions; requires dietary restrictions to avoid hypertensive crises with tyramine and has potential interactions with many medications.

maolate.definition: Not a recognized medical term in standard dictionaries; please verify spelling.

chlorphenesin carbamate.definition: A centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant; the carbamate derivative of chlorphenesin used to relieve muscle spasms by depressing central nervous system activity.

chlorphenesin.definition: A centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant that depresses the central nervous system to relieve muscle spasm; commonly encountered as chlorphenesin carbamate in combination cough/cold preparations.

map.definition: An estimate of the average arterial pressure over a single cardiac cycle, used as an indicator of tissue perfusion; commonly approximated by (systolic blood pressure + 2 × diastolic blood pressure) divided by 3.

maple bark disease.definition: There is no widely recognized medical condition by this name. If you meant maple syrup urine disease, it is an inherited metabolic disorder due to deficiency of the branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase complex, causing accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, and valine and a characteristic maple-syrup odor in urine; untreated, it can lead to brain injury.

cryptostroma corticale.definition: A saprophytic fungus (ascomycete) of the Xylariaceae that colonizes damp maple wood, causing maple bark disease in maples; inhalation of its spores can trigger hypersensitivity pneumonitis in susceptible individuals (maple bark pneumonitis).

branched chain ketoaciduria.definition: A rare inherited metabolic disorder caused by deficiency of the branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, leading to accumulation of the branched-chain amino acids valine, leucine, and isoleucine and their corresponding α-ketoacids in blood and urine; presents in infancy with poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, hypotonia, and a distinctive maple-syrup odor in urine; without treatment can cause seizures, coma, and neurodevelopmental disability; managed by dietary restriction of branched-chain amino acids (emphasizing leucine), thiamine supplementation in some cases, and prompt treatment of metabolic crises.

maprotiline.definition: A tetracyclic antidepressant that primarily inhibits norepinephrine reuptake and has antihistaminic/anticholinergic properties; used to treat depression and associated with sedation, dry mouth, constipation, orthostatic hypotension, and a risk of seizures and cardiac arrhythmias.

maprotiline hydrochloride.definition: A salt form of a tetracyclic antidepressant that inhibits presynaptic norepinephrine reuptake, increasing NE transmission; used to treat major depressive disorder and associated with sedation and seizure risk.

maraviroc.definition: Selective CCR5 receptor antagonist antiretroviral that blocks HIV-1 entry into CD4+ T cells by inhibiting the CCR5 co-receptor; active only against CCR5-tropic HIV-1 and used as part of combination antiretroviral therapy after tropism testing.

ccr5-tropic hiv.definition: A form of HIV that preferentially uses the CCR5 coreceptor on CD4+ T cells to enter cells (R5-tropic); CCR5 antagonists are effective only against R5-tropic virus, while CXCR4-tropic or dual-tropic viruses are not targeted by these drugs.

marax.definition: No standard medical term by that spelling; it may be a brand name for a medication rather than a term with a single definition. If you can provide the active ingredient or the context (e.g., allergy/cold remedy vs. a sedative/anxiolytic), I can give a precise definition.

ephedrine sulfate.definition: A salt form of a sympathomimetic amine with direct alpha/beta-adrenergic agonist effects and indirect action by releasing norepinephrine; used as a decongestant, bronchodilator, and vasopressor to raise blood pressure in hypotensive states.

marezine.definition: A brand name for meclizine, an oral antihistamine used to prevent and treat motion sickness and vertigo; it blocks H1 receptors to reduce nausea and dizziness.

cyclizine.definition: A first-generation histamine H1 receptor antagonist with anticholinergic properties used as an antiemetic for motion sickness and vertigo; commonly causes drowsiness.

cyclizine hydrochloride.definition: A first‑generation antihistamine antiemetic (H1 receptor antagonist) used to prevent and treat nausea and vomiting due to motion sickness, vertigo, and postoperative conditions; common adverse effects include drowsiness, dry mouth, and blurred vision.

marcaine.definition: A brand-name, long-acting amide local anesthetic (bupivacaine) used for regional anesthesia and postoperative pain relief; it blocks sodium channels to prevent nerve conduction and is commonly used in epidurals and nerve blocks.

bupivacaine hydrochloride.definition: A hydrochloride salt form of bupivacaine, a potent amide-type local anesthetic used for regional anesthesia and analgesia. It reversibly blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in nerve membranes, preventing conduction of nerve impulses.

weill-marchesani syndrome.definition: A rare genetic connective tissue disorder characterized by disproportionately short stature with brachydactyly and joint stiffness, and ocular features including microspherophakia with lens subluxation (ectopia lentis), resulting in high myopia and glaucoma risk; inheritance is typically autosomal recessive, with some cases due to autosomal dominant mutations.

marchesani’s syndrome.definition: A rare genetic disorder characterized by short stature, brachydactyly, and microspherophakia with lens dislocation leading to high myopia and glaucoma; associated with mutations in ADAMTS10 or ADAMTS17.

marchiafava-micheli disease.definition: A rare demyelinating disorder of the corpus callosum, historically linked to chronic alcohol use and malnutrition, characterized by symmetric demyelination and necrosis of the corpus callosum (and sometimes adjacent white matter), with neuropsychiatric and motor symptoms; MRI typically shows bilateral callosal lesions with T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and diffusion changes.

marchi’s globule.definition: A small spherical intracellular inclusion body observed in tissue sections, formed by accumulation of a specific substance (such as lipid or protein) as part of a metabolic, degenerative, or storage process; its exact meaning depends on the tissue and disease context.

marchi’s method.definition: I can’t locate a standard medical definition for “Marchi’s method.” Could you share the medical field or context where you saw it (e.g., surgery, imaging, dermatology), or confirm the spelling (Marchi vs. Marèi)? I’ll refine once clarified.

marcus gunn pupil sign.definition: A relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) characterized by reduced pupillary constriction, or paradoxical dilation, when light is directed into the affected eye during the swinging flashlight test, indicating optic nerve or severe retinal disease.

marcus gunn pupil.definition: Relative afferent pupillary defect due to unilateral optic nerve or retinal disease; decreased afferent input from the affected eye causes reduced direct and consensual pupillary constriction, producing a relative dilation during the swinging flashlight test.

march fracture.definition: A stress fracture of a metatarsal bone of the foot (most often the second metatarsal) caused by repetitive loading during marching or running; presents as focal forefoot pain and tenderness, often with initially normal radiographs, diagnosed by MRI or bone scan and treated with rest and gradual return to activity.

metatarsal stress fracture.definition: A small crack in one of the foot's metatarsal bones caused by repetitive stress or overuse, typically presenting as focal forefoot pain and tenderness that worsens with activity.

ebola virus.definition: An enveloped, filamentous, negative-sense RNA virus of the genus Ebolavirus in the Filoviridae family that causes Ebola virus disease—a severe, often fatal viral hemorrhagic fever in humans and nonhuman primates; transmitted through contact with infected blood or body fluids, contaminated materials, or sexual contact.

marburg virus.definition: A member of the Filoviridae family that causes a severe viral hemorrhagic fever; zoonotic spillover from fruit bats with subsequent human-to-human transmission via contact with contaminated bodily fluids; the virus has a negative-sense, single-stranded RNA genome.

hemorrhagic lesions.definition: Lesions resulting from extravasation of blood into the skin or mucosa due to rupture or increased vascular permeability; non-blanching, and include petechiae (tiny spots), purpura, and ecchymoses; may arise from trauma, vasculitis, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, infection, or medications.

respiratory obstruction.definition: Blockage or narrowing of the airways in the respiratory tract that impedes airflow and gas exchange; may be partial or complete and caused by foreign body aspiration, edema, inflammation, trauma, infection, allergic reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis), tumors, or other airway pathology.

viral meningitis.definition: An inflammation of the meninges caused by a viral infection, typically milder than bacterial meningitis, presenting with fever, headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia; CSF usually shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose and only mildly elevated protein; management is supportive and most people recover fully without lasting problems.

marginal gingiva.definition: That portion of the gingiva surrounding a tooth at the cervical area, forming the free (unattached) gingival margin and extending from the cementoenamel junction to the mucogingival junction.

bevel.definition: An oblique or slanted edge or surface formed by cutting at an angle; in medical contexts, the bevel refers to the angled cutting edge of a surgical blade or needle tip, designed to ease entry and produce a clean incision.

butt.definition: A colloquial term for the buttocks—the two rounded, fleshy prominences at the posterior pelvis, consisting of skin and fat overlaying the gluteal muscles (gluteus maximus, medius, and minimus); they help bear weight when seated and enable hip extension, abduction, and rotation, while stabilizing the pelvis during gait.

marginal gyrus.definition: On the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere, the marginal gyrus (gyrus marginalis) is the portion of the cingulate gyrus that forms the margin along the cingulate sulcus.

marginal placenta previa.definition: A placental position in which the placental edge extends to the margin of the internal cervical os but does not cover it.

placental sinus.definition: A dilated maternal blood space in the decidua basalis of the placenta that communicates with the intervillous space and is part of the maternal circulation surrounding the chorionic villi.

marginal sinus.definition: A venous sinus located in the marginal zone of the spleen, at the interface between white pulp and red pulp; it drains blood from the central arterioles into the red pulp and participates in splenic filtration and immune surveillance.

marginal sinus rupture.definition: Rupture of a marginal sinus is tearing of a small venous channel that runs along the edge of a tissue (most commonly the placenta), causing bleeding at the margin.

occlusal surface.definition: The chewing surface of a posterior tooth (premolars and molars) that comes into contact with the opposite dentition during biting, featuring cusps, grooves, and ridges for grinding food.

marginal ridge.definition: A raised, rounded border along the mesial and distal margins of a tooth's occlusal (chewing) surface, forming the boundary of the chewing surface.

margin of safety.definition: A pharmacology/toxicology metric defined as the ratio of the toxic (or lethal) dose that affects a given percentage of individuals (TD50 or LD50) to the therapeutic dose that achieves the desired effect (ED50); a larger value indicates a wider safety margin and a safer drug, closely related to the therapeutic index.

ld1.definition: The dose of a substance that is lethal to 1% of a defined population, used in toxicology to describe lethality on a dose–response curve and to help estimate higher lethal doses such as LD50.

ed99.definition: In pharmacology and toxicology, the dose required to produce the specified effect in 99% of individuals in a population; it’s the 99th percentile of the dose–response curve and is used to characterize potency and safety margins, analogous to ED50.

dose-response relationship.definition: A relationship in pharmacology and toxicology in which the magnitude of a drug’s effect increases with increasing dose until a maximum effect is reached; the curve’s position and steepness reflect the drug’s potency and efficacy.

marie’s hypertrophy.definition: Not a widely recognized medical term. Hypertrophy is the enlargement of an organ or tissue due to an increase in the size of its cells, typically in response to increased functional demand or hormonal stimulation (e.g., skeletal muscle hypertrophy with training, cardiac hypertrophy with hypertension).

hypertrophic pulmonary osteopathy.definition: A paraneoplastic syndrome characterized by digital clubbing and painful periostitis (new bone formation along the periosteum) of the long bones, most often secondary to intrathoracic malignancies such as bronchogenic carcinoma; may also be seen with other lung diseases and can improve with treatment of the underlying condition.

marie-strümpell arthritis.definition: A chronic inflammatory rheumatic disease of the axial skeleton (spine and sacroiliac joints) characterized by inflammatory back pain and progressive spinal stiffness, often associated with HLA-B27 and possible extra-articular features (e.g., uveitis).
