marinesco-sjögren syndrome.definition: An autosomal recessive multisystem disorder characterized by congenital cataracts, hypotonia with proximal muscle weakness, developmental delay, short stature, skeletal abnormalities, and cerebellar ataxia; caused by SIL1 gene mutations leading to impaired protein folding in the endoplasmic reticulum.

marinol.definition: A brand-name synthetic delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) used as an antiemetic for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting and as an appetite stimulant in AIDS-related anorexia.

mass spectrometry.definition: An analytical technique that ionizes chemical species and separates the resulting ions by their mass-to-charge ratio to identify, characterize, and quantify molecules in a sample.

mass spectrum.definition: A plot produced by a mass spectrometer showing the relative abundance of detected ions as a function of their mass-to-charge ratio (m/z); used to identify and characterize substances based on molecular weight and fragmentation patterns.

mass transfer.definition: The movement of material from one location to another driven by gradients in concentration or chemical potential (such as concentration or pressure differences), occurring via diffusion, convection (bulk flow), and membrane transport; a fundamental mechanism governing the exchange and distribution of substances (e.g., gases, nutrients, drugs) between body compartments.

massive transfusion syndrome.definition: An iatrogenic syndrome of bleeding and organ dysfunction caused by rapid, large-volume transfusion of blood products, dominated by dilutional coagulopathy from loss of platelets and clotting factors, citrate-related hypocalcemia, hypothermia, and accompanying acid–base and electrolyte disturbances. Common clinical definitions include transfusing about one blood volume (roughly 10 units of PRBCs) in 24 hours or ≥4 units within 1 hour with ongoing bleeding.

massive lung collapse.definition: A large-scale collapse of aerated lung tissue (massive atelectasis) due to airway obstruction, external compression, or surfactant deficiency, resulting in nonventilated, airless lung segments and impaired gas exchange.

masochist.definition: A person who derives sexual arousal or pleasure from experiencing pain, humiliation, or submission, often within a sexual context; in clinical psychology, masochism is a paraphilia, and when recurrent and distressing or impairing it may be diagnosed as masochistic disorder.

masochistic personality disorder.definition: A historical, now obsolete, diagnosis describing a pervasive pattern of seeking and tolerating humiliation and domination, often with sexual arousal from pain or humiliation and accompanying self-deprecating, submissive, and dependent personality traits; not recognized as a formal disorder in DSM-5.

masked facies.definition: A mask-like facial expression with reduced spontaneous facial movement and blinking (hypomimia), giving an expressionless, rigid face commonly seen in Parkinsonian syndromes.

parkinsonian facies.definition: Facial expression typical of Parkinson disease: reduced spontaneous facial movement (hypomimia) and decreased blinking, producing a masklike or expressionless face due to bradykinesia and rigidity of facial muscles.

hurler-like signs.definition: A cluster of clinical features resembling Hurler syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type I), typically including coarse facial features with gargoyle-like facies, skeletal dysplasia (dysostosis multiplex), joint stiffness, short stature, hepatosplenomegaly, and developmental delay (often with corneal clouding).

pseudo-hurler polydystrophy.definition: An obsolete term for Morquio syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type IV, MPS IV), a recessive lysosomal storage disorder due to N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase (GALNS) deficiency, causing accumulation of keratan sulfate and chondroitin-6-sulfate with skeletal dysplasia, short stature, joint abnormalities, and usually preserved intelligence.

scheie’s syndrome.definition: A mild-to-moderate form of mucopolysaccharidosis type I (MPS I) caused by alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency, presenting in childhood with skeletal abnormalities (dysostosis multiplex), joint stiffness, coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, corneal clouding, and typically milder or later-onset cognitive involvement compared with Hurler syndrome.

dermatan sulfate.definition: A sulfated glycosaminoglycan (GAG) component of proteoglycans in connective tissue, composed of repeating disaccharides of iduronic acid and N-acetylgalactosamine with variable sulfation; it contributes to extracellular matrix structure and collagen fibrillogenesis, and has anticoagulant activity by enhancing inhibition of thrombin via dermatan sulfate–specific cofactors (notably heparin cofactor II).

isocarboxazid.definition: An irreversible, nonselective monoamine oxidase inhibitor antidepressant that increases brain levels of serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine by inhibiting MAO-A and MAO-B; used for major depressive disorder when other treatments have failed and requires dietary tyramine restriction to reduce risk of hypertensive crisis.

marplan.definition: A brand-name irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor antidepressant (isocarboxazid) used to treat major depressive disorder; it increases brain serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine by inhibiting MAO-A and MAO-B, with dietary tyramine restrictions to prevent hypertensive crisis and numerous drug interactions.

internal os.definition: The opening at the superior end of the cervical canal that communicates with the uterine cavity, marking the boundary between the endocervical canal and the uterine cavity.

masseteric nerve.definition: A motor branch of the anterior division of the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve that innervates the masseter muscle; it exits the infratemporal fossa via the mandibular notch to enter the deep surface of the masseter and may convey proprioceptive fibers from the temporomandibular joint.

masseter muscle.definition: A thick, quadrangular muscle of mastication that elevates the mandible to close the jaw; it originates from the inferior border of the zygomatic arch and inserts on the lateral surface and angle of the mandible; innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3).

marshall-marchetti-krantz procedure.definition: An older surgical procedure for female stress urinary incontinence in which the bladder neck and proximal urethra are suspended to the pubic symphysis (pubourethral urethropexy) via sutures passed through the anterior vaginal wall to provide urethral support during increases in intra-abdominal pressure.

retropubic incision.definition: An incision made in the lower abdomen just above the pubic symphysis into the retropubic (preperitoneal) space behind the pubic bone to access the bladder, prostate, or pelvic organs without entering the peritoneal cavity.

vesicourethropexy.definition: A surgical procedure to suspend or fix the bladder neck and proximal urethra to the pelvic ligaments or pubic bone to restore urethral support and prevent stress urinary incontinence due to urethral hypermobility.

pilonidal cyst.definition: A hair-containing cyst or sinus located in the midline of the natal cleft near the coccyx, caused by hair penetration into the skin and subsequent chronic inflammation; it may become infected, presenting with pain and drainage, and is treated with incision and drainage for an abscess or surgical excision of the sinus tract.

pancreatic cyst.definition: An abnormal fluid-filled sac within the pancreas; may be a true cyst (epithelial-lined) or a pseudocyst (lacking a true lining), often arising after pancreatitis or pancreatic injury; management depends on size, symptoms, and cyst type.

marsupialize.definition: To surgically convert a closed cavity or cyst into an open pouch by suturing its edges to the surrounding skin, creating a continuous drainage opening.

brown dog tick.definition: A species of hard-bodied tick that commonly parasitizes dogs and can transmit pathogens such as Ehrlichia canis (canine ehrlichiosis) and Babesia vogeli (canine babesiosis); thrives in warm climates and can be found indoors, including kennels and homes.

rhipicephalus sanguineus.definition: A species of hard tick (Ixodidae) commonly known as the brown dog tick; a parasite of dogs worldwide and a vector for several pathogens, including Ehrlichia canis and Babesia canis; it can complete its life cycle indoors in warm climates.

conor’s disease.definition: Definition not found for "Conor's disease." Could you confirm the spelling or provide more context (e.g., symptoms or related condition)?

kenya fever.definition: A fever in the context of travel to or residence in Kenya, most commonly due to malaria; a mosquito-borne illness caused by Plasmodium species transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes.

indian tick fever.definition: A tick-borne protozoal disease of cattle (tropical theileriosis) caused by Theileria annulata, transmitted by Hyalomma ticks; characterized by fever, lymphadenopathy, anemia, weight loss, and edema, with potential fatality if untreated.

tick fever.definition: A fever resulting from infection transmitted by ticks; not a single disease but a category of tick-borne illnesses (e.g., rickettsioses such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever, Lyme disease, anaplasmosis, ehrlichiosis, babesiosis). It typically features fever with malaise, headache, and muscle aches; diagnosis relies on exposure history and laboratory tests (serology, PCR); treatment depends on the specific pathogen, with doxycycline commonly used for many bacterial tick-borne diseases.

takayasu’s arteritis.definition: A rare granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, causing stenosis, occlusion, or aneurysmal dilatation; typically presents in young women with systemic symptoms and diminished or absent peripheral pulses; treated primarily with corticosteroids and other immunosuppressants.

marcus gunn’s syndrome.definition: A relative afferent pupillary defect due to optic nerve or retinal disease, in which the affected pupil has reduced constriction to light and may appear to dilate when light is swung between eyes (as shown by the swinging flashlight test).

mastalgia.definition: Breast pain or tenderness, often cyclic and related to the menstrual cycle; commonly benign.

mast cell leukemia.definition: A very rare, aggressive hematologic malignancy in which malignant mast cells clonally proliferate, predominantly in the bone marrow and often circulate in the blood; it represents a high-burden form of systemic mastocytosis and is typically associated with mediator-related symptoms and organ involvement, with a poor prognosis.

mastocytoma.definition: A localized, benign neoplasm of the skin composed of mast cells; typically a solitary cutaneous lesion in infants or young children, presenting as a reddish-brown or yellowish nodule that may urticate when stroked.

mastocarcinoma.definition: A malignant neoplasm arising from mast cells (immune cells derived from the bone marrow that participate in allergic and inflammatory responses); may present as localized skin lesions or systemic disease and is diagnosed histologically with mast cell markers (e.g., tryptase, CD117/c-kit).

mammary gland.definition: A pair of modified sweat glands in mammals that produce milk for offspring; located in the breasts; organized into lobes and lobules drained by ducts; lactation is regulated by hormones such as prolactin and oxytocin.

chronic suppurative otitis media.definition: Chronic suppurative otitis media is a chronic infection of the middle ear and mastoid cavity characterized by persistent or recurrent ear discharge (otorrhea) through a perforated tympanic membrane for at least about 6 weeks, often with conductive hearing loss; it is typically classified into tubotympanic (safe) and atticoantral (unsafe, often with cholesteatoma) types.

mastoiditis.definition: An infection and inflammation of the mastoid air cells in the temporal bone, usually a complication of acute otitis media, characterized by fever, ear pain, and swelling or tenderness behind the ear, with potential for abscess or intracranial complications if untreated.

mastoid cells.definition: An air-filled system within the mastoid portion of the temporal bone, lined by mucosa and connected to the middle ear via the aditus ad antrum; these cells help aerate the middle ear and drain secretions.

mastoidectomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which part or all of the mastoid air cells in the temporal bone are removed or opened to treat disease (such as mastoiditis or cholesteatoma) or to gain access to the middle and inner ear for repair.

drainage catheter.definition: A flexible tube inserted into a wound, body cavity, or abscess to remove unwanted fluids (such as pus, blood, or serous exudate) or to decompress an area, often used postoperatively; it may drain passively or be connected to suction.

pectoral muscles.definition: The pectoral muscles are chest muscles on the anterior thorax, primarily the pectoralis major and pectoralis minor; they move the shoulder girdle and upper limb—pectoralis major flexes, adducts, and medially rotates the humerus, while pectoralis minor protracts and depresses the scapula to stabilize it against the thorax.

tympanic antrum.definition: An air-filled recess in the temporal bone behind the tympanic (middle ear) cavity; part of the middle ear air-cell system that communicates with the tympanic cavity and the mastoid air cells.

toluidine blue.definition: A basic histology dye used to stain acidic tissue components and to demonstrate metachromasia; commonly used to identify mast cell granules and to screen for dysplastic or malignant oral lesions.

mastoid air cells.definition: A network of air-filled spaces within the mastoid portion of the temporal bone, connected to the middle ear via the mastoid antrum and aditus ad antrum; lined with mucosa and involved in ventilating the middle ear and draining secretions, which can become inflamed or infected (mastoiditis).

maternal antibody.definition: Antibodies transferred from mother to fetus or infant (primarily IgG via the placenta and IgA via breast milk) that provide passive immunity in early life; they decline over months and can interfere with certain infant vaccine responses.

maternal immunity.definition: Passive immunity conferred to a fetus or newborn by the mother, mainly through transplacental transfer of IgG antibodies and antibodies in breast milk, providing temporary protection against infections in early life.

maternal-infant bonding.definition: The emotional and social connection between a mother and her infant, formed through sensitive, responsive caregiving and affectionate interactions, beginning in the early postpartum period and influencing the infant’s sense of security and later attachment style.

postnatal.definition: Relating to the period after childbirth; occurring after delivery and including postpartum care during roughly the first six weeks.

pediatric.definition: Relating to the medical care of children, from birth through adolescence; pertaining to pediatrics.

radical mastectomy.definition: An extensive surgical procedure for breast cancer in which the entire breast is removed along with overlying skin and nipple–areolar complex, the chest wall muscles (typically the pectoralis major and sometimes minor), and regional axillary lymph nodes; historically known as the Halsted procedure and now largely replaced by less extensive approaches.

simple mastectomy.definition: A surgical procedure that removes the entire breast tissue, including the nipple-areolar complex, without removal of axillary lymph nodes or chest wall muscles; commonly performed for breast cancer treatment or risk reduction, often followed by reconstruction.

puerperium.definition: The postpartum period after delivery during which the uterus involutes and the reproductive tract returns to its pre-pregnant state, typically lasting about six weeks (42 days).

rooming-in.definition: An hospital practice in which the newborn stays in the same room as the mother (instead of a separate nursery) after birth, around the clock, to promote bonding, initiate and support breastfeeding, and involve parents in care; exceptions are made for medical or safety reasons.

autoimmune_disease.definition: A disease in which the immune system mistakenly identifies healthy tissues and organs as threats and responds by attacking and destroying them.

maternal_mortality.definition: The death of a woman during pregnancy or within 42 days after termination, due to causes related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management.

ectopic_pregnancy.definition: A pregnancy in which the fertilized egg implants outside the uterine cavity, most commonly in the fallopian tube; it can cause tubal rupture and life-threatening hemorrhage and requires urgent medical evaluation.

spina_bifida.definition: A congenital defect in which part of the spinal column fails to develop completely, leaving part of the spinal cord exposed.

alpha_fetoprotein.definition: A glycoprotein produced mainly by the fetal liver and yolk sac; used clinically as a pregnancy biomarker (maternal serum AFP) to screen for neural tube defects and multiple gestations, and in adults as a tumor marker for hepatocellular carcinoma and certain germ cell tumors; elevated levels may indicate these conditions.

neural_tube_defects.definition: A group of congenital malformations caused by incomplete closure of the neural tube during early embryonic development, usually within the first 28 days after conception, resulting in defects of the brain and/or spinal cord (e.g., spina bifida, anencephaly, encephalocele).

maternal_inheritance.definition: Transmission of genetic material from the mother to offspring, most notably mitochondrial DNA, which is inherited almost exclusively from the mother (paternal contributions are typically not transmitted).

maternal_effect.definition: A genetic phenomenon in which the offspring's phenotype is determined by the mother's genotype because she provides during oogenesis the mRNA and proteins that direct early development, so the offspring's phenotype reflects the mother's genotype rather than its own.

mendelism.definition: The theory of heredity based on Gregor Mendel's principles, stating that traits are controlled by discrete genes that segregate during gamete formation and assort independently, leading to predictable inheritance patterns (Mendelian or particulate inheritance).

inheritance.definition: The transmission of genetic information and traits from parents to offspring, following genetic inheritance patterns (e.g., autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked) and including inherited disorders.

frontal.definition: Relating to the forehead; pertaining to the bone at the front of the skull; in anatomy, describing the plane that divides the body into anterior and posterior regions.

zygomatic.definition: Pertaining to the zygomatic bone (cheekbone) or the zygomatic arch.

zygomaticotemporal.definition: A sensory branch of the maxillary division (V2) of the trigeminal nerve that passes through the zygomatic bone to supply sensation to the skin of the temple and lateral forehead; it also gives a communicating branch to the lacrimal nerve, conveying parasympathetic fibers to the lacrimal gland.

zygomaticofacial.definition: Relating to the zygomatic bone and the facial region; in anatomy, the zygomaticofacial nerve supplies sensation to the skin of the cheek.

canine_fossa.definition: A shallow concavity on the anterior surface of the maxilla, just above the canine tooth and beneath the infraorbital rim, overlying the anterior wall of the maxillary sinus.

maxillary_artery.definition: A terminal branch of the external carotid artery that supplies the deep face and maxilla; it courses through the infratemporal fossa and divides into three parts (mandibular, pterygoid, and pterygopalatine) with branches that include middle meningeal, inferior alveolar, posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, greater palatine, and sphenopalatine arteries.

maxillary_nerve.definition: The sensory second division (V2) of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) that carries sensation from the midface (lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip, maxillary teeth, and palate) and gives branches such as infraorbital, zygomatic, and posterior superior alveolar nerves after exiting the foramen rotundum.

infraorbital_nerve.definition: A sensory branch of the maxillary division (CN V2) of the trigeminal nerve; travels through the infraorbital canal and exits the infraorbital foramen to supply sensation to the cheek, lower eyelid, upper lip, lateral nose, and the maxillary gingiva/teeth via its alveolar branches.

palatine_process.definition: It is the horizontal projection of the maxilla that forms the anterior portion of the hard palate; it joins with the contralateral palatine process at the midline to complete the bony roof of the mouth and separate the oral and nasal cavities.

maxillary_sinus.definition: An air-filled, pyramidal cavity within the maxilla, one of the paranasal sinuses, lined with respiratory epithelium and draining into the middle nasal meatus.

retainer.definition: A dental appliance worn after orthodontic treatment to maintain tooth alignment and prevent relapse; it can be fixed to teeth or removable.

tofflemire.definition: A dental instrument: a metal matrix-band retainer used to hold a matrix band around a tooth during restorative procedures, ensuring proper proximal contact and contour, especially for class II restorations.

compound.definition: A substance formed by the chemical combination of two or more elements; in medicine, a preparation containing two or more active ingredients.

carious.definition: Relating to dental caries (tooth decay); decayed or prone to decay of a tooth.

sockets.definition: A hollow cavity in bone or tissue designed to receive another structure; examples include the dental socket (alveolar socket) that holds a tooth, the orbital socket that houses the eye, and, in prosthetics, a molded cavity that fits over a residual limb.

passages.definition: Anatomical channels or cavities through which substances move or are transported within the body (for example, air through the nasal passages and food through the gastrointestinal tract).

parotid_gland.definition: A major salivary gland located just in front of and below the ear, producing serous saliva that drains into the mouth via Stensen's duct.

retroposition.definition: Backward displacement or posterior placement of a body part or organ from its normal anatomical position; a repositioning toward the back that may be congenital or acquired.

retrusion.definition: Backward displacement or retraction of a structure from its normal position; commonly used to describe posterior positioning of the mandible relative to the maxilla.

may-hegglin anomaly.definition: A rare autosomal dominant MYH9-related disorder characterized by macrothrombocytopenia (abnormally large platelets) and neutrophil inclusions known as May-Hegglin bodies; bleeding tendency is usually mild to moderate, and some individuals have associated renal or sensorineural hearing abnormalities due to the underlying MYH9 mutation.

maxillary tuberosity.definition: A rounded bony eminence on the posterior aspect of the maxilla, behind the last upper molar, forming the posterior boundary of the maxillary sinus and providing attachment for the buccinator muscle.

posterior superior alveolar nerve.definition: A sensory branch of the maxillary division (V2) of the trigeminal nerve; it arises from the maxillary nerve in the pterygopalatine fossa and enters the maxilla to innervate the pulp and supporting structures of the maxillary molars (and usually the buccal gingiva over these teeth) as well as the mucosa of the maxillary sinus.

maxillary vein.definition: A deep vein in the infratemporal fossa that drains the pterygoid venous plexus and surrounding deep facial structures; it accompanies the maxillary artery and typically drains into the retromandibular vein, contributing to the formation of the internal jugular venous system.

maxillodental.definition: Relating to the upper jaw (maxilla) and the teeth.

maxillofacial.definition: Relating to the maxilla (upper jaw) and facial bones; used to describe the anatomy of the face and the medical specialty (maxillofacial surgery) that treats diseases, injuries, and defects of the jaws and face.

maxillofacial dysostosis.definition: Congenital craniofacial malformation involving underdevelopment of the maxilla and other midfacial structures, often with mandibular hypoplasia, zygomatic hypoplasia, downslanting palpebral fissures, ear anomalies, and sometimes cleft palate; typically due to failure of neural crest cell migration during embryogenesis (as seen in Treacher Collins syndrome).

maxillofacial prosthesis.definition: A prosthetic device used to rehabilitate the maxillofacial region by replacing missing or defective hard and soft tissues of the jaw and face, to restore function (speech, swallowing, chewing) and aesthetics after trauma, cancer surgery, or congenital defects; includes intraoral obturators, tongue prostheses, and extraoral facial prostheses (nasal, orbital, auricular).

maxillofacial surgery.definition: A surgical specialty focused on the diagnosis and surgical treatment of diseases, injuries, and defects of the face, mouth, jaws, and surrounding soft tissues.

maxillofacial syndrome.definition: An umbrella term for a constellation of abnormalities affecting the maxillofacial region (jaw, palate, facial bones, and surrounding soft tissues), often seen in craniofacial syndromes and may include deformities, malocclusion, and functional impairments.

maxillofacial trauma.definition: Injury to the facial skeleton and soft tissues of the maxillofacial region caused by trauma, including fractures of the mandible and midface, dental injuries, and associated soft-tissue damage.

maxillomandibular.definition: Pertaining to or involving both the maxilla (upper jaw) and the mandible (lower jaw).

maxillomandibular relation.definition: The three‑dimensional spatial relationship between the maxilla and mandible, defined by the mandible’s position relative to the maxilla (often in centric relation), including vertical dimension and anteroposterior and transverse alignment, used to establish occlusion in dental rehabilitation and denture fabrication.

maxillotomy.definition: A surgical procedure involving partial cutting (osteotomy) of the maxilla (upper jaw) to gain access to the midface or to mobilize the maxilla for reconstructive or orthognathic procedures.

mayo scissors.definition: A heavy, blunt-tipped surgical scissor with straight or curved blades, used for cutting dense or fibrous tissue (such as fascia) during surgery.

mazindol.definition: A central nervous system stimulant and anorectic agent used historically for short-term obesity management; mazindol inhibits the reuptake of norepinephrine (and dopamine) in the CNS, leading to increased catecholamine activity and appetite suppression; adverse effects include tachycardia, hypertension, insomnia, anxiety, and potential for abuse.

morbilli.definition: Measles; a highly contagious viral illness caused by the measles virus (a Morbillivirus) characterized by fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots, and a maculopapular rash; transmitted by respiratory droplets and preventable by vaccination (MMR).

immune serum globulin.definition: A sterile preparation of concentrated antibodies derived from pooled human serum, used to provide passive immunity against infections or to modulate immune responses (includes products such as IVIG and hyperimmune globulins).

mcburney's incision.definition: A muscle-splitting oblique incision in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen used for appendectomy, typically placed at McBurney's point (one-third of the distance from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus).

mcburney's sign.definition: Tenderness to palpation at McBurney's point (approximately one-third of the distance from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus), an examination finding that suggests acute appendicitis.

gingival margin.definition: Edge of the gingiva that surrounds a tooth, marking the coronal boundary of the gingival sulcus and separating the tooth from the gingival tissue.

occlusal trauma.definition: An injury to the periodontium caused by occlusal forces; primary trauma occurs from excessive force on a tooth with normal support, while secondary trauma occurs from normal forces on a tooth with reduced supporting bone.

canines.definition: Pointed teeth at the corners of the dental arches, between the incisors and premolars; typically four in adult humans, with a long root and a single pointed crown, used to tear food and guide the bite.

third molar.definition: The most posterior permanent molar in each quadrant of the jaw, commonly called a wisdom tooth; the last molar to erupt, typically during late adolescence or early adulthood, and often impacted or associated with crowding or pathology, sometimes requiring extraction.

mcmurray's sign.definition: A clinical test for meniscal tears of the knee in which the examiner flexes the knee, then extends it while rotating the tibia; a palpable or audible click or pain along the joint line (positive sign) suggests a meniscal tear (external rotation tests the medial meniscus, internal rotation tests the lateral meniscus).

medial meniscus.definition: A C-shaped fibrocartilaginous structure in the knee on the medial (inner) side that cushions the joint by distributing load and absorbing shock between the femur and tibia; it contributes to joint stability and is attached to the joint capsule and medial collateral ligament.

meniscal tear.definition: A tear of the meniscus, the knee’s fibrocartilaginous cartilage between the femur and tibia, usually caused by twisting or degenerative changes, leading to knee pain, swelling, reduced motion, and sometimes mechanical symptoms such as locking or catching; treatment ranges from rest and physical therapy to surgical repair or partial meniscectomy depending on the tear and symptoms.

mcmurray's test.definition: A provocative knee examination used to detect meniscal tears. The patient lies supine with the knee flexed to about 90 degrees; the examiner rotates the tibia and extends the knee to stress the menisci—external rotation stresses the medial meniscus and the test is positive if a click, clunk, or reproducible joint-line pain is felt/present.

temporomandibular.definition: Relating to the temporal bone of the skull and the mandible (jaw); used to describe the temporomandibular joint and conditions affecting it.

labial.definition: Relating to the lips; pertaining to the labia (the lips of the vulva) or to the lips of the mouth.

vestibular surface.definition: A tooth surface oriented toward the oral vestibule; on anterior teeth it is the labial surface (lip-facing) and on posterior teeth it is the buccal surface (cheek-facing).

live vaccine.definition: A vaccine containing a live, weakened form of a pathogen that can replicate in the vaccinated person and elicit a strong, often long-lasting immune response with usually mild or no illness; not suitable for severely immunocompromised individuals due to risk of disease or reversion.

subacute sclerosing panencephalitis.definition: A rare, progressive encephalitis caused by a persistent measles virus infection, typically developing years after measles; it presents with cognitive and behavioral decline, myoclonus, seizures, and motor deterioration, with a poor prognosis and no curative treatment. Diagnosis is supported by elevated measles antibodies in CSF and characteristic EEG findings.

whole blood.definition: Blood that has not been separated into its component parts; it contains plasma and cellular elements (red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets) and is collected with an anticoagulant for direct transfusion or future component separation.

paramyxovirus.definition: An enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA virus of the family Paramyxoviridae; includes measles virus, mumps virus, and parainfluenza viruses; commonly causes respiratory tract infections.

mmr.definition: A combined live attenuated vaccine that provides immunity to measles, mumps, and rubella; typically given in two doses in childhood.

meatus acusticus externus.definition: A canal in the external ear that extends from the auricle to the tympanic membrane; about 2.5 cm long in adults; lined with skin containing hair, ceruminous and sebaceous glands; the lateral one-third is cartilage and the medial two-thirds is bone; conducts sound to the tympanic membrane and protects the middle ear.

meatus acusticus internus.definition: A short bony canal in the petrous part of the temporal bone that transmits cranial nerves VII (facial) and VIII (vestibulocochlear) and the labyrinthine artery from the posterior cranial fossa to the inner ear.

internal acoustic meatus.definition: A bony canal in the petrous portion of the temporal bone that transmits CN VII (facial nerve) and CN VIII (vestibulocochlear nerve), along with the labyrinthine artery, from the posterior cranial fossa to the inner ear.

meatuses.definition: A natural opening or canal within bone or soft tissue that provides a passage to another cavity or duct; examples include the external auditory canal (ear canal) and the passages beneath the nasal conchae.

meatal stenosis.definition: An abnormal narrowing of the external opening of the urethra (the urethral meatus), causing a diminished urinary stream and sometimes spraying, dysuria, or recurrent infections. Causes include scar tissue from inflammation, infection, trauma, or instrumentation; treatment options include dilation, meatotomy/meatoplasty, or surgical reconstruction.

meatorrhaphy.definition: Surgical suturing and repair of a meatus (an anatomical opening, such as the urethral or nasal meatus).

meatoscopy.definition: A visual examination of a bodily meatus (an external opening such as the nasal or urethral meatus) using a speculum or endoscope to inspect for mucosal pathology, obstruction, or other abnormalities.

meclofenamate.definition: A fenamate-type nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that inhibits cyclooxygenase, reducing prostaglandin synthesis to relieve pain and inflammation (e.g., in osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis); commonly causes gastrointestinal irritation and is contraindicated in active peptic ulcers or significant GI bleeding.

meclofenamate sodium.definition: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that is the sodium salt of meclofenamic acid; used to relieve pain and inflammation in conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis by inhibiting cyclooxygenase and reducing prostaglandin synthesis.

meclomen.definition: A brand-name nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that inhibits cyclooxygenase enzymes, reducing prostaglandin synthesis to relieve pain and inflammation in conditions such as osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis.

whipworm.definition: A parasitic infection of the human large intestine caused by the nematode Trichuris trichiura; acquired by ingesting embryonated eggs in contaminated soil or food, it can cause abdominal pain, diarrhea, and in heavy infections, rectal prolapse.

roundworm.definition: A nematode (roundworm); a slender, cylindrical, unsegmented worm. In humans, it refers to intestinal parasitic nematodes such as Ascaris lumbricoides and Enterobius vermicularis, which can cause ascariasis and enterobiasis.

insulin-like growth factor-1.definition: A peptide hormone produced primarily by the liver in response to growth hormone; it mediates growth-promoting effects by stimulating cell proliferation and differentiation in bone, muscle, and other tissues, acting via the IGF-1 receptor. It is part of the GH–IGF axis and is structurally similar to insulin.

growth factor.definition: A naturally occurring protein or peptide that binds to specific receptors on target cells to stimulate cellular growth, proliferation, differentiation, or survival; it regulates development, tissue maintenance, and wound healing.

antibodies to growth hormone.definition: Immunoglobulins that bind growth hormone, potentially neutralizing its activity; they can arise after exposure to recombinant growth hormone therapy and may diminish the therapeutic response.

visual impairment.definition: A decrease in vision that significantly limits daily functioning and cannot be fully corrected with standard glasses, contact lenses, or routine medical treatment.

tonsillar hypertrophy.definition: Enlargement of the palatine tonsils (lymphoid tissue of the oropharynx) due to lymphoid hyperplasia, often from recurrent or chronic infection or immune stimulation; may cause sore throat, dysphagia, snoring, and, in severe cases, obstructive sleep apnea.

meconium aspiration.definition: A respiratory condition in which a newborn inhales meconium-stained amniotic fluid into the lungs around birth, causing airway obstruction, chemical pneumonitis, and potentially respiratory distress or persistent pulmonary hypertension.

meconium peritonitis.definition: Chemical peritonitis caused by leakage of sterile meconium into the peritoneal cavity due to fetal or neonatal intestinal perforation, typically occurring in utero or shortly after birth.

meconium plug syndrome.definition: A neonatal distal colon obstruction caused by an inspissated meconium plug in the rectum or distal colon, leading to failure to pass meconium and abdominal distension; usually relieved with rectal disimpaction via glycerin or saline enemas (or contrast enema) and supportive care, with good prognosis when not associated with other conditions like Hirschsprung disease or meconium ileus.

meglumine diatrizoate.definition: An iodinated, water-soluble contrast medium composed of the meglumine salt of diatrizoic acid; a high-osmolar radiopaque agent used to enhance X-ray and CT imaging, administered intravenously, intra-arterially, intrathecally, or intraluminally depending on the study.

sodium diatrizoate.definition: A water-soluble iodinated contrast agent; the sodium salt of diatrizoic acid, used to enhance radiographic visualization in imaging studies (e.g., CT, fluoroscopy, angiography), typically administered intravenously or intra-arterially.

postmortem examination.definition: Systematic examination of a deceased person to determine the cause and manner of death and to identify disease processes; typically includes external inspection, internal examination with organ dissection, and sampling for histopathology, toxicology, and other tests as indicated.

meconium periorchitis.definition: A neonatal condition in which meconium from the peritoneal cavity tracks through a patent processus vaginalis into the scrotum, causing sterile chemical periorchitis (granulomatous inflammation) around the testis and scrotal swelling.

meckel's cartilage.definition: A cartilaginous bar of the first pharyngeal arch in the developing mandible that largely degenerates, with remnants forming the malleus and incus of the middle ear and the dorsal part contributing to the sphenomandibular ligament.

nuclear scan.definition: A nuclear medicine imaging study in which a small amount of radioactive material (radiopharmaceutical) is administered to the patient and images are captured with a gamma camera (or PET scanner) to assess the function and/or structure of organs based on tracer uptake.

meckel's diverticulum nuclear scan.definition: A nuclear medicine study that uses technetium-99m pertechnetate to detect ectopic gastric mucosa within a Meckel's diverticulum (usually in the ileum), commonly performed to evaluate painless lower gastrointestinal bleeding in children.

monckebergs.definition: A form of arteriosclerosis characterized by calcification of the tunica media of medium-sized arteries (medial calcific sclerosis), causing stiff, noncompressible arteries with usually preserved luminal diameter; most common in older adults and associated with diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease.

sternotomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which a vertical incision is made through the sternum to access the heart and mediastinal structures; the sternum is divided (often with a saw) and then wired or otherwise fixed shut after the operation.

mediastinoscopy.definition: A surgical procedure in which a mediastinoscope is inserted through a small incision above the sternum to inspect and biopsy mediastinal structures, particularly lymph nodes, for diagnostic or cancer-staging purposes.

calcaneal.definition: Pertaining to the calcaneus, the heel bone.

trochanteric.definition: Relating to the trochanter, the bony prominence on the proximal femur (e.g., the greater and lesser trochanters).

medial.definition: Towards the middle of the body.

cubital.definition: Relating to the elbow; anatomical term for the region around the elbow (the cubitus).

basilic.definition: Relating to the basilic vein, a large superficial vein of the upper limb that runs medially along the forearm and arm and drains into the axillary vein; commonly used for venipuncture and as a site for arteriovenous fistula in hemodialysis.

palmar.definition: Relating to the palm of the hand; pertaining to the palmar (volar) surface of the hand.

digital.definition: Relating to a digit (finger or toe); performed with the fingers; pertaining to the digits.

tibial.definition: Relating to the tibia, the shinbone; the larger, weight-bearing bone of the lower leg.

td50.definition: The median toxic dose — the dose of a substance that produces a defined toxic effect in 50% of a defined population under specified conditions; the endpoint must be clearly defined (e.g., a particular adverse effect or organ toxicity). It is analogous to LD50 (lethal dose) but refers to toxicity rather than death.

ld50.definition: A measure of acute toxicity defined as the lethal dose that would kill 50% of a defined test population (usually expressed as mg/kg), dependent on species, route of exposure, and experimental conditions.

ed50.definition: The dose of a drug that produces the intended therapeutic effect in 50% of individuals in a population; the median effective dose used as a measure of drug potency.

induction of labor.definition: The deliberate initiation of labor by medical or mechanical means to achieve vaginal delivery before spontaneous labor begins.

psoriasis vulgaris.definition: A chronic immune-mediated skin disorder presenting with recurrent, well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales, commonly on the scalp, elbows, and knees; due to increased keratinocyte turnover and inflammatory T-cell–driven pathology.

medicamentosus.definition: Pertaining to medicines; containing or administered as medicines; medicinal or therapeutic.

medicated bougie.definition: A bougie that is coated or impregnated with a medication for local delivery to a mucosal surface during dilation or instrumentation.

medicated enema.definition: A preparation in which a therapeutic drug is delivered by enema to act on the rectum and distal colon; used to treat conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease or hemorrhoids, and may include agents like corticosteroids (e.g., hydrocortisone, budesonide) or other medications.

medicated bath.definition: A therapeutic bath in which water contains a medicated preparation (such as antiseptics, keratolytics, anti-inflammatory agents, or soothing agents) intended to treat skin conditions or deliver medication through the skin.

ophthalmic medications.definition: Ophthalmic medications are drugs formulated for administration to the eye or periocular tissues to diagnose, treat, or manage ocular conditions. They are typically delivered as topical preparations (eye drops, ointments, gels) but may also be injections or implants, and include lubricants for dry eye, antimicrobials for infections, anti-inflammatories, antiglaucoma agents, mydriatics and miotics, antivirals/antifungals, and anesthetics.

interpleural.definition: Between the pleural membranes (the parietal pleura lining the chest wall and the visceral pleura covering the lungs), i.e., in the pleural region between pleural layers. The more common term for this space is intrapleural.

intraosseous.definition: Situated within bone or introduced into bone; relating to the bone marrow cavity, commonly used to describe delivering fluids or medications through the bone (intraosseous access).

dermatological disorders.definition: A broad category of diseases and conditions affecting the skin and its appendages (hair and nails) and mucous membranes, including inflammatory, infectious, neoplastic, genetic, and autoimmune disorders that manifest as rashes, lesions, itching, scaling, color changes, or structural changes.

physiology.definition: The branch of biology that studies how living organisms function—the processes and mechanisms by which cells, tissues, and organ systems perform, regulate, and coordinate life activities.

gastrointestinal system.definition: A series of hollow organs and associated glands that break down food, absorb nutrients, and eliminate waste. It includes the mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, and rectum, plus accessory organs such as the liver, biliary system, and pancreas.

inoculations.definition: Introduction of a vaccine or antigen into the body to stimulate an immune response and provide immunity against a disease.

pathology.definition: The underlying abnormalities that contribute to or are characteristic of a disease.

otic medications.definition: Drugs formulated for topical administration into the ear (usually as ear drops) to treat conditions of the external ear canal and middle ear, including infections (antibiotics, antifungals), inflammation (corticosteroids/anti-inflammatory agents), and pain relief; use with caution in a perforated eardrum and per labeled directions.

administration.definition: The act of giving a drug or other therapeutic agent to a patient, by a specified route and dose.

ventricular reservoir.definition: A surgically implanted device consisting of a ventricular catheter connected to a subcutaneous reservoir, used to access the brain's ventricular system for cerebrospinal fluid sampling or for intraventricular administration of medications.

medication error.definition: A preventable event in the medication-use process that may cause or lead to inappropriate medication use or patient harm, including errors in prescribing, transcribing, dispensing, administering, or monitoring.

route.definition: The path by which a substance enters or moves through the body, especially the method of administration of a drug (e.g., orally, intravenously, topically).

formulation.definition: The process of designing and preparing a drug product by combining an active ingredient with excipients to produce a specific dosage form (e.g., tablet, capsule, solution, cream) with desired stability and release characteristics.

condition.definition: A medical problem, like a disease or an illness.

drug allergies.definition: Drug allergies are immune-mediated adverse reactions to medications caused by hypersensitivity of the immune system to a drug or its metabolites. They are distinct from nonimmune adverse drug reactions and can present with symptoms ranging from mild skin rashes to life-threatening anaphylaxis.

sensitivities.definition: Sensitivities refers to the state of being easily reactive to stimuli; in medicine, it commonly means allergic or immunologic sensitivity to substances, and in testing, the ability of a test to correctly identify those with a condition (test sensitivity).

nursing intervention.definition: An evidence-based action performed by a nurse to support or improve a patient’s health status, usually specified in the nursing care plan and aimed at achieving defined outcomes (e.g., administering medications, wound care, patient education, monitoring, and safety measures).

prescription.definition: An order from your doctor, nurse, or physician assistant for drugs or other treatment.

pharmacy.definition: The science and practice of preparing, dispensing, and ensuring the safe and effective use of medications; also the establishment where medications are prepared and dispensed.

medication order.definition: A formal directive from a licensed clinician to administer a specific medication to a patient, detailing the drug, dose, route, frequency, and duration.

prescribing.definition: The act of authorizing the use of a drug or treatment by issuing a prescription, detailing the medication, dose, route, frequency, duration, and instructions for use and monitoring.

medication reconciliation.definition: A formal, systematic process used at care transitions (admission, transfer, discharge) to obtain and document a complete, accurate list of a patient’s medications (name, dose, route, frequency), compare it with new orders, identify and resolve discrepancies, and ensure safe, continuous medication therapy.

home medications.definition: Medications taken by a patient at home, including prescription drugs, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and other self-administered therapies used to treat, prevent, or manage health conditions outside of a formal healthcare setting.

admission.definition: The formal process of admitting a patient to a hospital or healthcare facility for evaluation, diagnosis, treatment, or observation, including bed assignment and the creation of an admission note.

orders.definition: A clinician's directive to perform a medical action or set of actions (such as prescribing a drug, ordering laboratory tests, imaging, or procedures) that is documented in the patient’s chart and carried out by the health care team.

accuracy.definition: The degree to which a measurement or diagnostic test result reflects the true value; for diagnostic tests, the proportion of all results that are correct (true positives and true negatives) among all individuals tested.

patient safety.definition: The avoidance, prevention, and mitigation of harm to patients that can result from the healthcare process, including errors, near misses, and adverse events, achieved through safe system design, standardized practices, proactive reporting, and a culture of safety.

therapeutic effects.definition: The intended, beneficial response produced by a treatment (drug, procedure, or therapy) that improves health, relieves symptoms, cures disease, or slows progression; contrasted with adverse or undesired effects.

adverse effects.definition: Unwanted, harmful, or unintended effects caused by a drug, therapy, or medical intervention, occurring in addition to the intended therapeutic effect; they may require monitoring, dose adjustment, modification of therapy, or discontinuation.

restraint.definition: An intervention that restricts a person’s freedom of movement or access to their body or surroundings to prevent harm to the individual or others; it can be physical (holding or immobilization), mechanical (restraining devices, bed rails), or chemical (sedation). Use should follow the least-restrictive principle, be time-limited, and be subject to ongoing monitoring and documentation.

medicinal treatment.definition: A therapeutic approach that uses medications to prevent, treat, or alleviate disease and its symptoms.

pharmacological agents.definition: A chemical substance that has a pharmacological effect on living organisms and is used to diagnose, treat, prevent, or study disease; in clinical terms, a drug.

medicolegal.definition: Relating to the legal aspects of medical practice; concerns the intersection of medicine and law, including issues such as malpractice liability, informed consent, patient confidentiality, and regulatory compliance.

medigap.definition: A private supplemental health insurance policy offered to people with Original Medicare to help pay for costs not covered by Parts A and B, such as deductibles, coinsurance, and copayments; it generally does not cover prescription drugs, which require a separate Part D plan.

medihaler-epi.definition: A brand-name epinephrine auto-injector used for emergency treatment of anaphylaxis; delivers a pre-measured intramuscular dose of epinephrine via a spring-activated needle when pressed against the outer thigh.

mediocarpal.definition: Pertaining to the middle portion of the carpus (the wrist); in anatomy, referring to the midcarpal region or the joint between the proximal and distal carpal rows.

mediolateral.definition: Pertaining to or oriented along the axis from the midline (medial) toward the side (lateral) of the body; used to describe directions or incisions that extend from medial to lateral.

meditation.definition: A family of contemplative practices that train attention and awareness, typically by focusing on a chosen object such as the breath, a sound, or a mantra, or by cultivating nonjudgmental awareness of thoughts and sensations, with the aim of promoting relaxation, emotional regulation, and self-awareness. Evidence suggests potential benefits for stress, anxiety, depression, and chronic pain, though results vary.

meditation therapy.definition: Therapeutic use of meditation practices (e.g., mindfulness, breath-focused or mantra-based techniques) to cultivate attention and acceptance, reduce autonomic arousal, and promote relaxation; used as an adjunct to conventional care to reduce stress and anxiety, alleviate pain, improve sleep, and support emotional well-being.

small intestine disease.definition: A disease of the small intestine (the portion of the GI tract between the stomach and colon) encompassing inflammatory, infectious, malabsorptive, obstructive, and neoplastic disorders; symptoms often include abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and malnutrition.

medium-chain fatty acid.definition: A fatty acid with a carbon chain of 6–12 carbons; more rapidly absorbed and oxidized for energy than long-chain fatty acids, and commonly found in coconut and palm kernel oils.

mcfa.definition: A fatty acid with a carbon chain length of 6–12 carbons that is absorbed directly into the portal circulation and rapidly oxidized for energy.

medium-chain triglyceride.definition: A triglyceride with medium-chain fatty acids (typically 6–12 carbon atoms); rapidly absorbed and oxidized for energy, and commonly used as a dietary fat supplement (MCT oil).

mct.definition: A dietary fat consisting of glycerol esterified with medium-chain fatty acids (typically 6–12 carbon atoms); absorbed directly into the portal circulation and rapidly oxidized for energy, commonly used in medical nutrition and for fat malabsorption or ketogenic-diet applications.

medius.definition: Latin for "middle"; in anatomical usage, an adjective indicating a structure located toward the midline or between other parts; used in compound names to denote relative position.

mefenamic acid.definition: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) of the fenamate class used to relieve mild to moderate pain, including menstrual cramps, by inhibiting cyclooxygenase and reducing prostaglandin synthesis.

mefoxin.definition: A second-generation cephalosporin antibiotic administered IV or IM that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin‑binding proteins; used to treat and prevent infections caused by susceptible organisms, including certain intra‑abdominal, gynecologic, and skin/soft tissue infections and for surgical prophylaxis.

cefoxitin sodium.definition: A parenteral salt form of cefoxitin, a second‑generation cephalosporin antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to penicillin‑binding proteins. It has activity against certain gram‑positive cocci and many anaerobes (including Bacteroides species) and is used to treat intra‑abdominal, gynecologic, and skin/soft tissue infections, as well as for perioperative prophylaxis (notably colorectal surgery). Adverse effects can include hypersensitivity reactions, diarrhea, rash, and potential superinfection.

mefr.definition: Peak expiratory flow achieved during a forced exhalation in spirometry, used to assess airway obstruction and overall pulmonary function.

megabladder.definition: An abnormally enlarged urinary bladder caused by chronic urinary retention or impaired detrusor contractility, often from bladder outlet obstruction or neurogenic/bladder dysfunction.

megacystis.definition: An abnormally enlarged urinary bladder, often due to bladder outlet obstruction (e.g., posterior urethral valves) or neurogenic bladder.

megacycle.definition: An obsolete unit of frequency equal to one million cycles per second; essentially the same as 1 megahertz (MHz).

megahertz.definition: A unit of frequency equal to one million cycles per second; commonly used to describe the operating frequency of ultrasound devices and other radio or wireless communication systems.

megakaryocyte.definition: A large bone marrow cell that produces platelets (thrombocytes) by fragmentation of its cytoplasm; derived from megakaryoblasts under thrombopoietin signaling during thrombopoiesis.

megakaryocytic.definition: Relating to megakaryocytes, the large bone marrow cells that produce platelets by cytoplasmic fragmentation.

megalencephalic.definition: Relating to megalencephaly; having an abnormally large brain.

megalencephalous.definition: A condition in which the brain is abnormally large (megalencephaly), typically presenting with macrocephaly in infancy and potentially associated with developmental delay, seizures, and certain overgrowth syndromes.

megaloblast.definition: A large erythroblast in the bone marrow with delayed nuclear maturation (nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony) due to impaired DNA synthesis, most often from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.

megalocystis.definition: A markedly enlarged urinary bladder due to dilation of the bladder lumen, typically arising from urinary tract obstruction or detrusor underactivity; can be congenital or acquired.

megalocyte.definition: An abnormally large cell, usually a red blood cell or its erythroid precursor, observed in megaloblastic disorders such as vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.

megalocytic interstitial nephritis.definition: Not a standard term; likely refers to giant cell (megalocytic) interstitial nephritis, a form of tubulointerstitial nephritis characterized by multinucleated interstitial giant cells, often drug-induced or granulomatous, which can present with acute kidney injury and is diagnosed by renal biopsy; management focuses on stopping the offending agent and may include corticosteroids.

medullary chemoreceptor.definition: Central (medullary) chemoreceptors are neurons in the medulla oblongata that sense changes in cerebrospinal fluid pH (hydrogen ion concentration), primarily reflecting arterial CO2 levels, and adjust ventilation accordingly to regulate CO2 and pH.

medullary sponge kidney.definition: Medullary sponge kidney is a congenital disorder characterized by dilation of the collecting ducts in the renal medulla (ductal ectasia), giving a sponge-like appearance on imaging; it predisposes to nephrocalcinosis, nephrolithiasis, hematuria, and recurrent urinary tract infections.

medulla spinalis.definition: The spinal cord: a cylindrical structure of nervous tissue within the vertebral canal that transmits sensory and motor signals between the brain and the body and contains reflex circuits; it extends from the medulla oblongata to about the L1–L2 level (conus medullaris) in adults.

neur al tube.definition: The neural tube is the embryonic precursor to the brain and spinal cord, formed by the closure of the neural plate during neurulation.

neural fold.definition: One of the raised borders of the neural plate that elevate and fuse along the midline to form the neural tube during neurulation in early embryonic development.

neural groove.definition: A groove along the dorsal midline of the developing neural plate during neurulation; it deepens as the neural folds elevate and fuse to form the neural tube.

neural plate.definition: A thickened region of the embryonic ectoderm on the dorsal surface that serves as the initial structure of neurulation; its cells invaginate and fold to form the neural groove and ultimately the neural tube (brain and spinal cord).

michaelis-gutmann bodies.definition: Intracytoplasmic, concentric, calcified inclusions within macrophages (von Hansemann cells) seen in malakoplakia; formed from partially digested bacterial remnants with calcium and iron deposits; pathognomonic for malakoplakia.

kidney stone.definition: A hard mineral deposit formed in the kidney from substances in urine (nephrolithiasis); stones are often calcium-based but can be uric acid, struvite, or cystine, and they may cause severe flank pain, hematuria, and urinary obstruction, sometimes passing spontaneously.

urographic techniques.definition: A range of radiologic methods for imaging the urinary tract (kidneys, ureters, and bladder) using contrast media to evaluate anatomy and function; includes intravenous/excretory urography, retrograde urography, voiding cystourethrography, and modern CT or MR urography.

toxic megacolon.definition: A life-threatening complication of inflammatory or infectious colitis characterized by nonobstructive dilation of the colon (typically >6 cm on radiographs) with systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, anemia, dehydration) and radiographic evidence of colonic distension; management includes bowel rest, IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, electrolyte correction, and urgent decompression, with colectomy if medical therapy fails or perforation occurs.

genital cancer.definition: A cancer that originates in the genital organs (including the penis, vulva, or vagina); most commonly squamous cell carcinoma, with risk factors such as HPV infection and smoking, and presents as a persistent lesion, mass, bleeding, or pain, treated according to site and stage.

renal carcinoma.definition: Malignant tumor arising from kidney tissue, typically from the renal cortex or tubular epithelium; presents variably with hematuria, flank pain, or an abdominal mass, though many cases are asymptomatic until advanced; primary treatment is nephrectomy with or without regional lymph node dissection, with targeted or immune therapies used for advanced disease.

renal pyramids.definition: Cone-shaped tissue masses in the renal medulla containing the loops of Henle and collecting ducts; they drain urine from the cortex to the minor calyces via the papillae, with apices facing the renal pelvis and bases adjacent to the renal columns.

arcuate vessels.definition: Arcuate vessels are the arcuate arteries and veins that arch along the corticomedullary junction of the kidney at the base of the renal pyramids, supplying and draining the renal cortex and giving rise to interlobular (cortical) vessels.

megalomania.definition: A delusion of grandeur involving an inflated sense of self-importance, power, or wealth; an unreal belief in one's extraordinary abilities or influence, often seen in mania or narcissistic pathology.

meissner's corpuscle.definition: A rapidly adapting encapsulated mechanoreceptor located in the dermal papillae of glabrous skin (notably fingertips) that detects light touch and fine textures with small receptive fields.

meissner's plexus.definition: A network of neurons in the submucosa of the gastrointestinal tract that is part of the enteric nervous system; it provides secretomotor and vasomotor innervation to the mucosa, regulating glandular secretion, local blood flow, and mucosal function, and communicates with the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus to coordinate intestinal activity.

megaloureter.definition: A congenital dilation of the ureter caused by deficiency or absence of the ureteral smooth muscle, resulting in a dilated, poorly peristaltic ureter that can obstruct urinary drainage and lead to hydronephrosis.

megaureter.definition: An abnormal dilation of the ureter, usually due to distal obstruction or vesicoureteral reflux, resulting in a widened ureter that can be unilateral or bilateral and may be associated with hydronephrosis.

dactylomegaly.definition: Enlargement of one or more digits (fingers or toes).

megavitamin therapy.definition: Administration of vitamins in doses well above recommended daily allowances, often touted in alternative medicine to treat or prevent various conditions; for most diseases, robust evidence of benefit is lacking, and risks include vitamin toxicity and adverse effects, especially from fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and potential interactions with medications.

meige's disease.definition: A focal cranial dystonia characterized by involuntary eyelid spasm (blepharospasm) and oromandibular dystonia (involuntary movements of the jaw, mouth, and tongue), causing facial grimacing and functional impairment; often idiopathic and progressive, with botulinum toxin injections being a common treatment.

meigs' syndrome.definition: A triad of a benign ovarian tumor (most commonly a fibroma) with ascites and pleural effusion that resolves after surgical removal of the tumor.

ovarian fibroma.definition: A benign ovarian tumor composed of fibrous connective tissue (fibroblasts with collagen) arising from the ovarian stroma; typically presents as a unilateral, solid, firm mass and may be associated with Meigs syndrome (ascites and pleural effusion) that resolves after removal.

melkersson-rosenthal syndrome.definition: A rare neurocutaneous granulomatous disorder characterized by recurrent or persistent orofacial swelling (cheilitis granulomatosa), episodes of facial nerve palsy, and fissured tongue (lingua plicata); the classic triad is often incomplete.

facial swelling.definition: Puffiness or enlargement of the facial soft tissues due to accumulation of excess fluid in the interstitial spaces (edema); caused by local processes such as inflammation, infection, or trauma, or by systemic conditions such as kidney or heart disease, liver disease, or allergic reactions. Presentation varies by cause.

fissured tongue.definition: A benign condition in which the dorsum of the tongue shows multiple deep grooves or fissures; usually asymptomatic but debris can accumulate and cause irritation or halitosis; no specific treatment aside from good oral hygiene.

palpebral gland.definition: An eyelid gland; glands in the eyelid include the Meibomian (tarsal) glands that secrete lipids forming the tear film’s oily layer, as well as Zeis (sebaceous) glands and Moll (apocrine) glands at the eyelid margin.

tarsal gland.definition: Sebaceous glands located in the tarsal plate of the eyelids (Meibomian glands) that secrete meibum, an oily lipid-rich substance that lubricates the ocular surface and reduces tear evaporation.

melena neonatorum.definition: A benign neonatal condition in which a newborn passes black, tarry stools (melena) due to swallowing maternal blood during delivery; it is not caused by neonatal GI disease and typically resolves spontaneously within the first few days of life without treatment.

melanism.definition: An abnormal increase in melanin production leading to darker pigmentation of the skin, hair, or other tissues; in animals, often results in unusually dark coat color.

melanosis.definition: An abnormal accumulation or deposition of melanin pigment in tissues, causing brown to black discoloration; not a disease itself, but a descriptive term for pigment changes (e.g., melanosis coli, hepatic melanosis).

melanosis coli.definition: Pigment deposition in the colonic mucosa causing brown-black discoloration, due to accumulation of lipofuscin within macrophages in the lamina propria, most commonly from chronic stimulant laxative use (e.g., senna); benign and reversible after cessation.

melanomata.definition: Plural of melanoma; a malignant neoplasm of melanocytes, most commonly arising in the skin, that can invade locally and metastasize; typically presents as an irregular, pigmented skin lesion and is diagnosed by biopsy.

melanocytic nevus.definition: Benign pigmented skin lesion resulting from clonal proliferation of melanocytes; commonly called a mole. It is typically well circumscribed and symmetric, arising in the epidermis and/or dermis (subtypes: junctional, compound, and dermal nevi, depending on the depth of melanocyte nests).

amelanic melanoma.definition: A melanoma that lacks pigment due to little or no melanin production by malignant melanocytes; presents as a nonpigmented lesion that can be pink, red, or skin-colored and may resemble benign conditions, potentially delaying diagnosis and treatment.

juvenile melanoma.definition: Malignant melanoma occurring in children; a cancer of melanocytes that is rare in the pediatric population, often arising de novo or from a preexisting nevus; diagnosed by biopsy; treated with surgical excision with adequate margins; prognosis depends on stage.

nodular melanoma.definition: A highly aggressive subtype of cutaneous melanoma characterized by early vertical growth and rapid invasion into deeper tissues, usually presenting as a rapidly enlarging, dome-shaped, pigmented (often blue-black) or nonpigmented nodule that may ulcerate; radial growth is limited or absent.

cutaneous melanoma.definition: A malignant tumor of melanocytes arising in the skin; typically presents as an irregular, evolving pigmented lesion and may metastasize to regional lymph nodes and distant organs.

superficial spreading melanoma.definition: A form of cutaneous melanoma characterized by initial radial (horizontal) growth along the epidermis, presenting as an irregular, asymmetrical, multicolored pigmented lesion on sun‑exposed skin; it commonly enlarges over time and may progress to vertical invasion and metastasis.

primary melanoma.definition: A malignant melanoma that originates at its primary site (most commonly the skin) rather than representing metastases from another melanoma.

melanomatosis.definition: A descriptive term for widespread, multifocal involvement by malignant melanoma, typically with numerous pigmented skin lesions and often indicating disseminated or metastatic disease.

melanosome.definition: A membrane-bound lysosome-related organelle in melanocytes that synthesizes and stores melanin pigment and facilitates its transfer to keratinocytes, contributing to skin, hair, and eye color.

melanotic carcinoma.definition: A malignant neoplasm of melanocytes that often contains melanin pigment; historically called melanotic carcinoma, this is today usually referred to as malignant melanoma.

melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infan.definition: A rare, pigmented neoplasm of infancy derived from neural crest cells, typically arising in the anterior maxilla; presents as a rapidly enlarging, pigmented gingival/alveolar mass. Histology shows a biphasic population of small neuroectodermal cells and larger melanin-containing epithelial-like cells; it is locally aggressive but usually benign, with complete surgical excision and close follow-up to monitor for recurrence.

melanoblast.definition: Embryonic neural crest–derived precursor cells that migrate to the epidermis and hair follicles and differentiate into melanocytes, the pigment-producing cells that synthesize melanin.

melanoblastoma.definition: A neoplasm consisting of melanoblasts (immature melanocytes); an historical or obsolete term for a melanocytic tumor, with modern terminology usually referring to melanoma or benign nevus.

melanoderm.definition: Hyperpigmentation of the skin due to increased melanin production or deposition, resulting in darker skin coloration.

melanophore.definition: A pigment-containing skin cell in some animals (notably fish, amphibians, and reptiles) that stores melanin and can change color by moving pigment granules within the cell; analogous to mammalian melanocytes.

melanoameloblastoma.definition: A rare pigmented odontogenic tumor variant in which melanin pigment is present within the tumor (epithelium and/or stroma), resulting in a pigmented ameloblastoma; histology shows conventional ameloblastomatous features with accompanying melanocytic pigment.

melanin.definition: A brown to black pigment that occurs in hair, skin, and eye color; it is responsible for tanning upon sun exposure.

melanocyte.definition: A pigment-producing cell in the epidermis that synthesizes melanin and transfers it to nearby keratinocytes, contributing to skin, hair, and eye color; derived from neural crest cells.

melanocyte-stimulating hormone.definition: A peptide hormone derived from proopiomelanocortin (POMC) that stimulates melanocytes to produce melanin, increasing skin and hair pigmentation; it also has anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects and exists in several forms (e.g., alpha-, beta-, and gamma-MSH).

msh.definition: Peptide hormone derived from proopiomelanocortin (POMC) that stimulates melanin synthesis in melanocytes by activating melanocortin receptors (primarily via the α-MSH form).

melanuria.definition: A condition in which melanin pigment is excreted in the urine, causing dark or black urine; most often associated with malignant melanoma or other melanin-producing tumors.

melasma.definition: A common, benign hyperpigmentation of the face characterized by symmetric brown-to-gray-brown patches on sun-exposed areas (cheeks, forehead, upper lip, chin) due to increased melanin production by melanocytes in the epidermis and/or dermis; commonly triggered by UV exposure and hormonal factors such as pregnancy or estrogen-containing therapy.

melasma gravidarum.definition: Pregnancy-associated facial hyperpigmentation due to hormonal changes (estrogen and progesterone) and sun exposure, presenting as symmetric brown patches on the cheeks, forehead, and sometimes above the upper lip; typically fades after delivery but may persist in some individuals.

melas syndrome.definition: A mitochondrial genetic disorder presenting with stroke-like episodes, lactic acidosis, and encephalopathy due to mtDNA mutations (most commonly MT-TL1), often with myopathy, seizures, hearing loss, diabetes, and cardiomyopathy.

melatonin.definition: Something made by the pineal gland that affects how well you sleep. Manmade and natural melatonin can be found in stores as pills.

melon-seed body.definition: A small, oval, seed-shaped lesion or body; typically used to describe seed-like calcifications or nodules seen in imaging or histology, with the exact diagnosis depending on the tissue context.

meloxicam.definition: A COX‑2 selective nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to relieve pain and inflammation in conditions such as osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis; it works by inhibiting cyclooxygenase‑2, reducing prostaglandin synthesis. Common adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset, ulcers or bleeding, renal impairment, and cardiovascular risk, and it is typically taken orally.

memantine.definition: Memantine is a noncompetitive NMDA receptor antagonist used in the treatment of moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease; it protects neurons by reducing glutamate-induced excitotoxicity and is taken orally.

vesicoureteral reflex.definition: A condition in which urine flows backward from the bladder into the ureter(s) and sometimes the kidney due to an incompetent vesicoureteral junction, increasing the risk of urinary tract infections and potential kidney damage; commonly diagnosed in children and graded I–V, with management ranging from observation and antibiotic prophylaxis to surgical correction for higher-grade reflux.

membrana tectoria.definition: A gelatinous, avascular extracellular membrane in the cochlea that covers the organ of Corti; attached to the spiral limbus, with the outer hair cell stereocilia embedded in it, aiding mechanical stimulation of hair cells during sound vibration.

occipitoaxial ligament.definition: A ligament connecting the occipital bone to the axis (C2) at the craniovertebral junction, helping stabilize that region.

membrana tympani.definition: A thin, semitransparent membrane that forms the boundary between the external ear canal and the middle ear; it vibrates in response to sound and transmits mechanical energy to the auditory ossicles, enabling hearing.

membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.definition: A pattern of glomerular injury characterized by mesangial and endocapillary proliferation with thickened, duplicated glomerular basement membranes (tram-track appearance) due to immune complex deposition or complement-mediated injury; clinically may present with proteinuria, hematuria, edema, and varying renal dysfunction; etiologies include infections (e.g., hepatitis B or C), cryoglobulinemia, and C3 glomerulopathy.

membranous nephropathy.definition: An immune complex–mediated glomerular disease in which subepithelial immune deposits cause thickening of the glomerular basement membrane, classically presenting with nephrotic-range proteinuria; it can be primary (idiopathic, often associated with anti-PLA2R antibodies) or secondary to infections, drugs, autoimmune diseases, or malignancy.

membranous pharyngitis.definition: Inflammation of the pharynx accompanied by the formation of a pseudomembrane (membranous coating) on the pharyngeal mucosa, commonly seen with diphtheria or other severe bacterial infections.

membranous stomatitis.definition: A form of stomatitis characterized by the formation of a membrane (pseudomembrane) on the oral mucosa, with surrounding inflammation; etiologies include infectious conditions such as candidiasis or diphtheria and other inflammatory processes.

multip le endocrine neoplasia.definition: A group of inherited, usually autosomal dominant syndromes in which tumors develop in multiple endocrine glands, often due to germline mutations in specific genes, with distinct tumor spectra for the different subtypes (e.g., parathyroid/pituitary/pancreatic tumors in one type; medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma in another).

menadione.definition: A synthetic form of vitamin K (vitamin K3), chemical name 2-methyl-1,4-naphthoquinone; historically used as a vitamin K supplement but rarely used today due to toxicity concerns.

mendelson's syndrome.definition: Chemical pneumonitis caused by aspiration of acidic gastric contents into the lungs during anesthesia, most classically in obstetric patients; can cause cough, dyspnea, hypoxemia, and radiographic infiltrates, and may progress to ARDS.

ménière's disease.definition: A disorder of the inner ear characterized by recurrent episodes of vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and a sense of fullness in the affected ear, often linked to endolymphatic hydrops.

bacterial meningitis.definition: An acute infection and inflammation of the meninges (the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord) caused by bacteria, most commonly Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, or Listeria monocytogenes; it presents with fever, headache, neck stiffness, and often altered mental status, and requires urgent intravenous antibiotics to prevent serious complications.
