microinjection.definition: A technique that delivers minute amounts of a substance directly into a cell (often into the cytoplasm or nucleus) using a fine glass micropipette attached to a micromanipulator; commonly used for genetic modification, embryo manipulation, and targeted delivery in research and assisted reproduction.

microinjector.definition: A device designed to deliver very small, precisely controlled volumes of liquid into a biological target—such as a single cell or tissue—typically via a microneedle or micropipette, used for microinjection of substances (e.g., genes, dyes, drugs) in research and clinical applications.

microinvasive.definition: A lesion in which malignant cells have breached the epithelial basement membrane and extended into the underlying stroma to only a minimal extent, with invasion typically measured in millimeters and far less than in conventional invasive cancer.

microinvasive carcinoma.definition: A malignant epithelial neoplasm with invasion into the surrounding stroma that is present only as microscopic foci and is extremely limited in extent, typically defined as invasion beyond the basement membrane of about 1 mm or less (definitions vary by organ).

microleakage.definition: Microscopic passage of fluids, bacteria, or ions through gaps at a restoration–tooth or implant interface due to an imperfect seal, potentially leading to secondary caries, sensitivity, and restoration failure.

microliter.definition: A microliter is a unit of volume equal to one millionth of a liter (10^-6 L); it equals 0.001 milliliters (mL) or 1 cubic millimeter (mm^3).

microlith.definition: A very small calcified stone (calculus) formed by mineral salts; a microscopic stone that may occur within a body duct, gland, or tissue.

micromanipulation.definition: Manipulation of microscopic biological samples (e.g., cells or embryos) under a microscope using precision microinstruments and micromanipulators, often for procedures such as microinjection or aspiration.

micromanipulator.definition: A precision mechanical device that enables fine, controlled movement of microscopic objects or instruments under a microscope, typically with micrometer- or sub-micrometer-resolution adjustments (e.g., for microinjection, electrophysiology, or cell manipulation).

micromelic.definition: A form of dwarfism characterized by marked shortening of all limb segments (short-limbed dwarfism), with a relatively normal trunk.

micrometer.definition: A metric unit of length equal to one micrometer (1 μm), i.e., one millionth of a meter; used in microscopy to express the size of microscopic biological structures and to calibrate imaging instruments.

micromillimeter.definition: Not a standard SI unit; a micromillimeter is a nonstandard length equal to 1 × 10^-9 meters (one nanometer), since micro (10^-6) times a millimeter (10^-3 m) equals 10^-9 m. Rarely used in practice.

micromyeloblastic.definition: Relating to abnormally small myeloblasts, the immature precursors of granulocytes in the bone marrow; the term is not commonly used in modern hematology.

micron.definition: A metric unit of length equal to one millionth of a meter (10^-6 m), used to measure very small distances such as cell and microorganism dimensions.

micronor.definition: An oral contraceptive containing the progestin norethindrone (0.35 mg) used as a progestin-only pill (mini-pill); it prevents pregnancy primarily by thickening cervical mucus and thinning the endometrium, with some suppression of ovulation, and must be taken at roughly the same time every day.

micronutrient.definition: A nutrient required in small amounts for normal metabolic function, growth, and development; includes vitamins and trace minerals.

microorganism.definition: A microscopic living organism, such as bacteria, archaea, fungi, protozoa, or certain algae.

micropenis.definition: A congenital condition in which the penis is abnormally small for age, typically defined as a stretched penile length more than 2.5 standard deviations below the mean for age; can be due to hormonal deficiencies or disorders of sexual development.

microphage.definition: An older term for small phagocytic leukocytes, typically neutrophils and eosinophils, that ingest and destroy bacteria and other pathogens during acute inflammation (in contrast to larger tissue macrophages).

microphallus.definition: An abnormally small penis, usually defined as a stretched penile length significantly below the mean for age, often due to hypogonadism or disorders of sexual development.

microphthalmos.definition: An abnormal, congenital reduction in the size of the eyeball (globe) with reduced axial length, typically causing high refractive error and visual impairment; it may be unilateral or bilateral and can be associated with other ocular or systemic anomalies.

microphthalmia.definition: A congenital anomaly in which one or both eyeballs are abnormally small, often with reduced visual acuity; may be isolated or part of a syndrome and can be associated with other ocular anomalies such as coloboma.

microplasia.definition: A developmental abnormality in which a tissue or organ is smaller or less well developed than normal, due to insufficient cell growth or differentiation; often considered a form of hypoplasia.

micropodia.definition: A congenital condition in which the fingers or toes are abnormally small due to hypoplasia of the digital bones and soft tissues; may occur as an isolated finding or with other limb anomalies.

microprolactinoma.definition: A prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma less than 10 mm in diameter that causes hyperprolactinemia and related symptoms such as galactorrhea, amenorrhea/oligoamenorrhea, and infertility.

microprosopus.definition: An archaic or obsolete term describing a relatively small facial skeleton; not a recognized or commonly used medical diagnosis in modern practice.

micropsia.definition: A perceptual distortion in which objects are perceived as smaller than their true size; a type of metamorphopsia that can occur with migraines, temporal lobe epilepsy, brain lesions, or certain drugs, and is described as part of Alice in Wonderland syndrome.

micropuncture.definition: A technique using a very fine needle to puncture a small vessel or tubular structure to gain access or obtain samples, designed to minimize tissue injury and complications during procedures such as vascular access.

microreentry.definition: Reentry confined to a microscopic region of myocardium, forming a self-sustaining reentrant circuit when a wavefront re-enters tissue after a localized conduction block, typically around micro-scale obstacles such as fibrosis or tissue heterogeneity.

microscope.definition: A device that uses lenses to magnify small objects beyond the naked eye, enabling detailed observation of cells, tissues, and microorganisms; common types include light microscopes and electron microscopes.

microscopy.definition: Observation of specimens using a microscope to magnify and resolve structures too small to see with the naked eye; includes modalities such as light, fluorescence, confocal, and electron microscopy.

microshock.definition: An electrical injury caused by a very small current delivered directly to the heart through a conductive pathway (such as implanted leads or exposed catheters), bypassing skin resistance, which can induce dangerous cardiac arrhythmias (e.g., ventricular fibrillation).

microsomal.definition: Pertaining to endoplasmic reticulum–derived vesicles formed when cells are disrupted; these vesicles contain enzymes, notably cytochrome P450, that catalyze drug metabolism.

microsome.definition: A small vesicle-like fragment of the endoplasmic reticulum obtained from disrupted cells after differential centrifugation; contains membrane-bound enzymes, notably cytochrome P450, and is used in in vitro studies of drug metabolism and xenobiotic processing.

microsomia.definition: An abnormal condition in which an organism or a body part is smaller than normal; in newborns it typically refers to fetal growth restriction with birth size (weight or length) below the 10th percentile for gestational age (small-for-gestational-age).

microsphere.definition: A small spherical particle used in medicine as an embolic agent or drug/radiopharmaceutical carrier; typically 10–1000 micrometers in diameter, made of materials such as gelatin, glass, or polymer, and used to occlude blood vessels or deliver localized therapy.

microspherocytosis.definition: An abnormal finding in which red blood cells appear as small, spherical (spherocytes) on a peripheral blood smear, reflecting loss of membrane surface area without a corresponding decrease in cell volume; these cells have reduced deformability and increased susceptibility to hemolysis, seen in hereditary spherocytosis and other forms of hemolytic anemia.

microsporida.definition: A phylum of obligate intracellular, spore-forming unicellular parasites, historically considered fungi, that infect a wide range of hosts—including humans—and cause microsporidiosis, especially in immunocompromised individuals.

microsporidiosis.definition: An infection caused by Microsporidia—obligate intracellular, spore-forming parasites (fungi)—that primarily affects immunocompromised hosts. It commonly presents with chronic diarrhea and weight loss from gastrointestinal infection and can involve the eye or disseminate to other organs. Diagnosis is by detecting spores in stool or tissue with special stains or PCR; treatment includes antiparasitic therapy and immune reconstitution.

microstomia.definition: An abnormal reduction in mouth opening (oral aperture), which can be congenital or acquired and may impair eating, speech, and dental care.

microsurgery.definition: Surgery performed under magnification with specialized microinstruments to repair or reconstruct very small structures—typically nerves and blood vessels—often involving microvascular anastomoses, nerve repair, or free tissue transfer.

microsurgical.definition: Relating to microsurgery; procedures performed under magnification with an operating microscope and microinstruments to repair or manipulate very small structures (e.g., nerves, blood vessels, or delicate tissues).

epididymal.definition: Relating to the epididymis, the coiled duct at the back of the testis where sperm mature and are stored.

mesa.definition: Not a recognized medical term; there is no standard medical definition for "mesa."

audouinii.definition: A dermatophyte fungus species that causes tinea capitis (scalp ringworm), most often in children, transmitted by close contact or contaminated objects and presenting with scalp scaling and patchy hair loss.

canis.definition: A Latin word meaning dog; used in biological taxonomy to designate the genus that includes domestic dogs and wolves.

gypseum.definition: An epithet used in fungal species names, particularly for dermatophytes associated with gypsum-containing soils; these soil-dwelling fungi can infect skin, hair, and nails in humans and animals.

ambiguous.definition: Open to more than one interpretation; unclear or lacking a single, definite meaning.

micrognathic.definition: Relating to or characterized by an abnormally small mandible (lower jaw).

micronodular.definition: Relating to or composed of very small nodules; consisting of discrete, tiny nodular lesions.

microtubule organizing center.definition: A cellular structure that nucleates and anchors microtubules, organizing the microtubule cytoskeleton and guiding spindle formation during cell division. In animal cells the centrosome—composed of a pair of centrioles and surrounding pericentriolar material—acts as the primary organizing center, while other organisms use spindle pole bodies or non-centrosomal organizing centers.

mtoc.definition: Not a standard medical term; there is no widely accepted definition in medical dictionaries. If you provide the full form or context, I can give a precise definition.

basal body.definition: A centriole-like organelle at the base of a cilium or flagellum that nucleates and anchors the axoneme, organizing the microtubule array for the cilium or flagellum.

microvascular.definition: Relating to the smallest blood vessels of the circulatory system (capillaries, arterioles, and venules) and to the microcirculation that mediates tissue perfusion and exchange of nutrients, gases, and waste.

microvilli.definition: Microscopic, fingerlike projections of the apical plasma membrane on certain epithelial cells (notably intestinal enterocytes and renal tubular cells) that increase surface area to facilitate absorption; each projection contains a core bundle of actin filaments and forms part of the brush border.

electron microscope.definition: A microscope that uses a beam of electrons instead of light to illuminate a specimen, providing far higher resolution and magnification; includes transmission and scanning electron microscopes and typically requires vacuum and specialized specimen preparation (often metal coating).

microwave interstitial system.definition: A system that delivers microwave energy through interstitially placed antennas or probes to heat and destroy targeted tissue, typically for tumor ablation, with imaging guidance and a microwave generator regulating energy delivery.

microwave-generated hyperthermia system.definition: A device that delivers microwave energy to body tissues to generate controlled heating (hyperthermia) in a targeted area, typically raising temperatures to about 39–45°C to enhance the effectiveness of radiation or chemotherapy; can be external (antenna/applicator array) or interstitial, with temperature monitoring and feedback control.

microwave thermography.definition: A noninvasive imaging technique that uses microwave energy to assess tissue properties (such as dielectric permittivity and conductivity) and/or temperature distributions, producing images that reflect internal tissue characteristics; primarily used in research and not widely adopted for routine clinical practice.

micturition reflex.definition: A reflex arc that coordinates urination: bladder wall stretch activates afferent fibers to the sacral spinal cord, triggering parasympathetic-mediated detrusor contraction and relaxation of the internal urethral sphincter; the external urethral sphincter is under voluntary control via the pudendal nerve.

micturition syncope.definition: A fainting episode triggered by urination, typically a vasovagal syncope occurring during or immediately after voiding, due to reflex bradycardia and hypotension from increased vagal tone and decreased sympathetic activity.

micu.definition: A hospital unit that provides continuous, highly specialized monitoring and organ-support for critically ill medical patients, including invasive lines, mechanical ventilation, vasoactive medications, and renal replacement therapy; typically separate from surgical ICUs.

minimal infecting dose.definition: The smallest quantity of a pathogenic organism (or its infectious unit) sufficient to establish infection in a susceptible host, and it varies with the organism, exposure route, and host factors.

midamor.definition: An oral potassium-sparing diuretic that blocks epithelial sodium channels in the distal nephron (collecting ducts), increasing sodium and water excretion while conserving potassium; used to treat hypertension and edema and to prevent hypokalemia when used with other diuretics.

midarm circumference.definition: Measurement of the circumference of the upper arm taken at the midpoint between the shoulder (acromion) and the elbow (olecranon); used to assess nutritional status and body composition.

midaxillary line.definition: A vertical anatomical line on the lateral chest that passes through the apex of the axilla; used as a surface landmark to describe the location of thoracic structures and to position leads or auscultation sites.

midazolam hydrochloride.definition: An injectable, water-soluble salt of the benzodiazepine midazolam used for sedation, anxiolysis, amnesia, and anesthesia induction; it enhances GABA-A receptor activity, providing rapid-onset, short-acting effects with risks of respiratory depression and hypotension, especially with other CNS depressants.

midbody.definition: A transient structure formed during late mitosis and cytokinesis, consisting of tightly bundled antiparallel microtubules with associated proteins at the center of the dividing cell; it forms between the daughter cells and coordinates the final abscission of the plasma membranes.

midcarpal.definition: The articulation between the proximal and distal rows of the carpal bones in the wrist; a synovial joint that allows mainly gliding movements with flexion and extension and some radial/ulnar deviation.

midclavicular line.definition: An imaginary vertical line drawn downward from the midpoint of the clavicle on each side, used as an anatomical landmark to describe chest surface anatomy (e.g., heart outline and apex beat along the left midclavicular line).

middle costotransverse ligament.definition: Not a standard anatomical term. If used, it would refer to a component of the thoracic costotransverse ligament complex—a connective tissue band that helps stabilize the costotransverse joint by linking a rib to the transverse process of the vertebra. Standard anatomy more commonly cites the superior costotransverse, lateral (costotransverse), and posterior costotransverse ligaments.

middle cuneiform bone.definition: A small, wedge-shaped tarsal bone in the foot, the middle (intermediate) cuneiform lies between the medial and lateral cuneiforms and articulates proximally with the navicular and distally with the base of the second metatarsal (and with the adjacent cuneiforms), helping form the transverse arch of the foot.

pharyngotympanic tube.definition: A narrow canal that connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx, equalizes air pressure on the tympanic membrane, and allows drainage of middle-ear secretions; it is normally closed and opens during swallowing or yawning; also known as the Eustachian tube.

epitympanic recess.definition: A recess of the middle ear (epitympanum/attic) located above the tympanic cavity in the petrous temporal bone; bounded by the tegmen tympani, it contains the head of the malleus and the body of the incus and communicates with the mastoid air system via the aditus to the antrum.

middle lobe syndrome.definition: A pattern of recurrent infection and/or atelectasis of the right middle lobe due to obstruction or impaired drainage of the middle lobe bronchus, often from mucus plugging, inflammation, bronchial stenosis, or extrinsic compression.

obstructive pneumonitis.definition: An inflammatory pattern in lung tissue distal to an obstructed airway, usually due to blockage by a tumor, mucus plug, or foreign body; may be accompanied by atelectasis or post-obstructive pneumonia.

antituberculosis chemotherapy.definition: A structured medical therapy for tuberculosis that uses a combination of anti-tuberculous drugs to kill Mycobacterium tuberculosis, prevent resistance, and reduce transmission. In drug-susceptible TB, the typical regimen consists of an initial intensive phase of 2 months with four drugs (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) followed by a continuation phase of about 4 months with isoniazid and rifampin.

tuberculous inflammation.definition: A chronic granulomatous inflammation caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, characterized by aggregates of epithelioid macrophages with Langhans-type giant cells surrounded by lymphocytes, often with central caseous necrosis; driven by a Th1-mediated immune response and IFN-γ–activated macrophages, and commonly affecting the lungs but possible in other tissues.

small cardiac vein.definition: A small cardiac vein is a cardiac vein that drains venous blood from the right atrium and right ventricle, runs in the right coronary sulcus, and empties into the coronary sinus.

middle molecule.definition: A category of solutes with intermediate molecular weight (about 0.5–60 kilodaltons) that are not efficiently removed by standard dialysis; examples include β2-microglobulin.

midface.definition: The middle third of the face, consisting of the maxilla and zygomatic bones and their soft tissues, including the cheeks, infraorbital region, and nasal base.

midoccipital.definition: Situated at or near the midline of the occipital bone; pertaining to the middle region at the back of the skull.

midodrine.definition: An oral prodrug whose active metabolite desglymidodrine is an alpha-1 adrenergic receptor agonist used to treat symptomatic orthostatic hypotension by increasing vascular tone and blood pressure.

midparental height.definition: An estimate of a child’s eventual adult height, derived from the heights of the biological parents; typically calculated as the average of the parents’ heights, sometimes adjusted for the child’s sex.

midpelvic contraction.definition: A condition in which the midportion of the maternal pelvis is constricted, reducing the obstetric diameter at the midpelvic plane and obstructing fetal descent during labor, often contributing to labor dystocia or arrest of descent. It is one of the pelvic constrictions (inlet, midpelvis, outlet) that can cause cephalopelvic disproportion.

midposition.definition: A position halfway between two extreme positions; in clinical use, it denotes a neutral, midline posture—for example, the eye in a resting, straight-ahead gaze or a fetus lying with the presenting part aligned with the maternal midline rather than flexed or extended.

midforceps.definition: An obstetric instrument—one of the forceps types—applied when the fetal head is at midpelvic level to facilitate vaginal delivery by traction and rotation.

trial forceps.definition: A pair of obstetric forceps used to attempt an instrumental vaginal delivery by grasping the fetal head to provide traction and rotation; used when conditions are favorable and progress is insufficient, with escalation if delivery cannot be achieved safely.

failed forceps.definition: An obstetric situation in which attempts to deliver the fetus with obstetric forceps are unsuccessful, prompting cessation of forceps use and alternative delivery methods (e.g., vacuum extraction or cesarean section) to complete delivery.

midgut loop.definition: A U-shaped loop of the developing midgut that temporarily herniates into the umbilical cord during embryogenesis due to rapid intestinal growth; it rotates about 270 degrees as it returns to the abdomen.

midgut volvulus.definition: An acute twisting of the midgut around its mesentery, typically due to intestinal malrotation, causing intestinal obstruction and mesenteric vascular compromise that can lead to bowel ischemia if not promptly treated; emergent surgical detorsion (often with a Ladd procedure) is required.

midgut volvulus neonatorum.definition: A life-threatening condition in newborns in which the midgut twists around the superior mesenteric artery due to intestinal malrotation, causing bowel obstruction and risking bowel ischemia; presents with bilious vomiting and abdominal distention and requires urgent surgical reduction (typically the Ladd procedure).

midsternum.definition: The central portion of the sternum (the body, or corpus sterni) between the manubrium above and the xiphoid process below; forms the main anterior part of the thorax.

midstream catch urine specimen.definition: A urine specimen collected after the patient begins urinating using a clean-catch technique to minimize contamination from distal urethral and genital flora; collected midstream into a sterile container for urinalysis and culture.

midwifery.definition: A health profession focused on the care of pregnancy, labor and birth, and the postpartum period. It includes prenatal care, continuous support during labor, safe birth, and early postpartum and newborn care, with an emphasis on normal pregnancies and prevention, typically provided by trained midwives who may practice independently or in collaboration with obstetric clinicians.

midwife.definition: A health professional who provides care to pregnant people before, during, and after childbirth, including prenatal care, labor and birth support, and postpartum/newborn care; midwives may be certified nurse-midwives (CNMs) or independent practitioners (CMs/CPMs).

mif.definition: A proinflammatory cytokine produced by macrophages and other cells that promotes immune and inflammatory responses by inhibiting macrophage migration and stimulating production of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, and by counter-regulating glucocorticoids.

macrophage migration inhibition factor.definition: A proinflammatory cytokine produced by activated T cells and macrophages that inhibits macrophage migration in vitro and modulates macrophage activation and inflammatory responses, including counteracting glucocorticoid action.

migration inhibitory factor.definition: A pro-inflammatory cytokine produced by activated T cells and macrophages; it promotes innate and adaptive immune responses, counteracts glucocorticoid-mediated immunosuppression, and was originally identified as a factor that inhibits macrophage migration.

migration inhibitory factor test.definition: An in vitro immunological assay in which leukocytes exposed to a specific antigen show inhibited macrophage migration due to release of a migration-inhibiting factor by sensitized T cells, indicating a cell-mediated immune response to that antigen.

mif test.definition: An older in vitro immunology assay that evaluates cell-mediated immunity by measuring whether sensitized T-lymphocytes release a factor that inhibits macrophage migration; historically used to detect delayed-type hypersensitivity to antigens such as tuberculin, but now largely superseded by modern tests.

miglitol.definition: An oral α-glucosidase inhibitor that delays digestion of carbohydrates in the small intestine, reducing postprandial glucose excursions in type 2 diabetes; often used with diet therapy and other antidiabetic agents. Common adverse effects are gastrointestinal, including flatulence, diarrhea, and abdominal discomfort.

miglustat.definition: A small-molecule iminosugar that inhibits glucosylceramide synthase, reducing glycosphingolipid synthesis; used as substrate-reduction therapy for certain lysosomal storage disorders, notably Niemann-Pick disease type C and Gaucher disease type 1.

phonophobia.definition: Sensitivity to noise, often experienced during a migraine attack.

ru-486.definition: A competitive progesterone receptor antagonist (mifepristone) used to medically terminate early pregnancy by blocking progesterone action, causing decidual breakdown and detachment of the pregnancy; typically followed by misoprostol to induce uterine contractions, effective up to about 10 weeks of gestation depending on guidelines.

endoscopic.definition: Relating to endoscopy; performed with an endoscope to visualize the interior of hollow organs or body cavities.

miliary.definition: Of or relating to millet seeds; in medicine, describing a diffuse distribution of numerous minute nodules (about 1–2 mm) that resemble millet seeds, as seen in conditions such as miliary tuberculosis.

tartrate.definition: A salt or ester of tartaric acid (an naturally occurring dihydroxybutanedioic acid; tartrates include potassium hydrogen tartrate and calcium tartrate).

phenobarbital.definition: A long-acting barbiturate anticonvulsant and sedative-hypnotic that enhances GABA-A receptor–mediated inhibition; used to treat certain seizures and as a sedative or preanesthetic agent.

triptan.definition: A class of selective serotonin 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonist medications used to abort acute migraine attacks; they cause constriction of intracranial blood vessels and inhibit release of inflammatory neuropeptides (eg, CGRP), reducing migraine pain.

diphosphate.definition: Two phosphate groups joined by a phosphoanhydride bond, forming the pyrophosphate moiety; found in nucleotide diphosphates (e.g., ADP) and as inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi); acts as a high-energy intermediate in biosynthetic and energy-transfer reactions and is hydrolyzed to two inorganic phosphate (Pi).

endometracin.definition: Not found in standard medical dictionaries; likely a misspelling of “endometrial,” meaning relating to the endometrium, the mucous membrane lining of the uterus.

hortons.definition: A vasculitis of medium- to large arteries, most commonly the temporal arteries, occurring in adults over ~50 years, causing new headaches, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, and possible vision loss; often with elevated inflammatory markers and treated urgently with high-dose corticosteroids to prevent blindness.

polyarthritis.definition: Inflammation of five or more joints, typically occurring as part of an inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis.

millerabbott.definition: A long, flexible enteric tube with two inflatable balloons used to decompress the gastrointestinal tract, especially in bowel obstruction; inserted nasogastrically and advanced by alternately inflating the balloons, with suction applied to remove gas and fluids.

pyrazinamide.definition: A first-line antitubercular drug; a prodrug converted to pyrazinoic acid by the mycobacterial enzyme pyrazinamidase and active mainly against dormant Mycobacterium tuberculosis, aiding sterilization and shortening TB therapy when used with other anti-TB drugs.

mikulicz.definition: An eponym for bilateral enlargement of the lacrimal and salivary glands; in current practice, this presentation is associated with IgG4-related disease, with historical links to Sjögren's syndrome.

aphthae.definition: Small, shallow, painful ulcers of the mucous membranes, most commonly on the oral mucosa (recurrent aphthous stomatitis); they typically have a gray or yellowish base with a surrounding red halo and usually heal spontaneously within 1–2 weeks.

milia.definition: Small, benign keratin-filled cysts that appear as tiny white bumps on the skin; occur when keratin becomes trapped beneath the epidermis, most commonly on the face and in newborns. They are non-inflammatory and typically resolve spontaneously within weeks to months, though persistent lesions can be removed by a dermatologist.

profunda.definition: Latin adjective meaning "deep"; in anatomy, used to describe a structure that lies deeper within a region, away from the surface (e.g., the deep femoral artery).

sutton.definition: A medical eponym referring to a clinical finding or disorder named after a clinician with the surname Sutton; the exact definition depends on which Sutton eponym is being invoked, so a precise meaning requires contextual specification.

antishock.definition: An intervention or device intended to prevent or treat shock by increasing venous return and central perfusion, historically achieved with inflatable anti‑shock trousers that compress the legs and abdomen to raise circulating blood volume.

garment.definition: An item of clothing worn on the body; in medical contexts it may refer to specialized garments such as compression stockings or postoperative garments used to support healing and reduce edema.

magnesia.definition: A basic oxide of magnesium (MgO) used medically as an antacid and laxative; the term also refers to magnesium hydroxide preparations (milk of magnesia) used for similar purposes.

milliary.definition: Resembling millet seeds; in medical terms used to describe numerous tiny nodules (about 1–2 mm in diameter) scattered throughout an organ, most often the lungs, as seen in miliary tuberculosis or disseminated metastases.

miller's syndrome.definition: Rare congenital craniofacial disorder characterized by hypoplasia of the mandible and midface (mandibulofacial dysostosis), often with malar hypoplasia and airway/feeding difficulties; historically described within the mandibulofacial dysostosis spectrum and overlapping Treacher Collins syndrome.

malar hypoplasia.definition: Underdevelopment of the zygomatic (malar) bones, resulting in a flattened cheek region and midface hypoplasia.

downslanting palpebral fissures.definition: A descriptive facial feature in which the outer corners of the eyes (lateral palpebral fissures) slope downward relative to the inner corners (medial canthi); used to describe certain dysmorphic phenotypes and genetic syndromes.

cup-shaped ears.definition: A congenital malformation of the external ear in which the pinna is cupped or funnel-shaped, often with reduced cartilage and an abnormal contour; may occur as an isolated anomaly or as part of a syndrome.

lower lid ectropion.definition: An outward turning of the lower eyelid margin away from the eyeball, resulting in conjunctival exposure, tearing, irritation, and potential corneal drying or injury.

postaxial limb deficiencies.definition: A congenital limb reduction defect in which structures on the postaxial (ulnar or fibular) side of a limb are missing or underdeveloped (e.g., ulna or fibular elements and postaxial digits), often with limb shortening; part of the spectrum of longitudinal limb deficiencies and contrasted with preaxial (radial/tibial) deficiencies.

syndactyly.definition: A congenital condition in which two or more digits are fused together, either by skin and soft tissue (simple) or by bone and deeper structures (complex); can be isolated or part of a syndrome, often due to failure of apoptosis between developing digital rays, and is usually treated with surgical separation when function or appearance is affected.

heart defects.definition: A broad category of structural abnormalities of the heart present at birth (congenital heart defects) that disturb normal blood flow, including septal defects, valve malformations, and abnormal connections between vessels.

postaxial acrofacial dysostosis.definition: A rare congenital disorder in the acrofacial dysostosis spectrum characterized by craniofacial (facial) anomalies from first- and second-arch developmental disturbances and postaxial (ulnar-side) limb defects, typically involving hypoplasia or aplasia of the fifth finger and ulna‑ray structures, with variable involvement of other craniofacial features.

retropubic prostatectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove the prostate gland through an anterior abdominal (retropubic) approach, typically performed for localized prostate cancer; commonly called radical retropubic prostatectomy and may include removal of surrounding tissues and regional lymph nodes.

millin operation.definition: I can’t find a medical term spelled “millin operation.” Could you check the spelling or give context (anatomy area, condition, or who the procedure is named after)? If you meant a similarly spelled term (e.g., “Miller operation” or “Millin procedure”), I can define that once clarified.

milroy's disease.definition: An inherited congenital form of primary lymphedema presenting at birth or in early infancy, with bilateral edema of the feet and legs due to developmental defects of the lymphatic vessels, most often caused by autosomal-dominant mutations in the FLT4 (VEGFR-3) gene.

congenital lymphedema.definition: A primary lymphedema that is present at birth or in early infancy due to congenital maldevelopment or dysfunction of the lymphatic system, leading to impaired lymph drainage and swelling (often of the lower limbs); edema is typically nonpitting and may worsen with standing or activity, with Milroy disease (congenital lymphedema type I) a classic form linked to VEGFR3 (FLT4) mutations.

milroy's edema.definition: A congenital form of primary lymphedema due to developmental defects in the lymphatic system (lymphatic hypoplasia/dysplasia), presenting at birth or in infancy with bilateral swelling of the legs; often inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.

nonne-milroy-meige syndrome.definition:
There is no widely recognized medical syndrome by that exact name in standard references; it may be a misspelling or a nonstandard combination of two distinct conditions.

- Milroy disease (congenital hereditary lymphedema): A congenital form of lymphedema presenting at birth or in early infancy, typically affecting the legs with non-pitting edema; most commonly due to mutations in FLT4/VEGFR3; inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.

- Meige syndrome (oromandibular dystonia with blepharospasm): A focal dystonia characterized by involuntary contractions of the facial muscles, especially the eyelids (blepharospasm) and the jaw/tongue/face (oromandibular dystonia); usually begins in adulthood and can be treated with botulinum toxin injections.

miltown.definition: A brand name for meprobamate, a prescription anxiolytic and sedative that acts as a central nervous system depressant; used to treat anxiety disorders but can cause drowsiness and has potential for dependence and withdrawal with long-term use.

tic.definition: A sudden, rapid, recurrent, nonrhythmic motor movement or vocalization.

mind-body medicine.definition: A field of health care that emphasizes bidirectional interactions between the mind and body, using evidence-based techniques such as meditation, mindfulness, relaxation, biofeedback, yoga, hypnosis, and cognitive-behavioral strategies to improve health, reduce symptoms, and prevent illness.

fludrocortisone.definition: A synthetic corticosteroid with potent mineralocorticoid activity used to replace aldosterone in adrenal insufficiency and to treat orthostatic hypotension; it promotes sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion in the distal renal tubules, increasing blood volume.

mineral oil.definition: A colorless, odorless petroleum-derived hydrocarbon oil used medically as an oral laxative and topically as a lubricant or emollient; it coats stool to prevent water loss and ease passage, but can interfere with absorption of fat-soluble vitamins and may cause lipid pneumonia if aspirated.

miner's elbow.definition: Inflammation and swelling of the olecranon bursa at the tip of the elbow due to chronic friction or pressure (typical of mining work with prolonged elbow resting on surfaces), often presenting as a tender swelling; usually aseptic but may become septic if infected.

miner's cramp.definition: A painful, transient cramp of the hand and forearm muscles due to prolonged, repetitive gripping and overuse, historically seen in miners; typically relieved by rest and changes in activity.

miner's pneumoconiosis.definition: An occupational lung disease caused by inhalation of coal dust, leading to deposition of carbon-laden dust in the lungs with nodular interstitial fibrosis in the upper lobes, which can progress to extensive fibrosis (progressive massive fibrosis) and restrictive ventilatory impairment.

minerva cast.definition: A rigid immobilization cast extending from the scalp to the upper thorax that immobilizes the head, neck, and upper spine to stabilize the cervical region, historically used for cervical spine fractures, infections, or postoperative stabilization.

minerva jacket.definition: A rigid cervicothoracic orthosis (brace) that immobilizes the head, neck, and upper spine, worn as a jacket around the torso to stabilize the cervical spine after injury or surgery (and used in some scoliosis treatment regimens).

minimal brain dysfunction.definition: A historical term for a presumed mild, non-specific neurological dysfunction in children, typically presenting with attention, learning, behavior, and coordination problems; the category is largely obsolete and has been superseded by modern diagnoses such as ADHD, specific learning disorders, and developmental coordination disorder.

minipress.definition: A selective alpha-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist used to treat hypertension; it lowers blood pressure by relaxing vascular smooth muscle and reducing peripheral resistance, and is also used off-label for PTSD-related nightmares and certain vasospastic conditions.

prazosin hydrochloride.definition: An oral, selective alpha-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist (the hydrochloride salt) used to treat hypertension by vasodilation of peripheral vessels; it is also used off-label for PTSD-related nightmares and can cause orthostatic hypotension.

minocycline hydrochloride.definition: A hydrochloride salt form of minocycline, a broad-spectrum tetracycline antibiotic that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by reversibly binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit; used to treat acne vulgaris and a variety of infections.

minocin.definition: A tetracycline antibiotic used to treat a variety of infections, notably acne vulgaris; it inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by reversibly binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit, blocking attachment of tRNA.

minocycline.definition: A broad-spectrum tetracycline antibiotic that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by reversibly binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit, blocking tRNA attachment; used for acne, rosacea, and various infections; generally bacteriostatic with risks including photosensitivity and, in pregnancy or young children, tooth discoloration and bone effects; contraindicated in pregnancy and children under 8.

minor arterial circle of iris.definition: A small arterial ring on the anterior surface of the iris near the pupillary margin formed by anastomoses of the anterior ciliary arteries; it supplies the iris stroma and the pupillary region.

minor hysteria.definition: An outdated term historically used to describe mild hysterical symptoms, such as exaggerated emotional reactions or non-specific physical complaints with no identifiable organic cause; in modern psychiatry these presentations are more accurately described as conversion disorder, somatic symptom disorder, or benign emotional disturbances.

minor renal calyx.definition: A cup-shaped structure at the apex of a renal pyramid that receives urine from the papilla and drains into the major calyx; it is the smallest of the renal calyces.

minor surgery.definition: A surgical procedure that is relatively simple and less invasive than major surgery, typically performed on an outpatient basis under local anesthesia or light sedation, involving small incisions or minimal tissue manipulation with a short recovery and low risk.

lordosis.definition: An inward (anterior) curvature of the spine, most commonly in the lumbar region; a normal part of spinal alignment (the cervical and lumbar regions are lordotic). When exaggerated, it is called hyperlordosis (swayback) and may be associated with posture, obesity, pregnancy, or muscle imbalance.

idiopathic nephrotic syndrome.definition: Nephrotic syndrome of unknown etiology after thorough evaluation, characterized by heavy proteinuria (nephrotic-range), hypoalbuminemia, edema, and often hyperlipidemia; in children, the most common underlying cause is minimal change disease.

lipoid nephrosis.definition: A nephrotic syndrome—predominantly in children—characterized by edema, hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia, and heavy proteinuria; classically due to minimal-change disease with normal glomeruli on light microscopy and podocyte foot-process effacement on electron microscopy.

nil disease.definition: An unrecognized or obsolete medical term with no widely accepted current definition; likely a misspelling or historical label for another condition. If you can share context (symptoms, region, era), I can help identify the intended condition.

proximal tubules.definition: A segment of the nephron in the kidney, comprising the proximal convoluted tubule and proximal straight tubule; the primary site of reabsorption of most filtered solutes and water (roughly 65–70% of NaCl and water, nearly all glucose and amino acids, bicarbonate) and of secretion of organic acids and bases, contributing to acid-base balance.

tetracycline hydrochloride.definition: The hydrochloride salt form of tetracycline, a broad-spectrum antibiotic that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by reversibly binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit; used to treat infections caused by susceptible bacteria; adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset, photosensitivity, and teeth discoloration in developing teeth; contraindicated in pregnancy and in children under 8.

minoxidil.definition: A potent arteriolar vasodilator and ATP‑sensitive potassium (K_ATP) channel opener used topically to promote hair growth in androgenetic alopecia; orally, it acts as a last‑line antihypertensive for refractory hypertension. Common adverse effects include hypertrichosis (excessive hair growth), edema, and tachycardia.

refractory hypertension.definition: Uncontrolled hypertension that persists despite adherence to a maximal antihypertensive regimen—typically at least four to five medications from different classes, including a diuretic.

severe refractory hypertension.definition: Uncontrolled high blood pressure that persists despite adherence to an optimized regimen of at least four antihypertensive medications from different classes (including a diuretic) at maximally tolerated or high doses, typically with severe elevations (for example, systolic ≥180 mmHg or diastolic ≥110 mmHg).

androgenic alopecia.definition: Androgenic alopecia is the most common form of hair loss, caused by genetic susceptibility and androgen-driven miniaturization of scalp hair follicles, resulting in patterned thinning of hair (male-pattern in men and diffuse crown thinning in women).

dissecting aortic aneurysm.definition: A tear in the intimal layer of the aorta that allows blood to dissect between wall layers, creating a false lumen; a life-threatening emergency typically presenting with sudden, severe chest or back pain and potential malperfusion of organs. It is classified by location as Stanford Type A (ascending aorta) or Type B (descending aorta).

salt and water retention.definition: Retention of sodium (salt) and water by the body, causing fluid overload and edema; commonly due to impaired renal sodium excretion or hormonal factors (eg, excess aldosterone or antidiuretic hormone) in conditions like heart failure, cirrhosis, or nephrotic syndrome.

excessive hair growth.definition: Excessive hair growth anywhere on the body; can be congenital or acquired and localized or generalized, often related to hormonal imbalance, medications, or genetic factors.

gi disorders.definition: An umbrella term for diseases and conditions that affect the digestive tract from the mouth to the anus and its accessory organs, presenting with symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, heartburn/reflux, diarrhea, constipation, bloating, weight loss, or GI bleeding.

mintezol.definition: A brand name for thiabendazole, a broad‑spectrum benzimidazole antiparasitic (anthelmintic) used to treat parasitic worm infections; it works by inhibiting microtubule formation in helminths, disrupting their glucose uptake and energy metabolism.

tiabendazole.definition: An anthelmintic in the benzimidazole class used to treat intestinal nematode infections (e.g., hookworm, roundworm, whipworm, Strongyloides) and, topically, certain fungal infections. It acts by binding parasite beta-tubulin, inhibiting microtubule formation and glucose uptake, leading to immobilization and death of the parasite.

minute ventilation.definition: The total volume of air entering and leaving the lungs per minute; equal to tidal volume times respiratory rate (approximately 5–8 liters per minute at rest).

mitral insufficiency.definition: A condition in which the mitral valve fails to close tightly, allowing blood to flow backward from the left ventricle into the left atrium during systole.

mitral murmur.definition: An abnormal heart sound produced by turbulent flow across the mitral valve, usually heard best at the apex; can indicate mitral regurgitation (holosystolic blowing murmur radiating to the axilla) or mitral stenosis (diastolic rumble with an opening snap).

mitral commissurotomy.definition: A surgical procedure to relieve mitral valve stenosis by dividing the fused commissures of the mitral valve to widen the valve orifice and restore blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle; traditionally performed as a closed or open commissurotomy (valvotomy).

mitral gradient.definition: Transmitral diastolic pressure gradient: the pressure difference between the left atrium and left ventricle across the mitral valve during diastole, used to assess the severity of mitral stenosis; measured by Doppler echocardiography as peak and mean gradients.

atrioventricular valve.definition: A heart valve between an atrium and its ventricle (the mitral valve on the left and the tricuspid valve on the right) that prevents backflow of blood from the ventricle to the atrium during ventricular contraction.

semilunar valve.definition: Either of the two crescent-shaped heart valves at the bases of the aorta and pulmonary artery, with three cusps, that prevent backflow of blood from the arteries into the ventricles during diastole.

mitral atresia.definition: A rare congenital heart defect in which the mitral valve orifice is absent or imperforate, preventing flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle. It is usually associated with a small or underdeveloped left ventricle (hypoplastic left heart) and often with single-ventricle physiology, leading to early cyanosis. Management is complex and may involve staged surgical palliation (e.g., Norwood-style procedures) or heart transplantation, depending on anatomy.

anterior descending coronary artery.definition: A branch of the left coronary artery that travels in the anterior interventricular groove and supplies the anterior wall of the left ventricle and most of the interventricular septum; also known as the left anterior descending (LAD) artery.

left atrial appendage.definition: An ear-shaped pouch of the left atrium that can form thrombi, especially in atrial fibrillation, and is a target for occlusion to reduce embolic stroke risk.

apex of left ventricle.definition: The conical, distal tip of the left ventricle formed by the LV free wall; typically located at the left fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line and corresponding to the point of maximal impulse on palpation.

refractory congestive heart failure.definition: Refractory congestive heart failure is heart failure that remains symptomatic and/or progresses despite optimized guideline-directed medical therapy and diuretic treatment, typically corresponding to persistent functional limitation (NYHA class III–IV), often requiring escalation to advanced therapies such as inotropic support, mechanical circulatory support, or heart transplantation.

rheumatic endocarditis.definition: An inflammatory valvulitis occurring in acute rheumatic fever, characterized by sterile verrucous vegetations along the lines of closure on the mitral (and often aortic) valves, as part of pancarditis; can lead to chronic rheumatic heart disease with valvular stenosis or regurgitation.

adrenal cortex carcinoma.definition: A malignant tumor arising from the adrenal cortex of the adrenal gland; it may secrete steroids (cortisol, androgens, or aldosterone) causing endocrine symptoms, or be nonfunctioning; often presents as an abdominal mass with pain or weight loss and can metastasize; treatment typically involves surgical resection, with adjuvant mitotane chemotherapy or radiation in selected cases.

epigastric distress.definition: Discomfort or pain localized to the epigastric region (the upper central abdomen beneath the sternum), often described as burning, pressure, fullness, or aching; may be associated with nausea, belching, or heartburn. Etiologies range from benign GI conditions such as gastritis, GERD, and peptic ulcer disease to more serious illnesses, including pancreatitis or myocardial ischemia, depending on the clinical context.

balanced anesthesia.definition: A technique in which multiple drugs from different classes (analgesics, sedatives/hypnotics, and muscle relaxants) are used together to achieve anesthesia, analgesia, amnesia, and muscle relaxation with lower doses of each agent, aiming for better hemodynamic stability and fewer adverse effects.

anxiety-depressive disorder.definition: A condition in which prominent symptoms of both anxiety and depression are present and cause clinically significant distress or impairment, but do not meet full criteria for a separate anxiety or depressive disorder. Common features include excessive worry or fear, restlessness, and fatigue (anxiety) along with persistent low mood or anhedonia, sleep disturbance, and poor concentration (depression), typically lasting several weeks.

malignant lymphoma.definition: A cancer originating in lymphocytes of the lymphatic system, typically presenting as painless lymph node enlargement; encompasses Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

malignant mesenchymoma.definition: A malignant soft-tissue neoplasm characterized by the presence of two or more distinct malignant mesenchymal components within a single tumor, arising from divergent differentiation; historically used to describe mixed sarcomas but not a distinct entity in current classifications.

ribonucleoprotein.definition: A macromolecular complex of RNA bound to protein that forms functional units involved in RNA-guided cellular processes (e.g., ribosomes for protein synthesis, snRNPs for RNA splicing).

esophageal hypomotility.definition: A motor disorder of the esophagus characterized by reduced strength and/or frequency of distal peristaltic contractions, resulting in impaired bolus transit and symptoms such as dysphagia; typically detected by esophageal manometry as low-amplitude, weak, or nonpropagating peristaltic waves.

mixed culture.definition: A culture that contains more than one species of microorganism growing together, i.e., a polymicrobial culture, which may indicate infection with multiple pathogens or sample contamination.

mixed lymphocyte culture.definition: A laboratory test in which lymphocytes from two individuals are cultured together to assess histocompatibility; if donor alloantigens stimulate the responder lymphocytes to proliferate, it indicates immunologic incompatibility and alloreactivity, informing transplant compatibility.

mixed dentition.definition: The developmental stage in which both primary (deciduous) teeth and permanent teeth are present in the mouth; it begins with eruption of the first permanent molars around age 6 and ends with the shedding of the last primary tooth in adolescence.

dust pneumoconiosis.definition: A form of occupational lung disease caused by chronic inhalation of mineral dusts (such as coal, silica, or metal dust), resulting in interstitial fibrosis and progressive impairment of lung function.

cusp.definition: A pointed projection or eminence on a structure; in dentistry, the pointed elevation on the chewing surface of a tooth (especially molars and premolars); in anatomy, one of the leaflets of a cardiac valve.

papillary muscles.definition: Threads of cardiac muscle in the ventricles that attach to the chordae tendineae and pull the atrioventricular valves (between the atria and ventricles) closed during ventricular contraction to prevent valve prolapse.

mobitz i heart block.definition: A type of second-degree atrioventricular (AV) block in which the PR interval gradually lengthens with each beat until a P wave is not conducted and a QRS complex is dropped; the cycle then restarts. It is usually AV nodal in origin and can be caused by increased vagal tone, certain medications, or AV nodal disease (Wenckebach phenomenon).

mobitz ii heart block.definition: Intermittent non-conducted atrial impulses (P waves) with no preceding PR interval prolongation, typically due to disease of the His–Purkinje system; results in dropped QRS complexes and carries a high risk of progression to complete heart block, often requiring permanent pacing.

monooctanoin.definition: A monoglyceride in which octanoic acid is esterified to glycerol; one fatty acid chain is attached to the glycerol backbone.

moctanin.definition: Not found in standard medical dictionaries; it may be a misspelling or an extremely obscure term. If you can share the context (disease, drug, or field where you saw it), I can help identify the correct term and provide a precise definition.

modafinil.definition: A wakefulness-promoting agent (CNS stimulant) prescribed for excessive daytime sleepiness due to narcolepsy, obstructive sleep apnea/hypopnea syndrome, and shift work sleep disorder; the exact mechanism is not fully understood but likely involves dopaminergic pathways and possibly the orexin system, with generally lower abuse potential than classic stimulants.

drug abuse.definition: The misuse of illegal drugs or the inappropriate or excessive use of prescription or other legal drugs for nonmedical purposes, leading to harm, dependence, or adverse health and social outcomes.

abnormal vision.definition: Any vision that is not normal, including decreased visual acuity, blurred or distorted vision, double vision (diplopia), or loss or disruption of the visual field.

mouth ulcer.definition: An oral mucosal sore that is usually small and painful, often with a white or yellow center surrounded by a red border; it typically heals within 1–2 weeks and can be caused by minor trauma, infections (such as herpes simplex), nutritional deficiencies, or aphthous (canker) ulcers.

thirst.definition: A physiological sensation and drive to drink fluids, triggered by increased plasma osmolality or decreased extracellular fluid volume, detected by hypothalamic osmoreceptors and baroreceptors to restore hydration.

obstructive sleep apnea.definition: A disorder marked by heavy snoring and interrupted breathing during sleep. It increases the risk of developing high blood pressure and having a stroke and is more common in people who are obese.

mixed sleep apnea.definition: A form of sleep-disordered breathing in which an apnea event contains both obstructive and central components: it begins with obstructed airflow with continued respiratory effort, followed by a central pause with little or no respiratory effort.

pancreatic lipase.definition: An enzyme secreted by the pancreas into the small intestine that hydrolyzes dietary triglycerides into monoglycerides and free fatty acids, enabling fat absorption; its activity is enhanced by colipase and bile salts.

jaw thrust.definition: A technique to open the airway by displacing the mandible forward (jaw thrust), moving the tongue away from the pharynx to relieve obstruction; used in unconscious or apneic patients and in trauma to maintain a patent airway.

modified barium swallow.definition: A fluoroscopic radiographic assessment of swallowing in which the patient ingests barium-coated liquids and solids of varying consistencies to visualize the oral and pharyngeal swallow, assess airway protection, and evaluate swallow safety (penetration or aspiration) and efficiency.

radiological examination.definition: A diagnostic imaging study in which internal body structures are visualized using radiologic techniques (such as X-ray, fluoroscopy, CT, or MRI) to aid diagnosis and treatment planning.

plantigrade position.definition: A posture or gait in which the entire sole of the foot is in contact with the ground (heel through toes).

physical therapy.definition: The treatment of pain and weakness with exercise.

chorionic gonadotropins.definition: A placental glycoprotein hormone produced after implantation by placental trophoblasts; stimulates the corpus luteum to secrete progesterone, maintaining the uterine lining in early pregnancy; detectable in pregnancy tests and used clinically to induce ovulation or to support luteal function in fertility treatments.

morning sickness.definition: A common condition in pregnancy characterized by nausea, with or without vomiting, usually beginning in the first trimester and thought to be related to hormonal changes (notably increased hCG and estrogen); it often resolves by mid-pregnancy.

left ventricular dysfunction.definition: Impaired pumping function of the left ventricle, causing reduced cardiac output and/or elevated filling pressures; may be systolic (reduced ejection fraction) or diastolic (impaired filling) dysfunction.

moexipril.definition: An oral angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor used to treat hypertension; a prodrug converted in the body to the active moexiprilat that inhibits ACE, reducing angiotensin II–mediated vasoconstriction and aldosterone secretion.

digestive tract disorders.definition: Digestive tract disorders are diseases and conditions that affect any part of the alimentary canal (from the mouth to the anus), altering its structure or function. They include inflammatory, infectious, autoimmune, metabolic, neoplastic, functional, and motility disorders, and commonly cause symptoms such as abdominal pain, indigestion, dysphagia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, GI bleeding, or weight loss.

sleeping difficulties.definition: Difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep or experiencing non-restorative sleep, resulting in daytime distress or impairment; can be acute or chronic and may be due to medical, psychiatric, lifestyle, or environmental factors.

anaphylactic reactions.definition: A serious allergic reaction that happens quickly and can be fatal.

monckeberg's arteriosclerosis.definition: Calcification of the tunica media of medium- to small-sized arteries (medial calcific sclerosis), causing stiff, noncompressible vessels with preserved luminal diameter; a form of arteriosclerosis that differs from atherosclerosis by lack of significant intimal plaque and luminal narrowing, and is associated with aging, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease.

monilethrix.definition: An inherited hair shaft disorder in which hair fibers show a beaded (nodal) appearance with alternating constrictions and enlargements (internodes), leading to fragile, easily breakable hair; often due to mutations in hair keratin genes (KRT81, KRT83, KRT86) and DSG4 (typically autosomal dominant).

orodigitofacial dysostosis.definition: An older term for mandibulofacial dysostosis (Treacher Collins syndrome), a congenital craniofacial disorder caused by defective development of neural crest–derived structures of the first pharyngeal arch, leading to hypoplasia of the mandible and zygomatic arches, downward-slanting palpebral fissures, eyelid colobomas, ear anomalies with conductive hearing loss, and other facial abnormalities. Most cases are autosomal dominant with variable expressivity, commonly due to mutations in the TCOF1 gene.

oral-facial-digital syndrome type ii.definition: A rare autosomal recessive congenital syndrome characterized by anomalies of the mouth, facial structures, and digits, typically including oral abnormalities (such as tongue and dental anomalies), facial dysmorphism, and limb malformations (e.g., polydactyly or brachydactyly).

palatal.definition: Relating to the palate, the roof of the mouth.

mody.definition: A monogenic form of diabetes caused by heterozygous mutations in a single gene (most commonly HNF1A, HNF4A, GCK, or HNF1B), inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, typically presenting before age 25 with hyperglycemia from beta-cell dysfunction and often with preserved insulin production; treatment varies by subtype and may include sulfonylureas or lifestyle management.

maturity-onset diabetes of youth.definition: A monogenic, autosomal-dominant form of diabetes caused by heterozygous mutations in a single gene that impairs beta-cell insulin secretion, typically presenting before age 25 and often misdiagnosed as type 1 or type 2 diabetes; treatment varies by subtype, with some forms responsive to sulfonylureas and others requiring little to no treatment (e.g., GCK-MODY).

molluscum contagiosum.definition: A common, benign skin infection caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus (a poxvirus) that presents as small, firm, dome-shaped, flesh-colored papules with a central dimple; highly contagious via direct contact and fomites; typically self-limited, resolving over several months, though treatments such as curettage, cryotherapy, or cantharidin may hasten clearance.

diphtheria toxoid.definition: An inactivated form of the diphtheria toxin used as a vaccine antigen to elicit protective immunity against diphtheria; produced by chemical inactivation (toxoid) so it cannot cause disease, and is used in vaccines such as DTaP and Tdap.

monobactam.definition: A class of beta-lactam antibiotics characterized by a single, monocyclic beta-lactam ring; they inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis by binding to penicillin-binding proteins, with activity primarily against aerobic Gram-negative bacteria and limited activity against Gram-positive organisms (aztreonam is the representative member).

monilia.definition: A yeast-like fungal pathogen, now usually referred to as Candida albicans, that commonly colonizes human mucous membranes and skin but can cause opportunistic infections such as oral thrush and vaginal candidiasis.

monistat.definition: A brand-name topical antifungal containing miconazole nitrate, used to treat vaginal yeast infections (candidiasis) and other superficial fungal infections; available in single-, 3-, or 7-day regimens.

monkeypox.definition: An acute viral infection caused by the Monkeypox virus, an Orthopoxvirus. It is zoonotic and transmits through close contact with infected animals or people, presenting with fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy, and a progressive vesiculopustular rash that usually lasts 2–4 weeks; management is supportive, with antivirals available and smallpox vaccination providing cross-protection.

mao inhibitor.definition: A class of antidepressants that inhibits the enzyme monoamine oxidase, increasing brain levels of serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine by reducing their breakdown; dietary and drug interaction precautions are necessary due to the risk of hypertensive crisis with tyramine.

tyramine.definition: A naturally occurring monoamine formed by the decarboxylation of tyrosine; found in certain foods (e.g., aged cheeses, fermented products, wine); it can induce release of norepinephrine and may cause hypertensive crises in individuals taking monoamine oxidase inhibitors.

monobenzone.definition: A topical depigmenting agent that permanently destroys melanocytes, producing irreversible depigmentation of the skin; used in extensive vitiligo but associated with significant risk of dermatitis and sensitization.

monoblast.definition: A relatively large, immature precursor of the monocyte lineage in the bone marrow that differentiates into promonocytes and eventually into monocytes/macrophages.

monoblastic leukemia.definition: An acute myeloid leukemia in which the malignant blasts are monoblasts (monocytic lineage), usually accounting for a majority of bone marrow and peripheral blood blasts; classified as AML-M5 (acute monocytic leukemia). Often presents with rapid marrow failure and extramedullary involvement (gum hypertrophy, skin lesions). Immunophenotype shows monocytic markers such as CD11c, CD14, and CD64.

naegeli's leukemia.definition: Definition not found for that exact name in standard medical dictionaries; it may be a misspelling or nonstandard term. If you meant leukemia in general: a malignant proliferation of hematopoietic cells in the bone marrow with accumulation of abnormal white blood cells and impaired production of normal blood cells; it is typically classified as acute or chronic, and by cell lineage as lymphoid or myeloid.

monocytopenia.definition: Monocytopenia is a decreased number of circulating monocytes, a type of white blood cell involved in phagocytosis and immune defense.

monocytosis.definition: An elevation of monocytes in the peripheral blood, typically defined as an absolute monocyte count above the normal reference range (often >0.8–1.0 x 10^9/L); it can occur with infections, inflammatory or autoimmune diseases, and certain hematologic conditions.

monocytic leukopenia.definition: A decrease in the absolute count of monocytes (the monocytic lineage) in the peripheral blood, contributing to overall leukopenia.

mononuclear leukocyte.definition: White blood cells with a single, non-segmented nucleus and little to no cytoplasmic granules; includes lymphocytes and monocytes, which mediate adaptive immunity (B and T cells) and phagocytosis/antigen presentation (monocytes/macrophages).

mononuclear cell.definition: A white blood cell with a single, non-lobed nucleus (a mononuclear leukocyte), typically including lymphocytes and monocytes; contrasts with granulocytes that have multilobed nuclei.

monospot test.definition: A rapid serologic test that detects heterophile antibodies in the blood to help diagnose infectious mononucleosis (usually due to Epstein-Barr virus); the test uses animal red blood cells to detect antibody-mediated agglutination.

monosodium urate.definition: The sodium salt of uric acid; it can crystallize and deposit in joints and soft tissues, a hallmark of gout and hyperuricemia.

monosodium urate monohydrate.definition: A hydrated salt of uric acid (monosodium urate) in which one molecule of water is incorporated per urate unit; these crystals can precipitate in joints and soft tissues, triggering the inflammatory attacks of gout.

monosomy x.definition: A chromosomal disorder in females caused by loss of one X chromosome (most often 45,X), known as Turner syndrome; features commonly include short stature, gonadal dysgenesis with infertility, and various congenital anomalies such as cardiovascular defects and lymphedema.

monosomic.definition: Having only one copy of a chromosome in a cell or organism, instead of the normal two.

monospecific.definition: Relating to a single antigenic specificity; an antibody or serum that binds only one antigen or epitope (monospecific antibody) as opposed to polyclonal antibodies that recognize multiple epitopes.

monospecific antibody.definition: An antibody that recognizes only one epitope (antigenic determinant) on a given antigen, providing highly specific binding; typically produced by a single B‑cell clone (monoclonal) for uniform specificity.

monosome.definition: A chromosome that exists in a cell in only one copy rather than the normal two in a diploid genome (the chromosomal state known as monosomy).

accessory chromosome.definition: A chromosome that is not essential for viability or normal development and exists in addition to the standard chromosome set; an extra, dispensable chromosome (often called a B or supernumerary chromosome) that is variably present among individuals and may carry genes affecting fitness, virulence, or adaptation.

monozygotic twins.definition: Monozygotic twins are twins that develop from a single fertilized egg (zygote) that splits into two embryos, resulting in two genetically identical individuals.

monozygosity.definition: The state of being derived from a single zygote; typically used to describe identical twins that arise when a fertilized egg splits into two embryos, yielding genetically nearly identical offspring.

siamese.definition: Historically used to describe twins born physically connected to one another due to incomplete splitting of a single fertilized egg during early embryogenesis; the site and extent of fusion vary, and separation surgery may be feasible depending on shared organs and tissues. The modern term is conjoined twins.

monovular.definition: Originating from a single ovum; used to describe monozygotic (identical) twinning.

monovular twins.definition: Twins that develop from a single fertilized egg that splits into two embryos, resulting in two genetically identical individuals. Depending on when the split occurs, they may have separate placentas and membranes or share one placenta and/or amniotic sacs (e.g., dichorionic diamniotic, monochorionic diamniotic, or monochorionic monoamniotic pregnancies).

monovulatory.definition: Describing an ovulation pattern in which only one oocyte is released during a single menstrual cycle.

omphalopagus.definition: A type of conjoined twinning in which two fetuses are joined at the abdomen (umbilical region), typically sharing the liver and parts of the gastrointestinal tract, while maintaining separate hearts.

monomphalus.definition: A congenital condition characterized by the presence of a single umbilicus.

omphalus.definition: The umbilicus (navel); the central area of the abdomen where the umbilical cord attached during fetal development.

symmelia.definition: A congenital anomaly in which two or more limbs or limb segments are fused together, resulting from incomplete separation of limb buds during embryogenesis; may involve soft tissues and bones and can affect one or both extremities.

monopodial.definition: A growth pattern along a single, dominant axis in which the main stem continuously elongates and bears lateral branches from its upper portions, rather than being terminated and replaced by successive axes (opposite of sympodial).

sirenomelia.definition: A rare congenital malformation in which the legs are fused (often described as a mermaid-like deformity) with severe caudal anomalies, commonly accompanied by renal agenesis or hypoplasia, genital abnormalities, and a single umbilical artery; caused by disruption of caudal mesoderm development during early embryogenesis.

tripodial symmelia.definition: A rare congenital limb fusion in which three limb projections arise from a common base, giving a tripod-like configuration; a form of symmelia (limb fusion).

sympus.definition: Not a recognized medical term in standard medical dictionaries.

monopus.definition: Not a recognized medical term; no standard medical definition exists.

monocyte.definition: A large white blood cell of the monocyte lineage that circulates in blood and, after migrating into tissues, differentiates into macrophages or dendritic cells; involved in phagocytosis and antigen presentation as part of the innate immune response.

monocular diplopia.definition: Double vision that persists when the affected eye is viewed alone (with the other eye closed), caused by an optical defect in that eye such as uncorrected refractive error (e.g., astigmatism), corneal irregularity, cataract, or lens abnormality.

monocular vision.definition: Vision in one eye; seeing with a single eye, with absence or suppression of input from the other eye, typically resulting in reduced depth perception due to loss of binocular cues.

monocular strabismus.definition: A unilateral misalignment of the visual axes in which one eye is consistently deviated and the other eye fixates, with no switching of fixation between the eyes.

monobasic acid.definition: A monoprotic (monobasic) acid is an acid that donates a single proton (H+) per molecule in aqueous solution.

monobasic potassium phosphate.definition: An inorganic salt of potassium and phosphoric acid (KH2PO4) that functions as a buffering agent and mineral supplement, supplying potassium and phosphate in medical and pharmaceutical preparations.

monobasic sodium phosphate.definition: An inorganic salt—the monosodium salt of phosphoric acid (NaH2PO4). In solution it provides the dihydrogen phosphate anion (H2PO4−) and acts as a weak acid buffer; used as a buffering agent and acidity regulator in foods and medicines, and as a source of phosphate in certain pharmaceutical preparations.

monosaccharide.definition: The simplest form of carbohydrate; a single sugar molecule that cannot be hydrolyzed into smaller sugar units. Common examples include glucose, fructose, and galactose.

monro-kellie doctrine.definition: A principle stating that the cranial vault is a fixed-volume compartment containing brain tissue, blood, and cerebrospinal fluid; the total volume is constant, so an increase in one component must be offset by a decrease in others to keep intracranial pressure stable. When compensatory capacity is exhausted, intracranial pressure rises, increasing the risk of brain herniation.

monteggia fracture.definition: A fracture of the proximal ulna with dislocation of the radial head at the radiocapitellar joint, typically with anterior radial-head dislocation; commonly classified by Bado into four types.

radial dislocation.definition: Displacement of the radius from its normal articulations with adjacent bones, most commonly at the elbow (radial head dislocation) or at the wrist (distal radioulnar or radiocarpal dislocations).

ankle mortise joint.definition: A socket formed by the distal tibia and fibula that houses the talus; the true ankle joint (tibiotalar joint) within the ankle mortise, enabling dorsiflexion and plantarflexion.

mons pubis.definition: A rounded pad of fatty tissue overlying the pubic symphysis that forms the anterior part of the vulva; it is covered with skin and becomes hair-bearing after puberty, cushioning the pubic bones and protecting underlying structures.

mons veneris.definition: A rounded fatty eminence over the pubic symphysis (pubic bone) forming part of the female external genitalia; also known as the mons pubis. It provides cushioning over the pubic bone and becomes covered with pubic hair after puberty.

montgomery strap.definition: A postoperative dressing method using two long fabric straps attached to the sides of a wound dressing; the straps wrap around the body and tie to secure the dressing, allowing frequent, atraumatic changes without removing the entire dressing.

mood.definition: A persistent emotional state that colors a person’s perception and experience of the world; unlike transient affect, mood is maintained over hours to days and can be normal or altered in mood disorders (e.g., depressive, manic).

moon face.definition: A rounded, full, puffy facial appearance due to fat redistribution and fluid retention associated with hypercortisolism (Cushing syndrome) or chronic glucocorticoid therapy.

angular conjunctivitis.definition: A chronic conjunctival infection localized at the lateral (outer) canthus, characterized by fissuring and crusting at the corner of the eye with discharge; most often caused by Moraxella species (eg, Moraxella lacunata) and commonly associated with blepharitis, treated with topical antibiotics.

corneal infections.definition: An infectious inflammation of the cornea, the clear front surface of the eye, caused by bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites. It typically presents with eye pain, redness, tearing or discharge, sensitivity to light, and reduced vision, and can lead to corneal ulcers or scarring if untreated. Management depends on the organism and severity and usually involves targeted antimicrobial therapy (topical and/or systemic) under urgent ophthalmologic care.

morbilliform.definition: A maculopapular, measles-like eruption—usually symmetric and diffuse, starting on the trunk and spreading to the face and limbs; commonly due to drug reactions or viral infections.

moro reflex.definition: A primitive neonatal startle response elicited by a sudden stimulus (e.g., a loud noise or loss of support): the infant first extends and abducts the arms with spread fingers, then flexes and adducts the arms toward the midline (often crying). It typically disappears by about 4–6 months of age.

morphine sulfate.definition: A potent opioid analgesic that is a mu-opioid receptor agonist used to relieve moderate to severe pain; available in oral and injectable formulations, among others; carries risks of respiratory depression, sedation, constipation, nausea, and a high potential for dependence and withdrawal.
