natriuretic peptides.definition: A family of peptide hormones mainly released by the heart in response to cardiac wall stretch; they promote natriuresis and diuresis, vasodilation, and inhibition of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, and BNP/NT-proBNP are used clinically as biomarkers of heart failure.

natriuretic peptides test.definition: A blood test that measures natriuretic peptides—most commonly BNP (brain natriuretic peptide) or NT-proBNP (N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide)—released by the heart in response to myocardial stretch; used to aid diagnosis and assessment of heart failure, differentiate cardiac from noncardiac causes of dyspnea, and guide prognosis and management.

natural antibody.definition: Antibodies that circulate without prior exposure to antigen, typically germline-encoded IgM produced by B-1 cells; they are polyreactive and recognize common microbial motifs and altered-self epitopes, providing immediate, broad innate-like defense and aiding clearance of apoptotic cells without requiring T-cell help.

natural childbirth.definition: The process of labor and vaginal delivery achieved with minimal medical intervention, often without pharmacologic pain relief (such as epidural anesthesia) and routine procedures, relying on nonpharmacologic pain management, mobility, and continuous labor support.

lamaze.definition: A method of childbirth preparation that uses controlled breathing, relaxation, and partner-assisted coaching to help manage pain and anxiety during labor.

natural dentition.definition: The patient’s own native teeth in the mouth, i.e., the natural dentition as opposed to teeth replaced by artificial prostheses such as dentures or dental implants.

natural family planning method.definition: A group of fertility-awareness–based methods used to plan or prevent pregnancy by identifying the fertile window through observation of natural signs such as cervical mucus and basal body temperature; intercourse is avoided or contraception used on days of high fertility.

calendar method.definition: A natural family planning method in which a woman’s fertile window is estimated by tracking the length of her menstrual cycles over several months and identifying the likely days of ovulation; intercourse or unprotected sex is avoided or protected during those predicted fertile days to prevent pregnancy. Effectiveness depends on regular cycles and accurate cycle tracking.

ovulation method.definition: A fertility awareness–based method of family planning that identifies the likely time of ovulation by observing physiological signs (such as changes in cervical mucus and basal body temperature) and/or using an ovulation predictor test, to determine the fertile window for contraception or conception.

symptothermal method.definition: A fertility awareness-based method that combines daily monitoring of cervical mucus changes with basal body temperature to pinpoint ovulation and identify fertile days for family planning.

natural foods.definition: Foods that are in or near their natural state, subjected to minimal processing and free from artificial additives such as colors, flavors, or preservatives; note that the term “natural” in labeling is not universally standardized.

natural immunity.definition: Non-specific, immediate defense present from birth (innate immunity) that protects against a broad range of pathogens via physical barriers, phagocytes, natural killer cells, and soluble factors; it lacks pathogen-specific memory.

naturalistic illness.definition: An illness concept that attributes disease to natural biological causes (e.g., pathogens, genetics, physiological dysfunction, environmental factors) and explains symptoms within biomedical or naturalistic frameworks rather than to personalistic or supernatural agents.

nk cell.definition: Natural killer cells are cytotoxic lymphocytes of the innate immune system that recognize and kill virus-infected and tumor cells without prior exposure, primarily by releasing perforin and granzymes; they can also mediate antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity via Fc receptors.

natural pacemaker.definition: A cluster of specialized cells in the right atrium—the sinoatrial node—that generates regular electrical impulses to set the heart rate and coordinate cardiac contractions; the primary natural pacemaker of the heart, with rate modulated by autonomic input.

natural radiation.definition: Ionizing radiation that originates from natural sources in the environment, including cosmic rays from space, terrestrial radionuclides in soil and rocks, radon gas in air, and internal radionuclides within the human body; it constitutes the natural background radiation to which all living beings are exposed.

natural selection.definition: A process in evolution whereby heritable traits that enhance survival or reproductive success become more common in a population over generations, while deleterious traits diminish.

naturetin.definition: Not a recognized medical term; no standard medical definition exists. It may be a misspelling or a brand name. Please provide context or check the spelling.

naturopath.definition: A practitioner who uses naturopathy, a holistic approach to health care that emphasizes natural therapies and lifestyle changes to support the body's innate healing ability.

naturopathic medicine.definition: Naturopathic medicine is a system of primary care that emphasizes the body's innate healing ability and uses natural, noninvasive therapies (e.g., lifestyle modification, nutrition, botanical medicines, physical medicine, and mind–body approaches); the scope of practice and licensure vary by country and jurisdiction.

naturopathy.definition: A form of alternative medicine that emphasizes natural, noninvasive therapies and the body's inherent ability to heal, often employing lifestyle modification, nutrition and dietary changes, herbal remedies, supplements, and various physical or hydrotherapy modalities; evidence for some practices is limited and varies by modality.

nausea and vomiting of pregnancy.definition: An often benign, pregnancy-related condition characterized by nausea with or without vomiting, typically beginning in the first trimester and usually resolving by mid-pregnancy; thought to be driven by hormonal changes (notably human chorionic gonadotropin and estrogen). In severe cases it can progress to hyperemesis gravidarum, requiring medical treatment.

hyperemesis gravidarum.definition: An extreme form of nausea and vomiting during pregnancy characterized by severe and persistent vomiting that leads to dehydration, weight loss, and electrolyte disturbances, often requiring medical treatment and nutritional support.

navane.definition: A brand-name antipsychotic medication (thiothixene) of the thioxanthene class used to treat schizophrenia; it acts as a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist (a typical antipsychotic) and may cause extrapyramidal side effects.

thiothixene.definition: An older, typical antipsychotic of the thioxanthene class used to treat schizophrenia; it antagonizes dopamine D2 receptors in the brain, reducing psychotic symptoms. Common adverse effects include extrapyramidal symptoms, sedation, and anticholinergic effects.

navelbine.definition: A brand-name chemotherapy drug (vinorelbine); a semi-synthetic vinca alkaloid that inhibits microtubule polymerization, blocking mitosis; used to treat non-small cell lung cancer and metastatic breast cancer; administered intravenously.

vinorelbine.definition: A semi-synthetic vinca alkaloid chemotherapy agent that binds tubulin and inhibits microtubule polymerization, blocking mitosis and causing cell death. It is used to treat certain cancers, most notably non-small cell lung cancer and metastatic breast cancer; given by intravenous infusion, with side effects including myelosuppression, nausea, constipation, fatigue, and neuropathy.

navicular pads.definition: A small cushioned insert placed on the plantar surface of the foot beneath the navicular region to support the medial longitudinal arch and reduce pronation; used in foot orthotics for flat feet or navicular-related pain.

neck righting reflex.definition: A primitive infant reflex in which turning the head to one side elicits a rolling movement of the body so that the trunk and limbs align with the head, helping to maintain head–body orientation as motor control develops.

ankylostomiasis.definition: A hookworm infection caused by nematodes (Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus), acquired by skin penetration or ingestion of larvae from contaminated soil; it causes chronic intestinal blood loss and iron-deficiency anemia, with abdominal pain and growth impairment in children in heavy infections.

necrotizing enterocolitis.definition: Life-threatening gastrointestinal disease of newborns, especially preterm infants, characterized by inflammation and necrosis of the intestinal wall that can lead to perforation and sepsis; presents with feeding intolerance, abdominal distension, and sometimes bloody stools; managed with bowel rest, broad-spectrum antibiotics, supportive care, and surgery if necrosis or perforation occurs.

neck dissection.definition: A surgical procedure to remove lymph nodes (and sometimes adjacent neck structures) to treat or prevent metastasis from cancers of the head and neck; it can be radical or selective, depending on the extent of tissue removal.

cervical lymph nodes.definition: Cervical lymph nodes are lymph nodes in the neck that filter lymph from the head and neck and participate in immune responses; they drain lymph from the scalp, face, oral cavity, pharynx, and thyroid and are organized into superficial and deep groups along the jugular chain.

radical neck dissection.definition: A surgical operation for head and neck cancer in which all ipsilateral cervical lymph node levels I–V are removed en bloc together with the sternocleidomastoid muscle, internal jugular vein, and spinal accessory nerve.

neck of femur.definition: A narrow, oblique segment of the proximal femur that connects the femoral head to the femoral shaft; lies just distal to the head and is intracapsular within the hip joint, and is a common site of hip fractures.

neck of gastric gland.definition: The middle portion of a gastric gland, located between the isthmus (upper part) and the base; it is lined by mucous neck cells and is involved in mucus secretion to protect the gastric mucosa.

neck of uterus.definition: A narrow, cylindrical lower portion of the uterus that opens into the vagina; it contains the cervical canal and serves as the passage between the uterine cavity and the vaginal canal.

intranasal medications.definition: Medications administered through the nasal mucosa (typically as sprays, drops, or powders) to achieve local nasal effects or systemic effects via rapid absorption, often avoiding hepatic first-pass metabolism.

nebulize.definition: To convert a liquid medication into a fine mist or aerosol that can be inhaled, typically delivered by a nebulizer to administer medication to the lungs.

atomizer.definition: A device that converts a liquid medication into a fine aerosol or mist for inhalation, enabling delivery to the respiratory tract; commonly used in inhalation therapy and with nebulizers.

nec.definition: Cell or tissue death resulting from irreversible injury, typically due to ischemia (reduced blood supply), toxins, infection, or trauma; it can lead to loss of function in the affected area and may provoke inflammatory responses.

niacin equivalent.definition: Units that express total dietary niacin activity from both preformed niacin and niacin produced from tryptophan; calculated as NE = mg of niacin + (mg of tryptophan)/60. Therefore, 1 NE equals 1 mg of niacin or 60 mg of tryptophan, and NE is used in nutrition labeling and dietary references to reflect available niacin.

acute bronchospasm.definition: A sudden tightening of the muscles around the airways, leading to acute narrowing of the bronchi and reversible airflow obstruction, commonly presenting with wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath.

atrioventricular heart block.definition: A condition characterized by impaired conduction of electrical impulses from the atria to the ventricles through the AV node and His-Purkinje system, causing slowed or blocked ventricular activation. It is graded by degree: first-degree (prolonged PR interval), second-degree (intermittent failure of conduction; Mobitz I or II), and third-degree (complete heart block with AV dissociation).

brudzinski sign.definition: A sign of meningeal irritation in which passive flexion of the neck produces involuntary flexion of the hips and knees, commonly seen with meningitis.

cervicothoracolumbar orthosis.definition: A spinal brace that extends from the neck to the lower back to immobilize and stabilize the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine for treatment of instability, fractures, deformities, or postoperative immobilization.

mesenteric vessels.definition: Arteries and veins contained in the mesentery that supply and drain the intestines; the major vessels are the superior mesenteric artery and vein, and the inferior mesenteric artery and vein, which drain into the portal venous system.

bowel wall.definition: Anatomical layers forming the intestinal wall: mucosa (epithelium with lamina propria and muscularis mucosae), submucosa, muscularis propria (inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle with the enteric myenteric plexus), and serosa or adventitia.

abdominal decompression.definition: Relief of elevated intra-abdominal pressure, typically achieved by surgically opening the abdomen (decompressive laparotomy) to treat abdominal compartment syndrome, often with temporary abdominal closure and planned staged closure.

whole blood transfusion.definition: Transfusion of donor blood without separating its components, providing red cells, plasma, platelets, and other elements in one unit to rapidly restore circulating volume and oxygen-carrying capacity during massive hemorrhage; now largely replaced by component therapy.

broad-spectrum antibiotics.definition: An antibiotic with activity against a wide range of bacteria, including many Gram-positive and Gram-negative species, often used empirically when the causative organism is unknown or polymicrobial; may disrupt normal flora and promote resistance.

periarteritis nodosa.definition: A systemic necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries with transmural inflammation and fibrinoid necrosis, leading to aneurysm formation and organ ischemia; commonly affects the kidneys, skin, and peripheral nerves and is historically associated with hepatitis B infection, with treatment typically including corticosteroids and immunosuppressants.

progressive systemic sclerosis.definition: A chronic autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by progressive fibrosis of the skin and internal organs (most often the lungs, heart, kidneys, and gastrointestinal tract) due to vasculopathy and immune dysregulation; a form of systemic sclerosis with variable skin involvement (limited or diffuse) and organ progression.

necrobiotic granulomas.definition: A type of granulomatous inflammation in which areas of tissue necrosis (necrobiotic change) are surrounded by a ring of histiocytes, often arranged in a palisading pattern; commonly seen in granuloma annulare and necrobiosis lipoidica.

necrobiosis lipoidica.definition: A chronic, diabetic-associated granulomatous skin disorder presenting with well-demarcated, atrophic, yellow-brown plaques—usually on the shins—where degenerating collagen (necrobiosis) is surrounded by palisading granulomatous inflammation; lesions may ulcerate and are associated with diabetes mellitus.

nedocromil.definition: A mast cell stabilizer that inhibits degranulation and mediator release from mast cells, used prophylactically for allergic asthma and conjunctivitis; administered as an inhaled or ophthalmic preparation and not for acute relief.

nedocromil sodium.definition: A mast cell stabilizer that prevents degranulation of mast cells and release of mediators (such as histamine) in allergic reactions; used prophylactically for allergic conjunctivitis and rhinitis, and in some formulations as an adjunct for asthma; typically given as ophthalmic drops or an inhaled formulation.

nefazodone.definition: An antidepressant in the serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor (SARI) class that blocks 5-HT2A receptors and inhibits serotonin reuptake; used for major depressive disorder but associated with rare, severe hepatotoxicity, leading to restricted or withdrawn use in many countries.

nefazodone hydrochloride.definition: An oral antidepressant of the serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor (SARI) class that blocks 5-HT2 receptors and inhibits serotonin reuptake; used to treat major depressive disorder and carries a risk of severe hepatotoxicity, often not used as first-line therapy.

intralesional corticosteroids.definition: Delivery of corticosteroids by injection directly into a lesion to reduce local inflammation and immune activity; commonly used in dermatology for conditions such as keloids, hypertrophic scars, warts, and granulomatous skin diseases (often triamcinolone acetonide).

negative end-expiratory pressure.definition: A ventilatory setting in which the pressure in the airways at the end of expiration is below ambient atmospheric pressure (negative end-expiratory pressure), the opposite of positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP); it is not a standard clinical practice and can promote venous return but risks alveolar collapse and worsened oxygenation.

neep.definition: Not a recognized medical term; there is no standard medical definition for "neep".

pion radiotherapy.definition: A form of radiotherapy in which beams of pions (pi mesons) are produced by accelerators and directed at a tumor to deliver ionizing radiation, with energy deposited along the pion’s path in tissue; historically explored in research settings but not used in routine clinical practice.

pion.definition: Not a recognized medical term; in particle physics, a pion is a light meson composed of a quark and an antiquark that mediates the strong nuclear force between nucleons.

low birth weight.definition: Birth weight less than 2,500 grams (5 pounds, 8 ounces), regardless of gestational age; it can result from preterm birth or fetal growth restriction.

umbilical catheter.definition: A catheter inserted through the umbilicus into a newborn’s vessels for central venous or arterial access, typically used in neonates for administration of fluids and medications, blood sampling, and hemodynamic monitoring.

necrotizing enteritis.definition: A severe inflammatory disease of the intestines in which portions of bowel tissue undergo necrosis, typically due to bacterial toxins or ischemia, and which may progress to perforation, peritonitis, and sepsis.

gingival papillae.definition: The interdental gingival tissue occupying the space between adjacent teeth; a wedge-shaped projection of gingiva that fills the embrasure and helps seal the gingival sulcus, protecting the underlying periodontal tissues.

necrotizing angiitis.definition: A form of vasculitis characterized by necrotizing inflammation of arterial walls (often with fibrinoid necrosis), typically involving medium- to small-sized vessels and causing vessel damage, thrombosis, aneurysm formation, and tissue ischemia.

t cell lymphoblastic leukemia.definition: An aggressive acute lymphoblastic leukemia characterized by malignant proliferation of immature T lymphoblasts (TdT-positive) that express T-lineage markers (eg, CD2, CD3, CD7), often presenting with bone marrow failure and a mediastinal/thymic mass; treated with intensive multi-agent chemotherapy and CNS prophylaxis.

t cell lymphoblastic lymphoma.definition: An aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma consisting of malignant immature T-lymphoblasts (TdT-positive, typically CD3/CD7-positive) that typically presents as a mediastinal thymic mass in children and young adults; may involve bone marrow and CNS; represents the lymphoblastic form of T-cell leukemia/lymphoma and is treated with intensive multiagent chemotherapy.

neonatal abstinence syndrome.definition: A withdrawal syndrome in newborns caused by in utero exposure to opioids (and other substances), presenting with irritability, high‑pitched cry, feeding difficulties, tremors, sweating, yawning, sneezing, vomiting, diarrhea, and sleep disturbances, and sometimes requiring pharmacologic treatment and supportive care.

negative-pressure ventilator.definition: An older mode of mechanical ventilation that uses subatmospheric pressure around the chest to cause thoracic expansion and draw air into the lungs, typically delivered by an enclosing shell (e.g., iron lung or cuirass); largely replaced by positive-pressure ventilation.

nelaton’s dislocation.definition: An old/obsolete term for anterior dislocation of the femoral head from the acetabulum, typically with the leg held in flexion, abduction, and external rotation.

nembutal.definition: A brand-name barbiturate (pentobarbital) that acts as a central nervous system depressant; used medically as a sedative and hypnotic, for anesthesia induction, and, in some jurisdictions, for humane euthanasia or execution.

neggram.definition: A brand name for nalidixic acid, a synthetic quinolone antibiotic used to treat infections caused by Gram-negative bacteria, especially urinary tract infections; it inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II).

neonatal conjunctivitis.definition: Inflammation of the conjunctiva in a newborn within the first 28 days of life, most often due to infection acquired during birth (notably Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis), presenting with red eye, discharge, and eyelid crusting and requiring prompt antimicrobial therapy.

neonatal mortality.definition: The death of a live-born infant within the first 28 days of life, typically reported as the neonatal mortality rate per 1,000 live births in a population.

neonatal thermoregulation.definition: Physiological process by which a newborn maintains a stable core body temperature despite environmental temperature changes, primarily via nonshivering thermogenesis from brown adipose tissue, metabolic heat production, and peripheral vasoconstriction; neonates are at high risk of hypothermia due to large surface area‑to‑volume ratio, thin skin, and limited brown fat, so environmental protection is crucial.

nbas.definition: A neonatal behavioral assessment scale: a standardized tool used to evaluate a newborn’s neuromotor and behavioral repertoire and responsiveness to environmental stimuli, developed by Brazelton. It assesses domains such as habituation, social-interactive behavior, motor organization, state regulation, autonomic stability, and attention to stimuli.

dexamethasone phosphate.definition: A water-soluble phosphate ester prodrug of dexamethasone used for parenteral administration; rapidly hydrolyzed in vivo to active dexamethasone, providing potent anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressant (glucocorticoid) effects.

neocortex.definition: A six-layered portion of the cerebral cortex, the evolutionarily newer part of the cortex, located over the brain's hemispheres and responsible for higher-order functions such as sensory perception, cognition, language, and voluntary motor control.

neocerebellum.definition: The lateral hemispheres of the cerebellum that plan and coordinate complex, learned voluntary movements; they receive input from the cerebral cortex via the pontine nuclei and send output to motor planning areas through the thalamus and dentate nucleus.

neoglottis.definition: A neoglottis is the reconstructed glottic opening created after laryngeal removal (such as total laryngectomy); it consists of the pharyngoesophageal segment and surrounding tissues that serves as the new sound source or constrictor for voice production in esophageal or tracheoesophageal speech.

pseudoglottis.definition: A false glottic opening — an airway space that resembles the glottis but is formed by non-glottic structures (such as mucosal folds, the epiglottis, edema, or a mass) and does not represent the true vocal-fold opening.

alaryngeal.definition: Without a larynx; relating to speech produced without using the larynx, typically via esophageal speech or other methods after laryngectomy.

neoblastic.definition: Relating to neoblasts (primitive, undifferentiated stem cells capable of differentiating into multiple cell types) or to the formation of new tissue from such cells; describes active tissue regeneration or growth.

neoantigen.definition: A tumor-specific antigen formed by somatic mutations in cancer cells, creating novel peptide sequences not found in normal tissues and capable of being presented by MHC molecules and recognized by T cells.

neoadjuvant.definition: A therapy given before the primary treatment (usually before surgery) to shrink a tumor or destroy microscopic disease, with the aim of improving surgical outcomes or enabling less extensive treatment.

enterobius vermicularis.definition: A parasitic nematode (pinworm) that infects humans, causing enterobiasis; the most common helminth infection in children, characterized by nocturnal perianal itching from female worm egg-laying; transmitted by ingesting eggs on contaminated hands, food, or surfaces; diagnosed by a perianal swab (tape test); treated with antiparasitic medications such as mebendazole or albendazole, with hygiene measures to prevent reinfection.

strongyloides stercoralis.definition: An intestinal nematode that causes strongyloidiasis in humans; infection begins when filariform larvae penetrate the skin, with autoinfection allowing chronic persistence. Clinical features range from asymptomatic to dermatitis, gastrointestinal and pulmonary symptoms, and potentially life-threatening hyperinfection in immunocompromised individuals; diagnosed by detection of larvae in stool or duodenal samples or serology; treated with ivermectin (preferred) or albendazole.

nematodiasis.definition: A parasitic infection caused by nematodes (roundworms); transmitted by ingestion of eggs or larvae or by skin penetration, leading to gastrointestinal or tissue disease with symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, anemia, malnutrition, or eosinophilia, depending on the species.

upper respiratory tract.definition: Anatomical region comprising the nose, nasal cavities, paranasal sinuses, and pharynx (plus often the larynx), forming the upper airway that conducts air to the lower respiratory tract while warming, humidifying, and filtering inspired air and supporting speech and smell.

neisseria sicca.definition: A Gram-negative diplococcus that resides as part of the normal flora of the oropharynx and upper respiratory tract; typically nonpathogenic but can rarely be involved in opportunistic infections.

neonatology.definition: A medical subspecialty of pediatrics focused on the medical care of newborns, especially ill or premature infants, during the neonatal period (the first 28 days of life).

neonatal unit.definition: A hospital unit devoted to the medical care of newborn infants, especially those who are premature or ill, providing specialized monitoring, therapies, and support (including intensive care when needed).

nephroangiosclerosis.definition: Hardening and sclerosis of the small renal arteries and arterioles caused by chronic hypertension (often with atherosclerosis), leading to hyaline arteriolosclerosis, ischemic glomerulosclerosis, and progressive chronic kidney disease.

nephrocalcinosis.definition: Deposition of calcium salts in the kidney parenchyma (cortex and/or medulla), producing renal calcifications detectable on imaging; often due to disorders of calcium, phosphate, or oxalate metabolism and may be associated with kidney disease.

uremic gingivitis.definition: A gingival inflammatory condition seen in advanced kidney failure, characterized by diffuse redness and swelling of the gingiva with easy bleeding and sometimes ulceration; thought to result from accumulation of uremic toxins in saliva that irritate gingival tissues and impair healing, and it commonly improves with dialysis or renal transplantation.

embryonal sarcoma.definition: A rare, high-grade malignant tumor of mesenchymal origin composed of undifferentiated embryonal cells; most often occurring in children and frequently arising in the liver; treated with surgical resection when possible, followed by multiagent chemotherapy.

teratocarcinoma.definition: A malignant germ cell tumor composed of a teratoma component plus embryonal carcinoma; a mixed non-seminomatous germ cell tumor arising from pluripotent germ cells, typically aggressive with metastatic potential.

meningioma.definition: A tumor arising from the meninges (the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord), typically benign and slow-growing, originating from arachnoid cap cells and usually dural-based (an extra-axial lesion); most are WHO grade I, with less common atypical (grade II) and anaplastic/malignant (grade III) variants, and symptoms arise from compression of adjacent neural tissue.

spongioblastoma.definition: Historically, spongioblastoma referred to glioblastoma multiforme, a malignant primary brain tumor of astrocytic origin (WHO Grade IV) characterized by rapid growth, necrosis, and microvascular proliferation.

neurofibrosarcoma.definition: Malignant tumor of the peripheral nerve sheath arising from Schwann cells or related cells; often associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 and may develop from plexiform neurofibromas. It is an aggressive sarcoma with local invasion and potential metastasis, usually treated with wide surgical excision, with adjuvant radiotherapy and/or chemotherapy in selected cases.

neurogenic sarcoma.definition: A malignant tumor arising from nerve tissue, typically from Schwann cells of the peripheral nerve sheath; historically termed neurogenic sarcoma and now usually called malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST), often associated with neurofibromatosis type 1.

myxosarcoma.definition: A malignant soft-tissue sarcoma characterized by abundant myxoid (mucoid) extracellular matrix with malignant mesenchymal cells, often arranged in a loose, gelatinous stroma.

osteoma.definition: A benign bone tumor composed of mature, well-differentiated bone tissue; most commonly arising on the skull or facial bones, it is usually slow-growing and asymptomatic, with treatment typically by observation or surgical excision if symptomatic or cosmetically undesirable.

osteogenic sarcoma.definition: A malignant primary bone tumor characterized by malignant mesenchymal cells that produce osteoid (bone matrix); the most common primary malignant bone tumor, typically arising in the metaphyses of long bones in adolescents and young adults, with aggressive local growth and potential for lung metastasis.

synovioma.definition: A tumor arising from the synovial membrane lining joints, bursae, or tendon sheaths; the term is historical and is now largely superseded by more specific diagnoses such as synovial sarcoma (malignant) or other synovial tumors for benign lesions.

synovial sarcoma.definition: A malignant soft tissue sarcoma most often arising near joints of the extremities; it frequently shows biphasic histology with spindle cells and epithelial-like cells and is associated with a characteristic t(X;18) chromosomal translocation (SS18-SSX fusion), reflecting its origin from mesenchymal tissue rather than synovial tissue.

leiomyosarcoma.definition: A malignant tumor of smooth muscle cells arising in tissues such as the uterus, gastrointestinal tract, or soft tissue; a sarcoma characterized by spindle cells with smooth muscle differentiation and a potential for local invasion and distant metastasis.

afferent renal artery.definition: Not a standard term. If meant to refer to the nephron, the intended vessel is the afferent arteriole: a small arteriole that delivers blood to the glomerulus for filtration, arising from renal-artery branches (e.g., interlobular/cortical radial arteries) and draining into the efferent arteriole to help regulate glomerular filtration rate.

malpighian corpuscle.definition: A renal corpuscle in the nephron consisting of a glomerulus (tuft of capillaries) enveloped by Bowman's capsule; the site of the first-stage filtration of blood to form filtrate.

nephronophthisis.definition: A rare autosomal recessive kidney disease characterized by chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis with corticomedullary cyst formation, leading to progressive kidney failure most often in childhood or adolescence; it is considered a ciliopathy.

nephrolithotomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which an incision is made into the kidney to remove kidney stones (renal calculi).

nephrolith.definition: A stone formed in the kidney from crystallized minerals in urine; a renal calculus that can cause flank pain, hematuria, and potential obstruction or infection.

nephrolithic.definition: Relating to kidney stones; pertaining to nephroliths or nephrolithiasis; describing the presence or formation of stones in the kidney.

nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.definition: A disorder in which the kidneys fail to respond to antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin), resulting in an inability to concentrate urine and thus polyuria and polydipsia; it can be hereditary or acquired (e.g., from lithium therapy or certain kidney diseases).

nephrogenic rests.definition: A focus of residual embryonic nephrogenic (metanephric) tissue in the kidney; these rests resemble Wilms tumor histologically and are considered precursor lesions that can give rise to Wilms tumor (nephroblastomatosis when widespread).

nephrogenous.definition: Relating to the kidney or to kidney development; arising from renal tissue.

nephrogram.definition: Radiographic imaging of the kidneys obtained after intravenous contrast administration, during which the renal parenchyma is opacified to evaluate renal perfusion, morphology, and excretory function.

nephrography.definition: Radiographic examination of the kidneys in which contrast medium is used to outline the renal parenchyma and collecting system, primarily to evaluate anatomy and pathology of the kidneys; historically a part of intravenous urography (IVU).

nephrolytic.definition: Relating to the destruction or dissolution of kidney tissue; an agent or process that lyses renal tissue.

water-seal drainage.definition: An external chest drainage device in which a chest tube is connected to an underwater seal chamber that acts as a one-way valve, allowing air or fluid to drain from the pleural space while preventing air from re-entering; commonly part of a three-chamber system (collection, water-seal, suction).

thoracoabdominal incision.definition: A single incision that extends from the thorax into the abdomen to provide exposure of both the chest and abdominal cavities for procedures involving organs in both regions.

crossmatched.definition: Pertaining to donor blood that has undergone a crossmatch test with the recipient's serum to confirm compatibility and reduce the risk of transfusion reactions.

carcinomatous pericarditis.definition: Malignant inflammation of the pericardium caused by metastatic cancer cells involving the pericardium, often presenting with an exudative (frequently hemorrhagic) pericardial effusion and risk of cardiac tamponade.

neostigmine bromide.definition: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (quaternary ammonium) that increases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction; used to treat myasthenia gravis, reverse nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade after anesthesia, and manage postoperative ileus or urinary retention. It does not readily cross the blood–brain barrier.

neo-synephrine.definition: A brand-name drug for phenylephrine, an α1-adrenergic receptor agonist that causes vasoconstriction; used as a nasal decongestant, a vasopressor to raise blood pressure, and a mydriatic in ophthalmology.

polymyxin b sulfate.definition: An antibiotic from the polymyxin class (mixture of polymyxin B1 and B2) produced by Bacillus polymyxa that binds to lipopolysaccharides and phospholipids in the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, disrupting membrane integrity and causing bacterial death; the sulfate salt is used for parenteral and topical formulations, typically for severe or multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infections, but it can cause nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity.

bacitracin zinc.definition: A topical antibiotic preparation containing bacitracin in the form of a zinc salt; used to prevent or treat minor skin infections and to prevent infection in minor wounds; it inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis and is primarily active against Gram-positive bacteria; systemic absorption is minimal when applied to the skin.

neosporin.definition: A brand-name over-the-counter topical antibiotic ointment containing bacitracin, neomycin, and polymyxin B used to prevent infection in minor skin injuries; may cause allergic reactions in some individuals, particularly those sensitive to neomycin.

nephropexy.definition: A surgical procedure to fix a mobile kidney in place by anchoring it to the posterior abdominal wall to prevent nephroptosis.

nephroptosis.definition: Downward displacement of the kidney when standing due to laxity of the kidney’s supporting tissues, sometimes called a floating kidney; it can be asymptomatic or cause flank pain and urinary symptoms, with management ranging from observation to surgical nephropexy in symptomatic cases.

nephrorrhaphy.definition: Surgical suturing of the kidney to repair renal injury or to approximate and secure renal tissue.

nephroscope.definition: A specialized endoscope used to visualize the interior of the kidney, inserted percutaneously or through the urinary tract to inspect the renal pelvis and calyces, often used to perform lithotripsy or stone retrieval.

nephrostomy.definition: A procedure that creates an opening from the kidney's renal pelvis to the skin to drain urine, typically via a percutaneous catheter to relieve urinary obstruction or hydronephrosis.

nephrostomy catheter.definition: A catheter placed percutaneously into the renal pelvis to drain urine externally, typically through the skin and connected to a collection bag; used to bypass ureteral obstruction or to drain an obstructed, hydronephrotic, or infected kidney for temporary or long-term urinary drainage.

nephrostoma.definition: A surgically created opening from the kidney to the skin that allows urine to drain externally, usually maintained by a tube inserted into the renal collecting system.

nephrostomata.definition: Plural form of a surgically created opening into the kidney that allows urine drainage or access to the renal collecting system.

nephrotomography.definition: A tomographic radiographic technique that yields cross-sectional images of the kidneys by taking a series of X-ray exposures at different focal planes; used to evaluate renal anatomy and pathology such as stones or masses, but now largely supplanted by CT urography.

nephrotomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which the kidney is incised (an incision into renal tissue), typically to remove renal stones or to drain a renal abscess.

nephroureterolithiasis.definition: Presence of stones in both the kidney and the ureter, often causing flank pain, hematuria, and possible urinary obstruction.

neptazane.definition: A brand-name oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (methazolamide) used to lower intraocular pressure in glaucoma by reducing aqueous humor formation; also has diuretic effects.

neri's sign.definition: I can’t locate a reliable definition for “Neri's sign” in standard medical references. Could you share the clinical context (specialty or scenario) or confirm the spelling? I can try again or suggest similarly named signs.

plantar nerves.definition: Nerves supplying the plantar (sole) aspect of the foot, chiefly the medial plantar nerve and lateral plantar nerve (branches of the tibial nerve), which provide motor innervation to intrinsic plantar muscles and sensory innervation to the sole and toes.

nerve entrapment.definition: Entrapment of a peripheral nerve by surrounding tissues (such as fascia, muscle, tendon, ligament, or bone) causing chronic compression and neuropathic symptoms such as pain, numbness, tingling, and sometimes weakness in the nerve’s distribution; symptoms may worsen with activity or posture and improve with rest or decompression.

nerve conduction test.definition: A diagnostic test that measures the speed and strength of electrical impulses traveling through a peripheral nerve by stimulating the nerve and recording the response, used to assess peripheral neuropathies, nerve injuries, and related disorders.

endoneurium.definition: An innermost connective tissue layer that surrounds and isolates each individual peripheral nerve fiber (axon) within a nerve fascicle; composed of a delicate basement membrane and reticular tissue with capillaries and Schwann cell processes.

epineurium.definition: The outermost connective tissue sheath of a peripheral nerve, surrounding the entire nerve and its fascicles; made of dense irregular connective tissue and containing blood vessels (vasa nervorum) and adipose tissue, providing protection and structural support.

nerve graft.definition: A surgical procedure in which a segment of nerve is transplanted to bridge a gap in a damaged peripheral nerve, typically using an autograft or allograft, with microsurgical joining of the nerve ends to restore axonal continuity and function.

ngf.definition: A neurotrophic protein that supports the survival, growth, and function of certain neurons—especially sympathetic and nociceptive (pain-sensing) neurons—and signals through TrkA receptors (and p75NTR) to promote neurite outgrowth and survival.

nerve root.definition: A portion of a spinal nerve that emerges from the spinal cord, consisting of the dorsal (sensory) root and ventral (motor) root; the dorsal root contains the dorsal root ganglion, and the two roots unite to form the mixed spinal nerve as it exits the intervertebral foramen.

nerve plexus.definition: A network of intersecting nerves formed by the joining and redistribution of adjacent ventral rami of spinal nerves, which then give rise to the peripheral nerves that innervate a body region (e.g., cervical, brachial, lumbar, and sacral plexuses).

iliosacral.definition: Relating to the ilium and sacrum; pertaining to structures or joints involving both bones (e.g., the iliosacral joint).

peripheral nervous system.definition: The parts of the nervous system outside of the brain, brain stem, and spinal cord.

sensory endings.definition: Terminal portions of sensory neurons that detect stimuli (mechanical, thermal, chemical, or nociceptive) and transduce them into nerve impulses; they can be free nerve endings or encapsulated receptor structures.

nervimotor.definition: Relating to the nerves that innervate skeletal muscles and to the neural control of voluntary muscle movement.

kidney pelvis.definition: The renal pelvis is the funnel-shaped dilation of the ureter inside the kidney that collects urine from the major calyces and narrows to form the ureter; it lies in the renal sinus.

sensory.definition: Relating to the senses or to sensation; pertaining to perception of stimuli, especially via sensory receptors and afferent nerves.

somatic.definition: Relating to the body rather than the mind; also used for body cells (the soma) and for the somatic nervous system that controls voluntary movement.

medullary plate.definition: A nonstandard anatomical term; when used, it may refer to a thin bony plate lining the medullary (marrow) cavity of a bone (the endosteal plate) or, more commonly, be a misnomer for the epiphyseal (growth) plate.

medullary tube.definition: An archaic term for the neural tube, the embryonic precursor to the brain and spinal cord.

neural tube formation.definition: Embryologic process during early development in which the flat neural plate folds and fuses to form the neural tube, the precursor to the brain and spinal cord; primary neurulation forms most of the tube, secondary neurulation forms the caudal portion, and closure occurs at the neural (anterior and posterior) neuropores.

spina bifida cystica.definition: A form of neural tube defect in which a cystic sac protrudes through a defect in the vertebral arch, usually containing meninges and cerebrospinal fluid (meningocele) or meninges, CSF, and neural tissue (myelomeningocele).

cranial meningocele.definition: A congenital herniation of the meninges through a skull defect, forming a cerebrospinal fluid–filled sac; brain tissue is usually not involved.

cranioschisis.definition: A rare congenital malformation in which there is a fissure or cleft in the skull (calvarial defect) with exposed brain tissue due to failure of the skull to close over the brain.

neuralgic amyotrophy.definition: An acute inflammatory brachial plexopathy, often following a viral illness, presenting with sudden severe shoulder girdle pain followed by weakness and wasting of proximal arm muscles (notably deltoid and rotator cuff); thought to be autoimmune and typically self-limited with recovery over weeks to months. Also known as Parsonage–Tottenham syndrome.

parsonage-turner syndrome.definition: An acute brachial neuritis (neuralgic amyotrophy) presenting with sudden, severe shoulder girdle pain that is followed by weakness and muscle wasting in one arm; believed to be inflammatory/immune-mediated injury to the brachial plexus, often preceded by a viral illness; typically self-limited with gradual recovery over weeks to months and managed with analgesia and physical therapy.

neural ectoderm.definition: The portion of the embryonic ectoderm that gives rise to the nervous system, including the brain and spinal cord (from the neural tube), and, at the neural plate border, neural crest cells that form peripheral nerves and other neural derivatives.

enteric ganglia.definition: Clusters of neuron cell bodies within the enteric nervous system of the gastrointestinal tract (in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses) that coordinate intrinsic digestive functions such as motility, secretion, and blood flow, largely functioning independently of the central nervous system.

schwann cells.definition: A glial cell of the peripheral nervous system that forms the myelin sheath around peripheral nerve axons (myelinating form) or supports unmyelinated fibers (non-myelinating form); derived from neural crest and essential for rapid conduction and nerve regeneration.

occipital region.definition: The posterior region of the head, overlying the occipital bone and extending from the back of the skull toward the neck.

n-acetylneuraminic acid.definition: A nine-carbon acidic monosaccharide derivative of neuraminic acid, N-acetylated; the principal form of sialic acid found at the terminal position of glycoproteins and glycolipids in many vertebrates, where it participates in cell–cell recognition and interactions with pathogens.

neuraminic acid.definition: A family of nine-carbon acidic sugars known as sialic acids; they are typically located at the terminal positions of glycoprotein and glycolipid chains on animal cell surfaces, bearing a negative charge at physiological pH and mediating cell–cell and host–pathogen interactions, including binding by influenza viruses; neuraminidases can cleave these residues.

neuraminidase.definition: An enzyme on the surface of a virus.

neuraminidase spikes.definition: Surface glycoprotein spikes on influenza virions containing neuraminidase enzyme activity; they cleave sialic acid residues from host cell receptors (and from viral glycoproteins), allowing release and spread of newly formed virions and preventing virion aggregation, working in concert with hemagglutinin to regulate attachment and release.

sialidosis.definition: A rare autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme neuraminidase (NEU1), leading to accumulation of sialylated glycoproteins and oligosaccharides in tissues; two main forms are Type I (adult-onset with myoclonus/ataxia) and Type II (congenital/infantile with dysmorphism and organomegaly).

galactogialidosis.definition: A rare autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of neuraminidase and beta-galactosidase due to a defect in protective protein/cathepsin A, leading to accumulation of sialylated glycoproteins and oligosaccharides in tissues; it has a variable clinical spectrum from infantile to late-onset neurodegenerative features.

dysostosis multiplex.definition: A constellation of abnormal skeletal development due to certain lysosomal storage disorders, most notably mucopolysaccharidoses, producing widespread skeletal dysplasia involving the skull, spine, chest, pelvis, and long bones, with characteristic radiographic features such as thickened calvaria, J-shaped sella turcica, oar-shaped ribs, and short stature.

npu.definition: A national-level poison information and toxicology service that provides expert clinical guidance on poisoning exposures, coordinates toxicology testing and case management, and disseminates poison-related safety information to healthcare professionals.

neufeld nail.definition: Definition not found in standard medical dictionaries. It may be a misspelling or an uncommon/obsolete term. Could you provide context or check the spelling? If you meant a different nail sign (e.g., Mees' lines, Beau's lines, Lindsay nails, clubbing), I can define that.

neufeld angled nail.definition: A type of intramedullary orthopedic implant—a metal rod inserted into the medullary canal of a long bone to stabilize a fracture, designed with an angled profile to match the bone’s curvature and provide angular stability across the fracture.

nesiritide.definition: A recombinant human B-type natriuretic peptide given intravenously for the acute, decompensated heart failure to promote vasodilation, natriuresis, and diuresis, thereby reducing preload and afterload and improving dyspnea; adverse effects include hypotension and potential renal impairment; not indicated for chronic heart failure.

orthopedic surgery.definition: A surgical specialty focusing on disorders of the musculoskeletal system (bones, joints, ligaments, tendons, and muscles), treated with both operative procedures and nonoperative care.

neurocytolysin.definition: A cytolytic toxin that lyses neurons.

neurocytolysis.definition: The destruction or lysis of neurons (nerve cells), resulting in neuronal loss.

neurocytoma.definition: A rare, low-grade neuronal tumor of the central nervous system that most often arises within the ventricular system (usually the lateral ventricles near the foramen of Monro). It shows neuronal differentiation on histology and is mainly treated with surgical resection; radiotherapy may be used for residual or recurrent disease, and prognosis is generally favorable.

neuroenteric canal.definition: A transient embryologic channel that briefly connects the amniotic cavity with the primitive gut through the developing notochord, allowing communication between ectoderm and endoderm during early development; it typically closes by the end of the third week. Abnormal persistence or closure can give rise to neurenteric cysts or duplications.

neuresthenia.definition: Historically, a condition characterized by chronic fatigue and weakness with irritability, headaches, sleep disturbances, and concentration problems attributed to nervous exhaustion; not a precise diagnosis in modern medicine and often reclassified under anxiety, depression, or chronic fatigue–related disorders.

neurectomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which a nerve or part of a nerve is removed or cut to interrupt nerve conduction, typically performed to relieve intractable pain, nerve entrapment, or other neuropathic symptoms.

schwann sheath.definition: A sheath formed by Schwann cells surrounding a peripheral nerve fiber; it constitutes the neurilemma (the outer cytoplasmic layer of the Schwann cell) and helps insulate the axon and support peripheral nerve regeneration.

neurilemmal.definition: Relating to the neurilemma, the Schwann cell–derived cytoplasmic layer that surrounds a peripheral nerve axon and forms the outer sheath (neurolemma).

neurilemmatic.definition: Relating to the neurilemma, the outer, cytoplasmic layer of a Schwann cell that surrounds a peripheral nerve axon and its myelin sheath.

neurilemmatous.definition: Relating to the neurilemma, the outermost layer of the nerve-fiber sheath formed by Schwann cells that surrounds peripheral nerves.

neurinomas.definition: Benign tumors of the nerve sheath arising from Schwann cells (schwannomas); typically encapsulated and slow-growing, occurring along cranial or peripheral nerves, often solitary; multiple lesions can occur in neurofibromatosis type 2 and related conditions, with treatment usually surgical excision or observation depending on symptoms.

neurinomata.definition: A benign tumor arising from Schwann cells of the peripheral nerve sheath (schwannoma/neurilemmoma); typically encapsulated and slow-growing, it may cause nerve compression and neurological symptoms depending on its size and location.

neuritic plaque.definition: An extracellular deposition of beta-amyloid protein in brain tissue, typically forming a dense core surrounded by dystrophic neurites and glial reaction; a histopathologic hallmark of Alzheimer's disease.

neuritides.definition: Inflammation of a nerve or nerves (neuritis); typically presents with pain along the affected nerve, sensory disturbances (numbness, tingling), and sometimes weakness; caused by infections, autoimmune/immune-mediated processes, toxins, or demyelinating conditions.

neuroacanthocytosis.definition: A group of rare neurodegenerative disorders characterized by acanthocytes (spur cells) in peripheral blood and a prominent movement disorder (often chorea with dystonia), accompanied by psychiatric and cognitive symptoms; includes chorea-acanthocytosis (VPS13A mutation) and McLeod syndrome (XK mutation).

neuroanatomy.definition: The study of the structure of the nervous system, including the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves, and the organization of neurons, glia, and neural pathways.

neuroarthropathy.definition: Progressive destructive degeneration of a joint caused by peripheral neuropathy, in which impaired sensation and proprioception permit repeated microtrauma, leading to inflammation, bone resorption, joint instability, and progressive deformity—most commonly in the feet and ankles.

neurobiology.definition: The branch of biology that studies the structure and function of the nervous system, including neurons and glial cells, synaptic signaling, neural circuits, development, and how these processes give rise to behavior, sensation, and cognition.

neuroblast.definition: An immature neuron derived from neural crest cells that differentiates into a mature neuron, typically in the developing peripheral/autonomic (sympathetic) nervous system.

neuroblastomata.definition: A malignant tumor composed of neuroblasts derived from neural crest cells, most often occurring in children and typically arising in the adrenal medulla or sympathetic nervous system; histology shows small round blue cells with Homer Wright rosettes.

pepper's syndrome.definition: I can’t find a standard medical term “pepper’s syndrome.” Could you confirm the spelling or provide context? If you meant a known craniosynostosis syndrome, I can provide a concise definition once clarified.

neurobrucellosis.definition: Infection of the nervous system by Brucella species, usually occurring in the setting of systemic brucellosis, presenting as meningitis or meningoencephalitis with possible radiculopathy or myelopathy. Clinically, patients may have fever, headache, and focal or cognitive neurologic deficits. CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with elevated protein and low glucose; diagnosis is supported by positive Brucella serology or culture in blood and/or CSF. Treatment requires prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (e.g., doxycycline plus rifampin with an aminoglycoside or TMP-SMX), typically for 6–12 weeks or longer.

neurocanal.definition: Not a standard medical term; literally a “nerve canal” would refer to a passage in the nervous system through which neural elements (nerves or nerve roots) or cerebrospinal fluid pass. In practice, more precise terms are the spinal canal (vertebral canal) and the neural foramina that transmit nerve roots.

neurocardiogenic syncope.definition: A reflex-mediated fainting due to abnormal autonomic control (vasovagal response) that causes a rapid drop in heart rate and blood pressure, reducing cerebral perfusion and leading to transient loss of consciousness, often triggered by prolonged standing, emotional distress, pain, or heat.

neurocele.definition: A cystic lesion of the nervous system, representing dilation or cystic degeneration of neural tissue; an archaic or rarely used term for a neural cyst.

neurocoele.definition: An abnormal cystic sac or herniation of nervous tissue through a defect in the surrounding structures.

neurocentral.definition: Relating to the junction between the neural (vertebral arch) and central (vertebral body) portions of a vertebra; used to describe the neurocentral junction or neurocentral synchondrosis, a temporary cartilaginous joint in developing vertebrae that ossifies with age.

neurocentrum.definition: A neural center within the central nervous system; a cluster or aggregation of neurons that functions as an integrative processing unit, coordinating sensory input and motor output. The term is primarily used in invertebrate neuroanatomy to describe centralized ganglia or brain-like centers.

neurocheck.definition: A rapid bedside neurological assessment used to monitor for acute changes in brain function, typically evaluating level of consciousness, pupil response, motor strength, sensation, and orientation/mental status.

neurochemistry.definition: The study of chemical processes and substances that influence nervous system function, including neurotransmitters, neuromodulators, and their receptors, and how these chemicals regulate neural signaling and brain activity.

neuroepithelioma.definition: A malignant tumor of neuroepithelial origin, typically composed of primitive neuroectodermal cells with neuroectodermal differentiation; historically used for certain CNS and retinal tumors, but many cases are now classified as primitive neuroectodermal tumors or other CNS neoplasms.

neuroepithelial tumor.definition: A neoplasm arising from neuroepithelial tissue of the central nervous system, derived from neural/glial or ependymal cells (e.g., gliomas, ependymomas, choroid plexus tumors).

neurofibril.definition: A thread-like filament that forms part of a neuron's cytoskeleton, contributing to its structural integrity and shape.

cafe-au-lait spots.definition: Flat, pigmented skin macules (light brown patches) present at birth or in early childhood; usually benign, but multiple or larger patches can be associated with neurofibromatosis type 1.

recklinghausen's disease.definition: A genetic neurocutaneous disorder (neurofibromatosis type 1) characterized by multiple café-au-lait macules, benign nerve sheath tumors (neurofibromas), axillary/inguinal freckling, Lisch nodules in the iris, and various skeletal/CNS abnormalities; caused by pathogenic variants in the NF1 gene and inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with variable expressivity.

von recklinghausen's disease.definition: A genetic autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder due to NF1 gene mutations on chromosome 17; its hallmark features include multiple café-au-lait macules, axillary/inguinal freckling, cutaneous neurofibromas, and iris Lisch nodules, with variable expressivity and risk of optic glioma and other tumors.

neurogen.definition: Not a standard medical term. If used, it’s usually shorthand for neurogenesis or neurogenic processes—the generation or production of new nerve cells (neurons) in the nervous system. Neurogenesis occurs in regions like the adult hippocampus (dentate gyrus) and the subventricular zone, and is involved in learning, memory, and neural repair. The adjective neurogenic describes something that generates nerve tissue or neurons.

neurogenesis.definition: The process by which new neurons are generated from neural stem or progenitor cells; in humans it primarily occurs during development, with limited neurogenesis in adulthood confined to specific regions (most notably the hippocampus) and modulated by factors such as aging, environment, and activity.

neurogenic arthropathy.definition: Progressive, noninflammatory degenerative joint disease caused by peripheral neuropathy and loss of protective sensation, leading to repeated unnoticed trauma and resulting joint destruction and deformity (commonly referred to as Charcot joint).

neurogenic bladder.definition: A bladder dysfunction resulting from brain, spinal cord, or peripheral nerve injury that disrupts normal neural control of the bladder and sphincter, causing storage and/or voiding problems such as incontinence or urinary retention.

neurogenic claudication.definition: A symptom complex of leg pain, numbness, or weakness provoked by walking or standing and relieved by sitting or flexing the spine; caused by compression or ischemia of the lumbosacral nerve roots within a narrowed lumbar spinal canal (lumbar spinal stenosis).

neurogenic fracture.definition: A fracture resulting from underlying nervous system disease or injury that weakens bone or impairs protective sensation, leading to fracture after minimal trauma (common in neuropathic joints or paralytic limbs).

neurogenic hoarseness.definition: A voice change caused by disturbance of neural control of the vocal folds, usually from injury or dysfunction of the vagus nerve or one of its branches (recurrent laryngeal nerve), leading to vocal fold paresis or paralysis and a breathy, weak, or hoarse quality due to impaired glottic closure.

neurogenic impotence.definition: Erectile dysfunction due to impairment of the neural pathways that mediate erection (central, spinal, or autonomic/somatic nerves), often from diabetes, spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, or pelvic surgery/radiation.

neurogenic shock.definition: A distributive shock caused by loss of sympathetic vasomotor tone (most often from acute spinal cord injury above T6) leading to widespread vasodilation and hypotension with relative bradycardia; skin is warm and dry early in the course due to vasodilation.

neuroglial.definition: Relating to neuroglia, the glial cells that support, protect, and nourish neurons in the central and peripheral nervous systems.

neurography.definition: An imaging technique to visualize nerves, particularly peripheral nerves, typically using MR neurography to assess nerve anatomy and pathology.

neurohormone.definition: A hormone produced and released by neurons (neurosecretory cells) into the bloodstream, typically from the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary, to act on distant target organs.

neurohypophyseal hormone.definition: A hormone released by the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis); synthesized in hypothalamic neurons and secreted into the bloodstream. The two principal examples are oxytocin and vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone).

neuroimmunology.definition: A field that studies the interactions between the nervous system and the immune system, including how immune signals influence neural function and behavior, how neural pathways regulate immune responses, and how inflammation and immune processes contribute to neurological diseases.

neurolemma.definition: The outer cytoplasmic envelope of a peripheral nerve fiber formed by Schwann cells; it surrounds the myelin sheath, contains the Schwann cell nucleus and cytoplasm, and participates in nerve regeneration.

neurolepsis.definition: A historical term for the state produced by neuroleptic (antipsychotic) drugs, involving marked reduction in psychomotor activity and blunting of affect (drug-induced indifference/catalepsy).

neurolepsy.definition: An obsolete or rarely used term historically referring to a neurological condition involving seizures or epileptic-like activity; not part of current standard medical terminology.

neurolept.definition: An antipsychotic medication that reduces psychotic symptoms by blocking dopamine D2 receptors in the brain; commonly used to treat schizophrenia and other psychoses.

neuroleptanalgesia.definition: A state of analgesia and sedation produced by the combination of a neuroleptic (antipsychotic) drug with an opioid analgesic, yielding diminished perception of pain, blunted emotional response, and reduced motor activity with minimal autonomic disturbance compared with general anesthesia.

neuroleptic.definition: A class of antipsychotic drugs used to treat psychosis; they primarily block dopamine D2 receptors in the brain, reducing psychotic symptoms, but frequently cause extrapyramidal side effects (and other dopamine-related adverse effects). Historically called typical antipsychotics.

neuroendocrine.definition: Relating to the interface between the nervous and endocrine systems; describing cells that receive neural input and secrete hormones into the bloodstream in response to neural signals.

neuroendoscope.definition: A rigid or flexible endoscope designed for visualization and access to the brain or spinal canal, used to diagnose conditions or perform minimally invasive neurosurgical procedures.

neuroendoscopy.definition: A minimally invasive neurosurgical technique using a rigid or flexible endoscope inserted through a burr hole or natural opening to visualize the brain's ventricular system and surrounding spaces, enabling diagnostic visualization and therapeutic procedures such as endoscopic third ventriculostomy, biopsy, fenestration of membranes or cysts, and removal of intraventricular lesions.

neurotransmitter.definition: A chemical messenger released by nerve cells that transmits messages to nearby other nerve cells.

neuromodulator.definition: A substance released by neurons that modulates the activity of other neurons or synapses by altering neurotransmitter release or receptor responsiveness, producing slower, longer-lasting effects that can affect multiple neurons or circuits (often via volume transmission).

neuronavigation.definition: A computer-assisted guidance system that uses preoperative brain imaging (MRI/CT) with real-time tracking to map anatomy and guide neurosurgical instruments for precise localization and safety.

neural canal.definition: The hollow passage within the vertebral column formed by the vertebral foramina that contains the spinal cord and its meninges; it extends from the foramen magnum to the sacral region.

cranial nerve lesions.definition: Damage or dysfunction of one or more of the twelve cranial nerves, producing corresponding sensory, motor, or autonomic deficits depending on the affected nerve.

neurosecretory cells.definition: Neurosecretory cells are specialized neurons that synthesize neurohormones and release them into the bloodstream (often via the hypothalamic–pituitary portal system or the posterior pituitary), thereby linking the nervous and endocrine systems. For example, hypothalamic magnocellular cells release oxytocin and vasopressin into the posterior pituitary.

neurosecretory.definition: Relating to nerve cells that synthesize and secrete hormones (neurohormones) into the bloodstream as part of the neuroendocrine system.

telangiectodes.definition: An abnormal dilation of small blood vessels near the surface of the skin or mucous membranes, producing visible fine red or purple lines or webs; can be idiopathic or associated with systemic vascular conditions such as rosacea or hereditary vascular disorders.

malignant syndrome.definition: A life‑threatening hypermetabolic syndrome usually caused by antipsychotic drugs (dopamine D2 blockade), presenting with high fever, severe generalized rigidity, autonomic instability, and altered mental status, often with marked elevation of creatine kinase.

neurolinguistic programming.definition: A controversial, pseudoscientific approach that asserts altering language and mental imagery can change neural pathways and behavior; lacks robust scientific evidence and is not an evidence-based medical treatment.

neurolinguistics.definition: A multidisciplinary field that studies how the brain supports language—its perception, production, and acquisition—exploring the neural substrates of phonology, syntax, and semantics and how brain injury affects language abilities.

neurology.definition: The study of the nervous system.

neurologic.definition: Relating to the nervous system; pertaining to the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves, including their structure, function, and disorders.

spinal nerves.definition: A mixed peripheral nerve of the peripheral nervous system formed by the union of a dorsal (sensory) and ventral (motor) root at a given spinal level; it exits the vertebral canal through the intervertebral foramen and divides into dorsal and ventral rami to carry sensory information to and motor commands from the spinal cord to the trunk and limbs (31 pairs: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal).

multipolar neuron.definition: Neuron with many dendritic processes and a single axon; the most common neuron type in the vertebrate central nervous system, receiving input from numerous neurons and transmitting the integrated signal along its axon to target cells.

bipolar neuron.definition: A neuron with two processes—one dendrite and one axon—emanating from opposite sides of the cell body; typically involved in specialized sensory pathways (e.g., retinal and olfactory neurons).

unipolar neuron.definition: A neuron with a single process that divides into two branches—a peripheral process carrying impulses from sensory receptors and a central process carrying impulses into the CNS; typically a pseudounipolar sensory neuron found in dorsal root ganglia.

cholinergic receptor.definition: A receptor that binds acetylcholine (and related agonists) to mediate cholinergic signaling; two main types are nicotinic receptors (ligand-gated ion channels) and muscarinic receptors (G protein–coupled receptors), found at neuromuscular junctions, autonomic ganglia, and in various central and peripheral tissues.

tabes dorsalis.definition: A late neurosyphilitic syndrome in which degeneration of the dorsal columns and dorsal roots of the spinal cord causes sensory ataxia, loss of proprioception and vibratory sense, lancinating pains, a broad-based gait, and a positive Romberg sign, often with pupillary abnormalities (Argyll Robertson pupils).

computerized tomogram.definition: An imaging study that produces cross-sectional images of the body by using rotating X-ray beams and computer reconstruction of the collected data.

neuromuscular.definition: Relating to the interaction between the nervous system and skeletal muscles, including motor neurons, the nerve-to-muscle junction where nerve signals trigger muscle contraction, and the muscle fibers themselves; encompasses processes of neural transmission to muscle and disorders affecting this nerve–muscle interface.

nmes.definition: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation: a rehabilitation technique that uses transcutaneous electrical impulses delivered via surface electrodes to activate motor nerves and evoke muscle contractions, with goals including improving muscle strength, preventing atrophy, and facilitating functional movement.

metocurine.definition: A long-acting nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent used to produce skeletal muscle relaxation during anesthesia; a derivative of tubocurarine with prolonged duration and potential histamine release causing hypotension.

pancuronium.definition: A long-acting nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent (an aminosteroid) used to induce skeletal muscle paralysis during anesthesia and mechanical ventilation. It works by competitive blockade of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction; given IV, with effects lasting roughly 60–90 minutes and reversible by acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (e.g., neostigmine) or sugammadex. Adverse effects can include tachycardia and mild blood pressure changes due to its vagolytic properties, with minimal histamine release compared to some older agents.

tubocurarine.definition: A nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent derived from curare that competitively inhibits nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the motor end plate, producing flaccid paralysis and skeletal muscle relaxation; used to facilitate intubation and surgical relaxation, with a relatively long duration and potential histamine release–related hypotension.

succinylcholine.definition: A depolarizing neuromuscular blocker that acts as an agonist at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, causing initial fasciculations followed by rapid, short‑lasting skeletal muscle paralysis. It is used to facilitate rapid sequence intubation and other brief procedures; onset is about 30–60 seconds and duration roughly 5–10 minutes, with rapid inactivation by plasma cholinesterase. Notable risks include malignant hyperthermia and transient hyperkalemia in at‑risk individuals; contraindicated in patients with known pseudocholinesterase deficiency or certain neuromuscular disorders.

neuromuscular blocking agent.definition: A drug that interferes with transmission of nerve impulses at the neuromuscular junction, producing skeletal muscle relaxation and paralysis; used to facilitate intubation and surgical procedures and classified as depolarizing or nondepolarizing, with reversal achieved by acetylcholinesterase inhibitors or specific reversal agents.

nondepolarizing agents.definition: A class of neuromuscular blocking drugs that competitively inhibit acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors on the motor end plate, preventing depolarization and causing flaccid paralysis; unlike depolarizing blockers, they do not cause initial fasciculations and their effects are reversed by acetylcholinesterase inhibitors.

depolarizing blocking agents.definition: A class of neuromuscular-blocking drugs that mimic acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors on the motor endplate, causing an initial fasciculation followed by sustained depolarization and desensitization of the receptor, producing rapid, short-duration flaccid paralysis; the prototype is succinylcholine, and its effect wears off with plasma cholinesterase metabolism. Adverse effects include hyperkalemia, malignant hyperthermia, bradyarrhythmias, and increased intraocular or intracranial pressure.

myelinated nerve fiber.definition: An axon insulated by a multilayered myelin sheath produced by Schwann cells (peripheral nervous system) or oligodendrocytes (central nervous system), which increases the speed of electrical impulse conduction via saltatory conduction, with interruptions at nodes of Ranvier that facilitate rapid signal transmission.

neuropore.definition: Two openings at the cranial (anterior) and caudal (posterior) ends of the developing neural tube in early embryogenesis; they normally close as the neural tube forms. Failure to close can result in neural tube defects such as anencephaly (cranial) or spina bifida (caudal).

neuropraxia.definition: A mild nerve injury (Seddon type I) with transient conduction block due to focal demyelination, while the axon remains intact; typically caused by compression or mild stretch and usually followed by full recovery within days to weeks.

neurosarcoidosis.definition: A form of sarcoidosis in which noncaseating granulomatous inflammation affects the nervous system—brain, spinal cord, meninges, or cranial nerves—leading to diverse neurologic symptoms (e.g., headaches, cranial neuropathies, seizures, meningitis, cognitive changes). Diagnosis relies on clinical and radiologic evidence with exclusion of other causes, and biopsy may show noncaseating granulomas; treatment typically starts with corticosteroids, with additional immunosuppressants for refractory disease.

neuroradiography.definition: Radiographic imaging of the brain and spinal cord using X-rays, typically with contrast to visualize the ventricles, subarachnoid spaces, or neural pathways; historically included procedures such as ventriculography and myelography.

neuroradiology.definition: A subspecialty of radiology focused on the imaging and diagnosis of diseases of the nervous system (brain, spinal cord, spine, and head/neck nerves) and the associated vasculature, using modalities such as MRI, CT, and angiography, and including endovascular and other interventional procedures.

neurophysin.definition: A carrier protein produced by hypothalamic neurons that binds and transports the neurohypophysial hormones vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone) and oxytocin to the posterior pituitary; two main forms exist, with neurophysin I binding oxytocin and neurophysin II binding vasopressin.

neuroplasticity.definition: Neuroplasticity is the brain's ability to reorganize its structure, function, and connections in response to learning, experience, or injury, through mechanisms such as synaptic strengthening or weakening, formation or pruning of synapses, and, in some regions, the growth of new neurons.

neuroplasty.definition: A surgical procedure to repair or reconstruct a damaged peripheral nerve to restore sensory or motor function, often by freeing the nerve from scar tissue (neurolysis), repairing its ends (neurorrhaphy), or bridging gaps with grafts.

neuroplegia.definition: Paralysis arising from damage or dysfunction of a nerve, leading to loss of motor function (and often sensation) in the distribution of that nerve.

neural tissue.definition: Tissue of the nervous system composed of neurons and glial cells; specialized for reception, integration, and transmission of electrical and chemical signals.

neuronal antibody.definition: An autoantibody directed against neuronal antigens (often targeting neuronal cell-surface receptors or intracellular neuronal proteins) and implicated in autoimmune neurological disorders such as autoimmune encephalitis.

sle.definition: Chronic autoimmune disease characterized by autoantibody production and immune complex–mediated inflammation that can affect multiple organs, most often the skin, joints, kidneys, and hematologic or nervous systems; course is marked by flares and remissions; common features include fatigue, arthralgia, malar rash, photosensitivity, nephritis, and cytopenias; management includes antimalarials, corticosteroids, and immunosuppressants.

neuropsychiatrist.definition: A clinician who specializes in disorders at the interface of neurology and psychiatry, diagnosing and treating psychiatric symptoms that arise from brain disease or injury (or neurological conditions that affect behavior, mood, and cognition).

neuropsychiatry.definition: A subspecialty at the interface of neurology and psychiatry that studies and treats mental, behavioral, and cognitive disorders arising from brain disease, including psychiatric symptoms in neurological illness and neurodegenerative conditions.
