nsb.definition: Binding that occurs to a surface or receptor in the absence of a specific interaction with the intended target, causing background signal; mitigated by blocking steps, stringent washing, optimized reagent concentrations, and proper negative controls.

nubain.definition: A semi-synthetic opioid analgesic (nalbuphine) that acts as a kappa-opioid receptor agonist and mu-opioid receptor antagonist; used for moderate to severe pain and obstetric analgesia, with a ceiling effect on respiratory depression and potential to precipitate withdrawal in opioid-dependent individuals.

posaconazole.definition: An antifungal triazole medication used to treat and prevent invasive fungal infections; it inhibits fungal lanosterol 14-α-demethylase, reducing ergosterol synthesis and disrupting fungal cell membrane integrity.

nucleolus.definition: A dense, non-membrane-bound structure inside the nucleus where ribosomal RNA (rRNA) genes are transcribed and ribosome subunits begin to assemble; it contains ribosomal DNA repeats and associated proteins and forms around active rRNA gene clusters (nucleolar organizer regions).

nucleoplasm.definition: The gel-like substance inside the cell nucleus (excluding the nucleolus) that surrounds chromatin and contains ions, enzymes, and proteins; the medium for nuclear processes such as DNA replication and transcription.

nucleocytoplasmic.definition: Relating to the cell nucleus and cytoplasm; describing processes or transport of molecules between the nucleus and cytoplasm via nuclear pore complexes.

nucleocytoplasmic ratio.definition: Proportion of the nucleus size to the cytoplasm size in a cell; a higher ratio indicates a larger nucleus relative to cytoplasm, commonly seen in immature or malignant cells.

radionuclide organ imaging.definition: A nuclear medicine imaging technique in which a radiopharmaceutical is administered to a patient and its distribution within an organ is captured by a gamma camera or PET scanner to assess structure, function, perfusion, or metabolism.

nucleocapsid.definition: A protein–nucleic acid complex that forms the inner core of a virus particle, consisting of the viral genome bound to nucleocapsid (nucleoprotein) proteins; it is distinct from the viral envelope.

nucleochylema.definition: A historical or less common term for the nucleoplasm—the viscous, protein-rich fluid inside the cell nucleus that surrounds chromatin and the nucleolus.

nucleochyme.definition: An obsolete or nonstandard term referring to the fluid content of the cell nucleus (nucleoplasm), the gel‑like substance surrounding chromatin and containing nuclear proteins.

nucleolus organizer.definition: A chromosomal region containing tandem repeats of ribosomal RNA gene sequences that directs the formation of the nucleolus by transcribing rRNA.

nucleosome.definition: A basic unit of DNA packaging in eukaryotes, consisting of about 147 base pairs of DNA wrapped around a histone octamer (two each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4), forming a bead-on-a-string chromatin structure, with linker DNA and histone H1 helping organize higher-order fibers.

nucleic acid.definition: Biopolymers made of nucleotide monomers that store, transmit, and direct genetic information; the main types are DNA and RNA, encoding information in sequences of bases (A, C, G, T in DNA; A, C, G, U in RNA).

nucleotide.definition: The basic building block of nucleic acids, consisting of a nitrogenous base attached to a five‑carbon sugar (deoxyribose in DNA or ribose in RNA) and one to three phosphate groups; nucleotides link to form DNA and RNA.

nucleoside.definition: A molecule consisting of a nitrogenous base covalently attached to a five‑carbon sugar (ribose in RNA or deoxyribose in DNA) via a glycosidic bond, without any phosphate groups. Nucleosides are the precursors to nucleotides and become nucleotides when one or more phosphate groups are added.

nucleoside analog.definition: A synthetic compound that mimics a natural nucleoside but has structural changes (on the sugar or base) that, after cellular phosphorylation, can be incorporated into nucleic acids or otherwise disrupt nucleic acid synthesis, often terminating DNA/RNA elongation; used as antiviral and anticancer agents.

nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibit.definition: A class of antiretroviral drugs that inhibit HIV reverse transcriptase by acting as nucleoside analogs; they are activated by host cell kinases to active triphosphate forms and terminate viral DNA synthesis upon incorporation, thereby preventing viral replication.

nucleoside monophosphate kinase.definition: A family of enzymes that phosphorylate nucleoside monophosphates (NMPs) to their corresponding diphosphates (NDPs) using ATP (or another nucleoside triphosphate) as the phosphate donor, thereby helping maintain cellular nucleotide pools.

dna amplification.definition: Production of many copies of a specific DNA sequence using enzymatic amplification, most commonly polymerase chain reaction (PCR), enabling detection, analysis, or downstream applications.

nucleic acid amplification.definition: A set of laboratory methods that selectively amplify a specific nucleic acid sequence, producing many copies from a minute initial amount to enable detection, quantification, or analysis. Common examples include polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and related techniques (such as RT-PCR for RNA and loop-mediated isothermal amplification), which use primers and enzymes to replicate the target sequence, resulting in exponential amplification.

nucleic acid amplification test.definition: A laboratory assay that detects a pathogen by amplifying its nucleic acids (DNA or RNA) to detectable levels, typically using PCR or RT-PCR, enabling sensitive and specific diagnosis from clinical specimens.

5'-nucleotidase.definition: A membrane-bound hydrolase that dephosphorylates 5'-nucleotides (e.g., AMP) to the corresponding nucleosides (e.g., adenosine) and inorganic phosphate, thereby regulating extracellular adenosine levels and purinergic signaling.

5'-nucleotidase test.definition: A laboratory test that measures the serum activity of 5'-nucleotidase, an enzyme that is elevated in cholestasis or biliary obstruction and is used to differentiate cholestatic (biliary) jaundice from hepatocellular injury when evaluating abnormal liver tests.

nucleus pulposus.definition: The gel-like shock-absorbing central portion of each spinal disc.

pulposus.definition: A soft, gel-like material that forms the inner core of an intervertebral disc.

vertebral disk.definition: A fibrocartilaginous cushion between adjacent vertebral bodies in the spine that absorbs and distributes loads and allows limited motion; it comprises an outer ring of annulus fibrosus and an inner gelatinous nucleus pulposus, and can degenerate or herniate.

nuclear pores.definition: A large protein complex that spans the nuclear envelope and forms selective channels, allowing bidirectional transport between the nucleus and cytoplasm. Small molecules diffuse through these channels passively, while larger proteins, RNAs, and ribonucleoprotein particles require active, receptor‑mediated transport mediated by karyopherins (importins/exportins) and the Ran GTPase system.

histone.definition: A family of highly basic nuclear proteins that package and organize DNA into chromatin by forming nucleosomes around an octameric core; they regulate DNA accessibility and processes such as transcription, replication, and repair.

nucleohistone.definition: A complex of DNA wrapped around histone proteins that constitutes the basic unit of chromatin (the nucleosome).

nucleoprotein.definition: A complex of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) with protein; forms the structural and functional unit of chromatin and various ribonucleoprotein particles, and in viruses constitutes the nucleocapsid.

co-60.definition: A radioactive cobalt isotope that decays with emission of gamma rays (half-life ~5.27 years) and is used as a gamma-ray source in external-beam radiotherapy (teletherapy) and for sterilization/irradiation.

nuhn's gland.definition: There is no widely recognized gland by that name in standard human anatomy; the term likely represents a misspelling or a nonstandard/local name rather than a defined anatomical structure.

nummular dermatitis.definition: A chronic, relapsing form of eczema presenting with multiple, well-demarcated coin-shaped plaques that are intensely itchy and inflamed, most commonly on the arms and legs; lesions may be scaly, crusted, or vesicular.

nummular psoriasis.definition: A chronic psoriasis variant characterized by well-circumscribed, coin-shaped (round) erythematous plaques with silvery scales, typically on the limbs; may resemble tinea corporis and often relapses.

null cell.definition: A lymphocyte that lacks surface markers of both B and T cells (CD19/CD20 and CD3 negative), typically referring to natural killer (NK) cells; part of the innate immune system that can destroy virally infected or malignant cells without prior sensitization.

nnrti.definition: A class of antiretroviral drugs that inhibits HIV reverse transcriptase by binding to an allosteric site on the enzyme, blocking synthesis of viral DNA from RNA; they are non-nucleoside inhibitors and do not require phosphorylation.

stavudine.definition: A nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) antiretroviral drug used to treat HIV infection; a thymidine analog that inhibits HIV-1 reverse transcriptase and terminates viral DNA synthesis.

ddi.definition: A drug–drug interaction is a change in the effect of one drug when another drug is present, potentially increasing toxicity or decreasing efficacy. It can be pharmacokinetic (altering absorption, distribution, metabolism, or excretion) or pharmacodynamic (altering the drug's effect at its target).

ddc.definition: I couldn’t find a standard medical definition for “ddc.” Could you share the full term or the clinical context (e.g., specialty, disease, or procedure) so I can provide the correct definition?

3tc.definition: A nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) used to treat HIV-1 infection and chronic hepatitis B; it is phosphorylated intracellularly to an active triphosphate form and inhibits viral DNA synthesis by causing chain termination during replication.

nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhi.definition: A class of antiretroviral drugs that inhibit HIV-1 reverse transcriptase by binding to an allosteric site, blocking synthesis of viral DNA; they do not require phosphorylation to become active and are used in combination therapy for HIV infection.

adenoviruses.definition: A group of nonenveloped, icosahedral, double-stranded DNA viruses in the family Adenoviridae that infect humans and other vertebrates, causing a range of illnesses including acute respiratory infections, conjunctivitis, pharyngitis, and gastroenteritis; transmission is via respiratory droplets, fecal-oral spread, or direct contact, and infections are usually self-limited but can be severe in immunocompromised individuals.

isolation.definition: The separation and confinement of a person who is infected or potentially infectious from others to prevent transmission of disease, usually involving designated rooms and protective precautions.

sertoli cell.definition: A sustentacular cell in the seminiferous tubules of the testis that supports and nourishes developing germ cells, forms the blood–testis barrier via tight junctions, and regulates spermatogenesis by secreting factors such as inhibin and androgen-binding protein in response to FSH.

nurse cell.definition: A specialized germline cell that nourishes the developing oocyte during oogenesis by supplying cytoplasm, RNAs, proteins, and organelles; in organisms like Drosophila, nurse cells are polyploid and connected to the oocyte via ring canals to transfer these materials.

outbreaks.definition: A sudden increase in the number of cases of a disease in a specific geographic area or population, above the normally expected baseline for a defined period, often indicating ongoing transmission and potential clustering.

nutcracker esophagus.definition: An esophageal motility disorder characterized by excessively vigorous, high-amplitude esophageal contractions during swallowing with preserved peristaltic sequence and normal lower esophageal sphincter relaxation, usually diagnosed by esophageal manometry; patients often present with chest pain or dysphagia.

nutcracker phenomenon.definition: Compression of the left renal vein between the abdominal aorta and the superior mesenteric artery, causing venous hypertension of the left kidney. It is typically asymptomatic (nutcracker phenomenon); when symptoms such as hematuria, left flank pain, or orthostatic proteinuria are present, it is called nutcracker syndrome.

nutcracker syndrome.definition: Compression of the left renal vein between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery, causing left renal venous hypertension with symptoms such as left flank pain, hematuria, and sometimes a left-sided varicocele or pelvic congestion; diagnosed by imaging (e.g., Doppler ultrasound, CT or MR venography) and managed based on severity, ranging from observation to surgical or endovascular relief in symptomatic cases.

nutmeg poisoning.definition: A toxic syndrome caused by ingesting large quantities of nutmeg (Myristica fragrans), due to psychoactive constituents such as myristicin and elemicin. It presents with gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain), neurological and behavioral changes (dizziness, confusion, agitation, delirium, perceptual disturbances), and autonomic effects (tachycardia, hypertension, dry mouth). Symptoms typically begin several hours after ingestion and are usually self-limited, resolving within 24–72 hours with supportive care.

nutrient.definition: A substance that comes from food, including proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins, minerals, and water.

megaloblastic.definition: Pertaining to megaloblasts; describing enlarged, immature red blood cell precursors (megaloblasts) in bone marrow due to impaired DNA synthesis, most often from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.

sleep.definition: An reversible state of perceptual disengagement and reduced responsiveness, in which voluntary movement is limited and brain activity cycles through non-REM and REM stages; sleep supports restoration, memory consolidation, and metabolic regulation and is governed by circadian and homeostatic mechanisms.

nyctophobia.definition: An irrational, excessive fear of darkness or the night that causes anxiety, distress, and avoidance of dark environments; typically classified as a specific phobia.

nux.definition: Latin for "nut"; refers to Nux vomica, the seed of Strychnos nux-vomica, containing toxic alkaloids (strychnine and brucine) and historically used as a stimulant/purgative; now mainly used in highly diluted homeopathic preparations.

vomica.definition: An archaic medical term for a tuberculous cavity in the lung (a cavitary lesion) produced by caseous necrosis, typically communicating with a bronchus and containing purulent material.

rhodopsin.definition: A light-sensitive G protein-coupled receptor in retinal rod cells formed by opsin bound to 11-cis-retinal; it initiates visual phototransduction when activated by light.

obex.definition: The caudal point of the floor of the fourth ventricle where it narrows to form the central canal of the spinal cord; marks the border between the medulla oblongata and the spinal cord near the foramen magnum.

obstetrician.definition: A doctor who cares for women who are expecting a baby.

obstetrix.definition: A historical term for a female obstetrician or midwife who assists with pregnancy and childbirth.

obstruction series.definition: A radiographic imaging series used to evaluate suspected intestinal obstruction, typically including upright and supine abdominal radiographs (often with a chest radiograph) to assess bowel gas patterns, bowel dilatation, air-fluid levels, and signs of perforation.

obstructive uropathy.definition: A condition in which urine flow is obstructed anywhere along the urinary tract, leading to dilation of the urinary system (hydronephrosis) and potential renal impairment; causes include stones, bladder outlet obstruction (e.g., benign prostatic hyperplasia), ureteral or urethral strictures, tumors, or congenital anomalies.

obstructive biliary cirrhosis.definition: A form of secondary biliary cirrhosis caused by long-standing obstruction of the bile ducts, leading to cholestasis and progressive biliary fibrosis that culminates in cirrhosis (often due to gallstones, biliary strictures, or bile duct tumors).

obstructive constipation.definition: A constipation caused by a mechanical obstruction of the colon or rectum (such as fecal impaction, tumor, stricture, volvulus, or hernia) that prevents stool passage, often with abdominal distension and cramping; differs from functional constipation due to slow transit or withholding.

obstructive hydroureter.definition: A dilation of the ureter caused by an obstruction to urine flow, resulting in urine accumulation proximal to the obstruction; commonly due to a ureteral stone, stricture, tumor, or external compression.

obstructive jaundice.definition: Obstructive jaundice is jaundice caused by blockage of bile flow, typically from an obstruction in the biliary tract (e.g., gallstones, tumors, or strictures), leading to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and clinical features such as pale stools and dark urine.

obstructive nephropathy.definition: Renal impairment and structural kidney damage caused by obstruction to urinary outflow (anywhere along the urinary tract), leading to hydronephrosis and increased intrarenal pressure; it can be acute or chronic and unilateral or bilateral, and may be reversible with prompt relief of the obstruction.

oculocutaneous albinism.definition: An inherited (typically autosomal recessive) disorder characterized by reduced or absent melanin production in the skin, hair, and eyes, leading to hypopigmented appearance and ocular abnormalities such as reduced visual acuity, nystagmus, and photophobia.

occipital artery.definition: A branch of the external carotid artery that runs posteriorly to supply the posterior scalp and occipital region, giving off branches to surrounding muscles and the mastoid region, and a posterior meningeal branch to the dura.

occipital sinus.definition: A small dural venous sinus that runs along the occipital bone within the falx cerebelli (at the internal occipital crest) and drains blood from the occipital region and cerebellum into the confluence of sinuses.

occipital condyles.definition: Two rounded projections on the inferior surface of the occipital bone that articulate with the superior articular facets of the atlas (C1), forming the atlanto-occipital joints; they support the skull and enable nodding and slight lateral movement of the head.

occipital condyle syndrome.definition: A rare skull-base syndrome characterized by occipital neuralgia with ipsilateral hypoglossal nerve (cranial nerve XII) palsy due to a lesion at the occipital condyle, most commonly from metastasis or other skull-base pathology.

occipitization.definition: A congenital fusion of the first cervical vertebra (atlas) with the occipital bone (atlantooccipital assimilation), resulting in limited movement at the craniocervical junction and may be asymptomatic or associated with craniovertebral anomalies such as basilar invagination.

occipitobregmatic.definition: Relating to the occipital bone and the bregma; in skull measurements, the distance from the occipital pole to the bregma (an anteroposterior diameter of the fetal skull).

occipital anchorage.definition: A form of orthodontic skeletal anchorage in which a fixed anchor is attached to the occipital bone (posterior skull) to provide a stationary point against which teeth are moved, improving control of tooth movement and reducing unwanted reciprocal movement; also known as skull-based anchorage.

greater occipital nerve.definition: A sensory nerve formed by the dorsal (posterior) ramus of C2 that provides cutaneous innervation to the posterior scalp from the occipital region up to the vertex; it usually pierces the semispinalis capitis muscle and accompanies the occipital artery.

obturator sign.definition: Pain in the lower abdomen elicited by internal rotation of the flexed right hip; a positive sign suggesting irritation of the obturator nerve or obturator internus muscle from intraperitoneal inflammation, commonly seen in acute appendicitis with a pelvic appendix.

obturator nerve.definition: A nerve of the lumbar plexus (L2–L4) that enters the thigh via the obturator canal and divides into anterior and posterior branches to supply the medial thigh adductors (adductor longus, adductor brevis, gracilis, and the adductor part of adductor magnus) and obturator externus, with a small sensory distribution to the medial thigh and articular branches to the hip joint.

obturator membrane.definition: A fibrous membrane that fills the obturator foramen of the hip bone, closing the foramen except for the obturator canal, through which the obturator nerve and vessels pass; it attaches to the margins of the foramen on the pubis and ischium.

obturator muscles.definition: Two hip rotator muscles—the obturator externus and obturator internus. They arise from the margins of the obturator foramen and membrane and pass through the lesser sciatic foramen; externus inserts on the trochanteric fossa of the femur, internus on the medial surface of the greater trochanter. They laterally rotate the thigh at the hip and help stabilize the femoral head in the acetabulum. Innervation: obturator externus by the obturator nerve; obturator internus by the nerve to obturator internus (L5–S2).

obturator canal.definition: A short canal in the superior pubic ramus at the edge of the obturator foramen through which the obturator nerve, artery, and vein pass from the pelvis to the medial thigh.

obstetric position.definition: Describes how the fetus is oriented within the uterus and birth canal during labor, including lie (longitudinal vs. transverse), presenting part (cephalic, breech, shoulder), and fetal position relative to the maternal pelvis (for example, occipitoanterior or occipitoposterior).

episiotomy repair.definition: An operative procedure to close an episiotomy incision in the perineum after vaginal delivery, typically by layered suturing of vaginal mucosa, perineal muscles, and skin with absorbable sutures to restore anatomy and promote healing.

elliot forceps.definition: A type of obstetric instrument (forceps) used to assist vaginal delivery by grasping the fetal head and guiding it through the birth canal during the second stage of labor.

simpson forceps.definition: A historical obstetric instrument: a pair of curved forceps used to assist vaginal delivery by grasping the fetal head and applying traction/rotation during the second stage, typically for outlet or low-forceps deliveries and named after James Young Simpson.

tucker-mclean forceps.definition: An obstetric instrument: a specialized pair of curved metal blades with handles used to grasp the fetal head during operative vaginal delivery and to apply controlled traction under obstetric supervision.

paracervical block.definition: A regional anesthesia technique in which local anesthetic is injected around the cervix (paracervical region) to block sensory nerves supplying the uterus and cervix, providing analgesia for gynecologic procedures such as dilation and curettage or early abortion.

renal calculi.definition: Kidney stones are hard mineral concretions that form in the kidneys from dissolved urinary salts; they are commonly composed of calcium salts (e.g., calcium oxalate or calcium phosphate), uric acid, or struvite, and they can cause flank pain, hematuria, and sometimes urinary obstruction.

foreign body ingestion.definition: The ingestion of a nonfood object into the gastrointestinal tract, typically accidentally, which may pass spontaneously but can cause obstruction, mucosal injury, or perforation depending on the object's size, shape, and location.

pickwickian syndrome.definition: A disorder in which severe obesity causes hypoventilation, resulting in chronically elevated daytime arterial carbon dioxide (hypercapnia) and reduced oxygen levels (hypoxemia), usually with sleep-disordered breathing; often associated with headaches, daytime sleepiness, pulmonary hypertension, and polycythemia.

inferior nuchal line.definition: A curved ridge on the external surface of the occipital bone, located inferior to the superior nuchal line; it marks the lower border of the nuchal lines and provides an attachment site for neck muscles.

superior nuchal line.definition: A curved ridge on the external (posterior) aspect of the occipital bone, extending laterally from the midline; it serves as an attachment site for the trapezius muscle and the nuchal ligaments.

external occipital protuberance.definition: A midline prominence on the external surface of the occipital bone at the posterior skull, just above the foramen magnum; it serves as the attachment site for the nuchal ligament and as a landmark for neck muscle origins.

occipitofrontal.definition: Relating to the occipital and frontal regions of the skull; commonly used to describe the occipitofrontalis muscle, which has occipital and frontal bellies connected by the galea aponeurotica and moves the scalp and eyebrows.

occipitomastoid.definition: Relating to the occipital bone and the mastoid portion of the temporal bone; refers to the occipitomastoid suture between them.

occipitoparietal.definition: Relating to the occipital and parietal bones of the skull; the junction where these bones meet (the suture between the occipital and parietal bones).

ectopic acth syndrome.definition: A form of Cushing's syndrome caused by nonpituitary tumors that secrete adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) ectopically, leading to excessive cortisol production by the adrenal glands; commonly associated tumors include small cell lung carcinoma and bronchial carcinoids.

occult blood test.definition: Test used to detect hidden blood in a sample, most often stool, to screen for colorectal cancer or to identify gastrointestinal bleeding; performed by guaiac-based assays or fecal immunochemical tests.

occult carcinoma.definition: A malignant neoplasm (carcinoma) that is not clinically evident or detectable by routine imaging, typically diagnosed only by histology or after presenting as metastatic disease with an unknown primary.

occult fracture.definition: A fracture that is not evident on initial plain radiographs despite clinical suspicion, often requiring repeat imaging or advanced modalities (MRI, CT, or bone scan) to confirm.

ochronosis.definition: Ochronosis is the deposition of pigment produced from homogentisic acid in connective tissues (notably cartilage), causing blue-black discoloration and progressive degenerative arthritis; seen in alkaptonuria.

ocular hypertelorism.definition: A condition in which the distance between the orbits (bony eye sockets) is abnormally wide, leading to widely spaced eyes; often associated with congenital craniofacial anomalies and quantified by an increased interorbital distance.

ocular dysmetria.definition: Ocular dysmetria is the overshooting (hypermetria) or undershooting (hypometria) of eye movements toward a target during rapid eye movements (saccades), reflecting cerebellar dysfunction and resulting in inaccurate fixation or pursuit.

ocular herpes.definition: An eye infection caused by herpes simplex virus (usually HSV-1), affecting the cornea or conjunctiva. Symptoms include redness, pain, tearing, light sensitivity, and possible vision changes; can cause dendritic corneal ulcers and keratitis. If untreated, it can threaten vision. Treated with antiviral medications; recurrence is common.

octreotide.definition: A synthetic analogue of somatostatin that inhibits the secretion of several hormones and peptides (notably growth hormone, insulin, glucagon, and various gastrointestinal hormones); used to treat acromegaly, certain neuroendocrine tumors (e.g., carcinoid syndrome, VIPoma), severe diarrhea/flushing, and to prevent variceal bleeding.

octreotide scan.definition: A nuclear medicine imaging procedure in which radiolabeled octreotide, a somatostatin analogue, is injected and detected with a gamma camera to visualize tumors that express somatostatin receptors (most notably neuroendocrine tumors).

octinoxate.definition: A chemical ultraviolet B sunscreen filter used in many sunscreens and cosmetic products; it absorbs UVB radiation to help protect the skin from sunburn. Also known as octyl methoxycinnamate.

octisalate.definition: An ester (octyl salicylate) formed from salicylic acid and 1-octanol; used in sunscreens as a UVB-absorbing filter and as a skin-conditioning emollient.

octocrylene.definition: An oil-soluble ultraviolet filter used in sunscreens to absorb UVB and UVA radiation; it is photostable and enhances broad-spectrum coverage and water resistance.

octigravida.definition: A woman who has been pregnant eight times (gravida 8), regardless of the outcome of those pregnancies.

octylmethoxycinnamate.definition: A UVB-filtering compound used in many sunscreens; an ester of p-methoxycinnamic acid and 2-ethylhexanol (octinoxate) that absorbs ultraviolet B radiation to protect the skin.

ornithine carbamoyltransferase.definition: An enzyme of the urea cycle that catalyzes the transfer of a carbamoyl group from carbamoyl phosphate to ornithine, forming citrulline; deficiency leads to hyperammonemia and may cause orotic aciduria.

vipoma.definition: A rare pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor that secretes vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), causing profuse watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome), often with dehydration and weight loss.

vipomas.definition: An uncommon pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor that secretes vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), causing profuse watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome).

sandostatin.definition: A brand-name formulation of octreotide; a synthetic somatostatin analog used to treat acromegaly and various hormone-secreting tumors by inhibiting release of growth hormone and other peptides; administered by injection (short-acting and long-acting formulations available).

arteriovenous malformations.definition: Abnormal connections between arteries and veins, usually caused by a birth defect.

convergent strabismus.definition: A form of strabismus in which the eyes deviate inward toward the nose (esotropia) due to imbalance of the extraocular muscles or their innervation; it can be present in infancy or develop later and may be constant or intermittent.

trigonocephaly.definition: A form of craniosynostosis caused by premature fusion of the metopic suture, resulting in a triangular, keeled forehead and a narrow anterior skull.

orbital hypotelorism.definition: A congenital finding in which the orbits are abnormally close together (reduced interorbital distance); often associated with midline facial anomalies such as holoprosencephaly and other midline defects.

ocular melanoma.definition: A malignant neoplasm of melanocytes arising within the eye, most often from the choroid (uveal tract); it is the most common primary intraocular malignant tumor in adults.

neuromuscular disease.definition: Disorders that affect the nerves controlling voluntary muscles or the muscles themselves, including motor neurons, neuromuscular junctions, and skeletal muscle, leading to weakness, fatigue, and impaired movement.

oculocerebral-hypopigmentation syndrome.definition: A rare neurocutaneous disorder characterized by reduced melanin in the skin, hair, and eyes (oculocutaneous hypopigmentation) occurring with congenital or early-onset brain abnormalities and neurological impairment; features may include visual problems with nystagmus or strabismus, developmental delay or intellectual disability, seizures, and structural brain anomalies. The exact criteria vary, and the term is used inconsistently in the literature.

cross syndrome.definition: A brainstem lesion–induced pattern in which cranial nerve findings appear on the same side as the lesion while motor and/or sensory signs occur on the opposite side.

lowe's syndrome.definition: A rare X-linked genetic disorder caused by mutations in the OCRL gene, characterized by congenital cataracts, neurodevelopmental impairment, and proximal renal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi-type).

decreased visual acuity.definition: A reduction in the clarity or sharpness of vision, typically demonstrated by reduced acuity on an eye chart, which can result from refractive error, ocular disease, media opacity (e.g., cataracts), or neural/optic pathway abnormalities.

oculoglandular syndrome.definition: A granulomatous conjunctivitis with ipsilateral regional lymphadenopathy (most often preauricular), classically caused by Bartonella henselae infection (cat-scratch disease).

cat-scratch disease.definition: A zoonotic infection caused by Bartonella henselae transmitted through cat scratches or bites, presenting with tender regional lymphadenopathy near the exposure site, often with fever and malaise; usually self-limited in healthy individuals. Treatment is typically supportive, though antibiotics such as azithromycin may shorten illness in some cases or be used for severe disease.

oculogyric crisis.definition: An acute dystonic reaction featuring sustained, involuntary upward deviation of the eyes due to contraction of the extraocular muscles, commonly caused by dopamine antagonist medications (e.g., antipsychotics or metoclopramide) and treatable with anticholinergic therapy or by stopping the offending drug.

neuroleptic malignant syndrome.definition: A rare, life-threatening reaction to dopamine D2 receptor–antagonist (neuroleptic) medications or to withdrawal of dopaminergic therapy, characterized by rapid onset of severe hyperthermia, generalized “lead-pipe” rigidity, autonomic instability, altered mental status, and markedly elevated creatine kinase from rhabdomyolysis. Management includes stopping the offending drug, aggressive supportive care (cooling, hydration, electrolyte management), and often with agents like dantrolene or bromocriptine if needed.

breast engorgement.definition: Painful swelling, firmness, and tenderness of the breasts caused by engorged milk and increased vascular and lymphatic congestion, typically occurring in the early postpartum period when milk is not being removed efficiently or breastfeeding is interrupted.

hostility.definition: An affective state or personality trait involving persistent anger, antagonism, and a readiness to undermine, devalue, or attack others; commonly expressed as hostile attitudes or aggressive behavior.

ocusert.definition: A sustained-release ocular insert containing pilocarpine placed in the lower conjunctival fornix to deliver pilocarpine gradually over several days for glaucoma management.

odaxetic.definition: Relating to the jaw; pertaining to the jawbone or temporomandibular joint.

oddi's sphincter.definition: A ring of circular smooth muscle surrounding the hepatopancreatic ampulla (major duodenal papilla) that regulates the flow of bile and pancreatic juice into the duodenum and prevents reflux into the biliary and pancreatic ducts.

oesophagectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove all or part of the esophagus, typically for esophageal cancer or severe disease, followed by reconstruction to restore continuity of the digestive tract (most often by pulling the stomach up to connect to the remaining esophagus or by interposing a segment of intestine).

oesophagitis.definition: Inflammation of the esophagus, commonly caused by gastroesophageal reflux, infection, or irritation from medications; presents with painful swallowing and chest discomfort, and is treated by addressing the underlying cause (e.g., acid suppression for reflux, antimicrobials for infection, or stopping offending drugs).

oesophagoscopy.definition: Endoscopic examination of the esophagus using a flexible or rigid endoscope to visualize the esophageal mucosa, obtain biopsies, remove foreign bodies, or perform therapeutic interventions (e.g., dilation or stent placement).

oestriol.definition: A weak estrogen produced mainly by the placenta during pregnancy; one of the three principal estrogens in humans (along with estradiol and estrone) that supports pregnancy and fetal development, and whose maternal levels are used as a marker in prenatal screening.

olanzapine.definition: A second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic used to treat schizophrenia and bipolar disorder; it antagonizes dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors and is associated with weight gain and metabolic side effects.

psychotic disorders.definition: A group of mental disorders characterized by psychosis—loss of contact with reality—manifested by delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thinking (speech), disorganized or catatonic behavior, and negative symptoms; includes schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders, typically onset in late adolescence to early adulthood, and treated with antipsychotic medications, psychotherapy, and social support.

odontogenesis.definition: Teeth development during embryogenesis, arising from reciprocal signaling between the oral epithelium and neural crest–derived mesenchyme to form the tooth germ and eventually the enamel, dentin, pulp, cementum, and supporting structures.

odontoblast.definition: A specialized cell of the dental pulp that synthesizes dentin and has long cellular processes that extend into dentinal tubules; they originate from the dental papilla.

ghost teeth.definition: An informal term in dentistry for a tooth or teeth that appear faint, translucent, or radiolucent on radiographs, giving a ghost-like appearance; may result from extreme hypomineralization, extensive resorption, dentin/enamel defects, or imaging artifacts, and is not a standard diagnostic term.

odontogenesis imperfecta.definition: A hereditary defect in dentin formation that produces discolored (opalescent), brittle teeth prone to rapid wear and fracture; enamel is usually normal but teeth are structurally weak due to faulty dentin.

dentigerous cyst.definition: A developmental odontogenic cyst that surrounds the crown of an unerupted or developing tooth, caused by fluid accumulation between the reduced enamel epithelium and the tooth crown; commonly associated with impacted teeth (especially mandibular third molars) and appears as a well-defined radiolucent lesion. Treatment typically involves surgical enucleation with removal of the involved tooth.

eruption cyst.definition: A soft tissue odontogenic cyst (fluid-filled swelling) over an erupting tooth, presenting as a bluish, painless swelling of the gingiva that usually resolves spontaneously as the tooth erupts; treatment is typically observation unless infection or obstruction occurs.

primordial cyst.definition: An odontogenic cyst that develops in the location where a tooth would have formed but did not; it arises from residual dental lamina epithelium and typically presents radiographically as a radiolucent jaw lesion in the area of a missing or unerupted tooth (most often in the mandible).

odontogenic keratocyst.definition: A developmental odontogenic cyst that originates from dental lamina remnants; it is lined by a parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelium with a palisaded basal layer and a keratin-filled lumen, and it frequently recurs after treatment, typically in the posterior mandible.

gingival cyst of the newborn.definition: Benign developmental cysts on the gingiva of newborns arising from remnants of the dental lamina (rests of Serres); keratin-filled cysts presenting as small white to yellow nodules on the alveolar ridges, usually multiple and self-resolving within weeks.

odontogenic fibroma.definition: A benign odontogenic tumor composed of fibrous connective tissue with variable amounts of inactive odontogenic epithelium, derived from odontogenic ectomesenchyme; often occurs intraosseously in the jaws, may be associated with a tooth, and typically presents radiographically as a radiolucent lesion (unilocular or multilocular) with a good prognosis after surgical excision.

odontogenic fibrosarcoma.definition: A rare malignant odontogenic tumor characterized by fibrosarcoma-like malignant mesenchymal stroma, typically with residual odontogenic epithelium; it may arise de novo or from malignant transformation of an odontogenic fibroma, and it shows local invasiveness with potential for metastasis.

odontogenic myxoma.definition: A benign, locally aggressive odontogenic tumor derived from dental mesenchyme, composed of a myxoid (mucoid) stroma with scattered stellate and spindle-shaped cells; most often located in the mandible and presenting as a multilocular radiolucent lesion with possible tooth displacement; treated by surgical excision with careful margins due to recurrence risk.

compound odontoma.definition: A benign odontogenic tumor (hamartoma) consisting of multiple tooth‑like structures (denticles) formed from enamel, dentin, cementum, and pulp, usually within a fibrous capsule.

complex odontoma.definition: A benign odontogenic tumor consisting of a disorganized mass of dental tissues (enamel, dentin, cementum) with no recognizable tooth-structure, most often located in the posterior mandible and treated with surgical excision.

odontoid vertebra.definition: The second cervical vertebra (C2) of the spine, with a peg-like odontoid process (dens) projecting upward to articulate with the atlas (C1), forming the atlantoaxial joint that enables head rotation.

odontology.definition: The scientific study of the structure, development, and diseases of the teeth and related oral tissues; the field of dental science.

periodontium.definition: A collection of tissues that surround and support the teeth, including the gingiva (gums), periodontal ligament, cementum, and alveolar bone.

odontoperiosteum.definition: The dental periosteum; a specialized periosteal membrane covering the alveolar bone adjacent to teeth, containing fibrous connective tissue with blood vessels and osteogenic cells, and involved in tooth eruption, remodeling of the supporting bone, and periodontal support.

toothache.definition: A pain in or around a tooth, typically resulting from dental problems such as tooth decay, pulpitis or abscess, gum disease, or tooth eruption; the pain may be sharp, throbbing, or persistent and may be provoked by temperature, pressure, or sweet stimuli.

oculus dexter.definition: The Latin term meaning “right eye”; used to denote the right eye in medical documentation and prescriptions (often abbreviated as OD).

oleandrism.definition: A poisoning caused by exposure to the oleander plant (Nerium oleander) and its cardiac glycosides, leading to GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain) and potentially life-threatening cardiac effects such as bradycardia, arrhythmias, and hyperkalemia.

olecranon process.definition: A prominent bony projection on the proximal ulna that forms the posterior point of the elbow; it serves as the insertion site for the triceps brachii tendon and participates in elbow articulation with the humerus.

proximal radioulnar joint.definition: A synovial pivot joint at the proximal forearm where the head of the radius articulates with the radial notch of the ulna; stabilized by the annular ligament (and the interosseous membrane), it allows rotation of the radius around the ulna (pronation and supination) during forearm movement.

olfaction.definition: A sense of smell defined by the detection of volatile odorant molecules by olfactory receptor neurons in the nasal olfactory epithelium, with signals transmitted via the olfactory nerve (CN I) to the brain for odor perception.

olfactory tract.definition: A bundle of myelinated axons from the olfactory bulb (mitral and tufted cell axons) that transmits olfactory information to the primary olfactory cortex, including the piriform and entorhinal cortices (via the lateral and medial olfactory tracts).

olfactory center.definition: An area of the brain responsible for processing olfactory (smell) information, primarily the primary olfactory cortex (piriform cortex) in the temporal lobe, with connections to the entorhinal cortex, amygdala, and orbitofrontal cortex that mediate odor perception, memory, and emotional associations.

olfactory cortex.definition: A region of the cerebral cortex involved in processing olfactory (smell) information; it receives direct input from the olfactory bulb and supports odor perception, discrimination, and odor-associated memory.

olfactory foramen.definition: A small opening in the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone that transmits olfactory nerve fibers (Cranial Nerve I) from the nasal cavity to the olfactory bulb.

olfactory hallucination.definition: A false perception of smell in the absence of an odor source, sometimes described as phantosmia.

olfactory lobe.definition: A brain structure involved in the sense of smell, typically referring to the olfactory bulbs and adjacent olfactory cortex that receive input from olfactory receptor neurons and relay olfactory information to higher brain centers.

olfactory organ.definition: The sensory organ for the sense of smell, located in the nasal cavity; it comprises the olfactory epithelium with olfactory receptor neurons and supporting/basal cells, whose axons form the olfactory nerve to the olfactory bulb.

olfactory receptors.definition: Olfactory receptors are G protein-coupled receptors on the cilia of olfactory sensory neurons in the nasal epithelium; they bind volatile odorant molecules and initiate intracellular signaling that transmits odor information to the brain.

oligemia.definition: A decreased volume of blood in a tissue or region, resulting in reduced tissue perfusion.

oligoclonal banding.definition: A pattern on cerebrospinal fluid electrophoresis showing discrete IgG bands present in CSF but absent in serum, indicating intrathecal IgG synthesis; most commonly associated with multiple sclerosis and other inflammatory central nervous system diseases.

oligodactyly.definition: A congenital condition in which a hand or foot has fewer than the normal number of digits, due to absence or underdevelopment (hypoplasia) of one or more digits.

oligodendroblastoma.definition: A rare pediatric brain tumor composed of oligodendrocyte-like cells with scattered primitive neuroepithelial (neuroblast) elements; historically described as a variant of oligodendroglioma, with management typically including surgical resection followed by adjuvant radiotherapy and/or chemotherapy depending on histology and grade.

oligodendrocyte.definition: A glial cell in the central nervous system that forms and maintains the myelin sheath around several axons, insulating them and increasing the speed of nerve impulse conduction; unlike Schwann cells, it can myelinate multiple axons.

oligodendroglia.definition: A type of glial cell in the central nervous system that forms and maintains the myelin sheath around axons by extending processes that wrap around segments of CNS axons; this myelination speeds nerve conduction and supports axonal integrity.

oligodendroglioma.definition: A type of diffuse glioma arising from oligodendrocytes in the brain; typically slow-growing and often presenting with seizures; histology shows round cells with perinuclear halos ("fried-egg" cells) and is commonly associated with 1p/19q codeletion and IDH mutations; graded as II or III, and treated with surgical resection followed by radiotherapy and chemotherapy.

oligodontia.definition: A developmental condition defined by the congenital absence of six or more permanent teeth (excluding third molars); it represents a severe form of hypodontia and can be nonsyndromic or associated with syndromes such as ectodermal dysplasia.

oligogenic.definition: A pattern of inheritance in which a trait or disorder is influenced by mutations in a small number of genes, with the phenotype resulting from the combined effects of variants at these loci rather than from a single gene.

oligomenorrhea.definition: Infrequent menstrual bleeding defined by cycles longer than about 35 days, resulting in fewer than eight periods per year; often due to hormonal imbalances or systemic conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome, thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia, significant weight loss, or intense physical activity.

oligonucleotide.definition: A short nucleic acid molecule (DNA or RNA), typically 2–100 nucleotides long, used in molecular biology for primers, probes, sequencing, and diagnostic or therapeutic applications.

oligopeptide.definition: A short chain of amino acids linked by peptide bonds, typically containing a small number of residues (roughly 2–20), shorter than a polypeptide; oligopeptides can function as signaling molecules, hormones, or fragments of larger proteins.

oligopnea.definition: Abnormally shallow breathing with decreased tidal volume; a reduced depth of respirations.

oligosaccharide.definition: A carbohydrate consisting of a small number of monosaccharide units (typically 3–10) linked by glycosidic bonds; shorter than a polysaccharide.

oligospermia.definition: A condition characterized by a lower-than-normal sperm count in semen, typically defined as fewer than about 15 million sperm per milliliter, which can impair male fertility.

oligozoospermia.definition: A condition in which there is a low concentration of sperm in semen, typically defined as fewer than 15 million sperm per milliliter, which can contribute to male infertility.

oligotroph.definition: An organism, especially a microorganism, that grows best in very low nutrient concentrations and is adapted to efficiently utilize scarce resources, often with slower growth in nutrient-poor environments.

olisthy.definition: Not a recognized medical term in standard dictionaries; likely a misspelling of listhesis or spondylolisthesis, which denotes forward displacement of one vertebra over another.

olivary body.definition: An oval-shaped gray-matter nucleus in the medulla oblongata of the brainstem; provides climbing-fiber input to the cerebellum and participates in motor coordination and motor learning.

olivopontocerebellar.definition: Relating to degeneration of the inferior olive, the pons, and the cerebellum.

olivopontocerebellar atrophy.definition: A progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by degeneration of neurons in the inferior olivary nucleus, the pons, and the cerebellum, resulting in cerebellar-type ataxia, dysarthria, and other cerebellar signs; historically described as a component neuropathologic pattern of multisystem atrophy.

ollie rs disease.definition: A rare nonhereditary skeletal disorder characterized by multiple enchondromas (benign cartilaginous tumors) within the bones, typically presenting in childhood; it can cause limb deformities and fractures and carries a risk of malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma.

olliers dyschondroplasia.definition: A nonhereditary mosaic skeletal disorder characterized by multiple enchondromas (benign cartilaginous tumors) within the bones—particularly the metaphyses and diaphyses of long bones—causing deformities and fractures and carrying an increased risk of malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma.

olmesartan medoxomil.definition: An antihypertensive prodrug in the angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB) class; it is converted to the active metabolite olmesartan, which selectively blocks the AT1 receptor to produce vasodilation and lower blood pressure.

omalgia.definition: Pain in a bone; bone pain (ostealgia/ostalgia).

omalizumab.definition: A humanized monoclonal antibody that binds IgE, blocking its interaction with FcεRI on mast cells and basophils; used to treat moderate-to-severe allergic asthma and chronic spontaneous urticaria.

omarthritis.definition: That spelling does not correspond to a standard medical term. If you meant a degenerative joint disease caused by loss of articular cartilage, with joint pain, stiffness, and reduced mobility (often in the knees, hips, hands, or spine), a concise definition is: A degenerative joint disease characterized by progressive loss of articular cartilage, subchondral bone changes, and synovial inflammation leading to pain and decreased range of motion. Would you like me to define another term or confirm the intended term?

omental appendix.definition: A small, fat-filled peritoneal projection on the surface of the greater omentum, analogous to the epiploic appendages along the colon.

omentectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove all or part of the omentum, a fatty peritoneal fold that drapes over abdominal organs (usually the greater omentum), often performed to treat or prevent cancer spread or during certain abdominal surgeries.

ommaya reservoir.definition: A surgically implanted subcutaneous reservoir connected to a ventricular catheter that provides access to cerebrospinal fluid for repeated sampling or intraventricular administration of medications (often chemotherapy).

opca.definition: An historical neurodegenerative disorder with progressive degeneration of the olivary nuclei, pons, and cerebellum, causing cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria, and nystagmus; historically used to describe olivopontocerebellar degeneration within related ataxic or multisystem disorders.

omphalitis.definition: An infection of the umbilicus (navel), most often in newborns, characterized by redness, swelling, warmth, tenderness, and discharge around the umbilical stump; can progress to cellulitis or sepsis if untreated; treated with systemic antibiotics.

omphalosite.definition: Not a recognized medical term in standard medical dictionaries. If you meant omphalocele: a congenital defect in which abdominal contents protrude through the umbilicus; if you meant omphalitis: infection of the umbilical stump.

omphalomesenteric.definition: Relating to the yolk sac (omphalos) and the primitive midgut during embryonic development; used to describe structures connecting the yolk sac to the gut, such as the omphalomesenteric (vitelline) duct.

omphalodidymus.definition: Not a recognized medical term; derived from omphalos (navel) and didymus (twin/paired). If encountered, it would imply a duplicated or paired structure at the umbilicus, but it has no established clinical definition.

gastrodidymus.definition: A nonstandard term; etymologically, it would imply a duplicated or paired gastric (stomach) structure, but there is no accepted medical definition or usage in current literature.

vitelline.definition: Relating to the yolk; in embryology, describing the yolk sac and its associated vessels and ducts, including the vitelline duct that connects the yolk sac to the midgut.

tumorigenesis.definition: The process by which normal cells acquire genetic and epigenetic alterations that lead to malignant transformation and the formation and growth of tumors.

sarcomagenesis.definition: The process by which malignant mesenchymal tumors (sarcomas) develop from normal connective tissue cells through genetic and epigenetic alterations that drive malignant transformation.

melanonychia.definition: A darkening of the nails caused by increased melanin production in the nail matrix, typically presenting as a longitudinal pigmented band; most cases are benign or drug/trauma-related, but changes in width, color, or irregularity can signal subungual melanoma and require evaluation.

choroidoretinitis.definition: Inflammation of the choroid and retina, a form of posterior uveitis; may result from infectious or autoimmune processes and presents with decreased vision and retinal/choroidal lesions.

cordotomy.definition: A neurosurgical procedure in which a portion of the spinal cord's pain-conducting pathways (the spinothalamic tract) is lesioned or interrupted to relieve intractable pain, typically performed unilaterally at the anterior spinal cord to block contralateral pain sensation.

ondinescurse.definition: A rare and potentially fatal disorder in which a person may stop breathing, especially at night. Also called congenital central hypoventilation syndrome.

spica.definition: A rigid cast or splint that immobilizes the hip and leg(s) by encircling the torso, used to treat hip fractures or dislocations and after hip surgery.

ovocenter.definition: Not a standard medical term; it would generally refer to the central region of an oocyte, typically the nucleus (germinal vesicle), but the word is not widely used in anatomy or embryology.

oocyst.definition: A thick-walled, spore-like cyst of certain coccidian protozoa (e.g., Isospora, Eimeria, Toxoplasma) that contains invasive sporozoites and is shed in feces; it sporulates in the environment to become infectious.

oocyesis.definition: An archaic term for pregnancy; the state of carrying a developing embryo in the uterus.

oogamy.definition: A form of sexual reproduction in which a large, non-motile female gamete (egg) fuses with a small, motile male gamete (sperm).

onlay.definition: A graft or prosthetic placed on the surface of a structure (eg, the exterior of a tooth or tissue), rather than embedded within it; in dentistry, an indirect restoration that covers one or more cusps of a tooth.

osteodysplasia.definition: A developmental abnormality of bone tissue characterized by defective formation or remodeling, leading to structurally abnormal bones; a general term for bone dysplasia rather than a specific disease.

onycholysis.definition: Separation of the nail plate from the nail bed, usually starting at the distal edge and progressing proximally; commonly caused by trauma, fungal infection (onychomycosis), psoriasis, thyroid disease, or chemical exposure.

onychodystrophy.definition: Abnormal nail growth or degeneration, resulting in changes to the nail plate’s shape, thickness, texture, or color (nail dystrophy); can arise from trauma, infection, or systemic diseases.

onychogryphosis.definition: A chronic nail deformity in which the nail plate becomes thickened and overgrown with pronounced curvature, often resembling a ram's horn; commonly affects the great toenail and is associated with trauma, vascular disease, or fungal infection, with management including careful debridement and, if needed, surgical nail removal.

onychopathology.definition: The study and pathology of nail diseases; abnormalities and disorders affecting the fingernails and toenails.

onychia.definition: Inflammation of the nail apparatus (primarily the nail matrix and nail bed) that leads to nail plate discoloration, deformity, or loss; can be acute (often infectious) or chronic.

onychotillomania.definition: A compulsive tendency to pick at the nails and surrounding cuticles, often leading to nail damage, nail bed injury, or infection; a type of body-focused repetitive behavior related to trichotillomania and dermatillomania.

onychotomy.definition: An incision into the nail, typically through the nail plate or nail bed, made to relieve pressure, drain a subungual hematoma, or facilitate exposure of the nail bed.

onychohelcosis.definition: No widely recognized definition exists for this term in standard medical references; it may be a misspelling or an obscure/obsolete term. If you meant onychomycosis (fungal nail infection), it is defined as a fungal infection of the nails, usually causing discoloration, thickening, and detachment of the nail from the nail bed. If you have context or a source, I can help identify the intended term.

omohyoid.definition: A neck infrahyoid (strap) muscle consisting of superior and inferior bellies joined by an intermediate tendon; it depresses the hyoid bone and larynx during swallowing and speaking.

pegaspargase.definition: A PEGylated form of the enzyme asparaginase used in the treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia; it depletes circulating asparagine by hydrolyzing it to aspartate and ammonia, thereby starving leukemic cells that require extracellular asparagine; pegylation prolongs the enzyme's half-life and reduces immunogenicity.

oncaspar.definition: A pegylated form of L-asparaginase used in chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia; it depletes circulating asparagine by hydrolyzing it to aspartic acid and ammonia, thereby inhibiting protein synthesis in leukemic cells; the PEG moiety prolongs half-life and reduces immunogenicity.

oogonium.definition: A primitive diploid germ cell of the ovary that gives rise to primary oocytes during oogenesis; in humans, oogonia proliferate during fetal life and then enter meiosis to become primary oocytes.

primary oocyte.definition: Diploid ovarian germ cell formed from an oogonium; after DNA replication it is arrested in prophase I of meiosis and, upon ovulation, completes the first meiotic division to form a secondary oocyte and a first polar body (meiosis II proceeds only after fertilization).

secondary oocyte.definition: A haploid female gamete produced from a primary oocyte after completion of meiosis I during oogenesis; it is released in ovulation and, upon fertilization, completes meiosis II to become a mature ovum (with the extrusion of a second polar body) and is arrested at metaphase II until fertilization.

ova.definition: The female gametes; mature haploid egg cells produced by oogenesis in the ovaries, released during ovulation; fertilization by a sperm forms a zygote.

zona pellucida.definition: A glycoprotein-rich extracellular layer that surrounds mammalian oocytes and early embryos; produced by the oocyte and surrounding follicle cells, it mediates sperm binding and the acrosome reaction and helps prevent polyspermy after fertilization.

primary follicle.definition: An early stage of an ovarian follicle in which the oocyte enlarges and is surrounded by a layer (later multiple layers) of cuboidal granulosa cells; the zona pellucida forms around the oocyte and the theca layer begins to develop.

growing follicle.definition: A developing ovarian follicle that is maturing during the follicular phase, increasing in size under FSH stimulation as the oocyte and surrounding granulosa and theca cells proliferate, progressing toward ovulation.

mature follicle.definition: A mature ovarian follicle (Graafian follicle) is a fully developed ovarian follicle, about 18–25 mm in diameter, containing a mature oocyte and a fluid-filled antrum; it ruptures at ovulation to release the oocyte and becomes the corpus luteum.

polar body.definition: A small haploid cell produced during oogenesis as a byproduct of meiosis; extruded from the oocyte with minimal cytoplasm and usually degenerates, not participating in fertilization. It is formed as the first polar body after meiosis I and the second polar body after meiosis II.

first polar body.definition: A small haploid cell produced during the first meiotic division of oogenesis, formed along with the secondary oocyte; it contains little cytoplasm and usually degenerates, and is not involved in fertilization.

second polar body.definition: A small haploid cell produced during the second meiotic division of oogenesis; it is extruded from the oocyte and discarded, containing the chromosomes not retained by the ovum.

sporozoan.definition: An obsolete grouping of protozoan parasites (now largely classified as Apicomplexa) that are obligate intracellular parasites and produce sporozoites as part of their life cycles.

parasite.definition: An animal or plant that lives off another animal or plant.

sporozoites.definition: The infectious, motile stage of certain Apicomplexan parasites (e.g., Plasmodium, Toxoplasma) formed in the vector; transmitted to a vertebrate host where it invades host cells (such as hepatocytes in malaria) and initiates infection.

opening wedge osteotomy.definition: An osteotomy in which a wedge-shaped gap is opened on one side of a bone to correct angular deformity or realign a joint; the gap is stabilized with internal fixation and may be filled with bone graft or substitute.

osteotomy.definition: An operation in which bone is cut to change its alignment or shorten or lengthen it.

tendon transfer.definition: A surgical procedure in which a functional tendon is detached from its original insertion and reattached at a new location to restore or improve movement lost due to nerve injury, muscle weakness, or deformity.

salpinx.definition: The fallopian tube (uterine tube); a slender canal that transports ovulated eggs from the ovary to the uterus, typically lined with ciliated epithelium and smooth muscle, and usually the site of fertilization.

ovariectomy.definition: Surgical removal of one or both ovaries.

oophoroma.definition: A tumor of the ovary; a neoplasm arising from ovarian tissue, which may be benign or malignant.

oophorocytosis.definition: Not a recognized medical term; if used, it would suggest an abnormal increase in ovarian cells (likely oocytes) within the ovary, but there is no standardized definition or established clinical significance in medical literature.

oophorosalpingectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove an ovary together with its accompanying fallopian tube (unilateral or bilateral).

oophorosalpingitis.definition: Inflammation of the ovary and fallopian tube, typically part of pelvic inflammatory disease, caused by ascending infection; characterized by pelvic pain and adnexal tenderness, with potential for infertility or ectopic pregnancy due to tubal scarring.

open-drop anesthesia.definition: A historical method of inhalational general anesthesia in which a volatile anesthetic liquid (often ether) is dripped onto an absorbent material in the patient’s mask, allowing vapors to be inhaled from an open system with no sealed circuit or precise vapor concentration control.

ether.definition: A colorless, volatile, highly flammable liquid historically used as a general inhalational anesthetic; it induces anesthesia when inhaled but is largely obsolete due to flammability and risks of cardiac and respiratory complications.

chloroform.definition: A volatile, colorless, sweet-smelling organochlorine liquid formerly used as a general anesthetic; inhalation induces anesthesia but carries serious risks of respiratory depression, cardiac arrhythmias, liver toxicity, and death.

open-heart surgery.definition: A surgical procedure to repair or replace structures of the heart (most commonly valves or coronary arteries) via a chest opening (usually a median sternotomy), with the patient connected to a heart-lung machine to temporarily take over circulation and keep the heart still during the operation.

open fracture.definition: A fracture in which the broken bone communicates with the external environment through an open skin wound, exposing bone and surrounding tissues (also called a compound fracture).

open wound.definition: A break in the skin or mucous membrane with exposure of underlying tissues, typically caused by trauma, that may bleed and has a risk of infection; healing may occur with primary closure or by secondary intention.

operative field.definition: The region of tissue exposed and prepared for a surgical procedure—the site where incisions are made and the operation is performed, kept sterile and protected from contamination.

operating microscope.definition: An optical instrument that provides magnified, stereoscopic, well-illuminated visualization of the surgical field to enable precise microsurgical dissection; it offers adjustable magnification and a sterile, stable setup.

operon.definition: A cluster of genes in prokaryotes that are transcribed together from a single promoter into a polycistronic mRNA and regulated by an operator, allowing coordinated expression of genes involved in a common pathway.

operator gene.definition: A regulatory DNA sequence in a prokaryotic operon that binds a repressor to block RNA polymerase and regulate transcription of the operon's downstream genes.

regulator gene.definition: A gene that encodes a product—typically a transcription factor or regulatory RNA—that modulates the expression of other genes by activating or repressing transcription or altering RNA stability/translation.

opening of ileocecal valve.definition: An opening between the ileum and the cecum guarded by the ileocecal valve, acting as a sphincter to regulate the passage of intestinal contents from the ileum into the cecum and to prevent reflux of colonic contents into the ileum.

ophidiophobia.definition: A persistent, irrational fear of snakes (a specific phobia) characterized by avoidance of snakes and marked anxiety or panic when exposed to snakes or reminders of snakes.

ophidia.definition: An historical zoological term for snakes; an outdated taxonomic group that encompassed snakes, now classified as Serpentes within Squamata.

insula.definition: A region of the cerebral cortex located deep within the lateral sulcus, comprising anterior, middle, and posterior parts; it processes interoceptive signals, emotion, autonomic regulation, and taste.

allophthalmia.definition: Not a standard medical term; there is no recognized condition named allophthalmia. It may be a misspelling or confusion with anophthalmia (congenital absence of one or both eyes) or microphthalmia (an abnormally small eye).

echinophthalmia.definition: An obsolete or nonstandard term describing inflammatory disease of the eye (ophthalmia), historically thought to involve irregular or nodular surface changes; not used in contemporary medical practice.

polemophthalmia.definition: An ophthalmic inflammatory condition; inflammation of the eye, typically conjunctival infection with discharge.

gonococcal infection.definition: A sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae, typically affecting mucous membranes of the genitourinary tract, rectum, or pharynx. Many infections are asymptomatic; when symptoms occur, they may include urethral or vaginal discharge and dysuria. If untreated, it can lead to pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and disseminated gonococcal infection. Diagnosis is by nucleic acid amplification testing or culture; treatment follows current antibiotic guidelines.

ophthalmic herpes zoster.definition: Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in the ophthalmic (V1) division of the trigeminal nerve, causing shingles with a vesicular rash on the forehead and around the eye and commonly leading to ocular involvement (conjunctivitis, keratitis, uveitis) that can threaten vision; urgent antiviral therapy is recommended.

ophthalmic nerve.definition: A division of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V1) that is purely sensory; it traverses the superior orbital fissure and supplies sensation to the forehead, eyelids, cornea, conjunctiva, nasal mucosa, and adjacent orbital structures, with major branches including the frontal, nasociliary, and lacrimal nerves.

ophthalmic vein.definition: A vein that drains venous blood from the eye and orbital contents; the principal channel is the superior ophthalmic vein, which drains into the cavernous sinus, with the inferior ophthalmic vein draining the lower orbit into the cavernous sinus or pterygoid venous plexus.

superior ophthalmic vein.definition: A vein draining blood from the orbit and eyeball, coursing from the superomedial orbit through the superior orbital fissure to drain into the cavernous sinus; it receives tributaries from the supraorbital and supratrochlear regions and communicates with facial veins.

inferior ophthalmic vein.definition: A venous vessel draining the inferior aspect of the orbit; it collects blood from the floor of the orbit and lower eyelid and typically drains into the cavernous sinus (often via the inferior orbital fissure or via the superior ophthalmic vein), with possible communications to the pterygoid plexus or facial venous system.

ophthalmic vesicle.definition: An early embryonic outpocketing of the forebrain (optic/ophthalmic vesicle) that develops into the retina and other ocular structures; it induces lens formation and later invaginates to form the optic cup.

optic vesicle.definition: Paired lateral outgrowths of the forebrain neural tube that give rise to the retina; they invaginate to form the optic cup and contribute to the development of the optic nerve.

ophthalmodynamometer.definition: A hand-held instrument that applies calibrated external pressure to the eyeball to temporarily occlude or modulate the central retinal artery, used to estimate intraocular pressure and assess retinal arterial pressure.

ophthalmodynia.definition: A symptom consisting of pain in or around the eye (ocular pain).

opisthognathism.definition: A jaw relation in which the mandible is positioned posteriorly relative to the maxilla (mandibular retrusion), often contributing to a convex facial profile.

opisthoporeia.definition: Backward bending of the spine (hyperextension) due to tonic or dystonic muscle contractions, yielding a rigid, backward-arched posture.

intrahepatic bile duct.definition: Bile ducts located within the liver that collect bile produced by hepatocytes from the canaliculi and drain it into the left and right hepatic ducts, which then join to form the common hepatic duct.

thiamine deficiency.definition: A deficiency of thiamine (vitamin B1) caused by inadequate intake, malabsorption, or increased requirements, leading to beriberi (dry or wet) and Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome.

cranial polyneuropathy.definition: Dysfunction or degeneration of multiple cranial nerves resulting in simultaneous or sequential cranial nerve palsies (e.g., ophthalmoplegia, facial weakness, bulbar symptoms) often due to inflammatory, infectious, autoimmune, toxic, metabolic, or demyelinating processes.

opportunistic infection.definition: An infection that you get because you are already weak.

opportunistic pathogen.definition: An organism that ordinarily does not cause disease in a healthy host but can cause infection when the host's immune defenses are impaired or when it is introduced into normally sterile sites.

pancreatic secretions.definition: Exocrine pancreatic juice: a bicarbonate‑rich fluid containing digestive enzymes (amylase, lipase, proteases such as trypsin/chymotrypsin) secreted into the duodenum; neutralizes gastric acid and provides optimal pH for digestion. Secretion is stimulated by secretin and cholecystokinin (and vagal input).

biliary secretions.definition: Digestive fluid produced by the liver and secreted into the biliary tract; composed of bile acids (bile salts), bilirubin, cholesterol, phospholipids, and electrolytes; functions to emulsify fats and aid digestion; stored in the gallbladder and released into the duodenum via the common bile duct in response to meals.

opium tincture.definition: An alcoholic tincture of opium (Laudanum) historically used as a potent opioid analgesic and antidiarrheal; produced by dissolving opium in ethanol to yield a solution containing multiple opium alkaloids, chiefly morphine.

opium alkaloids.definition: A group of naturally occurring, nitrogen-containing alkaloids derived from the opium poppy (Papaver somniferum) that act as agonists at opioid receptors to produce analgesia and other narcotic effects; the principal members are morphine, codeine, and thebaine, with others such as noscapine and papaverine having different pharmacologic actions.

papaverine.definition: An alkaloid vasodilator derived from the opium poppy; it inhibits phosphodiesterase enzymes, increases cyclic AMP and cyclic GMP, and relaxes smooth muscle to dilate vessels; used to treat vasospasm in various vascular beds and as an antispasmodic for smooth muscle.

papaverine hydrochloride.definition: A salt form of the opium-derived alkaloid papaverine; a non-narcotic vasodilator and smooth-muscle relaxant that inhibits phosphodiesterase, increasing cAMP/cGMP levels to relax vascular and other smooth muscles. Used to relieve vasospasm of vessels and smooth-muscle spasm in the gastrointestinal, biliary, and urinary tracts.

opioid receptor.definition: A G protein–coupled receptor that binds endogenous opioid peptides and exogenous opioids, mediating analgesia and various other effects; major subtypes include μ (mu), δ (delta), κ (kappa), and nociceptin receptors.

mu receptor.definition: A G protein–coupled opioid receptor that binds endogenous opioids and exogenous opioids, mediating analgesia and other opioid effects (euphoria, respiratory depression) via Gi/o signaling.

kappa receptor.definition: A G protein–coupled receptor of the opioid receptor family that preferentially binds kappa opioid ligands (including endogenous dynorphins); activation produces analgesia (notably spinal), diuresis, and dysphoria, via Gi/Go signaling that inhibits adenylyl cyclase and modulates ion channels.

delta receptor.definition: One of the three classical opioid receptors; a G protein–coupled receptor that binds endogenous enkephalins and certain opioids. Activation yields analgesia and modulates mood and autonomic function by inhibiting adenylyl cyclase and decreasing neuronal excitability; distributed in brain and peripheral tissues.

dynorphins.definition: A class of endogenous opioid peptides derived from prodynorphin that preferentially activate κ-opioid receptors and modulate pain signaling, stress responses, and mood; includes dynorphin A and dynorphin B.

opiate antagonist.definition: A drug that blocks opioid receptors (primarily μ receptors), preventing or reversing the effects of opioid agonists; used to treat opioid overdose and in opioid dependence management, and can precipitate withdrawal in dependent individuals.

opsonin.definition: A molecule that coats a pathogen to enhance its recognition and ingestion by phagocytes; opsonins include antibodies (e.g., IgG) and complement fragment (e.g., C3b) that bind to phagocyte receptors.

opsonization.definition: A process in which pathogens are coated with opsonins (e.g., IgG antibodies and complement fragment C3b), tagging them for recognition by phagocyte receptors (Fc and complement receptors) and thereby enhancing phagocytosis and clearance.

opsonize.definition: To mark a pathogen for ingestion and destruction by phagocytes by binding opsonins (such as antibodies like IgG or complement components like C3b) to its surface, thereby enhancing recognition by Fc and complement receptors on phagocytes.

fifth metacarpal.definition: One of the five metacarpal bones of the hand; the bone of the little finger that extends from the distal carpal row to the proximal phalanx of the little finger. Its base articulates with the hamate and capitate, and its head with the proximal phalanx; neck fractures are a common injury (boxer's fracture).

hook of the hamate.definition: Hook-shaped projection of the hamate bone on the palmar aspect of the wrist; forms part of the boundary of Guyon's canal and acts as a pulley for the flexor tendons of the little finger.

opponens digiti minimi.definition: A hypothenar intrinsic hand muscle that opposes the little finger by drawing the fifth metacarpal anteriorly toward the palm; innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
