saline solution.definition: A sterile isotonic solution of sodium chloride in water, typically 0.9% w/v NaCl (normal saline), with osmolarity similar to body fluids; used for intravenous fluid therapy, wound irrigation, and as a diluent for medications.

salt solution.definition: A solution in which salt (sodium chloride) is dissolved in water; commonly used as saline for hydration (intravenous fluids), wound irrigation, and cleansing.

paraffin.definition: A white, waxy hydrocarbon mixture derived from petroleum that is solid at room temperature and melts when heated; in medicine, it is used as an embedding medium for tissue specimens in histology and in therapeutic paraffin bath treatments to soften skin.

shortwave diathermy.definition: A physiotherapy modality that uses shortwave radiofrequency energy (typically 27.12 MHz) to produce deep heating of tissues, delivered via capacitive or inductive applicators to increase blood flow, tissue extensibility, and pain relief.

microwave diathermy.definition: A physical therapy modality that uses microwave‑frequency electromagnetic energy to heat body tissues, producing deep tissue heating for therapeutic effects such as pain relief and increased tissue extensibility.

electrical stimulation.definition: The application of controlled electrical impulses to nerves or muscles to evoke physiological responses for diagnostic, therapeutic, or rehabilitative purposes (e.g., pain relief, muscle activation, or tissue healing).

massage.definition: A manual therapy involving the manipulation of soft tissues (muscle, fascia, tendons, and ligaments) by hands or mechanical devices to promote relaxation, reduce muscle tension, improve circulation and range of motion, and relieve pain.

therapeutic exercises.definition: A clinician-prescribed regimen of physical activities designed to restore movement, strength, endurance, and function after illness or injury; it includes range-of-motion and stretching, strengthening, balance and proprioception training, and aerobic conditioning, and is tailored and progressed to reduce pain and disability.

physiotherapy.definition: Physiotherapy is a health-care discipline that uses exercise, manual therapy, education, and physical modalities to restore movement and function, relieve pain, and prevent disability after injury or illness.

physocele.definition: Not a recognized medical term in standard dictionaries; please check spelling or provide context for the intended condition. If you meant related terms, I can define those (e.g., hydrocele, pyocele, or physis-related terms).

physocephaly.definition: Not a recognized medical term; no established definition in standard medical references. If you meant plagiocephaly or another cephalic condition, I can provide definitions for those.

physometra.definition: Gas within the uterus; the presence of air in the uterine cavity, typically detected on imaging and may result from recent uterine instrumentation or abortion, uterine rupture, infection with gas-forming organisms, or a fistulous connection with the bowel.

physiognomy.definition: The practice of inferring a person’s character or personality from facial features; historically linked to discredited theories and, in medicine, to describing facial signs of disease, but not scientifically reliable.

ultrasonic heat.definition: Heat produced in tissues when exposed to high-frequency ultrasound energy, due to absorption of acoustic energy and its conversion to thermal energy; used therapeutically (therapeutic ultrasound) to raise tissue temperature, improve blood flow, and increase tissue extensibility.

salicylate.definition: A salt or ester of salicylic acid; a class of compounds derived from salicylic acid.

cholinesterase.definition: An enzyme that hydrolyzes acetylcholine and other choline esters, thereby terminating transmission at cholinergic synapses; there are two main forms, one at neural/neuromuscular junctions and one in plasma.

depolarizing.definition: Causing depolarization of a cell membrane; making the interior less negative (more positive) and increasing excitability by increasing inward positive current, often through sodium influx; in pharmacology, a depolarizing agent briefly activates receptors to trigger an action potential.

blocking.definition: An obstruction or interruption of a normal physiological pathway or signal; in medicine, it commonly refers to the deliberate stoppage of nerve conduction (as in a nerve block) to produce anesthesia or analgesia, or to other interruptions of conduction or flow.

phytanic acid storage disease.definition: An inherited peroxisomal metabolic disorder in which phytanic acid cannot be adequately oxidized, leading to accumulation of phytanic acid in plasma and tissues; most commonly referred to as Refsum disease, and typically presenting with retinitis pigmentosa, neuropathy/ataxia, deafness, and ichthyosis; managed by dietary restriction of phytanic acid.

refsum syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal recessive peroxisomal metabolic disorder caused by deficiency of phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase (impaired phytanic acid alpha-oxidation) leading to accumulation of phytanic acid; clinical features include retinitis pigmentosa, cerebellar ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, and anosmia, with treatment focusing on dietary restriction of phytanic acid and plasmapheresis in some cases.

phytohemagglutinin.definition: A plant lectin (glycoprotein) from beans that binds specific carbohydrate residues on cell surfaces, causes red blood cell agglutination, and acts as a mitogen to stimulate lymphocyte proliferation (particularly T cells); raw beans contain it and cooking denatures the toxin.

phytolectin.definition: A carbohydrate-binding protein produced by plants that binds specific sugars on cell surfaces and can cause agglutination of cells; commonly found in seeds and legumes; can be an anti-nutritional factor and may be toxic in raw form; heat denatures it and inactivates it.

pia-arachnoid.definition: Leptomeninges consisting of the pia mater and arachnoid mater; these inner meninges envelop the brain and spinal cord and form the subarachnoid space, which contains cerebrospinal fluid.

pigmented villonodular synovitis.definition: A benign but locally aggressive proliferative disorder of the synovium and tendon sheaths characterized by pigmented, hemosiderin-laden villous and nodular synovial proliferation; presents with joint swelling and pain, most often in the knee; occurs in localized or diffuse forms; treated with surgical synovectomy (with possible adjuvant radiotherapy in diffuse disease).

pigeon chest.definition: A chest wall deformity in which the sternum and adjacent costal cartilages protrude outward, giving a birdlike (pigeon) appearance; usually noticed in childhood or adolescence and may be associated with connective tissue disorders. Most cases are cosmetic, but severe deformities can cause respiratory or functional symptoms. Management ranges from observation in mild cases to bracing in skeletally immature patients and surgical correction for significant deformities.

pigeon breeder lung.definition: A form of hypersensitivity pneumonitis (extrinsic allergic alveolitis) caused by inhalation of avian proteins from pigeons (from droppings, feathers, and secretions), leading to inflammatory lung disease that can cause cough and dyspnea; chronic exposure may progress to fibrosis.

bird breeder lung.definition: A hypersensitivity pneumonitis caused by inhalation of avian antigens (feathers, droppings, or secretions) from birds, commonly seen in bird breeders; characterized by cough and dyspnea after exposure and often improves with antigen avoidance, though acute, subacute, or chronic forms with interstitial lung involvement can occur.

hen worker lung.definition: A hypersensitivity pneumonitis from inhaled avian antigens encountered by poultry workers (eg, hen dander, droppings, and feathers). Acute exposure causes flu‑like symptoms (fever, cough, dyspnea) that improve with antigen avoidance; chronic exposure can lead to progressive interstitial lung disease, managed with exposure avoidance and, for inflammatory episodes, corticosteroids.

pilonidal fistula.definition: A chronic fistulous tract that extends from a pilonidal sinus to the skin surface—usually in the sacrococcygeal region—often containing hair and inflammatory or purulent material and draining, frequently requiring surgical management.

pilonidal cystectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove a pilonidal cyst and any associated sinus tracts in the sacrococcygeal region, typically performed to treat pilonidal disease; the wound may be closed primarily or left to heal by secondary intention.

piles.definition: A condition of swollen veins in the lower rectum and anus (hemorrhoids), which may be internal or external and can cause bleeding, itching, and discomfort.

herpangina.definition: An acute, self-limited viral illness caused by Coxsackie A viruses, presenting with fever, sore throat, and painful vesicular or ulcerative lesions on the posterior oropharynx (soft palate, uvula, and tonsillar pillars); most common in children, with transmission via fecal-oral or oral-oral routes and typically lasting 3–7 days.

piedra.definition: Chronic superficial fungal infection of hair shafts characterized by the formation of firm nodules along the hair; pale nodules are caused by Trichosporon spp and dark nodules by Piedraia hortae.

piedra bortae.definition: A chronic superficial fungal infection of hair shafts caused by the fungus Piedraia hortae, characterized by hard, dark pigmented nodules encasing hair shafts (most often on scalp hair) and occurring in tropical climates; treatment typically involves shaving the affected hair and antifungal therapy.

black piedra.definition: A superficial fungal infection of hair shafts caused by Piedraia hortae, characterized by hard, black pigmented nodules along the hair shaft (usually on scalp or facial hair) with hair breakage; treated by removing infected hairs and using topical or systemic antifungal therapy.

white piedra.definition: A superficial fungal infection of hair shafts caused by Trichosporon species (formerly Trichosporon beigelii), characterized by soft white-to-pale nodules encasing hair shafts (often on the scalp, beard, or mustache); the hair shaft remains intact and nodules may be easily removed. Treatment includes removing the affected hair and using topical antifungal agents (e.g., selenium sulfide or ketoconazole), with systemic antifungals for extensive or persistent cases.

trichosporon beigelii.definition: An etiologic fungus of the genus Trichosporon that causes white piedra, a superficial infection of hair shafts with white to pale nodules encasing the hair.

pierre robin syndrome.definition: A congenital condition typically characterized by micrognathia (small mandible) with glossoptosis (posterior displacement of the tongue), often resulting in airway obstruction and commonly associated with a cleft palate; it can occur in isolation or as part of a syndrome due to mandibular hypoplasia causing airway compromise.

piedmont fracture.definition: Not a widely recognized term in standard medical references. If referring to a distal tibial plafond fracture (an ankle-involving fracture of the distal tibia), it is a fracture of the distal tibia that extends into the ankle joint, typically from high-energy trauma, often with articular surface disruption and possible comminution; management frequently requires surgical fixation.

venous congestion.definition: An increase in venous pressure with pooling of blood in the venous system of a tissue or organ due to impaired outflow, leading to venous engorgement and interstitial edema; commonly caused by heart failure, venous obstruction, or valvular incompetence.

denticulate ligament.definition: A pair of triangular extensions of the pia mater that project laterally from the spinal cord and attach to the arachnoid and dura mater, stabilizing the cord within the dural sac by limiting lateral movement.

pigeon-toed.definition: An in-toeing condition in which the feet point inward toward the midline during standing or walking; common in young children and frequently resolves with growth.

pilonidal.definition: Relating to a hair-containing sinus or cyst in the sacrococcygeal region (near the tailbone), typically arising when hair penetrates the skin and causes chronic inflammation, infection, and drainage through a sinus tract.

dermoid.definition: An ectoderm-derived lesion containing skin-like elements (hair, sebaceous and sweat glands), usually presenting as a benign cyst lined by keratinizing squamous epithelium.

pilosebaceous.definition: Relating to a hair follicle and its sebaceous gland; the pilosebaceous unit.

pilus.definition: A hair-like, extracellular appendage on many bacteria that mediates attachment to surfaces or other cells; a conjugative (sex) pilus in some species transfers DNA between bacterial cells.

sebum.definition: An oily secretion produced by sebaceous glands in the skin, rich in lipids such as triglycerides, wax esters, squalene, and free fatty acids, that lubricates and waterproofs hair and skin, helps maintain the skin barrier, and has antimicrobial properties.

pimeloma.definition: A malignant proliferation of clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow, typically presenting with bone pain, anemia, hypercalcemia, renal dysfunction, and lytic bone lesions; when widespread, it is called multiple myeloma.

pimelopterygium.definition: Not found in standard medical dictionaries; likely a misspelling or an extremely rare/obsolete term. If you can share the context (anatomical area or condition), I can help locate a close match or provide a definition for a related term.

pimelorrhea.definition:
Not a recognized medical term; no standard definition in reputable medical sources. If you meant:
- pyorrhea (pyorrhoea): pus discharge from a dental pocket or gingival inflammation (historically used for periodontal disease).
- urethral or penile discharge: drainage from the urethra due to infection or inflammation.

If you have a different spelling, please share it and I’ll look it up.

tourette.definition: When you make unusual movements or sounds.

qt.definition: A measurement on an electrocardiogram that spans from the start of the Q wave to the end of the T wave, reflecting the duration of ventricular depolarization and repolarization; commonly corrected for heart rate.

tardive.definition: Late-appearing; developing after prolonged exposure to a drug or long-term treatment, especially referring to tardive dyskinesia, a late-onset movement disorder associated with chronic dopamine receptor–blocking therapy.

pimple.definition: A small inflamed skin lesion caused by blockage of a hair follicle and its oil gland, commonly seen in acne; may be a red, raised papule or a pus-filled pustule.

pin.definition: A slender metal fastener used in orthopedic procedures to hold bone fragments in proper alignment during healing; often a percutaneously inserted Kirschner wire (K-wire) or similar pin.

pinprick.definition: A small puncture wound made by a pin or needle, used to test sharp-pain sensation in a neurological examination.

carateum.definition: A spirochete; the etiologic agent of pinta, a chronic contagious treponemal skin infection presenting with hypopigmented patches.

pioglitazone.definition: An oral thiazolidinedione antidiabetic agent that activates PPAR-γ to improve insulin sensitivity in type 2 diabetes; adverse effects include weight gain, edema, risk of heart failure, hepatotoxicity, and possible bladder cancer with long-term use; liver function monitoring advised and use is discouraged in active liver disease or symptomatic heart failure.

piperacillin.definition: A broad-spectrum penicillin antibiotic (an ureidopenicillin) that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins; used to treat a wide range of infections caused by susceptible bacteria and often combined with a beta-lactamase inhibitor (eg, tazobactam) to extend activity against beta-lactamase–producing organisms.

pipecuronium.definition: A long-acting, nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent (aminosteroid) used to produce skeletal muscle paralysis during general anesthesia; it acts as a competitive antagonist at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, with onset in a few minutes and a duration of action of roughly 1–2 hours.

pipette.definition: A laboratory instrument used to measure and transfer precise volumes of liquid, typically a slender tube or disposable tip with calibrated markings; micropipettes enable very small volume transfers.

pipracil.definition: A broad-spectrum parenteral penicillin antibiotic (carboxypenicillin) that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis; active against many Gram-negative bacteria including Pseudomonas aeruginosa and various Gram-positive cocci; used for serious infections caused by susceptible organisms and usually given by intravenous administration.

piriform.definition: Pear-shaped; having the shape of a pear; used in anatomy to describe structures that are wider at one end and taper toward the other.

piriformis.definition: A small flat muscle in the gluteal region that originates from the anterior surface of the sacrum and inserts on the superior border of the greater trochanter of the femur; it laterally rotates the thigh and, when the hip is flexed, abducts it. It is innervated by the ventral rami of the sacral nerves (L5–S2). Clinically, it can irritate or compress the sciatic nerve, causing buttock or leg pain.

pirogoff.definition: A historical ankle-level amputation (Pirogoff operation) in which the talus is removed and the calcaneus is cut, rotated to lie against the distal tibia, and fused to it to form a weight-bearing stump with the heel pad, a modification of Syme's amputation.

pirquet.definition: A historical cutaneous tuberculin test in which a small amount of tuberculin is applied to the skin and the surface is lightly scratched (scarified) to promote uptake; the site is read after about 48–72 hours for a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction indicative of prior exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It has largely been replaced by standardized intradermal tests such as the Mantoux test.

nitidus.definition: Latin adjective meaning "shiny" or "bright"; used in medical descriptions to denote a glossy or polished appearance and is not itself a disease name.

pinguecula.definition: A small, yellowish, benign thickening of the bulbar conjunctiva near the cornea (usually on the nasal side), caused by degenerative changes from UV exposure; typically asymptomatic and not cancerous.

pinealectomy.definition: A surgical removal of the pineal gland (pineal body), typically performed to treat pineal region tumors; removal abolishes melatonin production and can disrupt circadian rhythms.

pinealoma.definition: A tumor of the pineal gland, located in the pineal region of the brain; most often a germ cell tumor (e.g., germinoma), and it can cause obstructive hydrocephalus and Parinaud syndrome.

lichen.definition: A composite organism formed by a symbiotic association of a fungus (the mycobiont) with a photosynthetic partner (usually green algae or cyanobacteria), producing a thallus that grows on surfaces such as rocks, bark, or soil.

pinocytosis.definition: A form of endocytosis in which the cell ingests extracellular fluid and dissolved solutes by forming small vesicles from the plasma membrane; a non-specific uptake often referred to as "cell drinking" (distinct from phagocytosis).

pinocyte.definition: A cell that performs pinocytosis, taking up extracellular fluid and dissolved solutes by inward folding of the cell membrane to form pinocytic vesicles.

piskacek's sign.definition: An early sign of pregnancy characterized by a palpable lateral bulge with softening and enlargement of the uterus at the site of implantation (typically near the uterine cornua), usually detectable around 6 weeks gestation.

pisohamate ligament.definition: A fibrous band extending from the pisiform to the hook of the hamate in the wrist; forms part of the boundary of the canal of Guyon and helps create the space through which the ulnar nerve and artery pass.

pisometacarpal ligament.definition: A ligament that extends from the pisiform bone to the base of the fifth metacarpal on the palmar side of the hand, helping stabilize the pisiform against the metacarpal base and contributing to ulnar-side carpal stability.

pit and fissure cavity.definition: A dental caries lesion that forms in the pits and fissures of tooth enamel (usually on occlusal surfaces), often starting in enamel and potentially extending into dentin, and commonly managed with fissure sealants or direct restorations.

pit and fissure sealant.definition: A thin layer of plastic painted onto teeth to prevent decay. Also called dental sealant.

pithing.definition: A procedure to rapidly destroy the brain (and often the brainstem) of an animal by inserting a sharp instrument through the skull (typically via the foramen magnum), causing immediate insensibility and death; historically used in slaughter and certain research contexts.

pitocin.definition: A synthetic form of the hormone oxytocin used to induce or augment labor and to prevent or treat postpartum hemorrhage by stimulating uterine contractions; typically given IV or IM.

pitressin.definition: A brand-name preparation of vasopressin, a peptide hormone (antidiuretic hormone) that acts as a vasopressor and antidiuretic agent to raise blood pressure and promote water reabsorption; used to treat central diabetes insipidus, reduce esophageal variceal bleeding, and as an adjunct vasopressor in shock.

pitting edema.definition: A form of edema in which swelling leaves a persistent indentation (pit) when the swollen area is pressed with a finger; reflects excess interstitial fluid due to fluid overload or low plasma oncotic pressure, commonly from heart failure, liver or kidney disease, venous insufficiency, or malnutrition.

pituicyte.definition: Specialized glial cell of the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) derived from astrocytes that surrounds and supports the nerve terminals of hypothalamic neurons and helps maintain the local extracellular environment.

hypothalamic releasing factors.definition: Peptide hormones produced by the hypothalamus that stimulate the anterior pituitary to secrete its trophic hormones; they travel via the hypophyseal portal system to regulate ACTH, TSH, LH/FSH, and GH secretion. Examples include corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH), gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), and growth hormone–releasing hormone (GHRH).

somatotropin.definition: A polypeptide hormone produced by the anterior pituitary gland that stimulates growth and metabolic processes in tissues; its actions are largely mediated by IGF-1. Deficiency causes growth failure; excess leads to gigantism in children and acromegaly in adults.

thyrotropin-like hormone.definition: A hormone with thyrotropic activity that stimulates the thyroid gland to synthesize and release thyroid hormones (T4 and T3) by binding to the TSH receptor; it can refer to endogenous thyroid-stimulating hormone or to agents that mimic its action.

placental accreta.definition: An abnormal implantation in which placental tissue adheres directly to the muscular layer of the uterus (the myometrium) due to defective decidualization, causing firm attachment and potential incomplete placental separation at delivery (can predispose to severe hemorrhage).

placental insufficiency.definition: A condition in which the placenta fails to adequately transfer oxygen and nutrients from the mother to the fetus, usually due to impaired placental perfusion or placental pathology, leading to fetal growth restriction and increased risk of fetal distress or stillbirth.

placental dystocia.definition: Difficulty in the delivery of the placenta after birth (third stage of labor), typically due to impaired placental separation or abnormal placentation, which can lead to a retained placenta and postpartum hemorrhage.

placental infarct.definition: An area of placental tissue necrosis caused by ischemia from obstructed maternal blood flow (often due to thrombosis of placental vessels), typically wedge-shaped and pale.

intervillous thrombi.definition: A thrombus (blood clot) within the intervillous space of the placenta—the maternal blood–filled spaces between the chorionic villi. It reflects coagulation in these spaces and is a finding in placental pathology, sometimes associated with placental infarction or maternal vascular insufficiency.

placental membranes.definition: Two fetal membranes—the amnion (inner membrane lining the amniotic cavity) and the chorion (outer fetal membrane surrounding the chorionic villi)—that enclose the developing fetus and the amniotic sac and contribute to placental development.

placental hormones.definition: Hormones produced by the placenta that regulate fetal growth and development and maternal physiology to sustain pregnancy; examples include human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), human placental lactogen (hPL), progesterone, estrogens, and placental corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH).

hypophyseal infantilism.definition: An instance of pituitary dwarfism due to hypopituitarism, in which the anterior pituitary fails to produce adequate growth hormone (and other hormones), leading to markedly short stature and delayed or absent puberty with otherwise normal intelligence.

pituitary snuff.definition: Not a recognized medical term; no standard definition in medical dictionaries.

pituitary stalk.definition: A slender neurovascular connection between the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland (infundibulum) that contains hypothalamic nerve axons projecting to the posterior pituitary and the hypophyseal portal vessels transporting releasing and inhibiting hormones to the anterior pituitary.

trochoid joint.definition: A uniaxial synovial joint in which the round or cylindrical surface of one bone rotates within a ring formed by another bone and its ligament, allowing rotation around a single axis (for example, the atlantoaxial joint and proximal radioulnar joints).

radial notch.definition: A shallow concave depression on the lateral aspect of the ulna at the proximal end (near the coronoid process) that articulates with the head of the radius to form the proximal radioulnar joint.

pkd.definition: A genetic disorder characterized by the development of numerous fluid-filled cysts in the kidneys, often causing kidney enlargement and progressive renal dysfunction; most commonly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern (ADPKD), with a rarer autosomal recessive form (ARPKD).

prausnitz-kustner test.definition: An historical in vivo assay to detect allergen-specific IgE by passive transfer of serum containing IgE into the skin of a nonallergic recipient, followed by exposure to the allergen; a wheal-and-flare reaction at the site indicates the presence of specific IgE in the donor serum.

premature junctional complex.definition: A premature contraction arising from an ectopic focus in the atrioventricular (AV) junction that occurs earlier than the next expected beat; the QRS is typically narrow, and the P wave may be absent or inverted with retrograde atrial activation (and may appear before, during, or after the QRS depending on conduction).

pityriasis alba.definition: A common, benign hypopigmented facial patch seen in children and adolescents, characterized by dry, fine scaling on the cheeks that is lighter than the surrounding skin; often associated with dry skin and atopy, and usually self-limited, resolving with time and regular moisturization (and sun protection).

pityriasis rubra pilaris.definition: A rare chronic inflammatory skin disorder characterized by follicular hyperkeratosis and erythematous, scaly plaques that may coalesce with islands of spared skin; commonly involves the palms and soles and can progress to erythroderma.

pityriasis lichenoides chronica.definition: A chronic variant of pityriasis lichenoides characterized by recurrent crops of small, scaling papules that persist for weeks to months and may heal with residual hyperpigmentation.

pityriasis nigra.definition: A historical pigmentary skin disorder characterized by dark, hyperpigmented patches; traditionally attributed to a superficial fungal infection and often equated with pityriasis versicolor, though the term is now rarely used in modern dermatology.

placental membrane.definition: The placental membrane typically refers to the fetal membranes—the amnion and chorion—that envelop the developing fetus, forming the amniotic sac, and together with placental villi create the barrier between maternal and fetal blood while permitting exchange.

planar xanthoma.definition: Flat, yellowish skin plaques caused by lipid-laden macrophages in the dermis; associated with hyperlipidemia or lipoprotein disorders (e.g., familial hypercholesterolemia, dysbetalipoproteinemia), and may involve eyelids (xanthelasma) or extensor surfaces.

placental dysfunction.definition: Impaired placental function that reduces the delivery of oxygen and nutrients to the fetus, often associated with fetal growth restriction and pregnancy complications such as preeclampsia.

postmature infant.definition: A newborn delivered after 42 completed weeks of gestation (gestational age ≥42 weeks); often associated with placental aging and increased risk of perinatal complications such as hypoglycemia, dehydration, and meconium aspiration.

placental scan.definition: A prenatal ultrasound examination of the placenta that assesses its position, structure, and blood flow (often with Doppler) to detect abnormalities such as placenta previa, placental abruption, or placental insufficiency.

placental stage of labor.definition: The third stage of labor; the interval from the birth of the infant to the expulsion of the placenta and fetal membranes, typically lasting 5–30 minutes and managed with controlled cord traction and uterotonic agents to prevent postpartum hemorrhage.

placental thrombosis.definition: A thrombus within the placental vessels that reduces placental blood flow, potentially causing placental infarction and fetal compromise.

placental transmission.definition: Transplacental transmission is the passage of substances—such as infectious agents or maternal antibodies—from the maternal circulation across the placenta into the fetal circulation during pregnancy; it can lead to congenital infection or provide passive neonatal immunity via transfer of IgG antibodies.

placenta previa partialis.definition: A form of placenta previa in which the placental edge partially covers the internal cervical os, with implantation in the lower uterine segment; typically presents with painless third-trimester vaginal bleeding and often necessitates cesarean delivery.

placenta soufflé.definition: An audible soft blowing vascular sound heard over the uterus in late pregnancy, caused by placental blood flow through the intervillous spaces; it is synchronous with the maternal pulse and usually disappears after placental delivery.

placenta succenturiate.definition: A placenta with one or more separate accessory lobes (succenturiate lobes) that are connected to the main placental mass by blood vessels; these lobes may be delivered separately or retained, increasing the risk of postpartum hemorrhage and retained placental tissue.

plafond fracture.definition: A fracture of the distal tibial plafond, the articular surface of the tibia at the ankle; typically caused by a high-energy axial load and often involves intra-articular extension with potential joint incongruity and instability, frequently requiring surgical fixation depending on displacement.

plagiocephaly.definition: A condition characterized by asymmetrical flattening of the skull, typically in infants, due to external pressure on the developing head (most often from prolonged back-lying); may be associated with neck muscle tightness (torticollis) and often improves with time or repositioning, sometimes helmet therapy.

plagiocephalism.definition: An abnormal skull shape with asymmetrical contour, typically caused by external molding in infancy (deformational plagiocephaly), resulting in flattening on one side of the head and a parallelogram-shaped appearance when viewed from above.

pneumonic plague.definition: An acute, highly contagious form of plague caused by Yersinia pestis infection of the lungs, transmitted by respiratory droplets; presents with fever, rapid-onset pneumonia with dyspnea and chest pain, and often productive cough with hemoptysis; high mortality if not promptly treated with appropriate antibiotics.

septicemic plague.definition: A form of plague characterized by systemic infection with Yersinia pestis in the bloodstream, often presenting with fever, weakness, abdominal pain, vomiting, and rapid progression to septic shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation; may cause purpura and skin necrosis and can occur with or without buboes, requiring urgent antibiotic therapy.

plaquenil sulfate.definition: A sulfate salt form of hydroxychloroquine, a synthetic 4-aminoquinoline antimalarial drug used to prevent and treat malaria and to manage autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis.

malacoplakia.definition: A chronic granulomatous inflammatory disorder of the urinary tract (most often the bladder) caused by defective macrophage killing of bacteria, leading to foamy macrophages with Michaelis–Gutmann bodies; commonly associated with Escherichia coli infection and immunosuppression; managed with prolonged antibiotics and sometimes surgical debulking.

melanoplakia.definition: A pigmented plaque on mucosal surfaces (most commonly the oral mucosa) due to increased melanin deposition or melanocytic activity; similar in appearance to leukoplakia but pigmented. Most lesions are benign, but persistent or changing pigmentation should be evaluated to exclude melanoma or other pigmented neoplasms.

plane xanthoma.definition: Flat or slightly elevated yellow plaques in the skin formed by lipid-laden macrophages (histiocytes) in the dermis; a type of cutaneous xanthoma commonly associated with hyperlipidemia or lipid metabolism disorders (e.g., xanthelasma on the eyelids).

xanthoma planum.definition: Flat, yellowish cutaneous plaque (planar xanthoma) composed of lipid-laden macrophages (foamy histiocytes) in the dermis; often on the eyelids or other flat skin areas and frequently associated with hyperlipidemia or lipid metabolism disorders.

xanthelasmatosis.definition: A benign lipid deposition disorder of the eyelids characterized by yellowish plaques (xanthelasmata) in the dermis due to cholesterol-laden macrophages; often associated with dyslipidemia and lipid disorders and typically a cosmetic concern that may prompt evaluation for underlying lipid abnormalities.

planoconcave lens.definition: A lens with one planar surface and one concave surface; a diverging lens that causes incoming light rays to spread apart, with a negative focal length and typically forms a virtual, upright image.

planoconvex lens.definition: A transparent optical lens with one flat (plano) surface and one convex surface; it is a converging lens (positive focal length) used to focus or collimate light in optical instruments and ophthalmic applications.

plantar fascia.definition: Connective tissue in the foot which joins the heel bone to the ball of the foot.

plantar calcaneocuboid joint.definition: A synovial joint between the plantar surfaces of the calcaneus and cuboid bones, forming part of the transverse tarsal (Chopart) joint and allowing small gliding movements that contribute to foot flexibility and stability during gait.

plantar calcaneonavicular ligament.definition: A strong plantar ligament running from the sustentaculum tali of the calcaneus to the navicular bone; it supports the head of the talus and maintains the medial longitudinal arch of the foot, acting like a spring during weight-bearing.

plantar fasciitis.definition: When the thick tissue on the bottom of your foot (called plantar fascia) gets swollen.

plantar flexion.definition: Movement at the ankle that points the toes downward; the sole moves toward the ground (as in standing on tiptoe). It is the opposite of dorsiflexion.

plantar grasp reflex.definition: A primitive neonatal reflex in which stimulation of the sole causes the toes to curl downward and grasp; it typically integrates by about 9–12 months of age.

plantar neuroma.definition: Entrapment neuropathy of a plantar digital nerve in the forefoot, most often the nerve between the third and fourth toes, presenting as burning or sharp pain in the ball of the foot with numbness or tingling in the toes, typically worsened by weight-bearing and tight footwear.

plantar reflex.definition: A superficial reflex elicited by stroking the plantar surface of the foot; the normal response is toe flexion (plantar flexion). An abnormal extensor plantar response (Babinski sign) — extension of the big toe with fanning of the other toes — suggests an upper motor neuron or corticospinal tract lesion.

plantar wart.definition: A wart on the sole of the foot, caused by a virus.

plantar warts.definition: Benign epidermal growths on the sole of the foot caused by human papillomavirus infection (commonly HPV types 1, 2, or 4). They appear as rough, well-circumscribed lesions on weight-bearing areas and may show tiny black dots (thrombosed capillaries); they can be painful with walking. Diagnosis is clinical; treatments include topical salicylic acid, cryotherapy, cantharidin, laser, or occlusion. Many lesions resolve spontaneously over months to years, though recurrence is common and they are contagious.

plantaris.definition: A small, vestigial muscle of the posterior leg with a long, slender tendon that runs between the gastrocnemius and soleus and often blends with the Achilles tendon to insert on the calcaneal tuberosity; it acts as a weak plantarflexor of the foot and a minor knee flexor, and its tendon is sometimes used as an autograft in reconstructive surgery.

plasma cell leukemia.definition: A rare, aggressive plasma cell malignancy characterized by clonal plasma cells circulating in the peripheral blood; diagnostic criteria include an absolute circulating plasma cell count ≥2 × 10^9/L or plasma cells comprising ≥20% of peripheral white blood cells. It can be primary (de novo) or secondary to multiple myeloma and typically presents with anemia, fatigue, infections, and organomegaly; prognosis is poor and treatment involves systemic anti-myeloma therapy.

bence jones proteinuria.definition: Urinary excretion of free immunoglobulin light chains (Bence Jones proteins) from clonal plasma cells, most often in multiple myeloma; detectable by urine protein electrophoresis or sulfosalicylic acid test rather than routine dipstick.

wright-stain marrow smear.definition: A bone marrow aspirate smear stained with Wright stain (a Romanowsky-type stain) used to evaluate marrow cellularity and the morphology and differential counts of hematopoietic cells, including detection of blasts and dysplastic features.

plasmacytomas.definition: A solitary tumor composed of clonal plasma cells, arising in bone (solitary plasmacytoma of bone) or soft tissue (extramedullary plasmacytoma); a localized form of plasma cell neoplasm that may progress to multiple myeloma, diagnosed by biopsy with systemic evaluation, and often treated with radiotherapy for localized disease.

peripheral plasma cell myeloma.definition: Not a standard term; it may be used to refer to either plasma cell leukemia (malignant clonal plasma cells circulating in peripheral blood) or an extramedullary plasmacytoma (localized plasma cell tumor outside the bone marrow).

therapeutic plasmapheresis.definition: A procedure in which plasma is removed from the blood and replaced with a substitute (e.g., albumin or donor plasma) to remove pathogenic substances such as autoantibodies, immune complexes, or toxins from the circulation; used in certain autoimmune, hematologic, and neurologic disorders.

gamma globulins.definition: A class of serum globulins consisting of immunoglobulins (antibodies) produced by plasma cells; includes IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, and IgE and mediates humoral immunity; on electrophoresis, they form the gamma globulin fraction.

plasminogen.definition: A circulating glycoprotein zymogen produced by the liver that is the inactive precursor of plasmin; it is activated to plasmin by plasminogen activators such as tissue-type plasminogen activator (tPA) or urokinase (uPA), and plasmin then degrades fibrin and other proteins to promote fibrinolysis.

plasminogen activator.definition: A serine protease that catalyzes the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin, the enzyme responsible for dissolving fibrin clots; examples include tissue-type plasminogen activator (tPA) and urokinase-type plasminogen activator (uPA).

plasminogen activator inhibitor 1.definition: A serine protease inhibitor (serpin) that inhibits tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) and urokinase-type plasminogen activator (uPA), thereby reducing plasmin generation and fibrinolysis; produced by endothelial and other cells (encoded by SERPINE1).

plasminogen test.definition: A laboratory test that measures plasminogen in blood, either its quantity (antigen level) or its functional activity, to assess the fibrinolytic system and detect plasminogen deficiency or dysplasminogenemia.

plasminogen deficiency.definition: An extremely rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficient plasminogen levels or function due to PLG gene mutations, leading to impaired fibrinolysis and deposition of fibrin on mucous membranes; most characteristically presents as ligneous conjunctivitis with pseudomembranes on other mucosal surfaces (airways, GI, genitourinary tract). Management includes plasminogen replacement and supportive care.

plasmosome.definition: Not a widely recognized medical term; no standard definition exists in contemporary medical dictionaries. It may be a misspelling or an obscure/obsolete term.

plasmodia.definition: A group of intracellular protozoan parasites transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes that cause malaria; their life cycle includes a liver (hepatic) stage and a red blood cell (erythrocytic) stage, leading to periodic fevers and hemolytic anemia.

ovale malaria.definition: Malaria caused by infection with the protozoan parasite Plasmodium ovale, transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes; it typically presents with intermittent fever (every 48 hours) and may relapse due to dormant liver stages (hypnozoites), usually with milder illness than falciparum malaria.

vivax malaria.definition: Malaria caused by infection with Plasmodium vivax; it typically presents with fever paroxysms every 48 hours (tertian fever) and may relapse due to dormant liver-stage hypnozoites, transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes.

black-water fever.definition: A complication of malaria characterized by intravascular hemolysis and hemoglobinuria (dark urine), with fever, anemia, and possible acute kidney injury; historically associated with falciparum malaria and quinine therapy.

pharyngeal mucosa.definition: The mucous membrane lining the pharynx, featuring respiratory epithelium (pseudostratified ciliated columnar) in the nasopharynx and stratified squamous epithelium in the oropharynx and laryngopharynx, with a lamina propria containing glands and lymphoid tissue; it protects, moistens, and filters incoming air and participates in immune defense.

platelet aggregation.definition: The clumping together of platelets in the blood to form a platelet plug at sites of vascular injury, driven by platelet activation (e.g., by ADP, thromboxane A2, thrombin) and fibrinogen bridging via GPIIb/IIIa receptors; a central step in hemostasis and thrombosis.

platelet aggregation test.definition: A laboratory test that assesses platelet function by measuring the extent and rate of platelet aggregation in response to specific activators (e.g., ADP, collagen, epinephrine, ristocetin, arachidonic acid), typically using light transmission aggregometry in platelet-rich plasma.

platelet count.definition: A laboratory measurement of the number of platelets in the blood, typically reported as platelets per microliter (platelets/µL); used to evaluate bleeding risk and diagnose conditions such as thrombocytopenia or thrombocytosis.

platelet antibody detection test.definition: An in vitro assay that detects antibodies directed against platelet surface antigens in a patient’s blood, used to diagnose immune-mediated thrombocytopenias and alloimmune platelet disorders; common methods include MAIPA (monoclonal antibody–specific immobilization of platelet antigens), ELISA for platelet-associated antibodies, and flow cytometry–based assays.

platelet antibody detection.definition: A laboratory test that detects antibodies directed against platelet surface antigens in a patient’s blood, indicating immune-mediated platelet destruction or alloimmunization (e.g., in immune thrombocytopenia, posttransfusion purpura, or neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia).

idiopathic thrombocytopenia purpura.definition: An autoimmune disorder in which antibodies target platelets, causing their destruction and resulting in thrombocytopenia with mucocutaneous bleeding such as purpura or petechiae; it is often acute in children and can be chronic in adults.

posttransfusion purpura.definition: An immune-mediated thrombocytopenia that occurs about 5–10 days after a blood transfusion, caused by recipient antibodies against platelet antigens (often HPA-1a) that destroy transfused and/or autologous platelets, leading to acute purpura and mucosal bleeding.

neonatal thrombocytopenia.definition: A condition in newborns defined by a platelet count below 150,000 per microliter, associated with an increased risk of bleeding; it results from reduced platelet production or increased destruction and can be due to prematurity, infection/sepsis, birth complications, DIC, or immune/alloimmune mechanisms such as maternal anti-platelet antibodies.

drug-induced thrombocytopenia.definition: A decrease in circulating platelets caused by exposure to a medication, usually due to immune-mediated platelet destruction or impaired platelet production, which typically resolves after the offending drug is stopped.

paroxysmal hemoglobinuria.definition: A condition characterized by episodic intravascular hemolysis with hemoglobinuria due to complement-mediated destruction of red blood cells, caused by a clonal expansion of hematopoietic cells lacking GPI-anchored proteins (CD55/CD59) from a PIGA mutation; features include dark urine (often in the morning), anemia, and an increased risk of thrombosis.

immunological thrombocytopenia.definition: A disorder in which the immune system produces autoantibodies against platelets, causing their destruction and reduced production, leading to thrombocytopenia and an increased risk of mucocutaneous bleeding (e.g., petechiae, easy bruising). It can be primary or secondary to another condition.

wiskott-aldrich syndrome.definition: A rare X-linked recessive primary immunodeficiency caused by mutations in the WAS gene encoding WASP, leading to defective actin cytoskeleton remodeling in hematopoietic cells. It presents with eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, and recurrent infections due to combined humoral and cellular immunodeficiency, often with low IgM and elevated IgA/IgE and an increased risk of autoimmunity and malignancy.

glycogen storage disorders.definition: An inherited group of metabolic diseases caused by enzymatic defects in glycogen metabolism—either glycogen synthesis or glycogen breakdown—that lead to abnormal glycogen accumulation or structure in tissues, especially liver and skeletal or cardiac muscle, with clinical features such as hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, growth delay, muscle weakness, and/or cardiomyopathy, varying by subtype.

plasma thromboplastin antecedent.definition: An intrinsic pathway coagulation factor, historically termed plasma thromboplastin antecedent, now known as factor XI. It circulates as a zymogen and is activated to XIa, which helps activate factor IX; deficiency prolongs the activated partial thromboplastin time and can cause mild to moderate bleeding (hemophilia C).

cleft lip and cleft palate repair.word: cleft lip and cleft palate repair
cleft lip and cleft palate repair.definition: Staged surgical correction of congenital fissures of the upper lip and/or palate; lip repair (cheiloplasty) restores lip continuity and symmetry, while palate repair (palatoplasty) closes the cleft in the palate to improve feeding, speech, nasal function, and facial aesthetics, with possible later procedures (e.g., alveolar bone grafts and orthodontics) as needed.

uveoplasty.definition: A surgical procedure to repair or reconstruct the uveal tract (iris, ciliary body, and choroid) of the eye, typically to correct defects or restore normal anatomy and function after trauma or disease.

bronchoplasty.definition: A surgical procedure to repair or reconstruct a bronchus to restore airway patency, typically for bronchial stenosis or injury; may involve resection of a bronchial segment with end-to-end anastomosis or patch grafting.

z-plasty.definition: A surgical technique used to release scar contractures and reorient a scar by creating two triangular flaps in a Z-shaped incision and transposing them to lengthen and realign the scar.

y-plasty.definition: A reconstructive surgical technique in which a Y-shaped incision is made to create tissue flaps that are rearranged to widen a narrowed lumen or release a scar contracture, thereby lengthening or expanding the affected tissue segment.

tissue graft.definition: A tissue graft is a piece of tissue transplanted from one site to another to replace missing or damaged tissue; it may be autograft (from the same person), allograft (from another person), or xenograft (from another species) and relies on revascularization to survive after transfer.

skin grafting.definition: A surgical procedure in which skin is transplanted from a donor site to a recipient site to replace damaged or missing skin; most commonly autologous, and the graft can be split-thickness or full-thickness.

chemical peeling.definition: A dermatologic procedure in which a chemical solution is applied to the skin to cause controlled exfoliation and injury to the epidermis (and sometimes upper dermis), promoting regeneration and improvement of texture, pigment, and wrinkles; depth is categorized as superficial, medium, or deep depending on the agent and technique.

tattooing.definition: The practice of inserting pigment into the dermis by needle punctures to create a permanent mark on the skin.

grafting.definition: A surgical procedure in which tissue is transplanted from one site to another or from a donor to a recipient to replace damaged tissue or promote healing.

plasma volume extender.definition: An intravenous fluid that increases the volume of the blood plasma in the intravascular compartment, used to treat hypovolemia or shock from fluid loss. It includes crystalloids (e.g., normal saline, lactated Ringer's) and colloids (e.g., albumin, dextrans, gelatin, hydroxyethyl starch).

plasma volume.definition: The liquid, cell-free component of blood in the circulatory system; the extracellular fluid portion that remains after removing cellular elements; contains water, proteins (including albumin), electrolytes, and nutrients; typically about 3 liters in an average adult.

volume expander.definition: A substance administered intravenously to increase circulating blood volume in hypovolemia; includes crystalloids (e.g., normal saline, lactated Ringer's) and colloids (e.g., albumin, dextrans).

renin assay.definition: A laboratory test that measures the amount or activity of renin in blood (plasma renin activity or direct renin concentration), used to assess the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and aid in evaluating hypertension, including suspected renovascular disease or primary hyperaldosteronism.

plasma renin assay.definition: A laboratory assay that measures renin in plasma, either as plasma renin activity (PRA) or direct renin concentration (DRC). It assesses the activity of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and aids in evaluating hypertension etiologies and guiding management (often interpreted with aldosterone to compute the aldosterone-to-renin ratio).

renin activity.definition: The catalytic activity of renin, a kidney-derived protease that cleaves angiotensinogen to form angiotensin I in the renin–angiotensin system, thereby regulating blood pressure and electrolyte/fluid balance; commonly reported as plasma renin activity or direct renin concentration.

pra.definition: An in-lab measure of the enzymatic activity of renin in plasma, reflecting the activity of the renin–angiotensin system; used to evaluate hypertension, suspected renovascular disease, and disorders of sodium balance; reported as ng/mL/hour and influenced by posture, sodium intake, and medications. If you meant a different meaning (e.g., progressive retinal atrophy in animals), please specify.

primary hyperaldosteronism.definition: A disorder in which the adrenal cortex autonomously secretes aldosterone (renin-independent), causing sodium retention, potassium loss, metabolic alkalosis, suppressed renin activity, and hypertension; most often due to an aldosterone-producing adenoma or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia.

secondary hyperaldosteronism.definition: An increase in aldosterone secretion driven by activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system in response to decreased effective arterial blood volume or renal perfusion (e.g., heart failure, cirrhosis with ascites, nephrotic syndrome, renovascular disease, dehydration). Plasma renin activity is elevated, distinguishing it from autonomous (primary) overproduction of aldosterone.

renal hypertension.definition: A form of secondary hypertension caused by kidney disease or reduced renal perfusion, typically due to renal parenchymal disease or renovascular disorders, in which decreased renal function or perfusion activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, leading to elevated blood pressure.

renovascular hypertension.definition: A form of secondary hypertension caused by decreased renal perfusion due to renal artery stenosis, which stimulates renin release and activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, resulting in elevated systemic blood pressure. It is most commonly due to atherosclerosis in adults and fibromuscular dysplasia in younger patients.

adrenal disease.definition: Disorders of the adrenal glands that disrupt the production of their hormones (cortisol, aldosterone, and adrenal androgens from the cortex; catecholamines from the medulla), leading to a range of systemic effects. Examples include Addison disease (adrenal insufficiency), Cushing syndrome, primary hyperaldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, and adrenal tumors.

plethysmogram.definition: A tracing obtained by plethysmography that records changes in volume within a body part (usually blood volume) over time, used to assess blood flow and vascular function.

plethysmograph.definition: An instrument that measures changes in volume within an organ or body part, typically by sensing changes in blood volume using methods such as photoplethysmography (light-based) or impedance plethysmography (electrical impedance).

pleural biopsy.definition: A procedure in which pleural tissue is removed for histologic examination to diagnose pleural disease.

pleural rub.definition: A coarse, scratching or grating sound heard with auscultation when inflamed pleural surfaces rub against each other during respiration, typical of pleuritis (pleurisy).

pleuropericardial rub.definition: A friction rub from inflammation of both the pleura and pericardium, producing a scratchy, grating sound on auscultation that may be heard best at the left lower sternal border and suggests concurrent pleuritis and pericarditis.

pleuropericardial membranes.definition: Embryologic membranes formed by pleuropericardial folds that separate the pericardial cavity from the pleural cavities in the thorax; they contain the phrenic nerves and pericardiophrenic vessels and contribute to the development of the fibrous pericardium.

pleuroperitoneal cavity.definition: An embryologic space between the developing pleural and peritoneal cavities that is closed off by the pleuroperitoneal membranes to separate the thoracic and abdominal cavities and contribute to diaphragm formation.

pleuroperitoneal hiatus.definition: An embryologic opening between the pleural and peritoneal cavities of the developing diaphragm (the posterolateral pleuroperitoneal canal), normally closed by the pleuroperitoneal membranes; if it remains patent, it can lead to posterolateral diaphragmatic hernia (Bochdalek).

pleuropneumonia.definition: An infection of the lung that also involves the pleura, causing pleuritis (inflammation of the pleural membranes) and usually pleural effusion; can be complicated by empyema.

pplo.definition: Pleuropneumonia-like organism: a historical label for cell-wall–deficient bacteria in the Mycoplasma group, associated with pleuropneumonia in animals and atypical pneumonia in humans.

pleuropericardial.definition: Relating to both the pleura (the membranes surrounding the lungs) and the pericardium (the sac surrounding the heart); in embryology, membranes that separate the pericardial cavity from the pleural cavities.

pleuroperitoneal.definition: Relating to the pleural (thoracic) cavity and the peritoneal (abdominal) cavity; involving or connecting the thoracic and abdominal serous cavities.

pleurothotonos.definition: A dystonic posture in which the trunk is persistently laterally flexed (often with rotation) due to involuntary contractions of the trunk muscles.

plexiform.definition: Pertaining to or resembling a plexus; network-like or branched. In pathology, used to describe lesions or tumors that grow diffusely in a web-like, interwoven pattern along nerves or tissues.

plexor.definition: A small hammer used to strike the pleximeter to elicit a deep tendon reflex.

pleximeter.definition: A small flat surface used on the body during clinical percussion to receive the percussion blow from the hammer and transmit vibrations to the underlying tissues.

plica.definition: A fold or ridge of a membrane or tissue; in anatomy, a thin fold of synovial membrane or peritoneum.

plicae.definition: A fold or ridge of tissue, especially a mucosal fold in a hollow organ, that increases surface area or creates compartments (for example, the circular folds—plicae circulares—of the small intestine).

plication.definition: The folding or pleating of tissue, especially a surgical technique in which a section of tissue is folded and sutured upon itself to shorten, narrow, reinforce, or reduce the size of an organ.

mithramycin.definition: An antineoplastic antibiotic (plicamycin) produced by Streptomyces plicatus that binds to DNA and inhibits RNA synthesis; historically used to treat hypercalcemia of malignancy and certain germ cell tumors but limited today by severe toxicity.

plerocercoid.definition: A larval stage of certain cestodes (tapeworms) that follows the procercoid stage and develops in the tissues of the second intermediate host (often fish); it is the infectious form for the definitive host and can cause sparganosis in humans or develop into an adult tapeworm after ingestion, depending on the species.

pleuritis.definition: Inflammation of the pleura, the two-layer serous membranes surrounding the lungs and lining the chest wall, typically causing sharp chest pain that worsens with deep breathing or coughing and may be accompanied by a pleural friction rub; often due to infection, autoimmune disease, or other pleural or pulmonary conditions.

pleomorphism.definition: A variation in the size and shape of cells or microorganisms; in microbiology it refers to bacteria that lack a fixed shape, and in pathology it describes tumor cells with marked variability in size and form, indicating abnormal morphology.

pleiotropy.definition: A single gene influences multiple distinct phenotypic traits that are not necessarily related, often through a shared biochemical pathway or regulatory effect.

pleiotropic.definition: Relating to pleiotropy; describing a single gene or mutation that influences multiple, distinct phenotypic traits.

pleochromatic.definition: Exhibiting color changes; appearing as different colors when viewed from different angles or under polarized light due to anisotropic light absorption.

pleomorphic.definition: Characterized by variation in shape and size; lacking a uniform morphology in cells or organisms.

ploidy.definition: The number of complete chromosome sets in a cell or organism; commonly described as haploid (n, one set), diploid (2n, two sets), or polyploid (more than two sets, e.g., triploid 3n, tetraploid 4n).

ploid.definition: A combining form meaning “having a specified number of complete chromosome sets,” used to describe the ploidy level of a cell or organism (e.g., haploid, diploid, polyploid).

polyploid.definition: An organism or cell with more than two complete sets of chromosomes (more than the diploid number); polyploidy includes triploidy (3n), tetraploidy (4n), etc., and is common in plants but rare in animals.

plummer\u00027s disease.definition: A form of hyperthyroidism caused by autonomous, usually multinodular thyroid nodules that secrete thyroid hormone independently of TSH; also called toxic multinodular goiter.

koilonychia.definition: A nail deformity in which the nails become thin and concave (spoon-shaped), commonly associated with iron-deficiency anemia and other chronic iron deficiency states.

esophageal webs.definition: Thin membranous projections of the esophageal mucosa that extend into the lumen, typically in the proximal esophagus, which can cause intermittent dysphagia to solids; often associated with iron-deficiency anemia/Plummer–Vinson syndrome and treated with endoscopic dilation if symptomatic.

bronchial carcinoma.definition: A malignant neoplasm arising from the epithelium of the bronchial airways (bronchi), i.e., bronchogenic carcinoma; a form of lung cancer typically subdivided into small cell and non-small cell types.

thoracentesis.definition: An invasive procedure in which a needle or thin catheter is inserted into the pleural space to remove pleural fluid or air, usually to diagnose or relieve pleural effusion or pneumothorax.

podagra.definition: An acute gouty arthritis of the big toe (usually at the first metatarsophalangeal joint) caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition from hyperuricemia.

premenstrual tension.definition: A syndrome of physical and emotional symptoms that typically occur during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle and resolve with the onset of menstruation; commonly includes irritability, tension, anxiety, mood swings, breast tenderness, and bloating.

hematite pneumoconiosis.definition: A pneumoconiosis caused by inhalation of hematite (iron oxide) dust, typically seen in iron ore workers; it involves iron deposition in the lungs and usually causes little to no fibrosis or functional impairment.

pneumococcal meningitis.definition: A bacterial meningitis caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus), characterized by meningeal inflammation with fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and often altered mental status; requires prompt empiric IV antibiotics.

pneumococcal nephritis.definition: An immune complex–mediated glomerulonephritis that follows pneumococcal infection (such as pneumonia or meningitis), presenting as an acute nephritic syndrome with hematuria, proteinuria, edema, and usually hypertension; caused by deposition of antigen–antibody immune complexes in the glomeruli with complement activation; most cases are self-limited with recovery over weeks.

pneumococcal pneumonitis.definition: An inflammation of the lung tissue caused by infection with Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus), representing pneumococcal pneumonia.

pneumococcal disease.definition: Infections caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus), including pneumococcal pneumonia, meningitis, bacteremia/sepsis, otitis media, and sinusitis.

pneumococcal vaccine polyvalent.definition: A vaccine containing capsular polysaccharides from multiple serotypes of Streptococcus pneumoniae, used to induce antibodies and protect against pneumococcal disease (commonly the 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine).

pneumococcus.definition: A gram-positive, encapsulated diplococcus (Streptococcus pneumoniae) that commonly causes pneumonia, meningitis, otitis media, and bacteremia; part of the normal nasopharyngeal flora in some individuals.

pentamidine isethionate.definition: An antiprotozoal diamidine antimicrobial used to treat Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and certain protozoal infections (notably visceral leishmaniasis); administered parenterally (and by inhalation for PCP prophylaxis); it binds to DNA and inhibits parasite replication; adverse effects include nephrotoxicity, hypotension, pancreatitis, hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia, and electrolyte disturbances.

trimethoprim.definition: An antibiotic that inhibits bacterial dihydrofolate reductase, blocking folic acid synthesis and DNA replication; commonly used in combination with sulfamethoxazole (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) to treat urinary tract infections and other infections.

trimetrexate.definition: A lipophilic antifolate anticancer drug that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, reducing tetrahydrofolate and impairing thymidylate and purine synthesis required for DNA replication; used in cancer chemotherapy, typically with leucovorin (folinic acid) rescue to limit toxicity.

pneumopericardium.definition: Air in the pericardial cavity surrounding the heart, often due to chest trauma, thoracic surgery, or invasive procedures; large amounts can compress the heart and cause cardiac tamponade.

pneumoperitoneum.definition: The presence of free gas within the peritoneal cavity, most often due to perforation of a hollow viscus (e.g., stomach, duodenum, or intestines); typically detected on imaging as free intraperitoneal air and may indicate a surgical emergency.

pneumatocele.definition: A thin-walled, air-filled cavity within the lung parenchyma that develops after pulmonary infection (classically Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia) or trauma and often resolves spontaneously.

pneumocephalus.definition: Air or gas within the cranial cavity, typically resulting from head trauma, skull base fracture, neurosurgery, or infection; may be asymptomatic or cause headache and focal neurologic deficits, and in tension pneumocephalus can cause mass effect, with diagnosis by CT imaging.

pneumoencephalocele.definition: A congenital herniation of brain tissue and meninges through a skull defect, in which the herniated sac is air-filled rather than CSF-filled.

pneumogram.definition: A graphic recording of respiratory movements or airflow obtained with a pneumograph, used to assess breathing rate, depth, and effort.

pneumatogram.definition: A radiographic study produced by insufflating gas (air or CO2) into a hollow body cavity to outline its walls and contents for diagnostic visualization; historically associated with pneumography and pneumoencephalography, but the term is rarely used today.

pneumogastric nerve.definition: An old term for the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X); a mixed nerve that provides parasympathetic innervation to the heart, lungs, and much of the digestive tract, and carries sensory information from thoracic and abdominal viscera as well as motor input to the pharynx and larynx.

retinopexy.definition: A surgical procedure to reattach a detached retina by creating a chorioretinal adhesion around retinal breaks, usually with laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy, sometimes in combination with scleral buckling or vitrectomy.

pneumatic retinopexy.definition: A minimally invasive outpatient procedure to repair rhegmatogenous retinal detachment in which an expansile gas bubble is injected into the vitreous cavity to tamponade the retinal break, followed by laser photocoagulation or cryopexy to seal the tear.

tourniquet.definition: A device placed around a limb to compress soft tissue and occlude blood flow, used to control severe bleeding or to create a bloodless surgical field; prolonged use risks tissue ischemia.

pneumatic tourniquet.definition: A device consisting of an inflatable cuff connected to a pump used to occlude arterial blood flow in a limb, creating a bloodless surgical field or controlling bleeding; the cuff is inflated to a pressure typically above systolic blood pressure and released when no longer needed.

nasointestinal.definition: A flexible tube inserted through the nose and advanced into the small intestine (duodenum or jejunum) for enteral feeding or decompression, typically used when gastric access is unsuitable or risk of aspiration is high.

pneumonectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove an entire lung, usually for cancer or severe disease, involving division of the main bronchus and pulmonary vessels.

pneumonopathy.definition: A broad term referring to any disease or pathology of the lung; a lung disorder or pulmonary disease.

pneumonopleuritis.definition: Inflammation of the lung together with inflammation of the adjacent pleura (pleuritis), i.e., pneumonia with pleural involvement, often accompanied by pleural effusion.

pneumonotherapy.definition: A historical or nonstandard term referring to therapy directed at the lungs or pulmonary diseases; it is not part of contemporary, widely accepted medical terminology.

ventriculography.definition: A radiographic study in which contrast material is injected into the cerebral ventricles to visualize the ventricular system, typically to evaluate hydrocephalus or intraventricular anatomy and pathology.

podalgia.definition: Foot pain; pain located in the foot, arising from causes such as trauma, overuse, neuropathy, inflammatory or degenerative joint disease, or mechanical abnormalities.

podalic version.definition: An obstetric maneuver in which the fetus is rotated inside the uterus so that the presenting part becomes the feet (feet-first) or buttocks, facilitating breech delivery; can be performed by internal manipulation through the cervix or by external abdominal manipulation.

podophyllotoxin.definition: A plant lignan from Podophyllum species that inhibits tubulin polymerization, causing mitotic arrest; used topically to treat verrucae (external warts, including genital warts) and serves as a precursor to the anticancer drugs etoposide and teniposide.

pep syndrome.definition: I can’t find a standard medical definition for “PEP syndrome.” Could you clarify what PEP stands for in your context (e.g., post-exposure prophylaxis)? If you provide the exact acronym or context, I can give a precise definition.

rothmund-thomson syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal recessive genodermatosis characterized by early-onset poikiloderma with telangiectasias on sun-exposed skin, sparse hair and eyebrows/eyelashes, growth retardation, and skeletal abnormalities (often radial ray defects); there is an elevated risk of osteosarcoma and other cancers; usually caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in RECQL4.

poikiloderma.definition: A pattern of chronic, mottled skin changes characterized by reticulate hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation with telangiectasia and epidermal atrophy, typically on sun-exposed areas.

poikiloderma of civatte.definition: A chronic actinic (sun-induced) dermatosis of the neck and cheeks presenting with reticulate hyperpigmentation, telangiectasia, and dermal atrophy on sun-exposed areas, typically sparing the perioral region; most common in middle-aged to older women.

poikiloderma congenitale.definition: An extremely rare congenital or infancy-onset hereditary disorder characterized by lifelong poikiloderma—a reticulated pattern of hypopigmentation and hyperpigmentation with skin atrophy and telangiectasia—often accompanied by photosensitivity; the phenotype can vary and may include additional congenital anomalies depending on the specific hereditary form.

poikilocytosis.definition: Abnormal variability in red blood cell shapes seen on a peripheral blood smear, reflecting diverse erythrocyte morphologies that occur in various anemias and bone marrow disorders.

polioencephalitis.definition: Inflammation of brain tissue (encephalitis), potentially occurring with poliovirus infection as part of poliomyelitis; the term is used to describe brain involvement beyond the spinal cord.

poland's syndrome.definition: A rare congenital disorder characterized by unilateral absence or hypoplasia of the pectoralis major muscle, often with ipsilateral chest wall asymmetry and upper-limb anomalies (such as syndactyly or brachydactyly) and nipple/breast hypoplasia.

poland's anomaly.definition: A rare congenital condition characterized by unilateral absence or underdevelopment of the pectoralis major muscle on the chest, often with ipsilateral chest wall and rib abnormalities and sometimes with upper‑limb malformations (e.g., brachydactyly or syndactyly); believed to result from disrupted embryonic development of the subclavian artery on the affected side.

endocrinopathy.definition: Any disorder of the endocrine glands or the hormonal system, characterized by abnormal hormone production, secretion, or action that disrupts metabolic processes.

poison oak.definition: An allergenic plant of the Toxicodendron genus whose urushiol oil causes allergic contact dermatitis; exposure produces a pruritic, erythematous, vesicular rash often in streaks, with possible swelling, that typically begins 12–72 hours after contact and is treated with thorough washing, avoidance of further exposure, and topical corticosteroids (systemic steroids for severe cases).

poison sumac.definition: A poisonous plant in the Anacardiaceae family (Toxicodendron vernix) whose urushiol-containing sap causes an allergic contact dermatitis after skin contact, typically presenting with itching, redness, swelling, and vesicular rash in exposed areas; commonly found in swampy, wet areas of eastern North America.

poison ivy dermatitis.definition: A form of allergic contact dermatitis caused by urushiol oil from Toxicodendron species (poison ivy, poison oak, poison sumac). It presents as a pruritic, erythematous vesicular rash that often appears in a linear pattern at the contact site, developing hours to days after exposure. Management includes washing contaminated skin and objects, avoiding scratching, topical corticosteroids for mild cases, and systemic corticosteroids for extensive or facial involvement.

rhus dermatitis.definition: A type IV hypersensitivity reaction causing an allergic contact dermatitis to urushiol oil from Rhus plants (poison ivy, poison oak, poison sumac). It presents as a pruritic, erythematous, vesicular rash at the exposure site, often with swelling, typically beginning 12–72 hours after contact and may spread by autoinoculation; it is not contagious.

urushiol.definition: An oily allergenic resin found in Toxicodendron species (poison ivy, poison oak, poison sumac); a mixture of catechol derivatives (urushiols) that penetrates skin and binds to proteins to form hapten–protein complexes, provoking allergic contact dermatitis (type IV hypersensitivity).

root canal filling.definition: An endodontic material and technique used to fill and seal a cleaned and shaped root canal after instrumentation, typically gutta-percha with sealer to prevent reinfection.

podogram.definition: A tracing or image of the plantar (sole) aspect of the foot used in podiatry to assess arch height, plantar pressure distribution, and to guide orthotic design or footwear modifications.

podotrochilitis.definition: Inflammation of the podotrochlear (navicular) apparatus of the horse, including the navicular bone, navicular bursa, and surrounding soft tissues; a common cause of chronic forelimb lameness often referred to as navicular disease.

pogonion.definition: A cephalometric landmark; the most anterior point on the contour of the chin (mandibular symphysis), used to assess chin projection in craniofacial analysis.

subspinale.definition: A cephalometric landmark on the midline of the maxilla, defined as the deepest point on the curvature of the maxillary alveolar process between the anterior nasal spine (ANS) and the incisor region; used as the A-point in cephalometric analyses to characterize maxillary position.

porion.definition: A cephalometric landmark at the uppermost point on the margin of the external auditory meatus; used with orbitale to define the Frankfort horizontal plane.

point of maximum impulse.definition: The point on the chest wall where the heartbeat is most strongly felt, representing the left ventricular apical impulse during systole; normally located at the left 5th intercostal space along the midclavicular line, with a displaced location suggesting cardiomegaly or other cardiac pathology.

pseudopodium.definition: A temporary cytoplasmic projection of a cell, especially an amoeboid cell, used for locomotion and feeding, formed by rapid cytoskeletal (actin) rearrangement.

polioencephalomeningomyelitis.definition: A central nervous system inflammatory disease involving the gray matter of the brain (polioencephalitis), the meninges (meningitis), and the spinal cord (myelitis).

polioencephalomyelitis.definition: Inflammation of the gray matter of the brain and spinal cord.

polioencephalopathy.definition: An encephalopathy involving the brain's gray matter; in veterinary contexts it commonly denotes a gray-matter necrosis process (often due to thiamine deficiency or sulfur/toxin exposure) that produces neurologic signs such as ataxia, circling, and head pressing.

poliovirus vaccine, inactivated.definition: An injectable vaccine containing inactivated poliovirus types 1, 2, and 3; it cannot replicate and induces systemic neutralizing antibodies to prevent poliomyelitis, though it does not reliably induce intestinal mucosal immunity and requires multiple doses/boosters.

topv.definition: No widely recognized medical term matches this acronym; it may be an acronym, a misspelling, or a context-specific abbreviation. Please provide context or the full form.

salk vaccine.definition: An inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV) developed by Jonas Salk, containing killed poliovirus types 1–3, administered by injection to prevent poliomyelitis.

polio vaccine.definition: A vaccine to prevent poliomyelitis by inducing immunity to poliovirus; available as inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV) given by injection or oral poliovirus vaccine (OPV) given by mouth, protecting against infection with poliovirus serotypes 1, 2, and 3 and the risk of paralytic disease.

poliomyelitis vaccine.definition: A vaccine that prevents poliomyelitis by inducing immunity to poliovirus; available as the inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV) given by injection or the oral poliovirus vaccine (OPV) given by mouth.
