reifenstein's syndrome.definition: A form of partial androgen insensitivity syndrome caused by mutations in the androgen receptor gene, resulting in undervirilization of 46,XY individuals with testes (often undescended) and a spectrum of external genitalia from mild hypospadias to female-appearing genitalia; usually inherited in an X-linked pattern.

dactylitis.definition: Inflammation of an entire finger or toe, causing diffuse swelling (often described as a sausage-like digit); can result from infectious, inflammatory, or vascular processes, and is classically seen in vaso-occlusive crises in sickle cell disease.

sacroiliac joints.definition: The joints between the sacrum and ilium on each side of the pelvis; they are irregularly shaped synovial (plane) joints that transmit weight from the spine to the pelvis with limited gliding motion, stabilized by strong ligaments (anterior, posterior, and interosseous sacroiliac ligaments).

ankles.definition: A hinge-like joint between the distal ends of the tibia and fibula and the talus (foot), enabling mainly dorsiflexion and plantarflexion; stabilized by the joint capsule and strong ligaments, including the medial and lateral collateral ligaments.

feet.definition: Plural of foot; the distal portion of the lower limb from the ankle to the toes, bearing body weight and enabling standing, walking, and balance; composed of the hindfoot, midfoot, and forefoot, including the tarsal bones, metatarsals, and phalanges.

regurgitant murmur.definition: An abnormal heart murmur caused by backward (regurgitant) flow of blood across a heart valve due to valvular insufficiency; typically heard as a blowing, high-pitched sound that may be holosystolic (e.g., mitral or tricuspid regurgitation) or early diastolic (e.g., aortic or pulmonary regurgitation).

noses.definition: A prominent facial structure consisting of bone and cartilage that forms the external portion of the upper airway, with two nostrils that direct air into the nasal cavities and host olfactory receptors for the sense of smell; it conditions inspired air by warming, humidifying, and filtering.

tracheal cartilage.definition: C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage that form the anterior and lateral walls of the trachea, keeping the airway patent; the open posterior portion is bridged by the trachealis muscle and connective tissue to allow flexibility during swallowing.

renal adenocarcinoma.definition: A malignant tumor of the kidney arising from glandular (epithelial) cells; however, true renal adenocarcinomas are rare, and most primary kidney cancers are renal cell carcinomas arising from renal tubular epithelium.

renal angiography.definition: An invasive imaging procedure in which contrast material is injected directly into the renal arteries via a catheter, with radiographic imaging used to visualize the renal vasculature—commonly to assess renal artery stenosis, aneurysms, or vascular malformations and to guide interventional procedures.

remote afterloading.definition: A brachytherapy technique in which sealed radioactive sources are remotely loaded into applicators or catheters after they are placed, using an afterloading device to minimize staff radiation exposure and enable precise dose delivery.

head and neck tumors.definition: A group of tumors arising in the head and neck region (including the oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, nasal cavity and sinuses, salivary glands, and nearby structures); most malignant tumors here are squamous cell carcinomas, often linked to tobacco, alcohol, and HPV, presenting with local symptoms such as a lump, ulceration, difficulty swallowing, hoarseness, nasal bleeding, or obstruction, and diagnosed by biopsy and imaging with treatment determined by site and stage through a multidisciplinary approach (surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy).

vaginal tumors.definition: Abnormal growths arising from vaginal tissue that can be benign (e.g., polyps, fibromas, vascular lesions) or malignant, with primary vaginal cancers being rare and most often squamous cell carcinoma; they can also represent metastases from other sites. Diagnosis typically involves biopsy and imaging, with treatment depending on histology and stage.

cervical tumors.definition: Cervical tumors are abnormal growths arising from the cervix, the lower part of the uterus that opens into the vagina. They can be benign (e.g., polyps or cysts) or malignant, with malignant cases most commonly cervical cancer (typically squamous cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma). Diagnosis involves clinical examination and tests such as Pap smear, HPV testing, colposcopy, and biopsy.

remifentanil.definition: A potent, ultra–short‑acting synthetic opioid analgesic (mu‑opioid receptor agonist) used for intraoperative and procedural analgesia. It has a rapid onset and very short duration because it is rapidly metabolized by nonspecific plasma and tissue esterases; its effects dissipate quickly after infusion ends. Administered intravenously, often by continuous infusion during anesthesia; adverse effects include respiratory depression, hypotension, and chest wall rigidity at high doses.

renal biopsy.definition: A procedure in which a small sample of kidney tissue is removed, usually by percutaneous needle biopsy under imaging guidance, for microscopic examination to diagnose kidney disease or monitor a kidney transplant.

open biopsy.definition: A surgical procedure in which a tissue sample is removed through an incision for histopathologic examination, usually larger than a needle biopsy and may be incisional (partial) or excisional (complete).

percutaneous biopsy.definition: A biopsy obtained by inserting a needle through the skin to collect tissue for histopathologic examination, typically guided by imaging such as ultrasound, CT, or fluoroscopy.

radiology department.definition: A hospital department that performs diagnostic imaging (X-ray, CT, MRI, ultrasound, nuclear medicine) and image-guided interventional procedures; staffed by radiologists and radiologic technologists who acquire and interpret images to aid diagnosis and treatment.

dye contrast study.definition: A radiologic procedure in which a radiopaque contrast dye is introduced into a body part (such as the GI tract, urinary tract, or vessels) to visualize anatomy and assess patency, flow, or morphology on X-ray, fluoroscopy, or CT.

biopsy needle.definition: A needle designed to obtain a tissue or cellular sample for diagnostic testing; commonly a fine-needle aspiration needle or a core-needle biopsy needle, used with imaging guidance to harvest cells or tissue for histopathologic examination.

lower pole.definition: The inferior or bottom portion of an organ; for example, the lower pole of the kidney is the kidney’s inferior aspect, typically containing the lower calyces.

renal vessels.definition: The renal vessels are the arteries and veins that supply and drain the kidneys: renal arteries arise from the abdominal aorta to perfuse the kidneys, while renal veins drain venous blood from the kidneys into the inferior vena cava.

pressure bandage.definition: A bandage applied tightly around a wound or limb to exert external pressure, typically using an elastic compression bandage to help stop bleeding, limit swelling, and secure a dressing.

urinary output.definition: The volume of urine excreted by the kidneys per unit time, used to assess renal function and fluid balance; in adults, normal urine output is about 0.5 mL/kg/hour (roughly 30–60 mL/hour).

nephritic calculus.definition: Renal calculus (kidney stone): a hard mineral deposit that forms in the kidney from crystallized substances such as calcium oxalate, calcium phosphate, uric acid, or struvite; it may cause flank or groin pain, hematuria, and sometimes urinary obstruction or infection.

major renal calyx.definition: A funnel-shaped chamber of the kidney's collecting system formed by the convergence of two or more minor calyces; it collects urine from the minor calyces and drains into the renal pelvis.

adipose renal capsule.definition: A layer of adipose tissue surrounding the kidney, also called perirenal fat or the adipose capsule, located between the renal capsule and the surrounding renal fascia; it cushions and insulates the kidney and helps hold it in place within the retroperitoneum.

renal cast.definition: An elongated cylindrical sediment formed in the renal tubules and excreted in urine, composed largely of Tamm‑Horsfall protein with varying inclusions (cells or debris); its presence indicates tubular pathology or reduced tubular flow, with types including hyaline, granular, cellular (RBC or WBC), and waxy casts.

epithelial casts.definition: Urinary casts composed of renal tubular epithelial cells, indicating tubular epithelial damage or necrosis (tubular injury), often seen with acute tubular necrosis or nephrotoxic or inflammatory renal injury.

hyaline casts.definition: A colorless, transparent urinary cast composed primarily of Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein with no cellular material; the most common cast in urine and a nonspecific finding that can occur with concentrated urine, dehydration, fever, exercise, or various renal conditions.

waxy casts.definition: Broad, pale, waxy-appearing urinary casts formed by degeneration of hyaline or granular casts; typically indicate chronic kidney disease with reduced urine flow and advanced renal failure.

urinary cast.definition: A cylindrical structure formed by the precipitation of protein (primarily Tamm-Horsfall protein) in the renal tubules that is excreted in urine; its type (hyaline, granular, cellular, waxy, fatty) reflects the underlying renal condition.

adenocarcinoma of the kidney.definition: A malignant tumor composed of gland-forming (adenocarcinomatous) cells arising in the kidney. Primary renal adenocarcinoma is exceedingly rare; most adenocarcinomas involving the kidney are metastases from a primary tumor elsewhere, or represent glandular differentiation within a renal/urothelial tumor.

clear cell carcinoma of the kidney.word: clear cell carcinoma of the kidney
clear cell carcinoma of the kidney.definition: Malignant tumor of the kidney arising from the proximal renal tubular epithelium, characterized by tumor cells with clear cytoplasm due to lipid and glycogen content; the most common subtype of renal cell carcinoma and frequently associated with VHL gene alterations.

renal cortex.definition: The outer region of the kidney, just beneath the renal capsule, containing the glomeruli and most nephron tubules (proximal and distal convoluted tubules) and serving as the site of glomerular filtration and initial urine formation.

renal cortical necrosis.definition: A rare, catastrophic form of acute kidney injury marked by widespread coagulative necrosis of the renal cortex due to cortical microvascular thrombosis (often in the setting of DIC, shock, sepsis, pancreatitis, or obstetric complications), with relative sparing of the medulla and typically irreversible loss of renal function.

septic abortion.definition: An abortion (spontaneous or induced) complicated by intrauterine infection of the uterus and products of conception, typically presenting with fever, abdominal pain, uterine tenderness, and foul-smelling vaginal discharge; treated with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and evacuation of infected tissue to prevent sepsis.

retained fetus.definition: A condition in which a fetus remains within the uterus after fetal death or after delivery has begun, with the fetus not being expelled; management may require medical induction or surgical removal to prevent complications such as infection or hemorrhage.

renal tuberculosis.definition: A form of genitourinary tuberculosis in which infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis primarily involves the kidney, usually from hematogenous spread. It causes granulomatous inflammation with caseating necrosis and can lead to papillary necrosis, calyceal ulcers, ureteral strictures, hydronephrosis, sterile pyuria, and hematuria; treated with standard anti-tuberculous therapy.

nephrotuberculosis.definition: Tuberculosis of the kidney, typically part of genitourinary TB arising from hematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis from a primary focus; it causes granulomatous inflammation of the renal parenchyma and may present with sterile pyuria, hematuria, flank pain, and potential progressive renal impairment.

renal tubular acidosis.definition: A group of disorders characterized by impaired renal acidification leading to a normal-anion-gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis due to defective acid secretion or bicarbonate reabsorption in the tubules; subtypes include distal (type 1), proximal (type 2), and hyperkalemic (type 4).

oliguric.definition: Relating to or marked by abnormally low urine production, typically defined as urine output less than 400 mL per day in adults.

retarded growth.definition: A condition in which growth occurs at a slower rate than normal for age and sex, resulting in shorter stature or smaller body size; often due to malnutrition, chronic disease, endocrine disorders (eg, hypothyroidism or growth hormone deficiency), or genetic factors.

excessive urination.definition: Polyuria is the production of abnormally large volumes of urine, typically defined as urine output greater than about 2.5 liters per day in adults; it can be caused by diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus, diuretic use, or increased fluid intake.

renal nanism.definition: Abnormally small kidneys due to congenital underdevelopment of renal parenchyma (renal hypoplasia); characterized by reduced nephron number and potentially impaired renal function, can be unilateral or bilateral.

renal replacement lipomatosis.definition: A rare condition in which renal parenchyma is replaced by adipose tissue, typically due to long-standing obstruction and chronic inflammation (often from nephrolithiasis), resulting in an atrophic, nonfunctional kidney with fatty replacement of the renal sinus and perirenal spaces.

renal pseudotumor.definition: A benign imaging finding in which normal renal parenchyma or contour variants mimic a renal mass (most commonly due to the cortical columns called the columns of Bertin or other focal cortical bulges), not a true neoplasm.

bertins column hypertrophy.definition: A benign enlargement of the normal colonic mucosal folds known as Bertin's columns; thickening of these vertical intraluminal mucosal folds in the colon seen on imaging, which can mimic a mass or polyp but represents an anatomic variant rather than a true lesion.

dromedary hump.definition: A single, convex bony prominence on the skull (temporal bone/sella region) seen on imaging, representing a normal anatomic variant rather than pathology.

renal papilla.definition: The apex of a renal pyramid; the site where urine from the collecting ducts drains into the minor calyx through openings of the papillary ducts (Ducts of Bellini).

renal plasma flow.definition: The volume of plasma that flows through the kidneys per minute; in a healthy adult it is about 600 mL/min and is estimated clinically by PAH clearance as the effective renal plasma flow, with RPF ≈ RBF × (1 − hematocrit).

renal sinus cyst.definition: A benign, fluid-filled cyst located in the renal sinus, the central part of the kidney containing the pelvicalyceal system. It is typically a simple, noncommunicating cyst and is often found incidentally on imaging; large cysts can cause flank pain or hydronephrosis by mass effect.

renal sinus lipomatosis.definition: Benign overgrowth of adipose tissue in the renal sinus and peripelical space, often with thinning of the renal parenchyma; commonly detected incidentally on imaging and may mimic hydronephrosis or a renal mass.

replacement lipomatosis.definition: A nonstandard term describing the replacement of normal tissue by adipose (fat) tissue, leading to fatty replacement and possible Enlargement or dysfunction of the affected area. In general, lipomatosis refers to diffuse or nodular overgrowth of fat rather than a malignant tumor.

renal artery endarterectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove atherosclerotic plaque from the renal artery via arteriotomy, restoring blood flow to the kidney and treating renovascular hypertension or renal ischemia.

collecting tubules.definition: The collecting tubules are the nephron segment that receives filtrate from distal tubules and funnels it into the collecting ducts; they regulate final urine concentration and acid–base/electrolyte balance, mainly via hormone-regulated water reabsorption (ADH/vasopressin) and electrolyte transport.

renal fascia.definition: A dense fibrous envelope around the kidney and adrenal gland that encloses perirenal fat and separates the perirenal space from the anterior and posterior pararenal spaces; typically described as having an anterior layer (Gerota's fascia) and a posterior layer (Zuckerkandl's fascia).

renal fat.definition: Adipose tissue surrounding the kidney, primarily the perirenal (perinephric) fat within the renal fascia (Gerota's fascia), that cushions the kidney and serves as an energy reserve.

granulomatous inflammation.definition: An organized, chronic inflammatory response in which macrophages transform into epithelioid cells and may fuse to form multinucleated giant cells, aggregating into granulomas surrounded by lymphocytes; this reaction walls off persistent pathogens or foreign substances and may show caseation necrosis (as in tuberculosis) or noncaseating granulomas (as in sarcoidosis).

serum chloride.definition: The concentration of chloride ions (Cl−) in the blood plasma; the major extracellular anion that helps maintain osmotic balance and acid–base homeostasis. Normal serum chloride is typically about 96–106 mEq/L.

urinary bicarbonate.definition: The amount of bicarbonate (HCO3−) excreted in urine; normally minimal since the kidneys reabsorb nearly all filtered bicarbonate, but it increases with bicarbonate wasting (e.g., proximal renal tubular dysfunction) or after a bicarbonate load.

urine specific gravity.definition: A measure of the density of urine relative to the density of water, reflecting the urine’s concentration and the kidney’s ability to concentrate or dilute urine. It typically ranges from about 1.005 to 1.030 in healthy individuals and increases with dehydration or higher solute load.

juxtaglomerular apparatus.definition: Specialized structure in the kidney at the vascular pole of the glomerulus that regulates glomerular filtration rate and systemic blood pressure via tubuloglomerular feedback and the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system; it includes juxtaglomerular (renin-secreting) cells of the afferent arteriole, macula densa cells of the distal tubule, and extraglomerular mesangial cells.

renal angiogram.definition: An invasive imaging procedure in which a catheter is inserted into the renal artery and iodinated contrast is injected to produce radiographic images of the renal vasculature (selective renal angiography), used to evaluate renal artery anatomy and pathology such as stenosis, aneurysm, occlusion, or arteriovenous malformation/fistula.

percutaneous transluminal angioplasty.definition: A minimally invasive procedure in which a catheter with a balloon at its tip is threaded to a narrowed or blocked artery and the balloon is inflated to widen the vessel, improving blood flow; often used to treat coronary artery disease and may include stent placement.

rendu-osler-weber syndrome.definition: An autosomal-dominant hereditary vascular disorder characterized by mucocutaneous telangiectasias and visceral arteriovenous malformations, leading to recurrent epistaxis, iron-deficiency anemia, and potential AVM-related complications in the lungs, liver, and brain.

hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia.definition: A dominantly inherited vascular disorder characterized by mucocutaneous telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations in multiple organs (commonly lungs, liver, and brain), causing recurrent epistaxis, gastrointestinal bleeding, and AVM-related complications.

thiazide diuretic.definition: A class of diuretic drugs that inhibit the sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule of the nephron, reducing sodium reabsorption and increasing urine output; used to treat hypertension and edema, and commonly associated with hypokalemia.

polythiazide.definition: A thiazide-like diuretic that inhibits NaCl reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule, increasing urinary excretion of sodium and water; used to treat hypertension and edema and can cause hypokalemia and other electrolyte disturbances.

renin-angiotensin system.definition: A hormone cascade that regulates blood pressure, vascular resistance, and fluid and electrolyte balance. In response to reduced renal perfusion, renin release cleaves hepatic angiotensinogen to angiotensin I; angiotensin-converting enzyme then converts it to angiotensin II, a potent vasoconstrictor that stimulates aldosterone release, increasing sodium and water reabsorption and elevating blood pressure.

renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.definition: A hormonal system that regulates blood pressure and fluid/electrolyte balance through renin release, conversion of angiotensinogen to angiotensin II, vasoconstriction, and aldosterone-mediated sodium and water retention, with negative feedback once perfusion and volume normalize.

angio­tensin-converting enzyme.definition: An enzyme that converts the inactive form of the protein angiotensin (angiotensin I) to its active form—angiotensin II. Usually abbreviated as ACE.

repaglinide.definition: An oral meglitinide antidiabetic agent that stimulates rapid, meal-related insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells by closing ATP-sensitive potassium channels; used to treat type 2 diabetes mellitus and taken prior to meals, with a risk of hypoglycemia if meals are skipped or delayed.

reovirus.definition: A nonenveloped, icosahedral double-stranded RNA virus with a segmented genome in the family Reoviridae; human infections are typically mild or asymptomatic, and reoviruses include mammalian reovirus used as a model organism and studied for oncolytic therapy.

genital tract.definition: A reproductive system comprising the organs and ducts through which gametes are produced, matured, and transported; in males, the testes, epididymides, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate, and penis; in females, the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, vagina, and external genitalia.

genitourinary system.definition: The organs of the urinary and reproductive systems, including kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra, plus the gonads and genitalia, responsible for urine production, storage, elimination, and reproductive function.

delaviridine.definition: A non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) used in combination antiretroviral therapy for HIV-1 infection; it noncompetitively inhibits HIV-1 reverse transcriptase, blocking the synthesis of viral DNA. Administered orally; its use has diminished due to drug interactions and rapid resistance.

ridge.definition: An elongated, narrow raised crest or border on a bone or other anatomical surface; a raised linear elevation that marks a boundary between structures.

cementoclastic.definition: Relating to cementoclasts, the cells that resorb cementum (the mineralized tissue covering tooth roots); involved in physiological or pathological root resorption.

dentinoclastic.definition: Relating to the resorption or destruction of dentin; capable of dissolving dentin, typically by odontoclasts.

cheyne-stokes.definition: A periodic breathing pattern with a crescendo–decrescendo of tidal volume followed by a brief pause in breathing (apnea), commonly seen in severe heart failure or central nervous system disorders.

kussmaul.definition: A deep, labored breathing pattern with a regular rhythm and increased tidal volume (hyperpnea), seen in severe metabolic acidosis as a compensatory mechanism to blow off CO2 (e.g., diabetic ketoacidosis).

biot.definition: A pattern of irregular, unpredictable respiration with clusters of shallow breaths followed by periods of apnea, typically indicating brainstem dysfunction or increased intracranial pressure.

hyperpnea.definition: An increased depth of breathing, typically with a corresponding rise in ventilation, in response to heightened metabolic demand (e.g., exercise or metabolic acidosis); differs from tachypnea, which is rapid breathing with normal or shallow depth.

medullary.definition: Relating to the medulla—the inner part of an organ; used for structures such as the brain's medulla oblongata, the kidney's renal medulla, or the bone marrow-containing medullary (cavity) region.

neuropsychiatric.definition: Relating to the interrelationship between neurology and psychiatry; conditions in which neurological disease or injury produces psychiatric symptoms or behavioral and mental health disturbances.

respiratory assessment.definition: A systematic clinical evaluation of the respiratory system to assess breathing status and lung function, typically including patient history (e.g., dyspnea, cough), observation of breathing effort, auscultation of breath sounds, percussion, and measures of oxygenation/ventilation (e.g., pulse oximetry, arterial blood gases).

peripheral paresthesia.definition: An abnormal sensory sensation (such as tingling, prickling, numbness, or burning) resulting from irritation or damage to peripheral nerves, typically in a specific nerve or dermatomal distribution.

neuro-muscular.definition: Relating to the nervous system and the muscles, including how nerve impulses control muscle contraction via motor neurons and the neuromuscular junction, and disorders affecting this nerve–muscle connection.

blood gases.definition: An analysis of the oxygen and carbon dioxide content and acid–base status of the blood, typically obtained from arterial blood gas testing to measure pH, PaO2, PaCO2, and HCO3−, to assess gas exchange and acid-base balance.

throat culture.definition: A diagnostic test in which a swab from the back of the throat is cultured on appropriate media to detect bacterial organisms causing pharyngitis (most commonly group A Streptococcus); results take about 24–48 hours and help confirm infection and guide antibiotic treatment.

nasopharyngeal cultures.definition: A diagnostic procedure in which material collected from the nasopharynx (typically via a swab or aspirate) is cultured in the laboratory to detect and identify pathogenic bacteria or viruses responsible for respiratory infections or to assess asymptomatic carriage.

gastric washings.definition: A procedure in which saline is instilled into the stomach and the resulting fluid is aspirated to obtain gastric contents for cytology, culture, or chemical analysis (often to detect malignant cells or infections).

lung scans.definition: Imaging studies of the lungs used to visualize anatomy and assess function, typically including chest radiographs (X-ray), CT, MRI, PET, or nuclear medicine ventilation–perfusion scans, for diagnosing or evaluating infections, tumors, clots, scarring, and other lung conditions.

exogenous surfactant.definition: A preparation of pulmonary surfactant derived from animal or synthetic sources that is administered intratracheally to the lungs to replace deficient endogenous surfactant in preterm infants with neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, improving lung compliance and oxygenation.

parenteral therapy.definition: A method of delivering nutrients, fluids, and medications by routes other than the gastrointestinal tract, typically by injection or infusion (e.g., intravenous, intramuscular, or subcutaneous), used when the GI tract cannot be used.

nipple feeding.definition: An infant feeding method in which milk is delivered through a nipple (the breast or a bottle teat) and the infant sucks to extract the milk.

respiratory distress syndrome of the new.word: respiratory distress syndrome of the newborn
respiratory distress syndrome of the new.definition: A neonatal lung disease caused by deficiency of pulmonary surfactant, leading to alveolar collapse (atelectasis), decreased lung compliance, and hypoxemia; most common in preterm infants; managed with respiratory support and exogenous surfactant therapy.

idiopathic respiratory distress syndrome.definition: An acute, noncardiogenic form of respiratory failure with sudden onset of severe hypoxemia and diffuse bilateral infiltrates on chest imaging, in which no underlying cause is identified; due to increased alveolar-capillary permeability and diffuse alveolar damage, and managed with supportive care (including lung-protective ventilation and careful fluid management) while evaluation for occult precipitating factors continues.

retinopathy of prematurity.definition: An eye disease of premature infants in which abnormal retinal blood vessel development can cause scarring and retinal detachment, potentially leading to blindness; risk factors include very low birth weight and oxygen exposure; treatment options include laser therapy, cryotherapy, and sometimes anti-VEGF injections.

rsv-igiv.definition: A preparation of pooled human immunoglobulin given intravenously to provide passive immunity against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV); historically used for RSV prophylaxis in high‑risk infants, now largely superseded by palivizumab.

opiates.definition: Natural alkaloids derived from opium latex (e.g., morphine, codeine) that bind opioid receptors to produce analgesia and euphoria; they are a subset of opioids and can cause respiratory depression, constipation, and dependence.

tracheal deviation.definition: An abnormal displacement of the trachea from the midline due to intrathoracic pathology; it deviates toward the side of lung collapse or fibrosis, and away from the side of tension pneumothorax or large pleural effusion.

crepitations.definition: Crackling or bubbling sounds heard on chest auscultation, produced by air passing through fluid-filled or inflamed small airways or alveoli; commonly described as crackles or rales and heard in conditions such as pneumonia, heart failure, bronchitis, and interstitial lung disease.

friction rubs.definition: An abnormal, high-pitched, scratching or grating auscultatory sound produced by the rubbing of inflamed serous membranes (pleura or pericardium) against one another; pleural friction rub is typically heard during inspiration, while pericardial friction rub is heard in the cardiac cycle (often best at the left sternal border).

nostril flaring.definition: Widening of the nostrils (nares) during inspiration, a compensatory mechanism to reduce nasal airway resistance and improve airflow, commonly seen with increased work of breathing or airway obstruction.

retractions.definition: Inward pulling of the chest wall during inspiration (intercostal, supraclavicular, or sternal areas), a sign of increased work of breathing and potential respiratory distress, commonly due to airway obstruction, pneumonia, bronchiolitis, or asthma.

airways.definition: The tubes that take air in and out of your lungs.

hemidiaphragms.definition: One of the two muscular halves of the diaphragm that separate the thoracic and abdominal cavities; each contracts during inspiration to enlarge the thoracic cavity and is innervated by the phrenic nerve.

intercostals.definition: Muscles between the ribs that aid breathing by expanding and contracting the thoracic cage; external fibers elevate the ribs during inspiration, while internal and innermost fibers depress them during expiration, innervated by the intercostal nerves.

sternomastoids.definition: A pair of prominent neck muscles that originate from the sternum and clavicle and insert on the mastoid process; they rotate the head to the opposite side and flex the neck.

chemoreceptors.definition: Sensor cells that detect chemical stimuli (such as oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH) and convert these signals into neural activity to regulate physiological processes. Peripheral examples include the carotid and aortic bodies that monitor arterial blood gases and pH; central sensors in the brainstem respond mainly to CO2-induced changes in cerebrospinal fluid pH to modulate respiration.

central chemoreceptors.definition: Chemoreceptive neurons in the medulla oblongata that detect changes in cerebrospinal fluid pH, which reflect arterial CO2 levels; increased CO2 lowers CSF pH and stimulates ventilation; they are primarily responsive to hypercapnia and relatively insensitive to hypoxemia.

peripheral chemoreceptors.definition: Sensory receptors located in the carotid and aortic bodies that detect changes in arterial O2, CO2, and pH and transmit afferent signals to the brainstem to regulate ventilation; they mediate the hypoxic ventilatory response and complement central chemoreceptors.

hering-breuer reflex.definition: A vagally mediated reflex triggered by stretch of the lungs during inflation; pulmonary stretch receptors send impulses via the vagus nerve to the medullary respiratory centers, inhibiting inspiratory activity to terminate inspiration and prevent overinflation. It is more prominent in infants and less active during normal adult breathing.

respiratory quotient.definition: The ratio of carbon dioxide produced to oxygen consumed by the body during metabolism (VCO2/VO2), reflecting the predominant substrate being oxidized; typically ~0.7 for fat, ~0.8 for protein, and ~1.0 for carbohydrate.

respiratory rhythm.definition: The intrinsic, rhythmic pattern of breathing generated by brainstem respiratory centers (the central pattern generator) that coordinates the cyclic activation of inspiratory and expiratory muscles to produce regular breathing, modulated by chemical sensors (CO2, O2) and higher neural inputs.

airway patency.definition: The condition in which the upper and lower airways are open and free of obstruction, allowing adequate airflow for respiration.

chest radiograph.definition: A chest radiograph (chest X-ray) is an imaging study that uses X-rays to produce a two‑dimensional image of the chest, allowing evaluation of the lungs, heart size and contour, mediastinal structures, bones, and pleural spaces for infection, edema, injury, or other pathology.

lower respiratory tract infection.definition: Infections of the airways and lungs below the larynx (bronchitis, bronchiolitis, pneumonia) caused by viral or bacterial pathogens, typically presenting with cough, sputum production, fever, and dyspnea.

respiratory tract infection.definition: An infection of any part of the respiratory tract (upper or lower), usually viral in origin but can be bacterial, presenting with cough, fever, nasal congestion or discharge, sore throat, and sometimes shortness of breath or chest symptoms.

iga deficiency.definition: A primary immunodeficiency characterized by very low or absent serum immunoglobulin A (IgA) with normal IgG and IgM levels; many individuals are asymptomatic, but may have recurrent mucosal infections, allergies, autoimmune diseases, or, rarely, anaphylactic reactions to IgA-containing blood products.

fluid overload.definition: A state of excess body fluid (volume overload) resulting from an imbalance between fluid intake/retention and excretion, commonly due to heart, kidney, or liver disease or excessive IV fluids, and manifested by edema, weight gain, hypertension, and potentially dyspnea or pulmonary edema.

injection site inflammation.definition: Localized inflammatory response at the site of a parenteral injection, characterized by redness, swelling, warmth, and pain; may result from local irritation by the needle or injected solution and is usually self-limited, though infection or hypersensitivity can cause more persistent symptoms.

passive immunization.definition: Administration of preformed antibody-containing preparations to confer immediate, short-term protection or treatment against a specific pathogen or toxin, without triggering an active immune response or yielding long-lasting immunologic memory.

respiratory tract.definition: An air‑conducting system of the upper and lower airways that transports air to the lungs, conditions it (warms, humidifies, and filters), and facilitates gas exchange in the alveoli; includes the nose, nasal cavity, sinuses, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, and alveolar units.

tracheitis.definition: Inflammation of the trachea, usually acute, caused by infection or irritation, presenting with cough and often accompanied by fever, throat soreness, or hoarseness.

respiratory zone.definition: The portion of the respiratory system where gas exchange occurs, comprising the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs, and alveoli; oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveolar air.

retained placenta.definition: Failure to deliver the placenta within about 30 minutes after birth, or retention of placental tissue in the uterus after delivery, which can cause postpartum hemorrhage and may require manual removal or other intervention.

placental perfusion.definition: Flow of maternal blood through the placental intervillous spaces, enabling exchange of oxygen, nutrients, and waste between mother and fetus across the placental barrier.

extrauterine life.definition: Life outside the uterus; the period beginning at birth when the fetus is no longer in utero.

temazepam.definition: A short-acting benzodiazepine hypnotic used for the short-term treatment of insomnia; enhances GABA-A receptor–mediated inhibition to promote sleep, with potential for daytime sedation, cognitive impairment, dependence, and withdrawal with prolonged use.

tooth restoration.definition: A dental procedure to restore a damaged or decayed tooth to its normal shape, function, and appearance, typically using fillings, inlays/onlays, crowns, or veneers.

restoration contour.definition: In dentistry, restoration contour is the three-dimensional shape and margins of a dental restoration (e.g., a filling or crown) designed to mimic natural tooth anatomy, maintain proper proximal contacts and emergence profile, and support function, esthetics, and periodontal health.

restoration of cusps.definition: A dental procedure to reconstruct damaged cusps of a posterior tooth using restorative materials to restore cusp height, contour, and occlusion.

retention cyst.definition: A cyst formed when a gland's duct is obstructed, causing secretions to be retained and the duct to dilate, resulting in a cyst lined by glandular (ductal) epithelium.

retention groove.definition: A groove created in a tooth surface or restoration to provide mechanical retention for a dental prosthesis or restoration, by increasing surface area and friction to resist dislodgement.

retention form.definition: Features of a prepared tooth cavity designed to prevent the restoration from being dislodged by functional forces, typically through undercuts and converging walls that provide a mechanical lock for the restorative material.

retention pin.definition: A small surgical pin inserted to provide mechanical retention for a restoration or to stabilize and maintain alignment of bone fragments during healing.

restrictive disease.definition: A category of disorders characterized by reduced ability of the lungs to expand, resulting in decreased total lung capacity (TLC); caused by diseases of the lung parenchyma, pleura, chest wall, or neuromuscular system, and typically shows reduced FVC with a normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio.

respiratory therapy.definition: A healthcare specialty that evaluates and treats patients with breathing or cardiopulmonary disorders, using techniques such as airway management, oxygen therapy, inhaled medications, chest physiotherapy and airway clearance, pulmonary rehabilitation, and mechanical ventilation support.

respiratory system.definition: The anatomical system responsible for breathing, bringing air into the lungs for gas exchange (oxygen in, carbon dioxide out); it includes the airways (nose/mouth, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi), the lungs with alveoli, and the respiratory muscles (diaphragm and intercostals).

retinal tear.definition: A break in the neurosensory retina, typically due to vitreous traction, that can permit fluid to collect under the retina and lead to retinal detachment; treated with laser photocoagulation or cryopexy to seal the tear, or with surgical repair if detachment occurs.

retinal fissure.definition: An embryologic groove in the inferior part of the developing optic cup (the choroidal/optic fissure) that normally closes during development; failure to close can result in ocular coloboma.

photoreceptors.definition: Specialized retinal cells that detect light and convert it into electrical signals; the two main types are rods (vision in low light) and cones (color vision and high visual acuity).

hair cells.definition: A sensory receptor cell of the inner ear bearing apical stereocilia; deflection of the hair bundle by fluid movement opens mechanically gated ion channels, converting mechanical stimuli into neural signals and enabling hearing (cochlear) and balance (vestibular) functions.

reticular lamina.definition: Part of the basement membrane produced by underlying connective tissue, lying deep to the basal lamina and composed mainly of reticular fibers (type III collagen); it anchors the basement membrane to the surrounding connective tissue via anchoring fibrils (type VII collagen) and provides structural support.

reticular membrane.definition: An ultra-thin membrane composed of a network of reticular fibers (mostly type III collagen) that provides structural support and a filtration/anchoring framework in various tissues, often serving as a basement-like layer beneath epithelium or as part of connective tissue networks in organs such as lymphoid tissue.

median column reticular nuclei.definition: Not a standard anatomical term; if used, it would refer to neurons in the midline (median) portion of the brainstem reticular formation—a diffuse arousal and regulatory network with widespread projections to the thalamus and spinal cord, modulating consciousness, autonomic function, and motor tone.

medial column reticular nuclei.definition: A group of brainstem neurons located along the medial portion of the reticular formation; part of the diffuse arousal and motor regulation networks, integrating somatic and autonomic information with projections to the spinal cord and cortex.

lateral column reticular nuclei.definition: Not a standard anatomical term. If referring to the lateral reticular nucleus of the brainstem, it is a brainstem reticular formation nucleus located laterally that participates in relaying and modulating somatosensory and motor signals to the spinal cord and cerebellum, contributing to motor coordination and autonomic regulation.

reticular nucleus of the thalamus.definition: A thin shell of GABAergic neurons surrounding the thalamus that provides inhibitory modulation of thalamic relay nuclei; it receives input from cortex and thalamus and projects to other thalamic nuclei (not to cortex), thereby shaping thalamocortical signaling and rhythms.

retinocerebral angiomatosis.definition: A congenital neurocutaneous vascular disorder characterized by angiomatous malformations of the retina and brain (leptomeningeal angiomas), often with an ipsilateral facial port-wine stain, leading to seizures, focal neurologic deficits, and retinal vascular abnormalities.

retinochoroiditis.definition: Inflammation of the retina and choroid (the posterior uveal tract) of the eye; may be infectious or noninfectious and can present with focal retinal lesions and vitritis, often affecting vision.

retinodialysis.definition: Not a recognized medical term; no standard definition exists.

retinol equivalent.definition: A unit of vitamin A activity expressed as the amount of retinol that would produce the same biological effect; used to express the vitamin A activity of foods or supplements containing retinol or provitamin A carotenoids (conversion factors exist for carotenoids; this concept is now usually referred to as Retinol Activity Equivalents, RAEs).

retinoschisis.definition: Splitting of the retinal tissue into separate layers with intraretinal cystic cavities (schisis), most often in the nerve fiber layer; can be congenital or acquired (notably X-linked juvenile retinoschisis) and may cause decreased visual acuity.

retinoscope.definition: An ophthalmic instrument, handheld, used to perform retinoscopy by projecting a beam of light into the pupil and observing the movement of the retinal reflex to estimate refractive error and guide prescription of corrective lenses.

retinoblastoma.definition: A rare cancer of the eye in children.

retinoblastomata.definition: The plural of retinoblastoma; a malignant tumor of the retina, typically occurring in early childhood.

reticulum cell sarcoma.definition: A malignant neoplasm of reticular (reticuloendothelial) cells of lymphoid tissue; an historical label for what today would be classified as a histiocytic/non-Hodgkin lymphoma within the lymphoid malignancy spectrum.

reticulum.definition: A network or mesh-like structure; in anatomy, the reticulum is the second compartment of the ruminant stomach, located between the rumen and omasum.

eosinophilic granuloma.definition: A focal form of Langerhans cell histiocytosis presenting as a solitary bone lesion, characterized by infiltration of Langerhans cells with a prominent eosinophilic inflammatory component; most common in children and usually has a good prognosis when limited to one site.

hand's disease.definition: This term isn't a standard medical one. A disease of the hand refers to any pathological condition affecting the hand’s tissues—skin, joints, tendons, nerves, or bones—that causes pain, swelling, deformity, weakness, or impaired function. Etiologies may be inflammatory, degenerative, infectious, vascular, or neoplastic. If you meant a specific hand condition, please specify and I can define that.

reticulin.definition: A fine network of type III collagen fibers that provides supportive stroma for organs such as the liver, bone marrow, and lymphoid tissue; produced by reticular cells and highlighted by silver stains.

reticuloendothelioma.definition: An obsolete term for a malignant neoplasm of the reticuloendothelial (mononuclear phagocyte) system, arising from macrophages and related cells; historically used to describe histiocytic malignancies such as malignant histiocytosis or histiocytic sarcoma, often involving lymphoid tissues, liver, spleen, and bone marrow. Modern terminology more often specifies histiocytic sarcoma or related disorders.

reticuloendotheliosis.definition: Historically, a broad term for diseases of the reticuloendothelial (mononuclear phagocyte) system, involving dysfunction or proliferation of macrophages in organs such as the liver, spleen, lymph nodes, and bone marrow, leading to impaired phagocytic clearance and immune regulation.

reticulosarcoma.definition: An old term for a malignant neoplasm arising from cells of the reticuloendothelial (mononuclear phagocyte) system, principally histiocytes/macrophages; today such tumors are usually described as histiocytic sarcoma or, depending on lineage, as other non-Hodgkin lymphomas or dendritic cell sarcomas.

internal limiting membrane.definition: A thin basement membrane on the inner surface of the retina, formed primarily by Müller cell endfeet, constituting the retina's innermost layer and serving as the boundary between the retina and the vitreous.

stratum opticum.definition: The layer of the retina that contains the unmyelinated axons of retinal ganglion cells as they converge to form the optic nerve.

nerve fiber layer.definition: The inner retinal layer composed of the unmyelinated axons of retinal ganglion cells as they course toward the optic nerve head, located between the inner limiting membrane and the ganglion cell layer.

ganglion cell layer.definition: The layer of the retina that contains the cell bodies of retinal ganglion cells; their axons form the optic nerve, and this layer lies between the nerve fiber layer and the inner plexiform layer.

inner plexiform layer.definition: A retinal layer between the inner nuclear layer and the ganglion cell layer where bipolar, amacrine, and ganglion cells form synapses; it houses the synaptic sites that underlie the ON and OFF pathways and retinal signal processing.

inner nuclear layer.definition: A retinal layer that houses the cell bodies of bipolar, horizontal, and amacrine neurons (and Müller glial cells), located between the outer plexiform layer and the inner plexiform layer.

outer plexiform layer.definition: A retinal layer where photoreceptor terminals (rods and cones) form synapses with the dendrites of bipolar and horizontal cells, located between the outer nuclear layer and the inner nuclear layer.

outer nuclear layer.definition: The layer of the retina that contains the cell bodies (nuclei) of photoreceptor cells (rods and cones), located between the outer limiting membrane and the outer plexiform layer.

external limiting membrane.definition: A thin retinal layer formed by adherens junctions between Müller glial cells and photoreceptor inner segments, located at the boundary between the outer nuclear layer and the photoreceptor layer.

retinitis.definition: Inflammation of the retina, the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye, which may result from infectious, autoimmune, or inflammatory disorders and can lead to vision impairment or loss if untreated.

atherosclerotic vascular disease.definition: Atherosclerotic vascular disease is a progressive condition in which lipid-rich plaques develop in arterial walls (atherosclerosis), causing narrowing and stiffening of arteries and reduced blood flow, which can result in ischemia or infarction in affected organs (commonly coronary, carotid, and peripheral arteries).

paradoxical incontinence.definition: Leakage of urine that occurs in the setting of retention or high bladder pressure, often due to overflow from detrusor underactivity or bladder outlet obstruction; the leak happens despite the bladder not being able to store urine fully, creating a paradox between retention and leakage.

retin-a.definition: A topical retinoid containing tretinoin, a vitamin A derivative used to treat acne and reduce signs of photoaging by increasing skin cell turnover and stimulating collagen production; commonly causes irritation (redness, peeling, dryness) and is contraindicated in pregnancy.

tretinoin.definition: A retinoid comprising all-trans retinoic acid; used topically to treat acne and reduce signs of photoaging, by promoting epidermal turnover and normalizing keratinization; systemically, all-trans retinoic acid is used as differentiation therapy for acute promyelocytic leukemia.

methylene blue.definition: A blue thiazine dye used medically to treat methemoglobinemia by reducing methemoglobin back to hemoglobin; also used as a diagnostic or histologic staining agent in medical procedures.

thrombolytic agent.definition: A drug that dissolves blood clots by activating the body's fibrinolytic system, typically converting plasminogen to plasmin to degrade fibrin. Used in acute thrombotic conditions (e.g., myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, ischemic stroke) within specific time windows.

mesenteritis.definition: Inflammation of the mesentery, the fold of peritoneum that attaches the intestines to the posterior abdominal wall; a broad term that includes conditions such as mesenteric panniculitis and sclerosing mesenteritis, with inflammatory changes in mesenteric fat that may include fat necrosis and fibrosis.

sclerosis.definition: When tissues in your body get hard and thick.

sternal.definition: Relating to the sternum, the flat bone that forms the central part of the chest and anchors the rib cage.

retractor.definition: A surgical instrument used to hold back tissue to expose the operative field, either handheld or self-retaining.

retrograde.definition: In medicine, moving or occurring in the opposite direction to the normal physiological flow; used to describe backward movement or backward flow (e.g., retrograde blood flow) and, in neurology, retrograde amnesia refers to loss of previously formed memories.

retroauricular.definition: Relating to or situated behind the ear.

retrobulbar.definition: Relating to or located behind the eyeball; an anatomical region behind the eye.

urethrography.definition: Radiographic imaging of the urethra in which contrast material is introduced to visualize the urethral lumen and detect injuries, strictures, or other abnormalities (retrograde or antegrade approaches).

pelves.definition: The two pelvic bones forming the pelvic girdle; each consists of the fused hip bones (ilium, ischium, and pubis) that join with the sacrum and coccyx to form the bony ring supporting the trunk and enclosing the pelvic organs.

methysergide.definition: An ergot alkaloid–derived serotonin receptor antagonist (primarily 5-HT2) used for migraine prophylaxis; long-acting and associated with fibrotic adverse effects with prolonged use.

retroflexion.definition: A bending backward of an organ from its normal position; in gynecology, it refers to the uterus being tilted posteriorly (the fundus points toward the spine) rather than forward.

retroplacental.definition: Located behind the placenta; relating to or occurring in the space between the placental implantation site and the uterine wall.

rett.definition: A rare X-linked dominant neurodevelopmental disorder caused by variants in the MECP2 gene, typically affecting females. After a period of apparently normal development, there is regression with loss of purposeful hand skills and spoken language, emergence of stereotypic hand movements (e.g., wringing), gait abnormalities, decelerating head growth, seizures, and autistic features; management is supportive and multidisciplinary.

retrolental.definition: Located behind the crystalline lens of the eye; describing tissues, structures, or conditions posterior to the lens.

retromammary.definition: Relating to or located behind the breast tissue; the retromammary space is the potential space between the mammary gland and the pectoralis major muscle.

space.definition: An area or interval in the body between structures; it may be an actual space (a cavity) or a potential space that is normally closed but can become real if fluid, air, or tissue accumulates.

retromolar.definition: Situated posterior to the last molar tooth; describing anatomy or a region behind the molar (e.g., the retromolar area behind the mandible).

residual.definition: Something that remains after the main part has been removed or after a treatment or process; the remainder left behind. In medicine, it can refer to persistent cancer cells after therapy (residual disease) or to the volume of air remaining in the lungs after maximal exhalation (residual volume).

retromylohyoid.definition: Located behind the mylohyoid muscle; i.e., in the region posterior to the floor of the mouth (the retromylohyoid area).

retroperitoneum.definition: The retroperitoneum is the posterior compartment of the abdominal cavity, located behind the peritoneum. It contains organs and structures such as the kidneys and ureters, adrenal glands, most of the pancreas, portions of the duodenum, ascending and descending colon, and the great vessels (aorta and inferior vena cava), along with associated nerves, lymphatics, and connective tissue.

retrocecal.definition: Located behind the cecum; a structure that lies posterior to the cecum.

retrocaecal.definition: Situated behind the cecum; describing an anatomical position posterior to the caecum.

retropharyngeal.definition: Situated behind the pharynx; pertaining to the retropharyngeal space, the potential space between the pharyngeal wall and the prevertebral fascia.

peritonsillar.definition: Located around the tonsil; pertaining to the tissues or space immediately surrounding a tonsil.

htlv-1.definition: A human retrovirus of the Deltaretrovirus genus that infects CD4+ T lymphocytes and is transmitted via sexual contact, blood exposure, and from mother to child (breast milk). Most infections are asymptomatic, but a minority develop adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma or tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP); lifelong infection with no vaccine; diagnosis relies on serology and confirmatory nucleic acid testing.

retrovirus.definition: A retrovirus is an enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus that uses reverse transcriptase to convert its RNA into double-stranded DNA, which then integrates into the host genome as a provirus, enabling persistent infection (examples include HIV-1 and HTLV-1).

reyes syndrome.definition: An acute, life-threatening pediatric syndrome of encephalopathy with hepatic dysfunction and fatty liver changes that typically follows a viral infection and has been linked to aspirin use.

reverse transcriptase.definition: An RNA-dependent DNA polymerase that synthesizes complementary DNA (cDNA) from an RNA template; essential for retroviral replication and widely used in molecular biology to convert RNA into DNA for cloning, sequencing, and gene expression analyses.

rna-dependent dna polymerase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the synthesis of DNA using an RNA template (reverse transcription), essential for retroviral replication and used in molecular biology to convert RNA into complementary DNA.

reverse transcriptase inhibitor.definition: A drug that inhibits reverse transcriptase, the viral enzyme that converts RNA into DNA, thereby blocking replication of retroviruses such as HIV; includes nucleoside/nucleotide RT inhibitors (NRTIs) and non-nucleoside RT inhibitors (NNRTIs).

trendelenburg.definition: A position in which the patient lies on their back with the body tilted so that the head is lower than the feet (the feet are elevated above the head); used to improve venous return and for certain surgical procedures.

reversible brain syndrome.definition: Not a standard medical term; used to describe a spectrum of conditions causing transient cerebral dysfunction that fully or nearly fully resolves after addressing a reversible underlying cause (e.g., metabolic disturbances, toxin or drug effects, or reversible vascular/edema processes such as PRES or RCVS).

reversible obstructive airway disease.definition: A form of obstructive airway disease in which airway obstruction is reversible, usually evidenced by a meaningful rise in FEV1 (e.g., >12% and ≥200 mL) after bronchodilator administration; commonly seen in asthma and other bronchial hyperresponsiveness disorders.

exanthematous rash.definition: A widespread, symmetric red maculopapular eruption of the skin, typically resulting from a systemic infection (most commonly viral) or a drug-induced reaction.

fatty degeneration.definition: Intracellular accumulation of fat droplets (primarily triglycerides) within parenchymal cells due to an imbalance between lipid uptake/esterification and oxidation/export; most commonly affects the liver, heart, or skeletal muscle and is often reversible when the underlying cause is addressed.

liver biopsy.definition: A procedure to obtain a small sample of liver tissue for microscopic examination to diagnose liver disease, assess injury or fibrosis, and monitor response to therapy; samples can be collected percutaneously, transjugularly, or by laparoscopy.

mortality.definition: The rate at which deaths occur in a population over a specified period; the incidence of death expressed as a rate (e.g., deaths per 1,000 or 100,000 people per year).

hypertonic solutions.definition: A solution with higher osmolality than the intracellular fluid, causing water to move out of cells and leading to cell shrinkage (crenation). Clinically, hypertonic solutions (e.g., hypertonic saline) draw water from cells and are used to treat hyponatremia or cerebral edema; monitor for hypernatremia and volume overload.

revlimid.definition: A brand-name immunomodulatory drug (IMiD) whose generic form is lenalidomide; used orally to treat multiple myeloma and various hematologic cancers (e.g., mantle cell lymphoma, follicular lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, certain myelodysplastic syndromes). It modulates the immune response, inhibits angiogenesis, and reduces malignant cell growth. It carries risks of birth defects and blood-related toxicity and is typically available under restricted-use programs.

reyataz.definition: An antiretroviral protease inhibitor used to treat HIV-1 infection, typically given with ritonavir to boost levels in combination ART; it inhibits HIV protease, preventing viral maturation; common adverse effects include indirect hyperbilirubinemia with jaundice, and it has notable interactions with gastric acid–reducing agents and other CYP3A4 substrates.

embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma.definition: A malignant tumor of skeletal muscle–lineage cells (rhabdomyoblasts) arising from primitive muscle precursors; the most common soft tissue sarcoma in children, with varying rhabdomyoblastic differentiation and immunohistochemical positivity for myogenic markers (e.g., desmin, myogenin). It commonly occurs in the head and neck, genitourinary tract, or trunk and is treated with multimodal therapy (surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy) depending on stage and site.

alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma.definition: A malignant soft tissue sarcoma of skeletal muscle differentiation with an alveolar histologic pattern, commonly driven by PAX3-FOXO1 or PAX7-FOXO1 gene fusions; it occurs primarily in children and adolescents and tends to have a more aggressive course than embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma.

pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma.definition: A rare, high‑grade histologic variant of rhabdomyosarcoma seen mainly in adults, defined by marked cellular pleomorphism with rhabdomyoblastic differentiation; it typically lacks the defining translocations of other RMS subtypes and shows immunohistochemical positivity for muscle markers such as desmin, myogenin, and MyoD1.

rhabdomyoblastoma.definition: Malignant neoplasm composed predominantly of rhabdomyoblasts, the immature precursors of skeletal muscle, indicating skeletal muscle differentiation (most often seen in embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma).

head and neck.definition: An anatomical region comprising the skull and brain, including the face and sensory organs, plus the neck (cervical spine and associated soft tissues), together housing the upper airway, esophagus, and major nerves and vessels.

sinus pain.definition: Pain or pressure in the facial areas over the paranasal sinuses, usually due to inflammation of the sinus mucosa with impaired drainage (acute or chronic sinusitis); commonly accompanied by nasal congestion and facial tenderness.

rhesus factor.definition: A protein antigen (D antigen) on the surface of red blood cells that defines Rh blood group status; presence indicates Rh-positive, absence indicates Rh-negative. In pregnancy, an Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive fetus can develop antibodies against the D antigen, potentially causing hemolytic disease of the newborn if not prevented.

influenza vaccination.definition: An immunization against seasonal influenza that uses inactivated or attenuated influenza virus antigens (or recombinant hemagglutinin) to stimulate an immune response and provide protection for the current flu season, usually given annually as an intramuscular injection or nasal spray.

varicella vaccination.definition: A live attenuated vaccine that protects against Varicella zoster virus (chickenpox); administered as a multi-dose series (commonly two doses in childhood) and to certain adults, it reduces the risk of varicella infection and its complications.

barium x-ray.definition: A diagnostic radiographic examination in which the patient ingests a radiopaque barium sulfate contrast that coats the lining of the gastrointestinal tract, allowing X-ray images to delineate the esophagus, stomach, and intestines to detect structural or mucosal abnormalities.

icp monitor.definition: A device implanted to measure intracranial pressure and guide management of raised ICP; common forms include intraventricular catheters (which can drain CSF) and intraparenchymal sensors that provide continuous pressure readings.

disinfection.definition: Process of reducing or eliminating pathogenic microorganisms on inanimate objects or surfaces to levels considered safe; does not necessarily destroy all microorganisms or spores and is distinct from sterilization (which aims to eliminate all forms of microbial life) and antisepsis (which applies to living tissue).

rh_antiserum.definition: An anti-D immunoglobulin preparation (Rh(D) immune globulin) used to prevent Rh alloimmunization in Rh-negative individuals exposed to Rh-positive red blood cells, typically given to pregnant Rh-negative women at about 28 weeks gestation and within 72 hours after delivery or any event causing fetomaternal hemorrhage.

rhesus_factor.definition: A protein antigen (the D antigen) on the surface of red blood cells that determines the Rh blood group; presence of the antigen indicates Rh positivity, while its absence indicates Rh negativity. Clinically important for transfusion compatibility and for the risk of hemolytic disease of the newborn in pregnancy.

rheumatic_fever.definition: An inflammatory autoimmune response that develops after infection with Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes), usually after untreated or inadequately treated strep throat; features migratory polyarthritis, carditis (which can lead to rheumatic heart disease), chorea, subcutaneous nodules, and erythema marginatum. Treated with antibiotics and anti-inflammatory therapy.

rheumatic_heart_disease.definition: Chronic valvular heart disease caused by rheumatic fever following a group A Streptococcus infection; most commonly affects the mitral valve, causing stenosis or regurgitation and leading to heart failure and other complications.

rheumatic_arteritis.definition: Not a standard or recognized medical term; if used, it would imply inflammation of arteries in the setting of rheumatic disease, but there is no distinct entity by that name.

rheumatic_endocarditis.definition: A type of endocarditis that occurs as part of acute rheumatic fever, caused by an autoimmune reaction to group A Streptococcus infection, resulting in inflammation of the heart valves (most often the mitral and aortic valves) with small vegetations along their lines of closure that can lead to chronic valvular disease.

rheumatic_carditis.definition: Inflammation of the heart due to acute rheumatic fever, typically involving the endocardium, myocardium, and pericardium (pancarditis), often leading to rheumatic valvular disease.

rheumatic_chorea.definition: An immune‑mediated neurological manifestation of acute rheumatic fever presenting with abrupt, irregular involuntary choreiform movements (often of the face and limbs), hypotonia, and emotional/behavioral disturbances, typically appearing weeks after a streptococcal throat infection.

sydenhams_chorea.definition: An autoimmune choreiform movement disorder that develops after a streptococcal infection as part of acute rheumatic fever; characterized by rapid, involuntary, irregular movements (chorea), emotional lability, and hypotonia, often resolving over weeks to months.

retinal_detachment.definition: When part of your eye pulls away from its normal position.

rhegmatogenous.definition: Relating to rupture or tearing; in ophthalmology, a retinal detachment that results from a retinal break allowing vitreous fluid to accumulate under the retina.

rheumatic_nodules.definition: Subcutaneous nodules seen in acute rheumatic fever; painless, firm nodules over extensor surfaces and pressure points (e.g., elbows, knees, Achilles tendons) representing granulomatous inflammation with central fibrinoid necrosis; one of the major Jones criteria and typically resolve with treatment.

subcutaneous_nodules.definition: Firm, raised lumps beneath the skin caused by inflammatory, granulomatous, or metabolic processes; most commonly rheumatoid nodules in rheumatoid arthritis, but they can also occur with sarcoidosis, gout (tophi), infections, and other systemic diseases; they are typically non-tender.

migratory_polyarthritis.definition: A pattern of inflammatory arthritis in which pain, swelling, and limitation shift from one joint to another, with each affected joint involved for a limited period before symptoms migrate to a different joint.

erythema_marginatum.definition: A nonpruritic, evanescent, ring-shaped erythema with sharply defined margins and central clearing, typically seen in acute rheumatic fever.

aortic_stenosis.definition: When the valve for your aorta doesn't open enough and blocks the flow of blood to your heart.

mitral_valve_stenosis.definition: Occurs when the mitral valve between the 2 halves of the heart does not fully open, so less blood flows to the body.

chordae_tendineae.definition: Tendinous cords that connect the leaflets of the atrioventricular valves (mitral and tricuspid) to the papillary muscles in the ventricles, preventing prolapse of the valve leaflets during ventricular systole.

rheumatoid_arteritis.definition: An inflammatory vasculitis associated with rheumatoid arthritis in which immune-mediated inflammation damages arterial walls, potentially causing skin lesions, neuropathy, and organ ischemia; occurs most often in long-standing RA and is treated with immunosuppressive therapy in addition to controlling the arthritis.

rheumatoid_coronary_arteritis.definition: An uncommon inflammatory vasculitis of the coronary arteries seen in rheumatoid arthritis, potentially causing stenosis, thrombosis, myocardial ischemia, or infarction.

rheumatoid_pneumoconiosis.definition: A syndrome in which rheumatoid arthritis coexists with pneumoconiosis (most often coal workers’ pneumoconiosis), leading to multiple well-defined pulmonary nodules on radiographs and potential progressive dyspnea.

caplans_syndrome.definition: A constellation of rheumatoid arthritis with pneumoconiosis (most often coal workers' pneumoconiosis) characterized by the development of multiple, round, well-defined pulmonary nodules seen on chest radiographs or CT in patients with occupational dust exposure.

strumpell_marie_disease.definition: A chronic inflammatory rheumatic disease that primarily affects the spine and sacroiliac joints, causing inflammatory back pain, stiffness, and progressive fusion of the spine. It is historically associated with Pierre Marie and Strümpell and corresponds to what is now commonly called ankylosing spondylitis.

sjogrens_syndrome.definition: A chronic autoimmune disease characterized by lymphocytic infiltration and destruction of exocrine glands, especially lacrimal and salivary glands, causing dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and dry mouth (xerostomia); can occur alone (primary) or with other autoimmune diseases (secondary) and may have systemic manifestations such as arthritis, fatigue, and organ involvement.

rheumatoid_spondylitis.definition: An inflammatory manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis affecting the spine, most often the cervical region, presenting with neck pain and stiffness from synovitis of spinal joints, with possible erosions and instability (e.g., atlantoaxial subluxation) and risk of spinal cord compression.

latex_fixation_test.definition: A serologic assay in which latex beads coated with antigen are used to detect specific antibodies in a patient’s serum by visible agglutination; historically used for various infections but now largely outdated.

c_reactive_protein.definition: A liver-produced pentameric acute-phase protein whose blood levels rise rapidly in response to inflammation or tissue injury; used as a non-specific marker of inflammation in clinical practice and to monitor disease activity or treatment response.

synovial_membranes.definition: A specialized vascular connective tissue lining the inner surface of synovial joints, tendon sheaths, and bursae that secretes synovial fluid to lubricate and nourish articular cartilage.

feltys_syndrome.definition: A rare complication of long-standing rheumatoid arthritis characterized by neutropenia and splenomegaly, often with anemia, leading to an increased risk of recurrent infections.

pulmonary_disease.definition: A broad category of disorders affecting the lungs or respiratory system, leading to impaired ventilation or gas exchange (e.g., asthma, COPD, pneumonia, interstitial lung disease).

gold_salts.definition: A class of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) historically used to treat rheumatoid arthritis; these gold-containing compounds (e.g., injectable sodium aurothiomalate and oral aurothioglucose) modulate immune and inflammatory processes in the joints. Common adverse effects include dermatitis, mucosal ulcers, nephrotoxicity, and cytopenias.

antineoplastic_drugs.definition: Chemotherapeutic agents used to treat cancer by inhibiting the growth or survival of malignant cells; they work by damaging DNA, inhibiting cell division, or blocking signaling pathways, and include cytotoxic chemotherapy drugs as well as targeted therapies.

rh_immune_globulin.definition: An anti-D immunoglobulin preparation derived from human plasma used to prevent Rh (D) alloimmunization in Rh-negative individuals after exposure to Rh-positive red blood cells; administered prophylactically during pregnancy and after events that may cause fetomaternal bleeding (e.g., delivery, abortion, miscarriage, trauma) to prevent hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn in future pregnancies. Also known as Rho(D) immune globulin.

group_a_beta_hemolytic_streptococci.definition: Beta-hemolytic, gram-positive cocci arranged in chains that belong to Lancefield group A; the prototype species is Streptococcus pyogenes. They cause pharyngitis, skin/soft-tissue infections (e.g., impetigo, cellulitis), scarlet fever, and can lead to rheumatic fever and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

beta_hemolytic_streptococci.definition: Streptococcal bacteria that produce beta-hemolysis on blood agar, showing complete lysis of red blood cells around colonies with a clear zone; they are classified by Lancefield groups (A, B, C, F, G) and include clinically important species such as Streptococcus pyogenes (group A) and Streptococcus agalactiae (group B).

scarlet_fever.definition: A disease caused by a germ (or virus) that gives you a red rash. Also called scarlatina.

rheumatic_scoliosis.definition: An acquired scoliosis that arises from inflammatory or destructive spinal involvement in rheumatic diseases (such as rheumatoid arthritis), rather than from idiopathic factors.

gastrorrhaphy.definition: Surgical suturing or repair of the stomach, typically to close a gastric wound or perforation.

botryoid_rhabdomyosarcoma.definition: An embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma variant characterized by grape-like (botryoid) polypoid masses arising in mucosal-lined hollow organs (most commonly vagina or bladder), composed of rhabdomyoblasts with myogenic differentiation.

vitreous_fluid.definition: The clear, gel-like substance that fills the vitreous cavity of the eye; it helps maintain the eye’s shape, transmits light to the retina, and supports the retina. It is composed primarily of water with collagen and hyaluronic acid.

rhinedema.definition: Edema of the nasal tissues (nasal mucosa and turbinates) causing nasal congestion and obstruction, commonly seen with allergic rhinitis, infections, sinusitis, or trauma.

rhitidosis.definition: A condition characterized by wrinkling and folding of the skin, typically due to aging, sun exposure, and loss of skin elasticity.

rh positive.definition: Presence of the D antigen (Rh factor) on red blood cells; individuals with this antigen are categorized as having a positive Rh status.

rhinocort.definition: An intranasal corticosteroid spray containing budesonide used to treat nasal symptoms of allergic and nonallergic rhinitis by reducing inflammation of the nasal mucosa (relieving sneezing, itching, congestion, and runny nose).

rhinoentomophthoromycosis.definition: A chronic fungal infection of the nasal passages and surrounding facial tissues caused by Entomophthorales fungi (most commonly Conidiobolus coronatus), characterized by progressive nasal obstruction, facial swelling, and tissue destruction, occurring mainly in tropical regions.

rhinocerebral zygomycosis.definition: A rapidly progressive angioinvasive fungal infection of the nasal sinuses with potential orbital and cerebral involvement, caused by zygomycete fungi (order Mucorales). It most often occurs in diabetics or immunocompromised individuals and presents with sinusitis, facial swelling, black necrotic eschars in the nasal mucosa or palate, fever, and cranial nerve signs. Management requires prompt surgical debridement and systemic antifungal therapy plus control of underlying risk factors.

rhinolaryngitis.definition: Inflammation of the nasal mucosa and the laryngeal mucosa, typically seen in upper respiratory tract infections; symptoms may include nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, throat irritation, hoarseness, and cough.

rhinolith.definition: A calcified mass within the nasal cavity formed around a nidus (such as a foreign body or inspissated mucus); it often causes unilateral nasal obstruction, foul discharge, and epistaxis and may lead to chronic sinusitis; treatment is surgical removal.

rhinolithiasis.definition: A calcified concretion that forms in the nasal cavity around a central nidus (often a foreign body or inspissated mucus), causing unilateral nasal obstruction and discharge and sometimes epistaxis; removed endoscopically.

rhinologist.definition: A physician who specializes in the medical and surgical management of diseases of the nose and paranasal sinuses; a subspecialist of otolaryngology (ENT) focused on rhinology.

rhinology.definition: A medical specialty focusing on the nose and paranasal sinuses, including the diagnosis and treatment of nasal obstruction, rhinitis, sinusitis, and other nasal disorders.

rhinomanometer.definition: An instrument that measures nasal airway resistance by recording the pressure–flow relationship across the nasal passages during breathing, used to assess nasal obstruction and airflow dynamics.

rhinomycosis.definition: A fungal infection of the nasal mucosa and often the paranasal sinuses (sinonasal mycosis), commonly due to Aspergillus or Mucorales species.

rhinopathy.definition: A disease or pathological condition of the nose, encompassing disorders of the nasal mucosa, cavities, or nasal structures; not limited to inflammatory processes.

rhinophycomycosis.definition: A fungal invasion of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses—typically mucormycosis—occurring mainly in immunocompromised individuals; it can cause tissue necrosis and spread to surrounding structures, requiring urgent antifungal therapy and surgical debridement.

rhinophyma.definition: A severe, disfiguring form of rosacea in which the nasal sebaceous glands and supporting tissue undergo hypertrophy, producing a thickened, enlarged, bulbous nose with a rough, irregular surface.

rhinorrhagia.definition: Bleeding from the nasal cavity; epistaxis.
