pancreatic secretion.definition: An alkaline pancreatic juice produced by the exocrine pancreas, containing digestive enzymes (amylase, lipase, proteases such as trypsinogen) and bicarbonate-rich fluid, secreted by acinar and ductal cells and delivered to the duodenum via the pancreatic duct; regulated by secretin (stimulates bicarbonate) and cholecystokinin (stimulates enzyme secretion) in response to a meal.

sedative-hypnotics.definition: A class of central nervous system depressants that produce calming (sedative) and sleep-inducing (hypnotic) effects; used for anxiety, agitation, and insomnia but carry risks of tolerance, dependence, respiratory depression, and overdose. Includes benzodiazepines, barbiturates, and non‑benzodiazepine sleep aids (Z-drugs).

rapid eye movement sleep.definition: A period of intense brain activity during sleep, often associated with dreams; named for the rapid eye movements that occur during this time. Also called dreaming sleep.

dependence.definition: Physiological and psychological reliance on a substance or behavior, marked by tolerance (needing more to achieve the same effect), withdrawal symptoms on cessation, and a compulsive pattern of use or engagement despite adverse consequences.

buspirone.definition: An azapirone anxiolytic used to treat generalized anxiety disorder; it acts as a partial agonist at serotonin 5-HT1A receptors, has a gradual onset over several weeks, and a relatively low risk of dependence compared with benzodiazepines; common adverse effects include dizziness, headache, and nausea, and it should not be used with monoamine oxidase inhibitors.

zolpidem.definition: Rapid-acting sedative-hypnotic used for short-term treatment of insomnia, especially difficulty falling asleep; a nonbenzodiazepine (Z-drug) that enhances GABA-A receptor activity to promote sleep. Common adverse effects include daytime drowsiness and dizziness; risks include tolerance, dependence, withdrawal, and complex sleep-related behaviors.

zaleplon.definition: A short-acting nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic of the Z-drug class used for short-term treatment of insomnia, particularly trouble falling asleep; it acts as a GABA-A receptor agonist with selectivity for the alpha-1 subunit, promoting rapid sleep onset with minimal daytime sedation.

nonbarbiturate-nonbenzodiazepine sedativ.definition: A class of nonbarbiturate, nonbenzodiazepine hypnotics used to treat insomnia; examples include zolpidem, zaleplon, and eszopiclone. They act on GABA-A receptors to induce sleep with a relatively rapid onset and short duration of action, but can cause daytime sedation, dependence, and complex sleep-related behaviors.

benzodiazepine derivative.definition: A compound chemically related to benzodiazepines that shares the 1,4-benzodiazepine core with various substituents; it acts as a positive allosteric modulator of the GABA-A receptor, producing anxiolytic, sedative-hypnotic, anticonvulsant, and muscle-relaxant effects.

segmental bronchus.definition: A tertiary bronchus that supplies a single bronchopulmonary segment of the lung; it branches from a lobar (secondary) bronchus and represents the third generation of the airway in the tracheobronchial tree.

segmental fracture.definition: A fracture in which two separate fracture lines isolate a middle segment of bone, resulting in three or more fragments with a free-floating intermediate piece.

segmental reflex.definition: A reflex arc in which the sensory input and motor output are mediated within a single spinal segment, so the reflex is largely localized to that segment (often via a monosynaptic connection) with minimal involvement of higher CNS centers.

segmental spinal artery.definition: An artery that originates from a segmental branch (typically a posterior intercostal or lumbar artery) and enters the vertebral canal through the intervertebral foramen to supply the spinal cord and nerve roots, via radicular branches to the roots and medullary branches that reinforce the anterior and/or posterior spinal arteries.

segmental medullary arteries.definition: Arteries arising from segmental arteries (eg, intercostal, lumbar, or sacral arteries) that enter the spinal canal via the intervertebral foramina to reinforce the spinal arteries, especially the anterior spinal artery; they are typically called radiculomedullary arteries, with the great radicular artery of Adamkiewicz being a notable example.

spinal cord segments.definition: An anatomical division of the spinal cord corresponding to each pair of spinal nerves; each segment gives rise to a dorsal (sensory) and a ventral (motor) root and contains part of the gray matter (including motor neurons) and surrounding white matter. In humans there are 31 segments: C1–C8, T1–T12, L1–L5, S1–S5, and Co1.

vertebral arteries.definition: Two arteries that arise from the subclavian arteries, ascend through the transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae, enter the skull via the foramen magnum, and join to form the basilar artery; they supply the brainstem, cerebellum, and posterior cerebral regions.

deep cervical arteries.definition: Arteries arising from the costocervical trunk that ascend posteriorly to supply the deep neck muscles and surrounding vertebral region, and that anastomose with the occipital and vertebral arteries.

posterior intercostal arteries.definition: Arteries that run along the inferior border of each rib in the posterior thorax, supplying the intercostal muscles, overlying skin, and parietal pleura of the corresponding intercostal space; there are 11 pairs on each side. The first two typically originate from the supreme intercostal artery (a branch of the costocervical trunk), and the remaining arise from the thoracic aorta.

lumbar arteries.definition: Arteries arising from the posterior aspect of the abdominal aorta in the lumbar region (usually four pairs) that supply the posterior abdominal wall and adjacent structures; each gives a dorsal branch to the back muscles and skin and a spinal (radicular) branch that enters the vertebral canal via the intervertebral foramen to supply the meninges, vertebrae, and spinal cord.

intervertebral foramina.definition: An opening on each side between adjacent vertebrae through which the spinal nerve exits the vertebral canal; formed by the superior notch of the lower vertebra and the inferior notch of the upper vertebra, and containing the dorsal root ganglion and the mixed spinal nerve.

radicular arteries.definition: Arteries that accompany the spinal nerve roots as they exit the spinal cord, supplying the nerve roots and their coverings; they arise from segmental arteries (e.g., intercostal, lumbar, lateral sacral) and are classified as anterior (ventral) radicular arteries and posterior radicular arteries.

segmental hyalinizing vasculitis.definition: A histopathologic pattern of small- to medium-vessel vasculitis in which segments of the vessel wall show hyaline (glassy) thickening and degeneration, often from immune-complex–mediated injury, with inflammatory infiltrate; the involvement is segmental (discontinuous) along the vessel rather than uniform.

segmented neutrophil.definition: A mature neutrophil with a segmented (multi-lobed) nucleus, typically 2–5 lobes, a type of polymorphonuclear leukocyte that phagocytoses bacteria as part of the innate immune response.

blastomeres.definition: A cell formed by the mitotic divisions (cleavage) of a fertilized egg (zygote) during early embryogenesis; blastomeres are the daughter cells resulting from zygotic cleavage prior to morula formation.

segmentation method.definition: A process used to partition a medical image or dataset into distinct regions corresponding to anatomical structures or tissue types, enabling measurements, analysis, and visualization; it can be manual, semi-automatic, or automatic.

segmentation nucleus.definition: A multi-lobed nuclear morphology where the nucleus appears split into two or more connected lobes; characteristic of mature neutrophils (polymorphonuclear leukocytes).

cleavage nucleus.definition: A nucleus observed in a cell during embryonic cleavage; it undergoes mitotic division as the zygote rapidly divides to form blastomeres, with little to no cytoplasmic growth between divisions.

metameres.definition: A serially repeated body segment in a segmented animal; a unit of the body plan that typically contains its own nerves, muscles, and other organ components.

seitelberger’s disease.definition: A historic neurodegenerative storage disorder characterized by the accumulation of lipofuscin-like material (ceroid lipofuscin) within neurons, leading to progressive dementia, motor decline, seizures, and vision loss, typically in childhood; now classified among the neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses (Batten disease).

infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy.definition: An autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder of infancy characterized by early hypotonia and developmental delay with progressive motor and cognitive decline, optic atrophy, and seizures; neuropathology reveals neuroaxonal spheroids (axonal swellings) throughout the central nervous system, typically due to biallelic mutations in PLA2G6.

seizure precautions.definition: Seizure precautions are safety measures to protect a person from injury during a seizure and to facilitate prompt management; they include clearing the area of hazards, loosening restrictive clothing, protecting the head, not restraining the person or placing objects in the mouth, turning the person onto their side after the seizure ends, timing and documenting the event, monitoring airway and breathing, and ensuring access to emergency equipment and prescribed rescue medications.

seizure management.definition: An approach to preventing, recognizing, and treating seizures, including immediate first-aid during a seizure, emergency management of prolonged seizures with benzodiazepines, diagnostic workup to identify underlying causes, and long-term antiseizure therapy with safety measures tailored to the seizure type.

seizure threshold.definition: The level of neuronal excitability or stimulus required to provoke a seizure; a lower threshold indicates greater susceptibility to seizures, while a higher threshold indicates lower susceptibility. It can be modulated by genetics, sleep, medications, metabolic state, and brain injury.

seizure control.definition: The prevention or reduction of seizure frequency, duration, and severity in people with seizure disorders, typically achieved with antiseizure medications, lifestyle and trigger management, and, when indicated, surgical or neuromodulatory therapies.

selective angiography.definition: A radiologic procedure in which a catheter is guided into a specific artery and iodinated contrast is injected to visualize that artery and its branches, enabling imaging of a targeted vascular territory for diagnosis or intervention.

selective estrogen receptor modulator.definition: A class of compounds that bind estrogen receptors and act as agonists in some tissues (e.g., bone) and antagonists in others (e.g., breast), producing tissue-selective modulation of estrogen signaling; used in hormone-related cancer therapy and osteoporosis prevention (e.g., tamoxifen, raloxifene).

serm.definition: A class of drugs that bind estrogen receptors and produce tissue-specific effects, acting as agonists in some tissues (e.g., bone) and antagonists in others (e.g., breast tissue); used in estrogen receptor–positive breast cancer and osteoporosis prevention (examples: tamoxifen, raloxifene).

selective iga deficiency.definition: Very low or absent serum and secretory IgA with normal levels of other immunoglobulins; a common primary immunodeficiency. Many individuals are asymptomatic, but some experience recurrent mucosal infections (especially sinopulmonary and gastrointestinal), allergies or autoimmune diseases, and there is an increased risk of anaphylaxis to IgA-containing blood products.

selective immunoglobulin deficiency.definition: A primary immunodeficiency in which one immunoglobulin class is reduced or absent while others are normal, most commonly IgA; individuals may have increased susceptibility to mucosal infections and sometimes allergic or autoimmune conditions, though many are asymptomatic.

selective mutism.definition: An anxiety disorder of childhood characterized by a persistent inability to speak in certain social settings (such as school) despite speaking in other contexts, often due to fear of embarrassment. Not attributable to a speech or language disorder; onset typically before age 5 and can interfere with education and social functioning. Treatment usually involves behavioral therapy (e.g., CBT with gradual exposure), family involvement, and sometimes medication for coexisting anxiety.

selective neuronal necrosis.definition: Selective neuronal necrosis describes death of particular neuron types that are especially vulnerable to insults (such as hypoxia/ischemia, metabolic disturbances, or excitotoxic injury), resulting in necrosis of those populations while neighboring neurons are relatively preserved.

ssri.definition: A class of antidepressants that selectively inhibits the reuptake of serotonin (5-HT) into presynaptic neurons, increasing serotonin levels in the synaptic cleft; used to treat major depressive disorder and various anxiety disorders.

selenomethionine.definition: An organic form of selenium in which selenium substitutes for sulfur in the amino acid methionine; it is a major dietary source of selenium and can be non-specifically incorporated into body proteins in place of methionine, acting as a selenium reservoir that can be metabolized to other selenium compounds.

selenious acid.definition: An inorganic oxoacid of selenium (selenious acid) with the chemical formula H2SeO3; selenium is in the +4 oxidation state; a weak diprotic acid that forms selenite (SeO3^2−) salts on deprotonation.

percutaneous catheter.definition: A flexible tube inserted through the skin into a blood vessel or body cavity to provide access for infusion or withdrawal of fluids, administration of therapies, drainage, or monitoring.

xeroradiography.definition: A radiographic method in which X-ray exposure creates a latent electrostatic image on a xerographic (photoconductive) plate, which is developed with dry toner to produce a high-contrast, edge-enhanced image, typically transferred to paper; historically used for mammography and other radiographs but largely replaced by modern film/screen and digital radiography.

parathyroid tumors.definition: Neoplasms arising from the parathyroid glands; they are most often benign solitary adenomas but can be hyperplastic (involving multiple glands) or malignant (parathyroid carcinoma). They typically secrete excess parathyroid hormone, causing primary hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcemia and symptoms such as kidney stones, bone pain, fatigue, constipation, polyuria, and neuropsychiatric changes. Treatment is surgical removal, with histology distinguishing adenoma, hyperplasia, and carcinoma.

urogenital infections.definition: An umbrella term for infections affecting the urinary tract and/or genital organs, caused by bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites; includes urinary tract infections (cystitis, urethritis, pyelonephritis) and genital tract infections (vaginitis, cervicitis, balanitis, prostatitis, epididymitis); symptoms depend on site and may include dysuria, urinary frequency/urgency, discharge, itching, pelvic or lower abdominal pain, and fever.

squamous carcinoma.definition: A malignant neoplasm arising from squamous epithelium, characterized by squamous differentiation (keratinization and intercellular bridges); it commonly affects skin and mucosal surfaces and has the potential for local invasion and metastasis.

squamous epithelioma.definition: A malignant neoplasm arising from squamous epithelium, typically a squamous cell carcinoma of the skin or mucous membranes.

urinary meatus.definition: The external opening of the urethra through which urine exits the body; in males it is located at the tip of the penis, and in females it lies between the clitoris and the vaginal opening.

kidney infection.definition: An infection of the kidney caused by bacteria ascending from the urinary tract, leading to renal inflammation; commonly presents with fever, flank or groin pain, and urinary symptoms, and is treated with antibiotics.

renal disorders.definition: An umbrella term for diseases that affect kidney structure or function, causing impaired filtration, accumulation of waste, and disturbances of electrolyte and fluid balance; examples include acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease, glomerular and tubular disorders, nephrolithiasis, and obstructive nephropathy.

semicircular canal.definition: One of three looped channels in the inner ear’s vestibular system filled with endolymph that detects angular (rotational) head movements via hair cells in the ampulla, helping maintain balance.

crista ampullaris.definition: In the inner ear, a sensory receptor in the ampulla of each semicircular canal; it contains hair cells embedded in a gelatinous cupula and detects angular (rotational) acceleration via deflection of hair bundles in response to endolymph movement.

ethmoid cells.definition: Air-filled, mucosa-lined cavities within the ethmoid bone (the ethmoid labyrinth), part of the paranasal sinuses; arranged into anterior, middle, and posterior groups and draining into the middle nasal meatus.

ethmoid infundibulum.definition: An air-filled, funnel-shaped passage in the lateral wall of the nasal cavity formed by the uncinate process of the ethmoid bone; it serves as the drainage conduit from the frontal sinus (via the frontonasal duct) and the anterior ethmoid air cells into the middle meatus.

plica semilunaris conjunctivae.definition: A small crescent-shaped fold of bulbar conjunctiva at the medial canthus of the eye, representing a vestigial remnant of the nictitating membrane (third eyelid).

semilunar hiatus.definition: A crescent-shaped groove in the lateral wall of the middle meatus of the nasal cavity, forming part of the ostiomeatal complex and serving as the drainage pathway for the maxillary sinus (via the maxillary sinus ostium and infundibulum).

bulla of the ethmoid bone.definition: A rounded prominence on the lateral wall of the middle nasal meatus formed by the middle ethmoidal air cells; marks the ostium of the middle ethmoidal sinus.

seminal vesicle cyst.definition: A cystic dilation of the seminal vesicle, typically due to obstruction of the seminal vesicle/ejaculatory duct or congenital maldevelopment; may be isolated or associated with ipsilateral renal agenesis (as in Zinner syndrome); often asymptomatic but can cause pelvic pain, hematospermia, painful ejaculation, or infertility; managed from observation to surgical drainage or excision if symptomatic.

seminal vesiculitis.definition: Inflammation of the seminal vesicles, usually due to bacterial infection; presents with perineal or pelvic pain, fever, painful ejaculation, dysuria, or hematospermia, and is often associated with prostatitis. Diagnosis is clinical with supporting urinalysis and imaging; treated with targeted antibiotics and supportive care.

seminiferous cords.definition: A transient embryologic structure in the developing testis: solid cords of germ cells (gonocytes) surrounded by Sertoli cells that later canalize to form the seminiferous tubules.

seminiferous epithelium.definition: A germinal epithelium lining the seminiferous tubules of the testes, composed of Sertoli cells and developing germ cells (spermatogonia, spermatocytes, spermatids) and supporting spermatogenesis; forms part of the blood–testis barrier.

seminomas.definition: A malignant germ cell tumor of the testis, typically presenting as a painless testicular mass in young men; histology shows uniform cells with clear cytoplasm arranged in a “fried-egg” pattern, and it is highly radiosensitive with high cure rates after orchiectomy plus radiotherapy or chemotherapy. Serum AFP is usually normal, though beta-hCG may be elevated in some cases due to scattered trophoblastic cells, and metastasis commonly involves retroperitoneal lymph nodes.

sperm count.definition: A measurement of how many sperm cells are present in a given volume of semen, usually expressed as millions of sperm per milliliter; used in semen analysis to evaluate male fertility (low counts are called oligospermia).

semen analysis.definition: A laboratory test of a semen sample to evaluate male fertility by measuring semen volume, sperm concentration and total count, motility, morphology, and other parameters such as pH and liquefaction time.

cricoid pressure.definition: A technique in which backward pressure is applied to the cricoid cartilage to occlude the esophagus against the cervical spine, with the aim of preventing regurgitation and aspiration during induction of anesthesia or airway management.

sellick maneuver.definition: A technique used during airway management where firm backward pressure is applied to the cricoid cartilage to compress the esophagus against the vertebral bodies, with the aim of reducing the risk of regurgitation and aspiration during induction of anesthesia or rapid sequence intubation.

foley catheter.definition: A flexible indwelling urinary catheter inserted through the urethra (or occasionally via a suprapubic route) and secured by an inflatable balloon to drain urine continuously from the bladder.

self-retaining catheter.definition: A urinary catheter inserted through the urethra into the bladder and secured in place by an inflatable retention balloon near the catheter tip, allowing continuous drainage and preventing accidental withdrawal.

semiautomatic external defibrillator.definition: A device used to treat sudden cardiac arrest by delivering an electrical shock to the heart; it analyzes the heart rhythm, charges automatically when a shock is indicated, and requires the operator to press a button to deliver the shock.

semicomatose.definition: State of severely depressed consciousness between stupor and coma, with markedly reduced responsiveness to external stimuli; the patient may only respond to strong or painful stimuli and is usually not oriented or able to engage in purposeful activity.

semiconscious.definition: Partially conscious; an impaired state between waking and unconsciousness in which the person can be aroused by stimuli but has limited awareness and responsiveness.

stupor.definition: A state of lethargy and unresponsiveness.

obtundation.definition: Obtundation is a decreased level of consciousness characterized by dulled arousal and reduced responsiveness to stimuli, with slower thinking and replies; it lies between lethargy and stupor.

selsun.definition: A brand-name topical shampoo containing selenium sulfide used to treat dandruff (seborrheic dermatitis) and, sometimes, tinea versicolor by antifungal action; applied to wet hair, left on the scalp for several minutes, then rinsed.

selzentry.definition: Maraviroc, a CCR5 receptor antagonist antiretroviral used with other HIV therapies to treat HIV-1 infection in adults and in children aged 2 years and older who have CCR5-tropic virus; it is not active against CXCR4-tropic or dual/mixed-tropic HIV and requires tropism testing before starting. It can cause hepatotoxicity and drug interactions with potent CYP3A inhibitors or inducers.

urethral crest.definition: A longitudinal mucosal crest on the posterior wall of the prostatic urethra, formed by the folds of the prostatic ducts; it runs along the prostatic urethra and bears the openings of the prostatic ducts on its sides near the verumontanum.

ejaculatory ducts.definition: Two short ducts formed by the union of the ductus deferens and the seminal vesicle ducts; they traverse the prostate and open into the prostatic urethra, delivering semen during ejaculation.

sims' position.definition: A left lateral decubitus position in which the patient lies on the left side with the left leg extended and the right knee flexed toward the chest; the left arm is positioned behind the body and the right arm in front. It is used for rectal examinations and enema administration.

semi-fowler's position.definition: A bed position in which the patient lies supine with the head of the bed elevated to about 30 to 45 degrees (often with the knees supported or flexed).

semirecumbent.definition: A position in which a patient lies on their back with the head and upper body elevated, typically about 30–45 degrees, rather than fully horizontal.

semispinalis.definition: A deep back muscle in the transversospinalis group, comprising the capitis, cervicis, and thoracis portions; it extends the head and vertebral column and, when contracting unilaterally, rotates the spine to the opposite side.

semisupine.definition: A body position in which a person lies on their back with the head and trunk elevated somewhat, producing a semi-reclining (partially upright) posture.

semisynthetic.definition: A drug or compound derived from a natural product that has been chemically modified to improve properties such as potency, spectrum of activity, or pharmacokinetics.

semicircular duct.definition: A membranous duct inside one of the semicircular canals of the inner ear; filled with endolymph and containing hair cells in the ampulla that detect angular (rotational) head movements.

gastric contents.definition: A semi-liquid mixture in the stomach composed of ingested food, swallowed saliva, and gastric secretions (gastric juice containing acid, mucus, and digestive enzymes) that is churned by gastric motility to form chyme.

seneciosis.definition: A hepatic disease caused by poisoning with pyrrolizidine alkaloids from Senecio (groundsel) plants, leading to hepatic veno-occlusive disease (sinusoidal obstruction syndrome) and progressive liver injury.

senecio.definition: A genus of flowering plants in the Asteraceae family; some species contain hepatotoxic pyrrolizidine alkaloids that can cause liver injury, including veno-occlusive disease, when ingested.

ragwort.definition: A toxic flowering plant in the Asteraceae (daisy) family that contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids and can cause severe liver damage in grazing livestock and humans when ingested; a common pasture weed and contaminant of stored hay.

senile cataract.definition: A cataract arising from aging of the lens, causing progressive opacification and painless decline in vision; treated by surgical removal of the cloudy lens with intraocular lens implantation (commonly by phacoemulsification).

senile dental caries.definition: An age-related form of dental caries seen in older adults, typically involving exposed root surfaces due to gingival recession and reduced salivary flow; caused by demineralization of root dentin (and cementum) with potential cavitation if untreated.

senile tremor.definition: A benign postural tremor of the hands that commonly occurs with advancing age; typically mild, most evident when the hands are held outstretched or during activity, and not generally associated with a neurodegenerative disease.

senile vaginitis.definition: A postmenopausal atrophic vaginitis due to estrogen deficiency, causing thinning and drying of the vaginal epithelium with decreased lubrication, irritation or itching, burning, and dyspareunia; often with minimal discharge and an increased vaginal pH, increasing infection risk.

senile wart.definition: A benign, pigmented epidermal lesion seen in older adults, classically presenting as a waxy, “stuck-on” plaque or nodule; commonly referred to as seborrheic keratosis. It is not contagious and is rarely malignant; usually asymptomatic but may itch or be irritated, with treatment offered for cosmetic reasons (e.g., cryotherapy or curettage).

senility.definition: A historically used, non-specific term for age-related cognitive decline, including memory loss and confusion, often associated with dementia; not a precise medical diagnosis.

sennetsu fever.definition: A rare, mild, self-limited febrile illness caused by an Ehrlichia species transmitted by ingestion of raw or undercooked fish; presents with fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and mild hepatitis; diagnosed serologically or by PCR; usually resolves without antibiotics, though doxycycline can be used in more severe cases.

ehrlichia sennetsu.definition: An obligate intracellular Gram-negative bacterium of the genus Ehrlichia that causes Sennetsu fever in humans; transmitted by ingestion of raw fish, resulting in a mild febrile illness with fever, malaise, and sometimes lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly.

senopia.definition: An age-related decline in near vision caused by decreased accommodation of the crystalline lens (often due to lens hardening), typically starting in the 40s; presents with difficulty focusing on close objects and the need for reading glasses. Also known as presbyopia.

nucleus gracilis.definition: A nucleus in the dorsal medulla oblongata containing the second-order neurons of the dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway for the lower body; it receives input from the gracile fasciculus and sends crossed axons (internal arcuate fibers) that form the medial lemniscus to the thalamus, mediating fine touch, vibration, and conscious proprioception from the lower limbs and trunk.

nucleus cuneatus.definition: Paired somatosensory nuclei in the dorsal medulla oblongata that receive fine touch and proprioception from the upper limbs and upper trunk (via the fasciculus cuneatus) and project second-order fibers that decussate to form the medial lemniscus.

fasciculus gracilis.definition: A dorsal column–medial lemniscus ascending sensory tract that transmits fine touch, vibration, and proprioception from the lower body (below T6) to the gracile nucleus in the medulla, where fibers decussate to form the medial lemniscus.

fasciculus cuneatus.definition: A dorsal-column tract that conveys discriminative touch, vibration, and proprioception from the upper limbs and upper trunk above the T6 level; it ascends ipsilaterally to the medulla and synapses in the nucleus cuneatus, after which the pathway continues via the dorsal-column–medial lemniscus to the thalamus.

dorsal spinocerebellar tract.definition: An ascending somatosensory pathway that carries unconscious proprioceptive information from muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs of the lower body to the ipsilateral cerebellum; fibers originate in Clarke's column (nucleus dorsalis) in the spinal cord, ascend in the dorsal funiculus, and terminate in the ipsilateral cerebellar cortex via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.

ventral spinocerebellar tract.definition: An ascending spinal tract that transmits unconscious proprioceptive information from the limbs to the cerebellum; its fibers originate from spinal interneurons, cross to the contralateral side in the spinal cord and again in the brainstem, and enter the cerebellum via the superior cerebellar peduncle to aid in coordinating movement.

spinocerebellar tract.definition: A set of ascending spinal pathways that carry unconscious proprioceptive information about limb and trunk position and movement from the spinal cord to the cerebellum to help coordinate posture and movement.

delayed sensation.definition: A delay in the perception of a sensory stimulus after its application, resulting in sensation occurring later than expected; may arise from peripheral neuropathy, nerve injury, demyelination, or central processing abnormalities and can affect touch, temperature, pain, or proprioception.

referred sensation.definition: A sensory perception perceived at a location other than the actual source of stimulation or pathology, caused by convergence of afferent fibers from different tissues onto shared central neurons, leading to mislocalization of the sensation.

sensory receptor.definition: A specialized cell or nerve ending that detects a specific stimulus (e.g., light, sound, touch, chemical) and transduces it into an electrical signal conveyed to the central nervous system.

sensorineural.definition: Relating to the sensory (cochlear) and neural (auditory nerve) components of hearing; in audiology, a type of hearing loss caused by damage to the inner ear or auditory pathway rather than the outer or middle ear.

sensorimotor therapy.definition: A body-based therapeutic approach that aims to improve emotional and cognitive function by integrating sensory processing with motor function, typically through movement, grounding, and awareness of bodily sensations to regulate the nervous system.

sensory processing.definition: The process by which the nervous system receives, interprets, and integrates sensory information from the body and environment to produce appropriate perception and behavior.

sensory deprivation.definition: A condition in which sensory input is reduced or eliminated, leading to decreased stimulation of the senses (such as sight, hearing, or touch) and potentially causing perceptual, cognitive, or emotional changes; prolonged deprivation can cause disorientation, anxiety, or hallucinations.

sensory pathway.definition: A neural pathway that carries sensory information from peripheral receptors to the central nervous system, typically via a sequence of three neurons (first-order from receptor to CNS, second-order within the CNS, and third-order to the cerebral cortex) for conscious perception.

antibiotic sensitivity test.definition: A laboratory test that determines which antibiotics are effective against a bacterial isolate by measuring growth inhibition in the presence of different drugs (e.g., disk diffusion or minimum inhibitory concentration), guiding appropriate antimicrobial therapy and detecting resistance.

dissection.definition: The careful cutting and separation of tissues along natural planes to expose anatomy for study or surgical exposure; also used to describe a tear in the wall of a blood vessel with separation of its layers (as in aortic dissection).

lymphatic drainage.definition: Drainage of interstitial fluid, proteins, and waste products from tissues into the lymphatic system, which transports them through progressively larger lymphatic vessels and returns them to the venous circulation; essential for fluid balance and immune function.

breast tumor.definition: An abnormal growth or lump in the breast tissue resulting from uncontrolled cell proliferation; it may be benign (noncancerous), such as a fibroadenoma or cyst, or malignant (cancerous), such as breast carcinoma, which can invade surrounding tissues and spread to other parts of the body.

virchow's node.definition: A left supraclavicular lymph node enlargement that often indicates metastatic disease from intra-abdominal malignancies, most commonly gastric cancer; may also be caused by pancreatic, colorectal, ovarian, or other cancers, and typically presents as a hard, non-tender lump in the left supraclavicular region.

seoul virus.definition: An Old World hantavirus carried by the brown rat (Rattus norvegicus) that can cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in humans, transmitted via inhalation or contact with infected rodent urine, feces, or saliva.

somatosensory evoked potential.definition: A neurophysiologic test in which electrical stimuli are delivered to a peripheral nerve and the resulting evoked responses are recorded along the somatosensory pathways to the cortex, assessing the integrity and conduction of the dorsal columns and central somatosensory pathways (measured by latency and amplitude). Used for intraoperative monitoring and evaluation of sensory pathway function.

separating spring.definition: A small orthodontic appliance—a metal spring placed between neighboring teeth to apply a gentle separating force, thereby widening the interproximal space to allow for banding or subsequent tooth movement; removed once adequate space is achieved.

separating wire.definition: A slender, temporary wire placed between adjacent teeth to exert gentle, continuous pressure that separates the teeth to create space for orthodontic bands or other dental procedures; it is typically removed after space is achieved.

separation agent.definition: A substance used to facilitate separation of tissue planes or other surfaces during a medical procedure by reducing friction or adhesion, or by chemically loosening attachments.

separation anxiety.definition: An excessive, developmentally inappropriate fear or distress about being apart from home or attachment figures, causing significant impairment in functioning; commonly manifests in children as clinginess, reluctance to go to school or away from a caregiver, nightmares about separation, and somatic complaints.

separator.definition: An object or substance used to create or maintain a boundary between two adjacent tissues or substances, such as a dental separator that creates space between teeth or a gel used to separate plasma from cells during centrifugation.

space maintainer.definition: A dental appliance used to preserve the space left by an early loss of a tooth, primarily in children, to prevent adjacent teeth from shifting and to maintain space for the eruption of the permanent tooth; it can be fixed (e.g., band-and-loop, lingual holding arch) or removable.

serum erythropoietin.definition: The circulating glycoprotein hormone erythropoietin, produced mainly by the kidneys, that stimulates red blood cell production in the bone marrow; serum levels reflect erythropoietic activity and are used to evaluate and manage anemia.

septorhinoplasty.definition: A surgical procedure that combines septoplasty (straightening the nasal septum) and rhinoplasty (reshaping the nose) to improve nasal airflow and facial appearance.

septostomy.definition: A surgical or percutaneous procedure to create or enlarge an opening in a septum (the wall between two chambers), thereby establishing or increasing communication between the compartments; commonly performed as an atrial septostomy to improve blood mixing in certain congenital heart defects.

septra.definition: A combination antibiotic of trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole; used to treat a range of bacterial infections (e.g., urinary tract infections, bronchitis) and to prevent or treat Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, by inhibiting bacterial folate synthesis.

cotrimoxazole.definition: A fixed-dose antibiotic combining sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim; it inhibits two consecutive steps in bacterial folate synthesis, producing a synergistic bactericidal effect. Used to treat a range of infections such as urinary tract infections, certain respiratory infections, otitis media, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis or treatment.

septic sore throat.definition: A historical term for a severe throat infection (pharyngitis/tonsillitis) accompanied by systemic illness or sepsis; not a precise modern diagnosis—today's practice classifies by etiology (eg, streptococcal pharyngitis) or by presence of sepsis.

de morsier's syndrome.definition: A congenital disorder of GnRH deficiency with defective olfactory development, presenting as hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia or hyposmia; caused by defective migration of GnRH-releasing neurons and olfactory neurons, often with olfactory bulb hypoplasia or aplasia; puberty is delayed or absent.

transparent septum.definition: Not a standard medical term. If used descriptively, it would refer to a septum with unusually thin, translucent tissue (such as a nasal, interatrial, or interventricular septum) that allows light or imaging to pass through; there is no distinct anatomical structure officially named "transparent septum."

septuplet.definition: One of seven offspring born in a single delivery.

endotoxins.definition: A lipopolysaccharide component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria that is released upon bacterial cell death; it activates the host inflammatory response (via TLR4), commonly causing fever and, in severe cases, septic shock.

exotoxins.definition: Secreted protein toxins produced by living bacteria that damage host cells or disrupt physiological processes; they are usually highly potent and act at specific cellular targets, and are distinct from endotoxins that are part of the bacterial cell wall and released upon lysis.

vasopressors.definition: Drugs that cause vasoconstriction and raise blood pressure by stimulating vascular smooth muscle adrenergic receptors (primarily alpha-1), thereby increasing systemic vascular resistance; used to treat hypotension in shock, during anesthesia, and other critical-care settings.

volume expanders.definition: Agents used to increase intravascular volume in patients with hypovolemia or shock, thereby restoring preload and tissue perfusion. They include crystalloids (e.g., normal saline, balanced crystalloids) that rapidly distribute into the interstitial space, and colloids (e.g., albumin, synthetic starches) that largely stay intravascular; in some cases, blood products are used as volume expanders.

gi system.definition: A series of connected organs responsible for ingestion, digestion, absorption of nutrients, and elimination of waste; comprises the alimentary canal (mouth, esophagus, stomach, small and large intestines, anus) and accessory organs such as the liver, pancreas, and gallbladder.

pullularia pullulans.definition: An environmental, pigmented, yeast-like fungus (historically named Pullularia pullulans; now usually Aureobasidium pullulans). It is a saprophyte on damp surfaces and can rarely cause opportunistic infections in humans; it produces the extracellular polysaccharide pullulan.

graphium.definition: Not a recognized term in standard medical terminology; it does not refer to any anatomy, disease, or procedure in medicine.

optic disc hypoplasia.definition: Congenital underdevelopment of the optic nerve head, resulting in a smaller-than-normal optic disc with thinning of the retinal nerve fiber layer and diminished visual function. It can affect one or both eyes and is often associated with midline brain abnormalities such as septo-optic dysplasia.

growth deficiency.definition: Growth deficiency is a failure to achieve normal growth in height or size for age and sex, due to hormonal, nutritional, chronic disease, genetic, or psychosocial factors.

ser-ap-es.definition: I can’t locate a medical term matching that spelling. Could you confirm the correct spelling or provide context (anatomical area, condition, or language)? If you meant a different term, I can define it.

serax.definition: A benzodiazepine anxiolytic (oxazepam) used for short-term relief of anxiety and for alcohol withdrawal; it enhances GABA-A receptor activity, producing calming and sedative effects; adverse effects include drowsiness and dizziness, with risk of dependence and withdrawal. Use with caution in pregnancy, the elderly, and liver disease.

serentil.definition: A brand-name phenothiazine antipsychotic used to treat schizophrenia; a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist in the brain, with common adverse effects including extrapyramidal symptoms and sedation.

iproniazid.definition: An irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) antidepressant formerly used to treat depression; it increases brain monoamine levels by inhibiting MAO and is associated with dietary tyramine interactions and hepatotoxicity, now largely obsolete.

radioactive substance.definition: A substance containing unstable atomic nuclei that decay spontaneously, emitting ionizing radiation (alpha, beta, and gamma rays) and releasing energy; these materials can be natural or man-made and are used in medicine, research, and industry.

serevent.definition: A brand-name inhaled long-acting beta-2 agonist (LABA) bronchodilator used for maintenance therapy in asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD); it relaxes airway smooth muscle to prevent bronchospasm and provides prolonged bronchodilation (about 12 hours); not for relief of acute bronchospasm and typically used in combination with an inhaled corticosteroid.

serial casting.definition: A nonoperative method of gradually correcting a deformity or contracture by applying a sequence of casts, each positioned to move the limb a little further toward the desired alignment; casts are changed at set intervals to allow soft-tissue lengthening and progressive realignment.

serial dilution.definition: A stepwise process in which a sample is diluted in a series of successive, fixed-ratio dilutions (for example 1:10), so that the concentration is progressively reduced and can be measured or quantified in subsequent assays.

serial extraction.definition: An orthodontic technique in which a planned sequence of tooth removals is performed to create space and guide the eruption and alignment of the remaining teeth in a growing patient.

space management.definition: An approach to planning, organizing, and optimizing the use of physical space in healthcare settings (e.g., wards, clinics, operating rooms, imaging suites) to improve patient safety, workflow, throughput, and efficient use of equipment and staff.

tipping.definition: An angular movement of a tooth (or other structure) produced by directional forces, in which the crown shifts relative to the root (tilting) rather than the entire tooth translating as a unit.

serine protease inhibitor.definition: A molecule that inhibits serine proteases (enzymes that cleave peptide bonds using an active-site serine), typically a protein such as a serpin, which blocks proteolysis and helps regulate processes like coagulation, inflammation, and digestion.

serpin.definition: A superfamily of proteins that inhibit serine proteases by a suicide substrate mechanism: each inhibitor presents a reactive center loop that, when cleaved by a protease, undergoes a conformational change that traps and inactivates the protease. They regulate proteolytic cascades in coagulation, fibrinolysis, inflammation, and immunity; examples include α1-antitrypsin and antithrombin III.

sermorelin.definition: A synthetic peptide comprising the first 29 amino acids of human growth hormone–releasing hormone (GHRH) that stimulates the anterior pituitary to release growth hormone; used to assess GH secretory capacity and to treat growth hormone deficiency, though cosmetic anti-aging use is not FDA-approved in many places.

sertraline.definition: An antidepressant in the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) class that increases serotonin levels in the brain by inhibiting the serotonin transporter (SERT); used to treat major depressive disorder and several anxiety-related conditions (e.g., OCD, panic disorder, PTSD, social anxiety disorder, and premenstrual dysphoric disorder).

seroconversion.definition: When you become immune to a disease or show signs of the disease after being infected.

serodiagnosis.definition: A diagnosis based on detection of specific antibodies or antigens in a patient’s blood serum, typically using serologic tests to identify infection or immune-mediated conditions.

serofibrinous pericarditis.definition: An inflammatory pericarditis in which the pericardial exudate is serous with fibrin strands, producing a serofibrinous coating on the visceral and parietal pericardium and often a friction rub; commonly seen with rheumatic fever, viral infections, or uremia and may progress to fibrinous adhesions.

serofibrinous pleurisy.definition: Inflammation of the pleura with a serous pleural effusion that contains fibrin, producing a serofibrinous exudate and potentially leading to adhesions between the pleural surfaces.

seroimmunity.definition: Immunity conferred by antibodies present in the blood (serum), typically passive immunity acquired through transfer of immune serum or immunoglobulin-containing preparations, providing immediate but usually temporary protection rather than active, self-generated immunity.

serological.definition: Pertaining to the study of serum and immune responses, including diagnostic tests that detect antibodies or antigens in the blood.

serological test.definition: A laboratory test that detects antibodies or antigens in blood to indicate exposure to a pathogen, active or past infection, or immune status.

serologist.definition: A laboratory scientist who specializes in serology, the study of serum and its immune components, especially tests that detect antibodies or antigens in blood.

serology.definition: A test that looks for the strength of a reaction to a disease or substance.

seroma.definition: A pocket of lymphatic fluid that builds up at an incision after surgery.

seromycin.definition: Not a standard medical term; no widely recognized definition in medical dictionaries. It may be a misspelling or a brand name. Please provide context or confirm the spelling.

seronegative.definition: Relating to the absence of detectable specific antibodies in the blood serum against a particular antigen; i.e., a negative serology test for that disease.

seropositive.definition: Having detectable antibodies in the blood serum against a specific pathogen or antigen, indicating prior exposure, infection, or immune response; a positive serologic test result.

seroprevalence.definition: The proportion of individuals in a population who have detectable antibodies to a specific pathogen at a defined time, as determined by serologic testing; reflects prior exposure or vaccination and is used to estimate immunity or exposure levels, usually expressed as a percentage.

seroprophylaxis.definition: Prophylaxis achieved by administering serum containing antibodies to provide immediate, temporary protection against a specific infectious agent (passive immunization).

seropurulent.definition: Containing both serum and pus; a purulent exudate that includes serous (serum-like) fluid.

seroreversion.definition: The loss of detectable pathogen-specific antibodies in a person who was previously seropositive, resulting in negative serology as antibody titers fall below the assay’s threshold.

serovaccination.definition: Administration of immune serum or immunoglobulins containing antibodies against a specific pathogen to confer immediate, temporary protection or treatment; a form of passive immunization rather than active immunity.

serpent ulcer.definition: An ulcer characterized by snake-like, serpiginous (creeping) margins that enlarge slowly over time, typically reflecting a chronic infectious or granulomatous process.

serpiginous ulcer.definition: A chronic, slowly enlarging ulcer with serpentine (snake-like), undulating margins that creep or spread across the skin.

serrate.definition: Having a saw-toothed edge or margin; characterized by sharp, tooth-like projections along the edge.

serrated suture.definition: A surgical suture with a serrated or barbed surface along its length to grip tissue and resist pull-out, thereby distributing tension and enabling knotless tissue approximation in some applications.

serratia.definition: A genus of Gram-negative, rod-shaped, facultatively anaerobic bacteria in the Enterobacteriaceae family; many species are opportunistic pathogens causing nosocomial infections such as urinary tract infections, pneumonia, and wound infections; some species produce a characteristic red pigment (prodigiosin).

serratus posterior.definition: Two thin muscles on the posterior thorax: the serratus posterior superior, which elevates ribs 2–5 to aid inspiration, and the serratus posterior inferior, which depresses ribs 9–12 to aid expiration; both are innervated by the anterior rami of the corresponding thoracic intercostal nerves and act as accessory muscles of respiration.

sertoli-cell–only syndrome.definition: A histopathologic condition of the testis in which the seminiferous tubules contain only Sertoli cells and lack germ cells, causing impaired or absent spermatogenesis and usually azoospermia.

serum carnosinase deficiency.definition: A rare autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by mutations leading to deficient activity of serum carnosinase (CNDP1), resulting in markedly elevated levels of the dipeptide carnosine in serum and tissues; it commonly presents in infancy with developmental delay, hypotonia, and seizures.

serum globulin.definition: A group of globular proteins in blood serum other than albumin, comprising immunoglobulins (antibodies) and various nonimmune globulins; forms the serum globulin fraction (often separated into alpha, beta, and gamma globulins by electrophoresis) and participates in immunity, transport, and other physiological roles.

sgot.definition: An enzyme (aspartate aminotransferase) that catalyzes the transfer of an amino group from aspartate to alpha-ketoglutarate; elevated serum levels indicate hepatocellular injury or muscle damage and it is used in liver function testing. It was historically measured in blood as SGOT (serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase).

serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase.definition: An enzyme (also called aspartate aminotransferase, AST) that catalyzes the transfer of an amino group from aspartate to α-ketoglutarate to form oxaloacetate and glutamate; found mainly in liver, heart, and skeletal muscle, with elevated serum levels indicating hepatocellular injury or muscle/heart damage.

serum neuritis.definition: An inflammation of a peripheral nerve believed to be mediated by immune factors in the serum (e.g., autoantibodies or immune complexes), typically causing pain, sensory disturbance, and weakness along the affected nerve's distribution.

serum osmolality.definition: A measure of the solute concentration of blood serum, expressed in milliosmoles per kilogram (mOsm/kg); determined primarily by sodium, glucose, and urea, and used to assess hydration status and fluid balance.

serum urea nitrogen.definition: A measure of the amount of nitrogen in the blood as urea; used as a rough indicator of renal function and hydration, reported as blood urea nitrogen (BUN). Levels are influenced by kidney function, hepatic urea synthesis, protein intake, and hydration status; normal ranges are lab-dependent but typically about 7–20 mg/dL (2.5–7.1 mmol/L) in adults. Elevated levels suggest reduced kidney function, dehydration, or high protein metabolism, while low levels may occur with severe liver disease or malnutrition.

severe acute respiratory syndrome.definition: An acute viral respiratory illness caused by a coronavirus that typically begins with fever, myalgia, and dry cough and can progress to pneumonia and respiratory failure; transmitted mainly by close person-to-person contact via respiratory droplets; associated with outbreaks in the early 2000s that were contained by public health measures.

sevelamer.definition: A non-calcium, non-absorbed phosphate binder used to treat hyperphosphatemia in chronic kidney disease by binding dietary phosphate in the gastrointestinal tract and preventing its absorption (available as sevelamer carbonate or sevelamer hydrochloride).

phosphate binder.definition: A medication taken with meals that binds dietary phosphate in the gastrointestinal tract, forming insoluble complexes and preventing phosphate absorption to lower serum phosphate levels, commonly used to treat hyperphosphatemia in chronic kidney disease.

serous membrane.definition: A thin, slippery membrane composed of mesothelium (simple squamous epithelium) backed by connective tissue that lines closed body cavities and covers the surfaces of organs within them, producing serous fluid to reduce friction.

serous fluid.definition: A clear, pale-yellow, watery fluid produced by serous membranes and contained in serous cavities (pleural, pericardial, peritoneal); formed mainly by ultrafiltration of plasma with low protein content and serves to lubricate and cushion organ surfaces.

sesamoid bone.definition: A small independent bone embedded within a tendon or joint capsule, most commonly found in the hands and feet; sesamoids protect tendons from wear and improve mechanical leverage by changing the tendon’s angle, with the patella (kneecap) as the largest example.

sesamoid.definition: A small nodular bone embedded within a tendon near a joint, protecting the tendon from wear and improving its mechanical efficiency by altering the tendon’s angle of pull (the patella is the largest example).

sesame oil.definition: A vegetable oil pressed from sesame seeds (Sesamum indicum); rich in unsaturated fats and minor antioxidants (sesamol, sesamin); used for cooking and as a topical emollient or carrier oil; may cause allergic reactions in sesame-allergic individuals.

casein.definition: A family of phosphoproteins that are the major protein components of milk, comprising about 80% of the protein in bovine milk. They form a gel or curd when acidified or exposed to rennet and bind calcium and phosphate; they are used in cheese production and as a dietary protein source.

sars-cov.definition: An enveloped, positive-sense RNA coronavirus that caused the 2002–2003 SARS outbreak; it belongs to the Coronaviridae family and enters human cells via the ACE2 receptor, with transmission mainly through respiratory droplets.

enzyme immunoassay.definition: An immunoassay that uses an enzyme-labeled antibody (or antigen) to generate a measurable signal—usually a color change—upon substrate addition, allowing detection and quantification of a specific antigen or antibody (as in ELISA).

cell culture.definition: To take cells or tissues from your body and watch them grow.

reverse transcription polymerase chain r.definition: A laboratory method that converts RNA into complementary DNA (cDNA) using reverse transcriptase, followed by amplification of specific DNA sequences by PCR to detect or quantify RNA expression or viral RNA.

serum antibody.definition: An antibody circulating in the blood serum; produced by B cells after exposure to an antigen; mediates humoral immunity by binding specific antigens, neutralizing pathogens, and facilitating their clearance (e.g., via opsonization or complement activation). Includes immunoglobulin classes such as IgG, IgM, and IgA.

barr body.definition: An inactivated X chromosome in female somatic cells, appearing as a small, dense, dark-staining body in the nucleus due to X-chromosome inactivation (Lyonization) to balance X-linked gene expression with males.

sex chromatin.definition: A densely staining structure in the nucleus of most female somatic cells that represents the inactivated X chromosome (Barr body) as a result of X-chromosome inactivation; normally absent from male cells.

turner's syndrome.definition: A condition where a person's X chromosome is missing or partly missing. Only occurs in females.

sex-linked ichthyosis.definition: A genetic skin disorder caused by deficiency of the enzyme steroid sulfatase (STS) on the X chromosome, leading to defective desquamation and persistent, dark, plate-like scales (ichthyosis) most evident on the trunk and proximal limbs; inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern.

calcaneal epiphysitis.definition: Inflammation of the calcaneal growth plate (epiphysis) at the heel in growing children and adolescents, usually due to repetitive stress or overuse; presents as heel pain near the back of the heel that worsens with activity and improves with rest (often referred to as calcaneal apophysitis or Sever's disease).

hypophosphatemic vitamin d-resistant ric.definition: An inherited disorder characterized by renal phosphate wasting causing hypophosphatemia and rickets (in children) or osteomalacia (in adults), typically resistant to conventional vitamin D therapy; most commonly due to mutations in PHEX leading to X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets.

x-linked recessive disorders.definition: A category of inherited disorders caused by pathogenic variants on genes on the X chromosome with a recessive pattern of inheritance. Males are typically affected because they have only one X chromosome; females are usually asymptomatic carriers unless they have two mutant alleles or skewed X-inactivation. Transmission: affected fathers pass the mutant X to all daughters (who become carriers) and to no sons; carrier mothers have a 50% chance to pass the mutant allele to each son (often affected) and to daughters (carriers).

x-linked dominant conditions.definition: A pattern of inheritance in which a pathogenic variant on the X chromosome is sufficient to cause disease with one mutated copy; it can affect both sexes but is often more severe in males. An affected father passes the variant to all daughters but to no sons, while an affected mother has about a 50% chance of passing the variant to each child (male or female).

mosaic.definition: In medicine, the presence of two or more genetically distinct cell populations within a single individual, usually arising from a postzygotic genetic mutation; may produce patchy or segmental clinical features.

sex chromosome mosaic.definition: Two or more populations of cells with different sex chromosome karyotypes in the same person, arising after fertilization (postzygotic) due to mitotic nondisjunction or chromosomal loss/gain; common examples include 45,X/46,XX or 46,XY/46,XX, with clinical features varying by the distribution and proportion of the different cell lines.

histocompatible bone marrow transplantat.definition: A transplantation of hematopoietic stem cells from an HLA-matched donor to a recipient, enabling donor-derived marrow to reconstitute the recipient's blood and immune system after conditioning therapy.

maternal immunoglobulin.definition: Antibodies produced by the mother that are transferred to the fetus/newborn, mainly immunoglobulin G across the placenta, providing passive immunity during early life.

carbaryl.definition: A broad-spectrum carbamate insecticide that inhibits acetylcholinesterase by carbamylation, leading to accumulation of acetylcholine and cholinergic toxicity; used in agriculture for pest control.

sezary syndrome.definition: A leukemic variant of cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma (CTCL) characterized by diffuse erythroderma, generalized lymphadenopathy, and circulating malignant T cells with cerebriform (Sezary) nuclei; part of the mycosis fungoides disease spectrum.

shaken baby syndrome.definition: A form of inflicted traumatic brain injury in infants/young children caused by violent shaking (often with impact), leading to intracranial hemorrhages (especially subdural hematoma), retinal hemorrhages, brain injury, and possible permanent neurologic damage or death; commonly referred to as abusive head trauma (AHT).

sexual dysfunction.definition: A problem with any area of a person’s sexual response that causes distress.

sexual aversion disorder.definition: A persistent or recurrent avoidance of sexual contact with a partner due to intense fear, disgust, or anxiety about sex, resulting in distress or impairment.

sexual asphyxia.definition: A practice in which a person deliberately restricts oxygen to the brain during sexual activity to increase arousal or intensity, often by ligature or choking (also known as autoerotic asphyxiation); it carries a high risk of hypoxic brain injury, coma, or death.

anorectal herpes.definition: Anorectal herpes is a herpes simplex virus infection of the anal and rectal mucosa, most often due to HSV-2 (less commonly HSV-1), presenting with painful vesicular or ulcerative lesions in the anorectal area with possible rectal pain, tenesmus, and discharge; diagnosed by PCR or viral culture and treated with antiviral therapy such as acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir.

genital candidiasis.definition: A fungal infection of the genital tract caused by Candida species (most commonly Candida albicans), presenting with pruritus and irritation; in women, vulvovaginal candidiasis with thick white discharge, and in men, balanitis. Diagnosis is clinical and can be confirmed by microscopy or culture; treatment with topical or oral antifungals (eg, azoles such as fluconazole or clotrimazole).

chlamydial infections.definition: An infection caused by intracellular bacteria of the genus Chlamydia (primarily Chlamydia trachomatis), usually sexually transmitted and affecting the genitourinary tract; many infections are asymptomatic and diagnosed by nucleic acid amplification tests; treated with antibiotics such as doxycycline or azithromycin.

venereal disease.definition: An outdated term for infections transmitted through sexual contact; today these are referred to as sexually transmitted infections (STIs) or sexually transmitted diseases (STDs).

cerebral blood vessels.definition: The arteries, veins, and capillaries that supply and drain the brain, forming the cerebral circulation and delivering oxygen and nutrients to neural tissue while removing carbon dioxide and metabolic wastes.

pigment changes.definition: Alterations in skin, hair, or mucosal coloration due to changes in pigment production, distribution, or deposition—most commonly hyperpigmentation (increased pigment) or hypopigmentation (decreased pigment)—caused by inflammation, hormonal factors, medications, sun exposure, or systemic diseases.

nail changes.definition: Changes in the nails' appearance or structure, including alterations in color, thickness, curvature, surface (ridging or pitting), or nail bed separation, which may indicate local trauma or a range of dermatologic or systemic diseases.

uterine hemorrhaging.definition: Profuse or abnormal vaginal bleeding arising from the uterus; can occur during pregnancy (antepartum or postpartum hemorrhage) or in nonpregnant states, and may reflect obstetric, gynecologic, or systemic pathology, potentially requiring urgent evaluation and treatment.

gametes.definition: Haploid reproductive cells that unite during fertilization to form a zygote; produced by meiosis; in animals, sperm and ova; in plants, pollen and ovules.

cervical secretions.definition: A mucus secreted by the cervix; its volume and viscosity vary with hormonal changes across the menstrual cycle, aiding lubrication and, during the fertile period, facilitating sperm movement.

urethral culture.definition: A laboratory test in which a sample from the urethra is cultured to identify bacterial pathogens causing urethral infection and to determine antibiotic susceptibilities.

rectal culture.definition: A laboratory test in which a rectal sample (usually a swab or stool specimen) is cultured on selective media to detect and identify pathogenic microorganisms causing anorectal or enteric infection and to guide antimicrobial therapy.

cervical culture.definition: A laboratory diagnostic test in which a cervical specimen is cultured on appropriate media to grow and identify pathogenic organisms causing cervical infection, most commonly Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis.

foam test.definition: A simple qualitative bedside test in which a sample is vigorously shaken to induce foam; persistent foam suggests the presence of surface-active substances (notably protein) and has been used as a rough screen for proteinuria, though it is non-specific and superseded by more reliable tests.
