steppage gait.definition: A high-stepping gait caused by dorsiflexor weakness or paralysis (commonly peroneal nerve palsy), in which the leg is lifted high with exaggerated knee and hip flexion to clear the toes during the swing phase.

stepping reflex.definition: A neonatal primitive reflex in which, when an infant is held upright with the feet touching a solid surface, the legs perform alternating stepping movements; it typically disappears by about 2 months of age as higher CNS pathways mature and reappears later as voluntary walking.

step reflex.definition: A primitive neonatal reflex in which, when held upright with the feet touching a solid surface, the infant makes rhythmic stepping movements with the legs; it is present at birth and typically disappears by about 2 months of age, later reappearing as voluntary walking.

step wedge.definition: A calibration device for radiography consisting of a series of blocks with increasing thickness (or density) to produce a stepped density gradient on an image, used to assess and adjust exposure, detector response, and film processing quality.

penetrometer.definition: A device that measures the resistance of a material or tissue to penetration by a calibrated probe, providing a quantitative assessment of hardness or strength.

sterapred.definition: A brand name for prednisone, a synthetic glucocorticoid corticosteroid that reduces inflammation and suppresses the immune system when taken systemically, used to treat inflammatory and autoimmune conditions.

sterile field.definition: A designated area prepared with sterile drapes and supplies that is kept free of microorganisms and used for handling sterile instruments during procedures to prevent infection.

sterile water for inhalation.definition: A sterile, pyrogen-free, additive-free water intended for inhalation therapy, used to dilute nebulized medications or to humidify inspired air; not suitable for parenteral administration.

sterile water for injection.definition: Sterile water for injection is sterile, pyrogen-free water intended for dissolving or diluting drugs for parenteral administration; it contains no additives or electrolytes and should not be given by itself, but used to reconstitute injectable medications prior to administration.

sterilize.definition: To render an object free from all viable microorganisms, including spores, typically by destruction or removal of organisms through methods such as heat, chemicals, or irradiation.

sternoclavicular.definition: Relating to the sternum and clavicle; specifically, the sternoclavicular joint is the articulation between the medial end of the clavicle and the manubrium of the sternum.

sternocostal.definition: Relating to the sternum and the ribs or their costal cartilages; e.g., sternocostal joints are the articulations between the sternum and the costal cartilages of the true ribs.

sternomastoid.definition: A neck muscle that originates from the sternum and medial clavicle and inserts on the mastoid process; it flexes the neck and rotates the head to the opposite side; innervated by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), and can assist with deep respiration when the head is fixed.

sternopericardial ligaments.definition: Fibrous bands that anchor the fibrous pericardium to the sternum, stabilizing the heart within the mediastinum by limiting anterior movement.

sternothyroideus.definition: A thin infrahyoid neck muscle that depresses the thyroid cartilage (and thus the larynx) during swallowing and speaking; it originates from the posterior surface of the manubrium sterni and inserts into the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage.

gladiolus.definition: The central, elongated portion of the sternum between the manubrium and the xiphoid process.

costoclavicular ligament.definition: A strong band extending from the costal tubercle of the first rib to the inferior surface of the clavicle, stabilizing the sternoclavicular joint and limiting elevation of the clavicle.

interclavicular ligament.definition: A strong fibrous band that unites the medial ends of the clavicles across the superior chest (spanning the jugular notch); it stabilizes the sternoclavicular joints by preventing excessive downward depression and separation of the clavicles.

sternal angle.definition: A palpable bony ridge at the junction of the manubrium and the body of the sternum (manubriosternal joint), at the level of the second costal cartilage; serves as a key thoracic landmark, marking the approximate level of the tracheal bifurcation and the origin of the aortic arch.

anterior sternoclavicular ligament.definition: A thickened band of the sternoclavicular joint capsule on the anterior aspect that reinforces the joint and limits anterior displacement of the clavicle (anterior dislocation).

first costal cartilage.definition: A hyaline cartilage segment that connects the proximal end of the first rib to the manubrium of the sternum, forming the first costosternal articulation (a primary cartilaginous joint, typically a synchondrosis) that provides an elastic attachment for the rib cage.

sternutation.definition: The act of sneezing; a sudden, forceful expulsion of air from the lungs through the nose and mouth, usually triggered by irritation of the nasal mucosa.

sneeze.definition: A sudden, forceful expulsion of air from the nose and mouth caused by irritation of the nasal mucosa; a reflex triggered by irritants such as dust, pollen, infections, or other nasal irritants that helps clear the nasal passages.

steroid acne.definition: A form of acneiform eruption caused by systemic or topical corticosteroid or anabolic steroid use; characterized by sudden onset of monomorphic inflammatory papules and pustules, often on the face and trunk, with few or no comedones, and typically resolves or improves after withdrawal or tapering of the offending steroid.

steroid-cell antibody.definition: An autoantibody directed against steroid-producing cells (such as adrenal cortical cells), described in some autoimmune endocrinopathies; its clinical utility is limited and its pathogenic role is not well defined.

steroid hormone.definition: A hormone derived from cholesterol that is lipid-soluble and diffuses across cell membranes to bind intracellular receptors, thereby regulating gene transcription; examples include cortisol, aldosterone, estradiol, progesterone, and testosterone.

steroid hormone therapy.definition: Administration of exogenous steroid hormones (such as estrogens, progestins, androgens, glucocorticoids, or mineralocorticoids) to replace deficient hormones or to modulate hormonal activity for therapeutic benefit.

steroidogenesis.definition: The biosynthesis of steroid hormones from cholesterol, through enzymatic steps that convert cholesterol to pregnenolone and onward to corticosteroids, mineralocorticoids, and sex steroids in steroidogenic tissues such as the adrenal cortex, gonads, and placenta.

sterol.definition: A steroid alcohol; a class of lipids containing a steroid nucleus with a hydroxyl group, such as cholesterol.

sterility assurance level.definition: The probability that a given unit remains non-sterile after a sterilization process; it quantifies the effectiveness of the sterilization, with commonly accepted targets around 10^-6 (one non-sterile unit per one million produced units).

reed-sternberg cell.definition: A large atypical B lymphocyte with two prominent, mirror-image nuclei and eosinophilic nucleoli (owl's-eye appearance), found in classical Hodgkin lymphoma and typically CD15 and CD30 positive.

sternoclavicular joint.definition: An articulation between the medial end of the clavicle and the manubrium of the sternum (and the first costal cartilage) forming a synovial saddle-type joint that allows multiaxial movement of the clavicle (elevation/depression, protraction/retraction, and rotation); stabilized by the sternoclavicular ligaments (anterior and posterior), the interclavicular ligament, and the costoclavicular ligament, often with an articular disc that subdivides the joint capsule.

sternocostal articulation.definition: The joints between the sternum and the costal cartilages of the true ribs (ribs 1–7). The first sternocostal joint is a synchondrosis (immovable), while ribs 2–7 articulate with the sternum via synovial plane joints that allow limited gliding during respiration.

bone marrow puncture.definition: A procedure in which a needle is inserted into a bone marrow cavity (most commonly the posterior iliac crest) to aspirate or obtain a core sample of marrow for laboratory examination of hematologic disorders.

internal mammary node.definition: A lymph node along the internal thoracic (internal mammary) vessels near the sternum; part of the parasternal lymph node group that drains the medial breast and anterior chest wall and communicates with mediastinal nodes. It may be involved in breast cancer metastasis.

sternal puncture.definition: A procedure in which a needle is inserted through the sternum to obtain a bone marrow aspirate or biopsy for diagnostic evaluation; historically used for hematologic disorders but now rarely performed due to risk, with iliac crest marrow aspiration preferred.

stereotactic mammography.definition: A breast imaging technique that uses two mammographic views taken at different angles to triangulate the exact three-dimensional location of a lesion in the breast, enabling targeted biopsy or localization procedures.

herpes simplex virus type i.definition: A double-stranded DNA virus in the Herpesviridae family that commonly causes orofacial infections (cold sores and gingivostomatitis); it establishes lifelong latent infection in sensory neurons (often the trigeminal ganglion) and can reactivate periodically, transmitted by direct contact with infected saliva or lesions.

diaphragmatic surface of the liver.definition: Convex, smooth, superior surface of the liver that faces the diaphragm; it is largely peritoneum-covered except for the bare area where the liver is in direct contact with the diaphragm, and anteriorly it is divided into right and left lobes by the falciform ligament.

nasal passage.definition: A nasal passage is the space inside the nose through which air flows during breathing; it is lined with mucous membrane and cilia to warm, humidify, and filter the inspired air.

sternum puncture.definition: A procedure in which a needle is inserted into the sternum to obtain bone marrow aspirate or biopsy for diagnostic evaluation; historically performed but now rarely used due to risk to mediastinal structures, with the posterior iliac crest often preferred.

sternheimer-malbin stain.definition: A two-reagent supravital stain used in urine sediment microscopy to enhance visualization of cells, bacteria, casts, and crystals; nuclei are stained blue/purple and cytoplasm pink to orange against a pale background.

urinalyses.definition: A test of urine used to detect and evaluate diseases such as diabetes, urinary tract infections, and kidney problems.

crystal violet.definition: A dark purple triphenylmethane dye used as the primary stain in the Gram stain procedure to differentiate bacteria by cell wall properties; Gram-positive bacteria retain the stain after alcohol decolorization due to a thick peptidoglycan layer, whereas Gram-negative bacteria do not.

safranin.definition: A basic red dye used as a counterstain in Gram staining; it stains decolorized Gram-negative bacteria pink/red.

benign lymphocytic meningitis.definition: A self-limited aseptic meningitis in which cerebrospinal fluid shows a predominance of lymphocytes with negative bacterial cultures, typically caused by a viral infection (e.g., enteroviruses), and with full recovery.

sterile meningitis.definition: A form of meningitis in which no bacterial pathogen is detected in CSF cultures (aseptic meningitis); most commonly caused by viral infections, but it can also result from medications, chemical irritation, or autoimmune processes, and typically presents with fever, headache, neck stiffness, with CSF showing lymphocytic predominance and negative bacterial cultures.

simple meningitis.definition: Inflammation of the meninges without evidence of bacterial infection or significant systemic illness, most commonly aseptic/viral in origin and typically presenting with headache, fever, and neck stiffness.

stereotactic.definition: Techniques using a three-dimensional coordinate system to locate targets within the body for precise diagnostic or therapeutic interventions, often with image guidance or a fixed frame (e.g., in stereotactic neurosurgery or radiosurgery).

stereotactic surgery.definition: A neurosurgical technique that uses a three‑dimensional coordinate system and imaging guidance (often with a stereotactic frame or frameless navigation) to locate precise targets within the brain or other body parts and perform procedures such as biopsy, lesioning/ablation, or implantation of devices with minimal damage to surrounding tissue.

stereotaxic surgery.definition: A surgical technique that uses a three-dimensional coordinate system and imaging guidance to precisely locate targets inside the brain (or body) and guide procedures such as biopsy, lesioning, drug injection, or stimulation.

stereotaxic instrument.definition: A device that provides a fixed three-dimensional coordinate system to accurately locate predefined intracranial targets and guide instruments (such as needles or probes) to those targets during neurosurgical procedures.

stereotaxic neuroradiography.definition: A radiographic method that employs a stereotactic apparatus to define three‑dimensional coordinates for precise localization of brain targets on neuroradiographic images, facilitating targeted biopsy, lesioning, or electrode implantation.

stereotaxic radiosurgery.definition: Noninvasive radiation therapy that uses precise, image-guided targeting to deliver a high dose of ionizing radiation to a small, well-defined lesion (often in the brain) in a single session or a few fractions, minimizing exposure to surrounding tissue; delivered with systems such as Gamma Knife, linear accelerator (LINAC), or CyberKnife.

stereotaxic radiography.definition: A radiographic localization method that uses a fixed stereotactic frame to acquire X-ray images from multiple angles, enabling precise three-dimensional localization of a brain target for biopsy or neurosurgical procedures.

stereoradiograph.definition: A radiographic image produced by stereography, consisting of two X-ray images taken from slightly different angles that, when viewed together (often with a stereoscope), produce a perception of depth and a three-dimensional view of structures.

stereoradiography.definition: A radiographic technique in which two X-ray images are taken from slightly different angles to produce a stereoscopic (3D) view of anatomy, enabling more accurate measurements and assessment of spatial relationships.

stereoscopic radiograph.definition: A radiographic technique in which two images of the same object are taken from slightly different angles and viewed together as a stereo pair to produce a perception of depth and a three-dimensional view of the anatomy.

stereoscopic microscope.definition: A dissecting microscope designed for low-magnification viewing that provides a three-dimensional image by using two separate optical paths for each eye; it has a relatively long working distance and is used to examine and manipulate larger or opaque specimens (e.g., tissues, insects, plant parts) and for dissection or microsurgical prep.

stereomicroscope.definition: A binocular microscope designed for low-magnification, three-dimensional viewing of opaque specimens, providing depth perception through two separate optical paths to each eyepiece; commonly used for dissection, manipulation, and inspection of samples, with a long working distance and flexible illumination.

stereognostic.definition: Relating to the ability to recognize objects by touch; the capacity to identify objects through tactile sensation alone (tactile recognition of form).

nonparalytic.definition: Not causing paralysis; without loss of voluntary muscle function.

ophthalmological examination.definition: A systematic clinical evaluation of the eye and visual system, including history, external inspection, visual acuity testing, pupil reactions, intraocular pressure measurement, and assessment of ocular structures and movements.

gaze.definition: The direction and steadiness of the eyes’ line of sight toward a target, produced by coordinated eye movements.

ocular muscles.definition: Muscles that move the eyeball; the six extraocular muscles—superior, inferior, medial, and lateral rectus; and superior and inferior oblique—originate in the orbit and insert on the sclera, innervated by CN III, CN IV, and CN VI, coordinating horizontal, vertical, and rotational (torsional) eye movements.

streptococcus faecalis.definition: An enterococcal species; a Gram-positive, catalase‑negative coccus that forms pairs or short chains and is part of normal intestinal flora, capable of causing opportunistic infections such as endocarditis, urinary tract infections, biliary tract infections, and intra‑abdominal infections; notable for intrinsic and acquired antibiotic resistance, including vancomycin‑resistant strains.

neonatal sepsis.definition: A systemic bacterial infection in a newborn (0–28 days old), presenting with illness signs such as fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, poor feeding, lethargy, or apnea; diagnosed by positive blood culture and treated with empiric intravenous antibiotics.

strepticemia.definition: A bloodstream infection caused by Streptococcus species (streptococcal bacteremia), a form of septicemia that can lead to disseminated infection and sepsis.

streptosepticemia.definition: A septicemia caused by Streptococcus species; presence of Streptococcus bacteria in the bloodstream leading to systemic infection.

penicillin g benzathine.definition: A long-acting, slow-release intramuscular form of penicillin G that provides sustained penicillin levels for an extended period; used to treat syphilis and for rheumatic fever prophylaxis.

strawberry gallbladder.definition: A gross (macroscopic) appearance of the gallbladder in which the mucosa shows multiple pinpoint hemorrhages (petechiae), giving a strawberry-like red-spotted surface typically seen with acute or hemorrhagic cholecystitis due to mucosal inflammation and congestion.

strangulated hemorrhoid.definition: A prolapsed internal hemorrhoid whose venous outflow is constricted at the anal canal, causing ischemia and intense, continuous anal pain; the affected tissue may become edematous, discolored, and can necrose if not promptly treated.

strangulated hernia.definition: A hernia in which the protruded tissue (often intestine) becomes trapped and its blood supply is compromised, causing ischemia and risk of necrosis; it is a surgical emergency.

straight-leg-raising test.definition: A physical examination maneuver used to assess lumbar nerve root irritation or disc herniation. The patient lies supine and the clinician raises the straightened leg (hip flexed with knee extended). Reproduction of radiating pain or paresthesias in the sciatic distribution, typically between about 30 and 70 degrees, indicates a positive test and suggests nerve root compression (e.g., disc herniation); hamstring-only tightness pain is non-specific.

slr.definition: A physical examination maneuver used to assess lumbar nerve root irritation or sciatic pain. The patient lies on their back and the examiner lifts an extended leg; pain that radiates down the leg, particularly below the knee, suggests a positive test and possible lumbar disc herniation or nerve root compression.

hamstrings.definition: A group of muscles on the back of the thigh (semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and the long and short heads of the biceps femoris) that flex the knee and extend the hip; they originate from the ischial tuberosity (short head of the biceps from the femur) and are innervated by the sciatic nerve.

sciatica.definition: Pain along the course of the sciatic nerve (which runs from the buttock, down the back and side of the leg, and into the foot and toes), often because of a herniated disk.

edgewise orthodontic appliance.definition: A fixed orthodontic appliance consisting of bonded brackets and a rectangular archwire that sits in a bracket slot (edgewise) and is ligated to the teeth to apply controlled forces for tooth movement; the traditional metal braces system developed by Angle.

arch wire.definition: A slender orthodontic wire that runs through the brackets (and usually connects to molar bands) and delivers continuous, controlled forces to teeth to guide their movement toward proper alignment during orthodontic treatment.

brackets.definition: A pair of punctuation marks used to enclose added information, clarifications, or editorial insertions within text; in medical writing, they often denote editor-added clarifications or corrections.

tibialis posterior.definition: A muscle of the deep posterior compartment of the leg that inverts and plantarflexes the foot and supports the medial arch; it originates from the posterior surfaces of the tibia and fibula and inserts on the navicular and medial cuneiforms, innervated by the tibial nerve.

stratum lucidum.definition: A thin, clear layer of the epidermis found only in thick skin (palms and soles), located between the stratum granulosum and stratum corneum, consisting of flattened, dead keratinocytes rich in eleidin that keratinize to form a tougher barrier.

stratified epithelium.definition: A type of epithelium composed of two or more cell layers with the deepest layer in contact with the basement membrane; its primary function is protection against abrasion and mechanical stress, with the surface cells varying (squamous, cuboidal, or columnar) by region.

streptococcal angina.definition: An acute tonsillitis caused by infection with Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus), typically presenting with sudden-onset sore throat, fever, tonsillar exudates, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and painful swallowing.

coronary embolism.definition: An embolus that travels to a coronary artery and occludes it, usually a thrombus from the left heart (e.g., due to atrial fibrillation or valvular disease), causing acute myocardial ischemia or infarction; less commonly from endocarditis vegetations, paradoxical emboli, or other embolic sources.

streptococcemia.definition: The presence of Streptococcus species in the bloodstream (streptococcal bacteremia), typically arising from an invasive streptococcal infection and potentially leading to sepsis or metastatic infections.

pancreatic islet cell tumor.definition: An endocrine neoplasm of the pancreas arising from the islets of Langerhans, typically a neuroendocrine tumor that may secrete hormones (functional) such as insulin or gastrin or may be nonfunctional, with variable malignant potential.

strongyloidiasis.definition: An intestinal parasitic infection caused by the nematode Strongyloides stercoralis, acquired through skin contact with contaminated soil; larvae migrate via the lungs to the gut and can autoinfect, causing a chronic infection that may be asymptomatic or include GI symptoms, with immunosuppressed individuals at risk for hyperinfection or disseminated disease. Diagnosis is by stool/duodenal samples or serology, and treatment is typically with ivermectin (or albendazole in some cases).

loeffler's syndrome.definition: A self-limited pulmonary eosinophilic syndrome marked by peripheral eosinophilia and transient migratory pulmonary infiltrates, usually due to larval migration of helminths (classically Ascaris lumbricoides) through the lungs.

stress ulcer.definition: A gastric or duodenal mucosal ulcer that develops in the setting of severe physical stress (e.g., critical illness, trauma, burns, sepsis) due to reduced mucosal blood flow and protection, often presenting with GI bleeding.

regional ileitis.definition: A form of Crohn disease involving the ileum, especially the terminal ileum, characterized by chronic transmural inflammation with skip lesions and potential fistulas, strictures, and malabsorption.

membrane stripping.definition: A procedure in obstetrics in which a clinician inserts a gloved finger through the cervix to separate the amniotic membranes from the lower uterine segment, stimulating prostaglandin release to initiate or accelerate labor; may cause mild vaginal bleeding or contractions.

stripping of membranes.definition: A procedure in late pregnancy in which a clinician inserts a finger through the cervix to separate the amniotic membranes from the lower uterus, releasing prostaglandins to ripen the cervix and stimulate labor; it may shorten time to delivery but can cause discomfort, vaginal bleeding, and carries a small risk of membrane rupture or infection.

dental procedures.definition: An umbrella term for the diagnostic, preventive, restorative, and surgical interventions performed by a dentist to diagnose, prevent, treat, and manage diseases and conditions of the teeth, gums, and supporting oral structures (examples include prophylaxis, fillings, crowns, root canal therapy, extractions, implants, and periodontal therapy).

scar tissue removal.definition: Removal or reduction of fibrous scar tissue that forms after injury or surgery, typically to restore function or improve cosmetic appearance; techniques may include surgical excision or revision, laser therapy, dermabrasion, or enzymatic treatment, with variable outcomes and potential for recurrence.

tissue grafts.definition: A surgical transplantation of tissue from one site to another to replace or repair damaged tissue, which may be autologous (from the same person), allogeneic (from another person), isogeneic (from an identical twin), or xenogeneic (from a different species); success depends on revascularization and integration with the host tissue.

incision of a joint capsule.definition: A surgical procedure involving making an incision in the joint capsule to expose the joint or to release contracted or diseased capsule tissue.

saphenous vein stripping.definition: A surgical procedure in which the saphenous vein (usually the great saphenous vein) is tied off and removed from the leg to treat varicose veins and chronic venous insufficiency.

oxytocin challenge test.definition: An obstetric test in which a controlled infusion of oxytocin induces uterine contractions while fetal heart rate is monitored; a negative result (no repetitive late decelerations) suggests fetal well-being, whereas a positive result (late decelerations with contractions) indicates possible placental insufficiency and fetal risk.

stress echocardiography.definition: A noninvasive imaging test in which ultrasound of the heart is performed at rest and during stress (exercise or pharmacologic) to detect inducible ischemia by monitoring changes in regional wall motion and overall function.

stress radiography.definition: A radiographic technique in which controlled stress is applied to a joint (manual or device-applied) while X-rays are taken to assess instability and ligament laxity by revealing abnormal displacement or angular change under load. Common examples include varus/valgus and anterior/posterior stress views of the knee or flexion-extension views of the spine.

thallium stress test.definition: A nuclear imaging test in which a radioactive thallium tracer is injected during rest and during stress (exercise or pharmacologic) to image myocardial perfusion and detect ischemia or scar.

exercise electrocardiogram.definition: A diagnostic test in which the heart's electrical activity is recorded by electrocardiography during graded physical exercise (usually on a treadmill or stationary bike) to assess cardiac function and detect ischemia or arrhythmias; also known as an exercise treadmill test.

amygdaloid complex.definition: An almond-shaped group of nuclei in the anterior temporal lobe (the amygdala), a key limbic system structure that processes emotions (especially fear), assigns emotional significance to stimuli, and mediates autonomic and memory-related responses via connections with the hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and hypothalamus.

smooth muscle.definition: An involuntary, nonstriated muscle tissue that forms the walls of hollow organs and blood vessels (such as the GI tract, airways, vessels, bladder, and uterus); composed of spindle-shaped cells with a single nucleus and no sarcomeres, it contracts slowly and continuously under autonomic nervous system and hormonal control.

stria terminalis.definition: A major output pathway of the amygdala; a fiber tract that runs along the caudate nucleus to the hypothalamus and bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, conveying emotional–autonomic information and coordinating endocrine and autonomic responses to fear and stress.

myofascial.definition: Relating to the muscle tissue (myo) and the fascia surrounding and enveloping it.

strümpell-marie disease.definition: An inherited neurodegenerative disorder characterized by slowly progressive spastic weakness and stiffness of the legs due to degeneration of the corticospinal tracts (hereditary spastic paraplegia).

rheumatoid spondylitis.definition: An inflammatory manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis affecting the spine, most often the cervical region, with synovitis and erosion of the facet joints and supporting ligaments, causing neck pain and stiffness and potentially atlantoaxial instability or spinal cord compression.

spondylitis ankylopoietica.definition: Chronic inflammatory rheumatic disease primarily affecting the spine and sacroiliac joints, causing inflammatory back pain and progressive spinal stiffness that may culminate in fusion of the vertebrae (bamboo spine); commonly linked to HLA-B27 and may have extra-articular manifestations such as uveitis.

strychnine poisoning.definition: A toxic condition produced by exposure to strychnine, a highly potent glycine receptor antagonist that disinhibits motor neurons, causing painful generalized muscle spasms and seizures, with facial grimacing (risus sardonicus), lockjaw (trismus), and opisthotonos; death may result from respiratory failure or exhaustion.

opisthotonus.definition: A severe, sustained backward arching of the trunk and neck caused by tonic contraction of the back extensor muscles; commonly seen in tetanus and can occur with severe meningitis or brain injury.

stryker wedge frame.definition: A wedge frame is a rigid surgical accessory used to hold, position, or create a wedge-shaped gap or angle in bone during orthopedic procedures; a Stryker wedge frame refers to Stryker’s version of this instrument, typically used to maintain precise angular correction or graft placement during reductions, osteotomies, or distraction.

stuartnatal plus.definition: Definition not found in standard medical dictionaries. If you mean a prenatal vitamin product, a prenatal vitamin is a dietary supplement containing essential nutrients for pregnancy (eg, folic acid, iron, calcium, iodine) to support maternal health and fetal development; taken as directed during pregnancy to reduce certain risks.

studer neobladder.definition: An orthotopic urinary diversion using a detubularized ileal segment fashioned into a low-pressure reservoir, with ureters implanted into the reservoir and the neobladder connected to the urethra to allow near-normal continence and spontaneous voiding after radical cystectomy.

residual limb.definition: The portion of a limb that remains after amputation; it forms the stump that is fitted with a prosthesis and includes the remaining bone, soft tissue, nerves, and skin.

stump hallucination.definition: A phantom perceptual phenomenon in amputees where the residual limb is perceived as present and may exhibit sensory experiences (pain, tingling, warmth, pressure) or movements, despite the limb’s absence.

stump pain.definition: Pain localized to the residual limb after amputation, caused by tissue injury, nerve irritation or neuroma, inflammation, infection, edema, or prosthetic fit problems; can be nociceptive or neuropathic and is distinct from phantom limb pain.

stunned myocardium.definition: A transient, reversible impairment of myocardial contractility following a period of ischemia that persists after restoration of normal blood flow (reperfusion) but with preserved viability and no irreversible necrosis; typically resolves within hours to days.

styloid.definition: A slender, pointed projection from a bone, often serving as an attachment site for ligaments and muscles.

stylohyoideus.definition: A slender neck muscle that originates from the styloid process of the temporal bone and inserts onto the hyoid bone; it elevates and retracts the hyoid during swallowing.

stylohyoid ligament.definition: A fibrous band extending from the styloid process of the temporal bone to the hyoid bone, helping to suspend and stabilize the hyoid.

stylohyoid bone.definition: A vestigial or ossified segment of the stylohyoid ligament that creates a bony connection between the styloid process of the temporal bone and the hyoid bone; it is an anatomical variant and, when elongated, can contribute to Eagle syndrome.

stylomandibular ligament.definition: A fibrous band extending from the styloid process of the temporal bone to the angle of the mandible; one of the temporomandibular joint ligaments that helps restrict excessive protrusion of the mandible.

stylus.definition: A slender, pointed projection on a bone or tissue; in anatomy, a stylus is a small spike-like projection, and it can also refer to a sharp, rod-shaped instrument used in certain medical procedures.

styptic.definition: A topical astringent used to stop minor bleeding by constricting blood vessels and promoting coagulation; commonly applied to shaving nicks and cuts, often in a styptic pencil containing alum (potassium aluminum sulfate) or ferric subsulfate.

subacromial.definition: Relating to the area beneath the acromion of the shoulder; the subacromial space lies below the acromion and above the head of the humerus and contains the subacromial bursa and the tendons of the rotator cuff.

sbe.definition: A form of infective endocarditis with subacute onset and slow progression, typically caused by low-virulence organisms such as viridans streptococci; presents with fever, fatigue, malaise, and a new or changing heart murmur and may cause embolic phenomena; managed with prolonged intravenous antibiotics and, in selected cases, surgical valve repair or replacement.

vegetations.definition: An irregular mass on a heart valve or endocardial surface composed of fibrin, platelets, inflammatory cells, and microorganisms; characteristic of infective endocarditis.

osler's nodes.definition: Tender, subcutaneous nodules on the fingertips or toes seen in infective endocarditis; caused by immune complex deposition in the small vessels (type III hypersensitivity).

janeway lesions.definition: Non-tender, hemorrhagic or erythematous macules on the palms and soles seen in infective endocarditis, caused by septic microemboli from valvular vegetations.

splinter hemorrhages.definition: Small, linear subungual hemorrhages that run along the nail bed, caused by tiny capillary bleeds in the nail matrix; often due to minor trauma but can be associated with systemic conditions such as infective endocarditis or vasculitis.

bacteriological examination.definition: A laboratory procedure in which a clinical specimen is examined for bacteria, typically by microscopy and staining, culture to isolate the organisms, and subsequent identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing.

antibiotic prophylaxis.definition: Administration of antibiotics to prevent infection, typically given before exposure to a procedure or situation that could introduce bacteria (e.g., preoperative prophylaxis to reduce surgical site infection).

isoprinosine.definition: A medication with immunomodulatory and antiviral properties; used in some countries for certain viral infections; mechanism purportedly involves enhanced cell-mediated immunity and interferon activity; evidence of clinical benefit is limited and it is not approved by the FDA.

interferon alfa.definition: A type I cytokine that binds to cell-surface receptors to induce antiviral, antiproliferative, and immunomodulatory effects. It is used as an injectable therapy for certain viral infections (notably hepatitis B and C) and select malignancies (e.g., hairy cell leukemia, Kaposi sarcoma, malignant melanoma).

subaortic stenosis.definition: A congenital narrowing of the left ventricular outflow tract just below the aortic valve, usually due to a fibrous membrane or fibromuscular ridge, causing a fixed obstruction to flow from the left ventricle and often presenting with a systolic murmur and left ventricular hypertrophy.

subaortic.definition: Located below the aorta; in cardiac anatomy, referring to structures in the left ventricular outflow tract just below the aortic valve.

subaponeurotic.definition: Under the galea aponeurotica; pertaining to the loose areolar layer between the epicranial aponeurosis and the pericranium of the skull, a potential space that can accumulate blood in scalp injuries.

subarachnoid anesthesia.definition: A neuraxial anesthesia in which a local anesthetic is injected into the subarachnoid space (intrathecal) via a spinal needle, producing reversible loss of sensory and motor function below the injection level for lower abdominal, pelvic, and lower limb procedures; onset is rapid and effect is dense, with possible hypotension and postdural puncture headache.

subarachnoid cistern.definition: An enlargement of the subarachnoid space where cerebrospinal fluid pools around the brain and spinal cord, bounded by the arachnoid and pia mater; examples include the cisterna magna and lumbar cistern.

sah.definition: A hemorrhage into the subarachnoid space surrounding the brain, usually from rupture of a cerebral aneurysm or head injury; presents with a sudden, severe headache ('thunderclap'), neck stiffness, and sometimes loss of consciousness; requires urgent neuroimaging and prompt treatment to control bleeding and prevent rebleeding.

subclavian catheter.definition: A central venous catheter inserted through the subclavian vein to provide long-term or rapid venous access for infusions, parenteral nutrition, blood products, or hemodialysis.

subclavian steal syndrome.definition: Proximal subclavian artery stenosis or occlusion causing retrograde flow in the ipsilateral vertebral artery to perfuse the arm, resulting in vertebrobasilar ischemia and arm claudication during exertion.

subclavian trunk.definition: A lymphatic trunk that drains lymph from the upper limb and superficial thoracic structures, typically emptying into the venous angle at the junction of the subclavian and internal jugular veins.

subcapital fracture.definition: Fracture of the femoral neck occurring immediately below the femoral head, within the hip joint capsule (intracapsular); typically results from a fall in elderly individuals and carries a high risk of avascular necrosis due to disruption of the retinacular arteries.

subcapsular cataract.definition: A cataract that forms in the subcapsular region of the lens, just beneath the lens capsule—most commonly in the posterior subcapsular area; it causes glare and decreased visual acuity, often progressing more rapidly than other cataract types, with risk factors including steroid use, diabetes, intraocular inflammation, trauma, or radiation.

subcapsular hematoma.definition: A collection of blood beneath the capsule surrounding an organ (the subcapsular space), typically from trauma or vascular rupture, that can compress the underlying tissue (e.g., subcapsular hepatic or splenic hematoma).

subcapsular space.definition: A potential space between an organ’s capsule and the underlying parenchymal tissue in which fluid or blood can accumulate.

intracranial calcification.definition: An abnormal deposition of calcium salts within intracranial tissues detectable on imaging, which can be physiologic (e.g., pineal gland and choroid plexus calcifications) or pathologic, associated with infections, metabolic disorders, vascular or neoplastic processes, or neurodegenerative diseases.

cerebral cortex atrophy.definition: Progressive loss of neurons and thinning of cortical tissue in the cerebral cortex, leading to reduced cortical thickness and brain volume, often with widening of sulci and ventricular enlargement, seen in aging and various neurodegenerative or metabolic disorders.

port-wine-colored capillary hemangioma.definition: A congenital capillary malformation of the superficial dermal vessels presenting as a flat, well-demarcated pink-to-purple patch at birth that tends to darken and enlarge with age; common on the face or neck and often treated with pulsed-dye laser.

angioma of the choroid.definition: A benign vascular tumor of the choroid (uveal tract) consisting of an abnormal proliferation of choroidal blood vessels; typically presents as a localized reddish-orange lesion beneath the retina and can cause serous retinal detachment and vision loss.

new cutaneous hemangiomas.definition: New cutaneous hemangiomas are recently appearing benign vascular skin lesions caused by proliferation of cutaneous blood vessels, typically presenting as red to purple papules or nodules. They can be infantile hemangiomas that proliferate after birth or acquired lesions in adults (e.g., cherry angiomas); most are asymptomatic but may ulcerate or bleed, with management depending on size, location, and symptoms.

live measles virus.definition: A viable measles virus (genus Morbillivirus) that is capable of replication in host cells; in vaccine use it denotes an attenuated (weakened) live virus that can induce protective immunity with typically little or no illness.

epileptic stupor.definition: A state of severely reduced consciousness and responsiveness that occurs during an epileptic seizure (ictal stupor), in which the patient is largely unresponsive to external stimuli and exhibits diminished spontaneous movement; consciousness usually returns after the seizure ends, though a postictal period of confusion may follow.

hypoglossal nerves.definition: A pair of motor cranial nerves (the twelfth cranial nerves) that innervate the tongue muscles, enabling tongue movement. They arise from the hypoglossal nuclei in the medulla oblongata and exit the skull through the hypoglossal canal; they supply the intrinsic tongue muscles and most extrinsic tongue muscles (e.g., genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus; palatoglossus is supplied by CN X). Lesions cause tongue weakness and deviation toward the side of the lesion.

arachnoid space.definition: Interval between the arachnoid mater and the pia mater, filled with cerebrospinal fluid and containing connective tissue trabeculae; the site of CSF circulation around the brain and spinal cord.

arteriovenous malformation.definition: Abnormal connections between veins and arteries, usually caused by a birth defect.

endovascular procedure.definition: A minimally invasive vascular intervention performed inside a blood vessel using catheters and imaging guidance to diagnose or treat vascular disease, including angioplasty with or without stent placement, stent-graft repair of aneurysms, embolization, thrombectomy, and catheter-directed thrombolysis.

thoracic_duct.definition: The main lymphatic vessel that drains lymph from most of the body into the left subclavian vein; it originates from the cisterna chyli in the abdomen and ascends through the thorax, collecting chyle from intestinal and other lymphatics before emptying at the junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins.

right_lymphatic_duct.definition: A lymphatic vessel that drains lymph from the right upper limb, right side of the head and neck, and right thorax, and empties into the venous system at the right venous angle (junction of the right internal jugular and right subclavian veins).

first_rib.definition: The uppermost, short, broad true rib of the thorax that forms part of the superior thoracic inlet; its head articulates with the bodies of T1 (and the T1–T2 disc) and its costal cartilage joins the manubrium of the sternum. It serves as a landmark and conduit for the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus and provides attachment for scalene muscles.

costoclavicular_ligament.definition: A strong ligament connecting the inferior surface of the clavicle to the costal cartilage of the first rib, stabilizing the sternoclavicular joint and limiting elevation of the clavicle.

conoid_ligament.definition: A short, strong ligament extending from the conoid tubercle on the inferior clavicle to the base of the coracoid process of the scapula; it is the medial component of the coracoclavicular ligament and stabilizes the acromioclavicular joint by preventing superior displacement of the clavicle.

brachial_plexus.definition: A network of nerves that are rooted at the cervical spine and provide sensation and movement to the shoulder and arm.

fifth_cervical_nerves.definition: A spinal nerve of the cervical region arising from the C5 segment and exiting above the C5 vertebra; it contributes to the brachial plexus, providing motor innervation to shoulder girdle muscles (e.g., deltoid, supraspinatus) and sensory innervation to the lateral shoulder and upper arm.

sixth_cervical_nerves.definition: The sixth cervical nerve is a spinal nerve of the cervical region (C6) that exits the intervertebral foramen between the C5 and C6 vertebrae; it contributes to the brachial plexus and provides motor innervation to upper-limb muscles and sensory input from the lateral forearm and thumb.

pectoralis_major.definition: A thick, fan-shaped chest muscle with clavicular and sternocostal heads; it originates from the medial half of the clavicle, the sternum, and the upper six costal cartilages, and inserts on the lateral lip of the bicipital (intertubercular) groove of the humerus. It adducts and medially rotates the humerus; the clavicular head flexes the arm, while the sternocostal head extends it from a flexed position. Innervation is by the medial and lateral pectoral nerves (C5–T1).

pectoralis_minor.definition: A thin, triangular chest muscle beneath the pectoralis major; it originates from the 3rd–5th ribs and inserts on the coracoid process of the scapula. It protracts and downwardly rotates the scapula, stabilizes it against the thoracic wall, and assists in elevating the ribs during deep inspiration.

serratus_anterior.definition: Fan-shaped muscle on the lateral chest wall that protracts and stabilizes the scapula and assists in upward rotation; innervated by the long thoracic nerve (C5–C7).

subclinical.definition: Not producing noticeable symptoms; a disease or condition that is present but not clinically evident, detectable only by laboratory tests, imaging, or other objective methods, and may progress to clinical illness.

impaired_glucose_tolerance.definition: A prediabetic state defined by a 2-hour plasma glucose of 140–199 mg/dL (7.8–11.0 mmol/L) after a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test, with fasting glucose typically below 126 mg/dL, indicating increased risk of progression to type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

subclinical_diabetes.definition: A nonstandard term for diabetes that is not yet clinically evident and is detected only by laboratory tests showing hyperglycemia or impaired glucose metabolism, with no noticeable diabetes symptoms.

orthomolecular_medicine.definition: An alternative medical approach that proposes disease prevention and treatment by optimizing health through targeted nutrient supplementation, often involving megadoses of vitamins and minerals; its efficacy is not supported by robust evidence and it can carry risks from excessive intake.

subcollateral_gyrus.definition: An anatomical brain gyrus located below the collateral sulcus on the temporal lobe, adjacent to the parahippocampal gyrus (part of the limbic system).

subcostales.definition: Musculi subcostales are small, thin muscles on the inner surface of the thoracic wall that originate on the inner aspect of a lower rib and insert on the inner surface of the rib two or more levels below; they depress the ribs during forced expiration and are supplied by the intercostal nerves.

internal_intercostal_muscles.definition: Muscles between adjacent ribs, lying deep to the external intercostals, with fibers that run obliquely downward and forward; they depress the ribs during expiration (interosseous part) and, via the interchondral portion, can elevate the ribs during forced inspiration, aiding thoracic volume changes.

subcostal_nerve.definition: The ventral ramus of the twelfth thoracic spinal nerve (T12); a motor and sensory nerve that runs below the 12th rib, supplying the abdominal wall muscles (external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis) and providing cutaneous sensation to the lower anterior abdominal wall.

spinal_nerve_t12.definition: The 12th thoracic spinal nerve; the ventral ramus forms the subcostal nerve, which exits below the 12th rib and supplies motor innervation to the abdominal wall muscles (external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis) and sensory innervation to the skin of the lower anterior abdominal wall and surrounding hip region.

subcrepitant_rale.definition: A soft, low-pitched crackling lung sound heard on inspiration during auscultation, weaker than crepitant crackles and typically associated with mild interstitial edema, subsegmental atelectasis, or bronchitic secretions.

crackling_rale.definition: An adventitious lung sound consisting of brief, discontinuous crackling noises heard on inspiration (and sometimes expiration) caused by the reopening of collapsed or fluid-filled small airways or alveoli; seen with atelectasis, pneumonia, interstitial edema/heart failure, or fibrosis.

periodontal_pocket.definition: A pathologically deepened gingival sulcus due to inflammatory destruction of the periodontal ligament and supporting tissues, with apical migration of the junctional epithelium and often bone loss; typically measured as a pocket depth greater than 3 mm.

subcutaneous_fascia.definition: Layer of loose connective tissue and fat beneath the dermis, forming the superficial fascia; it binds the skin to underlying tissues, contains cutaneous nerves and vessels, and allows the skin to move over deeper structures.

entomophthromycosis.definition: A rare fungal infection caused by fungi of the order Entomophthorales (notably Basidiobolus ranarum or Conidiobolus spp.), presenting as chronic subcutaneous nodules or rhinofacial swelling after traumatic inoculation from soil or decaying vegetation; treated with itraconazole or potassium iodide.

basidiobolae.definition: Plural form of Basidiobolus, a genus of environmental fungi in the order Entomophthorales; Basidiobolus species, notably Basidiobolus ranarum, can cause basidiobolomycosis, a rare fungal infection affecting subcutaneous tissue and, less commonly, the gastrointestinal tract.

subcutaneous_emphysema.definition: Air or gas in the subcutaneous tissues, often from trauma, pneumothorax, esophageal or gastrointestinal perforation, or barotrauma; presents with swelling and palpable crepitus and usually resolves once the underlying cause is treated.

fat_necrosis.definition: Death of adipose tissue due to trauma or enzymatic fat hydrolysis (notably pancreatic lipase in pancreatitis), with necrotic adipocytes and saponification (calcium soap deposition), often accompanied by inflammation and fibrosis and may present as a palpable mass in tissues such as breast or subcutaneous fat.

adiponecrosis.definition: Necrosis (death) of adipose tissue due to compromised blood supply or external injury, often with an inflammatory reaction; can occur after trauma or injections and may mimic cancer on imaging when involving the breast or subcutaneous tissue.

subcutaneous_neonatorum.definition: Not a standard medical term. If taken literally, it would refer to a subcutaneous (beneath the skin) condition in a newborn (neonate), such as subcutaneous edema, hemorrhage, or inflammation, but there is no established disease named “subcutaneous neonatorum.”

intradermal_test.definition: A diagnostic skin test in which a small amount of antigen is injected into the dermis to elicit a localized reaction, used to assess hypersensitivity (e.g., tuberculin skin test or intradermal allergy testing).

bartholins_duct.definition: A duct of the Bartholin's (greater vestibular) gland that carries lubricating mucus from the gland to the vestibule of the vagina, opening at the posterior part of the vaginal introitus.

duct_of_rivinus.definition: One of the numerous small excretory ducts of the sublingual salivary gland that open along the floor of the mouth (sublingual folds); collectively called Rivini's ducts.

sublingual_duct.definition: A duct of the sublingual salivary gland that drains saliva into the floor of the mouth; there are multiple small ducts (ducts of Rivinus) and a major duct (often called Bartholin's duct) that opens at the sublingual caruncle.

sublingual_caruncle.definition: A small mucosal papilla on the floor of the mouth on each side of the lingual frenulum; it is the ductal opening site for saliva from the submandibular gland (and, to a lesser extent, the sublingual glands).

sublingual_fold.definition: One of a pair of mucosal folds on the floor of the mouth formed by underlying sublingual gland tissue; they run laterally from the lingual frenulum and contain the openings of the sublingual ducts.

sublingual_gland.definition: A small salivary gland located in the floor of the mouth beneath the tongue; the smallest of the three major salivary glands, it predominantly secretes mucous saliva and drains into the oral cavity via multiple sublingual ducts (Rivinus) and Bartholin's duct.

submandibular_duct.definition: The excretory duct of the submandibular gland that carries saliva from the gland to the floor of the mouth, opening at the sublingual caruncle near the lingual frenulum.

submandibular_gland.definition: A major salivary gland located beneath the floor of the mouth; it produces most of the resting (unstimulated) saliva and drains via Wharton’s duct into the oral cavity.

subcutaneous_mastectomy.definition: A surgical procedure in which the breast tissue is removed while preserving the skin envelope and the nipple-areolar complex; often used for prophylaxis in high-risk individuals or for select breast cancer cases to allow immediate reconstruction.

reconstruction.definition: A surgical procedure aimed at restoring form and function of a body part after injury, disease, or removal, typically using tissue transfer (flaps or grafts), implants, or other reconstructive techniques.

subcutaneous_nodule.definition: A palpable lump in the subcutaneous tissue beneath the skin, typically a discrete, rounded or oval lesion that may be mobile or fixed; can arise from benign processes such as lipoma or epidermoid cyst, inflammatory nodules, or less commonly malignant tumors or metastases.

sternal_notch.definition: A depression in the upper part of the sternum between the clavicles, marking the junction of the manubrium and the body of the sternum; also called the suprasternal or jugular notch and serves as an anatomical landmark.

brachiocephalic_vein.definition: One of two large veins formed behind the sternoclavicular joints by the union of the internal jugular and subclavian veins; they drain blood from the head, neck, and upper limbs (and upper thorax) and join to form the superior vena cava.

subclavian_vein.definition: Large deep vein that drains blood from the upper limb and adjacent thoracic wall; it continues from the axillary vein at the lateral border of the first rib, runs beneath the clavicle, and joins the internal jugular vein to form the brachiocephalic (innominate) vein.

carotid_artery.definition: One of two major blood vessels found on either side of the neck. The carotid arteries supply blood to the brain.

nasal_meatus.definition: A groove or passage within the nasal cavity beneath a nasal concha; there are three meatuses—the superior, middle, and inferior meatuses—that channel airflow and provide openings for the paranasal sinuses and the nasolacrimal duct.

mastoid_air_cells.definition: A network of air-filled spaces within the mastoid portion of the temporal bone, lined by mucosa and communicating with the middle ear via the aditus ad antrum; they aerate and drain the middle ear and mastoid, and can be involved in mastoiditis.

acoustic_meatus.definition: A canal within the temporal bone that conducts sound from the external ear to the tympanic membrane; the external auditory canal is about 2.5 cm long and lined with skin bearing hair and ceruminous glands.

infraglottic.definition: Below the glottis; located inferior to the vocal cords (the subglottic region of the larynx).

subiculum.definition: A major output structure of the hippocampus (part of the hippocampal formation), located at the border between CA1 and the entorhinal cortex; it contains pyramidal neurons and projects to various cortical and subcortical targets, relaying hippocampal information important for memory formation and spatial navigation.

hippocampal_formation.definition: A neural structure in the medial temporal lobe comprising the hippocampus proper, dentate gyrus, and subiculum; crucial for consolidation of long-term declarative memories and spatial navigation.

parahippocampal_gyrus.definition: A region of the limbic system on the medial temporal lobe that wraps around the hippocampus and is involved in memory formation and retrieval, contextual association, and scene/spatial processing.

ammon_horn.definition: A region of the hippocampus in the medial temporal lobe, comprising four subfields (CA1–CA4) collectively known as the Cornu Ammonis; essential for memory formation and spatial navigation.

subintimal.definition: Situated beneath the intima (the innermost layer) of a blood vessel; relating to the subintimal space between the intima and media.

subendocardial_infarction.definition: An ischemic myocardial infarction limited to the inner (subendocardial) portion of the heart wall (nontransmural infarct), usually due to partial coronary occlusion or low-flow states; ECG typically shows ST-segment depression and T-wave inversion rather than pathologic Q waves.

subepicardium.definition: The layer immediately beneath the epicardium (visceral pericardium) of the heart, composed of loose connective tissue and adipose tissue that contains portions of the coronary vessels and lies between the epicardium and the myocardium.

subepicardial.definition: Situated beneath the epicardium (the outer layer of the heart wall); the subepicardial region lies between the epicardium and the myocardium.

subepithelial_hematoma.definition: A localized collection of blood beneath an epithelial surface, usually resulting from trauma and rupture of subepithelial vessels, presenting as a raised, bruise-like area under the mucosa or skin.

renal_pelvis.definition: A funnel-shaped collecting portion of the kidney that gathers urine from the calyces and channels it into the ureter; located in the renal sinus at the hilum; lined by transitional epithelium and contains smooth muscle to facilitate propulsion of urine toward the bladder.
