hepaticdysfunction.definition: Hepatic dysfunction is impaired liver function, in which the liver cannot adequately perform its metabolic, detoxification, bile production, and synthetic duties, often evidenced by abnormal liver tests such as elevated transaminases and bilirubin.

erythrocythemia.definition: An elevated red blood cell mass or concentration in the circulating blood, typically evidenced by an increased hematocrit; may be primary (polycythemia vera) or secondary to hypoxia, smoking, or increased erythropoietin, and it can raise blood viscosity and risk of thrombosis.

ureteral.definition: Pertaining to the ureter, the muscular tube that transports urine from the kidney to the bladder.

testicularvein.definition: A vein that drains venous blood from the testes; the pampiniform plexus forms the testicular veins, with the right testicular vein draining into the inferior vena cava and the left into the left renal vein.

renalvein.definition: A vein that drains deoxygenated blood from the kidney and returns it to the inferior vena cava.

inferiorvenacava.definition: A large vein that returns deoxygenated blood from the lower body to the right atrium of the heart; formed by the union of the common iliac veins, it ascends through the abdomen and thorax, collecting blood from the hepatic, renal, lumbar, and iliac veins before entering the heart.

tetanus immune serum.definition: An antitoxin preparation containing antibodies against the tetanus toxin, used to provide immediate passive immunity after suspected exposure to Clostridium tetani; it neutralizes circulating toxin and is typically derived from equine or human donor antibodies.

tetanus infection.definition: A serious disease caused by a bug (bacteria) that lives in the soil. It causes muscles to spasm. Also called lockjaw.

exposure.definition: The state of being subjected to a potentially harmful agent or environmental factor (e.g., an infectious agent, chemical, or ionizing radiation), which may lead to disease or injury; exposure is determined by the presence and degree of contact with the agent.

tetanus treatment.definition: A medical regimen to manage tetanus caused by Clostridium tetani, including wound debridement, administration of tetanus immunoglobulin to neutralize unbound toxin, antibiotics (commonly metronidazole), vaccination with tetanus toxoid if not up to date, and comprehensive supportive care to control muscle spasms, autonomic instability, and respiratory failure.

tetanus immune globulin.definition: A preparation of anti-tetanus immunoglobulin (antibodies) that provides immediate, temporary passive immunity by neutralizing tetanus toxin; used for post-exposure prophylaxis or wound management in individuals with uncertain or incomplete vaccination, typically given alongside active tetanus vaccination.

tetanus toxoid.definition: An inactivated form of the tetanus toxin used as the antigen in vaccines to induce protective immunity against tetanus; the immunizing component of tetanus-containing vaccines such as DTaP, Td, and Tdap.

tetanolysin.definition: A hemolysin produced by Clostridium tetani; a pore-forming cytolysin that lyses red blood cells and other cell membranes, contributing to tissue damage during tetanus; not the tetanus neurotoxin.

equine serum.definition: Serum derived from horses; the liquid portion of blood obtained after coagulation and centrifugation, containing horse proteins and antibodies. Used in the production of antisera and as a reagent in diagnostics and research.

calcium metabolism.definition: Calcium metabolism is the set of physiological processes that maintain calcium balance and homeostasis in the body, including intestinal absorption of dietary calcium, storage and remodeling of calcium in bone, and renal excretion, regulated chiefly by parathyroid hormone, vitamin D (calcitriol), and calcitonin.

alkaline salts.definition: Salts that produce an alkaline (basic) solution in water due to hydrolysis of the conjugate base of a weak acid; they are typically formed when a strong base neutralizes a weak acid (e.g., sodium carbonate, sodium bicarbonate).

gastric tetany.definition: A form of tetany precipitated by gastric disturbances—historically due to prolonged vomiting or gastric suction—that causes metabolic alkalosis with decreased ionized calcium and subsequent neuromuscular irritability (e.g., muscle cramps and carpopedal spasm).

hyperventilation tetany.definition: Tetany caused by acute respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation; decreased ionized calcium due to increased binding of calcium to albumin at higher pH, leading to neuromuscular irritability (e.g., perioral numbness, tingling, carpopedal spasms).

hypocalcemic tetany.definition: Neuromuscular hyperexcitability due to low serum calcium, presenting with involuntary muscle contractions (tetany), paresthesias, cramps, and carpopedal spasm; may show Chvostek and Trousseau signs and can progress to laryngospasm or seizures; caused by hypocalcemia from hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, CKD, or pancreatitis.

discoloration of teeth.definition: An alteration of tooth color from its normal translucency, caused by intrinsic factors (stains within the tooth such as tetracycline exposure, fluorosis, aging dentin) or extrinsic factors (surface stains from coffee, tea, tobacco, red wine, and pigment-rich foods), resulting in yellow, brown, gray, or black hues.

superinfections.definition: An infection that develops during treatment for another infection or after it, caused by a different microorganism than the initial one—often due to disruption of normal microbial flora (e.g., antibiotic-associated yeast infections or colonization by resistant bacteria).

phototoxicity.definition: A nonimmune, dose-dependent adverse reaction in which light exposure (typically UV or visible light) after absorption of a photosensitizing substance (such as certain drugs or chemicals) causes tissue injury via energy transfer and reactive oxygen species formation, producing a sunburn-like eruption.

tetraparesis.definition: Weakness of all four limbs (both arms and legs) with reduced voluntary muscle strength, caused by disease or injury of the central or peripheral nervous system.

autonomic dysreflexia.definition: An acute, potentially life-threatening syndrome in people with high-level spinal cord injury characterized by sudden, severe hypertension due to unopposed sympathetic activity below the level of injury in response to a noxious stimulus (e.g., bladder distention, bowel impaction); requires immediate removal of triggers and rapid blood pressure control.

impaired peristalsis.definition: Decreased or poorly coordinated peristaltic contractions of the gastrointestinal tract, resulting in inadequate propulsion of luminal contents and slowed or incomplete transit.

spinal cord edema.definition: An abnormal accumulation of fluid within the spinal cord parenchyma causing swelling of the cord, which can be cytotoxic or vasogenic in origin and may result from trauma, ischemia, infection/inflammation, or mass effect, often visible as T2 hyperintensity on MRI.

spinal x-ray.definition: A plain radiograph (X-ray) of the spine used to visualize vertebrae and their alignment to assess fractures, degenerative changes, scoliosis, or other spinal abnormalities.

apansystolic murmur.definition: Not a standard medical term. If you meant pansystolic (holosystolic) murmur: a murmur that begins at S1 and continues through S2, lasting the entire systole. It is commonly due to mitral regurgitation, tricuspid regurgitation, or a ventricular septal defect; best heard at the left lower sternal border (MR may radiate to the axilla).

feeding difficulties.definition: A range of problems that interfere with achieving adequate oral nutrition, including dysfunctional sucking/swallowing, poor appetite, or feeding aversion, often due to medical, developmental, or behavioral factors.

squat position.definition: A posture in which the hips and knees are flexed, the person lowers the body toward the floor so the buttocks rest near or on the heels, and the feet are flat on the floor; the torso is upright or slightly forward-leaning.

aorta malposition.definition: An abnormal position or course of the aorta away from its normal left-sided, midline location, including aberrant arch configurations or displacement to the right, often described in congenital heart disease and vascular anomalies.

tetrodotoxism.definition: A life-threatening poisoning caused by tetrodotoxin, a potent neurotoxin found in pufferfish, that blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and prevents neuronal action potentials, leading to paresthesias, weakness, dizziness, and possible respiratory arrest.

tetrodotoxin.definition: A potent marine neurotoxin that blocks voltage-gated sodium channels on nerve and muscle membranes, inhibiting action potential propagation and leading to paresthesias, weakness, and potentially life-threatening respiratory failure after ingestion of contaminated seafood such as pufferfish.

texas catheter.definition: An external, noninvasive urinary collection device for men: a condom‑style sheath placed over the penis and secured with tape or strap, connected to a drainage bag to collect urine; used to manage urinary incontinence without urethral catheterization.

spinal block.definition: An anesthesia technique in which a local anesthetic is injected into the intrathecal (subarachnoid) space to produce rapid, dense sensory and motor blockade of the lower body for surgical anesthesia or analgesia.

topical anesthesia.definition: A local anesthetic applied to the surface of the skin or mucous membranes to temporarily block nerve conduction and produce numbness in superficial tissues for minor procedures.

ophthalmic vasoconstrictor.definition: A drug preparation for topical use in the eye that constricts conjunctival blood vessels to reduce redness and ocular swelling; commonly contains alpha-adrenergic agonists (e.g., phenylephrine) or imidazoline derivatives (e.g., naphazoline, tetrahydrozoline). Use is for short-term relief of redness due to irritation; potential adverse effects include rebound hyperemia, local irritation, and systemic cardiovascular effects; use caution in glaucoma, hypertension, or other cardiovascular disease, and avoid prolonged use.

thalamic.definition: Relating to the thalamus, the brain structure that relays sensory and motor signals to the cerebral cortex and participates in consciousness, sleep, and alertness.

thalamic syndrome.definition: A central pain syndrome caused by a thalamic lesion (most often after stroke), characterized by initial contralateral sensory disturbance that later evolves into chronic pain with dysesthesia and allodynia; may include other sensory, motor, or autonomic abnormalities.

thalamic peduncle.definition: A bundle of axons connecting the thalamus to other brain regions (commonly the brainstem or the cerebral cortex), forming part of the pathways that relay sensory, motor, and integrative information through the thalamus.

malignant hyperphenylalaninemia.definition: A rare form of hyperphenylalaninemia caused by defects in tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) metabolism (e.g., dihydropteridine reductase deficiency), leading to elevated phenylalanine with impaired synthesis of dopamine and serotonin; it mimics phenylketonuria but is not due to phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency and requires BH4 supplementation and neurotransmitter replacement in addition to dietary phenylalanine restriction.

tetrahydrobiopterin.definition: A pterin-derived cofactor required by aromatic amino acid hydroxylases (phenylalanine hydroxylase, tyrosine hydroxylase, tryptophan hydroxylase) and by nitric oxide synthases; enables the synthesis of phenylalanine to tyrosine and the monoamine neurotransmitters (dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin) as well as nitric oxide. Deficiency impairs these pathways.

transforming growth factor.definition: A family of secreted cytokines (including TGF-α and TGF-β) that regulate cell growth, differentiation, and extracellular matrix production; they signal through serine/threonine kinase receptors and SMAD transcription factors to modulate gene expression, playing key roles in development, wound healing, fibrosis, and immune regulation.

total hip arthroplasty.definition: A surgical procedure in which the hip joint is replaced with a prosthetic implant, typically replacing both the femoral head and the acetabulum to relieve pain and restore mobility in end-stage hip disease or severe fracture.

tetraploidy.definition: A form of polyploidy in which a cell contains four complete sets of chromosomes (4n) rather than the normal two (2n); it arises from genome duplication without cell division or from failure of cytokinesis after mitosis, and is usually lethal in most human tissues, though it can occur transiently in certain tissues (such as placenta) or in neoplasia.

thecoma.definition: A benign ovarian tumor arising from the theca interna cells (a sex cord–stromal tumor) that often secretes estrogen, potentially causing abnormal uterine bleeding and endometrial hyperplasia; usually unilateral.

thalamotomy.definition: A neurosurgical procedure in which a targeted region of the thalamus is lesioned or ablated to disrupt abnormal thalamocortical circuits and relieve tremor or other movement disorders; historically via radiofrequency ablation, now also by radiosurgery or laser-based methods.

theobromine.definition: A bitter alkaloid of the methylxanthine class found in cacao beans and chocolate; a milder central nervous system stimulant with diuretic, vasodilator, and bronchodilator properties, similar to caffeine but less potent; toxic to dogs and some other animals in significant amounts.

thallium.definition: A chemical element (Tl, atomic number 81): a soft, malleable, highly toxic post‑transition metal. In medicine, radioactive thallium (notably thallium-201) is used in nuclear cardiology for myocardial perfusion imaging.

thelarche.definition: The onset of breast development (breast budding), typically the first physical sign of puberty in females, caused by estrogen acting on breast tissue.

thelioma.definition:
No widely recognized medical term by that spelling; it may be a misspelling. Possible intended terms and concise definitions:

- A tumor of glial cells in the central nervous system (brain or spinal cord). 
- A ovarian stromal tumor arising from the theca interna cells, often estrogen-producing.

If you can provide context or the correct spelling, I can give a precise definition.

thelium.definition: A layer of epithelial cells that lines or covers body surfaces and cavities.

thecal.definition: Relating to the theca; specifically, of or relating to the thecal sac—the dura mater envelope surrounding the spinal cord and containing cerebrospinal fluid.

thenar.definition: The fleshy mass on the palm at the base of the thumb, formed by the intrinsic thumb muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis, and opponens pollicis) that enable thumb movements such as opposition, abduction, and flexion.

iridium-192.definition: A radioactive isotope used as a sealed radiation source in brachytherapy for cancer treatment; it emits high-energy gamma rays (with beta emissions) and has a half-life of about 74 days.

strontium-90.definition: A radioactive isotope that decays by beta emission to yttrium-90, with a half-life of about 28.8 years; it is bone-seeking and can pose radiation hazards if ingested or inhaled.

thebesian.definition: Tiny intramyocardial veins that drain directly into the heart chambers (most often the right atrium and right ventricle), bypassing the larger coronary venous system.

alpha-globin.definition: A globin chain that is one of the two components of adult hemoglobin; encoded by HBA1 and HBA2 genes on chromosome 16; pairs with beta-globin to form HbA (α2β2).

beta-globin.definition: The beta-globin chain is the beta subunit of hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells. It is encoded by the HBB gene and pairs with two alpha-globin subunits to form adult hemoglobin (HbA, α2β2). Mutations in HBB can cause beta-thalassemia and contribute to sickle cell disease.

raynaud disease.definition: A vasospastic disorder of the small arteries and arterioles in the fingers and toes, causing transient color changes (white/pale, blue, then red) and numbness or pain in response to cold or emotional stress; usually primary but may be secondary to autoimmune or connective tissue diseases.

thermokeratoplasty.definition: A procedure in which controlled heat is applied to corneal tissue to cause collagen shrinkage and reshape the cornea, thereby altering its refractive power to correct refractive errors.

thermotherapy.definition: The therapeutic use of heat applied to body tissues to raise tissue temperature, causing vasodilation, increased blood flow, reduced muscle spasm and pain, and improved tissue healing and range of motion; delivered by superficial modalities (hot packs, warm baths, paraffin) or deep heating modalities (diathermy, ultrasound heating).

thermography.definition: A noninvasive imaging modality that records infrared radiation emitted by the body's surface to create temperature maps, highlighting abnormal heat patterns associated with inflammation, vascular changes, or nerve dysfunction.

thermoreceptor.definition: A sensory receptor that detects changes in temperature; primarily free nerve endings in the skin (cold and warm receptors) that transduce thermal energy into neural signals conveyed to the brain, contributing to the perception of temperature and thermoregulation.

thermogenic center.definition: A hypothalamic region that acts as the body's thermoregulatory center, coordinating heat production and heat loss to maintain core temperature. It primarily involves the preoptic area of the anterior hypothalamus as the thermostat, integrating thermal inputs and triggering autonomic responses (vasomotor changes, sweating, shivering) and sympathetic-driven brown adipose tissue thermogenesis as needed.

thermoinhibitory center.definition: A hypothalamic region (often the anterior hypothalamus/preoptic area) that suppresses heat-production mechanisms and promotes heat loss; it mediates cooling responses such as cutaneous vasodilation and sweating and inhibits shivering when body temperature is high.

thermoregulatory center.definition: A neural mechanism in the hypothalamus (primarily the preoptic nucleus of the anterior hypothalamus) that monitors body temperature and coordinates autonomic, endocrine, and behavioral responses to maintain normothermia.

peripheral vascular disorders.definition: A group of disorders affecting the peripheral vascular system—arteries, veins, and capillaries outside the heart and brain—that impair blood flow and tissue perfusion to the limbs, potentially causing claudication, edema, ulcers, or ischemia.

thermocautery.definition: The use of heat from a heated instrument to coagulate and seal tissue or to destroy tissue, commonly to stop bleeding (hemostasis) or ablate tissue.

thermodilution.definition: A technique to measure cardiac output by injecting a known amount of cold saline into the right atrium and recording the resulting downstream temperature change (usually in the pulmonary artery) to calculate flow using the Stewart–Hamilton equation.

paquelin's cautery.definition: A hand-held electric cautery device in which a heated metal tip is used to cut or coagulate tissue; an early form of electrocautery developed by Paquelin.

thermoradiotherapy.definition: An oncologic treatment that combines hyperthermia (raising tumor tissue temperature to about 39–43°C) with ionizing radiation to enhance radiation-induced tumor cell death by increasing radiosensitivity, improving tumor oxygenation, and disrupting DNA repair; used as an adjunct to radiotherapy for some solid tumors.

thermoradiography.definition: An imaging technique that uses infrared thermography to map surface temperature and radiography to visualize underlying anatomy, aiming to correlate thermal patterns with structural changes.

hookworms.definition: Parasitic nematodes (mainly Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus) that infect humans when filariform larvae in contaminated soil penetrate the skin; they migrate to the lungs, are swallowed, and mature in the small intestine, where they attach to the mucosa and feed on blood, causing iron-deficiency anemia and abdominal symptoms.

roundworms.definition: Nematodes (phylum Nematoda) are slender, cylindrical, unsegmented worms; many species are parasitic in humans and animals and cause helminth infections. They have a complete digestive tract and a pseudocoelom, and transmission occurs via ingestion of eggs or larvae or through skin penetration, depending on the species.

pinworms.definition: Small white parasitic nematodes (Enterobius vermicularis) that infect the human large intestine; females migrate to the perianal region at night to lay eggs, causing perianal itching. Transmission is fecal-oral; diagnosis is typically by perianal tape test; treatment includes albendazole, mebendazole, or pyrantel pamoate, with treatment of household contacts and reinforced hygiene.

threadworms.definition: A small parasitic nematode (Enterobius vermicularis) that causes enterobiasis (pinworm infection) in humans; infection occurs by ingesting eggs shed around the anus, producing nocturnal perianal itching; diagnosis is typically by a perianal swab (tape test) and treatment with antihelminthic medications such as mebendazole, albendazole, or pyrantel pamoate.

thiamin.definition: A water-soluble B vitamin essential for carbohydrate metabolism; it serves as a coenzyme in energy production, especially glucose oxidation; deficiency can cause beriberi and Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome.

thiaminase.definition: An enzyme that degrades thiamine (vitamin B1), leading to thiamine deficiency; found in certain plants, bacteria, and fish.

thiazine-eosinate.definition: A thiazine-based dye in an eosinate salt form used as a histological stain or fluorescent dye for tissue visualization.

eosin.definition: A red, acidic dye used in histology as the counterstain in hematoxylin–eosin (H&E) staining; it stains basic (eosinophilic) structures such as cytoplasm, collagen, and red blood cells pink to red.

thiemia.definition: I can’t locate a recognized medical term spelled “thiemia.” It may be a misspelling or an abbreviation. Could you share the context (field or source) or the correct spelling? I can provide the definition once clarified.

thiethylperazine.definition: An antiemetic drug, a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist in the phenothiazine class, used to prevent or treat nausea and vomiting; may cause extrapyramidal symptoms and sedation.

parkinson's.definition: A movement disorder that occurs when the brain does not produce enough of a chemical.

malate.definition: A salt or ester of malic acid. In biochemistry, it is a four-carbon dicarboxylate anion that serves as an intermediate of the citric acid cycle, formed from fumarate and oxidized to oxaloacetate; it also participates in cytosolic–mitochondrial redox shuttles.

thioamide.definition: An organic compound in which the carbonyl oxygen of an amide is replaced by sulfur, producing a thiocarbonyl group (R-C(=S)-NR'R''); in pharmacology, the term often refers to antithyroid drugs such as methimazole and propylthiouracil that inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis.

thiouracil.definition: A thiourea derivative used as an antithyroid medication; it inhibits thyroid peroxidase, blocking iodination of tyrosine and the coupling of MIT and DIT, thereby reducing synthesis of thyroid hormones (T3 and T4). Historically used to treat hyperthyroidism; largely superseded by newer thioamide antithyroid drugs.

methylthiouracil.definition: An antithyroid thioamide drug that inhibits thyroid peroxidase, thereby decreasing synthesis of thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) in hyperthyroidism; used to treat thyrotoxicosis; potential adverse effects include agranulocytosis and hepatotoxicity.

carbimazole.definition: An antithyroid thionamide that inhibits thyroid peroxidase, reducing synthesis of thyroid hormones (T3 and T4); a prodrug of methimazole used to treat hyperthyroidism such as Graves' disease.

thiobarbituric.definition: Relating to thiobarbituric acid or its sulfur-containing derivatives; barbiturate compounds in which one or more carbonyl oxygens are replaced by sulfur.

thiobarbiturate.definition: A thiobarbiturate is a barbiturate in which a sulfur atom replaces one of the ring oxygens, producing a highly lipid-soluble, rapidly acting sedative-hypnotic used chiefly for anesthesia induction (examples include thiopental and thiamylal).

thioctic.definition: An antioxidant and mitochondrial cofactor that is a naturally occurring organosulfur compound; soluble in both water and fat and used as a dietary supplement, notably for diabetic neuropathy.

thioester.definition: A thioester is an organic compound in which an acyl group is bonded to sulfur (R-CO-S-R′); the sulfur analog of an ester, formed when a carboxylic acid reacts with a thiol (as in acyl-CoA thioesters in metabolism).

thioesters.definition: An acyl derivative in which the alkoxy oxygen of a carboxylic ester is replaced by sulfur, giving a carbonyl attached to sulfur (R–C(=O)–S–R'). These compounds are key acyl-transfer intermediates with relatively high-energy bonds that facilitate transfer of acyl groups in metabolism (e.g., acetyl–CoA).

thioethanolamine.definition: A thiol-containing amine that is the thiol analog of ethanolamine, with the structure HS-CH2-CH2-NH2.

thioflavine.definition: A fluorescent histology dye used to stain amyloid fibrils; binds to beta-pleated sheet–rich structures and exhibits enhanced fluorescence upon binding, enabling detection of amyloid deposits in tissue sections.

thiopental.definition: A rapid-onset, ultra-short-acting intravenous barbiturate used to induce anesthesia; it rapidly produces loss of consciousness within seconds and has a duration of about 5–10 minutes. It depresses CNS activity and can cause hypotension, respiratory depression, and apnea; its use for induction has largely been supplanted by propofol.

thioridazine.definition: A phenothiazine-class typical antipsychotic used to treat schizophrenia; a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist with a high risk of extrapyramidal symptoms, retinal pigment changes with long-term use, and QT interval prolongation.

thomsen's.definition: A hereditary myotonia congenita caused by mutations in the CLCN1 gene encoding the skeletal muscle chloride channel (ClC-1); typically autosomal dominant, it features delayed muscle relaxation after contraction (myotonia) present from birth and a warm-up phenomenon with a nonprogressive course.

ventriculostomy.definition: A neurosurgical procedure in which a catheter is placed into the brain's ventricular system (usually the lateral ventricle) to drain cerebrospinal fluid and control intracranial pressure, commonly via an external ventricular drain.

chiasmatis.definition: Not a standalone term; it is the Latin genitive form of chiasma. It is used in anatomy to denote “of the crossing” (as in anatomical names). In the visual system, it relates to the optic chiasm, the X-shaped crossing of the optic nerve fibers in the brain.

interpeduncular.definition: Situated between the cerebral peduncles of the midbrain; pertaining to the interpeduncular fossa.

thiry-vella.definition: A surgically created cutaneous fistula in which a loop of small intestine is exteriorized to the skin and fitted with two catheters (one for drainage and one for irrigation) to provide controlled external drainage and irrigation of luminal contents, facilitating healing of an enterocutaneous wound.

thigh.definition: The region of the lower limb between the hip and knee joints (the upper leg), containing the femur and the thigh muscles arranged into anterior (quadriceps), posterior (hamstrings), and medial (adductor) compartments; its muscles extend and flex the knee and assist with hip movement.

propofol.definition: A short-acting intravenous anesthetic agent used for induction and maintenance of general anesthesia and for procedural sedation; it produces rapid onset and short duration of hypnosis by potentiating GABA-A receptor activity; common adverse effects include hypotension, respiratory depression, and pain at the injection site; rarely, prolonged high-dose use can lead to propofol infusion syndrome.

thoraces.definition: The plural of thorax; the chest region of the body between the neck and the abdomen, containing the heart and lungs and protected by the rib cage.

thoracoacromial artery.definition: A short trunk of the axillary artery (second part) that divides into four branches—pectoral, clavicular, deltoid, and acromial—to supply the pectoral region, deltoid muscle, and shoulder girdle.

thoracocentesis.definition: A procedure in which a needle or catheter is inserted through the chest wall into the pleural space to remove pleural fluid or air for diagnostic analysis or therapeutic relief of pleural effusion or pneumothorax.

thoracic aorta.definition: Descending portion of the aorta within the thoracic cavity, extending from the aortic arch to the aortic hiatus in the diaphragm; it travels through the posterior mediastinum and gives off branches to the esophagus, bronchi, intercostal spaces, and mediastinal structures, continuing as the abdominal aorta.

bronchial artery.definition: A systemic artery that furnishes oxygenated blood to the conducting airways and other supporting tissues of the lungs (the bronchial tree), typically arising from the thoracic aorta (often as the left bronchial artery) or adjacent intercostal arteries, and sometimes forming anastomoses with branches of the pulmonary circulation.

esophageal artery.definition: Artery that supplies the esophagus; esophageal arteries arise from several sources along its length—upper from the inferior thyroid arteries, middle from branches of the thoracic aorta and bronchial arteries, and lower from the left gastric and inferior phrenic arteries.

posterior intercostal.definition: Relating to the posterior intercostal arteries, veins, or nerves that run along the posterior aspect of the intercostal spaces in the thorax; these structures supply and innervate the thoracic wall.

subcostal.definition: Situated beneath a rib; relating to or located below the costal margin.

superior phrenic.definition: Arteries that arise from the thoracic aorta (often from the inferior phrenic arteries) and supply the superior surface of the diaphragm; paired vessels that anastomose with the inferior phrenic arteries.

alimentary duct.definition: The digestive tract from the mouth to the anus through which ingestion, digestion, absorption, and elimination of food occur.

thoracic fistula.definition: An abnormal, epithelialized tract within the thorax that connects thoracic structures or cavities to another surface (such as the skin or pleural space), typically causing persistent drainage or air passage.

thoracic kyphosis.definition: An outward (posterior) curvature of the thoracic portion of the spine; when exaggerated, it is called hyperkyphosis, producing a rounded upper back.

thoracic medicine.definition: A medical specialty focused on diseases of the thorax—primarily the lungs, pleura, mediastinum, and chest wall—encompassing the diagnosis, medical management, and long-term care of respiratory and related cardiopulmonary conditions, often overlapping with pulmonology/internal medicine; surgical aspects are typically managed by thoracic surgery.

thoracic nerves.definition: The ventral rami of the 12 thoracic spinal nerves (T1–T12). They give rise to the intercostal nerves (T1–T11) and the subcostal nerve (T12), supplying motor innervation to the intercostal muscles and sensory innervation to the thoracic wall and upper abdomen.

intercostal nerves.definition: Ventral rami of thoracic spinal nerves (T1–T11, with T12 as the subcostal nerve) that run in the intercostal spaces, providing motor innervation to the intercostal muscles and sensory innervation to the thoracic and upper abdominal skin; they give off lateral and anterior cutaneous branches.

subcostal nerve.definition: A ventral ramus of the twelfth thoracic spinal nerve (T12) that runs below the 12th rib; it provides motor innervation to the abdominal wall muscles (external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis) and sensory innervation to the skin of the lower anterior abdominal wall.

cervical disk.definition: A fibrocartilaginous cushion between the vertebral bodies of the cervical spine that absorbs shock and allows neck movement; it consists of a nucleus pulposus surrounded by an annulus fibrosus and can degenerate or herniate, causing neck pain or radiculopathy.

thoracic parietal node.definition: A lymph node located in the chest wall that drains lymph from thoracic somatic structures (such as the intercostal spaces and pleura) and communicates with mediastinal nodes; part of the parietal (somatic) thoracic lymph node group and may be involved in metastasis from thoracic malignancies.

sternal nodes.definition: A group of lymph nodes located along the sternum (parasternal or internal thoracic nodes) that drain lymph from the anterior chest wall and the medial portions of the breast.

intercostal nodes.definition: A group of lymph nodes located along the intercostal spaces of the thoracic wall; they drain lymph from the intercostal spaces and thoracic wall to the posterior mediastinal nodes, and then to the thoracic duct (left) or the right lymphatic duct (right).

diaphragmatic nodes.definition: A group of lymph nodes located on the diaphragmatic surface of the diaphragm (along the inferior aspect and near the crura). They drain lymph from the diaphragmatic peritoneum and adjacent abdominal and thoracic regions, with efferents typically passing to the phrenic nodes and then to mediastinal lymphatic trunks.

anterior mediastinal nodes.definition: A group of lymph nodes located in the anterior part of the mediastinum (prevascular nodes) that drain the thymus and other anterior mediastinal structures; they are part of the mediastinal lymphatic drainage and can be involved by thymic tumors or anterior mediastinal lymphoma.

tracheobronchial nodes.definition: A group of lymph nodes situated in the mediastinum around the trachea and the origins of the main bronchi (including paratracheal and carinal/inferior tracheobronchial nodes). They drain lymph from the lungs and lower airways and are a key nodal station for thoracic cancers.

thoracic spine.definition: A section of the vertebral column comprising twelve vertebrae (T1–T12) in the mid-back, which articulates with the ribs via costal facets, contributes to the thoracic kyphosis, and encloses and protects the spinal cord and nerve roots.

thoracic vertebra.definition: One of the twelve vertebrae of the mid-back (T1–T12) that articulates with ribs via costal facets on the vertebral body and (for ribs 1–10) on the transverse processes; typical features include a heart-shaped body, a long downward-sloping spinous process, and superior/inferior articular facets oriented in the coronal plane.

thoracic wall.definition: A bony and muscular enclosure forming the boundary of the thoracic cavity, built from the thoracic cage (ribs, costal cartilages, sternum, thoracic vertebrae) with surrounding intercostal muscles and fascia; it protects thoracic organs and assists respiration by expanding and contracting the chest.

transversus thoracis.definition: A thin muscle on the inner surface of the anterior chest wall arising from the posterior lower sternum and xiphoid, inserting into the costal cartilages of ribs 2–6; it depresses these cartilages to assist expiration.

thoracobronchotomy.definition: A surgical procedure involving an incision into a bronchus through the thoracic cavity (a bronchotomy performed via thoracotomy).

thoracomyodynia.definition: Pain in the chest wall muscles (thoracic musculature), usually due to strain, overuse, injury, or inflammation; presents as localized chest wall tenderness and can mimic cardiac chest pain.

thoracodorsal nerve.definition: A motor branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus (typically C6–C8) that innervates the latissimus dorsi muscle; it enables shoulder extension, adduction, and internal rotation, and injury can weaken these movements.

thoracodynia.definition: Pain located in the chest (thoracic region); chest pain.

thoracolumbar junction.definition: A region of the spine where the thoracic and lumbar curvatures meet, typically around the T11–L2 levels; a biomechanically transitional zone between thoracic kyphosis and lumbar lordosis that is prone to injury such as compression fractures in osteoporosis.

tlso.definition: A thoracolumbosacral orthosis; a rigid or semirigid back brace that immobilizes the thoracic, lumbar, and sacral spine to provide external stabilization after injury, surgery, or deformity, typically worn around the torso from the mid-chest to pelvis.

thoracopathy.definition: A general term for disease or pathology of the thorax (chest); a non-specific description rather than a specific medical entity.

thoracoplasty.definition: A surgical procedure in which multiple consecutive ribs are removed to collapse the chest wall and obliterate the pleural space, historically used to treat chronic empyema (often due to tuberculosis).

thoracoscopy.definition: A minimally invasive procedure in which a thoracoscope is inserted through small chest-wall incisions into the pleural cavity to visualize the thoracic organs and perform diagnostic or therapeutic interventions (e.g., biopsy, drainage, or resection); when used for surgery, it is commonly called video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS).

thoracostomy.definition: A surgical procedure that creates an opening into the thoracic cavity to drain air, fluid, or blood from the pleural space, typically accomplished by inserting a chest tube (tube thoracostomy) to treat pneumothorax or pleural effusion.

thoracostomy tube.definition: A chest tube inserted through the chest wall into the pleural space to drain air or fluid and allow the lung to re-expand; used for conditions such as pneumothorax, pleural effusion, and hemothorax.

thorazine.definition: A phenothiazine class antipsychotic used to treat schizophrenia and other psychoses; also used as an antiemetic and sedative. It works primarily by blocking dopamine D2 receptors in the brain.

thought broadcasting.definition: A delusional belief, common in psychosis, that one’s private thoughts are being transmitted to and accessible by others, as if broadcast aloud or read by those nearby.

thought insertion.definition: Delusional belief that thoughts are being placed into one’s mind by an external agent or force; the person experiences these thoughts as not originated by themselves and may feel controlled or monitored.

thought transference.definition: The delusional belief that one’s thoughts are being transmitted to or read by others through mental means (telepathy), a psychotic symptom sometimes described as thought broadcasting/transmission.

thought.definition: The mental process of considering, reasoning, and forming ideas; the content of cognition, including ideas, beliefs, and plans, expressed in thinking, speech, and behavior.

threadworm.definition: A small intestinal nematode parasite (Enterobius vermicularis) that causes enterobiasis; presents with nocturnal perianal itching; transmitted by ingestion or inhalation of eggs on contaminated hands or surfaces; diagnosed by perianal adhesive tape test; treated with albendazole or mebendazole.

acanthocheilonema perstans.definition: A human parasitic nematode that causes subcutaneous filariasis; transmitted by Culicoides biting midges, with adults dwelling in subcutaneous tissues and microfilariae circulating in peripheral blood. Infections are often asymptomatic but may cause pruritus, dermatitis, or subcutaneous nodules; diagnosis is by detecting microfilariae in blood, and treatment typically involves antifilarial medications such as diethylcarbamazine or ivermectin.

threadworm infection.definition: An intestinal helminth infection caused by Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm), characterized by perianal itching (often worse at night), possible mild abdominal discomfort, and transmission via ingestion of eggs; diagnosed by perianal swab/tape test or stool exam; treated with antihelminthics such as mebendazole, albendazole, or pyrantel pamoate, along with hygiene measures to prevent reinfection.

thready pulse.definition: A pulse that is weak and easily obliterated on palpation, often described as thread-like; it indicates reduced stroke volume or poor peripheral perfusion, commonly due to hypovolemia, dehydration, or shock.

thromboangiitis.definition: Inflammation with thrombosis of small- to medium-sized arteries and veins, producing segmental occlusive vasculitis of the extremities and strongly linked to tobacco use.

thromboangiitis obliterans.definition: A nonatherosclerotic inflammatory vasculitis of small- to medium-sized arteries and veins in the extremities, marked by segmental thrombosis and occlusion that cause ischemia; strongly associated with tobacco use and typically affecting young to middle-aged smokers; management centers on complete smoking cessation.

glanzmann thrombasthenia.definition: A rare autosomal recessive platelet function disorder caused by deficiency or dysfunction of the platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (integrin αIIbβ3) receptor, leading to defective platelet aggregation and mucocutaneous bleeding despite a normal platelet count; aggregation is impaired with ADP, collagen, and epinephrine, while ristocetin-induced aggregation is normal.

thrombocystis.definition: Not a standard medical term; there is no established definition in contemporary medical references. It may be a misspelling or historical term related to platelets, commonly confused with thrombocytosis (elevated platelets) or thrombocytopenia (decreased platelets).

thromboarteritis.definition: An inflammatory, segmental vasculitis of small- to medium-sized arteries and veins, most often in the extremities, characterized by thrombosis of the vessel lumen and inflammatory microabscesses; strongly associated with tobacco use and may cause claudication, ischemia, ulcers, and gangrene. Also known as thromboangiitis obliterans.

nasopharyngeal culture.definition: A microbiology test in which a sample from the nasopharynx is plated on culture media and incubated to grow and identify the causative pathogen of a respiratory infection or to detect asymptomatic carriage.

right primary bronchus.definition: A mainstem airway that carries air from the trachea into the right lung; it is shorter, wider, and more vertical than the left main bronchus and divides into the right upper, middle, and lower lobar bronchi.

left primary bronchus.definition: Main airway arising from the lower trachea that enters the left lung and divides into the left upper and left lower lobe bronchi; it is longer, narrower, and more horizontal than the right main bronchus.

thromboplastic.definition: Capable of initiating thrombosis; pertaining to thromboplastin (tissue factor) that activates the coagulation cascade, especially via the extrinsic pathway.

thrombocyst.definition: Not a standard medical term; if used, it refers to a cyst containing a thrombus (blood clot) or a cyst that has undergone thrombosis.

thrombocythemia.definition: A condition characterized by an abnormally high number of platelets in the blood, which may be reactive (secondary) or due to a myeloproliferative neoplasm such as essential thrombocythemia.

thrombocytopathy.definition: A disorder of platelet function in which platelets fail to aggregate and form a proper hemostatic plug despite a normal platelet count, leading to easy mucocutaneous bleeding; it can be congenital or acquired (e.g., drug-induced).

thromboembolic.definition: Relating to a thrombus that has broken loose and traveled through the bloodstream to occlude a distant blood vessel (embolic obstruction).

thromboendarterectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove a thrombus (blood clot) and occlusive atherosclerotic plaque from the interior of a diseased artery to restore blood flow.

thrombogenesis.definition: The formation of a thrombus (blood clot) within a blood vessel, involving activation of the coagulation cascade and platelets with fibrin deposition to stabilize the clot.

thrombogenic.definition: Tending to promote thrombosis; capable of initiating or promoting the formation of a blood clot.

thromboid.definition: Resembling or relating to a thrombus (blood clot).

thrombokinase.definition: An enzymatic complex that activates prothrombin to thrombin during coagulation; typically the prothrombinase complex composed of factor Xa and factor Va with calcium on a phospholipid surface.

thrombopathy.definition: A disorder of platelet function causing defective primary hemostasis and an increased risk of bleeding; it may be congenital or acquired.

thrombopenia.definition: A condition characterized by a lower-than-normal platelet count in the blood, leading to impaired hemostasis and an increased risk of bleeding; typically defined as a platelet count below 150,000 per microliter (150 x 10^9/L).

thrombophilia.definition: A predisposition to abnormal blood clot formation, usually due to inherited or acquired factors, resulting in an increased risk of venous thromboembolism (e.g., deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism) and, less commonly, arterial clots.

thrombophlebitis migrans.definition: A migratory, recurrent superficial thrombophlebitis characterized by tender, inflamed superficial veins that appear at different sites over time, often as a paraneoplastic sign indicating occult malignancy (most commonly pancreatic adenocarcinoma).

thromboxane-a.definition: A potent prostanoid produced by activated platelets from arachidonic acid via cyclooxygenase, promoting platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction; it is rapidly hydrolyzed to the inactive metabolite thromboxane B2.

thromboxane-a2.definition: A potent vasoconstrictor and promoter of platelet aggregation synthesized by activated platelets from arachidonic acid via cyclooxygenase-1 and thromboxane synthase; rapidly inactivated to TXB2 and acts on TP receptors to enhance aggregation and vasoconstriction; inhibited by aspirin.

thromboxane-b2.definition: An inactive, stable metabolite of thromboxane A2 produced by platelets; formed by hydrolysis of TXA2; used as a biomarker of thromboxane A2 production and platelet activation; thromboxane A2 is a potent vasoconstrictor and promoter of platelet aggregation.

angiograms.definition: A radiographic imaging study of the blood vessels obtained after injecting contrast material (usually via catheter) to visualize arteries and veins and identify blockages, aneurysms, or other vascular abnormalities.

thymic.definition: Relating to the thymus, a lymphoid organ in the anterior mediastinum where T lymphocytes mature.

thymectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove the thymus gland, often performed for myasthenia gravis or thymic tumors.

thymoma.definition: A tumor arising from thymic epithelial cells in the anterior mediastinum; typically slow-growing and encapsulated, it may be benign or malignant; commonly associated with paraneoplastic syndromes such as myasthenia gravis; treatment usually involves surgical resection, with adjuvant radiotherapy or chemotherapy for invasive or unresectable disease.

thymomata.definition: A tumor of the thymus arising from thymic epithelial cells; can be benign or malignant and is often associated with paraneoplastic syndromes such as myasthenia gravis.

thymidine.definition: A deoxyribonucleoside consisting of the pyrimidine base thymine attached to a deoxyribose sugar; one of the four nucleosides of DNA, pairing with adenine and serving as the precursor to dTMP and dTTP for DNA synthesis.

thymidine kinase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the phosphorylation of thymidine to thymidine monophosphate (dTMP) using ATP as the phosphate donor; a key enzyme in the pyrimidine salvage pathway of DNA synthesis, existing in cytosolic (TK1) and mitochondrial (TK2) forms.

digeorge syndrome.definition: A congenital genetic disorder caused by a microdeletion at chromosome 22q11.2, resulting in thymic hypoplasia with T-cell immunodeficiency, hypocalcemia from parathyroid aplasia, and congenital heart defects (often conotruncal), with variable facial features, palate abnormalities, and developmental or neuropsychiatric issues.

thrombotapheresis.definition: A therapeutic apheresis procedure designed to remove thrombi or prothrombotic factors from the blood, with the treated blood returned to the patient.

thymocytes.definition: Immature T lymphocytes that develop in the thymus; they arise from bone marrow precursors and undergo T-cell receptor gene rearrangement and thymic selection to mature into CD4+ helper or CD8+ cytotoxic T cells.

cricothyroid.definition: Relating to the cricoid and thyroid cartilages; used to describe the cricothyroid joint or the cricothyroid muscle, which tilts the thyroid cartilage forward to tense the vocal cords.

thyrocricotomy.definition: A surgical airway procedure in which an opening is made through the thyroid and cricoid cartilages to access the trachea, typically performed when cricothyrotomy is not feasible or feasible due to neck anatomy.

thyroid function test.definition: Thyroid function tests are blood tests that assess thyroid gland activity by measuring circulating levels of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and thyroid hormones, typically free T4 (and sometimes free T3); this panel helps diagnose and monitor hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism and guide treatment.

subclavian arteries.definition: A pair of major arteries supplying blood to the upper limbs and portions of the neck and thorax; the right subclavian artery arises from the brachiocephalic trunk and the left from the aortic arch, and each becomes the axillary artery at the lateral border of the first rib.

scalenus anterior.definition: A neck muscle that originates from the anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C3–C6 and inserts on the first rib; it elevates the first rib during inspiration and helps flex and laterally bend the neck.

suprascapular.definition: Situated above the scapula; of or relating to the suprascapular nerve.

transverse cervical.definition: Relating to structures crossing the neck; most often refers to either the neck vessel that travels laterally across the base of the neck to supply the trapezius (a branch of the thyrocervical trunk), or to the cutaneous nerve from the cervical plexus that innervates the anterior neck skin.

inferior thyroid.definition: An anatomical term referring to structures in the lower portion of the thyroid region, most commonly the inferior thyroid artery, a branch of the thyrocervical trunk that supplies the lower thyroid.

thyroglossal.definition: Relating to the thyroid gland and the tongue; in embryology, describing the thyroglossal duct, a transient tract that extends from the foramen cecum at the base of the tongue to the developing thyroid.

thyrolingual.definition: Relating to the thyroid gland and the tongue; most often describes thyroid tissue located at the base of the tongue as a result of incomplete embryologic descent of the thyroid.

thyrohyoid membrane.definition: A fibrous membrane spanning from the greater horn of the hyoid bone to the superior border of the thyroid cartilage, forming part of the anterior wall of the larynx and containing the foramen thyroideum through which the superior laryngeal vessels and the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve pass.

follicular carcinomas.definition: Malignant thyroid neoplasms arising from follicular cells, distinguished from benign follicular adenomas by invasion of the capsule and/or blood vessels; well-differentiated carcinomas that predominantly spread hematogenously (to bone and lung) and are typically treated with thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine, with prognosis depending on extent of invasion and metastasis.

anaplastic carcinomas.definition: A malignant epithelial tumor composed of highly undifferentiated (anaplastic) cells with marked pleomorphism and loss of differentiation; typically shows high mitotic activity and an aggressive clinical course.

medullary carcinomas.definition: A malignant neoplasm defined by a medullary histologic appearance that can arise in several organs (most commonly the thyroid and breast). It typically forms sheets or nests of malignant cells and often has a prominent inflammatory/lymphoid stromal component; prognosis and treatment depend on the organ of origin.

total thyroidectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove the entire thyroid gland (both lobes and the isthmus) through a neck incision, often resulting in lifelong thyroid hormone replacement therapy.

remnant ablation.definition: Destruction of residual tissue left after surgical removal, most commonly thyroid tissue after thyroidectomy, typically achieved with radioactive iodine ablation to eradicate remaining cells and facilitate follow-up monitoring.

radioisotope scanning.definition: A nuclear medicine imaging technique in which a radioactive tracer (radiopharmaceutical) is administered to the patient and its gamma emissions are detected to produce images showing the distribution and function of a targeted organ or tissue.

radioisotope uptake.definition: The process by which a tissue or organ absorbs and concentrates a radioactive tracer (radioisotope-labeled compound) from the bloodstream, allowing imaging and assessment of physiological function, metabolism, or receptor activity based on the amount of radioactivity uptake.

iodine therapy.definition: A medical treatment using radioactive iodine (usually I-131) given orally that concentrates in thyroid tissue to deliver targeted radiation and destroy thyroid cells; used to treat hyperthyroidism (e.g., Graves’ disease, toxic nodular goiter) and to ablate residual thyroid tissue after surgery for differentiated thyroid cancer.

tri-iodothyronine.definition: One of two types of major thyroid hormone manufactured by the thyroid gland. It contains three iodine atoms. Also known as T3.

liothyronine sodium.definition: A man-made version of the thyroid hormone triiodothyronine.

colloid goiter.definition: A non-toxic goiter in which the thyroid follicles are markedly distended with colloid, with minimal follicular hyperplasia and flattened epithelium; typically due to impaired thyroid hormone synthesis, most often from iodine deficiency.

nontoxic colloid goiter.definition: Diffuse enlargement of the thyroid gland in which follicles are distended with colloid and thyroid function is normal or not hyperactive (non-toxic/euthyroid goiter), typically seen with iodine deficiency.

radiation thyroiditis.definition: Inflammation of the thyroid gland caused by exposure to ionizing radiation (such as neck irradiation or radioactive iodine therapy), often presenting with tender thyroid enlargement and may be followed by transient thyrotoxicosis and later hypothyroidism; typically resolves over weeks to months, though permanent thyroid dysfunction can occur.

pretibial myxedema.definition: A localized, non-pitting dermopathy of the shins characterized by thickened, waxy skin due to mucopolysaccharide (glycosaminoglycan) accumulation in the dermis, seen in Graves disease; also called Graves dermopathy.

toxic nodular goiter.definition: An enlarged thyroid gland with nodules that produce excess thyroid hormone. This type of goiter is to blame for hyperthyroidism in many people over 60.

plummer's disease.definition: A form of hyperthyroidism caused by autonomous, hyperfunctioning thyroid nodules (toxic multinodular goiter) that secrete thyroid hormones independent of TSH stimulation, leading to thyrotoxicosis.

thyroglobulin test.definition: A blood test that measures thyroglobulin, a protein produced by thyroid tissue, used primarily as a tumor marker to monitor for residual or recurrent differentiated thyroid carcinoma after thyroid surgery; results can be affected by anti-thyroglobulin antibodies and the patient’s TSH level.

frozen section.definition: A rapid intraoperative pathological examination of a small tissue specimen that has been flash-frozen and cut into thin sections for quick microscopic evaluation to guide surgical decisions.

ultrasonic examination.definition: An imaging study that uses high-frequency sound waves via a transducer to produce real-time images of internal structures; commonly used to evaluate organs, tissues, fetal development, and blood flow (with Doppler), and to guide procedures.

thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins.definition: Autoantibodies that stimulate the thyroid by binding the TSH receptor, mimicking TSH and causing increased thyroid hormone production (hyperthyroidism); most commonly associated with Graves disease.

thyrotropin-releasing hormone.definition: A hypothalamic tripeptide neurohormone that stimulates the anterior pituitary to release thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and, to a lesser extent, prolactin.

thyroid-stimulating hormone assay.definition: A laboratory test that measures the level of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in the blood, usually by immunoassay, to evaluate thyroid gland function and guide treatment of thyroid disorders; TSH levels rise in hypothyroidism and fall in hyperthyroidism due to pituitary feedback.

scintiscanning.definition: A nuclear medicine imaging technique in which a small amount of radioactive tracer is administered and a gamma camera detects the emitted radiation to produce functional images of organs or tissues.

iodine uptake.definition: The rate at which thyroid tissue absorbs iodide from the bloodstream via the sodium-iodide symporter, enabling thyroid hormone synthesis; clinically assessed by radioactive iodine uptake tests to evaluate thyroid function.

iodine excretion.definition: The elimination of iodine from the body, primarily as iodide excreted in urine; small losses occur in sweat and feces, and urinary iodine excretion reflects recent iodine intake and body iodine stores.

atomic bomb exposure.definition: Exposure to ionizing radiation resulting from a nuclear detonation, including prompt radiation and fallout, that can cause acute radiation syndrome, tissue damage, burns, and an increased long-term risk of cancer.

protein-bound iodine.definition: A historical laboratory assay that measures the portion of circulating iodine bound to serum proteins (primarily thyroxine-binding globulin) as an indirect indicator of thyroid hormone levels; elevated protein-bound iodine suggested hyperthyroidism and reduced levels suggested hypothyroidism. The test has largely been replaced by direct TSH, free T4, and free T3 measurements.

butanol-extractable iodine.definition: A fraction of total iodine in a sample that can be solubilized into n-butanol during a liquid-liquid extraction, typically representing organoiodine compounds or iodine bound to organic matter rather than inorganic iodide/iodate.

istmus of the thyroid gland.definition: A narrow band of thyroid tissue that connects the right and left lobes, located anterior to the trachea and crossing the midline at roughly the level of the second to fourth tracheal rings.

lateral lobe.definition: A lobe situated on the side (lateral aspect) of an organ; a distinct anatomical subdivision separated from other lobes by fissures or boundaries.

pyramidal lobe.definition: A small, pyramidal extension of thyroid tissue that arises from the thyroid isthmus and extends upward toward the hyoid bone; a normal anatomical variant and a remnant of the thyroglossal duct.

thyroid dermoid cyst.definition: A rare benign cystic lesion of the thyroid region arising from ectodermal tissue, typically lined by keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium with skin adnexal structures (e.g., hair follicles, sebaceous glands) within or adjacent to the thyroid gland.

thyroid dermopathy.definition: A skin manifestation of Graves disease presenting as nonpitting, thickened skin (often on the pretibial area) due to glycosaminoglycan deposition in the dermis.

thyroglossal duct.definition: An embryologic tract that connects the developing thyroid gland to the floor of the tongue at the foramen cecum; it normally obliterates during development, but remnants can lead to thyroglossal duct cysts or fistulous tracts.

thyroglossal duct cyst.definition: A congenital midline neck mass resulting from persistence of the thyroglossal duct tract; it typically presents in children as a painless, mobile lump that moves with swallowing and tongue protrusion and may become infected. Definitive management is surgical excision, classically the Sistrunk procedure (removal of the cyst, tract, and part of the hyoid bone).

thyroid-storm.definition: An acute, life-threatening form of thyrotoxicosis due to excessive thyroid hormone release, usually triggered by stress (infection, surgery, trauma), presenting with fever, marked tachycardia, agitation or delirium, and potential heart failure or shock; requires urgent ICU management with antithyroid medication, beta-blockade, corticosteroids, iodine after antithyroid therapy, and treatment of the precipitating cause.

antithyroid.definition: A substance or drug that suppresses thyroid function by inhibiting the synthesis or release of thyroid hormones; used to treat hyperthyroidism.

acute-respiratory-distress.definition: A severe, rapidly developing form of respiratory failure caused by diffuse alveolar-capillary injury leading to noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, reduced lung compliance, and hypoxemia; commonly triggered by critical illness (e.g., sepsis, pneumonia, trauma, aspiration) and typically managed with supportive care including lung-protective mechanical ventilation and treatment of the underlying cause.

heart-failure.definition: When your heart can't pump enough blood. Also called congestive heart failure or CHF.

thyroid-crisis.definition: An acute, life-threatening thyrotoxicosis due to abrupt, extreme elevation of circulating thyroid hormones, usually precipitated by a stressor such as infection, surgery, or trauma; features include high fever, tachycardia, hypertension, agitation or delirium, GI symptoms, and potential shock; requires urgent ICU management with antithyroid drugs, inorganic iodine after thioamide therapy, beta-blockers, glucocorticoids, cooling, and aggressive supportive care.

thyroid-ultrasound.definition: A noninvasive imaging modality that uses high-frequency ultrasound to visualize the thyroid gland, assess size and structure, detect nodules or cysts, characterize masses, and guide procedures such as fine-needle aspiration; it does not assess thyroid function.

thyroid-nodules.definition: A discrete lesion within the thyroid gland that can be solid or cystic; most nodules are benign and nonfunctioning, but some may be hyperfunctioning or malignant. Evaluation typically includes clinical assessment, thyroid function testing, ultrasound characterization, and fine-needle aspiration biopsy if indicated.

thyroid-mass.definition: A lump or enlargement arising from the thyroid gland (a thyroid nodule or goiter); most are benign, but some may be malignant; evaluation typically includes neck ultrasound and, if indicated, fine-needle aspiration biopsy.

thyrolar.definition: A brand-name thyroid hormone replacement medication consisting of a fixed 4:1 ratio of levothyroxine (T4) to liothyronine (T3); used to treat hypothyroidism.

thyroliberin.definition: A hypothalamic releasing hormone that stimulates the anterior pituitary to release thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and prolactin.

anterior-pituitary-gland.definition: An endocrine component of the pituitary that forms its anterior lobe; it synthesizes and secretes multiple hormones (growth hormone, prolactin, ACTH, TSH, LH, and FSH) under hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting control via the hypothalamic–pituitary portal system, and it is derived from Rathke's pouch.

thyrotropin-releasing-hormone.definition: A hypothalamic tripeptide hormone that stimulates the anterior pituitary to release thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and prolactin.

trh.definition: A hypothalamic releasing hormone that stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and prolactin.

thyrotropin-releasing-hormone-test.definition: A provocative diagnostic procedure in which synthetic thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) is administered to stimulate the pituitary to secrete TSH (and prolactin); changes in TSH (and prolactin) levels after TRH administration are measured to evaluate hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis function and help distinguish hypothalamic from pituitary causes of central hypothyroidism.

trh-stimulation-test.definition: An endocrine test in which synthetic thyrotropin-releasing hormone is given to stimulate the pituitary to release thyroid-stimulating hormone, with measurement of TSH (and sometimes prolactin) before and after; used to assess the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid axis and to distinguish central from primary hypothyroidism. Often less commonly used today.

tetraiodothyronine.definition: A thyroid hormone produced by the thyroid gland that contains four iodine atoms; serves as a prohormone to triiodothyronine (T3); is converted to T3 in peripheral tissues and helps regulate basal metabolic rate, growth, and development.

thyroxine-binding-globulin.definition: A liver-produced thyroid hormone transport glycoprotein with high affinity but low capacity for binding thyroxine (T4) and, to a lesser extent, triiodothyronine (T3), thereby serving as a circulating reservoir and modulating the free hormone fraction.

thyroxine-binding-globulin-test.definition: A blood test that measures the concentration of thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) in the serum to help interpret total thyroid hormone levels and distinguish changes due to TBG from true thyroid dysfunction; TBG levels can be elevated with estrogen exposure or pregnancy and decreased with liver disease, nephrotic syndrome, or certain genetic variants.

transient-ischemic-attack.definition: Happens when the blood supply to the brain is blocked briefly. Also called a TIA.

tiagabine.definition: An anticonvulsant that inhibits the GABA transporter GAT-1, increasing brain GABA levels; used as adjunctive therapy for partial-onset seizures.

ticlopidine.definition: An antiplatelet drug that prevents the formation of blood clots.

ticarcillin.definition: An extended-spectrum penicillin antibiotic (an antipseudomonal penicillin) that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins; active against many Gram-negative bacteria, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa; commonly given with clavulanate (ticarcillin-clavulanate) to inhibit beta-lactamases.

tic-douloureux.definition: Pain from a disorder of the trigeminal nerve, the chief sensory nerve of the face. Also called trigeminal neuralgia.

trigeminal-neuralgia.definition: Pain from a disorder of the trigeminal nerve, the chief sensory nerve of the face. Also called tic douloureux.

tick-bite.definition: A puncture wound produced by a tick attaching to the skin; ticks may transmit pathogens that cause tick-borne diseases (e.g., Lyme disease), with possible local skin reaction and, if infected, systemic symptoms such as fever or malaise.

tick-borne-relapsing-fever.definition: An infectious disease caused by Borrelia spirochetes transmitted by soft ticks (Ornithodoros), characterized by repeated febrile episodes separated by afebrile intervals due to antigenic variation of the spirochetes.

tick-borne-rickettsiosis.definition: A group of tick-borne diseases caused by Rickettsia species transmitted by hard ticks; they typically present with acute fever, headache, myalgias, and a rash (often starting on the wrists/ankles) and may include an eschar at the bite site, due to endotheliotropic vasculitis. Diagnosis is via serology or PCR, and treatment is doxycycline (with alternatives such as rifampin in pregnancy).

rocky-mountain-spotted-fever.definition: A tick-borne rickettsial disease caused by Rickettsia rickettsii; presents with fever, headache, malaise, and myalgias, often followed by a spreading rash; transmitted by Dermacentor ticks; can be severe or fatal without prompt doxycycline treatment.

lyme-disease.definition: A tick-borne infectious disease caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, transmitted by Ixodes ticks. Early manifestations commonly include an expanding erythema migrans rash and flu-like symptoms; if untreated, it can lead to intermittent arthritis, facial palsy, meningitis, and other neurologic or cardiac complications.

q-fever.definition: A zoonotic infection caused by the intracellular bacterium Coxiella burnetii, typically acquired by inhaling contaminated aerosols from birth products or excreta of infected livestock (cattle, sheep, goats). It causes an acute febrile illness with flu-like symptoms and may involve the liver (hepatitis) or lungs (pneumonitis); a chronic form can develop, most commonly endocarditis, especially in those with underlying heart disease.

tick-fever.definition: A febrile illness transmitted to humans by the bite of an infected tick; caused by a variety of tick-borne pathogens (including bacteria such as Rickettsia and Borrelia, and protozoa such as Babesia) and typically presenting with fever, headache, malaise, and sometimes a rash. Diagnosis is clinical plus laboratory testing where available; treatment often includes doxycycline for suspected rickettsial infection; prevention centers on avoiding tick bites and performing tick checks.

myasthenia-gravis.definition: An autoimmune neuromuscular disorder characterized by fatigable weakness of voluntary muscles due to autoantibodies against acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction (often with thymic abnormalities); symptoms worsen with activity and improve with rest and commonly involve ptosis, diplopia, and bulbar weakness.

tetanus-immune-globulin.definition: An antibody preparation derived from human plasma containing immunoglobulins against Clostridium tetani toxin, used to provide immediate passive immunity by neutralizing circulating toxin in people exposed to tetanus or at risk; used for post-exposure prophylaxis or treatment and often given with tetanus toxoid to allow active immunity to develop.

trimethobenzamide-hydrochloride.definition: An antiemetic drug; the hydrochloride salt of trimethobenzamide, a benzamide derivative that acts centrally to suppress nausea and vomiting.

tigecycline.definition: A broad-spectrum glycylcycline antibiotic derived from tetracycline that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit (bacteriostatic) and is active against many tetracycline-resistant organisms; used to treat complicated skin and intra-abdominal infections and some cases of community-acquired pneumonia, administered intravenously.

anaphylactic-reactions.definition: An acute, life-threatening IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction that occurs rapidly after exposure to an allergen, causing widespread mediator release from mast cells and basophils with symptoms such as urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, laryngeal edema, hypotension, and potential shock; requires immediate treatment with epinephrine and airway/circulatory support.

aspartate-aminotransferase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the transfer of an amino group from aspartate to α-ketoglutarate, producing oxaloacetate and glutamate; predominantly located in liver and heart; serum levels are used as a marker of hepatocellular injury and other tissue damage.

alanine-aminotransferase.definition: An intracellular enzyme predominantly in the liver that catalyzes the transamination between L-alanine and α-ketoglutarate to form pyruvate and glutamate; clinically, serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) is a sensitive indicator of hepatocellular injury, with elevated levels suggesting liver damage.

blood-urea-nitrogen.definition: A laboratory measure of the nitrogen content in blood in the form of urea, a waste product of protein metabolism excreted by the kidneys; used to assess renal function. Elevated levels indicate reduced kidney function or dehydration, while low levels occur with liver disease or malnutrition (normal range roughly 7–20 mg/dL or 2.5–7.1 mmol/L, depending on the laboratory).

lactic-acid.definition: Ácido orgánico débil (C3H6O3) formado durante la fermentación de azúcares y, en el cuerpo humano, por la glucólisis anaeróbica en músculo; su forma ionizada es lactato; puede acumularse en sangre durante el ejercicio intenso o la hipoxia y, en exceso, provocar acidosis láctica.

alkaline-phosphatase.definition: An enzyme (EC 3.1.3.1) that hydrolyzes phosphate groups from phosphomonoesters, with optimum activity at alkaline pH; produced mainly by the liver (bile ducts) and bone, also in kidney, intestine, and placenta; serum activity is used as a marker of hepatobiliary disease and bone turnover.

peripheral-edema.definition: Swelling of the limbs (most often the feet and ankles) due to excess fluid accumulation in the interstitial tissues, typically caused by impaired venous return, fluid overload, or systemic conditions such as heart, kidney, or liver disease, or lymphatic obstruction.

pathological-fractures.definition: A fracture that occurs in a bone weakened by disease (e.g., osteoporosis, metastatic cancer, infection, or metabolic bone disorders), often with little or no trauma, reflecting underlying pathology rather than normal mechanical forces.

bone-pain.definition: Pain that originates from bone or the periosteum, typically described as a deep, dull, aching or throbbing sensation; it can result from fractures, osteomyelitis, bone tumors or metastasis, and metabolic bone diseases (e.g., osteoporosis, Paget disease), and may be worsened by weight bearing or movement.

radioiodine-scanning.definition: A nuclear medicine imaging study in which a small dose of radioactive iodine (usually I-123 or I-131) is given and a gamma camera images the thyroid to assess iodine uptake and distribution, aiding evaluation of thyroid function, nodules, hyperthyroidism, and possible metastasis.

radioactive-iodine.definition: A radioactive form of iodine that can be used as a tracer during a radioactive iodine uptake test or a radioactive thyroid scan. Much larger amounts are used in the treatment of hyperthyroidism.

thyroglobulin-testing.definition: A blood test that measures thyroglobulin, a thyroid-derived protein, used mainly as a tumor marker to monitor for residual or recurrent differentiated thyroid carcinoma after thyroidectomy and ablation; ideally it remains low or undetectable, but rising levels suggest recurrence and interpretation can be affected by anti-thyroglobulin antibodies.

well-differentiated-thyroid-cancer.definition: A thyroid cancer composed of tumor cells that resemble normal thyroid follicular cells and retain features of thyroid differentiation; it primarily includes papillary and follicular carcinomas and generally has a relatively favorable prognosis with appropriate treatment.

thyrotropin-alfa.definition: Recombinant human thyroid-stimulating hormone used to raise circulating TSH levels for diagnostic radioiodine imaging and thyroglobulin testing, or to prepare for radioactive iodine therapy in differentiated thyroid cancer, without requiring thyroid hormone withdrawal.

thyrotrophic-hormone.definition: A pituitary gland–secreted glycoprotein hormone that stimulates the thyroid gland to synthesize and release thyroid hormones (thyroxine/T4 and triiodothyronine/T3); its release is regulated by hypothalamic thyrotropin-releasing hormone and inhibited by circulating thyroid hormones.

thyroid-stimulating-hormone.definition: A hormone secreted into the bloodstream by the pituitary gland that stimulates the thyroid gland. Doctors measure levels of TSH to determine whether a person’s thyroid hormone levels are normal.

thyrotoxic-crisis.definition: An acute, life-threatening exacerbation of thyrotoxicosis marked by sudden fever, marked tachycardia, tachypnea or shock, agitation or delirium, and GI symptoms, often with heart failure; precipitated by stress such as infection, surgery, or trauma; requires rapid, multi-pronged therapy with antithyroid drugs (e.g., propylthiouracil), followed by iodine, a beta-blocker, corticosteroids, and aggressive supportive care plus treatment of the inciting trigger.

thyrotoxic-myopathy.definition: A proximal myopathy syndrome caused by thyrotoxicosis (excess thyroid hormone), presenting with symmetric proximal muscle weakness and mild muscle wasting; typically improves when hyperthyroidism is treated.

thyrotoxin.definition: An uncommon, nonstandard term for a substance that damages or disrupts thyroid gland function or thyroid hormone synthesis, release, or action; not a formally defined medical term.

patellar-ligament.definition: A strong, flat band that extends from the inferior pole of the patella to the tibial tuberosity, forming part of the knee's extensor mechanism and transmitting quadriceps force to the tibia to extend the knee.

quadriceps-femoris.definition: A large extensor muscle group of the anterior thigh comprising four heads (rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, vastus intermedius) that extends the knee; the rectus femoris also flexes the hip. Innervated by the femoral nerve.

extensor-digitorum-longus.definition: A muscle of the anterior compartment of the leg that dorsiflexes the foot and extends the lateral four toes (digits 2–5); it originates from the tibia and fibula with the interosseous membrane and inserts into the extensor expansions of the toes, innervated by the deep fibular (peroneal) nerve.

tibialis-anterior.definition: A muscle of the anterior compartment of the leg that dorsiflexes the foot at the ankle and inverts the foot; it originates from the lateral surface of the tibia and the interosseous membrane and inserts on the medial cuneiform and base of the first metatarsal.

peroneus-longus.definition: A muscle of the lateral compartment of the leg that originates from the head and shaft of the fibula and inserts on the base of the first metatarsal and the medial cuneiform; it everts the foot and plantarflexes the ankle, and helps support the transverse arch. Innervated by the superficial peroneal nerve.

peroneus-brevis.definition: A muscle of the lateral compartment of the leg that everts the foot and assists in plantarflexion; its tendon inserts on the tuberosity of the base of the fifth metatarsal, passing behind the lateral malleolus.

peroneus-tertius.definition: A small muscle of the anterior leg that dorsiflexes and everts the foot; it typically originates from the distal fibula and interosseous membrane and inserts on the base of the fifth metatarsal, and it may be absent in some individuals. Innervation is by the deep fibular (peroneal) nerve.
