uterus bicornis.definition: A congenital uterine malformation with partial failure of fusion of the paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts, resulting in a uterus with two distinct horns and often a heart-shaped fundus; may have a single cervix (unicollis) or two cervices (bicollis).

vaccinia immune globulin.definition: An antibody preparation derived from human plasma containing anti-vaccinia antibodies, used for passive immunization to treat severe reactions to smallpox vaccination (e.g., disseminated vaccinia, eczema vaccinatum) and as post-exposure therapy for suspected vaccinia infection.

vaccinotherapeutics.definition: The use of vaccines or vaccine-based strategies to treat an existing disease by stimulating an immune response against disease-associated antigens (therapeutic vaccines), such as in cancer immunotherapy.

autovaccine.definition: A vaccine prepared from pathogens isolated from an individual patient (an autologous or autogenous vaccine) and used to immunize that patient against future infections caused by the same organism.

enterovaccine.definition: A vaccine intended to elicit immunity against enteroviruses, a group of RNA viruses that includes poliovirus, coxsackieviruses, and echoviruses; polio vaccines are the best-known example.

heterovaccine.definition: A vaccine produced from an antigen or pathogen originating in a species different from the recipient, used to immunize against a disease (historically exemplified by the vaccinia/cowpox–derived smallpox vaccine).

vacuum assisted closure.definition: A wound-healing therapy that applies controlled negative pressure to a sealed wound via a special dressing and vacuum device, removing exudate and edema and promoting granulation tissue formation and wound closure.

vacutainer.definition: A sterile evacuated blood-collection system used in phlebotomy to draw a precise volume of blood; the vacuum within the tube draws blood into the tube when the needle punctures the stopper, with tubes containing anticoagulants or clot activators depending on the test.

vacutainer tube.definition: A sterile evacuated blood collection tube used with a vacutainer needle; it contains a predefined vacuum to draw a specific volume of blood and may contain additives (e.g., EDTA, heparin, or a clot activator) to preserve or prepare the sample.

vaginography.definition: A radiographic study in which contrast material is introduced into the vagina to visualize its anatomy and detect abnormalities such as vaginal fistulas, septa, diverticula, or post-surgical leaks.

vaginolabial.definition: Relating to both the vagina and the labia; pertaining to the region encompassing the vaginal opening and the surrounding labial folds.

vaginoperineoplasty.definition: A surgical procedure combining vaginoplasty and perineoplasty to reconstruct and tighten the vaginal opening and surrounding perineal tissues, usually after childbirth-related trauma or to correct vaginal laxity and perineal defects.

valvotomy.definition: A surgical procedure to relieve valvular stenosis by incising a narrowed heart valve (often a commissurotomy) to widen the valve orifice and improve blood flow.

valsalva.definition: A maneuver in which a person forcibly exhales against a closed airway (with mouth and nose blocked or glottis closed), increasing intrathoracic pressure; used to equalize ear pressure, assess autonomic function, or terminate certain supraventricular tachycardias.

valproate.definition: A salt or ester of valproic acid used as an anticonvulsant and mood stabilizer; commonly prescribed for epilepsy, bipolar disorder, and migraine prophylaxis.

valproic.definition: Relating to valproic acid; a commonly used anticonvulsant and mood stabilizer for epilepsy and bipolar disorder, and sometimes used for migraine prophylaxis.

pantothenic.definition: Relating to pantothenic acid (vitamin B5), a water-soluble B vitamin essential for the synthesis of coenzyme A and fatty acid metabolism; pantothenic acid is widely found in foods and deficiency is rare.

valganciclovir.definition: An antiviral prodrug of ganciclovir with enhanced oral bioavailability used to prevent and treat cytomegalovirus (CMV) infections, especially in transplant recipients; it is converted in vivo to ganciclovir and then to ganciclovir triphosphate, which inhibits viral DNA polymerase and DNA replication.

valisone.definition: A brand-name topical corticosteroid preparation used to treat inflammatory skin conditions, reducing inflammation, itching, and redness by suppressing the skin’s inflammatory response; may contain a glucocorticoid such as betamethasone valerate.

valium.definition: A benzodiazepine (diazepam) used to treat anxiety, muscle spasms, seizures, and symptoms of alcohol withdrawal; it enhances GABA activity at the GABA-A receptor, producing sedative, anxiolytic, anticonvulsant, and muscle-relaxant effects.

vault.definition: A dome-shaped part of the skull that encloses the brain; the calvaria, formed by the frontal, parietal, temporal (squamous part), and occipital bones.

labium.definition: A lip or lip-like margin; in anatomy, a fold that forms part of an opening (such as the mouth or the female external genitalia); in insects, a lower lip formed by fused mouthparts.

prosthetic_valve.definition: An artificial heart valve implanted to replace a diseased native valve, restoring unidirectional blood flow; it can be mechanical (durable, usually requiring lifelong anticoagulation) or bioprosthetic (tissue-based, lower thrombogenic risk but shorter durability) and may be implanted surgically or via transcatheter methods such as TAVR.

biological_valve.definition: A prosthetic heart valve made from biological tissue (usually porcine or bovine) used to replace a diseased heart valve; a bioprosthetic valve that generally does not require long-term anticoagulation but has finite durability due to structural degeneration.

displacement.definition: The movement of a body part from its normal anatomical position; in orthopedics, a displaced fracture means the bone fragments are out of alignment.

heart_block.definition: A condition in which the electrical impulses between the atria and ventricles are delayed or blocked, most often at the AV node or below (AV block), causing bradycardia and a range of symptoms from none to syncope; classified into first-, second-, or third-degree AV block.

valvule.definition: A small valve; a diminutive valve that regulates fluid flow in a duct or vessel and prevents backflow.

valvular.definition: Relating to a valve; pertaining to heart valves or other biological valves.

valvular_endocarditis.definition: Infection of one or more heart valves, usually due to bacteria or fungi, with vegetations on the valve leaflets that can cause valve dysfunction (regurgitation or obstruction) and may lead to embolic complications; treated with prolonged IV antibiotics and sometimes surgery.

chronic_endocarditis.definition: A prolonged infection of the endocardial surface of the heart (usually the valves) caused by relatively low-virulence microorganisms, leading to insidious symptoms, formation of valvular vegetations, and potential valvular dysfunction, embolization, and heart failure.

valvular_heart_disease.definition: Disorder of one or more heart valves (mitral, aortic, tricuspid, or pulmonary) that results in abnormal valve function—stenosis (narrowing) or regurgitation (incompetence)—leading to disrupted blood flow through the heart and potential symptoms such as shortness of breath, fatigue, or edema; diagnosed mainly by echocardiography and treated with medical therapy, valve repair, or valve replacement.

aortic_valve.definition: A valve on the left side of the heart that acts as a one-way gate, opening to allow blood to leave the left ventricle and closing to prevent blood from leaking back into that ventricle.

mitral_valve.definition: The valve that controls the one-way flow of blood from the left atrium to the left ventricle.

aortic_regurgitation.definition: A valvular heart disease in which the aortic valve fails to close properly, allowing retrograde blood flow from the aorta into the left ventricle during diastole, causing left ventricular volume overload and potentially heart failure; it can be acute or chronic and may result from valve or aortic root pathology (e.g., bicuspid aortic valve, rheumatic disease, endocarditis, aortic root dilation).

mitral_regurgitation.definition: A condition in which the mitral valve does not close properly during systole, allowing blood to leak backward from the left ventricle into the left atrium. It can be primary (valvular degeneration or rheumatic disease) or secondary (due to left ventricular dilation or ischemia). Severity ranges from asymptomatic to heart failure and may be managed medically or with valve repair/replacement or catheter-based repair.

pulmonary_stenosis.definition: A structural narrowing of the right ventricular outflow tract to the pulmonary artery, most commonly at the pulmonary valve (valvular stenosis) but can be subvalvular or supravalvular, resulting in obstructed blood flow from the right ventricle and potential right heart strain; often congenital.

tricuspid_stenosis.definition: A narrowing of the tricuspid valve opening that restricts diastolic blood flow from the right atrium to the right ventricle, usually due to rheumatic disease but can arise from carcinoid syndrome, congenital valve anomalies, or prior endocarditis; it leads to right‑sided venous congestion and is typically associated with a diastolic murmur at the left lower sternal border (often with an opening snap and increased with inspiration).

valvular_regurgitation.definition: Backward flow of blood through a heart valve due to incomplete closure; also known as valvular insufficiency or incompetence, which can affect any valve (mitral, aortic, tricuspid, or pulmonary).

valvular_stenosis.definition: A narrowing of a heart valve that prevents it from opening fully, resulting in restricted blood flow and increased pressure load on the heart.

congenital_defects.definition: Anomalies present at birth arising from abnormal fetal development or inherited genetic factors, affecting body structure or function and ranging from minor to life-threatening.

congenital_cardiac_anomaly.definition: A heart defect present at birth due to abnormal development of the heart or great vessels, encompassing a wide range of structural abnormalities (e.g., septal defects, outflow tract or valve malformations) that can alter blood flow and oxygenation, and may range from asymptomatic to life-threatening, often requiring medical or surgical management.

bacterial_endocarditis.definition: An infection of the endocardial surface of the heart (usually the heart valves) caused by bacteria, typically following bacteremia; it often presents with fever and a new or changing heart murmur, and can cause embolic phenomena, valvular destruction, heart failure, or other complications. Diagnosis relies on blood cultures and imaging (e.g., echocardiography); treatment requires prolonged intravenous antibiotics, with surgery in selected cases.

calcium_deposits.definition: An abnormal deposition of calcium salts in soft tissues, typically from dystrophic calcification in damaged tissue or metastatic calcification due to elevated calcium or phosphate levels; it can occur in arteries, joints, kidneys, and other tissues and may be asymptomatic or cause pain, stiffness, or organ dysfunction, often visible as radiopaque deposits on imaging.

fused_commissures.definition: A condition in which the commissures—the junctions where paired structures meet (for example, the corners of the mouth or the eyelids)—are abnormally fused or adherent, resulting in restricted movement and possible cosmetic deformity.

porcine_valve.definition: A bioprosthetic heart valve derived from porcine (pig) tissue, typically pig aortic valve leaflets, processed and implanted to replace a diseased human valve; functions like a native valve but usually requires little to no long-term anticoagulation and has limited durability compared with mechanical valves.

artificial_valve.definition: Prosthetic device implanted to replace a diseased heart valve, restoring unidirectional blood flow. It can be mechanical (durable, usually requiring lifelong anticoagulation) or bioprosthetic (tissue-based).

cardiac_valve.definition: A heart valve that maintains unidirectional blood flow by opening to allow movement from atria to ventricles (AV valves) or from ventricles to the great arteries (semilunar valves) and closing to prevent backflow; the AV valves are mitral and tricuspid, while the semilunar valves are aortic and pulmonary.

intracardiac_pressure.definition: Pressure within the heart chambers (atria and ventricles) throughout the cardiac cycle, measured by intracardiac catheterization to assess hemodynamics and cardiac function.

pulmonary_circulation.definition: The movement of blood from the right ventricle through the pulmonary arteries to the lungs for gas exchange, returning oxygenated blood to the left atrium via the pulmonary veins.

peripheral_circulation.definition: The circulation of blood to the peripheral tissues—principally the limbs and skin—through the arterial, capillary, and venous networks, providing oxygen and nutrients and removing carbon dioxide and waste products.

cardiac_arrhythmia.definition: An abnormality of the heart's rhythm caused by disturbances in the heart’s electrical conduction, resulting in a heartbeat that is too fast, too slow, or irregular.

heart_failure.definition: When your heart can't pump enough blood. Also called congestive heart failure or CHF.

cardiogenic_shock.definition: A condition in which the heart's pumping ability is severely compromised, leading to inadequate systemic perfusion and hypotension; commonly due to acute myocardial infarction or other acute cardiac dysfunction and requiring inotropic/vasopressor support and treatment of the underlying cause, with possible mechanical circulatory support if refractory.

cardiotonics.definition: Agents that increase the heart's contractile force (positive inotropes), thereby raising cardiac output. They are used in heart failure and acute decompensation and include cardiac glycosides (e.g., digoxin), catecholamines (e.g., dobutamine, dopamine), phosphodiesterase inhibitors (e.g., milrinone), and calcium sensitizers (e.g., levosimendan).

valvuloplasty.definition: A procedure to repair or widen a diseased heart valve that has become narrowed (valvular stenosis) to improve blood flow, performed either surgically (open valvuloplasty) or via catheter with balloon dilation (percutaneous valvuloplasty).

balloon_tipped_catheter.definition: A catheter with a small inflatable balloon near its tip that, when filled with sterile fluid, anchors the catheter in place (such as in the bladder for urinary drainage) or assists navigation/occlusion within a vessel or heart chamber.

vincristine_sulfate.definition: A vinca alkaloid chemotherapy agent that inhibits tubulin polymerization, blocking microtubule formation and arresting cells in metaphase to prevent mitosis; used to treat various hematologic malignancies and solid tumors; administered intravenously; major adverse effects include neurotoxicity and constipation; intrathecal administration is contraindicated due to risk of fatal neurotoxicity.

beclomethasone_dipropionate.definition: An inhaled corticosteroid used to prevent and control asthma and allergic rhinitis; a prodrug converted in the lungs to its active metabolite beclomethasone-17-monopropionate, exerting anti-inflammatory effects by glucocorticoid receptor activation; administered by inhalation or intranasal spray; common adverse effects include oropharyngeal candidiasis, hoarseness, and cough.

vancomycin_hydrochloride.definition: A glycopeptide antibiotic used to treat serious gram‑positive infections (e.g., MRSA); it inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to the D-Ala‑D‑Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursors and is given IV for systemic infections or orally for C. difficile infection—adverse effects include nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, and red man syndrome if infused too rapidly.

staphylococcal_infections.definition: An infection caused by Staphylococcus species (most often Staphylococcus aureus), ranging from localized skin and soft-tissue infections such as boils and abscesses to invasive diseases including pneumonia, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, bacteremia, endocarditis, and toxic shock syndrome; spread is via direct contact, and many strains are resistant to antibiotics (notably MRSA), complicating treatment.

pseudomembranous_colitis.definition: Inflammation of the colon caused by Clostridioides difficile infection, usually after antibiotic exposure, marked by pseudomembrane formation on the colonic mucosa and symptoms of watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and fever; diagnosed by stool toxin testing or visualization of pseudomembranes on colonoscopy.

clostridium_difficile.definition: A Gram-positive, spore-forming, anaerobic bacterium that overgrows in the colon after antibiotic use, producing toxins A and B and causing antibiotic-associated diarrhea and colitis, including pseudomembranous colitis; transmitted via spores, especially in healthcare settings.

van_den_bergh_test.definition: A chemical test for bilirubin in serum that uses diazotized sulfanilic acid to form azobilirubin, historically used to quantify bilirubin and differentiate direct (conjugated) from indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin.

bilirubin_test.definition: A laboratory test that measures the level of bilirubin in the blood (usually as total bilirubin and its fractions—direct/conjugated and indirect/unconjugated—to assess liver function, hemolysis, biliary obstruction, or jaundice, including in newborns).

varicella_zoster_virus.definition: A double-stranded DNA herpesvirus (alpha-herpesvirus) that causes varicella (chickenpox) on primary infection and herpes zoster (shingles) upon reactivation; it establishes lifelong latency in sensory dorsal root and cranial ganglia and is transmitted by respiratory droplets or contact with vesicular fluid.

varicella_vaccine_live.definition: Live attenuated vaccine containing varicella-zoster virus used to prevent varicella (chickenpox); given by subcutaneous injection, usually in a two-dose schedule; contraindicated in pregnancy and in individuals with severe immunodeficiency or active moderate to severe illness; common side effects include injection-site pain and fever; rare serious adverse events.

varicella_zoster_immune_globulin.definition: A human-derived immunoglobulin preparation containing antibodies to varicella-zoster virus, used as postexposure prophylaxis to prevent varicella in susceptible individuals (such as newborns, pregnant women, and immunocompromised patients) by providing temporary passive immunity; should be given within about 96 hours of exposure.

zoster_immune_globulin.definition: A preparation of human antibodies against varicella-zoster virus used after exposure to prevent varicella infection or reduce its severity in susceptible individuals; administered intramuscularly within a short window after exposure; derived from pooled human plasma; not effective for treatment of active varicella or herpes zoster.

herpes_zoster.definition: A disease that causes painful sores on your skin. It is caused by the same bug (or virus) that causes chickenpox. Also called shingles.

desciclovir.definition: Not a recognized antiviral drug; likely a misspelling of penciclovir, a guanine analogue antiviral used to treat herpes simplex virus infections. It is phosphorylated to an active form in infected cells and inhibits viral DNA polymerase, reducing viral replication.

valaciclovir.definition: An antiviral prodrug of acyclovir that is rapidly absorbed and converted to acyclovir in the body; it inhibits viral DNA polymerase, reducing replication of herpesviruses, and is used to treat and prevent infections caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV-1 and HSV-2) and varicella-zoster virus (chickenpox and shingles).

postherpetic_neuralgia.definition: Nerve pain caused by the herpes zoster virus, also known as shingles.

varicose.definition: Relating to varicose veins; veins that are enlarged, tortuous, and bulging due to valve failure in the veins, most commonly in the legs.

varicose_aneurysm.definition: Not a standard medical term; if used, it suggests a venous aneurysm—a focal dilation of a vein—in the setting of varicose veins. True aneurysms are arterial; venous aneurysms are rare and management depends on size, location, and risk of thrombosis.

varicose_ulcer.definition: A venous leg ulcer resulting from chronic venous insufficiency and venous hypertension, typically on the lower leg near the medial malleolus; commonly associated with varicose veins, edema, and skin changes, and managed with compression therapy and wound care while addressing the underlying venous insufficiency.

varicose_vein.definition: A dilated, tortuous superficial vein, most often in the legs, caused by venous valvular incompetence and chronic venous hypertension, leading to venous reflux and pooling; may cause visible bulging veins, pain, heaviness, swelling, and skin changes or ulcers in advanced cases.

stasis_ulcer.definition: A chronic venous insufficiency–related ulcer of the lower leg caused by sustained venous hypertension, typically occurring near the medial malleolus and associated with edema, skin changes (e.g., hemosiderin staining, lipodermatosclerosis), and slow healing.

venous_insufficiency.definition: A condition in which the veins have difficulty returning blood from the legs to the heart due to venous valvular incompetence or obstruction, leading to venous hypertension with symptoms such as edema, leg heaviness or aching, skin changes, and sometimes venous ulcers.

venous_stasis_ulcers.definition: Chronic lower-extremity ulcers caused by venous insufficiency and venous hypertension; typically occur near the medial malleolus, associated with edema, hemosiderin deposition and dermatitis; heal slowly with compression therapy, wound care, leg elevation, and management of venous hypertension; recurrence is common if underlying venous disease persists.

trendelenburgs_test.definition: A clinical test to evaluate strength of the hip abductors (gluteus medius/minimus) and the superior gluteal nerve. The patient stands on one leg; a positive result is indicated when the pelvis drops on the non–weight-bearing (opposite) side, indicating weakness of the abductors on the stance leg.

duplex_ultrasound.definition: A noninvasive imaging study that combines standard B-mode ultrasound with Doppler ultrasound to visualize blood vessels and assess the speed and pattern of blood flow, used to evaluate arterial and venous disease such as stenosis, occlusion, or thrombosis.

stripping.definition: A surgical procedure to remove a vein (usually the great or small saphenous vein) by tying off the ends and drawing the vein out through small incisions, typically to treat varicose veins.

compression_stockings.definition: Graduated compression stockings are medical hosiery that apply the greatest pressure at the ankle and gradually decrease up the leg to improve venous return, reduce edema, and help prevent venous thromboembolism; used for chronic venous insufficiency, varicose veins, edema, and postoperative prophylaxis, with varying compression levels and requiring proper fitting.

postphlebitic_syndrome.definition: A chronic venous insufficiency following a deep vein thrombosis, due to valvular damage that impairs venous return; characterized by persistent leg swelling, aching or heaviness, varicose veins, skin changes (such as hyperpigmentation and lipodermatosclerosis), and sometimes venous ulcers, with management including compression therapy, leg elevation, exercise, wound care, and sometimes venous surgery or endovenous procedures.

polycythemia_vera.definition: A chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by clonal erythroid proliferation causing increased red blood cell mass and hematocrit, typically with low erythropoietin levels; often associated with a JAK2 mutation and an elevated risk of thrombosis.

erectile_dysfunction.definition: A persistent or recurrent inability to obtain or maintain an erection sufficient for sexual activity.

diminished_vision.definition: A reduction in visual acuity or visual field resulting in vision that is not normal; may be due to refractive error, ocular diseases (e.g., cataract, glaucoma, macular degeneration), or optic/neurological conditions.

abnormal_ejaculation.definition: A broad term describing ejaculation that deviates from normal patterns, encompassing premature ejaculation, delayed ejaculation, anejaculation, and retrograde ejaculation; may result from hormonal imbalance, neurologic or pelvic nerve injury, diabetes or other medical conditions, medications (notably antidepressants), or psychological factors, and can affect sexual satisfaction and fertility.

abnormal_dreams.definition: Distressing, frightening, or otherwise atypical dream experiences that occur with unusual frequency or content and disrupt sleep or daytime functioning; often categorized as nightmares and can be related to stress, anxiety, trauma, depression, sleep deprivation, medications, or an underlying sleep disorder.

weight_gain.definition: An increase in body weight, typically due to an energy surplus (calories consumed exceeding calories burned), resulting in increased fat mass and/or body water; can occur with medications, medical conditions, or changes in fluid balance.

gastroesophageal_reflux_disease.definition: A chronic condition in which stomach contents reflux into the esophagus, producing troublesome symptoms (e.g., heartburn, regurgitation) and/or esophageal mucosal injury, often due to lower esophageal sphincter dysfunction; treated with lifestyle changes, acid-suppressive therapy (PPIs or H2 blockers), and sometimes surgery.

cardiovascular_collapse.definition: A sudden, life-threatening failure of the circulatory system marked by profound hypotension and inadequate tissue perfusion, resulting in organ dysfunction; most often seen in shock from hemorrhage, infection, myocardial failure, or cardiac arrhythmia.

epinephrine_hydrochloride.definition: An injectable salt form of epinephrine (adrenaline) that acts as a rapid-acting sympathomimetic agent by stimulating alpha- and beta-adrenergic receptors, causing vasoconstriction and increased cardiac output. Clinically, it is used to prolong local anesthesia via vasoconstriction and as a vasopressor in anaphylaxis, severe hypotension, and cardiac arrest.

adrenal_glands.definition: Glands that sit on top of each kidney and secrete stress hormones.

3-methoxy-4-hydroxymandelic_acid.definition: A substituted mandelic acid (a phenylglycolic acid) in which the benzene ring bears a methoxy group at the 3-position and a hydroxyl group at the 4-position relative to the side chain.

vanillylmandelic_acid.definition: A major end product of catecholamine metabolism (from epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine) formed in the liver and other tissues and excreted in urine; historically used as a diagnostic marker for pheochromocytoma due to increased catecholamine turnover, though plasma free metanephrines are now preferred for screening.

varicosis.definition: A condition characterized by dilated, tortuous superficial veins, most often in the legs, due to chronic venous insufficiency and venous hypertension from valvular incompetence; commonly referred to as varicose veins.

hepatic porphyria.definition: A group of inherited disorders of heme biosynthesis in which the liver is the primary site of excess porphyrin production, leading to accumulation of porphyrin precursors and a spectrum of symptoms ranging from acute neurovisceral attacks to photosensitive skin lesions, depending on the subtype.

varioliform gastritis.definition: A gastritis characterized by multiple pinhead-sized, varioliform (pox-like) erosions or shallow ulcers on the gastric mucosa, giving a dotted, vesicular appearance on endoscopy; a descriptive endoscopic pattern rather than a distinct disease subtype.

cluster headache.definition: A short-lived, extremely painful headache that occurs repeatedly over a period of a few weeks or months and then disappears for months or years.

vasospastic angina.definition: A type of chest pain caused by transient constriction of a coronary artery (vasospasm) that temporarily reduces blood flow to the heart, causing reversible myocardial ischemia; episodes often occur at rest and may be accompanied by transient ST-segment elevations on ECG, and the condition can occur with or without underlying atherosclerosis. Treated primarily with calcium channel blockers and nitrates.

acute heart failure.definition: An abrupt or rapidly progressive deterioration of cardiac function with new or worsening symptoms and signs of heart failure, frequently presenting with pulmonary or systemic congestion and requiring urgent medical therapy.

cerebral ischemia.definition: Reduced blood flow to brain tissue causing insufficient oxygen and glucose delivery, leading to neuronal dysfunction or death; it can be global (hypoperfusion) or focal (ischemic stroke) due to arterial occlusion.

vascular pole.definition: Region of Bowman's capsule adjacent to the glomerulus where the afferent and efferent arterioles enter and exit; the opposite region is the urinary pole, where the proximal tubule begins.

vascular endothelium.definition: A thin monolayer of flattened endothelial cells lining the interior surface of all blood vessels, forming a selective barrier between blood and the vessel wall and regulating vascular permeability, blood flow, coagulation, and inflammatory responses through vasoactive mediators such as nitric oxide and endothelin.

vascular endothelial growth factor.definition: A signaling protein that promotes angiogenesis by binding to receptors on vascular endothelial cells, stimulating their proliferation, migration, and the formation of new blood vessels; it also increases vascular permeability and is upregulated by hypoxia via HIF-1α.

vegf.definition: A signaling protein that promotes angiogenesis (growth of new blood vessels) and increases vascular permeability; produced by various cell types in response to hypoxia and plays key roles in development and wound healing, but can contribute to tumor growth and retinal/neovascular diseases.

vascularity.definition: The presence, distribution, and density of blood vessels within tissues or organs, reflecting the tissue's blood supply and perfusion; used to describe how well a tissue, organ, or lesion is supplied with blood.

vascularized graft.definition: A graft in which the transplanted tissue retains its vascular supply or is reanastomosed to blood vessels, allowing immediate or rapid revascularization and survival after transfer.

pedicle flap.definition: A vascularized tissue flap transferred to a nearby defect while remaining attached to its original blood supply via a pedicle (stalk), allowing continued perfusion as it is rotated or advanced and later may be divided.

epididymides.definition: Two coiled ducts along the posterior aspect of each testis that store and mature spermatozoa and transport them to the vas deferens.

vasectomy.definition: A type of surgery that prevents a man from being able to make a woman pregnant.

vasovasostomy.definition: A surgical procedure to reverse a vasectomy by reconnecting the severed ends of the vas deferens to restore sperm flow and fertility.

vasovagal syncope.definition: A transient loss of consciousness caused by a brief drop in cerebral perfusion due to a vasovagal reflex, commonly called fainting.

vasovagal.definition: Reflex-mediated reduction in heart rate and blood pressure due to vagal stimulation, leading to transient cerebral hypoperfusion and fainting, commonly triggered by emotional distress, pain, or prolonged standing.

vasomotor.definition: Relating to the nerves that regulate the diameter of blood vessels, thereby controlling vascular tone through vasoconstriction and vasodilation.

vasodepressor syncope.definition: A form of neurally mediated syncope in which a sudden reduction in systemic vascular resistance due to peripheral vasodilation causes a drop in blood pressure and cerebral perfusion, with little or no compensatory slowing of the heart.

vasoparesis.definition: Partial loss or impairment of vasoconstriction of blood vessels due to autonomic (sympathetic) dysfunction, resulting in impaired regulation of vascular tone and blood pressure.

vasoparalysis.definition: A term not widely used in standard medical dictionaries; it would describe paralysis or loss of function of vascular smooth muscle, leading to impaired regulation of vascular tone and destabilized blood pressure.

vasomotor reflex.definition: A neural reflex that regulates vascular tone by changing the diameter of systemic blood vessels through autonomic (primarily sympathetic) outflow in response to changes in blood pressure, helping to maintain mean arterial pressure.

vasomotor center.definition: A region in the medulla oblongata that regulates autonomic vascular tone by modulating sympathetic outflow to blood vessels, thereby controlling peripheral resistance and blood pressure; it integrates inputs from baroreceptors and higher brain centers.

vasoconstrictive.definition: Causing constriction of blood vessels, which reduces their diameter and increases vascular resistance, potentially raising blood pressure.

vasoganglion.definition: A vascular ganglion; a cluster of nerve cell bodies in the autonomic nervous system that supplies innervation to blood vessels, helping regulate vascular smooth muscle tone and blood flow.

vip.definition: A neuropeptide that functions as a neurotransmitter and hormone, causing vasodilation and stimulating water and electrolyte secretion in the gut and pancreas; it also relaxes smooth muscle and modulates immune activity.

vasoactive intestinal peptide.definition: A 28‑amino‑acid neuropeptide that acts as a neurotransmitter and hormone; causes vasodilation, stimulates secretion of water and electrolytes in the intestines, inhibits gastric acid secretion, relaxes smooth muscle, and modulates immune responses via VPAC1/VPAC2 receptors.

trimethaphan.definition: An intravenous nicotinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist that blocks autonomic ganglia (a ganglionic blocker), causing rapid, dose-dependent hypotension; historically used to control severe hypertension or to facilitate anesthesia, but now largely obsolete due to severe autonomic side effects and unpredictable hemodynamics.

vasotec.definition: A brand-name ACE inhibitor containing enalapril, used to treat hypertension and heart failure by inhibiting the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II.

nodular vasculitis.definition: A form of panniculitis presenting with tender subcutaneous nodules on the lower legs; histology shows lobular panniculitis with vasculitis, often described as erythema induratum of Bazin and thought to be a hypersensitivity reaction to infection (e.g., tuberculosis).

lateral condyle of the tibia.definition: Proximal, lateral part of the tibia forming the lateral half of the tibial plateau; it articulates with the lateral femoral condyle to contribute to the knee joint and serves as an attachment site for the lateral meniscus and joint capsule.

medial supracondylar line.definition: A bony ridge on the distal femur on the medial side, extending from the medial epicondyle toward the shaft (toward the linea aspera); it marks the medial boundary of the popliteal surface.

medial intermuscular septum.definition: A fibrous partition on the medial side of the arm that extends from the medial supracondylar ridge of the humerus to the medial epicondyle, dividing the arm into anterior (flexor) and posterior (extensor) muscle compartments.

capsule of the knee joint.definition: A fibrous envelope surrounding the knee joint, consisting of an outer fibrous capsule and an inner synovial membrane; it attaches to the articular margins of the femur, tibia, and patella, encloses the synovial cavity, and is reinforced by extracapsular and intracapsular ligaments. The inner synovial membrane lines the capsule and secretes synovial fluid.

vastus internus.definition: A muscle of the quadriceps femoris group that lies deep to the rectus femoris, between the vastus medialis and vastus lateralis; it assists knee extension and is innervated by the femoral nerve.

vater association.definition: Nonrandom constellation of congenital malformations including vertebral defects, anal atresia, tracheoesophageal fistula with esophageal atresia, and renal anomalies; often with additional cardiac, limb, or other defects, and related to the VACTERL association.

vertebral defects.definition: Abnormal development or structure of one or more vertebrae—typically congenital (e.g., hemivertebra, wedge vertebra, segmentation defect) or acquired—that can cause spinal deformities (scoliosis, kyphosis), instability, and potential neural compromise.

tracheoesophageal fistula.definition: An abnormal connection between the trachea and esophagus that allows air and secretions to pass between the airway and the digestive tract; it can be congenital (often with esophageal atresia) or acquired and commonly presents with coughing, choking, and aspiration during feeding, often requiring surgical repair.

radial dysplasia.definition: Congenital deficiency or underdevelopment (hypoplasia/aplasia) of the radius (radial ray), often with bowing of the ulna and resultant radial deviation of the hand; may involve thumb hypoplasia or absence and other carpal abnormalities; collectively part of the radial longitudinal deficiency spectrum.

vater-pacini corpuscles.definition: A rapidly adapting mechanoreceptor in the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, composed of an onion-like lamellated capsule surrounding a sensory nerve ending, that detects high-frequency vibration and changes in pressure.

kinesioceptors.definition: Proprioceptive sensory receptors that monitor limb position and movement by detecting stretch and tension in muscles, tendons, and joints (e.g., muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, and joint receptors).

pvb.definition: A regional anesthesia technique in which a local anesthetic is injected near the spinal nerves as they emerge from the intervertebral foramina, producing unilateral sensory and sympathetic blockade for analgesia of the chest wall or abdomen.

velban.definition: A brand-name vinblastine sulfate; a vinca alkaloid chemotherapy agent that inhibits microtubule formation by binding tubulin, thereby blocking mitosis; used to treat various cancers.

velcade.definition: A proteasome inhibitor used in cancer treatment; it blocks the 26S proteasome, causing accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins and promoting apoptosis of malignant plasma cells, mainly in multiple myeloma and mantle cell lymphoma.

bortezomib.definition: A proteasome inhibitor used in cancer therapy that blocks the 26S proteasome, causing accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins and triggering apoptosis in malignant cells; commonly used to treat multiple myeloma and mantle cell lymphoma. Administered by subcutaneous or intravenous injection.

velosef.definition: A brand-name cephalosporin antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis.

vdrl.definition: A non-treponemal serologic test for syphilis that detects reagin antibodies (anti-cardiolipin) using a cardiolipin-lecithin-cholesterol antigen; used for initial screening and monitoring of treatment, with results reported as reactive/nonreactive and titers, and typically followed by confirmatory treponemal testing due to possible false positives.

vdrl test.definition: A non-treponemal serologic test for syphilis that detects reagin antibodies to cardiolipin-lecithin-cholesterol antigen; used for initial screening and monitoring treatment, with results reported as a titer. Positive results are non-specific and require confirmation with a treponemal-specific test (e.g., FTA-ABS, TPPA).

vein ligation and stripping.definition: A surgical treatment for varicose veins in which an incompetent superficial leg vein (usually the greater or small saphenous vein) is tied off (ligated) near its junction with deeper veins to prevent reflux, and then the vein is removed (stripped) from the leg through incisions.

median antebrachial vein.definition: A superficial vein of the forearm that runs along the midline of the anterior forearm, arising from the palmar venous plexus and typically draining into the median cubital vein (with occasional drainage into the basilic or cephalic veins).

radial vein.definition: A pair of deep forearm veins that accompany the radial artery on the lateral aspect of the forearm; drain blood from the lateral forearm and hand and typically join the ulnar veins to form the brachial vein.

digital vein.definition: A vein that accompanies a digital artery in a finger (a proper digital vein); it drains venous blood from the finger into the palmar/dorsal venous networks, ultimately returning blood to the forearm via the superficial or deep venous system.

metacarpal vein.definition: Veins that accompany the metacarpal arteries in the metacarpal region of the hand; part of the hand's superficial venous drainage, draining blood from the metacarpal bones and surrounding tissues into the dorsal venous network and ultimately into the superficial veins such as the cephalic or basilic.

vegetative endocarditis.definition: Endocarditis characterized by vegetations on heart valves or endocardial surfaces; vegetations are clumps of fibrin, platelets, inflammatory cells, and microorganisms, typically caused by microbial infection (infective endocarditis) and may lead to valvular dysfunction and systemic emboli.

vectorcardiogram.definition: A vectorcardiogram is a recording that depicts the three-dimensional magnitude and direction of the heart's electrical vectors during the cardiac cycle, typically derived from standard ECG by transforming leads into three orthogonal components (X, Y, and Z) to produce vector loops; it helps assess the electrical axis and conduction patterns.

vectorcardiography.definition: A method of recording the heart's electrical activity as three-dimensional vectors, illustrating the magnitude and direction of depolarization and repolarization (QRS and T vectors) by deriving orthogonal leads from the standard ECG to form a vectorcardiogram.

venezuelan hemorrhagic fever.definition: A viral hemorrhagic fever caused by Guanarito virus (an arenavirus) transmitted primarily from rodent reservoirs to humans; presents as an acute febrile illness with malaise, myalgia, and hemorrhagic manifestations, and can have a high case-fatality rate; geographically restricted to Venezuela.

gingival bleeding.definition: Bleeding from the gums, typically due to inflammation of the gingival tissues (gingivitis) or periodontal disease, and can also occur after trauma, aggressive brushing, hormonal changes, infections, or disorders of blood clotting.

deep tendon reflexes.definition: A stretch reflex elicited by tapping a tendon, causing a brief contraction of the corresponding muscle; part of the spinal reflex arc and used to assess neuromuscular integrity.

neurological deterioration.definition: An abrupt decline in neurological function, typically evidenced by reduced level of consciousness and/or new or worsening focal deficits, often due to edema, ischemia or hemorrhage, mass effect, infection, metabolic disturbance, or systemic illness.

stylet.definition: A slender, stiff guide inserted into a catheter, needle, or tube to provide rigidity and steerage during insertion; removed after the device is properly placed.

ethyl alcohol.definition: A clear, colorless two-carbon alcohol (C2H5OH) that is the principal alcohol in alcoholic beverages; a central nervous system depressant, used as a solvent and antiseptic, and metabolized in the liver to acetaldehyde and then acetate.

antimicrobial ointment.definition: A topical preparation applied to the skin or mucous membranes that contains antimicrobial agents (e.g., antibiotics or antiseptics) to kill or inhibit microorganisms and help prevent or treat infection.

venom immunotherapy.definition: A form of allergen immunotherapy in which controlled, gradually increasing doses of insect venom extract are administered (typically by subcutaneous injection) to desensitize the immune system and reduce the risk of systemic allergic reactions to future stings; treatment is usually continued for several years (commonly 3–5) and has high efficacy in preventing severe reactions.

venomous snake.definition: A snake that produces venom in specialized glands and injects it via hollow fangs, causing envenomation that can injure tissue, disrupt organ function, or be fatal.

venospasm.definition: A sudden, involuntary constriction of a vein resulting in narrowing of the venous lumen and reduced blood flow, which can hinder IV access or infusion.

venostasis.definition: Venostasis, or venous stasis, is the slowing or stagnation of venous blood flow, typically due to impaired venous return or venous obstruction, which can lead to edema and an increased risk of venous thrombosis.

venothrombotic.definition: Relating to venous thrombosis; the formation of a blood clot within a vein that can obstruct venous blood flow.

venotomy.definition: An incision into a vein to gain access to the venous lumen for diagnostic or therapeutic vascular procedures, such as cannulation, repair, or thrombectomy.

venous access device.definition: A device that provides access to the venous system for delivering medications, fluids, blood products, or parenteral nutrition, and/or for drawing blood; examples include peripheral IV cannulas, central venous catheters (CVCs), peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs), and implanted venous ports.

venous stasis dermatitis.definition: A chronic inflammatory skin condition of the lower legs caused by chronic venous insufficiency and venous hypertension, characterized by edema, brown hemosiderin staining, pruritic eczematous changes, scaling, and may progress to lipodermatosclerosis or venous ulcers.

elastic bandages.definition: A stretchable fabric bandage that provides adjustable compression to a limb or joint, used to control swelling, support injured tissues, and secure dressings.

nerve damage.definition: Injury or dysfunction of a nerve causing impaired signal transmission, leading to sensory deficits (numbness, tingling), motor weakness or paralysis, or autonomic changes in the region supplied by the affected nerve. Causes include trauma, compression, inflammation, ischemia, metabolic disorders (e.g., diabetes), infection, or toxins; prognosis varies with extent and location.

scar tissue.definition: Fibrous connective tissue that forms during wound healing to replace normal tissue; composed mainly of collagen, it provides structural repair but with reduced strength, elasticity, and function compared with the original tissue; it can be raised (hypertrophic) or extend beyond the wound (keloid).

cardiac aneurysm.definition: A localized dilation or bulging of the heart wall, most commonly of the left ventricle, due to weakening after myocardial damage (often from a prior heart attack), resulting in a noncontractile segment that may impair function and predispose to heart failure, arrhythmias, thromboembolism, and rupture.

interventricular foramen.definition: An opening in the brain's ventricular system that connects the lateral ventricle to the third ventricle, allowing cerebrospinal fluid to flow from the lateral ventricle into the third ventricle; also known as the foramen of Monro.

foramen vesalius.definition: An obsolete or rarely used label for a skull opening; not a standard, widely recognized foramen in modern anatomy. Its location and contents vary by source, and many texts do not use this term. If you have a specific reference, share it and I can interpret from that context.

venous sinus.definition: A large, thin-walled, valveless venous channel between layers of dura mater that collects cerebral venous blood and drains it toward the internal jugular veins.

ventriculofallopian tube shunt.definition: An experimental or historical surgical procedure in which cerebrospinal fluid is diverted from a brain ventricle into the fallopian tube, intended to treat hydrocephalus; not used in standard practice.

ventriculoperitoneal shunt.definition: A surgically implanted CSF-diverting device that drains cerebrospinal fluid from the brain's ventricles to the peritoneal cavity to treat hydrocephalus; it typically includes a ventricular catheter, a valve, and a distal catheter tunneled under the skin to the peritoneum.

ventriculoperitoneostomy.definition: A neurosurgical procedure to divert cerebrospinal fluid from the cerebral ventricle into the peritoneal cavity, typically to treat hydrocephalus.

ventriculopleural shunt.definition: A cerebrospinal fluid shunt that diverts CSF from the brain’s ventricles into the pleural space via a distal catheter and valve, allowing absorption of CSF by the pleural membranes; used for hydrocephalus when peritoneal drainage is unsuitable, but carries risks such as pleural effusion, pneumothorax, and shunt obstruction/infection.

ventriculovenous shunt.definition: A CSF shunt that diverts cerebrospinal fluid from a cerebral ventricle into the venous system (often a cranial venous sinus or jugular vein) to treat hydrocephalus, typically with a valve to regulate flow.

ventricular bigeminy.definition: An arrhythmia in which a premature ventricular contraction occurs on every other beat, producing a repeating pattern of normal beat followed by a PVC, with wide QRS complexes and usually a compensatory pause.

premature ventricular beat.definition: An ectopic heartbeat that originates in the ventricles and occurs earlier than the next expected normal heartbeat. It typically presents with a wide QRS complex, usually without a preceding P wave, and is often followed by a compensatory pause. It can be benign, especially in healthy individuals, but may indicate underlying cardiac or metabolic issues in others.

ventricular block.definition: A disturbance of electrical conduction within the ventricles that slows or blocks impulse transmission to the ventricular myocardium, most commonly due to a bundle-branch block or intraventricular conduction delay; produces a widened QRS complex on ECG and may cause asynchronous ventricular contraction.

foramina of magendie.definition: Median openings of the fourth ventricle that permit cerebrospinal fluid to exit the ventricular system into the subarachnoid space.

foramina magendie.definition: A median aperture of the fourth ventricle; a single opening on the dorsal aspect of the fourth ventricle through which cerebrospinal fluid exits the ventricular system into the subarachnoid space (cisterna magna).

magendie.definition: A French physiologist who, with Charles Bell, described that dorsal spinal nerve roots carry sensory information while ventral roots carry motor information (dorsal–ventral nerve law). The eponym is also associated with the median aperture of the fourth ventricle, through which cerebrospinal fluid flows into the subarachnoid space.

luschka.definition: Small bile ducts located in the gallbladder fossa that drain liver tissue directly into the biliary system; they can be encountered and injured during cholecystectomy, potentially causing postoperative bile leakage.

ventricular compliance.definition: The distensibility of the ventricle during diastole, defined as the change in volume for a given change in filling pressure (dV/dP); high compliance means easy filling at low pressures, while low compliance indicates a stiff ventricle requiring higher filling pressures.

ventricular dysfunction.definition: Impaired ability of a heart ventricle to contract and/or relax (systolic and/or diastolic dysfunction), affecting one or both ventricles and often causing reduced cardiac output and elevated filling pressures.

ventricular ejection.definition: The phase of the cardiac cycle during which the ventricles contract and expel blood into the aorta and pulmonary artery, occurring during systole when the semilunar valves are open and ending with their closure. It includes rapid and reduced ejection phases.

ventricular escape.definition: A rhythm originating from ventricular pacemaker tissue that takes over when higher cardiac pacemakers fail or conduction is blocked, producing a slow rate (typically ~20–40 beats per minute) with broad QRS complexes and often reduced cardiac output. It serves to maintain some heart function in the setting of complete or high-grade conduction block.

ventricular extrasystole.definition: A premature heartbeat arising from an ectopic focus in the ventricles, producing an early, wide QRS complex on ECG and often a compensatory pause; usually benign in healthy individuals but may indicate underlying cardiac disease if frequent or symptomatic.

ventricular flutter.definition: An extremely fast, regular ventricular tachyarrhythmia occurring at roughly 250–350 beats per minute, often with a sine-wave ECG appearance; it is highly unstable and commonly degenerates into ventricular fibrillation if not promptly treated, requiring emergent defibrillation or synchronized cardioversion.

ventricular gallop.definition: An extra heart sound (S3) heard in early diastole after S2, produced by rapid ventricular filling; commonly associated with increased volume load or reduced ventricular compliance, as seen in heart failure, but may be normal in children and young adults.

ventricular gradient.definition: An electrophysiologic concept describing the spatial gradient of ventricular electrical activity during the cardiac cycle; in vectorcardiography, it often refers to the net ventricular gradient—the vector sum of the QRS (depolarization) and T (repolarization) vectors—representing the overall magnitude and direction of ventricular activation and recovery.

ventricular pacing.definition: An artificial electrical stimulation of the ventricles by a pacemaker to depolarize the ventricular myocardium and maintain an adequate heart rate when the heart's intrinsic conduction is slow or blocked.

ventricular remodeling.definition: Structural and functional changes in the ventricle (usually the left) following injury or chronic hemodynamic stress, including alterations in size (dilation or hypertrophy), wall geometry, and myocardial tissue (fibrosis and extracellular matrix remodeling); these changes can be adaptive at first but often become maladaptive, impairing contractile function and promoting heart failure.

ventricular rhythm.definition: A cardiac rhythm that originates from ventricular tissue (below the AV node), usually slower than normal when higher pacemakers fail and typically producing wide, abnormal QRS complexes on ECG.

vsd.definition: One or more holes in the septum, the muscular wall separating the right and left sides of the heart.

ventricular standstill.definition: A state in which the ventricles have no electrical activity and no mechanical contraction, producing no cardiac output; ECG shows absence of QRS complexes (electrical standstill), typically corresponding to asystole.

venturi effect.definition: A pressure drop that occurs when a fluid flows through a constricted section, due to increased velocity (Bernoulli principle); in medicine, this principle is exploited by devices such as the Venturi mask to entrain ambient air and deliver a fixed fraction of inspired oxygen.

venule.definition: A small vessel that collects blood from capillaries and drains it into veins.

venulitis.definition: Inflammation of the venules, the smallest veins; a form of small-vessel vasculitis that may cause localized redness, warmth, tenderness, and sometimes purpura, and can be secondary to infection, immune-complex–mediated processes, or systemic vasculitis.

venular.definition: Relating to or resembling a venule, the small vessel that drains blood from capillary beds into a vein.

visual-evoked potential.definition: An electrophysiologic test that records the brain's electrical response to visual stimuli (usually pattern-reversal or flash) from scalp electrodes, used to assess the function of the visual pathway from the retina to the occipital cortex.

vep.definition: An electrophysiological test that records the brain's electrical response to visual stimuli (such as flashing lights or pattern-reversed checkerboards) to assess the integrity of the visual pathways from the retina to the occipital cortex.

vepesid.definition: Brand-name chemotherapy drug (etoposide) that inhibits topoisomerase II, causing DNA damage and cancer cell death; used to treat various cancers and administered orally or by IV infusion.

vp-16.definition: An antineoplastic drug (etoposide), a semi-synthetic derivative of podophyllotoxin that inhibits topoisomerase II, causing DNA strand breaks and blocking cell division; used in various chemotherapy regimens for cancers such as testicular cancer, small-cell lung cancer, and lymphomas; administered orally or IV; common adverse effects include bone marrow suppression, nausea, mucositis, and alopecia.

veratrum.definition: A genus of toxic perennial flowering plants in the Melanthiaceae family, containing veratrine alkaloids that affect voltage-gated sodium channels; historically used as an antihypertensive and emetic, but now rarely used due to high toxicity.

verbal aphasia.definition: An expressive language disorder due to brain injury (usually in the dominant frontal language area) causing nonfluent, effortful speech with relatively preserved comprehension and impaired repetition.

verbal language.definition: The spoken form of human language conveyed through articulated sounds and grammar to communicate meaning; encompasses phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, and pragmatics, and is distinct from nonverbal language such as gestures or sign language.

verdeso.definition: Not a recognized medical term; no standard medical definition exists. It may be a misspelling or a non-English word. If you have context or the source, I can help identify the intended term or provide a definition for a related term.

veregen.definition: A prescription topical ointment containing sinecatechins, a green tea (Camellia sinensis) extract, used to treat external genital and perianal warts caused by human papillomavirus; it exerts antiviral and immunomodulatory effects and is applied to affected skin as directed, with potential local skin irritation.

vergence.definition: The coordinated, disconjugate movement of both eyes in opposite directions to maintain single binocular vision; it includes convergence (inward turning for near objects) and divergence (outward turning for far objects).

vernal conjunctivitis.definition: A bilateral, seasonal allergic conjunctivitis seen mainly in children and young adults, with intense itching, tearing, redness, and photophobia during spring and summer; often linked to atopy and characterized by prominent papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva and limbal involvement.

vernal keratoconjunctivitis.definition: A chronic allergic inflammatory disorder of the ocular surface, most common in children and adolescents, characterized by severe itching, tearing, redness, and mucous discharge; features include cobblestone papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva, limbal involvement with Trantas dots, and, in severe cases, corneal shield ulcers; it is usually seasonal (spring/summer) but may be perennial in atopic individuals.

verner-morrison syndrome.definition: A syndrome caused by a vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)–secreting pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (VIPoma), characterized by profuse watery diarrhea with hypokalemia and achlorhydria (the WDHA triad); also known as VIPoma syndrome or pancreatic cholera.

pancreatic diarrhea.definition: Diarrhea caused by pancreatic exocrine insufficiency resulting in fat malabsorption; stools are steatorrheic—bulky, greasy, pale, and foul-smelling—and often associated with weight loss and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies; may improve with pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy.

vernet’s syndrome.definition: Jugular foramen syndrome: an ipsilateral palsy of cranial nerves IX, X, and XI due to a lesion at the jugular foramen, typically causing dysphagia, hoarseness and diminished gag reflex (IX/X), and weakness of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius (XI).
