plexiform neuroma.definition: A benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor that grows along the length of a nerve, involving multiple fascicles (a nerve plexus); most often associated with neurofibromatosis type 1, it can be infiltrative and carries a risk of malignant transformation to malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor.

appendix vermiformis.definition: A narrow blind-ended tube attached to the cecum in the lower right abdomen, containing lymphoid tissue; its precise function is unclear, but it is thought to contribute to gut immunity; inflammation causes appendicitis.

vermifuge.definition: An anthelmintic drug that facilitates the expulsion of intestinal worms from the body, usually by paralyzing or immobilizing the parasites so they can be passed in the stool; contrasted with a vermicide, which kills the worms.

vermicular.definition: Relating to or resembling a worm; worm-shaped.

vermilion.definition: Red, hairless, highly vascular mucous membrane of the lips that forms the visible portion of the lips; the vermilion border is the junction between lip mucosa and the adjacent skin.

vermilion border.definition: The mucocutaneous boundary between the red, highly vascularized portion of the lips (vermilion) and the adjacent facial skin; the edge where lip mucosa meets skin.

verocytotoxin.definition: A potent AB5 bacterial toxin produced by Shigella dysenteriae type 1 and some Escherichia coli strains that inhibits protein synthesis by depurinating the 28S rRNA of the 60S ribosomal subunit; it can cause hemorrhagic colitis and hemolytic-uremic syndrome.

verrucae.definition: A benign epidermal skin lesion caused by human papillomavirus infection of keratinocytes, presenting as a rough, keratinized papule or plaque; commonly known as warts and often occurring on the hands or feet.

vernix caseosa.definition: A protective, waxy, cheese-like coating covering the fetal and newborn skin, composed of sebum and shed epithelial cells; formed in utero and helps moisturize and waterproof the skin, protecting it from amniotic fluid, typically diminishing after birth.

jugular foramen syndrome.definition: A focal cranial nerve syndrome due to pathology at the jugular foramen causing ipsilateral palsy of IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), and XI (spinal accessory) nerves, typically with dysphagia, hoarseness, loss of gag reflex, palate weakness, and weakness of the sternocleidomastoid/trapezius muscles; if the hypoglossal nerve (XII) is also involved, the condition is called Collet-Sicard syndrome.

basilar.definition: Located at or forming the base; in anatomy, pertaining to the base of a structure (e.g., basilar artery at the base of the brainstem or basilar membrane of the cochlea).

dorsal spine.definition: The posterior aspect (back) of the vertebral column; the dorsal side of the spine, including the spinous processes along the back of each vertebra.

twelfth rib.definition: The lowest rib of the thoracic cage; a floating (false) rib with no anterior attachment to the sternum, articulating posteriorly with the T12 vertebra (head) and the transverse process of T12.

spinal subarachnoid spaces.definition: A potential space within the spinal meninges between the arachnoid and pia mater that contains cerebrospinal fluid and the cauda equina nerve roots; it extends from the foramen magnum to the filum terminale and is continuous with the cranial subarachnoid space.

pulmonary vascular obstructive disease.definition: A group of disorders characterized by obstruction to blood flow through the pulmonary vasculature (arteries and/or veins), leading to increased pulmonary vascular resistance and commonly pulmonary hypertension.

folium vermis.definition: A leaf-like fold of the cerebellar cortex located on the vermis (the midline portion of the cerebellum), contributing to the cerebellum's folded surface.

vermis cerebelli.definition: Midline, narrow portion of the cerebellum that connects the two cerebellar hemispheres; contains the medial cerebellar cortex and is primarily involved in coordination of trunk posture and gait via spinocerebellar inputs.

verruca acuminata.definition: A sexually transmitted infection caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), typically types 6 and 11, presenting as soft, moist, cauliflower-like warty lesions on the genital or perianal skin or mucosa; often asymptomatic but may cause pruritus or bleeding and is treated with topical therapies, cryotherapy, or surgical removal.

verruca vulgaris.definition: A common wart caused by human papillomavirus infection of the epidermis, presenting as rough, raised, hyperkeratotic papules most often on the hands or fingers; benign and contagious.

verruca plana.definition: Flat warts caused by human papillomavirus infection, presenting as smooth, flat-topped, flesh-colored papules that often occur in clusters on the face, hands, or shins; common in children and young adults.

verruca senilis.definition: An age-related benign skin lesion (seborrheic keratosis) that appears as a well-demarcated, pigmented, waxy or "stuck-on" plaque, commonly occurring on the trunk, face, or extremities of older adults.

verrucous carcinoma.definition: A well-differentiated, low-grade variant of squamous cell carcinoma characterized by a slow-growing, exophytic, cauliflower-like lesion that invades locally with a pushing margin and has a relatively low metastatic potential; most commonly arising in the oral cavity, larynx, skin, or genitourinary tract.

verrucous dermatitis.definition: A chronic inflammatory skin condition presenting with thickened, wart-like (verrucous) plaques resulting from long-standing dermatitis or irritation; it is a descriptive pattern seen in several eczematous or contact-related dermatoses rather than a single disease entity.

cantharidin.definition: A potent vesicant and terpenoid toxin produced by blister beetles (family Meloidae); used topically to induce a controlled skin blister for treatment of certain lesions such as warts and molluscum contagiosum, but can cause severe local skin injury and systemic toxicity if ingested or absorbed; should be applied only by a clinician.

laser excision.definition: A surgical procedure in which focused laser energy is used to cut, vaporize, or excise tissue to remove a lesion or diseased tissue, often with coagulation to reduce bleeding.

liquid nitrogen.definition: A colorless, odorless cryogenic liquid formed by cooling nitrogen gas to −196°C (−321°F); used in medicine for cryotherapy, cryosurgery, and cryopreservation of tissues and cells, and can cause severe frostbite and tissue damage on contact as well as asphyxiation risk in poorly ventilated spaces.

internal podalic version.definition: An obstetric maneuver in which, with ruptured membranes, the clinician reaches through the cervix into the uterus to grasp the fetus and rotate or deliver it feet- or buttocks-first (podalic presentation) to facilitate vaginal delivery in a breech or transverse lie (often used for a second twin).

external version.definition: A procedure in obstetrics where a clinician uses external manual pressure on the abdomen to rotate the fetus from a breech or transverse lie to a head-down (cephalic) presentation, usually performed near term to facilitate vaginal delivery or to avoid cesarean delivery.

total breech extraction.definition: An obstetric maneuver for vaginal breech delivery in which the entire fetus is delivered through the birth canal by traction on the presenting part, with the trunk and limbs delivered before the head.

vertebral arch.definition: The posterior part of a vertebra that encircles the vertebral foramen; formed by the pedicles and laminae, it protects the spinal cord and serves as attachments for muscles and ligaments.

vertebral foramen.definition: An opening in a vertebra formed by the vertebral arch and body, through which the spinal cord and its meninges pass; collectively, the vertebral foramina form the vertebral canal.

vertebral groove.definition: A groove on a vertebra that accommodates or directs a nerve or blood vessel as it passes along the spine.

vertebral notch.definition: A notch on the superior or inferior border of a vertebra's pedicle that forms the intervertebral foramen with the corresponding notch of the adjacent vertebra, through which a spinal nerve exits the spinal canal.

vertebral rib.definition: One of the ribs that has no anterior attachment to the sternum and articulates only with the vertebral column (typically the 11th and 12th ribs); commonly called a floating rib.

false rib.definition: Ribs that do not attach directly to the sternum with their own costal cartilage; ribs 8–10 attach to the cartilage of the rib above, while ribs 11–12 (floating ribs) have no anterior attachment.

true rib.definition: One of the first seven pairs of ribs that attach directly to the sternum via costal cartilage.

vertebrocostal.definition: Relating to the vertebrae and the ribs; pertaining to the joints where the ribs articulate with the thoracic vertebrae (costovertebral and costotransverse joints).

vertebrocostal rib.definition: A rib that articulates with the thoracic vertebrae at the costovertebral joints; its head has two articular facets for the bodies of adjacent vertebrae, and its tubercle articulates with the transverse process of the corresponding vertebra.

vertebrosternal rib.definition: One of the true ribs (ribs 1–7) that attach directly to the sternum via their costal cartilages.

vertebral angiography.definition: An imaging procedure in which a contrast agent is selectively injected into the vertebral arteries (usually via catheter) to visualize their flow and branches on fluoroscopic imaging, used to evaluate vertebral artery anatomy and pathology such as stenosis, dissection, occlusion, or aneurysm.

vertebral-basilar system.definition: The vertebrobasilar system is the posterior circulation of the brain, supplied by the vertebral arteries that join to form the basilar artery and by its branches, delivering blood to the brainstem, cerebellum, and posterior cerebral cortex.

sacral vertebrae.definition: Five sacral vertebrae (S1–S5) that usually fuse to form the sacrum, a triangular bone at the base of the spine that forms the posterior pelvic wall and transmits body weight to the pelvis; it articulates superiorly with L5 and inferiorly with the coccyx.

coccygeal vertebrae.definition: Small vertebrae that form the coccyx (tailbone); typically four rudimentary vertebrae that fuse in adulthood to constitute the terminal portion of the vertebral column.

vertebral subluxation complex.definition: An unproven chiropractic concept describing a cluster of vertebral segment dysfunction and nerve interference, including altered joint motion, soft-tissue changes, and impaired neural function believed to affect overall health.

verteporfin.definition: A photosensitizing benzoporphyrin derivative used in photodynamic therapy to selectively occlude abnormal choroidal neovascular membranes in diseases such as neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration; activated by specific laser light to generate reactive oxygen species and cause vessel occlusion.

ocular histoplasmosis.definition: A syndrome of eye disease linked to prior Histoplasma capsulatum exposure, characterized by multiple peripheral punched-out chorioretinal scars (histo spots), often with peripapillary scarring; macular involvement can occur and choroidal neovascularization may lead to vision loss. It represents scar tissue from past infection rather than active infection.

pathological myopia.definition: A severe, progressive elongation of the eyeball with degenerative changes of the retina, choroid, and sclera that causes progressive visual loss and increases the risk of retinal detachment and myopic maculopathy, typically associated with high refractive error (approximately −6 diopters or more).

vesicular mole.definition: A hydatidiform mole characterized by vesicular (grape-like) chorionic villi with hydropic degeneration; a gestational trophoblastic disease typically arising from fertilization of an empty ovum by paternal sperm, usually representing a complete mole with no viable fetus.

vesical fistula.definition: An abnormal communication between the urinary bladder and another organ or the skin, through which urine drains abnormally (e.g., vesicovaginal, vesicocutaneous, or vesicoenteric fistulas).

vesical glands.definition: Small mucous glands in the wall of the urinary bladder that secrete mucus to lubricate and protect the bladder mucosa.

vesical hematuria.definition: Blood in the urine originating from the urinary bladder.

vesical lithotomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove stones from the urinary bladder by making an incision in the bladder (cystotomy).

vesical reflex.definition: An involuntary reflex of the urinary bladder in which stretch of the bladder wall by urine activates afferent pathways that trigger detrusor muscle contraction via parasympathetic (pelvic) nerves, promoting micturition; mediated at the sacral spinal cord (S2–S4) and modulated by higher centers.

vesical sphincter.definition: A smooth muscle ring at the bladder neck (internal urethral sphincter) that constricts the bladder outlet to maintain continence and prevent retrograde ejaculation; it relaxes during micturition under parasympathetic input.

vesicare.definition: A brand-name antimuscarinic (solifenacin) used to treat overactive bladder by reducing bladder muscle contractions, thereby decreasing urge incontinence, urgency, and frequency.

vesicoabdominal.definition: Relating to the urinary bladder and the abdomen; describing an anatomical relationship or surgical approach that involves both the bladder and the abdominal region.

vesicocele.definition: A herniation or protrusion of the urinary bladder through a defect in the pelvic floor or abdominal wall (i.e., a bladder hernia).

vesicoureteral reflux.definition: A condition in which urine flows backward from the bladder into the ureter and possibly the kidney due to failure of the vesicoureteral junction to close properly; commonly seen in children and associated with an increased risk of recurrent urinary tract infections and renal scarring, graded I–V by severity.

vesicovaginal fistula.definition: An abnormal connection between the urinary bladder and the vagina, causing continuous leakage of urine through the vagina; commonly caused by obstetric trauma during childbirth, pelvic surgery, or radiation.

vesicula.definition: A small sac or bladder-like cavity; a diminutive anatomical pouch used to describe small fluid-filled structures or glands (for example, the seminal vesicle).

vesiculitis.definition: Inflammation of a vesicle; in urology, inflammation of the seminal vesicles (seminal vesiculitis) often due to infection.

vesiculography.definition: A radiographic imaging procedure of the seminal vesicles in which radiopaque contrast is injected into the vesicles (via the vas deferens or ejaculatory ducts) to visualize them and assess for obstruction, rupture, or other pathology, often in evaluation of male infertility.

vesiculotympanitic.definition: Relating to vesicles on the tympanic membrane; describing a tympanic membrane that bears vesicles (bullae), as seen in bullous myringitis.

voiding cystourethrography.definition: An imaging study in which contrast is instilled into the bladder and radiographs are obtained during voiding to evaluate the bladder and urethra for vesicoureteral reflux and other lower urinary tract abnormalities.

vestibular ganglions.definition: The sensory ganglia of the vestibular division of cranial nerve VIII that contain the cell bodies of vestibular afferent neurons; they receive input from the semicircular canals and otolithic organs and project to the vestibular nuclei.

vestibulo-ocular reflex.definition: An eye movement reflex that stabilizes vision during head movement by generating rapid, compensatory eye movements in the opposite direction of head motion, mediated by the vestibular apparatus (semicircular canals and otolith organs) and integrated in brainstem circuits with cerebellar modulation.

vestibuloplasty.definition: A surgical procedure to deepen the oral vestibule by repositioning the mucosa (often with grafts or flaps) to create a longer, deeper sulcus for improved denture retention and prosthetic function.

sulcoplasty.definition: A surgical procedure to repair or reconstruct a sulcus—a groove or furrow in tissue or an organ—aimed at restoring normal anatomy or function after trauma, disease, or congenital defects.

false vocal cord.definition: Mucosal folds in the larynx located above the true vocal cords; they do not vibrate to produce sound and mainly protect the airway and assist in swallowing by helping to close the laryngeal inlet.

navicular fossa.definition: A dilated, funnel-shaped portion of the penile (spongy) urethra located within the glans penis, just proximal to the external urethral meatus.

vaginal orifice.definition: The external opening of the vagina (the vaginal introitus), through which the vaginal canal opens to the exterior; part of the vulva.

frenulum of pudendal labia.definition: A small mucous membrane fold that joins the inner surfaces of the labia minora at the anterior part of the vestibule (the front of the vaginal opening).

lesser vestibular gland.definition: Small mucous-secreting glands on the anterior wall of the vaginal vestibule near the external urethral meatus; they secrete lubrication into the vestibule and are homologous to the male prostate (parauethral/paraurethral glands, also called Skene's glands).

scarpa's ganglion.definition: The vestibular ganglion: the sensory neuron cell bodies of the vestibular portion of the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII), located in the internal auditory canal; it relays balance and spatial orientation information from the inner ear (semicircular canals, utricle, and saccule) to the brain.

vestibular neuritis.definition: An acute, unilateral peripheral vestibular disorder caused by inflammation of the vestibular nerve, producing sudden severe vertigo with nystagmus, nausea, and gait imbalance, typically with preserved hearing (unlike labyrinthitis).

vestibular toxicity.definition: Damage to the vestibular apparatus or vestibular pathways caused by toxic agents, resulting in vertigo, dizziness, imbalance, and abnormal vestibulo-ocular reflex; commonly drug-induced (e.g., aminoglycoside antibiotics, platinum-based chemotherapy).

vestibule of the ear.definition: Central chamber of the inner ear within the bony labyrinth that connects the cochlea with the three semicircular canals; it contains the utricle and saccule (otolith organs) and is involved in detecting linear acceleration and head position.

vestibule of the mouth.definition: The space between the lips and cheeks externally and the teeth and gingiva internally, forming the oral vestibule; it communicates with the oral cavity proper and is divided into maxillary and mandibular vestibules.

vestibule of the aorta.definition: A smooth-walled portion of the left ventricle immediately beneath the aortic valve, forming the proximal part of the left ventricular outflow tract and channeling blood from the LV into the ascending aorta; it is distinct from the trabeculated body of the ventricle.

herpes simplex virus type 1.definition: A double-stranded DNA virus of the Herpesviridae family that commonly causes orolabial herpes (cold sores) and can establish latent infection in the trigeminal ganglion with periodic reactivation.

herpes simplex virus type 2.definition: Double-stranded DNA virus of the Herpesviridae family that primarily causes genital herpes; transmitted sexually and establishes latent infection in sensory ganglia with recurrent outbreaks of painful genital ulcers; managed with nucleoside analog antivirals such as acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir.

vidarabine.definition: A purine nucleoside analog antiviral (Ara-A) that inhibits viral DNA polymerase, used to treat certain herpesvirus infections (notably herpes simplex and varicella-zoster viruses) and some ophthalmic infections; historically given systemically or topically, but largely superseded by acyclovir.

adenine arabinoside.definition: A purine nucleoside analog antiviral agent that inhibits viral DNA synthesis by blocking viral DNA polymerase; active against herpes simplex virus and varicella-zoster virus infections; phosphorylated intracellularly to an active triphosphate form.

vidaza.definition: A brand-name chemotherapy drug (azacitidine) used to treat myelodysplastic syndromes; it is a hypomethylating agent that inhibits DNA methyltransferase, leading to DNA hypomethylation and reactivation of silenced genes, administered by subcutaneous injection or intravenous infusion in cycles.

videoendoscopy.definition: A procedure in which an endoscope equipped with a video camera and light transmits real-time images to a monitor, allowing visualization, documentation, and assessment of internal passages or cavities.

videolaparoscopy.definition: A minimally invasive surgical technique in which a laparoscope with a video camera is inserted into the abdominal cavity to visualize the operative field on a video monitor, allowing procedures through small incisions.

videostroboscopy.definition: A diagnostic procedure in which a flexible or rigid endoscope is used with a synchronized strobe light to visualize vocal-fold vibration during phonation, allowing assessment of glottic closure, vibratory pattern, mucosal wave, and any lesions.

video display terminal.definition: A device with a video display used to present computer-generated information (such as patient records, monitoring data, or test results) at a clinician's workstation, typically with input controls to interact with the computer system.

vinorelbine tartrate.definition: A semi-synthetic vinca alkaloid chemotherapy agent in the tartrate salt form; inhibits tubulin polymerization, blocking microtubule assembly and causing mitotic arrest (G2/M) with apoptosis. Used primarily for non–small cell lung cancer and certain breast cancers; given intravenously.

vineberg's operation.definition: An early myocardial revascularization method in which a segment of the internal mammary (internal thoracic) artery is implanted into the ischemic heart muscle (usually the left ventricle) to promote neovascularization and collateral blood supply; largely obsolete with modern bypass grafting.

villous.definition: Relating to villi, the small finger-like projections on mucosal surfaces (especially the intestinal lining) that increase surface area for absorption; describes tissue bearing these projections or conditions affecting them, such as atrophy of the mucosal projections.

villous adenoma.definition: Colorectal adenomatous polyp with villous (frond-like) projections lined by dysplastic epithelium; a premalignant lesion with a higher risk of progression to colorectal cancer than tubular adenomas, especially when large or with high-grade dysplasia.

villous carcinoma.definition: A malignant epithelial tumor characterized by slender, finger-like (villous) projections of neoplastic glands; in colorectal pathology it usually refers to an adenocarcinoma with prominent villous architecture, often arising from a preexisting villous adenoma and associated with a higher risk of invasion and metastasis than tubular-type cancers.

villous chorion.definition: That portion of the chorion that bears chorionic villi; the fetal component of the placenta comprising villous projections that invade the maternal decidua and mediate maternal–fetal exchange.

villous papilloma.definition: Benign epithelial tumor with finger-like (villous) projections from a mucosal surface; a papilloma with villous architecture, and in the colon/rectum such lesions are often called villous adenomas, which have a higher malignant potential than tubular polyps.

vibrio cholerae.definition: A curved, motile, Gram-negative bacterium that is the etiologic agent of cholera; it colonizes the small intestine and produces cholera toxin, causing profuse watery diarrhea and dehydration, transmitted via contaminated water or food, with epidemic strains in serogroups O1 and O139.

vibrio parahaemolyticus.definition: A curved, Gram-negative, halophilic bacterium of marine origin; a common cause of seafood-associated gastroenteritis, typically acquired by eating raw or undercooked seafood, resulting in watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, nausea, and vomiting; infections are usually self-limiting.

vibrio vulnificus.definition: A pathogenic halophilic Gram-negative curved bacterium from marine environments that causes severe wound infections and septicemia, typically after exposure of an open wound to seawater or consumption of raw shellfish (especially oysters); it has high mortality in patients with liver disease or immunocompromised status.

intrathecal administration.definition: Delivery of a drug directly into the intrathecal (subarachnoid) space around the spinal cord to reach the cerebrospinal fluid, bypassing the blood–brain barrier.

vasoactive intestinal polypeptide.definition: A 28-amino-acid neuropeptide that functions as a potent vasodilator and stimulates secretion of water and electrolytes from the intestinal and pancreatic mucosa; it also relaxes smooth muscle and modulates immune responses via VPAC1 and VPAC2 receptors.

viremia.definition: The presence of viruses in the blood.

viral cultures.definition: A laboratory test in which a specimen is inoculated into susceptible cell cultures to allow replication of viable virus, enabling isolation and identification of the infecting virus; used to diagnose active viral infections; results may take several days to weeks.

vira-a.definition: The presence of viruses in the bloodstream, indicating a systemic viral infection; detectable by nucleic acid tests (such as PCR) or viral culture.

central ulceration.definition: Ulceration that occurs at the center of a lesion or structure, presenting as a crater-like area of tissue loss with surrounding inflammation or granulation tissue.

virchow’s node.definition: A left supraclavicular lymph node that enlarges due to metastatic cancer, most commonly from gastric or other intra-abdominal malignancies; a classic sign known as Troisier's sign.

bk virus.definition: A nonenveloped double-stranded DNA virus of the Polyomaviridae family that commonly infects children, remains latent in renal tissue, and reactivates during immunosuppression to cause nephropathy in kidney transplant recipients and hemorrhagic cystitis in hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients.

hepatitis f.definition: A historically proposed but unconfirmed hepatitis virus; not recognized as a distinct hepatitis pathogen by major health authorities, and the term is largely obsolete.

hepatitis g.definition: A blood-borne flavivirus (GBV-C), also called hepatitis G virus; infection is typically asymptomatic and has not been clearly linked to hepatitis or clinically significant liver disease; transmitted via parenteral routes (blood, needles) and sometimes sexually; there is no vaccine and no routine testing.

hepatitis h.definition: Not a recognized form of viral hepatitis; there is no disease entity or virus officially designated as “Hepatitis H” in current medical taxonomy. If encountered, the term likely refers to non-A–E hepatitis or results from mislabeling of another liver condition.

clay-colored stools.definition: A pale, clay-colored stool caused by a lack of bile pigments reaching the gut, typically due to biliary obstruction or liver/bile duct disease (e.g., gallstones, cholestasis, hepatitis).

dark urine.definition: Urine that appears darker than normal, typically ranging from deep yellow to brown; most often due to concentrated urine from dehydration, but it can also indicate underlying conditions such as bleeding in the urinary tract (hematuria), elevated bilirubin (bilirubinuria) from liver or biliary disease, or the presence of myoglobin, as well as effects from certain foods, drugs, or supplements.

viral load.definition: Quantitative measure of the amount of virus present in a defined volume of a biological sample, commonly blood, usually reported as copies per milliliter (or international units per milliliter). It reflects viral replication activity and is used to monitor infection severity and treatment response (e.g., HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C).

viral pneumonia.definition: Pneumonia caused by a viral infection of the lungs, characterized by inflammation of the lung parenchyma with symptoms such as fever, cough, and shortness of breath, and often diffuse interstitial or patchy consolidations on chest imaging.

chick embryo.definition: A developing vertebrate in a fertilized chicken egg (Gallus gallus domesticus); widely used as a model organism to study embryology and organogenesis.

fluorescent antibody.definition: A reagent in which an antibody is conjugated to a fluorescent dye, used to detect specific antigens by binding them and visualizing under fluorescence microscopy (direct or indirect immunofluorescence).

microscopic examination.definition: An analysis of a specimen (tissue, cells, or body fluids) prepared on a slide and examined under a microscope to assess cellular detail and tissue architecture for diagnostic purposes.

skin tests.definition: Tests that evaluate skin reactivity to specific antigens by applying or injecting them into the skin and observing the reaction; used to diagnose allergies (e.g., skin-prick or intradermal tests for IgE-mediated sensitivities) and contact dermatitis (patch testing), as well as to infer prior exposure to certain pathogens (e.g., the tuberculin skin test for tuberculosis).

virtual endoscopy.definition: A noninvasive imaging technique that uses CT or MR data to generate three-dimensional reconstructions of a hollow organ’s interior lumen, producing a simulated endoscopic view to visualize mucosal surfaces without inserting an instrument.

perivascular spaces.definition: CSF-filled, pial-lined spaces surrounding penetrating brain vessels as they enter the parenchyma; they contain interstitial fluid and are typically incidental and benign, though enlargement can occur with aging or certain diseases and may mimic pathology on MRI when enlarged.

virchow-robin spaces.definition: Perivascular spaces around penetrating cerebral arteries as they enter the brain parenchyma; CSF-filled compartments that accompany vessels and are normal anatomical structures, which can enlarge with aging or small vessel disease and be seen on MRI.

situs inversus viscerum.definition: Congenital condition in which the major thoracic and abdominal organs are arranged as a mirror image of their normal positions; in situs inversus totalis, all viscera are reversed, including dextrocardia (heart on the right).

visceral cavity.definition: An anatomical space in the body that houses the internal organs (viscera); for example, the thoracic cavity contains the heart and lungs, while the abdominal cavity contains digestive organs.

visceral afferent fibers.definition: Afferent sensory nerve fibers that carry information from visceral organs to the central nervous system, including stretch, chemical stimuli, and pain; these fibers travel with autonomic nerves (general visceral afferents) and project to brainstem nuclei or the spinal cord to mediate visceral reflexes and sensations.

visceral efferent system.definition: The motor component of the autonomic nervous system that sends efferent impulses from the CNS to visceral effectors (smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands) via sympathetic and parasympathetic pathways, regulating involuntary functions such as heart rate, digestion, and glandular secretion.

cerebrospinal nerves.definition: Not a standard term; if used, it refers to the cranial and spinal nerves—the peripheral nerves that originate from the brain and spinal cord and connect the central nervous system to the body, transmitting motor, sensory, and autonomic information.

somatic afferent fibers.definition: Sensory nerve fibers that convey information from somatic structures (skin, muscles, joints, and body walls) to the central nervous system, transmitting modalities such as touch, pressure, temperature, pain, and proprioception.

liver function.definition: A set of metabolic, synthetic, detoxification, excretory, storage, and immune activities performed by the liver, including processing nutrients, producing bile and plasma proteins, detoxifying drugs and toxins, and storing glycogen and vitamins.

visceral larva migrans.definition: A zoonotic infection caused by migrating nematode larvae (most commonly Toxocara canis or Toxocara cati) in humans, resulting from ingesting eggs that hatch and disseminate to visceral tissues (often liver and lungs) with eosinophilic inflammation. Acquired from soil contaminated with dog or cat feces; can present with hepatomegaly, fever, eosinophilia, and occasionally ocular or CNS involvement.

strongyloides.definition: A genus of parasitic nematodes (roundworms) that infect humans and other mammals; the clinically important species causes strongyloidiasis. Transmission occurs when filariform larvae in contaminated soil penetrate the skin; autoinfection can allow chronic infection. Symptoms range from none to abdominal pain, diarrhea, urticaria, and pulmonary involvement; dissemination or hyperinfection can occur in immunosuppressed individuals. Treatment options include ivermectin or albendazole.

nematodes.definition: A phylum of elongated, unsegmented roundworms with a pseudocoelom and a tough cuticle, possessing a complete digestive tract; many species are free-living in soil or water, while numerous species are parasitic in plants and animals, including humans.

podocytes.definition: Specialized visceral epithelial cells of the renal glomerulus that encircle glomerular capillaries with interdigitating foot processes (pedicels) and slit diaphragms, forming part of the glomerular filtration barrier; they regulate filtration and maintain capillary permeability, and damage can lead to proteinuria.

urinary space.definition: Not a standard anatomical term; when used, it refers to the cavity or lumen of the urinary tract that contains urine—the spaces within the kidney (renal pelvis and calyces), ureter, bladder, and urethra.

visceral leishmaniasis.definition: A systemic protozoal infection caused by the Leishmania donovani complex transmitted by sandflies, characterized by fever, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, weight loss, and high mortality if untreated.

visceral lymph node.definition: A lymph node that drains lymph from internal organs (viscera) rather than from the body wall; typically located along arteries supplying the viscera and feeding into central lymphatic trunks (e.g., celiac, superior/inferior mesenteric, or intestinal trunks).

visceral nervous system.definition: The component of the nervous system that innervates and regulates internal organs (viscera) through autonomic (sympathetic and parasympathetic) efferents and visceral afferents, including the enteric nervous system; it controls involuntary visceral functions such as heart rate, digestion, vascular tone, and glandular secretion.

visceral efferent fibers.definition: Autonomic motor nerve fibers that innervate visceral organs (smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands), carrying efferent impulses from the CNS via preganglionic and postganglionic neurons of the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions to regulate involuntary visceral functions.

nonstriated muscle.definition: An involuntary, nonstriated muscle tissue that forms the walls of hollow organs and vessels; it contracts slowly and without conscious control, regulated by the autonomic nervous system.

visceral obesity.definition: An excessive accumulation of visceral fat around internal abdominal organs (intra-abdominal adiposity), as opposed to subcutaneous fat, associated with increased risk of metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, fatty liver disease, and cardiovascular disease.

visceral fat.definition: Fat that lies beneath the abdominal wall, in the spaces surrounding the liver, intestines, and other organs. Sometimes called belly fat or abdominal adiposity.

visceral pain.definition: Pain arising from internal organs (viscera) due to distension, inflammation, or ischemia; typically poorly localized and diffuse, often described as dull or cramping, and may be referred to other body regions.

nociceptors.definition: Nerve endings that detect pain and transmit pain information to the brain and spinal cord.

visceral peritoneum.definition: The portion of the peritoneum that covers the external surfaces of abdominal and pelvic viscera; a serous membrane continuous with the parietal peritoneum, forming mesenteries, omenta, and peritoneal ligaments.

mesenteries.definition: A double layer of peritoneum that suspends the intestines from the posterior abdominal wall and contains the vessels, nerves, and lymphatics supplying the intestines.

omenta.definition: Two folds of peritoneum that connect the stomach to other abdominal organs; there are two main parts: a large, fatty apron that hangs from the stomach and drapes over the intestines, and a shorter ligamentous fold that connects the stomach to the liver. They contain fat and immune tissue, help localize and limit intraperitoneal infections, and provide a conduit for vessels and ligaments between the stomach and surrounding structures.

ligaments of the liver.definition: Peritoneal folds that connect the liver to surrounding structures (diaphragm, anterior abdominal wall, stomach, and duodenum) and help stabilize its position within the upper abdomen. Classic examples include the falciform ligament (with the ligamentum teres hepatis in its free edge), the coronary and triangular ligaments anchoring to the diaphragm, and the hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments forming the lesser omentum.

bursa omentalis.definition: An omental bursa (lesser sac) is a potential space of the peritoneal cavity located posterior to the stomach and the lesser omentum; it communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow).

lesser peritoneal cavity.definition: A potential space in the peritoneal cavity, the lesser sac (omental bursa), located posterior to the stomach and lesser omentum; it communicates with the greater sac via the epiploic foramen of Winslow.

visceral protein status.definition: Visceral protein status is the assessment of hepatic-synthesized plasma proteins (commonly albumin, transferrin, prealbumin/transthyretin, and retinol-binding protein) to gauge protein-energy nutritional status; these markers reflect liver protein synthesis and are affected by inflammation and hydration, so they may not directly reflect total body protein stores.

viscerosomatic reaction.definition: A reflex interaction in which visceral organ pathology or visceral afferent stimulation elicits somatic (musculoskeletal) responses—such as muscle tension, tenderness, or postural changes—via autonomic and spinal reflex pathways.

viscerosomatic.definition: Relating to the interaction between visceral organs and the somatic nervous system, especially where visceral pathology or stimuli produce reflexes or symptoms in somatic tissues (musculoskeletal or skin) via shared spinal-segment innervation.

visceromotor.definition: Relating to the motor control of the viscera; autonomic (visceral) efferent pathways that stimulate smooth muscle contraction and glandular secretion in internal organs.

viscerocranium.definition: The facial portion of the skull comprising the bones of the face (maxillae, zygomatic, nasal, lacrimal, palatine, inferior nasal conchae, vomer, and mandible) derived from the pharyngeal arches, forming the viscerocranium.

visceropleural.definition: Relating to the visceral pleura, the inner pleural membrane that covers the surface of the lungs (as opposed to the parietal pleura which lines the chest wall).

visceral reflex.definition: A reflex arc mediated by the autonomic (visceral) nervous system in which visceral sensory input triggers an automatic response in visceral effectors (smooth muscle or glands) via autonomic efferent pathways, typically without conscious awareness.

amsler grid.definition: A tool used to check for vision problems, particularly macular degeneration. The grid looks like graph paper with a dot in the center.

visual field defect.definition: A deficit or loss of part of the visual field in one or both eyes, due to disease of the retina, optic nerve, or brain’s visual pathways; may present as scotoma, hemianopia, quadrantanopia, or tunnel vision.

retinal detachments.definition: Retinal detachment is the separation of the retina from its underlying support tissues (the retinal pigment epithelium and choroid), allowing fluid to accumulate between them and causing loss of vision. It can be rhegmatogenous (from a retinal tear or hole letting fluid under the retina), tractional (from scar tissue pulling the retina away), or exudative (from inflammation or vascular leakage without a tear). Symptoms include sudden or progressive vision loss, new floaters, flashes of light, or a curtain-like shadow over part of the visual field. It is an ophthalmic emergency requiring prompt evaluation and treatment (e.g., laser photocoagulation or cryopexy to seal tears, scleral buckle, pars plana vitrectomy, or pneumatic retinopexy) to reattach the retina.

vascular occlusion.definition: Blockage or closing of a blood vessel that interrupts blood flow to the tissues it supplies, potentially causing ischemia or tissue damage. It can involve arteries or veins and may result from thrombosis, embolism, vasospasm, or external compression.

optic radiations.definition: Projection fibers of the visual pathway carrying information from the lateral geniculate nucleus to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe; subdivided into the superior (parietal) and inferior (Meyer’s) radiations, with lesions causing contralateral homonymous visual field defects.

visual pathway.definition: The neural route carrying visual information from the retina to the brain's primary visual cortex, via the optic nerve, optic chiasm, optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus, and optic radiations.

visual agnosia.definition: A failure to recognize or identify visually presented objects despite intact visual acuity and elementary vision, usually due to posterior cortical damage; individuals can see features but cannot interpret or name the objects.

visual-spatial agnosia.definition: An impairment of higher-order visual processing in which a person cannot accurately interpret the spatial relationships of objects in the visual field, despite normal basic vision; individuals have difficulty judging distances, depth, orientation, and organizing or copying spatial layouts, often due to damage to the parietal cortex.

eidetic image.definition: A vivid, detailed mental image of a visual scene that closely resembles the original view and persists briefly after the scene is no longer present; more common in children and not equivalent to a true photographic memory.

visual memory.definition: The ability to encode, store, and retrieve visual information—images, scenes, and visual details—within the memory system.

visual imagery.definition: The mental representation and manipulation of visual information in the absence of external visual input; the ability to "see" pictures or scenes in the mind, used in memory, planning, and cognitive tasks.

visualization.definition: The process of forming or obtaining a visual image of internal body structures, typically through imaging techniques (e.g., X-ray, CT, MRI, ultrasound, endoscopy) for diagnostic assessment or treatment planning.

visual accommodation.definition: Adjustment of the crystalline lens’ shape by ciliary muscle action to change the eye’s optical power, enabling focused vision of objects at different distances.

toxic confusional psychoses.definition: An acute delirium-like state produced by exposure to a toxin or poisoning, marked by sudden onset of confusion, inattention, disorientation, perceptual disturbances (often hallucinations), and fluctuating consciousness, typically reversible with removal of the toxin and treatment of the underlying cause.

focal brain diseases.definition: A neurological condition in which pathology is localized to a discrete region of the brain, causing focal neurological deficits or symptoms that map to the function of the affected area; typically due to focal lesions such as stroke, tumor, hemorrhage, abscess, trauma, or localized inflammation/demyelination.

visken.definition: A nonselective beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist (beta-blocker) with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity, used to treat hypertension and angina; it blocks both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors and has partial agonist activity.

pindolol.definition: A nonselective beta-adrenergic blocker with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (ISA) used to treat hypertension and angina; it has partial beta-agonist activity, which can reduce bradycardia risk but may provoke bronchospasm and mask signs of hypoglycemia.

vistaril.definition: A brand-name form of hydroxyzine (hydroxyzine pamoate), a sedating antihistamine used to treat anxiety and tension, relieve itching due to allergic conditions, and serve as a preoperative sedative.

hydroxyzine pamoate.definition: A salt form of hydroxyzine, an H1-blocking antihistamine with sedative, anxiolytic, antiemetic, and antipruritic properties; used to treat anxiety and tension, pruritus from allergic conditions, and to provide sedation or premedication in anesthesia.

beta blocker.definition: A class of medications that block beta-adrenergic receptors (primarily β1 in the heart and β2 in the airways), producing decreased heart rate, reduced myocardial contractility, slower AV conduction, and lower blood pressure; used to treat hypertension, angina, certain arrhythmias, and some forms of heart failure; common side effects include bradycardia, fatigue, and bronchospasm with nonselective agents.

viscosity.definition: A measure of a fluid's resistance to flow due to internal friction between its molecules; higher viscosity means the fluid is thicker and flows more slowly.

viscous.definition: Having a high resistance to flow; thick and sticky in consistency; a property of fluids characterized by high viscosity.

viscid.definition: Having a thick, sticky, adhesive consistency; viscous and slow to flow.

viscoelasticity.definition: A material property in which deformation under load has both viscous (time-dependent flow) and elastic (recoverable) components; the response depends on loading rate and duration, often exhibiting creep, stress relaxation, and hysteresis.

viscus.definition: An internal organ, especially one within a body cavity (the viscera), as distinguished from the walls of that cavity.

pernicious_anemia.definition: A form of anemia in which red blood cells enlarge and decrease in size due to an inability to properly absorb vitamin B12.

megaloblastic_anemia.definition: Fewer than normal healthy red blood cells in circulation, caused by a lack of folate or vitamin B12. Red cells become large and deformed, and are unable to carry oxygen efficiently.

liver_dysfunction.definition: An impairment of the liver's ability to perform its normal metabolic, synthetic, and detoxification functions, often due to acute or chronic liver injury or disease, leading to abnormal laboratory tests and clinical signs such as jaundice, coagulopathy, or encephalopathy.

zollinger_ellison_syndrome.definition: A condition caused by a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma), usually in the pancreas or duodenum, leading to excessive gastric acid production and refractory peptic ulcers, often with diarrhea and malabsorption; it may be associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1).

inflammatory_bowel_disease.definition: A chronic, relapsing inflammatory disorder of the gastrointestinal tract, comprising Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.

malabsorption_syndromes.definition: A group of disorders in which the small intestine absorbs nutrients inadequately due to mucosal damage or functional defects in digestion or transport, leading to chronic diarrhea or steatorrhea, weight loss, abdominal symptoms, and nutritional deficiencies (e.g., iron, calcium, vitamins A, D, E, K, and B12).

hemorrhagic_disease_of_the_newborn.definition: A neonatal bleeding disorder caused by deficiency of vitamin K, leading to impaired activation of vitamin K–dependent coagulation factors (II, VII, IX, X); occurs in early (within 24 hours), classical (days 1–7), or late (2–12 weeks) forms and is preventable by vitamin K prophylaxis at birth.

piebald.definition: Having patches of unpigmented (white) skin and hair interspersed with normally pigmented areas; in medical genetics, this pattern is seen in a rare congenital condition caused by abnormal melanocyte development, leading to depigmented patches often with a white forelock.

vitamin_a.definition: An essential fat-soluble vitamin (retinoids) required for normal vision, immune function, and epithelial cell growth and differentiation; deficiency can cause night blindness and xerophthalmia, while toxicity can occur with excessive intake.

betacarotene.definition: A red-orange pigment in plants that serves as a provitamin A carotenoid; the body converts it to vitamin A (retinol) as needed.

vitamin_a1.definition: A fat-soluble form of vitamin A present in animal tissues (retinol); essential for vision (rhodopsin function), immune competence, and maintenance of epithelial tissues; activity is expressed as retinol activity equivalents (RAE).

vitamin_a2.definition: 3,4-dehydroretinol, a fat-soluble form of vitamin A (vitamin A2) found mainly in freshwater fish; functions as a retinoid precursor to retinal and retinoic acid, supporting vision, growth, and epithelial and immune health; its metabolic conversion and tissue distribution differ from vitamin A1 and it is less common in humans.

vitamin_b1.definition: A water-soluble B vitamin (thiamine) that serves as a coenzyme for carbohydrate metabolism, crucial for energy production; deficiency causes beriberi and Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome.

vitamin_b2.definition: A water-soluble B vitamin that functions as a coenzyme in redox reactions (as FAD and FMN), essential for energy production from carbohydrates, fats, and proteins, and for the maintenance of skin, mucous membranes, and vision. Found in dairy products, eggs, meat, fortified cereals, and green vegetables; deficiency causes ariboflavinosis (angular stomatitis, glossitis, dermatitis).

vitamin_b6.definition: A water-soluble B vitamin (pyridoxine) that is converted to the active coenzyme pyridoxal phosphate and functions as a cofactor in numerous enzymatic reactions, especially amino acid metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis; also involved in heme biosynthesis and the conversion of tryptophan to niacin. Deficiency can cause sideroblastic anemia, glossitis, dermatitis, and peripheral neuropathy; excess intake can cause sensory neuropathy.

vitamin_b9.definition: Water-soluble vitamin (folate) essential for one-carbon metabolism and DNA synthesis; necessary for cell division and fetal neural tube development. Deficiency can cause megaloblastic anemia and neural tube defects; found in leafy greens and legumes; supplemental form is folic acid.

vitamin_b12.definition: An essential water-soluble vitamin (cobalamin) required for DNA synthesis and normal nervous system function; obtained mainly from animal-derived foods and stored in the liver. Deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and peripheral neuropathy and can result from pernicious anemia, malabsorption, gastric surgery, or inadequate intake.

folic_acid.definition: A water-soluble B vitamin (vitamin B9) essential for DNA synthesis and cell division; crucial for fetal neural tube development and prevention of neural tube defects; deficiency can cause megaloblastic anemia.

alpha_tocopherol.definition: The most biologically active form of vitamin E; a fat-soluble antioxidant that protects cell membranes from oxidative damage by scavenging free radicals.

phylloquinone.definition: A fat-soluble vitamin (vitamin K1) derived from leafy greens; acts as a cofactor for gamma-carboxylase, enabling gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues in coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X and in proteins C and S; essential for normal blood coagulation.

protopic.definition: A brand-name tacrolimus ointment (topical calcineurin inhibitor) used to treat atopic dermatitis (eczema) by suppressing T-cell activation and inflammatory cytokine production.

ultraviolet_radiation.definition: A form of electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths about 10–400 nanometers, shorter than visible light, emitted by the sun and some artificial sources. It is divided into UV-A, UV-B, and UV-C; exposure can cause DNA damage, sunburn, photoaging, and skin cancer. UV-C is largely absorbed by the atmosphere. Uses include sterilization and phototherapy.

stain.definition: A chemical dye or solution applied to tissues or cells to impart color, enabling visualization and differentiation of structures under microscopy; used in histology and microbiology (e.g., hematoxylin and eosin stain, Gram stain).

dye.definition: A colored substance used to stain tissues, cells, or specimens to enhance contrast for microscopic examination or diagnostic visualization.

blood_pressure.definition: The force of your blood pressing against the walls of your arteries. The high number (systolic pressure) measures when your heart beats and the low number (diastolic pressure) measures between beats.

vitamin_d.definition: A hormone that plays a key role in ensuring the absorption of calcium from the intestines.

vitamin_d2.definition: Ergocalciferol; a fat-soluble form of vitamin D derived from plant sources that, after hepatic and renal activation, increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption and supports bone mineralization; used to prevent or treat vitamin D deficiency.

vitamin_d3.definition: A fat-soluble vitamin produced in the skin from cholesterol after UVB exposure; it is converted in the liver to 25-hydroxyvitamin D and in the kidney to the active form calcitriol, which regulates calcium and phosphate homeostasis and promotes bone mineralization; deficiency causes rickets or osteomalacia, and excess can lead to hypercalcemia.

vitamin_c.definition: An important vitamin that helps the body grow and repair itself. It is found in many fruits and vegetables.

vitrectomy.definition: A microsurgical procedure in which part of the vitreous humor of the eye is removed and then replaced with sterile saline or some other fluid.

vogt-spielmeyer disease.definition: A juvenile-onset neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL), an inherited lysosomal storage disorder causing progressive neurodegeneration with seizures and vision loss; historically known as Batten disease.

vogt-koyanagi-harada syndrome.definition: A multisystem autoimmune inflammatory syndrome against melanocytes, presenting as bilateral granulomatous panuveitis with exudative retinal detachments, often accompanied by meningitis-like symptoms, tinnitus or hearing loss, and integumentary changes such as vitiligo, alopecia, and poliosis.

harada syndrome.definition: An autoimmune multisystem granulomatous uveitis presenting with bilateral exudative retinal detachments and choroidal thickening, often accompanied by meningitis‑like symptoms and integumentary changes (vitiligo, poliosis, alopecia); commonly described as Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease.

vitreous cavity.definition: The large, gel-filled space within the eyeball behind the lens and in front of the retina, containing the vitreous humor and helping maintain the globe’s shape and optical properties.

vitreous membrane.definition: A thin fibrocellular membrane enclosing the vitreous body of the eye; the vitreous cortex comprises an anterior hyaloid membrane (between the vitreous and the lens/ciliary body) and a posterior hyaloid membrane (facing the retina).

vitreous degeneration.definition: Age-related breakdown of the vitreous body of the eye, characterized by liquefaction (syneresis) of the gel and aggregation of collagen fibers, leading to floaters and potential posterior vitreous detachment with risk of retinal tears.

retinochoroidal detachment.definition: An ocular condition in which the retina and choroid detach from the sclera due to fluid accumulation in the suprachoroidal space, often secondary to hypotony, intraocular inflammation, or postoperative choroidal effusion.

uveomeningitis.definition: Inflammation of the uveal tract (uveitis) occurring together with inflammation of the meninges (meningitis); may reflect an infectious or inflammatory underlying process and typically requires evaluation for systemic etiologies.

neuronal ceroid-lipofuscinosis.definition: A group of inherited neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders characterized by accumulation of autofluorescent lipofuscin-like material in neurons and other cells, leading to progressive vision loss, seizures, cognitive decline, and motor deterioration, typically presenting in childhood or adolescence.

volkmann's paralysis.definition: Ischemia-induced fibrosis and contracture of the forearm muscles, typically following arterial injury or compression (often after a supracondylar fracture of the humerus), resulting in permanent flexion contractures of the fingers and wrist and impaired hand function.

volkmann's ischemic contracture.definition: A permanent flexion contracture of the forearm and hand caused by ischemic necrosis and fibrous replacement of the forearm flexor muscles after severe ischemia (often from compartment syndrome or arterial injury), resulting in a claw-like hand deformity and impaired hand function.

voluntary abortion.definition: An induced abortion performed at the request of the pregnant person, typically for nonmedical reasons; synonymous with elective abortion.

volitional tremor.definition: A tremor that occurs during voluntary, goal-directed movement and increases in amplitude as the limb approaches the target, typical of cerebellar dysfunction (also known as an intention tremor).

vivactil.definition: A brand-name tricyclic antidepressant (protriptyline) used to treat depressive illness; it blocks the reuptake of norepinephrine (and to a lesser extent serotonin) and has anticholinergic and sedative effects, with potential side effects such as dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention, tachycardia, dizziness, and drowsiness.

vivisection.definition: The practice of performing operations on living animals for experimental purposes to study biological processes, such as anatomy, physiology, or pathology, often to observe the effects of interventions.

voiding urethrography.definition: A radiographic study in which contrast material is introduced into the urinary tract and X-ray images are obtained during urination to visualize the urethra and assess for urethral injury, stricture, or other abnormalities (often part of voiding cystourethrography).

vocal apparatus.definition: Anatomical structures involved in voice production, including the larynx with the vocal folds that vibrate to generate phonation and the upper vocal tract (pharynx, oral and nasal cavities, and articulators) that modify the sound into speech.

true vocal cord.definition: One of the paired mucosal folds in the larynx that vibrate to produce phonation; formed by the vocal ligament and underlying vocalis muscle, covered by stratified squamous epithelium.

vocal ligament.definition: An elastic tissue band within the true vocal cord formed by the deep layer of the lamina propria (the vocal ligament), lying between the epithelium and the thyroarytenoid muscle; it provides elasticity and tensile strength for phonation.

vocal folds.definition: Two mucosal folds in the larynx (the true vocal cords) that vibrate as air passes through the glottis to produce phonation; composed of stratified squamous epithelium with a vocal ligament and underlying thyroarytenoid muscle, whose adduction and tension shape pitch and voice.

vocal fremitus.definition: Palpable vibration transmitted to the chest wall when the patient speaks, assessed during thoracic examination to evaluate lung tissue density; normally symmetric, with increased vibration in pulmonary consolidation (e.g., lobar pneumonia) and decreased vibration with pleural effusion or pneumothorax.

vocal cord dysfunction.definition: A condition in which the vocal cords adduct (close) during inspiration, causing transient upper airway obstruction with symptoms such as shortness of breath and wheezing; often misdiagnosed as asthma and diagnosed by laryngoscopy showing paradoxical vocal fold movement.

vocal cord nodule.definition: A small, benign, callus-like growth on the true vocal cords resulting from chronic voice misuse or overuse (phonotrauma); usually bilateral and located at the anterior/glottic region, causing hoarseness and roughness, with management typically by voice therapy and vocal hygiene; surgical removal is considered if therapy fails or the lesion persists.

screamer's nodule.definition: Not a standard medical term; if used, it likely refers to a vocal fold nodule (singer’s nodule): a small, benign, often bilateral callus on the anterior two-thirds of the vocal cords caused by chronic phonotrauma (e.g., loud shouting or screaming). It commonly presents with hoarseness and is usually managed with voice rest, hydration, and speech-language therapy, plus avoiding vocal strain to prevent recurrence.

teacher's nodule.definition: A benign, localized lump or thickening of soft tissue on the hand or fingers caused by chronic repetitive use or friction (e.g., extensive writing or gripping), resembling a callus rather than a distinct disease.

bronchophony.definition: An auscultatory finding in which spoken voice sounds are transmitted with greater clarity and loudness through the chest wall, typically over areas of lung consolidation (e.g., pneumonia).

bronchial obstruction.definition: Blockage of a bronchus or the bronchial airways resulting in reduced or absent airflow to a portion of the lung; can be due to mucus plugging, foreign body, tumor, edema, or inflammatory swelling, potentially causing atelectasis or hypoxemia.

volvulus neonatorum.definition: A twisting of the intestine in a neonate around its mesentery causing acute intestinal obstruction and risk of bowel ischemia, typically due to malrotation; presents with bilious vomiting and abdominal distension and requires urgent surgical management.

fecal vomiting.definition: Vomiting of feculent material (feces-like content) due to retrograde movement of intestinal contents, typically from distal small-bowel or colonic obstruction or from a gastrocolic fistula.

nonpassage of stools.definition: Inability to pass stool, typically due to constipation or bowel obstruction; obstipation is the severe form with no passage of stool or gas.

interarytenoid notch.definition: A small gap between the arytenoid cartilages at the posterior aspect of the larynx, forming part of the interarytenoid space and occupied by the interarytenoid muscles.

base of tongue.definition: Posterior third of the tongue, located in the oropharynx behind the sulcus terminalis; contains the lingual tonsils and is continuous with the anterior two-thirds, contributing to swallowing and taste sensation for the posterior tongue (innervation by glossopharyngeal nerve).

vomeronasal organ.definition: A chemosensory structure in the nasal cavity that detects pheromones and other chemical signals; in many species it transmits information to the accessory olfactory bulb and influences social and reproductive behaviors; in humans it is largely vestigial or nonfunctional.

vomiting agents.definition: Substances that induce vomiting by stimulating the emetic reflex, either via gastric irritation or activation of central emetic centers; historically used to treat poisoning but now used only under medical supervision due to risks such as aspiration.

adamsite.definition: A highly toxic organoarsenic vomiting agent used historically as a chemical warfare agent; inhalation or contact causes rapid irritation of the eyes, nose, throat, and lungs, with coughing, tearing, and severe vomiting leading to temporary incapacitation.

diphenylchlorarsine.definition: A highly toxic organoarsenic vesicant chemical warfare agent that irritates and damages the eyes, skin, and mucous membranes of the respiratory tract; historically used as a blistering agent in chemical warfare.

diphenylcyanoarsine.definition: A volatile organoarsenical chemical warfare/riot-control agent that irritates mucous membranes and can cause coughing, eye irritation, nausea, and vomiting after inhalation.

gastric reflux.definition: Backward flow of stomach contents into the esophagus due to lower esophageal sphincter dysfunction, often causing heartburn and regurgitation and potentially leading to esophagitis or gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

reflex emesis.definition: An involuntary vomiting reflex triggered by stimulation of the GI tract, vestibular system, or chemoreceptor trigger zone, coordinated by the vomiting center in the medulla with retching and abdominal contractions to expel gastric contents.

glycogen storage disease type ia.definition: A congenital autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by deficiency of hepatic glucose-6-phosphatase (G6PC), impairing glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and thus glucose production. It presents with severe fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia, and is commonly known as von Gierke disease; management centers on preventing hypoglycemia with frequent carbohydrate intake (e.g., uncooked cornstarch).

glucose-6-phosphatase.definition: A microsomal enzyme of the endoplasmic reticulum that hydrolyzes glucose-6-phosphate to glucose and inorganic phosphate, enabling glucose release into the bloodstream during gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis; deficiency causes von Gierke disease (glycogen storage disease type I).

glycogen metabolism.definition: The synthesis and breakdown of glycogen, the storage form of glucose, primarily in liver and skeletal muscle; includes glycogenesis (glycogen formation) and glycogenolysis (glycogen breakdown), regulated by hormones and energy status via enzymes such as glycogen synthase and glycogen phosphorylase.

hemangioblastomas.definition: A rare, usually benign, highly vascular tumor of the central nervous system, most often arising in the cerebellum and composed of numerous capillaries with a sparsely cellular, lipid-rich stromal component; can also occur in the retina or spinal cord, and is sometimes associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease. WHO grade I; best treated by surgical resection.

cerebellar hemispheres.definition: Two lateral parts of the cerebellum (left and right), separated by the midline vermis; they contain the lateral cerebellar cortex and white matter, including the dentate nucleus, and coordinate voluntary limb movements, motor planning, and motor learning with predominantly ipsilateral control.

spinal cord lesions.definition: Localized areas of damage or abnormal tissue within the spinal cord, resulting in neurological deficits (motor, sensory, and autonomic) below the level of the lesion; causes include trauma, ischemia, infection, demyelinating/inflammatory diseases, tumor, and compressive processes.

wagr syndrome.definition: A genetic syndrome caused by deletion of chromosome 11p13 encompassing WT1 and PAX6 genes, characterized by Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, and intellectual disability; often presents in early childhood with an elevated risk of Wilms tumor.

genitourinary abnormalities.definition: A broad term for disorders of the genital and urinary tracts, including congenital malformations and other abnormalities of the kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra, and external genitalia.

brachydactyly.definition: Congenital shortening of the fingers and toes caused by shortened phalanges (and sometimes metacarpals/metatarsals); can occur as an isolated finding or as part of various syndromes, often inherited (commonly autosomal dominant).

cardiac malformation.definition: A congenital abnormality of the heart's structure present at birth, including defects of the walls, valves, or great vessels, that can impair blood flow and heart function.

wagstaffe's fracture.definition: An avulsion fracture of the distal radius at the radial styloid, produced by traction from the brachioradialis tendon; a small bone fragment that can occur with distal radius injuries and is managed based on fragment size and joint stability (immobilization or surgical fixation).

organ transplant.definition: A surgical procedure in which a diseased or failing organ is removed and replaced with a healthy organ donated by another person, from a living or deceased donor.

waldeyer's throat ring.definition: A circular arrangement of lymphoid tissue in the pharyngeal mucosa (nasopharynx and oropharynx) comprising the pharyngeal (adenoids), tubal, palatine, and lingual tonsils, providing immune surveillance by sampling inhaled and ingested antigens and mounting immune responses.

palatine tonsils.definition: Paired lymphoid tissues in the oropharynx between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches; a component of Waldeyer's ring that samples antigens from the oropharynx and mounts local immune responses; can become enlarged or inflamed in tonsillitis.

lingual tonsils.definition: Aggregates of lymphoid tissue located at the posterior third of the tongue (the base), forming part of Waldeyer's ring and participating in immune defense against oral antigens.

tonsillar ring.definition: A ring of lymphoid tissue in the pharynx (Waldeyer's ring) formed by the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids), palatine tonsils, lingual tonsils, and tubal tonsils, providing immune surveillance of inhaled or ingested antigens.

lymphoid ring.definition: A ring-shaped collection of lymphoid tissue in the pharynx that surrounds the openings of the oral and nasal cavities; known as Waldeyer’s ring, it consists of the pharyngeal (adenoids), palatine, and lingual tonsils and serves as a first line of immune defense by sampling inhaled and ingested antigens.

varicella-zoster virus.definition: The bug (virus) that causes chicken pox.

varicella-zoster immune globulin.definition: A preparation of human antibodies against varicella-zoster virus used as passive postexposure prophylaxis to prevent varicella infection or reduce its severity after exposure, especially in susceptible newborns, pregnant women, and immunocompromised individuals; given intramuscularly within about 10 days of exposure.

vzig.definition: An immunoglobulin preparation containing antibodies against varicella-zoster virus administered after exposure to varicella to prevent infection or lessen disease in susceptible, high-risk individuals (e.g., pregnant women, newborns, or immunocompromised patients); given within about 96 hours of exposure.

von willebrand factor.definition: A large multimeric glycoprotein produced by endothelial cells and megakaryocytes that mediates platelet adhesion to damaged endothelium by binding to exposed collagen and platelet glycoprotein Ib, and that also stabilizes circulating factor VIII.

vascular permeability factor.definition: A signal protein that stimulates angiogenesis (growth of new blood vessels) and increases capillary permeability; produced by many cells in response to hypoxia or inflammation, best known as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF).

vra.definition: A behavioral hearing test for infants and young children in which a head-turn toward a sound is reinforced by a visual reward (e.g., lights or toys), used to estimate auditory thresholds typically from about 6 months to 2–3 years.

visual response audiometry.definition: A behavioral hearing test for infants and young children in which the child is conditioned to look toward a sound source; a visual reward (e.g., a lighted toy or video) is presented when the response occurs to reinforce it, allowing estimation of hearing thresholds across frequencies. Also known as visual reinforcement audiometry.

retinal dysplasia.definition: A congenital developmental anomaly of the retina characterized by disorganized retinal lamination with rosettes and folds, often leading to reduced visual function and an increased risk of retinal detachment.

agyria.definition: Absence of the normal gyri (convolutions) of the cerebral cortex, resulting in a smooth brain surface; a severe form of lissencephaly often associated with developmental delay and seizures.

waldeyer's ring.definition: A circular arrangement of lymphoid tissue in the pharynx that protects the entry to the upper respiratory and digestive tracts by trapping pathogens and initiating immune responses; it includes the pharyngeal (adenoids), palatine, and lingual tonsils (and sometimes the tubal tonsils).
