simple vulvectomy.definition: A surgical procedure to remove the vulva (external female genitalia), typically for vulvar cancer or precancerous lesions, usually without removal of nearby organs or inguinal lymph nodes (more extensive disease may be treated with radical vulvectomy).

vulvar dystrophy.definition: An umbrella term describing degenerative or dystrophic changes of vulvar skin or mucosa, typically arising from chronic dermatoses (e.g., lichen sclerosus or lichen planus) and presenting with thinning or thickening of tissue, discoloration, itching, pain, and potential scarring; not a single discrete diagnosis.

vulvodynia.definition: Pain in the vulva that may or may not be brought on by touch or pressure.

candida vaginitis.definition: An infection of the vagina caused by Candida species (most commonly Candida albicans), presenting with vulvovaginal itching and irritation and a thick, white discharge; diagnosed clinically or by microscopy/culture and treated with antifungal therapy (e.g., topical azoles or a single-dose oral fluconazole).

encephalocele.definition: A neural tube defect in which brain tissue and meninges herniate through a defect in the skull, forming a sac-like protrusion, most often in the occipital region; may be associated with hydrocephalus and neurodevelopmental impairment.

hard syndrome.definition: No widely recognized medical syndrome by that name; it may be a misspelling or misnomer for another condition. If you have context (symptoms, affected system, or related terms), I can help identify the likely diagnosis.

walker lissencephaly.definition: Severe congenital brain malformation with lissencephaly (smooth brain), typically seen in Walker-Warburg syndrome—a fatal congenital muscular dystrophy with brain and eye abnormalities.

walker warburg syndrome.definition: A severe congenital muscular dystrophy (dystroglycanopathy) marked by brain malformations (most often type II lissencephaly/cobblestone cortex with cerebellar hypoplasia), ocular abnormalities, and profound neonatal hypotonia, typically fatal in infancy.

warburg syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal recessive congenital neuro-ophthalmic disorder characterized by severe ocular anomalies (e.g., microphthalmia or anophthalmia with optic nerve/retinal abnormalities), brain malformations (notably microcephaly and pontocerebellar hypoplasia), developmental delay, and growth retardation; commonly due to biallelic mutations in Rab-related genes such as RAB3GAP1 or RAB3GAP2.

wandering atrial pacemaker.definition: An irregular atrial rhythm caused by the pacemaker site shifting among atrial foci (often including the SA node), producing at least three different P‑wave morphologies with varying PR intervals and a heart rate typically <100 bpm.

atrial pacemaker.definition: A device implanted to deliver electrical impulses to the atrial myocardium to initiate atrial contraction, used to treat bradycardia from sinoatrial node dysfunction or other conduction disorders; may be a standalone atrial pacemaker or the atrial component of a dual-chamber pacemaker.

geographic tongue.definition: A benign migratory condition of the tongue characterized by irregular, map-like red patches with white or pale borders that change location over time due to depapillation of the filiform papillae; usually asymptomatic or with mild burning, and typically requires no treatment unless symptomatic.

wandering rash.definition: A rash that changes location on the skin over time, with lesions appearing in new areas as others fade; commonly described in urticaria (hives) and other inflammatory skin conditions, and is a descriptor rather than a specific diagnosis.

wandering spleen.definition: A rare condition in which the spleen is abnormally mobile due to congenital or acquired laxity or absence of its supporting ligaments, allowing it to migrate from the left upper quadrant to other parts of the abdomen or pelvis. It can lead to torsion of the splenic pedicle with infarction and acute abdomen; management ranges from splenopexy to preserve the spleen to splenectomy if there is infarction or nonviable tissue.

wallenberg syndrome.definition: A lateral medullary infarct, usually from occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery, producing vertigo and nystagmus, ipsilateral facial loss of pain and temperature, contralateral body loss of pain and temperature, ipsilateral dysphagia and hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus), ataxia, and often Horner syndrome.

wallerian degeneration.definition: Degeneration of the portion of a damaged axon distal to the injury site, with breakdown of the axon and its myelin followed by clearance; in the peripheral nervous system, regrowth may occur along Schwann cell–guided pathways, while regeneration in the central nervous system is limited.

horner's syndrome.definition: A disorder caused by disruption of the sympathetic pathways to the eye and face, resulting in ipsilateral ptosis (drooping eyelid), miosis (pupil constriction), and facial anhidrosis; may include apparent enophthalmos and arises from lesions along the oculosympathetic pathway (central, preganglionic, or postganglionic).

watershed infarct.definition: A cerebral infarct at the border zones between major cerebral artery territories (eg, between MCA-ACA or MCA-PCA), typically due to systemic hypoperfusion; affects cortical and subcortical (white matter) watershed regions.

adrenal hemorrhage.definition: Bleeding into one or both adrenal glands, often due to trauma, sepsis with coagulopathy, anticoagulation, or perioperative stress; it can cause adrenal insufficiency if extensive.

syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic h.word: syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic h.definition: A condition in which excess antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) activity causes excess free water reabsorption in the kidneys, producing dilutional hyponatremia with low serum osmolality and inappropriately concentrated urine, typically with euvolemia and normal renal, adrenal, and thyroid function.

complement fixation reaction.definition: A serologic assay in which antigen–antibody complexes fix (consume) complement; if specific antibody is present, the complement is used up and the indicator system shows no hemolysis (positive result), whereas absence of antibody allows hemolysis (negative result).

complement fixation.definition: An immunologic reaction in which antigen–antibody complexes fix complement, rendering it unavailable to lyse target cells; used in serologic testing to detect the presence of specific antibodies.

waters method.definition: A radiographic projection of the skull used to visualize the paranasal sinuses, particularly the maxillary sinuses, by positioning the head to obtain an unobstructed view of the sinuses; commonly used to evaluate sinusitis and facial trauma.

water-soluble contrast medium.definition: An iodinated contrast agent that dissolves in water and is used to enhance radiographic imaging of hollow organs and spaces; it is excreted by the kidneys and is generally less irritating than oil-based contrast if leakage occurs, but can cause osmotic effects and renal toxicity in susceptible individuals.

wedge pressure.definition: A measurement of left atrial pressure obtained by inflating a balloon on a pulmonary artery catheter and wedging it in a distal branch; the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) approximates left atrial pressure and left-sided filling pressures. Normal is about 6–12 mmHg.

wedge resection.definition: A surgical procedure in which a wedge-shaped segment of tissue is removed, usually to excise a localized lesion while preserving as much surrounding tissue as possible (e.g., a peripheral lung nodule in pulmonary wedge resection).

granulomatosis vasculitis.definition: A form of systemic vasculitis characterized by necrotizing granulomatous inflammation of the upper and lower airways and necrotizing vasculitis of small- to medium-sized vessels, often associated with PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA); commonly involves the sinonasal tract, lungs, and kidneys.

saddle-nose deformity.definition: A deformity in which the nasal dorsum collapses or is flattened, producing a saddle-shaped profile due to loss or destruction of nasal septal cartilage (often from trauma, inflammatory diseases such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis, or infections).

chest discomfort.definition: Chest discomfort is a subjective sensation of pain, pressure, tightness, or fullness in the chest region, which may result from cardiac causes (e.g., angina, myocardial infarction), noncardiac causes (e.g., gastroesophageal reflux disease, esophageal spasm, musculoskeletal strain), or pulmonary conditions; urgent evaluation is warranted if the discomfort is sudden or severe or accompanied by symptoms such as shortness of breath, sweating, fainting, or radiation to the arm, jaw, or back.

renal involvement.definition: Renal involvement refers to the involvement or impact of a disease process on the kidneys, evidenced by impaired kidney function (e.g., reduced GFR or elevated creatinine), urinalysis abnormalities (proteinuria or hematuria), hypertension, or histologic kidney damage due to the systemic condition.

webbed neck.definition: A congenital condition in which the skin on the neck forms web-like folds from the shoulders to the nape, producing a broad, short neck; commonly associated with Turner syndrome and Noonan syndrome.

webbed penis.definition: A congenital anomaly in which skin from the scrotum extends onto the penile shaft, forming a web-like band between the penis and scrotum.

webbed toes.definition: A congenital condition in which two or more toes are fused together by skin and soft tissue, sometimes extending to the bones; it can be partial (skin only) or complete (bone involvement) and may occur in isolation or with other anomalies.

weigert-meyer rule.definition: In a duplicated renal collecting system, the ureter from the upper pole inserts into the bladder more medially and inferiorly (often ectopic or obstructed), while the lower-pole ureter inserts more laterally and superiorly (more commonly associated with vesicoureteral reflux).

weigert-meyer law.definition: In complete renal duplication, the ureter draining the upper renal pole inserts into the bladder inferomedially (often with a ureterocele and obstruction), while the lower-pole ureter inserts superolaterally and is more prone to vesicoureteral reflux.

double ureter.definition: A congenital anomaly in which a kidney has two ureters draining it; it can be complete, with two separate ureters draining separately into the bladder, or partial, with duplication of the proximal ureter forming a duplex collecting system that may merge before entering the bladder.

ischial bursae.definition: Ischial bursae are synovial-fluid–filled sacs located over the ischial tuberosities that cushion and facilitate gliding between the ischial tuberosities and the overlying gluteal muscles (primarily the gluteus maximus) and proximal hamstring tendons; inflammation can cause ischial bursitis, often from prolonged sitting.

weaver's bottom.definition: Inflammation of the ischial bursa (ischial bursitis) caused by repetitive pressure or friction from prolonged sitting, historically seen in weavers; presents as localized buttock pain and tenderness over the ischial tuberosity, worsened by sitting and relieved by standing. Treatment includes rest, padding, NSAIDs, and corticosteroid injection if needed.

weber's tuning fork test.definition: A bedside screening test for unilateral hearing loss in which a vibrating tuning fork is placed on the midline of the forehead; sound lateralizes to the affected ear in conductive loss, to the unaffected ear in sensorineural loss, and is heard equally with normal hearing.

weber's sign.definition: I can’t find a standard definition for “Weber's sign” in trusted medical references. Please share the context (spelling, specialty, or where you saw it). If you meant a different term (e.g., Weber’s test), I can provide that definition.

weber syndrome.definition: A ventral midbrain infarct involving the cerebral peduncle causing ipsilateral oculomotor nerve palsy with contralateral hemiparesis; typically due to occlusion of perforating branches of the posterior cerebral artery (also known as superior alternating hemiplegia).

wet bulb thermometer.definition: An instrument in which the thermometer's bulb is covered with a wick kept moist; evaporation cools the bulb, and the difference between its reading and a dry-bulb thermometer's reading is used (in a psychrometer) to determine relative humidity and dew point.

marchesani's syndrome.definition: A rare hereditary connective tissue disorder characterized by ocular lens abnormalities (microspherophakia with potential lens subluxation causing myopia and risk of secondary glaucoma) and systemic features such as short stature, brachydactyly, and joint stiffness.

nasal discharge.definition: Mucus produced by the nasal mucosa that drains from the nose; it can be clear and watery or thick and discolored, and may result from viral or bacterial infection, allergic rhinitis, irritants, or sinus disease.

welt.definition: A raised, itchy patch on the skin caused by superficial dermal edema, commonly arising from an allergic reaction or insect bite; often described as a wheal or hive.

wet dressing.definition: A dressing that is moistened with saline or another suitable solution and placed over a wound to maintain a moist environment, promote healing, and facilitate debridement; when used as a wet-to-dry dressing, it is kept wet during application and allowed to dry, then removed to pull away debris.

eosinophilic cellulitis.definition: A rare inflammatory skin condition, also known as Wells syndrome, characterized by sudden onset of pruritic, edematous, erythematous plaques that may resemble urticaria; histology shows an eosinophil-rich dermal infiltrate with flame figures; lesions typically resolve over weeks to months but may relapse, and treatment often involves corticosteroids or other anti-inflammatory agents.

wenckebach heart block.definition: Progressive prolongation of the PR interval with each beat until a beat is dropped (a nonconducted P wave with no QRS), after which the cycle repeats; an AV nodal second-degree block that is often benign and may be related to high vagal tone or certain drugs.

progressive spinal muscular atrophy.definition: A genetically inherited neurodegenerative disorder caused by loss of anterior horn motor neurons in the spinal cord and brainstem, leading to progressive symmetric proximal muscle weakness and atrophy, fasciculations, and respiratory insufficiency; most commonly due to biallelic deletions of the SMN1 gene with disease severity modified by SMN2 copy number; inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.

infantile spinal muscular atrophy.definition: A severe form of spinal muscular atrophy that begins in infancy (Werdnig–Hoffmann disease) caused by degeneration of anterior horn cells in the spinal cord, presenting with flaccid hypotonia and progressive paralysis with respiratory failure; typically autosomal recessive and often fatal in early childhood.

familial spinal muscular atrophy.definition: A hereditary neuromuscular disorder caused by degeneration of motor neurons in the spinal cord (and brainstem), leading to progressive proximal muscle weakness and atrophy; most forms are autosomal recessive due to SMN1 gene mutations, with severity influenced by SMN2 copy number.

hoffmann’s atrophy.definition: Definition not found in standard medical dictionaries. Could you provide alternate spelling or context (neurology, pediatric, etc.) so I can help clarify?

floppy infant syndrome.definition: A newborn or young infant with marked generalized hypotonia (decreased muscle tone) and poor resistance to movement, often with weak suck and poor head control; it reflects a broad range of potential underlying causes, including neuromuscular, central nervous system, metabolic, infectious, or genetic disorders.

werlhof’s disease.definition: A historical name for idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (immune thrombocytopenia), an autoimmune disorder characterized by isolated thrombocytopenia and mucocutaneous bleeding due to autoantibody-mediated destruction of platelets.

werner’s syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal recessive premature-aging syndrome caused by WRN gene mutations encoding a RecQ helicase; onset in young adulthood with cataracts, alopecia and hair graying, skin atrophy, short stature, diabetes mellitus, osteoporosis, and increased cancer and atherosclerotic disease risk, leading to shortened life expectancy.

wernicke’s encephalopathy.definition: An acute neurologic emergency caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, most often in individuals with alcohol use disorder or malnutrition. It presents with acute confusion, ocular motor abnormalities (e.g., ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus), and gait ataxia; urgent thiamine replacement is essential to prevent progression to Korsakoff syndrome.

korsakoff’s syndrome.definition: A chronic memory disorder caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, usually from long-term alcohol use, characterized by severe anterograde amnesia with confabulation and disorientation (often with retrograde memory loss), due to damage to the mammillary bodies and thalamus; memory impairment may persist despite thiamine treatment.

wernicke’s aphasia.definition: A fluent receptive (Wernicke’s) aphasia due to damage to Wernicke’s area in the dominant hemisphere; speech is fluent but often meaningless or paraphasic, with severely impaired comprehension and repetition, and patients are typically unaware of their deficits.

broca’s aphasia.definition: Nonfluent expressive aphasia due to damage to Broca’s area in the dominant frontal lobe (inferior frontal gyrus). Speech is slow, halting, and telegraphic; comprehension is relatively preserved; repetition is impaired; writing is often reduced; may be accompanied by apraxia of speech.

wernicke’s center.definition: A region of the dominant left temporal lobe, typically the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus, essential for language comprehension; damage results in fluent but nonsensical speech with poor understanding (receptive aphasia).

sensory speech center.definition: A region of the dominant hemisphere's temporal lobe (posterior superior temporal gyrus) involved in understanding spoken language; damage causes receptive (sensory) aphasia with fluent but often nonsensical speech and impaired comprehension.

wernicke’s field.definition: A cortical region in the dominant (usually left) hemisphere responsible for language comprehension, located in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus.

wernicke’s zone.definition: A language-processing region in the dominant hemisphere, located in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus and adjacent temporoparietal cortex; essential for comprehension of spoken language. Damage causes fluent but nonsensical speech and poor comprehension (Wernicke's aphasia).

wernicke syndrome.definition: An acute neuropsychiatric emergency caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, most often in malnourished or alcohol-dependent individuals, characterized by ophthalmoplegia/eye movement abnormalities, ataxia, and confusion; urgent thiamine replacement is essential to prevent progression to Korsakoff syndrome or coma.

west nile encephalitis.definition: An inflammatory brain infection caused by West Nile virus transmitted by mosquitoes, ranging from fever and headache to severe encephalitis with confusion, seizures, and focal neurologic deficits; diagnosed by West Nile virus–specific antibodies (IgM) or RNA in CSF/serum and treated with supportive care; prevention focuses on mosquito bite avoidance.

west nile fever.definition: An infection caused by West Nile virus transmitted by mosquitoes; most infections are asymptomatic. When symptoms occur, the illness typically includes fever, headache, malaise, and myalgias (often with a rash), and rare cases involve neuroinvasive disease such as meningitis or encephalitis; management is supportive and there is no specific antiviral therapy or widely available human vaccine. Prevention focuses on reducing mosquito exposure.

west nile virus.definition: A disease that you can get from a mosquito bite that can be very mild or very serious (if it affects your brain).

west nile virus testing.definition: Laboratory assays used to diagnose West Nile virus infection, typically by detecting virus-specific IgM antibodies in serum or cerebrospinal fluid (often with confirmatory neutralization testing), and by detecting viral RNA with RT-PCR during acute illness; may also include virus isolation or serologic confirmation.

If you share the medical specialty or a more precise spelling, I can give a precise definition.

west’s syndrome.definition: An early-life epileptic encephalopathy characterized by clusters of infantile spasms, a chaotic hypsarrhythmia EEG pattern, and developmental regression or psychomotor delay, often associated with an underlying brain disorder.

chronic alcoholism.definition: A long-standing pattern of excessive alcohol consumption leading to physical dependence, withdrawal symptoms, tolerance, and adverse health and social consequences; commonly equated with alcohol use disorder or alcohol dependence.

widal’s test.definition: A serologic test for typhoid fever that detects antibodies against Salmonella typhi—specifically the O (somatic) and H (flagellar) antigens—in a patient’s serum; agglutination indicates antibody presence, and rising titers in paired sera suggest acute infection. The test has limited sensitivity and specificity and can yield false positives after vaccination or with other Salmonella infections.

agglutination test.definition: A serologic assay in which antigen-coated particles (e.g., latex beads or red blood cells) clump together (agglutinate) in the presence of a specific antibody, or vice versa, indicating a positive result for that antigen or antibody; used to detect or quantify pathogens, antibodies, or blood group antigens.

sympathetic ganglia.definition: Ganglia of the sympathetic nervous system located along the sympathetic trunk (paravertebral ganglia); they contain postganglionic neuron cell bodies that receive preganglionic fibers and project to various organs to mediate sympathetic (fight-or-flight) responses.

pancreaticojejunostomy.definition: A surgical anastomosis between the pancreatic remnant (or pancreatic duct) and the jejunum that allows pancreatic secretions to drain into the small intestine.

whipple’s disease.definition: An uncommon chronic systemic infection caused by the bacterium Tropheryma whipplei, presenting with malabsorption and weight loss often with diarrhea and may include arthralgias, fever, and CNS or cardiac involvement; diagnosed by PAS-positive macrophages in intestinal mucosa and PCR for T. whipplei; treated with prolonged antibiotic therapy (commonly IV ceftriaxone followed by oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole).

whistling face syndrome.definition: A rare congenital muscular disorder characterized by a distinctive whistled lip appearance and microstomia, accompanied by multiple distal limb contractures (distal arthrogryposis); often caused by MYH3 gene mutations with autosomal dominant inheritance.

whitaker test.definition: An invasive urology pressure‑flow test that measures intrapelvic pressure while saline is infused into the renal pelvis to distinguish obstructive from nonobstructive hydronephrosis; a steep rise in pressure with infusion indicates obstruction, while a flat pressure–volume curve suggests no obstruction.

wbc.definition: A nucleated blood cell of the immune system that circulates in blood and tissues, defending the body against infection through phagocytosis, antibody production, and other immune responses; normal circulating counts are roughly 4,000–11,000 per microliter.

leukocyte cast.definition: A cylindrical renal tubule cast composed of white blood cells embedded in a proteinaceous matrix, indicating renal tubular inflammation or infection such as acute interstitial nephritis or pyelonephritis.

white blood cell cast.definition: A urinary cast composed of white blood cells that forms in the renal tubules, indicating renal parenchymal inflammation or infection (e.g., acute pyelonephritis or tubulointerstitial nephritis).

white corpuscle.definition: A white blood cell (leukocyte), a blood cell of the immune system that defends the body against infection; produced in the bone marrow and circulating in blood and lymphatic tissues; includes granulocytes, lymphocytes, and monocytes.

white gold.definition: An alloy of gold mixed with white metals such as palladium, nickel, or silver to produce a white or pale-gray color; commonly used in jewelry and often rhodium-plated to enhance brightness.

whitehead.definition: A closed comedo (non-inflammatory acne lesion) caused by blockage of a hair follicle by sebum and keratin, with the opening closed, producing a small white or flesh-colored bump on the skin.

white thrombus.definition: A platelet-rich thrombus that forms at sites of high shear or arterial injury; composed mainly of platelets (and von Willebrand factor) with relatively little fibrin, giving a pale or white appearance and often causing arterial occlusion.

white willow bark.definition: A natural product from the bark of Salix alba (white willow) containing salicin, a glycoside that is metabolized to salicylic acid and provides analgesic, antipyretic, and anti-inflammatory effects; historically used for pain and fever, with potential adverse effects including GI irritation and bleeding risk. Avoid in children with viral illnesses due to risk of Reye syndrome.

salicin.definition: A glycoside found in willow bark that is hydrolyzed to salicyl alcohol and glucose; it is metabolized to salicylic acid, the active anti-inflammatory and analgesic metabolite.

whitepox.definition: Not a standard medical term in reputable references; there is no established clinical definition. If encountered, it may be used informally to describe a poxvirus-related skin infection with whitish lesions or crusts, but this usage is not validated and context is needed.

bremsstrahlung radiation.definition: Electromagnetic radiation produced when a high-energy charged particle, typically an electron, is decelerated or deflected by the electric field of atomic nuclei, causing emission of photons; also called braking radiation; a primary source of X-rays in radiography and high-energy physics interactions.

white ramus communicans.definition: Myelinated preganglionic sympathetic fibers that exit the spinal nerve via the ventral root and white ramus to the sympathetic trunk (paravertebral ganglia) to synapse on postganglionic neurons; part of the thoracolumbar outflow (T1–L2).

lichen sclerosus et atrophicus.definition: Chronic inflammatory dermatosis characterized by thinning and whitening of the skin with sclerotic, porcelain-white plaques, most often in the genital and perianal area; causes pruritus, pain, fissuring, and possible scarring; more common in prepubertal girls and postmenopausal women; histology shows epidermal atrophy with dermal sclerosis and a lichenoid inflammatory infiltrate.

white substance.definition: In anatomy, white substance (often called white matter) refers to the myelinated nerve fibers of the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord). It appears white due to the myelin sheath and enables rapid transmission of neural signals between gray-matter regions and between the brain and spinal cord.

antegrade pyelography.definition: Radiographic imaging in which contrast material is injected directly into the renal collecting system (renal pelvis) in an antegrade direction, typically via percutaneous nephrostomy or renal puncture, to visualize the ureter and kidney for assessment of obstruction or injury.

mammillary bodies.definition: Two small paired nuclei on the posterior hypothalamus, part of the limbic system; they receive input from the hippocampus via the fornix and project to the anterior thalamic nuclei via the mammillothalamic tract, contributing to memory formation and recollection.

aqueducts.definition: A narrow canal or passage within an organ; in neuroanatomy, the slender channel in the midbrain that connects the third and fourth ventricles, enabling cerebrospinal fluid to flow between them.

hodgkin’s lymphoma.definition: A type of cancer that grows in a part of your immune system (your lymph nodes). Also called Hodgkin's disease.

b-cell neoplasms.definition: Malignant proliferations of B-lymphocytes or their precursors, arising at various stages of B-cell differentiation. They include mature B-cell lymphomas (eg, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, follicular lymphoma, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma) and precursor B-cell neoplasms (eg, B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma); they are defined by clonal B-cell expansion and expression of B-cell–associated markers such as CD19 and CD20, with prognosis and treatment varying by subtype.

t-cell neoplasms.definition: Malignant neoplasms arising from T lymphocytes (T cells), including T-cell leukemias and T-cell lymphomas, characterized by clonal proliferation of neoplastic T cells in blood, bone marrow, lymphoid tissues, and often extranodal sites, with expression of T‑cell markers.

world health organization.definition: A specialized agency of the United Nations dedicated to international public health, coordinating global health policy, disease surveillance, and emergency response.

real classification.definition: Not a standard medical term; if encountered, it could refer to a classification system that groups diseases or patient states using observed, real-world clinical data and criteria rather than theoretical assumptions or surrogate markers.

lymphoid neoplasms.definition: Malignant clonal proliferations of lymphoid cells arising from B-, T-, or NK-cell lineages, encompassing lymphomas (including Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin) and lymphoid leukemias, typically involving lymphoid tissues and/or peripheral blood.

windpipe.definition: A tube that extends from the larynx to the bronchi, conducting air to the lungs; supported by C-shaped cartilage rings and lined with ciliated epithelium.

agglutinins.definition: A substance, typically an antibody, that causes agglutination by cross-linking antigens on the surface of cells or particles, resulting in visible clumping; most agglutinins are IgM antibodies against red blood cell antigens (e.g., ABO/Rh), though IgG and other agents can also act as agglutinins.

excretory urogram.definition: A radiographic study of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder obtained after intravenous administration of radiocontrast, used to assess anatomy and excretory function of the urinary tract.

wilsons disease.definition: An autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, leading to impaired biliary copper excretion and accumulation of copper in the liver, brain, and other tissues.

winckel disease.definition: I can’t find a standard medical definition for “Winckel disease.” Could you confirm the spelling or provide context (organ system, symptoms, or who described it)? If you meant a similar term like Winkelmann disease, Winkler disease, or Wernicke’s disease/encephalopathy, I can define that precisely.

neural deafness.definition: A form of hearing loss due to damage or dysfunction of the neural components of hearing—typically the auditory nerve (cranial nerve VIII) or central auditory pathways—resulting in impaired perception of sound despite normal outer and middle ear function.

wood's lamp.definition: A handheld ultraviolet light used in dermatology to illuminate skin under UV-A, causing certain substances to fluoresce and aiding in diagnosing fungal infections (e.g., tinea versicolor) and pigmentary disorders.

atrioventricular conduction.definition: The propagation of electrical impulses from the atrioventricular (AV) node to the ventricles via the AV bundle (His bundle) and Purkinje fibers, coordinating ventricular depolarization and contraction.

radiofrequency ablation.definition: A minimally invasive procedure that uses heat generated by radiofrequency energy delivered through a needle or catheter to destroy targeted tissue by coagulative necrosis.

wolffian body.definition: A transient embryonic kidney (the mesonephros) in vertebrate development, consisting of mesonephric tubules that drain into the Wolffian (mesonephric) ducts; it functions as the interim kidney and, in males, contributes to the development of parts of the male reproductive tract.

wolff-chaikoff effect.definition: A temporary inhibition of thyroid hormone synthesis caused by a large excess of iodide, due to inhibition of thyroid peroxidase activity and organification of iodine; normal hormone synthesis often resumes after a few days despite continued iodide exposure (the escape phenomenon).

receptive aphasia.definition: A language disorder in which spoken language is fluent but comprehension is severely impaired, with frequent paraphasias and nonsensical speech; usually due to damage to Wernicke's area (posterior superior temporal gyrus) in the dominant hemisphere.

withdrawal syndrome.definition: A set of physical and psychological symptoms that occur after abrupt reduction or cessation of a substance to which the person has developed dependence, reflecting withdrawal from that substance; common features include autonomic signs (sweating, tachycardia), tremor, anxiety, agitation, nausea/vomiting, insomnia, and headache.

withdrawal bleeding.definition: Vaginal bleeding that occurs after the withdrawal of exogenous hormones (most often when stopping combined estrogen–progestin contraception or progestin therapy), representing shedding of the endometrium due to loss of hormonal support.

coitus interruptus.definition: A method of contraception in which the penis is withdrawn from the vagina before ejaculation to prevent semen from entering the vagina. It has a high typical-use failure rate due to timing errors and the presence of sperm in pre-ejaculate, and it provides no protection against sexually transmitted infections.

stanozolol.definition: A synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid derived from dihydrotestosterone; 17α-alkylated to allow oral administration, used medically for certain conditions such as hereditary angioedema but commonly encountered as a performance-enhancing drug, with risks including liver toxicity and androgenic side effects.

winstrol.definition: A synthetic anabolic steroid derived from dihydrotestosterone; a 17α-alkylated compound used medically for certain conditions such as hereditary angioedema and, outside approved indications, as a performance-enhancing drug; associated with liver toxicity, adverse lipid changes, and virilizing effects.

parietal-occipital.definition: Relating to the boundary region between the parietal and occipital lobes of the brain.

healing.definition: A physiological process by which damaged tissue is repaired and function is restored, typically involving inflammation, tissue proliferation, and remodeling; may involve regeneration of native tissue or scar formation.

primary intention.definition: Healing of a clean wound in which the edges are approximated and closed (primary closure), leading to rapid healing with minimal granulation tissue and scar formation.

compressed air.definition: Air that has been pressurized above atmospheric pressure by a compressor, used to power pneumatic medical devices and equipment.

regulator.definition: A molecule, protein, or gene product that modulates the activity of genes, proteins, or signaling pathways to regulate a biological process. In genetics, a regulator influences the expression of other genes.

work of breathing.definition: The energy expended by the respiratory muscles to move air in and out of the lungs, determined by airway resistance and the elastic properties (compliance) of the lungs and chest wall.

oxygen consumption.definition: Rate at which the body's tissues consume oxygen per unit time (typically measured as VO2, in milliliters of O2 per minute); reflects metabolic demand and the balance between oxygen delivery and utilization.

acute illness.definition: An illness characterized by abrupt onset and relatively short duration, with symptoms that are often severe and progress rapidly, typically resolving within days to weeks.

ergonomics.definition: The scientific study and application of designing workplaces, tools, and tasks to fit human physical and cognitive capabilities, with the aim of reducing injury and improving safety, comfort, and productivity.

occupational therapy.definition: The kind of treatment that helps you relearn everyday activities.

wound clip.definition: A small surgical device, usually stainless steel, applied across a wound to approximate and hold the edges together for healing; commonly called a skin clip and typically removed after the incision has healed.

skin staple.definition: A small metal fastener used to close a skin wound or surgical incision by approximating the edges; applied with a stapling device and later removed, typically made of stainless steel or titanium.

culture and sensitivity.definition: An infectious-disease lab test where a specimen is cultured to identify the causative pathogen and then tested for antibiotic susceptibility to determine which drugs are effective (sensitive) or ineffective (resistant), guiding appropriate therapy.

wound culture.definition: A laboratory test in which a sample from a wound is cultured on appropriate media to detect and identify infectious organisms and to determine their antimicrobial susceptibilities to guide treatment.

giemsa stain.definition: A differential, Romanowsky-type stain used on blood and bone marrow smears to visualize cellular morphology and parasites; it stains nuclei blue-purple and cytoplasm pink to gray, aiding identification of malaria parasites and differential leukocyte counts.

wright-giemsa stain.definition: A differential hematology stain that combines Wright's stain with Giemsa stain to color blood and bone marrow cells on smears, enhancing nuclear detail and cytoplasmic characteristics of leukocytes, platelets, and parasites for morphology assessment and differential counts.

sterile irrigating solution.definition: A sterile, nonpyrogenic isotonic saline solution (commonly 0.9% sodium chloride) or other sterile irrigation fluid used to rinse wounds, surgical sites, or body cavities to remove debris and reduce contamination.

sterile.definition: Free from all living microorganisms; aseptic. Also used to describe infertility—unable to have children.

enterostomal.definition: Relating to a stoma formed from the intestine; pertaining to an enterostomy, a surgically created opening between the intestinal tract and the body surface for drainage or diversion of feces.

continence.definition: The ability to voluntary retain and release urine and/or stool, i.e., control urinary and/or fecal elimination until an appropriate time.

enterostomal therapist.definition: A healthcare professional, usually a nurse, who specializes in the care of patients with ostomies (stomas) and intestinal fistulas, providing education, appliance fitting and management, skin protection, and rehabilitation for effective stoma care.

reticuloendothelial disorders.definition: Disorders of the reticuloendothelial system (the mononuclear phagocyte system) involving macrophages in liver, spleen, bone marrow, and lymph nodes, characterized by impaired phagocytic function or abnormal storage/processing of internalized material, often presenting with hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, and systemic inflammatory or storage features.

juvenile xanthogranuloma.definition: A benign, self-limited non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis of infancy/early childhood, presenting as solitary or a few yellow-orange cutaneous papules or nodules (often on the head/neck) that frequently spontaneously regress; histology shows lipid-laden histiocytes with Touton giant cells.

xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis.definition: A rare chronic inflammatory disease of the gallbladder characterized by xanthogranulomatous (foamy macrophage–rich) granulomatous inflammation of the gallbladder wall with cholesterol clefts and fibrosis, often presenting as marked wall thickening and mass-like lesions that can mimic gallbladder cancer; typically associated with gallstones and definitively diagnosed histologically after cholecystectomy.

xanthoma disseminatum.definition: A rare non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis presenting with widespread yellow-brown papules and nodules on the skin and mucous membranes; typically normolipemic and may be associated with diabetes insipidus from hypothalamic involvement.

xanthoma multiplex.definition: Multiple yellowish papules or nodules composed of lipid-laden foam cells in the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, seen in inherited disorders of lipid metabolism (hyperlipidemia), commonly with familial hypercholesterolemia or dysbetalipoproteinemia.

xanthelasma palpebrarum.definition: Yellowish cholesterol-rich plaques on the eyelids (typically near the inner canthus) formed by lipid-laden macrophages in the dermis; often associated with hyperlipidemia or liver disease, though lipid levels can be normal; benign but may indicate an underlying lipid disorder and can be removed for cosmetic reasons or to address lipids.

xanthochromia.definition: A yellowish discoloration of cerebrospinal fluid (and other fluids) caused by bilirubin from the breakdown of red blood cells, indicating prior or ongoing hemorrhage; in CSF, it typically appears hours after hemorrhage and can be detected by spectrophotometric analysis.

xanthochromic.definition: Having a yellowish coloration caused by bilirubin; in clinical use, it describes yellow cerebrospinal fluid indicative of prior intracranial bleeding (e.g., subarachnoid hemorrhage).

xanthoderma.definition: Yellow discoloration of the skin due to accumulation of carotenoids in the skin (carotenemia); often from excessive intake of carotene-rich foods or supplements and is typically benign and reversible, with sclerae usually remaining white.

xanthinuria.definition: A rare inherited disorder of purine metabolism caused by deficiency of xanthine oxidoreductase (xanthine dehydrogenase), sometimes due to molybdenum cofactor deficiency, leading to low uric acid levels and accumulation of xanthine with risk of xanthine stones.

xanthine oxidase.definition: An enzyme in purine metabolism that catalyzes the oxidation of hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid, often generating reactive oxygen species; inhibited by allopurinol.

xanthan gum solution.definition: An aqueous preparation in which xanthan gum—a high-molecular-weight anionic polysaccharide produced by Xanthomonas campestris—is dispersed and hydrated to form a thick, viscous, shear-thinning solution used as a thickening and stabilizing agent in pharmaceuticals and foods.

microfilaria.definition: A larval stage of filarial nematodes that circulates in the host's blood or skin and is transmitted to a vector; produced by adult worms and used in diagnosis of filarial infections.

wuchereria bancrofti.definition: A parasitic nematode that causes bancroftian lymphatic filariasis in humans; transmitted by mosquitoes; adults inhabit the lymphatic vessels and can cause lymphatic dysfunction with lymphedema and, in chronic cases, elephantiasis. Diagnosis is by detecting microfilariae in blood or by antigen tests; treatment includes antifilarial therapy (e.g., diethylcarbamazine) and, in some regimens, albendazole, along with vector-control measures.

immunodeficiency syndrome.definition: A disorder in which the immune system is deficient or dysfunctional, resulting in increased susceptibility to infections, particularly opportunistic infections, and a higher risk of malignancies and autoimmune phenomena.

alprazolam.definition: An oral short-acting benzodiazepine anxiolytic that enhances GABA-A receptor–mediated inhibition, used to treat anxiety disorders (e.g., generalized anxiety disorder and panic disorder). It can cause sedation, dependence and withdrawal, and should be used with caution and for short durations, especially in older adults or with other CNS depressants.

xanax.definition: A brand-name benzodiazepine (alprazolam) used to treat anxiety disorders and panic disorder; it enhances GABA-A receptor–mediated inhibition in the brain to provide anxiolytic and sedative effects; common adverse effects include drowsiness and dizziness; it carries risk of dependence and withdrawal; should be used under medical supervision.

wymox.definition: A brand-name antibiotic product; the exact active ingredient varies by formulation and is used to treat bacterial infections.

penicillin g procaine.definition: A long-acting intramuscular antibiotic formulation in which penicillin G is combined with procaine to provide slower, prolonged release of penicillin G for treating susceptible infections; must be given by deep IM injection and should not be administered intravenously due to risk of serious adverse reactions.

wycillin.definition: A brand name for a penicillin antibiotic (usually penicillin V potassium), an oral, narrow-spectrum beta-lactam agent used to treat mild to moderate infections caused by susceptible bacteria.

wydase.definition: An enzyme preparation (hyaluronidase) that cleaves hyaluronic acid in the extracellular matrix to increase tissue permeability, thereby enhancing dispersion and absorption of injected drugs. Often used to facilitate subcutaneous or intradermal injections.

wytensin.definition: Not a recognized term in standard medical dictionaries; no established definition. It may be a misspelling or a brand name. If you can share context (drug class, condition, or region), I can help identify the correct term and provide its definition.

radiocarpal articulation.definition: A synovial ellipsoidal joint between the distal radius (with its articular disc) and the proximal carpal row (primarily the scaphoid and lunate; the triquetrum to a lesser extent); the principal wrist joint that permits flexion, extension, and radial and ulnar deviation.

extensor muscles.definition: Any muscle or group of muscles that extends a joint, increasing the angle between the bones; most are on the posterior (dorsal) aspect of limbs and act opposite to flexor muscles.

writer's cramp.definition: A focal dystonia causing involuntary contractions of the hand and forearm specifically during writing, leading to cramping, tremor, or an awkward grip; it is a task-specific disorder sometimes called writer's or occupational cramp.

graphospasm.definition: A focal dystonia characterized by involuntary contractions of the hand and forearm muscles during writing, producing distorted or illegible handwriting (writer's cramp).

wrist ganglion.definition: A benign, fluid-filled cyst arising from a joint capsule or tendon sheath in the wrist, most commonly on the dorsal aspect; it contains gelatinous mucinous fluid and may fluctuate in size.

wryneck.definition: A condition in which the neck muscles contract involuntarily, causing the head to tilt to one side and rotate to the opposite side; can be congenital or acquired.

xanthoma eruptivum.definition: A cutaneous eruption of small yellow-to-orange papules caused by markedly elevated triglycerides; due to lipid-laden macrophage (foam cell) deposition in the dermis, typically appearing on the buttocks, shoulders, and extensor surfaces and resolving with triglyceride lowering.

eruptive xanthoma.definition: A type of xanthoma characterized by crops of small (about 1–4 mm) yellow‑orange papules with a red halo, typically on the buttocks, shoulders, and extensor surfaces, due to markedly elevated triglyceride levels; caused by deposition of lipid‑laden macrophages in the dermis, and usually resolves with reduction of triglycerides.

xanthoma palpebrarum.definition: Yellowish plaques on the eyelids formed by lipid-laden macrophages in the dermis; commonly bilateral and associated with dyslipidemia or cholestatic liver disease, often a cosmetic concern and may prompt evaluation of lipid levels.

xanthomasarcoma.definition: Not a widely used term; when used, it denotes a malignant mesenchymal tumor (sarcoma) with xanthomatous (lipid-laden histiocyte) features — effectively a xanthomatous variant of soft tissue sarcoma.

xanthomasarcomata.definition: A malignant mesenchymal tumor in which the cancer cells show xanthomatous (lipid-laden, foamy) cytoplasm; a xanthomatous variant of sarcoma.

tendon sheath.definition: A tubular synovial membrane surrounding a tendon, forming a fluid-filled sheath that lubricates movement and reduces friction, especially in the fingers and wrist.

aponeuroses.definition: A broad, flat sheet of dense connective tissue that serves as a tendon-like attachment for a muscle, connecting it to bone, other muscles, or fascia.

xanthoma striatum palmare.definition: Palmar xanthoma presenting as yellow-orange plaques or linear stripes along the palmar creases of the hands, caused by lipid deposition in the dermis; classically associated with dysbetalipoproteinemia (type III hyperlipoproteinemia) and may indicate increased cardiovascular risk.

xanthoma tendinosum.definition: An accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages in tendons (most often the Achilles) forming a thickened, nodular xanthoma associated with familial hypercholesterolemia and elevated LDL cholesterol.

hereditary lipid storage disease.definition: A group of inherited lysosomal storage disorders (lipidoses) caused by deficient lysosomal enzymes or lipid transport, leading to accumulation of lipid substances within cells and progressive dysfunction of multiple organs (often including the liver, spleen, nervous system, and bones).

xanthomatosis bulbi.definition: A rare ocular condition in which lipid-laden macrophages (foam cells) deposit within the tissues of the eyeball (the globe), producing yellowish xanthomatous lesions and potentially impairing vision, often in association with systemic hyperlipidemia or lipid storage disorders.

xanthoma tuberosum.definition: A type of xanthoma characterized by firm, yellowish nodules on extensor surfaces (commonly elbows, knees, and buttocks) due to focal accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages in the dermis; often associated with dyslipidemias, particularly dysbetalipoproteinemia (type III hyperlipoproteinemia).

tuberous xanthoma.definition: Firm yellow-orange nodules or plaques on extensor surfaces (such as elbows and knees) caused by deposition of lipid-laden macrophages in the dermis; commonly associated with hyperlipidemia or lipoprotein disorders.

xanthoma tuberosum multiplex.definition: Multiple yellowish, firm nodules on extensor surfaces (e.g., elbows, knees, buttocks) formed by lipid-laden macrophage deposits in the dermis, typically associated with underlying hyperlipidemia such as familial hypercholesterolemia.

xanthomonas.definition: A genus of Gram-negative, rod-shaped, aerobic bacteria in the family Xanthomonadaceae, primarily plant pathogens that cause a range of crop diseases; many species produce a characteristic yellow pigment (xanthomonadin).

xanthomonas maltophilia.definition: Historically, a name for Stenotrophomonas maltophilia; a Gram-negative, nonfermenting, aerobic bacillus that is an opportunistic, nosocomial pathogen with intrinsic resistance to multiple antibiotics.

stenotrophomonas maltophilia.definition: A Gram-negative, aerobic, nonfermenting bacillus that is an opportunistic pathogen, commonly causing infections in hospitalized or immunocompromised patients (e.g., pneumonia, bacteremia, urinary tract and wound infections); it has intrinsic resistance to many antibiotics, including most beta-lactams and aminoglycosides, and is typically treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, with alternatives chosen based on susceptibility (e.g., fluoroquinolones or minocycline).

xanthopsia.definition: A color vision disturbance in which colors appear yellow; a form of chromatopsia commonly associated with digoxin (digitalis) toxicity.

carotenosis.definition: A benign condition of yellow-orange skin discoloration due to elevated carotene levels in the blood, usually from excessive intake of carotene-rich foods or supplements; sclerae are not affected and the color fades with reduced intake.

lipemia.definition: An abnormal increase in blood lipids, causing plasma to appear milky or turbid due to excess chylomicrons and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins; commonly related to hyperlipidemia or recent fat intake and may interfere with laboratory tests.

paraproteinemia.definition: The presence of a monoclonal immunoglobulin (paraprotein) in the serum or urine, produced by a clonal population of plasma cells or B lymphocytes, typically seen in disorders such as MGUS, multiple myeloma, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia.

lipoid storage diseases.definition: An inherited group of metabolic disorders in which lipids accumulate abnormally within cells, especially in lysosomes, due to deficiencies of enzymes or transport proteins required for lipid degradation or trafficking, leading to progressive multisystem disease with organomegaly and organ-specific dysfunction.

xanthosis of retina.definition: Yellow discoloration of the retina due to lipid or cholesterol deposition in retinal tissues (often with lipid-laden macrophages), typically associated with systemic lipid disorders; not a widely used standalone clinical diagnosis.

xanthotoxin.definition: A naturally occurring furanocoumarin (psoralen) found in certain plants such as Ammi majus and Ruta graveolens; it is a photosensitizing compound that, upon exposure to UVA radiation, intercalates into DNA and forms cross-links, a mechanism used in PUVA therapy but which can cause phytophotodermatitis.

xanthurenic acid.definition: A metabolite of tryptophan formed in the kynurenine pathway of its catabolism; it can be detected in urine and has been studied as a biomarker of disorders affecting tryptophan metabolism.

xanthurenic aciduria.definition: A rare metabolic abnormality in which xanthurenic acid is excreted in the urine due to a disturbance in the kynurenine pathway of tryptophan metabolism, often related to vitamin B6 deficiency or related enzymatic defects.

xenodiagnosis.definition: An infectious-disease diagnostic method in which a susceptible vector is allowed to feed on a person suspected of infection, and the vector is subsequently examined for the presence of the pathogen to determine whether the person is infected. It has historically been used for diagnosing Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) and other infections, though it is largely supplanted by direct tests.

xenogenous.definition: Originating from a different species; foreign to the host; referring to materials or organisms derived from another species.

xenoantibody.definition: An antibody produced against antigens from a different species (xenogeneic antigens); involved in immune responses to xenogeneic tissues and a major mediator of hyperacute rejection in xenotransplantation.

xenoantigen.definition: An antigen derived from a different species that is recognized as foreign by the recipient's immune system, often triggering an immune response and acting as a barrier in xenotransplantation (e.g., alpha-gal epitopes).

xenobiotic.definition: A chemical substance that is foreign to a biological system and not normally produced by or present in the body, such as drugs, environmental pollutants, and pesticides.

xenobiotics.definition: A chemical substance that is foreign to a biological system or to the body's normal biochemistry; includes drugs, environmental pollutants, pesticides, and other synthetic compounds not endogenously produced.

xenogenesis.definition: Interbreeding between individuals of different species resulting in offspring; interspecies hybridization.

xenology.definition: The study of xenografts and xenotransplantation: the transplantation of organs or tissues across species, and the associated immunologic, ethical, and clinical considerations.

xenoma.definition: A hypertrophied host cell induced by infection with certain microsporidian parasites, containing numerous intracellular spores; a distinctive histopathological lesion seen in microsporidial infections of invertebrates and sometimes fish.

xenon.definition: A chemical element and inert noble gas used as an inhaled anesthetic in select settings, with rapid onset and recovery due to low blood-gas solubility and minimal cardiovascular and respiratory depression, though its use is limited by high cost and availability.

xenon-133.definition: A radioactive isotope of the noble gas xenon (Xe-133) with a half-life of about 5.3 days that emits gamma radiation and is inhaled as a radiotracer for pulmonary ventilation imaging (ventilation scans) in nuclear medicine, and occasionally used for cerebral perfusion imaging.

xenoparasite.definition: A parasite that infects or resides in a host belonging to a different species than its usual host (cross-species parasitism).

xenophobia.definition: Irrational fear of or aversion to people from other countries or cultures, often with hostility, prejudice, or discriminatory behavior toward outsiders.

xenopsylla.definition: A genus of parasitic fleas (order Siphonaptera) that commonly infest mammals, particularly rodents; species such as Xenopsylla cheopis are important vectors for plague (Yersinia pestis) and murine typhus.

xenopsylla cheopis.definition: A hematophagous flea of rats (Siphonaptera) that parasitizes rodents and other mammals; a primary vector of Yersinia pestis, transmitting plague to humans via bite, often after the flea becomes blocked with bacteria in the proventriculus.

xenotype.definition: An organism's genetic or phenotypic profile derived from a different species, such as in xenotransplantation; not a widely used or standard medical term.

xerogram.definition: An image produced by xeroradiography; a radiographic image created on a photoconductive plate that is developed with toner to yield a high-contrast, edge-enhanced radiograph, historically used but now largely obsolete in favor of digital imaging.

xerography.definition: A dry copying process in which an electrostatic charge is used to form an image on a photosensitive surface; the latent image is developed with dry toner, transferred to paper, and fixed by heat to produce a permanent copy.

xeromammogram.definition: A historical breast-imaging technique in which the breast tissue is dehydrated (dried) with a solvent to remove water content, increasing radiographic contrast and improving visualization of calcifications; largely obsolete with modern mammography.

xeromammography.definition: A historical method of breast imaging that uses xerography to produce a high-contrast, edge-enhanced radiographic image on a photoconductive plate after X-ray exposure; largely obsolete today in favor of conventional film and digital mammography.

xerotic eczema.definition: A form of dermatitis driven by severe skin dryness (xerosis), presenting with dry, scaly, and often fissured skin with itching; commonly affects the lower legs in older adults and is treated with regular emollients, gentle cleansing, and avoidance of irritants.

xerotic keratitis.definition: A keratitis caused by severe dryness of the ocular surface (xerosis), leading to corneal epithelial breakdown and inflammation; symptoms commonly include irritation, a foreign body sensation, photophobia, and sometimes corneal ulcers, typically in the context of dry eye disease or vitamin A deficiency (xerophthalmia).

xiphoid appendix.definition: Not a recognized anatomical term; may refer to either the xiphoid process or the vermiform appendix. The xiphoid process is the small cartilaginous projection at the inferior end of the sternum that ossifies with age; the vermiform appendix is a narrow, blind-ended tube attached to the cecum in the large intestine.

xiphisternum.definition: Small, variably cartilaginous projection at the inferior end of the sternum; the lowest part of the sternum that ossifies with age and serves as an attachment site for the diaphragm and abdominal muscles.

ensiform cartilage.definition: The cartilaginous, blade-shaped portion at the inferior end of the sternum (the xiphoid cartilage), which forms the xiphoid process and may ossify with age.

ensiform process.definition: A small, inferior projection of the sternum; initially cartilaginous and that ossifies with age, serving as an attachment site for the diaphragm and abdominal muscles.

xiphopagus.definition: A form of conjoined twins in which the two individuals are joined at the xiphoid process of the sternum (the lower part of the sternum), typically with a connection at the anterior chest/upper abdomen.

x-linked.definition: Relating to a gene located on the X chromosome; inheritance follows the X chromosome and can show distinct patterns depending on whether the mutation acts in a recessive or dominant manner.

x-linked bulbospinal neuropathy.definition: An X-linked inherited neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive degeneration of bulbar (brainstem) and spinal motor neurons, causing dysarthria, dysphagia, and proximal limb weakness; predominantly affects males, with female carriers often asymptomatic or mildly affected.

x-linked mucopolysaccharidosis.definition: A rare X-linked recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of iduronate-2-sulfatase, leading to accumulation of dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate in tissues and resulting in multiorgan disease with features such as coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, skeletal abnormalities, airway obstruction, and progressive developmental delay.

x-linked dominant inheritance.definition: An inheritance pattern in which a pathogenic variant on the X chromosome is sufficient to cause disease in individuals with one mutated copy. Affected fathers pass the mutation to all daughters but no sons; affected mothers have a 50% chance of passing it to each child (both sexes). In females, expression is often variable due to X-inactivation, while affected males are typically more severely affected.

x-linked recessive inheritance.definition: A pattern of genetic transmission in which a pathogenic variant on the X chromosome causes disease that predominantly affects males; females are usually asymptomatic carriers. Affected males inherit the mutation from carrier mothers and pass the mutated X to all daughters (who become carriers) but not to sons; transmission from father to son does not occur. Rarely, females can be affected due to skewed X-inactivation or underlying abnormalities.

x-linked ichthyosis.definition: An X-linked recessive skin disorder caused by deficiency of the enzyme steroid sulfatase (STS) on the X chromosome, leading to accumulation of cholesterol sulfate in the stratum corneum and generalized, dark, plate-like scales that are often evident at birth; scales are most prominent on the trunk and proximal limbs, and management includes regular moisturizers and keratolytics.

xolair.definition: A monoclonal antibody that binds to IgE, preventing its interaction with the high-affinity IgE receptor on mast cells and basophils, thereby reducing allergic inflammation; approved for moderate-to-severe persistent allergic asthma and chronic idiopathic urticaria; administered by subcutaneous injection.

roentgen ray.definition: An old term for X-ray radiation, the high-energy electromagnetic radiation used in radiographic imaging.

x-radiation.definition: A form of high-energy, ionizing electromagnetic radiation (wavelength roughly 0.01–10 nanometers) produced by X-ray tubes and other sources; it penetrates body tissues to form images but can ionize atoms and cause cellular/DNA damage, requiring careful use and shielding.

x-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome.definition: An X-linked primary immunodeficiency caused by mutations in SH2D1A (SAP) or XIAP that impairs regulation of immune responses to Epstein-Barr virus–infected B cells; it presents with severe EBV-induced mononucleosis-like illness, uncontrolled B-cell proliferation, hypogammaglobulinemia, and an increased risk of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and lymphoma.

b-cell lymphoma.definition: A cancer of B lymphocytes in the lymphatic system; a heterogeneous group of lymphomas (mostly non-Hodgkin) that can be indolent or aggressive, with subtypes including diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, follicular lymphoma, mantle cell lymphoma, and Burkitt lymphoma.

lymphoproliferative syndrome.definition: An umbrella term for disorders marked by abnormal proliferation of lymphocytes (B, T, or NK cells) due to immune dysfunction or immunosuppression, ranging from benign lymphoid hyperplasia to malignant lymphoproliferative diseases, often EBV-associated and seen with transplantation, HIV, or other immunosuppressive states.

contraction.definition: Muscle contraction is the shortening of muscle fibers with generation of force in response to stimulation, driven by actin–myosin cross-bridge cycling and ATP use, enabling movement (skeletal), heartbeat (cardiac), and regulation of organ flow (smooth).

fetal skull.definition: A skull of a developing fetus whose cranial bones are incompletely ossified and separated by sutures and fontanelles, making the cranium flexible to mold during passage through the birth canal; ossification continues after birth.

cephalopelvic relationship.definition: The fit between the fetal head and the maternal pelvis that determines whether the head can pass through the birth canal during labor; an unfavorable cephalopelvic relationship (eg, head too large or pelvis too small) can lead to cephalopelvic disproportion and obstructed labor.

radiological technologist.definition: A licensed or certified allied health professional who performs diagnostic imaging procedures (most commonly X-ray radiography), positions patients, selects exposure factors, operates imaging equipment, ensures radiation safety, and processes images under a physician’s orders; may specialize in radiography, fluoroscopy, CT, or mammography.

bouba.definition: Not a recognized medical term; there is no standard medical definition.

buba.definition: A swollen, tender lymph node caused by infection of the lymphatic system, often associated with bubonic plague; commonly located in the groin, armpit, or neck and may be painful and suppurate.

parangi.definition: Definition not found in trusted medical dictionaries. Please verify spelling or provide context so I can help identify the term.

patek.definition: There is no recognized medical term named 'patek' in standard medical dictionaries.

pian.definition: A distressing sensory and emotional experience arising from actual or potential tissue damage, acting as a protective signal that prompts withdrawal from danger and fosters healing.

trisomy x.definition: An X-chromosome aneuploidy in females caused by an extra X chromosome (47,XXX); most have normal development and fertility, but some exhibit tall stature and mild learning or language delays.

xxxy syndrome.definition: A rare sex chromosome aneuploidy in males in which there are three X chromosomes and one Y chromosome (often described as 48,XXXXY or XXXY). It typically presents with developmental delay and intellectual disability, hypotonia, speech and language delays, hypogonadism with small testes and infertility, skeletal anomalies, and behavioral or psychiatric problems.

xxy syndrome.definition: A chromosomal disorder in males due to an extra X chromosome (47,XXY), typically causing hypogonadism and infertility, tall stature with long limbs, small testes, gynecomastia, and learning or language difficulties.

xyy syndrome.definition: A sex chromosome aneuploidy in males due to an extra Y chromosome; most individuals have normal sexual development and fertility, but may be taller than average and show mild language or learning difficulties and a slightly higher risk of behavioral problems such as ADHD.

xxx syndrome.definition: No widely recognized medical syndrome by this name; appears to be a placeholder or fictional term. If you provide the correct term or more context, I can define it.

yellow fever vaccine.definition: A live attenuated vaccine (based on the 17D strain) that prevents yellow fever; given as a single subcutaneous injection, it provides long‑lasting immunity and is used for travelers to endemic areas and for international travel certification.

nail syndrome.definition: An umbrella term for a range of nail abnormalities that may occur as primary nail disorders or as manifestations of dermatologic, systemic, or genetic diseases; not a single disease.

pulmonary disorders.definition: Pulmonary disorders refer to diseases of the lungs and lower respiratory tract that impair ventilation and/or gas exchange. They include obstructive conditions (e.g., asthma, COPD), restrictive lung diseases (e.g., pulmonary fibrosis), infections (e.g., pneumonia), vascular disorders (e.g., pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension), and pleural diseases (e.g., pleural effusion, pleuritis).

yerba maté.definition: A caffeinated infusion prepared from the dried leaves of Ilex paraguariensis; traditionally consumed as a social drink in parts of South America; contains caffeine and related compounds; may cause stimulant effects such as insomnia and tachycardia and can interact with other stimulants or medications.

depurative.definition: An agent or therapy that purges or cleanses the body of toxins, typically by promoting elimination or detoxification and historically described as purifying the blood.

yersinia.definition: A genus of Gram-negative, non-spore-forming bacilli that are facultatively anaerobic; pathogenic members cause plague and various enteric infections, transmitted by fleas or ingestion of contaminated food or water.

yersinia arthritis.definition: A form of reactive (post-infectious) arthritis triggered by infection with Yersinia enterocolitica or Yersinia pseudotuberculosis after an enteric illness, characterized by sterile inflammatory arthritis (often asymmetric oligoarthritis of the knees and ankles) that may be accompanied by enthesitis and extra-articular features such as conjunctivitis or urethritis.

yersinia enterocolitica.definition: Yersinia enterocolitica is a gram-negative, non-spore-forming bacillus that causes yersiniosis—a food- and waterborne enteric infection typically acquired from contaminated pork—characterized by fever, abdominal pain, and diarrhea; it can mimic appendicitis due to mesenteric adenitis and may lead to bacteremia in immunocompromised individuals; it is capable of growing at refrigeration temperatures.

yersinia pseudotuberculosis.definition: A Gram-negative, facultatively anaerobic bacillus that causes yersiniosis in humans, typically presenting with fever and mesenteric lymphadenitis that can mimic appendicitis; transmitted by ingestion of contaminated food or contact with infected animals.

yersiniosis.definition: An infection caused by Yersinia enterocolitica (and occasionally Yersinia pseudotuberculosis) characterized by acute gastroenteritis with diarrhea, fever, and abdominal pain that can mimic appendicitis; commonly acquired through undercooked pork, contaminated milk, or contaminated water, and typically self-limited in healthy individuals with antibiotics reserved for severe disease.

erythema multiforme.definition: An acute, self-limited mucocutaneous hypersensitivity reaction characterized by symmetric target-like skin lesions, often with mucosal involvement; commonly triggered by herpes simplex virus infections or certain drugs and typically resolves in 2–6 weeks.

y-fracture.definition: A fracture pattern in which the bone is split into three fragments that form a Y-shaped configuration, typically resulting from high-energy trauma and often indicating comminution with potential joint involvement. If you can specify the bone or context, I can give a more precise description.

y-linked.definition: Relating to genes located on the Y chromosome; a pattern of inheritance in which traits are passed from father to son via the Y chromosome and are not transmitted to females.

yodoxin.definition: No widely recognized medical definition exists; it may be a brand name or an obscure/archaic term rather than a standard medical substance.

yohimbine hydrochloride.definition: A salt form of yohimbine, an indole alkaloid that acts as a selective alpha-2 adrenergic receptor antagonist, increasing sympathetic outflow; used, where prescribed, for erectile dysfunction and as a stimulant, with potential adverse effects including hypertension, tachycardia, and anxiety.

yohimbe.definition: The bark of the West African tree Pausinystalia johimbe (syn. Corynanthe johimbe); contains the alkaloid yohimbine and is used traditionally as an aphrodisiac and in dietary supplements, but can cause hypertension, tachycardia, anxiety, and drug interactions.

pausinystalia yohimbe.definition: A West African tree of the Rubiaceae family whose bark contains the alkaloid yohimbine; extracts have been used medically for erectile dysfunction but can cause hypertension, tachycardia, and anxiety.

yolk membrane.definition: A thin envelope surrounding the yolk of an ovum (egg), forming a boundary between the yolk and the surrounding fluids.

omphalomesenteric duct.definition: An embryologic connection between the yolk sac and the midgut (the yolk stalk) that normally regresses/obliterates by about the 7th week of gestation; persistence can give rise to Meckel’s diverticulum or other vitelline duct anomalies.

morula.definition: An early embryonic stage consisting of a solid ball of blastomeres produced by cleavage of a fertilized egg, typically containing 16–32 cells and forming before the blastocyst (around day 4–5 after fertilization).

yolk sphere.definition: A yolk sphere is a spherical mass of yolk (nutrient-rich lipid and protein droplets) within an oocyte or early embryo, serving as a nutrient reserve for the developing embryo, especially in species with abundant yolk (oviparous).

primitive blood plasma.definition: The liquid extracellular component of blood in which cells and platelets are suspended; about 55% of blood volume; composed mainly of water with dissolved electrolytes, nutrients, hormones, wastes, and a variety of proteins such as albumin, globulins, and coagulation factors.

cerebrohepatorenal syndrome.definition: A theoretical or rarely used designation for concurrent dysfunction of the brain, liver, and kidneys, typically in the setting of severe liver failure with hepatic encephalopathy and hepatorenal syndrome; not a widely recognized or distinct clinical entity.

zellweger's syndrome.definition: A rare autosomal recessive peroxisomal biogenesis disorder caused by mutations in PEX genes, leading to defective formation of peroxisomes and accumulation of very long‑chain fatty acids; infancy onset with hypotonia, craniofacial dysmorphism, hepatomegaly, seizures, and severe neurodevelopmental impairment, often fatal within the first year.

zenker's diverticulum.definition: A false diverticulum of the pharyngoesophageal junction arising through Killian’s dehiscence (between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus muscles); it presents with dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, and halitosis, and is typically diagnosed by barium swallow and treated surgically (diverticulectomy with cricopharyngeal myotomy or endoscopic stapling).

young's operation.definition: Could you specify the medical field or context? “Young’s operation” can refer to different procedures in different specialties, and I want to give you the correct definition. For example, is it in ophthalmology, ENT, dentistry, or another area? If you have the condition or a nearby term, that would help too.

y-set.definition: Not a standard medical term; there is no widely accepted definition in medical literature.

y-tubing.definition: An intravenous administration set with a Y-shaped junction that allows two solutions (a primary infusion and a secondary piggyback) to be delivered through a single IV line, typically enabling quicker administration of medications without disconnecting the primary infusion.

yttrium.definition: An element with atomic number 39; a silvery-white transition metal in the rare-earth category. Its radioactive isotope is used in targeted radiotherapy for cancer.

ytterbium.definition: A chemical element in the lanthanide series (symbol Yb, atomic number 70); not used as a therapeutic drug and has no standard medical indications, primarily used in alloys and specialized optics/electronics.

yttrium-90.definition: A radioactive isotope of yttrium (mass number 90) that decays by beta emission with a half-life of about 64 hours, used in targeted radiotherapy (e.g., Y-90–labeled antibodies and Y-90 microspheres) to deliver localized cytotoxic radiation to tumor cells.

esophageal ulcers.definition: Focal breaks or ulcers in the mucosa of the esophagus caused by injury or infection (e.g., gastroesophageal reflux, herpes simplex virus or cytomegalovirus infection, pill-induced injury, caustic ingestion, radiation); commonly present with odynophagia and chest pain and may bleed.

suicidal tendencies.definition: An inclination or risk to commit suicide, typically evidenced by thoughts of death, a wish to die, or an intent or plan to end one’s life; commonly seen as a symptom or risk factor in mood disorders and other psychiatric conditions and requiring risk assessment.

ibritumomab tiuxetan.definition: A monoclonal antibody directed against CD20 on B cells, conjugated to the chelator tiuxetan and labeled with the radiometal yttrium-90, used as targeted radiotherapy for CD20-positive non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

zavesca.definition: An oral iminosugar drug that inhibits glucosylceramide synthase, thereby reducing the synthesis and accumulation of glycosphingolipids; used as substrate-reduction therapy for Niemann-Pick disease type C (and historically explored for Gaucher disease).

zdv.definition: A nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) used in antiretroviral therapy for HIV infection; it inhibits viral DNA synthesis, leading to chain termination and reduced viral replication.

z-line.definition: An anatomical and endoscopic boundary where the esophageal squamous epithelium transitions to gastric simple columnar epithelium at the gastroesophageal junction; endoscopically seen as the squamocolumnar junction. It can be displaced or irregular in conditions such as Barrett's esophagus.

z-disk.definition: A boundary structure of the sarcomere in skeletal and cardiac muscle that anchors thin (actin) filaments and connects to titin and desmin, marking the borders of the sarcomere.

z-chromosome.definition: A sex chromosome in species with ZW sex-determination (e.g., birds and some reptiles); the Z chromosome is the larger chromosome present in both sexes, with males typically ZZ and females ZW, and it carries many genes important for development; traits linked to it (Z-linked) often show sex-biased expression due to differences in gene dosage.
